Addressing numerous engineering challenges necessitates predicting realization-to-realization variability or refining descriptions of modeled quantities, which often requires sampling from unknown high-dimensional spaces containing millions of degrees of freedom. Although methods exist for sampling from probability density functions (PDFs) with known shapes, handling unknown distributions typically demands various approximations. This paper introduces a data-driven approach using generative adversarial networks (GANs) to simultaneously manage the sampling process and infer the underlying distribution. GANs achieve this by training two competing neural networks to create a generator capable of effectively producing samples matching the training distribution. Practically, sampling from conditional distributions is often required; however, when conditioning variables are continuous, data scarcity (often only a single point per value) makes estimating the conditional distribution difficult. To resolve this, the proposed work employs an a priori estimation of the PDF's conditional moments. The study compares two techniques for computing these moments: stochastic estimation and an external neural network, noting that either method is applicable. The algorithm is validated through the deconvolution of a filtered turbulent flow field. Results demonstrate that all proposed algorithm versions effectively sample the target conditional distribution with minimal degradation in sample quality compared to state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, this procedure serves as a metric for assessing the diversity of samples generated by a conditional GAN (cGAN) conditioned on continuous variables.

This paper investigates specific regularity characteristics linked to the initial value problem (IVP) defined by:
\begin{equation}\label{main1} \left\{ \begin{array}{ll}
\partial_{t}u-\partial_{x_{1}}(-\Delta)^{\alpha/2} u+u\partial_{x_{1}}u=0,
\quad 0< \alpha\leq 2,& \\ u(x,0)=u_{0}(x),\quad x=(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n})\in
\mathbb{R}^{n},\, n\geq 2,\quad t\in\mathbb{R},& \\ \end{array} \right.
\end{equation}
where $(-\Delta)^{\alpha/2}$ represents the $n$-dimensional fractional Laplacian. We demonstrate that solutions to this IVP, starting from initial data within an appropriate Sobolev space, display a local smoothing effect in the spatial variable corresponding to $\frac{\alpha}{2}$ derivatives, holding true almost everywhere in time. A primary challenge in establishing this regularizing effect arises from the mismatch between the non-local nature of the operator and the local property being analyzed, necessitating novel approaches. To circumvent these complications, we employ a perturbation strategy by substituting $(-\Delta)^{\frac{\alpha}{2}}$ with $(I-\Delta)^{\frac{\alpha}{2}}$. Utilizing pseudo-differential calculus, this approach proves that solutions become locally smoother by $\frac{\alpha}{2}$ derivatives across all spatial directions. As a secondary result, we leverage this specific smoothing phenomenon to demonstrate that additional regularity present in the initial data on certain distinguished subsets of Euclidean space is propagated by the solution flow at infinite speed.

We demonstrate that the Remote Point Problem (RPP), originally formulated by Alon et al. [APY09], admits an $NC^2$ algorithm using $\epsilon$-bias spaces over $F_2$, matching the parameters of [APY09]. We extend the RPP to arbitrary fixed groups $G$ by substituting $F^n$ with $G^n$. For Abelian groups, we provide an $NC^2$ solution leveraging $\epsilon$-bias spaces, whereas for nonabelian groups, we present a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm. Furthermore, we establish a link between these results and the construction of expanding generator sets for $G^n$. All proposed algorithms for the RPP attain parameters essentially identical to those in [APY09].

Although recent Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems have shown enhanced performance, transcription mistakes remain inevitable. In critical fields like healthcare, where ASR aids clinical documentation, these errors can be highly consequential. Consequently, identifying ASR errors is an essential initial step to stop their propagation into downstream applications. We introduce a novel end-to-end approach for ASR error detection based on audio-transcript entailment. To our knowledge, this is the first study to frame the problem as an end-to-end entailment task between an audio segment and its corresponding transcript. Our hypothesis is that error-free recognition implies a bidirectional entailment between the audio and transcript, whereas errors disrupt this relationship. The model employs an acoustic encoder and a linguistic encoder to represent speech and text, respectively, fusing these encoded features to predict entailment. Given that our experiments utilize doctor-patient dialogues, special attention is devoted to medical terminology. Our model achieves Character Error Rates (CER) of 26.2% for all transcription errors and 23% for medical errors, representing 12% and 15.4% improvements over a strong baseline, respectively.

Comparing galaxy populations across vast cosmic timescales requires addressing various observational effects. This study utilizes a sample of 166 nearby galaxies that hosted Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) and were observed via the AMUSING survey using the MUSE integral field spectrograph. We investigate systematic errors and biases in host stellar mass estimates as redshift increases, issues often neglected in SNe Ia cosmological analyses. By simulating observations across redshifts of 0.1 < z < 2.0 using four photometric bands (griz, comparable to the DES-SN program), we estimated host galaxy properties throughout cosmic history. Our results indicate that stellar masses are systematically underestimated at higher redshifts, primarily due to variations in rest-frame wavelength coverage, with discrepancies reaching 0.3 dex near z~1. We applied newly derived redshift-dependent corrections to adjust stellar masses for a known sample of SN Ia hosts and subsequently derived cosmological parameters. The findings reveal that these corrections exert a minimal influence on the resulting parameters: the mass step ($\Delta_M$) decreases by approximately 0.004 (6% lower), the dark energy equation of state ($w$) shifts by $\Delta w \sim 0.006$ (0.6% higher), and $\Omega_m$ increases by no more than 0.001 ($\sim$0.3%), all within the model's uncertainties. Although the identified systematic error in host stellar mass estimation does not significantly alter derived cosmological parameters, it represents a crucial source of error that must be corrected as the field advances into an era of precision cosmology.

This study investigates two types of small spin-1/2 clusters: edge-shared tetrahedra and octahedra, incorporating Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions under a longitudinal magnetic field. We analyze the magnetization and electric polarization of these systems as functions of magnetic and electric fields at low temperatures using exact numerical diagonalization. Our findings align well with recent analyses by J. Štréčka and K. Karlová. We demonstrate that polarization behavior mirrors magnetization curves, including sequential intermediate plateaus, and reflects stepwise changes in ground-state phase transitions. Additionally, we observe that polarization significantly influences the magnetic field dependence of magnetization. Beyond this, we examine isothermal strategies such as cooling rates, the magnetocaloric effect (MCE), and the electrocaloric effect (ECE) for both models. Given the importance of high-performance electrocaloric materials in condensed matter physics, we specifically report on the ECE of these spin-1/2 Heisenberg clusters. We conclude that the edge-shared tetrahedra exhibit a significantly higher reversible temperature change capability under an external electric field compared to the octahedra, making it a promising candidate for cooling and heating applications.

We categorize the closed ideals of bounded operators on the Banach spaces $\left(\bigoplus_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \ell_2^n\right)_{c_0} \oplus c_0(\Gamma)$ and $\left(\bigoplus_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \ell_2^n\right)_{\ell_1} \oplus \ell_1(\Gamma)$ for all uncountable cardinals $\Gamma$.

Facial Expression Recognition (FER) in uncontrolled environments remains a highly difficult challenge. Although recent studies have investigated Vision Transformers (ViTs) for FER, their performance generally lags behind Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). This underperformance stems from the difficulty in training new modules from scratch due to a lack of inductive bias, which often causes models to focus on occluded or noisy regions. While TransFER, a prominent transformer-based approach, mitigates this issue through multi-branch attention dropping, it incurs significant computational costs. In contrast, we introduce two Attentive Pooling (AP) modules—Attentive Patch Pooling (APP) and Attentive Token Pooling (ATP)—that directly filter out noisy features. Designed to highlight the most discriminative information while suppressing irrelevant data, APP selects the most informative patches within CNN features, whereas ATP eliminates unimportant tokens in ViTs. Since these modules are straightforward to implement, contain no learnable parameters, and intuitively lower computational overhead by focusing exclusively on key features, they effectively enhance performance. Qualitative analyses validate our approach's rationale and efficacy, while quantitative evaluations on six in-the-wild datasets demonstrate superiority over current state-of-the-art methods.

This work investigates Ising Field Theory, representing the scaling limit of the Ising model near the Curie critical point, specifically within a pure imaginary external magnetic field. Our focus centers on the intricate structure of the Yang-Lee edge singularity. While the dominant singular behavior is governed by the Yang-Lee fixed point, corresponding to the minimal conformal field theory ${\cal M}_{2/5}$, the detailed fine structure of subleading singular terms arises from an effective action containing a spectrum of irrelevant operators. Leveraging numerical data derived from the "Truncated Free Fermion Space Approach," we estimate the couplings for the two least irrelevant operators. The first is the operator $T{\bar T}$; we utilize the universal characteristics of the $T{\bar T}$ deformation to determine the contributions of higher orders in the associated coupling parameter $\alpha$. The second operator is the descendant $L_{-4}{\bar L}_{-4}\phi$ of the relevant primary field $\phi$ within ${\cal M}_{2/5}$. This operator holds particular significance as the lowest-dimension operator that disrupts the integrability of the effective theory. Furthermore, we derive the analytic properties of the particle mass $M$ (defined as the inverse correlation length) as a function of the complex magnetic field.

This study presents a measurement of the time-integrated $CP$ asymmetry for $D^0\rightarrow K^0_S K^0_S$ decays. Utilizing approximately $2$ fb$^{-1}$ of data from $pp$ collisions at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV recorded by the LHCb collaboration between 2015 and 2016, the analysis selects $D^0$ candidates via the decay chain $D^{\ast +} \rightarrow D^0 \pi^+$ to tag the meson's flavor based on the pion's charge. The $D^0 \rightarrow K^{+}K^{-}$ channel, known for its well-established $CP$ asymmetry, serves as a calibration reference. The resulting $CP$ asymmetry for $D^0\rightarrow K^0_S K^0_S$ is found to be \begin{equation*} \mathcal{A}^{CP}(D^0\rightarrow K^0_S K^0_S) = (4.3\pm 3.4\pm 1.0)\%, \end{equation*} with the first error being statistical and the second systematic. When combined with prior LHCb results obtained at lower center-of-mass energies, the updated measurement yields \begin{equation*} \mathcal{A}^{CP}(D^0\rightarrow K^0_S K^0_S) = (2.3\pm 2.8\pm 0.9)\%. \end{equation*}

This paper offers a concise introduction to the theory of causal fermion systems. Following an examination of the theory's historical context and a review of essential physical preliminaries, we explore the core concepts behind the fermionic projector principle and elucidate its relationship to causal fermion systems. Finally, we present an overview of the theory's primary structures.

Although Deep Learning models have demonstrated significant potential for automatically creating polyphonic music, guiding these models to achieve specific objectives remains a major challenge. This paper introduces a generative Deep Learning framework capable of composing music with a predefined sentiment. Beyond generation, the model also functions for sentiment analysis on symbolic music. We assessed its classification accuracy using a novel dataset of video game soundtracks, and the results indicate strong performance. Furthermore, a user study confirmed that listeners perceived the generated music as having the intended emotional tone, though negative sentiments were sometimes found to be ambiguous.

Building on our previous research, this study provides a comprehensive structural analysis of a representative selection of nearby spiral and early-type galaxies from the KINGFISH/SINGS survey. Bulge photometric parameters are derived via bulge-disc decomposition using the GALFIT algorithm, applying previously established corrections for projection and dust to determine intrinsic structural and photometric properties. We examine key bulge scaling relations and black hole connections in the B band, distinguishing between observed and intrinsic values. Our findings indicate that dust and inclination significantly alter parameters in the Kormendy relation for spirals, with late-type galaxy bulges following a steeper slope than those of early-type galaxies. Furthermore, combining the Kormendy relation with a bulge Sérsic index ($n_b$) threshold fails to achieve a definitive morphological separation. While the $n_b$-bulge-to-total flux ratio ($B/T$) and $B/T$-stellar mass can distinguish between late- and early-type galaxies, using these metrics to separate bulge morphologies is challenging due to distribution overlaps and large value spreads. We confirm two distinct intrinsic relations linking bulge luminosity (or absolute magnitude) to the Sérsic index for late- and early-type galaxies, whereas the relationships between black hole mass ($M_{BH}$) and bulge luminosity show no statistically significant difference at p<0.05. Within measurement uncertainties, the intrinsic $M_{BH}$-$n_b$ relations appear statistically similar across all bulge types.

Sequence-level knowledge distillation (SKD) in non-autoregressive neural machine translation (NAT) typically relies on autoregressive models (AT) as teachers, yet NAT systems often produce shorter outputs than their AT counterparts. This study introduces an SKD approach utilizing perturbed length-aware positional encoding, applied to the Levenshtein Transformer student model. On the WMT14 German-to-English task, this method achieved a peak BLEU score 2.5 points higher than the standard Levenshtein Transformer, while also generating longer sentences than baseline NAT models.

This study examines the random access challenge within delay-constrained heterogeneous wireless networks. As an initial exploration of this emerging issue, we analyze a two-user network transmitting delay-sensitive data to an access point (AP) over a shared, unreliable collision channel. In this setup, User 1 employs ALOHA, while we optimize the random access strategy for User 2. A key complexity arises because User 2 lacks knowledge of User 1's state yet must maximize the system's timely throughput. This collaborative spectrum-sharing approach aligns with DARPA's vision for dynamically balancing future supply and demand [1], [2]. Initially, we introduce a Markov Decision Process (MDP) formulation to establish a model-based upper bound, serving as a metric to quantify the performance gap of various schemes. Subsequently, we apply reinforcement learning (RL) to develop TSRA, an R-learning-based [3]-[5] random access protocol. Extensive simulations demonstrate that TSRA achieves performance nearly matching the upper bound and outperforms the existing DLMA [6] baseline, which addresses delay-unconstrained heterogeneous networks. All source code is accessible at https://github.com/DanzhouWu/TSRA.

The growing demand for automated visual monitoring in areas like smart surveillance, traffic management, and intelligent environments drives the need to enhance active visual monitoring techniques. Historically, this task relied on a modular pipeline involving detection, filtering, and control. This paper reframes active visual monitoring as a supervised imitation learning problem, utilizing deep learning to directly map visual inputs to camera movements, thereby integrating computer vision and control into a cohesive solution. An end-to-end deep convolutional neural network is trained to serve as the camera controller, learning the full processing pipeline required to track multiple targets and estimate their density from a single image. Experimental findings demonstrate that this approach is robust to varying conditions and outperforms traditional methods in both the number of monitored targets and monitoring speed, achieving up to 25 FPS. Consequently, it offers a practical and cost-effective solution for multi-target active monitoring in surveillance and smart-environment contexts.

This paper proposes that the ages of reported measles cases can serve as a basis for estimating the volume of undetected infections. Surprisingly, even when age data is recorded only to the nearest year, it is possible to generate underreporting estimates at the rapid two-week intervals characteristic of measles transmission dynamics. The methodology is illustrated using the extensively analyzed United Kingdom dataset covering sixty cities, which documents the shift to universal healthcare in 1948 and thus offers a compelling case study for infectious disease surveillance. Finally, the paper concludes with a brief discussion on adapting this approach for contemporary applications.

The correlation between the abundance ratios of certain chemical species and stellar age suggests that atmospheric abundances could serve as indicators for determining a star's age. Although these chemical clocks have been calibrated using solar twins, open clusters, and red giants, their effectiveness in identifying coeval stars within a broad field population (a concept known as chemical tagging) remains unproven. Since wide binaries consist of stars sharing a common origin, they offer ideal settings for evaluating the utility of chemical clocks for dating field stars. By analyzing a new sample of five binaries and compiling data from 31 additional systems found in the literature, we tested the applicability of these clocks. Our findings confirm the established observation that wide binary components exhibit more chemically consistent profiles than random pairs. Furthermore, we demonstrate for the first time that abundance ratios specifically designed as chemical clocks are even more uniform among wide binary components than their standard [X/Fe] ratios. Additionally, the pair HIP 34426/HIP 34407 suggests that chemical clocks may remain consistent among coeval stars even when individual elemental abundances differ. If chemical clocks are indeed reliable age indicators, this would provide the first statistically significant, quantitative proof that wide binaries in the Galactic field are coeval, thereby validating extensive existing literature based on this assumption. Finally, our results strongly indicate that chemical clocks contain crucial data regarding stellar birthplaces and chemical evolution, leading us to propose that incorporating them into chemical tagging strategies could enhance the identification of currently dissolved stellar groups.

In 1982, the KEK electron-positron injector LINAC began injecting particles into the Photon Factory (PF) light source. Over the subsequent 39 years, this facility has supported numerous major projects, including TRISTAN, PF-AR, KEKB, and SuperKEKB. By May 7, 2020, its cumulative operational time had reached 200,000 hours, an achievement we are deeply proud of, thanks to the sustained efforts of our predecessors. Construction of the injector LINAC commenced in 1978, leading to its commissioning for PF in 1982 with a 2.5 GeV electron beam. Concurrently, a positron generator linac was built for the TRISTAN collider, followed by the commissioning of the slow positron facility in 1992. With the launch of the KEKB asymmetric-energy collider in 1998, which utilized direct energy injections, advanced techniques such as two-bunch acceleration and simultaneous injection were developed. Following the Great East Japan earthquake, which severely damaged the LINAC's soft structure, a three-year recovery period ensued before work on the SuperKEKB project resumed. The resulting simultaneous top-up injection into four storage rings now significantly contributes to both elementary particle physics and photon science.

We introduce Leapfrog, a Coq-based framework designed to verify the equivalence of network protocol parsers. This approach relies on an automata-based model for P4 parsers and employs an algorithm that symbolically computes a compact bisimulation representation through "leaps." The verification process utilizes a certified compilation chain that translates first-order entailments into low-level bitvector conditions, which are then discharged using standard SMT solvers. Consequently, Leapfrog enables fully automatic, push-button proofs of parser equivalence. We provide mechanical proofs for the core metatheory supporting our method, covering essential transformations and multiple optimizations. Evaluation across various practical case studies demonstrates that Leapfrog requires minimal configuration and no manual intervention. Notably, our largest case study applies Leapfrog to validate translation from automata to hardware pipelines performed by a third-party compiler. Ultimately, Leapfrog advances the goal of verifying all parsers for critical network infrastructure and opens avenues for future work, such as verifying relational properties related to security.

Neural networks present a privacy hazard because they can memorize and inadvertently expose training data. Our findings demonstrate that both discriminative multi-layer perceptrons and convolutional neural networks, when trained on standard imaging benchmarks, retain unique data instances that appear only once. We have developed a methodology specifically for scenarios where sensitive training data is inaccessible, such as in medical imaging contexts. In this framework, the observer identifies a unique feature but lacks access to the original training set, model parameters, or the feature's label. We introduce a scoring mechanism that estimates a model's vulnerability to a specific unique feature by analyzing the Kullback-Leibler divergence between output distributions generated from modified out-of-distribution images. Our results indicate that standard overfitting mitigation techniques fail to stop the memorization of unique features. Furthermore, images containing these unique features exert high influence independently of their other attributes. We also observe substantial variability in memorization outcomes based on the random seed used during training. These findings suggest that neural networks threaten the privacy of rare, private information. This risk is particularly acute in healthcare, where sensitive patient data can be retained in models even after imperfect sanitization efforts.

The LHCb experiment analyzed proton-proton collision data at center-of-mass energies of 7, 8, and 13 TeV, with integrated luminosities of 1, 2, and 6 fb$^{-1}$, respectively, to search for baryon- and lepton-number violating decays of $B^0\to p\mu^-$ and $B^0_s\to p\mu^-$. No significant signals were observed for these processes, leading to the establishment of the first-ever upper limits on their branching fractions: ${\cal B}(B^0\to p\mu^-)<2.6\,(3.1)\times10^{-9}$ and ${\cal B}(B^0_s\to p\mu^-)<12.1\,(14.0)\times10^{-9}$ at 90% and 95% confidence levels, respectively.

This study examines decays of $B$ and $K$ mesons resulting in a pseudo-scalar or vector meson alongside missing energy. Under the Standard Model (SM), such processes arise from flavor changing neutral currents (FCNC) involving two neutrinos in the final state. This paper analyzes experimental upper limits on these modes and treats the discrepancy between these bounds and SM predictions as a probe for new light invisible particles. Specifically, we investigate scenarios where a new symmetry mandates the production of these particles in pairs. We first derive a general low-energy effective Lagrangian describing FCNC couplings to two dark sector particles with spins zero, one-half, and one. Subsequently, we provide numerical estimates of the constraints on these interactions, revealing that an effective new physics scale ranging from ${\cal O}(10)$ to ${\cal O}(10^{11})$ GeV can be accessed, with the precise reach heavily dependent on the interaction structure and the invisible particle's mass. For the decay $K^+\to \pi^+ \displaystyle{\not} E$, our constraints account for the signal region selection of NA62, while for $B^+\to K^+ \displaystyle{\not} E$, we incorporate the $q^2$-dependent efficiency of Belle II.

Traditional Hasting-Metropolis reversible schemes often suffer from prohibitively long convergence times when applying Monte Carlo simulations to particle systems with singular kernels, such as hard or soft spheres, particularly near phase transitions. To address this, efficient event-chain Monte Carlo (ECMC) algorithms were developed, utilizing non-reversible continuous-time Markov processes. However, the lack of a theoretical framework to prove invariance and ergodicity for these non-reversible schemes, unlike discrete-time ones, hindered the extension of ECMC to more complex systems. This work characterizes ECMC-generated Markov processes as piecewise deterministic, enabling the proposal of more general schemes, such as those involving direction refreshment. Furthermore, we demonstrate the invariance of the correct stationary distribution and establish the ergodicity of the processes for both soft- and hard-sphere systems, specifying a density condition for the latter.

We present a novel, streamlined proof of the fractional Korn's inequality for domains within $\mathbb{R}^d$. Furthermore, we establish a framework that derives Korn's inequality directly from the corresponding Hardy-type inequality.

This presentation introduces SymDefFix, a constraint-based repair methodology. Building upon ExtractFix [3], SymDefFix substitutes its dynamic analysis phase—used for error detection and identifying potential fix locations—with symbolic execution. We begin by outlining our modifications to ExtractFix and their rationale, followed by an illustrative example.

Data privacy has been a significant concern for decades; although numerous techniques have been created to safeguard individual privacy, privacy breaches continue to occur. In 2006, Cynthia Dwork introduced Differential Privacy, offering robust theoretical assurances for data protection. While many companies and research institutions have developed libraries implementing Differential Privacy, users are still required to manually tune privacy parameters to achieve differentially private results. This paper addresses that challenge by minimizing the number of tunable parameters. We developed a DP-framework that evaluates differentially private outputs across three Python-based DP libraries. Furthermore, we introduced GRAM-DP, a new and highly accessible DP library. This allows individuals without prior knowledge of Differential Privacy to protect dataset privacy while still publishing statistical results publicly.
This paper derives uniform large deviation estimates of exponential nature and demonstrates the H\"older continuity of Lyapunov exponents for random non-invertible cocycles with constant rank.

This study introduces a real-time motion training system designed for skydiving, where aerial maneuvers are executed by altering body posture to deflect surrounding airflow. Natural learning is notoriously slow because of unfamiliar free-fall dynamics, stress-induced suppression of kinesthetic feedback, and the complexity of required movements. The core concept involves augmenting the learner with an automatic control system capable of performing trained activities as if it had direct access to the learner's body as an actuator. This supportive system provides three specific visual cues: 1. Feedback on the current body posture; 2. The target posture needed to achieve the desired maneuver; and 3. A prediction of future inertial position and orientation if the current posture is maintained. By enabling novices to maintain stability in free-fall and comprehend unfamiliar environmental dynamics, the system accelerates early skill acquisition. This paper reports on a Proof-of-Concept experiment where humans controlled a virtual skydiver in a computer simulation using their own bodies. Without the aid of this system, the task would have been impossible; however, the system enabled all participants to succeed on their first attempt.

This paper demonstrates that disabling rotational motion for users operating telepresence robots can enhance the sensation of presence or "being there." Immersive telepresence is defined as a setup where a user wearing a head-mounted display controls a mobile robot fitted with a 360° camera in a remote location, enabling both locomotion and social interaction. By preventing the perception of rotation through the display while the user remains stationary, this approach mitigates sensory mismatch, a primary cause of VR-induced sickness. We conducted a user study (N=32) on a physical Dolly mobile robot platform, replicating a prior simulation-based study. Unlike the simulated results, our physical study found no statistically significant difference in reported VR sickness or preferred rotation mode (unwinding versus automatic) among participants. Nevertheless, subjects still favored the unwinding condition and rated it as producing a stronger sense of presence, which is crucial for natural communication. Furthermore, we found that participants on the real robot perceived distances similarly to those in simulation, providing additional evidence that VR serves as an effective research platform for robotics and human-robot interaction.

By leveraging large-scale ab initio calculations, we establish novel constraints on recoil corrections in the $\beta$ decay of $^8$Li through a robust correlation with its ground state quadrupole moment. These findings are critical for enhancing the sensitivity of high-precision experiments aimed at investigating weak interaction theory and searching for physics beyond the Standard Model (BSM). Furthermore, our computations predict a $2^+$ state within the $\alpha+\alpha$ system that is energetically reachable via $\beta$ decay yet remains unobserved in the experimental $^8$Be spectrum; this state significantly influences recoil corrections and $\beta$ decay dynamics across $A=8$ systems. Although modeling this $2^+$ state and its associated $0^+$ state has historically been challenging due to their cluster structure and collective correlations, the ab initio symmetry-adapted no-core shell-model framework renders these calculations feasible.

Ultra-peripheral heavy ion collisions offer an optimal environment for discovering exotic hadrons due to their low event multiplicity and the potential for effective background suppression. We suggest investigating four-quark states generated via photon-photon fusion at a nucleon pair center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=5.5~{\rm TeV}$. Specifically, we target states that would serve as definitive proof for the compact tetraquark model. Our analysis indicates that the $X(6900)$, a probable $cc\bar{c}\bar{c}$ compact configuration, is an ideal candidate for this search, with an estimated production cross section between approximately $250$ nb and $1150$ nb, contingent upon its quantum numbers. Additionally, we highlight the significance of ultra-peripheral collisions in searching for the scalar and tensor counterparts of the $X(3872)$, which are predicted by the diquarkonium model but remain unobserved. Confirming such a flavor-spin multiplet would provide strong support for the compact tetraquark model.

For over four hundred years, single, double, and triple pendulums have served as fundamental experimental benchmarks for investigating dynamical behavior. These systems display diverse phenomena, ranging from the simple harmonic motion of a single pendulum to the chaotic dynamics found in multi-arm configurations. When subjected to external forces, even a single pendulum can exhibit chaos, offering a straightforward model of a damped-driven system. A defining characteristic of all multi-armed pendulums is the presence of index-one saddle points, which facilitate trajectory transport and provide a mechanical analog for complex transport phenomena, including biological locomotion and solar system dynamics. Furthermore, pendulum systems are widely utilized to develop and validate both linear and nonlinear control strategies, with added arms increasing the complexity of the problem. This work presents comprehensive designs for constructing and operating a high-performance, multi-link pendulum on a cart. Despite numerous existing experimental setups, the literature lacks extensive documentation on the design, construction, and operation of such systems. The resulting apparatus is highly flexible, supporting a broad spectrum of benchmark problems in dynamical systems modeling, system identification, machine learning, and control. To foster reproducible research, we have made the entire system open-source, providing 3D CAD files, introductory code, and datasets. Additionally, we explore the potential for remote operation to allow global researchers to access and utilize the system.

A primary objective in quantum key distribution (QKD) is to achieve the transmission of unconditionally secure keys across long distances. Prior research indicates that the key rate of point-to-point QKD is constrained by a secret key rate capacity bound, necessitating quantum repeaters for higher rates. In 2018, the twin-field (TF) QKD protocol was introduced as a significant solution to surpass this linear secret key capacity limit. This article offers a comprehensive survey of recent advancements in this field, covering security proofs for phase-matching QKD and other TF-QKD variants, theoretical analyses under realistic conditions, and recent experimental demonstrations.

This research explores the extreme value theory concerning a specific class of random sequences, defined as the all-time suprema of aggregated self-similar Gaussian processes incorporating a trend. The study is driven by both its theoretical significance and potential practical applications. We examine both stationary and non-stationary sequences, distinguishing between cases where trend functions are identical or distinct. Our findings demonstrate that a sequence of appropriately normalized $k$th order statistics converges in distribution to a limiting random variable. Depending on three conditions derived from the model parameters, this limit may be a negative log-transformed Erlang distributed variable, a Normal variable, or a mixture of these forms, a phenomenon notably similar to that observed in stationary Normal sequences. Furthermore, we establish that the moments of these normalized $k$th order statistics converge to the moments of their respective limiting distributions. These results facilitate the analysis of various properties of these sequences, highlighting unique characteristics within extreme value theory for this class of random processes.

We demonstrate that for a finite group $G$ with exponent $n$, any irreducible representation $\rho$ that can be realized over $\mathbb{R}$ is also realizable over the field $E:=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)\cap\mathbb{R}$, which consists of real cyclotomic numbers of order $n$. Furthermore, we outline an algorithmic method to convert a realization of $\rho$ over $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)$ into one defined over $E$.

Future human space exploration planning must account for designing environments that foster positive interpersonal communication and social dynamics within crews. Could embodied social robots enhance the overall team interaction experience in space? On Earth, social robots have demonstrated effectiveness in offering companionship, reducing stress and anxiety, strengthening social bonds, boosting team performance, and resolving conflicts among groups. This paper introduces a series of novel research questions investigating social human-robot interactions during long-duration space missions.

While extensive research has examined digital trigger patterns for backdoor poison attacks and their defenses, "physical backdoors"—which utilize physical objects as triggers—have only recently been recognized and possess distinct characteristics that render existing digital defenses ineffective. Current research into physical backdoors is hindered by the scarcity of large datasets containing real images of physical objects paired with their classification targets, as constructing such data is both laborious and time-consuming. This work aims to overcome the accessibility barriers in studying physical backdoor attacks by hypothesizing that naturally occurring, physically co-located objects already exist within popular datasets like ImageNet. By carefully relabeling these instances, they can be converted into training samples for physical backdoor attacks. We propose a scalable method to identify these potential trigger subsets and the specific classes they can compromise, designating them as "natural backdoor datasets." Our approach successfully detects natural backdoors in widely available datasets, yielding models with behavioral performance equivalent to those trained on manually curated sets. Furthermore, we have released our code to enable the research community to generate their own datasets for investigating physical backdoor attacks.

Domain Adaptive Object Detection (DAOD) aims to learn a domain-invariant transformation by modeling the joint distribution of images and labels from a labeled source domain, enabling label estimation for target domain images. While current approaches typically assume flawless source annotations, real-world large-scale datasets frequently suffer from annotation errors caused by instance ambiguity. These errors distort the source distribution and significantly impair the performance of domain adaptive detectors. This paper introduces the first formulation of noisy DAOD and proposes the Noise Latent Transferability Exploration (NLTE) framework to mitigate this challenge. The framework comprises three key components: 1) Potential Instance Mining (PIM), which uses eligible proposals to recover instances incorrectly labeled as background; 2) the Morphable Graph Relation Module (MGRM), which models the adaptability and transition probabilities of noisy samples using relation matrices; and 3) Entropy-Aware Gradient Reconcilement (EAGR), which integrates semantic information into the discrimination process to ensure that gradients from both noisy and clean samples align toward learning domain-invariant representations. Extensive evaluations on benchmark DAOD datasets with noisy source annotations demonstrate the effectiveness of NLTE. Notably, NLTE achieves an 8.4% improvement in mAP under 60% annotation corruption, performance that nearly matches the theoretical upper bound of training on a clean source dataset.

This addendum establishes an existence and uniqueness theorem for mild solutions to semilinear stochastic partial differential equations driven by both Wiener processes and Poisson random measures. Utilizing the semigroup approach with locally monotone coefficients, the framework accommodates pseudo-contractive semigroups. This work extends an earlier study by the author, which was restricted to equations driven solely by Wiener processes and required the semigroup to be a contraction.

Although automatic machine translation (MT) metrics are extensively employed for system-level evaluation across large test sets, their reliability at the segment level—distinguishing high-quality from poor translations—remains uncertain. This study examines the utility of these metrics in identifying successful machine translation components within larger platforms executing downstream tasks. We assess the segment-level performance of prevalent metrics, including chrF, COMET, and BERTScore, across three cross-lingual downstream tasks: dialogue state tracking, question answering, and semantic parsing. Given that only monolingual, task-specific models were available for each task, we analyzed the correlation between a metric's capacity to predict translation quality and the ultimate success or failure of the task in a Translate-Test configuration. Our findings indicate that all evaluated metrics show negligible correlation with extrinsic evaluations of downstream outcomes. Furthermore, we observe that scores generated by neural metrics lack interpretability, largely due to undefined value ranges. Consequently, our analysis recommends that future MT metrics be engineered to output error labels instead of scores to better support extrinsic evaluation.

We investigate the upper limits on the dark matter fraction attributed to primordial black holes (PBHs) possessing non-zero spin, utilizing the absorption signature within the global 21-cm signal at a redshift of approximately $z \sim 17$. As mass and spin are intrinsic characteristics of black holes, they significantly influence the evaporation rate; when these black holes evaporate, they inject energy into the intergalactic medium, heating the gas and altering the amplitude of the 21-cm absorption feature. Consequently, this absorption feature offers a robust method for constraining PBHs. Our analysis evaluates projected constraints on the dark matter fraction for both spinning and non-spinning PBHs, revealing that limits are tighter for spinning variants. Furthermore, by comparing these bounds with other observational data, we identify the most stringent lower mass constraint, indicating that extremal spinning PBHs could constitute the entirety of dark matter up to a mass of $6.7 \times 10^{17}$ g.

Consider a finite simple connected graph $G = (V, E)$. We define $G$ as realizing a code of the form $0^s_1 1^t_1 0^s_2 1^t_2 \dots 0^s_k 1^t_k$ if it can be constructed from this code via a specific rule. Notable classes of graphs, including threshold and chain graphs, exemplify this property. This paper introduces computationally efficient methods for calculating significant graph-theoretical invariants. Specifically, we offer an efficient algorithm to find the metric dimension of both threshold and chain graphs. Additionally, we compute the threshold dimension and restricted threshold dimension for threshold graphs. The study also examines $L(2, 1)$-coloring in these graph classes. Furthermore, we derive a formula that determines the $\lambda$-chromatic number for any threshold graph $G$. Finally, we present an algorithm to calculate the $\lambda$-chromatic number for chain graphs.

This paper investigates the second eigenvalues of closed hyperbolic surfaces with large genus. We demonstrate that for every closed hyperbolic surface $X_g$ of genus $g$ where $g\geq 3$, the second eigenvalue $\lambda_2(X_g)$ satisfies $\frac{\mathcal{L}_2(X_g)}{g^2} < \lambda_2(X_g) < C \cdot \mathcal{L}_2(X_g)$, where $C$ is a uniform positive constant; notably, both bounds are optimal in the limit as $g\to \infty$. Here, $\mathcal{L}_2(X_g)$ denotes the minimal length of simple closed multi-geodesics that divide $X_g$ into three regions. Additionally, we analyze the ratio $\frac{\lambda_2(X_g)}{\mathcal{L}_2(X_g)}$ for random hyperbolic surfaces of large genus, proving that as $g\to \infty$, a typical hyperbolic surface $X_g$ exhibits a ratio uniformly comparable to $\frac{1}{\ln(g)}$.

This paper examines a general framework for a pure exchange economy characterized by differential information. Within this model, the states of nature are represented by a complete probability measure space, agents by a finite measure space, and commodities by Euclidean space. Assuming standard and suitable conditions regarding agents' attributes, the study establishes results concerning the continuity and measurability of the aggregate preferred correspondence, following Aumann's approach in [4]. Leveraging these findings alongside additional methods, the authors demonstrate the existence of a maximin rational expectations equilibrium (maximin REE) within the proposed economic model.

The Sierpinski gasket possesses a locally isometric ramified self-covering. A semifinite spectral triple is then established on the ensuing solenoidal space, with its primary geometric characteristics analyzed.

A vertex coloring $\varphi$ of a graph $G$ is defined as odd when, for every non-isolated vertex $x$, there is at least one color $c$ such that the number of neighbors of $x$ assigned color $c$ is odd. The odd chromatic number, $\chi_o(G)$, represents the smallest number of colors required for an odd coloring of $G$. This concept was recently introduced by Petru\v{s}evski and \v{S}krekovski in their work on colorings with neighborhood parity conditions. This paper explores fundamental properties of this new parameter, characterizes acyclic graphs and hypercubes based on their odd chromatic numbers, derives multiple upper bounds related to degeneracy and maximum degree, and presents several open questions and problems.

The expansion of digital archives and the advancement of algorithms for automatic text and speech analysis have opened new avenues for fundamental phonetic research. These empirical methods enable the statistical testing of a broader range of hypotheses regarding phonetic variation and its conditioning factors, including geographical and dialectal differences. This paper presents this perspective and suggests challenging automatic analysis methods with a phenomenon that is typically difficult to observe: vowel length contrast. Specifically, we examine Wolof, an under-resourced language from Sub-Saharan Africa. We introduce multiple features to finely assess the degree of length contrast across various conditions, such as read versus semi-spontaneous speech and standard versus dialectal Wolof. Our fully automated measures, applied to over 20,000 vowel tokens, demonstrate that these features can effectively distinguish the varying degrees of contrast for each vowel. Notably, our findings indicate that vowel contrast is reduced in semi-spontaneous speech and in non-standard semi-spontaneous dialects.

Medical vision-and-language pre-training offers a viable method for extracting effective representations from medical images and text, yet few studies have focused on advancing this domain. This paper introduces a self-supervised learning framework utilizing multi-modal masked autoencoders (M$^3$AE), which acquire cross-modal knowledge by reconstructing randomly masked pixels and tokens from images and texts. The approach relies on three key designs: first, acknowledging the disparity in information density between modalities, we apply distinct masking ratios, utilizing a significantly higher rate for images than for text; second, we leverage features from diverse layers of both visual and textual inputs to handle varying levels of abstraction during reconstruction; third, we employ specialized decoders for each modality, specifically a Transformer for vision and a multi-layer perceptron for language. To support comprehensive evaluation and future research, we establish a medical vision-and-language benchmark comprising three tasks. Experimental outcomes confirm the method's efficacy, achieving state-of-the-art performance across all downstream tasks. Additionally, we perform detailed analyses to validate the effectiveness of various components and pre-training configurations. The source code is accessible at~\url{https://github.com/zhjohnchan/M3AE}.

This research investigates the formation of heavy multiquark states in heavy ion collisions at the LHC. We posit that these states emerge at the conclusion of the quark-gluon plasma phase and subsequently interact with light hadrons within the hadron gas phase. Using the coalescence model, we calculate initial multiplicities, while effective Lagrangians are employed to characterize the interactions. Our findings indicate that the initial abundance of molecular states exceeds that of tetraquarks by two orders of magnitude. Subsequent interactions within the hadron gas decrease the number of molecules and increase the number of tetraquarks by a factor of two in both instances. Even at kinetic freeze-out, the disparity between the two remains substantial.

Inductive logic programming constitutes a machine learning paradigm grounded in mathematical logic, designed to derive logic programs from examples and background knowledge. This project enhances the Popper ILP system by incorporating multi-task learning. We implement leading-edge methods alongside novel strategies to boost search efficiency. Moreover, we introduce "constraint preservation," a technique that elevates performance across all approaches. By enabling the system to transfer knowledge between updates to the background knowledge set, constraint preservation minimizes redundant computational effort. Additionally, it facilitates a shift from the current state-of-the-art iterative deepening search to a more efficient breadth-first search method. Finally, we investigate curriculum learning techniques, demonstrating their promising advantages for the field.

In the context of the SOS (solid-on-solid) model featuring an external field and integer-valued spins on a Cayley tree, every (gradient) Gibbs measure is associated with a boundary law—an infinite-dimensional vector function defined on the tree's vertices—that satisfies a non-linear functional equation. While recent studies have identified translation-invariant and height-periodic (non-normalisable) solutions to this equation, our objective is to discover non-height-periodic and non-normalisable boundary laws for the SOS model. These solutions enable the construction of non-probability Gibbs measures. We explicitly derive several such non-normalisable boundary laws and simplify the problem by reducing it to solving a non-linear, second-order difference equation. Furthermore, we provide both analytical and numerical examinations of this difference equation.

This paper aims to demonstrate that Eilenberg-type correspondences arise from combining Birkhoff's theorem for (finite) algebras with duality. We examine algebras within a monad T defined on a category D, focusing on the (pseudo)varieties of these T-algebras, which are also referred to in the literature as varieties of finite algebras. Two foundational theorems characterizing these structures are central to our approach: Birkhoff's theorem and its finite counterpart, known as Reiterman's theorem. Under mild assumptions, we establish a categorical version of Birkhoff's theorem for (finite) algebras, creating a one-to-one mapping between (pseudo)varieties of T-algebras and (pseudo)equational T-theories. Furthermore, if C is the category dual to D and B is the comonad on C dual to T, we derive a one-to-one correspondence between (pseudo)equational T-theories and their duals, the (pseudo)coequational B-theories. Instances of these (pseudo)coequational B-theories have previously been investigated in language theory as "varieties of languages" to define Eilenberg-type correspondences. Ultimately, we establish a one-to-one correspondence between (pseudo)varieties of T-algebras and (pseudo)coequational B-theories, thereby revealing the fundamental nature of Eilenberg-type correspondences.

The study identifies time-dependent central potentials that are integrable and possess linear and quadratic first integrals distinct from those derived from angular momentum, demonstrating that earlier solutions to this problem were incomplete. These findings are utilized to derive integrable time-dependent oscillators, generalized Kepler potentials with time dependence, a category of integrable binary systems featuring variable mass, as well as time-dependent Yukawa and interatomic potentials. Furthermore, the research integrates a novel class of integrable potentials and determines their associated wavefunctions.

The ALICE experiment's measurements of charm meson production multiplicity in p-p collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 7$ TeV and 13 TeV were analyzed using the Pythia 8 event generator. This investigation examined partonic-level processes, specifically varying color reconnection modes and rope hadronization. The study found that Pythia 8's predictions for the relative yields ($\rm Yield/\langle Yield \rangle$) of D-mesons and $J/\psi$ across different relative charged particle multiplicities and transverse momentum ($p\textsubscript{T}$) ranges align reasonably well with ALICE data within a microscopic framework. Additionally, the model generated predictions for B meson relative yields over $p\textsubscript{T}$ intervals ($1 < p_{T} < 20$ GeV/$c$) for p-p collisions at both $\sqrt{s} = 7$ TeV and $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV.

Microbiology culture reports are vital for clinical and public health decisions, yet their complex, semi-structured free-text format often hinders secondary data utilization. To address this, we developed and validated an open-source package that ingests these reports, identifies positive cultures, and outputs a list of bacteria mapped to SNOMED-CT codes. Our rule-based natural language processing algorithm was trained on microbiology reports from two electronic health record systems within a large healthcare organization and subsequently validated externally using manually annotated data from two other institutions. The algorithm achieved F-1 scores exceeding 0.95 across all classification tasks in both validation sets. The resulting Python package, MicrobEx, is designed for reuse and adaptation by individual institutions as an upstream processing step for various clinical applications, including machine learning research, clinical decision support, and disease surveillance.

The Expected Improvement (EI) algorithm stands out as a leading optimization strategy under uncertainty, valued for its simplicity and efficiency. However, its theoretical foundations remain insufficiently explored, particularly regarding the convergence of the standard EI approach with a fixed incumbent in noisy environments within Gaussian process bandit optimization. This paper addresses this open problem by introducing a new EI variant where the standard incumbent is defined using the Gaussian process predictive mean. We demonstrate that this algorithm converges and attains a cumulative regret bound of $\mathcal O(\gamma_T\sqrt{T})$, with $\gamma_T$ representing the maximum information gain over $T$ observations. Building on this, we propose an "Improved GP-EI" algorithm that converges more rapidly than existing methods. Notably, our variants eliminate the need for prior knowledge of the RKHS norm and the noise's sub-Gaussianity parameter, requirements often present in previous literature. Empirical results confirm the superiority of our algorithms against several baseline methods.

By coupling the metric to an additional spin-two field, a pathology-free phase of massive gravity can be achieved. We examine the gravitational field generated by a static, spherically symmetric object by deriving an exact solution that extends the Schwarzschild metric to massive gravity. Beyond the standard $1/r$ term, the primary influences of this new spin-two field include a modification to the body's total mass and the introduction of a new power-law term, whose magnitude depends on the source's mass and radius. Because these alterations are contingent upon the source, they result in a dynamical violation of the Strong Equivalence Principle. Depending on the specific coupling details, the power-law term could dominate either at large distances or in the ultraviolet regime, an effect that remains even when the extra field's dynamics are decoupled.

This paper provides a detailed description of invertible functions on the Drinfeld symmetric space over $K$, where $K$ is a finite extension of $\mathbb{Q}_p$. We establish a correspondence between these functions and specific distribution spaces defined over the profinite set of $K$-rational points of projective space. Our approach involves constructing a map from these distributions to the invertible functions, utilizing techniques developed by Schneider-Stuhler, Iovita-Spiess, and de Shalit. We demonstrate that this map aligns with the isomorphisms previously established by these authors for computing étale and de Rham cohomology in degree 1; this compatibility ensures that our map is an isomorphism. Consequently, we obtain a $\mathbb{Z}$-structure for these cohomology groups.

The widespread accessibility of remote sensing data has drawn significant attention to developing models capable of interpreting this complex information. Specifically, hyperspectral images (HSI) provide spectral details, while LiDAR offers elevation data, creating a need for further research into effectively fusing these distinct data sources. This paper proposes a method that leverages semantic understanding to dynamically integrate features from both sources. We utilize separate capsule network branches to extract features from HSI and LiDAR, while enhancing the Canonical Capsule approach by improving self-supervised loss functions and adapting random rigid rotation techniques for high-dimensional scenarios. Canonical Capsule performs object decomposition through permutation-equivariant attention, a process that is self-supervised via training on randomly rotated object pairs. Following the semantic fusion of HSI and LiDAR features, the method achieves unsupervised extraction of combined spectral-spatial-elevation representations. Experimental validation using two real-world HSI and LiDAR datasets demonstrates that the proposed multi-branch, high-dimensional canonical capsule algorithm is highly effective for semantic understanding. These results indicate that the model successfully extracts features from both data types, outperforming existing models in the unsupervised extraction of multi-source remote sensing data.

Computational color constancy serves as a critical preprocessing stage in numerous camera systems, aiming to neutralize illumination effects and recover the true colors of objects. While recent deep learning approaches have achieved state-of-the-art performance in terms of average error metrics, they struggle with extreme samples, resulting in significant inaccuracies. This paper addresses that limitation by aggregating diverse deep learning methods based on their output uncertainty. We quantify the relative uncertainty of each approach via Monte Carlo dropout and derive the final illumination estimate by summing individual model outputs, weighted by the inverse logarithm of their respective uncertainties. This proposed framework achieves state-of-the-art results on the INTEL-TAU dataset.

We introduce a finite-order system of recurrence relations designed to calculate the permanent of circulant matrices featuring a band of $k$ arbitrary-value diagonals above a uniform matrix, specifically for $k = 1, 2,$ and $3$. Our approach includes a derivation method grounded in the permanents of matrices with defects. This proposed system of linear recurrence equations with variable coefficients serves as a potent analytical tool for circulant permanents, enabling their rapid linear-time computation and the determination of their asymptotic behavior in the limit of large matrix sizes. Resolving this asymptotic problem is a fundamental open challenge; solving it would be of immense significance for the unified analysis of numerous $\#P$-hard problems found in nature, spanning areas such as many-body physics, critical phenomena, quantum computing, quantum field theory, chaos theory, fractals, graph theory, number theory, combinatorics, and cryptography.

This study investigates the laser-driven acceleration of electrons from overdense hydrogen clusters, achieving energies up to 13 MeV in the forward laser direction and several hundred keV in an outer ring-like structure. Employing cryogenic hydrogen enables high repetition rates and allows for the analysis of how source parameters, such as temperature and gas flow, influence the process. The robust, outer ring-like electron population, which persists despite variations in laser and target conditions, appears at low electron densities around $3\times10^{16}$ cm$^{-3}$. At higher densities, an additional central electron spot emerges in the forward direction. Three-dimensional particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations indicate that both electron populations primarily originate from ponderomotive scattering.

This article models and analyzes the propagation of COVID-19 across Germany, Japan, India, and specific Indian states heavily affected by the pandemic, namely Delhi, Maharashtra, West Bengal, Kerala, and Karnataka. Utilizing data from Worldometers and the COVID-19 India website spanning April 2020 to July 2021, we focus on critical periods marked by severe outbreaks. Our approach employs the classic susceptible-infected-removed (SIR) framework, enhanced by three key adaptations: (a) resetting susceptible and infected populations during data-driven surges, secondary waves, or outbreaks; (b) treating effective transmission and recovery rates as time-dependent variables; and (c) refining death estimates by integrating model solutions with recorded data to approximate fatalities between surge events. We present findings on current infection statuses in the studied regions and specific metrics for India and Japan. The proposed model dynamically adapts to recorded data to explain past trends and forecast future numbers of infected, recovered, removed, and deceased individuals, while also estimating time-varying infection and recovery rates. These capabilities allow for the prediction of future reproduction numbers. Consequently, this approach aids in recommending intervention strategies and mitigation policies to control infection and mortality rates, thereby reducing the global impact of the pandemic and enhancing public wellbeing.

Addressing the critical demand for algorithmic transparency, Explainable AI (XAI) has become a central focus in AI research. This paper introduces BayLIME, a new Bayesian extension to the LIME framework, one of the most prevalent XAI methods. Unlike standard LIME, BayLIME leverages prior knowledge and Bayesian reasoning to enhance consistency across repeated explanations of individual predictions and increase robustness regarding kernel configurations. Furthermore, BayLIME surpasses current state-of-the-art methods (including LIME, SHAP, and GradCAM) in explanation fidelity by effectively integrating prior information from diverse XAI techniques and verification and validation (V&V) approaches. We validate the advantageous properties of BayLIME through both theoretical analysis and comprehensive experiments.

Kernel methods are foundational to classical machine learning and have recently been formally linked to quantum mechanics. To comprehend the benefits of quantum machine learning, one must distinguish between classical kernels and non-classical ones. Building on a recent phase space nonclassicality witness, this paper derives a corresponding witness for quantumness within continuous-variable systems. We examine how kernel nonclassicality influences data distributions in feature space and the impact of imperfect state preparation. Additionally, we demonstrate that non-classical kernels enable quantum advantages in parameter estimation. Ultimately, our work underscores the importance of phase space correlation functions in differentiating classical from quantum machine learning.

Hybrid beamforming (HBF) integrates analog beamforming utilizing phase-shifted arrays in the radio frequency domain with digital beamforming in the baseband domain. Typically, these phase-shifted arrays consist of numerous phase shifters, which, due to manufacturing constraints, inevitably introduce phase and gain errors. This paper investigates how such imperfect phase shifters affect multiuser mmWave massive MIMO systems, assuming a wireless channel characterized by Rice fading. We establish an upper bound for the achievable sum rate under these imperfections, noting that this bound becomes highly accurate when the base station's antenna count significantly exceeds the number of users. Our findings indicate that phase-shifting and gain errors impose a performance ceiling. To address this, we propose a novel channel estimation and hybrid beamforming technique that achieves this goal with minimal training overhead. This method demonstrates strong performance in scenarios with few channel paths and a high Rician K-factor—conditions common in outdoor mmWave environments. Furthermore, we balance performance against training overhead to ensure the algorithm remains effective across a wider variety of propagation conditions.

Many scientific disciplines are currently grappling with a reproducibility crisis. For the emerging field of quantum software engineering, it is crucial to prioritize robust reproducibility practices from the outset. However, the creation of reproduction packages is almost entirely absent, and practical guidance on constructing them is scarce—a significant issue given that many contributors come from non-computer science backgrounds. This article proposes a solution through a "1-2-3" approach to reproducibility engineering for quantum experiments. By utilizing a meta-generation mechanism, we create reproduction packages that are DOI-secure, durable over time, and free from external dependencies. These packages are designed to meet the standards of professional and academic societies using only project-specific artifacts, such as source code, measurement data, and configuration files, while minimizing the time researchers need to invest. Our method ensures long-term traceability even if the underlying quantum hardware becomes unavailable. By significantly reducing technical barriers, we aim to encourage the widespread adoption of reproduction packages in quantum experiments and facilitate the participation of researchers without a computer science background.

Decision-making under uncertainty and dynamic constraints is a prevalent challenge in optimal control, reinforcement learning, and increasingly, online learning. In online learning, an agent's performance is typically evaluated using regret, which measures the difference between the agent's actual decisions and the optimal decisions made in hindsight. Although regret is a valuable metric, assessing the stability of the closed-loop system is equally critical when dealing with dynamical systems. This work demonstrates that for linear systems with adversarial disturbances, linear regret guarantees asymptotic stability for linear state feedback policies, regardless of whether the system is time-invariant or time-varying. Conversely, we establish that bounded-input bounded-state (BIBS) stability, combined with the summability of state transition matrices, ensures the presence of linear regret.

This work investigates transient phenomena occurring within the subgap region of a series-connected double quantum dot system bridging superconducting and normal metallic leads, with a specific focus on the evolution of the superconducting proximity effect. For an uncorrelated nanostructure, we derive explicit formulas for time-dependent occupancies in both dots, charge currents, and electron pairing induced individually and between the dots. We demonstrate that initial configurations significantly influence these dynamical processes, particularly the emergence of in-gap bound states upon coupling the double quantum dot to superconducting reservoirs. Specifically, the superconducting proximity effect is temporarily suppressed when the quantum dots are initially singly occupied, a phenomenon known as {\it triplet}/{\it Andreev blockade} that has recently been observed experimentally in double quantum dots embedded within Josephson [D. Bouman et al., Phys. Rev. B 102, 220505 (2020)] and Andreev [P. Zhang et al., arXiv:2102.03283 (2021)] junctions. Furthermore, we examine correlation effects using the lowest-order decoupling scheme and time-dependent numerical renormalization group calculations. The competition between repulsive Coulomb interactions and the superconducting proximity effect results in the renormalization of in-gap quasiparticles, accelerating quantum oscillations and narrowing the transient phenomenon region, while the dynamical Andreev blockade remains prominent in the weak inter-dot coupling limit. Finally, we suggest feasible methods to detect the characteristic time-scales that could be observable via Andreev spectroscopy.

Achieving real-time holistic scene understanding would enable machines to perceive their surroundings with significantly greater detail than is currently feasible. Although panoptic image segmentation has advanced the field toward this objective, such data must be mapped to a 3D environment to be effectively utilized. This paper explores techniques for the sequential 3D reconstruction of static scenes from panoptic segmentations, with a specific focus on real-time performance; the proposed algorithm must operate strictly online at high frame rates and remain scalable for large, practical environments. By employing a straightforward yet potent data-association strategy, we surpass previous online-only approaches. Our method achieves frame rates suitable for real-time applications and demonstrates scalability to larger settings. The source code and additional demonstrations are publicly available at: \url{https://tutvision.github.io/Online-Panoptic-3D/}

The mechanisms governing gamma-ray emission and particle acceleration during the prompt phase of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) remain unresolved; therefore, unambiguous physical modeling requires a definitive identification of the emission process. A prime example is the synchrotron emission observed during the intense flare of GRB 160821A at 135 seconds into the prompt phase. This study demonstrates that the radiating electron distribution in this flare begins as very narrow but subsequently evolves into a power-law tail of accelerated electrons, marking the first-ever identification of particle acceleration onset within a GRB jet. This flare aligns with a delayed energy release from the central engine that triggers an external shock upon interacting with a pre-existing ring nebula from a Wolf-Rayet progenitor star. Consequently, relativistic forward and reverse shocks form, creating two distinct emission zones with comparable characteristics. Particle acceleration is confined exclusively to the forward shock as it penetrates the dense nebular material. In this region, the magnetization drops below the critical threshold, enabling Fermi acceleration. Based on this, we derive a bulk Lorentz factor of $420 \leq \Gamma \leq 770$ and an emission radius of approximately $10^{18}$ cm, suggesting a tenuous circumburst environment. Observing the initiation of particle acceleration thus provides novel, independent constraints on flow properties and theories regarding particle acceleration in collisionless astrophysical shocks.

With the expansion of networked control systems and the increasing complexity of inter-subsystem interactions, ensuring their resilience has become increasingly critical. Recently, redefining classical system and control concepts through graph theory has emerged as a promising and significant research domain. This paper provides an overview of graph-theoretic approaches for assessing the resilience of such systems. We examine various distributed algorithms applied to networked environments and evaluate their resistance to adversarial actions by analyzing the structural characteristics of their underlying networks. Furthermore, we introduce methods to quantify attack severity and reinterpret traditional robustness concepts from a graph-theoretic perspective to counteract malicious impacts. Additionally, we address other security challenges in networked control systems that leverage graph theory for analysis, concluding with suggestions for future research directions in this field.

Generating random numbers is essential for many critical domains, such as cryptography, scientific simulations, and industrial testing. While True Random Number Generators (TRNGs) derive genuine randomness from physical entropy sources, they often require specialized hardware and suffer from high latency. To achieve high-bandwidth, low-latency TRNGs on standard devices, recent research has proposed using DRAM as an entropy source. Despite promising results from previous studies, integrating these mechanisms into real systems presents specific hurdles. We have identified three primary challenges: (1) RNG operations can impair overall system performance by slowing concurrent applications due to interference between random number generation and standard memory access within the memory controller; (2) this interference compromises system fairness by unfairly favoring applications with heavy random number usage; and (3) applications relying on random numbers face significant slowdowns caused by high latency. We introduce DR-STRaNGe, an end-to-end system architecture for DRAM-based TRNGs that addresses these issues by: (1) isolating RNG requests from regular memory requests in the controller to minimize interference, (2) enhancing fairness through an RNG-aware memory scheduler, and (3) concealing high latency via a buffering mechanism paired with a novel DRAM idleness predictor that accurately detects idle periods. Evaluation using 186 multiprogrammed workloads shows that, compared to an RNG-oblivious baseline, DR-STRaNGe boosts the average performance of non-RNG and RNG applications by 17.9% and 25.1%, respectively. Furthermore, it increases average system fairness by 32.1% and cuts average energy consumption by 21%.

The inspiral of supermassive black-hole binaries within gas-rich environments is propelled by accretion discs, with viscous forces generally aligning the black holes' spins to the disc's orbital angular momentum. Recent studies introduced an iterative method to model this alignment and the subsequent non-linear evolution of warped discs, predicting that spins either fully align or reach a critical obliquity beyond which warp equations fail. This paper demonstrates that such a critical threshold marks the onset of disc breaking, where the disc fragments into two or more distinct parts. Utilizing 3D hydrodynamical simulations, we (i) validate the semi-analytic model's predictions and (ii) reveal a more complex behavior, including unsuccessful, single, and multiple disc breaks. Furthermore, we identify hydrodynamic features like spiral arms that can stabilize the disc against breaking even past the critical limit. Our findings indicate that when disc breaking occurs, the alignment between the black holes and the disc is either hindered or entirely prevented during the binary's inspiral.

This research investigates nonperturbative flavor correlations between leading and next-to-leading charged hadron pairs inside jets at the Electron-Ion Collider (EIC). We propose a charge correlation ratio observable, denoted as $r_c$, which differentiates between same-sign and opposite-sign charged pairs. Through Monte Carlo simulations employing various event generators, we analyze $r_c$ across multiple kinematic variables and different hadron species combinations, demonstrating the feasibility of these measurements at the EIC. The proposed precision study on hadronization aims to offer new constraints on hadronization models and ultimately foster a more robust quantitative, and potentially analytic, comprehension of nonperturbative QCD dynamics.

This study examines how aerosols influence the micro- and macro-physical characteristics of marine stratocumulus clouds over the Western North Atlantic Ocean (WNAO) using large-eddy simulations (LES) and in-situ data from two cold air outbreak (CAO) events in February and March 2020 as part of the ACTIVATE campaign. The LES successfully replicates vertical profiles of liquid water content (LWC), effective radius ($r_{eff}$), and cloud droplet number concentration ($N_c$) obtained from fast cloud droplet probe (FCDP) measurements for both cases. Additionally, the findings demonstrate that aerosols modify cloud properties ($N_c$, $r_{eff}$, and LWC) through prescribed bulk hygroscopicity and aerosol size distribution traits. Specifically, $N_c$, $r_{eff}$, and liquid water path (LWP) exhibit positive correlations with both bulk hygroscopicity and aerosol number concentration ($N_a$), whereas cloud fractional cover (CFC) remains unaffected by these aerosol characteristics across the two cases. By adjusting aerosol size distribution parameters (number concentration, width, and geometric diameter), the study isolates aerosol impacts on cloud properties from meteorological influences. Furthermore, LES outputs were used to assess cloud properties in two reanalysis datasets, ERA5 and MERRA-2. While ERA5 accurately captures the temporal evolution of LWP and total cloud coverage within the study area during both CAO events, MERRA-2 tends to underestimate these metrics.

I investigate a population model where the reproduction rate $\lambda$ is subject to inheritance and mutation, creating a tension between short-term advantages for rapid reproducers and a mechanism that disperses agglomerations of individuals. This system is a variation of the triplet annihilation model proposed decades ago by R. Dickman [Phys. Rev. B~{\bf 40}, 7005 (1989)], where organisms (treated as "particles") reproduce and diffuse across a lattice but are annihilated if and only if they occupy three consecutive sites. When diffusion rates fall below a specific threshold, the population exhibits two distinct "survival strategies": (i) rare reproduction ($0 < \lambda < \lambda_{c,1}$), where a sparse density of diffusing particles makes triplets extremely uncommon, and (ii) frequent reproduction ($\lambda > \lambda_{c,2}$). In the intermediate range between $\lambda_{c,1}$ and $\lambda_{c,2}$, no active steady state exists. Within the rare-reproduction regime, a mutating $\lambda$ triggers stochastic boom-and-bust cycles; reproduction rates rise locally but eventually cause extinction in those areas as $\lambda$ becomes too high. However, the global population persists because other regions maintain reproduction rates that have not yet drifted upward.
