Over the last ten years, significant advancements in experimental research on exclusive meson photoproduction from protons and comprehensive multi-channel amplitude analyses have led to the identification of several anticipated new nucleon resonances. This breakthrough was largely driven by $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ photoproduction results obtained using the CLAS detector at Jefferson Lab. The presentation will explore further developments by integrating exclusive meson photo- and electroproduction data from protons. The discovery of a new nucleon excited state, $N'(1720)3/2^+$, derived from combined analyses of $\pi^+\pi^-p$ photo- and electroproduction data, alongside other resonances found in photo- and hadroproduction studies, highlights the promising potential of this emerging research direction for uncovering additional resonances.

Constraints on new-physics (NP) involving first-generation quark-lepton interactions are highly significant due to the extensive array of complementary measured processes and observables. Recent indications of such NP effects have emerged, notably as a deficit in first-row CKM unitarity—the Cabibbo angle anomaly—and the CMS excess in $q\bar q\to e^+e^-$. Because any such NP would inevitably influence low-energy parity violation searches, including atomic parity violation, parity-violating electron scattering, coherent neutrino-nucleus scattering, and electroweak precision observables, a combined analysis is essential to evaluate potential NP interpretations. This article examines the interplay among LHC searches, the Cabibbo angle anomaly, electroweak precision data, and low-energy parity violation by analyzing all simplified models yielding tree-level effects in first-generation quark-lepton interactions. By matching these models to the Standard Model effective field theory, we derive master formulae based on Wilson coefficients, conduct a comprehensive phenomenological analysis of existing constraints, demonstrate how future parity violation measurements can distinguish between different NP scenarios, and project the sensitivity achievable with upcoming experiments.

This study investigates the properties of rotating neutron stars undergoing a phase transition to quark matter. The hadronic phase is analyzed using the density-dependent relativistic mean-field (DD-RMF) model, whereas the Vector-Enhanced Bag (vBag) model describes the quark matter. Key stellar characteristics—including mass, radius, moment of inertia, rotational frequency, the Kerr parameter, and other critical metrics—are examined to assess the impact of quark matter inclusion. Results indicate that for the DD-LZ1 and DD-MEX parameter sets, the maximum mass of a rotating neutron star in a pure hadronic phase is approximately $3M_{\odot}$, which drops to roughly $2.6M_{\odot}$ upon transitioning to quark matter, aligning with recent GW190814 constraints. Conversely, for the DDV, DDVT, and DDVTD sets, the maximum mass decreases to satisfy the $2M_{\odot}$ limit. Calculations show that the moment of inertia diminishes as mass increases across various DD-RMF parameter sets, consistent with observational data. Additionally, other derived quantities vary with the bag constant, suggesting that quark presence within neutron stars helps constrain these values to refine the Equation of State (EoS). Ultimately, combining theoretical models with precise measurements of uniformly rotating neutron stars could yield significant insights into the high-density region of the EoS.

These lecture notes support a six-hour mini-course on SPDEs delivered at the University of Oxford in April/May 2021. The primary emphasis is an exposition of the variational method applied to monotone and coercive SPDEs. The notes also include a review of essential concepts in functional analysis, operator theory, and stochastic analysis on Hilbert spaces, along with supplementary references. The final chapter explores the pathwise approach.

Polar crystal surfaces are critical to the functionality of numerous materials and have been the subject of extensive research over several decades. This article introduces a theoretical framework that advances current models by treating the surrounding solution environment with the same importance as the crystal itself, a perspective particularly beneficial for analyzing processes like solution-based crystal growth. By modeling the polar crystal as a series of parallel plate capacitors within a solution, the study derives the equilibrium adsorbed surface charge density through the minimization of the system's free energy. Drawing a parallel to the well-established divergence of surface energy in polar crystals at zero temperature, the authors demonstrate that in a solution environment, the "polar catastrophe" appears as a diverging free energy penalty when the system is perturbed from equilibrium. Extending beyond existing theories, the formulation predicts that fluctuations in the adsorbed surface charge density diminish as crystal thickness increases. Furthermore, the work elucidates how an electric displacement field arises as an electrostatic boundary condition in the commonly used slab geometry, a phenomenon rooted in the geometry itself rather than periodic boundary conditions. This insight provides a more robust theoretical foundation for recent findings indicating that standard "slab corrections" inadequately describe, even qualitatively, polar crystal surfaces in solution.

This paper addresses the challenge of computing approximate Nash equilibria in continuous-action games without access to gradient information, a scenario typical in reinforcement learning where environments function as black boxes. Our approach leverages zeroth-order optimization, integrating smoothed gradient estimators with equilibrium-finding dynamics. We represent player strategies using artificial neural networks, specifically employing randomized policy networks to model mixed strategies. These networks accept both observations and noise as inputs, enabling the flexible representation of arbitrary, observation-dependent continuous-action distributions. Modeling such mixed strategies is essential for addressing continuous-action games that do not possess pure-strategy equilibria. We assess our method's performance using a game-theoretic approximation of the Nash convergence metric, which quantifies the potential gain from unilateral strategy changes. Applications include continuous Colonel Blotto games, single and multi-item auctions, and a visibility game. Experimental results demonstrate that our method efficiently identifies high-quality approximate equilibria and reveal that the dimensionality of input noise significantly impacts performance. To our knowledge, this work represents the first solution for general continuous-action games with unrestricted mixed strategies in the absence of gradient information.

This paper explores the challenge of receiving text messages via a communication channel that is both noisy and expensive. While the noise necessitates redundancy, the high cost restricts how much redundancy can be employed. I begin by applying established decoding techniques for noisy signals, specifically compressed sensing, and then strive to minimize redundancy through random projections. This process continues until the number of orthogonal vectors exceeds the dimensionality of the space. Contrary to expectations, the method does not fail or produce noise; instead, it successfully decodes messages, either perfectly or nearly so. I remain uncertain as to why this approach functions, which serves as my primary motivation for adopting a narrative style over traditional scientific prose (the secondary motivation being a desire to move away from semi-formal writing).

Recently, reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-assisted wireless communications have garnered considerable interest. This study examines the physical layer security of downlink RIS-aided transmissions for randomly positioned users facing a multi-antenna eavesdropper. To highlight the benefits of RIS networks, we analyze two practical scenarios: communication with and without RIS. In both cases, stochastic geometry is employed to derive the exact probability density function (PDF) and cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the received signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio. These derived functions are then utilized to assess key security metrics, including secrecy outage probability, the probability of nonzero secrecy capacity, and the average secrecy rate. Monte-Carlo simulations are performed to verify the accuracy of the analytical findings. When compared to conventional MIMO systems, RIS-aided networks demonstrate superior physical layer security performance. Notably, security is significantly enhanced by increasing the number of reflecting elements in the RIS. However, RISs with a small number of elements fail to improve system performance when non-line-of-sight (NLoS) path loss is low.

This preface introduces the SIGMA special issue titled "Tensor Models, Formalism and Applications," available at http://www.emis.de/journals/SIGMA/Tensor_Models.html. The issue compiles eight comprehensive and current reviews on random tensor models. These articles offer both accessible introductions for a broad audience and detailed accounts of the latest advancements in the field. The preface serves as a concise overview of random tensors, highlighting them as the natural extension of random matrices into higher dimensions.

The initial observations of the $z>10$ universe by the $JWST$ have revealed a surprising number of bright galaxy candidates, with CEERS-1749 representing the most extreme example. Photometry spanning $0.6-5\mu$m indicates this exceptionally luminous ($\approx$26 mag) object is located at $z\approx17$, suggesting it is a massive system with an $M_{\rm{UV}}\approx-22$ and stellar mass of $\approx5\times10^{9}M_{\rm{\odot}}$ that formed only $\sim220$ Myrs after the Big Bang. The density of such galaxies would contradict nearly all early galaxy evolution models within the $\Lambda$CDM framework. However, compelling environmental data supports an alternative redshift of $z\approx5$; all three nearest neighbors within $<2.5$" exhibit photometric redshifts near $z\approx5$. Additionally, CEERS-1749 may reside in a $z\approx5$ protocluster that is more than five times overdense relative to the field. Strong emission lines at $z\approx5$ from either a quiescent galaxy with ionized gas or a dusty starburst could explain its photometry. These lines at $z\approx5$ artificially enhance the $>2\mu$m flux, creating an apparent blue slope and a prominent break in the spectral energy distribution (SED). Such a "disguised" contaminant is only viable within a narrow redshift range ($\Delta z\lesssim0.1$), implying that the volume available for similar interlopers is likely not a significant issue for $z>10$ searches, especially with medium-band filters. If confirmed at $z\approx5$, CEERS-1749 would represent either the highest-redshift quiescent galaxy or one of the lowest-mass dusty galaxies ever detected. Given that both potential redshift scenarios could disrupt current models of early galaxy evolution, spectroscopic follow-up of this source is essential.

Spacecraft navigation and the three-dimensional reconstruction of celestial bodies heavily rely on imagery. When a camera's orientation is known, both tasks reduce to a triangulation problem based on extracted line-of-sight (LOS) vectors. This paper offers a thorough examination of the historical development and theoretical underpinnings of triangulation. It surveys various classical algorithms, covering suboptimal linear approaches suitable for numerous LOS measurements and the optimal Hartley-Sturm method designed for only two measurements. The study demonstrates that the optimal solution for multiple measurements can be achieved without iteration by solving a linear system through the newly proposed Linear Optimal Sine Triangulation (LOST) method. Notably, both LOST and the Hartley-Sturm polynomial method yield identical results when limited to two measurements. The performance of these diverse algorithms is evaluated through numerical examples, such as planetary terrain relative navigation, angles-only optical navigation at Uranus, the 3-D reconstruction of Notre-Dame de Paris, and angles-only relative navigation.

Spin polarization measurements from heavy-ion collisions have enabled new phenomenological studies of spin dynamics in relativistic fluids. While theoretical predictions for global polarization align with experimental data, significant discrepancies remain regarding local polarization. We demonstrate that the covariant theory of relativistic quantum fluids at local equilibrium necessitates an additional, non-dissipative term in the spin polarization vector, proportional to the thermal shear, a factor previously neglected. Incorporating this contribution, alongside an enhanced approximation for the local equilibrium density operator expansion, reestablishes quantitative agreement between theory and experiment.

We demonstrate that the posterior distribution of parameters in a hidden Markov model, characterized by parametric emission distributions and a discrete, known state space, converges asymptotically to a normal distribution. The primary innovation of our proof lies in its reliance on a testing condition, where the sequence of test functions is derived from an optimal transportation inequality.

This research addresses the design of interval-valued observers capable of concurrently estimating system states and identifying unknown dynamic models for partially unknown nonlinear systems subject to dynamic unknown inputs and bounded noise. By integrating affine abstraction techniques, nonlinear decomposition functions, and a prior data-driven approach for over-approximating unknown dynamics, the proposed observer recursively calculates the upper and lower bounds of estimate intervals, which are mathematically guaranteed to encompass the true augmented states. Subsequently, the observer utilizes observed output and measurement data to iteratively refine these intervals by discarding estimates inconsistent with the measurements. Furthermore, the observer adjusts the over-approximation of the unknown model dynamics based on the updated interval estimates. Additionally, we establish sufficient conditions ensuring the uniform boundedness of the estimate interval widths—thereby guaranteeing observer stability—in the form of tractable (mixed-)integer programs with finitely countable feasible sets.

Rather than relying on conventional uniform sampling, time encoding transforms continuous-time signals into streams of trigger events, forming the basis of Event-Driven Sampling (EDS). These data-driven EDS models offer superior power efficiency and time resolution, drawing inspiration from biological nervous systems. However, if an analog signal exceeds a predefined dynamic range, EDS produces sparse trigger times, resulting in aliasing-induced recovery distortion. Drawing on the Unlimited Sensing Framework (USF), this paper introduces a novel EDS architecture called Modulo Event-Driven Sampling (MEDS), which inserts a modulo nonlinearity before acquisition. In MEDS, this nonlinearity folds high-dynamic-range inputs into lower amplitudes, thereby preventing distortion. Specifically, we utilize the asynchronous sigma-delta modulator (ASDM), a technique previously employed for low-power analog-to-digital conversion. This new MEDS approach is made possible by a recent generalization of the modulo operation known as modulo-hysteresis. We develop a mathematically guaranteed recovery algorithm for bandlimited inputs based on a specific sampling rate criterion and establish bounds for reconstruction errors. Furthermore, we move beyond numerical simulations to present the first hardware validation of this method, bridging the gap between theoretical concepts and practical implementation while confirming the foundational principles of our work.

First, we demonstrate that indefinite Sasakian manifolds cannot accommodate any screen conformal $r$-null submanifolds tangent to the structure vector field. Consequently, we introduce a specific category of null submanifolds termed {\it contact screen conformal} $r$-null submanifolds within indefinite Sasakian manifolds. We establish several characterization theorems for this class, notably proving their existence in indefinite Sasakian space forms possessing constant holomorphic sectional curvatures of $-3$.

This note calculates Leibniz algebra deformations for the 3-dimensional nilpotent Lie algebra $\mathfrak{n}_3$ and contrasts them with its Lie deformations, revealing three additional Leibniz deformations. Furthermore, we outline the versal Leibniz deformation of $\mathfrak{n}_3$ along with its corresponding versal base.

Collisions of heavy ions at low beam energies may uncover the complex phase structure of QCD under conditions of non-zero temperature and density. This structure includes phases characterized by spatial periodicity, where the energy spectrum resembles a moat, reaching its minimum at a non-zero momentum on a spherical surface. We propose that if the matter generated in these collisions passes through such a phase, it will exhibit a distinct momentum dependence in particle yields and their correlations. Specifically, we analyze a quantum pion liquid phase to calculate these metrics at the freeze-out surface. These findings offer an initial framework for systematically investigating spatially modulated phases within heavy-ion collision experiments.

Empirical evidence indicates that computing systems built from segregated single processors face significant performance constraints when cooperating and communicating. Von Neumann, in his seminal "First Draft," cautioned that an excessively fast processor undermines his simple procedural approach (though not his underlying computing model) and noted that applying the classic computing paradigm to simulate neuronal functions is fundamentally flawed. Amdahl further observed that large-scale machines with numerous processors possess inherent disadvantages. Since Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) consist of heavily interconnected components constructed from devices designed for conventional computing, and since they attempt to replicate biological processes using inappropriate technological means, their achievable computational performance remains conceptually limited. The specific workloads generated by AI systems result in exceptionally low payload computational efficiency, restricting the size of these systems to just above the "toy" level; consequently, the scaling of processor-based ANNs follows a strongly nonlinear trajectory. Amidst the growing proliferation of ANNs, this work proposes methods to predict device or application efficiency in advance. By analyzing published data, we demonstrate that data transfer time plays a critical role in determining both ANN performance and feasibility. The discussion examines how major theoretical bottlenecks—specifically ANN layer structures and their technical communication implementations—impact efficiency. Starting from von Neumann's original model while accounting for transfer time alongside processing time, the paper derives an appropriate interpretation and application of Amdahl's Law, showing that, under this framework, Amdahl's Law accurately describes the behavior of ANNs.

We introduce a framework in which a gauge symmetry breaking phase transition, occurring just above the electroweak scale, facilitates baryogenesis akin to the Standard Model's electroweak mechanism. This scenario is concretely realized through the breaking of $SU(2)_R \times U(1)_X \rightarrow U(1)_Y$. The inclusion of new chiral fermions charged under this extended symmetry, which possess non-zero lepton numbers, renders the $B-L$ symmetry anomalous. This new lepton sector exhibits substantial flavor-dependent CP violation, comparable to the CKM phase, yet avoids generating significant electric dipole moments for Standard Model particles. Dynamics arising from the first-order phase transition, specifically bubble wall evolution and $SU(2)_R$ sphalerons, produce a lepton asymmetry that is subsequently converted into a baryon asymmetry via standard electroweak sphalerons. In contrast to Standard Model electroweak baryogenesis, this new phase transition can be strongly first-order, and the CP violation remains unsuppressed by Yukawa couplings, thereby enabling the generation of the observed asymmetry. The model is testable through collider searches for new particles and gravitational wave detection. Furthermore, one of the new leptons serves as a dark matter candidate, and the framework can be extended into a left-right symmetric theory to address the strong CP problem.

Drawing upon the distinctive nonclassical nature of two-photon interactions driven by entangled photons, we establish a novel, comprehensive Förster-type framework for entangled two-photon resonance energy transfer (E2P-RET). This approach addresses systems involving inhomogeneous, dispersive, and absorptive media characterized by arbitrary space- and frequency-dependent dielectric functions, applicable to donors and acceptors of any size. Within this theoretical model, two uncoupled particles are simultaneously excited by a temporally entangled field comprising two virtual photons generated via three-level radiative cascade decay in a donor. The temporal entanglement induces frequency anticorrelation within the virtual photon field and eliminates one of the time-ordered excitation pathways. Consequently, this mechanism yields an enhancement in the E2P-RET rate exceeding three orders of magnitude compared to scenarios with uncorrelated photons. Leveraging our new formulation, we introduce an effective rate coefficient, $K_{E2P}$, to characterize E2P-RET. This coefficient illustrates how energy transfer can be amplified or inhibited based on parameters within the radiative cascade and variations in the donor-acceptor frequency differences.

We demonstrate that for any $2$-colouring of the edges of $K_\mathbb{N}$, there exists a monochromatic infinite path $P$ whose vertex set $V(P)$ possesses an upper density of at least ${(12+\sqrt{8})}/{17} \approx 0.87226$, and we establish that this bound is optimal. This result resolves a problem posed by Erd\H{o}s and Galvin.

Nanomechanical resonators featuring ultra-high quality factors have emerged as a cornerstone of fundamental research, facilitating measurements beneath the standard quantum limit and the creation of long-lasting quantum states. This work proposes that these resonators can enable the high spatial resolution detection of electron and nuclear spins, thereby laying the groundwork for future nanoscale magnetic resonance imaging devices. The article outlines the hurdles that must be addressed to realize this vision and suggests potential solutions.

Millimeter-wave self-backhauled small cells are fundamental to future wireless networks. Their widespread deployment promises to boost data throughput, lower latency, and facilitate efficient data transfer between access and backhaul layers, offering flexibility that optical fibers cannot match. Although their potential is significant, achieving optimal operation in dense self-backhauled environments remains a critical challenge, especially regarding radio resource management (RRM). This paper introduces RadiOrchestra, a comprehensive RRM framework that jointly optimizes beamforming, rate selection, user association, and admission control for these networks. The framework addresses real-world constraints, including base station hardware limits (such as computational power and discrete rate options), the dynamic nature of backhaul links, and interference. Modeled as a nonconvex mixed-integer nonlinear program—a notoriously difficult problem to solve—we propose three algorithms that balance computational complexity with solution optimality. Additionally, we establish upper and lower bounds to define the system's performance limits. Through evaluations across various scenarios, we demonstrate the viability of implementing practical self-backhauling in upcoming network architectures.

Quantitative and qualitative (QQ) computer experiments are widely utilized across scientific and engineering fields, yet creating effective emulators for them remains a significant challenge. This article introduces an easily interpretable Gaussian process (EzGP) model designed to capture variations in computer models across different combinations of qualitative factors. Built on an additive Gaussian process framework, this approach offers the flexibility needed to handle heterogeneity arising from multiple qualitative inputs. Furthermore, we present two variants of the EzGP model to enhance computational efficiency when dealing with high-dimensional and large datasets. The advantages of these models are demonstrated through various numerical simulations and a real-world data application.

This work introduces a quantum field theoretical framework for investigating vacuum neutrino oscillations within curved spacetime, examining the complex relationship between field quantization and mixing in such environments to establish novel oscillation formulas. These formulas are explicitly calculated for spatially flat FLRW metrics characterizing universes dominated by radiation and a cosmological constant. Additionally, transition probabilities are assessed using the Schwarzschild black hole metric, demonstrating that Hawking radiation influences neutrino oscillations. Finally, we confirm that our findings align with prior analyses when the quantum mechanical limit is applied.

We establish a decomposition theorem for the cohomological Chow group of 0-cycles on the double of a quasi-projective $R_1$-scheme over a field along a closed subscheme, expressed in terms of the scheme's Chow groups both with and without modulus. This result significantly generalizes the decomposition theorem by Binda-Krishna. As applications, we demonstrate a moving lemma for Chow groups with modulus and derive an analogue of Bloch's formula for 0-cycles with modulus on singular surfaces, thereby extending a prior result by Binda-Krishna-Saito.

Using Keck/HIRES, we observed the Rossiter-McLaughlin effect of WASP-107b during one transit, determining the sky-projected angle between its orbital plane and the star's rotation axis to be $|\lambda| = {118}^{+38}_{-19}$ degrees. This result confirms a previously hinted misaligned or polar orbit, further establishing WASP-107b as a hot Neptune in a polar orbit around a cool star. Notably, it is the fourth known planet with such an orbit to have a distant companion. We investigated various dynamical mechanisms that could have caused this high obliquity, concluding that both nodal precession and disk dispersal-driven tilting can account for the observed geometry, whereas Kozai-Lidov cycles are inhibited by general relativity. Although both scenarios require an initial mutual inclination between the planets, nodal precession demands a significantly larger angle; for WASP-107, this angle lies near the limit of future detection via Gaia astrometry. Because nodal precession is independent of stellar type while disk dispersal-driven tilting is not, distinguishing between these models is most effectively achieved by analyzing population-level statistics. Furthermore, discovering and studying more systems analogous to WASP-107 will clarify whether the distribution of hot-Neptune obliquities represents a split between aligned and polar populations or reflects a uniform sampling of angles during nodal precession cycles.

Achieving high performance for both regular and irregular computations on GPUs relies fundamentally on fine-grained balancing of workloads and resources. This dissertation presents an extensive survey of current load-balancing methods to develop a new abstraction that overcomes the challenges of scheduling computations on GPUs. We introduce a GPU-specific, fine-grained load-balancing abstraction that separates load balancing from work processing, supporting both static and dynamic schedules via a programmable interface. Previously, unlocking GPU potential for irregular problems required tightly coupled, application-specific load-balancing strategies. Our proposed open-source framework aims to enhance programmer productivity when creating irregular-parallel algorithms on GPUs and to improve overall application performance by facilitating rapid experimentation with various existing load-balancing techniques. Leveraging insights gained from balancing irregular workloads, we developed Stream-K, a work-centric parallelization approach for matrix multiplication (GEMM) and related dense linear algebra operations. Unlike contemporary tile-based decompositions, our method partitions an equal share of aggregate inner loop iterations among physical processing elements, ensuring near-perfect resource utilization regardless of how efficiently output tiling quantizes across processors. On GPU architectures, our Stream-K implementation of GEMM achieves peak speedups of up to 14x and 6.7x, delivering higher and more consistent average performance across 32K GEMM problem geometries compared to state-of-the-art libraries like CUTLASS and cuBLAS.

The primary critique of average-case analysis is the lack of knowledge regarding the probability distributions of real-world inputs, suggesting that results derived from random models fail to reflect practical performance. Fundamentally, this objection questions external validity by assuming that algorithmic behavior observed on simplified, idealized models does not extend to actual real-world scenarios. This paper initiates a systematic investigation into external validity by evaluating six graph algorithms across 2,745 sparse real-world networks based on two key attributes: heterogeneity (variance in degree distribution) and locality (the propensity for edges to connect nearby vertices). We contrast these findings with performance on generated networks that exhibit varying levels of locality and heterogeneity. Our results indicate that performance observed in idealized network models translates remarkably well to real-world networks. Furthermore, heterogeneity and locality emerge as the fundamental properties influencing the performance of numerous graph algorithms.

Entanglement represents a holistic characteristic of multipartite quantum systems, characterized by the formation of nonclassical correlations among subsystems. While most entanglement generation processes are driven by coherent interaction Hamiltonians and evolve temporally—implying a temporal direction for entanglement creation—dissipative structure theory guides the time evolution of non-equilibrium systems. By dissipating energy into the environment, such systems spontaneously generate order from disorder, a phenomenon known as self-organization. This study investigates a novel approach to generating entanglement by applying principles of dissipative structure theory to quantum systems. In this framework, subsystem entanglement arises through dissipation-structured correlations. This method necessitates a non-equilibrium initial state and cooperative dissipation, making it applicable across various waveguide-coupled quantum architectures.

This study demonstrates that a 3-3-1 model incorporating new heavy right-handed neutrinos as $SU(3)_L$ singlets can concurrently account for lepton flavor-violating decays of the SM-like Higgs boson, charged lepton flavor-violating transitions such as $e_b\rightarrow e_a\gamma$, and electron $(g-2)_e$ anomalies, all in agreement with recent experimental findings. Within this framework, the model's prediction for the muon $(g-2)_{\mu}$ discrepancy relative to the Standard Model can achieve a magnitude of $10^{-9}$. Furthermore, the decay rates for the Standard Model-like Higgs boson into $\tau e$ and $\tau\mu$ final states can reach values on the order of $\mathcal{O}(10^{-4})$.

The introduction of default Bayesian hypothesis tests has provided researchers in applied disciplines with a robust and principled framework for hypothesis evaluation. Nevertheless, these standard tests often necessitate a compromise by enforcing a rigid, one-size-fits-all methodology that may lack the adaptability required to address the specific problems scientists find most significant. This tutorial presents a flexible strategy for extending a particular default test—the JZS t-test (Rouder et al., 2009)—which is gaining traction in social and behavioral sciences. By leveraging two key theoretical concepts, the Savage-Dickey density ratio (Dickey and Lientz, 1980) and encompassing priors (Klugkist et al., 2005), alongside MCMC sampling implemented through the user-friendly R package Greta, this approach offers a versatile solution. Through a detailed mathematical exposition and practical examples, the tutorial equips readers with a generalizable workflow adaptable to their own research challenges.

This note aims to demonstrate that the symplectic mapping class groups of numerous K3 surfaces possess infinite generation. Unlike previous methods, our proof avoids Floer-theoretic tools and instead adopts the strategy of Kronheimer, relying on invariants obtained from Seiberg-Witten equations.

To validate ab initio nuclear structure theory, researchers have successfully measured, for the first time, the lifetime of the second 2+ state in neutron-rich 20O as tau(2+_2 ) = 150(+80-30) fs, alongside an estimated lifetime for the corresponding state in 16C. These results were derived using a new Monte Carlo method capable of determining nuclear state lifetimes in the tens-to-hundreds femtoseconds range by analyzing Doppler-shifted gamma-transition line shapes from low-energy transfer and deep-inelastic reactions involving 18O (7.0 MeV/u) + 181Ta. This required the exceptional sensitivity provided by the AGATA gamma-tracking array, combined with the PARIS scintillator array and the VAMOS++ magnetic spectrometer. The measured experimental lifetimes align with ab initio predictions for 20O using the valence-space in-medium similarity renormalization group with two- and three-nucleon interactions, and for 16C using the no-core shell model. This study demonstrates that high-precision gamma spectroscopy, which yields electromagnetic observables, is a powerful tool for evaluating the accuracy of first-principles nuclear calculations, offering a necessary complement to traditional benchmarks based on nuclear energies. Furthermore, this experimental methodology will be crucial for measuring short lifetimes in uncharted regions of the nuclear chart, such as r-process nuclei, once high-intensity ISOL-type beams are accessible.

MPI applications typically initialize with a fixed number of ranks that remain constant throughout execution. Although developers can manually increase ranks by dynamically spawning processes, this approach introduces significant complexity. Achieving malleability in MPI \cite{b20} would enable HPC applications to match the elasticity found in cloud environments. This paper proposes code-agnostic methods to modify the rank of an MPI program, utilizing checkpointing to halt execution and resume the application with an updated state. Specifically, we investigate increasing the rank of an MPI program using ExaMPI as the underlying implementation.

Let C1 and C2 be codes with code distance d. Codes C1 and C2 are defined as weakly isometric if there exists a mapping J from C1 to C2 such that for any x and y in C1, the condition d(x,y) = d holds if and only if d(J(x),J(y)) = d. It is evident that two codes are weakly isometric precisely when their minimal distance graphs are isomorphic. This paper establishes that for Preparata codes of length n ≥ 2^12, weak isometry is equivalent to code equivalence. A similar result is demonstrated for punctured Preparata codes of length at least 2^10 - 1.

While recent studies on fair regression have introduced new fairness concepts and approximation techniques for scenarios involving continuous target variables and sensitive attributes, they have universally assumed that training and testing data follow identical distributions. This assumption frequently fails in practice due to sample selection bias between these datasets. To address this, we propose a framework for fair regression that accounts for sample selection bias, specifically when dependent variable values for certain training samples are missing due to an underlying hidden process. Our approach integrates the classic Heckman model for bias correction with Lagrange duality to ensure fairness across multiple fairness definitions. The Heckman model characterizes the selection mechanism and utilizes the Inverse Mills Ratio (IMR) to mitigate selection bias. We formulate various fairness notions using inequality and equality constraints, then apply Lagrange duality to convert the primal problem into a dual convex optimization task. For two common fairness metrics—mean difference and mean squared error difference—we derive explicit formulas that bypass iterative optimization, while for Pearson correlation, we establish the conditions required for strong duality. Experiments on three real-world datasets confirm the method's efficacy in balancing both utility and fairness.

The Hyper-Suprime Cam Subaru Strategic Program (HSC-SSP) has demonstrated success through its extensive sky coverage in previous years. Leveraging this capability, we present initial findings from our investigation of vast over- and under-dense structures at redshifts $z = 0.3$–$1$, utilizing the second Public Data Release. This dataset includes optical 5-band photometric information for approximately eight million sources brighter than $i < 23$ mag across roughly $360$ square degrees. We have confirmed known superclusters and identified candidate titanic over- and under-dense regions extending out to $z=1$. Mock data analysis indicates that density peaks likely contain one or more massive dark matter haloes ($>10^{14}$ M$_\odot$) at the corresponding redshift, while density troughs appear largely devoid of massive haloes over scales exceeding $10$ comoving Mpc. Furthermore, density peaks and troughs at $z<0.6$ correspond to positive and negative weak lensing signals, respectively, as observed in mean tangential shear profiles, showing strong agreement with full-sky weak lensing simulations. Future extensive spectroscopic surveys will be capable of resolving these colossal structures in three dimensions. Grid-point data regarding number density across the entire survey field will be accessible via the HSC-SSP data release website (https://hsc.mtk.nao.ac.jp/ssp/data-release/).

Real-time estimation of fluid dynamics within a centrifugal pump is a complex challenge that long-standing methods, such as Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD), cannot meet due to their high computational costs. Instead, this study employs a projection-based reduced-order model (ROM). Utilizing this ROM, a real-time observer is developed to estimate temporally and spatially resolved velocity and pressure fields throughout the pump. To accommodate moving rigid bodies during the reduction process, the entire fluid-solid domain is modeled as a fluid. A greedy algorithm is utilized to identify the minimal set of optimal measurement locations. Robust observability is guaranteed through an extended Kalman filter, which relies on a time-varying observability matrix derived from the nonlinear velocity ROM. The paper presents results for both velocity and pressure ROMs, based on unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) CFD simulations of a 2D centrifugal pump model, alongside the performance outcomes of the extended Kalman filter.

Mobile Edge Computing (MEC), by decentralizing computation, caching, and network management to the edge, is poised to be a cornerstone of 5G and future 6G networks. However, due to rapidly expanding computational needs, no single MEC model can adequately deliver high-quality intelligent services to end-user equipment (UEs). To overcome this limitation, this article proposes an Air-Ground Collaborative MEC (AGC-MEC) architecture. This framework unites all accessible MEC servers across both aerial and terrestrial domains within the envisioned 6G ecosystem, utilizing diverse collaboration methods to optimize service delivery for UEs. The paper first outlines the AGC-MEC architecture and details three representative use cases. Subsequently, it examines four primary challenges associated with AGC-MEC alongside their proposed solutions. Furthermore, a case study on collaborative service placement is presented to demonstrate the efficacy of the strategy. Finally, the article identifies several promising avenues for future research in AGC-MEC.

This paper establishes the existence of the $n$-point boundary Green's function, with exponent $\frac8\kappa -1$, for chordal SLE$_\kappa$ when $\kappa\in(0,8)$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the convergence is uniform across compact sets and that the Green's function is continuous. Additionally, we provide bounds for the Green's function up to a multiplicative constant.

Traditional heuristic search methods depend on manually crafted or algorithmically generated heuristics. While neural networks (NNs) offer a modern capability to learn intricate mappings from states to cost-to-go estimates, their slow individual inference speed creates significant overhead that can severely hinder planning efficiency in optimized search algorithms. Although recent studies have leveraged NN batch processing to reduce this overhead without sacrificing suboptimality bounds, these approaches typically employ a "blocking" strategy during batch construction and neglect readily available, fast-to-compute admissible heuristics (such as classical ones). We present Non-Blocking Batch A* (NBBA*), a bounded suboptimal technique that lazily computes NN heuristics in batches while simultaneously permitting expansions guided by non-NN heuristics. We demonstrate that this nuanced yet critical modification can drastically reduce the number of required expansions compared to existing blocking methods, with performance outcomes closely tied to the informational gap between the batch-derived NN heuristic and the rapid non-NN alternative.

This document presents two measurements from the LHCb experiment concerning mixing and $CP$ violation in charm decays. The first quantifies the mixing observable $y_{CP}-y_{CP}^{K\pi}$ within two-body $D^0$ decays, and the second investigates direct $CP$ violation in $D^+_{(s)}\rightarrow\eta^{(')}\pi^+$ decays.

We introduce GeoRefine, a robust and precise depth refinement framework designed for geometrically consistent dense mapping from monocular sequences. This system comprises three core components: a hybrid SLAM module integrating learning-based priors, an online depth refinement stage utilizing self-supervision, and a global mapping component based on TSDF fusion. By design, GeoRefine operates online and ensures high robustness and accuracy through (i) a strengthened hybrid SLAM that incorporates learning-based optical flow and/or depth estimates; (ii) self-supervised losses that exploit SLAM outputs to maintain long-term geometric consistency; and (iii) a deliberate system architecture that prevents degenerate scenarios during online depth refinement. Comprehensive evaluations across multiple public datasets demonstrate that GeoRefine achieves absolute relative depth errors as low as 5%.

This paper presents the current status of the ALICE Time-Of-Flight (TOF) detector, comparing its operational performance during the Run 1 (2009–2013) and Run 2 (2015–present) data collection periods. The detector's Particle IDentification (PID) capabilities are analyzed in the context of enhanced calibration, which achieved a timing resolution of 56 ps.

A central issue in decision theory involves combining individual rankings and ratings to form a collective assessment. We present a novel aggregation technique within the framework of the 2007 MSOM student paper competition. This specific scenario presents two distinct difficulties: first, because each paper was assessed by only a tiny fraction of the judges, the resulting collective evaluation is extremely sensitive to the subjective scales used; second, judges submitted both cardinal (ratings) and ordinal (rankings) evaluations. Our contribution is a robust new methodology that simultaneously integrates these two types of evaluations into a unified collective result. This approach is especially effective for incomplete evaluation scenarios, where individuals assess only a strict subset of the available items. Furthermore, this method holds potential value for managerial decision-making contexts, such as committees selecting projects from extensive pools or capital budgeting tasks involving multiple priorities.

Particle physics research heavily depends on computing and data services, establishing e-infrastructure as a cornerstone of collaborative efforts. However, establishing and managing distributed computing systems can present significant hurdles for smaller-scale collaborations. The Light Dark Matter eXperiment (LDMX) is an upcoming small-scale accelerator project designed to detect dark matter within the sub-GeV mass range. Completing the detector's design requires Monte-Carlo simulations of anticipated physical phenomena. To optimize resource usage across partner institutes and enhance both scalability and reproducibility, a pilot project for distributed computing was proposed. This paper details the selected lightweight distributed architecture, covering the necessary requirements, component integration procedures, and insights gained from testing the pilot system with large-scale simulations. By prioritizing the use of existing technologies to minimize new software development and deploying only non-intrusive elements at participating sites, the pilot demonstrated that leveraging current components can drastically cut the effort required to build and maintain a distributed e-infrastructure, thereby making it feasible for smaller research teams.

Nucleon form factors offer essential insights into nucleon characteristics. When experimental observables are precisely measured, these form factors act as benchmark values for lattice computations. Conversely, lattice-derived results provide crucial theoretical input for interpreting experimental data, such as in neutrino-nucleus scattering. This review examines recent advancements in calculating nucleon form factors using lattice methods and highlights their significance for upcoming experiments.

Although theoretical progress has been made, current PAC-Bayesian frameworks for meta-learning fail to adequately account for performance gains in few-shot learning, where target tasks have very few training examples. This discrepancy stems from an unrealistic assumption in existing theories that the distribution of examples in observed tasks matches that of target tasks, a condition seldom met in practice. By relaxing this constraint, we propose two PAC-Bayesian bounds specifically designed for few-shot learning. These bounds not only recover two established meta-learning algorithms (MAML and Reptile), thus aligning practical methods with PAC-Bayesian theory, but also yield a novel, computationally efficient PACMAML algorithm. Experimental results on multiple few-shot benchmarks demonstrate that PACMAML surpasses existing meta-learning approaches.

Three existing QCD models within (1+1) dimensions are analyzed and expanded using light-front coordinates, revealing that a high-momentum pion possesses an infinite spatial extent along its direction of motion.

Let $H$ denote a graph. The generalized outerplanar Turán number of $H$, represented as $f_{\mathcal{OP}}(n,H)$, signifies the maximum count of $H$ subgraphs within an $n$-vertex outerplanar graph. Considering $P_k$ as the path graph with $k$ vertices, this paper determines the precise value of $f_{\mathcal{OP}}(n,P_4)$ and provides the optimal asymptotic estimate for $f_{\mathcal{OP}}(n,P_5)$. Furthermore, it identifies and characterizes all outerplanar graphs that contain exactly $f_{\mathcal{OP}}(n,P_4)$ copies of $P_4$.

This paper investigates frame-like characteristics of a wave packet system through the lens of hyponormal operators on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions, expressed via relative hyponormality, for a system to constitute a wave packet frame within $L^2(\mathbb{R})$. Furthermore, we prove a characterization of hyponormal operators utilizing tight wave packet frames, which contrasts with Djordjevi$\acute{c}$'s approach relying on the Moore-Penrose inverse of a bounded linear operator possessing a closed range. Finally, we examine linear combinations of wave packet frames derived from hyponormal operators.

Hot-rolling is a metal forming technique that creates a target cross-section from an input workpiece through a series of plastic deformations, where each step involves a stand of opposing rolls with specific geometries. Currently, experts design the rolling sequence—comprising the order of stands and roll geometries—based on prior experience, refining it through an expensive trial-and-error method. While Finite Element Method (FEM) simulations are increasingly used to improve efficiency and test potential sequences with high accuracy, their long computation times restrict practical application. We introduce a supervised learning approach to predict how a given workpiece deforms under specific roll geometries. This model is trained on a large dataset of procedurally generated FEM simulations, which are provided as supplementary material. The resulting predictor operates four orders of magnitude faster than FEM simulations, achieving a Jaccard Similarity Index of 0.972 compared to simulation ground truth and 0.925 against real-world measured deformations. We also present preliminary findings on utilizing this predictor for the automatic planning of rolling sequences.

For integers $k>0$ and $0<r \leq \Delta$ (with the constraint $r \leq k$), a conditional $(k,r)$-coloring of a graph $G$ refers to a proper $k$-coloring where each vertex $v$, having degree $d(v)$, is connected to at least $\min\{r, d(v)\}$ neighbors of distinct colors. The minimum integer $k$ satisfying this condition for a graph $G$ is defined as the $r$th order conditional chromatic number, denoted by $\chi_r(G)$. The discussion first presents findings regarding $\chi_r(G)$ for various values of $r$, including exact values and bounds. Subsequently, the specific $\chi_r(G)$ values are determined for several parameterized graphs, including the windmill graph, the line graph of a windmill graph, the middle graphs of friendship and cycle graphs, the line graph of a friendship graph, the middle graph of a complete $k$-partite graph, the middle graph of a bipartite graph, and the gear graph. Finally, the concept of \emph{unique conditional colorability} is introduced, along with associated results.

Fairness in resource allocation is a well-established field, featuring concepts such as envy-freeness (EF), along with its relaxations, proportionality, and max-min share (MMS). Extensive research exists regarding both the existence and computational complexity of these notions. However, existing algorithms typically assume that agents truthfully report their valuations, an assumption that often fails in real-world web-based fair division settings where agents act strategically to maximize individual utility. This paper investigates strategy-proof mechanisms without monetary transfers that uphold various fairness criteria. While it is known that truthful mechanisms for EF, MMS, and proportionality are impossible under additive valuations, we demonstrate that truthful mechanisms for EFX do not exist and that current EF1 algorithms are susceptible to manipulation. Furthermore, focusing on single-minded agents, we introduce a Serial Dictatorship Mechanism that is strategy-proof and satisfies all fairness criteria except for EF.

Collaborating swarms of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) leveraging ad-hoc networking to coordinate actions hold promise for advancing research areas like autonomous disaster zone exploration, demand-responsive network provisioning, and near-field packet delivery within Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITSs). However, the high relative mobility inherent in these robotic networks often causes existing routing protocols to fail in adapting their decision-making to dynamic network topologies. To address this, we introduce Predictive Ad-hoc Routing fueled by Reinforcement learning and Trajectory knowledge (PARRoT), a novel machine learning-based protocol that incorporates future motion predictions of mobile agents into routing decisions by utilizing mobility control data. Comprehensive network simulations evaluate the proposed approach, demonstrating that PARRoT outperforms established protocols by achieving significantly greater robustness and substantially reduced end-to-end latency.

Natural language interfaces (NLIs) for databases have seen substantial growth in both academic and industrial sectors over recent years. Although recent surveys highlight diverse approaches within these systems, there has been no systematic comparison against a standardized benchmark to rigorously assess their functional capabilities and expressive power. This paper provides an overview of 24 recently developed database NLIs, evaluating each against a curated set of ten sample questions to illustrate their respective strengths and limitations. The systems are categorized into four methodological groups: keyword-based, pattern-based, parsing-based, and grammar-based. Our analysis reveals that keyword-based systems suffice for simple queries, whereas addressing complex questions involving subqueries requires parsing to identify structural dependencies. While grammar-based systems demonstrate the highest overall power, they remain heavily reliant on manually crafted rules. Beyond this systematic evaluation of major systems, we extract key lessons essential for designing NLIs capable of answering a broad spectrum of user questions.

This paper introduces a conceptual design study utilizing external calibrators for 21 cm experiments aimed at detecting the globally averaged radiation from the Epoch of Reionization (EoR). Using external calibrators, rather than the internal ones typical in current EoR studies, enables the elimination of instrumental effects—such as beam patterns, receiver gain fluctuations, and system instability—provided that conventional three-position switch measurements are conducted within brief time intervals. Additionally, the proposed design situates the antenna system within an underground anechoic chamber featuring an open/closing ceiling to maximize the reduction of environmental interference, including radio frequency interference (RFI) and ground radiation or reflections. However, analysis suggests that three of the four proposed external calibrators, comprising two indoor artificial transmitters and one outdoor celestial source (Galactic polarization), do not fulfill the study's objectives. Instead, the diurnal motion of Galactic diffuse emission emerges as the most viable external calibrator, for which an observational strategy and an algorithm for extracting the EoR signal have been detailed.

Chalermsook et al. [SODA'21(arXiv:2007.07862)] recently introduced vertex sparsifiers for $c$-edge connectivity, a concept that has enabled parameterized algorithms for network design and spurred dynamic algorithms for $c$-edge st-connectivity [Jin and Sun FOCS'21(arXiv:2004.07650)]. This work investigates a natural generalization: vertex sparsifiers for $c$-hyperedge connectivity. We construct a sparsifier whose size equals the state-of-the-art bound for standard graphs. Specifically, for a hypergraph $G=(V,E)$ with $n$ vertices, $m$ hyperedges, $k$ terminals, and a parameter $c$, we demonstrate the existence of a hypergraph $H$ with only $O(kc^{3})$ hyperedges that maintains all minimum cuts (up to value $c$) among every subset of terminals. This achieves the optimal $O(kc^{3})$ edge bound established for normal graphs by [Liu'20(arXiv:2011.15101)]. Furthermore, $H$ can be built in almost-linear time $O(p^{1+o(1)} + n(rc\log n)^{O(rc)}\log m)$, where $r=\max_{e\in E}|e|$ denotes the rank of $G$ and $p=\sum_{e\in E}|e|$ represents the total size of $G$. Alternatively, if the size is relaxed to $O(kc^{3}\log^{1.5}(kc))$ hyperedges, construction is achievable in $\text{poly}(m, n)$ time.

This study examines the oracle complexity of sampling from heavy-tailed target densities with polynomial decay by applying the Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm to specific transformations of these densities. We introduce a particular class of closed-form transformation maps, proven to be diffeomorphisms, which are especially advantageous for creating efficient diffusion-based samplers. We define the exact subset of heavy-tailed densities capable of achieving polynomial-order oracle complexities regarding dimension and inverse target accuracy, accompanied by illustrative examples. Furthermore, we elucidate the connection between our assumptions and functional inequalities—specifically super and weak Poincaré inequalities derived from non-local Dirichlet forms involving fractional Laplacian operators—which characterize the heavy-tailed equilibrium densities of certain stable-driven stochastic differential equations.
We investigate the automorphism groups of finite-dimensional cyclic Leibniz algebras, examining the interconnections among these groups, modules over associative rings, and Leibniz algebras.

This study investigates how peculiar velocities of both observers and Type Ia supernova host galaxies induce correlated fluctuations in observables, thereby influencing cosmological parameter estimation. Utilizing the CosmicFlows-3 dataset, we demonstrate that at low redshifts, corrections for peculiar velocities within the JLA catalogue have been systematically underestimated. By querying an N-body simulation spanning a horizon scale, we find that an observer situated in an environment akin to our local Universe perceives correlations between supernovae in the JLA catalogue that are 2 to 8 times stronger than those seen by a randomly placed observer. Consequently, standard covariances underestimate the impact of coherent motion among supernova host galaxies. Contrary to prior claims that peculiar velocities negligibly affect cosmological parameter estimation, we show that accounting for these correlations causes JLA data to favor significantly lower dark energy density values compared to the standard $\Lambda$CDM model. A joint fit designed to simultaneously constrain cosmological parameters and bulk flow reveals a bulk flow magnitude of approximately 250 km/s extending beyond 200/h Mpc. Therefore, the local bulk flow must be treated as an essential nuisance parameter in analyses of the supernova Hubble diagram.

Expansion testing determines if an $n$-node graph possesses an expansion of at least $\Phi$ or differs significantly from any such graph. We introduce a quantum expansion tester with complexity $\widetilde{O}(n^{1/3}\Phi^{-1})$, which improves upon the classical $\widetilde{O}(n^{1/2}\Phi^{-2})$ method by Goldreich and Ron [Algorithmica '02]. Our approach merges two quantum speedups: the $\widetilde{O}(n^{1/3}\Phi^{-2})$ result by Ambainis, Childs, and Liu [RANDOM '11] and the $\widetilde{O}(n^{1/2}\Phi^{-1})$ advancement by Apers and Sarlette [QIC '19]. The latter strategy relies on a quantum fast-forwarding technique, which we enhance by first expanding a seed set within the graph. To achieve this, we employ an evolving set process from graph clustering research to generate a suitably local seed set.

Beliefs that hold significant sway are fundamental to comprehending how individuals approach political reasoning and decision-making. This study introduces a novel methodology for assessing the impact of political beliefs within broader belief system networks, leveraging recent developments in psychometric network analysis and research on network influence. Applying the most recent European Social Survey data, we illustrate this technique using a belief network that maps support for regimes across 29 European nations, encompassing views on regime performance, core principles, institutions, and political figures. Our findings indicate that the average influence of beliefs correlates with both the consistency and connectivity of the belief network. Furthermore, the influence of particular beliefs—such as Satisfaction with Democracy—at the national level exhibits a significant negative correlation with external metrics from the same domain, like the Liberal Democracy index, implying that highly influential beliefs often address urgent political concerns. These results demonstrate that network-derived metrics of belief influence, calculated from extensive survey data, can serve as a fresh indicator in comparative political research, thereby creating new pathways to integrate psychometric network methods into political science methodologies.

This article addresses the $c$-dispersion problem within a metric space $(X,d)$. Given a set $P=\{p_{1}, p_{2}, \ldots, p_{n}\}$ of $n$ points in this space, we define $cost_{c}(p,S)$ for any $p \in P$ and subset $S \subseteq P$ as the sum of distances from $p$ to its $c$ nearest neighbors in $S \setminus \{p\}$, where $c \geq 1$ is a fixed integer. For a subset $S$, $cost_{c}(S)$ is defined as $\min_{p \in S}\{cost_{c}(p,S)\}$. The $c$-dispersion problem involves a set $P$ of $n$ points and a positive integer $k$ (where $c+1 \leq k \leq n$); the goal is to identify a subset $S \subseteq P$ of cardinality $k$ that maximizes $cost_{c}(S)$. We introduce a straightforward polynomial-time greedy algorithm that achieves a $2c$-factor approximation for this problem in general metric spaces. This improves upon the best-known result of $2c^2$ for the Euclidean case in $\mathbb{R}^2$ (Amano and Nakano, CCCG, 2018). Furthermore, we establish that the $c$-dispersion problem is $W[1]$-hard in metric spaces.

Utilizing the quantum master equation framework, this study examines the nonlinear electric conductivity of graphene subjected to static electric fields across different chemical potential shifts. Simulation outcomes indicate that rising field strength initially suppresses effective conductivity, a phenomenon attributed to carrier depletion resulting from significant displacements within the Brillouin zone. However, once the field strength surpasses $1$~MV/m, conductivity begins to rise, as Landau--Zener tunneling mechanisms overcome the carrier depletion. Leveraging this nonlinear conductivity behavior, the research further investigates charge transport driven by few-cycle THz pulses to demonstrate the potential for ultrafast electric current control in matter.
This scientific paper focuses on investigating the T-matrix, specifically the set of composite numbers defined as 6h ± 1, and explores its applications within number theory.

Human-in-the-loop (HiL) reinforcement learning is increasingly popular in fields characterized by vast state and action spaces as well as sparse rewards, primarily because it enables agents to incorporate human guidance. Beyond simply accepting advice, sequential decision-making agents must also communicate the degree to which they have integrated human input. Furthermore, these agents need to offer a mechanism for HiL operators to examine specific pieces of advice that were overridden in pursuit of the broader environmental goals. We define the "Advice-Conformance Verification" problem, which mandates that RL agents provide assurances to HiL partners regarding the extent of adherence to their suggestions. To facilitate this dialogue, we introduce the "Preference Tree," a tree-based lingua franca designed to support this exchange. Our approach is evaluated using two scenarios involving good and bad advice within MuJoCo's Humanoid environment. Experimental results demonstrate that our method offers an interpretable solution to the Advice-Conformance Verification problem by clearly indicating whether the agent is following human advice. Finally, we validate our approach through a user study involving 20 participants.

Since the initial survey on blockchain was released in 2017, the volume of such publications has grown significantly, creating a dilemma for newcomers regarding which papers to read, who publishes them, their nature, publication frequency, length, citation impact, and collaboration patterns. These inquiries prompted an analysis of blockchain survey trends. This study presents a bibliometric examination of 801 blockchain surveys and review papers published over the past five years. We evaluated these works across various dimensions, including publication type, venue and publisher, references, citations, length, categories, publication year, geographical origin, authors, and collaborative networks, uncovering several key insights. To our knowledge, this represents the first study of its kind, aiming to offer a deeper understanding of the field.

Web archive analytics involves utilizing publicly available web pages and their historical changes for research, constrained only by organizational limitations. To illustrate the complexity of this endeavor, the paper's first section contextualizes the "Global Datasphere"—the total captured, created, and replicated data—against other critical datasets, including the public internet and the portion preserved by the Internet Archive. Recently, the Webis research group, which includes the authors, finalized an agreement with the Internet Archive to download a significant portion of its web archive for scholarly use. The second part of the paper details the infrastructure developed to process this vast data resource. The project aims to host approximately 8 petabytes of web archive data sourced from the Internet Archive and Common Crawl, with the objective of augmenting existing large-scale web corpora and creating an unbiased subset of the 30 petabytes held by the Internet Archive.

Unlike traditional knowledge graphs, commonsense knowledge graphs (CKGs) such as Atomic and ASER comprise significantly more nodes derived from loosely structured text. While this characteristic allows them to address a wide array of natural language queries related to commonsense, it also presents distinct challenges for automated construction techniques. Beyond detecting missing relations between existing nodes, these methods must also uncover absent nodes represented by textual descriptions of various real-world entities. To manage the vast number of entities inherent in commonsense, we propose a conceptualization approach within CKG construction, treating text-mentioned entities as instances of specific concepts or vice versa. We generate synthetic triples through this conceptualization process and frame the task as triple classification, utilizing a discriminative model enhanced by knowledge transferred from pretrained language models and refined via negative sampling. Experimental results indicate that our approach effectively identifies plausible triples, expanding the knowledge graph with diverse and novel nodes and edges.

This research investigates state consensus within linear shift-invariant, discrete-time, homogeneous multi-agent systems (MASs) operating over time-varying graphs. A new method utilizing the small gain theorem is introduced to develop consensus control protocols for both neutrally stable and neutrally unstable MASs, assuming uniformly connected graphs. The study demonstrates that state consensus is attainable for neutrally stable MASs under a weak uniform observability condition, whereas neutrally unstable MASs require a strong uniform observability condition to achieve consensus. Two numerical examples are provided to validate these consensus findings.

Mobile robots are advancing quickly and are increasingly utilized in industrial settings, yet significant challenges persist regarding their practical deployment, including the requirement for costly hardware and high energy consumption. This study presents a low-cost indoor mobile robot platform that operates without LiDAR or GPU components. We developed an autonomous navigation architecture capable of delivering real-time performance on this platform using an RGB-D camera and a budget-friendly single-board computer. The comprehensive system integrates SLAM, global path planning, ground segmentation, and motion planning. Specifically, our proposed ground segmentation method generates a traversability map from raw depth images to ensure safe navigation for low-profile robots. By employing both rule-based and learning-based navigation policies utilizing this map, our system processes sensor data and other autonomous driving modules simultaneously, achieving a control command refresh rate of 18Hz, which is faster than many competing systems. Simulation tests indicate that our methods outperform current state-of-the-art navigation approaches under constrained computational resources. Furthermore, we validate the system's practicality by demonstrating successful autonomous operation in an indoor environment.

It has been established that Gage's area-preserving flow can smoothly evolve a centrosymmetric star-shaped initial curve into a convex shape within finite time and transform it into a circle as time approaches infinity.

This paper introduces GINCO, a novel training dataset designed for automatic genre identification. Derived from 1,125 crawled Slovenian web documents totaling 650,000 words, the dataset features manual genre annotations created using a new schema that prioritizes label clarity and high inter-annotator agreement based on existing frameworks. GINCO encompasses various web-specific challenges, including machine-translated text, encoding errors, and multiple content types within single documents, thereby allowing for the evaluation of classifiers under realistic conditions. Preliminary machine learning experiments reveal that (1) pre-Transformer models struggle significantly with these phenomena, achieving macro F1 scores near 0.22, whereas Transformer-based models reach approximately 0.58, and (2) multilingual Transformer models perform comparably to monolingual models, overturning previous findings that favored monolingual approaches on standard NLP tasks.

On 3-dimensional Euclidean space, the vorticity of a vector field is typically defined as its curl. This paper generalizes that notion to compact, oriented Riemannian manifolds of arbitrary dimension $n$ and investigates various properties of this generalized operation. We demonstrate that every vector field on a compact Riemannian manifold possesses a unique Helmholtz decomposition and prove that any smooth vector field defined on an open neighborhood of such a manifold satisfies a Stokes-type identity.

Current state-of-the-art maximum entropy models for texture synthesis utilize statistics derived from image representations generated by convolutional neural networks (CNNs). These representations excel at capturing complex structures in textures, surpassing traditional wavelet-based approaches. Conversely, while neural networks dominate, wavelets provide meaningful multi-scale structural detection, such as edges. This paper introduces a new family of statistics based on non-linear wavelet representations, which can be interpreted as a specific case of a one-layer CNN employing a generalized rectifier non-linearity. These statistics markedly enhance the visual quality of prior classical wavelet-based models, enabling the generation of syntheses comparable to state-of-the-art results for both grayscale and color textures.

This project investigates the relationship between non-local pressure within massive neutron stars (MANs)—which counteracts core gravitational collapse—and ECSK dark energy, driven by spin-torsion coupling between quark fields and spacetime at ultra-high densities exceeding nuclear levels. The introduction of ECSK dark energy into MAN cores, along with its anti-gravitational resistance to collapse, suggests the potential existence of neutron stars within the unobserved mass range of $[2.16M_{\odot},5M_{\odot}]$. By deriving the ECSK TOV equation, we determine the local pressure of the MAN ambient medium, while the negative pressure of the ECSK dark energy is calculated from the Lagrangian. These values allow us to examine the hydrostatic equilibrium of both the core and ambient medium. If this equilibrium holds true for the unobserved mass gap within the ECSK framework, it would indicate that our model successfully predicts this extensive, previously unseen mass spectrum in astrophysical contexts.

Current pre-main-sequence models frequently omit critical early stellar physics, such as accretion processes, resulting in inadequate model grids and systematic errors. This study investigates enhanced and existing methods for asteroseismically modeling pre-main-sequence delta Scuti stars. We generated an extensive grid of pre-main-sequence models that incorporates the early accretion phase, using these equilibrium models to compute theoretical frequency spectra. These spectra facilitated an evaluation of various techniques for modeling echelle diagrams to identify the most robust approaches. Utilizing Petersen diagrams, we developed a straightforward algorithm to derive echelle diagrams from observed pulsation frequencies. We demonstrate that relying on model grids with deficient physical inputs and flawed modeling strategies leads to underestimated uncertainties and systematic errors in derived stellar parameters. A re-analysis of HD 139614 yields stellar parameters distinct from those reported by Murphy et al. (2021). Model comparisons between our findings and the previous study, employing Akaike and Bayesian information criteria, provide strong evidence favoring a 6-day model with fixed accretion parameters—which produces stellar parameters nearly identical to those of our 10-day model—over the approach used by Murphy et al. (2021), while results for the 10-day model remain inconclusive. Overall, our methodology offers tight constraints on stellar parameters (ΔR ~ 0.05 R⊙, Δ log g <~ 0.01, and ΔM★ ~ 0.1 M⊙). The rigorously tested modeling frameworks and automated echelle diagram extraction enable the future investigation of numerous pre-main-sequence delta Scuti stars, promising more reliable stellar parameter determinations.

Axie Infinity presents a complex card game with an extensive action space, rendering it challenging for standard Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms to solve. We introduce a hybrid RL framework designed to acquire both action representations and game strategies. To circumvent the computational burden of evaluating every possible move within the vast action set, our approach assesses only a fixed-size subset of actions, determined by the learned representations. We benchmark our method against two other baseline approaches, focusing on sample efficiency and winning rates. Empirical results demonstrate that our method outperforms the others, achieving both the highest winning rate and superior sample efficiency.

While edge computing is vital for remote environments, traditional hardware lacks optimization for deep neural networks. The Google Edge TPU addresses this as an emerging accelerator that delivers cost, power, and speed efficiency for both prototyping and production. This overview examines the Edge TPU platform, showcases tasks successfully completed with it, and outlines the deployment steps required for models. Beyond handling standard computer vision tasks, the Edge TPU outperforms other accelerators when entire models are deployed to it. Integrating the Edge TPU directly into cameras enables seamless primary data analysis. Ultimately, the Edge TPU represents a maturing system that has demonstrated its utility across a wide range of applications.

The classical Cauchy rigidity theorem for convex polytopes states that if two such polytopes possess isometric developments, they must be congruent. Essentially, this means we can determine whether two polyhedra are isometric by examining their developments alone. In this paper, we investigate a related question: whether the developments of two convex polyhedra in Euclidean 3-space are sufficient to determine if they are affine-equivalent or not.

Light field (LF) technology offers a promising approach for delivering high-quality virtual reality (VR) content, yet its substantial data volume necessitates efficient compression strategies. This paper introduces an LF image coding method leveraging view synthesis and quality enhancement. Rather than transmitting all LF views, the proposed scheme encodes and sends only a sparse set of reference views, while synthesizing the remaining views at the decoder. These transmitted views are compressed using the Versatile Video Coding (VVC) standard and serve as references for reconstructing the dropped views. The selection of non-reference views is optimized via rate-distortion analysis based on VVC temporal scalability. Reconstructed dropped views are generated using the LF dual discriminator GAN (LF-D2GAN) model. Furthermore, a quality enhancement step is applied at the decoder to ensure consistent view quality and facilitate smooth navigation. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior coding performance, outperforming state-of-the-art LF compression techniques with a -36.22% improvement in BD-BR and a 1.35 dB gain in BD-PSNR. The project's web page can be found at https://naderbakir79.github.io/LFD2GAN.html.

Road safety is paramount, particularly for autonomous vehicles, necessitating the early and effective detection and communication of disruptive events. This paper introduces a system utilizing an off-the-shelf deep neural network to identify and classify unsigned (non-placarded) and physical road incidents visible in imagery. To facilitate the organization of these events, we established a taxonomy for unsigned physical incidents and selected eight specific target categories. A dataset comprising 12,000 images sourced from publicly available web resources was assembled, and a convolutional neural network was fine-tuned to recognize these eight incident types. The resulting model achieves recognition accuracy exceeding 90%. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the system generalizes well across different spatial contexts within the United Kingdom when trained on geostratified data, maintaining over 90% accuracy; however, adapting the model to visually dissimilar environments necessitates the collection of spatially distributed data. Please note that this is a pre-print of a paper accepted for IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Vehicles (T-IV), currently in production with a DOI link pending.

This article introduces a novel approach to geophysical data collection and management using a near real-time peer-to-peer network. It provides a concise overview of the underlying motivations, the technology involved, and a specific application for gathering data from GNSS stations.
