However, by employing multiple spectral lines that span different optical depths, we can infer magnetic fields across nearly horizontal surfaces in regions of low plasma $\beta$, enabling the derivation of free energy, magnetic topology, and other relevant quantities. Building on recent successful suborbital magnetic field measurements by the CLASP2 instrument, we argue that a modest space-based telescope could significantly advance efforts to predict solar eruptions. We also demonstrate in an Appendix that difficulties related to blended lines are minimal.

Moving mesh techniques aim to redistribute a mesh systematically. This application aligns with the challenge of identifying a diffeomorphic mapping between density measures. Practically, this involves restructuring an existing grid to achieve higher resolution in specific areas while preventing mesh tangling, which highlights the value of diffeomorphic mapping approaches. For exact diffeomorphic mappings on a sphere, Optimal Transport is a primary tool, capable of mapping between even non-continuous source and target densities. However, Optimal Information Transport has recently been rigorously developed to facilitate both exact and inexact diffeomorphic mappings by solving a simpler partial differential equation.

This manuscript presents the first direct comparison of Optimal Transport and Optimal Information Transport applied to adaptive mesh problems on a sphere. We also demonstrate how to extend these computations to broader manifolds. Our comparison utilizes provably convergent solvers, a significant challenge for both problems due to missing boundary conditions and the absence of a comparison principle in the associated PDE formulation. Results indicate that Optimal Information Transport yields superior outcomes and offers greater ease of generalization for moving mesh tasks. Consequently, before Optimal Transport can be recommended for challenging moving mesh scenarios, further research is required to improve the accuracy of its solvers on spheres and to establish a framework for generalization to other manifolds.

Resolving interacting binaries is typically difficult because their separations fall within the milli-arcsecond range, making them hard to distinguish at any wavelength. However, recent progress in optical interferometry has enhanced our capacity to identify components in such systems, allowing for the direct calculation of physical parameters. Utilizing the Navy Prototype Optical Interferometer, we generated the first images that resolve all three components of the well-known Algol triple system. Specifically, we successfully separated the tertiary component from the binary pair and simultaneously resolved the eclipsing binary, which is the nearest and brightest of its kind in the sky. We provide revised orbital elements for the system and have corrected the 180-degree ambiguity in the position angle of Algol C. Furthermore, our directly determined magnitude differences and masses for this triple star system align with previous results derived from light curve modeling.

To address the security and privacy vulnerabilities inherent in centralized cloud services, edge computing networks have been deployed to distribute storage and computing resources to the network's periphery. Nevertheless, the constrained capabilities of edge devices create significant hurdles in areas such as data encryption, user privacy, and data authorization. Blockchain technology, currently a leading solution for distributed networks, resolves data consistency issues and is widely applied in sectors including cryptocurrency, smart grids, and the Internet of Things. This study examines the security and privacy challenges within edge computing networks, specifically analyzing how blockchain offers solutions regarding data authorization, encryption, and user privacy. We elaborate on the advantages of integrating blockchain with edge computing, demonstrating how this synergy effectively manages data authorization and encryption while enhancing the system's scalability without compromising security or privacy. Finally, we identify future research directions concerning storage, workload, and latency challenges in this domain.

Visual classification is categorized into two types: coarse-grained and fine-grained. Coarse-grained tasks involve distinguishing between highly dissimilar categories, such as cats versus dogs, whereas fine-grained tasks deal with highly similar classes, like specific bird species or vehicle makes and models. Unlike coarse-grained methods, fine-grained classification typically demands expert annotation, leading to higher costs. To address this, numerous approaches have been developed to automatically identify the most discriminative regions using local features, relying solely on image-level labels to lower annotation expenses. However, most existing solutions depend on multi-stage architectures that prevent end-to-end training. Consequently, we introduce a novel plug-in module compatible with various common backbones, including CNNs and Transformers, designed to extract strongly discriminative regions. This module generates pixel-level feature maps and fuses filtered features to boost performance in fine-grained visual classification. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed module surpasses state-of-the-art methods, achieving accuracy rates of 92.77% on CUB200-2011 and 92.83% on NABirds. Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/chou141253/FGVC-PIM.git.

We extend the Nakajima-Yoshioka blowup formula to determine partition functions that enumerate bound state spectra for half-BPS Wilson loop operators within 5d and 6d supersymmetric field theories. When placed on the blowup $\hat{\mathbb{C}}^2$ within the $\Omega$-background, the partition function for a Wilson loop operator factorizes into two distinct components under localization. This factorization establishes a framework of blowup equations specific to Wilson loop operators. We detail the formulation of these equations and their solution to compute the relevant partition functions. Furthermore, we validate this approach by explicitly deriving Wilson loop partition functions across various 5d and 6d theories, comparing the outcomes with established results and anticipated dualities.

Freezing of Gait (FOG), a profoundly disabling symptom of Parkinson's Disease, is closely linked to falls and diminished independence, yet the underlying patho-physiological mechanisms remain largely unclear. This study integrates time series analysis with mathematical modeling to investigate the dynamics of FOG, specifically examining the shift from stepping in place to freezing. We interpret this transition as an escape from an oscillatory attractor toward an equilibrium attractor state. By deriving a discrete-time, discrete-space Markov chain from experimental data and partitioning its state space into communicating classes, we pinpoint the onset of freezing. This approach enables the development of a methodology to computationally estimate both the time until freezing occurs and the phase within the oscillatory stepping cycle for patients undergoing Freezing Episodes (FE). Furthermore, this methodology is versatile and applicable to any time series data exhibiting transitions between distinct dynamic regimes, including forward walking patterns in individuals with FOG.

This study examines the essential function of uniform measures in the strict formulation of nonabelian lattice theories. It derives the fundamental requirements these measures must satisfy to guarantee consistency, positivity, and a mass gap. Additionally, the influence of non-generic strata on the characteristics of the Hamiltonian lattice potential is explored.

This study examines the interfacial dynamics between two immiscible viscous fluids within a Hele-Shaw cell, specifically focusing on the impact of a thin wetting film trailing the displaced fluid. This film introduces a nonlinear relationship between the interfacial velocity and the pressure drop. The analysis covers two scenarios: injection-driven flow, characterized by expansion, and lifting plate flow, characterized by contraction. We specifically explore how wetting effects can be leveraged to control fingering instabilities in these distinct setups. Using linear stability theory, we determine the necessary time-dependent injection rates $Q(t)$ for expansion and lifting speeds ${\dot b}(t)$ for contraction to regulate the number of emerging fingers. Our findings suggest that accounting for wetting requires larger magnitudes of $Q(t)$ and ${\dot b}(t)$ compared to non-wetting approaches. Furthermore, a spectrally accurate boundary integral method is employed to validate these control protocols in the fully nonlinear regime, confirming that the proposed injection and lifting strategies are viable for prescribing the resulting pattern morphologies when a wetting film is present.

Investigating signatures of quantum chaos in experimentally accessible many-body systems is a highly active area of research. In these systems, the spectral form factor (SFF)—the Fourier transform of the two-level spectral correlation function—is expected to display random matrix theory (RMT) characteristics, specifically a "ramp" followed by a "plateau" at sufficiently late times. Recently, a generic early-time deviation from RMT behavior, termed the "bump," has been identified in toy models like random quantum circuits and spin chains representing many-body quantum chaos. This study demonstrates the "bump-ramp-plateau" sequence in the SFF for several paradigmatic, stroboscopically driven cold atom models involving interacting bosons in optical lattices and spinor condensates. Our findings reveal that the scaling of the many-body Thouless time ($t_{\text{Th}}$)—marking the onset of the RMT ramp—and the growth of the bump amplitude with atom number are considerably slower in effectively zero-dimensional chaotic spinor gases compared to one-dimensional optical lattices, highlighting the influence of locality on many-body quantum chaos. Furthermore, both the $t_{\text{Th}}$ scaling and the bump amplitude exhibit greater sensitivity to changes in atom number than to variations in system size, irrespective of hyperfine structure, symmetry classes, or driving protocols. We derive SFF scaling functions indicating power-law behavior for the bump regime in quantum chaotic cold-atom systems. Finally, we propose an interference measurement protocol suitable for probing the SFF in laboratory settings.

In plasmas following a thermal quench, whether mitigated or unmitigated, the power equilibrium primarily involves Ohmic or collisional heating versus radiative cooling. For an atomic mixture $\{n_\alpha\}$ where $\alpha$ denotes the species, this balance determines the plasma temperature, the ion charge state distribution $\{n_\alpha^i\}$ (with $i$ as the charge number), and consequently the parallel electric field $E_\parallel$ via the electron temperature $T_e$ and charge state distribution. Since the threshold electric field for runaway avalanche growth, $E_{av}$, is likewise determined by the atomic mixture, ion charge state distribution, and the resulting electron density $n_e$, the power balance between Ohmic heating and radiative cooling places a strict constraint on the plasma conditions required to prevent and minimize runaways during the rapid termination of a fusion-grade tokamak plasma.

Recently, Transformer-based AutoRegressive (AR) models have demonstrated performance comparable to, or even surpassing, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) for full-image generation. However, directly adapting these AR models to modify specific local regions often leads to issues such as loss of global context, sluggish inference speeds, and information leakage from local guidance. To overcome these challenges, we introduce the Image Local Autoregressive Transformer (iLAT), a new framework designed to enhance locally guided image synthesis. iLAT employs a novel Local Autoregressive (LA) Transformer, which integrates attention masks and convolutional mechanisms to learn new local discrete representations. This architecture enables the efficient synthesis of local image regions using essential guidance cues. We evaluated iLAT across various tasks, including pose-guided person synthesis and face editing, where both quantitative and qualitative assessments confirm the model's effectiveness.

Researchers have examined several models for quantifying network reliability, typically defining it as the probability that a randomly failing graph remains connected. This study strengthens such a model by evaluating the likelihood that the surviving graph is not only connected but also "cop-win"—meaning a single cop can guarantee capturing a robber in the Cops and Robber pursuit-evasion game. Specifically, for a graph $G$ where nodes function independently with probability $p$ and edges function only if both endpoints do, the node cop-win reliability, denoted $\text{NCRel}(G,p)$, represents the probability that the operational nodes form a cop-win subgraph. The goal is to identify graphs $G$ with $n$ nodes and $m$ edges that maximize this reliability across all $p \in [0,1]$ compared to any other graph $H$ with the same parameters; such graphs are termed "uniformly most reliable." We demonstrate that uniformly most reliable graphs exist for both unicyclic and bicyclic graphs, contrasting with the current lack of known sparse graphs that maximize standard node reliability.

It is generally believed that blockchain systems cannot interact with external services because every node must maintain a deterministic state. However, this paper challenges that preconception by demonstrating a method that allows blockchain and distributed ledger technologies to initiate calls to external systems directly from the blockchain/DLT itself.

In neural machine translation (NMT), back-translation is commonly used to leverage target language monolingual data for synthesizing additional parallel training sets, a technique proven to enhance NMT performance, particularly for low-resource language pairs and domains. However, sufficient large-scale monolingual data in specific target domains or languages is not always accessible for generating extensive synthetic parallel corpora. This study introduces a novel approach to create substantial synthetic parallel data by utilizing minimal in-domain monolingual data. We fine-tune a pre-trained GPT-2 model on this limited in-domain monolingual corpus to produce a large volume of synthetic in-domain monolingual text, which is subsequently used for back-translation or forward translation to yield synthetic in-domain parallel data. Preliminary experiments across three language pairs and five domains demonstrate the method's efficacy in generating fully synthetic yet valuable in-domain parallel data to improve NMT across all configurations. Furthermore, we observe promising outcomes in extreme adaptation scenarios for personalized NMT.

Consistency training regularizes models by ensuring that predictions for original and perturbed inputs remain similar. While previous studies have introduced various augmentation techniques for perturbation, they are model-agnostic, often resulting in perturbed samples that are too easy for the model to classify, thereby limiting their regularization effectiveness. To address this, we propose an augmentation strategy that introduces discrete noise designed to maximize the divergence between predictions. This virtual adversarial discrete noise is generated by replacing a small fraction of tokens while maintaining the original semantics as much as possible, which efficiently shifts the model's decision boundary. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses other consistency training baselines—such as those using text editing, paraphrasing, or continuous noise—on semi-supervised text classification tasks and robustness benchmarks.

Recent research has sought to resolve the biological implausibility of the standard backpropagation (BP) algorithm. Although methods like feedback alignment, direct feedback alignment, and their variants (e.g., sign-concordant feedback alignment) offer solutions to the weight transport problem, their efficacy is still debated due to remaining unresolved issues. This study investigates whether random backpropagation can be implemented using only mechanisms observed in neuroscience. We introduce a hypothetical framework featuring a novel microcircuit architecture and compatible Hebbian learning rules. This architecture, which includes three cell types and two synaptic connectivity patterns, utilizes local feedback connections to compute and propagate error signals, enabling the training of multi-layer spiking neural networks with a globally defined spiking error function. Furthermore, we apply local Hebbian rules within specific compartments to update synaptic weights, facilitating supervised learning in a biologically plausible way. From an optimization perspective, we demonstrate that this framework is equivalent to sign-concordant feedback alignment. Benchmarking on datasets such as MNIST and CIFAR10 reveals that the proposed method achieves accuracy comparable to standard backpropagation.

Given a subgroup $H$ of the fundamental group $\pi_{1}(X,x_{0})$, we first introduce the notion of a strong $H$-SLT space, which extends the strong SLT space concept relative to $H$. Subsequently, we examine the existence of covering maps for such spaces and demonstrate that a semicovering map qualifies as a covering map when the strong $H$-SLT property holds. Furthermore, we establish conditions ensuring the equivalence of the whisker and lasso topologies on $\widetilde{X}_{H}$, alongside an analysis of the relationship between open subsets of $\pi_{1}^{wh}(X,x_{0})$ and $\pi_{1}^{l}(X,x_{0})$. Finally, we provide illustrative examples to validate the definition and utility of strong $H$-SLT spaces.

This study examines the statistical properties of the convex hull generated by a single run-and-tumble particle (RTP), or persistent random walker, in a two-dimensional space. Recently, RTPs have attracted considerable attention for their biological relevance in modeling bacterial motion. We analyze two distinct statistical ensembles: one where the total number of tumbles $n$ is fixed, and another where the total observation time $t$ is fixed. After establishing benchmarks for the perimeter, we investigate the statistical behavior of the convex hull's area. By leveraging connections to extreme value statistics, we derive exact analytical formulas for the mean area under both ensembles. For the fixed-time ensemble, the mean area exhibits a scaling form dependent on $\gamma t$ (where $\gamma$ is the tumbling rate), with the scaling function calculated precisely. Notably, this system displays a crossover from $\sim t^3$ scaling at short times ($t \ll \gamma^{-1}$) to $\sim t$ scaling at long times ($t \gg \gamma^{-1}$). Conversely, in the fixed-number ensemble, the mean area grows linearly with $n$ when $n \gg 1$. All analytical predictions are corroborated by numerical simulations.

We introduce a shuffle model differential privacy (DP) protocol for frequency estimation that attains an error of $\omega(1)\cdot O(\log n)$, nearly matching central-DP accuracy, while requiring only $1+o(1)$ messages per user. This highlights a sharp transition, given that a lower bound of $\Omega(n^{1/4})$ applies when users are restricted to a single message. While similar results were previously established only for domain sizes $B=o(n)$, our approach handles large domains by employing an efficient shuffle-DP method to detect heavy hitters (frequent elements). This heavy hitter detection protocol utilizes $o(1)$ messages per user and identifies all such elements in polylogarithmic time relative to $B$. By integrating our frequency estimation and heavy hitter detection mechanisms, we address the $B$-dimensional 1-sparse vector summation problem in high-dimensional settings where $B=\Omega(n)$, achieving the optimal central-DP mean squared error of $\tilde O(n)$ with $1+o(1)$ messages per user. Beyond improvements in error and message count, our protocols also enhance message size and execution time, remain straightforward to implement, and experimental evidence shows they offer order-of-magnitude gains over previous approaches.

When quantum states undergo an adiabatic traversal along a closed loop, they acquire a geometric phase known as the Berry phase, which relies on the trajectory rather than the speed of movement. This phase parallels the Aharonov-Bohm phase derived from electromagnetic vector potentials and is mathematically described using an Abelian gauge potential termed the Berry connection. Wilczek and Zee expanded this framework to encompass non-Abelian phases, defined by the gauge-independent Wilson loop and arising from non-Abelian gauge potentials. Leveraging an atomic Bose-Einstein condensate, we engineered a non-Abelian SU(2) gauge field created by a Yang monopole situated at the center of a five-dimensional parameter space. By adiabatically encircling this monopole, we characterized the Wilczek-Zee phase through the Wilson loop, which was found to depend on the solid angle subtended by the path—a generalization of Stokes' theorem. This achievement represents the first observation of a Wilson loop generated by a non-Abelian point source.

This paper examines the definition of conserved quantities within asymptotically locally de Sitter spacetimes. We propose defining holographic charge analogues at future and past infinities, as well as on other Cauchy surfaces $I_t$, by integrating over the intersections of timelike surfaces $C$ with these Cauchy surfaces. Typically, the charges $Q^t$ assigned to a Cauchy surface $I_t$ vary depending on the choice of $C$; however, in the absence of gravitational flux, these charges remain independent of $C$. Conversely, when a net gravitational flux enters or exits the spacetime region bounded by $C_1$, $C_2$, and two Cauchy surfaces, the difference $\Delta Q^t(C_1, C_2) = Q^t(C_1)-Q^t(C_2)$ shifts by an equivalent amount.

In natural language, referring to objects across varying levels of specificity serves as a core pragmatic strategy for efficient contextual communication. To investigate how such reference systems emerge in artificial agents, we introduced a new communication task called the hierarchical reference game. This simplified environment treats concepts as abstractions derived from primitive attributes like color, shape, and style; combining these attributes yields concepts that range from general (e.g., "circle") to specific (e.g., "red dotted circle"). Within this framework, agents must communicate at different hierarchical levels dictated by the context. Our findings indicate that agents successfully learn to play the game and can generalize to previously unseen concepts. To achieve abstraction, they employ both implicit strategies (excluding irrelevant details) and explicit strategies (signaling that certain attributes are irrelevant). Furthermore, the emergent communication protocols mirror the compositional structure of the concept hierarchy, suggesting that the necessity of developing hierarchical reference systems drives the emergence of compositionality.

Sparsification shrinks network size while maintaining key structural and statistical characteristics. Although various algorithms exist across different contexts, this work offers the first systematic conceptual and experimental comparison of *edge sparsification* techniques across a diverse range of network properties. The study demonstrates that these methods essentially function by assigning importance scores to edges and subsequently filtering them globally based on those scores. Additionally, we introduce a novel approach called *Local Degree*, which retains edges connected to local hub nodes. The evaluation, conducted on 100 Facebook social networks, examines properties such as diameter, connected components, community structure, and multiple node centrality metrics. Using the open-source NetworKit suite, our implementations reveal that numerous network properties can be preserved even when reducing the edge set to approximately 20% of its original size. Furthermore, these experiments differentiate the behavior of various methods, identifying which is best suited for specific properties. Our *Local Degree* method proves efficient for large-scale networks and outperforms previously proposed methods across a broader spectrum of properties.

Conversational Recommender Systems (CRS) utilize natural language interactions to recommend appropriate products to users, making the comprehension of user preferences and the development of effective item representations essential. Although previous research has explored these areas, most approaches rely on learning item representations from isolated conversations, overlooking item popularity derived from broader interactions. Furthermore, these methods often struggle to efficiently capture user preferences due to the limited information contained within a single dialogue. Drawing inspiration from collaborative filtering, we introduce COLA, a collaborative augmentation method designed to simultaneously enhance item representation learning and user preference modeling. By constructing an interactive user-item graph across all conversations, COLA enriches item representations with user-aware data, specifically item popularity. To refine user preference modeling, the method retrieves similar conversations from the training set, leveraging shared items and attributes to augment user representations via a gating mechanism. Extensive evaluations on two benchmark datasets confirm the method's efficacy, with code and data accessible at https://github.com/DongdingLin/COLA.

This study explores the application of deep representation learning (DRL) to speech enhancement (SE). While the efficacy of deep neural networks (DNNs) largely hinges on the quality of learned data representations, DRL's role is frequently overlooked in existing DNN-driven SE approaches. To achieve superior speech enhancement, we introduce a two-stage DRL-based method utilizing adversarial training. In the initial stage, we disentangle latent variables, as decoupled representations facilitate better speech generation by the DNN. Specifically, we employ a $\beta$-variational autoencoder (VAE) to derive speech and noise posterior estimates and associated representations from the input signal. However, because these posteriors and representations are intractable and rely on conditional assumptions for estimation, their accuracy cannot be guaranteed, potentially compromising final signal estimation performance. To mitigate this, the second stage incorporates adversarial training to minimize the impact of imperfect posterior estimates on signal reconstruction, thereby enhancing estimation accuracy and increasing the algorithm's robustness against such inaccuracies. Consequently, improved SE performance is realized. Experimental findings demonstrate that this strategy enables comparable DNN-based SE algorithms to achieve higher scores in short-time objective intelligibility (STOI), perceptual evaluation of speech quality (PESQ), and scale-invariant signal-to-distortion ratio (SI-SDR). Furthermore, the proposed algorithm surpasses several recent competitive SE methods.

Using light-cone QCD sum rules, we examine the isovector axial vector and pseudoscalar form factors of the $\Delta$ baryon. Our numerical results indicate that these form factors are accurately described by an exponential function. Furthermore, we compare our findings with predictions derived from Lattice QCD, Chiral Perturbation Theory, and the Quark Model.

Boron nitride emerges as a highly promising candidate for nanotechnology, characterized by its graphene-like two-dimensional structure, insulating properties, and exceptional stability. Recently, it has garnered significant interest as a substrate for growing and isolating graphene, as well as for its inherent ultraviolet (UV) lasing capabilities. Much like carbon, one-dimensional boron nitride nanotubes (BNNTs) have been both theoretically predicted and successfully synthesized. In this study, we employ first-principles simulations to conclusively demonstrate three key findings: first, BN nanotubes retain the highly efficient UV luminescence observed in hexagonal boron nitride; second, applying an external perpendicular electric field reduces the electronic gap while maintaining UV lasing, albeit with lower yield; third, defects within BNNTs enable tunable light emission ranging from the UV to the visible spectrum, controlled by a transverse electric field (TEF). These results lay the groundwork for practical optoelectronic devices based on BN nanotubes, offering a straightforward implementation that eliminates the need for specialized doping or intricate growth processes.

Earlier work established precise connections between the characteristics of a linear time-invariant control system and those of an anomaly detector designed to measure the impact of a stealthy attacker. A crucial initial step in this framework is accurately calibrating the detector to a target false alarm rate during normal operation, usually by adjusting a threshold parameter. While previous studies were limited to Gaussian noise, this work extends the calibration methodology to chi-squared anomaly detectors for non-Gaussian noise distributions. Our approach utilizes a Gaussian Mixture Model to approximate arbitrary noise profiles, maintaining analytical tractability and offering an insightful interpretation as a combination of multiple chi-squared detectors responding to various Gaussian disturbances.

Lately, a unified adversarial learning framework for image-to-image translation has garnered significant attention from computer vision researchers. Despite their empirical achievements, these successes currently lack robust theoretical explanations regarding their underlying mechanisms. This paper re-examines the model through a novel geometrical lens, providing a comprehensive interpretation of intriguing yet ambiguous experimental observations. Additionally, by expanding the definition of generalization in generative adversarial networks to a broader scope, we derive a condition to regulate the model's generalization capacity. Based on this condition, we offer practical recommendations for model architecture and dataset curation to guide future empirical studies.

This paper investigates the challenges of achieving asymptotic and finite-time cluster synchronization in time-varying delayed neural networks using pinning impulse and hybrid controllers, respectively. Based on Lyapunov stability theory and the Lyapunov-Razumikhin approach, a new sufficient condition for asymptotic cluster synchronization is derived. Similarly, by applying finite-time stability theory and hybrid control techniques, a sufficient criterion for finite-time cluster synchronization is established. To address time-varying delays and reduce control expenses, pinning pulse control is employed to facilitate asymptotic cluster synchronization. Following the pinning control framework, a progressive hybrid control strategy is designed to achieve finite-time cluster synchronization. Finally, an example is provided to validate the theoretical findings.

Close-in planets locked in a 1:1 mean motion resonance undergo significant tidal forces from their host star. This study presents an analytical framework tailored to model the tidal evolution of such systems, utilizing a Hamiltonian formulation of the constant time-lag tidal model that expands upon the existing formalism for point masses. Our findings indicate that tidal dissipation in these co-orbital systems drives them toward either Lagrange or anti-Lagrange configurations, contingent on specific system parameters. Nevertheless, regardless of the parameter range or initial conditions, both configurations are ultimately unstable; however, the timescale required for system destruction may exceed the star's lifetime. Additionally, we offer a straightforward criterion to assess whether a known close-in exoplanet could possess an undetected co-orbital companion.

A mathematical model represents a physical system based on unknown parameters, where calibration involves assigning values to these parameters using observations, recognizing the model as an imperfect representation of reality. General Bayesian inference extends traditional Bayesian methods by substituting the log-likelihood in Bayes' theorem with a negative loss function. The proposed methodology applies this general Bayesian framework to model calibration, where the resulting posterior distributions estimate parameter values that minimize the L2 norm of the discrepancy between the mathematical model and the actual physical system.

This study addresses the design of a circularly polarized Fabry-Pérot cavity (FPC) antenna for S-band sensing, utilizing the spatial distribution of peripheral roughness on the unit cell's partially reflecting surface as a key optimization parameter. Since full-wave solver evaluations for each candidate design are computationally prohibitive, we introduce a deep generative adversarial network (GAN) to create a surrogate model trained on input-output pairs of antenna configurations and their resulting radiation patterns. Leveraging this GAN framework enables the rapid assessment of numerous design candidates, ultimately yielding an antenna with an axial ratio of 0.4 dB, a gain of 7.5 dB, and a bandwidth of 269 MHz.

Image denoising focuses on recovering a clean image from one corrupted by noise. Model-based methods offer strong generalization across varying noise levels and high interpretability, whereas learning-based approaches, while often delivering superior results, typically lack these qualities. This paper introduces WINNet, a wavelet-inspired invertible network designed to merge the strengths of wavelet-based and learning-based techniques. WINNet integrates K-scale lifting-inspired invertible neural networks (LINNs) with sparsity-driven denoising and noise estimation networks. Drawing from the wavelet lifting scheme, the LINN architecture learns a non-linear, perfectly reconstructible redundant transform to aid in noise removal. The denoising component performs sparse coding, while the noise estimation module analyzes the input to adaptively adjust LINN soft-thresholds. The LINNs generate a redundant multi-scale representation, which is then reconstructed into a denoised image by applying the inverse transform to the cleaned detail channels alongside the original coarse channel. Simulation results indicate that WINNet is highly interpretable, exhibits robust generalization to unseen noise levels, and achieves competitive performance in both blind and non-blind denoising as well as image deblurring.

Video Question Answering (VQA) represents a recently emerged and challenging endeavor within Computer Vision. Prior to VQA, various visual information retrieval methods, such as Video Captioning/Description and Video-guided Machine Translation, were developed. VQA facilitates the extraction and interpretation of temporal and spatial data from video scenes. This survey examines numerous methods and datasets related to the VQA task. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first survey dedicated to the VQA task.

This study introduces approximation techniques for time-dependent thermal radiative transfer within high energy density physics. The approach utilizes a multilevel quasidiffusion framework, coupling high-order radiative transfer equations (RTE) with low-order quasidiffusion (VEF) equations for the moments of specific intensity. Since data storage in thermal radiative transfer (TRT) tasks between time steps is heavily influenced by the dimensionality of the radiation intensity grid functions, the authors apply approximate implicit methods with reduced memory to the time-dependent Boltzmann equation. The high-order RTE is discretized temporally using the backward Euler (BE) scheme, where the high-dimensional intensity from the preceding time level is approximated via low-rank proper orthogonal decomposition (POD). An alternative implementation applies POD to the remainder term of the intensity's P2 expansion. The accuracy of these approximate implicit solutions is contingent upon the POD rank. Ultimately, the proposed methods effectively decrease storage demands for time-dependent problems, and numerical results from a Fleck-Cummings TRT test case are provided to demonstrate their efficacy.

Unmeasured confounding often prevents the identification of causal effects from a postulated model; however, we can pursue partial identification by determining the upper and lower bounds of a target causal quantity across all solutions consistent with the specified structural assumptions. A promising approach to deriving these bounds involves constrained optimization that searches over all causal models compatible with the available evidence, a method pioneered by Balke and Pearl (1994) for discrete data. While this approach guarantees tight bounds, it presents significant computational hurdles. To address this, researchers have turned to algorithms that sacrifice tightness for efficiency or to impose restrictions on the model class. This paper introduces a novel alternative inspired by belief propagation: we enforce compatibility between a causal model's marginals and the observed data without constructing a global causal model. We refer to the set of these locally consistent marginals as the causal marginal polytope. Since global independence constraints vanish when examining small, tractable dimensional marginals, this framework necessitates a reevaluation of how causal knowledge is elicited and expressed. We present an explicit algorithm and implementation for this concept, evaluating its practical utility through numerical experiments.

We present an energetic framework that accounts for the distinctive twisting dynamics of spindle-shaped polymer microparticles exhibiting nematic order, which differ significantly from standard nematics in spindle geometries. Building on our prior geometric model—derived from experimental data and demonstrating that twist patterns follow loxodrome spirals [Ansell et al., Phys. Rev. Lett., 123, 157801 (2019)]—this study first analyzes a spindle-shaped surface. We demonstrate that the observed loxodrome twisting can be described by the Frank free energy of a nematic system augmented with a term that constrains the length of the integral curves. Subsequently, we extend this model to the bulk phase and investigate the parameter regimes where the twisted loxodrome solution remains energetically optimal.

We introduce a geometric method for analyzing the Lieb-Schultz-Mattis theorem in quantum many-body systems featuring discrete spin-rotation symmetries and lattice inversion or rotational symmetry, without requiring translational invariance. By applying symmetry twisting to a $(d-1)$-dimensional plane, we demonstrate that any $d$-dimensional inversion-symmetric spin system with a half-integer spin at the inversion center exhibits a doubly degenerate spectrum. Similarly, we prove that generalized rotation-symmetric spin models possessing a projective representation at the rotation center display analogous degeneracy under symmetry twisting. We contend that these spectral degeneracies preclude the existence of a unique, symmetric, gapped ground state smoothly connected to product states in the original untwisted systems, thereby establishing generalized inversional and rotational Lieb-Schultz-Mattis theorems that do not rely on lattice translation symmetry. This proposed framework also encompasses traditional Lieb-Schultz-Mattis theorems that include translational symmetry.

Thermal transport and quantum thermodynamics at the nanoscale are currently attracting significant interest, especially within the realm of quantum technologies. It is anticipated that experiments pertinent to these technologies will operate in the non-linear regime. Building upon prior findings from the linear response regime regarding an Aharonov-Bohm (AB) interferometer used as a heat engine, this study investigates the non-linear regime. We demonstrate that this mesoscopic quantum device exhibits tunability, substantial efficiency, and thermopower, thereby validating the promising potential of AB rings for creating highly efficient thermal machines in the fully quantum domain.

Originating in linear algebra, the concept of zero forcing has been extensively explored by graph theorists and algebraists alike. This process involves initiating vertex activation on a graph $G$ from a specific set, where an active vertex with exactly one inactive neighbor compels that neighbor to become active. A subset $S\subset V(G)$ is defined as a zero forcing set if starting with only vertices in $S$ active eventually activates the entire graph. The zero forcing number is the cardinality of the smallest such set. Although minimum zero forcing sets are typically unique only in edgeless graphs, we examine a relaxed uniqueness criterion: for any two minimum sets in $G$, there exists an automorphism mapping one to the other. We characterize the trees satisfying this property by leveraging properties of minimum path covers. Furthermore, we analyze four variations of uniqueness related to Grundy domination concepts, which emerged from domination games but share strong ties to zero forcing. For each variation, we identify graphs possessing a single Grundy dominating set of that type and forests satisfying the weaker isomorphism-based uniqueness condition. These characterizations enable the development of efficient algorithms to recognize the respective classes of forests.

We determine the genus of the galaxy distribution within two-dimensional slices of the SDSS-III BOSS catalog to restrict the cosmological parameters that dictate the Universe's expansion history. The BOSS data are segmented into twelve concentric shells spanning redshifts $0.25 < z < 0.6$, and we repeatedly calculate the genus from the resulting two-dimensional galaxy density fields by varying the cosmological parameters used to derive the distance-redshift relation for each shell. Additionally, we indirectly reconstruct the two-dimensional genus amplitude using three-dimensional genus measurements from the SDSS Main Galaxy Sample, focusing on low-redshift galaxies ($z < 0.12$). By merging low- and high-redshift measurements, we identify the cosmological model that minimizes the redshift evolution of the genus amplitude, relying on the principle that this quantity should remain conserved. As a distance metric, this test is sensitive to the matter density parameter ($\Omega_{\rm m}$) and the dark energy equation of state ($w_{\rm de}$). Combining high- and low-redshift data with Planck CMB results yields constraints of $w_{\rm de} = -1.05^{+0.13}_{-0.12}$ and $\Omega_{\rm m} = 0.303 \pm 0.036$. Future constraints will be strengthened by incorporating higher-redshift data and combining additional low-redshift datasets.

This review examines recent advancements in quantum glasses, emphasizing their equilibrium behavior and the connection between glassy dynamics and localization effects, along with notable links to the SYK model.

A cover of an associative ring $R$ (which may lack unity or commutativity) consists of a collection of proper subrings whose union is $R$ as sets. When such a cover exists, $\sigma(R)$ denotes the cardinality of the smallest such cover, and $R$ is termed $\sigma$-elementary if $\sigma(R)$ is strictly less than $\sigma(R/I)$ for every nonzero two-sided ideal $I$. For unital rings, the unital covering number $\sigma_u(R)$ is defined as the size of a minimal cover by subrings containing the identity element $1_R$ (provided one exists), and $R$ is $\sigma_u$-elementary if $\sigma_u(R) < \sigma_u(R/I)$ for all nonzero two-sided ideals. This paper classifies all $\sigma$-elementary unital rings and computes their covering numbers. Leveraging this classification, we further categorize all $\sigma_u$-elementary rings and establish that $\sigma_u(R) = \sigma(R)$ for any $\sigma_u$-elementary ring $R$. Additionally, we demonstrate that for any ring $R$ without unity possessing a finite cover, there exists a unital ring $R'$ such that $\sigma(R) = \sigma_u(R')$, thereby providing a complete enumeration of integers that serve as covering numbers. Finally, defining $\mathscr{E}(N)$ as the set of integers $m \le N$ that are covering numbers of some ring, we prove that $|\mathscr{E}(N)| = \Theta(N/\log(N))$, indicating that the vast majority of integers are not covering numbers.

Federated learning (FL) facilitates predictive model training on Internet of Things (IoT) devices by eliminating the energy, time, and privacy costs associated with data collection. We define the utility of an IoT device as the ratio of its learning gain to its participation cost. Given device heterogeneity, both the local learning cost and model quality vary across devices and can change over time. We demonstrate that sharing a single global model leads to utility unfairness due to these variations. Typically, the central server lacks visibility into individual device computation and transmission expenses, rendering it incapable of resolving this unfairness; furthermore, devices may exploit this information asymmetry to minimize their own costs and maximize utility. To address this, we propose regulating the quality of the global model distributed to devices in each round based on their specific contributions and expenditures. This approach utilizes differential privacy to limit information leakage regarding learning contributions. Additionally, we develop adaptive computation and transmission policies for each device to manage its expenditure and alleviate utility unfairness. Experimental results indicate that the proposed scheme reduces the standard deviation of device energy costs by 99% compared to the benchmark, while the standard deviation of training loss remains approximately 0.103.

We contend that ocean general circulation models and observations derived from Ekman or geostrophic balance approximate the Lagrangian-mean ocean velocity field averaged over surface waves. This represents the total time-averaged velocity responsible for advecting tracers, particles, and water parcels. This view challenges the common assumption in ocean transport studies that numerical models and dynamical balance-based observations estimate the Eulerian-mean velocity—the time-averaged velocity at a fixed location, which accounts for only a portion of the total ocean velocity. Our argument relies on the similarity between the large-scale, wave-averaged Lagrangian-mean momentum equations and the momentum equations solved by "wave-agnostic" general circulation models that ignore surface wave effects. We strengthen this position by comparing a realistic, global, "wave-agnostic" general circulation model against a wave-averaged Lagrangian-mean model at eddy-permitting 1/4° resolution, demonstrating that the resulting wave-agnostic velocity field is nearly identical to the wave-averaged Lagrangian-mean velocity.

Identifying named entities within legal documents serves as a fundamental prerequisite for advancing various legal artificial intelligence tools. Unlike standard entities such as persons, organizations, and locations, named entities in legal contexts are more granular and distinct. This paper presents a novel corpus comprising 46,545 annotated legal named entities categorized into 14 specific legal entity types, alongside the development of a baseline model for extracting these entities from judgment texts.

As efforts to boost efficiency intensify, interdependence and complexity have emerged as hallmark traits of modern networks, spanning both engineered and natural domains. Graph theory serves as a prevalent framework for modeling these networks and assessing their resilience against disruptions. Specifically, pinpointing critical nodes or links can significantly enhance system robustness and highlight key performance determinants. However, most current critical node identification methods rely on iterative processes that examine every node and link, leading to high computational costs and network-specific analyses. Furthermore, inherent uncertainties within the graphical model constrain the effectiveness of these traditional techniques. To address these limitations, we introduce a Bayesian graph neural network framework for node classification that offers computational efficiency and systematically integrates uncertainty. Rather than training directly on the observed graph, the model computes a Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimate of the graph structure using observed topology and target node labels. Additionally, Monte-Carlo dropout is employed to capture epistemic uncertainty. Simulation results demonstrate the framework's accuracy and its substantial reduction in computational complexity.

This manuscript establishes the Bernstein inequality and advances the theory of holonomic D-modules for two specific settings: rings of invariants of finite groups in characteristic zero, and strongly F-regular finitely generated graded algebras with FFRT in prime characteristic. In both scenarios, the rings themselves, their localizations, and their local cohomology modules are proven to be holonomic. Furthermore, we demonstrate that holonomic D-modules within this context possess finite length. These findings are derived from a broader formulation of Bernstein filtrations.

This study introduces mCube, a multinomial multi-state micro-level reserving model. We develop a unified framework to model the temporal and payment dynamics of IBNR and RBNS claims, as well as IBNR claim counts, utilizing multinomial distributions for the time component and spliced mixture models for the payment component. The model's superior performance is demonstrated using a real-world dataset from a major insurer covering bodily injury claims. Results indicate that the proposed model generates a best estimate distribution that accurately centers around the true reserve value.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) are susceptible to adversarial examples, which cause incorrect predictions through the injection of subtle perturbations. This research investigates the transferability of these examples, a critical factor for real-world scenarios where target model architectures or parameters remain hidden. While previous studies indicate that adversarial examples often overfit their generating surrogate models—thereby reducing transfer attack effectiveness against diverse targets—we introduce a new method called Reverse Adversarial Perturbation (RAP) to address this overfitting. Rather than minimizing the loss of a single point, RAP seeks adversarial examples within a region characterized by uniformly low loss values by applying worst-case perturbations at every optimization step. Formulated as a min-max bi-level optimization problem, RAP enhances the iterative attack process to produce more stable adversarial examples that are less sensitive to decision boundary shifts, effectively curbing surrogate model overfitting. Extensive experiments confirm that RAP substantially improves adversarial transferability and can be seamlessly integrated with various existing black-box attack techniques to further enhance performance. In tests against the Google Cloud Vision API, RAP achieved a 22% improvement in targeted attack success rates compared to baseline methods. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/SCLBD/Transfer_attack_RAP.

Sensor-based Human Activity Recognition (HAR), which involves identifying daily human behaviors using wearable or embedded sensors, serves as a critical component for numerous real-world applications in smart homes, personal healthcare, and urban planning. As the deployment of these applications expands, a significant challenge emerges: enabling HAR systems to autonomously acquire new activities over extended periods without requiring complete re-engineering. This issue, known as continual learning, has gained substantial traction in computer vision, where various solutions have been developed. This paper investigates the extent to which these continual learning methods can be adapted for the HAR domain. Specifically, we introduce a general framework to assess the performance of such techniques across diverse, commonly used HAR datasets. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive empirical analysis of their computational costs and their efficacy in addressing HAR-specific challenges, namely sensor noise and data scarcity. The results offer valuable insights into their applicability and propose future research directions for HAR systems. Our code, models, and data are accessible at https://github.com/srvCodes/continual-learning-benchmark.

This paper introduces a computationally efficient, end-to-end trainable deep neural network (CEDNN) that incorporates spatial attention maps derived from difference images. The process begins with generating a difference image via image processing, followed by the creation of five binary difference images using various thresholds to serve as spatial attention maps. To minimize model complexity, group convolution is employed, while skip connections and $1\times1$ convolutions ensure robust performance even within a shallow architecture. Spatial attention maps are selectively input to each block, allowing feature maps to concentrate more effectively on task-relevant regions. Furthermore, training the model for different numbers of Action Units (AUs) requires only adjustments to the classifier parameters. The framework is easily adaptable to varying datasets with minimal computational overhead. Extensive experiments on the DISFA+ and CK+ datasets demonstrate that the proposed CEDNN significantly outperforms traditional deep learning approaches and achieves superior results compared to state-of-the-art AU detection methods. Additionally, the network features a compact size, high processing speed, and low hardware requirements.

Recommender systems significantly shape the information users encounter on platforms like social media, thereby affecting their beliefs, choices, and behaviors. Simultaneously, these systems generate considerable economic value for various stakeholders. As the influence of such AI-driven technologies on individuals, organizations, and society expands, fairness has become a focal point of inquiry. Nevertheless, research dedicated to fairness in recommender systems remains an emerging field. This survey begins by examining the core concepts and definitions of fairness introduced recently in this domain. Subsequently, based on a review of over 150 academic papers, we provide an overview of how current research operationalizes these issues, covering methodologies, fairness metrics, and algorithmic strategies. Our analysis of recent literature reveals distinct research gaps: specifically, many computer science studies rely on highly abstract problem formulations and frequently fail to deeply explore underlying normative assumptions or define what constitutes a fair recommendation within specific application contexts. These findings underscore the need for increased interdisciplinary collaboration to address fairness in recommendation systems more comprehensively and effectively.

We introduce a two-stage deep reinforcement learning algorithm designed to tackle difficult control challenges. While deep RL has proven effective for high-dimensional continuous control tasks, it often fails on problems characterized by sparse rewards or sensitive dynamics. Our proposed method addresses this by decomposing the task into two phases: motion planning and motion imitation. In the planning phase, a feasible trajectory is computed by directly sampling the state space using approximated dynamics, avoiding the inefficiency of exploring random control signals. Subsequently, the imitation phase trains a control policy to replicate this planned motion under realistic sensor and actuation constraints. We show that this framework successfully solves complex problems like rocket navigation and quadrupedal locomotion, which are intractable using standard Markov Decision Process formulations. A supplementary video is available at: https://youtu.be/FYLo1Ov_8-g

Due to the time-consuming and error-prone nature of manual volumetric measurements of fetal structures in MRI, automatic segmentation is essential. Segmenting the placenta and accurately delineating the fetal brain for gyrification analysis pose significant challenges owing to the placenta's indistinct boundaries and the intricate folding of the fetal brain cortex. This study investigates the application of Contour Dice loss to address both issues, benchmarking it against alternative boundary losses and the standard combination of Dice and Cross-Entropy losses. The proposed loss function is calculated efficiently for individual slices using erosion, dilation, and XOR operations, featuring a novel formulation similar to the Contour Dice metric. Results indicate that combining Dice loss with Contour Dice loss produced superior outcomes for placenta segmentation. In fetal brain segmentation, the optimal approach was the combination of Dice and Cross-Entropy losses, which outperformed other boundary losses, with the Dice and Contour Dice combination ranking second.

This study examines continuous-time stochastic differential games involving numerous players, where costs and dynamics are coupled via the empirical distribution of states and controls, assuming open-loop control strategies. We establish regularity conditions ensuring that, if a finite-player game possesses a Nash equilibrium, the sequence of equilibria and associated state processes obey a Sanov-type large deviation principle. This finding relies on the existence of a Lipschitz continuous solution to the master equation of the corresponding mean field game and utilizes concentration inequalities for Lipschitz forward-backward stochastic differential equations (FBSDEs). The theorem also extends to cooperative (central planner) scenarios, with a detailed analysis provided for the linear-quadratic case.

Electrochemical effects in ferroelectrics are highly significant for catalysis and sensing, with recent research emphasizing the interplay between ferroelectric polarization, applied surface voltage, and switching history. This study employs systematic Kelvin probe microscopy to investigate how relative humidity and polarization switching history influence surface charge dissipation in Pb(Zr$_{0.2}$Ti$_{0.8}$)O$_3$ thin films. By applying physically constrained unsupervised machine learning via Dictionary Learning, we examine the interaction between surface charges and ferroelectric domains, uncovering a complex network of voltage-driven physical processes responsible for signal decay. Furthermore, a Fitzhugh-Nagumo reaction-diffusion model provides additional perspective on these behaviors, elucidating the contributions of lateral charge spread and passivation within the Dictionary Learning framework.

We investigate heat transport through a harmonic chain of charged particles featuring transverse degrees of freedom under a uniform magnetic field. For an open chain coupled to heat baths at its ends, we derive a nonequilibrium Green's function formulation for the heat current. This expression utilizes two distinct Green's functions, representing scattering processes either within or between the two transverse waves. The magnetic field induces two phonon bands in the isolated system, allowing the net transmission to be expressed as a sum of two terms, each corresponding to one band. We derive exact current expressions for the thermodynamic limit under both free and fixed boundary conditions. In this limit, at low frequencies ($\omega$), the effective transmission exhibits $\omega^{3/2}$ and $\omega^{1/2}$ dependencies for fixed and free boundaries, respectively. This contrasts with the zero magnetic field scenario, where transmission follows $\omega^2$ and $\omega^0$ dependencies for the respective boundary conditions, a behavior attributable to the quadratic low-frequency phonon dispersion.

We present the initial findings from an ALMA band 3 spectroscopic survey focused on the most luminous submillimeter galaxies (SMGs) within the COSMOS field. Drawing from a parent sample of 260 ALMA-detected SMGs identified in the AS2COSMOS survey, this study analyzes 18 primary SMGs with 870 $\mu$m flux densities ranging from $S_{870}=12.4-19.3$ mJy. Emission lines were detected in 17 of these sources, yielding redshifts between $z=2$ and $z=5$, with a median value of ${3.3\pm0.3}$. Our data confirm a trend where SMGs exhibiting brighter $S_{870}$ fluxes reside at higher redshifts. Additionally, we analyzed five fainter companion SMGs and secured a line detection for one. Combined with prior research, our results suggest that for SMGs meeting our selection criteria, their brightest companions are physically associated with the primary in at least 40% of cases, indicating that mergers contribute to triggering star formation. By modeling foreground gravitational fields, we find that fewer than 10% of the primary SMGs are strongly lensed with magnifications $\mu>2$. Spectral analysis reveals that approximately 90% of the primary SMGs exhibit line profiles better fit by double Gaussians, with a median peak separation of $430\pm40$ km s$^{-1}$. These parameters allow for estimates of average baryon mass, which, when paired with line dispersion measurements, places our primary SMGs on a mass-$\sigma$ correlation similar to that of local early-type galaxies. Finally, the number density of our $z>4$ primary SMGs is calculated as $1^{+0.9}_{-0.6}\times10^6$ cMpc$^{-3}$, implying they may serve as progenitors for massive quiescent galaxies at $z\sim3-4$.

Recent research indicates that deep neural networks are susceptible to adversarial examples, yet existing defense mechanisms fail to address this issue fundamentally. This paper provides a theoretical proof establishing an upper bound on the error caused by adversarial noise for neural networks utilizing identity mappings; however, in practical computations, these networks lose this bound and remain vulnerable. Using analogous reasoning, we clarify why adversarial examples can deceive other deep neural networks featuring skip connections. Additionally, we demonstrate that a novel class of deep neural networks known as Neural ODEs (Chen et al., 2018) possesses a weaker upper bound, which limits the magnitude of output changes. Consequently, Neural ODEs exhibit inherent robustness against adversarial examples. We evaluate Neural ODEs against ResNet across three white-box attacks (FGSM, PGD, DI2-FGSM) and one black-box attack (Boundary Attack). Finally, our results indicate that the natural robustness of Neural ODEs surpasses that of networks trained using adversarial training techniques like TRADES and YOPO.

Multi-spectral imagery holds immense value for remote sensing because materials that look identical in greyscale or RGB formats often display distinct spectral signatures. When combined with advanced deep learning techniques, this data type offers significant potential for diverse applications, including humanitarian aid and disaster recovery. Although current deep learning models rely heavily on large-scale annotated datasets like ImageNet, existing multi-spectral image collections lack comparable annotation volumes. Rather than depending on transfer learning with limited labels, we utilize complex-valued co-domain symmetric models to classify real-valued multi-spectral images. Experiments conducted on 8-band xView data demonstrate that our ultra-lean model, trained from scratch without data augmentation, surpasses ResNet architectures enhanced with data augmentation and modified transfer learning on the same dataset. This study marks the first demonstration of the benefits of complex-valued deep learning applied to real-valued multi-spectral data.

To address biases in search ranking and enable training with user interaction data, unbiased learning to rank has been introduced. However, real-world search engines typically display only the top $k$ most relevant documents from a candidate set, discarding the rest. This practice often leads to the simultaneous occurrence of position bias and sample selection bias. Current unbiased learning to rank methods either target a single bias type or address these two biases through separate components, thereby ignoring their interconnections. In this study, we examine the mechanisms and relationships between position bias and sample selection bias using a causal graph framework. Building on this analysis, we propose Causal Likelihood Decomposition (CLD), a unified approach designed to mitigate both biases concurrently within top-$k$ learning to rank. CLD decomposes the log-likelihood of biased data into an unbiased term reflecting only relevance and additional terms associated with biases, effectively separating relevance from both position and sample selection biases. An unbiased ranking model is derived by maximizing the overall likelihood using the unbiased term. We also extend this method to pairwise neural ranking. The advantages of CLD include its theoretical rigor and a unified framework applicable to both pointwise and pairwise unbiased top-$k$ learning to rank. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CLD, along with its pairwise neural extension, outperforms baseline methods by effectively mitigating both biases. Furthermore, empirical studies confirm that CLD remains robust against variations in bias severity and click noise.

Determining the critical parameters of metals remains a significant challenge, both experimentally due to the extreme temperatures required and theoretically because of complex many-body interactions. Furthermore, experimental observations reveal that these systems display a pronounced asymmetry in their binodal. Recent theoretical advancements have introduced new similarity laws derived from the Zeno line and Boyle parameters, yielding critical properties for atomic and molecular systems that align exceptionally well with experimental data. Employing the recently developed Expanded Wang-Landau (EWL) simulation technique, we have evaluated the grand-canonical partition function across a broad spectrum of conditions for eleven FCC and HCP metals (Ag, Al, Au, Be, Cu, Ir, Ni, Pb, Pd, Pt, and Rh) modeled using many-body interaction potentials. This approach enables the calculation of the binodal, Zeno line, and Boyle parameters, which subsequently allow for the determination of critical properties for these systems. Additionally, we propose two scaling laws for the enthalpy and entropy of vaporization, identifying critical exponents of 0.4 and 1.22, respectively, for these laws.

Cell-to-cell heterogeneity underpins various (patho)physiologically significant outcomes, including cell fate determination and resistance to chemotherapy. The role of metabolism, especially that of mitochondria, is increasingly acknowledged as a key driver of this heterogeneity. Since most eukaryotic cells contain multiple copies of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) per cell—with each molecule potentially exhibiting sequence variations—intra-cellular mitochondrial diversity is feasible. This intra-cellular variation can propagate to create inter-cellular differences, potentially fueling cellular noise. This review examines the origins of mitochondrial heterogeneity, encompassing variations among mitochondria within a single cell and differences between ostensibly identical cells, from both genetic and non-genetic standpoints, alongside the connections between mitochondrial genotypes and phenotypes. We address the homeostasis of mtDNA copy numbers, the prevalence of intra-cellular mtDNA mutations (termed "microheteroplasmy"), and advancements in understanding inter-cellular mtDNA mutations ("macroheteroplasmy"). Additionally, we highlight how mitochondrial supercomplexes, cristae architecture, pH levels, and cardiolipin may act as amplifiers of the genotype-phenotype relationship. The discussion also covers mitochondrial membrane potential and network dynamics as sources of heterogeneity and their impact on the mitochondrial genome. Finally, we reconsider mitochondrial complementation as a mechanism to mitigate genotype-phenotype links, informed by recent experimental findings. The variety of mitochondrial heterogeneity sources and their growing recognition as contributors to cellular heterogeneity underscore the necessity for future single-cell mitochondrial analyses within the framework of cellular noise research.

Comprehending how high-energy radiation and stellar winds influence planetary atmospheres is essential for interpreting the characteristics of close-in exoplanets. By analyzing transiting exoplanets through the triplet of metastable helium lines at 10830 Å, researchers can investigate extended atmospheres and escape mechanisms on a per-planet basis. We utilized NIRSPEC on Keck to observe a single transit of WASP-107b at this wavelength. Our data provided significant post-transit coverage for the first time, revealing excess absorption lasting more than an hour after fourth contact. These findings support a model of a comet-like tail stretching approximately 7 planetary radii, roughly equivalent to twice the Roche lobe radius. Such tails are predicted by 3D simulations of atmospheric escape, especially when accounting for interactions with intense stellar winds, and have previously been detected at 10830 Å in at least one other exoplanet. Given that WASP-107b exhibits both the largest mid-transit absorption signal and the most extended tail observed at this wavelength, it stands as a pivotal subject for studying atmospheric escape.

We introduce Diffstar, a smooth parametric framework designed to model the in-situ star formation history (SFH) of galaxies. Unlike traditional SFH models that interpret spectral energy distributions (SEDs), Diffstar is defined directly by fundamental aspects of galaxy formation physics. The model posits that star formation is driven by gas accretion onto dark matter halos, relying on a parametric description of halo mass assembly known as Diffmah. It incorporates parameters for the star formation efficiency ($\epsilon_{\rm ms}$) and the consumption timescale ($\tau_{\rm cons}$), while also accounting for quenching events at time $t_{\rm q}$ and potential subsequent rejuvenation. When applied to galaxies from the IllustrisTNG (TNG) and UniverseMachine (UM) simulations, Diffstar accurately reproduces average stellar mass histories with a precision of approximately 0.1 dex across most cosmic epochs. Comparing TNG and UM using these common physical parameters reveals four key differences: (i) UM exhibits less efficient and more bursty star formation than TNG; (ii) UM galaxies possess longer gas consumption timescales; (iii) rejuvenation is common in UM but rare in quenched TNG galaxies; and (iv) in both simulations, the distributions of $\epsilon_{\rm ms}$, $\tau_{\rm cons}$, and $t_{\rm q}$ show a shared dependence on halo mass and strong correlations with halo assembly history. [Abridged]

It has been proposed that most red supergiant (RSG) progenitors of Type II-P supernovae (SNe) are surrounded by substantial circumstellar material (CSM) at the moment of explosion. The density of this CSM far exceeds that typically observed around field RSGs, suggesting a brief period of heightened mass loss preceding the event. However, the duration over which this material accumulates remains uncertain: does it result from a decades-long `superwind' with a mass-loss rate of $\dot{M} \sim10^{-3}\,{\rm M_\odot\,yr^{-1}}$, or from an outburst lasting less than a year with $\dot{M}\sim10^{-1}\,{\rm M_\odot\,yr^{-1}}$? In this study, we simulate spectra for RSGs experiencing these mass-loss episodes and show that, in both cases, the CSM attenuates optical flux by more than a factor of 100 and near-infrared flux by a factor of 10. We contend that the `superwind' scenario is untenable because it would obscure the progenitor heavily for decades before explosion, contradicting observations of II-P progenitors within 10 years of core-collapse. Consequently, our findings support abrupt outbursts occurring less than a year before explosion as the cause of early optical radiation in II-P SNe. Based on this, we predict that RSGs will exhibit significant photometric variability in both optical and infrared bands during the weeks to months leading up to core-collapse.

Crystals of manganese, tellurium, and selenium exhibit chiral properties. To investigate how variations in chirality influence the characteristics of these elemental samples, crystallographic analyses must distinguish between two enantiomorphic, physically distinct structural variants. However, due to inherent constraints in kinematical X-ray scattering, detecting chirality effects in single-element crystals via standard X-ray diffraction is highly challenging. This paper demonstrates that dynamical Kikuchi diffraction within a scanning electron microscope is capable of sensing the local chirality in crystals of individual chemical elements. We successfully assign chirality in $\beta$-manganese and determine the specific sense of crystal chirality by analyzing the Kikuchi diffraction patterns of the trigonal structures found in tellurium and selenium.

This review examines recent advancements in applying machine learning to molecular modeling and simulation. Following a concise introduction to the foundations, components, and workflow of standard supervised learning methods for chemical tasks, we present state-of-the-art examples and key application areas. Furthermore, we explore how machine learning complements, supports, and enhances conventional physics-based computational approaches. Finally, we identify current challenges and future research directions necessary for establishing machine learning as a mainstream tool in chemical engineering.

By addressing questions 19.23 and 19.24 in the Kourovka notebook, we build polycyclic groups featuring torsion of any specified length and provide instances of finitely presented groups where the quotients formed by their torsion subgroups fail to be finitely presented.

This study investigates the electrical and spin characteristics of monolayer MoSi2X4 (where X = N, P, As, and Sb) under vertical strain. Band structure analysis reveals that MoSi2N4 is an indirect semiconductor, while the remaining compounds are direct semiconductors. Vertical strain was applied to modulate electrical properties, causing the bandgap to reach a maximum before decreasing under both tensile and compressive conditions. Significant spin-splitting is observed in the valence band at the K-point, whereas the primary conduction band exhibits negligible splitting. Conversely, the second conduction band shows substantial spin-splitting and shifts downward under vertical strain, resulting in large spin-splitting at both conduction and valence band edges. The projected band structure and projected density of states elucidate the origins of these spin-splitting phenomena, all of which can be regulated by vertical strain.

Current methods for detecting machine-generated text primarily rely on binary classification to distinguish between human and machine-written content. In the scientific publishing sector, where such models screen submitted manuscripts, misclassification risks harming authors, particularly since the legitimate use of assistive technologies like translation tools may be incorrectly flagged as machine-generated. To address this, our study simulates this scenario by evaluating a state-of-the-art detector trained on the DAGPap22 dataset using machine-translated passages from Scielo, discovering that the model performs no better than random chance. Consequently, we propose a novel framework for dataset creation that enables a more granular detection approach by categorizing the specific technology used (e.g., translation versus paraphrase), leading to the development of the SynSciPass dataset. When we retrained the DAGPap22-trained model on SynSciPass, we demonstrated that it becomes more robust to domain shifts and capable of identifying the specific generation technology employed. However, we conclude that existing datasets remain insufficiently comprehensive and realistic for predicting model performance in real-world scenarios, specifically regarding manuscript submissions from diverse or novel distributions, the analysis of full scientific texts rather than isolated passages, and the complex interplay of appropriate and inappropriate natural language generation uses.

Accurate polyp localization is vital for early cancer detection during gastrointestinal endoscopy. Unlike still images, endoscopic videos provide richer contextual data but present greater challenges, particularly due to camera movement rather than a fixed camera-object setup, which causes substantial background fluctuations between frames. Additionally, severe internal artifacts, such as fluid flow within the body or tissue specular reflections, can drastically alter frame quality. These issues impede video-based models from effectively aggregating features across neighboring frames for improved predictions. To address these problems, we introduce Spatial-Temporal Feature Transformation (STFT), a multi-frame collaborative framework. Spatially, STFT reduces inter-frame variations in camera-moving scenarios through feature alignment using proposal-guided deformable convolutions. Temporally, it employs a channel-aware attention module to simultaneously assess the quality and correlation of adjacent frames, enabling adaptive feature aggregation. Empirical results demonstrate the method's effectiveness and stability; for instance, STFT enhances the still-image baseline FCOS by 10.6% and 20.6% in comprehensive F1-scores for polyp localization on the CVC-Clinic and ASUMayo datasets, respectively, while surpassing state-of-the-art video-based methods by 3.6% and 8.0%. The code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/lingyunwu14/STFT}.

Following the LHCb Collaboration's announcement of five narrow $\Omega^0_c$ excited resonances, we suggest an interpretation grounded in the Chiral Quark Soliton Model. Our argument posits that three of these resonances correspond to negative-parity excitations of the ground-state SU(3) sextets, whereas the remaining two, characterized by the smallest widths, are exotic pentaquarks belonging to the SU(3) $\overline{\mathbf{15}}$. We begin with a concise review of the model and an examination of the proposed $\Theta^+(1540)$, then demonstrate how to extend the framework to heavy baryons. By testing this approach against the ground-state $\overline{\mathbf{3}}$ and ${\mathbf{6}}$ heavy baryons, we explore various excitation modes within the Chiral Quark Soliton Model.
