Our analysis confirms that the model supports two excited $\overline{\mathbf{3}}$ states in the charm sector that have been experimentally observed, before concluding with a discussion on potential assignments for the LHCb $\Omega^0_c$ states.

This study examines explicit and implicit difference equations alongside the associated infinite-horizon linear-quadratic optimal control problem. We establish feasibility conditions for the optimal control problem and prove the existence and uniqueness of optimal controls under assumptions that are less restrictive than those found in standard literature, which typically rely on algebraic Riccati equations. To achieve this, we propose and analyze a discrete-time Lur'e equation and its corresponding Kalman-Yakubovich-Popov (KYP) inequality. We demonstrate that the solvability of the KYP inequality can be characterized by the spectral properties of a specific palindromic matrix pencil. Furthermore, the deflating subspaces of this pencil are utilized to construct solutions for the Lur'e equation. These findings are adapted from the continuous-time framework, though this transition introduces several additional technical challenges.

With data visualizations becoming more prevalent in mass communication, designers increasingly aim to capture viewer attention and encourage deeper engagement, goals linked by prior research to emotional activation, specifically affective arousal. Motivated by this, the present study initiates an investigation into the design factors that influence arousal. We assembled a corpus of 265 data visualizations and executed a crowdsourcing experiment involving 184 participants. Participants rated the affective arousal evoked by the visualizations (with all textual content blurred to eliminate semantic influence) and explained their reasoning. From this data, we first qualitatively analyzed user comments to identify a set of arousal-related design features. Subsequently, these features were converted into computable variables, and regression models were built to quantitatively determine which features significantly contribute to affective arousal. This exploratory research ultimately identified four design features—such as colorfulness and the number of distinct visual channels—that were cross-validated as key correlates of affective arousal.

The Rubik's cube, a renowned puzzle where movable faces generate a group through their operations, serves as the basis for a generalization to any 3-valent map. We establish an upper bound for the size of the associated group, which we conjecture to be optimal.

Over the past few years, multi-view learning technologies have garnered significant attention across diverse applications. Because these methods leverage compatible and complementary data from multiple perspectives, they often outperform traditional single-view approaches in most scenarios. Nevertheless, current research lacks a sufficient unified framework, and efficiently integrating multi-view information remains a formidable challenge. This paper introduces a novel multi-view learning framework designed to consolidate existing graph embedding techniques into a single formulation by incorporating a graph consensus term. Specifically, the method independently analyzes the graph structure within each view to maintain the diversity inherent in graph embedding, while simultaneously utilizing heterogeneous graphs to construct the consensus term and capture inter-view correlations. This dual approach allows for the concurrent consideration of both diversity and complementary information across different views. Furthermore, the proposed framework is applied to develop the Multi-view Locality Linear Embedding (MvLLE), a multi-view extension of Locality Linear Embedding that can be efficiently solved using an alternating optimization strategy. Empirical evaluations on six benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

This study investigates the potential production of Dark Matter particles and a hypothetical gauge boson, the Z'$', within the Mono-Z'$' framework at the Large Hadron Collider. The analysis focuses on events characterized by dimuons and significant missing transverse momentum. Data were derived from CMS open samples, comprising both recorded proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 8 TeV in 2012 and corresponding Monte Carlo simulations, covering an integrated luminosity of 11.6 fb$^{-1}$. Results were interpreted using two benchmark scenarios: a simplified Dark Higgs model and the effective field theory formalism of the Mono-Z'$' model. No evidence for Dark Matter candidates was observed; therefore, 95% confidence level exclusion limits were established for the Z'$' mass and the effective field theory cutoff scale.

The advancement of technology increasingly envisions robots interacting with people in daily life. Human-robot collaboration (HRC) represents an approach that investigates interactions between humans and robots to achieve shared goals at both cognitive and physical levels. Typically, HRC research constructs a cognitive model that gathers inputs from the environment and users, processing and converting them into actionable information for the robot. Machine learning offers a promising recent method for developing these cognitive models and behavioral blocks within HRC. Accordingly, this paper presents a comprehensive literature review on the application of machine learning techniques in human-robot collaboration. It selects and analyzes 45 pivotal papers, proposing a classification of studies based on collaborative task types, evaluation metrics, and modeled cognitive variables. Furthermore, a detailed examination explores various families of machine learning algorithms, their characteristics, and the sensing modalities employed. Key observations highlight the necessity for machine learning algorithms to integrate time dependencies. Finally, the salient features of these works are cross-analyzed to identify trends in HRC and provide guidelines for future research, contrasting them with HRC aspects not covered in the review.

Microlocation is essential for converting conventional structures into intelligent infrastructure. This process involves determining the position of any entity with extreme precision, often down to the centimeter level. Effective implementation demands technologies that offer high detection accuracy, energy efficiency, broad coverage, affordability, and accessibility. This article explores various microlocation-enabling technologies, methods, and services, explaining how they can expedite the integration of the Internet of Things (IoT) within smart buildings. Furthermore, we address existing challenges and review specific signal processing filtering techniques to ensure the seamless incorporation of these microlocation solutions into IoT-equipped environments. Finally, the study includes an experiment utilizing Bluetooth Low-Energy (BLE) beacons for microlocation purposes.

Controller reduction is a well-established topic within control theory, yet numerous open questions persist. Specifically, there are scarce results concerning the order reduction of general non-observer based controllers and the corresponding quantification of closed-loop performance. Recent advancements in model-free policy optimization for Linear Quadratic Gaussian (LQG) control have underscored the significance of this issue. This paper first introduces a new set of sufficient conditions guaranteeing that a perturbed controller maintains internal stability. Leveraging this finding, we demonstrate methods for reducing the order of general non-observer based controllers via balanced truncation and modal truncation. Additionally, we derive explicit bounds on the LQG performance of the resulting reduced-order controllers. For single-input-single-output (SISO) systems, we propose a novel reduction technique by truncating unstable modes. We validate our theoretical findings through numerical simulations. Ultimately, these results offer essential tools for designing direct policy search algorithms in control problems involving partial observations.

Entity typing involves categorizing entity mentions within specific texts. The conventional classification-based approach suffers from two significant limitations: first, it cannot assign entities to types outside a predefined set, and second, it struggles with few-shot and zero-shot scenarios where long-tail types lack sufficient training examples. To address these issues, we introduce a novel Generative Entity Typing (GET) paradigm. This method utilizes a pre-trained language model (PLM) to generate multiple possible types for an entity's role within a given text. However, PLMs often produce coarse-grained types after fine-tuning on entity typing datasets, and our training data is heterogeneous, comprising a small fraction of human-annotated samples and a larger portion of low-quality auto-generated data. To resolve these challenges, we apply curriculum learning (CL) to train our GET model on this diverse dataset. The curriculum dynamically adjusts through self-paced learning, adapting to the model's understanding of type granularity and data heterogeneity. Extensive experiments across various languages and downstream tasks demonstrate that our GET model outperforms state-of-the-art entity typing models. The source code is available at https://github.com/siyuyuan/GET.

This article primarily investigates the utility of incorporating four-wave mixing or Kerr nonlinearity modulation within a nonuniform grating structure characterized by gain and loss. To achieve this, we introduce an inhomogeneous system where the nonlinearity of the $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric grating is modulated. Our findings indicate that this scheme is viable only under the assumption that the nonlinearity and its associated modulation terms are self-defocusing. To minimize the intensity threshold required for steering, we adopt a negative chirping sign and operate at a wavelength exceeding the Bragg wavelength. Combined with these parameters, launching light from the rear of the device drastically lowers the critical intensity to approximately 0.015, representing the lowest switching intensity reported to date for nonlinear $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric gratings. Furthermore, ramp-like stable states persist within the broken $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric regime despite modulation of the nonlinearity index, regardless of the light's incident direction.

Utilizing light-driven plasmonic enhancement to boost chemical reactions on metal catalysts offers a viable path toward highly selective and efficient transformations. While research has historically centered on late transition metals like Au, Ag, and Cu, recent attention has shifted toward earth-abundant elements such as Mg, which demonstrate intriguing hydrogenation chemistry relevant to hydrogen storage. This study investigates the optical, electronic, and catalytic characteristics of Mg nanoclusters containing up to 2057 atoms through time-dependent density functional tight-binding and density functional theory simulations. The findings indicate that Mg nanoclusters can generate highly energetic hot electrons reaching up to 4 eV. Electronic structure analysis reveals that these hot electrons align energetically with the states of physisorbed molecular hydrogen; populating these states facilitates hydrogen dissociation. Furthermore, the study suggests that hot electrons can also promote the reverse process—hydrogen evolution on metallic Mg—via a distinct mechanism. Consequently, from a theoretical standpoint, Mg nanoclusters exhibit significant potential for light-driven hydrogen storage and release.

We examine the empirical autocovariance matrix at a non-zero lag derived from a multivariate complex Gaussian stationary time series, noting that its spectral analysis aids in specific statistical tasks, such as white noise testing. This study investigates the asymptotic behavior of these spectral measures when both the series dimension and observation window length increase simultaneously at the same rate. Utilizing a general framework for the spectral analysis of large random non-Hermitian matrices, we first determine the probabilistic behavior of the small singular values of shifted autocovariance matrices. These findings subsequently inform the large-sample behavior of the empirical spectral measure at any lag, with matrix orthogonal polynomials on the unit circle serving as a fundamental tool in this analysis.

This article investigates the existence of an absorbing-state phase transition in an Abelian process that extends the Activated Random Walk (ARW). For a vertex transitive graph $G=(V,E)$, each site $x \in V$ is assigned a capacity $w_x \ge 0$, representing the number of inactive particles it can contain, where the collection $\{w_x\}_{x \in V}$ consists of i.i.d. random variables. We demonstrate that for amenable graphs, the model undergoes an absorbing state phase transition when $\mathbb E[w_x]<\infty$, whereas it fixates for all $\lambda>0$ if $\mathbb E[w_x]=\infty$. Furthermore, in the case where $\mathbb E[w_x]<\infty$, we establish bounds for the critical density that align with those found in the classical Activated Random Walk.

Time series forecasting is a vital predictive technique applicable to diverse problems. Specifically, predicting indoor temperatures enables more efficient HVAC usage in homes, thereby enhancing energy efficiency. To achieve this, the paper details the implementation of an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) algorithm on a low-cost system-on-chip to create an autonomous, intelligent wireless sensor network. Utilizing resource-constrained 8051MCU microcontrollers, the study employs a Wireless Sensor Network (WSN) to monitor and forecast indoor temperatures within a smart home. An on-line learning strategy based on the Back-Propagation (BP) algorithm was developed for real-time time series analysis. This approach trains the model with incoming data in real-time, avoiding the need to store vast historical datasets or rely on prior knowledge. To validate this method, a simulation study using a Bayesian baseline model was conducted to compare performance and accuracy against a real-world application database. The paper's primary contribution is a novel algorithm derived from the BP method, with a detailed focus on overcoming the challenge of executing a computationally intensive algorithm within a simple architecture limited by minimal hardware resources.

Yang et al. [Nature 576, 248 (2019)] established a comprehensive theoretical framework for nanoscale electromagnetism utilizing Feibelman parameters. This approach encapsulates the quantum effects of optically excited electrons at material interfaces into two complex, frequency-dependent parameters, which are integrated into modified Maxwell boundary conditions known as mesoscopic boundary conditions. While these modifications can theoretically be applied to any Maxwell solver, the specific implementation details vary depending on the computational method used. This paper details the application of mesoscopic boundary conditions within a boundary element method, employing a Galerkin scheme and Raviart-Thomas shape functions to represent tangential electromagnetic fields at the interface. Our simulations demonstrate perfect agreement with Mie theory that includes Feibelman parameters, and show that the computational cost remains minimal for typical scenarios.

This informal report details my research endeavors, collaborations, and experiences during my tenure in the Naval Research Laboratory's (NRL) Advanced Graduate Research Program (AGRP), also known as Sabbatical, spanning October 2008 to September 2009. Rather than providing technical specifics of individual projects, this document offers a broad perspective on how my contributions supported ongoing research initiatives. My aim is to highlight the significance of interdisciplinary approaches in scientific inquiry and demonstrate how the AGRP enables such opportunities.

This study introduces a macroscopic method for automatically identifying speech sound disorders (SSD) in children. While SSD typically involves persistent articulatory and phonological errors regarding specific phonemes—usually detected by analyzing individual phones or words—we propose a subject-level approach. Instead of focusing on discrete errors, we extract holistic representations from long utterances formed by concatenating multiple test words. By applying speaker verification techniques and deep neural network-generated posterior features, we derive various comprehensive representations. A linear classifier is then trained to distinguish disordered speech from normal speech. Experimental results on detecting SSD in Cantonese-speaking children demonstrate that this proposed method outperforms previous approaches that rely on fusing phone-level detection results. Specifically, using articulatory posterior features to generate i-vectors from multi-word utterances yields an unweighted average recall of 78.2% and a macro F1 score of 78.0%.

Acknowledging the importance of spectrally efficient secure non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA), this study introduces a new quality of service (QoS)-aware secure NOMA framework designed to maximize secrecy fairness among untrusted users. In a system comprising a base station (BS) and two users, a novel decoding sequence is established to guarantee security for both parties. The primary objective is to minimize the maximum secrecy outage probability (SOP) while adhering to BS transmit power constraints and satisfying individual QoS requirements. Closed-form expressions for pair outage probability (POP) and the optimal power allocation (PA) that minimizes POP are derived. Analytical formulas for the SOP of both users are presented, and individual SOP minimization problems are addressed using generalized-convexity concepts. Additionally, high signal-to-noise ratio approximations of the SOP and their corresponding asymptotically optimal solutions are identified. A globally optimal solution from a secrecy fairness perspective is achieved with low computational complexity, alongside a tight approximation that offers analytical insights. Numerical findings reveal that the globally optimized PA ensures secrecy fairness and yields performance improvements of approximately 55.12%, 69.30%, and 19.11% relative to fixed PA and individual users' optimal PAs, respectively. Finally, the paper examines the tradeoff between secrecy fairness and QoS requirements.

Augmented reality (AR) enables the integration of visualizations within real-world environments, facilitating situated analysis of live data in their spatial context. However, the necessity to adapt existing methods and develop novel approaches for this domain introduces new evaluation challenges for researchers. Beyond traditional performance metrics, eye tracking has emerged as a powerful tool for both qualitative and quantitative assessment of visualizations. This discussion examines the specific challenges and opportunities presented by eye tracking in evaluating situated visualizations. We propose that expanding gaze-based evaluation methodologies into this field will yield fresh insights into human perception and interaction with augmented reality visualizations.

For any bivariate scalar function that is locally Lipschitz continuous and directionally differentiable, a subgradient can always be constructed from its directional derivatives along the four cardinal directions, organized as a "compass difference." While the resulting subgradient belongs to Clarke's generalized gradient when the function is nonconvex, the finding appears novel even for convex functions. No specific functional form or additional assumptions are necessary, although the result is strengthened if the function is also L-smooth according to Nesterov's definition. For specific optimal-value functions and parametric solutions of differential equations, these findings may offer the only known method to compute a subgradient. Furthermore, these results indicate that centered finite differences converge to a subgradient for bivariate nonsmooth functions. As a dual finding, it is shown that any compact convex set in two dimensions includes the midpoint of its interval hull. Illustrative examples are provided, and it is demonstrated that these results do not directly generalize to functions with more than two variables or sets in higher dimensions.

Climate change has led to a rise in the frequency and intensity of extreme precipitation events, yet accurately forecasting their likelihood on seasonal timescales remains a significant challenge. This study introduces a method for predicting the quantiles of maximum daily precipitation for each week up to six months in advance by utilizing the Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT) model. Experiments conducted across two regions compare TFT outputs against two baselines: climatology and a calibrated ECMWF SEAS5 ensemble forecast (S5). The findings indicate that at a six-month lead time, TFT predictions significantly outperform those of S5 regarding quantile risk, while demonstrating a modest overall improvement over climatology. Additionally, the TFT model effectively captures deviations from normal conditions that climatology fails to detect.

We investigate the $s$-wave kaon-nucleon bound state with strangeness $S=-1$ using the Bethe-Salpeter formalism under ladder and instantaneous approximations. By solving the Bethe-Salpeter equation for this bound state, we derive the corresponding Bethe-Salpeter amplitude. Our findings demonstrate that a $K^-p$ bound state exists within this framework. Furthermore, we analyze the bound state's decay width using Bethe-Salpeter techniques, determining a mass of 1422 MeV and a decay width notably smaller than that of $\Lambda(1405)$. These results suggest the possibility of additional structures contributing to the observed resonance.

Comprehending the overarching narrative of video content, such as films and television series, directly from raw data remains a formidable challenge. Contemporary Video Question Answering (VideoQA) frameworks frequently rely on external human-generated resources, including scripts, plot summaries, descriptions, or knowledge bases. This study introduces a novel methodology capable of deriving a complete story understanding without such auxiliary inputs. The core innovation involves leveraging dialogue: unlike previous approaches, we process dialogue as a noisy signal that is transformed into textual descriptions through summarization, mirroring how recent techniques handle video. Each modality is independently encoded by transformers, and a straightforward fusion mechanism integrates all modalities, employing soft temporal attention to manage localization across extended inputs. Our model significantly surpasses state-of-the-art performance on the KnowIT VQA benchmark, achieving this without question-specific human annotations or manually crafted plot summaries. Notably, it even exceeds the performance of human evaluators who have not previously viewed the entire episodes. The code is accessible at https://engindeniz.github.io/dialogsummary-videoqa.

Resonant excitation-based energy acquisition plays a critical role in both chemical and biological systems. This study investigates the intramolecular resonant absorption of polarized mid-infrared pulses by bulk and surface water through molecular dynamics simulations. The resulting heating, driven by OH stretching vibrations, occurs rapidly, generating a temperature jump exceeding 100 K upon irradiation with a 1 ps pulse having a peak intensity of 0.5 V/nm. A general anisotropic effect emerges due to the preferential resonant excitation of either symmetric or asymmetric OH stretching modes, contingent upon the alignment between water molecule orientations and the pulse's polarization direction. Specifically, when water molecules possess a preferred dipole orientation—imposed by static electric fields or spatial confinement—that aligns parallel to the pulse polarization, energy absorption is dominated by the symmetric stretching mode (approx. 99 THz). Conversely, in the perpendicular configuration, the asymmetric stretching mode (approx. 101 THz) proves more efficient. Given that oriented water molecules are ubiquitous in chemical and biological contexts, these insights into orientation-dependent intramolecular vibrational excitation hold particular significance for understanding energy absorption and transitions in related biochemical processes.

This paper examines the characterizations of rectifying and osculating curves situated on a smooth surface, utilizing the reference frame $\{\vec{T},\ \vec{N},\ \vec{T}\times\vec{N}\}$. We determined the components of the position vectors for these curves along the vectors $\vec{T}$, $\vec{N}$, and $\vec{T}\times\vec{N}$, subsequently analyzing their invariance under surface isometries. The results demonstrate that such invariance holds if and only if either the curve's normal curvature remains invariant or the curve's position vector aligns with the tangent vector of the curve.

This document is part of a series of whitepapers from the USQCD collaboration. In it, we explore the potential of lattice QCD within neutrino-oscillation physics, a field that necessarily involves nucleon and nuclear structure. Beyond examining relevant lattice-QCD computations of nucleon and nuclear matrix elements, we also address the interaction with nuclear models. This initiative of lattice-QCD calculations is pertinent to both existing and forthcoming neutrino experiments, growing in significance as we approach the eras of LBNF/DUNE and HyperK.

This study examines the spectral characteristics of balanced trees and dendrimers to consolidate and enhance current findings. We derive a semi-factorized expression for their characteristic polynomials and subsequently determine their spectra using these factors. Finally, we investigate the energy behavior of dendrimers and calculate lower and upper bound approximations.

Deep reinforcement learning (RL) relies heavily on deep neural networks to create effective internal representations, yet these methods often struggle with high sample complexity, making the quality of initial input representations critical for performance. This paper leverages the inherent graph structure of underlying Markov decision processes (MDPs) to integrate topological information for improved state representation. Inspired by recent advancements in node representations for graph analytics, we examine how such methods can effectively encode MDP topology within Deep RL frameworks. We conduct a comparative study of four distinct classes of representation learning algorithms applied to grid-world navigation tasks, which serve as representative scenarios for broader RL challenges. Our results indicate that all tested embedding techniques surpass the conventional matrix-based representation of grid-world environments across all studied cases. Furthermore, we observe that graph convolution-based methods are less effective than simpler random walk-based approaches and graph linear autoencoders.

We present a spectral preparation strategy for quantum memory designed to optimize both bandwidth and efficiency within the high-field regime, where hyperfine structure is resolved, specifically in 167Er3+:Y2SiO5. In this material, we successfully implement the method by generating spectrally isolated features with 18 dB of absorption against a background noise level of less than 1 dB. Leveraging these features, we constructed an atomic frequency comb and achieved the storage of 200 ns pulses with 22% efficiency; this performance is currently constrained by background absorption resulting from laser instability. Finally, we outline the necessary experimental enhancements to achieve material limits characterized by O(1) second spin-state storage, O(100) MHz bandwidth, and efficiency exceeding 90%.

This paper presents an extensive survey of Natural Language Generation (NLG) research spanning the last twenty years, with a specific focus on data-to-text and text-to-text generation using deep learning, alongside emerging applications of the technology. The survey aims to: (a) provide a current synthesis of deep learning advancements in core NLG tasks and the architectures employed; (b) offer a detailed and thorough overview of various NLG tasks and datasets, while emphasizing evaluation challenges, including diverse methods and their interrelationships; and (c) underscore future research directions and recent issues stemming from the growing synergy between NLG and other AI domains, such as computer vision, text processing, and computational creativity.

Scripts, which are standardized sequences of events depicting routine daily activities, facilitate narrative comprehension by offering expectations, clarifying ambiguities, and supplying implicit details. Despite their utility, creating or extracting these scripts from text has historically been challenging. This study demonstrates, for the first time, that pre-trained neural language models can be fine-tuned to produce high-quality scripts at various granularities across diverse everyday scenarios, such as baking a cake. To achieve this, we assembled a substantial crowdsourced dataset of partially ordered scripts called proScript, containing 6.4k entries, which significantly outnumbers previous resources. We developed models that integrate language generation with structure prediction through two complementary tasks: (i) edge prediction, which organizes unordered events into a valid script given a scenario, and (ii) script generation, which creates both events and their structural order from a scenario alone. Experimental results indicate strong performance (e.g., an F1 score of 75.7 in edge prediction), showcasing a novel method to overcome prior obstacles in script collection, although human-level performance remains a goal for future improvement. Collectively, our proposed tasks, dataset, and models establish a promising new direction for acquiring script knowledge.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of diffusion processes modeling a single species subject to both demographic and environmental stochasticity. Without demographic noise, the system's asymptotic fate is dictated by the sign of $\Lambda_0$, the external Lyapunov exponent: $\Lambda_0<0$ leads to extinction, whereas $\Lambda_0>0$ results in convergence to a unique positive stationary distribution $\mu_0$. When demographic stochasticity is introduced with intensity $\epsilon$ and population size scaling as $\frac{1}{\epsilon^{2}}$ (for small $\epsilon>0$), extinction becomes almost surely finite. Consequently, analyzing the quasi-stationary distribution (QSD) $\mu_\epsilon$ is essential for understanding the dynamics. The existence and uniqueness of $\mu_\epsilon$ are established under mild conditions.

We examine the limit as the population size approaches infinity ($\epsilon\to 0$), demonstrating that $\Lambda_0$ remains pivotal:
1. If $\Lambda_0<0$, then $\mu_\epsilon$ converges to the Dirac measure $\delta_0$, the mean extinction time scales as $|\ln \epsilon|$, and the extinction rate associated with $\mu_\epsilon$ is lower-bounded by order $\frac{1}{|\ln\epsilon|}$.
2. If $\Lambda_0>0$, then $\mu_\epsilon$ converges to $\mu_0$, with the mean extinction time and the extinction rate scaling polynomially with $\frac{1}{\epsilon^{2}}$ and $\epsilon^{2}$, respectively.

Additionally, for $\Lambda_0>0$, we reveal a multiscale dynamic: the process rapidly approaches the QSD $\mu_\epsilon$ and subsequently relaxes to the extinction state after a polynomially long duration. We provide sharp asymptotic estimates in $\epsilon$ for the time the system spends near $\mu_\epsilon$.

We examine the ground state of the spin $S=1/2$ Heisenberg anti-ferromagnet on the Shuriken lattice, both with and without an external magnetic field. Using two-dimensional tensor network methods grounded in infinite projected entangled pair and simplex states, we analyze configurations with varying unit cell sizes. Our results demonstrate that a valence bond crystal, characterized by resonances across six-loop structures, constitutes the ground state at any finite bond dimension. This state yields the current lowest estimate for the ground state energy, $E_0/J = -0.4410 \pm 0.0001$, in the thermodynamic limit. Furthermore, under an applied magnetic field, we observe the formation of magnetization plateaus at $0$, $1/3$, and $2/3$ levels. These states maintain translation and point group symmetries but are distinguished by loop-four plaquette resonances.

Contramodules represent module-like algebraic systems equipped with infinite summation (and sometimes integration) operations that adhere to natural axioms. Originally formulated by Eilenberg and Moore in 1965 for coalgebras over commutative rings, these structures saw a brief revival after being largely overlooked for thirty years between 1970 and 2000. This overview examines various definitions and findings concerning contramodules, primarily drawing from our monographs and preprints (arXiv:0708.3398, arXiv:0905.2621, arXiv:1202.2697, arXiv:1209.2995, arXiv:1512.08119, arXiv:1710.02230, arXiv:1705.04960, arXiv:1808.00937). The discussion encompasses contramodules over corings, topological associative rings, topological Lie algebras, and topological groups, as well as semicontramodules over semialgebras and a "contra" analogue of the Bernstein-Gelfand-Gelfand category O. Additionally, several underived instances of the comodule-contramodule correspondence are explored.

Probabilistic language understanding models offer interpretability and structure, such as those modeling metaphor comprehension through latent topics and features; however, they are manually engineered for particular tasks. While large language models (LLMs) can execute diverse tasks via in-context learning, they lack the distinct structural clarity of probabilistic approaches. This paper employs chain-of-thought prompts to integrate probabilistic model structures into LLMs, guiding them to infer latent variables and reason about their interconnections to select suitable metaphor paraphrases. These selected variables and relationships are grounded in cognitive psychological theories of metaphor understanding. Applied to the two largest GPT-3 variants, these prompts demonstrate an ability to enhance paraphrase selection.

For any integer $n \geq 3$, we establish pointwise inversion formulae for Siegel transforms within the geometry of numbers that hold almost everywhere with respect to the Lebesgue measure. These results are highly general, applying to the Siegel transforms of any function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ that is even, compactly supported, Borel measurable, and lies in the intersection $L^1(\mathbb{R}^n) \cap L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$.

The division of graphs into multiple sections based on specific criteria, known as graph partitioning, is a fundamental concept in discrete mathematics that has been widely investigated. In the 1990s, Ando proposed that the vertices of any cubic graph could be split into two subsets that form isomorphic subgraphs. By combining probabilistic techniques with refined recolouring strategies, we demonstrate that Ando's conjecture holds true for all sufficiently large connected graphs.

We demonstrate that every positive solution to the Yamabe equation on an asymptotically flat $n$-dimensional manifold with a flatness order of at least $\frac{n-2}{2}$ and $n \le 24$ converges at infinity to either a fundamental solution of the Laplace operator on Euclidean space or a radial Fowler solution defined across the entire Euclidean space. The threshold flatness order of $\frac{n-2}{2}$ represents the minimal requirement for defining ADM mass in general relativity, while dimension 24 marks the boundary for the compactness of solutions to the Yamabe problem. Furthermore, we establish similar alternatives for bounded solutions when $n > 24$. These findings are achieved by deriving specific asymptotic behaviors near isolated singularities of Yamabe equation solutions under conditions where the metric exhibits a flatness order of at least $\frac{n-2}{2}$ at the singularity for $n < 24$, and where the solution's growth at the singularity does not exceed that of the fundamental solution of the flat metric Laplacian for $n > 24$. Our work extends previous findings by L. Caffarelli, B. Gidas, and J. Spruck, as well as N. Korevaar, R. Mazzeo, F. Pacard, and R. Schoen regarding conformally flat metrics; C.C. Chen and C. S. Lin concerning scalar curvature with suitable flatness at singular points; F. Marques for smooth non-conformally flat metrics in dimensions three, four, and five; and recent results by the second and third authors in dimension six.

This study employs non-commutative (NC) gauge theory of gravity to analyze the thermodynamics of a deformed Schwarzschild black hole (SBH), proposing a novel evaporation scenario. Initially, we characterized the Arnowitt-Deser-Misner (ADM) mass, Hawking temperature, and entropy of the NC SBH. Notably, non-commutativity eliminates the temperature's divergence and introduces a temperature difference between the poles and equator. These corrections also identify a new fundamental length scale at the Planck order, $\Theta \approx 2.257 \times 10^{-35}\,m$. In the final evaporation stage, NC corrections reveal a remnant entropy, $\hat{S}_0$, for the black hole. Furthermore, examining the heat capacity and Gibbs free energy highlights the impact of NC gauge theory on thermodynamic stability and phase transitions. Finally, we assessed how black hole pressure influences stability and phase transitions within NC spacetime. Our findings indicate that the NC parameter functions similarly to thermodynamic variables, demonstrating that the NC SBH undergoes a second-order phase transition.

A vector field is considered bounded when both its length and differential are bounded. Consider a non-compact connected manifold $M$ acted upon by an amenable group $G$ with an infinite-order element, where the action is cocompact and properly discontinuous. We prove a Poincaré–Hopf theorem for bounded vector fields on $M$ that satisfy a specific mild condition. The index of such a vector field is defined as an element within the module of coinvariants of bounded sequences on $G$, a concept that is straightforward to define. Consequently, if the Euler characteristic of the quotient space $M/G$ is non-trivial, the vector field must possess infinitely many zeros.

Deepfakes represent a malicious technique that superimposes a target's face onto original video footage, leading to severe issues such as copyright violations, misinformation, and public panic. Existing detection approaches primarily rely on appearance features, which are vulnerable to advanced manipulation, often resulting in high model complexity and sensitivity to noise. Furthermore, effectively mining and utilizing temporal features in manipulated videos remains an unresolved challenge. We introduce LRNet, an efficient and robust framework designed to detect Deepfakes by modeling precise geometric features over time. To improve the discriminative power of these geometric features, we developed a novel calibration module, and we implemented a two-stream Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) to fully leverage temporal dynamics. Compared to prior methods, our approach is lighter-weight and simpler to train. Additionally, the model demonstrates robustness against highly compressed or noise-corrupted videos. On the FaceForensics++ dataset, our method achieved an AUC of 0.999, maintaining a graceful performance drop of only 0.042 AUC when tested on highly compressed videos.

The hypothesis that Sommerfeld-enhanced $s$-wave dark matter (DM) annihilation explains both the cosmic-ray (CR) positron surplus and the thermal relic density is widely accepted. However, this model faces stringent limits from gamma-ray observations of dwarf spheroidal galaxies (dSphs) and cosmic microwave background (CMB) data, as the annihilation cross-section rises continuously with lower DM velocities, whereas dSph environments exhibit even slower DM speeds than the Galactic halo. To address this, we investigate Sommerfeld-enhanced $p$-wave DM annihilation, where the cross-section can be boosted at specific velocities but is strongly suppressed at extremely low velocities. We computed the velocity-dependent astrophysical factors ($J$-factors) for fifteen nearby dSphs in the context of this $p$-wave mechanism. Using the annihilation channel into $4\mu$ mediated by two light particles as a case study, we demonstrate that viable parameter spaces exist where this scenario simultaneously accounts for the CR positron excess and the DM relic density without conflicting with gamma-ray constraints from Fermi-LAT on dSphs or CMB limits from PLANCK.

Upcoming experiments offer the potential to test the neutrino flavor oscillation model with unprecedented precision. In this study, we investigate a scenario where the universe's dark matter consists of two components: a sterile neutrino and an extremely light dark matter particle. Utilizing a 3+1 neutrino flavor oscillation framework, we examine how this specific dark matter composition influences solar neutrino fluxes, energy spectra, and electron neutrino survival probabilities. Existing solar neutrino data enable us to establish an upper bound on the ratio of the light dark matter particle's mass ($m_\phi$) to its Fermi constant ($G_\phi$), requiring that $G_\phi/m_\phi$ remain below $10^{30}\; G_{\rm F}\; eV^{-1}$ to align with observations from Borexino, the Sudbury Neutrino Observatory, and Super-Kamiokande. Furthermore, in models featuring a very small Fermi constant, the amplitude of time variability must not exceed $3\%$ to remain consistent with current solar neutrino measurements. Additionally, we identify that future solar neutrino detectors, such as Darwin, which can accurately measure low-energy neutrino fluxes, will impose supplementary constraints on this class of models, complementing the limits derived from existing instruments.

Recent advancements have been observed in learning-based Multi-view Stereo (MVS) across both supervised and unsupervised domains. To leverage the strengths of each regarding accuracy and completeness while minimizing the need for costly labeled datasets, this study investigates a new semi-supervised MVS approach where only a minimal portion of the data includes dense depth ground truth. However, the inherent diversity of scenarios and flexible view configurations in semi-supervised MVS (Semi-MVS) often violate the fundamental premise of classic semi-supervised learning: that labeled and unlabeled data share the same label space and distribution. To address these challenges, we introduce SE-MVS, a novel semi-supervised MVS framework. In cases where the basic assumption holds, consistency regularization is employed to ensure model predictions remain consistent between original and randomly augmented samples through KL divergence constraints. For scenarios where the distribution gap undermines this assumption, we propose a new style consistency loss to mitigate negative effects by transferring the visual style of unlabeled samples to labeled ones, thereby narrowing the distribution gap. Additionally, the model's predictions on generated samples are further supervised using labels from the original labeled data. Experiments on the DTU, BlendedMVS, GTA-SFM, and Tanks&Temples datasets demonstrate the method's superior performance; specifically, SE-MVS outperforms both fully-supervised and unsupervised baselines using identical backbone network settings.

We present experimental results concerning laser-pulsed photoacoustic excitation in turbid polymer materials, aimed at determining sound velocity and identifying bulk inhomogeneities. The study details a system enabling direct wave speed measurement by engraving a fiducial pattern of black lines onto the sample's surface. Furthermore, we explain how this pattern improves sensitivity in detecting internal inhomogeneities, both of which are valuable for investigating soft matter systems, potentially including biological specimens. Finally, we report an experimental analysis on Grilon® samples under various conditions, highlighting the method's limitations.

This study introduces updated $^{12}$C + $^{12}$C reaction rates, provided as numerical tables with uncertainty estimates and analytical formulas ready for direct integration into stellar evolution codes. The paper also examines how these new rates influence carbon burning within stars. We calculated reaction rates using two cross-section extrapolation models: one grounded in the fusion-hindrance phenomenon and another incorporating both fusion-hindrance and a resonance, comparing our findings against previous data. Utilizing the GENEC stellar evolution code, we analyzed the effects of these rates on the carbon-burning phases of two distinct stellar model sets with initial masses of 12 M$_{\odot}$ and 25 M$_{\odot}$, selected to represent the diversity of massive stars. The effective temperatures for carbon burning in both model sets fall entirely within the range covered by current experimental data, eliminating the need for rate extrapolation. Despite potential differences in rates exceeding an order of magnitude at typical carbon-burning temperatures, the resulting changes to stellar structures during this phase remain modest due to the readjustment of stellar structure in response to altered nuclear reaction rates driving energy production. In the fusion-hindrance scenario, the carbon-burning phase occurs at central temperatures approximately 10% higher than in the hindrance-plus-resonance case, with the burning lifetime halved. However, this model loses more entropy, leading to an earlier transition into the degeneracy regime and affecting final evolution stages prior to core collapse. Additionally, the hindrance model yields up to 60% more neon. The impact of varying rates on the s-process during carbon burning is limited, altering final abundances of s-process elements by no more than 20% (specifically for cobalt).

This study investigates an optimal control problem for the Keller-Segel system with logistic reaction within two-dimensional domains, where the control acts bilinearly within the chemical equation. We establish the existence of an optimal control and derive a necessary optimality system. The primary innovation lies in allowing the control to be highly singular, while the state variables (cell density $u$ and chemical concentration $v$) remain in a weak functional setting; this approach is atypical for optimal control problems involving chemotaxis models, as noted by Guillén-González et al. in ESAIM Control Optim. Calc. Var. 26 (2020).

Extracting Drug-Drug Interactions (DDIs) involves creating either manual or automated systems to identify embedded information within biomedical literature. Due to the limitations and slow speed of manual methods, machine learning and deep learning approaches have gained prominence for this task. This study introduces a novel, general-purpose deep learning model that integrates Hierarchical Bidirectional LSTMs with two Attention Mechanisms. Based on the DDIExtraction-2013 corpus, this model surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods, achieving a macro F1-score of 0.785 and a precision of 0.80.

We present the Scalable ZX-calculus (SZX-calculus), a formal and concise graphical language designed for creating and verifying quantum computations. Building upon the ZX-calculus—a robust framework that graphically represents the core principles of quantum mechanics through a complete set of rewrite rules—the SZX-calculus addresses its limitation as a low-level language where each wire corresponds to only a single qubit, thereby restricting its capacity to manage complex, large-scale quantum evolutions. By extending the ZX-calculus to support qubit registers and enabling the compact representation of sub-diagrams using binary matrices, the SZX-calculus overcomes these constraints. We demonstrate the soundness and completeness of this system and illustrate its utility through two applications: graph states and error-correcting codes.

This study examines how thermo-optic effects impact the shape profiles of soliton crystals within optical Kerr microresonators. The research utilizes a model combining the Lugiato-Lefever equation with a one-dimensional heat diffusion equation, where the heat source is proportional to the average optical power. Through specific variable transformations, this system is converted into a set of coupled, first-order nonlinear ordinary differential equations. These equations are solved numerically to analyze the impact of thermo-optic phenomena on the optical field's amplitude and instantaneous frequency, as well as the temperature distribution inside the cavity. Results indicate that while thermo-optic effects do not hinder the formation of soliton crystals, significant thermal detuning reduces their amplitude. Furthermore, the model predicts a temperature profile within the cavity that remains largely unaffected by the specific spatio-temporal characteristics of the propagating soliton crystal, a distinctive trait of this approach.

We investigate a biological autoregulatory mechanism involving a protein that promotes its own transcription, focusing on a parameter regime where bistability would otherwise occur without fluctuations. Using path integral formulations alongside Master and Chapman-Kolmogorov equations, we determine the rate of rare transitions between locally stable states induced by fluctuations. Consistent with simpler models, this rate follows the form $\exp(S_0)\eta$, where $S_0$ represents a "barrier" and $\eta$ is a prefactor. We first compute $S_0$ and $\eta$ in the bursting limit, characterized by a very large ratio $\gamma$ of protein to mRNA lifetimes. In this limit, the calculation is nearly entirely analytical and aligns well with simulations. For finite $\gamma$, numerical methods are typically necessary; however, $S_0$ can be derived analytically to first order in $1/\gamma$, matching full numerical results for all $\gamma > 1$. Using a previously established method, we qualitatively explain the variation of the prefactor $\eta$ with $\gamma$, though our calculated value remains 15-20% higher than that observed in simulations.

Although numerous U.S. states have embraced cannabis legalization, the extent to which it drives the progression from tobacco e-cigarette usage to vaping cannabis remains uncertain. Given that cannabis vaping is linked to emerging pulmonary conditions and a surge in adolescent consumption, this study employs an observational approach to assess the causal impact of recreational legalization on fostering pro-cannabis sentiments among existing e-cigarette users. By gathering and analyzing Twitter data regarding opinions on cannabis and JUUL, a prominent e-cigarette brand, we apply weakly supervised learning to filter individual tweets and detect user stances. Our findings indicate that recreational cannabis legalization policies significantly contribute to the growth of pro-cannabis attitudes within the population already inclined toward e-cigarettes.

We extend the validity criterion for the infinitary proof system of multiplicative additive linear logic with fixed points, ensuring it accommodates both axioms and cuts. We demonstrate that this criterion is sound and possesses the cut elimination property. Furthermore, we examine its decidability, proving that while it is generally undecidable, it becomes decidable under specific constraints.

As converter-interfaced distributed generation systems become more prevalent, establishing local compliance criteria is essential to maintain small-signal stability within interconnected networks. Previously, device admittance passivity has served as such a local criterion to prevent resonances between these devices and the network's lightly damped oscillatory modes. However, common active and reactive power control strategies, including droop and virtual synchronous generator controls, inherently breach passivity constraints at low frequencies; while this does not guarantee instability, it renders admittance passivity unsuitable as a stability criterion for devices modeled with wide-band characteristics. To address this limitation, this paper introduces criteria based on admittance at higher frequencies and an alternative transfer function at lower frequencies. This alternative representation utilizes active and reactive power alongside the derivatives of voltage's polar components as interface variables. Furthermore, to enable separate analysis across frequency ranges, the paper proposes slow-fast separation in device dynamics as an additional constraint. Compliance with these proposed criteria is straightforward and can be easily verified using frequency response analysis.

This study evaluates the precision of measuring the Higgs boson yield for its decay into a pair of $Z$ bosons at the Circular Electron Positron Collider (CEPC). In the Higgsstrahlung process, which involves the associated recoil $Z$ boson, a total of three $Z$ bosons are produced; the analysis focuses on signal final states containing leptons, quarks, and neutrinos. After comparing two distinct analysis methods, a multivariate technique utilizing boosted decision trees achieves an estimated precision of 7.9% for the ${\sigma}_{\mathrm{ZH}}{\cdot}$BR($H \rightarrow ZZ^{*}$) measurement. Furthermore, the relative precision of the Higgs boson width is determined by combining this result with the precision of the inclusive \textit{ZH} cross section measurement.

Web archiving represents a distinctive collaboration between human agents and automated systems dedicated to preserving the web. Centuries-old archival appraisal theories are being adapted for the World Wide Web's sociotechnical landscape, though with mixed results. The interaction between archivists and bots regarding web content creates a unique, yet under-researched, Computer-Supported Cooperative Work (CSCW) challenge. To explore this domain, we performed semi-structured interviews with archivists and technologists directly responsible for selecting web content for preservation. These interviews revealed key themes that shape the appraisal process in web archives, some of which are embedded within heuristics and algorithms. Enhancing the transparency of web archive infrastructure for archivists, automated agents, and future researchers remains a significant challenge for both the CSCW and archival communities.

Within the 2021 DESY summer student program, transverse momentum-dependent (TMD) parton distributions derived via the Parton Branching (PB) method were merged with next-to-leading-order (NLO) calculations using the POWHEG technique. The resulting Drell-Yan (DY) transverse momentum spectra were computed, revealing strong agreement between theoretical predictions and CMS experimental measurements at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, specifically at low and intermediate DY $p_{\rm T}$. Additionally, a new scale selection option for this matching procedure has been integrated into the CASCADE event generator.

Sensitivity to obstructions represents a critical challenge for high-frequency wireless networks, including 5G millimeter wave and 6G sub-terahertz systems. Because these networks depend primarily on line-of-sight (LOS) connections, sudden blockages significantly jeopardize network reliability. Furthermore, when an LOS link is obstructed, the network must hand off the user to another LOS base station, a process that can introduce substantial latency, particularly if it involves searching a large codebook of narrow beams. A viable solution to these reliability and latency issues is to introduce proactivity into wireless networks. Proactivity enables the network to anticipate, especially dynamic, blockages and initiate user hand-offs in advance. This paper introduces a comprehensive machine learning framework for achieving such proactivity in wireless networks by leveraging visual data, such as images captured by RGB cameras at base stations. Specifically, the study proposes a vision-aided communication solution that employs bimodal machine learning to execute proactive blockage prediction and user hand-offs. The foundation of this approach is a deep learning algorithm trained on both visual and wireless data to forecast incoming blockages. The wireless network utilizes these predictions to proactively trigger hand-off decisions, thereby avoiding unnecessary latency. The algorithm was developed using a vision-wireless dataset created with the ViWi data-generation framework. Experimental results from two base stations equipped with different cameras demonstrate that the algorithm can accurately detect incoming blockages in approximately 90% of cases. This predictive capability directly translates to proactive hand-off accuracy, which also reaches around 87%. These findings underscore a promising avenue for enhancing high reliability and low latency in future wireless networks.

Machine learning practitioners devote considerable manual and computational effort to identifying appropriate learning rates for optimization algorithms. We offer a probabilistic justification, grounded in Gaussian inference, for widely used stochastic first-order methods. Notably, this framework recovers the Polyak step as a specific instance using a generalized metric. This inferential approach connects the learning rate to a dimensionless parameter that can be autonomously adjusted during training by a control mechanism. Empirical results demonstrate that the resulting meta-algorithm robustly adapts learning rates across a broad spectrum of initial values when tested on deep learning benchmarks.

A novel sequential sampling technique with unequal probabilities is introduced. Selection of individual units depends on their sequence of appearance, with a variant specifically designed for sampling from a continuous stream. At every step, the decision to include a unit is made based on its order in the stream, utilizing a sliding window of minimal size. Furthermore, the method enables the sample to be distributed across the population, with the degree of spread being adjustable.

**Background.** Pull requests serve as a standard mechanism for contribution and review in both industrial and open-source environments. A primary objective of code reviews is to identify defects, thereby enabling maintainers to seamlessly integrate external changes and facilitate discussions on contributions. **Objective.** This study aims to determine whether code quality is a decisive factor in pull request acceptance. Specifically, it investigates if issues such as code smells, antipatterns, and style violations within a pull request influence the likelihood of its approval by a project maintainer. **Method.** A case study was conducted across 28 Java open-source projects, examining 4.7 million code quality issues found in 36,000 pull requests. The analysis utilized Logistic Regression alongside seven machine learning algorithms, including Decision Tree, Random Forest, Extremely Randomized Trees, AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, and XGBoost. **Results.** Contrary to expectations, code quality was found to have no impact on pull request acceptance. Consistent with prior research, other factors—such as maintainer reputation and the significance of the delivered feature—appear to be more influential than code quality regarding acceptance. **Conclusions.** While the impact of developer reputation on acceptance has been previously studied, this work is the first to specifically examine whether code quality within pull requests affects their acceptance. We recommend that future research explore this topic further to identify if alternative metrics or tools could yield useful insights.

This research investigates cross-correlations between line intensity and weak lensing maps to detect axion-like particles (ALPs). The radiative decay of eV-mass ALPs generates cosmic background emissions in the optical and infrared spectra. Since line intensity mapping uniquely measures background emission at specific photon frequencies, it offers a distinctive method for this search. Should ALPs comprise a significant portion of cosmic dark matter, their decay signals would correlate with large-scale structures identified via weak gravitational lensing in galaxy surveys. We establish a theoretical framework to forecast these cross-correlations and evaluate the feasibility of detecting ALPs using upcoming galaxy-imaging and spectroscopic surveys. Under assumptions of data from SPHEREx and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), we determine that ALP decay signals could exceed astrophysical line counterparts at wavelengths around 3000 nm for particles with a mass of $m_a \sim 1\, \mathrm{eV}$ and a particle-to-two-photons coupling of $g_{a\gamma\gamma} \sim 1\times10^{-11}\, \mathrm{GeV}^{-1}$. Furthermore, we predict that a null result would establish a $2\sigma$ upper limit of $g_{a\gamma\gamma} \lesssim 10^{-11}\, \mathrm{GeV}^{-1}$ for eV-mass ALPs, enhancing current constraints by approximately a factor of ten. Finally, utilizing Fisher analysis, we forecast expected constraints on ALP parameters for SPHEREx and LSST, offering a strategic guide for utilizing large-scale structure data to search for ALP decay.

Brakerski et al. [BCM+18] established a framework for cryptographically testing individual untrusted quantum devices and proposed a protocol for certifiable randomness generation. Leveraging the leakage resilience inherent in the Learning With Errors problem, we tackle a critical unresolved issue from prior research: the efficiency of randomness generation. Our proposed protocol certifies $\Omega(n)$ fresh random bits within a constant number of rounds, where $n$ denotes a protocol parameter, with total communication scaling as $O(n)$, thereby approaching an optimal rate. Furthermore, the demonstration that the output is statistically random is both conceptually straightforward and technically elementary.

Which object detector best fits your context-sensitive requirements? Deep detectors leverage scene context in distinct ways. This study categorizes object detectors into three groups based on their context utilization: those with no context (RCNN via input cropping), those with partial context (two-stage methods via featuremap cropping), and those with full context (single-stage methods without cropping). We systematically assess the impact of context across these detector categories by constructing a fully controlled dataset with varying contextual conditions and analyzing context usage in deep detectors. Furthermore, we evaluate the effects of progressively removing background and foreground elements on the MS COCO dataset. Our findings indicate that both single-stage and two-stage detectors inherently utilize context through their extensive receptive fields, suggesting that the optimal detector choice often depends on the specific application context.

Stochastic gradient descent ascent (SGDA) and its derivatives have long served as the primary method for solving minimax problems. Yet, unlike the extensively researched stochastic gradient descent (SGD) under differential privacy (DP) constraints, the generalization capabilities of DP-SGDA remain largely unexplored. This study employs the algorithmic stability framework to analyze the utility of DP-SGDA across various scenarios. Specifically, within the convex-concave setting, we demonstrate that DP-SGDA attains an optimal utility rate regarding weak primal-dual population risk, covering both smooth and non-smooth scenarios. To our knowledge, this marks the first result establishing utility for DP-SGDA in the non-smooth case. Furthermore, we present a utility analysis for the nonconvex-strongly-concave setting, which is also the first of its kind concerning primal population risk. Notably, the convergence and generalization findings for this nonconvex setting are novel even without privacy constraints. Finally, numerical experiments validate the efficacy of DP-SGDA in both convex and nonconvex contexts.

This study investigates the physical properties and characteristics of radiation emitted from accretion disks situated within a rotating, traversable, axially symmetric wormhole spacetime of the Teo class. We graphically analyze marginally stable orbits and accretion efficiency for varying dimensionless spin parameters ($J/M^2$) between 0.2 and 1.5 and specific throat radii ($r_0$), comparing these findings with Kerr black holes sharing identical parameters, while also presenting the data in tabular form. Additionally, we plot the radiated energy flux $F(r)$, temperature profile $T(r)$, and emission spectra $\nu L(\nu)$ across different spin and throat radius values, and tabulate the critical frequency where luminosity peaks for various $J/M^2$ and $r_0$. Furthermore, utilizing ray-tracing techniques, we generate intensity maps of the accretion disk as seen by an asymptotic observer under two scenarios: first, when the disk and observer are on the same side, with comparisons to Kerr black hole images of equivalent parameters; second, when the disk and observer are separated by the throat. Ultimately, this research aims to facilitate the detection and differentiation of wormhole geometries from other compact astrophysical objects.

Single Stop Signal Reaction Times (SSRT), which measure the latency of the unobservable stopping process in the Stop Signal Task (SST), have previously been modeled using a nonparametric approach by Hans Colonius (1990) and a Bayesian parametric approach by Eric-Jan Wagenmakers and colleagues (2012). Both prior methods assumed that the preceding trial type (go/stop) had an equal impact on SSRT distributional estimation, failing to account for scenarios where this assumption is violated. This study introduces a model that addresses this gap by employing a two-state mixture model for the SSRT distribution. It compares Bayesian parametric single SSRT distributions against mixture SSRT distributions using stochastic order at both the individual and population levels, assuming an ex-Gaussian format. The results demonstrate that, relative to a single SSRT distribution, the mixture SSRT distribution exhibits greater diversity, positive skewness, and leptokurtosis, alongside a larger stochastic order. The magnitude of these discrepancies also varies based on the weight selection within the mixture model. Ultimately, the study confirms that mixture SSRT indices—whether treated as constants or distributions—are significantly larger than their single SSRT counterparts in the relevant order, representing a vital enhancement to SSRT estimation methods.

This paper introduces a parametric extension of generalized Euler sums, termed (alternating) parametric Euler $T$-sums. Utilizing contour integration and the residue theorem, we derive multiple explicit expressions for linear parametric Euler $T$-sums. Moreover, by leveraging these findings, we establish explicit formulae for Hoffman's (alternating) double $t$-values as well as Kaneko-Tsumura's (alternating) double $T$-values.

This work outlines the initial findings of a ground-based observing campaign designed to construct a grid of roughly 200 spectro-photometric standard stars (SPSS). These stars will achieve an internal accuracy of approximately 1% and sub-percent precision, anchored to the CALSPEC Vega and Sirius systems within a 1% margin, to support the absolute flux calibration for data collected by the European Space Agency's {\it Gaia} astrometric mission. The paper details the selection criteria, candidate list, survey strategy, and data analysis techniques employed. Furthermore, all candidates were monitored for constancy with a precision of about $\pm 5$ mmag. The current grid comprises approximately half of the intended final sample; it has already met the target accuracy, though precision is expected to improve significantly with future updates. This grid is intended to calibrate the spectra and photometry included in the {\it Gaia} (E)DR3 release.

This paper investigates the significance of context in forecasting the citation potential of sentences within academic papers. We frame this challenge as a sequence labeling problem addressed by a hierarchical BiLSTM architecture. Our contribution includes a novel benchmark dataset comprising more than two million labeled sentences. By maintaining sentence order and implementing document-level train/test splits, we enable the model to effectively integrate contextual information. We assess the proposed method across three benchmark datasets, with results demonstrating the advantages of leveraging context and contextual embeddings for predicting citation worthiness. Furthermore, error analysis offers insights into specific scenarios where context is critical for accurate prediction.

We introduce a new machine learning approach for sampling from high-dimensional probability distributions in Lattice Quantum Field Theories. Rather than relying on deep architectures common in this field, our method utilizes a single neural ODE layer and fully integrates the problem's inherent symmetries. Evaluations on the $\phi^4$ theory reveal that our model systematically surpasses existing flow-based methods in sampling efficiency, with particularly significant gains observed on larger lattices. Compared to prior baselines, we enhance the effective sample size metric from 1% to 91% on a $32\times 32$ lattice. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the model can simultaneously learn a continuous spectrum of theories, with learned results effectively transferring to larger lattices. These generalization capabilities highlight the superior potential of machine learning techniques over traditional MCMC-based approaches.

Inspired by the challenge of optimally harvesting natural resources, this research examines a control problem involving Volterra-type dynamics influenced by time-changed Lévy noises, which generally lack the Markovian property. To leverage the specific characteristics of this noise, we employ various information flows within a maximum principle framework. Specifically, we utilize backward stochastic differential equations (BSDEs) with time changes and apply the non-anticipating stochastic derivative defined in [15]. Consequently, we establish both sufficient and necessary conditions for a stochastic maximum principle.

Video conferencing applications (VCAs) have emerged as essential internet tools, a trend accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic, as global users depend on them for work, education, and telehealth. Consequently, analyzing the resource demands of various VCAs and their performance across diverse network conditions is increasingly vital. Key areas of inquiry include the speed requirements (upstream and downstream throughput) for high-quality experiences, resilience during temporary capacity drops, competitive behavior among applications, and the impact of usage modes (such as participant count) on resource utilization. This study examines three prominent platforms: Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams. Findings vary significantly across these services. First, average utilization on unconstrained links ranges from 0.8 Mbps to 1.9 Mbps. When capacity is temporarily reduced, some VCAs may take up to 50 seconds to return to a steady state. Additionally, proprietary congestion control mechanisms lead to unfair bandwidth distribution; for instance, in constrained environments, a single Zoom session can consume over 75% of available bandwidth when competing with other platforms like Meet or Teams. Furthermore, for certain VCAs, client utilization may drop as participant numbers rise, driven by reduced video resolution per stream. Finally, individual viewing preferences, such as pinning a speaker, can influence the upstream bandwidth usage of other participants.

The prompt production of $\chi_{c1}$ and $\chi_{c2}$ charmonium mesons was investigated in proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider with a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=7$ TeV. Utilizing 36 $\mathrm{pb^{-1}}$ of data recorded by the LHCb detector in 2010, these $\chi_c$ mesons were reconstructed via the decay chain $\chi_c\to J/\psi\,\gamma$, where $J/\psi \to \mu^+ \mu^-$. The ratio of the prompt production cross-sections, $\sigma(\chi_{c2})/\sigma(\chi_{c1})$, was measured as a function of the $J/\psi$ transverse momentum ($p_{\mathrm{T}}^{J/\psi}$) across the range of 2 to 15 GeV/$c$. At high $p_{\mathrm{T}}^{J/\psi}$, the findings align with next-to-leading order non-relativistic QCD predictions but remain consistently higher than those of the pure leading-order colour singlet model.

Materials inevitably harbor defects—such as vacancies, dislocations, voids, and cracks—upon their creation during manufacturing, which influence mechanical performance across various spatial and temporal scales. Consequently, it is essential to understand, model, and simulate the stochastic evolution of these micro-structural defects in real time to facilitate multi-scale coupling and trace uncertainty propagation from the atomistic level up to aging continuum mechanics. We propose a graph-based surrogate model for calculating dislocation mobility by representing an edge dislocation as a random walker that transitions between neighboring graph nodes according to a Poisson stochastic process. This network approach serves as a coarse-grained alternative to molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, generating dislocation trajectories that empirically determine jump rates. Our method successfully reproduces the original atomistic mobility estimates with significant improvements in both computational speed and accuracy. Additionally, the inherent stochastic framework captures the statistical distribution of dislocation mobility observed in the MD simulation, enabling the efficient transmission of material parameters and uncertainties across different scales.

Neuromorphic computing platforms are increasingly utilizing memristors arranged in crossbar arrays to achieve high-density, low-power synaptic storage, thereby enhancing the energy efficiency of Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs). However, we identify that long bitlines and wordlines within these crossbars induce parasitic voltage drops, leading to current asymmetry. Circuit simulations reveal that this asymmetry causes substantial variations in endurance. Consequently, the overuse of critical memristors with lower endurance can significantly shorten the operational lifetime of the crossbar. To address this, we introduce eSpine, a novel technique that extends device lifetime by integrating endurance variability into the mapping of machine learning workloads. This approach ensures that synapses with higher activation frequencies are assigned to memristors with superior endurance, while those with lower activation utilize less durable devices. The eSpine methodology operates in two stages: first, it employs the Kernighan-Lin Graph Partitioning algorithm to divide workloads into neuron and synapse clusters compatible with individual crossbars; second, it utilizes Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) to map these clusters to hardware tiles, optimizing synapse-to-memristor placement based on activation analysis. Evaluated on a state-of-the-art neuromorphic hardware model featuring phase-change memory (PCM) memristors across ten SNN workloads, eSpine demonstrates a marked improvement in effective lifetime.

The CMS Collaboration at the LHC reports a measurement of electroweak W boson production accompanied by two jets in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, utilizing an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$. This analysis focuses on the $\ell\nu$jj final state within a kinematic region characterized by a dijet invariant mass $m_\mathrm{jj}$ exceeding 120 GeV and jet transverse momenta $p_\mathrm{T j}$ greater than 25 GeV. Cross-section measurements for the electron and muon channels yield $\sigma_\mathrm{EW}$(Wjj) = 6.23 $\pm$ 0.12 (stat) $\pm$ 0.61 (syst) pb per channel, consistent with leading-order standard model expectations. The study further investigates additional hadronic activity in a signal-enriched sample and compares these findings with theoretical predictions. Additionally, a search for anomalous trilinear gauge couplings is conducted using this final state. Within an effective field theory framework involving dimension-six operators, 95% confidence level limits are established for the couplings: $-$2.3 $<$ $c_{\mathrm{WWW}}/\Lambda^2$ $<$ 2.5 TeV$^{-2}$, $-$8.8 $<$ $c_{\mathrm{W}}/\Lambda^2$ $<$ 16 TeV$^{-2}$, and $-$45 $<$ $c_{\mathrm{B}}/\Lambda^2$ $<$ 46 TeV$^{-2}$. Combining these results with previous CMS EW Zjj analyses refines the constraint on the $c_{\mathrm{WWW}}$ coupling to $-$1.8 $<$ $c_{\mathrm{WWW}}/\Lambda^2$ $<$ 2.0 TeV$^{-2}$.

Loop closure detection and subsequent relocalization constitute a critical component of visual navigation systems for intelligent autonomous vehicles. Current state-of-the-art methods predominantly address this problem unidirectionally, following the direction of prior motion, which often leads to failures when significantly similar perspective overlaps are absent. This study introduces a novel bi-directional approach to loop closure. For the first time, this enables relocalization even when traveling in the opposite direction, thereby substantially mitigating long-term odometry drift in scenarios lacking direct loops. We present a method for selecting training data from extensive datasets to adapt them for the bi-directional challenge. This data is utilized to train and validate two distinct CNN architectures for end-to-end loop closure detection and the regression of 6-DOF camera poses between views. The resulting technique offers significant benefits, particularly aiding real-world applications where direct loop closures are unavailable. We provide a rigorous empirical comparison against established approaches and evaluate our method using both outdoor and indoor data from the FinnForest and PennCOSYVIO datasets.

Recent literature has examined measurement scales in information retrieval (IR) experiments, advocating exclusively for uniform-step interval scales. Consequently, these authors suggest discarding or adapting established metrics like reciprocal rank, expected reciprocal rank, normalized discounted cumulative gain, and average precision to ensure their values fall on uniformly spaced points. This perspective casts past decades of IR evaluation in a negative light, contradicting the community's focus on practical experimentation and quantifiable progress. This paper challenges that stance. We contend that mapping categorical and ordinal data to points on a number line is valid whenever there is an external justification for selecting each specific target point. After reviewing the general roles of measurement scales and the nature of categorical, ordinal, interval, ratio, and absolute data, we illustrate how numeric mappings represent knowledge for the first two categories.
