Turning to IR, we argue that document rankings constitute categorical data, where an effectiveness metric serves to assign a single value representing the utility of a ranking for a user or population, with this utility expressible as a continuous ratio-scale variable. Therefore, we maintain that current IR metrics are well-founded and more meaningful in their existing form than in the proposed "intervalized" alternatives.

We provide a full classification of finite covers from a proper stacky curve to a proper orbifold curve that maintain the slope-stability of vector bundles under pullback. Let $f \colon \mathfrak{Y} \longrightarrow (X,P)$ denote such a cover, defined as a finite, surjective, and generically separable morphism from a proper stacky curve (which may not be smooth) to a proper orbifold curve. We define a cover $f$ as genuinely ramified if the induced homomorphism $f_* \colon \pi_1(\mathfrak{Y}) \longrightarrow \pi_1(X,P)$ on the étale fundamental groups is surjective. Our main result establishes that a cover $f$ is genuinely ramified if and only if the pullback $f^*E$ of any $P$-stable vector bundle $E$ on $(X, P)$ remains $\mu_{\mathfrak{Y}}$-stable on $\mathfrak{Y}$. Furthermore, we present additional equivalent criteria for genuine ramification, extending previous results that were limited to smooth curves.

This study examines a boundary value problem involving a second-order equation with variable coefficients defined within a multi-dimensional domain containing numerous small, closely spaced cavities arranged along a specific manifold. The linear dimensions of these cavities are of the same small order, though their geometries and spatial distributions remain arbitrary. The cavity boundaries satisfy a nonlinear Robin condition. We demonstrate that the solution to the perturbed problem converges to the solution of the corresponding homogenized problem in the $L_2$ and $W_2^1$ norms, with convergence uniform with respect to the $L_2$-norm of the equation's right-hand side. Furthermore, we derive estimates for the rates of this convergence.

An operator $T$ on a Banach space $X$ is termed super-recurrent if, for every open subset $U \subseteq X$, there exist a scalar $\lambda \in \mathbb{K}$ and a natural number $n$ such that $\lambda T^n(U)$ intersects $U$. This paper introduces and examines the concepts of super-rigidity and uniform super-rigidity, which are closely linked to super-recurrence. We analyze various properties of these operator classes and demonstrate that they exhibit characteristics similar to those of super-recurrent operators. Finally, we explore the specific case involving finite-dimensional spaces.

At the National Superconducting Cyclotron Laboratory, we measured the $\beta$-delayed proton ($\beta$p) and $\gamma$ emissions from $^{57}$Zn. Our findings determine a half-life of $43.6 \pm 0.2$ ms for $^{57}$Zn and a $\beta$p branching ratio of $(84.7 \pm 1.4)\%$. We also identified four transitions associated with the exotic $\beta$-$\gamma$-$p$ decay mode, marking the second such discovery in the $fp$-shell. Utilizing the $p/\gamma$ ratio to correct for isospin mixing, we determined the mass of $^{57}$Zn through the isobaric multiplet mass equation. Previously, it remained unclear if the rp-process could bypass the canonical waiting point $^{56}$Ni under conditions relevant to Type-I X-ray bursts. Our results definitively confirm the existence of this $^{56}$Ni bypass, showing that 14–17% of the rp-process flow follows this path.

This paper introduces a rank-one tensor modeling approach that provides a compact representation of the optimal IRS phase-shift vector to minimize feedback overhead. The core concept involves decomposing the phase-shift vector into a Kronecker product of smaller constituent vectors, referred to as factors. This proposed model enables the network to balance achievable data rates against feedback reduction by adjusting the factorization parameters. Simulation results demonstrate that the suggested phase-shift factorization significantly lowers feedback overhead and enhances data rates in certain scenarios compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

This work tackles the challenge of creating stabilizing control strategies for discrete-time nonlinear systems with the goal of minimizing an arbitrary cost function. While the System Level Synthesis (SLS) method provides an exact solution via convex programming when the system is linear and the cost is convex, finding a globally optimal solution for more complex cases generally remains intractable. To address this, we introduce a parametrization that captures every and only the stabilizing control policies for a specified time-varying nonlinear system, defined by the interaction between a strongly stabilizing base controller and a freely designed stable SLS operator. Leveraging this framework, we propose a Neural SLS (Neur-SLS) methodology that ensures closed-loop stability throughout and following parameter optimization without imposing constraint satisfaction requirements. By utilizing recent Deep Neural Network (DNN) architectures based on Recurrent Equilibrium Networks (RENs), we learn across a diverse class of nonlinear stable operators, with numerical examples validating the approach's effectiveness.

This work introduces the concept of fuzzy cardinal semantic transformation as a foundation for developing fuzzy semantic numeration systems. It addresses both the fuzziness inherent in the initial data—the cardinals of abstract entities—and the fuzziness of the parameters within cardinal semantic operators. Furthermore, cardinal semantic transformations are formulated for both discrete and continuous triangular fuzzy numbers. Finally, the principles governing the creation of a fuzzy common carry in multi-input cardinal semantic operators are established.

This study explores and validates the utility of Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) profiles for extracting seasonal height changes in polar CO2 snow and ice caps through a co-registration approach. Focusing on a prototype analysis of the residual south polar cap within the region [85.75°S, 86.25°S, 300°E, 330°E], our methodology involves recalculating MOLA footprint coordinates using an updated Mars Global Surveyor (MGS) ephemeris and a refined Mars rotation model. The reprocessed MOLA data for the South Pole (south of 78°S) is self-registered to create a consistent reference digital terrain model (DTM). Segments of these reprocessed profiles are then co-registered to this reference DTM to derive temporal height differences at both footprints and cross-overs. A proposed two-step Regional Pseudo Cross-over Adjustment (RPCA) procedure is subsequently applied to correct these height differences for temporal systematic biases and other residual errors. Unlike traditional methods, the pseudo cross-overs in this RPCA are constructed from profile pairs that may not physically intersect but are linked via the underlying DTM. The final CO2 snow/ice temporal height variations are determined by median-filtering the corrected height differences. The resulting height change time series achieves a precision of approximately 4.9 cm, with an estimated peak-to-peak variation of about 2 meters. Furthermore, a significant "pit" representing transient height accumulation of roughly 0.5 meters, centered at Ls=210° during southern spring, is identified. This method establishes the potential to map seasonal CO2 snow/ice height variations across the entire North and South polar regions of Mars.

Artificial neural networks (ANNs) have recently been utilized to solve partial differential equations (PDEs). This study examines the classic task of pricing European and American financial options by leveraging their respective PDE formulations. Rather than relying on traditional numerical methods such as finite element or difference approaches, we employ ANNs within an unsupervised learning framework. Through the minimization of an appropriate loss function, the ANN determines option values across all potential underlying stock prices at future time steps. Specifically, we resolve the linear Black-Scholes equation for European options and the linear complementarity problem formulation for American options. Additionally, the method accurately computes values for two-asset exotic options, highlighting the ANN's capability to handle high-dimensional valuation problems. The accuracy of the proposed approach is evaluated by comparing its results against analytic solutions or numerical reference solutions (with American option values benchmarked against finite element computations).

Pretrained Transformer models have become state-of-the-art solutions by leveraging textual context to enhance performance across various NLP tasks. However, despite their power, these models often demand specialized knowledge for specific applications. This paper contends that contextual data extracted from a knowledge graph (specifically Wikidata) offers sufficient signals to guide pretrained Transformers, thereby boosting their effectiveness in Named Entity Disambiguation (NED) within the Wikidata environment. We further hypothesize that this knowledge graph context can be standardized for Wikipedia and assess its impact on state-of-the-art NED models applied to the Wikipedia knowledge base. Our empirical findings confirm that the proposed KG context is generalizable to Wikipedia and that integrating such context into Transformer architectures significantly outperforms current baselines, including standard vanilla Transformers.

We propose and examine an explicit finite difference scheme for the Camassa-Holm shallow water equation, designed to accommodate general $H^1$ initial data and consequently manage peakon-antipeakon interactions. Under a specific condition that constrains the time step relative to the spatial discretization parameter, we demonstrate that the scheme converges strongly in $H^1$ to a dissipative weak solution of the Camassa-Holm equation.

This dissertation examines various facets of Device-to-Device (D2D) communications and their influence on key network performance metrics. We propose an architecture designed to facilitate collaboration among cellular users by effectively leveraging timely D2D opportunities. Initially, we present an analytical investigation into opportunistic out-of-band D2D communications, which demonstrates the significant potential of this approach to enhance the energy efficiency, fairness, and capacity of cellular networks, provided that groups of D2D users can be successfully formed and managed within the network. Subsequently, we introduce a protocol compatible with the latest IEEE and 3GPP standards, enabling the practical implementation of our proposal in current cellular infrastructure. To validate our analytical results, we utilize an experimental Software Defined Radio (SDR) testbed to evaluate our proposal in real-world scenarios. The experimental outcomes confirm the exceptional potential of opportunistic out-of-band D2D communications. Finally, we analyze the advantages and disadvantages of various D2D modes. Our findings indicate that, contrary to common assumptions, all D2D modes are complementary, with their specific benefits being contingent upon the scenario.

A recently introduced "agegraphic dark energy" aims to account for the dark energy-dominated universe. This study extends agegraphic dark energy models to curved universes while incorporating interactions between dark matter and dark energy. We demonstrate that these generalized models permit the equation of state of dark energy to cross the $w_D = -1$ threshold. Furthermore, in the specific limit where the universe is flat ($k = 0$), all prior findings regarding agegraphic dark energy in flat spacetime are recovered.

Dual Connectivity (DC) serves as a fundamental technique for maximizing the capabilities of heterogeneous cellular networks. Nevertheless, the 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) has implemented distinct mechanisms for DC across various Radio Access Technologies (RATs), which introduces complexity into Multi-RAT Radio Access Network (RAN) nodes. Additionally, supporting DC necessitates a high volume of control information exchange between these nodes. To mitigate these challenges, this paper proposes an SDN-based architecture for Multi-RAT RANs. This proposed design simplifies network interactions, enhances flexibility, and enables effective load balancing and mobility management. Furthermore, the study demonstrates a reduction in control signaling and an improvement in system performance relative to legacy architectures.

Mobile games enjoy immense popularity, captivating millions daily. Despite their often straightforward gameplay, creating them involves significant complexity and demands meticulous focus to ensure high user satisfaction and developer profitability. This paper introduces a model designed to analyze user session durations, enabling the assessment and optimization of game longevity, even during early development stages.

This study examines discrete-time risk-sensitive portfolio optimization over extended periods subject to proportional transaction costs. We demonstrate that within the framework of independent and identically distributed log-returns, a solution to a specific Bellman equation exists under minimal assumptions, enabling the characterization of optimal strategies for both risk-averse and risk-seeking scenarios. Furthermore, through numerical examples, we illustrate how analyzing the Bellman equation facilitates the construction or refinement of optimal trading strategies when transaction costs are present.

We introduce graded hyper-algebras for vector-valued Siegel modular forms to facilitate the analysis of their tensor products. Furthermore, we establish vector-valued Hecke operators defined at all rational places for these forms, acting within the hyper-algebras. These constructions serve as a bridge between classical and representation-theoretic perspectives on Siegel modular forms. By integrating the product structure with the action of Hecke operators, we demonstrate for elliptic modular forms that cusp forms of sufficiently high weight can be generated through products of just two fixed Eisenstein series. Consequently, this yields inclusions of cuspidal automorphic representations into the tensor product of global principal series.

This Thesis details my individual contributions to two separate domains within Flavour Physics: the recent experimental irregularities observed in B-meson decays and the enduring search for a theoretical account of lepton masses and mixings. It emphasizes the contemporary understanding of the Standard Model as an effective theory and highlights flavour's dual function as both a tool for detecting New Physics and an integral component of the physical puzzle itself. By examining two physics cases of differing natures together, I aim to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of Beyond Standard Model investigations. The work starts with a preliminary overview of Standard Model Effective Field Theories, presenting key theoretical matching results. The narrative then shifts to B-meson decay anomalies, where, following an introduction to Lepton Flavour Universality, I analyze the phenomenology of scalar leptoquarks as a specific Standard Model extension. Additionally, I outline the Effective Field Theory framework for Rank-One Flavor Violation to offer a broader, though less detailed, perspective on neutral-current anomalies. Finally, the Thesis addresses the Standard Model flavour puzzle by exploring an approach to resolving charged lepton mass hierarchies within supersymmetric modular invariant models of lepton flavour.

Recent research on algorithmic fairness has extensively examined the conflict between \textit{sufficiency} and \textit{separation}, metrics such as predictive value ratios and false positive or negative rates across different groups. Following the controversy surrounding the COMPAS criminal justice system, scholars established a theoretical proof demonstrating that simultaneously achieving both fairness criteria is impossible with an imperfect predictor unless label distributions are equal across groups. This paper explores the viable solutions that exist within this impossibility, arguing that recognizing a trade-off necessitates finding an optimal equilibrium. We refine existing theory and introduce a new objective function designed to balance \textit{sufficiency} and \textit{separation} while preserving comparable accuracy. Empirical validation through two case studies—one utilizing a multi-objective framework and the other fine-tuning an accuracy-optimized pre-trained model—demonstrates that this approach yields superior trade-offs compared to current alternatives.

This study investigates low-mass dilepton resonances within Higgs boson decays by analyzing the four-lepton final state. The analysis considers scenarios where the decay involves either a pair of beyond-the-standard-model particles or a single such particle alongside a Z boson. Data from proton-proton collisions recorded by the CMS detector at the CERN LHC are utilized, with an integrated luminosity of 137 fb$^{-1}$ at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. No significant deviation from standard model predictions is found. Consequently, 95% confidence level upper limits are established for model-independent Higgs boson decay branching fractions. Furthermore, constraints on the production of dark photons and axion-like particles, derived from two specific models, are presented.

The primary goal of person re-identification (re-ID) is to locate images of a specific individual within a gallery based on a single query image. Despite recent progress, learning features that are both identity-sensitive and invariant to viewpoint remains a significant hurdle due to the extensive variation in human poses. This paper introduces a re-ID framework that leverages the image synthesis capabilities of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), alongside pose clustering and feature fusion, to learn features that are robust to pose changes. The aim is to model an individual across various viewpoints and significant pose variations, subsequently extracting the most distinctive features from these diverse appearances. Specifically, the Pose Transformational GAN (pt-GAN) module is trained to synthesize images of a person in any specified pose. To determine which poses are most critical for discriminative feature extraction, a Pose Clustering module is introduced. The queried person is then modeled across multiple poses, with these features being effectively integrated via a Feature Fusion Network. The final re-ID architecture, comprising these three components, mitigates pose dependency in person re-ID. Furthermore, the proposed model demonstrates robustness against occlusion, scale, rotation, and illumination, offering a comprehensive framework for viewpoint-invariant feature learning. Experimental results on four benchmark datasets show that the proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art GAN-based approaches and achieves superior accuracy compared to other leading models.

This article examines the fundamental architecture for terahertz (THz) wireless links integrated with optical networks, targeting bandwidths exceeding 50 GHz. Achieving Tbps data rates with near-zero latency using this concept necessitates new design principles and breakthrough technologies. Specifically, we outline a strategy for baseband signal processing that encompasses both optical and wireless segments, utilizing an end-to-end (E2E) error correction method for the unified link. We detail two electro-optical baseband interface architectures currently under study: the transparent optical-link and the digital-link. The text also specifies THz wireless link requirements and outlines the core principles and research trajectories for developing next-generation transceiver frontends capable of ultra-high spectral efficiency through higher-order modulation schemes. Furthermore, we address the necessity of establishing a novel network information theory framework for THz networks that accounts for specific channel characteristics and interference types. Finally, we emphasize the critical role of pencil-beamforming (PBF) in mitigating propagation losses, alongside the associated physical layer and medium access control challenges.

This study examines gravastars, or gravitational vacuum stars, within non-minimally coupled models incorporating both electromagnetic and gravitational fields. We analyze two distinct non-minimal models to derive corresponding spherically symmetric exact solutions for the star's interior, which contains a dark energy condensate. Outside the star, our models reduce to the Einstein-Maxwell framework, yielding the Reissner-Nordström solution. The resulting physical quantities remain continuous and non-singular across specific parameter ranges, ensuring a seamless transition between the interior and exterior geometries at the stellar surface. We compute the matter mass, total gravitational mass, electric charge, and redshift for both models. Notably, except for redshift, these quantities depend on a subtle free parameter, $k$, specific to the model. Furthermore, in the second model, we observe that the redshift spans a wide range from zero to infinity, contingent upon the free parameter $\beta$.

Let $R$ denote a commutative ring; we elucidate the Beilinson-Bernstein localisation process for sheaves of homogeneous twisted differential operators on a smooth, separated, locally finite-type $R$-scheme. As an application, we provide a novel proof of Duflo's theorem, which characterizes the primitive ideals within the enveloping algebra of a complex semisimple Lie algebra.

Thermoelectric materials offer a pathway to capture wasted energy and reduce the power requirements of electronic devices. Effective heat-to-electricity conversion demands materials that exhibit high electronic conductivity alongside significantly suppressed thermal conductivity. While nanostructured materials largely meet this criterion, even when their bulk equivalents are inefficient, this study examines how many-body effects boost thermoelectric efficiency in graphene nanoribbons at low temperatures. Utilizing the Kane-Mele-Hubbard model under a mean-field approximation, we conduct a comprehensive numerical analysis of how electron-electron interactions influence the thermoelectric performance of both armchair and zigzag-edged graphene nanoribbons. The investigation covers two distinct regimes: trivial and topological insulators. Our findings indicate that electron-electron interactions are essential for generating interference phenomena that enhance the thermoelectric efficiency of these nanoribbons. Finally, we outline an experimental configuration designed to validate our conclusions.

The short-lived radioactive nuclide $^{26}$Al is responsible for the observed galactic diffuse gamma-ray emission at 1.8 MeV. Although various sources of $^{26}$Al have been investigated, including AGB stars, massive star winds, and supernovae, the role of very massive stars has not yet been examined. This study investigates the contribution of stellar winds from very massive stars (those with initial masses ranging from 150 to 300 M$_\odot$) to the $^{26}$Al enrichment of the galactic interstellar medium. We analyze $^{26}$Al production using both rotating and non-rotating stellar models within this mass range, covering metallicities of Z=0.006, 0.014, and 0.020. These findings are compared against a simplified Milky Way model that incorporates gradients in both star formation rate and metallicity. Our results suggest that very massive stars across the Z=0.006–0.020 metallicity range could be highly significant contributors to interstellar $^{26}$Al enrichment. Specifically, including very massive stars in the calculation increases the estimated contribution of massive star winds to the Galaxy's total $^{26}$Al inventory by approximately 150%. Despite their scarcity, very massive stars may play a crucial role in $^{26}$Al production and serve as key agents in galactic nucleosynthesis.

We provide the highest-fidelity spectrum of a planetary-mass object obtained to date. VHS 1256 b is a young brown dwarf companion with a mass less than 20 Jupiter masses, located at a wide separation of approximately 8 arcseconds (semi-major axis of 150 au). It shares photometric colors and spectroscopic characteristics with the directly imaged exoplanets HR 8799 c, d, and e. As an object in the transition from spectral type L to T, VHS 1256 b occupies a region on the color-magnitude diagram where substellar atmospheres shift from cloudy to clear. Using JWST's NIRSpec IFU and MIRI MRS modes, we observed the object across a range of 1 to 20 $\mu$m at resolutions between $\sim$1,000 and 3,700. Comparisons with template brown dwarf spectra, molecular opacities, and atmospheric models reveal the presence of water, methane, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, sodium, and potassium throughout various sections of the JWST spectrum. The spectral profile of VHS 1256 b is shaped by disequilibrium chemistry and clouds. Furthermore, we achieve the first direct detection of silicate clouds in a planetary-mass companion.

Video search has become the primary method users employ to find videos matching text queries on major short-video platforms. During the training of a query-video bi-encoder using online search logs, we observed a modality bias where the video encoder predominantly relies on text matching while overlooking other video modalities like vision and audio. This imbalance stems from two factors: the modality gap, where query-video text relevance is easier to learn due to shared text modality, and data bias, as most training samples are solvable through text alone. In this work, we present our strategies for enhancing the initial retrieval stage, specifically addressing this modality imbalance. We introduce MBVR (Modality Balanced Video Retrieval), featuring two core components: manually created modality-shuffled samples and a dynamic margin based on visual relevance, both designed to encourage balanced attention from the video encoder across all modalities. Extensive experiments on a real-world dataset demonstrate that our approach is both effective and efficient in mitigating modality bias. Furthermore, we deployed MBVR on a large-scale video platform, achieving statistically significant performance improvements over a highly optimized baseline in both A/B tests and manual GSB evaluations.

This study quantifies the chemical and kinematic properties of the Galactic disks using a sample of 119,558 giant stars, combining abundance and 3D velocity data from the APOGEE DR17 and Gaia EDR3 catalogs. A Gaussian Mixture Model is applied to separate high-$\alpha$ and low-$\alpha$ sequences based on metallicity by jointly analyzing chemical and kinematic data. This approach identifies and characterizes four disk components: h$\alpha$mp, h$\alpha$mr, l$\alpha$mp, and l$\alpha$mr, representing combinations of high/low $\alpha$ and metal-poor/metal-rich attributes. When integrated with spatial and stellar age data, these components align well with the two-infall formation model. The initial infall of turbulent gas rapidly creates the hot, thick h$\alpha$mp disk, followed by thinner h$\alpha$mr and l$\alpha$mr disks, while a subsequent gas accretion event forms the thinner, outermost l$\alpha$mp disk. Our findings suggest that the inside-out and upside-down scenarios effectively explain both the overall two-episode formation of the Galactic disk and the specific sequence of the three inner disks. Crucially, we uncover an inverse Age-[M/H] trend in the l$\alpha$mr disk, where younger stars are more metal-poor, indicating that rejuvenated gas from the second accretion increasingly dominates later star formation. Furthermore, recently formed stars converge toward [M/H]$\sim$-0.1 dex, demonstrating a thorough mixture of gas from both infall events.

Cache-coherent non-uniform memory access (ccNUMA) architectures allow parallel workloads to expand across thousands of cores and terabytes of memory. However, the elevated cost of remote memory accesses necessitates specific optimizations to effectively scale applications to high core counts and process data volumes exceeding typical server capacities. Just as applications require tuning for better cache usage, they also need optimization to enhance data locality on ccNUMA topologies. The initial step in this optimization process involves identifying performance bottlenecks, which requires either profiling tools or manual instrumentation. Despite this need, optimizing applications on large ccNUMA systems is hindered by a scarcity of mechanisms to capture and display actionable telemetry. This limitation stems partly from the proprietary nature of these interconnects and, more significantly, from the absence of a common, accessible (open-source) framework for developers and vendors to utilize.

This paper introduces an open-source, extensible framework capable of capturing high-rate on-chip events with minimal overhead (less than 10% single-core utilization). The framework supports both live and record modes, facilitating real-time monitoring as well as data capture for subsequent offline or post-workload analysis. Furthermore, it offers high-resolution visualization via a standards-compliant interactive web interface or a convenient textual interface designed for rapid analysis.

The rapid global dissemination of COVID-19, driven by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, has heightened concerns regarding the frequency of mutations throughout the viral genome. This study performs a partial replication of a 2021 investigation by Wang et al., which identified four substrains and eleven predominant mutations within the United States. By examining a subset of the original dataset, we successfully reconstruct Figure S1, reproducing the key features present in the initial publication. Additionally, we compile a summary of mutation profiles for all 26 identified proteins and validate that the spike protein accounts for approximately 24% of total recorded mutations. Our findings indicate that variables beyond protein length likely influence the per-protein mutation rate.

Observations of TeV halos surrounding nearby pulsars suggest that these objects inject substantial fluxes of high-energy electron-positron pairs into the interstellar medium, likely accounting for the majority of the cosmic-ray positron flux. This study utilizes the positron fraction measured by the AMS-02 Collaboration to limit the properties of the local pulsar population. For plausible model parameters, we achieve good agreement with the observed positron fraction up to energies of approximately $E_e \sim 300 \, {\rm GeV}$. At higher energies, the positron fraction is governed by a small number of pulsars, rendering precise predictions of the expected shape uncertain. The low-energy positron spectrum corroborates the conclusion that pulsars typically convert about $\eta \sim 5-20\%$ of their total spindown power into very high-energy electron-positron pairs, generating a particle spectrum with a hard spectral index of $\alpha \sim 1.5-1.7$. These pulsars generally exhibit spindown timescales on the order of $\tau \sim 10^4 \, {\rm years}$. Our optimal fits correspond to models where the radio and gamma-ray beams from pulsars are detectable to 28% and 62% of surrounding observers, respectively.

The commutativity degree of a finite group represents the likelihood that two elements selected uniformly at random commute. This concept naturally generalizes to finitely generated groups $G$: the commutativity degree $\text{dc}_S(G)$, defined relative to a specific finite generating set $S$, is calculated by examining the proportion of commuting pairs within expanding neighborhoods of the identity in the Cayley graph $\mathcal{C}(G,S)$. This study concentrates on restricted wreath products of the form $G = H \wr \langle t \rangle$, where $H$ is a non-trivial finitely generated group and the acting group $\langle t \rangle$ is infinite cyclic. Supporting a broader conjecture, we demonstrate that $\text{dc}_S(G) = 0$ for these groups, independent of the generating set $S$ chosen. This finding builds upon Cox's earlier work regarding lamplighter groups under specific generating sets. Furthermore, we establish an extension of Cox's primary auxiliary lemma: in sufficiently large homomorphic images of such wreath products, the image of the base group exhibits zero density with respect to particular generating set types.

Can a problem that is undecidable using classical resources become decidable with quantum resources? The anticipated answer is negative, as both classical and quantum frameworks operate as Turing theories and should theoretically fail to solve the Halting problem, which is unsolvable by any Turing machine. However, we offer an affirmative response to this question. We introduce a new logical structure capable of defining infinitely many such problems for any pair of distinct Turing theories, encompassing but not restricted to classical and quantum models. Crucially, other decision problems, including the Halting problem, remain unsolvable across all these theories. This seemingly paradoxical scenario is resolved by recognizing that the reducibility of the Halting problem shifts depending on the computational resources available within different theories. Finally, we propose a multi-agent game in which determining whether a player restricted to classical resources can win is undecidable, whereas a player with access to quantum resources possesses a perfect winning strategy.

This paper presents $\mathsf{CO}_3$, an algorithm designed to enhance communication efficiency in federated Deep Neural Network (DNN) training. The name $\mathsf{CO}_3$ reflects its three-stage processing pipeline, which mitigates communication overhead during the transmission of local gradients from remote users to the Parameter Server. These stages are: (i) gradient quantization via floating-point conversion, (ii) lossless compression of the quantized gradients, and (iii) correction of quantization errors. Each step is meticulously engineered to minimize accuracy loss in distributed DNN training under a fixed communication budget. Specifically, the design of steps (i) and (ii) relies on the assumption that DNN gradients follow a generalized normal distribution, an assumption that is empirically validated within the paper. For step (iii), an error feedback mechanism incorporating memory decay is employed to address quantization errors introduced in step (i). We posit that this coefficient, akin to the learning rate, can be optimally tuned to accelerate convergence. Numerical simulations demonstrate that $\mathsf{CO}_3$ achieves superior accuracy and enhanced stability while significantly reducing the communication payload.

There is currently substantial interest in supervised machine learning methods designed to streamline the time and effort required for manual seismic interpretation. Nevertheless, most effective supervised algorithms depend on vast quantities of annotated training data, and labeling large seismic volumes remains a tedious and resource-intensive endeavor. To overcome this challenge, we propose a weakly-supervised framework for predicting labels across diverse seismic structures. This method requires interpreters to select only a minimal set of exemplar images per subsurface class, after which a new similarity-based retrieval system extracts thousands of analogous images from the seismic volume. By operating under the assumption that visually similar images share the same class—a hypothesis confirmed in our results—we generate thousands of image-level labels. We subsequently introduce a novel weakly-supervised algorithm that refines these coarse image-level annotations into precise pixel-level labels, accurately localizing specific subsurface features. This strategy significantly simplifies the acquisition of labeled data needed to train supervised models for seismic interpretation. Applying our approach to the Netherlands Offshore F3 block yielded thousands of automatically labeled images with reasonably accurate pixel-level precision. We anticipate that this work will facilitate further advancements in machine learning-driven seismic interpretation.

This study investigates hidden-sector bosons ($\chi$) generated through the decay ${B^0\!\to K^*(892)^0\chi}$, where $K^*(892)^0$ decays into $K^{+}\pi^{-}$ and $\chi$ decays into $\mu^+\mu^-$. The analysis utilizes $pp$-collision data amounting to 3.0 fb$^{-1}$ recorded by the LHCb detector. Within the accessible mass interval of $214 \leq m({\chi}) \leq 4350$ MeV, no significant signal was detected. Consequently, upper limits were established for the branching fraction product $\mathcal{B}(B^0\!\to K^*(892)^0\chi)\times\mathcal{B}(\chi\!\to\mu^+\mu^-)$ as a function of the $\chi$ boson's mass and lifetime. For $\chi$ lifetimes under 100 ps, these limits reach approximately $10^{-9}$ across most of the mass spectrum, thereby setting the tightest constraints to date on numerous theories proposing additional low-mass bosons.

This study investigates transportability, a specific aspect of generalizability, by introducing metrics grounded in established statistical principles to predict how NLP model performance shifts across different contexts. Establishing a novel transportability measure could enhance the estimation of NLP system efficacy in new domains, proving essential when evaluating performance on unfamiliar tasks and settings. We illustrate the utility of lightweight domain similarity measures as transportability estimators through progressively complex examples, evaluating these proposed metrics within Named Entity Recognition and Natural Language Inference tasks.

This paper provides a theoretical overview of static source code analysis, covering its definition, applications, execution methods, intermediate representation formats, models, and prevalent techniques. It concludes by listing free and downloadable static analysis tools, including academic software developed by researchers. (Note: The article is written in Brazilian Portuguese.)

This study examines the one-loop renormalization of the electroweak Standard Model by adopting the leptonic effective weak mixing angle as an input parameter. We assess how this specific choice influences the predicted forward-backward asymmetry in the neutral current Drell-Yan process. Furthermore, the suggested input scheme facilitates the direct extraction of the effective leptonic weak mixing angle from experimental results.

Relying on an agent's uncertainty regarding the optimal policy serves as a robust exploration strategy in reinforcement learning, particularly within tabular environments where it often achieves near-optimal results. Conversely, in non-tabular contexts utilizing function approximators, deriving precise uncertainty estimates remains a significant challenge. This paper identifies that value estimates are frequently prone to bias and temporal inconsistency. Addressing these issues, we introduce a new method for quantifying uncertainty over the value function by establishing a distribution over temporal difference errors. This exploration signal accounts for state-action transitions to isolate value uncertainty stemming specifically from parameter uncertainty. Since this uncertainty metric conditions on transitions, it cannot be acted upon directly; instead, we integrate it as an intrinsic reward, framing exploration as a distinct learning problem driven by temporal difference uncertainties. We develop a specialized exploration policy designed to gather data from high-uncertainty regions, creating a curriculum that evolves smoothly during learning and disappears once value estimates become perfect. Evaluations on difficult exploration tasks, such as Deep Sea and Atari 2600, demonstrate that our approach effectively promotes both diverse and deep exploration.

This paper addresses few-shot open-set recognition (FSOR), aiming to develop systems that rapidly adapt to new classes using limited labeled data while effectively rejecting unknown negatives. Conventional large-scale open-set techniques often fail in FSOR scenarios due to data scarcity. Existing FSOR approaches typically calibrate few-shot closed-set classifiers to detect negative samples via thresholding; however, manually tuning these thresholds is difficult because rejection requirements vary across tasks. To overcome this, we introduce a task-adaptive negative class envisioning framework that embeds threshold tuning directly into the learning process. Specifically, we enhance the few-shot closed-set classifier by incorporating additional negative prototypes derived from few-shot examples. By leveraging correlations among few-shot classes during negative prototype generation, our method learns dynamic rejection boundaries tailored to specific FSOR tasks. Furthermore, we extend this approach to generalized few-shot open-set recognition (GFSOR), which handles classification of both few-shot and many-shot classes alongside negative rejection. Comprehensive experiments on public benchmarks demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed methods on both FSOR and GFSOR tasks.

Developers frequently utilize forking to extend existing projects, creating variants that share a common codebase but diverge to meet specific project needs. A notable benefit of this multiplicity is the ability to choose between different evolutionary paths driven by bug fixes. However, analyzing this decentralized information remains challenging. This study introduces a visualization tool designed to examine active changes in fork repositories that have not yet been merged back to the original source. Similar to GitHub's code frequency view, our visualization displays commit activities across multiple forks but exclusively highlights commits unique to those forks, with specific emphasis on bug fixes. To demonstrate its efficacy, we applied the tool to two scenarios: identifying forks from abandoned projects and locating bug fixes among forks. In the first scenario, we traced a fork continuing development on the suspended Obfuscator-LLVM project, displaying both the original repo and its most active derivative. In the second, we pinpointed a bug fix within a fork of the Clipy project, where our view clearly distinguished the patch made by the most active fork. As a novel ideas paper, we outline three research questions to inspire future real-world applications and goals for this visualization. A prototype is accessible at \textcolor{blue}{\url{https://naist-se.github.io/vissoft2022/}}.

Latency-sensitive and bandwidth-heavy stream processing applications are the primary sources of traffic on the Internet. Since these streams consist of continuous data elements requiring near real-time processing, Fog computing is employed to mitigate communication latency and network congestion by shifting computation to the network edge, complementing traditional Cloud services. However, the heterogeneity inherent in the Cloud-Fog continuum presents significant challenges for deploying and executing stream applications. This work introduces a two-sided stable matching model, termed Cloud-Fog to Data Stream Application Matching (CODA), designed to deploy distributed applications—structured as workflows of stream processing microservices—onto heterogeneous Cloud-Fog resources. In the CODA framework, microservices rank continuum resources based on stream processing time, whereas resources rank microservices according to their residual bandwidth. A stable many-to-one matching algorithm assigns microservices to resources based on these mutual preferences, aiming to minimize total stream processing time for the application and aggregate streaming traffic for the resources. The CODA algorithm was evaluated using both simulated and real-world Cloud-Fog scenarios, demonstrating a reduction in stream processing time of 11% to 45% and a decrease in streaming traffic of 1.3% to 20% compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches.

Grasping the kinematics and dynamics of drop spreading, pinching, and coalescence is vital for numerous applications including atomization, dispensing, coating, printing, spraying, and emulsification. Consequently, experimental research focuses on visualizing and characterizing how drops expand over time on substrates, how liquid bridges grow between merging drops, and how the radius of pinching necks diminishes during formation. Even for Newtonian fluids, the interaction of inertial, viscous, and capillary stresses generates various scaling laws, characterized by three limiting self-similar regimes: visco-inertial (VI), visco-capillary (VC), and inertio-capillary (IC). Although experiments often illustrate dimensional analysis methods, the absence of accurate pre-factors, transition points, and scaling exponents hinders quantitative analysis and material characterization. This tutorial review reexamines and synthesizes a comprehensive collection of landmark experimental studies on diverse Newtonian fluids. We demonstrate that shifting from VI, VC, and IC units to a system based on intrinsic timescales and lengthscales derived from all three material properties—viscosity, surface tension, and density, known as Ohnesorge units, yields a complementary framework. Our findings reveal that despite significant variations in topological features, timescales, and material properties, analyzing spreading, pinching, and coalescing drops using Ohnesorge units causes experimental datasets to collapse remarkably, underscoring the universal characteristics shared by these flows.

This study investigates a MIMO secure wireless communication system enhanced by physical layer security techniques involving artificial noise (AN). To further boost security, an intelligent reflecting surface (IRS) is integrated into the AN-aided framework, where the base station (BS), legitimate receiver (IR), and eavesdropper (Eve) all possess multiple antennas. The objective is to maximize the secrecy rate (SR) by jointly optimizing the transmit precoding (TPC) matrix at the BS, the AN covariance matrix, and the IRS phase shifts, subject to constraints on transmit power and unit modulus phase shifts. The resulting secrecy rate maximization (SRM) problem is formulated as a non-convex challenge with multiple coupled variables. To address this, we propose a block coordinate descent (BCD) algorithm that alternately updates the TPC matrix, AN covariance matrix, and phase shifts while ensuring the SR does not decrease. Specifically, the optimal TPC matrix and AN covariance matrix are derived using the Lagrangian multiplier method, while the optimal phase shifts are obtained via the Majorization-Minimization (MM) algorithm. Since all variables can be computed in closed form, the proposed algorithm demonstrates high efficiency. Furthermore, the SRM problem is extended to a more general scenario involving multiple IRSs, for which a BCD algorithm is also developed. Finally, simulation results confirm the effectiveness of the system's security enhancement through the use of IRS.

We establish a refinement of Raynaud's Theorem (the Manin-Mumford conjecture) applicable to abelian schemes defined over certain rings of integers. In this context, traditional torsion points are substituted with special 0-cycles, representing reductions modulo specific, potentially varying, primes of Galois orbits containing torsion points. The structure consists of two distinct parts: a flat/horizontal component and a vertical component. The irreducible components of the flat part correspond to the Zariski closure over the integers of torsion cosets within the generic fiber of the abelian scheme, whereas the vertical components arise from translates of abelian subvarieties originating from characteristic zero.

This brief paper introduces a numerical approach to optimize the conservative confidence bound for system reliability, utilizing tests on individual components. It serves as an alternative to the algorithmic methods discussed in Bishop and Povyakalo (RESS 2020). For a specified maximum number of component tests, this numerical method can generate an optimal test plan for any arbitrary system architecture. The optimization technique relies on linear programming, which is more efficient than the alternative integer programming approach. Furthermore, the optimization process requires execution only once for a given system structure, as the resulting solution can be reused to calculate an optimal integer test plan for varying maximum numbers of component tests. This methodology may have wider applicability to other optimization problems typically addressed using integer programming.

The study clarifies the mechanism behind the failure of the superhydrophobic state in submerged nanoscale textures that create a three-dimensional, interconnected vapor region. Designing such nanotextures is a critical challenge due to the significant simulation difficulties posed by the wide range of time and length scales involved. To address the long timescales associated with high free energy barriers, advanced atomistic simulations of rare events were employed. In these interconnected surface cavities, wetting initiates with the formation of a liquid finger between two pillars. This symmetry breaking causes a gentler curvature in the remaining liquid-vapor interface, subsequently triggering the wetting of adjacent pillars. This collective process, where multiple pillars wet simultaneously, could not be observed in prior atomistic simulations that utilized surface models with only a few pillars (typically just one). Interpreting these atomistic findings through a sharp-interface continuum model indicates that line tension, condensation, and other nanoscale effects play negligible roles under the simulated conditions.

We demonstrate that the anticipated duration of a hide-and-seek game on a Riemannian manifold governed by Brownian Motion constitutes a spectral invariant, specifically a zeta-regularized trace of the Laplacian. A comparable game can be played on Markov chains, yielding a spectral invariant recognized as Kemeny's constant. By exploring the parallels between these two frameworks, we illuminate the relationship between the regularized trace and Kemeny's constant. Our proof leverages the link between Green's functions and expected hitting times, alongside the fact that the regularized trace can be approximated through the Green's function.

The primary obstacle in transit photometry stems from noise within the photometric data, particularly for ground-based telescopes where atmospheric disturbances introduce significant interference. While employing large-aperture telescopes can substantially enhance the photometric signal-to-noise ratio (S/N), extracting transit signals from noisy stellar light curves and accurately determining transit parameters necessitate advanced noise reduction methods. This study details multi-band transit photometric follow-up observations of five hot-Jupiters—HAT-P-30 b, HAT-P-54 b, WASP-43 b, TrES-3 b, and XO-2 N b—conducted using the 2m Himalayan Chandra Telescope (HCT) at the Indian Astronomical Observatory in Hanle and the 1.3m J. C. Bhattacharya Telescope (JCBT) at the Vainu Bappu Observatory in Kavalur. Our rigorous noise mitigation strategy incorporates techniques such as Wavelet Denoising and Gaussian Process regression, which successfully eliminate both time-correlated and time-uncorrelated noise from the transit light curves. Furthermore, the application of our advanced modeling algorithms has enabled more precise and accurate estimations of the target exoplanets' physical properties compared to prior research.

With a known radial magnetic field distribution at the Sun's photosphere, established techniques allow for the calculation of a potential magnetic field in the corona. These potential fields are commonly utilized as inputs for solar wind models and to initialize magneto-frictional or full magnetohydrodynamic simulations of coronal and heliospheric magnetic structures. We present an enhanced magnetic field model that computes a magneto-frictional equilibrium under an imposed solar wind profile (such as Parker's solution or a comparable alternative). These "outflow fields" seem to approximate the actual coronal magnetic field more accurately than potential fields, require a similar computational time, and eliminate the necessity of imposing an artificial source surface. Consequently, they offer a practical alternative to potential field models for initializing time-evolving simulations or modeling the heliospheric magnetic field. We provide an open-source Python implementation in spherical coordinates and apply the model to data from Solar Cycle 24. The resulting outflow increases the open magnetic flux relative to the potential field model, thereby reducing the well-known discrepancy with in situ observations.

This study details the synthesis and comprehensive analysis of the structural and magnetic characteristics of polycrystalline NaVOAsO$_4$, utilizing x-ray diffraction, magnetization, electron spin resonance (ESR), $^{75}$As nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), and density-functional band structure calculations. An alternating spin-$1/2$ chain model effectively describes the temperature-dependent magnetic susceptibility, ESR intensity, and NMR line shifts, yielding an exchange coupling of $J/k_{\rm B}\simeq 52$ K and an alternation parameter of $\alpha \simeq 0.65$. Analysis of the high-field magnetic isotherm at $T=1.5$ K identifies a critical field of $H_{\rm c}\simeq 16$ T, corresponding to a zero-field spin gap of $\Delta_0/k_{\rm B}\simeq 21.4$ K. The activated behavior observed in both the NMR shift and spin-lattice relaxation rate at low temperatures further substantiates the existence of a singlet ground state. Notably, the spin chains do not align with the structural chains, and inter-chain couplings exhibit frustration. Given its relatively small spin gap, NaVOAsO$_4$ emerges as a promising candidate for future investigations under high magnetic fields.

Turbulent flows exhibit intricate dynamics driven by complex energy transfers between scales, non-stationary forces, and geometric limitations. This complexity gives rise to non-hyperbolic chaos, stochasticity, persistence that varies with the system state, and inherent unpredictability. These characteristics have hindered a complete description of the underlying turbulent (stochastic) attractor, which is essential for unraveling this complexity. In this work, we introduce a new framework to track how the structural features of phase-space trajectories evolve across scales, thereby achieving a full characterization of the attractor. We show that the properties of these dynamically invariant structures are scale-dependent. Specifically, in laboratory fluid experiments, we identify an intrinsic timescale arising purely from nonlinear interactions that governs the geometric and topological nature of phase-space trajectories. Due to the time- and scale-dependent variability of these attractors, we classify them as "chameleon attractors."

This report details measurements of charm mixing and $C\!P$ violation parameters derived from the decay-time-dependent ratio of $ D^0 \to K^+ \pi^- $ to $ D^0 \to K^- \pi^+ $ rates, alongside their charge-conjugate counterparts. The analysis utilizes $\overline{B}\to D^{*+} \mu^- X$ and charge-conjugate decays, with $D^{*+}\to D^0 \pi^+$, followed by $D^0\to K^{\mp} \pi^{\pm}$. Data from $pp$ collisions recorded by the LHCb experiment at center-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV, amounting to an integrated luminosity of 3 fb$^{-1}$, are examined under three scenarios: (i) mixing with $C\!P$ symmetry, (ii) mixing without direct $C\!P$ violation in Cabibbo-favored or doubly Cabibbo-suppressed amplitudes, and (iii) mixing permitting both direct $C\!P$ violation and $C\!P$ violation in the flavor eigenstate superpositions defining mass eigenstates. Additionally, these results are combined with data from a prior LHCb study of $D^0\to K \pi$ decays involving a disjoint set of $ D^{*+} $ candidates produced directly in $pp$ collisions. Across all analyses, the findings remain consistent with the hypothesis of $C\!P$ symmetry.

We demonstrate that Contrastive Learning (CL), encompassing a wide range of loss functions such as InfoNCE, can be unified into a coordinate-wise optimization framework involving network parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ and pairwise importance weights $\alpha$. In this setup, the \emph{max player} $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ learns representations to enhance contrastiveness, while the \emph{min player} $\alpha$ assigns greater weight to sample pairs with distinct identities but similar representations. This proposed framework, termed $\alpha$-CL, not only unifies diverse existing contrastive losses by varying the construction of $\alpha$, but also extrapolates to generate novel losses beyond established methods, thereby opening new avenues for loss design. These new losses achieve performance on CIFAR10, STL-10, and CIFAR-100 that is comparable to or superior to classic InfoNCE. Additionally, we conduct a detailed analysis of the max player, proving that for fixed $\alpha$, it is equivalent to Principal Component Analysis (PCA) in deep linear networks, where nearly all local minima are global, rank-1 solutions that recover optimal PCA. Finally, extending this analysis to 2-layer ReLU networks reveals that the fixed points of the max player can exhibit higher ranks.

This paper presents an approach for automatically generating a complete typographic font based on a limited set of characters. By extrapolating from a subset, we produce a full font containing the necessary characters for everyday use. The demand for automated Japanese font creation is high, as these fonts require over 1,000 characters; however, relying on professional typographers involves substantial time and financial costs. The proposed method serves as a valuable tool by allowing designers to avoid creating the majority of characters manually. The system utilizes strokes derived from provided samples to construct new characters, with these strokes extracted by leveraging a character skeleton dataset. The study offers three primary contributions: a novel stroke extraction technique applicable to both standard fonts and variations, a fully automated character construction process, and a method for selecting sample characters. We validate the approach by generating 2,965 characters across 47 fonts. Both objective and subjective evaluations confirm that the generated characters closely resemble handmade ones.

Shadow systems serve as approximations for reaction-diffusion problems derived from the limit of infinite diffusion coefficients, thereby simplifying the system and easing its analysis. This approximation's accuracy is evaluated across three temporal regimes: short durations accounting for the initial layer, long durations scaling with the diffusion coefficient as it approaches infinity, and the asymptotic state extending to $T = \infty$. This study concentrates on uniform error estimates within the long-time regime. By linearizing around a time-dependent shadow solution, we establish sufficient conditions to manage these errors. The methodology combines cut-off techniques, $L^p$-estimates, and stability criteria for the linearized shadow system. Furthermore, we demonstrate that extending these uniform error estimates globally in time may not be possible without imposing stricter assumptions on model linearization. The proposed approach is illustrated through reaction-diffusion equations coupled with ordinary differential equations (ODEs) and applied to a standard reaction-diffusion system. Finally, specific examples are provided to highlight the necessity and utility of the derived conditions.

This study introduces a sample of 14 hydrogen-rich superluminous supernovae (SLSNe II) discovered by the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) between 2018 and 2020. The selection includes all classified SLSNe with peak magnitudes brighter than $M_{g}<-20$ mag that exhibit broad, rather than narrow, Balmer emission lines, representing approximately 20% of all hydrogen-rich SLSNe identified during ZTF's Phase I. By analyzing their light curves and spectra alongside light-curve modeling, we seek to identify their energy sources. While the most luminous events closely resemble the prototype SN 2008es both photometrically and spectroscopically, others show stronger spectroscopic similarities to non-superluminous SNe II, particularly SNe II-L. Radioactive $^{56}$Ni decay is ruled out as the primary power source. Although light-curve models struggle to differentiate between circumstellar interaction (CSI) and a magnetar central engine, most SLSNe with available UV data display excess UV emission indicative of CSI, regardless of their photometric characteristics. Furthermore, the broad H$\alpha$ profiles of the brightest SLSNe II can be attributed to electron scattering within a symmetric circumstellar medium (CSM), whereas in other SLSNe II lacking narrow lines, the CSM appears confined and fully overtaken by the ejecta. CSI, potentially arising from mass loss during recent eruptions, is suggested as the dominant power source for most SLSNe II, with property diversity likely stemming from varying mass loss histories. However, given their radiated energy, the brightest SLSNe II may require an additional power source, possibly a combination of a central engine and CSI.

Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) relies on bag-level weak labels containing only presence or absence information, yet it suffers from a significant performance gap compared to fully supervised models, which hinders its practical use. To address this, this paper proposes a novel semi-weak label learning paradigm that serves as an intermediate solution. We define semi-weak labels as data where the presence or absence of a class is known alongside the exact count of each class, rather than just label proportions. We introduce a two-stage framework to tackle learning from these semi-weak labels, exploiting the fact that counting data is non-negative and discrete. Experiments were performed on generated samples from CIFAR-10, comparing our approach against fully-supervised, weakly-supervised, and Learning from Proportion (LLP) baselines. Our framework surpasses both the weakly-supervised and LLP baselines and achieves results comparable to the fully-supervised model. Additionally, comprehensive ablation studies were conducted to evaluate performance across different datasets, batch sizes, loss functions, architectural variations, bag sizes, and regularization techniques.

This study investigates methods for creating new music using a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) trained on a specific stylistic corpus. Rather than generating free improvisation through random latent sampling, we produce novel music by querying the network with input from a style distinct from its training data. This approach yields musical outputs with extended structural coherence that harmonize the query style with the network's learned characteristics. To regulate the degree of this stylistic blending, we introduce a noisy channel between the VAE's encoder and decoder, utilizing a bit-allocation algorithm derived from communication rate-distortion theory. Our experimental results offer fresh insights into the relationship between the representational and structural information within latent states and the query signal, indicating their potential utility for compositional applications.

Speech dereverberation plays a critical role in numerous speech technology applications, an area recently dominated by deep neural networks. While Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) have been adopted for sequence modeling in speech dereverberation, this study introduces a weighted multi-dilation depthwise-separable convolution to replace standard depthwise-separable convolutions within TCN architectures. This innovation allows the network to dynamically emphasize varying degrees of local information across its receptive field at each block. The resulting Weighted Multi-Dilation TCN (WD-TCN) consistently surpasses standard TCNs across different configurations. Furthermore, utilizing the WD-TCN offers a more parameter-efficient strategy for enhancing performance compared to simply increasing the number of convolutional blocks. The WD-TCN achieves its best improvement of 0.55 dB in scale-invariant signal-to-distortion ratio (SISDR) over the baseline, with the top-performing model reaching 12.26 dB SISDR on the WHAMR dataset.

This study aims to develop a mechatronic bipedal robot capable of navigating three-dimensional environments. The prototype features six actuated degrees of freedom (DoF): two per leg at the hip, controlling abduction/adduction and thigh flexion/extension, plus one DoF at the knee for shin flexion/extension. To enable dynamic underactuated walking, the robot utilizes point-feet legs. Each actuator assembly consists of a DC gear motor, a position encoder, a flexible joint creating a series elastic actuator, and a feedback controller for trajectory tracking. Topology optimization was applied to the shins to minimize overall mass, and the design was manufactured using 3D printing to create a functional prototype for actuator validation. Preliminary tests confirm the robot's ability to maintain a standing posture, paving the way for future research into dynamic control and trajectory generation for stable, periodic walking.

This study examines concentration characteristics of functions defined on random vectors within the discrete cube that satisfy either the stochastic covering property (SCP) or the strong Rayleigh property (SRP). Regarding SCP, we establish bounded-difference subgaussian inequalities that extend the work of Pemantle and Peres to matrix-valued contexts, thereby enhancing recent findings by Aoun, Banna, and Youssef. Under the stricter SRP assumption, we derive Bernstein-type inequalities for matrix-valued functions, which generalize previous bounds on linear combinations of positive definite matrices established by Kyng and Song. Additionally, we provide a detailed analysis of independent Bernoulli random variables conditioned on their sum, yielding strengthened estimates. These include modified log-Sobolev inequalities, Talagrand's convex distance inequality, and derived concentration results for convex functions and polynomials, alongside improved bounds for matrix-valued functions. These findings extend inequalities previously studied for the uniform measure on slices of the discrete cube by numerous researchers. Our methodology relies on recent advances by Hermon and Salez and employs a general framework centered on modified log-Sobolev inequalities over the discrete cube, a component that holds independent significance.

Currently, over 100,000 children in the U.S. foster care system await adoption through a semi-decentralized matching system managed by local agencies. Historically, agencies utilized a family-driven approach where prospective parents responded to caseworker announcements, but some have recently shifted to a caseworker-driven model where professionals actively identify suitable families. This paper introduces a new search-and-matching framework to analyze these processes using game theory. We demonstrate that equilibrium outcomes under threshold strategies form a lattice structure in both scenarios. Our primary theoretical finding indicates that family-driven search equilibria cannot Pareto dominate caseworker-driven ones, yet specific instances exist where a caseworker-driven outcome Pareto dominates all family-driven alternatives. Furthermore, when families exhibit sufficient impatience, the caseworker-driven approach benefits all children. Numerical simulations across a broad parameter range confirm that the majority of agents fare better under the caseworker-driven model.

This study introduces data-driven methods for forecasting the remaining useful life (RUL) of an aircraft engine fleet prone to various failure modes. The proposed approach utilizes a two-tier architecture of stacked Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs). The initial DCNN extracts a low-dimensional feature vector from normalized raw inputs, which is then fed into a second DCNN to estimate the RUL. Model selection was performed through Bayesian optimization employing a repeated random subsampling validation strategy. Consequently, this methodology secured third place in the 2021 PHM Conference Data Challenge.

The study of two-dimensional semiconductors has been revitalized recently by the identification of transition metal dichalcogenides. Within these materials, excitons control optical responses in the visible spectrum, offering significant potential for nonlinear spectroscopy. To model the coherence and polarization evolution of excitons following ultrafast excitation, we utilize an extended Bloch equation framework for a two-level system that incorporates a local field term representing exciton-exciton interactions. We compute four-wave mixing signals and examine how temporal and spectral characteristics vary with the delay between excitation pulses. Our analysis compares exact analytical solutions for ultrafast ($\delta$-shaped) pulses against numerical results for pulses of finite duration. When the nonlinear signal arises from two pulses, characteristic spectral line splittings are confined to short delays; however, with three-pulse excitation, these splittings, driven by the local field effect, endure for extended delays. We provide a clear explanation of these phenomena using the Bloch vector formalism and demonstrate how exciton occupation dynamics dictate the distinct four-wave mixing signals.

Decomposing network flows into weighted paths serves many purposes, ranging from optimizing specific metrics like path count, robustness, or length to satisfying bioinformatic needs where paths must reflect underlying data. However, on real-world inputs, no optimization criterion guarantees a unique correct decomposition. To address this, we propose identifying "safe paths"—subpaths that exist in every possible flow decomposition. While Ma, Zheng, and Kingsford previously tackled the issue of non-identifiability using a probabilistic framework and later introduced a quadratic-time algorithm for the AND-Quant problem (which generalizes safe path verification), we provide the first local characterization of safe paths in directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). This characterization enables a practical algorithm to find the complete set of safe paths. When evaluated on RNA transcript datasets against trivial methods (unitigs, extended unitigs) and the common greedy-width heuristic, our approach maintains perfect precision while achieving approximately 50% higher coverage than trivial algorithms. Although greedy-width offers better coverage, it suffers from significantly lower precision on complex graphs. Consequently, our algorithm outperforms greedy-width by roughly 20% on the F-Score metric for datasets containing many complex graphs. Furthermore, it demonstrates superior efficiency, being 3–5 times faster and using 1.2–2.2 times less space, making it a more effective and practical solution for bioinformatics applications involving flow decomposition.

All known gamma-ray sources with the highest energy levels are found within 0.5 degrees of exceptionally potent pulsars, prompting the inquiry into whether ultra-high-energy (UHE; $>$ 56 TeV) gamma emission is a universal characteristic of pulsars possessing high spin-down power. By utilizing four years of data from the High Altitude Water Cherenkov (HAWC) Gamma-Ray Observatory, we conducted a joint-likelihood analysis of ten such powerful pulsars to detect UHE gamma rays correlated with these positions. We report a significant detection ($>$ 3$\sigma$), suggesting that UHE gamma-ray emission is a generic trait of powerful pulsars. Furthermore, we examine the gamma-ray emission mechanisms and the implications of this finding, noting that the specific environment surrounding each pulsar seems to influence the magnitude of the emission.

Recent studies have increasingly focused on interference-aware routing (IAR) protocols to facilitate multiple concurrent transmissions in next-generation wireless systems. However, current IAR protocols often overlook node cooperation during route establishment, primarily because incentivizing cooperation and modeling such interactions are complex challenges. Furthermore, neighboring nodes cannot directly observe a node's cooperative behavior. To address these issues, this paper introduces a novel routing method that leverages node cooperation data to enhance edge computing-enabled 5G networks. The proposed metric evaluates both generated and received interference: the received interference component maintains the Signal-to-Interference-plus-Noise Ratio (SINR) above a required threshold along the route, while the generated interference component prioritizes nodes that minimize disruption to others. Simulation results demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms conventional routing protocols in ad hoc networks, achieving higher throughput and lower outage probabilities.

This study examines particles moving along fractional paths and employs fractional derivatives to expand the dynamic dimensions of Quantum Field Theory. We formulate the Lagrangians for fractional scalar, vector, and spinor fields to derive their propagators via the path integral method. Subsequently, we calculate typical tree-level and one-loop diagrams corresponding to QED scenarios. The results demonstrate the dependence of amplitudes on dimension. Furthermore, our one-loop calculations yield outcomes consistent with dimensional regularization as the dimension converges to the Standard Model value. Consequently, fractional path integrals can be viewed as an equivalent theoretical framework for regularizing divergences in standard Quantum Field Theory.

Recent literature has increasingly utilized Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to create unseen evasion samples, which are then integrated into original training datasets to enhance the detection capabilities of machine learning (ML) classifiers through adversarial training. However, the efficacy of these generated samples depends heavily on the quality of the available training data, a significant challenge in low-data domains such as medical imaging and cybersecurity where anomaly instances are scarce. To address this, we introduce the Evasion Generative Adversarial Network (EVAGAN), a novel GAN architecture specifically designed for low-data regimes to improve ML classifier detection via oversampling. EVAGAN uniquely functions by not only generating evasion samples but also employing its discriminator as an evasion-aware classifier. Using the Auxiliary Classifier GAN (ACGAN) as a benchmark, we evaluated EVAGAN on cybersecurity datasets (ISCX-2014, CIC-2017, and CIC-2018 botnets) and computer vision datasets (MNIST). Our results demonstrate that EVAGAN surpasses ACGAN in detection performance, training stability, and time complexity when handling unbalanced datasets. The EVAGAN generator rapidly learns to produce samples from the low-frequency class while simultaneously hardening its discriminator. Unlike traditional ML classifiers that require post-training security hardening after adversarial exposure to GAN-generated data, EVAGAN inherently eliminates this need. Experimental analysis confirms that EVAGAN serves as an efficient, evasion-hardened model for low-data scenarios in both cybersecurity and computer vision, with the source code available at HTTPS://www.github.com/rhr407/EVAGAN.

Identifying dark matter stands as a central goal in contemporary physics and cosmology, with numerous collaborations currently conducting or planning searches for axions. As the field advances toward next-generation detectors, a critical inquiry arises: can we uncover novel experimental configurations and identify them effectively? This work introduces a fresh methodology for experimental design by employing gradient descent algorithms to locate optimal detector architectures. We demonstrate the feasibility of this approach through a proof of principle study involving one-dimensional detectors, systematically adjusting bulk properties to determine the best design. Surprisingly, the algorithm-optimized detector outperformed the initial human-designed experiment. This success paves the way for exploring more intricate two- and three-dimensional designs across diverse materials and boundary geometries. Furthermore, it suggests the potential for utilizing advanced gradient descent algorithms to conduct a more comprehensive survey of the design landscape.

While deep learning diagnostic capabilities improve with more annotated data, acquiring large volumes through manual labeling is costly and laborious. Since clinical experts routinely evaluate diagnostic images and document their findings in reports, utilizing unlabelled examinations alongside these clinical reports offers a solution to the manual labeling bottleneck. We hypothesize that detection models can be effectively trained using a semi-supervised approach, where automatic annotations are generated from model predictions and refined by sparse information derived from clinical reports. To validate this, we developed clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) segmentation models, guiding automatic annotations based on the number of clinically significant findings noted in radiology reports. Our dataset comprised 7,756 prostate MRI scans, with 3,050 manually annotated. We assessed detection performance on 300 exams from an external center using histopathology-confirmed ground truth. Results showed that semi-supervised training increased the patient-based diagnostic area under the receiver operating characteristic curve from $87.2 \pm 0.8\%$ to $89.4 \pm 1.0\%$ ($P<10^{-4}$) and boosted lesion-based sensitivity at one false positive per case from $76.4 \pm 3.8\%$ to $83.6 \pm 2.3\%$ ($P<10^{-4}$). Furthermore, semi-supervised training proved to be 14 times more annotation-efficient for case-based performance and 6 times more efficient for lesion-based performance. These results confirm the feasibility of our training methodology. Source code is accessible at github.com/DIAGNijmegen/Report-Guided-Annotation, and the top-performing csPCa detection algorithm is available at grand-challenge.org/algorithms/bpmri-cspca-detection-report-guided-annotations/.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) serve as potent instruments for information compression and distillation. However, their immense scale and intricate architecture, characterized by billions of interdependent parameters, make direct microscopic examination challenging. Consequently, a prevalent approach involves isolating slow variables that smooth out the erratic fluctuations of rapid microscopic components.
