In this work, we uncover a comparable separation of scales within fully trained, finitely over-parameterized deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and fully connected networks (FCNs). We demonstrate that DNN layers interact exclusively through the second moments (kernels) of their pre-activations and activations, which exhibit nearly Gaussian fluctuations. While these kernels remain static in infinite-width DNNs, they dynamically adapt to data in finite-width networks, generating a manageable, data-informed Gaussian Process. This derived thermodynamic framework for deep learning offers precise predictions across diverse scenarios and introduces novel methodologies for the analysis and comprehension of DNNs broadly.

Recent advances have enabled text-to-speech (TTS) systems to generate audio nearly indistinguishable from human speech; however, their prosody often remains flatter and less expressive than natural speech. To enhance naturalness and variability, it is essential to disentangle speaker identity from prosody within these systems. This paper introduces a novel neural TTS model that addresses this challenge by conditioning a Tacotron2-like architecture on flow-normalized speaker embeddings and replacing the standard reference encoder with a learned latent distribution designed to capture intra-sentence prosodic variability. By eliminating the reliance on the reference encoder, the model effectively mitigates the common issue of speaker leakage, resulting in more distinctive synthesized outputs during inference. Quantitative evaluations demonstrate that the proposed model achieves significantly greater prosodic variance and improved speaker distinctiveness compared to baseline systems, all while maintaining high speaker intelligibility. Furthermore, the use of normalized speaker embeddings facilitates much richer speaker interpolation, substantially enhancing the distinctiveness of the interpolated voices.

The newly launched SRG mission's eROSITA X-ray telescope serendipitously detected the galaxy cluster A3408 ($z=0.0420$) while observing the AGN 1H0707-495 during a point source observation. Despite its luminosity and vast size, this cluster had not previously been detected by any contemporary X-ray observatory. A neighboring cluster, A3407 ($z=0.0428$), located to the northwest, appears to be in close proximity in projection ($\sim 1.7$ Mpc), suggesting the pair may be undergoing a pre- or post-merger phase.

We conducted a comprehensive X-ray analysis of A3408, generating particle-background-subtracted and exposure-corrected images along with surface brightness profiles across various sectors. Spectral analysis extended to $1.4r_{500}$, accompanied by a temperature map illustrating the intracluster medium (ICM) distribution. Furthermore, we utilized RASS data to estimate bulk properties for both A3407 and A3408 through growth curve analysis and scaling relations.

Imaging results reveal a complex morphology for A3408, characterized by a pronounced elongation along the SE-NW axis. Comparing surface brightness profiles in the four cardinal directions confirms that the NW and SE sectors exhibit significantly higher brightness than the SW and NE sectors. We derived a gas temperature of ${\rm k_B}T_{500}=(2.23\pm0.09)$ keV. The temperature profile indicates a hot core within $2'$ of the emission peak, with a temperature of ${\rm k_B}T=3.04^{+0.29}_{-0.25}$ keV. Using a mass-temperature relation, we iteratively calculated a mass of $M_{500}=(9.27\pm0.75)\times 10^{13}M_{\odot}$. The projected $r_{200}$ radii of A3407 and A3408 overlap, supporting the likelihood of ongoing interactions. A 2D temperature map shows higher temperatures in the western direction compared to the east.

A3407 and A3408 are likely in a pre-merger state, influencing ICM properties; specifically, elevated temperatures toward A3407 suggest adiabatic compression or shocks resulting from their interaction.

This study addresses the context aggregation challenge in semantic image segmentation. While current research primarily enhances pixel representations by aggregating contextual data within single images, these approaches overlook the value of pixel representations for specific classes that exist beyond the input image itself. To remedy this, the paper introduces a method to mine contextual information extending beyond individual images to further enrich pixel representations. First, a dynamically updated feature memory module is established to store dataset-level representations for various categories. Subsequently, the class probability distribution for each pixel representation is learned under the supervision of ground-truth segmentation masks. Finally, each pixel's representation is augmented by aggregating these dataset-level representations according to the corresponding class probability distribution. Additionally, leveraging the stored dataset-level representations, a representation consistency learning strategy is proposed to enable the classification head to better achieve intra-class compactness and inter-class dispersion. This method can be seamlessly integrated into existing segmentation frameworks, such as FCN, PSPNet, OCRNet, and DeepLabV3, yielding consistent performance gains. By mining contextual information beyond individual images, the proposed approach achieves state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmarks, including ADE20K, LIP, Cityscapes, and COCO-Stuff.

Based on the count of observed forward electron scattering events from the 1982 CERN-WA-066 beam dump experiment at the Big European Bubble Chamber, we establish constraints on millicharged dark states and particles possessing electric or magnetic dipole moments. These dark states, generated mainly via meson decays induced by the 400 GeV proton beam within the dump, result in upper mass limits extending to the GeV range due to the absence of excess events. Our findings surpass the sensitivity of bounds set by all other experiments, notably CHARM II.

Conversational agents are rapidly approaching human-level performance in open-domain dialogues, yet they often express insensitive, harmful, or nonsensical views that undermine user trust in the system's ethical integrity. Addressing these moral deviations is challenging due to the lack of universal moral standards and the existence of conflicting judgments for a single scenario. This study presents a novel resource designed not to dictate moral resolutions but to enable a systematic analysis of the values, intuitions, and moral judgments embedded in dialogue system outputs. The Moral Integrity Corpus (MIC) comprises 38,000 prompt-reply pairs annotated with 99,000 distinct Rules of Thumb (RoTs), where each RoT represents a specific moral belief explaining why a response might be deemed acceptable or problematic. We further categorize these RoTs using nine moral and social attributes and evaluate classification performance. Crucially, we demonstrate that current neural language models can automatically generate new RoTs that reasonably characterize unseen interactions, though they face difficulties in certain contexts. These results indicate that MIC will serve as a valuable tool for analyzing the implicit moral assumptions of language models and for flexibly benchmarking the ethical integrity of conversational agents. Data can be downloaded from https://github.com/GT-SALT/mic.

Deep Learning has driven significant research and development across diverse real-world data modalities, recently intensifying interest in the rapidly evolving intersection of Vision and Language. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of current trends in visual and linguistic research, examining task formulations, solutions for semantic perception and content generation, and specific task-related developments. It further discusses evaluation strategies, emerging challenges, and recent multi-disciplinary insights that are steering the field toward more modular and transparent intelligent systems. Ultimately, this survey highlights key directions in recent VisLang literature and explores the future trajectory of the field.

Although AI has seen recent advancements, comprehending stories remains an under-explored challenge. To address this, we have gathered, preprocessed, and made publicly available the Synopses of Movie Narratives (SyMoN) dataset, which includes 5,193 video summaries of popular films and television shows. SyMoN features naturalistic storytelling created by humans for human audiences, offering broader story coverage and more frequent references to mental states compared to similar video-language datasets. Unlike most existing video-text collections, SyMoN exhibits significant semantic gaps between visual and textual modalities, driven by reporting biases and descriptions of mental states. We have established benchmarks for video-text retrieval and zero-shot alignment on movie summary videos. Through SyMoN, we aim to provide a foundation for advancing multimodal story understanding.

This research addresses the challenge of detecting object instances within dynamic settings where human interaction causes frequent appearance variations, such as those resulting from object manipulation, occlusion, or background shifts. These factors create significantly greater intra-instance appearance variability compared to static scenarios. To investigate these difficulties, we introduced a novel benchmark comprising over 1,500 instances derived from the EPIC-KITCHENS dataset, featuring natural activities, alongside a comprehensive analysis. Experimental findings indicate that advancing performance requires (i) robustness to instance-specific appearance changes, (ii) the integration of both low-level (e.g., color, texture) and high-level (e.g., object category) features, and (iii) effective foreground feature selection when objects overlap.

We introduce a non-autonomous stochastic dynamical framework to characterize the seasonal and interannual fluctuations of the El Ni\~no-Southern Oscillation (ENSO). Model parameters are derived through systematic statistical inference utilizing partial observations limited to sea surface temperature data. This methodology successfully replicates the observed seasonal phase locking and associated uncertainties, alongside the highly non-Gaussian statistical properties of ENSO. Furthermore, we reconstruct the intermittent time series of latent processes, such as thermocline depth and wind bursts.

By employing the coefficients established by Bargmann and Moshinsky to decompose the su(3) algebra of three-dimensional Cartesian oscillator states into so(3) angular momentum submultiplets, we perform unitary rotations on finite pixellated "volume images" represented as three-dimensional Cartesian arrays. The process of converting between spherical and Cartesian bases translates the subgroup of rotations inherent in the spherical framework into rotations within the Cartesian framework. This enables the correct concatenation and inversion of these unitary transformations, ensuring that no information is lost.

This work develops a kinetic theory regarding microinstabilities in a cylindrical plasma generated by a cylindrical helicon wave with azimuthal symmetry ($m_{0}=0$). The theoretical framework relies on a linear integral equation derived for the Fourier-Bessel transform of the electrostatic potential. This equation captures the plasma's response to radial inhomogeneities present at both the macroscale, comparable to the helicon wave's radial structure, and the microscale, comparable to the electron thermal Larmor radius. The theory uncovers a novel macroscale phenomenon: a steady azimuthal rotation of electrons with a radially varying angular velocity, induced by the radial inhomogeneity of the helicon wave. By solving the integral equation for the electrostatic potential in the short-wavelength limit, a functional equation is obtained, which couples the potential with an infinite series of satellites separated by the helicon wave frequency. This serves as the fundamental equation for analyzing the dispersion characteristics of parametric and current-driven instabilities in radially inhomogeneous cylindrical helicon plasma. Furthermore, an analytical solution to the resulting dispersion equation is presented for the high-frequency kinetic ion acoustic instability in cylindrical helicon plasma, which arises from the combined effects of electron diamagnetic drift and the steady azimuthal rotation of electrons relative to ions, characterized by a radially inhomogeneous angular velocity.

Semantic segmentation remains a leading field within medical image computing. Remarkably, nnU-Net, first conceptualized in 2018, continues to deliver robust, ready-to-use solutions for diverse segmentation challenges and frequently serves as the foundation for algorithms that win competitions. In this study, we employed nnU-Net for the AMOS2022 challenge, which presented distinctive requirements: a massive dataset featuring 15 target structures and the necessity to process both MRI and CT scans. By fine-tuning hyperparameters, integrating residual connections into the encoder, and developing a bespoke postprocessing approach, we significantly outperformed the standard nnU-Net baseline. Our final ensemble model achieved Dice scores of 90.13 for Task 1 (CT) and 89.06 for Task 2 (CT+MRI) through 5-fold cross-validation on the training data.

Using a tablet, we experimentally measured how the magnetic field (B) varies with electrical current and axial distance (z) from a coil. Our data confirms the inverse cubic relationship between B and z with high precision ($B \propto z^{-3}$), allowing us to accurately determine the air permeability $\mu_{air}$. We observed this same dependence when replacing the coil with a magnet. Despite relying on straightforward data fitting for initial estimates, a more rigorous error analysis further validates our calculated value for $\mu_{air}$.

The upcoming circular high-energy collider is anticipated to be a lepton facility, either FCC-ee at CERN or CEPC in China. Nevertheless, civil engineering plans anticipate constructing detector caverns larger than those strictly necessary for lepton operations, enabling the installation of a hadron collider within the same tunnel without additional infrastructure. This design flexibility allows for the addition of specialized instrumentation along the cavern walls to detect new long-lived particles during lepton collider runs. Using heavy neutral leptons as a case study, we demonstrate that such an arrangement could enhance sensitivity to the squared mixing parameter by nearly half an order of magnitude.

Recent decades have seen studies suggesting that magnetic fields may influence galactic rotation curves, though their impact is generally minor compared to dark matter and baryonic matter. This letter revisits the magnetic field's effect on the Milky Way's rotation curve, demonstrating that the inner region could be significantly altered by it. Consequently, the previously proposed addition of an inner bulge component to explain inner rotation data is unnecessary, as the magnetic field alone accounts for the excess velocity observed between 5 and 50 parsecs from the Galactic center. Furthermore, our analysis constrains the strength of the central regular magnetic field's azimuthal component to approximately 50–60 $\mu$G, aligning with observational data.

Current limitations in understanding mitochondrial disease pathology render these conditions untreatable. To uncover the mechanisms underlying such pathologies, we examine mitochondrial protein expression in skeletal myofibres (SM) using Imaging Mass Cytometry (IMC). IMC generates high-dimensional, multi-channel pseudo-images that capture spatial variations in protein expression across tissues and subcellular regions. Analyzing these images statistically typically demands semi-automated annotation of thousands of SMs from patient muscle biopsy data. This study explores the application of deep learning (DL) directly to raw IMC data, bypassing manual pre-processing, statistical summaries, and traditional models. We first trained state-of-the-art computer vision DL models on all available image channels, both individually and in combination, observing accuracy levels that exceeded expectations. Subsequently, we employed advanced explainable AI techniques relevant to computer vision to determine the basis of these models' predictions. Several resulting visual explainability maps highlight image features that align with recent hypotheses regarding mitochondrial disease progression within myofibres.

Due to the irregular nature of data encountered in certain fluid mechanics problems, this study focuses on finding very weak solutions for the stationary Stokes problem with Navier-type boundary conditions within a three-dimensional exterior domain. This scenario models the movement of a viscous, incompressible fluid around an obstacle, allowing for slip along the obstacle's surface. Given that the flow domain is unbounded, the analysis is conducted in weighted Sobolev spaces to regulate the solutions' behavior at infinity. The primary objective is to establish both the existence and uniqueness of a very weak solution within a Hilbertian framework.

The recent observation of triple heavy vector boson production ($pp \to VVV$, where $V = W, Z$) opens a new avenue for precision measurements that could effectively probe the Yukawa couplings of first-generation light quarks. In this process, altered quark interactions with an off-shell Higgs boson cause the partonic cross-sections to rise sharply with energy, resulting in a distinct enhancement of the transverse momentum ($p_T$) distributions for the final-state leptons and quarks. We have quantified this phenomenon and evaluated the current and future $2\sigma$ sensitivities for the up, down, and strange quark Yukawa couplings. Specifically, our analysis indicates that the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) could achieve an $\mathcal{O}(400)$ sensitivity for the down quark Yukawa relative to Standard Model predictions, representing a tenfold improvement over existing sensitivities in this channel; the Future Circular Collider (FCC-hh) could further enhance this to $\mathcal{O}(30)$. These results offer constraints that are both competitive with and complementary to those derived from global fits and other on-shell methods. Furthermore, the triboson sensitivity at the HL-LHC is comparable to other LHC Higgs probes, effectively probing dimension-6 SMEFT operators suppressed by a scale of approximately $\mathcal{O}(1)$ TeV.

This paper introduces the MeLa-BitChute dataset, comprising over 3 million videos from 61,000 channels collected over 2.5 years (June 2019 to December 2021) from BitChute, a popular alternative to YouTube. The dataset includes extensive video-level metadata such as comments, channel descriptions, and view counts. You can access the MeLa-BitChute dataset at: https://dataverse.harvard.edu/dataset.xhtml?persistentId=doi:10.7910/DVN/KRD1VS.

By analyzing the extreme limits of disk motion, we have determined the surface magnetic field strengths ($B_0$) for the Z-source systems GX 17+2 and Cyg X-2. The derived values are approximately $(1\text{--}5)\times 10^8$ G for GX 17+2 and $(1\text{--}3)\times 10^8$ G for Cyg X-2, levels that are comparable to those found in millisecond X-ray pulsars and atoll sources. It is probable that the magnetic axis of Z-source neutron stars aligns parallel to their rotation axis, a configuration that likely explains the absence of observed pulsations in these systems.

The importance of word vector sequence ordering in text reading has been well-established in natural language processing (NLP). In contrast, the principles governing sequence ordering in computer vision (CV) remain underexplored, particularly regarding why "zigzag" flattening (ZF) is the default approach for arranging image patches in vision transformers (ViTs). Notably, ZF fails to preserve the invariance of feature point positions when decomposing multi-scale images. To address this, we investigate Hilbert fractal flattening (HF) as an alternative sequence ordering method for CV and compare it with ZF. HF has demonstrated superiority over other curves in maintaining spatial locality during multi-scale dimensional transformations and can be seamlessly integrated into most deep neural networks (DNNs). Extensive experiments show that HF delivers consistent and significant performance improvements across various architectures. Ultimately, we hope our findings inspire further research into image reading flattening strategies.

Although virtual reality research typically investigates user perception and performance as separate entities, the Action-Specific Perception (ASP) theory suggests that task performance directly influences an individual's perception of space and time relevant to that task. This study explores the relationship between performance and perception, specifically examining the impact of different tactile feedback modalities. A user study involving 24 participants required them to complete a Fitts's law target acquisition task using three distinct feedback types: visual, visuo-electrotactile, and visuo-vibrotactile. Participants executed 18 trials, varying by target size, distance, and feedback modality (3 sizes × 2 distances × 3 modalities). Perceptual assessments for size, distance, and movement time were conducted after each trial. Performance results indicated that electrotactile feedback yielded significantly higher accuracy than both visual and vibrotactile feedback, which produced the lowest accuracy. While electrotactile and visual feedback resulted in similar reaction times, vibrotactile feedback led to substantially slower responses. Although the patterns of perceptual differences mirrored the performance differences, none reached statistical significance; however, the data confirmed that performance does modulate perception. Significant action-specific effects on spatial and time perception were observed: variations in accuracy affected size and time perception, while changes in movement speed influenced distance perception. Additionally, the index of difficulty was found to impact perception. These findings underscore the critical role of haptic feedback in performance and highlight the necessity of accounting for action-specific effects on spatial and time perception in future virtual reality research.

Ram pressure stripping (RPS) is recognized as a primary environmental mechanism capable of depleting interstellar gas from galaxies within clusters. Typically, this process is modeled as a contest between the ram pressure exerted by the intracluster medium (ICM) and the gravitational anchoring force holding the galaxy's interstellar medium (ISM) in place. Nevertheless, the real-world stripping mechanism is often more intricate, influenced by complex gas physics including compression, geometrical self-shielding, and thermal cooling or heating. To determine if observed RPS signatures can be adequately explained by simple momentum transfer, we compared measured stripping radii of Virgo cluster galaxies across various RPS stages—derived from HI observations—with predicted gas truncation radii under specific conditions. For galaxies experiencing active RPS, we generally observed good alignment between predictions and measurements within the limits of uncertainty. Conversely, galaxies in early or late RPS phases, or those exhibiting additional environmental effects like tidal interactions or starvation, displayed notable discrepancies. Our findings suggest that the standard RPS relation functions reasonably well broadly when RPS is the dominant force and the surrounding environment is well-defined; otherwise, a more detailed examination of secondary mechanisms and local conditions is necessary to evaluate the impact of RPS on a given target.

An investigation into Beyond the Standard Model double-$\beta$ decay modes of $^{76}$Ge was conducted using data from the Phase II of the GERmanium Detector Array (GERDA) experiment at the Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso in Italy. This study established enhanced constraints on Majoron-mediated decays compared to prior $^{76}$Ge experiments, yielding half-life limits around $10^{23}$ years. Additionally, this work presents the first-ever limits on Lorentz invariance violation effects in $^{76}$Ge double-$\beta$ decay, constraining the isotropic coefficient $\mathring{a}_\text{of}^{(3)}$ to approximately $10^{-6}$ GeV. Furthermore, the first experimental bounds on light exotic fermions, such as sterile neutrinos, within the context of double-$\beta$ decay have been set.

We introduce a dynamical model for generic 2D crowds where individual agents perceive their local surroundings, including neighboring agents and domain boundaries, and can pursue static targets. This model integrates characteristics typical of various "active matter" systems, such as collision avoidance, agent alignment, and target-seeking behavior. Its novelty lies in naturally combining topological and metrical features based on the agent's local Voronoi diagram. Despite relying on only two parameters, the model successfully reproduces a broad spectrum of collective behaviors.

Millions of users globally leverage the advantages of data processing and sharing within cloud environments. Consequently, data security and privacy are essential prerequisites for such systems. The extensive utilization and exchange of data among users create opportunities for security vulnerabilities. This paper explores the cloud environment, examining its benefits, challenges, and emerging research trends specifically focused on the secure processing and sharing of data.

Let $k$ denote a perfect field with characteristic $p > 2$, and let $R := W(k)[\![t_1, \dots, t_d]\!]$ represent the power series ring constructed over the Witt vectors. Consider $X$ as a smooth, proper scheme defined over $R$. The primary objective of this paper is to generalize the classical Fontaine-Messing theory to the context where the base ring is $R$. Specifically, we establish comparison theorems linking the torsion crystalline cohomology of $X/R$ with its torsion \'etale cohomology within this framework.

We examine a planar Hamiltonian system defined by $Jz' = 
abla_z H(t,z)$, where the Hamiltonian $H: \mathbb{R} 	imes \mathbb{R}^2 	o \mathbb{R}$ is periodic in time, satisfies $
abla_z H(t,0) \equiv 0$, and exhibits asymptotic linearity of $
abla_z H(t,z)$ as $\vert z \vert 	o +\infty$. By re-examining index theory for linear planar Hamiltonian systems and applying the Poincaré-Birkhoff fixed point theorem, we establish that the nonlinear system possesses subharmonic solutions of sufficiently high order $k$, provided that the rotation numbers (or, equivalently, the mean Conley-Zehnder indices) of the linearizations at zero and at infinity differ. The results are applied to planar Hamiltonian systems derived from second-order scalar ordinary differential equations.

This study examines the double longitudinal-spin asymmetry in semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering (SIDIS) for dihadron production, where the total transverse momentum of the hadron pairs is integrated out. Specifically, we explore the source of the $\cos\phi_R$ azimuthal asymmetry by considering the interplay between the helicity distribution $g_1$ and the twist-3 dihadron fragmentation function $\widetilde{D}^{\sphericalangle}$. Using a spectator model, we compute the interference term $\widetilde{D}^{\sphericalangle}_{ot}$ arising from $s$-wave and $p$-wave contributions. We provide estimates for the $\cos\phi_R$ asymmetry under COMPASS kinematics, which are currently utilized in polarized deep inelastic scattering experiments. Additionally, predictions for this asymmetry at JLab 12GeV and a future Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) are presented. Our findings suggest that measuring the $\cos\phi_R$ asymmetry in SIDIS offers an optimal method for investigating the dihadron fragmentation function $\widetilde{D}^{\sphericalangle}$.

This study investigates CP violation within the phase-space distributions of $D^0$ and $\bar{D}^0$ decays into the $K^-\pi^+\pi^-\pi^+$ and $\pi^-\pi^+\pi^+\pi^-$ final states. The analysis utilizes a 2011 LHCb data set with an integrated luminosity of $1.0\text{ fb}^{-1}$ from $pp$ collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV. For the $K^-\pi^+\pi^-\pi^+$ channel, the four-body phase space is segmented into 32 bins, each containing roughly 1800 decays; no CP asymmetry exceeding 6.5% is found, and the $p$-value assuming no CP violation is 9.1%. Similarly, the $\pi^-\pi^+\pi^+\pi^-$ phase space is divided into 128 bins with approximately 2500 decays per bin, yielding a $p$-value of 41% under the no CP violation hypothesis, with no bin showing a CP asymmetry above 5.5%. All findings align with the hypothesis of no CP violation given the current sensitivity.

Convolutional neural networks (ConvNets) are utilized to explore phase transitions in two-dimensional complex plasmas. Langevin dynamics simulations generate particle configurations across diverse thermodynamic states, from which bitmap images representing two extreme conditions are created and used as training data for the ConvNet. This approach yields a phase diagram, and the trained model can subsequently be applied directly to video microscopy sequences to analyze melting processes in experimental settings.

We describe a method for constructing a proper holomorphic embedding $f\colon \Bbb P^1\setminus C\hookrightarrow \Bbb C^2$, where $C$ represents a Cantor set formed by iteratively removing increasingly narrow vertical and horizontal strips from a square with side length 2, thereby enabling the measure of $C$ to approach 4 arbitrarily closely.

This study re-examines the determination of branching fractions for heavy quarkonium decaying into light hadrons at $e^+e^-$ colliders. In such annihilation experiments, background contributions from the continuum amplitude and its interference with the resonance amplitude constitute irreducible sources of uncertainty. As experimental precision advances, these effects grow increasingly significant. While the continuum contribution can be readily subtracted using data collected off the resonance peak, the interference term relies on the relative magnitude and phase between the resonance and continuum amplitudes. To quantify these impacts, two ratios are introduced: $r_{R}^{f}$, representing the ratio of the interference contribution to the resonance term, and $r_{c}^{f}$, representing the ratio to the continuum term. Our findings indicate that $r_{R}^{f}$ may reach several percent for narrow resonances, whereas both $r_{R}^{f}$ and $r_{c}^{f}$ can be substantial for broad resonances. Consequently, for branching fraction measurements targeting percent-level or higher precision, the interference effect is critical and must be accurately measured or estimated.

This study investigates the energies and decay widths of exotic 7He nuclear states using an ab initio framework. The No-Core Shell Model (NCSM), combined with a specific extrapolation method, is employed to calculate the state spectrum, utilizing the well-validated Daejeon16 potential based on extensive data. The research applies a previously developed NCSM-based methodology that constructs an orthogonalized basis for cluster channels and matches the resulting cluster form factors with asymptotic wave functions to determine decay widths. The study demonstrates the approach's capability to compute partial decay widths for transitions into diverse channels characterized by varying fragmentation types, spins, relative angular momenta, and amplitudes. Finally, the obtained results are compared against other microscopic calculations.

Achieving atomic-scale smooth thin films is essential for the effective integration and operation of numerous multilayer devices. Yet, the inherent island-like growth mechanism often hinders the creation of such ultrasmooth surfaces for many critical functional materials. To address this challenge, we introduce a negative entropy-infusing technique that utilizes evanescent waves to boost downward interlayer diffusion of adatoms, thereby converting island-like growth into a layer-by-layer mode. We derived the governing equations for optical force and the reduced diffusion barrier, and numerical simulations of a simplified case confirm that this theoretical framework yields markedly improved surface morphologies.

Starting with a Lie algebroid equipped with a representation, we define a graded Lie algebra where its Maurer-Cartan elements correspond to relative Rota-Baxter operators. Utilizing the associated cohomology theory, we analyze infinitesimal deformations and the extendability of $n$-th order deformations to $(n+1)$-th order for these operators. Additionally, we construct a graded Lie algebra on the space of multi-derivations of a vector bundle, whose Maurer-Cartan elements represent left-symmetric algebroids. We demonstrate a homomorphism from the controlling graded Lie algebra of relative Rota-Baxter operators to that of left-symmetric algebroids, thereby inducing a natural homomorphism between their respective cohomology groups and deformation cohomology groups. As applications, we establish the controlling graded Lie algebra and cohomology theory for Koszul-Vinberg structures defined on left-symmetric algebroids.

Quantum computers utilize quantum bits and apply gate operations to execute computations. Although physicists aim to design arbitrary gates for quantum algorithms, physical constraints on the hardware limit the available gate set. Consequently, they must construct sequences from permitted gates that approximate the desired operations, a process known as quantum compiling. Austin Fowler introduced a method capable of finding optimal gate sequences in exponential time, though it remains practical for typical scenarios. This paper outlines several optimizations to his algorithm; while these enhancements do not alter its exponential complexity, they boost empirical performance by one to two orders of magnitude.

This study presents and assesses a new, highly effective computational method for quantitative finance using stylized examples. The approach relies on Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) and neural networks, with powerful open-source optimization libraries enabling efficient implementation even within high-dimensional frameworks. Applications to free-boundary problems associated with American and Bermudan options demonstrate both the method's capabilities and the challenges it may encounter. Furthermore, the influence of training data size is examined through a simplified Merton-type problem, while the classical option hedging scenario highlights the necessity of utilizing market generators or conducting a large number of simulations.

We introduce Adorym, an optimization-driven framework for reconstructing x-ray images. This system offers a versatile forward model, enabling a single codebase to support diverse imaging techniques, from near-field holography to fly-scan ptychographic tomography. Leveraging automatic differentiation for optimization, Adorym can flexibly refine experimental variables such as probe locations, multi-hologram alignment, and object tilts. Built with robust parallel processing capabilities, it facilitates the handling of large datasets on high-performance computing platforms. We validate the framework using multiple experimental datasets, demonstrating that parameter refinement leads to enhanced image quality.

We examined a hot strange star immediately following a supernova collapse, modeling it as a system of strange, up, and down quarks to determine its bulk properties at finite temperatures using a density-dependent bag constant. To parameterize this constant, we utilized results from our lowest-order constrained variational (LOCV) calculations of asymmetric nuclear matter. Our analysis of the strange star's structural properties across various temperatures reveals that the maximum mass diminishes as temperature rises. Furthermore, when comparing our findings with those derived from a fixed bag constant, we observed that the density-dependent approach yields higher maximum mass and radius values for the strange star.

This research investigates the link between song lyrics and mood using a data-driven approach. Our dataset comprises nearly one million songs, with mood associations sourced from user playlists on Spotify. We leverage state-of-the-art transformer-based natural language processing models to identify these associations. Our findings indicate that a pretrained transformer model operates effectively in a zero-shot setting, capturing song-mood relationships without additional training on our specific data. Additionally, we demonstrate that training the model on song-mood associations yields high accuracy in predicting these links for unseen songs. Furthermore, by comparing models utilizing lyrics versus acoustic features, we observe that the relative importance of lyrics in mood prediction varies depending on the specific mood. Finally, we validate whether the models capture human-like interpretations of lyrics and acoustics through an annotation task where humans judged the relevance of moods to songs based on these features.

This document summarizes the fifth edition of the CASE workshop, organized within the EMNLP 2022 conference. The event features regular papers, two keynotes, working papers from shared task participants, and task overview documents. The workshop unites diverse facets of event information gathering, bridging technical and social science disciplines. Beyond advancements in depth, the inclusion and acceptance of multimodal approaches highlight the expanding scope of this interdisciplinary field.

Reconstructing sky brightness from radio interferometers typically relies on gridding techniques, which function as histograms in spatial Fourier space. For measuring the Epoch of Reionisation (EoR) 21 cm power spectrum, extreme gridding resolutions are necessary to mitigate spectral contamination, a topic previously examined in other studies. Beyond resolution, the shape of the Fourier space spreading function (kernel) significantly impacts reconstructed power spectra. We analyzed this by decomposing the Murchison Widefield Array (MWA) instrumental beam into Gaussians and simulating the effects of varying kernel shapes and finite extents during gridding and de-gridding processes for optimal map making. Our findings for the MWA indicate that to measure the EoR using foreground avoidance, the kernel must extend to between 0.001% and 0.0001% of the maximum value. This threshold varies with beam shape; compact kernels can achieve similar contamination levels with much smaller extents, albeit with suboptimal error characteristics. However, simple calibration based on pixelated de-gridding results fails to recover the EoR regardless of kernel shape, due to catastrophic errors stemming from pixel resolution. Furthermore, incorporating an opaque horizon with widefield beams introduces substantial spectral contamination through a beam–horizon interaction that generates an infinitely extended kernel in Fourier space, which cannot be adequately represented. Consequently, our results suggest that simple calibration via de-gridded models and optimal map making are not feasible for extreme widefield instrumentation.

This study assessed LPRNet [1], a lightweight Convolutional Neural Network designed for automatic License Plate Recognition (LPR), across two datasets containing both real and synthetic license plate images. Performance was benchmarked against Tesseract [2], an Optical Character Recognition engine, using recognition accuracy and Levenshtein Distance as metrics. As an end-to-end framework, LPRNet exhibited robust capabilities on both datasets, achieving 90% and 89% accuracy on test sets of 1000 real and synthetic images, respectively. In contrast, Tesseract, which lacked training on real license plates, performed well only on synthetic data following pre-processing, reaching 93% accuracy. Furthermore, Pareto analysis of misclassified character frequencies identified specific characters responsible for the highest accumulated errors. Since license plate characteristics vary by region, LPRNet can be effectively trained to recognize characters from specific areas and datasets. Future research may explore applying transfer learning to leverage features learned by LPRNet and fine-tune the model using smaller, more recent license plate datasets.

This study investigates the shape transformations of hairy nanoparticles under confinement using molecular dynamic simulations, specifically focusing on their behavior within slits featuring either inert or attractive walls. The model assumes that only the polymer chains interact attractively with the walls. The analysis examines how wall interaction strength and slit width influence particle configuration. For attractive surfaces, novel structures emerge where chains bridge both walls, forming pillars, symmetrical and asymmetrical spools, and hourglasses. Additionally, in wide pores with strongly attractive walls, hairy particles adsorb onto a single surface to create "mound" or starfish-like structures.

This study examines a planner's optimal interventions affecting both players' standalone marginal utilities on a network and the weights of the links connecting them. The welfare-maximizing joint intervention demonstrates two key properties: (a) with a moderate budget (resulting in interior solutions), the adjustment in link weights between any pair of players is proportional to the product of their eigen-centralities; (b) with a sufficiently large budget, the optimal network structure simplifies to either a complete network under strategic complements or a complete balanced bipartite network under strategic substitutes. We find that the welfare impact of joint intervention is determined by the principal eigenvalue, whereas the distributional effect is reflected in the dispersion of the corresponding eigenvalues, known as eigen-centralities. When comparing joint intervention in this context to single interventions on standalone marginal utilities (as analyzed by Galeotti et al., 2020), we observe that joint intervention consistently achieves higher aggregate welfare but may increase inequality, underscoring a potential trade-off between overall welfare and distributional consequences.

Prolog is a prominent declarative programming language grounded in propositional Horn formulas, widely utilized in fields such as artificial intelligence, automated theorem proving, and mathematical logic. For many years, researchers have sought to expand Prolog's applicability to broader logical classes, leading to significant extensions like constraint logic programming and object-oriented logic programming. However, Prolog remains incapable of addressing problems involving arbitrary quantified Horn formulas. Specifically, Prolog's facts, rules, and queries do not permit variables with arbitrary quantification. This paper addresses that critical limitation by extending Prolog to handle quantified Boolean Horn formulas. This was accomplished by adapting the SLD-resolution proof system for these formulas and developing an efficient implementation model. Furthermore, the proposed implementation demonstrates support for first-order predicate Horn logic with arbitrary quantified variables. Additionally, this work introduces, for the first time, a declarative programming framework specifically designed for quantified Boolean Horn formulas.
I outline the initial efforts, dating back to the 1960s, to quantize General Relativity.

The assessment of complexity in neurophysiological signals has been extensively explored through various methods, particularly those rooted in information and dynamical systems theory. These investigations have highlighted a correlation with consciousness states, suggesting that wakefulness exhibits higher signal complexity, likely because the brain must process diverse sensorimotor data. Consequently, these theoretical frameworks are valuable for quantifying cognitive states. This study aimed to evaluate scalp and intracerebral electroencephalography (EEG), as well as magnetoencephalography (MEG), across different consciousness levels in subjects, including wakefulness, sleep stages, and epileptic seizures. Analysis employed both a statistical approach (Permutation Entropy) and a deterministic one (Permutation Lempel Ziv Complexity). The findings, visualized in complexity versus entropy graphs, indicate that entropy and complexity values peak during fully alert states and decrease as awareness or consciousness diminishes. These results were consistent across all three recording types. We propose that examining cognitive structure through complexity frameworks can uncover mechanistic aspects of brain dynamics related to altered states of consciousness, as well as normal and pathological conditions.

We introduce a straightforward formula to determine the minimal dimension of operators that generate any specific helicity amplitude. This approach streamlines the systematic identification of independent operators by constructing massless, non-factorizable on-shell amplitudes. Subsequently, Little-group constraints are solved algorithmically for every helicity configuration to derive a complete set of spinor structures with the lowest possible dimension. While this process is generally systematic, additional reductions utilizing momentum conservation, on-shell conditions, and Schouten identities are sometimes necessary; we present a systematic method to handle these requirements. By dressing these spinor structures with momentum dot products, we obtain the independent Lorentz structures for each helicity amplitude. We apply these methodologies to particles with spins ranging from 0 to 2. Furthermore, incorporating spin statistics and gauge symmetry selection rules allows us to enumerate operators containing gravitons alongside standard-model particles within the GRSMEFT effective field theory. Additionally, we catalog the independent spinor structures arising from operators involving only standard-model particles. In both scenarios, our analysis covers operators up to dimension eight.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) models have achieved state-of-the-art results in various knowledge-intensive NLP applications, including open-domain question answering and fact verification. However, these models are trained to produce final outputs based on retrieved passages that may be irrelevant to the query, a situation that encourages the learning of spurious cues or answer memorization. This study presents a method to integrate the evidentiality of passages—determining whether they contain valid evidence supporting the output—into the generator's training process. We propose a multi-task learning framework that simultaneously generates the final answer and predicts the evidentiality of each passage, utilizing a novel task-agnostic approach to create silver evidentiality labels for supervision. Experiments across five datasets spanning three knowledge-intensive tasks demonstrate that our evidentiality-guided generator significantly surpasses its direct counterpart of equivalent size and sets a new state-of-the-art on the FaVIQ-Ambig dataset. We attribute these performance gains to the combination of auxiliary multi-task learning and silver evidentiality mining techniques.

We present and experimentally validate an accreditation protocol that establishes an upper limit on the variation distance between the output distributions of noisy and ideal quantum computations. This method was applied to verify the results of twenty-four quantum circuits run on programmable superconducting hardware, covering a range from nine-depth circuits with ten qubits to twenty-one-depth circuits with four qubits. The protocol involves executing the target circuit alongside multiple random Clifford circuits, followed by post-processing of the Clifford outputs. Crucially, the number of required Clifford circuits is determined by the desired confidence and accuracy levels and remains independent of the target circuit's size or characteristics. Consequently, we demonstrate a practical and scalable approach for verifying the correctness of outputs from noisy quantum computers of any size, which serves as the definitive measure of their utility.

Impersonators play a significant role in generating and spreading content within Online Social Networks, particularly on Instagram. These malicious fake accounts mimic legitimate profiles and flood social media with deceptive material, making it increasingly difficult to distinguish authentic posts from inauthentic ones. This study examines three major communities containing verified legitimate accounts and identifies a group of 2.2K impersonator profiles responsible for nearly 10,000 posts, 68,000 comments, and 90,000 likes. By analyzing profile attributes and user behaviors, we categorize these impersonators into two clusters: "bot" and "fan." To differentiate between impersonator-created content and genuine posts, we introduce a Deep Neural Network architecture that evaluates "profile" and "post" features to classify content as "bot-generated," "fan-generated," or "genuine." Our research illuminates this phenomenon and offers valuable insights into bot-generated content, enhancing our understanding of how impersonators contribute to the production of fake material on Instagram.

The SemEval-2010 benchmark dataset has revitalized interest in automatic keyphrase extraction. Comprising scientific articles automatically converted from PDF to plain text, this dataset necessitates meticulous preprocessing to ensure that irrelevant text segments do not hinder extraction performance. While prior research has outlined various document preprocessing techniques, their specific influence on keyphrase extraction model efficacy remains unexamined. This study re-evaluates multiple keyphrase extraction models and quantifies their robustness against progressively advanced levels of document preprocessing.

The growing use of machine learning in atomic-scale simulations has spurred research into the mathematical characteristics of the transformation from atomic Cartesian coordinates to symmetric descriptors or features. This study examines how sensitive this mapping is to atomic displacements, revealing that combining symmetry with smoothness creates mappings with singular points where the Jacobian possesses null singular values, in addition to those arising from infinitesimal translations and rotations. These symmetry-induced singularities are beneficial as they ensure that regression models adhere to physical symmetry constraints. However, beyond these, we identify spurious singular points caused by mapping incompleteness; specifically, certain representations fail to guarantee that structurally distinct configurations map to unique feature vectors. Furthermore, excessive truncation of the infinite basis set used for discretization can introduce additional singularities.

The relationship between the fundamental groups $\pi_1(X)$ of complex quasi-projective varieties $X$ and their hyperbolicity is a central inquiry. This paper investigates this connection specifically when a linear representation $\varrho:\pi_1(X)\to GL_N(\mathbb{C})$ exists. First, under the conditions that $\varrho$ is big and its Zariski closure within $GL_N(\mathbb{C})$ forms a semisimple algebraic group, we demonstrate the existence of a proper Zariski closed subset $Z\subsetneqq X$. Any closed irreducible subvariety $V$ of $X$ not contained in $Z$ is of log general type, and any holomorphic map from the punctured disk $\Delta^*$ to $X$ whose image avoids $Z$ lacks an essential singularity at the origin. Consequently, $X$ itself is of log general type, and all entire curves $f:\mathbb{C}\to X$ are contained within $Z$. We present examples showing that these conditions are sharp. Second, if $X$ is a special or hyperbolically special quasi-projective manifold according to Campana's definition, we prove that the image $\varrho\big(\pi_1(X)\big)$ is virtually nilpotent. We further construct counterexamples demonstrating the optimality of this result, thereby refuting Campana's abelianity conjecture for quasi-projective manifolds. The proofs of these theorems rely on novel developments in non-abelian Hodge theory, geometric group theory, and Nevanlinna theory. Additionally, we establish the strong Green-Griffiths-Lang conjecture for quasi-projective varieties $X$ admitting a morphism $a:X\to A$ where $\dim X=\dim a(X)$ and $A$ is a semi-abelian variety, and we prove a reduction theorem for Zariski dense representations $\pi_1(X)\to G(K)$ where $G$ is a reductive group over a non-Archimedean local field $K$.

Rotational superradiance influences the behavior of numerous rotating natural systems by facilitating the stimulated or spontaneous removal of energy and angular momentum. While this phenomenon is thoroughly understood in relativistic contexts where dispersion is absent, it remains an essential factor in condensed matter systems, particularly for short-wavelength modes. This study investigates how dispersion alters superradiance through a representative model. Specifically, we examine the scattering of linear excitations within a Bose-Einstein condensate subject to a rotating, draining vortex flow, utilizing the complete Bogoliubov dispersion relation. Our findings demonstrate that dispersion inhibits energy and angular momentum extraction in two ways: by narrowing the superradiant bandwidth and by blocking high-angular momentum modes from undergoing superradiance.

We investigate the existence of large Willmore spheres $\Sigma$ with area constraints in a Riemannian $3$-manifold $(M,g)$ asymptotic to Schwarzschild, assuming the scalar curvature is non-negative and the Hawking mass is non-negative, where the inner radius $\rho$ is dominated by the area radius $\lambda$. We demonstrate that no such surfaces exist when $\log \lambda \ll \rho$, thereby resolving a question posed by G. Huisken.

Scientific fields are increasingly leveraging machine learning (ML) and deep learning models to expedite research breakthroughs, while high-performance computing (HPC) systems continue to expand capabilities through diverse hardware and massive scalability. There is an urgent requirement for fair and representative benchmarking standards for ML applications in real-world scientific contexts. MLPerf serves as a community-led initiative to evaluate ML workloads via end-to-end metrics. This paper introduces MLPerf HPC, a benchmark suite for large-scale scientific ML training developed by the MLCommons Association. We present findings from the inaugural submission round, featuring a varied array of the world's most significant HPC systems. By establishing a systematic framework for joint analysis, we compare these systems regarding data staging, algorithmic convergence, and compute performance. Consequently, we achieve a quantitative grasp of optimizations across subsystems—including data staging, on-node loading, compute-unit utilization, and communication scheduling—facilitating overall end-to-end performance gains exceeding 10× through system scaling. Crucially, our analysis reveals a scale-dependent interaction among dataset size, system memory hierarchy, and training convergence, highlighting the significance of near-compute storage. To address data-parallel scalability challenges at large batch sizes, we examine specific learning techniques and hybrid data-and-model parallelism effective for large-scale systems. Finally, we characterize each benchmark based on low-level memory, I/O, and network behaviors to inform extended roofline performance models in future iterations.

The Casimir And Non-Newtonian force EXperiment (CANNEX) utilizes a distinctive macroscopic parallel-plate configuration designed to ensure optimal sensitivity to interfacial forces and their gradients. Drawing on insights from the recently concluded proof-of-concept phase, we have initiated a redesign aimed at minimizing systematic errors and maximizing potential sensitivity. Proposed measurement targets include Casimir forces under both thermal equilibrium and non-equilibrium conditions, as well as hypothetical interactions involving axions, axion-like dark matter, and forces arising from chameleon or symmetron dark energy models. This article details the design specifications for the upcoming implementation stage of CANNEX and analyzes the anticipated experimental opportunities and limitations associated with the new setup.

Recent studies have shown that large quantum circuits can be fragmented into smaller, independent clusters with fewer qubits, executable on limited hardware, with classical post-processing combining these results to recover the original output. However, the runtime for such hybrid quantum-classical approaches scales exponentially with the number of cuts. We introduce Rotation-Inspired Circuit Cut Optimization (RICCO), an alternative strategy that lowers post-processing overhead by solving an optimization problem. RICCO applies unitary rotations at cut points to manipulate the quantum state, maximizing expectation values for specific observables while nullifying others. We validate RICCO's practical utility for the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) by classically simulating a small VQE instance and comparing it against an existing circuit-cutting technique.

This study explores the dynamical and geometric dimensions of deep learning. By presenting semi-invariant metrics for various standard layer configurations, we quantify discrepancies in data or decision functions. Leveraging non-commutative ergodic theorems with random layer maps, we demonstrate the existence of limits as the layer count approaches infinity. Furthermore, we investigate random initialization in conventional networks, revealing a notable cut-off phenomenon relative to network depth. This finding may guide the selection of optimal layer counts and initialization strategies for specific learning tasks. Ultimately, we aim to establish a geometric framework that enhances the theoretical comprehension of deep neural networks.

This study investigates how race and racial categories are integrated into algorithmic fairness frameworks. Existing methods often overlook the socially constructed nature of race, treating it instead as a static attribute. By framing race merely as an attribute rather than a structural, institutional, and relational phenomenon, these approaches risk minimizing the structural roots of algorithmic bias. To address this, we examine the historical development of racial categories and draw upon critical race theory, sociological insights, and lessons from public health, biomedical, and social survey research to ground our conceptualizations. We contend that researchers in algorithmic fairness must acknowledge the multidimensionality of race, rigorously examine how race is conceptualized and operationalized, prioritize the social processes that generate racial inequality, and incorporate the perspectives of those most impacted by sociotechnical systems.

We establish several findings regarding the fibers and images of rational maps originating from hyper-Kähler manifolds, with a specific focus on the minimal genus of curves within a fibration. The final section examines the rational map induced by a linear system on a hyper-Kähler fourfold that meets numerical criteria akin to those analyzed by O'Grady for fourfolds numerically equivalent to $K3^{[2]}$. We generalize his results to this broader setting.

This paper presents a novel and efficient local planning method that relies exclusively on depth data to improve both computational efficiency and performance for memoryless local planners. The proposed approach utilizes depth information to guide sampling, enabling the identification and removal of specific collision-prone trajectories from the motion primitive library. Specifically, by querying depth values, the endpoints of obscured primitives are detected and excluded from the sampling set, which substantially reduces the computational load associated with collision checking. Additionally, a steering mechanism based on depth data is introduced to effectively prevent autonomous vehicles from becoming trapped by large convex obstacles, thereby enhancing the overall autonomy of the planning system. This steering technique is theoretically proven to be complete in convex obstacle scenarios. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed DEpth based both Sampling and Steering (DESS) methods, they were implemented in a simulated environment where a quadrotor navigated through a cluttered area containing obstacles of varying sizes. The results indicate that the proposed approach significantly reduces local planner computation time, allowing for the evaluation of more trajectories and the discovery of optimal paths with lower costs. Furthermore, the average success rate across various testing scenarios, defined as the robot successfully reaching its destination, consistently exceeds 99.6%.

This study introduces SANDD (Segmented AntiNeutrino Directional Detector), a compact (9-liter), mobile plastic scintillator system doped with 0.1% 6Li, designed for near-field reactor monitoring with the capability to determine antineutrino direction. The detector integrates three distinct module types, for which a specialized Monte Carlo simulation code was created to validate individual performance before modeling the entire system. To isolate inverse beta decay events and suppress background noise, specific analysis cuts were implemented. Estimated efficiencies are 34.8% for neutron detection, 80.2% for positron detection, and 71.7% for coincidence detection, yielding an overall inverse beta decay detection efficiency of 20.05% (+0.2% statistical, +2.1% systematic). Furthermore, SANDD is predicted to achieve an azimuthal directional uncertainty of 20 degrees for every 100 detected antineutrino events.

Deep Neural Network (DNN) watermarking serves as a mechanism for verifying the provenance of DNN models, requiring robustness against attacks that generate surrogate models to bypass these verification checks. Although numerous schemes claiming such robustness have emerged, their validation has largely been isolated and limited to a narrow range of attacks. There remains a lack of systematic, empirical assessment against a unified and comprehensive suite of removal techniques, creating uncertainty that hinders practical deployment. This paper investigates the robustness of recently proposed, supposedly resilient watermarking schemes against an extensive array of removal attacks. We review literature methods categorized into three groups: (i) established removal attacks, (ii) surrogate model derivation techniques previously untested as removal attacks, and (iii) novel attacks, including the newly adapted Weight Shifting and Smooth Retraining. We introduce taxonomies for both watermarking schemes and removal attacks. Our empirical study features an ablation analysis across parameter sets for various attacks and schemes on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets. Surprisingly, our findings reveal that no surveyed scheme demonstrates practical robustness. We observe failures against adaptive attacks and previously unexamined surrogate derivation methods, indicating intrinsic flaws in current robustness evaluation practices. We conclude that watermarking schemes must be tested against a broader set of attacks using a more realistic adversary model. Our source code and comprehensive evaluation dataset are publicly available to enable independent verification of our conclusions.

This study introduces a distributed approach for detecting and mitigating attacks utilizing estimation across a multi-agent network, where agents gather partial system measurements that may be subject to biasing attacks. Notably, the system is assumed to be unobservable locally through measurements from any agent's immediate neighbors. Initially, under attack-free conditions, we demonstrate that the proposed distributed estimation remains unbiased with bounded mean-square deviation in the steady state. Subsequently, we develop a residual-based method for agents to locally identify potential attacks. Unlike existing deterministic thresholds that rely on an upper bound for noise support, our thresholds are defined probabilistically. Following the detection and isolation of compromised agents, a mitigation strategy grounded in the system's digraph is presented to substitute attacked measurements with observationally equivalent ones, thereby restoring lost observability. We employ graph-theoretic methods to categorize agents based on their measurements, distinguishing between those that recover system rank-deficiency and those that restore output-connectivity in the system digraph. Specific detection and mitigation protocols are outlined for each category, ensuring polynomial-order complexity suitable for large-scale applications. Simulations are provided to validate the theoretical findings.

IT Librae is an atypical eclipsing binary composed of two B-type stars located approximately 1 kpc above the galactic plane. Although the system was likely expelled from the galactic disk, the calculated time required to reach its present position surpasses the primary star's evolutionary lifespan. This study utilizes new high-dispersion spectroscopy and a precise light curve from the Kepler K2 mission to characterize the system and address this chronological inconsistency. By analyzing radial velocity data, we established a revised spectroscopic orbit and determined the effective temperatures of the components by comparing reconstructed and model spectra ($T_1 = 23.8 \pm 1.8$ kK, $T_2 = 13.7 \pm 2.5$ kK). Furthermore, modeling the K2 light curve with the Eclipsing Light Curve (ELC) code allowed us to calculate the inclination, yielding the component masses ($M_1 = 9.6 \pm 0.6 M_\odot$, $M_2 = 4.2 \pm 0.2 M_\odot$) and mean radii ($R_1 = 6.06 \pm 0.16 R_\odot$, $R_2 = 5.38 \pm 0.14 R_\odot$). The secondary star is found to be overluminous for its mass and appears to fill its Roche lobe, suggesting IT Librae is a post-mass transfer system where the current secondary acted as the donor. The primary star was rejuvenated through mass accretion, meaning its evolutionary age reflects the duration since the mass transfer phase. Therefore, the binary's true age exceeds the ejection time-of-flight, successfully resolving the timescale discrepancy.

Recent advances in opinion mining have introduced word embedding-based topic modeling techniques that achieve better coherence than traditional approaches. This paper illustrates how SocialVisTUM, an interactive visualization toolkit we developed, leverages these methods to map correlated topics within social media content. The system presents a graph where nodes represent topics and edges indicate their correlations, offering interactive details to facilitate the exploration of extensive text corpora. These details include representative words and sentences, topic and sentiment distributions, hierarchical clustering, and customizable topic labels. The toolkit automatically optimizes for coherence on custom datasets. We demonstrate its application using English social media data regarding organic food consumption, where the visualization corroborates findings from a qualitative consumer study. SocialVisTUM and its training protocols are available online.

We present two analytically tractable models designed to characterize dynamic effects in resonant light scattering from subwavelength particles. The first model extends the temporal coupled-mode theory, while the second utilizes the normal mode approach. Our analysis demonstrates that rapid changes in the incident pulse envelope can trigger unconventional, counterintuitive scattering dynamics driven by the interference of modes with distinct fast and slow relaxation rates. To validate these models, we apply them to the dynamic light scattering of a square-envelope pulse by an infinite circular $GaP$ cylinder, specifically when the carrier frequency is near the destructive interference point of Fano resonances. We identify and explain intense, sharp spikes in the scattering cross-section appearing immediately behind both the leading and trailing edges of the pulse. The spike following the pulse termination is attributed to electromagnetic energy released from the particle during prior scattering phases. We verify the high accuracy of these models by comparing them with direct numerical integration of Maxwell's equations. Furthermore, we outline the respective strengths and limitations of the models and discuss their potential application to other forms of dynamic resonant scattering.

The cores of dense primordial black hole clusters constitute an active region characterized by various scattering mechanisms. While some interactions result in single events, others occasionally produce bounded pairs that eventually develop into binary black holes (BBHs) emitting periodic gravitational waves. In contrast, single scattering events occurring at short distances, known as close hyperbolic encounters (CHE), generate intense gravitational wave bursts. This study presents the initial calculation of the stochastic gravitational wave background (SGWB) arising from unresolved CHE sources. Unlike BBH contributions, the low-frequency spectrum of the CHE-induced SGWB is sensitive to the redshift evolution of the event rate, offering a potential means to differentiate between primordial black holes and astrophysical origins. Furthermore, we demonstrate that third-generation ground-based detectors, such as the Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer, may possess the sensitivity to test the existence of CHE phenomena.

Training Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) is computationally intensive due to the recursive aggregation of data from neighboring nodes. To mitigate this overhead, prior research has introduced various neighbor sampling techniques that approximate aggregation using a limited subset of neighbors. While these approaches have effectively accelerated single-machine training, they are less effective in distributed environments, which are essential for handling large-scale real-world graphs. We discovered that existing sampling methods struggle in distributed settings, often leading to excessive communication of feature vectors between machines when implemented naively. To resolve this, we propose a communication-efficient neighbor sampling strategy. Our core approach involves assigning higher sampling probabilities to local nodes to minimize remote node access. We developed an algorithm to calculate these skewed local probabilities while ensuring that training convergence remains largely unaffected. Experimental results on node classification benchmarks demonstrate that our method significantly lowers communication costs for distributed GCN training with minimal impact on accuracy.

The study focuses on non-alternating Hamiltonian Lie algebras defined in three variables over a perfect field with characteristic 2. A classification is provided for non-alternating Hamiltonian forms within the algebra of divided powers in three variables, along with the associated simple Lie algebras. Specifically, it is demonstrated that a non-alternating Hamiltonian form can differ from its linear component in terms of equivalence. Furthermore, the proof establishes that simple Lie algebras arising from non-equivalent forms are not isomorphic.

Turbulence modeling holds the promise of transforming high-speed vehicle design by acting as a viable alternative to expensive and difficult ground and flight tests. However, the very assumptions that render turbulence modeling attractive compared to scale-resolved methods also limit its accuracy for practical high-speed applications, particularly in fully three-dimensional flows. This study presents a methodology to enhance turbulence modeling performance for a complex Mach 8.3, three-dimensional shock boundary layer interaction (SBLI) occurring in a double-fin configuration. A representative two-equation model incorporating low-Reynolds number terms serves as the test bed. Initial deficiencies in the baseline model are identified using benchmark cases, including a Mach 11.1 zero pressure gradient boundary layer and a Mach 6.17 flow over an axisymmetric compression corner. To address these issues, two coefficients are introduced to prevent the non-physical over-amplification of turbulence production and turbulence length-scale downstream of a shock. These coefficients utilize terms already present in the original model, thereby simplifying implementation and keeping computational costs stable. The coefficient values depend on upstream turbulence distributions, ensuring that modifications do not impair model predictions in simpler scenarios like attached boundary layers where such changes are unnecessary. Results demonstrate that these modifications significantly improve predictions of surface pressure and wall heat flux for the 3D SBLI case, which exhibits unique features absent in 2D studies, such as three-dimensional separation, skewed boundary layers, and centerline vortices. Finally, the study discusses considerations regarding inflow turbulence variable values and mesh resolution.

This paper investigates the dynamic sum-of-radii clustering problem, which involves selecting centers to group clients within a metric space while minimizing the combined cost of the centers and their cluster radii. The solution must adapt efficiently to clients arriving and departing, maintaining competitiveness against the optimal current solution. We introduce a data structure capable of sustaining a solution within a constant factor of the optimal cost for metric spaces with bounded doubling dimension, achieving a worst-case update time that is logarithmic in the problem's parameters.

As the second installment in a series dedicated to modeling the black hole (BH) mass function from stellar to supermassive scales, this study concentrates on (super)massive BHs by calculating their mass function across cosmic epochs from first principles. We examine two primary growth mechanisms expected to act synergistically in high-redshift, star-forming progenitors of local massive galaxies. The first involves gaseous dynamical friction, which drives stellar-mass BHs—formed during intense starbursts in gas-rich hosts—toward nuclear regions, rapidly building a central heavy seed ($M_\bullet\sim 10^{3-5}\, M_\odot$) within roughly $10^7$ years. The second mechanism is standard Eddington-limited accretion from a gas disk onto this seed, enabling the BH to reach (super)massive scales ($M_\bullet\sim 10^{6-10}\, M_\odot$) within the typical star-formation duration of $\lesssim 1$ Gyr. Our semi-empirical method is validated by successfully reproducing observed redshift-dependent bolometric AGN luminosity functions, Eddington ratio distributions, and the correlation between star formation and the bolometric luminosity of accreting central BHs. Subsequently, we derive the relic (super)massive BH mass function at various redshifts using a generalized continuity equation and compare these results with current observational data. Finally, we reconstruct the comprehensive BH mass function spanning from stellar to supermassive regimes, covering more than ten orders of magnitude in BH mass.

In contemporary software quality management, peer code reviews and continuous integration frequently operate in tandem. While existing research has examined how non-technical elements—such as reviewer workload, developer involvement, and patch size—influence the code review process, the specific effects of continuous integration remain underexplored. This paper presents an exploratory study analyzing 578,000 automated build entries to assess how these builds impact code reviews. Our findings indicate that builds passing successfully are more likely to spur new participation in pull request reviews. Furthermore, projects with frequent builds sustain a consistent level of reviewing activity over time, a stability rarely observed in projects built infrequently. Experiments involving 26,516 automated build entries demonstrate that our proposed model can predict 64% of the builds that subsequently trigger new code reviews.

This study shows that incorporating chemo-mechanical polishing (CMP) into standard photolithography enables the fabrication of silica microdisks with ultra-high quality factors exceeding $10^8$. When comparing the intrinsic optical quality factor measured at 970 nm, it becomes evident that the substantial reduction in surface roughness causes water molecule absorption at the cavity surface to become the primary mechanism for Q degradation at a wavelength of 1550 nm, surpassing Rayleigh scattering.

Microwave photonic graph states offer a viable method for establishing resilient quantum communication between distant superconducting chips via microwave photons. While Besse et al. [Nat. Commun. 11, 4887 (2020)] recently showed that one-dimensional graph states can be created with two transmon qubits, this paper proposes leveraging transmon qubits alongside additional microwave components to generate more intricate graph structures, specifically two-dimensional lattices and tree-like configurations. We evaluate performance across fixed- and tunable-frequency transmon qubits and various photonic qubit encoding schemes. Based on current experimental parameters, we estimate the fidelity of the resulting microwave graph states for each scenario and pinpoint the primary factors constraining performance.

We introduce a technique for deriving potential proofs of a query based on a specified Answer Set Programming (ASP) rule set. This approach utilizes an abductive process where the set of abducibles is automatically derived solely from the input rules, eliminating the need for the user to explicitly define this space. Starting with an optional set of user-provided facts, our method identifies any additional facts required to entail the query and outputs these inferred facts. Additionally, we provide a mechanism to generate a set of directed edges representing the query's justification graph. By employing various forms of implicit term substitution, the method can incorporate user-provided facts and appropriately adjust the abductive solutions. While previous abduction research has largely relied on goal-directed methods—which can lead to solvers that lack true declarativity—there has been limited work on implementing abduction within bottom-up solvers like Clingo. We present novel ASP programs that execute directly within Clingo to produce both abductive solutions and directed edge sets, all without requiring modifications to the underlying solving engine.

Positron Emission Tomography (PET) serves as a prevalent imaging technique for both clinical diagnostics and medical research. This study investigates the advantages of leveraging quantum entanglement in the linear polarization of the two positron annihilation photons used in PET, utilizing a combination of rigorous simulations and detailed experiments.
