Retail forecasting algorithms have become increasingly intricate, with modern techniques like machine learning introducing inherent complexity. Even established model families, such as exponential smoothing and ARIMA, have proliferated into numerous variants and forecasting profiles. This paper challenges the necessity of managing such vast model families. We argue that selecting parsimonious subsets of models does not compromise forecasting accuracy or the capacity to estimate uncertainty. Instead, we propose a framework that balances performance against computational expenses, focusing on a streamlined set of models. Empirical evidence confirms that this reduced set performs effectively. Furthermore, we convert these computational gains into monetary savings and environmental benefits, discussing the broader implications for large-scale retailers.

We obtain self-similar string solutions within a graph framework close to the onset of singularity formation, demonstrating that these solutions generalize to point-like singularities on M-branes and to radially symmetric configurations.

Materials often exhibit unexpected behaviors under unforeseen conditions; for instance, when Bismuth (Bi) was unexpectedly transformed into an amorphous phase ($a$-Bi), it became a superconductor below $10$ K. We explained why $a$-Bi superconducts while the crystalline ($c$-Bi) does not by computing their electronic properties, revealing that $a$-Bi possesses a higher electron density of states (eDoS) at the Fermi surface than $c$-Bi. Furthermore, we predicted an upper limit for the crystalline phase's superconducting critical temperature ($T_c$), a prediction confirmed experimentally within a year. We now investigate the effects of sub-atmospheric pressure (expansion) on both crystalline (Wyckoff structure) and amorphous Bi. Our findings show that expanding $c$-Bi enhances its metallic character, as the eDoS rises with volume for the Wyckoff structure, whereas the amorphous eDoS declines. Consequently, if the crystalline structure remains intact, expansion would increase its $T_c$, while $a$-Bi's $T_c$ would decrease. Laboratory expansion can be achieved through the chemical etching of Bi-based alloys, a process known as dealloying.

In compact exoplanetary systems, tidal interactions govern the long-term orbital and rotational evolution of both stars and planets. Within the convective envelopes of low-mass stars and giant gas planets, tidally excited inertial waves—restored by Coriolis acceleration—play a pivotal role in tidal dissipation, particularly during the early stages of system evolution, as they are excited and subsequently damped by mechanisms such as viscous friction. These waves are prone to nonlinear effects, notably the generation of zonal flows that induce differential rotation. This study employs realistic tidal body forcing to excite inertial waves via the residual action of the equilibrium tide within the wave momentum equation. Through 3D nonlinear hydrodynamical simulations of adiabatic, incompressible convective shells, we examine how nonlinear terms influence tidal flow characteristics and the redistribution of energy and angular momentum. Specifically, we identify and remove terms causing unphysical angular momentum evolution noted in prior numerical work. Our new framework reveals the development of robust, cylindrically sheared zonal flows that alter tidal dissipation rates compared to previous linear theoretical predictions. We show that the differential rotation induced by these flows clearly accounts for discrepancies between linear and nonlinear dissipation rates across many simulations. Furthermore, we emphasize the critical impact of corotation resonances and parametric instabilities of inertial waves on the tidal flow response, particularly under conditions of high tidal forcing amplitudes or low viscosity.

This paper investigates the fast rotation regime of the density-dependent incompressible Euler equations in two dimensions, accounting for the Coriolis force. Specifically, when initial densities represent small perturbations of a constant state, we demonstrate that the solutions converge to those of a quasi-homogeneous incompressible Euler system. Our proof utilizes a combination of uniform estimates in high-regularity norms and a compensated compactness argument to establish the limit. This methodology enables us to handle scenarios involving ill-prepared initial data.

This paper outlines the design methodology for modulated metasurface leaky-wave antennas (MMLWAs) capable of producing coaxial superpositions of vortex beams across multiple orbital angular momentum (OAM) states. Leveraging the Flat Optics (FO) technique and aperture field estimation (AFE), we establish an analytical framework to enable MMLWAs to generate various topological charges within the OAM regime. Additionally, spectral analysis derived from this model demonstrates that aperture symmetry influences mode purity, identifying a perfectly symmetric circular shape as the optimal configuration for high-purity vortex generation. This single-aperture antenna, equipped with an embedded monopole feed, serves as a viable alternative to more intricate vortex beam generators, such as spiral phase plates and circular antenna arrays.

Representing measured Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Functions (BRDFs) through low-dimensional parametric models remains a difficult task. Existing methods often lack interpretability, depend on restricted analytical approaches, or necessitate costly investigations involving test subjects. This study aims to define a parameterization space that combines the data-driven variability of measured BRDFs with the artistic control found in analytical parametric models. We introduce a machine learning framework utilizing a $\beta$-Variational AutoEncoder ($\beta$-VAE) to create an interpretable, disentangled parameter space. In this representation, each parameter governs a distinct generative factor independently of others. Following network training, we analyze the resulting space and interpret the learned factors through visual perception. Unlike many current methods that use perception to initially design parameters, our approach employs perceptual analysis post-hoc for interpretation. Additionally, our method eliminates the need for test subject trials. A key advantage of this disentangled parametrization is its ability to integrate new parameters alongside existing ones via post-processing, thereby enhancing the diversity of generatable appearances. Moreover, it offers more flexible and controllable material editing than traditional manifold exploration techniques. Finally, we provide a rendering interface that enables real-time material editing and interpolation based on this new system.

This paper investigates the quasinormal modes (QNMs) of massive Klein-Gordon fields within static Ba\~{n}ados-Teitelboim-Zanelli (BTZ) black holes by utilizing ladder operators derived from spacetime conformal symmetries. Given that the BTZ spacetime is locally isometric to three-dimensional anti-de Sitter space, these operators—which transform solutions of the massive Klein-Gordon equation into those with distinct mass squared values—can be constructed based on these conformal symmetries. We apply these ladder operators to the QNMs of the Klein-Gordon equation in the BTZ background, showing that they can shift the indices of QNM overtones. Under Dirichlet or Neumann boundary conditions at infinity, all overtone modes can be generated from a single fundamental mode. Additionally, we examine the scenario involving Robin boundary conditions.

Consider the first-order, one-dimensional $n \times n$ quasilinear strictly hyperbolic system $\partial_t u + F(u)\partial_x u = 0$, initialized with $u(x, 0) = \varepsilon u_0(x)$, where $\varepsilon > 0$ is small, $u_0(x) \not\equiv 0$, and $u_0(x) \in C_0^2(\mathbb{R})$. It is established that if at least one eigenvalue of $F(u)$ is genuinely nonlinear, then at the finite blow-up time $T_{\varepsilon}$, the derivatives $\partial_{t,x}u$ become unbounded while the solution $u$ remains small. For the 1D scalar case or $2 \times 2$ strictly hyperbolic systems (where $n=1$ or $2$), the blow-up mechanism for smooth solutions is well understood, characterized specifically by the divergence of $\partial_{t,x}u$. In this paper, we investigate the blow-up mechanism and the detailed singular behavior of $\partial_{t,x}u$ near the blow-up point for $n \times n$ ($n \geq 3$) strictly hyperbolic systems with a specific class of large initial data. Our findings rely on an efficient decomposition of $u$ along distinct characteristic directions, the introduction of modulated coordinates, and global weighted energy estimates.

We introduce a discrete method for addressing the problem of constructing polygons from broken sticks, which parallels the task of counting polygons with integer side lengths under specific Diophantine constraints. Specifically, we apply MacMahon's Partition Analysis to derive a generating function representing the set of segment sizes from a broken stick that satisfy these inequalities. Notably, this methodology demonstrates that for $n\geq k\geq 3$, the probability of failing to form a $k$-gon from a stick divided into $n$ pieces equals $n!$ divided by a product of linear combinations of partial sums of generalized Fibonacci numbers. This result addresses a problem that was previously difficult to generalize.

When water droplets interact with swollen, elastomeric surfaces, they can trigger capillary-mediated phase separation within wetting ridges. By employing laser scanning confocal microscopy, we observed the segregation of oligomeric silicone oil from a crosslinked silicone network during the steady-state sliding of water drops. Our findings reveal an inverse correlation between the height of the oil tip and the sliding velocity of the drop, a phenomenon explained by competing transport timescales involving oil molecular separation and the advection speed of the drop. Notably, in highly swollen networks, these separation rates approach the speed of diffusion observed in pure melts.

Gravitational wave detections from compact binary mergers have provided unique opportunities to test general relativity (GR) in dynamical, non-linear regimes. A primary focus among these tests involves constraining post-Newtonian (PN) phase corrections, whose values differ between standard GR and various alternative gravity theories, making their observational limits highly significant. Most existing analyses, which offer the tightest constraints, vary PN coefficients individually. Although this approach can detect specific deviations, it is a significant limitation because alternative theories typically introduce additional parameters. Consequently, corrections to PN coefficients should depend on these extra parameters, leading to strong correlations among the coefficients. This study presents an alternative analysis using data from the binary neutron star merger GW170817. Instead of varying coefficients individually, we employ a linear combination of non-GR parameters representing absolute deviations from the TaylorF2 approximant phase, constructed to correspond to uncorrelated directions in the parameter space (principal components of the covariance matrix). Our results show excellent agreement with GR, yielding an integral non-GR phase of $\Psi_{\mbox{non-GR}} = (0.447\pm253)\times10^{-1}$ and a deviation percentile from GR of $p^{\mbox{Dev-GR}}_{n}=25.85\%$.

In the current landscape of data-driven research, analyzing extensive datasets across heterogeneous computational clusters has become a standard daily practice for many scientists. Furthermore, ensuring the credibility of these findings requires that analyses be easily reproducible by the broader research community. While numerous technologies have emerged in recent years to support this goal, there remains a gap in open-source platforms that integrate them effectively. This paper presents and demonstrates SCHeMa, an open-source solution designed to enable the execution and reproducibility of computational analyses on heterogeneous clusters by utilizing containerization, experiment packaging, workflow management, and machine learning capabilities.

Driving in the wrong direction is a primary cause of global traffic congestion and accidents. Identifying such vehicles can significantly mitigate both collisions and gridlock. Given the rising adoption of real-time traffic management systems and the affordability of modern cameras, surveillance footage has emerged as a critical data source. This paper introduces an automated system designed to detect wrong-way vehicles using on-road surveillance video. The methodology operates in three phases: first, detecting vehicles within video frames via the You Only Look Once (YOLO) algorithm; second, tracking each vehicle within a designated region of interest using a centroid tracking algorithm; and third, identifying instances of wrong-way driving. YOLO offers high precision in object detection, while the centroid tracking method efficiently monitors moving objects. Experimental results using various traffic videos demonstrate that the proposed system successfully detects and identifies wrong-way vehicles under diverse lighting and weather conditions. Furthermore, the system is characterized by its simplicity and ease of implementation.

This study presents a learning model tailored for applications with constrained computational resources, emphasizing robustness and interpretability. Learning challenges can be framed as constrained stochastic optimization problems, where constraints stem primarily from model assumptions balancing complexity against performance. This balance is intrinsically linked to over-fitting, generalization capacity, and resilience against noise and adversarial attacks, relying on both model architecture and optimization techniques. We propose an online prototype-based learning algorithm grounded in annealing optimization, structured as an online gradient-free stochastic approximation method. This model functions as an interpretable, progressively expanding competitive-learning neural network suitable for supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning tasks. The annealing mechanism minimizes the need for hyper-parameter tuning, mitigates local minima issues, and ensures robustness regarding initial conditions. Simultaneously, it offers online management of the performance-complexity trade-off by incrementally increasing model complexity as required via an intuitive bifurcation process. Furthermore, the stochastic approximation framework facilitates the analysis of algorithmic convergence using dynamical systems and control theory, enabling integration with reinforcement learning to build an adaptive state-action aggregation scheme.

In the creation of communicative visualizations, designers typically prioritize cognitive learning goals—such as conveying patterns, relationships, or comparisons—while largely neglecting affective objectives. These affective aims involve influencing the audience's values, attitudes, or opinions, with potential outcomes ranging from fostering care for a subject to strengthening specific stances or prompting action. Because these goals are frequently viewed as compromising neutrality or engaging in politics, designers often struggle to articulate or formalize them. Although exceptions exist, such as advocacy graphics or persuasive maps, affective objectives remain rarely acknowledged or structured by visualization practitioners. Drawing on interviews with designers, this work extends existing frameworks that use learning objectives to describe communicative intent by incorporating a new set of affective learning objectives. This revised taxonomy empowers designers to clearly define and evaluate their goals in a principled manner, facilitates comparative analysis, and supports external critique. We demonstrate the taxonomy's utility through a critical examination of an affective visualization.

**Objective:** Performance models serve as vital resources for athletes and coaches aiming to refine training regimens and competition results. A recently introduced hydraulic performance model has demonstrated superior accuracy compared to traditional work-balance models in forecasting recovery during intermittent activity, specifically after being optimized for exercise recovery dynamics. This study hypothesizes that while the hydraulic model excels in recovery prediction, it compromises the accuracy of metabolic response forecasts, such as oxygen uptake ($\dot{V}_{\mathrm{O}_2}$).

**Methods:** We compared hydraulic model outputs against breath-by-breath $\dot{V}_{\mathrm{O}_2}$ measurements collected from 25 constant high-intensity exercise trials involving five participants (age $32\pm7.8$ years, mass $73.6 \pm 5.81$ kg, $\dot{V}_{\mathrm{O}_2\mathrm{max}} \; 3.59 \pm 0.62$ L/min). Participants exercised on a cycle ergometer to volitional exhaustion for durations ranging from 2 to 12 minutes. The analysis specifically targeted the kinetics of $\dot{V}_{\mathrm{O}_2}$ onset.

**Results:** On average, the hydraulic model forecasted peak $\dot{V}_{\mathrm{O}_2}$ approximately $216\pm113$ seconds prior to the observed data. Furthermore, the model failed to account for the $\dot{V}_{\mathrm{O}_2}$ slow component and erroneously assumed zero $\dot{V}_{\mathrm{O}_2}$ at the start of exercise.

**Conclusion:** Although the hydraulic model offers significant potential for predicting energy recovery, it is unsuitable for forecasting metabolic responses during high-intensity exercise. This research provides a more comprehensive view of the model's advantages and constraints. The associated data and code are available as open source.

Traffic congestion and stoppages are significant issues, making it essential to develop models that evaluate the efficiency of different traffic management standards. Our proposed model aims to simulate traffic flow realistically by integrating multiple variables, including passing conventions (such as the "right except to pass" or REP rule), system disruptions caused by accidents, the impact of available lanes under REP, and human factors like individual maximum speeds and passing tendencies. This was achieved by evolving an existing single-lane model into a multi-dimensional lattice that incorporates multiple lanes, passing rules, stochastic elements to represent individuality, and queuing rules for movement algorithms. Our findings indicate that the REP rule effectively raises the critical density a system can sustain. Furthermore, removing human variability through automation increases the sustainable critical density by 160%. While adding lanes boosts critical density, it does not alter the maximum efficiency of the speed distribution. Without automation, the optimal speed distribution for drivers' maximum speeds was identified as Beta(5,5). Additionally, in stable systems, accidents may trigger minor local jams but do not necessarily lead to global gridlock.

A leading hypothesis for superconductivity in iron-based superconductors (FeBSC) suggests that spin-fluctuation bosons, characterized by wave vectors connecting hole Fermi surfaces near the $\Gamma$ point and electron Fermi surfaces near the M points, drive electronic pairing. Neutron scattering data from all FeBSCs studied to date confirm these excitations, while band structure calculations reveal quasi-nested Fermi surfaces across the family, resulting in peaks in spin susceptibility at the requisite wave vectors. However, the newly discovered compound Sr$_{2}$VO$_{3}$FeAs presents a complex Fermi surface lacking obvious quasi-nesting features, leading to the conclusion that it deviates from the established paradigm and necessitates a reevaluation of the mechanisms behind superconductivity in FeBSCs. This paper demonstrates that the apparent complexity of the Fermi surface in Sr$_{2}$VO$_{3}$FeAs arises solely from vanadium-derived electronic states. By assuming that superconductivity in this material, consistent with other FeBSCs, originates within the FeAs layers and depends on the susceptibility of the iron-arsenic subsystem, I recalculated the bare susceptibility by weighting electronic states according to their iron character. This approach yields a susceptibility that robustly supports the existing quasi-nesting model.

As the scale of state-of-the-art language models grows, the demand for massive corpora has made the use of web data as a primary pre-training source a standard practice. This shift presents a significant challenge for NLP practitioners, who must now build highly optimized models and pipelines capable of pre-processing vast amounts of text. This task effectively requires classifying and filtering multilingual, heterogeneous, and noisy data at web scale. A critical component of this pre-processing pipeline is the removal of adult and harmful content. This paper investigates various methods for detecting such content within multilingual, heterogeneous web data. We first demonstrate that traditional harmful content detection methods, which often perform well on small, specialized datasets, tend to fail when applied to heterogeneous, noisy web-scale data. We then propose a perplexity-based approach with a unique twist: rather than training a small language model on a "clean" corpus to select documents with low perplexity (those resembling the clean data), we train solely on adult and harmful textual data. By selecting documents with perplexity values exceeding a specific threshold, this method virtually clusters documents into two distinct groups. This clustering greatly simplifies threshold selection and enables higher precision compared to traditional classification techniques for identifying adult and harmful content.

Participatory Design envisions democratic participation rooted in the belief that individuals possess the agency to imagine a shared future. However, this assumption often falters when working with vulnerable groups. Drawing from our experience facilitating activities designed to foster agentic future-envisionment among sex-trafficking survivors in Nepal, we observed that participants increasingly felt capable of driving change within their families and gained insight into engaging with institutional resources. Based on these findings, we contend that cultivating agency through intimate, personal interactions is a prerequisite before expecting broader political involvement. Specifically, for vulnerable populations, a core value of Participatory Design lies in the process itself, particularly when it empowers participants to see themselves as active agents in the wider world.

We perform a systematic calculation of polarized vector meson production in semi-inclusive deep inelastic lepton-nucleon scattering ($e^-N\to e^-VX$), focusing on the general case of high-energy neutral current electroweak interactions that induce parity-violating effects. Our analysis provides a comprehensive kinematic framework, demonstrating that the cross sections are defined by 81 structure functions. Furthermore, we apply a parton model approach to derive these structure functions in terms of transverse momentum dependent parton distribution functions and fragmentation functions at leading order and leading twist within perturbative quantum chromodynamics. At this level, 27 of the structure functions are nonzero, with 15 associated with the vector meson's tensor polarization and 13 arising from parity-violating contributions. Finally, we provide results and a preliminary numerical estimate for the vector meson's spin alignment.

Data from various spacecraft reveal energy spectral "breaks" occurring between 1-10 MeV in certain large CME-driven shocks, a feature that remains difficult for numerical models to replicate due to prohibitive computational costs. This study analyzes such breaks using Monte Carlo simulations of an isolated CME-driven shock, specifically examining the December 14, 2006 event. By varying scattering time parameters in the model to generate high-energy "tails" capable of surpassing the "break" threshold, we observed that these tails do not extend beyond the break range. Instead, they saturate near 5 MeV, suggesting an inherent energy spectral "cut-off" within isolated shocks. Consequently, we conclude that the formation of energy spectral "breaks" likely requires interaction with another shock, as isolated shocks do not exhibit this property.

We present a significant refinement of a theorem by Andrews and Newman, which states that the total sum of minimal excludants across all partitions of $n$ matches the count of distinct parts partitions of $n$ into two colors. Furthermore, we investigate the $k^{th}$ moments of minimal excludants by extending this established result. Finally, we offer an alternative proof for an elegant identity originally attributed to Hopkins, Sellers, and Stanton.

Beyond the persistent discrepancies observed in the muon $g-2$, $R_{K^{(*)}}$, and $R_{D^{(*)}}$ measurements by multiple independent groups, the CDF Collaboration has identified a further significant anomaly in the $W$-boson mass. These irregularities may be fundamentally connected and share a unified new-physics origin. This study proposes a simultaneous resolution to these issues using two scalar leptoquarks with comparable masses—one weak-singlet $S_1$ and one weak-triplet $S_3$—that interact via a Higgs portal. The model relies on only a limited number of new couplings and TeV-scale leptoquarks, rendering it testable at the LHC. We derive both lower and upper constraints on the leptoquark masses within this framework, based on existing LHC data and the requirement that all new couplings remain within the perturbative regime.

This study performs a statistical analysis of radial abundance patterns in the Galactic disk using a theoretical model of Galactic chemical evolution that accounts for spiral arm dynamics. Key findings include: 1) the average oxygen yield per core-collapse supernova (CC SNe), which occur primarily in spiral arms, is approximately 0.27 M$_{\odot}$; 2) the average iron yield from `tardy' Type Ia supernovae (SNeIa)—originating from older stars ($\gtrsim$100 Myr to several Gyr) that are not concentrated in spiral arms—is about 0.58 M$_{\odot}$; 3) the maximum iron yield from `prompt' SNeIa—stemming from younger stars ($\lesssim$100 Myr) located in spiral arms—does not exceed 0.23 M$_{\odot}$ per event; and 4) the corresponding mean iron production from CC SNe is capped at 0.04 M$_{\odot}$ per event. Collectively, short-lived supernovae (both core-collapse and prompt SNeIa) contribute roughly 85% of the iron in the Galactic disk. The relatively low oxygen yield per CC SNe event suggests an upper mass limit of approximately 23 M$_{\odot}$ for their progenitors; otherwise, the disk would exhibit excessive oxygen abundance. Furthermore, the fact that prompt SNeIa produce about 2.5 times less iron than tardy SNeIa challenges the notion that both sub-populations share the same physical origin. We propose that prompt SNeIa may instead resemble CC SNe and explore the consequences of this hypothesis.

Code search seeks to locate precise code fragments in response to natural language queries, thereby enhancing software productivity and quality. Given the vast volume of code repositories available on platforms like GitHub and Stack Overflow, accurately identifying and localizing relevant snippets is vital for developers. While deep learning has recently been extensively applied to various coding tasks, such as vulnerability detection and source code summarization, automated deep code search remains difficult due to the semantic disparity between natural language and programming code. Most current deep learning methods treat code and queries as flat sequences of tokens, often neglecting structural information. Although Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated effectiveness in learning program semantics, they struggle to capture global dependencies within the constructed graphs, which constrains their learning capacity. To overcome these limitations, this paper introduces GraphSearchNet, a novel neural framework designed to achieve effective and accurate source code search by jointly modeling the rich semantics of both source code and natural language queries. Specifically, we construct graphs for both the code and queries using Bidirectional Gated Graph Neural Networks (BiGGNN) to capture local structural details. Additionally, we augment BiGGNN with a multi-head attention mechanism to recover the global dependencies that BiGGNN overlooks, thereby improving overall model capacity. Extensive experiments on Java and Python datasets from the CodeSearchNet benchmark demonstrate that GraphSearchNet significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches.

We examine smooth projective morphisms $f:X\rightarrow S$ between $K$-varieties, where $K$ is a number field and $S$ is an open curve. We derive upper bounds for the Weil height $h(s)$ relative to the degree $[K(s):K]$ at specific points $s\in S(\bar{K})$ that are "exceptional" regarding the variation of Hodge structures $R^n(f^{an})_{*}(\Q_{X^{an}_{\C}})$, with $n=\dim X-1$. This analysis assumes that the generic special Mumford-Tate group of the variation is $Sp(\mu,\Q)$, the variation undergoes strong degeneration at a fixed point $s_0$ on a proper curve containing $S$, the Hodge conjecture is valid, and a "good arithmetic model" for the morphism $f$ exists over the ring $\mathcal{O}_K$.

**Background:** The Kidney Exchange Problem (KEP) focuses on pairing patients requiring transplants with compatible living donors. While broader participation by medical institutions would ideally enhance match success rates, current legal mandates enforce complex data protection policies that effectively bar smaller facilities from joining. Secure Multi-Party Computation (MPC) offers a technical solution that satisfies strict privacy requirements for sensitive health data while alleviating regulatory hurdles.

**Results:** We developed, implemented, and benchmarked SPIKE, an MPC-based privacy-preserving system for KEP that identifies donor-recipient pairs within a graph structure. SPIKE successfully matches 40 pairs in two-cycle configurations in under four minutes, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art protocol by a 400-fold improvement in runtime and delivering medically more robust outcomes.

**Conclusions:** This work demonstrates a robust, privacy-preserving approach to solving the KEP with practical performance. By utilizing MPC techniques to meet data protection standards technically, the system enables smaller healthcare providers to participate directly in kidney exchanges with significantly reduced legal procedures.

This paper is derived from a presentation given at the XIII Marcell Grossmann meeting. We summarize ongoing collaborative research with Giovanni Amelino-Camelia concerning momentum-dependent (Rainbow) metrics within a Relative Locality framework, demonstrating that this approach is equivalent to the Hamiltonian formalization of Relative Locality presented in arXiv:1102.4637.

Beyond finding equilibria, a primary objective in multiagent learning is acquiring rationalizable behavior, which involves avoiding actions that are iteratively dominated. Nevertheless, in the fundamental context of multiplayer general-sum games, current algorithms necessitate an exponential number of samples relative to the player count to learn rationalizable equilibria under bandit feedback. This paper introduces the first family of efficient algorithms capable of learning rationalizable Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) with sample complexities that are polynomial in every problem parameter, including the number of players. To accomplish this, we also propose a new, efficient method for identifying a single rationalizable action profile (which need not be an equilibrium), significantly improving upon the sample complexity achieved by Wu et al. (2021). Our approach integrates several innovative techniques to ensure both rationalizability and no (swap-)regret, such as a correlated exploration scheme and adaptive learning rates, which may hold independent value. We further validate our findings with a sample complexity lower bound that demonstrates the tightness of our guarantees.

This work investigates the topological characteristics of generalized two-dimensional (2D) Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) models. We demonstrate that a pair of Dirac points emerges within the Brillouin zone (BZ), forming a semimetallic phase. Notably, unlike conventional cases, the positions of these Dirac points are not fixed to high-symmetry points but can be adjusted via model parameters. Furthermore, the coalescence of these two Dirac points triggers a unique topological phase transition, resulting in either a weak topological insulator or a nodal-line metallic phase. We substantiate these findings by developing two specific models, designated as type-I and type-II 2D SSH models, and also explore feasible experimental setups for realizing these systems.

The geometry of rough, fractured, porous, and textured media is topologically intricate. While these media are frequently modeled using bundles of capillary tubes, angle-containing geometries offer a more realistic depiction of their internal structure. A fundamental component inherent to all such geometries is an open, wedge-like channel. According to classical capillarity theory, which neglects intermolecular interactions, a liquid entering a wedge with a concave liquid-gas interface must propagate indefinitely along its spine; this phenomenon is known as the Concus-Finn condition. However, this paper demonstrates that when surface forces are considered, steady-state rivulets violating the Concus-Finn condition can form within these channels. We introduce a straightforward model based on the disjoining pressure approach to analyze rivulet shapes in wedges and also examine a scenario where the wedge walls are soft and deformable under the influence of the liquid.

The recent Muon g-2 experiment at Fermilab has established robust limits on various new particle properties. By employing an effective field theory framework for higher-spin field interactions, we assess the impact of an electrically neutral, colour-singlet spin-3/2 fermion on $(g-2)_\mu$ and determine the resulting bounds on its mass and coupling strengths. These findings are juxtaposed with constraints on spin-1/2 fermions, including vector-like leptons from Standard Model extensions, excited leptons from composite models, and the charginos and neutralinos found in supersymmetry. In contrast to these spin-1/2 candidates, spin-3/2 particles yield only negligible contributions to the muon's anomalous magnetic moment.

This report offers theoretical backing for the continual learning approach known as **Elastic Weight Consolidation**, which was first introduced in the paper titled `Overcoming catastrophic forgetting in neural networks'. As one of the most frequently cited works on regularized continual learning methods, this document unpacks the core concept of its proposed objective function. We proceed with the assumption that the reader is already familiar with the fundamental terminology of continual learning.

Online review platforms serve as a primary channel for businesses to cultivate their brand and disseminate their messages. Existing research on the impact of these reviews has predominantly concentrated on single numerical indicators, such as ratings or sentiment scores. We contend that this single-cause approach suffers from three significant limitations: it focuses exclusively on isolated numerical factors while neglecting the distinct impacts of multiple attributes—like food quality and service—embedded within the text; it presumes no hidden confounders exist in observational data, such as individual consumer preferences; and it fails to account for indirect numerical effects that may negate the influence of textual reviews on revenue. Consequently, we propose an alternative framework that moves beyond single-cause estimation. In the presence of hidden confounders, we analyze multi-aspect textual reviews, specifically examining their total effects on revenue and their direct effects, where numerical ratings act as mediators. Leveraging recent advancements in machine learning and causal inference, we jointly estimate these hidden confounders and causal effects. Finally, we provide empirical evaluations using real-world data to highlight the strategic importance of distinguishing between multi-aspect effects when managing business operations.

We employ a unified approach to establish an isomorphism between direct sums of cyclotomic affine (and degenerate affine) Hecke algebras and cyclotomic BK-subalgebras, which represent a specific class of KLR-type algebras.

We present deep optical spectroscopic data for four blue-excess, dust-obscured galaxies (BluDOGs) discovered by the Subaru Hyper Suprime-Cam. BluDOGs represent a subset of dust-obscured galaxies (DOGs) characterized by extremely red colors ($i-[22])_{\rm AB} \geq 7.0$; Toba et al. 2015), distinguished by significant flux excesses in the optical $g$- and $r$-bands compared to power-law fits at longer wavelengths. While Noboriguchi et al. (2019) proposed that BluDOGs may signify the gas-rich major merger blowing-out phase, their detailed properties remain unclear due to a scarcity of spectroscopic data. Using Subaru/FOCAS and VLT/FORS2, we observed four BluDOGs at redshifts ranging from 2.2 to 3.3. The resulting spectra reveal broad emission lines with exceptionally large equivalent widths and a blue wing in the CIV profile. The average rest-frame equivalent widths for CIV lines reach $160\pm33$ $\mathrm{\mathring{A}}$, approximately seven times the mean value for typical type-1 quasars. Velocity profile full widths at half maximum (FWHM) span 1990 to 4470 ${\rm km\ s^{-1}}$, with asymmetric parameters of 0.05 and 0.25. These intense CIV lines substantially influence broad-band magnitudes, contributing to the observed blue excess in the spectral energy distributions. Estimated supermassive black hole masses fall between $1.1\times10^8$ and $5.5 \times 10^8$ $M_\odot$. Furthermore, inferred Eddington ratios exceed unity ($1.1< \lambda_{\rm Edd} < 3.8$), indicating that these BluDOGs reside in a rapidly evolving phase of supermassive black hole growth.

Maximal Independent Set (MIS) remains a cornerstone problem in distributed computing, having been extensively studied for over forty years. Despite this, the most efficient randomized algorithms still require $O(\log{n})$ rounds in the worst case for general graphs, while the established lower bound stands at $\Omega\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log{n}}{\log{\log{n}}}}\right)$ rounds. Consequently, improving upon the $O(\log{n})$ upper bound or proving tighter lower bounds has remained a persistent open challenge.

Our primary advancement demonstrates that MIS can be solved with a worst-case awake complexity of $O(\log \log n)$ rounds, which represents an exponential improvement over the traditional round complexity lower bound of $\Omega\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log{n}}{\log{\log{n}}}}\right)$. Specifically, we achieve two main results:

1. We introduce a randomized Monte Carlo distributed algorithm for MIS that computes a valid independent set with high probability in $O(\log\log{n})$ rounds of awake complexity. Although its traditional round complexity is $O(poly(n))$, these bounds apply within the $CONGEST(O(polylog n))$ model, where edges transmit $O(\log^3 n)$ bits per round.
2. We further demonstrate a trade-off where round complexity is significantly reduced at the expense of a marginal increase in awake complexity. This yields a randomized MIS algorithm with $O(\log \log n \log^* n)$ awake complexity and $O(\log^3 n \log \log n \log^*n)$ round complexity, also within the $CONGEST(O(polylog n))$ model.

This paper introduces a theoretical framework for intersubband absorption that accounts for electronic ground state correlations within a doped GaAs/Al$_{35}$Ga$_{65}$As quantum well system. By concentrating on the Coulomb interactions between carriers at low temperatures, we demonstrate that ground state correlations cause significant renormalization and broadening of the absorption spectrum. Specifically, at T = 1 K, the full width at half maximum can increase by as much as threefold. Furthermore, incorporating electron-phonon scattering markedly diminishes the relative influence of these electronic correlations.

Dataset bias and spurious correlations often severely hinder the generalization capabilities of deep neural networks. While previous approaches have tackled this issue through alternative loss functions or sampling strategies targeting rare patterns, we introduce a novel strategy: adjusting the network architecture to embed inductive biases that enhance robustness against dataset bias. We present OccamNets, a design inherently biased toward simpler solutions. This architecture incorporates two specific inductive biases: first, it prefers using the minimum necessary depth for each individual example, and second, it favors utilizing fewer image locations for predictions. Although OccamNets lean toward simpler hypotheses, they retain the capacity to learn more complex ones when required. Experimental results show that OccamNets match or exceed the performance of state-of-the-art methods operating on architectures lacking these specific biases. Additionally, combining OccamNets with existing state-of-the-art debiasing techniques yields further performance improvements.

Symmetry class D two-dimensional disordered topological superconductors display diverse phenomena, including the diffusive thermal metal (DTM), Anderson insulator (AI), and thermal quantum Hall (TQH) phases. Through numerical analysis of a lattice model for this class D superconductor, we examine the phase diagram, emphasizing transitions between these states and their corresponding universal critical behaviors. Our findings confirm a repulsive tricritical point where the three phases converge. By numerically assessing the localization length, conductance (or conductivity), and density of states at various critical points and the tricritical point, we characterize the system's behavior. We conclude that the DTM-TQH and DTM-AI metal-insulator transitions share the same universality class, while the tricritical point belongs to a distinct one.

We demonstrate that a hallmark of gravity's quantum nature is the quantum mechanical squeezing of the relative motion between two identical masses with respect to their common mode. Since gravitational interaction relies exclusively on the relative positions of these masses, this squeezing is theoretically equivalent to quantum entanglement between them. However, experimentally, observing this squeezing is more practical than directly detecting entanglement. To facilitate this, we propose an optical interferometric scheme designed to test and potentially refute hypothetical models of gravity.

We utilize $\textit{Planck}$ LFI and $\textit{WMAP}$ polarization data within a Bayesian CMB analysis framework to limit the extent of polarized anomalous microwave emission (AME) at large angular scales. Synchrotron emission is modeled using a power-law spectral energy distribution, while the combined signal of AME and thermal dust is fitted via linear regression against $\textit{Planck}$ HFI 353 GHz data. This template-based approach enables constraints on polarized AME with minimal assumptions regarding its frequency dependence. Although cosmic microwave background fluctuations are ignored, simulations confirm their impact on the results is negligible. We observe that the confidence limit for the AME polarization fraction depends on the prior for the polarized synchrotron spectral index. Specifically, for priors steeper than $\beta_{\mathrm{s}} = -3.1\pm0.1$, an upper limit of $p_{\mathrm{AME}}^{\rm max}\lesssim 0.6\,\%$ is established at $95\,\%$ confidence, whereas a prior of $\beta_{\mathrm{s}}=-3.0\pm0.1$ yields a nominal detection of $p_{\mathrm{AME}}=2.5\pm1.0\,\%$ ($95\,\%$ confidence). Consequently, the current data cannot robustly constrain both polarized synchrotron emission and AME simultaneously; our primary outcome is a constraint on the AME polarization fraction explicitly dependent on $\beta_\mathrm{s}$. Future improvements to these limits will require combining existing $\textit{Planck}$ and $\textit{WMAP}$ observations with high-sensitivity low-frequency measurements from experiments like C-BASS and QUIJOTE.

Observations in cosmology and astrophysics reveal magnetic fields spanning all scales. To account for these, it is hypothesized that primordial seed fields, generated during early universe events such as inflation, phase transitions, or turbulent phases, were subsequently amplified by dynamos. A prominent mechanism for seed field generation is the Biermann battery, initially proposed for astrophysical objects, which requires non-parallel gradients in both electron number density and pressure. This article introduces a analogous mechanism for generating seed fields within an inhomogeneous chiral plasma. Relying on the chiral anomaly, our approach utilizes inhomogeneities in chiral chemical potential and temperature. We examine various scenarios for the emergence of these inhomogeneities and determine that the resulting seed field strength ranges from a few nano-Gauss to several hundred nano-Gauss, depending on the specific epoch of generation.

An analysis of proton-proton collision data, with an integrated luminosity of 9$fb^{-1}$ gathered by the LHCb detector from 2011 to 2018, reveals a new narrow charmonium state, the $X(3842)$ resonance, through its decays into $D^0\bar{D}^0$ and $D^+D^-$. The measured mass and natural width are \begin{eqnarray*}
m_{X(3842)} & = & 3842.71 \pm 0.16 \pm 0.12 MeV/c^2\,, \Gamma_{X(3842)} & = &
2.79 \pm 0.51 \pm 0.35 MeV\,, \end{eqnarray*} where the first error represents statistical uncertainty and the second systematic uncertainty. The observed narrow width and mass values support the interpretation of this state as the previously unobserved spin-3 $\psi_3\mathrm{\left(1^3D_3\right)}$ charmonium. Furthermore, this study reports the first observation of prompt hadroproduction for the $\psi(3770)$ and $\chi_{c2}(3930)$ states, with their parameters determined as \begin{eqnarray*} m_{\psi(3770)} & = & 3778.1 \pm 0.7 \pm 0.6
MeV/c^2\,, m_{\chi_{c2}(3930)} & = & 3921.9 \pm 0.6 \pm 0.2 MeV/c^2\,,
\Gamma_{\chi_{c2}(3930)} & = &36.6 \pm 1.9 \pm 0.9 MeV\,, \end{eqnarray*} where the first uncertainty is statistical and the second is systematic.

This work examines rational representations of a connected linear algebraic group $\mathbb G$ defined over a field $k$ with positive characteristic $p > 0$. We define a natural extension, denoted $M \mapsto \Pi(\mathbb G)_M$, of $\pi$-point support theory to $\mathbb G$-modules for finite group schemes $G$. We demonstrate that this approach is fundamentally equivalent to a more "intrinsic" and "explicit" support theory, $M \mapsto \mathbb P\mathfrak C(\mathbb G)_M$, applicable to algebraic groups of exponential type, which relies on 1-parameter subgroups $\mathbb G_a \to \mathbb G$. Furthermore, we generalize this support theory to bounded complexes of $\mathbb G$-modules, expressed as $C^\bullet \mapsto \Pi(\mathbb G)_{C^\bullet}$. We also introduce the tensor triangulated category $StMod(\mathbb G)$, constructed as the Verdier quotient of the bounded derived category $D^b(Mod(\mathbb G))$ modulo the thick subcategory of mock injective modules. Our proposed support theory adheres to all standard properties required for a support theory within $StMod(\mathbb G)$. As an application, we utilize the mapping $C^\bullet \mapsto \Pi(\mathbb G)_{C^\bullet}$ to classify $(r)$-complete, thick tensor ideals of $stmod(\mathbb G)$ based on $stmod(\mathbb G)$-realizable subsets of $\Pi(\mathbb G)$, and similarly to classify $(r)$-complete, localizing subcategories of $StMod(\mathbb G)$ in terms of $StMod(\mathbb G)$-realizable subsets of $\Pi(\mathbb G)$.

We investigate various limits of exactly solvable vector and matrix fermionic quantum mechanical models featuring quartic interactions at finite temperature. These systems maintain a $U(1)\times SU(N)\times SU(L)$ symmetry classically, and we examine them using bosonization methods that introduce both scalar (singlet) and matrix (non-singlet) bosonic fields. In the vector limits $(N,1)$ and $(1,L)$, the resulting bosonic path integrals correspond to fermionic Fock space Hamiltonians defined via quadratic Casimirs and supplementary terms related to the Cartan subalgebra, thereby clarifying the symmetries retained by scalar and matrix bosonizations at the quantum level. For non-singlet bosonization, we establish an equivalence between the vector model and the Polychronakos+Frahm spin model, utilizing this connection to calculate the free energy. Furthermore, we determine the eigenvalue distribution in the large $N,L$ limit where $\alpha = L/N$ remains constant. The system exhibits a third-order phase transition as temperature varies, which admits an analytical characterization in the $\alpha\gg1$ regime. Our analysis concludes by identifying the critical curve in parameter space marking the transition of the eigenvalue distribution from a single to a double cut.

We introduce an inverse seesaw model based on a hidden $U(1)$ gauge symmetry, which naturally accommodates distinct hierarchies among neutral fermion mass scales. These hierarchies arise from theoretical requirements and experimental bounds. The framework necessitates that Majorana exotic masses be generated at the one-loop level, while experimental constraints on lepton flavor violations (LFVs), such as $\mu\to e\gamma$, demand a strong suppression of Dirac mass terms. To achieve such small Majorana masses, we incorporate exotic fermions and bosons, which also yield interesting phenomenological consequences, including contributions to the muon anomalous magnetic moment, a dark matter candidate, LFVs, and deviations in leptonic $Z$ decays. We perform a numerical analysis of these phenomena, incorporating neutrino oscillation data, to delineate the allowed parameter regions. Furthermore, we examine the dark matter candidate in scenarios involving both fermions and scalar bosons, focusing on the lighter mass range of 10 GeV or less. In these cases, the primary contributions stem from the hidden gauge sector interactions, and we present the corresponding allowed ranges for both possibilities.

This research investigates how the polytropic index—the ratio of specific heats for a perfect gas—influences detonation structure through two-dimensional numerical simulations. To isolate gasdynamic effects, a simplified Arrhenius kinetic model is employed, with the activation energy normalized by shock temperature held constant to ensure uniform reaction rate sensitivity across all mixtures. This approach separates chemical effects from gasdynamic ones. The findings indicate that mixtures with lower polytropic indices exhibit enhanced convective mixing compared to those with higher indices, a metric assessed via Lagrangian tracers. Furthermore, low polytropic index mixtures demonstrate shorter reaction lengths than their high index counterparts. Additionally, within the studied parameter range, Mach stem bifurcation in detonations caused by jetting is identified as a mechanism primarily driven by gasdynamics.

This work investigates the quantification of genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) for general multipartite states. By leveraging constraints on entanglement distributions, we derive a set of inequalities applicable to $N$-partite pure states, demonstrating that the bipartite entanglement between any single part and the rest cannot surpass the sum of entanglements among the remaining partners. Based on these inequalities, we introduce "concurrence triangles" and construct GME measures using the geometric mean area of these triangles. These measures are non-increasing under local operations and classical communication (LOCC) and effectively distinguish separable from entangled components in non-genuinely entangled pure states. For mixed states, we define GME measures via the convex roof extension and present a detection witness utilizing state purifications. Finally, detailed examples demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed GME measures.

This study offers a quantitative assessment of inertial range statistics generated by the Entropic Lattice Boltzmann Method (ELBM) within 3D homogeneous and isotropic turbulence. ELBM represents a promising mesoscopic framework for investigating fully developed turbulent flows, distinguished by its inherent scalability and unconditional stability. In the hydrodynamic limit, ELBM aligns with the Navier-Stokes equations augmented by an additional eddy viscosity term [1]. Building on this macroscopic formulation, we developed a novel hydrodynamical model suitable for Large-Eddy Simulation (LES) closure. Unlike traditional models, this approach is not positive definite, enabling the reproduction of backscatter events where energy transfers from subgrid to resolved scales. We present a statistical comparison of both mesoscopic and macroscopic entropic models derived from the ELBM approach, validating them against fully resolved Direct Numerical Simulations (DNS). Furthermore, we compare ELBM performance with the established Smagorinsky closure. Our findings indicate that ELBM extends the energy spectrum scaling range while maintaining simulation stability. Regarding higher-order inertial range observables, the accuracy of ELBM is demonstrated to be comparable to other methodologies, including the Smagorinsky model.

Bayesian optimization has significantly advanced the state of the art across various AI domains by efficiently optimizing black-box processes. It intelligently navigates vast and intricate design spaces while minimizing the costly evaluations of the underlying functions. Materials science faces a remarkably similar challenge: optimizing material properties within expansive synthesis or processing design spaces, where each evaluation demands expensive experiments or simulations. Although Bayesian optimization is a prevalent solution for such tasks, there is currently minimal intersection between the two research communities addressing these shared concepts. This survey aims to bridge that gap by reviewing Bayesian optimization applications in materials science, thereby fostering cross-disciplinary collaboration and preventing redundant efforts. Furthermore, we identify shared challenges and potential avenues for joint research initiatives.

Scanning devices frequently generate incomplete point clouds due to occlusions, prompting the need for completion techniques that reconstruct full shapes from partial inputs. Current approaches fall into supervised and unsupervised categories, yet both depend heavily on abundant 3D complete point clouds, which are notoriously difficult to acquire. This paper introduces Cross-PCC, an unsupervised completion framework that eliminates the need for any 3D complete data. Instead, it leverages 2D images of complete objects, which are far easier to capture. To exploit complementary information from these images, the method extracts 2D features from a single-view RGB image and employs a fusion module to integrate them with 3D features derived from the partial point cloud. To ensure the predicted shape aligns correctly, the system projects predicted points onto the 2D plane and constrains their positions using foreground pixels from silhouette maps. Additionally, a proposed view calibrator reduces outliers by shifting points projected into background regions back into the foreground based on the single-view silhouette. To our knowledge, Cross-PCC represents the first point cloud completion method that requires no 3D supervision. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art unsupervised methods and achieves performance comparable to supervised techniques. The source code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/ltwu6/cross-pcc.

For distinct odd primes $p$ and $q$, the Catalan curve $C_{p,q}$ is defined by the affine equation $y^q = x^p - 1$. This article constructs the Sato-Tate groups associated with the Jacobians of these curves to analyze the limiting distributions of the normalized coefficients of their L-polynomials. These Catalan Jacobians are characterized as nondegenerate, simple varieties with noncyclic Galois groups acting on their endomorphism fields over $\mathbb{Q}$, rendering them compelling subjects for Sato-Tate group research. The study calculates both statistical and numerical moments for the resulting limiting distributions and establishes the Galois endomorphism types of the Jacobians by employing a combination of established and novel methods.

The vectorial nonlinearity of a vector-valued function is defined as its distance from the set of affine functions. In 2017, Liu, Mesnager, and Chen proposed a conjecture regarding a general upper bound for vectorial linearity. Subsequently, Carlet established a lower bound expressed in terms of differential uniformity. This paper refines Carlet's lower bound using an elementary approach that leverages the property that the level sets of APN functions constitute Sidon sets. Additionally, we provide a survey of Sidon sets within elementary abelian 2-groups and investigate the completeness problem for Sidon sets derived from hyperbolas and ellipses in the finite affine plane.

Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) and their derivatives have demonstrated remarkable efficacy across numerous recommendation scenarios. Nevertheless, many current GCN architectures rely on recursive aggregation across all connected nodes, creating substantial computational overhead that limits their scalability for large-scale recommendation systems. To address this, we introduce FlatGCN, a model that delivers superior performance with significantly reduced complexity. Our contributions are threefold: first, we present a streamlined yet potent GCN architecture that utilizes a single flattened layer to aggregate neighborhood information, replacing the recursive approach; this parameter-free aggregation step allows for parallel pre-computation, thereby conserving memory and processing resources. Second, we develop an informative neighbor-infomax sampling strategy that identifies the most valuable neighbors by evaluating node correlations through a rigorous metric. Third, we propose a layer ensemble technique that enhances the expressiveness of learned representations by combining layer-wise neighborhood features at the final stage. Comprehensive experiments across three datasets confirm that our model not only substantially outperforms existing GCN approaches but also achieves training efficiency gains of up to several orders of magnitude.

A theoretical study examines modulational instability (MI) and dust-acoustic rogue waves (DARWs) within a four-component dusty plasma comprising inertial, negatively charged, massive heavy (or light) cold (or hot) dust grains, alongside super-thermal electrons and non-thermal ions. Utilizing the reductive perturbation method to derive the nonlinear Schrödinger equation, the analysis identifies two distinct modes: fast and slow dust-acoustic modes. The conditions governing MI and the emergence of associated DARWs are shown to be substantially altered by factors such as the non-thermality of ions ($\alpha$), super-thermality of electrons ($\kappa$), the density ratio of non-thermal ions to cold dust ($\mu_i$), and the mass ratio of cold to hot dust ($\sigma$). Finally, the study briefly outlines the implications of these findings for both space and laboratory plasmas.

This study explores the utility of Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) for identifying new physics within the dark matter power spectrum, specifically focusing on evolving dark energy and General Relativity modifications. Following the introduction of a novel method for quantifying classification uncertainty in BNNs, we trained two networks on simulated matter power spectra generated by the public $\tt{ReACT}$ code. These simulations cover the $k$-range $\left(0.01 - 2.5\right) \, h \mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$ and redshift bins $\left(0.1,0.478,0.783,1.5\right)$ with noise characteristics similar to Euclid. The first network classifies spectra into five categories: $\Lambda$CDM, $f(R)$, $w$CDM, Dvali-Gabadaze-Porrati (DGP) gravity, and a "random" class, while the second is trained to separate $\Lambda$CDM from all non-$\Lambda$CDM models. Both networks achieved approximately 95% accuracy across training, validation, and test sets. Furthermore, both demonstrated the ability to detect deviations from $\Lambda$CDM not present in their training data, illustrated using spectra generated with the growth-index $\gamma$. We quantified the networks' constraining power by determining the minimum deviation from $\Lambda$CDM required for the noise-averaged non-$\Lambda$CDM classification probability to reach at least $2\sigma$. The resulting limits are $f_{R0} \lesssim 10^{-7}$, $\Omega_{rc} \lesssim 10^{-2}$, $-1.05 \lesssim w_0 \lesssim 0.95$, $-0.2 \lesssim w_a \lesssim 0.2$, and $0.52 \lesssim \gamma \lesssim 0.59$. By training a specialized network to distinguish exclusively between $\Lambda$CDM and $f(R)$ spectra, the constraint on $f(R)$ can be tightened, allowing detection of a non-zero $f_{R0}$ at $\mathcal{O}\left(10^{-8}\right)$ with greater than $2\sigma$ confidence. We anticipate that future advancements, such as incorporating smaller length scales or additional $\Lambda$CDM extensions, will further enhance the capability of BNNs to uncover new physics in cosmological data.

This study addresses the iterative resolution of symmetric saddle-point matrices featuring a singular leading block. We propose a novel ideal positive definite block diagonal preconditioner, resulting in a preconditioned operator characterized by four distinct eigenvalues. Additionally, we present several methods to render this preconditioner practical, and we demonstrate the efficacy of our methodology through numerical experiments.

Fast Lyapunov Indicators (FLIs) are functions defined on the tangent fiber of the phase space for both continuous and discrete dynamical systems, computed through a finite sequence of dynamical iterations. Over the past decade, these indicators have become essential in numerical analyses for identifying phase-space resonances and, more recently, the stable and unstable manifolds associated with normally hyperbolic invariant manifolds. This paper presents an analytic framework describing the evolution of tangent vectors for orbits starting near the stable-unstable manifolds of a hyperbolic saddle point within an area-preserving map. This representation elucidates why FLIs successfully detect the stable-unstable manifolds of all fixed points meeting a specific criterion; for those that do not, a suitably adjusted FLI remains effective for detection. Furthermore, the proposed method enables manifold identification with a precision that scales linearly with integration time. The approach is demonstrated by addressing the critical challenge of detecting the tube manifolds associated with Lyapunov orbits at the L1 and L2 points in the circular restricted three-body problem.

This study investigates both prompt-like and long-lived dark photons ($A^{\prime}$) generated in proton-proton collisions at a 13 TeV center-of-mass energy, utilizing $A^{\prime}\to\mu^+\mu^-$ decay channels and an integrated luminosity of 1.6 fb$^{-1}$ from the LHCb detector. The search for prompt-like $A^{\prime}$ spans masses from the dimuon threshold up to 70 GeV, whereas the long-lived $A^{\prime}$ analysis focuses on the low-mass interval of 214 to 350 MeV. No signal evidence was observed, leading to the establishment of 90% confidence level exclusion limits on the $\gamma$-$A^{\prime}$ kinetic-mixing parameter. These results set the most stringent constraints to date for prompt-like dark photons in the range $10.6 < m(A^{\prime}) < 70$ GeV and match the best existing limits for $m(A^{\prime}) < 0.5$ GeV. Additionally, this marks the first search for long-lived dark photons to achieve sensitivity through a displaced-vertex signature.

We introduce the concept of "instance reducibility" between predicates, a notion frequently utilized in reverse constructive mathematics. This framework allows for the comparison and classification of diverse principles within this field, including formal Church's thesis, Brouwer's Continuity principle, the Fan theorem, the Law of Excluded Middle, the Limited Principle of Omniscience, Function choice, and Markov's principle. We demonstrate that instance degrees constitute a frame, defined as a complete lattice where finite infima distribute over set-indexed suprema. These degrees are equivalent to the frame of upper sets of truth values, ordered by the reverse Smyth partial order. In our analysis of the lattice's structure, we observe that the subobject classifier embeds into it via two distinct methods: one monotone and one antimonotone. Furthermore, the $\lnot\lnot$-dense degrees correspond exactly to those reducible to the degree of the Law of Excluded Middle.

We provide an explicit formulation of instance degrees within a relative realizability topos, designating them as "extended Weihrauch degrees." This naming is appropriate because, in Kleene-Vesley realizability, $\lnot\lnot$-dense modest instance degrees align precisely with standard Weihrauch degrees. These extended degrees enhance the structure of Weihrauch degrees by introducing computable infima and suprema, an implication operator, mechanisms for controlling parameter access and result computation, and by broadening the overall scope of Weihrauch reducibility.

This work examines high-dimensional extensions of the maximum flow and minimum cut problems within the framework of simplicial complexes, delivering both algorithmic approaches and hardness proofs. By interpreting flows and cuts topologically through the simplicial (co)boundary operator, these problems are formulated as linear programs that serve as duals. Unlike standard graphs, complexes with integer capacity constraints can exhibit fractional maximum flows, and we demonstrate that finding a maximum integral flow is NP-hard. Additionally, we introduce a combinatorial definition of a simplicial cut that appears more natural for optimization contexts, proving that computing such a cut is also NP-hard. However, we identify specific conditions under which the linear programming solution corresponds to a combinatorial cut. For $d$-dimensional simplicial complexes embedded in $\mathbb{R}^{d+1}$, we present algorithms based on the dual graph, where maximum flow corresponds to shortest path computation and minimum cut corresponds to minimum cost circulation. Finally, we analyze the Ford-Fulkerson algorithm in this setting, establishing its correctness and proposing a heuristic that ensures termination.

This study evaluates the performance of a downlink multi-user multiple-input multiple-output (MU-MIMO) non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) system. To minimize hardware complexity and leverage antenna diversity, the work employs a transmit antenna selection (TAS) strategy alongside equal-gain combining (EGC) receivers. Furthermore, Weibull-distributed fading channels are utilized to model propagation medium non-linearities, while also encompassing Rayleigh and exponential models as specific instances. Exact closed-form expressions are derived for key performance indicators, including outage probability (OP) and average bit error rate (ABER), accompanied by an asymptotic analysis for both metrics. Additionally, precise formulas for the probability density function (PDF) and cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the end-to-end signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) are established. Notably, findings reveal that in high-SNR conditions, the ABER for all users except the nearest one reaches a performance floor determined exclusively by the power allocation coefficient and modulation type, remaining independent of channel statistics or the number of transmit and receive antennas. To the authors' knowledge, this specific scenario has not been previously analyzed in the literature. Finally, Monte-Carlo simulations are conducted to validate the accuracy of all derived expressions.

Perturbative effective potentials encounter infrared (IR) divergences in gauges containing massless Goldstone bosons at their minima, such as Landau or Fermi gauges; however, this issue is resolved through appropriate resummation of the Goldstone propagators. When the potential minimum arises radiatively, achieving gauge-independence at the minimum similarly necessitates resummation. We demonstrate that the resummation technique which eliminates the IR divergence also resolves the gauge-dependence problem, explicitly illustrating this within the Abelian Higgs model under Fermi gauge. During this analysis, we identify an IR divergence specific to the location of the minimum in Fermi gauge that has been overlooked in recent studies. We confirm that physical observables remain calculable in this gauge and further present a method to eliminate this divergence via field redefinition. These findings extend to the Standard Model as well.

This work introduces a numerical investigation of an asymmetric dumbbell model, where "molecules" are formed by linking two Lennard-Jones spheres of unequal sizes via a rigid bond. Using the radius of the larger (A) particle as the reference scale, we provide data on the structure and dynamics of the liquid phase for bond lengths of 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, and 0.5, alongside corresponding data for the plastic-crystal phase at bond lengths of 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3. Structural properties are examined through the AA, AB, and BB radial distribution functions, while dynamic behavior is assessed using the mean-square displacements of A and B particles over time and the rotational time-autocorrelation function. Aligned with the systems' strong virial potential-energy correlations, both structure and dynamics exhibit approximate isomorph invariance when expressed in reduced units. Conversely, these properties show significant variation along isotherms even for a fixed 20% density change. Notably, the rotational time-autocorrelation function, which theoretical predictions suggest should not be isomorph invariant due to the fixed bond length, demonstrates greater variation along isotherms than along isomorphs. These results offer the first validation of isomorph theory for plastic crystals, revealing that isomorph invariance holds more strongly in this phase than in the liquid phase of asymmetric-dumbbell models.

The computational difficulties involved in employing Wigner functions to detect non-classical characteristics of states are resolved through the use of generating functions. This approach enables the calculation of Wigner functions for photon-subtracted states across any number of subtracted photons. The analysis covers both the formal definition of these states using ladder operators and their experimental realization via heralded photon detections. These methods are illustrated by examining photon subtraction applied to squeezed thermal and squeezed Fock states. Furthermore, generating functions are utilized to determine the photon statistics of these states, thereby uncovering various dependencies on their parameters.

This study analyzes a stochastic SIR (susceptible, infective, recovered) epidemic model situated on a social network. The network structure follows an Erdős–Rényi random graph, but susceptible individuals adjacent to infectious nodes may sever or rewire these links during the epidemic. We derive large-population limits that establish convergence for the initial branching process phase and, under the assumption of a major outbreak, for the subsequent epidemic phase, which approaches a deterministic model equivalent to a specific pair approximation. Additionally, we obtain law of large numbers results for the final size of a major outbreak. Two key findings emerge across various parameter configurations: (i) the limiting proportion of infected individuals can exhibit a discontinuity at the critical infection rate $\lambda_c$, resulting in an abrupt jump from zero to a positive value, and (ii) when rewiring is restricted to uninfected individuals, this discontinuity causes the final infected fraction to leap from $0$ to $1$ as $\lambda$ crosses $\lambda_c$.

Contrastive learning (CL) typically demands a vast number of negative samples; for example, MoCo requires 65,536. In dictionary-free frameworks, performance often lags because the negative sample size (NSS) is constrained by the mini-batch size (MBS). To separate NSS from MBS, many CL architectures utilize dynamic dictionaries, with the MoCo family being the most prominent. MoCo specifically employs a momentum-based queue dictionary, which we analyzed in detail regarding its size and consistency. We observe that the InfoNCE loss in MoCo implicitly guides anchors toward their positive counterparts with varying penalty strengths, identifying this inter-anchor hardness-awareness as a key driver for the need for large dictionaries. These insights prompted us to streamline MoCo v2 by eliminating both its dictionary and momentum mechanisms. Leveraging a dual-temperature InfoNCE loss, our simplified frameworks, SimMoCo and SimCo, surpass MoCo v2 by a significant margin. Furthermore, this work narrows the divide between CL and non-CL approaches, fostering a more unified perspective on these two dominant paradigms in self-supervised learning. The code is accessible at: https://bit.ly/3LkQbaT.

Coastal erosion involves the loss of land due to destructive tides, currents, and sea waves. Significant initiatives have utilized structures like breakwaters and groynes to mitigate these impacts. This study tackles the issue by employing shape optimization methods for these obstacles. We simulate wave propagation toward the coastline using two-dimensional porous Shallow Water Equations augmented with artificial viscosity. The permeable shape of the obstacle is optimized via a specific cost function to reduce wave height and velocity along the shore. Unlike approaches relying on finite-dimensional design spaces, this method is grounded in shape calculus.

Real-world graphs often exhibit edge correlations tied to distance, yet these relationships are inhomogeneous. Although the Chung-Lu model and geometric random graph models are valued for their simplicity, they fail to fully capture the complexity of such networks. This paper introduces a generalized geometric random graph model designed to retain key graph-theoretic properties of real-world networks. We validate this model by applying it to a graphical representation of the Drosophila Medulla connectome.

Employing a state-of-the-art combination of dynamical mean-field theory and density functional theory, we conducted a systematic investigation into the temperature and pressure-dependent electronic structure of the ferromagnetic quantum critical candidate CeRh$_6$Ge$_4$. At pressures of -3.9 GPa and -8.3 GPa, variations in Ce-4$f$ occupation, local magnetic susceptibility, and low-frequency electronic self-energy indicate that the Ce-4$f$ electrons remain localized; conversely, at 6.5 GPa and 13.1 GPa, these metrics reveal an itinerant character. As external pressure is released, the characteristic temperatures linked to coherent Kondo screening gradually diminish to zero near 0.8 GPa, signaling a local quantum critical point. Notably, the momentum-resolved spectral function demonstrates that even within the localized regime, highly anisotropic $\mathbf{k}$-dependent hybridization between Ce-4$f$ and conduction electrons persists along the $\Gamma$-A direction, resulting in a hybridization gap. Our calculations predict eight Fermi surface sheets on the local-moment side and six on the Kondo coherent side. Furthermore, the self-energy at 0.8 GPa aligns well with a marginal Fermi-liquid form, leading to resistivity that varies linearly with temperature.

Biological adaptation has always been intertwined with mathematical, engineering, and physical concepts. In 1932, Cannon applied an engineering perspective on regulation in "The Wisdom of the Body," and Selye expanded this in 1938 by introducing the concept of "adaptation energy." While the literal interpretation of this term as physical energy has sparked debate, Selye's phenomenological theory, though not expressed in mathematical language, was easily formalized within thermodynamics to yield verifiable predictions. During the 1980s, researchers investigated how correlation and variance dynamics evolve in systems adapting to environmental loads, discovering a universal effect: prior to the appearance of obvious stress symptoms, both variance and volatility increase alongside correlation during a crisis. This phenomenon has been confirmed over thirty years through observations of diverse groups, including humans, mice, plants, and financial markets. Recent experiments in the last decade have further validated these findings across gene networks in cardiology and oncology, as well as the dynamics of depression and clinical psychotherapy. Consequently, several modeling systems have emerged, including a thermodynamic-like theory for ensembles and various models for individual adaptation. Historically, the first model group relied on Selye's adaptation energy and fitness estimates, while the other two groups are grounded in hidden attractor bifurcation and advection-diffusion models for population distribution in physiological attribute spaces. This overview explores these models and experimental results, beginning with foundational works, emphasizing findings from the last ten years, and addressing open questions.

The cosmological constant puzzle, typically regarded as a naturalness issue, is effectively resolved by the $S$-matrix approach to quantum gravity and string theory. We highlight how this resolution impacts the Hierarchy Problem concerning the disparity between weak and Planck scales. By removing the landscape of de Sitter vacua and eternal inflation, the $S$-matrix framework creates a direct conflict with explanations relying on anthropic selection or cosmological relaxation for the Higgs mass, thereby intensifying the Hierarchy Problem. This development bolsters arguments for new physics emerging near the weak scale while simultaneously raising the possibility that the hierarchy arises from consistency requirements between the $S$-matrix, the Standard Model, and gravity.

Automating the large-scale parametric fitting of multicomponent spectra is a critical but often overlooked component of high-throughput quantification for material and chemical composition.
