To streamline the annotation of spectroscopic and diffraction datasets containing hundreds to thousands of entries, we introduce a systematic methodology designed for high-performance computing environments, leveraging the MapReduce model and task-based parallelization. Implemented in software, this approach demonstrates linear computational scaling relative to the number of spectral components, validated using multidimensional datasets from photoemission spectroscopy and powder electron diffraction. This solution facilitates the efficient creation of high-quality annotations and online spectral analysis, serving as a versatile foundation for closed-loop experimental systems across various analytical techniques in materials science and chemistry.

We introduce a neuro-symbolic pipeline for visual question answering (VQA) on the CLEVR dataset, which features images of object-filled scenes accompanied by related queries. Our approach encompasses three main components: (i) training neural networks to classify objects and predict bounding boxes within CLEVR scenes, (ii) conducting statistical analyses on prediction distributions to establish thresholds for high-confidence outputs, and (iii) converting questions and high-confidence predictions into logic programs to derive answers via an ASP solver. By utilizing choice rules, we accommodate both deterministic and non-deterministic scene encodings. Experimental results indicate that non-deterministic encodings yield strong performance even when neural networks are trained suboptimally, surpassing the deterministic method; this is crucial for constructing robust VQA systems in the face of imperfect network predictions. Additionally, we demonstrate that limiting non-determinism to reasonable options enables more efficient implementations compared to related neuro-symbolic approaches with minimal accuracy loss. This research is currently under review for publication in TPLP.

The evolution of a localized vortex in stably stratified flow, under the Boussinesq approximation, is examined through the lens of fluid impulse theory. The governing equations for the temporal evolution of fluid impulse possess an integro-differential nature, with stratification effects manifesting as convolution integrals involving the impulse components and time-dependent "memory" functions. These functions were computed for scenarios where an external parallel shear flow varies solely in the direction of gravity and is perturbed by localized two- and three-dimensional disturbances. Solutions to these evolution equations indicate that, for both disturbance types, there exists a range of Richardson numbers where the fluid impulse associated with the disturbance grows exponentially. The upper bounds of this range are approximately Ri ~ 1.23 for two-dimensional cases and Ri ~ 0.89 for three-dimensional cases. Furthermore, both scenarios exhibit a critical Richardson number (around Ri ~ 0.3); beyond this threshold, the solution displays oscillatory behavior. While such oscillations have been noted in turbulent flows, this study demonstrates that they are an intrinsic characteristic of a non-wavy localized vortex within a stably stratified shear flow. This paper was originally written in 2001 and has been published without subsequent modifications or additions.

Real-world datasets with skewed distributions present significant hurdles for current object detection systems. Furthermore, detector samplers cause shifts in training label distributions, and the overwhelming ratio of background to foreground samples severely degrades foreground classification performance. To address these problems, this paper introduces Logit Normalization (LogN), a straightforward method that self-calibrates detector logits in a manner analogous to batch normalization. Generally, LogN is training- and tuning-free (requiring no additional training or tuning), agnostic to model and label distributions (ensuring broad generalization across different detectors and datasets), and plug-and-play (allowing direct application without complex modifications). Extensive experiments on the LVIS dataset demonstrate that LogN outperforms state-of-the-art methods when combined with various detectors and backbones. We also conduct in-depth analyses of LogN's different facets. Additional experiments on ImageNet-LT highlight its competitiveness and generalizability. LogN serves as a robust baseline for long-tail object detection and is anticipated to inspire future research in this domain. The code and trained models will be made publicly available at https://github.com/MCG-NJU/LogN.

This paper introduces a scalable "Trustworthy Container Repository" (TCR) designed to store software container images, including those for Docker. Leveraging authenticated data structures based on index-ordered Merkle trees (IOMTs), the TCR ensures users of containers hosted in untrusted environments receive guarantees of 1) Integrity, 2) Availability, and 3) Confidentiality. The system's trust model relies on a low-complexity, tamper-resistant trusted module. IOMTs enable this module to efficiently monitor a virtually limitless number of container images, thereby delivering the necessary security assurances. Simulations of the proposed system demonstrate its scalability, exhibiting logarithmic time complexity even at $2^{25}$ (32 million) container images. The study includes both algorithmic details and proof-of-concept software implementations of the TCR infrastructure.

An abstractive snippet is a newly generated text summary displayed on search engine results pages, distinct from conventional extractive snippets that merely copy phrases and sentences verbatim from web pages. This approach not only bypasses copyright concerns but also enables personalization. While prior evaluations suggest abstractive snippets match extractive ones in user acceptance and expressiveness, the critical challenge remains: can they be automatically generated with adequate quality? This paper presents a novel method for abstractive snippet generation by identifying two large-scale sources for distant supervision: anchor contexts and web directories. By mining ClueWeb09 and ClueWeb12 for anchor contexts and leveraging the DMOZ Open Directory Project, we created the Webis Abstractive Snippet Corpus 2020. This corpus contains over 3.5 million $\langle$query, snippet, document$\rangle$ triples, where the snippets serve as substitutes for genuine query-biased abstractive summaries. We introduce a bidirectional abstractive snippet generation model and evaluate its performance, the corpus quality, and the generated snippets using standard metrics, crowdsourcing, and comparisons against state-of-the-art methods. Results indicate that our new data sources and proposed model successfully produce usable, query-biased abstractive snippets while significantly reducing text reuse.

This work details the full structure of azimuthal dependences and polarization observables in two-hadron production during $e^+e^-$ annihilation, utilizing a transverse momentum dependent (TMD) framework based on the helicity formalism. It comprehensively incorporates leading-twist TMD fragmentation functions (TMD-FFs) for spin-1/2 hadrons. Furthermore, the analysis examines the polarizing FF and its derivation from Belle data regarding the transverse polarization of $\Lambda$ baryons. Finally, the study offers predictions for SIDIS processes at the EIC.

We present a comprehensive error analysis for the low-rank approximation of arbitrary real matrices, addressing both spectral and Frobenius norms. Initially, we establish deterministic error bounds under minimal assumptions. Subsequently, we derive expected error bounds for non-standard Gaussian scenarios, accommodating a non-zero mean and a general covariance structure for the random matrix. This analysis extends and refines the spectral and Frobenius norm error bounds previously introduced by Halko, Martinsson, and Tropp. Furthermore, we examine the Randomized Singular Value Decomposition, applying our expected error bounds specifically to this context. Finally, numerical experiments using a synthetic instructional dataset validate the tightness of the newly derived error bounds.

This work generalizes prior findings on Putinar's Positivstellensatz for cylindrical sets of the form $S \times \mathbb{R}$ to specific instances involving sets of type $S \times \mathbb{R}^r$. These extensions incorporate the parameter $r$ and the degree of polynomials relative to the unbounded variables in $\mathbb{R}^r$. The identified special cases align with scenarios where the cone of non-negative polynomials coincides with the cone of sums of squares, and explicit degree bounds are established.

Galaxy clusters contain hot, diffuse plasma that emits X-rays, characterized by a magnetically tangled field with energy nearly equal to that of turbulent motions \cite{zweibel1997, Vacca}. In the cluster cores, temperatures remain unexpectedly high despite radiative cooling times being much shorter than the Hubble time \cite{cowie1977,fabian1994}. Although heating from central active galactic nuclei (AGN) \cite{fabian2012,birzan2012,churazov2000} is thought to account for most of the energy, there is ongoing debate regarding whether heat conduction from the surrounding bulk to the core contributes significantly \cite{narayan2001,ruszkowski2002,kunz2011}, particularly given the tangled magnetic fields. Notably, sharp temperature gradients observed in cold fronts suggest that thermal conduction is highly suppressed \cite{markevitch2007}. To investigate heat conduction within a magnetized, turbulent plasma, we simulated such conditions using a laser laboratory experiment. Our results demonstrate a reduction in local heat transport by at least two orders of magnitude, producing significant temperature variations on small spatial scales consistent with observations of cluster plasmas \cite{markevitch2003}.

Recent analyses of Planck data have suggested the possibility that our universe is not spatially flat. Motivated by this renewed focus on non-zero spatial curvature, we revisit light propagation in such a universe and derive gauge-invariant expressions for key cosmological probes: luminosity distance, galaxy clustering, weak gravitational lensing, and cosmic microwave background anisotropies. Due to the positional dependence of the spatial metric, light propagation in a non-flat universe is significantly more complex than in a flat one. By incorporating all relativistic effects, including vector and tensor contributions, we obtain the necessary expressions for these probes and explicitly confirm their gauge invariance. While we compare our findings to any existing literature on non-flat universes, this study constitutes the first comprehensive investigation of these probes in such a context. Our developed theoretical framework for non-flat universes will be essential for constraining spatial curvature in future large-scale surveys.

Wikipedia stands as one of the web's most visited sites, serving millions of daily users who turn to it for diverse information. Despite its importance in addressing these information needs, the underlying reasons why users visit remain largely unexplored. This paper aims to address that gap by integrating a survey of Wikipedia readers with an analysis of server logs. Drawing from initial survey data, we developed a taxonomy of Wikipedia use cases across multiple dimensions, encompassing user motivations, the depth of knowledge sought, and prior familiarity with the topics. Subsequently, we measured the frequency of these use cases through a large-scale survey of live Wikipedia users, gathering nearly 30,000 responses. Our analysis reveals a wide array of drivers for visits, including current events, media coverage, personal curiosity, academic or professional requirements, and boredom. Furthermore, we cross-referenced survey answers with users' digital footprints in Wikipedia's logs to identify behavioral patterns linked to specific use cases. For example, users driven by boredom or random exploration tend to navigate long, rapid sequences of pages, while those using the site for school or work spend more time on individual articles focused on subjects like science. These findings deepen our understanding of reader motivations and behaviors on Wikipedia, offering valuable insights for developers enhancing user experience, editors catering to reader needs, third-party services accessing Wikipedia content, and researchers developing tools such as recommendation engines.

We introduce a novel class of quantum fluids termed Stiefel liquids, constructed from $2+1$-dimensional nonlinear sigma models defined on the target space $SO(N)/SO(4)$ and augmented by Wess-Zumino-Witten terms. These Stiefel liquids represent a category of critical quantum fluids exhibiting remarkable characteristics, including expansive emergent symmetries, a cascading structure, and nontrivial quantum anomalies. Our analysis demonstrates that the established deconfined quantum critical point and the $U(1)$ Dirac spin liquid are unified as specific instances of Stiefel liquids, corresponding to $N=5$ and $N=6$, respectively. Moreover, we posit that Stiefel liquids with $N>6$ are non-Lagrangian; under renormalization group flow, they approach infrared conformal fixed points that defy description by any renormalizable continuum Lagrangian. Such non-Lagrangian states transcend the conventional parton gauge mean-field theory framework used in condensed matter physics to study exotic quantum liquids. The inherent inability to construct these states via (conventional or parton-like) mean-field methods implies that traditional approaches struggle to determine whether a non-Lagrangian state can emerge from a specific ultraviolet system, such as a lattice spin model. To address this, we propose that a quantum state is emergible from a lattice system if its quantum anomalies satisfy the constraints imposed by (generalized) Lieb-Schultz-Mattis theorems. Guided by this hypothesis, we identify that certain non-Lagrangian Stiefel liquids can be realized in frustrated quantum spin systems—such as those on triangular or Kagome lattices—through the interplay between non-coplanar magnetic orders and valence-bond-solid orders.

This work examines conjugate and Lagrange dualities in the context of abstract convexity for composite optimization problems. We establish sufficient conditions for a zero duality gap in conjugate duality, while employing the intersection property to achieve the same result for Lagrange duality. Additionally, we elucidate the relationship between the Lagrange and conjugate duals, supported by examples involving both convex and weakly convex functions.

Closed-loop brain stimulation involves capturing neurophysiological signals like electroencephalography (EEG), rapidly detecting specific neural events, and delivering precise auditory, magnetic, or electrical interventions to modulate brain activity. While this approach holds significant promise for fundamental neuroscience and clinical uses such as rehabilitating impaired memory, current systems are often costly, bulky, and lack experimental flexibility. This article introduces Portiloop, a portable, low-cost, deep learning-driven closed-loop system designed to target specific brain oscillations. We first detail open-hardware solutions built from off-the-shelf components, followed by the provision of a lightweight neural network and an automated algorithm that optimizes hyperparameters for desired oscillatory targets. The system's efficacy is demonstrated through real-time sleep spindle detection, achieving performance comparable to offline expert consensus on the Massive Online Data Annotation (MODA) dataset. To foster further innovation in closed-loop neuroscience, the software and hardware plans are released as an open science resource for the community.

Meta-materials, characterized by unique optical properties, represent a significant area of study within advanced physics. They possess the capability to manipulate light and wave propagation to generate electromagnetic spaces, distinguished by natural hyperbolic and non-convex plasmons. This paper investigates the optical properties of the three-layer Beryllium-Graphene-Beryllium (BeCBe) structure, demonstrating that it exhibits hyperbolic plasmons within the terahertz (THz) frequency range alongside non-convex plasmons. Our findings indicate that plasmon energy propagation predominantly occurs along the qy axis in the hyperbolic region. Furthermore, an elliptic case is observed exclusively at 1029.71 THz. The hyperbolic region initiates at 289.31 THz, marking the onset of the first and narrowest hyperbolic window. Due to the high density of free electrons in the BeCBe plasmonic material, the presence of the visible region within the third hyperbolic window results in an elevated plasma frequency.

Call Graphs, serving as a rich data source, are utilized in various applications, notably for detecting security vulnerabilities. Although numerous studies demonstrate that Call Graphs significantly enhance analysis accuracy, current ecosystem-scale tools such as Dependabot operate at the package level without leveraging Call Graphs. Applying Call Graphs to ecosystem-wide scenarios remains impractical due to scalability constraints inherent in Call Graph generators. Typically viewed as a form of "full program analysis," generating Call Graphs produces massive graphs and incurs high computational costs. Consequently, this exhaustive approach is unsuitable for ecosystem-level analysis because the potential combinations of how artifacts interact within a full program explode in number. Therefore, incremental analysis is essential. While existing research covers various types of incremental program analysis, none specifically addresses Call Graph generation across an entire ecosystem. This paper introduces an incremental implementation of the CHA algorithm capable of generating Call Graphs on-demand by stitching together previously extracted partial Call Graphs for libraries. Preliminary evaluation results indicate that this proposed method scales effectively and surpasses the performance of OPAL, the most scalable existing framework.

This study presents a measurement of the jet mass distribution for hadronic decays of Lorentz-boosted top quarks. The analysis focuses on the lepton+jets channel of top quark pair ($\mathrm{t\bar{t}}$) production, where the lepton is either an electron or a muon. The decay products of the hadronic top quark are reconstructed into a single large-radius jet with transverse momentum exceeding 400 GeV. Data collected by the CMS detector during proton-proton collisions at the LHC amount to an integrated luminosity of 138 fb$^{-1}$. The differential $\mathrm{t\bar{t}}$ production cross section, differentiated by jet mass, is unfolded to the particle level to determine the top quark mass. Calibration of the jet mass scale is achieved using the hadronic W boson decay contained within the large-radius jet. By investigating angular correlations in jet substructure, uncertainties related to final state radiation modelling are minimized. These improvements result in enhanced precision, yielding a top quark mass measurement of 172.76 $\pm$ 0.81 GeV.

The propagation of Ultra-High-Energy Cosmic Rays (UHECRs) through a turbulent intergalactic magnetic field within the small-angle scattering regime is well-established for distances significantly exceeding the field's coherence length. However, diffusion theory fails in this context, and anomalous effects can emerge over shorter ranges, spanning from a few to 10–20 coherence scales. This study investigates UHECR propagation in this specific regime, which is particularly relevant for intermediate-mass UHECR nuclei and nG-level intergalactic magnetic fields possessing a 1 Mpc coherence scale. Our findings reveal that particle trajectories develop a complex, caustic-like structure characterized by significant deviations from isotropy. Consequently, flux measurements from a source at a fixed distance will vary depending on the observer's location.

We demonstrate that any effectively closed action of a finitely generated group $G$ on a closed subset of $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ can be realized as a topological factor of the $G$-subaction within a $(G \times H_1 \times H_2)$-subshift of finite type (SFT), regardless of the choice of infinite, finitely generated groups $H_1$ and $H_2$. Consequently, we establish that any group structured as a triple product $G_1 \times G_2 \times G_3$, where each $G_i$ is finitely generated and possesses a decidable word problem, supports a non-empty strongly aperiodic SFT. Furthermore, derived from this result, we prove the existence of non-empty strongly aperiodic SFTs for a broad class of branch groups, which explicitly encompasses the Grigorchuk group.

Binary matrices are prevalent in scientific research, where detecting significant patterns often involves comparing observed data against a null model. This study focuses on sampling binary matrices that adhere to specific row and column sum constraints. While previous methods have primarily utilized uniform sampling from this space, we propose modified elementwise swapping algorithms that generate samples based on a non-uniform probability distribution defined by a weight matrix, which assigns relative likelihoods to individual entries. We find that structural zeros (zeros in the weight matrix) typically hinder swapping algorithms unless they exhibit special monotonic properties. Through simulation studies and an analysis of a classic bird habitation dataset, we evaluate our algorithms and demonstrate the implications of using a non-uniform null model.

Recursive Neural Networks (RvNNs), which organize sequences based on their inherent hierarchical syntax, have demonstrated superior performance in various natural language processing tasks compared to models lacking structural biases. However, conventional RvNNs cannot autonomously infer latent structures from plain text. While several extensions have been introduced to mitigate this issue, they often depend on surrogate gradients or reinforcement learning, resulting in increased bias or variance. To address these drawbacks, we introduce the Continuous Recursive Neural Network (CRvNN), a backpropagation-compatible alternative that integrates a continuous relaxation of the induced structure. Our results show that CRvNN excels in demanding synthetic benchmarks, including logical inference and ListOps. Furthermore, on real-world applications such as sentiment analysis and natural language inference, CRvNN performs on par with or outperforms existing latent structure models.

Inspired by fluid dynamics applications related to the harmonic Bergman projection, our goal is to extend the theory of single and double layer potentials—from its established foundation in functions with $H^1_{\ell oc}$ regularity—to locally square integrable functions. Considering the requirements of numerical simulations where functions are typically defined on polygonal meshes, we aim to develop a theory that accommodates non-smooth domains, specifically those with Lipschitz continuous or polygonal boundaries.

We describe the computation of the leading-order quark Sivers function at low Bjorken $x$. Utilizing the high-energy scattering approximation and the operator framework established by Kovchegov and Sievert, we derive the primary contribution arising from the spin-dependent odderon, a result consistent with findings by Dong, Zhen, and Zhou. Subsequently, we evaluate this dominant term within the proton's diquark model to generate a small-$x$ estimate for the Sivers function.

Using first-principles calculations, we investigate the gate field effects on the Mn$_{12}$O$_{12}$(COOH)$_{16}$(H$_2$O)$_4$ | graphene | GaAs heterostructure. Our results indicate that under moderate doping conditions, electrons can be introduced into the single-molecule magnet Mn$_{12}$ but cannot be extracted. As the electron doping level rises, the magnetic anisotropy energy (MAE) of Mn$_{12}$ diminishes, driven by electron transfer from graphene to Mn$_{12}$ and shifts in the band alignment between the two. Specifically, at an electron doping level of $-5.00 \times 10^{13}\, \textrm{cm}^{-2}$, the MAE drops by approximately 18% relative to the undoped state. The band alignment between graphene and GaAs proves more responsive to electron doping than to hole doping, largely because the GaAs valence band lies near the Fermi level. Additionally, the GaAs substrate creates a minor bandgap in the supported graphene at zero gate field while maintaining a nearly strain-free configuration. We conclude by suggesting a vertical tunnel junction as a method to probe the gate-dependent MAE through electron transport measurements.

Subsampling is a widely adopted strategy to mitigate computational demands when analyzing large-scale datasets. While recent studies have focused on statistical models lacking explicit regularization, this paper introduces an efficient subsampling framework specifically for large-sample linear ridge regression. Unlike ordinary least squares, the ridge penalty creates a delicate balance between bias and variance. We first examine the asymptotic behavior of the subsampling estimator and subsequently propose minimizing the asymptotic mean squared error to achieve optimality. The derived subsampling probability incorporates both the ridge leverage score and the L2 norm of the predictors. To further lower the computational expense associated with calculating ridge leverage scores, we present an algorithm featuring efficient approximation techniques. Validation using both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrates that this approach achieves superior statistical accuracy and computational efficiency compared to existing subsampling methods.

This study extends the $\Delta$-CoVaR methodology to both conditional and unconditional frameworks by incorporating Expected Shortfall (ES) through quantile regression and adopting a broader definition of distress. The resulting $\Delta$-CoES metric complements $\Delta$-CoVaR and demonstrates superior efficacy in capturing short-term systemic risk fluctuations and distinguishing heterogeneity in risk contributions and inter-institutional linkages, owing to its enhanced robustness. These attributes offer significant economic value for regulators, risk managers, and market participants seeking greater sensitivity and granular insights to establish short-term capital adequacy and risk limits, detect fragile financial connections and institutions, or develop early warning systems for systemic risk. Furthermore, the $\Delta$-CoES is straightforward to estimate and aligns with contemporary regulatory standards like the FRTB. To empirically validate these statistical advantages and characteristics, the paper applies both $\Delta$-CoVaR and $\Delta$-CoES to a comprehensive dataset spanning from December 31, 1970, to December 31, 2020, comprising 1,564 US financial institutions, analyzing daily equity data within both systemic and network contexts. Additionally, the study utilizes a sample of nine US-based GSIBs to illustrate the $\Delta$-CoES's utility in pinpointing problematic financial linkages.

This document establishes the groundwork for VO and requirement refinement, model abstractions, and their instantiations, while also addressing VOs within the context of both abstractions and instantiations.

Metamorphic testing (MT) is a prevalent method for evaluating software when traditional oracles are unavailable. It relies on metamorphic relations (MRs)—connections between multiple inputs and their corresponding outputs—to identify faults. Since MRs differ in their fault-detection capabilities and often target the same defects, this paper introduces prioritization strategies to enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of MT during regression testing. We propose two specific approaches: fault-based and coverage-based prioritization. To assess these methods, we conducted experiments on three complex open-source software systems. The results demonstrate that our prioritization techniques significantly outperform the conventional practice of executing MR test cases ad-hoc, particularly regarding fault detection effectiveness. Furthermore, fault-based prioritization reduces the number of required source and follow-up test cases and lowers the average time to detect faults, ultimately saving time and resources in the testing process.

This submission addresses SemEval-2021 Task 5, focused on detecting toxic spans within text. Identifying these spans is a complex challenge due to the inherent subjectivity of toxicity and the fact that toxic content often arises not just from isolated insults, but from multi-word expressions where individual words may appear benign. Guided by the need to evaluate both single tokens and phrases, we investigated the efficacy of a multi-depth DistilBERT model, which leverages embeddings from various layers to determine per-token toxicity scores. Our quantitative findings indicate that incorporating information from multiple model depths significantly enhances performance. Additionally, we provide a qualitative analysis of our top-performing model.

We introduce a straightforward approach for creating giant lipid pseudo-vesicles, characterized by an oily cap and encapsulated within an agarose gel. This technique utilizes only a standard micropipette and depends on the formation of a water/oil/water double droplet within liquid agarose. Using fluorescence imaging, we analyze the resulting vesicles and confirm the existence and integrity of the lipid bilayer through the successful insertion of $\alpha$-Hemolysin transmembrane proteins. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these vesicles can be mechanically deformed without intrusion by indenting the gel surface.

This work investigates the linear convergence properties of generalized proximal point algorithms applied to monotone inclusion problems. Assuming either metric subregularity of the associated monotone operator or Lipschitz continuity of its inverse, we establish both Q-linear and R-linear convergence theorems. Additionally, this paper includes remarks comparing our findings with existing results in the literature.

This paper investigates Cotton solitons on almost Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds. We first examine the case where the potential vector field is pointwise collinear with the Reeb vector field, demonstrating that no such Cotton soliton exists. Subsequently, assuming the potential vector field is orthogonal to the Reeb vector field, we prove that on a non-Kenmotsu almost Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifold where the Reeb vector field is an eigenvector of the Ricci operator, the Cotton soliton is steady and the manifold is locally isometric to $\mathbb{H}^2(-4) \times \mathbb{R}$.

Excessive salt consumption among the general population leads to hypertension and associated health issues. This paper presents findings from ongoing research aimed at reducing salt intake through technological means, specifically focusing on user interfaces. The study investigates how visual and textual explanations within a search interface can influence preferences for salty foods. An online experiment involving 200 participants reveals that it is feasible to alter these preferences in food search results by pairing recipes with a visual taste map that accounts for salt-replacing herbs and spices when calculating overall saltiness.

Modeling binary light curves within gravitational microlensing formalism fundamentally requires solving the binary lens equation. Currently, the standard approach combines Newton's and Laguerre's methods, a technique originally proposed by Skowron & Gould (SG). In this paper, we present a rapid root-finding algorithm for univariate polynomials based on the Aberth-Ehrlich (AE) method, which was introduced in 1967 as an enhancement to Newton's method. The AE algorithm demonstrates superior speed compared to Newton's, Laguerre's, and Durand-Kerner methods, with the distinct advantage of computing all roots simultaneously. After refining the basic AE algorithm and analyzing its characteristics, we optimize it specifically for binary lens equations, which are fifth-degree polynomials with complex coefficients. Our optimized method achieves a speed improvement of approximately 1.8 to 2.0 times over the SG algorithm. Since determining magnification factors for both point-like and finite source stars necessitates solving the binary lens equation to locate image plane positions, this new approach significantly enhances the speed and accuracy of binary microlensing modeling.

The occurrence rate of sub-Saturns (planets with radii between $\sim$4 and $8R_{\oplus}$) increases with orbital period up to at least $\sim$300 days. This study proposes and evaluates the hypothesis that atmospheric mass loss drives the decline in sub-Saturn frequency closer to their host stars, converting them into sub-Neptunes ($\lesssim$4$R_{\oplus}$) more rapidly at shorter periods. Under this mass loss framework, the observed sub-Saturn occurrence can be used to deduce their intrinsic core mass function, which subsequently informs our understanding of gas giant cores. We find that a lognormal core mass function peaking near $\sim$10--20$M_{\oplus}$ aligns with the sub-Saturn period distribution, observational estimates of their cores, and gas accretion models. Our theory predicts that around rapidly rotating stars, close-in sub-Saturns should be approximately 50% less frequent and 30% more massive; this prediction is testable for stars younger than $\lesssim$500 Myr. Additionally, we forecast that the sub-Jovian desert will be less distinct and extend to shorter orbital periods around M dwarfs compared to solar-type stars (roughly 0.7 days versus $\sim$3 days). We further demonstrate that low-density "Super-Puff" sub-Saturns can persist today despite intense hydrodynamic escape if they formed with significantly larger atmospheres; for instance, Kepler 223 d likely began with an envelope 1.5 times the mass of its core and is currently shedding its atmosphere at a rate of $\sim$2$\times$10$^{-3}M_{\oplus}~\mathrm{Myr}^{-1}$. Should these theoretical predictions hold true observationally, the derived core mass function could also help constrain theories regarding the formation of gas-rich planetary cores.

The Dirac scotogenic model offers a sophisticated solution for generating small Dirac neutrino masses and mixing patterns, utilizing a single symmetry to ensure both the "Dirac nature" of neutrinos and the stability of dark matter. This study investigates the phenomenological consequences of the recent CDF-II $W$ boson mass measurement within this framework. We demonstrate that, in scenarios where dark matter is primarily an $SU(2)_L$ scalar doublet, it is impossible to simultaneously meet the requirements for dark matter relic density, the $m_W$ anomaly, and direct detection limits. However, distinct from the Majorana scotogenic model, the Dirac variant also incorporates an $SU(2)_L$ singlet scalar within the "dark sector." We find that if this singlet scalar serves as the lightest dark sector particle and constitutes the dark matter, then constraints from neutrino physics, dark matter observations, and oblique $S$, $T$, and $U$ parameters can all be satisfied for $W$ boson masses falling within the CDF-II range.

We introduce Pathways, a novel large-scale orchestration layer designed for accelerators. This system facilitates the exploration of emerging ML research concepts and architectures without compromising the performance of existing state-of-the-art models. Pathways employs a sharded, asynchronous dataflow graph where operators consume and generate futures, enabling the efficient gang-scheduling of heterogeneous parallel workloads across thousands of accelerators while managing data transfers via dedicated interconnects. By utilizing a new asynchronous distributed dataflow architecture, the control plane operates in parallel even when data plane dependencies exist. This engineering approach supports a single-controller model, simplifying the expression of complex parallelism patterns. We demonstrate that Pathways achieves performance parity (approximately 100% accelerator utilization) with leading systems on SPMD computations across 2048 TPUs. Furthermore, it delivers throughput comparable to SPMD configurations for Transformer models pipelined over 16 stages or sharded across two accelerator islands connected by a data center network.

Extended zigzag Schur algebras, which are conjectured to be Morita equivalent to RoCK blocks of classical Schur algebras, are quasi-hereditary algebras; we demonstrate that these algebras are Ringel self-dual.

This article introduces a novel generalization of the Genocchi numbers and Genocchi theorem. As a result, we derive several significant families of integer-valued polynomials that are closely linked to Bernoulli polynomials. Letting ${(B_n)}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ represent the sequence of Bernoulli numbers and ${(B_n(X))}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ denote the sequence of Bernoulli polynomials, we specifically establish that for every natural number $n$, the reciprocal polynomial of $\big(B_n(X) - B_n\big)$ takes integer values.

The selection of a parameter sharing strategy in multilingual machine translation models dictates how effectively the parameter space is utilized, thereby directly impacting final translation quality. Drawing inspiration from linguistic trees that depict interlanguage relatedness, a novel general approach to parameter sharing has recently been proposed. Its core principle involves leveraging these expert language hierarchies to construct multilingual architectures, where the degree of parameter sharing between languages is proportional to their closeness. In this study, we evaluate this concept using the Transformer architecture and reveal that, despite prior successes, inherent challenges exist in training such hierarchical models. We demonstrate that with a carefully selected training strategy, this hierarchical architecture can surpass both bilingual models and multilingual models that employ full parameter sharing.

Astrotourism offers fresh avenues for fostering sustainable socio-economic growth, safeguarding cultural heritage, and inspiring and educating people worldwide. This sector encompasses various activities, ranging from visiting observatories to traveling to remote locations to witness a clear, dark night sky. Through our UK-Namibian partnership, we are actively developing and promoting astrotourism in Namibia while simultaneously expanding its potential on a global scale.

Let $\varrho$ be a fixed integer greater than or equal to 2. We examine functions $H: \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ where, for each integer $n$, $H(n)$ is the result of applying one of $\varrho$ distinct affine-linear maps, selected based on $n \pmod{\varrho}$; these functions extend the well-known Collatz or $3x+1$ map. This paper develops a $p$-adic framework for analyzing the periodic points of $H$, a method applicable to the standard Collatz map and a broad class of its generalizations. When this approach is viable, it produces a function $\chi_{H}: \mathbb{Z}_{\varrho} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}_{q}$ (where $q \geq 2$ is an integer intrinsic to $H$) such that every integer in the image $\chi_{H}(\mathbb{Z}_{\varrho})$ is a periodic point of $H$, and every cycle of $H$ with length at least 2 includes at least one such integer. Furthermore, the $\chi_{H}$ formalism streamlines, unifies, and extends prior research on Collatz-type maps by various authors, laying the groundwork for future investigations into the periodic points of these maps using $p$-adic Fourier analysis, complex analysis, and probability theory.

This work continues the investigation into global solutions for the two-dimensional Prandtl system regarding unsteady boundary layers, specifically within Oleinik's class under favorable pressure conditions. First, employing an alternative approach distinct from [13], we provide a direct proof of the existence of a global weak solution via a direct BV estimate. Subsequently, we establish the uniqueness and continuous dependence on data for this weak solution in the context of the initial-boundary value problem. Finally, we demonstrate the regularity of these weak solutions and conclude with the global existence of smooth solutions.

First-Order Logic (FOL) serves as a potent reasoning instrument for program verification, with recent Ivy research demonstrating its effectiveness for parameterized distributed systems. Nevertheless, expressing common structures like ring topologies in FOL remains unexpectedly cumbersome. We introduce an FOL-based framework designed to specify distributed multi-process protocols in a process-local fashion alongside an implicit network topology. Within this framework, we offer an auto-active analysis method to reason about protocols locally and in a modular manner, aiming to align with how designers typically conceptualize and analyze such systems. By concealing the topology within the FOL structure, we streamline the modeling process, albeit at the cost of increased reasoning complexity. To address this, we employ a topology oracle to formulate a sound and relatively complete proof rule that transforms reasoning about the implicit topology into pure FOL, thereby eliminating the need to axiomatize the topology. Leveraging this rule, we derive a property that limits verification to a fixed number of processes, determined by the size of local neighborhoods. We illustrate the framework's application through two examples, including leader election on a ring.

Bird vocalizations span a spectrum from basic tones to intricate, multi-harmonic dynamic structures. Currently, the more complex calls remain largely enigmatic, particularly those of the scientifically significant corvid family, which includes jackdaws, crows, and ravens. While individual birds are capable of recognizing familiar conspecifics via their calls, the specific location within the signal where identity is encoded remains unclear. To investigate this, we analyzed a dataset of jackdaw calls using a hybrid of feature representations, specifically linear predictive coding (LPC) and the adaptive discrete Fourier transform (aDFT). Our results, derived from a classification framework, demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms standard spectrogram representations in identifying individual birds. Furthermore, by applying metric learning, we identified the specific time-frequency regions that most critically contribute to robust individual recognition. Ultimately, computational methodologies can guide our quest to decipher these complex biological signals.

The pre- and post-selected weak value, $\rm A_w$, has recently proven effective for detecting minute physical phenomena. While a reduction in post-selection probability theoretically enhances sensitivity, this relationship holds strictly when $\rm A_w$ is purely real or purely imaginary; in such cases, sensitivity correlates with the real or imaginary part of $\rm A_w$, respectively. However, when $\rm A_w$ is complex (plural), an anomalous behavior emerges where decreasing the post-selection probability can diminish sensitivity under specific pre- and post-selection conditions. Furthermore, practical limitations such as device imperfections and environmental instability within the Weak Value Amplification (WVA) protocol exacerbate this anomaly, leading to reduced sensitivity and systematic measurement errors compared to the standard scheme. Consequently, three viable strategies are proposed to mitigate these adverse effects whenever weak measurement transitions into a regime characterized by a plural weak value.

This study develops a method grounded in Fisher information (FI) to quantify maximum information gain and optimize experimental design within neutron reflectometry. Since the FI can be derived analytically in these experiments, it enables sub-second forecasts of parameter uncertainties. This capability supports real-time adjustments to experimental variables—such as measurement angles, duration, and contrast selection—based on specific parameters of interest. The FI establishes a lower bound for parameter estimation uncertainties, which diminish according to the inverse square root of measurement time, offering valuable insights for planning and scheduling. Given its computational efficiency, the FI can be recalculated repeatedly throughout an experiment to conserve beam time by identifying when sufficient data has been collected or to justify extending an experiment if more data is needed. The validity of this approach is confirmed via a simulation framework that accounts for instrument-specific incident flux profiles and by analyzing the structural properties of a phospholipid bilayer.

This study examines two optimization challenges concerning area-proportional rectangle contact representations for layered, embedded planar graphs. In these representations, vertices are depicted as interior-disjoint unit-height rectangles with specified widths, arranged in a single row per layer, while edges are ideally realized as contacts of positive length. Such representations are useful in semantic word or tag cloud visualizations, where semantically linked words are positioned closely together. Our objectives are to either maximize the count of realized rectangle contacts or minimize the total area of the representation, all while preventing false adjacencies. We introduce a network flow model for area minimization, a linear-time algorithm for maximizing contacts in two-layer graphs, and an integer linear programming (ILP) model for optimizing contacts in $k$-layer graphs.

Quantum interference among multiple pathways during molecular photodissociation frequently induces angular momentum polarization in atomic fragments, offering profound insights into fundamental physics. While the resulting orbital polarization in diatomic dissociation is well-established and aligns with quantum mechanical theory, coherent photofragment orbital polarization in polyatomic molecules remains an observed phenomenon lacking theoretical explanation and physical understanding. This study introduces a model for ozone photodissociation that highlights a novel aspect of the geometric phase. We demonstrate that this geometric phase effect enables coherent polarization in scenarios where it would typically disappear and suppresses it in cases where it might otherwise occur. Consequently, the model explains ozone measurements that have previously resisted interpretation and marks progress toward a deeper comprehension of coherent electronic excitation in polyatomic systems and the emerging role of the geometric phase.

Aluminum is a predominant material in superconducting quantum circuits and is currently the preferred superconductor for developing topological qubits. However, aluminum-based devices face significant limitations regarding magnetic field compatibility. This study addresses that constraint by demonstrating that heavy element adatoms, such as platinum (Pt), can more than double the critical field of thin aluminum films. Through tunnel junction experiments, we attribute this enhanced field resilience to spin-orbit scattering induced by Pt. Leveraging this property within semiconductor-superconductor hybrids, we show that InSb nanowires strongly coupled to Al/Pt films sustain superconductivity up to 7 Tesla. Furthermore, we confirm that the two-electron charging effect—a cornerstone of topological quantum computation—remains robust despite the presence of these heavy adatoms. Non-local spectroscopy in a three-terminal configuration reveals that the bulk of these hybrid devices remains free of sub-gap states. Additionally, we verify that semiconductor states proximitized by Al/Pt films retain their capacity for Zeeman splitting under an applied magnetic field. Given aluminum's established chemical stability and fabrication methods, the Al/Pt combination emerges as the ideal successor to pure Al systems and a compelling high-field alternative to other superconductors.

Distributional semantic models for noun-noun compounds (such as starfish, bank account, or houseboat) often overlook the critical impact of constituent polysemy, contrasting, for instance, the various senses of "star" in "starfish," "star cluster," and "star athlete." Rather than relying on semantic vectors that average across multiple meanings, these models require disambiguated constituent vectors to accurately capture how specific meanings contribute to the compound's overall definition. This paper introduces a novel solution to this word sense disambiguation challenge using set expansion. Adapting the methodology of Mahabal et al. (2018), originally intended for analogy tasks, we modified it to specifically address the disambiguation of compound constituents. Experimental results on a dataset of nearly 9,000 compounds (LADEC, Gagné et al. 2019) indicate that this approach is effective, although its performance varies depending on the frequency with which the compounds appear.

This research investigates the streaming instability of cosmic rays (CRs) ranging from GeV to 100 GeV and their damping within the turbulent interstellar medium (ISM). Our findings indicate that ion-neutral collisional damping governs the instability in weakly ionized molecular clouds, turbulent damping prevails in the highly ionized warm medium, and nonlinear Landau damping occurs in the Galactic halo. Notably, CR streaming velocity approaches the Alfvén speed only within the Galactic halo. Alfvénic turbulence is crucial for both suppressing the streaming instability and regulating CR diffusion through magnetic field line tangling; in super-Alfvénic turbulence, the effective mean free path in the observer's frame is set by the Alfvénic scale. Consequently, the diffusion coefficient is highly sensitive to the Alfvén Mach number, which varies widely across the multi-phase ISM. Furthermore, super-Alfvénic turbulence enhances the confinement of streaming CRs, regardless of the primary damping mechanism at play.

This study estimates that approximately $27.99(\pm2.15)\%$ of the UK population has experienced wheezing prior to their first birthday. Utilizing a cohort of $N=1184$, the Bernoulli Mixture Model was determined to perform optimally with $K=4$ clusters, effectively balancing cluster separability with interpretability. The model assumes that the probability of parents in the $j$th cluster reporting wheezing for their children at the $i$th age follows $P_{ij} \sim \text{Beta}(1/2, 1/2)$, cluster assignment probabilities follow $R \sim \text{Dirichlet}_K(\alpha)$, individual patient assignments follow $Z_n\ |\ R \sim \text{Categorical}(R)$, and wheezing events follow $X_{in}\ |\ P_{i,Z_n} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(P_{i,Z_n})$, where $i\in\{1,\dots,6\}$, $j\in\{1,\dots,K\}$, and $n\in\{1,\dots, N\}$. Clustering is executed via the E-M optimization algorithm. Results indicate that this approach efficiently categorizes patients into groups characterized by late-childhood, persistent, early-childhood, or absent/sporadic wheezing. Additionally, the method demonstrates independence from specific datasets and accommodates those containing missing entries.

Despite notable advancements in artistic style transfer, most current approaches struggle to maintain semantic integrity in a fine-grained, locally consistent way, particularly when transferring multiple artist styles within a single model. To address this limitation, we introduce a Stroke Control Multi-Artist Style Transfer framework. This framework employs a multi-condition single-generator architecture to facilitate multi-artist style transfer and incorporates an Anisotropic Stroke Module (ASM). The ASM dynamically adjusts style strokes between complex and simple regions, granting the network adaptive semantic consistency across diverse styles. Additionally, we propose a novel Multi-Scale Projection Discriminator designed for texture-level conditional generation. Unlike single-scale discriminators, our approach captures multi-scale texture cues to effectively differentiate a broad spectrum of artistic styles. Extensive experiments confirm the feasibility and effectiveness of our method, demonstrating that a single model can successfully transform photographs into distinct oil painting styles while preserving anisotropic semantic details and maintaining unique artistic characteristics. The code is publicly available at: https://github.com/neuralchen/ASMAGAN.

This study demonstrates that vector fields $b$ with a spatial derivative $D_xb$ satisfying an Orlicz summability condition possess a spatially continuous representative and are well-posed. Specifically, when sub-exponential summability is present, their flows also satisfy a quantitative version of the Lusin (N) condition. Moreover, we establish that if $D_xb$ meets a specific exponential summability criterion, the flow generated by $b$ exhibits Sobolev regularity, even without assuming that ${\rm div}_xb$ is bounded. These findings are subsequently applied to analyze the representation and Sobolev regularity of weak solutions to the Cauchy problem for both transport and continuity equations.

Image-text matching is a crucial multi-modal task with extensive applications, aiming to align images and text based on shared semantic content. Current methods fail to explicitly map different modalities into a unified space, and the widely adopted attention mechanisms in these models lack supervision. We introduce a novel attention scheme that projects image and text embeddings into a common space and directly optimizes attention weights toward evaluation metrics. This approach functions as a form of supervised attention without requiring additional annotations. It is trained using a new discrete-continuous action space policy gradient algorithm, which models complex action spaces more effectively than prior continuous-only methods. Experiments on two standard benchmark datasets, Flickr30k and MS-COCO, demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms previous approaches.

Fitting Parton Distribution Functions (PDFs) demands a unified framework that integrates extensive datasets from both theoretical predictions and experimental data. While data integration primarily involves standardizing formats, incorporating theoretical predictions is more complex due to the involvement of multiple components. Various independent groups develop distinct providers for different processes, utilizing diverse input parameters (runcards) and output structures (interpolation grids). Furthermore, because processes are measured across different scales, the PDF candidate requires DGLAP evolution, either calculated dynamically or precomputed into grids. Our goal is to automate all these steps within a single framework, making it a valuable resource for any PDF fitting group and potentially for broader phenomenological investigations.

From a requirements engineering perspective, identifying context-aware features necessitates context modeling, an initial phase designed to comprehend application environments and their impact on user tasks. However, practitioners often neglect this activity due to its inherent complexity. To address this gap, we developed xPACE and TASC Modeler, tools that automate context modeling using available contextual data. This demonstration paper introduces our data-driven approach, consisting of a contextual data processor (xPACE) and a context model generator (TASC Modeler), and reports on a successful evaluation of these tools within a software development project.

We enumerate all 97 pairs, each consisting of an almost affine Lie superalgebra and its desuperization, which is a hyperbolic Lie algebra. Among the 66 hyperbolic Lie algebras identified, 18 possess multiple superizations. Notably, the cosmological billiard trajectories associated with these paired structures remain identical.

This paper introduces a concept learning architecture allowing a robot to autonomously develop symbols through self-exploration with a variable number of objects. Our objective is to facilitate unconstrained concept learning, eliminating limitations regarding the quantity of interacted items or predefined symbolic frameworks. Consequently, the architecture must generate symbols for diverse entities, including graspable single objects, non-graspable object stacks, and other dynamic composite structures. To achieve this, we present a novel self-attentive predictive encoder-decoder network featuring binary activation layers. We validate this network using a robotic manipulation environment with a changing count of rigid objects. The system leverages the robot's continuous sensorimotor data to construct effect predictors and discrete symbolic structures representing interaction dynamics. Our results demonstrate that the robot acquires reasoning abilities to encode the interaction dynamics of varying object counts across different configurations using these discovered symbols. For instance, the robot can infer that multiple objects stacked atop another will move together if the base object is displaced. Furthermore, we show that these symbols enable goal-oriented planning by training a higher-level neural network capable of pure symbolic reasoning.

Code review stands as a premier best practice and a potent safeguard for software quality. Typically, experienced reviewers examine source code to offer constructive feedback, addressing nuances and edge cases that authors might overlook. This collaborative validation enhances code quality and reduces bug occurrences; however, due to the variability and limitations of individual expertise, the efficiency and effectiveness of this process require further enhancement. Currently, generating insightful review comments demands immense time and effort. This paper investigates the synergy of multiple practical review approaches to improve the code review process by introducing AUGER (AUtomatically GEnerating Review comments), a system utilizing pre-trained models. We assembled a dataset comprising 10,882 code changes drawn from 11 prominent Java projects. By employing Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer (T5) models, our framework synthesizes valuable knowledge during training, surpassing baseline methods by 37.38% in ROUGE-L scores. According to established metrics, 29% of the generated comments are deemed useful. The inference process completes in merely 20 seconds and supports further training. Additionally, case studies confirm performance improvements upon thorough analysis.

A graph is defined as $(k,t)$-regular when it is $k$-regular and the subgraph induced by the neighborhood of each vertex is $t$-regular. We establish new criteria for the existence of these graphs and present numerous examples.

The doubly charmed baryon $\Xi^{++}_{cc}$ was first detected by the LHCb collaboration in 2017. Previous studies predicted the branching fractions of two-body decays for doubly charmed baryons using the rescattering mechanism and examined certain $SU(3)_F$ relations within topological amplitudes. This work investigates the correlation between quark-level topological diagrams and hadron-level rescattering triangle diagrams in doubly charmed baryon decays. The validity of our framework is demonstrated by the fact that all twelve possible meson-baryon scattering structures appear exactly once each in the intermediate "topological-scattering" diagrams. Furthermore, the triangle diagrams derived from topological diagrams align with those obtained directly from the chiral Lagrangian. The relative magnitudes of rescattering contributions in the $C$, $C^\prime$, $E$, $E^\prime$, $P$, and $P^\prime$ diagrams, as determined by $SU(3)_F$ symmetry, match numerical analyses found in existing literature. Using the decay modes $\Xi^{++}_{cc}\to \Xi^+_c\pi^+$, $\Xi^{+}_{cc}\to \Xi^0_c\pi^+$, and $\Xi^{+}_{cc}\to \Xi^+_c\pi^0$ as examples, we demonstrate that isospin relations hold true when expressed through triangle diagrams.

Controlling the movement of colloids presents a significant challenge across disciplines, from materials science to biological systems. In this work, we introduce a flexible platform for defining colloidal migration by embedding energy landscapes within confined nematic liquid crystals. This is accomplished by inserting a wavy boundary featuring alternating hills and wells into the liquid crystal, which creates a smooth elastic energy field characterized by alternating splay and bend distortions. These domains produce stable regions that attract colloids and unstable regions that repel them over distances significantly larger than the particle radius. By harnessing the energy gradients near these loci, we direct colloid trajectories. We illustrate various facets of this control by examining transitions between defect configurations, guiding particles along specific paths, and utilizing multistable systems to transport particles to designated sites within the domain. These customized landscapes hold great potential for reconfigurable systems and microrobotics applications.

The relationship between thermodynamics, information, and work extraction is profound. Since the inception of thermodynamics, various iterations of Maxwell's demon have been proposed to clarify the second law, demonstrating the intrinsic links between thermodynamics, information, and work within thermal systems. This paper investigates energy extraction from a thermodynamic system adhering to detailed balance, performed by an agent possessing perfect information and employing an optimal strategy derived from the Bellman equation, specifically within the framework of Ising models. We designate these agents as "kobolds," distinguishing them from traditional Maxwell's demons, which are not required to satisfy detailed balance. This approach stands in sharp contrast to standard Monte Carlo algorithms, which select actions randomly at each step, making a comparison between kobolds and the Metropolis algorithm particularly relevant. Through both numerical and analytical examinations of various Ising models, we explore the characteristics of these optimal strategies and identify a transition in kobold behavior dependent on the parameter defining their strategy.

Recently, scaled relative graphs (SRGs) have been developed to assess the convergence of optimization algorithms within a two-dimensional Euclidean framework. This work establishes a link between SRGs and the traditional theory of input/output systems. We demonstrate that, under a specific coordinate transformation, the Nyquist diagram of an $L_2$ linear time-invariant (LTI) system represents the convex hull of its SRG. Furthermore, SRGs facilitate the visualization of approximations for static nonlinearities, such as describing functions and quadratic constraints, enabling the verification or refutation of system properties. Since interconnections of systems translate to graphical operations on their SRGs, this approach yields a straightforward, graphical proof of the classical incremental passivity theorem.

We conducted observations of 12CO (J=1-0 and 2-1), 13CO (J=1-0), and C18O (J=1-0) toward the supernova remnant (SNR) G22.7-0.2. These observations revealed a filamentary molecular gas structure, likely part of a larger complex moving at a VLSR of 75–79 km/s, surrounding the remnant's southern edge. Specifically, the high-velocity wing (77–110 km/s) observed in the 12CO (J=1-0 and J=2-1) emission provides strong evidence for the interaction between SNR G22.7-0.2 and the 75–79 km/s molecular clouds (MCs). Redshifted spectral profiles, indicative of shocked molecular gas, were detected at the southeastern boundary. This association between the remnant and the 77 km/s MCs suggests a near distance of 4.0–4.8 kpc, consistent with a position on the Scutum-Crux arm. We propose that SNR G22.7-0.2, SNR W41, and HII region G022.760-0.485 share the same distance and are linked to the GMC G23.0-0.4.

This study employs a Self-Explaining Neural Network (SENN) to automatically acquire concepts that are easily understandable by humans. By learning unsupervised concepts, the SENN's hidden layers retain verbalizable features essential for the output, a capability critical for adapting to real-world settings that demand explanations. However, the interpretability of SENN-generated concepts often diminishes in general applications, such as autonomous driving. To address this, the study integrates contrastive learning with concept learning to enhance both concept readability and task accuracy, resulting in a model named the Contrastive Self-Explaining Neural Network (C-SENN).

Let $M_R$ denote an injective right module over a ring $R$. The objective of this paper is to establish that the endomorphism ring $S = \text{End}(M_R)$ is quasi-duo if and only if $M_R$ is square-free.

This study evaluates three Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) algorithms: Variational Bayesian inference, Online Variational Bayesian inference, and the Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method known as Collapsed Gibbs sampling. By analyzing their time complexity and performance, we determine that Online Variational Bayesian inference is the most efficient algorithm while maintaining reasonably high accuracy.

We introduce a novel strategy that integrates deep learning with statistical physics to address combinatorial optimization challenges. Recent advanced techniques, particularly artificial neural networks, have proven highly effective for solving various physical tasks within quantum many-body systems, which are directly linked to combinatorial optimization problems. Specifically, we examine the classical Maximum Cut (MaxCut) problem by framing it as the search for the ground state of a quantum many-body system using artificial neural networks and deep learning. Our findings indicate that the exact solution obtained for the quantum system aligns perfectly with its classical MaxCut counterpart. As validation, we applied this approach to two random graphs of varying sizes—60 vertices with 885 edges and 100 vertices with 2,475 edges—achieving performance metrics of approximately 0.99 and 0.97, respectively, against known maximal cuts.

This concise textbook is designed for individuals new to the study, research, or development of optical coherence tomography (OCT), as well as those beginning to utilize it. The first chapter provides an overview of OCT's concepts and history. The second chapter details OCT technologies, covering mathematical principles, hardware implementation, design guidelines for components like interferometers and wavelength selection, and theories regarding resolution and sensitivity. The third chapter outlines examples of ophthalmic applications of OCT, while the final chapter offers guidance on subsequent learning steps.

Although polar codes offer capacity-achieving advantages and have been adapted for block fading channels, most existing constructions rely on complex iterative calculations. This paper presents a systematic framework to evaluate the error performance of polar codes under block and random mapping schemes. By introducing the novel concept of "split polar spectrum," we derive an upper bound on the error probability of polarized channels that explicitly links the diversity order $L$ to the block-wise weight distribution of the codeword. For block mapping with a specific diversity order of $L=2$, we develop an enumeration algorithm based on general MacWilliams identities to compute the exact split polar spectrum. In the case of random mapping with arbitrary diversity orders, we utilize uniform interleaving to approximate the split polar spectrum by integrating the polar spectrum with the probability of specific fading patterns for a given weight. Guided by design criteria aimed at achieving full diversity for gain and maximizing product distance for coding gain, we propose a construction metric called polarized diversity weight (PDW). This simple metric enables the design of polar codes for both mapping types that achieve performance comparable to or better than traditional methods in block fading environments.

Molecular dynamics simulations examined how hydrogenation and temperature influence the self-scrolling of two interacting nanoribbons around a carbon nanotube (CNT), focusing on three setups: (1) graphene/graphene/CNT, (2) graphene/graphane/CNT, and (3) graphane/graphane/CNT, where graphane denotes a fully hydrogenated graphene nanoribbon. Nanoscrolls, characterized by a papyrus-like spiral structure of rolled graphene layers, successfully formed in configurations (1) and (2) at temperature ranges of 300–1000 K and 300–600 K, respectively. In contrast, configuration (3) resulted in the nanoribbons wrapping the CNT without generating nanoscrolls.

The BB84 quantum key distribution protocol exhibits semi-device-independent security, meaning it remains secure even if only one party's device is constrained to a qubit Hilbert space. In this work, we establish an analytic lower bound for the asymptotic secret key rate of the entanglement-based BB84 variant, under the assumption that a single user employs unknown qubit POVMs. This result applies to collective attacks and simplifies to the established Shor-Preskill key rate when considering ideal BB84 correlations contaminated with varying levels of random noise.

This study conducts a comprehensive comparative analysis of fusion barriers for asymmetric nuclear collisions, utilizing various versions of the phenomenological proximity potential and other parametrizations within the proximity framework, extending to an asymmetry parameter of 0.23. A total of 12 distinct proximity potentials demonstrated robustness against experimental data from 60 reactions. The analysis indicates that both the surface energy coefficient and the radii of the colliding nuclei exhibit significant dependence on the asymmetry parameter. On average, all models successfully account for fusion barrier heights with an accuracy within ±10%. Furthermore, the potentials proposed by Bass (1980), AW (1995), and Denisov DP effectively describe fusion cross sections across both above- and below-barrier energy regimes.

This paper extends the approach introduced by Mertens et al. (2020, Biometrical Journal) to analyze censored lifetime (survival) data, incorporating imputation for missing values. The study addresses scenarios where missing data may exist in both calibration sets and future validation observations, with a specific focus on the Cox model. We outline methods for integrating imputation with predictive calibration in survival models subject to censoring and discuss their application in cross-validation. Our results broadly align with the initial study, which was limited to binary outcomes, confirming that prediction-averaging exhibits superior statistical properties—particularly reduced predictive variability—compared to directly applying Rubin's rules. Additionally, we explore distinct strategies for handling baseline hazards within Rubin's rules-based frameworks.

Recently, a maximal valence model was introduced to explain liquid-liquid phase transitions driven by polymerization in sulfur. This paper proposes a straightforward, general framework for describing liquid polyamorphism in single-component fluids by applying a maximum-valence approach to any arbitrary coordination number. The model incorporates three interaction types: i) van der Waals attraction between atoms, which creates a liquid-gas transition at low pressures; ii) the ability of atoms to form covalent bonds, leading to association; and iii) extra repulsive forces between atoms at their maximal valence and those at any other valence, which drive liquid-liquid phase separation. We demonstrate that this model yields liquid-liquid phase transitions for dimerization, polymerization, gelation, and network formation across coordination numbers z = 1 to 6, while also examining the boundaries of this generic model in generating fluid polyamorphism.

In reinforcement learning involving complex stochastic systems with multiple dynamic factors affecting output trajectories, it is beneficial to utilize information from historical samples gathered in prior iterations to speed up policy optimization. While classical experience replay enables agents to retain knowledge by reusing past observations, its uniform sampling strategy treats all data points equally, neglecting their varying significance. To address this, we introduce a general Variance Reduction-based Experience Replay (VRER) framework that selectively prioritizes the most relevant samples to refine policy gradient estimates. This adaptive mechanism assigns greater weight to historical data more likely to originate from the current target distribution. Both theoretical analysis and empirical results demonstrate that VRER accelerates the convergence to an optimal policy and boosts the performance of leading policy optimization methods.

Data-driven methodologies are widely utilized across various urban computing challenges. However, current research predominantly relies on data from restricted sources, limiting the ability to capture the inherent complexity of urban data derived from multiple entities and the inter-correlations between them. Therefore, a comprehensive and multifaceted dataset is essential to enable more extensive investigations in this domain. This paper introduces CityNet, a multi-modal urban dataset comprising data from 7 cities, each sourced from 3 distinct origins. We detail the generation process and fundamental characteristics of CityNet. Furthermore, to support its adoption, we conduct extensive machine learning experiments covering spatio-temporal forecasting, transfer learning, and reinforcement learning. These results serve as benchmarks for numerous tasks and methods while revealing internal correlations among cities and tasks within CityNet; leveraging these insights can enhance performance across various applications. Ultimately, we contend that CityNet, through its benchmarking framework and discovered correlations, will advance the field of urban computing by facilitating research into numerous sophisticated topics.

This work applies the mathematical framework developed by A. Plastino and M. C. Rocca (J. Phys. Commun. {\bf 2}, 115029, 2018) to Einstein's gravity (EG). We quantize EG using the Schwinger-Feynman variational principle, a more rigorous and suitable approach than the functional integral method when dealing with derivative couplings, building on the foundational efforts of Suraj N. Gupta and Richard P. Feynman. While we utilize the Einstein Lagrangian formulated by Gupta, we introduce a novel constraint distinct from Gupta's original one. This modification resolves the unitarity issues affecting the $S$-matrix in Gupta and Feynman's procedures and greatly simplifies constraint handling, thereby removing the necessity for ghost fields to ensure unitarity. Although our resulting approach is non-renormalizable, this limitation is addressed by employing the mathematical theory of Bollini et al., which was established on the works of Alexander Grothendieck and the theory of Ultradistributions by Jose Sebastiao e Silva (also termed Ultrahyperfunctions). Over approximately 25 years, these foundations have enabled the construction of a mathematical structure capable of quantizing non-renormalizable Field Theories; here, we specialize this theory for Einstein's gravity. Since we employ a Gupta-Feynman inspired Lagrangian, we successfully bypass the complexities typically associated with Yang-Mills theories.

Mixture of Experts (MoE) Transformers have recently demonstrated significant potential across various domains, primarily due to their unique advantages. First, these models expand capacity without escalating computational costs during either training or inference. Furthermore, as dynamic networks, they can adjust to the varying complexity of input instances found in real-world scenarios. This paper investigates an MoE-based architecture for speech recognition, termed SpeechMoE. To better regulate router activation sparsity and enhance the diversity of gate values, we introduce a sparsity L1 loss and a mean importance loss, respectively. Additionally, SpeechMoE employs a novel router architecture that integrates information from both a shared embedding network and the hierarchical representations of different MoE layers. Experimental findings indicate that SpeechMoE achieves a lower character error rate (CER) with comparable computational expenses relative to traditional static networks, delivering 7.0% to 23.0% relative CER improvements across four evaluation datasets.

This work investigates how information-bearing signals propagate and distribute within dynamical systems functioning as reservoir computers. Through multivariate correlation analysis applied to specific replica tests, we identify consistency spectra and capacities that offer a high-dimensional representation of the system's nonlinear functional dependence on inputs. When multiple inputs are present, a hierarchy of capacity metrics characterizes signal interference from each source, while time-resolved capacity for individual inputs forms a nonlinear fading memory profile. We demonstrate this methodology using various types of echo state networks.

The widespread presence of abusive language across various online platforms has created a significant need for automated detection systems capable of operating across multiple domains. While previous research has primarily focused on concatenating data from different platforms using Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM), this study approaches the challenge through the lens of domain generalization. We introduce SCL-Fish, a supervised contrastive learning algorithm integrated with meta-learning, designed to identify abusive language on previously unseen platforms. Experimental results demonstrate that SCL-Fish outperforms both ERM and existing state-of-the-art models. Furthermore, we show that SCL-Fish is highly data-efficient, achieving performance comparable to large-scale pre-trained models after fine-tuning for abusive language detection.

This study conducts a broad analysis of simplified models involving dark matter coannihilation with a strongly interacting particle, denoted as X. In these frameworks, dark matter depletion is primarily driven by the self-annihilation of X into quark and gluon pairs via strong interactions. Consequently, the phenomenology of such scenarios relies exclusively on the dark matter mass, the mass splitting between the dark matter and X, and the quantum numbers of X. We investigate cases where X is a scalar, fermion, or vector, and possesses color charges corresponding to a triplet, sextet, or octet. Our calculations of dark matter relic density constraints incorporate Sommerfeld corrections and bound state formation. Additionally, we assess restrictions arising from thermal equilibrium requirements, the lifetime of X, and both existing and anticipated LHC limits on X pair production. All constraints are systematically displayed within the plane defined by mass splitting versus dark matter mass.
