While relic density constraints may impose upper limits on the dark matter mass ranging from 2 TeV to over 10 TeV across various models, projected LHC bounds fall between 800 and 1500 GeV. Therefore, achieving comprehensive coverage of the strongly coannihilating dark matter parameter space would necessitate hadron colliders operating at significantly higher center-of-mass energies.

Anomaly detection remains a critical but difficult challenge in machine learning primarily because of the scarcity of labeled data. This paper introduces SLA$^2$P, a robust framework designed for unsupervised anomaly detection. The approach begins by extracting representative embeddings from raw inputs, which are then subjected to random projections; features resulting from different projections are treated as distinct pseudo classes. A classifier is subsequently trained on these transformed features using self-supervised learning. Furthermore, adversarial perturbations are applied to the transformed features to reduce the softmax scores of their predicted labels, with anomaly scores derived from the classifier's predictive uncertainty on these perturbed inputs. The underlying rationale is that, given the limited quantity and decentralized nature of anomalies, (1) the pseudo-label classifier prioritizes learning semantic patterns of normal data over anomalous data, and (2) normal data's transformed features exhibit greater robustness against perturbations compared to those of anomalies. As a result, perturbed anomalous features are poorly classified and yield lower anomaly scores than normal samples. Comprehensive experiments across image, text, and tabular benchmarks validate these findings, demonstrating that SLA$^2$P consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance in unsupervised anomaly detection.

Text-to-SQL has garnered significant interest from both the natural language processing and database communities due to its capacity to translate natural language semantics into SQL queries and its practical utility in creating natural language interfaces for database systems. The primary challenges in this domain involve encoding the meaning of natural language utterances, decoding them into SQL queries, and bridging the semantic gap between these two formats. While recent advancements have addressed these challenges to varying degrees, a comprehensive survey of the task remains absent. Consequently, this paper reviews recent developments regarding datasets, methodologies, and evaluation metrics to provide a systematic overview that tackles the aforementioned challenges and explores potential future research directions. We aim for this survey to act as a rapid reference to existing literature and to inspire further investigation.

Inspired by recent theoretical breakthroughs in dimensionality reduction, we apply the Block Markov Chain model to empirically investigate clustering within real-world sequential datasets. Clustering methods for Block Markov Chains offer theoretical optimality and function effectively in sparse data environments. However, despite these advantageous theoretical characteristics, their performance in realistic scenarios has not been thoroughly assessed.

We tackle this gap by examining the efficacy of these algorithms for exploratory data analysis of sequential data sourced from human DNA, written text, animal movement patterns, and financial markets. To assess the resulting clusters and the underlying model, we created a suite of evaluation instruments, including benchmarking, spectral noise analysis, and statistical model selection utilities. Alongside this paper, we release an efficient implementation of both the clustering algorithm and these new tools.

We discuss practical challenges arising from real-world data complexities. Ultimately, we demonstrate that the Block Markov Chain model, combined with our developed tools, yields meaningful insights for exploratory data analysis, even when dealing with the complexity and sparsity inherent in real-world datasets.

We establish a dispersive estimate for the elastic wave equation, thereby extending the established Strichartz estimates from the classical wave equation to the elastic context, including the derivation of endpoint estimates. To achieve this, we diagonalize the symbols associated with the Lamé operator and its semigroup, a process that also yields alternative and more streamlined proofs for prior results concerning perturbed elastic wave equations. Additionally, we derive uniform Sobolev inequalities for the elastic wave operator.

While most research on autonomous agents acquiring open-ended skill sets adopts a Piagetian view—where learning emerges from agent-environment interactions—this paper proposes coupling it with a Vygotskian perspective, which highlights how higher cognitive functions arise from internalizing socio-cultural transmissions. We introduce two contributions to foster skill acquisition in autotelic agents through this dual approach. First, we present "Help Me Explore" (HME), a novel social interaction protocol that integrates individual and socially guided exploration; in social phases, partners propose goals at the edge of an agent's knowledge, whereas in autotelic phases, agents either master discovered goals or autonomously rehearse unsuccessful social attempts. Second, we introduce GANGSTR, a graph-based autotelic agent designed for manipulation tasks that can break down goals into sequences of intermediate sub-goals. Our results demonstrate that when utilizing HME, GANGSTR surpasses its solitary learning constraints, successfully mastering highly complex configurations (such as stacks of five blocks) with minimal social intervention.

This study introduces a highly efficient representation of functions and differential operators derived from Fourier analysis. Leveraging this framework, we propose a variational hybrid quantum algorithm designed to address static, Schrödinger-type, Hamiltonian partial differential equations (PDEs). The approach employs space-efficient variational circuits that incorporate problem symmetries and utilizes both global and gradient-based optimization strategies. We evaluate the efficacy of these representation techniques by calculating the ground states of three specific PDEs: the one-dimensional quantum harmonic oscillator, along with transmon and flux qubits, assessing their performance on both ideal and near-term quantum hardware. Our results demonstrate that the developed Fourier methods achieve infidelities in the range of $10^{-4}$ to $10^{-5}$ using merely three to four qubits, highlighting the significant information compression capability of quantum computers. While practical fidelities are constrained by hardware noise and cost function evaluation errors in real devices, these limitations can be alleviated through error mitigation techniques.

This work addresses the challenge of simultaneously embedding a family of $n$-connected domains $\Omega_r\subset\Bbb P^1$, where no component of the complement $\Bbb P^1\setminus\Omega_r$ is a single point, into $\Bbb C^2$ via proper holomorphic maps. This is achieved by constructing a continuous mapping $\Xi\colon\bigcup_r\{r\}\times\Omega_r\to\Bbb C^2$ such that each slice $\Xi(r,\cdot)\colon\Omega_r\hookrightarrow\Bbb C^2$ constitutes a proper holomorphic embedding for every $r$. To accomplish this, the paper establishes and proves a parametric extension of both the Andersén-Lempert procedure and Carleman's Theorem.

This paper addresses key challenges in automatically verifying security protocols that rely on a dynamic root of trust, typically implemented through protected hardware like the TPM. We model the semantics of trusted computing platforms—including CPUs, TPMs, operating systems, and other critical components—along with their associated protocols using a classical process calculus compatible with ProVerif. As part of this formalization, we develop new equational theories to represent TPM-specific platform states and dynamically loaded programs. However, existing ProVerif capabilities struggle with such comprehensive models, particularly due to the expansive search space created by unbounded extensions of TPM registers. To overcome this, we introduce a transformation of the TPM process that streamlines the search space for automated verification without compromising relevant security properties. This approach enables the use of ProVerif on our proposed models, allowing for the automatic derivation of security guarantees for protocols operating within a dynamic root of trust environment.

Most solved dynamic structural macrofinance models are characterized as high-dimensional, complex non-linear and/or non-Gaussian state-space systems. We introduce an annealed controlled sequential Monte Carlo method designed to produce numerically stable, low-variance estimators for the likelihood function. This approach utilizes an annealing process to incrementally incorporate observational data and establishes globally optimal proposal distributions by resolving associated optimal control problems, thereby achieving zero variance in likelihood estimation. For parameter inference, we create a novel adaptive SMC$^2$ algorithm that integrates likelihood estimators derived from our annealed controlled sequential Monte Carlo framework. We offer a theoretical stability analysis highlighting the benefits of our methodology, along with asymptotic results regarding the consistency and convergence rates of our SMC$^2$ estimators. Furthermore, we demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed approach by estimating two widely recognized macrofinance models: a non-linear new Keynesian dynamic stochastic general equilibrium model and a non-linear non-Gaussian consumption-based long-run risk model.

We report Monte Carlo (MC) simulation findings regarding the miniTimeCube (mTC), a compact plastic-scintillator detector optimized for imaging fast neutrons within the 1–10 MeV range. Initially conceived for antineutrino detection, the mTC features 24 MultiChannel Plate (MCP) photodetectors encircling a 13 cm boron-doped plastic scintillator cube. Our simulations indicate that digitizing waveforms across the 1536 optically sensitive channels enables the spatiotemporal localization of individual neutron-proton scatters with precision of approximately 100 picoseconds and 5 mm. We introduce a Bayesian estimation framework for reconstructing multiple scattering events to determine the direction and energy of incident neutrons. Furthermore, we demonstrate how populations of reconstructed neutrons can be utilized to infer the direction and energy spectrum of nearby simulated neutron sources.

Unitarity requires that the final state of a black hole (the remnant within the event horizon after total evaporation) must be singular. By assuming a UV theory containing an infinite number of fields, we suggest that this singularity can be realized through a mechanism similar to how quantum mechanics describes dissipation.

The low-x gluon density within protons, and specifically within nuclei, remains poorly constrained, yet a deeper understanding of this structure is vital for LHC measurements and the design of future hadron collider experiments. Furthermore, non-linear QCD evolution effects are anticipated at low x, potentially resulting in gluon saturation and the formation of a universal hadronic state known as the color-glass condensate; however, these phenomena have not yet been definitively confirmed. Fortunately, LHC data can be leveraged to improve constraints on parton distribution functions (PDFs). In this regard, a Forward Calorimeter (FoCal) is proposed as an upgrade to the ALICE experiment, scheduled for installation during Long Shutdown 3. The primary objective of the FoCal proposal is to measure forward direct photons in both pp and p-Pb collisions to derive experimental constraints on proton and nuclear PDFs in previously unexplored low-x regions. Drawing on current insights from deep inelastic scattering (DIS) experiments and initial LHC findings, this discussion outlines the physics case for the detector. Although open charm measurements offer significant constraints, direct photon measurements would provide unique additional information. Achieving direct photon detection necessitates a novel electromagnetic calorimeter with exceptionally high granularity, and the innovative design concept of a high-resolution Si-W sandwich calorimeter is examined.

Cortical neurons operating in the fluctuation-driven regime are capable of ultrafast population encoding, yet the biophysical mechanisms behind this remain unclear. While reducing the sharpness of the action potential onset hinders this encoding, it is uncertain whether a sharp onset alone is sufficient. A prevailing hypothesis suggests that the sharp onset arises from the electrotonic separation between the action potential initiation site and the soma, and that this spatial distance also drives ultrafast encoding. To test this, we analyzed the linear response properties of model neurons with defined initiation sites. Our findings indicate that varying the axonal position of the initiation site has a minimal effect on the linear response function, failing to produce the high bandwidth and ultrafast response seen in actual cortical neurons. Additionally, the model's high-frequency response proved insensitive to input current correlation times, contradicting empirical data. However, increasing the voltage sensitivity of sodium channels at the initiation site successfully restored both observed phenomena. We offer an explanation for the dissociation between sharp action potential onsets and ultrafast responses. Furthermore, by exploring different soma sizes, we demonstrated how neuron morphology influences linear response. Ultimately, our results confirm that a sharp action potential onset is not sufficient for an ultrafast response. Considering recent findings on activity-dependent repositioning of the axon initial segment, our study predicts that a more distal initiation site may increase the sharpness of the somatic waveform but will not alter the linear response of neuronal populations.

The geometric configuration of zirconium isotopes remains an unresolved issue attracting significant attention. Recent analyses of STAR measurement data from relativistic heavy-ion collisions suggest non-zero $\beta_{30}$ in the ground state of $^{96}$Zr \cite{Zhang2021_arXiv2109.01631}, a finding that conventional nuclear structure models struggle to reconcile with their predictions of non-pear-like shapes. To address this discrepancy, we conduct systematic projection-after-variation calculations for $^{96}$Zr utilizing the multi-dimensionally constrained relativistic Hartree-Bogoliubov model. Our approach simultaneously considers all $\beta_{\lambda \mu}$ components where $\mu$ is even, presenting selected potential energy surfaces (PESs) along with projected PESs for specific angular momentum and parity states. Although mean-field calculations consistently predict reflection-symmetric ground states, static octupole deformations appear upon projection to the $0^+$ state. We determine that $\beta_{20}, \beta_{22}, \beta_{30},$ and $\beta_{32}$ are all required to describe the ground state, with their values varying substantially across excited states of different angular momenta and parities. These intricate structures arise from the competition among various shell structures within this mass region. Consequently, our findings indicate that both beyond-mean-field effects and exotic shapes are crucial for comprehending the structure of $^{96}$Zr.

The incorporation of games in educational settings is expanding steadily, yet challenges remain regarding the balance between play and learning, as well as maintaining student engagement. This study outlines methodologies for surveying and analyzing the needs necessary to develop educational games tailored for children aged 5 to 9. It presents a set of fundamental requirements designed to enhance game development and serve as a foundation for future projects. Future research could expand on this by exploring educational theories, the gamification of learning processes, and additional data collection techniques.

The collisional energy loss of a high-energy particle traversing a medium is primarily attributed to the medium's polarization by the particle's electromagnetic fields, with a minor portion lost as Cherenkov radiation. In chiral media, an extra energy loss component arises from the induction of an anomalous current proportional to the magnetic field, resulting in energy dissipation predominantly through \emph{chiral} Cherenkov radiation. Utilizing classical electrodynamics, which remains valid across a broad spectrum of particle energies, we calculate the collisional energy loss of fast particles within a homogeneous chiral plasma and apply these findings to both Quark-Gluon Plasma and Weyl semimetals. Specifically, in Weyl semimetals, the photon spectrum exhibits significant enhancement in the ultraviolet and X-ray ranges, facilitating experimental study. Our primary finding indicates that whereas collisional energy loss in non-chiral media varies slowly with energy $E$ (at most logarithmically), chiral Cherenkov radiation scales with $E^2$ when recoil effects are ignored and with $E$ when they are included.

This paper introduces a straightforward yet powerful method for estimating 3D poses of multiple individuals from multi-view imagery. Our proposed coarse-to-fine framework initially aggregates noisy 2D observations from various camera perspectives into 3D space, subsequently grouping them into distinct instances via a confidence-aware majority voting mechanism. The ultimate pose estimates are derived from an innovative optimization strategy that connects high-confidence multi-view 2D observations with 3D joint candidates. Furthermore, we employ a statistical parametric body model, such as SMPL, as a regularizing prior for these 3D joint candidates. Specifically, both the 3D poses and SMPL parameters are optimized simultaneously in an alternating manner. In this process, the parametric models assist in rectifying implausible 3D pose estimates and inferring missing joint detections, while the refined 3D poses, in turn, facilitate improved SMPL estimations. By establishing a link between 2D and 3D observations, our approach ensures both accuracy and generalization across different data sources, as it effectively decouples the final 3D pose from inter-person configurations and demonstrates greater robustness against noisy 2D detections. We systematically evaluate our method on public datasets, achieving state-of-the-art results. The source code and video demonstrations will be accessible on the project page: https://ait.ethz.ch/projects/2021/multi-human-pose/.

Girolami et al. [1,2] introduced local quantum uncertainty and interferometric power as geometric measures of quantum correlations. This paper aims to explore their properties in a unified framework using the metric-adjusted skew information proposed by Hansen [3].

Generative adversarial networks (GANs) have emerged as an effective approach for training deep generative neural networks. This paper introduces a GAN designed for continuous sequential data, specifically applied to a dataset of classical music. Our findings demonstrate that the generated music improves in quality with further training, we provide statistical analysis of the output, and we invite readers to assess the artistic quality by downloading the generated tracks.

The use of multiple workers to annotate data for machine learning has grown significantly in recent years, driven by the need to collect vast amounts of labeled data for complex models while minimizing the risk of noisy or incorrect labels. Whether utilizing large-scale crowd-sourcing platforms or smaller groups of high-expertise workers, various techniques exist to establish consensus and determine ground-truth labels. However, research into how specific task parameters influence these methods remains limited. Key parameters include the number of workers, their expertise levels, the size of the label taxonomy, and sample size. This paper evaluates Majority Vote, CrowdTruth, and Binomial Expectation Maximisation across different permutations of these parameters to better understand optimal settings for ground-truth inference. The results indicate that Expectation Maximisation and CrowdTruth only outperform Majority Vote under specific conditions, with many scenarios showing negligible differences between methods. The study provides guidance on which parameters favor each method, and the developed experimental framework allows for testing both existing and new approaches to achieve superior performance where current methods fall short. Ultimately, this work enhances the understanding of optimal parameters for crowd-sourcing tasks.

This study revisits the conformal anomaly in curved spacetime featuring antisymmetric torsion, incorporating previously overlooked critical details. For the first time, we derive a covariant solution for the effective action induced by the anomaly. This covariant action encompasses local terms that correspond to total derivatives within the conformal anomaly; the contribution of massless fermions to these terms is defined by a multiplicative anomaly, which arises from two distinct choices regarding the doubling of the spinor operator. Conversely, the nonlocal component of the anomaly-induced action remains free of ambiguities and possesses a low-energy limit that parallels the effective potential found in metric-scalar theories.

Inequalities play a crucial role within the study of number sequences and polynomials. The Bessenrodt--Ono inequality, which applies to partition numbers and Nekrasov--Okounkov polynomials, was only recently identified. This paper investigates the log-concavity (Turán inequality) and the Bessenrodt--Ono inequality concerning plane partitions and their associated polynomials.

Currently, online information systems predominantly depend on traditional username and password mechanisms for access control and data protection. However, driven by advancements in biometric technology and the rising prominence of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning, biometric security is gaining traction due to its enhanced usability. This study demonstrates the integration of machine learning-based face recognition into a web-based platform to leverage these usability improvements. It evaluates various combinations of detection and classification algorithms paired with FaceNet for face recognition tasks. The findings indicate that a specific pipeline—utilizing MTCNN for detection, FaceNet for embedding generation, and LinearSVC for classification—achieves superior performance with 95% accuracy compared to other configurations. Consequently, this optimized classifier has been embedded into the web system to facilitate user authentication.

Accurate quantification of facial keypoint displacement is essential for imaging ballistocardiography (BCG) to estimate heart rates effectively, while skin feature tracking allows for video-based assessment of motor decline in Parkinson's disease. Although traditional computer vision techniques such as Scale Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT), Speeded-Up Robust Features (SURF), and the Lucas-Kanade method (LK) have historically offered high efficiency and accuracy, they struggle with common deformations like affine local transformations and lighting variations. In the last five years, deep convolutional neural networks have surpassed these traditional approaches across most computer vision tasks. We introduce a feature tracking pipeline that utilizes a convolutional stacked autoencoder to locate the image crop most similar to a reference crop containing the target feature. This autoencoder learns to encode image crops into deep features specific to the object category it was trained on. Trained on facial images, the model was validated on manually labeled videos of faces and hands for general skin feature tracking. Tracking errors for distinctive skin features (moles) were negligible, with a $\chi^2$-test suggesting they might originate from manual labeling errors. With a mean error ranging from 0.6 to 4.2 pixels, our method outperformed all other techniques in every scenario except one and was the only approach that did not diverge. Ultimately, we conclude that our method generates superior feature descriptors for tracking, matching, and image registration compared to traditional algorithms.

Dementia encompasses a range of neurodegenerative disorders that impair memory and cognitive function, impacting an ever-growing segment of our aging global population. The use of automated analysis for linguistic, vocal, and paralinguistic markers has increasingly emerged as a promising method for detecting cognitive deterioration. In this study, we introduce a new longitudinal, multi-modal dataset gathered from individuals with mild dementia and age-matched controls over several months within a natural environment. This dataset includes spoken conversations (with a portion transcribed), along with typed and written thoughts, supplemented by extra-linguistic data such as pen movements and keystrokes. We provide a comprehensive description of the dataset and subsequently concentrate on a task utilizing the speech modality to differentiate between controls and those with dementia by leveraging the longitudinal characteristics of the data. Our experiments revealed statistically significant variations in session-to-session speech patterns between the control and dementia groups.

The Gauss map $g$ associated with a surface $\Sigma$ embedded in $\mathbb{R}^4$ maps into the Grassmannian of oriented 2-planes within $\mathbb{R}^4$, denoted as $G^+(2,4)$. We establish geometric conditions for the stability of minimal surfaces in $\mathbb{R}^4$ based on this map $g$. Specifically, we demonstrate that if the spherical area of the Gauss map, $|g(\Sigma)|$, is less than $2\pi$, the surface remains stable under deformations that preserve its boundary. This result resolves a question posed by Barbosa and Do Carmo regarding $\mathbb{R}^4$.

The rapid expansion of interest in semi-autonomous systems (SAS) stems from their utility as a framework for deploying autonomous technologies in environments where intermittent human intervention is necessary. This approach enables service robots and autonomous vehicles to function across a spectrum of autonomy levels, ensuring safety when human judgment is required. We introduce an introspective autonomy model that is continuously learned and refined through experience, determining the degree to which an agent can operate independently in specific contexts. Furthermore, we define a competence-aware system (CAS) that explicitly tracks its proficiency at various autonomy levels and incorporates available human feedback. A CAS utilizes experience to dynamically adjust its autonomy, aiming to maximize overall efficiency by accounting for the costs associated with human assistance. We examine the convergence characteristics of the CAS and present experimental findings from robot delivery and autonomous driving scenarios that highlight the advantages of this methodology.

Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT) models are distinguished by their exceptional performance on complex language tasks, yet they impose significant computational and storage burdens. Due to their enormous scale, running even the most accurate large GPT models often necessitates multiple high-performance GPUs, thereby restricting their practical utility. Although emerging efforts aim to alleviate these demands through model compression, current techniques struggle with the sheer scale and intricacy of GPT architectures. This paper introduces GPTQ, a novel one-shot weight quantization approach leveraging approximate second-order information, designed to achieve both high accuracy and efficiency. GPTQ successfully quantizes a 175-billion-parameter model in roughly four GPU hours, compressing weights to 3 or 4 bits with minimal loss in accuracy compared to the uncompressed baseline. This method more than doubles the compression efficiency of prior one-shot quantization techniques while maintaining precision, enabling the execution of a 175-billion-parameter model on a single GPU for the first time. Experimental results demonstrate end-to-end inference speedups of approximately 2x on high-end NVIDIA A100 GPUs and 4x on more cost-effective NVIDIA A6000 GPUs relative to FP16. The implementation is accessible at https://github.com/IST-DASLab/gptq.

This study presents a theoretical extension of the characteristic mode formulation to analyze a vertical electric dipole positioned above a lossy dielectric half-space. Since standard characteristic formulations fail to preserve the orthogonality of field modes over an infinite sphere, an alternative modal approach is introduced to ensure orthogonality for both current and field modes. The resulting modal data align closely with method of moments counterparts. Subsequently, the modes of an isolated dipole without a ground plane are utilized, via a linear combination of eigenvectors theory, to predict the influence of the lossy ground plane. Various heights relative to the ground plane are examined, and the proposed formulations are validated against direct modal solutions. This work elucidates how isolated modes interact to form perturbed modes within a lossy half-space, offering applications for modeling lightning fields and antenna path loss over lossy ground.

The quantum speed limit defines the maximum rate at which a quantum system transitions from an initial to a final state over time. In this work, we establish a generalized quantum speed limit (GQSL) for arbitrary evolution by employing a geometrical framework in quantum mechanics. This GQSL applies to quantum systems experiencing unitary, non-unitary, completely positive, and non-completely positive dynamics. When restricted to unitary time evolution, it simplifies to the standard quantum speed limit, specifically the Mandelstam-Tamm bound. Additionally, we derive a quantum speed limit for non-Hermitian quantum systems. To demonstrate these results, we calculated the quantum speed limit for both time-independent and time-dependent non-Hermitian systems, including the Bethe-Lamb Hamiltonian applied to a general two-level system.

We evaluate submodular and Jaccard techniques to diversify Amazon Music recommendations, finding that submodularity substantially enhances both recommendation quality and user engagement. In contrast to the Jaccard method, our submodular approach integrates item relevance scores into its optimization function, yielding a result that is both highly relevant and uniformly diverse.

This paper introduces reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-assisted unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) networks designed to leverage the agility of UAVs and the reflective capabilities of RIS to boost network performance. To maximize the energy efficiency (EE) of these networks, we jointly optimize UAV power allocation and RIS phase-shift matrices. We propose a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework to address this continuous optimization problem under time-varying channels in a centralized manner. Additionally, a parallel learning method is introduced to reduce the information transmission overhead associated with the centralized approach. Numerical results demonstrate that our proposed schemes significantly outperform conventional methods in terms of EE, flexibility, and processing time. Due to their ability to make instant decisions and adapt to dynamic environmental conditions and time-varying channels, the proposed DRL methods for RIS-assisted UAV networks are well-suited for real-time applications.

Although disfluency stems from spoken human language, it is predominantly treated as a uni-modal text-based Natural Language Processing (NLP) task. This paper introduces a new multimodal architecture for detecting disfluency in individual utterances, utilizing early-fusion and self-attention mechanisms to interact between text and acoustic data. Our proposed model employs a multimodal dynamic fusion network that integrates minimal additional parameters into standard text encoders found in existing research, thereby harnessing prosodic and acoustic cues embedded within speech. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on the widely recognized English Switchboard dataset for disfluency detection, significantly outperforming both prior unimodal and multimodal systems. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive qualitative analysis revealing that, unlike text-only models which are prone to spurious correlations, our system mitigates this issue by incorporating supplementary information from speech signals. All source code is made publicly available on GitHub.

Natural language is theoretically the ideal user interface for numerous domains; however, general models bridging natural language with specific domains remain nonexistent. Offering a natural language interface to relational databases could potentially engage the vast majority of users, regardless of their proficiency with query languages. Consequently, the emergence of deep learning has spurred extensive research into creating suitable natural language interfaces for relational databases. This survey reviews recent methods and models for generating SQL queries from natural language, covering architectures such as convolutional neural networks, recurrent neural networks, pointer networks, and reinforcement learning. Additionally, several datasets designed to address SQL query generation are analyzed and briefly summarized. Finally, the survey outlines the evaluation metrics used in the field, which primarily combine execution accuracy with logical form accuracy.
This study presents two series of unfolded abstract regular polytopes within Coxeter groups of type Bn; one series maintains a rank of 4, whereas the other encompasses ranks of arbitrary magnitude.

Semantic segmentation of polyps and depth estimation are critical challenges within endoscopic image analysis. A primary barrier to advancing research in these areas is the scarcity of annotated data. Since obtaining endoscopic annotations requires specialized expertise from expert endoscopists, the process is often costly, time-consuming, and difficult to coordinate. To mitigate this issue, we explore an active learning approach that reduces the number of required training samples by identifying the most discriminative and diverse unlabeled instances for specific tasks. While many existing active learning frameworks are task-agnostic and often sub-optimal for specific applications, this paper introduces a novel task-aware active learning pipeline tailored for semantic segmentation and depth estimation in endoscopy. Comparative experiments against competitive baselines demonstrate substantial performance improvements with our method. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/thetna/endo-active-learn.

This study investigates minimax optimization problems defined as $\min_x \max_y f(x,y)$, where the objective function $f(x,y)$ is $m_x$-strongly convex in $x$, $m_y$-strongly concave in $y$, and $(L_x,L_{xy},L_y)$-smooth. Zhang et al. previously established a lower bound on the gradient complexity for any first-order method as $\Omega\Bigl(\sqrt{\frac{L_x}{m_x}+\frac{L_{xy}^2}{m_x m_y}+\frac{L_y}{m_y}}\ln(1/\epsilon)\Bigr)$. In response, we introduce a novel algorithm achieving an upper bound of $\tilde{O}\Bigl(\sqrt{\frac{L_x}{m_x}+\frac{L\cdot L_{xy}}{m_x m_y}+\frac{L_y}{m_y}}\ln\left(1/\epsilon\right)\Bigr)$, with $L=\max\{L_x,L_{xy},L_y\}$. This result surpasses the prior best upper bound of $\tilde{O}\left(\sqrt{\frac{L^2}{m_x m_y}} \ln^3\left(1/\epsilon\right)\right)$ established by Lin et al. Our approach not only ensures a linear convergence rate but also offers a tighter dependence on condition numbers, particularly when $L_{xy}\ll L$, indicating weak interaction between $x$ and $y$. Furthermore, through reduction techniques, our findings yield improved bounds for both strongly convex-concave and convex-concave minimax optimization. In the specific case where $f$ is quadratic, we can refine the upper bound further, bringing it to match the lower bound up to a minor sub-polynomial factor.

In recent years, there has been a significant rise in two interconnected fields: mathematics for deep learning, which aims to deepen theoretical understanding and enhance robustness, and deep learning for mathematics, which employs deep learning algorithms to address mathematical challenges. The latter has driven the popularity of scientific machine learning, applying these algorithms to scientific computing tasks. Notably, numerous neural network architectures have been created to tackle specific classes of partial differential equations (PDEs). These methods leverage inherent PDE properties, outperforming classical feed-forward, recurrent, and convolutional neural networks. This advancement has profoundly influenced mathematical modeling, where parametric PDEs are essential for representing natural and physical processes in science and engineering. In this work, we review these methods, extending them for parametric studies and related inverse problems, while also demonstrating their relevance in various industrial applications.

Speciation is crucial for the vast biodiversity found on Earth. Evidence indicates that reproductive isolation most frequently emerges in allopatry, particularly within small populations, yet current theories fail to account for this relationship in the weak mutation regime. This study investigates a biophysical model of speciation grounded in the binding of transcription factors to DNA sites, demonstrating how the independent co-evolution of these elements across two allopatric lineages within a stabilizing landscape generates incompatibilities. Our findings offer a novel prediction for the monomorphic evolutionary regime that aligns with empirical data: smaller populations accumulate incompatibilities more rapidly. This occurs because: 1) smaller populations carry a higher initial drift load, meaning more sequences bind poorly than well, thus requiring fewer substitutions to reach incompatible phenotypic regions; and 2) divergence proceeds more slowly when population size exceeds the inverse of discrete fitness differences. Additionally, we observe that longer sequences develop incompatibilities faster in small populations but slower in large ones. Consequently, this biophysical model describes a robust mechanism for rapid reproductive isolation in small populations with long sequences, operating without the need for peak-shifts or positive selection.

The nucleon tensor charge, $g_T$, plays a crucial role in investigating tensor interactions beyond the Standard Model within neutron and nuclear $\beta$-decays, as well as in determining the quark electric dipole moment's (EDM) contribution to the neutron EDM. This work presents findings from the QCDSF/UKQCD/CSSM collaboration regarding $g_T$, derived via lattice QCD techniques and the Feynman-Hellmann theorem. Employing a flavor symmetry breaking approach, we systematically extrapolate to physical quark masses using ensembles across three distinct lattice spacings.

This study numerically examines how an asteroid's elongation influences the sensitivity of its surface to tidal forces during a distant planetary flyby outside the Roche limit. By evaluating surface slope changes in relation to shape elongation, spin period, and orbital parameters, we find that greater elongation typically correlates with increased slope variation, though the total area exhibiting such variation does not necessarily increase monotonically.

This study investigates a marketplace for trading Internet of Things (IoT) data intended for training machine learning models. Data, whether raw or processed, is delivered to the platform via a network, with pricing determined by the specific value the data contributes to the models. Within a game-theoretical framework, we examine data correlation to develop a simplified, distributed trading mechanism that prioritizes mutual benefits for both devices and the market. Our primary proposal is an efficient algorithm that tackles availability and heterogeneity in participation, alongside trust transfer and the economic valuation of data exchanges in IoT networks. The approach fosters collaboration among devices holding correlated data to prevent information leakage. Specifically, we formulate a network-wide optimization problem that maximizes the social value of coalitions among IoT devices with similar data types while minimizing costs associated with network externalities, such as leakage risks from correlation, and opportunity costs. We identify the problem structure as a distributed coalition game and resolve it using a simplified split-and-merge algorithm. Simulation outcomes demonstrate the effectiveness of this mechanism design in creating a trusted IoT data market, yielding an average payoff increase of up to 32.72% for each seller.

Rings of fractions and the related localization process represent the most significant technical instruments in commutative algebra. Krasner (m,n)-hyperrings serve as a generalization of (m,n)-rings. Given a commutative Krasner (m,n)-hyperring R, this research aims to introduce the concept of fractions generated by R and subsequently examine its fundamental properties.

Material systems are increasingly subjected to diverse performance requirements, encompassing mechanical, thermal, electrical, optical, acoustic, and flow characteristics. This article reviews the emerging domain of disordered hyperuniform composites and their distinctive multifunctional attributes. These disordered hyperuniform media represent exotic amorphous states of matter defined by a remarkable suppression of large-scale volume-fraction fluctuations relative to typical disordered materials. Compared to their periodic equivalents, such unconventional composites offer superior advantages, including direction-independent physical properties that are unique or nearly optimal, alongside enhanced robustness against defects. The discussion demonstrates that both disordered hyperuniform composites and porous media can be engineered to exhibit a wide range of extraordinary physical traits—spanning photonic, phononic, transport, chemical, and mechanical domains—that are only now being uncovered.

Recognizing words absent from training data remains a persistent challenge for automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems, yet no standardized approach exists for evaluating solutions to this issue. We introduce the use of the CommonVoice dataset to construct multi-lingual test sets featuring high out-of-vocabulary (OOV) rates compared to their training counterparts and release a new utility for computing pertinent performance metrics. Subsequently, we assess, within a hybrid ASR framework, the superior capabilities of subword models in identifying OOVs and the gains achievable by integrating OOV-word data into existing systems through WFST modifications. Furthermore, we propose an innovative method for adjusting subword-based language models to enhance OOV-word recognition. Our results demonstrate significant improvements in this area, and we have made both the dataset and accompanying code publicly available.

Masked image modeling (MIM) currently dominates previous pre-training strategies—such as image classification, instance contrastive learning, and image-text alignment—by delivering superior fine-tuning results. This paper demonstrates that the underperformance of these older methods can be substantially enhanced through a straightforward post-processing technique known as feature distillation (FD). FD transforms legacy representations into new ones that exhibit key characteristics, collectively termed "optimization friendliness," mirroring those found in MIM. These traits are identified and analyzed using specialized diagnostic tools focused on attention mechanisms and optimization dynamics. Leveraging these optimized properties, the updated representations achieve robust fine-tuning capabilities, rendering contrastive self-supervised learning methods nearly as competitive as state-of-the-art MIM algorithms. Additionally, CLIP models see marked improvements; for instance, a CLIP ViT-L model attains 89.0% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K. On larger scales, the 3-billion-parameter SwinV2-G model achieves new benchmark records on ADE20K semantic segmentation (61.4 mIoU) and COCO object detection (64.2 mAP), with gains of +1.5 mIoU and +1.1 mAP respectively. Crucially, this work enables future research to prioritize the generality and scalability of learned representations, as optimization friendliness can now be easily enhanced. The associated code is accessible at https://github.com/SwinTransformer/Feature-Distillation.
We construct an infinite family of real cyclotomic fields possessing non-trivial class groups. This finding extends the result presented in [1], as our family encompasses the one described therein.

We introduce a decoder designed to correct erasures in hypergraph product codes, a prominent family of quantum LDPC codes. Numerical simulations demonstrate that this decoder closely approximates the maximum likelihood decoder, requiring O(N^2) bit operations, where N represents the code length. Additionally, a probabilistic variant of the decoder can be executed with O(N^1.5) bit operations.

High-purity single photons with high generation rates are essential for numerous quantum technology applications. While various methods exist for their creation, heralded single photons derived from spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) remain the most prevalent approach. However, the generation rate of these heralded sources is constrained by the efficiency of detectors required to record coincidence events between photon pairs, which is typically lower than the individual single-photon counts obtained separately. This paper introduces a revised formula for calculating the second-order temporal correlation function, $g^{(2)}$, applicable to any fixed time window (bin), and details the experimental characterization of purity for both unheralded and heralded SPDC photons. We demonstrate that by selecting an appropriate time bin for a specific pump power, it is possible to generate single photons with $g^{(2)}(0) = 0$ at a higher rate and with very high probability, even without using heralding.

This study introduces a novel end-to-end framework for multi-talker audio-visual speech recognition, termed the Visual Context Attention Model (VCAM). By leveraging video data to associate decoded text with specific visible speakers, VCAM effectively addresses the label ambiguity inherent in most multi-talker systems, which often fail to correctly assign transcribed labels to individual talkers despite generating multiple label strings. Built upon a transformer-transducer architecture, the model was evaluated on a two-speaker overlapping speech dataset derived from YouTube videos. The results demonstrate that VCAM outperforms existing audio-only and audio-visual multi-talker automatic speech recognition systems.

Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), characterized by its use of small batches across multiple epochs, has long been the preferred method for training large, over-parameterized models. A prevailing hypothesis suggests that SGD's practical efficacy stems from an inherent regularization mechanism that steers the algorithm toward optimal solutions. The most theoretically robust setting for analyzing SGD is Stochastic Convex Optimization (SCO), where it is established that SGD achieves a learning rate of $O(1/\sqrt{n})$ given $n$ samples. This paper investigates SCO to examine the interplay between implicit regularization, batch size, and multi-epoch training. Our primary contributions are threefold: (a) We demonstrate that for any given regularizer, there exists an SCO problem where Regularized Empirical Risk Minimization (RERM) fails to learn, thereby invalidating implicit regularization as a sufficient explanation for SGD's success. (b) We establish a sample complexity gap between SGD and Gradient Descent (GD) on empirical loss, proving that for a specific SCO problem, GD with any step size or iteration count is limited to a suboptimal rate of at least $\widetilde{\Omega}(1/n^{5/12})$. (c) We introduce a multi-epoch variant of SGD used in practice and prove that it performs at least as well as single-pass SGD in the worst case, while significantly outperforming it on certain SCO problems. Furthermore, we extend these findings to the general learning setting by identifying a learnable problem across all data distributions where SGD strictly surpasses RERM regardless of the regularization function. Finally, we discuss the implications for deep learning and demonstrate a separation between SGD and Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) within two-layer diagonal neural networks.

Post-reionisation 21cm intensity mapping experiments aim to observe the spectral line of neutral hydrogen (HI) within dark matter haloes. Under the halo model, these discrete haloes trace the continuous dark matter density field down to a specific scale determined by the physical size of the haloes. This physical size establishes an exclusion region that imprints distinct signatures on the statistical properties of HI. We demonstrate how this exclusion effect, driven by finite halo size, alters the HI power spectrum, defining the halo's physical boundary via the splashback radius. Crucially, we find that the white noise-like feature present at the zero-momentum limit of the power spectrum is precisely eliminated when finite halo size is accounted for. This cancellation extends to all tracers of the dark matter density field, such as galaxies. Additionally, we show that exclusion caused by finite halo size produces a sub-Poissonian noise signature on large scales, a finding consistent with N-body simulation results.

Galaxy lenses are often modeled using elliptical mass distributions combined with external shear and isothermal spheres to represent secondary and line-of-sight galaxies. However, statistical data indicates that a portion of observed quads contradicts these assumptions, suggesting a need for dipole-like mass contributions relative to the light. Oversimplified assumptions regarding mass distribution shapes can lead to erroneous parameter recoveries, such as the Hubble constant ($H_0$). To address this, we developed tests using synthetic quad populations with varying deviations from elliptical shapes, fitting them with an ellipse-plus-shear model to measure the resulting $H_0$ values, excluding kinematic constraints. We conducted two fitting approaches: one using a single point source and another employing an array of sources to simulate extended objects. Additionally, we performed two model-free comparisons between our mock quads and the observed population. One key finding, previously unreported, is a statistical inconsistency where the image distance ratios relative to the lens center in observed quads exhibit a significantly wider range than those in synthetic or simulated quads. Considering this discrepancy, our mock populations indicate that biases in $H_0$ could reach approximately 10%.

The hypothesis that wave function collapse results from correlating interactions characteristic of measurements yields a stochastic collapse equation that avoids introducing new physical constants and adheres to conservation laws. This collapse operator relies on interaction (potential) energy, incorporating a variable timing parameter tied to the frequency at which individual interactions establish correlations. The approximate localization of physical systems arises from the distance-dependent nature of these interaction potentials. The equation maintains strict conservation of momentum and orbital angular momentum, while also satisfying energy conservation within the precision limits imposed by nonrelativistic energy descriptions. The potential extension of this proposal to a fully relativistic framework is also examined.

In quantum mechanics courses, students learn that a wave function encapsulates all knowable information regarding an isolated system. However, this perspective later appears challenged by the enigmatic density matrix, which introduces additional probabilities beyond those inherent in the wave function. This paper demonstrates that the density matrix can be harmonized with standard quantum mechanical descriptions by employing a two-particle entangled state, where a one-particle subsystem serves as a fundamental illustration. The apparent extra-quantum probabilities are attributed to the superposition coefficients of the quantum state vector, and the seemingly irreversible exponential decay of population is shown to align with the unitary time evolution of a pure state upon particle interaction. Consequently, this two-particle framework offers students a means to comprehend how the density operator, in all its complexity, arises from the principles of quantum mechanics.

Kaleidoscopic groups represent a newly defined class of permutation groups introduced by Duchesne, Monod, and Wesolek. Given a permutation group $\Gamma$, the kaleidoscopic construction yields a new group $\mathcal{K}(\Gamma)$ acting on a Ważewski dendrite, a compact space characterized by dense branching. This paper investigates the relationship between the topological dynamics of $\mathcal{K}(\Gamma)$ and those of $\Gamma$ specifically when $\Gamma$ is transitive. By establishing a Ramsey theorem for decorated rooted trees, we demonstrate that the universal minimal flow (UMF) of $\mathcal{K}(\Gamma)$ is metrizable if and only if $\Gamma$ is oligomorphic and its own UMF is metrizable. Furthermore, within a suitable model-theoretic context, we provide explicit computations of the UMF for $\mathcal{K}(\Gamma)$ under the condition that the UMF of a point stabilizer $\Gamma_c$ possesses a comeager orbit. Additionally, our findings identify a substantial collection of examples featuring non-metrizable UMFs with comeager orbits, thereby extending earlier research by Kwiatkowska and Duchesne regarding full homeomorphism groups.

We establish high-dimensional Gaussian comparison theorems applicable to standard $V$-fold cross-validated risk estimators. This achievement merges a recent stability-driven approach for the low-dimensional central limit theorem of cross-validation with a high-dimensional Gaussian comparison framework designed for sums of independent random variables. These findings offer novel perspectives on the joint sampling distribution of cross-validated risks, particularly in model comparison and tuning parameter selection scenarios where the count of candidate models and parameters exceeds the training sample size. Consequently, our work provides theoretical validation for recent methodological advances that utilize cross-validation to construct model confidence sets.

Spontaneous structural rearrangements are fundamental to the organization and function of intricate biomolecular systems. While physics-based simulations such as Molecular Dynamics (MD) theoretically allow for the investigation of these thermally driven processes at atomic resolution, they struggle with rare conformational transitions. This difficulty arises because simulating thermal fluctuations within metastable states requires an exponentially large allocation of computational resources. Path sampling techniques, such as Transition Path Sampling, offer a promising solution by directing computational efforts toward sampling these rare stochastic transitions between metastable states. However, a significant challenge in these methods is generating trajectories that access diverse regions of conformational space efficiently. To address these issues, we present a rigorous framework combining machine learning algorithms, classical MD simulations, and adiabatic quantum computing. First, utilizing functional integral methods, we derive a rigorous low-resolution model of system dynamics based on a limited set of molecular configurations generated via machine learning. Subsequently, a quantum annealing device explores the transition path ensemble of this low-resolution theory without applying unphysical biasing forces to guide the dynamics. We validated this approach using the D-Wave quantum computer by simulating a benchmark conformational transition within a state-of-the-art atomistic framework. Our findings demonstrate that the quantum computing component produces uncorrelated trajectories, thereby enhancing the sampling of the transition region in configuration space. These results establish a new paradigm for integrating machine learning and quantum computing into MD simulations.

Research into active matter has uncovered novel non-equilibrium collective behaviors, highlighting its potential as an emerging materials platform. However, most existing studies treat active matter as unregulated systems characterized by uniform microscopic energy input, termed activity. Conversely, functionality in biological materials arises from the local regulation and control of activity across space and time—a capability that has only recently become experimentally feasible for engineered active matter. Achieving functionality necessitates navigating the high-dimensional landscape of spatio-temporal activity patterns; yet, brute-force methods are unlikely to succeed without system-specific intuition. In this work, we employ reinforcement learning to induce net directional transport in a simulated system of Vicsek-like self-propelled disks by using a spotlight to enhance activity locally. The learned, time-varying activity patterns leverage the distinct physics governing strong and weak coupling regimes. Our findings demonstrate how reinforcement learning can uncover physically interpretable protocols for controlling collective behavior in non-equilibrium systems.

Existing question-answering systems often produce plausible but incorrect responses without offering supporting evidence or reasoning, a significant issue when users cannot easily verify the model's output, thereby undermining trust in machine learning. Drawing inspiration from real-world scenarios where complex questions are addressed by weighing opposing viewpoints (Irving et al., 2018), we constructed a dataset for multiple-choice QA featuring single arguments for both correct and incorrect options within a debate-style framework. This initial step aims to train models to generate explanations for two candidate answers. We utilized long contexts where experts familiar with the material crafted convincing justifications for pre-selected correct and incorrect answers, then evaluated whether these explanations enabled humans unfamiliar with the full context to identify the correct answer more accurately. Our results indicate that, in this specific setup, generated explanations did not enhance human accuracy; however, a baseline condition demonstrated that providing human-selected text snippets did improve performance. Based on these findings, we propose strategies to refine the debate setup for future data collection initiatives.

This study introduces the inaugural survey of quiet Sun features detected in hard X-rays (HXRs) using the Nuclear Spectroscopic Telescope Array (NuSTAR), a telescope equipped with focusing optics. The convergence of the recent solar minimum and NuSTAR's superior sensitivity created an ideal scenario for conducting the first HXR imaging spectroscopy across various quiet Sun features. Analyzing this HXR emission enables the detection or constraint of high-temperature (>5 MK) and non-thermal sources, offering insights into their connection to larger solar phenomena and their role in atmospheric heating. We detail observations from NuSTAR full-disk mosaics acquired on September 28, 2018, marking the start of the quiet Sun observing campaigns. These mosaics primarily captured steady X-ray bright points, an emerging flux region that later developed into an active region, and a brief jet. Our analysis reveals that the HXR spectra of these features are well-modeled by isothermal distributions with temperatures between 2.0 and 3.2 MK. By integrating NuSTAR data with softer X-ray data from Hinode/XRT and EUV data from SDO/AIA, we reconstructed the differential emission measures, confirming negligible significant emission above 4 MK. The NuSTAR HXR spectra further allowed us to constrain potential non-thermal emission consistent with a null detection. We determined that only the jet exhibited a potential non-thermal upper limit capable of powering observed heating; however, even in this case, the non-thermal electron distribution required a very steep slope (effectively mono-energetic) with a low-energy cutoff between 3 and 4 keV. Consequently, higher-temperature or non-thermal sources within typical quiet Sun features observed in this September 2018 dataset are found to be extremely weak, if they exist at all.

Understanding the link between intelligence and neural activity is critical for grasping how the human brain functions in both healthy and pathological states. While current literature successfully employs functional brain connectomes to predict cognitive metrics like IQ scores in diverse populations using machine learning, existing approaches typically flatten these connectome graphs into vectors, thereby ignoring their topological characteristics. To overcome this shortcoming and leverage emerging graph neural networks (GNNs), we developed a novel regression GNN model called RegGNN for IQ prediction based on brain connectivity. Additionally, we introduced a fully modular sample selection technique to identify the most effective training samples for the prediction task. Recognizing the computational cost of training such deep learning models, we further proposed a *learning-based sample selection* strategy that learns to prioritize training samples with the highest expected predictive power for unseen data. This method exploits the property that connectomes, represented as adjacency matrices, reside within the symmetric positive definite (SPD) matrix cone. Our findings demonstrate that RegGNN outperforms comparison methods in predicting full-scale and verbal IQ for autism spectrum disorder cohorts and achieves competitive results for neurotypical subjects via 3-fold cross-validation. Moreover, we established that our sample selection approach generalizes effectively to other learning-based methods, highlighting its broader utility beyond the specific GNN architecture.

We present theoretical predictions regarding the radio emission generated when a dark matter candidate annihilates into 2-lepton and 4-lepton final states. These predictions are then compared against existing measurements of sky temperature across various frequencies. Specifically, we compute the radio emission for dark matter candidates that annihilate into intermediate bosons, which subsequently decay into a 4-lepton channel with a thermal annihilation cross-section. Our analysis demonstrates that within the frequency range of $20\,{\rm MHz}$ to $5\,{\rm GHz}$, this indirect channel can yield a more prominent signature than direct annihilation into leptons.

This study investigates the natural vibrations of curved nano-beams and nano-arches, specifically those with piece-wise constant thickness that are weakened by stable cracks at the re-entrant corners of their steps. A new method utilizing the weightless rotating spring approach is developed to determine natural frequencies. The primary objective is to evaluate how eigenfrequencies respond to variations in the geometric and physical parameters of the nano-arch. The calculated results align well with findings from comparable research conducted by other scholars.

Extending our prior work, we establish Gersten's conjecture for the $p$-torsion subgroup of the generalized Brauer group defined over a henselian regular local ring of mixed characteristic $(0, p)$. Additionally, we demonstrate the $\mathbb{P}^{1}$-homotopy invariance of the generalized Brauer group, providing an analogue to the findings by Auel-Bigazzi-B\"{o}hning-Graf von Bothmer within mixed characteristic settings.

This work investigates the compactly supported rational cohomology of point configurations on wedge sums of spheres, analyzing natural actions by the symmetric group and the outer automorphism group $Out(F_g)$ of the free group. These representations connect closely to Hochschild-Pirashvili homology involving square-zero algebras and appear across diverse mathematical domains, ranging from curve moduli space cohomology to polynomial functors on free groups. We demonstrate that these cohomology representations constitute a polynomial functor and employ various geometric models to determine a significant portion of its composition factors. Furthermore, we fully compute these factors for all configurations with $n \leq 10$ particles. A key application of this analysis provides a novel super-exponential lower bound regarding the symmetric group action on the weight $0$ component of $H^*_c(M_{2,n})$.

The physical mechanisms driving multiwavelength emission from relativistic jets remain largely unclear, as modeling spectral energy distributions and light curves is insufficient to differentiate between competing theories. Polarization measurements in the X-ray and gamma-ray bands could offer unique insights into jet physics and radiation processes. Several forthcoming projects aim to obtain polarimetric data for the brightest X-ray sources, including active galactic nuclei (AGN) jets and gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). This paper details the creation of a new Monte-Carlo code named MAPPIES (Monte-Carlo Applications for Partially Polarised Inverse External-Compton Scattering), designed to simulate polarization-dependent Compton scattering in relativistic jets. Additionally, the study presents general findings regarding Compton polarization across both the Thomson and Klein-Nishina regimes.

We contend that geometrical scaling (GS), initially formulated for Deep Inelastic Scattering (DIS) at HERA, remains valid in proton-proton collisions at LHC energies and within the NA61/SHINE experimental data. Our analysis demonstrates that GS holds in DIS up to moderately large Bjorken $x$ values of approximately 0.1. Consequently, negative pion multiplicity $p_{\rm T}$ distributions measured by NA61/SHINE exhibit geometrical scaling in the mid-rapidity region. However, for non-zero rapidity ($y \ne 0$), distinct scaling violations emerge when one of the colliding partons possesses a Bjorken $x$ greater than or equal to 0.1. Furthermore, we posit that while geometrical scaling persists for identified particles, the scaling variable depends on transverse mass instead of $p_{\rm T}$.

To effectively model and assess large-scale quantum systems, such as quantum computers and quantum annealers, it is essential to measure their "quantumness." This paper explores dimensionless combinations of fundamental parameters in large, partially quantum coherent systems that can characterize this degree of quantumness. Through both analytical and numerical methods, we propose a specific metric for qubit systems undergoing adiabatic evolution, termed the accessibility index. When applied to the D-Wave One superconducting quantum annealing device, our analysis indicates that its operation resides firmly within the quantum domain.

Biological nervous systems utilize distributed components to sense, communicate, calculate, and execute movement, yet they face significant trade-offs regarding speed, precision, sparsity, noise, and saturation. Despite these constraints, the brain achieves exceptional control performance through a highly efficient layered architecture. This study introduces a driving task to examine how a mountain biker handles immediate trail bumps and adapts to directional changes. By manipulating the latency and precision of wheel control inputs, we simulated variations in neuronal properties within the control loop. The resulting speed-accuracy trade-offs (SATs) inspired a theoretical framework of layered control loops, where each physical level contains components with varying speeds and accuracies—mirroring nerve bundles with axons of diverse sizes. Our model elucidates why errors from a fast but imprecise reflexive layer (correcting bumps) and a slow but precise planning layer combine additively, and it demonstrates how to decompose errors into those caused by limited component speed and accuracy. These findings illustrate that diversity in neuronal properties across layers generates "diversity-enabled sweet spots" (DESSs), enabling the system to achieve both rapid and accurate control even when utilizing slow or inaccurate components.

Photogrammetry-derived point clouds often result in noisy and incomplete representations of reality. We introduce an evolutionary optimization framework capable of reconstructing the underlying geometry of objects from such data. This method leverages prior knowledge of the 3D structure to identify a set of primitive shapes that approximate the scene. By incorporating mechanisms that ensure high shape diversity and adapt the population size, the approach is effective for modeling both simple and complex environments. This study specifically examines cylinder approximations, detailing, evaluating, and comparing a suite of mutation operators optimized for exploring the search space. We evaluate the algorithm's robustness and limitations using synthetic examples and demonstrate its broad applicability through real-world applications in vegetation and industrial contexts.

Matching pursuit and Frank-Wolfe represent two foundational prototypes of greedy optimization. This paper adopts a unified perspective on both method classes, establishing the first explicit convergence rates for matching pursuit in an optimization context applicable to general atom sets. We demonstrate sublinear ($1/t$) convergence for both approaches on general smooth objectives and linear convergence when objectives are strongly convex, while also clarifying the relationships between algorithmic variants. The proposed algorithms and their convergence rates are affine invariant and require no assumptions regarding incoherence or sparsity.

The exponential suppression of quantum decay in a metastable vacuum arises from a tunneling action, which can be determined via the semi-classical approximation as the Euclidean action of a bounce connecting false and true vacuum states. In multi-field scenarios, locating this bounce is challenging because of its unique boundary conditions and the fact that the action corresponds to a saddle point rather than a minimum. A recently introduced alternative tunneling action, which avoids reliance on Euclidean bounces and matches standard results at its minimum, is now extended to multiple scalar fields. We show that applying this novel method substantially enhances the numerical computation of tunneling actions for multi-field potentials.

This research investigates the nonlinear dynamics of unstable flux compactifications by employing numerical relativity to resolve the Einstein equations in $D$ dimensions, incorporating a $q$-form field and a positive cosmological constant. We demonstrate that initially homogeneous flux compactifications are prone to instability, dynamically evolving into warped compactifications. In certain scenarios, this warping mechanism acts as a simplified model for slow-roll inflation, whereas other instances yield solutions that progress toward a singular state. Drawing parallels to dynamical black hole horizons, we utilize the geometric attributes of marginally trapped surfaces to define lower-dimensional vacua within these inhomogeneous and dynamic contexts. Our findings indicate that lower-dimensional vacua exhibiting a reduced expansion rate are dynamically preferred; furthermore, we identify spacetimes that experience a phase of accelerated expansion before transitioning into contraction.

Association schemes on triples (ASTs) serve as the ternary counterparts to classical association schemes, characterized by their ternary relations and adjacency algebras rather than binary ones. This survey outlines recent advancements in AST research, identifies open problems, proposes future research avenues, and presents several related findings. We examine the properties of ternary adjacency algebras within ASTs, focusing on those invariant under specific group actions and those derived from 2-designs and two-graphs. Furthermore, we introduce the concepts of fusion and fission for ASTs, illustrating these ideas with an example based on the AST generated by the affine special linear group $ASL(2,q)$.

This paper investigates combinatorial quantitative group testing (QGT) under noisy measurement conditions. The primary objective of QGT is to identify defective items within a dataset of size $n$ using counting measurements, where each measurement tallies the number of defects in a specific subset. Although existing literature typically addresses either probabilistic QGT with random noise or combinatorial QGT with noiseless data, this study focuses on combinatorial QGT with noisy measurements subject to adversarially added bounded noise. Since flawless detection is unattainable, the study employs a partial detection criterion. Given that the adversarial noise is bounded by $d_n = \Theta(n^\delta)$ and the detection goal allows for at most $k_n = \Theta(n^\kappa)$ errors, the research aims to determine the fundamental limit on the number of measurements, known as \emph{pooling complexity}, and to construct explicit measurement plans that achieve this optimal complexity alongside efficient decoding algorithms. First, it is demonstrated that the fundamental limit is $\frac{1}{1-2\delta}\frac{n}{\log n}$, up to a constant factor independent of $(n,\kappa,\delta)$, for the non-adaptive case when $0<2\delta\leq \kappa <1$, thereby refining the earlier findings of Chen and Wang [2]. Furthermore, an explicit deterministic non-adaptive measurement plan is presented with a pooling complexity of $\frac{1}{1-2\delta}\frac{n}{\log_{2} n}$ (up to a constant factor), which matches the theoretical limit. This plan features a decoding complexity of $o(n^{1+\rho})$ for any $\rho > 0$, representing a nearly linear complexity relative to the dataset size $n$.

We develop a streamlined presentation of Drinfeld super Yangians for special linear superalgebras corresponding to any Dynkin diagram, enabling the definition of a Hopf superalgebra structure on these Yangians. Leveraging the full Weyl group, we classify the Drinfeld super Yangians equipped with this structure. Furthermore, we establish an isomorphism between the completions of Drinfeld super Yangians and quantum loop superalgebras.

Determining the success of future tokamaks relies heavily on understanding the interaction between energetic particles and Alfv\'{e}n Eigenmodes (AEs). In the JET device, eight in-vessel antennas were deployed to actively investigate stable AEs across frequencies of 25–250 kHz and toroidal mode numbers with $\vert n \vert < 20$. Throughout the 2019–2020 deuterium campaign, nearly 800 plasma discharges yielded measurements of almost 7,500 resonances, including their frequencies ($f_0$), net damping rates ($\gamma < 0$), and toroidal mode numbers. Statistical analysis of this dataset indicates that both continuum and radiative damping rise with increasing edge safety factor and edge magnetic shear, particularly when non-ideal effects are accounted for. Furthermore, both the presence of stable AEs and their damping rates diminish as $\vert n \vert$ increases. Active antenna excitation proved ineffective in H-mode compared to L-mode, likely because steeper edge density gradients hinder accessibility and ELM-related noise complicates mode identification. A novel observation involved a marginally stable, edge-localized Ellipticity-induced AE detected during high-power auxiliary heating (ICRH and NBI up to 25 MW). NOVA-K kinetic-MHD simulations aligned well with experimental data regarding $f_0$, $\gamma$, and $n$, suggesting that continuum and electron Landau damping dominate in this scenario. Similar experimental and computational investigations are scheduled for recent hydrogen and current tritium campaigns to prepare for the forthcoming DT campaign.

Bit vectors serve as essential components for numerous succinct data structures. They are utilized to represent graphs, form a key element of text indices such as the wavelet tree, and encode ordered integer sequences via Elias-Fano codes. This functionality relies on answering two specific queries: rank and select. For a bit vector of length $n$, a rank query counts the 1-bits preceding a given position, while a select query, given a parameter $j$, identifies the location of the $j$-th 1-bit. Both queries can be resolved in $O(1)$ time with $o(n)$ additional space. Currently, the smallest uncompressed implementation, cs-poppy, achieves a space overhead of approximately 3.51% [Zhou et al., SEA 13]. This paper introduces an enhanced rank and select structure that maintains the same space overhead but improves query performance by up to 8% for rank operations and 16.5% for select operations compared to cs-poppy.

Scheduled for launch in the mid-2030s, the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) is an ESA flagship mission currently in Phase B development. As a space-based gravitational wave observatory targeting the millihertz frequency band, LISA aims to deepen our understanding of the universe by detecting diverse sources, including those at extreme redshifts ($z\sim 20$). On February 23, 2022, we convened the 1st *LISA in Greece Workshop*, supported by the Hellenic Space Center (HSC), to engage the Greek scientific and technological sectors in LISA-related opportunities. This white paper outlines the workshop's key outcomes, most notably the recruitment of 15 Greek researchers into the LISA Consortium, bringing the total Greek participation to 22. Additionally, we provide a roadmap detailing the future strategic actions of the Greek Gravitational Wave community regarding the upcoming LISA mission.

I introduce libcommute, a C++11/14/17 template library designed with expressiveness, extensibility, and performance as primary goals. It provides a domain-specific language for handling polynomial operators within quantum many-body theory and offers a toolkit for exact diagonalization software. The library supports common abstractions and algorithms through straightforward syntax, is thoroughly documented, and includes comprehensive unit tests. Additionally, libcommute is accompanied by Python 3 bindings named pycommute, which facilitate solving small-scale diagonalization tasks, rapid prototyping, and integrating high-performance libcommute cores into Python environments.

This study centers on minimizing $\alpha$-divergence within the context of Variational Inference.
