Specifically, we examine algorithms designed to optimize mixture weights for any mixture model, irrespective of prior knowledge regarding the distribution of the mixture component parameters. We provide a complete proof of convergence for the Power Descent algorithm (defined for all $\alpha \neq 1$) toward optimal mixture weights when $\alpha < 1$. Given that $\alpha$-divergence converges to the standard forward Kullback-Leibler divergence as $\alpha \to 1$, we extend the Power Descent to the $\alpha = 1$ case, demonstrating that it yields an Entropic Mirror Descent. This connection prompts an investigation into the relationship between Power Descent and Entropic Mirror Descent; utilizing first-order approximations, we introduce the Renyi Descent, a novel algorithm for which we establish an $O(1/N)$ convergence rate. Finally, we conduct a numerical comparison between the unbiased Power Descent and the biased Renyi Descent, discussing the relative advantages of each approach.

Exceeding the Nyquist rate boosts the spectral efficiency of pulse amplitude modulation by tolerating intersymbol interference (ISI), though this necessitates an equalizer at the receiver. Because the complexity of an optimal equalizer grows exponentially with the number of interfering symbols, practical implementations utilize truncated equalizers with limited memory, where residual interference is governed by the transmit filter and constrains overall performance. This study employs numerical optimization and prolate spheroidal wave functions to derive optimal time-limited pulses that minimize such residual interference. Relative to root raised cosine pulses, these new pulses reduce residual interference by an order of magnitude; specifically, a 32 dB reduction is realized with a four-symbol memory equalizer operating at 57% higher transmission rates. As a proof of concept, binary transmissions at 57% above the Nyquist rate demonstrate that the proposed pulse combined with a 4-state equalizer yields superior bit error rate performance compared to a root raised cosine pulse paired with a 128-state equalizer.

This study presents an unbiased minimum variance approach for painting CMB maps across both observed and unobserved sky regions. In unobserved areas, it produces CMB realizations matching the statistical characteristics of the expected signal, while in observed areas, it substantially reduces unwanted residuals, such as those caused by EB-leakage. The computational cost of this method scales as $\sim O(N_{side}^3)$, where $N_{side}$ denotes the map resolution parameter; this efficiency aligns with fast spherical harmonic transforms and vastly outperforms the traditional minimum variance method, which scales as $\sim O(N_{side}^6)$. Serving as the foundation for a suite of minimum variance estimators for CMB data analysis, this method paves the way for future research.

This study analyzes heavy flavor hadron decay electrons, separating charm and beauty contributions using a data-driven approach in $p+p$ and Pb+Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}}$ = 5.02 TeV at the LHC. We derived the transverse momentum ($p_{\mathrm{T}}$) spectra, nuclear modification factor ($R_{\mathrm{AA}}$), and azimuthal anisotropic flow ($v_2$) distributions for electrons originating from charm and beauty decays. Our findings reveal that electron $R_{\mathrm{AA}}$ from charm ($R_{\mathrm{AA}}^{\mathrm{c\rightarrow e}}$) and beauty ($R_{\mathrm{AA}}^{\mathrm{b\rightarrow e}}$) decays are suppressed at $p_{\mathrm{T}}$ > 2.0 and $p_{\mathrm{T}}$ > 3.0 GeV/$c$, respectively, in Pb+Pb collisions, indicating that charm and beauty quarks interact with and lose energy within the hot, dense medium. Furthermore, we observe less suppression in the electron $R_{\mathrm{AA}}$ from beauty decays compared to charm decays in the range of 2.0 < $p_{\mathrm{T}}$ < 8.0 GeV/$c$, a result consistent with a mass-dependent partonic energy loss scenario. A non-zero $v_2$ from beauty decays ($v_{2}^{\mathrm{b\rightarrow e}}$) is detected and aligns well with ALICE measurements. In the low $p_{\mathrm{T}}$ region (1.0 to 3.0 GeV/$c$), a discrepancy between RHIC and LHC results emerges at a 68% confidence level, suggesting varying degrees of thermalization for beauty quarks across different medium temperatures. Finally, between 3.0 and 7.0 GeV/$c$, $v_{2}^{\mathrm{b\rightarrow e}}$ deviates from the number-of-constituent-quark (NCQ) scaling hypothesis, implying that beauty quarks are unlikely to be fully thermalized in heavy-ion collisions at LHC energies.

The advent of NuSTAR, alongside the growing detection rate of binary black hole (BBH) mergers via gravitational waves (GW), has dramatically accelerated our comprehension of black holes. Despite being theoretically simple objects defined solely by mass and angular momentum, they continue to serve as enigmatic laboratories for exploring the universe's most extreme conditions. Although the last decade has yielded substantial progress, the distribution of black hole spins remains elusive. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of all known X-ray binary (XB) black holes observed by NuSTAR for which spin measurements via the "relativistic reflection" method were previously unavailable. By re-examining the full archival NuSTAR dataset for these sources, we determine ten new spin values: IGR J17454-2919 ($a=0.97^{+0.03}_{-0.17}$); GRS 1758-258 ($a=0.991^{+0.007}_{-0.019}$); MAXI J1727-203 ($a=0.986^{+0.012}_{-0.159}$); MAXI J0637-430 ($a=0.97\pm0.02$); Swift J1753.5-0127 ($a=0.997^{+0.001}_{-0.003}$); V4641 Sgr ($a=0.86^{+0.04}_{-0.06}$); 4U 1543-47 ($a=0.98^{+0.01}_{-0.02}$); 4U 1957+11 ($a=0.95^{+0.02}_{-0.04}$); H 1743-322 ($a=0.98^{+0.01}_{-0.02}$); and MAXI J1820+070 ($a=0.988^{+0.006}_{-0.028}$), with all uncertainties reported at the $1\sigma$ confidence level. We examine the consequences of these findings for the overall spin distribution of stellar-mass black holes in X-ray binaries and contrast this with BBH spin distributions, revealing a distinct discrepancy between the two. Furthermore, we evaluate the implications of our results for the reliability of the "relativistic reflection" technique and identify potential systematic uncertainties that could introduce bias into such measurements.

We explore various systems for identifying mathematical entities within English texts concerning category theory, serving as an initial phase for building a mathematical knowledge graph. By evaluating four distinct term extractors, we compare their outputs to highlight challenges inherent in constructing and assessing terms derived from noisy domain-specific text. Additionally, we provide access to two open corpora focused on research mathematics, specifically category theory: a smaller collection of 755 abstracts from the journal TAC (containing 3,188 sentences) and a larger dataset from the nLab community wiki (15,000 sentences).

This study addresses the open challenge of developing complete, concise, and explainable quantitative representations of microstructure for disordered heterogeneous material systems. Although existing data-driven approaches, such as deep generative models, have successfully achieved completeness and conciseness, they lack mathematically explainable latent representations. This research investigates representations built from three-point correlation functions, a specific form of spatial convolution. We demonstrate that diverse microstructures can be characterized by a concise subset of these correlations, which can be identified using Bayesian optimization. Finally, we show that this proposed representation can be directly applied to compute material properties via effective medium theory.

Bielliptic and quasi-bielliptic surfaces constitute one of the four categories of minimal smooth projective surfaces with Kodaira dimension $0$. This article establishes the automorphism schemes for these surfaces over algebraically closed fields of any characteristic, extending the work of Bennett and Miranda originally done over the complex numbers; furthermore, it identifies specific cases absent from the classification of bielliptic surface automorphism groups in characteristic $0$.

The virality of social media content is driven by several variables, specifically the content's subject, timing, and creator. Among these, the subject and timing are the most adjustable elements for optimizing reach. Since the title is the most flexible component of the content compared to the often static body, this paper investigates how titles influence popularity while accounting for posting time through an interpretable, attention-based model. Our method delivers state-of-the-art accuracy in forecasting post engagement across diverse communities, topics, and formats, maintaining a parsimonious design. By analyzing the model's attention weights, we uncover heterogeneous patterns showing how specific title words affect virality across different platforms. Ultimately, our findings underscore the significance of sentiment alignment, personal storytelling, and personality politics in driving content to become viral.

Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate remarkable capabilities through few-shot prompting, and the availability of commercial APIs like OpenAI's GPT-3 has accelerated their adoption in practical language tasks. Despite this, current research predominantly evaluates model accuracy on standard benchmarks, often neglecting reliability—a critical factor for preventing severe real-world consequences. Although reliability is a broad and somewhat ambiguous concept, this study breaks it down into four specific dimensions: generalizability, fairness, calibration, and factuality. We develop straightforward and effective prompts to assess GPT-3's reliability across these areas: 1) generalizing to out-of-domain scenarios, 2) balancing demographic distributions to mitigate social biases, 3) calibrating language model probabilities, and 4) updating the model's knowledge base. Our results indicate that with the right prompting strategies, GPT-3 significantly outperforms smaller supervised models on all four facets. To support further investigation, we make all processed datasets, evaluation scripts, and model predictions publicly available. These findings offer new perspectives on the reliability of prompting LLMs and provide practitioners with strategies to utilize large models like GPT-3 more dependably.

This paper details methodologies for constructing multilingual representation models that match the performance of current state-of-the-art systems while utilizing fewer parameters, thus facilitating greater adoption in resource-limited and practical contexts. We demonstrate that moving beyond English-centric bitexts, combined with a new sampling strategy designed to mitigate training data under-utilization, significantly enhances performance across various model sizes for both Electra and MLM pre-training objectives. We present XY-LENT (X-Y bitext enhanced Language ENcodings using Transformers), which achieves state-of-the-art results on five cross-lingual tasks across all model size bands. Specifically, the XY-LENT XL variant surpasses XLM-RXXL and competes with mT5 XXL while being five and six times smaller, respectively. Furthermore, we illustrate that our approach alleviates the curse of multilinguality, with XY-LENT XL attaining 99.3% GLUE and 98.5% SQuAD 2.0 scores compared to a state-of-the-art English-only model of equivalent size. Finally, we evaluate our models on extremely low-resource languages and argue that scaling alone is insufficient to improve performance in such scenarios.

This work introduces novel concepts, perspectives, and challenges regarding the measurement and control of open quantum systems through sequential schemes. We examine how protocols utilizing both repeated quantum measurements and dynamical decoupling pulses can achieve three key objectives: (i) confine and safeguard quantum dynamics against decoherence in line with Zeno physics; (ii) analytically determine the probability of transferring a quantum system to a target state via stochastic sequential measurements; and (iii) optimally reconstruct the spectral density of environmental noise sources by frequency-domain orthogonalization of the filter functions driving the designed quantum sensor. Accomplishing these tasks will improve our ability to observe and manipulate open quantum systems, thereby advancing quantum science and technology.

Shortest-path distance is a cornerstone of graph analytics and has been widely explored in research. However, many real-world scenarios impose quality constraints on edges, making it essential to determine the shortest distance between vertices $s$ and $t$ using only edges that meet specific quality criteria. This paper addresses this novel and significant challenge of quality-constrained shortest distance queries. We introduce an efficient index structure derived from 2-hop labeling methods. Leveraging a path dominance relationship that integrates both quality and length metrics, we prove the minimality of our proposed index. Furthermore, we develop a streamlined algorithm for query processing. Comprehensive experiments on real-world datasets confirm the efficiency and effectiveness of our approach.

Reinforcement learning (RL) serves as a prominent framework for sequential decision-making. Recent progress over the last ten years has driven breakthroughs in diverse fields, including robotics, video and board games, and chip design. However, the high sample inefficiency of deep RL methods remains a major barrier to their application in real-world scenarios. Transfer learning addresses this by allowing knowledge from one task to aid training on a new one, while curriculum learning focuses on ordering tasks or data to facilitate such transfers, enabling the solution of problems that would otherwise be too difficult. Designing an effective curriculum to enhance sample efficiency is a complex challenge. This thesis introduces a teacher-student curriculum learning framework where a teacher simultaneously selects tasks for a student agent, which in turn learns to solve them. This approach eliminates the need for manual curriculum design or human domain expertise. We evaluated the method on two benchmarks: the grid world and the demanding Google Football environment. Results demonstrate that our approach improves both the sample efficiency and generality of the student agent compared to standard tabula-rasa reinforcement learning.

In multicell massive MIMO non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) systems, base stations equipped with multiple antennas transmit radio frequency energy via the downlink, enabling Internet-of-Things (IoT) devices to harvest energy for uplink data transmission. This study examines the energy efficiency (EE) challenge within multicell massive MIMO NOMA networks utilizing wireless power transfer (WPT). To enhance network EE, we introduce a new joint resource allocation strategy encompassing power, time, antenna selection, and subcarrier assignment, ensuring optimal scheduling for both energy harvesting and data transmission phases. The analysis covers scenarios with both perfect and imperfect channel state information (CSI). Given quality-of-service (QoS) constraints, we formulate an EE maximization problem that is inherently non-convex. To address this, we employ nonlinear fractional programming to transform the problem into a convex form, followed by a distributed alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) approach for solution. Simulation outcomes indicate that the proposed algorithm converges rapidly with fewer iterations and delivers superior EE performance compared to existing methods.

Fluorescence microscopy has revolutionized modern biology by allowing the visualization of organisms at micrometer resolution; however, the diffraction limit hinders the resolution of sub-micron and nanometer features. Although various super-resolution techniques exist to overcome this barrier, they frequently demand costly optical equipment or specialized fluorophores. Recently, deep learning has emerged as a promising solution to lower these technical hurdles and generate super-resolution images directly from diffraction-limited data. Yet, conventional deep learning methods typically require thousands of images for training, a requirement that is often unattainable in biological research due to fluorophore photobleaching, phototoxicity, and dynamic cellular processes. Consequently, achieving super-resolution via deep learning with limited datasets remains a significant challenge. This study introduces a novel convolutional neural network approach capable of producing super-resolution images from small datasets. To validate the method, we utilized a training set of 750 images comprising 15 distinct fields-of-view (FOVs), with each FOV containing a single target image generated via the super-resolution radial fluctuation method. As anticipated, traditional super-resolution architectures failed to yield a functional model with this limited data. In contrast, our new approach successfully trained a network to achieve super-resolution from these few samples. Furthermore, this deep learning model holds potential for application across other biomedical imaging modalities, such as MRI and X-ray imaging, where acquiring large training datasets is equally difficult.

This paper examines the fair allocation of indivisible items within a unified model incorporating goods, chores, and copies. We address two primary research questions: (1) the existence of EFX and related fairness concepts for goods with copies, and (2) the existence of EFX and related concepts for chores. We establish a precise connection between these problems through two key contributions. First, we introduce a refined envy-based fairness notion called envy \emph{without commons} (denoted $\efxwc$ when applied to EFX). Second, we present a formal \emph{duality theorem} that links the existence of various (refined) fair allocation concepts for copies to their existence for chores. We illustrate the utility of this duality by characterizing EFX existence for chores via the dual environment and proving EFX existence for chores under leveled preferences. Additionally, we analyze the hierarchy among envy-freeness notions without commons and their $\alpha$-MMS guarantees, demonstrating, for instance, that any $\efxwc$ allocation ensures at least a $\frac{4}{11}$-MMS guarantee for goods with copies.

This study demonstrates that Bragg diffraction can be represented by classical light propagation within photonic lattices featuring a square power law refraction index coefficient. The system's dynamics are proven to be completely integrable, allowing for a closed-form description. We further analyze the trajectories of classical light as it propagates through these structures.
At the first order of perturbation theory, the correction to the electronic terms of a diatomic molecule is computed by considering the Pauli principle.

Clinical data on the longitudinal gross tumour volume (GTV) of head and neck cancer patients indicate that tumors of comparable pre-treatment size and stage can exhibit vastly different responses to identical radiotherapy fractionation regimens. Mathematical models of radiation response are frequently suggested to forecast treatment outcomes and enable the prescription of more personalized fractionation schedules. For clinical utility, such predictive models must strike a balance: they need sufficient detail to reflect the complex in vivo dynamics observed, yet remain simple enough for their parameters to be identifiable using the data typically available for calibration.

This paper demonstrates that models accounting for the spatiotemporal heterogeneity of intratumoural composition are superior at capturing observed in vivo dynamics compared to models focusing solely on tumour volume evolution. We compare the qualitative range of responses regarding GTV data during radiotherapy against observations from a cohort of head and neck cancer patients. Furthermore, synthetic data studies are employed to investigate issues of identifiability and uncertainty quantification. Our findings suggest that developing accurate, predictive mathematical models requires a dual approach: simultaneously advancing toward more detailed models—potentially incorporating tumour heterogeneity—and refining data metrics to better inform these models.

We provide a characterization of groups $G$ with order $p^7$ (where $p$ is a prime) such that not every element of the commutator subgroup $\gamma_2(G)$ is a commutator within $G$. In the process, we derive various structural properties for groups of this order.

The widespread adoption of machine learning in music has resulted in a readily available collection of pre-trained neural network (NN) models suitable for creative endeavors. This project details the development of an assistance tool tailored for live improvisation by laptop groups, aiming to utilize these off-the-shelf models to support individual musicians. Whether assisting novices in collaborating with experienced peers or enabling new creative expressions, the system integrates concepts from musical interfaces, generative music, and group performance into a web-based, networked solution. It provides performers with both high- and low-level controls to shape real-time note sequences generated by locally running NN models, while also allowing them to adjust their level of interaction with the generative assistance. Two test performances demonstrated the system's ability to cohesively support four musicians over a four-minute piece. However, iterative design processes revealed technical limitations specific to executing generative models within a JavaScript environment during live performance, primarily due to unavoidable processing overheads.

This work explores the evolution of parametric invariance across classical mechanics, quantum mechanics, statistical mechanics, and thermodynamics, with a specific focus on its connection to entropy. Originally utilized by Ehrenfest as a foundational principle for quantization rules in early quantum theory, and later adapted by Rayleigh to analyze vibrational pressure, our approach builds upon Rayleigh's methodology. We perform specific calculations of invariants within both classical and quantum frameworks, extending the concept of the Hertz invariant—a phase space volume—to systems with variable particle numbers. Furthermore, we demonstrate that slow parametric variations constitute an adiabatic process, thereby enabling the definition of entropy as a form of parametric invariance.

Research and development of through-wall radars focus on detecting, locating, and monitoring human activities within indoor spaces. However, electromagnetic waves passing through walls cause refraction, attenuation, multipath effects, and ghost targets, which distort radar signatures. By estimating wall properties such as dielectric profiles and thickness, these wall-induced effects can be removed from the radar data. This study proposes utilizing Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to derive wall characteristics from narrowband scattered electric fields measured on the transmitter's side of the wall. We show that these adversarial neural networks effectively address the highly nonlinear regression challenge even with limited training data, achieving up to 95% accuracy in estimating the dielectric profile and thickness of real walls using simulated training data generated by full-wave solvers.

Graphene is a superior candidate for Hall sensors because of its atomically thin form, high carrier mobility, and low carrier density. Nevertheless, to ensure reliable and durable performance across various environmental conditions, graphene devices require protection from their surroundings. This study introduces magnetic Hall sensors built on large-area, commercially available CVD graphene, shielded by exfoliated hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN). To link the graphene active regions to the outputs, we employed 1D edge contacts, which demonstrate stable and reliable electrical characteristics. The Hall sensors exhibit current-dependent sensitivities reaching up to 345 V/(AT). Furthermore, by adjusting the gate voltage to alter the carrier concentration and type within the graphene, the Hall sensitivity can be tuned.

Person re-identification (re-id) involves the difficult task of recognizing individuals across various camera viewpoints. Training a convolutional neural network (CNN) for this purpose typically demands extensive labeled datasets, necessitating the laborious manual matching of people between cameras. To mitigate the reliance on annotated data, we investigate a semi-supervised strategy that necessitates labeling only a fraction of the training data. We present a thorough review of person re-id research constrained by limited labels. Current methods in this domain are constrained by their dependence on features from multiple CNNs and the prerequisite of knowing the count of identities within the unlabeled data. To address these drawbacks, we introduce an approach utilizing part-based features derived from a single CNN, eliminating the need to know the label space (i.e., the number of identities). This enhances practical applicability and substantially lowers computational demands. Furthermore, we propose a PartMixUp loss designed to bolster the discriminative power of learned part-based features for pseudo-labeling in semi-supervised contexts. Our method surpasses state-of-the-art performance on three large-scale person re-id datasets and matches the efficacy of fully supervised techniques using merely one-third of the labeled identities.

In a spatially averaged inhomogeneous Universe, the backreaction term ${\cal Q}_\CD$ and the averaged spatial Ricci scalar $\average{\CR}$ can be combined to form an effective perfect fluid characterized by an energy density $\varrho_{\rm eff}^{\CD}$ and pressure $p_{\rm eff}^{\CD}$, which serve as novel sources for backreaction effects. To model the realistic evolution of these effects, we utilize the Chevallier-Polarski-Linder (CPL) parameterization for the equation of state (EoS) of this effective fluid. Addressing observations within this framework, we employ two distinct metrics for the late-time Universe: the standard Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) metric and a template metric featuring an evolving curvature parameter, as proposed by Larena et al. in \cite{larena2009testing}. By fitting the CPL backreaction model to type Ia supernova (SN Ia) data and observational Hubble parameter data (OHD) using both metrics, we observe that parameter tensions between the datasets are more pronounced when the template metric is used. Consequently, we conclude that the prescription for the geometrical instantaneous spatially-constant curvature $\kappa_{\CD}$ requires modification.

Sentence simplification enhances readability and comprehension through operations like splitting, deletion, and paraphrasing, yet the resulting sentence must remain logically entailed by the original. This study introduces a robust sequence-to-sequence model for sentence simplification that leverages a pointer-copy mechanism, subsequently refining its entailment and paraphrasing abilities through multi-task learning with auxiliary tasks for entailment and paraphrase generation. Additionally, we propose a novel 'multi-level' layered soft sharing strategy, wherein auxiliary tasks share specific layers of the main model—higher or lower levels—according to whether the task is primarily semantic or lexico-syntactic. We also implement a new multi-armed bandit training method that dynamically optimizes task switching during multi-task learning. Evaluations across multiple standard datasets show that our approach surpasses competitive simplification systems in both SARI and FKGL metrics as well as human assessments. Finally, we provide ablation studies examining alternative layer sharing techniques, comparisons between soft and hard sharing, dynamic multi-armed bandit sampling strategies, and the model's acquired entailment and paraphrasing proficiency.

We explore the characteristics of the $\Lambda$ hyperon within $\Lambda$-hypernuclei by employing an effective nuclear density functional theory grounded in low-energy effective field theory. This approach expands the energy density as a power series of Fermi momentum, resulting in multiple density dependencies for effective many-body interactions. Beginning with an effective density functional for nucleons, we derive parameters for two- and many-body $\Lambda$-$N$ interactions to supplement the nucleon functional, optimizing them against $\Lambda$-hypernuclear experimental data. This dataset encompasses energy levels for $\Lambda$ hyperons in $p$-, $d$-, and $s$-states across hypernuclei ranging from $_\Lambda^{16}$O to $_\Lambda^{208}$Pb. Our findings successfully account for most hypernuclear data through the inclusion of effective many-body interactions, with minor discrepancies observed in light hypernuclei. We apply this hyperon functional to analyze the binding energy of $\Lambda$ hyperons in neutron-rich $^{124-136}_\Lambda$Sn isotopes, which are candidates for upcoming measurements at J-PARC. Furthermore, our results demonstrate insensitivity to the density dependence of symmetry energy. We also investigate nuclear matter containing $\Lambda$ hyperons, noting that the hyperon threshold density is contingent upon nuclear matter properties.

Tongue twisters are sentences that carry meaning but are challenging to articulate. Automatically creating them is difficult because the output must simultaneously meet two criteria: phonetic complexity and semantic coherence. Moreover, defining phonetic difficulty is inherently complex, as it in natural tongue twisters arises from a diverse combination of elements like alliteration and homophony. This paper introduces PANCETTA: Phoneme Aware Neural Completion to Elicit Tongue Twisters Automatically. By utilizing phoneme embeddings to model phonetic difficulty, we train language models to produce original tongue twisters across two specific task configurations. To support this, we compiled the PANCETTA dataset, which comprises existing English tongue twisters. Through both automated and human assessments, alongside qualitative analysis, we demonstrate that PANCETTA successfully generates novel, phonetically challenging, fluent, and semantically coherent tongue twisters.

Utilizing a Riemann theta function alongside Hirota's bilinear method, we offer a clear and direct approach to explicitly generating double periodic wave solutions for both nonlinear differential and difference equations. By expressing an equation in bilinear form, its periodic wave solutions can be immediately derived through a unified theta function formula. We rigorously establish the connections between these periodic wave solutions and soliton solutions. The effectiveness of this proposed method is demonstrated across a range of nonlinear equations, including those featured in this study, as well as the shallow water wave equation, the (2+1)-dimensional Bogoyavlenskii-Schiff equation, and the differential-difference KdV equation.

This paper establishes multiple inequalities, including Sobolev, Poincaré, and logarithmic Sobolev types, that feature a generalized norm with precise extremal data and apply to certain symmetric functions. Our approach employs Ioku's transformation—a specific instance of $p$-harmonic transplantation—applied to symmetric functions.

Within the standard Bayesian framework, data are modeled as arising from a distribution defined by a parameter $\theta$ within a parameter space $\Theta$, accompanied by a prior distribution $\pi$. A Bayesian statistician expresses confidence that the true parameter equals $\theta_0$ via the posterior probability conditional on observed data. This study examines how the posterior belief in $\theta_0$ behaves when data are actually generated by a parameter $\theta_1$, which may differ from $\theta_0$. Leveraging stochastic orders, specifically likelihood ratio dominance, we analyze the monotonicity of posterior probabilities with respect to sample size as data arrive sequentially. While the posterior for $\theta_0$ is monotonically increasing (acting as a submartingale) when data originate from $\theta_0$, it does not necessarily decrease monotonically—neither in general nor in expectation—when data come from a distinct $\theta_1$. Indeed, the posterior may fluctuate repeatedly, even in elementary scenarios like independent and identically distributed coin tosses. We derive precise asymptotic rates for distributions belonging to the broad class of exponential families; these rates demonstrate that, for $\theta_1 \neq \theta_0$, the expectation of the $\theta_0$-posterior eventually becomes strictly decreasing. Furthermore, we establish that in several notable cases, this expectation functions as a log-concave, and therefore unimodal, function of the sample size. For the Bernoulli case, this result is achieved by deriving an inequality linked to Turán's inequality for Legendre polynomials.

Although TrustZone can isolate I/O hardware, it currently lacks support for modern I/O devices. Instead of porting traditional drivers, we propose a novel method to generate minimum viable drivers: developers execute a full driver while recording interactions between the driver and the device. These processed recordings, termed "driverlets," are replayed within the Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) at runtime to facilitate access to I/O devices.

Driverlets resolve two primary challenges—correctness and expressiveness—by leveraging a core construct known as an interaction template. This template guarantees the faithful reproduction of recorded I/O jobs (even when applied to new data), accommodates dynamic input values, and handles nondeterministic device behaviors. We have demonstrated driverlets across a range of sophisticated devices, making them accessible to TrustZone for the first time, to our knowledge. Experimental results indicate that driverlets are secure, straightforward to construct, and introduce acceptable performance overhead (ranging from 1.4x to 2.7x compared to native drivers). By bridging a critical gap in the TrustZone TEE, driverlets realize the long-awaited vision of secure I/O.

The LHCb detector has analyzed data from proton-proton collisions at the LHC, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 3/fb, to study Bs and B0 meson decays into J/\psi \pi +\pi -\pi +\pi - final states. For the first time, B^0_(s) -> J\psi f_1(1285) decays have been observed, and their branching fractions have been measured. Based on these rates, the mixing angle between the strange and non-strange components of the f_1(1285) wave function within the q-qbar structure model is determined to be \pm (24.0^{+3.1+0.6}_{-2.6-0.8}) degrees. The study also discusses the implications of these findings regarding the potential tetraquark nature of the f_1(1285).

Detecting fake news has become crucial during the ongoing pandemic, significantly affecting various facets of daily life. This paper introduces a solution for the shared task on English COVID-19 Fake News Detection, achieving a rank of 50th out of 168 submissions. Our approach performed within 1.5% of the top-ranked solution. The method utilizes a heterogeneous representation ensemble tailored for classification by incorporating an additional neural network head with multiple hidden layers. Furthermore, the paper includes comprehensive ablation studies that illustrate the proposed method's behavior and potential implications. The solution is open-source and can be accessed at \url{https://gitlab.com/boshko.koloski/covid19-fake-news}.

Standard transformer language model scaling typically involves training each model size from a random initialization. In contrast, we propose a staged training method that starts with a small model and gradually increases computational resources by applying a "growth operator" to expand the model's depth and width. By using the output of one stage as the initialization for the next, this approach reuses prior compute, enhancing efficiency. Each growth operator accepts the full training state—encompassing model parameters, optimizer state, and learning rate schedules—and generates a new state to continue training. We identify two critical properties of these operators: they preserve both the loss and the "training dynamics" (the rate at which loss decreases during training). While loss preservation is a known concept, this work is the first to highlight the significance of maintaining training dynamics. To determine the optimal stage schedule, we apply scaling laws from Kaplan et al. (2020) to pinpoint when training efficiency declines, thereby initiating a new stage for maximum compute savings. Empirical validation on autoregressive language models demonstrates up to 22% compute savings compared to a strong baseline trained from scratch. The code is accessible at https://github.com/allenai/staged-training.

We present the Minimum Shared-Power Edge Cut (MSPEC) problem. Given an undirected graph with edge weights and two distinguished nodes, $s$ and $t$, the objective is to determine an $s$-t cut by assigning "powers" to vertices; an edge is removed if the combined powers of its endpoints meet or exceed its weight. The goal is to minimize the total sum of these assigned powers. This problem generalizes a barrier coverage scenario in wireless sensor networks: specifically, finding the minimum total reduction in the radii of unit disks (centered within a rectangle) required to allow an intruder to traverse the area undetected, meaning the intruder can pass without entering any disk. This metric offers a more refined assessment of barrier coverage compared to simply counting the minimum number of disks needed to break the barrier. We propose a fully polynomial time approximation scheme (FPTAS) for MSPEC and provide polynomial-time solutions for specific instances where edge weights are uniform or vertex powers are limited to a bounded set. While MSPEC shares connections with network flow and matching problems, its exact computational complexity—whether it belongs to P or is NP-hard—remains unresolved.

Text-VQA's open-ended question answering frequently demands reading and reasoning about scene text that is either rarely encountered or entirely unseen. To tackle this zero-shot challenge, we propose leveraging external knowledge to enhance the comprehension of such text. We introduce a framework designed to extract, validate, and reason with knowledge using a standard multimodal transformer tailored for vision-language understanding. Empirical evidence and qualitative analysis demonstrate that incorporating external knowledge can emphasize instance-specific cues, thereby mitigating training data bias, improving the accuracy of answer entity types, and identifying multiword named entities. Our results, achieved under constraints of comparable upstream OCR systems and training data, match the state-of-the-art performance across three publicly available datasets.

The decoupling paradigm is gaining traction in speech enhancement by splitting the intricate spectrum estimation task into simpler sub-tasks, specifically magnitude recovery and residual complex spectrum estimation, thereby improving performance and interpretability. This paper introduces DBT-Net, a dual-branch federated framework for magnitude and phase estimation designed for monaural speech enhancement. The goal is to concurrently recover coarse and fine-grained spectral regions. From a complementary viewpoint, the magnitude estimation branch targets the filtering of dominant noise within the magnitude domain, whereas the complex spectrum purification branch focuses on inpainting missing spectral details and implicitly estimating phase information in the complex-valued domain. To enhance information exchange between branches, interaction modules are integrated to utilize features from one branch to suppress unwanted artifacts and restore missing components in the other. Departing from conventional RNNs and temporal convolutional networks for sequence modeling, we implement a novel attention-in-attention transformer architecture within each branch to optimize feature learning. Specifically, this structure comprises multiple adaptive spectro-temporal attention modules and an adaptive hierarchical attention module, enabling the capture of long-term time-frequency dependencies and the aggregation of intermediate hierarchical context. Extensive evaluations on the WSJ0-SI84 + DNS-Challenge and VoiceBank + DEMAND datasets confirm that the proposed method consistently surpasses previous state-of-the-art systems, achieving superior results in both speech quality and intelligibility.

We establish sufficient conditions for the solvability of state estimation in a class of nonlinear, time-varying control systems, which encompasses systems with triangular dynamics. The state estimation is achieved through a sequence of functionals that approximate the unknown state over a specified bounded time interval. Additionally, further assumptions ensure that the state estimation problem can be solved using a hybrid observer.

Although self-supervised speech representation learning (SSL) models are versatile for various downstream applications, they tend to overfit to the specific domain of their unlabelled training data. To address this, we introduce PADA (Pruning Assisted Domain Adaptation), a method that eliminates redundant weights from models pre-trained on extensive out-of-domain (OOD) datasets to create capacity for target-domain automatic speech recognition (ASR) fine-tuning. We explore several pruning strategies to identify these redundant weights, with a specific focus on comparing Task-Agnostic and Task-Aware approaches. Based on the latter, we propose a novel paradigm termed Cross-Domain Task-Aware Pruning (CD-TAW), which uniquely generates its initial pruning mask from a well-fine-tuned OOD model. When fine-tuned on a 2-hour subset of Switchboard data without language model decoding, our CD-TAW approach yields up to a 20.6% relative improvement in Word Error Rate (WER) compared to the baseline. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the critical design decisions underlying this methodology.

Identifying and quantifying a primordial non-Gaussian signature within the density field represents a primary objective for upcoming galaxy surveys, as this signal allows for the determination of early-universe physics and the restriction of cosmic inflation models. Moving beyond traditional methods that rely on restricted statistical summaries, we introduce a field-level strategy utilizing Bayesian forward-modeling of the complete three-dimensional galaxy survey. This approach naturally and self-consistently leverages the full scope of large-scale structure—including higher-order statistics, peculiar velocity fields, and scale-dependent galaxy bias—to extract the local non-Gaussianity parameter, $\fnl$. We validate our method using mock galaxy data designed to emulate \sdssiii{}-like surveys and additional \textit{Stage IV} datasets. These tests confirm that the method yields unbiased $\fnl$ values by effectively accounting for survey geometry, noise, and unknown galaxy biases. Our results indicate that for \sdssiii{}-like data, the method achieves $\sigma_{\fnl} \approx 8.78$, representing a roughly 2.5-fold improvement over existing constraints. Furthermore, simulations with next-generation mocks suggest that even greater precision is attainable with higher resolution. Finally, the method consistently marginalizes over all nuisance parameters and enables the inference of the three-dimensional primordial density field, opening avenues to investigate further signatures of primordial physics.

Maps are essential to the rapidly evolving field of autonomous driving. Our literature review of various map representations reveals that, despite the three-dimensional nature of the real world, 2D representations are frequently utilized to satisfy real-time performance requirements. However, achieving high situational awareness necessitates the use of 3D representations alongside semantic data. We demonstrate that our recently introduced hierarchical 3D grid mapping framework, UFOMap, satisfies these real-time constraints. Additionally, we illustrate its capability to efficiently support advanced functions, such as computing occluded spatial regions and aggregating outputs from semantic segmentation networks.

This paper establishes that minimal hypersurfaces for $n \geq 3$ and nonzero constant mean curvature hypersurfaces for $n \geq 2$, which are foliated by spheres within parallel horizontal hyperplanes in ${\mathbb{H}}^n \times \mathbb{R}$, are necessarily rotationally symmetric.

Understanding the superconductivity mechanism in iron-based superconductors necessitates a clear grasp of their electronic and superconducting gap structures. Yet, even for the extensively researched optimally-doped (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$, significant controversies persist regarding these features. We address these discrepancies by performing high-resolution angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) on the material using both Helium lamps and laser sources. Our findings reveal that the "flat band" near the Brillouin zone center in the superconducting state results from a combination of superconductivity-induced band back-bending and the folding of a band from the zone corner to the center. We provide direct evidence of this band folding in both the normal and superconducting states. By clarifying the origin of the flat band, we can accurately assign the three hole-like bands around the zone center and determine their superconducting gaps. Around the zone corner, we simultaneously observe a tiny electron-like band and an M-shaped band in both states. The derived gap size for these corner bands ($\sim$5.5 meV) is markedly smaller than those reported in previous ARPES studies. These results define a novel superconducting gap structure around the zone corner and resolve numerous longstanding controversies about the electronic and gap structures in optimally-doped (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$, offering fresh perspectives for developing theories on the superconductivity mechanism in iron-based superconductors.

Industrial Control Systems (ICSs) depend on vulnerable protocols and hardware to manage critical infrastructure. Previous research shows that well-resourced attackers with extensive system knowledge can alter sensor data to degrade process performance or cause complete plant shutdowns. Detecting such attacks typically involves iterating through every possible sensor value and running complex simulations to pinpoint optimal strategies, enabling adversaries to launch highly effective, undetected strikes on their first attempt. This study examines whether attackers lacking detailed system knowledge and simulation tools can achieve similar results. Specifically, we demonstrate that an attacker needing only abstract understanding of general information flows—rather than precise algorithms, operating parameters, or process models—can execute single-shot, near-optimal attacks that reliably shut down systems immediately. Validated across two use cases, our approach yields performance comparable to prior methods that relied on comprehensive system information and simulations.

Deep learning is revolutionizing numerous scientific and technological fields, including electron microscopy. This review provides a practical overview tailored for developers with minimal prior experience. First, we examine common applications of deep learning within electron microscopy. Next, we explore the necessary hardware and software for initiating deep learning projects and interfacing with electron microscopes. We then analyze neural network components, prevalent architectures, and their optimization techniques. Finally, we outline future directions for deep learning in electron microscopy.

We investigate specific abelian subcategories and torsion pairs within Abramovich and Polishchuk's heart. Furthermore, we establish stability conditions on a full triangulated subcategory $\mathcal{D}^{\leq 1}_S$ contained in $D(X\times S)$, where $S$ is any smooth projective variety. Additionally, we introduce the concept of $l$-th level stability, which extends both slope stability and Gieseker stability. We demonstrate that for every object $E$ in Abramovich and Polishchuk's heart, there exists a unique filtration composed of $l$-th level semistable factors, with phase vectors arranged in a decreasing lexicographic order.

In numerous reinforcement learning scenarios, the objective involves training a policy to control a fixed agent design in order to maximize cumulative reward, even though the agent's physical structure is seldom optimized for the specific task. This work investigates the potential of simultaneously learning an improved agent design tailored to the task alongside the policy itself. We introduce a modification to the widely used OpenAI Gym framework by parameterizing specific environmental components, enabling an agent to jointly optimize these parameters and its policy. Our results demonstrate that an agent can acquire a body structure better suited for the task, which also streamlines policy learning. Furthermore, the joint learning of policy and structure may reveal design principles beneficial for assisted design applications. Video demonstrations of the results are available at https://designrl.github.io/.

This paper examines the embedding problem for centrosymmetric matrices, representing higher-order extensions of the matrices found in Strand Symmetric Models. These models reflect the substitution symmetries inherent in the DNA double helix structure. Determining the embeddability of a transition matrix allows researchers to verify whether observed substitution probabilities align with a homogeneous continuous-time substitution model, including the Kimura, Jukes-Cantor, and general time-reversible models. Furthermore, the extension to higher-order matrices is driven by synthetic biology, which utilizes genetic alphabets of varying sizes.

Creating novel chemical compounds with specific pharmaceutical characteristics is a complex, multi-year endeavor that frequently results in new drugs failing to demonstrate efficacy. However, recent breakthroughs in deep generative modeling offer significant potential for generating and optimizing new molecules. This review provides a comprehensive overview of existing generative models, outlines essential biological and chemical terminology—including molecular representations required to grasp drug design and response—and details widely used chemical and biological databases along with modeling tools. Furthermore, we summarize the current landscape of generative modeling in drug design and response prediction, emphasizing both state-of-the-art methods and the field's prevailing limitations.

This paper presents our insights on the newly launched WILDS benchmark, a suite of ten datasets designed to foster robust models and training strategies capable of handling domain shifts. Through several experiments, we identify key findings that we consider vital for future research on WILDS, with a specific focus on the iWildCam and FMoW datasets. Our analysis reveals four critical points: (1) Performing distinct cross-validation for each evaluation metric is essential for both datasets; (2) iWildCam presents challenges in model development due to a weak correlation between validation and test performance; (3) Minor adjustments to hyperparameter training can significantly enhance baseline performance, particularly on FMoW; and (4) a strong correlation exists between specific domains and target labels, primarily observed in iWildCam. To our knowledge, these observations, despite their clear significance, have not been reported in prior work on these datasets. Our code is publicly available.

We highlight how the exponential parameterization of the quark mixing matrix inherently captures both the Cabibbo structure and the hierarchical characteristics of the Wolfenstein form. Furthermore, we generalize these findings to neutrino mixing by proposing an exponential generator for the tribimaximal matrix.

We gathered experimental thermal conductivity data from literature for ethylene glycol-based nanofluids to analyze the effects of concentration, temperature, and nanoparticle size. By applying statistical linear regression to the dataset, we evaluated four distinct nanoparticle types: alumina, titania, copper oxide, and carbon nanotubes. Our results indicate that statistical correlations align well with Maxwell's effective medium theory, even amidst significant data scatter. Thermal conductivity rises linearly with concentration and, specifically for carbon nanotubes, with temperature, while nanoparticle size exerts a notable influence on alumina and titania. The substantial variability in experimental results remains a primary challenge; therefore, we recommend rigorous characterization and measurement to accurately assess the potential of nanofluids.

This study establishes the general solution for the quinquevigintic functional equation and examines its stability within matrix normed spaces and matrix non-Archimedean fuzzy normed spaces, employing the fixed point method.

This document details the publication of ELKI, a Java-based open-source (AGPLv3) data mining framework, version 0.7.5. ELKI prioritizes algorithmic research, particularly in unsupervised techniques for clustering and outlier detection. To ensure high performance and scalability, it incorporates data index structures like the R*-tree, which significantly enhance efficiency. Designed for extensibility, ELKI invites researchers and students to contribute new methods. Furthermore, it provides a vast array of highly parameterizable algorithms to facilitate fair and straightforward evaluation and benchmarking. The paper begins by outlining the rationale behind this release and future development plans, followed by a summary of new features. An appendix is also included, offering a comprehensive overview of the system's implemented capabilities.

We examined the parametric seeding of a microresonator frequency comb (microcomb) using a pump laser featuring two electro-optic modulation sidebands. Our findings reveal that the spacing between the pump sidebands is exactly replicated across the entire optical spectrum of the microcomb. Furthermore, we achieved a record level of absolute line-spacing stability for microcombs, reaching $1.6\times10^{-13}$ at 1 second. Although parametric comb spectra are typically complex and often exhibit non-equidistant subcombs, our results indicate that parametric seeding can effectively control these subcombs and produce a strictly equidistant microcomb spectrum.

Gait recognition stands out as a premier remote identification technique, ideal for both medical uses and real-world surveillance. Among existing approaches, model-based methods are highly valued for their ability to remain invariant to scale and viewing angles. This work introduces $\mathcal{G}$lidar3DJ, the inaugural model-based gait recognition framework utilizing skeleton models derived from single-flash LiDAR sequences. While previous successful model-based systems rely on high-quality skeletal data from sources like Kinect and motion capture studios—making them impractical for non-laboratory settings—this method adapts to LiDAR's limitations. Although the noisy, low-resolution imaging process of LiDAR typically degrades performance in state-of-the-art skeleton-based systems by producing numerous outlier skeletons, we propose a rule-based filtering mechanism employing robust statistics to correct joint measurements. Quantitative results confirm the effectiveness of this approach in enhancing gait recognition accuracy.

Although the ground states of certain systems, such as organic molecules, are only weakly correlated, the ultrafast hole dynamics resulting from photoexcitation represent a highly correlated process. This work introduces a unified framework and an efficient matrix-based formulation of advanced non-equilibrium Green's function (NEGF) techniques, including second-Born, $GW$, and $T$-matrix approaches, both with and without exchange diagrams. Numerical simulations on a paradigmatic, exactly solvable molecular model highlight the limitations of existing NEGF methods. Subsequently, we develop a NEGF scheme grounded in the Faddeev treatment of three-particle correlations, demonstrating its exceptional superiority over established methods. Notably, this Faddeev-based NEGF approach scales linearly with the maximum propagation time, thereby enabling femtosecond simulations of large molecules.

We characterize the magnetic activity of M dwarfs to inform the planetary community about stellar energy inputs. Specifically, beyond the optical flare frequencies directly detected by TESS, we aim to estimate corresponding X-ray flare rates by leveraging the limited dataset of events observed simultaneously in both bands. We identified 112 M dwarfs with TESS magnitudes $\le$ 11.5, making them accessible for full habitable zone transit studies. These stars provided 1276 two-minute cadence light curves from the primary mission, which we analyzed for rotational modulation and flares. Our investigation explores the connection between rotation and flares, as well as flare characteristics such as the amplitude-duration relationship and cumulative flare frequency distributions (FFDs). Assuming a one-to-one correspondence between optical and X-ray flares, and utilizing published simultaneous Kepler/K2 and XMM-Newton studies, we estimated the X-ray energy output for our detected TESS events. Our calibration also incorporates the relationship between flare energies in the TESS and K2 bands. We detected over 2,500 optical flare events across approximately 32% of our targets, but determined reliable rotation periods for only 12 stars (about 11%). For these 12 targets, we present cumulative FFDs and their power-law fits. We constructed X-ray band FFDs by calibrating optical flare energies to X-rays. In the absence of directly observed X-ray FFDs for main-sequence stars, our predictions can serve as estimates for the high-energy input to planets orbiting typical fast-rotating early- or mid-M dwarfs.

"Recently, two distinct methods have been proposed to extend the supersymmetry technique within random matrix theory from Gaussian ensembles to general rotation-invariant ensembles: the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization formula. In this work, we demonstrate the equivalence of these two approaches by reducing integrals involving functions of supersymmetric Wishart matrices to integrals over quadratic supermatrices possessing specific symmetries."

The recent surge in commercial social virtual reality (VR) platforms marks a significant expansion in the adoption of consumer VR. These platforms adapt elements from traditional 2D virtual worlds, allowing users to engage in immersive experiences, interactive tasks, and avatar-based interactions. However, social VR introduces distinct features that differentiate it from other online spaces, such as full or partial body-tracking, novel ways to perform mundane daily acts (like sleeping), and immersive opportunities for exploring complex identities. This growing popularity has attracted major technology companies, each launching its own social VR ecosystem. Consequently, social VR has emerged as a research domain focusing on design strategies, communication modalities, nuanced activities, self-presentation, harassment, privacy, and self-disclosure. Current scholarship indicates that many unresolved questions remain regarding ethical research practices and priority areas within the field. Therefore, this paper offers an overview of modern social VR, critically examines existing research, outlines ethical considerations for studying these environments, and identifies unexplored avenues for future inquiry.

This study employs $\textit{ab initio}$ techniques to examine the spin-nonconserving relaxation of excitons via phonon coupling in two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides. By integrating the $\text{GW}$-Bethe-Salpeter equation method with density functional perturbation theory, we computed the electron-phonon and exciton-phonon coupling matrix elements responsible for spin-flip scattering in monolayer WSe$_{\text{2}}$, subsequently analyzing the microscopic mechanisms governing these scattering rates. Our findings indicate that phonons generate effective in-plane magnetic fields capable of flipping exciton spins, thereby creating relaxation pathways that complement spin-conserving processes. Furthermore, we determined the temperature-dependent relaxation times for spin-flip exciton-phonon interactions. This methodological framework and its analytical approach are adaptable for investigating other two-dimensional materials and may encourage experimental efforts to measure spin-flip exciton relaxation dynamics.

In computer science, a preprocessor (also known as a macro processor) is a utility that programmatically modifies its input, usually relying on inline annotations, to generate output intended for another program. These tools are integral to software development and document processing, serving to translate or expand programming and markup languages, as well as enabling conditional or pattern-driven generation of source code and text. Initially, preprocessors were basic string-replacement utilities bound to specific programming languages and domains. Although they have evolved into more capable, general-purpose instruments, these advanced tools often demand that users master intricate macro languages with unique syntactic rules. This paper introduces GPP, an extensible, general-purpose preprocessor whose primary strength lies in its ability to customize syntax and behavior to fit any specific preprocessing requirement. Consequently, GPP offers significant value for research applications, allowing it to be readily adapted for use with innovative markup, programming, and control languages.

We introduce an efficient algorithmic framework for generating multi-level hp-bases that employs a data-oriented strategy, easily scaling to any number of dimensions and offering a natural basis for performance-optimized implementations. By focusing exclusively on the bounding faces of finite elements while ignoring lower-dimensional topological details, we demonstrate the method's potential through a newly developed open-source library. First, we examine a Fichera corner, showing that the framework matches the classical p-version of the finite element method in terms of runtime and memory usage. Next, we perform a transient simulation involving dynamic refinement and derefinement, achieving the anticipated convergence rates alongside superior performance in both computational time and memory consumption.

Spatiotemporal predictive learning (ST-PL) seeks to forecast future frames based on restricted input sequences, offering wide-ranging real-world utility. Nevertheless, extracting representative spatiotemporal features for accurate prediction remains difficult, a challenge further compounded by the chaotic uncertainty inherent in consecutive frames during long-term forecasting. This study focuses on enhancing prediction accuracy by strengthening the alignment between prior contexts and the current state. To this end, we introduce the Detail Context Block (DCB), which isolates fine-grained details and refines the correlation between upper-level context states and current inputs. By combining the DCB with a standard ConvLSTM and proposing the Motion Details RNN (MoDeRNN), we capture detailed spatiotemporal features and improve the representation of latent states, yielding significant quality gains. Experiments conducted on the Moving MNIST and Typhoon datasets validate the proposed method's efficacy. MoDeRNN surpasses current state-of-the-art approaches in both qualitative and quantitative metrics while requiring reduced computational resources.

We investigate the dynamical characteristics of massive quiescent galaxies between redshifts $1.4 < z < 2.1$ by combining deep Hubble Space Telescope WFC3/F160W images with literature stellar velocity dispersion data and new near-infrared spectra from KMOS on the ESO VLT. Our analysis reveals that the dynamical-to-stellar mass ratio has risen by approximately 0.2 dex from $z = 2$ to today. We examine this trend within the framework of potential variations in the stellar initial mass function (IMF) and the dark matter fraction ($f_\mathrm{DM}$) enclosed within the galaxy's effective radius. By comparing our high-redshift sample to their probable low-redshift descendants, we determine that $f_\mathrm{DM}$ has grown by a factor exceeding 4 since $z \approx 1.8$, shifting from $6.6\pm1.0\%$ to roughly 24%. This finding remains robust regardless of the specific methodologies used for estimating dynamical masses or identifying progenitor-descendant pairs. Furthermore, we quantify IMF variations using the offset parameter $\alpha$, which represents the ratio of dynamical stellar mass to mass derived from a Chabrier IMF. We show that the correlation between stellar velocity dispersion and $\alpha$ observed in low-redshift quiescent galaxies already exists at $z = 2$. Consequently, we argue that future evolution driven primarily by minor mergers will maintain this relationship while substantially increasing the galaxies' overall size and stellar mass.

The inventory of semiconductor materials featuring spectroscopically identified self-interstitials remains extremely limited. For nearly twenty years, the M-center in 4H-SiC—a bistable defect underlying a family of electron traps—lacked a theoretical model capable of revealing its true significance. By employing advanced first-principles calculations alongside junction spectroscopy, we show that the characteristics of the M center, such as its bistability, annealing behavior, reconfiguration kinetics, and electronic levels, are consistent with those of the carbon self-interstitial.

This work reviews BABAR and Belle findings on branching fractions, rate asymmetries, and angular observables for B \to K(*)l+l- decays, alongside a discussion of new CDF results concerning B \to K(*){\mu}+{\mu}- branching fractions and angular observables. Additionally, the first search for B+ \to K+{\tau}+{\tau}- is introduced.

High-precision direct N-body simulations model tidal disruption events (TDEs) in dense nuclear star clusters hosting supermassive black holes (SMBHs), where stars approaching the SMBH are torn apart. These events provide insights into SMBH properties, accretion disks, and the surrounding stellar clusters. This study compares the rates of full tidal disruption events (FTDEs) against partial tidal disruption events (PTDEs). Unlike FTDEs, PTDEs leave behind a surviving object, termed a "leftover star." The simulations incorporate two novel factors: fluctuations in the leftover star's mass and radius, and changes in its orbital energy. Activating these factors reduces the FTDE count by approximately 28%, primarily due to the ejection of leftover stars from PTDEs originating at larger distances. Conversely, the PTDE rate is roughly 75% higher than the simple estimates from Stone et al. (2020), driven mainly by multiple PTDEs generated by leftover stars in the diffusive regime. Analysis of peak mass fallback rates reveals that 58% of PTDEs exceed the Eddington limit, with the number of super-Eddington PTDEs being 2.3 times greater than that of super-Eddington FTDEs.

The "downwards drifting" features seen in fast radio bursts (FRBs) may naturally result from a screen located downstream of a small initial dispersion region. This screen imprints temporally sharp yet broadband structures onto pulses that have already undergone dispersion, while the majority of the dispersion measure is accumulated further along the path to the observer. If this model holds, the frequency-dependent scaling of drift rates in repeating FRBs indicates that the emission is beamed away from our line of sight, with circum-burst plasma deflecting the beam toward us. This mechanism also accounts for the observed limited and variable bandwidths of the bursts, despite the broadband nature of the underlying emission. We outline the geometric constraints of this straightforward model in explaining much of the observed spectro-temporal phenomenology of FRBs, offer generic predictions, and discuss potential modulation mechanisms.

This article investigates deformations of conjugate self-dual Galois representations through two main avenues. First, we establish an R=T type theorem for such representations with coefficients in a finite field that satisfy a specific "rigid" condition. Second, we examine the rigidity property within the families of residue Galois representations associated with the symmetric powers of an elliptic curve and regular algebraic conjugate self-dual cuspidal representations.

We demonstrate that for Specht modules of the Hecke algebra associated with partitions having at most two parts, the transition matrix mapping the standard basis to the web basis is both unitriangular and exhibits a strong positivity property. This finding extends the work previously established by Russell--Tymoczko and Rhoades.

Let $K$ denote an imaginary quadratic field and $\mathcal{O}_K$ its ring of integers. A subset $\{a_1, a_2, \cdots,a_m\} \subset \mathcal{O}_K\setminus\{0\}$ is defined as a Diophantine $m$-tuple in $\mathcal{O}_K$ satisfying $D(-1)$ if the condition $a_i a_j - 1 = x_{ij}^2$ holds for all $1 \leq i < j \leq m$, where each $x_{ij}$ belongs to $\mathcal{O}_K$. In this work, we establish that no such Diophantine $m$-tuple exists within $\mathcal{O}_K$ when $m > 36$.

We conducted a comprehensive analysis of post-merger quark-formation mechanisms using full 3+1 dimensional general-relativistic hydrodynamic simulations of equal- and unequal-mass neutron-star binaries, with properties aligned with the GW170817 inspiral. This study utilized three equations of state (EoS) consistent with current pulsar data, derived from a new finite-temperature framework grounded in V-QCD, a non-perturbative gauge/gravity approach to Quantum Chromodynamics. Through this method, we identified three distinct post-merger phases where both mixed baryonic-quark matter and pure quark matter are produced. Specifically, a phase-transition-triggered collapse occurring within approximately 10 ms of the merger indicates that the softest EoS version is incompatible with the expected longer post-merger lifetime observed for GW170817. These findings highlight the critical role multi-messenger observations of binary neutron-star mergers play in constraining the nuclear matter equation of state, particularly under extreme conditions.

We introduce time-resolved scanning x-ray microscopy utilizing picosecond photo-excitation driven by a customized infrared pump laser within a scanning transmission x-ray microscope setup. Specifically, we visualize the laser-induced demagnetization and subsequent remagnetization of thin ferrimagnetic GdFe films, a process occurring over a few nanoseconds. By managing sample heat load through supplementary reflector and heat-sink layers, we achieve non-destructive measurements at a 50 MHz repetition rate. Near-field enhancement of the excitation and controlled annealing effects result in laterally heterogeneous magnetization dynamics, which we track with 30 nm spatial resolution. Our research establishes new avenues for investigating photo-induced dynamics at the nanometer scale across picosecond to nanosecond timescales, a capability with significant technological importance, particularly in magnetism.

This work introduces a four-field Virtual Element discretization for time-dependent resistive Magnetohydrodynamics equations in three dimensions, concentrating on the semi-discrete formulation. The method utilizes arbitrary polyhedral meshes and ensures that both velocity and magnetic fields remain divergence-free up to machine precision. Furthermore, we offer a comprehensive convergence analysis based on appropriate regularity assumptions, a finding supported by numerical experiments.

Drawing upon the recent FermiLab measurement of $(g-2)_{\mu}$ and the XENON1T collaboration's upper limit on electron-dark matter recoil, we re-examine the phenomenology of MeV-scale vector dark matter within a leptophilic Standard Model extension featuring a new spinor mediator. We explore a viable parameter space to assess the feasibility of light dark matter relic density and the muon's anomalous magnetic moment. Our analysis includes direct detection limits for DM-electron interactions and cosmological constraints on the model's parameters. We demonstrate that while the new $(g-2)_{\mu}$ bounds significantly restrict the model's parameter space, thermal light dark matter remains viable for masses in the range $\rm M_{DM}\sim 10^{-3}-10^{-1}~\rm GeV$.

This study introduces a new design for distributed interval observers tailored to linear time-invariant (LTI) discrete-time systems operating under bounded disturbances. The proposed algorithm enables each agent within a networked group to share locally computed interval-valued state estimates with its neighbors, coordinating updates through an intersection operation. It is demonstrated that these constructed framers inherently guarantee bounds on the system's true state trajectory, requiring no additional assumptions or constraints. Furthermore, necessary and sufficient conditions for the collective stability of the distributed observer are established to ensure the uniform boundedness of the observer error sequence. Specifically, it is shown that these conditions can be practically met using a constructive and distributed methodology. Additionally, an algorithm is provided to verify specific structural conditions for a given system, ensuring the existence of the proposed observer. Finally, simulation results illustrate the efficacy of the proposed method when compared to existing distributed observers in the literature.

This paper outlines a system design for executing longitudinal daily-task studies using consistent workers on Amazon Mechanical Turk. The system was utilized to investigate touch dynamics, and we detail the challenges, experiences, and lessons derived from this process. Participants installed our application on their Apple iOS devices and performed two daily tasks over a 31-day period. Each task required a series of scrolling or swiping gestures, from which behavioral metrics like movement speed and pressure were extracted.

Although completing these daily tasks did not involve additional interaction with the Mechanical Turk interface, workers were compensated through the platform. This approach contrasts with the typical rapid completion of one-off tasks common on Amazon Mechanical Turk. Consequently, this unconventional use of the platform led us to evaluate factors influencing long-term worker retention and engagement, specifically examining the effects of payment schedules (both amount and structure) and reminder notifications. Additionally, we explored the challenge of balancing informed consent with workers' preference for quick task completion. Our findings indicate that leveraging the Mechanical Turk platform for longitudinal daily studies is a viable strategy to supplement or replace traditional laboratory-based research.

We develop efficient algorithms for finding weakly Pareto optimal solutions in smooth, convex, and unconstrained multiobjective optimization problems within general Hilbert spaces. This is achieved by introducing a new inertial gradient-like dynamical system tailored for multiobjective settings, whose trajectories converge weakly to Pareto optimality. Discretizing this system produces an inertial multiobjective algorithm that generates sequences converging weakly to these solutions. By incorporating Nesterov acceleration, we create an algorithm with a superior convergence rate compared to the standard multiobjective steepest descent method (Algorithm 1).

Further efficiency gains are realized by eliminating the need to solve a quadratic subproblem to determine a common descent direction for all objectives—a requirement typical of first-order methods. Through an alternative discretization of our inertial gradient-like system, we derive an accelerated multiobjective gradient method that avoids solving a subproblem at each iteration (Algorithm 2). Although this method does not guarantee convergence in all cases, it delivers strong performance on test problems and outperforms standard steepest descent by two to three orders of magnitude in speed.

Current Bayesian phylogenetic inference relies on Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods with basic proposal mechanisms, which limits exploration efficiency and frequently necessitates extended runtime to achieve accurate posterior estimates. This paper introduces an alternative variational framework for Bayesian phylogenetic analysis. Our approach integrates subsplit Bayesian networks—a highly expressive graphical model for representing tree topology distributions—with a structured amortization of branch lengths across topologies to define a suitable variational family. We train this variational approximation using stochastic gradient ascent, employing distinct gradient estimators for continuous and discrete parameters to navigate the composite latent space inherent in phylogenetic models. Our results demonstrate that the variational method offers performance comparable to MCMC while significantly reducing computational demands through a more efficient exploration strategy enabled by variational inference. Furthermore, experiments on a benchmark of challenging real-world phylogenetic problems confirm the effectiveness and efficiency of our proposed methods.

This paper addresses the NP-complete imbalance problem within complete bipartite graphs, a challenge with significant applications in fields ranging from parallel computer architecture and VLSI design to computational biology and archaeology. We provide characterizations for optimal solutions to this problem on complete bipartite graphs, enabling a solution in $\mathcal{O}(\log(|V|) \cdot \log(\log(|V|)))$ time when the part cardinalities are known, and allowing verification of optimality in $O(|V|)$ time. Furthermore, we introduce a specific class of proper interval bipartite graphs where the imbalance problem can be solved in $\mathcal{O}(c \cdot \log(|V|) \cdot \log(\log(|V|)))$ time, with $c = \mathcal{O}(|V|)$, leveraging the established characterizations.

Biomedical word embeddings are typically pre-trained on unrestricted text corpora using neural techniques that capture both local and global distributional patterns. These embeddings are subsequently utilized in downstream tasks via diverse neural architectures optimized for specific objectives, which can further refine the embeddings.
