However, since 2018, the field has shifted significantly from static embeddings to contextual ones driven by language models such as ELMo, transformers (e.g., BERT, ULMFiT), and others. These dynamic embeddings offer the distinct advantage of distinguishing between homonyms and acronyms based on context. Nevertheless, static embeddings remain pertinent for low-resource environments, such as smart devices and IoT components, and for investigating lexical semantics from a computational linguistics standpoint. This paper presents a method for jointly learning word and concept embeddings by initially employing the skip-gram approach and subsequently fine-tuning them using correlation data derived from co-occurring Medical Subject Heading (MeSH) concepts within biomedical citations. This fine-tuning process utilizes the BERT transformer architecture in a two-sentence input configuration with a classification objective designed to capture MeSH pair co-occurrences. Essentially, we adapt a transformer architecture—usually employed for generating dynamic embeddings—to enhance static embeddings through concept correlations. We evaluate these optimized static embeddings across multiple datasets previously developed for word relatedness. Unlike prior efforts that selectively removed concepts and terms, we believe this study provides the most comprehensive evaluation of static embeddings to date, demonstrating consistent performance improvements across all metrics. We make our code and embeddings publicly available for downstream applications and research at: https://github.com/bionlproc/BERT-CRel-Embeddings

We introduce a decentralized algorithm enabling a robot swarm to collaboratively move objects of arbitrary shapes. The method initiates with a task allocation stage that sequentially assigns positions around the object, beginning from a seed robot that first contacts it. Unlike previous methods, our approach does not require prior knowledge of the object's geometry to achieve caging. To guide the object toward a destination, we calculate the necessary number of robots by analyzing the angular difference between the object and the target. Throughout transport, robots navigate a sequence of intermediate waypoints that define the required object poses at each step. We validate the approach in a physics-based simulator with up to 100 robots across three generic paths, and further demonstrate its efficacy in real-world scenarios using a group of KheperaIV robots.

Keywords: Collaborative transport, Task Allocation, Caging, Robot Swarms

Laser-generated plasmas serve as intense, transient X-ray sources frequently employed for time-resolved imaging and spectroscopy. Obtaining absolute measurements necessitates precise data regarding laser-to-X-ray conversion efficiencies, spectral characteristics, photon yield, and angular distribution. This study presents soft X-ray emission results from a thin silicon foil subjected to a sub-petawatt, picosecond laser pulse. The reported absolute measurements span a continuous, broad spectrum from 4.75 to 7.5 Angstroms (1.7–2.6 keV). The resulting X-ray spectrum comprises spectral line transitions from highly charged ions alongside broadband emission arising from recombination and free-free processes, where electrons decelerate within plasma electromagnetic fields. These quantitative findings are contrasted with particle-in-cell simulations, enabling the differentiation between bremsstrahlung and synchrotron contributions to the free-free emission. The study reveals strong agreement between experimental and simulation estimates of laser-to-bremsstrahlung conversion efficiency, underscoring the reliability of the experimental approach and the validity of the physical interpretation.

Over the past decade, in-memory columnar databases have become mainstream, significantly accelerating the processing of massive datasets through multi-core parallelism and in-memory compression, thus overcoming typical disk-based bottlenecks. However, storing all data in memory becomes prohibitively costly as volumes expand to the terabyte and petabyte scale. Consequently, efficient compression algorithms are employed to leverage multi-core parallelization for query processing. Various methods have been explored to compress column arrays following Dictionary Encoding. This paper introduces two novel compression optimizations—Block Size Optimized Cluster Encoding and Block Size Optimized Indirect Encoding—that outperform existing techniques. Additionally, we propose heuristics to select the most effective encoding among common compression schemes.

A deterministic finite-state automaton (FSA) functions as an abstract sequential machine that processes input symbols one by one. An FSA is defined as symmetric when its output remains unchanged regardless of the order in which input symbols are read, meaning the output is invariant under input permutations. This paper demonstrates a method to transform a symmetric FSA into an automaton-based divide-and-conquer algorithm where intermediate results do not exceed the memory size of the original automaton. In contrast, while a comparable result for general FSAs exists through functional composition, it requires an exponential increase in memory. This new approach holds significant applications for parallel processing and networks of symmetric FSAs.

This study presents the initial measurement of top quark spin asymmetry, which reflects top quark polarization, within $t$-channel single top quark production. The analysis utilizes a dataset of proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 8 TeV, yielding an integrated luminosity of 19.7 $\mathrm{fb^{-1}}$. A high-purity selection of $t$-channel single top quark events featuring an isolated muon is employed, with signal and background contributions determined through a data-driven fit. Following corrections for detector effects, a differential cross section is measured for an angular variable sensitive to polarization. Utilizing this differential distribution, a top quark spin asymmetry of $0.26 \pm 0.03 \texm{(stat)} \pm 0.10 \texm{(syst)}$ is extracted. This result aligns with the Standard Model prediction of 0.44, corresponding to a p-value of 4.6%.

We perform a canonical analysis of a covariant formulation of unimodular gravity using the connection representation. Subsequently, we apply the Dirac procedure to quantize the theory. We investigate the extent to which the Kodama state, known as a solution in quantum general relativity, can be extended within covariant unimodular gravity. Finally, we examine the distinctions among the quantum states of covariant unimodular gravity, standard unimodular gravity, and general relativity.

Hot subdwarf stars are essential objects for investigating binary evolution and atmospheric diffusion. Although machine learning has recently emerged as a popular approach for identifying these stars, current methods still face challenges regarding automation and precision. This study introduces a robust identification technique utilizing a convolutional neural network (CNN). We built a dataset based on spectral data from LAMOS DR7-V1 and developed a hybrid recognition framework comprising both an 8-class and a binary classification model. This model demonstrated a testing set accuracy of 96.17%. To further verify its reliability, we evaluated the model against a validation set of 835 Hot subdwarfs drawn from the identified LAMOST catalog (2428 entries, including repeats) that were excluded from training, achieving an accuracy of 96.05%. Leveraging this model, we processed all 10,640,255 spectra in LAMOST DR7-V1, resulting in a catalog of 2,393 Hot subdwarf candidates, with 2,067 already confirmed. Manual validation of the remaining candidates yielded 25 new Hot subdwarfs, bringing the model's overall accuracy to 87.42%. In summary, the proposed method effectively identifies specific spectra with high robustness and accuracy, making it suitable for large-scale spectral classification and the targeted search of specific astronomical objects.

We establish general conditions guaranteeing that Markov processes with absorption converge exponentially and non-uniformly in the total variation norm to a quasi-stationary distribution. Furthermore, we identify a subset of the distribution's domain of attraction through an integrability condition, demonstrate the existence of a right eigenvector for the process's semigroup, and confirm the existence and exponential ergodicity of the Q-process. These findings are extended to various models, including one- and multi-dimensional diffusions, pure jump continuous-time processes, reducible systems with multiple communication classes, perturbed dynamical systems, and discrete-time processes on discrete state spaces.

Deep Metric Learning (DML) seeks to construct representation spaces where semantic relationships can be defined via predefined distance metrics. Leading methods typically utilize class proxies as representative samples to enhance convergence and generalization. However, these proxy-based approaches exclusively optimize for distances between samples and their proxies. Due to the inherent non-bijectiveness of distance functions, this strategy often results in locally isotropic sample distributions, causing the loss of critical semantic context because local structures and intra-class sample relations remain unresolved. To address this, we introduce non-isotropy regularization ($\mathbb{NIR}$) for proxy-based DML. By employing Normalizing Flows, we enforce a unique translatability of samples from their respective class proxies, thereby explicitly shaping a non-isotropic distribution around them to optimize for. This approach enables proxy-based objectives to more effectively capture local structures. Extensive experiments demonstrate that $\mathbb{NIR}$ consistently improves generalization while achieving competitive and state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks, including CUB200-2011, Cars196, and Stanford Online Products. Furthermore, we observe that the superior convergence properties of proxy-based methods are maintained or even enhanced, rendering $\mathbb{NIR}$ highly attractive for practical applications. The code is available at https://github.com/ExplainableML/NonIsotropicProxyDML.

This study examines the matching numbers associated with the power graphs of finite groups. The power graph $P(G)$ is defined as an undirected simple graph where the vertex set consists of the group elements $G$, and adjacency exists between two elements if one is a power of the other. The paper establishes upper and lower bounds for these matching numbers, alongside specific conditions under which a power graph admits a perfect matching. Furthermore, a formula is provided to calculate the matching number for any finite nilpotent group. Additionally, leveraging elementary number theory, it is demonstrated that the matching number of the enhanced power graph $P_e(G)$—where adjacency is defined by both elements sharing a common power—equals the matching number of the standard power graph of $G$.

An $(n, k, r, t)$ information symbol locally repairable code ($(n, k, r, t)_i$ LRC) is defined as a code where every information coordinate can be recovered using at least $t$ disjoint repair sets, each comprising no more than $r$ additional coordinates. This study examines a specific subclass of such codes in which every repair set includes precisely one parity coordinate. The analysis focuses on systematic codes by utilizing the standard parity check matrix. Initially, structural characteristics of this matrix are established by highlighting relationships with the membership matrix and the minimum distance optimality of the code. Subsequently, various bounds associated with the code are proven using the parity check matrix. Furthermore, several constructions for optimal $(n, k, r, t)_i$ LRCs are presented, leveraging two Cayley tables of a finite field. Finally, the paper extends a known result regarding $q$-ary $(n, k, r)$ LRCs to the broader class of $q$-ary $(n, k, r, t)$ LRCs.

This study explores the impact of dark energy on atom-field interactions by examining the acceleration radiation of a freely falling atom near a Schwarzschild black hole (BH) within a spacetime containing a positive cosmological constant ($\Lambda$). Employing a fundamental quantum optics framework and assuming a Boulware vacuum for a scalar ($\text{spin}-0$) field, we numerically calculate the probability of an atom becoming excited and detecting a photon as it approaches the BH horizon. Our results indicate that the character of the emitted radiation is fundamentally shaped by the magnitude of $\Lambda$. Specifically, dark energy expands the BH horizon, thereby enhancing radiation emission. Furthermore, we observe an oscillatory, non-thermal spectrum in the presence of $\Lambda$, where the amplitude of these oscillations varies with both the BH mass and the atom's excitation frequency. We hypothesize that this phenomenon arises naturally from constrained motion dictated by the bifurcate Killing horizon of the spacetime. This scenario resembles the Parikh-Wilczek tunneling method for Hawking radiation, where additional contributions to the Boltzmann factor alter the flux's thermality. Such findings suggest that the field adheres to a modified energy-momentum dispersion relation in the classical regime of general relativity, potentially stemming from an effective low-energy signature of underlying quantum gravity. Ultimately, our results may offer novel perspectives on the complexities of dark energy physics.

This paper investigates resilient average consensus within multi-agent systems facing misbehaving nodes. To prevent consensus values from being compromised by such nodes, we propose a strategy that detects anomalies, mitigates their negative effects, and ensures resilient average consensus. We address general misbehavior categories, including deception attacks, accidental faults, and link failures. By utilizing two-hop communication data, we characterize the impact of misbehaving nodes in a distributed fashion and develop a deterministic detection-compensation-based consensus (D-DCC) algorithm featuring a decaying fault-tolerant error bound. Furthermore, to handle scenarios with intermittently available information caused by link failures, we introduce a stochastic extension called the stochastic detection-compensation-based consensus (S-DCC) algorithm. We demonstrate that both D-DCC and S-DCC enable nodes to achieve resilient average consensus asymptotically, with exact convergence for D-DCC and convergence in expectation for S-DCC. Additionally, we employ the Wasserstein distance to evaluate the accuracy of S-DCC, and extensive simulations are performed to validate the efficacy of the proposed algorithms.

Equivariant Graph Neural Networks (EGNs) effectively characterize the dynamics of multi-body physical systems. However, existing EGNs rely on flat message passing, which fails to capture the spatial and dynamical hierarchies inherent in complex systems, thereby restricting substructure discovery and global information fusion. To address this, we introduce Equivariant Hierarchy-based Graph Networks (EGHNs), composed of three core components: Generalized Equivariant Matrix Message Passing (EMMP), E-Pool, and E-UpPool. Specifically, EMMP enhances the expressivity of traditional equivariant message passing; E-Pool aggregates low-level node quantities into high-level clusters; and E-UpPool utilizes high-level information to refine the dynamics of low-level nodes. Consistent with their nomenclature, both E-Pool and E-UpPool maintain equivariance to satisfy physical symmetry requirements. Extensive experimental evaluations across multiple applications, including multi-object dynamics simulation, motion capture, and protein dynamics modeling, demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed EGHN.

We present the concept of a fundamental heap, an isotopy invariant applicable to compact orientable surfaces with boundaries embedded in 3-space. Defined via diagrams of surface ribbons—thickened trivalent graphs—this structure forms a group equipped with a ternary heap operation. We demonstrate that the free component of this heap has a rank equal to the number of the surface's connected components. The text examines how this invariant responds to boundary connected sums and the addition or removal of twisted bands, offering formulas that link the heap's generator count to Euler characteristics. Additionally, we detail the impact of stabilization, proving that for any finitely presented group, a corresponding surface ribbon exists whose fundamental heap is isomorphic to it, modulo extra free factors. The relationship between the fundamental heap and the Wirtinger presentation is also explored. Furthermore, we establish cocycle invariants for surface ribbons through mutually distributive cohomology and heap colorings, accompanied by explicit computations of both the fundamental heap and these cocycle invariants.

The growing demand for secure communication and cryptography necessitates random number generators that are dependable, rapid, and genuinely unpredictable. Quantum random number generation leverages the intrinsic randomness of quantum mechanics to produce truly unpredictable values, with a prominent method utilizing the quantum vacuum state. Although this approach is convenient, it has historically been constrained by slower generation speeds relative to other techniques. In this study, we achieved an unprecedented 100 Gbps generation rate through a custom co-design of opto-electronic integrated circuits and digital filtering to minimize side-information. This result establishes a new benchmark for vacuum-based quantum random number generation, surpassing previous records by a factor of ten. Additionally, our experimental findings are validated by an enhanced device-dependent security framework that remains robust against both classical and quantum side-information while accurately accounting for digitization non-linearity. This chip-scale, ultrafast, and secure random number generator offers significant potential for future communication and cryptographic applications.

Grasping the relaxation mechanisms within colloidal suspensions is vital for pinpointing factors that govern constituent mobility, evaluating macroscopic behavior across pertinent time and length scales, and revealing the foundational principles essential for formulation engineering. This study specifically examines how long-range ordering affects the relaxation dynamics of suspensions containing soft-repulsive rod-like particles capable of self-assembling into nematic and smectic liquid-crystalline phases. Utilizing Dynamic Monte Carlo simulations, we investigate how translational and orientational order influence the diffusion of these rods along specific directions dictated by the background phase morphology. To clarify the resulting dynamics, we evaluate their temperature dependence, as temperature can profoundly alter system relaxation times and the self-diffusion coefficients of the rods. Furthermore, calculating van Hove correlation functions enables us to identify rods that diffuse significantly faster than the average, with their concentration precisely tunable through appropriate temperature selection.

Building upon the research of Sun and Kechris-Quorning, we establish that every acylindrically hyperbolic group $G$ possesses a faithful, weakly mixing probability measure-preserving action $G \curvearrowright (X,\mathcal{B},\mu)$ that is not essentially free. Equivalently, every such group admits a nontrivial faithful IRS which is weakly mixing. Furthermore, we demonstrate that every non-elementary hyperbolic group also admits a characteristic random subgroup exhibiting these same properties.

The LHCb detector functions as a forward spectrometer located at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Its primary objective is to conduct high-precision measurements of CP violation and investigate the rare decays of beauty and charm hadrons. This paper details the performance of the LHCb sub-detectors and trigger system based on data collected between 2010 and 2012, confirming that the experiment successfully met its design criteria. The detector's exceptional performance has enabled the LHCb collaboration to publish a broad spectrum of physics results, highlighting LHCb's distinctive dual role as both a specialized heavy flavour experiment and a general-purpose detector operating in the forward region.

The "memory wall problem"—the notion that memory bandwidth is the primary bottleneck for computer performance—is frequently cited. However, this paper challenges that view by arguing that, given historical trends where storage capacity grows exponentially while access latency decreases linearly, the focus should shift to minimizing whole-system memory access latencies. This requires examining how legacy software design choices lead to unnecessary waste of memory bandwidth. Consequently, this study explores the feasibility of virtualizing the Memory Management Unit (MMU) for each application process, granting it direct access to its own page tables and exclusive control over its allocated memory, thereby bypassing the kernel. Under typical conditions, this approach yields nearly scale-invariant performance for memory allocation, allowing hundreds of megabytes to be allocated, moved, swapped, and freed in roughly the same time as kilobytes; for instance, an experimental allocator allocated 8MB ten times faster and resized a 128KB block to 256KB four-and-a-half times faster than conventional methods. Additionally, first-time page access latencies improved tenfold, and the elimination of kernel page fault calls prevented cache pollution, boosting overall application memory access latency and performance by up to 2x. Finally, applying binary patches to existing applications to utilize this technique resulted in near-universal performance gains without requiring recompilation.

Consider a product cone $(X,g)$ equipped with the metric $g=dr^2+r^2h$, where $X=C(Y)=(0,\infty)_r\times Y$ and the cross-section $Y$ is a closed Riemannian manifold of dimension $(n-1)$ with metric $h$. This work investigates the upper bounds of the heat kernel for the operator $L_V=-\Delta_g+V_0 r^{-2}$. In this setting, $-\Delta_g$ denotes the positive Friedrichs extension of the Laplacian on $X$, while the potential is given by $V=V_0(y) r^{-2}$, with $V_0\in\mathcal{C}^\infty(Y)$ being a real-valued function. A key condition is that the operator $-\Delta_h+V_0+(n-2)^2/4$ must be strictly positive on $L^2(Y)$. The proof introduces a novel element: the utilization of the Hadamard parametrix alongside the finite propagation speed property of the wave operator on $Y$.

Although the phase structure of the $U(1)\times U(1)$-symmetric Higgs theory remains debated, a recent study by Shyta, van den Brink, and Nogueira (Phys. Rev. Lett. 127, 045701, 2021) demonstrated that adding a Chern-Simons term leads to a second-order phase transition. This extended theory is dual to a topological field theory involving massless fermions and two gauge fields. This work expands on that duality, specifically examining critical current correlators and the nature of the critical point through bosonization duality. We show that current correlators linked to the $U(1)\times U(1)$ symmetry and the topological current match exactly, differing only by a universal prefactor that remains consistent across both $U(1)$ and $U(1)\times U(1)$ topological Higgs models. Furthermore, this duality provides additional evidence for a critical point in the bosonic Chern-Simons $U(1)\times U(1)$ Higgs model: a Schwinger-Dyson analysis of the fermionic dual reveals no dynamical mass generation. This absence of mass generation does not hold for the theory lacking the Chern-Simons term in the action.

The $n$-queens problem seeks to calculate $\mathcal{Q}(n)$, representing the count of arrangements where $n$ mutually non-attacking queens are placed on an $n \times n$ board. We demonstrate the existence of a constant $\alpha = 1.942 \pm 3 \times 10^{-3}$ satisfying the asymptotic relation $\mathcal{Q}(n) = ((1 \pm o(1))ne^{-\alpha})^n$. This constant $\alpha$ is defined as the solution to a convex optimization problem within $\mathcal{P}([-1/2,1/2]^2)$, the space of Borel probability measures on a square. Our primary advancement involves introducing "queenons," which are limit objects for $n$-queens configurations forming a convex subset of $\mathcal{P}([-1/2,1/2]^2)$. We define an entropy function quantifying the number of $n$-queens configurations approximating a specific queenon. The upper bound derivation employs the entropy method, while the lower bound relies on a randomized algorithm that generates a configuration near a designated queenon with entropy matching the upper bound's calculation. Consequently, enumerating $n$-queens configurations is achieved by maximizing the concave entropy function over the space of queenons. Furthermore, we establish a large deviations principle for $n$-queens configurations, facilitating the analysis of their typical structural properties.

This paper examines the anisotropic Hastings-Levitov model, denoted as AHL$(\nu)$. While earlier studies demonstrated that on bounded time-scales, the harmonic measure at the cluster's boundary converges to the solution of a deterministic ordinary differential equation in the small-particle limit, we investigate its evolution on logarithmically growing time-scales as particle size approaches zero. We establish that on this extended scale, the leading-order behavior of the harmonic measure becomes stochastic. Specifically, we identify a critical logarithmic time window where the harmonic measure flow, initiated from an unstable fixed point, evolves randomly toward a stable fixed point. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the entire trajectory can be fully characterized by a single Gaussian random variable.

Unsupervised image-to-image translation seeks to learn a mapping between source and target domains without relying on paired training images. However, a critical yet limiting assumption in this field is domain alignment; for instance, in a selfie-to-anime task, the anime domain must exclusively contain anime faces that correspond to images in the selfie domain. Acquiring such aligned datasets is often labor-intensive and requires significant effort. This paper addresses the challenge of translating between unaligned domains, which can occur for various reasons. To tackle this, we introduce an approach that selects images via importance reweighting, learning the weights and performing translation simultaneously and automatically. We evaluate our method against state-of-the-art techniques, presenting both qualitative and quantitative results across multiple unaligned domain tasks. Comprehensive empirical evidence highlights the validity of our problem formulation and the superior performance of our proposed method.

Polarized proton-proton collisions offer a leading-order method to access gluons, enabling the investigation of gluon spin-momentum correlations in transversely polarized protons and advancing our knowledge of the proton's three-dimensional structure. At $\sqrt{s}=200$ GeV, midrapidity open-heavy-flavor production is primarily driven by gluon-gluon fusion, which yields greater sensitivity to gluon dynamics compared to alternative channels. Using the PHENIX detector at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider, transverse single-spin asymmetries of electrons and positrons arising from heavy-flavor hadron decays are measured at midrapidity. These charge-separated measurements probe gluon correlators that can potentially be linked to gluon orbital angular momentum through theoretical models. Explicit constraints on these gluon correlators are derived for two distinct models, including one that had not previously been constrained.

Barrett is a Python package designed for processing and visualizing statistical inferences generated by the nested sampling algorithm MultiNest. Its primary advantage over competing tools is its ability to perform full out-of-core processing, enabling it to manage datasets of any size. This capability is realized through the use of the HDF5 data format.

Transformers have demonstrated significant success in natural language processing. Leveraging the potent self-attention mechanism, researchers have adapted transformer architectures for diverse computer vision applications, including image recognition, object detection, segmentation, pose estimation, and 3D reconstruction. This paper offers a comprehensive survey of existing literature on various architectural designs and training strategies for vision transformers, encompassing self-supervised learning techniques. The objective is to deliver a systematic review that highlights open research opportunities in this field.

Misinformation has emerged as a critical issue in recent years due to its widespread presence across information channels. While numerous NLP tasks have been developed in this field, with some systems achieving strong performance on English datasets, existing AI literature identifies automatic stance detection as a foundational step for combating misinformation. This study aims to extend the progress made in English to other languages, a challenging endeavor given the domain disparity between English and target tongues. We introduce a black-box, non-intrusive method that employs Domain Adaptation techniques to bridge this gap without requiring human expertise in the target language, leveraging both supervised and unsupervised low-quality data. Consequently, we achieve stance detection results for Zulu—the target language of this work—that rival those obtained in English. Additionally, we present a new stance detection dataset for Zulu. Our experiments demonstrate that utilizing English datasets alongside machine translation enhances performance across both English and other languages.

Unlike other formulations of the second law, the Clausius statement regarding the spontaneous flow of heat from cold to hot bodies applies to non-equilibrium systems, making it both more ambitious and ambiguous. We examine two specific scenarios where the plain version of this statement fails. First, in ergodic systems, while energy transfer generally aligns with the Clausius statement over coarse-grained time scales, it can exhibit anomalous directionality during intervals shorter than the thermalization time. Specifically, when a colder system contacts a hotter bath, its internal energy eventually increases but does so non-monotonically. Second, in non-ergodic systems, heat transfer may violate the Clausius statement at all time scales due to the emergence of localized vibrational modes. These two cases are demonstrated using a standard model of an isotope atom coupled to a semi-infinite harmonic atomic chain. The analysis relies on a Langevin equation for the isotope, assuming initial uncorrelated canonical states where the boundary atom is initially fixed and subsequently released. Under these conditions, the Langevin noise is non-stationary, and the fluctuation-dissipation relation takes a non-standard form.

This study explores the intersection between garbage-collected languages and those employing advanced type systems for safe manual memory management. While garbage collection traditionally underpins functional languages, type systems have increasingly been adopted in imperative languages to ensure memory safety. We leverage established techniques involving linear capabilities to safely access copyable references, though our specific application to tracing garbage collectors and data with explicit lifetimes represents a novel contribution. Although this research aligns with mixed linear/non-linear programming, the specific languages integrated in this work are Rust and JavaScript.

Multivalency is a fundamental feature across diverse biological systems and biorelevant applications, driven by the superselectivity that arises from cooperative multivalent binding. It is generally accepted that weak individual interactions enhance selectivity in multivalent targeting. However, through a combination of analytical mean field theory and Monte Carlo simulations, we demonstrate that in systems with highly uniform receptor distributions, peak selectivity is achieved at intermediate binding energies, often surpassing the limits observed in weak binding scenarios. This phenomenon stems from an exponential relationship between the bound fraction and receptor concentration, a dynamic influenced by both binding strength and combinatorial entropy. We delineate the specific parameter ranges where this exponential dependence manifests in single-site models. These insights provide fresh guidelines for the rational design of advanced drug delivery systems and introduce an additional dimension for comprehending biological processes governed by multivalency.

Blazars, which are active galaxies oriented with their jets toward Earth, radiate across the entire electromagnetic spectrum. While the one-zone model effectively accounts for both quiescent and flaring phases, it fails to explain observed radio emissions; consequently, extended jet models are required for a self-consistent description of the full spectrum. Specifically, kinetic frameworks for these extended jets can map the temporal and spatial evolution of particle species alongside their complete electromagnetic output. This paper presents preliminary findings from a newly developed hadronic extended-jet code. Since protons retain energy significantly longer than electrons, they facilitate energy transport over vastly greater distances, making them crucial for jet dynamics. Additionally, protons can generate extra leptons via pion and Bethe-Heitler pair production, offering an explanation for dominant leptonic radiation while simultaneously producing neutrinos. We will provide a comprehensive parameter study and offer insights into various blazar subclasses.

This study investigates the reset threshold of randomly generated deterministic automata. We propose that an automaton featuring a random mapping alongside two random permutation letters achieves a reset threshold of $\mathcal{O}\big( \sqrt{n \log^3 n} \big)$ with high probability. This observation builds upon Nicaud's 2014 breakthrough, which established a near-linear bound for a comparable scenario, alongside other related findings. While recent numerical analyses suggest the expected reset threshold may be closer to $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{n})$, no sublinear bound has yet been rigorously confirmed for any specific variant.

The Lotka-Volterra framework is commonly applied to describe dynamics between two species. In this study, we create synthetic datasets simulating competitive, mutualistic, and antagonistic relationships between two tumor cell lines and apply the Lotka-Volterra model to deduce the nature of these interactions. We confirm the model's structural identifiability and evaluate its practical identifiability across three experimental strategies: (a) observing a mixed population of both cell lines over time using a single dataset; (b) a sequential approach where growth rates and carrying capacities are derived from isolated cell line experiments before estimating interaction parameters from a mixed population experiment; and (c) a parallel design where all parameters are fitted simultaneously using data from two mixed populations. Beyond assessing practical identifiability, we examine how the choice of experimental design influences the model's predictive capacity, specifically its ability to fit data with initial ratios different from the calibration set. Our results indicate that the parallel calibration method is optimal. This approach is further validated using *in silico* data generated from a spatially-resolved cellular automaton model that incorporates oxygen consumption and variable interaction intensities. This work underscores the necessity for caution when interpreting parameter estimates from the spatially-averaged Lotka-Volterra model when calibrated against data from the cellular automaton model, as inherent baseline competition for space and resources within the automaton can cause discrepancies between the true interaction type used to generate the data and the interaction type inferred by the model.

This study investigates the quantum soft covering problem, focusing on how effectively a random codebook of a specific size can approximate the output state of a quantum channel. We consider a random codebook where codewords are independently drawn from a prior distribution and passed through a classical-quantum channel to mimic a target state. Our analysis demonstrates that if the codebook rate, sampled from an independent and identically distributed prior, exceeds the quantum mutual information, the expected trace distance between the resulting codebook state and the target state decreases exponentially, with an exponent defined by the sandwiched Rényi information. Conversely, when the rate falls below the quantum mutual information, the trace distance approaches one at an exponential rate. Comparable findings are achieved using random constant composition codebooks, where the error exponent is characterized by the sandwiched Augustin information. Furthermore, beyond standard large deviation analysis, our results extend to the moderate deviation regime, proving that the trace distance still vanishes asymptotically even when the codebook rate approaches the quantum mutual information moderately rapidly.

This paper investigates X-ray images of paintings that hide subsurface designs, such as those resulting from support reuse or compositional revisions, which combine signals from both surface and concealed layers. We introduce a self-supervised deep learning framework for image separation that processes these X-rays to generate two distinct hypothetical images: one representing the concealed artwork and the other containing only the visible painting's information. The proposed network comprises two modules: an analysis sub-network derived from learned coupled iterative shrinkage thresholding algorithms (LCISTA) via algorithm unrolling, and a synthesis sub-network utilizing linear mappings. Crucially, the learning process is entirely self-supervised, eliminating the need for paired datasets of mixed and separated images. We validate the method's efficacy on "Doña Isabel de Porcel" by Francisco de Goya, a painting known to contain hidden content.

As the COVID-19 pandemic progresses, misinformation spreads widely across social media, posing severe risks that necessitate effective detection and mitigation strategies. Recently, deep learning models utilizing natural language processing (NLP), particularly BERT, have demonstrated significant success in identifying such false information. This paper introduces an explainable NLP framework combining DistilBERT and SHAP (Shapley Additive exPlanations) to address COVID-19 misinformation, leveraging their efficiency and effectiveness. First, we assembled a dataset of 984 fact-checked claims regarding COVID-19, which was expanded to double its size through back-translation augmentation. Using DistilBERT on this augmented data yielded strong performance, achieving an accuracy of 0.972 and an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.993. Furthermore, our model performed well on a larger dataset from the AAAI2021 COVID-19 Fake News Detection Shared Task, recording an accuracy of 0.938 and an AUC of 0.985, outperforming traditional machine learning approaches. Second, to enhance public confidence in model predictions, we integrated SHAP to improve explainability. This approach was evaluated via a between-subjects experiment involving three conditions: text-only (T), text with SHAP explanations (TSE), and text with SHAP explanations plus source and evidence (TSESE). Participants showed significantly higher willingness to trust and share COVID-19-related information in the TSE and TSESE conditions compared to the T condition. These findings offer valuable insights for detecting COVID-19 misinformation and fostering greater public trust.

During the Internet-of-Things (IoT) era, Wireless Body Area Networks (WBANs) and their integration with big data infrastructure have garnered significant interest from the medical research community. Given that sensor nodes are low-powered devices requiring heterogeneous Quality-of-Service (QoS), the efficient management of extensive medical data is paramount in WBANs. Consequently, effective aggregation of large-scale medical data is essential. In response, we introduce a quality-driven and energy-efficient big data aggregation method for cloud-assisted WBANs. This approach proves cost-effective for both intra-BAN (Phase I) and inter-BAN (Phase II) communications. Comprehensive simulation results demonstrate that the proposed DEBA approach significantly enhances network efficiency regarding aggregation delay and cost when compared to existing schemes.

The significant enrollment in Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) has driven a rise in automated program repair techniques designed for introductory programming assignments (IPAs). These methods leverage correct student submissions from previous iterations to deliver automated, comprehensive, and personalized feedback. This paper introduces C-Pack-IPAs, an open-access benchmark comprising 25 distinct IPAs. It includes a test suite alongside semantically correct, semantically incorrect, and syntactically incorrect student programs for each assignment. Consequently, C-Pack-IPAs serves as a resource for evaluating new automated program repair frameworks—addressing both semantic and syntactic issues—that aim to assist novice programmers.

By applying the equivariance to families principle to a geometric family of Clifford module bundles under the action of a compact Lie group G, we establish an equivariant variant of Bismut's families index theorem on the differential Borel quotient of this geometric family.

Although inference accuracy is a vital performance indicator for deep neural networks (DNNs), it often fluctuates significantly across different test datasets and remains unknown in practice due to the absence of ground truth labels. This uncertainty has sparked major concerns regarding the reliability of DNNs, particularly in safety-critical domains. To mitigate these issues, this paper introduces a post-hoc processing method to monitor true inference accuracy on user-specific datasets. Specifically, we propose a neural network-based accuracy monitor that accepts the softmax probability outputs of a deployed DNN as input and directly predicts the correctness of its predictions, thereby estimating the true accuracy. This monitor can be pre-trained on application-relevant data and requires labeling only a small fraction (1% in our experiments) of the user's dataset for transfer learning. To enhance robustness, we utilize an ensemble of monitor models employing Monte-Carlo dropout. We validated our approach across various DNN architectures for image classification and traffic sign detection on multiple datasets, including those with adversarial samples. The results demonstrate that our accuracy monitor yields estimates closely aligned with true accuracy and surpasses existing baseline methods.

In supervised learning via neural networks, we assert and empirically demonstrate that performance improves when data distribution concentrates on regions where the target function has steep gradients. We formalize this premise using Taylor expansion to define a novel training distribution grounded in the function's derivatives. This approach leads to the development of Variance Based Samples Weighting (VBSW), a methodology that assigns weights to training points based on local label variance. VBSW is a general, scalable, and cost-efficient technique that substantially enhances the performance of diverse neural network architectures across classification and regression tasks involving image, text, and multivariate data. Experimental results confirm its efficacy across a spectrum of models, ranging from linear regressors to ResNet and BERT.

Driven by a rigidity-theoretic viewpoint on the Localization Problem in two dimensions, we present an algorithm to compute circuit polynomials within the algebraic rigidity matroid linked to the Cayley-Menger ideal for $n$ points in 2D. We define combinatorial resultants, a novel graph operation that encapsulates characteristics of the Sylvester resultant for two polynomials in this matroid. We demonstrate that every rigidity circuit admits a construction tree rooted in $K_4$ graphs derived from this operation. The algorithm executes algebraic elimination guided by this tree, leveraging classical resultants, factorization, and ideal membership tests. To validate its efficacy, we implemented the method in Mathematica; it solved an example in under 15 seconds, whereas a Groebner Basis computation required 5 days and 6 hours.

Although B. Hirshberg et al. have recently successfully utilized path integral molecular dynamics (PIMD) to simulate identical bosons and fermions, this work demonstrates that PIMD can be further developed to compute Green's functions and derive momentum distributions for spin-polarized fermions. Specifically, we highlight the potential of PIMD-calculated momentum distributions for studying various quantum systems, including the cold atom simulation of Mott insulators within the Fermi-Hubbard model.
We determine the cardinality of the set $G_{3}(n,x) = \{M \in GL_3(\mathbb{Z}_n) \mid perm(M) \equiv x \pmod{n} \}.$

This study introduces a new computational approach for resolving acoustic wave transmission issues involving composite scatterers, specifically penetrable obstacles featuring junctions or triple points. The continuous problem is formulated as a time-domain boundary integral method utilizing multiple traces, applicable to both two and three dimensions. Numerically, the two-dimensional non-conforming spatial discretization employs spectral elements derived from second-kind Chebyshev polynomials, with a convolution quadrature scheme executed in the complex frequency domain. Computational experiments demonstrate that multistep and multistage convolution quadrature achieve the anticipated convergence rates across various complex domains.

We employ a coherent fiber bundle to perform endoscopic absorption imaging on quantum gases. Our results indicate that the fiber bundle generates spurious noise primarily caused by strong coupling between adjacent cores. Through direct comparison with free-space imaging, we identify a maximum column density that can be accurately measured using this method and establish a simple criterion for estimating this limit. We demonstrate that by adhering to this threshold, precise quantitative data regarding the atomic system can be recovered, rendering the technique highly suitable for applications demanding environmental isolation.

We investigated the evolution of the correlated metallic state in LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices as a function of bilayer thickness using $\beta$-detected NMR with ion-implanted $^8$Li. Spin-lattice relaxation measurements conducted at 6.55 T identified two components of equal amplitude: one displaying metallic behavior with a $T$-linear $1/T_{1}$, and another exhibiting a more intricate temperature dependence. The metallic nature of the slow-relaxing component remains largely insensitive to changes in LaNiO$_3$ thickness, whereas the fast component shows significant sensitivity, particularly in the thinnest, most magnetic samples where it displays an inverse temperature dependence (increasing as $T$ decreases). The underlying causes of this bipartite relaxation are discussed.

Existing $B_c$ states are all situated below the open bottom-charm threshold, decay primarily via weak interactions, and have three dominant decay modes. This study examines the mass spectrum and strong decays of the $B_c(3S)$ states, which lie just above this threshold, utilizing the Bethe-Salpeter formalism and the $^3P_0$ model. Our numerical findings yield $M(B_c(3^1S_0))=7273\ {\rm MeV}$ and $M(B_c^*(3^3S_1))=7304\ {\rm MeV}$, along with the following partial widths: $\Gamma\left(B_c(3^1S_0)\to B^*D\right)=26.02^{+2.33}_{-2.21}\ {\rm MeV}$, $\Gamma\left(B_c^*(3^3S_1)\to BD\right)=3.39^{+0.27}_{-0.26}\ {\rm MeV}$, $\Gamma\left(B_c^*(3^3S_1)\to B^*D\right)=14.77^{+1.40}_{-1.33}\ {\rm MeV}$, and $\Gamma\left(B_c^*(3^3S_1)\to BD^*\right)=6.14^{+0.58}_{-0.54}\ {\rm MeV}$. In contrast to earlier non-relativistic studies, these results demonstrate that relativistic effects are significant for the exclusive strong decays of $B_c(3S)$. Consequently, we recommend searching for these $B_c(3S)$ states through their hadronic decays into $B$ and $D$ mesons in experimental facilities such as LHCb.

Tibaduiza et al. [Braz. J. Phys. 50, (2020)] recently examined, using an exact algebraic approach, the dynamics of a quantum harmonic oscillator that abruptly shifts from an initial frequency $\omega_0$ to $\omega_1$, subsequently returning to $\omega_0$ after a specific duration. In this study, we analyze the identical physical system via the Lewis-Riesenfeld method of dynamical invariants. Our investigation successfully reproduces the exact analytical formulas derived by Tibaduiza et al. for squeeze parameters, quantum fluctuations in position and momentum, and the transition probability amplitude from the ground state to arbitrary energy eigenstates, thereby confirming both our findings obtained through the LR method and their original results. Furthermore, we provide novel expressions for the mean energy, mean number of excitations, and transition probabilities, specifically for cases where the initial state is not the fundamental one. We demonstrate that the oscillator's mean energy post-jump is always greater than or equal to its pre-jump energy, even when $\omega_1 < \omega_0$. Additionally, we show that for specific time intervals between jumps, the oscillator can revert to its original initial state.

Deep Reinforcement Learning (RL) has become a potent approach for addressing various intricate and specialized control problems, though training generalist agents capable of rapid adaptation to novel tasks remains a significant hurdle. Recent breakthroughs in unsupervised RL indicate that pre-training agents using self-supervised intrinsic rewards can facilitate efficient adaptation. Nevertheless, the absence of a standardized benchmark has made it difficult to compare and advance these algorithms. To address this, we present the Unsupervised Reinforcement Learning Benchmark (URLB), which comprises two stages: reward-free pre-training followed by adaptation to downstream tasks using extrinsic rewards. Leveraging the DeepMind Control Suite, URLB offers twelve continuous control tasks across three domains for assessment and provides open-source code for eight prominent unsupervised RL methods. Our evaluation reveals that while current baselines show progress, they fail to fully solve the URLB challenges, prompting suggestions for future research directions.

Molecular dynamics simulations were utilized to investigate the microscopic causes of slow relaxation in supercooled Lennard-Jones liquids. These investigations reveal a direct link between the increase in the highest peak of the radial distribution function $g(r)$, the radial force originating from this peak, and density relaxation. By analyzing the free volume available to neighboring pairs for string-like motion, we established a relationship between the surface density of the spherical shell $\rho_{loc}$ surrounding a reference particle at the peak of $g(r)$ and the density relaxation time $\tau_\alpha$. Specifically, $\tau_\alpha \propto \exp(\rho_0/(\rho_0-\rho_{loc}))$, where dynamics diverge at $\rho_0$, a form analogous to the Vogel-Fulcher-Tammann (VFT) equation connecting $\tau_\alpha$ and temperature. This relationship holds effectively within the supercooled regime of the simulated model systems.

Queue length violation probability, representing the tail distribution of queue length, serves as a prevalent statistical quality-of-service (QoS) metric in wireless communications. Analyzing and optimizing this metric is crucial for time-sensitive networking (TSN) and ultra-reliable low-latency communications (URLLC), yet it remains an unresolved challenge. This paper investigates the tail distribution of queue length through a cross-layer design approach for wireless link transmission. Our findings indicate that under a finite average power constraint, the queue length violation probability can be driven to zero utilizing diversity gains; however, with limited receiver sensitivity, it exhibits a linear-decay-rate exponent as predicted by large deviation theory (LDT). Furthermore, we demonstrate that arbitrary-decay-rate queue length tails exist within Rayleigh fading channels under finite average power constraints. We subsequently generalize the sufficient conditions for communication systems falling into these three distinct scenarios. Additionally, we extend these results to analyze wireless link transmission in Nakagami-m fading channels, with numerical approximations validating our theoretical analysis.

We investigate non-equilibrium transport in graphene by applying a large direct current alongside a perpendicular magnetic field. This setup generates a robust in-plane Hall field within the graphene channel, causing Landau levels to tilt spatially. Consequently, the energy of cyclotron orbits in the bulk varies depending on the guiding center's position, allowing for the observation of several significant phenomena. Although Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations are predictably suppressed by the Hall field, new magnetoresistance oscillations appear near the charge neutrality point as a function of the direct current. As carrier density and direct current are varied, two oscillation branches with linear dispersions become apparent; their velocities closely match those of TA and LA phonon modes, suggesting phonon-assisted intra-Landau level transitions between neighboring cyclotron orbits. These findings provide unique avenues for studying non-equilibrium effects in two-dimensional materials and van der Waals heterostructures.

Addressing practical optimization challenges with today's quantum hardware requires hybrid quantum-classical (HQC) methodologies. This paper adapts a multi-cut Benders decomposition (BD) framework—originally designed to leverage multiple master problem (MP) solutions for generating valid cuts—to function as an HQC solver for general mixed-integer linear programming (MILP). The study examines various cut selection criteria and strategies for managing MP size by selectively adding cuts to the BD scheme via quantum computation. The proposed HQC algorithm is tested on the Unit Commitment (UC) problem, a representative optimization task in electrical power systems that could significantly benefit from quantum advancements. Finally, the effectiveness and computational feasibility of this approach are validated using the D-Wave Advantage 4.1 quantum annealer.

Research has examined how the QCD critical point influences the propagation of nonlinear waves using second-order causal dissipative hydrodynamics, where the critical point is integrated into the equation of state along with the scaling behaviors of transport coefficients and thermodynamic response functions. Near this critical point, nonlinear waves experience significant damping, potentially causing the Mach cone effects associated with the away-side jet to vanish. This damping could also amplify fluctuations in elliptic and higher-order flow coefficients. Consequently, the absence of Mach cone signatures and the increased fluctuations in flow harmonics observed in event-by-event analyses may serve as indicators of the critical endpoint.

Coudert et al. (SODA'18) demonstrated that assuming the Strong Exponential-Time Hypothesis, no algorithm running in ${\cal O}(2^{o(k)}n^{2-\epsilon})$ time exists to compute the diameter of $n$-vertex cubic graphs with clique-width at most $k$, for any $\epsilon > 0$. We introduce an algorithm that, given an $n$-vertex $m$-edge graph $G$ along with a $k$-expression, calculates all eccentricities in ${\cal O}(2^{{\cal O}(k)}(n+m)^{1+o(1)})$ time, thereby meeting their conditional lower bound. This approach can be adapted to compute both the Wiener index and the median set of $G$ within the same timeframe. Additionally, we develop a distance-labeling scheme for $n$-vertex $m$-edge graphs with clique-width at most $k$, requiring ${\cal O}(k\log^2{n})$ bits per vertex and constructible in ${\cal O}(k(n+m)\log{n})$ time from a $k$-expression. This scheme matches the label size achieved by Courcelle and Vanicat (DAM 2016) but offers a significantly better dependence on $k$. Consequently, we derive an ${\cal O}(kn^2\log{n})$-time algorithm for All-Pairs Shortest-Paths on $n$-vertex graphs with clique-width at most $k$, partially resolving an open question posed by Kratsch and Nelles (STACS'20).

Stochastic volatility (SV) models, which are nonlinear state-space models increasingly favored for analyzing heteroskedastic time series, face challenges in efficient estimation due to their numerous latent variables, resulting in a scarcity of user-friendly software. To address this gap, we present novel implementations of four SV models available through two new R packages. These packages include several unique, well-documented features. Unlike prior versions, the `stochvol` package now supports linear mean models, heavy-tailed SV, and SV with leverage, while the newly introduced `factorstochvol` package addresses multivariate SV. Both packages provide an intuitive interface using standard R generics alongside specialized methods. Computational performance is enhanced by linking R to C++ to handle intensive calculations. This paper offers a comprehensive discussion on Bayesian SV estimation and demonstrates the capabilities of the new software through multiple examples.

We introduce a divide-and-conquer filtering strategy that breaks down the state variable into low-dimensional parts, enabling the use of conventional particle filtering techniques, and then recursively combines these parts to reconstruct the complete filtering distribution. Unlike competing methods, this approach relies less on the factorization of transition densities and observation likelihoods, allowing it to handle a wider range of models. When benchmarked against state-of-the-art techniques, the proposed method performs comparably in scenarios where those methods work, and it successfully operates in contexts where they fail.

The Einstein Telescope (ET) is proposed as a third-generation gravitational wave (GW) detector with sensitivity ten times superior to that of the second-generation Advanced LIGO (aLIGO), enabling significantly more accurate measurements of GW source parameters. This study demonstrates the enhancement in parameter estimation precision from aLIGO to ET by analyzing measurement errors. Utilizing the frequency-domain TaylorF2 waveform model within the Fisher matrix method—a semi-analytic technique for estimating GW parameter uncertainties—we examined low-mass binary black holes with total masses $M\leq 16 M_{\odot}$ and effective spins ranging from $-0.9$ to $0.9$. Measurement errors for mass and spin were calculated using $10^4$ Monte-Carlo samples randomly distributed across the parameter space. Our results indicate that ET achieves a signal-to-noise ratio approximately 14 times higher than aLIGO for identical sources, yielding error ratios ($\sigma_{\lambda, \rm ET}/\sigma_{\lambda, \rm aLIGO}$) for chirp mass, symmetric mass ratio, and effective spin below 7% across all binaries. Furthermore, for equal-mass binary neutron stars with component masses of 1, 1.4, and 2 $M_{\odot}$, the error ratios for mass and spin parameters drop below 1.5%. Notably, ET significantly reduces the measurement error of tidal deformability ($\tilde{\Lambda}$), with error ratios between 3.6% and 6.1%.

This work introduces new constraints on the existence of general quantum maximum distance separable (QMDS) codes, establishing that for codes with local dimension $D$, distance $d \geq 3$, and length $n$, the inequality $n \leq D^2 + d - 2$ must hold. We derive their weight distributions and provide further limits based on Rains' shadow inequalities. Our primary findings extend existing bounds known for stabilizer QMDS codes and absolutely maximally entangled states, thereby validating the quantum MDS conjecture specifically for distance-three codes. Since the existence of QMDS codes corresponds to highly entangled subspaces where every vector possesses uniform $r$-body marginals and maximal dimension, our methodology applies directly to investigating multipartite entanglement.

This study introduces a decoupled characteristic Galerkin finite element approach for modeling autochemotactic pattern formation driven by growth in self-propelling bacteria. The proposed method employs a modified characteristic Galerkin technique to address the bacterial density equation, whereas the classical finite element procedure is applied to the system governing self-secreted chemical density and polarization dynamics. Under specific regularity assumptions, the convergence of this method is analyzed, and an associated error estimate is derived. Numerical experiments are conducted to validate the theoretical findings, and additionally, several novel wave-type pattern formations are discovered.

Causal relationships within a collection of variables are typically modeled using directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), where certain edge directions can be identified from observational or interventional data. Additional orientations are often achieved by iteratively applying Meek rules. The task of inferring edge orientations based on existing ones, known as Causal Orientation Learning (COL), is a frequent challenge in causal discovery. Since COL problems often need to be solved repeatedly, the direct application of Meek rules can be computationally expensive. Drawing inspiration from these rules, we introduce "Meek functions" designed to accelerate COL solutions. We demonstrate that these functions possess specific desirable properties that facilitate faster rule application. Specifically, we propose a dynamic programming (DP) approach to implement these functions. Furthermore, leveraging this DP method, we establish a lower bound on the number of edges orientable due to intervention and develop a technique to verify if oriented edges conform to a causal DAG. Experimental outcomes indicate that our proposed methods achieve superior performance in terms of execution time compared to prior approaches across various causal discovery tasks.

This study explores the connections between transverse momentum dependent parton distributions (TMDs) and generalized parton distributions (GPDs) using a light-front quark-diquark model inspired by soft wall AdS/QCD. The analysis reveals that many of these relationships maintain similar structures across various models. Specifically, a connection between the Sivers function and the GPD $E_q$ is derived within this framework via a lensing function. Additionally, quark orbital angular momentum is computed and contrasted with findings from other comparable models, with broader implications of the results discussed. The paper also outlines the interrelations among different TMDs within the proposed model.

This paper examines the boomerang uniformity of an infinite family of (locally-APN) power maps, demonstrating that over the finite field $\F_{2^n}$, the uniformity equals $2$ when $n \equiv 0 \pmod 4$ and $4$ when $n \equiv 2 \pmod 4$. Consequently, we establish that for this specific class of power maps, the differential uniformity strictly exceeds the boomerang uniformity.

X-ray binaries have long been considered potential sources of Galactic cosmic rays and neutrinos. Within these binary systems, the compact object serves as a possible site for cosmic-ray acceleration, while high-energy neutrinos may arise from interactions between cosmic rays and the jet, stellar wind, or companion star's atmosphere. This study presents a time-dependent analysis of high-energy neutrinos from X-ray binaries using 7.5 years of muon neutrino data from IceCube alongside X-ray observations. Finding no significant correlation, we establish upper limits on the neutrino fluxes from these sources and compare them with theoretical models.

This work examines the estimation of a regression function based on independent and identically distributed random variables, utilizing the $L_2$ error integrated against the design measure as the performance metric. We define estimates using over-parametrized deep neural networks where all weights are optimized via gradient descent. It is demonstrated that the expected $L_2$ error of these estimates converges to zero at a rate approximately equal to $n^{-1/(1+d)}$, provided the regression function is H\"older smooth with an exponent $p \in [1/2,1]$. Furthermore, for interaction models where the regression function is represented as a sum of H\"older smooth functions, each depending on only $d^*$ of the $d$ design components, the proposed estimates achieve the corresponding convergence rate in $d^*$ dimensions.

Spinoptronics relies heavily on precise control of photonic spin-orbit coupling within devices exhibiting strong optical nonlinearities. These systems could usher in a new era of optoelectronics by intertwining and interfacing the momentum and polarization properties of light with electronics. Nevertheless, electrically manipulating photons is challenging due to their charge neutrality, necessitating intricate electro-optic modulation of the surrounding medium. This study introduces electrically tunable microcavity exciton-polariton resonances operating at room temperature within a Rashba-Dresselhaus spin-orbit coupling environment. We demonstrate that combining various spin-orbit coupling fields with reduced cavity symmetry enables the tunable generation of Berry curvature, a defining feature of quantum geometric phenomena. To achieve this, we developed a novel hybrid photonic architecture featuring a two-dimensional perovskite layer integrated into a microcavity containing nematic liquid crystal. By merging electrical control over strong light-matter coupling with artificial gauge fields, our work successfully bridges spinoptronic devices with electronic systems.

Anomaly detection focuses on spotting deviant instances within a normal data distribution, a task where contrastive learning has proven effective by generating representations that facilitate clear anomaly discrimination. Nevertheless, under semi-supervised conditions where training sets contain unlabeled abnormal samples, existing contrastive methods typically suffer from two main drawbacks: 1) they neglect the comprehensive relationships among training data, causing suboptimal results, and 2) they rely on fine-tuning, which reduces efficiency. To resolve these challenges, this paper introduces a novel Hierarchical Semi-Supervised Contrastive Learning (HSCL) framework designed for contamination-resistant anomaly detection. HSCL hierarchically regulates three complementary relationships—sample-to-sample, sample-to-prototype, and normal-to-abnormal—to enhance the distinction between normal and abnormal samples through a thorough exploration of contaminated data. Furthermore, as an end-to-end learning approach, HSCL efficiently learns discriminative representations without the need for fine-tuning. The method achieves state-of-the-art results across various scenarios, including one-class classification and cross-dataset detection, with extensive ablation studies confirming the contribution of each relationship. The implementation code is accessible at https://github.com/GaoangW/HSCL.

Radical atoms in plasmas have long exhibited nonthermal velocity distributions characterized by significantly heavier tails than those predicted by the Maxwellian distribution. Historically, these distributions were represented using a two-temperature Maxwell model. In this study, I introduce a model grounded in the collisional energy cascade concept, originally explored within granular material physics. This process involves an ensemble of particles receiving energy input at high-energy levels, generating entropy through elastic collisions, and dissipating energy. For radical atoms, energy input arises from molecular dissociation via Franck-Condon energy or charge-exchange collisions with hot ions, while dissipation occurs through wall collisions. I demonstrate that the steady-state velocity distribution resulting from this collisional energy cascade can be approximated by the generalized Mittag-Leffler distribution, a one-parameter extension of the Maxwell distribution. This parameter quantifies the degree of nonthermality and correlates with the ratio of energy dissipation to entropy production. Finally, this model is validated against direct molecular dynamics simulations of a simplified gaseous system featuring energy input and dissipative wall interactions, as well as against observed velocity distributions of light radicals in plasmas.

We examine a matching scenario within a bipartite graph $G=(A\cup B,E)$, where nodes in set $A$ represent agents with partial order preferences over their neighbors, and nodes in set $B$ represent objects without preferences. Since matching size takes precedence over individual preferences, the focus is exclusively on maximum matchings. Any two maximum matchings can be evaluated through a head-to-head election among the agents. The objective is to determine an assignment $M$ that is not dominated by any other, a task known as the popular assignment problem, which extends the well-known popular matching problem.

Popular assignments do not always exist. We present a polynomial-time algorithm that determines the existence of a popular assignment for a given instance and computes one if it exists. For instances lacking a popular assignment, we address the problem of identifying an almost popular assignment, defined as one with the minimal unpopularity margin. We provide an $O^*(|E|^k)$ time algorithm to decide whether an assignment with an unpopularity margin of at most $k$ exists, and we demonstrate its near-optimality by proving the problem is $\mathsf{W}_l[1]$-hard with respect to parameter $k$.

Additionally, we investigate the minimum-cost popular assignment problem involving edge costs, establishing its $\mathsf{NP}$-hardness even when costs are restricted to $\{0,1\}$ and agents hold strict preferences. In contrast, we offer a polynomial-time algorithm for deciding the existence of a popular assignment under specified forced or forbidden edges, a result that remains valid even with partially ordered preferences. Our approaches are combinatorial and rely on LP duality, aiming to locate a suitable witness or dual certificate; if such a certificate cannot be found, we prove that the desired assignment is impossible within $G$.

Thorndike et al. (1975) introduced a novel and physically self-consistent theory for the ice thickness distribution, $g(h)$, that accounts for the dynamic and thermodynamic aggregate properties of the ice pack, establishing the conceptual foundation for sea-ice thickness categories in climate models. However, their approach lacked mathematical closure due to the use of an arbitrary redistribution function $\psi$ for mechanical deformation, a limitation acknowledged by the authors. Toppaladoddi and Wettlaufer (2015) resolved this closure issue by expressing $\psi$ in terms of $g(h)$, reformulating the theory as a Fokker-Planck equation that they solved analytically to quantitatively match observed winter $g(h)$ distributions. In this work, we extend that framework to incorporate open water by deriving a new boundary condition for the Fokker-Planck equation and coupling it with Semtner's (1976) observationally consistent sea-ice growth model to investigate the seasonal evolution of $g(h)$. Our results demonstrate that as ice thins, $g(h)$ shifts from a single-peaked to a double-peaked distribution, aligning with observational data. To elucidate the mechanism behind this transition, we develop a simplified system description using an equivalent Langevin equation and solve the resulting stochastic ordinary differential equation numerically. Furthermore, we solve the Fokker-Planck equation for $g(h)$ across various climatological scenarios to examine the evolution of the open-water fraction.

Over the past few years, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have proven highly effective across various domains, achieving unprecedented accuracy. However, their heavy computational demands have prevented standard CPUs from meeting real-time performance needs. Conversely, Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) have gained significant traction for accelerating CNN inference due to their capacity for custom parallel architectures and superior energy efficiency compared to GPUs. While current FPGA-based accelerators typically employ multiple convolutional layer processors (CLPs) tailored for specific layer subsets, the increasing complexity of CNN models makes optimizing FPGA resources for peak performance increasingly difficult. This paper introduces a novel CNN accelerator and an automated design framework that utilizes metaheuristic algorithms to partition FPGA resources for a Multi-CLP system. Specifically, the proposed tool leverages simulated annealing (SA) and tabu search (TS) to determine the optimal number and configuration of CLPs for a target FPGA, focusing on critical hardware specifications such as digital signal processors, block RAM, and off-chip memory bandwidth. Experimental evaluations using four benchmark CNN architectures on Xilinx VC707 and VC709 boards demonstrate the framework's promise, showing that the SA-/TS-based Multi-CLP approach delivers 1.31x to 2.37x higher throughput than existing state-of-the-art Single- and Multi-CLP methods.

We investigate a neutral exciton confined within a two-dimensional model p-i-n junction composed of MoSe$_2$ and phosphorene, employing a variational method applied to the effective mass Hamiltonian. The non-uniform electric field at the junction inhibits the separation of the center of mass. Our variational solution yields the exciton density in real space and incorporates the kinetic energy arising from exciton localization. For small potential steps across the junction, the exciton occupies a region significantly larger than the junction's nominal width, and its energy remains largely unaffected by the step size. When the exciton localizes within the junction, a dipole moment emerges due to the local electric field; however, this dipole moment scales linearly with the potential step only when the step is sufficiently large. Consequently, the energy's dependence on the step value is non-parabolic. Furthermore, we show that exciton localization does not occur precisely at the junction's center but rather shifts toward the side that is energetically more favorable for the heavier carrier, whether it be the electron or the hole.

This article extends our prior research, specifically the studies on maps from $X_0(N)$ to $\mathbb{P}^2$ (and broader contexts) constructed using modular forms of identical weight, as detailed in Muić (Monatsh. Math. 180, no. 3, 607–629, 2016) and Muić, Kodrnja (Ramanujan J. 55, no. 2, 393–420, 2021). In this brief note, we investigate the variations in the degrees of both the maps and the resulting curves as the underlying modular forms change.

This paper investigates the limiting spectral distribution of large-dimensional sample covariance matrices derived from symmetric random tensors, which consist of $\binom{n}{d}$ distinct products of $d$ variables selected from $n$ independent standardized random variables. We establish optimal sufficient conditions under which this distribution converges to the Marchenko-Pastur law when $d=d(n)$ and $n$ approaches infinity. Specifically, if the variables possess uniformly bounded fourth moments, our conditions simplify to $d^2=o(n)$. The proofs rely on a novel concentration inequality for quadratic forms in symmetric random tensors and a law of large numbers for elementary symmetric random polynomials.

This study introduces two enhancements to the Arrow-Hurwicz (AH) iteration designed to solve the incompressible steady Navier-Stokes equations more efficiently: grad-div stabilization and Anderson acceleration. Originally a classical approach for general saddle point linear systems, the AH method was adapted for Navier-Stokes problems in the 1970s and has recently regained attention. By integrating recent advancements in grad-div stabilization and divergence-free finite element methods with Anderson acceleration for fixed-point iterations, we aim to boost the AH algorithm's convergence. Both analytical and numerical findings indicate that while each technique individually improves convergence, their combined application produces an efficient and effective solver that rivals more traditional methods.

Accurate user interest modeling is vital for personalized news recommendation within online news platforms. While current methods predominantly rely on implicit feedback such as news clicks, this metric can be misleading, as users might click an article due to an engaging title only to find the content unappealing. Consequently, reading dwell time serves as a crucial indicator for modeling user interest, where brief durations often signal low or negative engagement. By integrating this inferred negative feedback, the quality of user modeling can be significantly enhanced. This paper introduces a neural news recommendation framework that incorporates implicit negative feedback by distinguishing between positive and negative clicks based on dwell time. We employ a combination of Transformer and additive attention networks to learn separate user representations from these distinct click types. Furthermore, we calculate both positive and negative click scores derived from the relevance between candidate news and the respective user representations, ultimately aggregating them into a final score. Additionally, we propose an interactive news modeling technique to capture the relationship between news titles and bodies. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves more precise user interest modeling for news recommendation.

Conventional methods for dynamical random matrix models typically focus on eigenvalue trajectories. By drawing an analogy from optics—specifically the duality between Fermat's principle (governing trajectories) and Huygens' principle (governing wavefronts)—we derive Hamilton-Jacobi dynamics for large random matrix ensembles. This framework yields a set of equations that uniformly describe a wide spectrum of random matrix models, encompassing both standard (Hermitian or unitary) cases and strictly non-normal dynamics.
