By applying community detection techniques, we quantify the structural patterns within these inputs. Our experiments indicate that as depth increases, inputs exhibit stronger affinities to other inputs belonging to the same class. We further employ matrix similarity metrics to compare affinity graphs across different layers. First, comparing a layer during training to its converged state reveals that shallower layers converge faster than deeper ones. Second, a pairwise analysis of the full architecture shows that as the network scales, it transitions from a state of moderate inter-layer similarity to one where layers within a block are more similar to each other than to layers in different blocks. Finally, by examining the learned affinity graphs of the network's final convolutional layer, we illustrate how an input's local neighborhood influences its classification.

The NL2Code task involves generating code that fulfills user requirements expressed in natural language, a critical and challenging endeavor that reflects AI-driven programming capabilities. Characterized by its versatility, diversity, and complexity, the task accommodates demands described in various languages, formats, and levels of detail. Motivated by these factors, we conducted this survey to explore how neural networks address NL2Code. We introduce a comprehensive framework capable of encompassing all existing studies in the domain, followed by a detailed analysis of current research within this structure. Additionally, we have developed an online platform to document these findings, tracking both existing and recent advancements in the field. Furthermore, we outline the prevailing challenges and future directions for NL2Code. Ultimately, we hope this survey will catalyze the field's continued evolution.

Numerical simulations face significant, well-documented challenges when dealing with localized nonhomogeneous material properties. These issues are exacerbated by large disparities in length scales, which complicate meshing and preconditioning, and become even more severe if the localized dynamic regions evolve over time. Overlapping domain decomposition methods, which operate by splitting the problem at the continuous level, offer a promising solution due to their implementation simplicity and computational efficiency. Consequently, this study aims to advance the mathematical theory of these methods at both continuous and discrete levels. Regarding the continuous formulation, we present a comprehensive convergence analysis. For the discrete case, we demonstrate that the method can be interpreted as a Gauss-Seidel scheme or a Neumann series approximation, thereby establishing a convergence criterion based on the system's spectral radius. Finally, we offer a spectral scaling argument supported by numerical evidence validating its justification.

We introduce HubbardNet, a deep neural network (DNN) model designed to variationally determine the ground and excited state wavefunctions for both one- and two-dimensional Bose-Hubbard systems. By applying this model to a square lattice containing $M$ sites, we derive the energy spectrum as an analytical function of the on-site Coulomb repulsion ($U$) and total particle number ($N$) through a single training process. This method eliminates the necessity of solving a new Hamiltonian for every distinct $(U,N)$ configuration. Our results demonstrate that the DNN-parametrized solutions align exceptionally well with exact diagonalization outcomes and offer superior computational scaling. These findings indicate that our model holds significant promise for efficiently and accurately computing the exact phase diagrams of many-body lattice Hamiltonians.

Atomically thin van der Waals heterostructures exhibit unique and emerging optoelectronic characteristics. As research into these quantum materials expands, comprehending the fundamental microscopic interfacial coupling mechanisms becomes critically vital. Utilizing multidimensional photoemission spectroscopy, we present a momentum- and layer-resolved perspective on the rapid transfer of electrons and energy between layers in a monolayer-WSe$_2$/graphene system. The dominant transfer mechanisms vary based on the optically prepared state: electron injection from graphene into WSe$_2$ occurs following the photoexcitation of quasi-free hot carriers in graphene, whereas an interfacial Meitner-Auger energy transfer process is established after exciting excitons in WSe$_2$. By analyzing the time-energy-momentum distributions of excited carriers through a rate-equation model, we differentiate these dynamic types and pinpoint the ultrafast conversion of WSe$_2$ excitons into valence band transitions in graphene. Microscopic calculations indicate that interfacial dipole-monopole coupling, which drives the Meitner-Auger energy transfer, prevails over traditional F\"orster- and Dexter-type interactions, aligning with experimental findings. This revealed energy transfer mechanism could facilitate novel device concepts based on hot carriers within van der Waals heterostructures.

We advance the generalization of the road (colouring) problem, originally formulated by Adler-Goodwyn-Weiss and resolved by Trahtman. Ashley-Marcus-Tuncel previously addressed this generalization, solving it for specific cases. We settle two new families of instances: one extends the original road problem using a solution approach consistent with Trahtman's, while the other builds upon a result by Ashley-Marcus-Tuncel through a distinct proof method. Additionally, we establish a universal property concerning the fiber product of specific graph homomorphisms, a finding that may hold independent significance. Finally, we present polynomial-time algorithms for the associated construction and decision tasks.

Modeling post-transcriptional regulation quantitatively remains a significant challenge within systems biology. An effective mechanical framework must accurately capture available spatio-temporal data regarding mRNA expression and protein concentrations to reconstruct continuous fields, necessitating rigorous parameter identification methods. A viable solution involves employing Gaussian processes as prior distributions for latent functions of mRNA and protein levels. This study utilizes a partial differential equation (PDE) mechanical model incorporating linear differential operators and latent functions; because these operators are linear, their physical constraints can be integrated directly into the kernel function. Bayesian inference for both PDE and Gaussian process kernel parameters is performed using Hybrid Monte Carlo methods. Consequently, the spatio-temporal distributions of protein concentration and mRNA expression are reconstructed without the need to explicitly solve the underlying partial differential equations.

We present experimental data quantifying how quantum coherence in the initial state of a qubit contributes to non-equilibrium entropy production when the system is subjected to both coherent driving and dissipation. This experimental validation relies on the precise manipulation of a nitrogen-vacancy defect's spin state within a diamond, supported theoretically by a generalized fluctuation theorem developed to monitor quantum coherence effects. Our findings offer strong evidence that the genuine quantum mechanical components contributing to the thermodynamics of non-equilibrium quantum processes can be accurately identified.

Developing methods to synthesize realistic cell shapes can facilitate the creation of training datasets, thereby enhancing cell tracking and segmentation in biomedical imaging. While deep generative models for cell shape synthesis demand a lightweight and flexible representation, standard voxel-based approaches are ill-suited for high-resolution tasks, and polygon meshes struggle to model topological changes like growth or mitosis. This study introduces the use of signed distance function (SDF) level sets for representing cell shapes. We train a neural network as an implicit representation of SDF values across a 3D+time domain, conditioning the model on a latent code to enable the generation of novel and unseen shape sequences. Our approach is validated both quantitatively and qualitatively using *C. elegans* cells undergoing growth and division, as well as lung cancer cells exhibiting complex filopodial protrusions. The results demonstrate that synthetic cells exhibit shape descriptors similar to real cells and that the model successfully generates topologically plausible sequences of intricate cell shapes in 3D+time.

A core challenge in differential privacy involves generating a privatized data structure from a dataset that supports accurate answers to a range of linear queries. While this issue has been extensively analyzed in static environments, this paper addresses the dynamic scenario, where data items are added or removed over time, necessitating the continuous release of data structures to enable querying at any moment. We introduce black-box methods to convert static differentially private mechanisms into dynamic ones, achieving only a polylogarithmic loss in utility. Notably, our approach provides the first such result for the fully-dynamic setting. For insertion-only scenarios, similar constructions previously existed; however, we enhance their performance specifically for sparse update streams.

We introduce a Modulation of Intensity with Zero Effort (MIEZE) configuration designed for high-resolution neutron spectroscopy, capable of handling momentum transfers up to 3 Å⁻¹, energy transfers up to approximately 20 meV, and achieving energy resolutions in the μeV range using both thermal and cold neutrons. MIEZE offers two key benefits over classical neutron spin-echo techniques. First, it enables the investigation of spin-depolarizing samples or those in strong magnetic fields without signal amplitude or intensity loss, thereby facilitating the study of spin fluctuations in ferromagnets and samples with significant spin-incoherent scattering. Second, multi-analyzer setups can be implemented with relatively minimal effort. Utilizing thermal neutrons extends the validity of the spin-echo approximation to shorter spin-echo times. Consequently, the thermal MIEZE option for extended ranges (TIGER) bridges the gap between classical neutron spin-echo spectroscopy and conventional high-resolution methods such as triple-axis, time-of-flight, and back-scattering techniques. To demonstrate the feasibility of TIGER, we detail an implementation at the RESEDA beamline at FRM II, utilizing an additional velocity selector, polarizer, and analyzer.

Over the past few years, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated exceptional efficacy across various real-world domains. To enhance model capacity, optimizing GNN topology design is crucial alongside the development of aggregation operations. Currently, two primary approaches exist for topology design. The first involves stacking aggregation layers to extract higher-level features, which often leads to performance degradation as depth increases. The second employs multiple aggregation operations within each layer, offering robust and independent local feature extraction but struggling to efficiently capture higher-level information. To leverage the advantages of both methods while mitigating their respective drawbacks, we introduce F$^2$GNN, a novel framework designed from a feature fusion perspective. Specifically, we propose a unified architecture that integrates existing topology designs with feature selection and fusion strategies. Furthermore, we develop a neural architecture search method built upon this framework, utilizing a search space composed of selection and fusion operations guided by an improved differentiable search algorithm. Experiments on eight real-world datasets confirm the effectiveness of F$^2$GNN. Additionally, our results demonstrate that F$^2$GNN successfully enhances model capacity and overcomes limitations of current topology designs, particularly by alleviating the over-smoothing issue through the adaptive utilization of features at different levels.

Neuroscientists typically theorize that the brain utilizes 3D spatial representations across various coordinate frames, such as head-, hand-, or world-centered systems. However, recent developments in reinforcement learning suggest a distinct and potentially superior model for understanding the biological mechanisms of spatial perception and navigation. This study examines reinforcement learning approaches where agents are rewarded for reaching target images without constructing an explicit 3D map. We evaluate whether such representations can support geometrically consistent tasks, specifically interpolating between learned locations by decoding feature vectors. We propose a manually designed representation engineered for high geometric consistency, showing that incorporating information about feature persistence during camera translation (e.g., distant objects remaining visible) enhances performance on these tasks. Crucially, these examples operate without relying on Cartesian (2D) spatial representations. Consequently, non-Cartesian, learned representations offer a significant impetus for neuroscience research seeking alternatives to the traditional "cognitive map."

The electronic configuration of magnetic lanthanide atoms is intriguing from a fundamental standpoint. These atoms possess electrons within a deeply buried, partially filled 4f shell situated beneath a fully occupied 6s shell. Strong relativistic correlations within this structure generate significant magnetic moments and substantial electronic orbital angular momentum. This pronounced angular momentum induces robust anisotropies, meaning orientation-dependent variations, in their mutual interactions. Such long-range molecular anisotropies are essential for proposals involving ultracold lanthanide atoms in spin-based quantum computing, the creation of exotic states in correlated matter, and the emulation of orbitronics used in magnetic technologies. However, short-range interactions and bond formation among these atomic species have not yet been thoroughly characterized, necessitating efficient relativistic computations. In this work, we present the first theoretical determination of the electronic and ro-vibrational states for heavy homonuclear lanthanide molecules, specifically Er₂ and Tm₂, utilizing advanced relativistic methods. Despite the intricate nature of their internal structure, we successfully calculated reliable spin-orbit and correlation-induced energy splittings across the 91 electronic potentials of Er₂ and the 36 potentials of Tm₂, which dissociate into two ground-state atoms. Through tensor analysis, we expanded the interatomic potentials using a sum of seven spin-spin tensor operators to facilitate future investigations. We present the strengths of these tensor operators as functions of internuclear distance and elucidate the relationships among them, which are derived from dispersive long-range interactions. Finally, we computed and analyzed low-lying ro-vibrational energy levels that are spectroscopically relevant using coupled-channels calculations.

Fabry-Perot interferometers have driven a wide array of scientific and technical applications, spanning from high-resolution spectroscopy and metrology to optical filtering and quantum light-matter interfaces. The ability to machine the end facets of optical fibers has facilitated the miniaturization of Fabry-Perot cavities. When integrated with fiber waveguide technology, this enables compact, open devices that offer advantageous scaling, mechanical stability, and a compact mode geometry. Consequently, Fiber Fabry-Perot Cavities (FFPCs) are expanding their utility across diverse fields such as cavity quantum electrodynamics, optomechanics, sensing, and nonlinear optics. This work provides a summary of the current state-of-the-art in FFPC-based devices, outlines their applications, and concludes with anticipated future research directions.

WorkingWiki is a free software extension for the MediaWiki platform that transforms wikis into robust environments for collaborating on publication-ready manuscripts and software initiatives. Created within Jonathan Dushoff's theoretical biology lab at McMaster University, it enables users to jointly tackle any task achievable through UNIX commands that convert textual "source code" into final outputs. Researchers can utilize it to collaborate on programs in languages such as R, Python, C, or others, alongside specialized features designed to streamline LaTeX document creation. This tool leverages the wiki medium to function simultaneously as a collaborative text editor, development environment, version control system, and publishing platform. Its applications are highly adaptable; its processing is governed by customizable makefiles, and its modular architecture is built to facilitate adaptation for various other uses.

We develop a quantum model featuring independent Stokes and anti-Stokes nonlinear interactions to investigate nonclassical correlations within the corresponding photon fields. This study elucidates how laser pump amplitude, the ratio of coupling constants, and the vibrational mode's population and losses influence these correlations. By analyzing the $ g^{(2)} $ intensity cross-correlation function, noise-reduction factor, two-mode principal squeezing variance, logarithmic negativity, non-classicality depth, steering parameter, and Bell parameter concurrently, we gain insight into the interplay between the Stokes and anti-Stokes fields. Furthermore, we identify conditions under which these fields consist exclusively of photon pairs—mirroring twin beams in parametric down-conversion—even when nonzero mean thermal phonon numbers are present.

We introduce a method for decomposing modal formulae within the context of processes exhibiting both nondeterminism and probability, based on Structural Operational Semantics. Our objective is to simplify the satisfaction verification of a formula for a process by checking whether its subprocesses satisfy specific formulae derived from this decomposition. To address the probabilistic behaviors of processes and the corresponding decomposition of their characterizing formulae, we develop a SOS-like framework capable of specifying the behavior of open distribution terms. Through this decomposition approach, we establish (pre)congruence formats for probabilistic bisimilarity, ready similarity, and similarity.

Although adjoint-based shape optimization typically depends on Eulerian flow formulations, Lagrangian particle methods are better suited for oceanographic sedimentation challenges, making their extension necessary. To address coastal erosion, this study conducts shape optimization for fluid dynamics governed by Lagrangian shallow water equations and discretized using smoothed particle hydrodynamics. The obstacle's geometry is optimized against a specific cost function to reduce shoreline wave heights through shape calculus. Various numerical scenarios will be simulated to validate these theoretical findings.

Over the last twenty years, numerous researchers have investigated {\it index $2$} Gauss sums, defined by the condition that the subgroup generated by the characteristic $p$ of the underlying finite field has index $2$ within the unit group of ${\mathbb Z}/m{\mathbb Z}$, where $m$ is the order of the associated multiplicative character. Yang and Xia (2010) provided a complete solution for evaluating these sums, establishing that certain nonzero integral powers of such sums reside in quadratic fields. Conversely, Chowla (1962), McEliece (1974), Evans (1977, 1981), and Aoki (1997, 2004, 2012) examined {\it pure} Gauss sums, for which some nonzero integral powers belong to the rational numbers. This paper investigates Gauss sums whose nonzero integral powers lie in quadratic fields; this category extends the concept of index $2$ Gauss sums and generalizes pure Gauss sums from the rational numbers to quadratic fields.

This study employs first-principles calculations to examine the geometrical stability and electronic properties of the graphdiyne nanosheet (Gdn-NS), confirming structural stability through phonon band structures and cohesive energy. The primary goal is to evaluate how Gdn-NS influences the odor quality of *Mangifera indica* L. (mangoes) across different ripening stages. Furthermore, the adsorption of specific volatiles—ethyl butanoate, myrcene, (E,Z,Z)-1,3,4,8-undecatetraene, and $\gamma$-octalactone—on Gdn-NS is analyzed using key parameters such as adsorption energy, Bader charge transfer, energy gaps, and variations in average energy gaps. The material's sensitivity to volatiles released at various ripening stages is also investigated via density of states spectra. Ultimately, these findings demonstrate that Gdn-NS, utilized through density functional theory, can effectively detect the ripening stage and odor quality of mangoes.

Printed materials remain a significant obstacle for blind, low-vision, and other print-disabled individuals. This study addresses the specific issue of accessibility regarding internal references to citations, footnotes, figures, tables, and equations. Although sighted readers can quickly navigate back and forth to locate referenced material, the linear nature of audio narration used by those with print disabilities makes tracking these references exceptionally difficult. We introduce a vision-based approach to identify referenced content and extract the necessary metadata, which will be utilized in future work to integrate content summaries directly into the audio stream. Testing our method on citations within scientific documents demonstrates its effectiveness on both born-digital and scanned files.

LSTMs and GRUs, which utilize gating mechanisms, are highly effective for modeling sequential data. Within these architectures, the forget gate, originally designed to regulate information flow within the hidden state, has recently been reinterpreted as a proxy for the state's time scale—specifically, the duration the network retains input information. Leveraging this perspective, researchers have proposed various parameter initialization strategies to leverage prior knowledge of temporal dependencies, thereby enhancing learnability. However, this interpretation depends on several unrealistic assumptions, such as the absence of inputs after a specific time point. This study re-examines the forget gate's interpretation under more realistic conditions. First, we extend the existing theory of gated RNNs to accommodate scenarios where inputs are provided sequentially. We then demonstrate that the view of the forget gate as a temporal representation holds true when the gradient of the loss with respect to the state decays exponentially as time progresses backward. Empirical results across multiple tasks confirm that existing RNNs satisfy this gradient condition during the initial training phase, aligning well with previous initialization techniques. Building on this insight, we introduce a method to construct RNNs capable of representing longer time scales than conventional models, which should improve the learnability of long-term sequential data. The efficacy of our approach is validated through experiments using real-world datasets.

Self-gravitating quantum matter appears across diverse cosmological and astrophysical contexts, ranging from the early universe to contemporary boson stars. This phenomenon is predicted by various theories, such as the Peccei-Quinn axion model and UltraLight (ULDM) or Fuzzy (FDM) dark matter frameworks. We examine the dynamical behavior of perturbations affecting the spherically symmetric soliton, which represents the ground state of the Schrödinger-Poisson system shared by these theories. By constructing eigenstates of the Schrödinger equation with the gravitational potential fixed at its ground state value, we demonstrate that these eigenstates qualitatively replicate key features observed in full ULDM simulations, including the soliton's "breathing" mode, the stochastic wandering of its center, and quadrupolar deformations. Furthermore, we show that the time evolution of the gravitational potential and its influence on perturbations can be effectively modeled using time-dependent perturbation theory. When applied to a synthetic ULDM halo, our formalism reveals significant eigenstate mixing, despite the relative stability of the overall density profile. These findings offer a novel analytical method for understanding the evolution of such systems and suggest pathways for more efficient approximate simulations.

This study introduces a multi-physics framework for numerically simulating physical systems characterized by the non-linear interaction of multi-phase reactive fluids and elastoplastic solids under conditions of high strain rates and significant deformation. In this approach, each state of matter is controlled by a unified system of non-linear, inhomogeneous partial differential equations solved concurrently on a single computational grid, eliminating the need for specialized handling of immersed boundaries. To achieve this, the governing equations for both solid mechanics and reactive multiphase fluid dynamics are formulated in an identical mathematical structure and discretized on a regular Cartesian mesh. All phase and material interfaces are modeled as diffuse boundaries. Furthermore, an interface-steepening method is applied at material fronts to preserve sharp interfaces while retaining the system's conservation properties. These algorithms are deployed within a highly parallelized, hierarchically adaptive mesh refinement environment and have been verified and validated against both numerical and experimental benchmarks. The results demonstrate strong alignment with experimental data and superior numerical performance relative to specific existing Eulerian methods, all without compromising conservation laws.

This study examines the spectrum of a discrete Schrödinger operator where the potential derives from a periodic version of the Anderson Model. To achieve this, we investigate the uniform hyperbolicity of the Schrödinger cocycle formed by $SL(2,R)$ transfer matrices. Specifically, for potentials arising from an alternating sequence of random values, we demonstrate that the almost sure spectrum comprises no more than four intervals.

Denoising autoencoder-based pretraining, such as BERT, surpasses autoregressive language modeling approaches by effectively modeling bidirectional contexts. However, BERT's reliance on masking input tokens leads to a neglect of dependencies between masked positions and creates a discrepancy between pretraining and fine-tuning. Addressing these advantages and drawbacks, we introduce XLNet, a generalized autoregressive pretraining method that (1) learns bidirectional contexts by maximizing the expected likelihood across all possible permutations of factorization orders and (2) resolves BERT's limitations through its autoregressive structure. Additionally, XLNet incorporates concepts from Transformer-XL, the leading autoregressive model, into the pretraining process. Empirically, under comparable experimental conditions, XLNet outperforms BERT on 20 tasks, often by significant margins, covering areas such as question answering, natural language inference, sentiment analysis, and document ranking.

Existing Deep Learning (DL) modules in Case-Based Reasoning (CBR) systems frequently fail to fully incorporate available domain knowledge, a gap that the emerging trend of Informed Machine Learning aims to address. This study explores the potential of embedding domain knowledge into Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) utilized for evaluating similarity among semantic graphs in process-oriented CBR applications. We implement this integration through two primary methods: first, by employing a specialized data representation and processing technique that encodes structural information regarding the semantic annotations of graph nodes and edges; and second, by constraining the GNN's message-passing mechanism with knowledge about valid node mappings. The evaluation compares the enhanced GNNs against standard models in terms of output quality and training duration. The findings demonstrate that both integration strategies yield superior quality, reduced training times, or a combination of both benefits in various configurations.

We develop a model to investigate the hydrodynamic interactions of active inclusions within curved biological membranes. This membrane is represented as a two-dimensional layer of highly viscous fluid, encased by external solvents with varying viscosities. The active inclusions are treated as point force dipoles, with the point dipole limit applied along a geodesic on the curved surface to account for orientation changes induced by curvature. We explicitly analyze a spherical membrane to derive an analytic solution for the flow produced by a single inclusion. Additionally, we demonstrate that the flow field exhibits an extra defect of negative index, a consequence of the membrane's topology absent in planar models. Finally, we examine the hydrodynamic interactions between pairs of inclusions across low and high curvature regimes, as well as in scenarios where the external fluid is confined. Our findings suggest that dipole aggregation occurs in curved biological membranes under strong confinement, regardless of whether the curvature is low or high. However, we observe that extremely high curvatures can disrupt this aggregation, even when strong confinement is present.

Let $X$ denote a genus $2$ curve among the $28$ Atkin-Lehner quotients of $X_0(N)$, with the condition that its Jacobian variety $J$ is absolutely simple. We demonstrate that the Shafarevich-Tate group of $J/\mathbb{Q}$ is trivial, thereby confirming the strong BSD conjecture for $J$.

We develop quantum algorithms designed to calculate physical observables for nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs) involving $M$ initial conditions. Leveraging an exact correspondence between nonlinear and linear PDEs established via the level set method, these novel algorithms for nonlinear Hamilton-Jacobi and scalar hyperbolic PDEs achieve a computational cost that remains independent of $M$, regardless of the degree of nonlinearity. Depending on the specific characteristics of the initial data, these methods can offer an exponential advantage in both the PDE's dimension and the accuracy of observable computations. Furthermore, for general nonlinear PDEs, a quantum advantage relative to $M$ becomes feasible as $M$ approaches infinity.

Projecting onto $\ell_p$ norm balls is a fundamental task in statistics and machine learning, but practical algorithms are currently restricted primarily to the cases where $p \in \left\{ 0, 1, 2, \infty \right\}$. This paper presents new, scalable techniques for projecting onto the $\ell_p$ ball for any $p>0$. For $p \geq1$, we resolve the univariate Lagrangian dual using a dual Newton method. For $p<1$, we devise a specific bisection strategy, supported by both theoretical analysis and empirical results demonstrating a negligible duality gap in this non-convex setting. We rigorously evaluate our methods empirically and apply them to large-scale regularized multi-task learning and compressed sensing.

We establish a straightforward analytical line integral formula to calculate the relaxation volume tensor for any interconnected dislocation network. This parameter quantifies the extent to which dislocations influence dimensional shifts and volumetric expansion in materials, underscoring their dual function as both generators of internal strain and agents of plastic deformation. To demonstrate the method's utility, we calculate the relaxation volume of a stacking fault tetrahedron frequently found in fcc metals, determine the volume of a distinctive tetrahedral arrangement composed of (a/2)<111> and a<001> dislocations in bcc metals, and assess the relative impact of extended dislocations on volume relaxation in heavily irradiated tungsten.

Because real-world Facial Expression Recognition (FER) datasets often suffer from ambiguous annotations—stemming from subjective crowdsourcing and the inherent similarity between different expressions—most prior approaches simplify the learning task by converting these uncertain labels into precise one-hot vectors and training models using end-to-end supervised learning. In this paper, we challenge this conventional training framework and argue that weakly supervised strategies, which utilize the original ambiguous annotations directly, offer a superior approach for training FER models.

This paper introduces the concepts of containment and avoidance for subsets within $\mathbb{R}^2$. We subsequently define a novel, continuous, and super-additive extremal function, denoted as $px(n, P)$ for subsets $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$. This function represents the supremum of the Lebesgue measure $\mu_2(S)$ for all open subsets $S \subseteq [0, n]^2$ that are $P$-free. We demonstrate that $px(n, P)$ subsumes the Zarankiewicz problem and, more broadly, the 0-1 matrix extremal function $ex(n, M)$ up to a constant factor. Specifically, we establish a natural mapping between finite subsets $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ and 0-1 matrices $M_P$, proving that $px(n, P) = \Theta(ex(n, M_P))$ for all finite $P$, where the bounding constants rely solely on the inter-point distances within $P$.

Furthermore, we examine bounded infinite subsets $P$ where $px(n, P)$ exhibits growth rates exceeding those of $ex(n, M)$ for any fixed 0-1 matrix $M$. In particular, we prove that $px(n, P) = \Theta(n^2)$ for any open subset $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$. We strengthen this result by showing that if $Q_P$ denotes the set of rational-coordinate points within any open subset $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$, then $px(n, Q_P) = \Theta(n^2)$. Additionally, we derive an extension of the Kővari–Sós–Turán theorem applicable to infinite subsets of $\mathbb{R}^2$. For subsets $P_{s, t, c} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ composed of $t$ horizontal line segments of length $s$, aligned vertically with consecutive segments separated by distance $c$, we establish that $px(n, P_{s, t,c}) = O(s^{\frac{1}{t}}n^{2-\frac{1}{t}})$, with the constant depending on $t$ and $c$. When $t=2$, we confirm that this bound is tight up to a constant factor dependent on $c$.

The literature extensively documents the difficulty of finding deterministic solutions for $\mathcal{NP}$-Hard Combinatorial Optimisation Problems (COP). While efficient non-deterministic approaches have been employed to address this challenge, the emergence of quantum technology suggests a new avenue for overcoming these tractability limits that warrants investigation. This study compares the performance of classical and quantum optimisation algorithms on two standard COPs: the Travelling Salesman Problem (TSP) and the Quadratic Assignment Problem (QAP). Specifically, it contrasts two classical methods—Branch and Bound (BNB) and Simulated Annealing (SA)—against two quantum algorithms: the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) and the Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm (QAOA). These algorithms were executed on both classical hardware and IBM's Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) systems, with specific problem encodings provided for the NISQ architecture. Experimental findings indicate that current classical devices significantly outperform available NISQ hardware, a result that aligns with and extends existing literature. To facilitate a more robust comparison between the two paradigms, this work introduces additional metrics focusing on computational time, feasibility, and solution quality. Results demonstrate that VQE outperforms QAOA across these metrics, likely due to the higher number of operations required by QAOA. Furthermore, the study examines the effect of a new set of basis gates on quantum optimisation techniques, finding no significant improvement. Finally, the paper outlines the limitations of current state-of-the-art IBM NISQ devices and proposes directions for future research.

Positive Lyapunov exponents quantify the asymptotic exponential separation of nearby trajectories within a dynamical system, serving not only as a measure of chaos but also, via the Ruelle inequality, as an upper bound for entropy that effectively gauges the complexity of active networks. We provide numerical evidence that for a broad category of active networks, the sum of their positive Lyapunov exponents is bounded by the sum of the positive exponents of the associated synchronization manifold—a quantity that is theoretically more accessible to compute. This result stems from the characteristic that, in these networks, information generation is driven more by node interactions than by network topology. Leveraging this inequality, we demonstrate how to forecast the behavior of a large-scale active network using data derived solely from a minimal system of two coupled nodes.

This study addresses heat conduction via vibrational modes between Langevin thermostats linked by a central anharmonic device capable of sustaining large temperature gradients and operating out of equilibrium. We introduce a self-consistent Green's function framework to model high-temperature and non-equilibrium transport, deriving an expression for heat current valid up to quartic anharmonicity (fourth-order potential energy). We demonstrate that incorporating quartic terms in the anharmonic potential is essential for accurately capturing thermal expansion and temperature dependence at the leading order of anharmonicity. This approach enables precise and efficient modeling of thermal transport in strongly non-equilibrium regimes that extend beyond perturbation theory.

This study introduces a novel analytical approach to derive an a priori estimate for weak solutions within a coupled steady-state dual-porosity-Navier-Stokes fluid flow model incorporating the Beavers-Joseph-Saffman interface condition. The primary benefit of this methodology is that both the a priori estimate and the existence result hold without reliance on small data assumptions or large viscosity restrictions. Consequently, the global uniqueness of the weak solution is achieved naturally.

We aim to enhance the factual accuracy of descriptions regarding exotic multiquark hadrons by employing the QCD sum rules approach for bound states of strongly interacting constituents. This method involves incorporating exclusively those contributions that may hold relevance for multiquark states into the correlation functions, which serve as the primary component of this framework. To demonstrate this pathway toward our objective, we examine the special case of tetraquark states, which are presumably the least complex.

Topological superconductivity in quasi-one-dimensional systems represents a new state of matter with potential applications in quantum computing. Despite extensive research, the experimental confirmation of this phase remains controversial, largely due to complications arising from magnetic fields, such as induced in-gap states, vortices, and alignment problems. In this work, we introduce a planar semiconductor-superconductor heterostructure as a viable platform to achieve topological superconductivity in a two-dimensional electron gas without requiring an external magnetic field. Instead, time-reversal symmetry is broken by applying a phase bias to the proximitizing superconductors, which can be accomplished using minimal fluxes or bias currents located away from the quasi-one-dimensional channel. This mechanism relies on the interference between the applied phase bias and the phase generated by strong spin-orbit coupling along closed electron paths. We validate this principle through both analytical modeling with a simplified system and numerical simulations of realistic devices. Our results demonstrate a robust topological phase diagram and provide explicit wavefunctions for Majorana zero modes. Furthermore, we address practical experimental challenges, confirming that this approach is feasible with current technological capabilities.

The size distribution of sunspots offers critical insights into how solar magnetic fields are generated and emerge. While prior research has mainly examined the total area of entire groups or individual spots, this study focuses on the internal organization of spot areas within groups. Specifically, we analyze the ratio, $\rm{R}$, between the area of the largest spot ($\rm{A_{big\_spot}}$) in a group and the group's total area ($\rm{A_{group}}$). Drawing on observations from the Kislovodsk, Pulkovo, and Debrecen observatories spanning solar cycles 17 through 24, we determined that when a group's area peaks, the largest spot typically comprises approximately 60% of the total group area. For roughly half of all groups, $\rm{R}$ falls between 50% and 70%. Additionally, $\rm{R}$ varies with $\rm{A_{group}}$, peaking at about 0.65 for groups with an area near $200\mu$Hem before stabilizing around 0.6 for larger groups. These results indicate a scale-invariant emergence pattern, offering an observational constraint on the emergence process. Furthermore, extrapolating these findings to larger sunspot groups suggests implications for the giant unresolved starspot features observed in Doppler images of highly active sun-like stars. Our data implies that such giant features consist of multiple spots, with the largest occupying approximately 55–75% of the total area.

In Multi-Label Text Classification (MLTC), a single sample may be associated with multiple classes, and it is commonly observed that these labels exhibit interdependencies. However, many existing approaches fail to account for these label relationships. This paper introduces a graph attention network-based model designed to capture the attentive dependency structure among labels. By utilizing both a feature matrix and a correlation matrix, the network identifies and explores critical label dependencies to generate specialized classifiers. These classifiers are applied to sentence feature vectors derived from a BiLSTM-based text extraction network, facilitating end-to-end training. The attention mechanism enables the system to assign varying weights to neighboring nodes for each label, thereby learning label dependencies implicitly. The proposed model's effectiveness is validated across five real-world MLTC datasets, where it achieves performance comparable to or superior to previous state-of-the-art methods.

This study benchmarks event-chain Monte Carlo (ECMC) algorithms for tethered hard-disk dipoles in two dimensions, aiming to facilitate their application to water models in molecular simulations. We analyze dipole rotation dynamics by examining the integrated autocorrelation times of polarization. The investigated non-reversible algorithms—straight, reflective, forward, and Newtonian ECMC—are all event-driven, differing solely in their update rules at event instances. Compared to the local reversible Metropolis algorithm, these methods achieve substantial speedups, though notable performance variations exist among the ECMC variants. Specifically, Newtonian ECMC demonstrates particular suitability for resolving the dynamical arrest that has hindered straight ECMC in three-dimensional dipolar models featuring Coulomb interactions.

Recent research has demonstrated that compiling functional programs into dense, serialized memory formats for recursive algebraic datatypes can produce substantial constant-factor performance gains in sequential contexts. However, maximizing data density inherently constrains parallel processing, creating a trade-off between the two. This paper argues that a practical, structured compromise can be achieved. We introduce Parallel Gibbon, a compiler that leverages both dense data representations and parallelism. We formalize the semantics of the parallel location calculus that supports this new implementation approach and prove its type safety. Furthermore, Parallel Gibbon outperforms existing compilers for purely functional programs utilizing recursive algebraic datatypes—such as those performing abstract-syntax-tree traversals common in compilers—in terms of parallel performance.

We demonstrate that compounds exhibiting $I$4/$mcm$ crystalline symmetry support three-dimensional semi-Dirac fermions. In contrast to established two-dimensional semi-Dirac points, the degeneracy of these three-dimensional counterparts remains intact even under spin-orbit coupling, shielded by nonsymmorphic symmetry—specifically, a screw rotation within the $a-b$ plane and a translation along the $c$ axis. This symmetry occurs in tetragonal perovskite oxides and can be achieved in thin films through epitaxial strain inducing $a^0a^0c^-$-type octahedral rotations. Notably, breaking time-reversal symmetry causes two pairs of Weyl points to emerge from the semi-Dirac points inside the Brillouin zone, while further lattice distortion amplifies the intrinsic anomalous Hall effect. Consequently, the capacity to modulate the Berry phase via epitaxial strain holds promise for advanced oxide-based electronic applications.

It is a well-established fact that translating songs and poems often disrupts rhythm and rhyme, leading to potential losses in semantic meaning. The *Bhagavad Gita*, an ancient Hindu philosophical scripture originally composed in Sanskrit, recounts a dialogue between Lord Krishna and Arjuna before the Mahabharata war. As a central sacred text and a primary component of the Vedic corpus, the *Gita* has attracted significant interest from Western scholars over the past two centuries, resulting in numerous translations into various languages. Despite this volume of work, there remains a scarcity of research validating the quality of these English versions. Recent advancements in deep learning-powered language models have not only facilitated translation but also enhanced the understanding of text through semantic and sentiment analysis. Motivated by these developments, our study presents a framework that evaluates selected Sanskrit-to-English translations of the *Bhagavad Gita* using semantic and sentiment analyses. We fine-tuned the state-of-the-art BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) model using a hand-labeled sentiment dataset. Our analysis covers specific chapters and verses across different translations. The results indicate that while the vocabulary and stylistic choices vary significantly among the translations, both sentiment analysis and semantic similarity demonstrate that the core message remains largely consistent.

This study addresses the sequential binary hypothesis testing problem within an adversarial setting utilizing data from $s$ sensors, where a subset of $c$ sensors is compromised and their observations can be arbitrarily manipulated. The system's performance is evaluated using the asymptotic Average Sample Number (ASN) needed to achieve a specific error probability threshold. The scenario is modeled as a game between a detector seeking to optimize performance and an adversary aiming to degrade it. We introduce a voting hypothesis testing rule alongside a flip attack strategy, demonstrating that they constitute an equilibrium pair for this game. Furthermore, we analyze the detection scheme's performance when the number of compromised sensors is unknown and validate our findings through simulations.

The Einasto profile is widely used to describe the density distribution of dark matter haloes, yet comprehensive dynamical analyses remain scarce due to the limited number of analytically calculable properties. This study aims to systematically examine the photometric and dynamical characteristics of the entire family of Einasto models across all parameter values. Employing the SpheCow numerical code, we investigated how key properties vary with the Einasto index ($n$), analyzing both isotropic configurations and radially anisotropic models utilizing the Osipkov-Merritt formalism. Our results indicate that models with $n < 0.5$ possess formal distribution functions that become negative in certain regions of phase space, rendering them physically unsupported by either isotropic or Osipkov-Merritt orbital structures. Conversely, models with $n \geq 0.5$ are dynamically viable under isotropic conditions or via Osipkov-Merritt anisotropy, provided the anisotropy radius exceeds a specific critical threshold. Since this critical radius decreases as $n$ increases, less centrally concentrated models permit greater degrees of radial anisotropy. In conclusion, the structural and dynamical study of galaxies and dark matter haloes should extend beyond purely analytical approaches; numerical tools like SpheCow enable the systematic investigation of a broader range of models, including various extensions of the Einasto profile.

Graph learning focuses on capturing intricate node relationships and the topological structures inherent in real-world graphs, such as social, academic, and e-commerce networks. Unlike traditional tabular data where nodes exist in non-Euclidean spaces, these graphs possess unique characteristics and rich information that facilitate deep exploration. Evolving from graph theory to data mining and now leveraging representation learning, the field has achieved remarkable success across diverse domains, including text, image, chemistry, and biology. Given its extensive practical potential, graph learning has emerged as a vital and promising frontier in machine learning, attracting thousands of studies and growing academic interest. Consequently, surveying valuable prior work is crucial. While previous researchers have produced impressive surveys, they often fail to logically connect related objectives, methods, and applications, or adequately address current scenarios and challenges driven by the field's rapid expansion.

In our previous work \cite{yu2021Finiteness}, we demonstrated that the planar four-vortex problem possesses only a finite number of stationary configurations, which include equilibria, rigidly translating states, relative equilibria, and collapse configurations. However, at that time, we could only prove the finiteness of collapse configurations under the condition that a specific collapse constant was prescribed. By advancing the analytical methods of Albouy-Kaloshin and Hampton-Moeckel to examine singularities, this paper establishes that the set of collapse configurations in the four-vortex problem is indeed finite in an absolute sense. This finding is particularly surprising, as the $N$-vortex problem admits infinitely many collapse configurations for both $N=3$ and $N=5$. Furthermore, we derive improved upper bounds for these collapse configurations compared to those presented in \cite{yu2021Finiteness}.

Sound Event Localization and Detection (SELD) involves identifying independent or overlapping sound sources, classifying them, and estimating their spatial directions during activity. Recently, neural networks have become the dominant approach for SELD, with convolutional recurrent neural networks (CRNNs) being particularly prominent. This paper describes a system entered into the Detection and Classification of Acoustic Scenes and Events 2020 Challenge, Task 3. The proposed algorithm utilizes a CRNN with rectangular filters designed to capture significant spectral features relevant to the task. To enhance performance scores and generalize the system to unseen data, the training dataset was expanded through data augmentation. Specifically, channel rotations and reflections in the First Order Ambisonic domain were employed; this technique preserves the physical relationships between channels while improving Direction of Arrival labels. Evaluation on the development dataset demonstrates that the proposed system surpasses baseline results, significantly reducing the Error Rate and increasing the F-score for location-aware detection.

Speech separation has proven effective for recognizing speech from multiple talkers. However, ad hoc microphone array setups, characterized by spatially distributed and asynchronous microphones with unknown geometry and count, introduce additional complexities. Previous research indicates that neural networks employing a spatial-temporal interleaving structure can efficiently leverage multi-channel signals from such arrays. This paper extends that approach to continuous speech separation. To facilitate separation for real-world continuous recordings, several techniques are introduced. First, a transformer-based network is utilized for spatio-temporal modeling of ad hoc array signals. Furthermore, two methods are proposed to address speech duplication issues that are particularly pronounced during single-talker segments in ad hoc scenarios. The first method involves device distortion simulation to reduce acoustic mismatches between simulated training data and actual recordings. The second method employs speaker counting to identify single-speaker segments and merge output channels accordingly. Experiments on AdHoc-LibiCSS, a new dataset comprising continuous recordings of concatenated LibriSpeech utterances captured by various devices, demonstrate that the proposed separation method significantly enhances automatic speech recognition (ASR) accuracy for overlapped speech while causing minimal performance degradation in single-talker segments.

We report the identification of 2013 VZ70, the first confirmed horseshoe coorbital companion of Saturn. Following 4.5 years of observation by the Outer Solar System Origins Survey (OSSOS), its orbit was precisely determined to show it is currently in horseshoe libration with the planet. This coorbital configuration will persist for at least thousands of years but is expected to terminate approximately 10,000 years from now. Consequently, 2013 VZ70 joins the known population of "transient coorbitals" around giant planets, marking the first prograde example for Saturn, whereas temporary retrograde coorbitals have previously been identified for both Jupiter and Saturn. We also introduce a theoretical steady-state model describing the scattering population of trans-Neptunian objects within the giant planet region (2–34 au), encompassing the temporary coorbital groups of all four giant planets. By subjecting this model to observational biases through survey simulations, we compare its predictions against actual detections from well-characterized outer Solar System surveys. Although the observed count of coorbitals relative to the scattering population exceeds model predictions, we demonstrate that the relative numbers of observed transient coorbitals across each giant planet align with a trans-Neptunian source.

Using topological current theory, we investigate the internal topological structure of defects within two-dimensional crystals. Our findings identify two distinct elementary point defect currents: one associated with dislocations and the other with disclinations. We further examine the topological quantization and evolution of these defects in 2D crystals. Finally, we compare our theoretical framework with Brownian-dynamics simulations of 2D Yukawa systems.

This paper presents an elementary derivation of the parametric solution to Euler and Elkies' equation, xyz(x+y+z) = a. Furthermore, we demonstrate that there exist infinitely many parametric solutions within Euler's and Elkies's family.

The intriguing connections between emerging physical phenomena, such as superconductivity, and the orbital, charge, and spin degrees of freedom of $3d$ electrons in transition metal compounds are explored here. We demonstrate the successful manipulation of superconductivity in the spinel oxide Li$_{1\pm x}$Ti$_2$O$_{4-\delta}$ (LTO) through ionic liquid gating. This approach establishes a dome-shaped superconducting phase diagram, revealing two insulating phases in both heavily electron-doped and hole-doped regions. The superconductor-insulator transition (SIT) observed in the hole-doping regime is attributed to the depletion of Ti valence electrons. Conversely, in the electron-doping regime, LTO displays an unexpected SIT rather than metallic behavior, despite an increased carrier density. Additionally, thermal hysteresis in the normal-state resistance curve indicates a first-order phase transition. By comparing transport and structural data of LTO with the spinel oxide superconductor MgTi$_2$O$_4$ and utilizing first-principles calculations to analyze the electronic structure, we hypothesize that the SIT and thermal hysteresis arise from enhanced $3d$ electron correlations and orbital ordering. A deeper understanding of the complex interplay between superconductivity and orbital ordering is expected to aid in uncovering the mechanisms behind unconventional superconducting pairing.

Modern implementations of the Maxwell-demon thought experiment utilize information-driven engines to correct thermal fluctuations. We present a straightforward design featuring a heavy colloidal particle suspended in water by an optical trap. By employing a precisely engineered feedback loop, our experimental "information ratchet" harnesses advantageous upward fluctuations to raise a weight against gravity, thereby storing potential energy without performing external work. Optimizing this ratchet's design for performance using a simple theoretical framework reveals that the rates of work storage and directed motion velocity are constrained solely by the engine's physical parameters: particle size, ratchet spring stiffness, motion-induced friction, and the medium's temperature. Significantly, since performance plateaus as observation frequency increases, the measurement process itself does not limit efficiency. Furthermore, the achieved power output and velocity exceed those of previously reported engines by at least an order of magnitude.
This paper illustrates the McKay quivers corresponding to groups of order 2, order 5, and order $2^3$ using diagrams of yinyang, wuxing, and bagua, respectively.

This Snowmass 2021 Topical Report for the Underground Facilities and Infrastructure Frontier examines synergies in research conducted at underground facilities, highlighting a wide array of scientific and engineering endeavors that extend beyond the physics-centric activities covered in other reports. These diverse research domains encompass nuclear astrophysics, geology, geoengineering, gravitational wave detection, biology, and potentially quantum information science in the near future. The report surveys these non-physics research areas that align with the goals of underground facilities and infrastructure. Given the extensive scope of these research objectives, a complete coverage is often impractical; therefore, introductory summaries are followed by references to key surveys and documents. The text further explores the shared, overlapping, and distinct infrastructure requirements of each field relative to the broader underground research community. Finally, any potential conflicts regarding usage type, site selection, or duration are explicitly identified.

We examine Einstein-Maxwell-Dilaton theory in $(2+1)$-dimensions, utilizing a dilatonic coupling $f(\phi) = \exp (-2\alpha \phi)$ between the scalar field and the Maxwell invariant to derive new exact rotating black hole solutions. The dilatonic parameter $\alpha$ influences the metric function, thereby altering the black hole's rotation characteristics, mass, and thermodynamic behavior. Our entropy calculations reveal that it remains strictly positive; furthermore, these dilatonic black holes can possess greater entropy than the standard BTZ black hole. Depending on specific parameters, a dilatonic BTZ-like black hole may be thermodynamically favored over the BTZ black hole, which corresponds to the case where $\alpha=0$.

Following the successful flight of the Ingenuity Mars helicopter, aerial exploration of Martian terrain has emerged as a key research focus. While current autonomous systems perform well in open environments, future missions aim to investigate caves and ancient lava tubes in the ongoing search for extraterrestrial life. This paper introduces an autonomous exploration mission utilizing a modified frontier approach, integrated collision avoidance, and risk-aware planning, specifically tailored for a custom-designed Mars Coaxial Quadrotor (MCQ) operating within a simulated Martian lava tube. A primary innovation is the system's ability to rapidly explore local areas and intelligently reposition globally when encountering dead ends, thereby optimizing battery consumption and maximizing explored volume. The proposed three-layer cost-based global re-positioning strategy facilitates quick redirection to previously partially observed areas to uncover new sections of the lava tube. The fully simulated mission accounts for Martian physical conditions, including low gravity, low surface pressure, and a thin atmosphere, demonstrating the scheme's effectiveness in challenging subterranean environments. Finally, the exploration-planning framework is validated through simulation by comparing its performance against a graph-based exploration planner.

This study introduces models aimed at quantifying how stellar activity influences exoplanet transit spectroscopy and atmospheric analysis across low (R = 100) and high (R = 100,000) spectral resolutions. We examine three model categories representing distinct planetary systems: a hot Jupiter orbiting an early-K star (HD 189733 b), a mini-Neptune around an early-M dwarf (K2-18 b), and terrestrial planets near a late M dwarf (TRAPPIST-1). By mapping photospheres with temperature and radial velocity data and integrating specific intensity stellar models, we generate transit spectra that account for stellar contamination, the Rossiter-McLaughlin effect (RME), and center-to-limb variations (CLV). Our findings indicate that at low resolution, water features in planets orbiting later-type stars often become indistinguishable from contamination; notably, various distributions of unocculted active regions can mimic planetary signals in late M dwarfs with comparable amplitudes. Consequently, characterizing atmospheres around late-type stars may remain degenerate with stellar activity unless active region parameters are constrained by supplementary data. For early-K stars, stellar contamination primarily appears as an optical slope resembling Rayleigh scattering. Across all scenarios, contamination introduces offsets in measured planetary radii. However, at high resolution, we demonstrate the ability to distinguish the origins of H2O and CO detection signals and resolve low-resolution degeneracies, provided there is sufficient radial velocity variation in the planet during transit and proper corrections for RME and CLV. Thus, high-resolution spectroscopy offers a pathway to mitigate stellar contamination issues in suitable systems.

To address the continuous COVID-19 crisis, we introduce a robust deep learning framework designed to detect both proper and improper mask usage in real-time video feeds. We developed and assessed two distinct methodologies for this purpose. The initial method combines a pre-trained face detector with a mask-wearing classifier trained on an extensive synthetic dataset. The second method employs a cutting-edge object detection network to simultaneously localize and classify faces in a single pass, fine-tuned using a limited set of labeled real-world images. The first pipeline reached 99.97% test accuracy on the synthetic data while maintaining 6 FPS on video inputs. Conversely, the second pipeline achieved an mAP(0.5) of 89% on real-world images with a processing speed of 52 FPS. We conclude that if a dataset with bounding-box annotations can be assembled, object detection architectures like YOLO and SSD are the optimal choice for this task, offering superior inference speeds and satisfactory performance on key metrics.

This work constructs the homotopy theory of semisimplicial sets using constructive methods that avoid point-set topology, thereby establishing a constructive model for $\omega$-groupoids. While much of the material is well-known folklore, the author provides novel constructive proofs for specific results: namely, that the unit of the free simplicial set adjunction consists of weak equivalences, and that the geometric and cartesian products of fibrant semisimplicial sets are weakly equivalent. The framework is subsequently extended to marked semisimplicial sets to create a constructive model for $(\omega, 1)$-categories.

Over the last decade, the remarkable achievements of deep neural networks (DNNs) have stemmed primarily from increased computational scale rather than insights drawn from biological intelligence. This study investigates whether these trends have similarly led to improved alignment with the visual strategies humans employ for object recognition. We examine two distinct yet related aspects of these strategies: the location of salient visual features within images and the mechanisms by which these features are utilized for categorization. By evaluating 84 DNNs trained on ImageNet against three independent datasets that measure human visual strategies, we identify a systematic trade-off between categorization accuracy and alignment with human perception. Specifically, as state-of-the-art DNNs achieve higher accuracy, they become progressively less aligned with human visual processes. To address this divergence, we introduce the "neural harmonizer," a general-purpose training procedure that simultaneously aligns DNN and human visual strategies while enhancing categorization performance. Our findings represent the first evidence that the scaling laws currently guiding DNN design are resulting in models that are poorer representations of human vision. We have made our code and data available at https://serre-lab.github.io/Harmonization to assist the community in developing more human-like DNNs.

VANET solutions typically employ aggregated graph representations to model vehicle interactions and utilize complex network measures to quantify topological features. However, this approach overlooks temporal dynamics between vehicles, leading to information loss or unrealistic behavioral modeling. To address this, the proposed work integrates both temporal graphs and temporal measures for VANET applications. Validating the model's viability involves a comparative analysis using five distinct real-world datasets, which demonstrates that aggregated modeling fails to effectively capture temporal network aspects. Subsequently, a network evaluation via simulation assesses the impact of temporal modeling on Road Side Unit (RSU) deployment. First, a solution based on the proposed temporal model is compared against a greedy algorithm utilizing an aggregated model for RSU placement; in a scenario with 70 RSUs, the temporal model achieves 77% coverage compared to 65% for the aggregated model. Second, the study evaluates aggregated and temporal measures as features within a genetic algorithm. The approach incorporating temporal betweenness yields superior results with 90% coverage, surpassing the 61% achieved by the aggregated measure in the same scenario.

Machine learning has become firmly established in experimental particle physics, enabling novel approaches to analyzing detector data. Enhancing the identification of signals within particle observatories is a critical data processing challenge that these methods could address. This study investigates the advantages of applying specialized machine learning techniques to classify signals in dual-phase noble gas time projection chambers. We present a comprehensive methodology, ranging from exploratory data analysis utilizing Gaussian mixture models and feature importance ranking to the development of predictive models based on standard neural networks and random forests. These models were validated against unlabelled simulated data from the LZ experiment, serving as a proxy for real-world data. Our predictive models achieved a global classification accuracy exceeding 99.0%, surpassing the performance of conventional algorithms tested on the same dataset. Additionally, the clustering analysis identified anomalies stemming from miscalculated signal properties, demonstrating the methodology's utility for data monitoring.

Air-Cherenkov telescopes have identified pulsations from an increasing number of Fermi-detected pulsars at energies exceeding 50 GeV. Notable sources include the Crab, Vela, PSR B1706-44, and Geminga, with the Crab and Vela exhibiting pulsed emission above 1 TeV. In certain instances, very-high-energy (VHE) emission appears as a high-energy extension of Fermi spectra, whereas in others, distinct higher-energy spectral components suggest the presence of separate emission mechanisms. We present findings from broad-band spectral modeling utilizing global magnetosphere fields and multiple emission processes, including synchro-curvature (SC) and inverse Compton scattered (ICS) radiation from accelerated primary particles, alongside synchrotron-self Compton (SSC) emission from lower-energy pairs. Our models predict three distinct VHE components: SC emission from primaries with tails extending to 100 GeV, SSC emission from pairs reaching several TeV, and ICS emission from primary particles accelerated in the current sheet, scattering pair synchrotron radiation at energies beyond 10 TeV. Our analysis suggests that H.E.S.S.-II and MAGIC have observed the high-energy tail of the primary SC component responsible for the Fermi spectrum in Vela, Geminga, and PSR B1706-44. Furthermore, we argue that H.E.S.S. has detected the ICS component peaking above 10 TeV from Vela. Future observations with HAWC and CTA could detect this emission component from the Crab and other pulsars, providing a direct measurement of maximum particle energies within pulsars.

The Bayesian statistical framework employs probability to quantify uncertainty regarding the processes that produce observed data. In this approach, probability distributions define the analysis, utilizing probabilistic rules to convert prior distributions for unknowns—including parameters, latent variables, and models—into posterior distributions once data is observed. Performing Bayesian analysis necessitates calculating integrals involving these distributions. Consequently, Bayesian computation focuses on evaluating such integrals, particularly in scenarios where analytical solutions are unavailable. This paper offers a chronological overview of Bayesian computational methods spanning the last two and a half centuries. Starting with the one-dimensional integral addressed by Bayes in 1763 and extending to modern challenges involving millions of unknowns, the text unifies computational problems within a single framework and describes all methods using consistent notation. The primary objective is to assist new researchers, as well as others interested in applying Bayesian methods to empirical research, in navigating the wide array of available computational techniques, understanding the specific contexts and reasons for their utility, and recognizing the inherent connections between them.

In contrast to telephone operators, who pay termination fees to connect to users on other networks, Internet Content Providers (CPs) currently do not compensate Internet Service Providers (ISPs) for the users they reach. Although this cross-subsidization has fostered content innovation at the network's edge, it diminishes access ISPs' incentives to invest in expanding capacity. Amidst criticisms of potential termination charges during the net neutrality debate, we propose a model allowing CPs to voluntarily subsidize the usage-based fees their traffic generates for end-users. By modeling regulated subsidization competition under a neutral network framework, we demonstrate that deregulating such subsidies could boost an access ISP's utilization and revenue, thereby reinforcing investment incentives. While this competition may disadvantage some CPs, our analysis indicates that the primary driver is high access prices rather than the presence of subsidies itself. Our findings suggest that subsidization competition will enhance the competitiveness and welfare of the Internet content market, though regulators may need to oversee access pricing if the ISP market lacks sufficient competition. Ultimately, we envision subsidization competition as a viable model for the future Internet.

This research investigates a distributed machine learning scenario involving an edge server and multiple agents within a wireless network, aiming to minimize a global function composed of the agents' individual loss functions through analog over-the-air model training. In this process, each agent simultaneously transmits its local gradient, modulated onto specific waveforms, to the edge server. The server then decodes a noisy, aggregated gradient from the received analog signal—distorted by channel fading and interference—to update the global model and distribute the updated parameters back to the agents for subsequent local computations. Given that electromagnetic interference typically follows a heavy-tailed distribution, we model its statistics using the $\alpha$-stable distribution. Consequently, the global gradient exhibits infinite variance, rendering conventional convergence analysis techniques, which depend on the existence of second-order moments, inapplicable. To address this, we develop a novel analytical framework to determine both the convergence rate and generalization error of the algorithm. Our findings demonstrate a dual impact of interference on the training process: negatively, heavy-tailed noise decelerates convergence, with heavier tails resulting in slower algorithmic performance; positively, however, such noise can enhance the generalization capability of the trained model, where heavier tails correlate with improved generalization. This counterintuitive result suggests that the traditional view of interference as purely detrimental to edge learning systems is obsolete, advocating instead for new strategies that leverage rather than merely suppress interference to optimize machine learning in wireless networks.

This research conducts a linear analysis of a turbulent methane-air jet flame to forecast how the reacting flow responds to upstream acoustic actuation. Within a linearized framework, capturing heat release fluctuations is essential for studying thermoacoustic instabilities and flame noise. Distinct from prior work, this study employs an active flame approach, which incorporates heat release oscillations induced by acoustic fluctuations. Implementing this approach linearly requires linearizing a combustion model; however, linearizing Large Eddy Simulation (LES) and Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) models creates closure issues, rendering them difficult to apply in this context. Conversely, Reynolds-averaged Navier Stokes (RANS) models effectively avoid these problems, making them ideal for this application. These RANS models were linearized around the temporal mean flow of the turbulent jet, which was derived using LES. An a priori analysis identified the linearized RANS-Eddy Break Up (EBU) model as the most appropriate choice for the specific setup, demonstrating high accuracy in reproducing LES-derived reaction rate fluctuations. Subsequently, the linearized governing equations, including the linearized EBU model for reaction rates, were solved for incoming acoustic perturbations. The resulting response modes indicate that reaction rate oscillations stem from Kelvin-Helmholtz vortex rings disturbing the jet flame. These findings align well with LES simulations regarding the mode shapes of both velocity and reaction rate fluctuations.

Image colorization is a recognized challenge within computer vision, primarily because the task is inherently ill-posed. Although researchers have developed various methods to automate this pipeline, the resulting images often appear unrealistic due to insufficient conditioning. This study proposes integrating textual descriptions as an auxiliary condition alongside the grayscale input to enhance colorization fidelity. To our knowledge, this represents one of the initial efforts to incorporate text-based conditioning into the colorization workflow. We introduce a novel deep network that accepts two inputs—the grayscale image and its corresponding encoded text—to predict the appropriate color gamut. Since textual descriptions contain information about object colors within the scene, the text encoding significantly improves the quality of the predicted hues. Our model was evaluated using various metrics and demonstrated superior performance compared to state-of-the-art colorization algorithms, both quantitatively and qualitatively.

We calculate the operator product expansion (OPE) coefficient $c_{112}$ for the operators $\mathcal{O}_1\sim\varphi$ and $\mathcal{O}_2\sim\varphi^2$ within the three-dimensional $\mathrm{O}(N)$ universality class and the Ising class ($N=1$), spanning dimensions $2 \leq d \leq 4$, by employing the nonperturbative functional renormalization group (FRG) under the Blaizot-M\'endez-Galain-Wschebor approximation. Our findings align exceptionally well with available exact solutions, conformal bootstrap estimates, and Monte-Carlo simulations, while the FRG method uniquely enables the determination of values across the entire investigated range of $d$ and $N$.

Lifelong object re-identification incrementally learns from a continuous stream of re-identification tasks, aiming to develop a universal representation that generalizes to both seen and previously unseen tasks. The primary challenge lies in ensuring the model can handle novel identities at inference time. To tackle this, we employ continual meta metric learning within the context of lifelong object re-identification. To mitigate catastrophic forgetting of prior tasks, we utilize knowledge distillation while investigating the impact of positive and negative pairs. Observing an antagonistic relationship between distillation and metric losses, we propose excluding positive pairs from the distillation process to enhance the robustness of model updates. Our proposed method, Distillation without Positive Pairs (DwoPP), is evaluated through extensive intra-domain experiments on person and vehicle re-identification datasets, as well as inter-domain experiments on the LReID benchmark. Results indicate that DwoPP significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art methods. The source code is available at: https://github.com/wangkai930418/DwoPP_code

This research investigates inference within linear models where the key parameter is a high-dimensional matrix. Specifically, we examine scenarios in which this matrix is well-approximated by a "spiked low-rank matrix," characterized by a rank that increases slowly relative to its dimensions and nonzero singular values that tend toward infinity. We demonstrate that this framework encompasses a wide range of latent-variable models, including applications in matrix completion, factor analysis, varying coefficient models, principal components analysis with missing data, and heterogeneous treatment effects.
