For inference, we introduce a novel "rotation-debiasing" technique designed for product parameters initially estimated via nuclear norm penalization. We establish general high-level results showing that our procedure yields asymptotically normal estimators. Furthermore, we outline specific low-level conditions that allow us to validate these high-level assumptions within a treatment effects context.

We introduce a correlated \textit{and} gate designed to propagate uncertainty and dependency through Boolean functions, as any such function can be decomposed into \textit{and} and \textit{not} operations. We posit that the \textit{and} gate constitutes a bivariate copula family, capable of generating bivariate Bernoulli random variables based on specified marginal probabilities and a target Pearson correlation coefficient. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this copula framework facilitates the propagation of uncertainty—represented as event probabilities, probability intervals, and probability boxes—even when dependency information is incomplete or entirely absent, expressed only as a correlation interval. These findings extend prior work by Fr\'echet regarding the conjunction of events with unknown dependencies. Finally, we illustrate an application involving uncertainty propagation through a fault tree for a pressure tank, accompanied by an open-source Julia library for executing uncertainty logic.

Let $G$ be a connected graph, where the eccentricity of a path $P$, denoted $\text{ecc}_G(P)$, represents the greatest distance from $P$ to any vertex in $G$. The \textsc{Central path} (CP) problem seeks a path with the minimum such eccentricity. Originally introduced by Cockayne et al. in 1981 to explore various graph centrality measures, CP admits a linear-time solution in trees but is NP-hard for numerous graph families, including chordal bipartite graphs, planar 3-connected graphs, and split graphs.

This work examines the path eccentricity of a connected graph $G$ as a parameter, defining $\text{pe}(G)$ as the eccentricity value of a central path $P$ in $G$. We establish tight upper bounds for $\text{pe}(G)$ across several graph classes, proving that $\text{pe}(G) \leq 1$ for biconvex graphs and $\text{pe}(G) \leq 2$ for bipartite convex graphs, alongside linear-time algorithms to identify these paths. Additionally, by analyzing longest paths, we derive tight upper bounds for $\text{pe}(G)$ in general graphs and $k$-connected graphs.

Finally, we explore the relationship between central paths and longest paths. We demonstrate that on trees and bipartite permutation graphs, a longest path is necessarily a central path. However, for superclasses of these graph types, we provide counterexamples showing this property does not always hold.

Artificial intelligence and semantic technologies are advancing and finding applications across diverse research fields, notably within education. Higher Education institutions aim to enhance student academic outcomes, making early intervention for at-risk students and a well-structured curriculum essential for success. While previous studies relied on traditional machine learning models to forecast student performance, this research addresses limitations in existing semantic technologies for Computer Science curricula, specifically regarding the accuracy and ambiguity of concept and course representation found in prior systematic reviews. To address these gaps, the study developed three implementations: predicting student performance based on previous semester marks, modeling course representations semantically to compute similarity, and identifying prerequisites between similar courses. For performance prediction, a combination of Genetic Algorithms and Long-Short Term Memory (LSTM) was utilized on a dataset from a Brazilian university comprising 248,730 records. In similarity measurement, BERT was employed to encode sentences, with cosine similarity calculating the distance between courses. Regarding prerequisite identification, TextRazor extracted concepts from course descriptions, followed by the use of SemRefD to quantify the prerequisite relationship between concepts. The study's outcomes include: (i) a significant improvement of 2.5% in dropout prediction accuracy over Manrique's work; (ii) the ability to uncover course similarities based on descriptions; and (iii) the identification of prerequisites across three compulsory courses at the School of Computing, ANU.

Currently, the production of active RF components, such as klystrons, relies on costly and labor-intensive machining and brazing procedures. This article examines the RF characteristics of X-band klystron cavities and integrated circuits fabricated using an innovative additive manufacturing approach. Components are 3D printed from 316L stainless steel via direct metal laser sintering, copper electroplated, and joined in a single brazing step. Both standalone cavities and integrated circuit assemblies were monitored throughout production. Measurements indicate that the untuned cavity frequency deviates by less than 5% from the target, with Q factors exceeding 1200. Tuning experiments revealed that unoptimized pins provide a 138 MHz tuning range without degrading the Q factor. System performance was simulated using the as-built cavity parameters and realistic tuning conditions. Collectively, these findings suggest that this method offers a promising route for the rapid and cost-effective fabrication of a new class of highly integrated, high-power vacuum devices.

Because the Landau problem involves a magnetic field that is uniformly distributed across the entire two-dimensional plane, three conserved quantities inevitably arise: two conserved momenta and one conserved orbital angular momentum for the electron, regardless of the specific gauge potential chosen. Consequently, the quantum eigenfunctions of the Landau problem can be derived by diagonalizing the Landau Hamiltonian alongside any one of these three conserved operators, allowing the eigenfunctions to be explicitly written for arbitrary gauge potentials. This paper aims to elucidate the significance of gauge choice within the Landau problem through this gauge-potential-independent framework, specifically to uncover the physical relevance of the concept of a gauge-invariant extension of the canonical orbital angular momentum, which has been proposed in recent literature concerning the nucleon spin decomposition problem. Ultimately, our analysis reveals a physically vacuous aspect of gauge symmetry.

Multi-person pose estimation typically relies on top-down or bottom-up paradigms, both of which are two-stage approaches that result in high computational costs and low efficiency. To address this, we propose a compact and efficient pipeline for multi-person pose estimation by representing human parts as points. Specifically, we introduce a novel body representation using an adaptive point set comprising the human center and seven joint-related points to capture human instances in a fine-grained manner. This representation effectively models various pose deformations and adaptively factors long-range displacements between the center and joints, enabling a single-stage differentiable network named AdaptivePose to precisely regress multi-person poses. During inference, our network removes the need for grouping and refinement steps, requiring only a single disentangling process to generate multi-person poses. Without complex additional components, we achieve the best speed-accuracy trade-offs of 67.4% AP / 29.4 fps using DLA-34 and 71.3% AP / 9.1 fps using HRNet-W48 on the COCO test-dev dataset.

We apply a recent frame-indifferent theory of diffusive momentum transport to locate internal barriers within wall-bounded turbulence. Constructed from the invariant manifolds of the velocity field's Laplacian, these barriers obstruct the viscous component of the instantaneous momentum flux. By utilizing level sets of single-trajectory Lagrangian diagnostics—specifically the trajectory rotation average and stretching exponent—we approximate interfaces for both vortical and internal wall-parallel momentum transport barriers (MTBs). These interfaces offer frame-indifferent alternatives to traditional velocity-gradient-based vortices and high-shear boundaries separating uniform momentum zones (UMZs). Our results indicate that these elliptic manifold approximations and MTBs are superior to standard vortices and UMZ interfaces at impeding diffusive momentum transport, implying that these momentum barriers represent physical features potentially responsible for coherence signatures observed in statistical and non-objective diagnostics. Furthermore, we present normalized trajectory metrics that enable unprecedented visualizations of objective coherent structures by mitigating strong turbulence biases.

Recent research has demonstrated significant advancements in GANs utilizing implicit neural representations (INRs)—multilayer perceptrons that output RGB values based on (x, y) coordinates. Unlike traditional 2D pixel arrays, INRs model images as continuous 2D signals, unlocking new possibilities for GAN applications such as zero-shot super-resolution and image outpainting. However, training current methods incurs high computational costs that scale linearly with image resolution, as they require MLP evaluations at every coordinate. To address this, we introduce a novel, scalable multi-stage patch-based training strategy that enables efficient training of INR-based GANs with a flexible computational cost independent of resolution. Specifically, our approach generates and discriminates in patches to capture local details while employing a new reconstruction loss to learn global structures, facilitating efficient GAN training. Experiments across multiple benchmark datasets confirm that our method improves baseline performance in terms of GPU memory usage while maintaining FID scores at acceptable levels.

We establish a higher weight generalization of the Gross-Zagier formula for CM cycles on Kuga-Sato varieties defined over the modular curve X(N). To achieve this, we demonstrate the modularity of these CM cycles by showing that the Hecke modules they generate are semisimple, with irreducible components linked to higher weight holomorphic cuspidal automorphic representations of GL2(Q). The derivation of the higher weight general Gross-Zagier formula relies on arithmetic relative trace formulas, while the proof regarding the modularity of CM cycles draws inspiration from arithmetic theta lifting.

Automated surgical activity recognition holds the promise of enhancing surgical device intelligence and streamlining workflows, thereby improving patient care and reducing costs when integrated into modern operating rooms. Although recent advancements have demonstrated strong performance in this area, the limited generalizability of existing models remains a significant hurdle to widespread adoption. This study investigates the generalizability of these models across different operating environments. We introduce a novel domain adaptation technique designed to boost model performance in new operating rooms using only unlabeled video data. Our method generates high-confidence pseudo-labels for unlabeled clips and trains the model on an augmented version of these segments. Furthermore, we extend this approach to a semi-supervised domain adaptation framework, incorporating a small set of labeled data from the target domain. Experimental results on a dataset comprising over 480 long surgical videos from two distinct operating rooms demonstrate that our proposed method consistently surpasses baseline approaches.

By formulating an ordinary differential equation derived from a specific type of meromorphic 1-form, we present an explicit method for constructing certain conformal metrics of constant curvature on Riemann surfaces featuring singularities. As a practical application, we classify one-dimensional constant curvature metrics on the sphere $S^{2}$ that possess two conical singularities, a result originally established by Troyanov in \cite{Tr89} via the use of projective connections.

We introduce a novel class of cosmological unified dark sector frameworks termed "Generalized Logotropic Models," which are governed by a free parameter $n$. The original logotropic model, as proposed by P.H. Chavanis in 2015, emerges as a specific instance of this generalized framework when $n=1$. Within this scenario, the cosmos contains a single generalized logotropic dark fluid (GLDF), where the pressure $P$ incorporates higher-order logarithmic dependencies on the rest-mass density $\rho_m$. The total energy density $\epsilon$ combines the rest-mass energy density $\rho_m c^2$ and the internal energy density $u$, which function as the dark matter energy density $\epsilon_m$ and dark energy density $\epsilon_{de}$, respectively. Our analysis examines the cosmological dynamics of these models by tracking the evolution of energy density, the scale factor, the equation of state parameter, the deceleration parameter, and the squared speed of sound. Results indicate that values of $n \le 3$ are preferred. Furthermore, we investigate the asymptotic behavior, demonstrating that the model exhibits phantom characteristics and follows three distinct evolutionary paths contingent on $n$. Specifically, $n \le 2$ results in a little rip, whereas $n > 2$ leads to a big rip. Additionally, we derive the big rip time as a function of $n$ without relying on any undetermined parameters.

Model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML) stands as one of the most influential and widely utilized meta-learning algorithms, demonstrating significant success across diverse learning tasks. However, its distinct architecture, characterized by nested inner-loop and outer-loop updates that handle task-specific and meta-model-centric learning respectively, results in an implicit learning objective that complicates straightforward interpretation. This paper offers a novel perspective on MAML's operational mechanism, revealing that it functions similarly to a meta-learner employing a supervised contrastive objective. Specifically, query features are attracted toward support features of the same class while being repelled by those of different classes, a contrastive behavior validated experimentally through cosine similarity analysis. Furthermore, we identify an undesirable interference term in standard MAML arising from random initialization and cross-task interactions. To mitigate this, we introduce a simple yet effective "zeroing trick." Extensive experiments on the mini-ImageNet and Omniglot datasets confirm consistent performance improvements, substantiating the efficacy of our proposed approach.

Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) is a highly effective deep reinforcement learning algorithm, particularly for continuous control tasks, yet its performance remains constrained by limited exploration capabilities. While classical reinforcement learning offers methods to balance exploration and data exploitation, their algorithmic complexity often prevents application in intricate environments. Focusing on continuous control tasks with dense rewards, this study examines the underlying assumptions of the standard Gaussian action exploration in PPO and elucidates how exploration efficacy impacts overall performance. To address these limitations, the paper introduces an uncertainty estimation-based mechanism to enhance exploration. By integrating this approach, we propose IEM-PPO, a variant of PPO equipped with an intrinsic exploration module designed for complex environments. Experiments conducted on the MuJoCo physical simulator benchmark multiple tasks, comparing IEM-PPO against both curiosity-driven exploration (ICM-PPO) and the original PPO. Results indicate that while IEM-PPO requires a longer training duration, it achieves superior sample efficiency, cumulative rewards, and demonstrates greater stability and robustness.

Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) are considered a promising component for future wireless networks due to their ability to adaptively control the propagation environment using low-cost passive elements. Nevertheless, traditional passive RIS units suffer from severe double path loss, limiting their gain to scenarios where receivers are in close proximity, and they fail to cover receivers located behind them. To overcome these practical limitations, this paper proposes a novel active RIS architecture capable of simultaneous reflection and transmission with active signal amplification, thereby significantly expanding coverage and improving the quality-of-service (QoS) for all users. We investigate the joint optimization of transmit beamforming and the design of this dual-functional active RIS within multiuser multiple-input single-output (MU-MISO) systems, addressing both sum-rate maximization and power minimization objectives. To resolve the inherent non-convexity of these problems, we develop efficient iterative algorithms that decompose the challenges into separate sub-problems, which are then solved using fractional programming and Riemannian-manifold optimization techniques. Simulation results confirm that the proposed dual-functional active RIS architecture and the associated algorithms outperform various benchmark schemes.

We introduce a technique for the adiabatic control of an atomic ensemble by establishing a decoherence-free subspace (DFS) inside a dissipative cavity. This is achieved by injecting a field into the cavity that destructively interferes with the ensemble's emission amplitude, thereby engineering a specific eigenstate of the system's Lindblad jump operators. Unlike earlier adiabatic DFS proposals, our approach generates a DFS even when collective decoherence is present. Consequently, we can create states with high multi-particle entanglement, which are valuable for quantum information science and metrology. Additionally, we present an optimized driving protocol that leverages insights from adiabatic criteria regarding potential diabatic evolution. This enables the system to reach a target state with exceptionally high fidelity on a timescale independent of the ensemble size. By adiabatically engineering the DFS eigenstate, our method facilitates faster state preparation compared to previous schemes that rely exclusively on dissipative damping to reach the desired state.

Primordial perturbations that deviate from Gaussian statistics on the distribution's tails often signal non-perturbative inflationary effects. This paper presents specific scenarios where the distribution tail becomes highly non-Gaussian despite the statistics remaining nearly Gaussian in the perturbative regime. We first examine an extension of ultra-slow-roll inflation featuring a transition phase, wherein the inflaton ascends a minute potential step at the conclusion of the non-attractor phase before settling into the slow-roll attractor. This example highlights the critical role of off-attractor dynamics during upward-step transitions. We subsequently extend this analysis to a different transition type involving two slow-roll stages linked by a small step. By conducting detailed perturbative and non-perturbative analyses of fluctuations generated around the step, we demonstrate that even tiny, non-trivial transitions can significantly influence large perturbations in the distribution's tail, while keeping perturbative non-Gaussianity minimal. Our findings suggest that non-Gaussian tails possess rich phenomenology previously overlooked in standard analyses. Furthermore, we investigate the implications of these tails for primordial black hole (PBH) formation, discovering that their mass fraction can be amplified by several orders of magnitude compared to Gaussian scenarios. Finally, we discuss a PBH formation mechanism specific to the upward-step inflation model, which relies on trapping the inflaton at the bottom of the step.

We hypothesize that both creativity and the perception of creativity are influenced, to a certain degree, by embodiment. This suggests that embodiment is crucial for Computational Creativity (CC) research; however, current studies in this area are limited, and the application of the concept remains vague. To address this gap, we conducted a systematic review and prescriptive analysis of papers presented at the International Conference on Computational Creativity. By adopting and expanding an existing embodiment typology, we aimed to clarify ambiguities by identifying and comparing various definitions of the concept. Furthermore, we gathered, contextualized, and highlighted the opportunities and challenges associated with integrating embodiment into CC as a research framework, while proposing key directions to advance the field of embodied CC.

This study presents the first calculation of interaction energy shifts and widths in kaonic atoms, utilizing microscopic $K^- N$ and $K^- NN$ potentials derived from $K^- N$ scattering amplitudes within SU(3) chiral coupled-channels models of meson-baryon interactions. These calculations incorporate in-medium modifications of free-space amplitudes arising from Pauli correlations. Evaluated across 23 nuclear species, the $K^-N+K^-NN$ potentials were compared against kaonic atom data, revealing a significant improvement in data description when $K^-NN$ absorption is included. However, achieving a $\chi^2$ comparable to that of phenomenological multi-nucleon potentials ($K^-N+$) requires an additional phenomenological term for $K^{-}-3N(4N)$ processes. The density dependence of this term highlights deficiencies in the current microscopic potentials, suggesting a need for further model refinement. Furthermore, the calculated branching ratios for $K^-N$ and $K^-NN$ absorption channels in the $^{12}$C$+K^-$ system align reasonably well with both historical bubble chamber data and recent findings from the AMADEUS Collaboration.

There is increasing focus on creating automated agents that collaborate with humans. Beyond task completion, these agents must act in ways humans prefer, necessitating clear communication of those preferences. Existing methods typically require users to define reward functions or engage in interactive queries comparing trajectories. Defining reward functions is difficult when an agent's internal logic is opaque, while interactive comparisons can be burdensome if users could express preferences using simpler symbolic concepts. This paper introduces PRESCA (PREference Specification through Concept Acquisition), a system enabling users to articulate preferences via familiar concepts. PRESCA maintains a shared vocabulary of such concepts, learning new ones if necessary. To enhance efficiency, it exploits causal links between new and existing concepts. Furthermore, the cost of learning new concepts is offset by integrating them into the shared vocabulary for future use. Evaluated in a Minecraft environment, PRESCA demonstrates its ability to effectively align agent behavior with user preferences.

MAPS (MMT Adaptive optics exoPlanet characterization System) represents an enhancement to the legacy 6.5m MMT adaptive optics system. Supported by NSF MSIP funding, the project encompasses (i) refurbishing the MMT Adaptive Secondary Mirror (ASM), (ii) implementing new high-sensitivity, high spatial-order visible and near-infrared pyramid wavefront sensors, and (iii) upgrading the Arizona Infrared Imager and Echelle Spectrograph (ARIES) and MMT High Precision Imaging Polarimeter (MMTPol) science cameras. This paper details the design and development of the visible pyramid wavefront sensor, which comprises an acquisition camera, a fast-steering tip-tilt modulation mirror, a double pyramid, a pupil imaging triplet lens, and a low-noise, high-speed frame-rate CCID75 camera. We will report on the hardware and software, present laboratory characterization results for the individual subsystems, and outline the on-sky commissioning plan.

We introduce a new reliability framework for aggregating energy service requests, grounded in consumer behavior and past energy request history. This model is designed to maximize incentives for providers, serving as a green strategy to boost IoT user engagement within crowdsourced energy-sharing ecosystems. Furthermore, we present adaptive and priority-based scheduling methods to compose the most dependable energy requests while optimizing provider incentives. Experimental evaluations were performed to assess these approaches, with results demonstrating their effectiveness.

This study presents a new molecular dynamics investigation into the collisional dynamics of particles near the exit of a two-dimensional silo. While most research on this granular system focuses on the bulk region, where contacts are long-lived and continuous approximations suffice for analyzing velocity distributions and mass flow, the area close to the exit differs significantly. There, density drops and contacts become instantaneous, making the collisional nature of the dynamics crucial and necessitating the specific analysis provided here. Notably, this region is where arches that obstruct flow in small apertures form. The findings reveal that the transition from the clogging regime (observed at small apertures) to the continuous flow regime is smooth regarding collisional variables, and particle velocity distributions remain unaffected. This suggests there is no critical outlet size that separates these two regimes, contradicting previous literature. Instead, the results support the alternative view that clogging can occur regardless of the outlet size.

We have calculated all coefficients for the most general 4-loop gauge and 3-loop Yukawa $\beta$-functions applicable to the broadest class of renormalizable four-dimensional theories. By employing a comprehensive parametrization of these $\beta$-functions, we compare the general expressions against those of established theories to restrict the values of unknown coefficients. Furthermore, Weyl consistency conditions supply the necessary additional constraints to finalize the determination.

Driven by advancements in artificial intelligence, particularly within speech recognition and machine translation, automatic speech-to-text and speech-to-speech translation have seen significant growth. While these systems are typically evaluated using automated metrics like BLEU to track release improvements or during evaluation campaigns, there is limited understanding of how end-users perceive their output or how they stack up against human performance in similar communicative scenarios. This paper reports on an experiment designed to assess a real-time speech translation engine by benchmarking it against professional simultaneous interpreters. Utilizing a framework originally developed for evaluating human interpreters, we conducted a manual assessment of both human and machine outputs. Our findings indicate that human interpreters outperformed the machine in terms of intelligibility, whereas the machine demonstrated slightly superior performance regarding informativeness. The study discusses its limitations and potential improvements to the evaluation framework. Despite these constraints, employing this framework marks a significant initial step toward a user-centric and communication-focused methodology for assessing real-time automatic speech translation.

This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the parameters affecting charge collection in partially depleted Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors (MAPS) featuring small electrodes (<25 μm²), fabricated using the TowerJazz 180 nm CMOS process. The findings offer crucial insights for optimizing the diode structure in the ALPIDE chip, which is integral to ALICE's second-generation Inner Tracking System, and provide a benchmark for future simulations of comparable devices. Key investigated variables include reverse substrate bias, epitaxial layer thickness, electrode dimensions, and the distance between electrodes and adjacent in-pixel electronics. Data from 28 μm pitch pixels demonstrate that rapid charge collection (under 10 ns) is achievable even in partially depleted configurations. Furthermore, the study quantifies how these parameters influence signal sharing and amplitude, underscoring the critical role of proper well spacing and the effects of reverse substrate bias.

This paper introduces a new online method for fusing depth maps that aggregates them within a latent feature space. Unlike prior techniques that rely on explicit scene representations such as signed distance functions (SDFs), our approach utilizes a learned feature representation for fusion. Central to this method is the decoupling of the internal scene representation used during fusion from the final output representation, achieved through a dedicated translator network. The proposed neural architecture comprises two primary components: a depth and feature fusion sub-network, succeeded by a translator sub-network that generates the ultimate surface representation (e.g., TSDF) required for visualization or further processing. Functioning as an online process, our method effectively manages high noise levels and is specifically robust against the gross outliers frequently encountered in photometric stereo-based depth maps. Empirical evaluations on both real and synthetic datasets show performance that surpasses current state-of-the-art methods, particularly in difficult scenarios characterized by significant noise and outliers.

Our research aims to develop an interface enabling multiple operators to collaboratively manage robot teams in complex scenarios, specifically investigating how inter-human communication influences the design space. We examined the effects of direct versus indirect communication on metrics including awareness, workload, trust, and usability. In our user study, participants either communicated verbally or conveyed their actions and intentions indirectly through the interface. The study involved 18 humans and 9 robots performing a collective transport task. Results indicate that integrating both direct and indirect communication yields the most effective approach for multi-human, multi-robot interaction.

Current multilateral negotiation protocols mandate complete consensus among all participants; however, we introduce a new protocol that permits partial consensus, enabling a subset of parties to finalize an agreement. We outline specific scenarios necessitating this approach and provide a formal description of the protocol.

The study utilizes bijections connecting invariants of indecomposable projective modules in specific Brauer configuration algebras with those linked to solutions of the Kronecker and four subspace problems to categorify integer sequences, as defined by Ringel and Fahr. Additionally, the dimensions of these Brauer configuration algebras and their respective centers, which play a role in these various processes, are provided.

A subset of the integer planar grid $[N] \times [N]$ is defined as corner-free if it lacks any triplet of the form $(x,y), (x+\delta,y), (x,y+\delta)$. While it is established that such sets possess a density that approaches zero as $N$ grows, the exact magnitude of this upper bound remains an open question. The prior best construction relied on Behrend's large subset of $[N]$ devoid of 3-term arithmetic progressions. This paper presents the first significant enhancement to that lower bound in many years. Our methodology draws from communication complexity theory, specifically addressing the 3-player exactly-$N$ problem, where participants must determine if $x+y+z=N$ given inputs $x,y,z$ and a fixed $N$. This marks the inaugural study of such a problem within the multiplayer Number On the Forehead (NOF) model. Despite its fundamental nature, the problem has seen no advancement over the years; although explicit protocols were recently discovered, they have not yet improved upon existing complexity bounds. The current work introduces the first improved protocol for the exactly-$N$ problem, representing the first major instance where algorithmic techniques in communication complexity successfully yield results in additive combinatorics.

In traditional communication frameworks, interference between transmitting endpoints is typically treated as detrimental noise that degrades signal integrity. Conversely, recent wireless applications have explored the benefits of allowing simultaneous transmission by intentionally managing and even leveraging signal interference. Prominent techniques such as non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA), joint source-channel coding, and computation codes are specifically engineered to harness this phenomenon, inspiring further foundational research ranging from network coding to consensus algorithms. Notably, federated learning represents an emerging distributed machine learning technology that facilitates simultaneous transmission. Although numerous independent applications for simultaneous transmission exist in the literature, they all fundamentally rely on the superposition property. This survey aims to highlight the interconnections among these studies and offer readers a comprehensive guide to wireless communication techniques that capitalize on signal superposition. By categorizing existing research according to its purpose and application domain, the survey outlines key contributions. It demonstrates that simultaneous transmission can deliver scalability, enhanced security, low latency, reduced complexity, and improved energy efficiency in specific distributed wireless scenarios, which are critical for the demands of emerging Internet of Things (IoT) applications.

Accurate and up-to-date knowledge of current information sources is vital for numerous applications, especially when status updates reach their destination after generation due to processing and communication delays. This timeliness is quantified by the age of information. This study investigates a multi-sensing network comprising multiple sources, servers, and a central monitor. Each source represents independent data, with its age tracked individually. For a specific source, servers independently sense it and forward updates to the monitor. Updates arrive at servers following Poisson processes, and each server transmits them to the monitor via a direct link modeled as a queue, where transmission times follow an exponential distribution. The analysis covers both homogeneous and heterogeneous rates for single-source scenarios, while restricting to homogeneous rates for multiple-source cases. We derive a closed-form solution for the average age of information under a last-come-first-serve (LCFS) queue with a single source and any number of homogeneous servers. Additionally, using a recursive approach, we obtain an explicit formula for the average age across any number of sources and homogeneous servers. Furthermore, we explore heterogeneous servers in a single-source context and provide algorithms to determine the average age of information.

Beyond merely replicating discriminatory patterns found in training datasets, machine learning models can also generate or intensify bias. We define this phenomenon as introduced unfairness and examine the scenarios that lead to it. Specifically, we introduce "introduced total variation" as a metric to quantify this type of unfairness and identify the graphical conditions that incentivize its occurrence. Our findings suggest that incorporating sensitive attributes as features eliminates the incentive for such variation when using well-behaved loss functions. Furthermore, adopting a causal framework reveals how path-specific effects clarify when certain pathways should be deemed fair.

Stellar oscillations may originate from topological mechanisms. We uncover this previously concealed characteristic by drawing a new analogy between stars and topological insulators. By formulating a Hermitian problem, we derive the formula for the stellar acoustic-buoyant frequency $S$ associated with non-radial adiabatic pulsations. Subsequent topological analysis links sign reversals in the acoustic-buoyant frequency to the presence of Lamb-like waves inside the star. These topological modes traverse the frequency gap, exhibiting gravity-mode behavior at low harmonic degrees $\ell$ and pressure-mode behavior at high $\ell$. We find that $S$ changes sign at least once throughout the interior of most stellar objects, implying that topological modes are widespread across the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram. Additionally, certain topological modes are predicted to become trapped in regions with strong local variations in internal structure.

Most current research on the average unexplained gender pay gap relies on overly restrictive linear forms of the Blinder-Oaxaca decomposition. Leveraging a substantial dataset of 1.7 million Swiss employees, this study examines how methodological advancements enabled by big data influence these estimates. We assess the sensitivity of the results concerning: i) the presence of observationally comparable male and female counterparts, ii) the flexibility of the wage equation when accounting for wage determinants, and iii) the selection of various parametric and semi-parametric estimators, including those incorporating machine learning. Our findings indicate that these three elements significantly impact the results. Specifically, enforcing comparability between genders and adopting a more flexible wage equation specification causes Blinder-Oaxaca estimates of the unexplained pay gap to fall by as much as 39%. Furthermore, semi-parametric matching produces estimates that are up to 50% lower than traditional Blinder-Oaxaca figures and demonstrate reduced sensitivity to the specific inclusion of wage determinants.
We demonstrate that specific quiver varieties are irreducible and consequently isomorphic to Hilbert schemes of points on the total spaces of the bundles $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-n)$ for $n \ge 1$.

As high-velocity clouds (HVCs) traverse the Galactic halo, they entrain ambient magnetic fields, creating stretched and draped magnetic structures at the cloud-halo boundary. This magnetized layer inhibits mixing between the cloud and the surrounding halo gas. While earlier numerical studies often simplified initial conditions by assuming spherically symmetric, uniform-density clouds, observations reveal that HVCs are actually clumpy and turbulent. Consequently, this study employs three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic simulations to examine the evolution of clouds with more realistic density distributions. In the parameter regime modeled, simple spherical clouds grow immediately from the simulation's onset, whereas clumpy clouds shed cold gas early on and only begin to grow if their metallicity is very low. Massive clumps within these clumpy clouds exhibit similarities to single uniform-density clouds, displaying distinct head-tail morphologies with draped magnetic fields; however, such similarities are marginal for clumps located in the cloud's wake. The presence of magnetic fields suppresses hydrodynamic instability growth along the direction of motion. Efficient radiative cooling results in a compact cloud featuring rich clumps and filaments condensed from the surrounding gas. Furthermore, the slope of the initial density power spectrum is closely linked to the internal density contrast of a clumpy cloud, thereby governing the rate at which material is expelled from the initial cloud and mixed with the halo gas.

Predictive policing originates from crime hotspot modeling. This paper illustrates the components of mathematical crime hotspot modeling and demonstrates that the underlying assumptions reinforce systemic racism within law enforcement. The objective of this study is to challenge this field of research not regarding its mathematical validity, but concerning the limitations of how the problem is defined.

This paper demonstrates that an order $m$, dimension 2 tensor is primitive if and only if its majorization matrix is primitive. Consequently, we derive the characterization of order $m$, dimension 2 strongly primitive tensors and establish bounds for their strongly primitive degree. Additionally, we investigate the properties of strongly primitive tensors where $n \geq 3$ and suggest several avenues for future research.

Existing quantum simulators face significant hurdles, including brief coherence times, operational noise, unreliable readout, and limited qubit connectivity. Variational quantum algorithms represent the most viable strategy for achieving quantum advantage in near-term simulations. This study investigates these algorithms across various connectivity configurations to simulate the ground states of long-range interacting systems and generate spin-squeezed states. We observe that as interactions extend over longer distances, algorithmic efficiency declines, resulting in reduced fidelity and a higher demand for optimization iterations; this inefficiency is particularly pronounced near critical points. Enhancing connectivity between distant qubits mitigates these issues, yielding better results with fewer quantum and classical resources. Our findings indicate that integrating circuit layers with varying connectivity levels can substantially boost performance. Notably, the sequence of these layers is critical, with placing long-distance connectivity layers at the circuit's outset outperforming other arrangements. This same circuit architecture is also applicable for variationally creating spin-squeezed states, which serve as essential resources for quantum metrology.

This paper highlights that DETR's one-to-one set matching results in sparse supervision for the encoder's output due to insufficient positive query assignments, which significantly hinders discriminative feature learning in the encoder and, conversely, impairs attention learning in the decoder. To address this issue, we introduce Co-DETR, a novel collaborative hybrid assignment training scheme designed to learn more efficient and effective DETR-based detectors through diverse label assignment strategies. This approach enhances the encoder's learning capacity in end-to-end detectors by training multiple parallel auxiliary heads under one-to-many label assignments, such as those used in ATSS, FCOS, and Faster R-CNN. Furthermore, we generate additional customized positive queries by extracting positive coordinates from these auxiliary heads to boost the training efficiency of positive samples within the decoder. During inference, these auxiliary heads are removed, meaning our method adds no extra parameters or computational overhead to the original detector and eliminates the need for hand-crafted non-maximum suppression (NMS). We conducted extensive experiments to evaluate our approach on various DETR variants, including DAB-DETR, Deformable-DETR, and H-Deformable-DETR. Specifically, we improved basic Deformable-DETR by 5.8% after 12 epochs and by 3.2% after 36 epochs. Additionally, we enhanced the state-of-the-art H-Deformable-DETR from 57.9% to 58.7% mAP on the MS COCO validation set. Remarkably, when combined with the large-scale MixMIM-g backbone containing 1 billion parameters, we achieved a 64.5% mAP on the MS COCO test-dev set, demonstrating superior performance with minimal additional data requirements. The code will be made available at https://github.com/Sense-X/Co-DETR.

Combining Vector Quantised Variational AutoEncoders (VQ-VAE) with autoregressive models for image generation has produced high-quality outputs; however, the strict progressive scanning order inherent to autoregressive sampling limits these models by preventing them from accessing global information. Conversely, Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM) operating in continuous domains effectively capture global context while maintaining high generation quality. Although discrete diffusion models have previously shown promise in text and low-resolution image tasks, this work demonstrates that leveraging a content-rich discrete visual codebook from VQ-VAE enables discrete diffusion models to produce high-fidelity images with global context. This approach compensates for the pixel-space limitations of classical autoregressive models. Furthermore, integrating discrete VAEs with diffusion models addresses two key drawbacks: the excessive size of conventional autoregressive models and the time-consuming sampling process of standard diffusion models. The study highlights that the quality of generated images relies heavily on the discrete visual codebook. Extensive experiments confirm that the proposed Vector Quantised Discrete Diffusion Model (VQ-DDM) achieves performance comparable to top-tier methods with low complexity. Additionally, VQ-DDM exhibits significant advantages over other vector-quantized autoregressive models in image inpainting tasks, all without requiring additional training.

By employing $\mu$-bubbles, we establish that for dimensions $3 \le n \le 7$, the connected sum of a Schoen-Yau-Schick $n$-manifold with any arbitrary manifold fails to support a complete metric with positive scalar curvature. Furthermore, we demonstrate that under specific conditions—namely, when $3 \le n \le 5$ and $1 \le m \le n-1$, or when $6 \le n \le 7$ and $m \in \{1, n-2, n-1\}$—the connected sum $(M^{n-m}\times \mathbb{T}^m) \# X^n$, where $X$ is an arbitrary manifold, does not admit a metric of positive $m$-intermediate curvature. This $m$-intermediate curvature represents a novel concept introduced by Brendle, Hirsch, and Johne that interpolates between Ricci and scalar curvature.

Machine learning models often fail to predict accurately when encountering inputs that differ significantly from their training data, a limitation that obstructs their use in critical sectors like healthcare and autonomous driving. While detecting shifts from the training distribution has become a focal point, with various out-of-distribution (OOD) detection methods proposed, many real-world applications involve temporal sequences of inputs. Current OOD detection techniques for time-series data frequently fail to leverage temporal dependencies or offer theoretical guarantees on detection reliability. To address this, we introduce a method that utilizes deviation from in-distribution temporal equivariance as a non-conformity measure within a conformal anomaly detection framework tailored for time-series data. By aggregating independent predictions from multiple detectors based on this measure using Fisher's method, we developed CODiT, a detector that provides rigorous guarantees on false detection rates for time-series data. We demonstrate CODiT's effectiveness by achieving state-of-the-art performance on computer vision datasets for autonomous driving and by successfully applying it to non-vision physiological data via experiments on the GAIT sensory dataset. The accompanying code, datasets, and trained models are accessible at https://github.com/kaustubhsridhar/time-series-OOD.

This paper introduces a new algorithm designed for a swarm of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to locate an unknown source without prior knowledge. Inspired by the Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) method, the proposed Acceleration-based PSO (APSO) addresses source-seeking challenges differently from conventional PSO, which relies on self- and social-cognition to update particle velocity; instead, APSO updates particle acceleration. Theoretical analysis demonstrates the stability and convergence of this approach, with conditions for the third-order update equations derived using the Jury stability test. High-fidelity simulations conducted in CoppeliaSim reveal that the APSO algorithm outperforms existing state-of-the-art PSO-based source-seeking methods. Results indicate that the proposed method excels under various conditions, including diverse UAV communication topologies, varying swarm sizes, different search region dimensions, restricted source movement, and the presence of measurement noise.

We examine a system of phase oscillators in the thermodynamic limit, which is modeled by a kinetic equation governing the phase distribution density. We introduce an ansatz for the circular moments (Kuramoto-Daido order parameters) that enables exact truncation at any chosen number of modes. In the specific case of a single mode, this ansatz aligns with the formulation by Ott and Antonsen [Chaos 18, 037113 (2008)]. Dynamics evolving on these extended manifolds support higher-dimensional behaviors, such as chaos, as illustrated by a simulation of a Josephson junction array. These results are further extended to oscillators characterized by a Cauchy-Lorentzian distribution of natural frequencies.

Storytelling, encompassing genres like fables, news, documentaries, and memoirs, can be defined as the transmission of connected, engaging incidents that collectively constitute a tangible process. Consequently, identifying the event sequences that embody these processes is a worthy goal, yet it presents a significant challenge. We attribute this difficulty to the inherent complexity of natural language, which blends a core narrative of key events with supplementary material such as background context, opinions, and pragmatic discourse elements that are essential but not central to the main event flow. To address this, we propose methods for isolating the primary event chain by removing non-essential sentences and non-salient events. Our approach's efficacy is validated by demonstrating its positive impact on downstream applications. Specifically, we show that pre-training large language models on these distilled chains enhances performance in tasks requiring a clear grasp of event sequences, namely narrative prediction and event-based temporal question answering. Both the observed improvements and ablation studies substantiate that our extraction technique successfully isolates critical event chains.

Despite decades of research into Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM), existing state-of-the-art techniques often face instability or inaccuracies in civilian settings due to insufficient features or inherent estimation drift. To address these challenges, we introduce a navigation system that integrates SLAM with prior-map-based localization. Specifically, we enhance SLAM by incorporating line and plane features, which are abundant and structurally prominent in civilian environments, thereby ensuring feature sufficiency and robust localization. Furthermore, we embed general prior map data to mitigate drift and boost accuracy. To prevent complex associations between prior information and local observations, we represent prior knowledge as low-dimensional structural priors, defined by relative distances and angles between geometric primitives. The localization process is modeled as a graph-based optimization problem involving sliding-window variables and factors derived from IMU data, heterogeneous features, and structural priors. We also derive analytical expressions for the Jacobians of various factors to eliminate the overhead of automatic differentiation. Additionally, an information-gain-based selection mechanism is employed to reduce computational costs by including only the most effective structural priors in the optimization. Finally, the framework has been rigorously evaluated using synthetic data, public datasets, and real-world UAV flight data collected during a building inspection mission. Results demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly enhances localization accuracy and robustness for autonomous robots in civilian applications.

All our understanding of the surrounding environment stems from light, a form of electromagnetic radiation. Astronomy leverages this radiation across the entire electromagnetic spectrum, utilizing various instruments to capture signals and identify their cosmic origins. These signals are processed to create images intended for public display. Astronomers recognize that such images inspire curiosity in viewers, reflecting a science dedicated to inclusivity and the dissemination of the universe's beauty to everyone. To achieve this, we employ innovative teaching methods and leverage current technologies to make knowledge accessible to underserved groups, such as visually impaired individuals in our country. Consequently, the AstroBVI project launched in Peru for the first time, supported by the Centro de Astronomía de la Universidad de Antofagasta and funded by the International Astronomical Union Office of Astronomy for Development (IAU-OAD). This initiative distributed 3D tactile galaxy images, enabling seven workshops in 2019 that reached various institutions and engaged over 160 participants with blindness and low vision. The significant interest demonstrated by these participants highlights the immense potential of 3D tactile materials in astronomy education.

The Soccer Simulation 2D League stands as a premier competition within the RoboCup framework, featuring matches between two squads of eleven players and a coach. Various foundational codes have been made available to the RCSS2D community, fostering the integration of multi-agent systems and AI techniques. This paper presents "Cyrus2D Base," an adaptation of the 2021 RoboCup champion's code. By synthesizing Gliders2D base V2.6 with the latest Helios version and incorporating key features from Cyrus2021, we have enhanced both performance and capability. Additionally, a Data Extractor has been integrated to streamline machine learning applications. Testing across diverse teams and scenarios confirms that this base code yields substantial advancements in both defensive and offensive strategies.

This paper offers a comprehensive review of symmetry-related literature concerning the eikonal equations $u_\mu u_\mu =0$ and $u_\mu u_\mu =1$, where lower indices on dependent variables represent derivatives ($\mu=0,1,2,..,n$) and summation is implied for repeated indices. We examine general solutions and symmetries of these equations, their connection to the reduction of higher-order partial differential equations (PDEs), and include several new results essential for this thorough presentation. Specifically, we analyze discrete symmetries, equivalence classes of solutions, and the relationship between symmetry solutions and general solutions. Furthermore, we detail the procedure for deriving general solutions using hodograph and contact transformations applied to the initial equations. The author presents new findings, notably a general solution for the eikonal equation applicable to an arbitrary number of spatial variables. Intended as both a reference resource and a practical manual, the work covers these topics in depth.

The elasticity of disordered and polydisperse polymer networks remains a fundamental, unresolved issue in soft matter physics. This study presents a simulation of such systems utilizing either trivalent or tetravalent crosslinks. These networks self-assemble through equilibrium simulations, yielding an exponential strand length distribution that mirrors experimental findings for randomly crosslinked systems. We observe that the network's fractal structure is determined by the initial density ($\rho_\text{init}$); however, systems sharing the same mean valence and $\rho_\text{init}$ exhibit identical structural characteristics. Furthermore, we calculate the long-time limit of the mean-squared displacement—termed the (squared) localization length—for both crosslinks and strand midpoints, demonstrating that the dynamics of long strands align well with the tube model. Finally, we establish a relationship between these two localization lengths at high densities and link the crosslink localization length to the system's shear modulus.

This work investigates the LHC's potential to detect new broad neutral resonances arising from two-photon fusion ($\gamma\gamma \to t\bar{t}$) that decay into top quark pairs. The study focuses on central exclusive $t\bar{t}$ production in proton-proton collisions ($pp \to p t\bar{t} p$), utilizing intact proton tagging via the PPS detector in CMS and the AFP detector in ATLAS within the semi-leptonic $t\bar{t}$ decay channel. Sensitivity results are translated into constraints on dimension-8 $\gamma\gamma t\bar{t}$ operators in the high-mass regime. By leveraging kinematic correlations between the intact protons and the reconstructed $t\bar{t}$ system, we achieve a 95% confidence level sensitivity to the couplings of these dimension-8 operators of $1.4 \cdot 10^{-11}~\mathrm{GeV}^{-4}$. This sensitivity to anomalous couplings can be significantly enhanced to approximately $7 \cdot 10^{-12}~\mathrm{GeV}^{-4}$ if future measurements determine proton time-of-flight with a precision of 20 ps. Furthermore, the ability to probe broad neutral resonances extends to masses around $1500~\mathrm{GeV}$ at 95% CL when utilizing timing information.

This study introduces OGCOSMO, a software tool developed using the High Level Design Methodology (HLDM). This approach prioritizes Very High Level (VHL) programming languages while reserving Intermediate Level (IL) languages specifically for time-critical processing tasks; in this case, Python serves as the VHL language and Fortran as the IL language. The core of OGCOSMO is the OGC\_lib package, which houses modules dedicated to analyzing cosmological and astrophysical phenomena, including comoving distances, the redshift-time relationship, cosmic star formation rates, dark matter halo number densities, and the mass functions of supermassive black holes (SMBHs). Currently under development, the software plans to add features for investigating the stochastic gravitational wave (GW) background generated by stellar collapses into black holes and SMBH binary systems. Furthermore, the authors demonstrate that the HLDM framework utilizing Python and Fortran constitutes a potent methodology for creating astrophysical software.

The product of two Mirkovic-Vilonen cycles represents a degeneration of their intersection, originally defined via the Beilinson-Drinfeld Grassmannian. This paper introduces a conceptually straightforward method for calculating this product within type $A$ by shifting the problem to the fusion of generalized orbital varieties through the Mirkovic-Vybornov isomorphism. As an application, we explicitly determine all cluster exchange relations in the coordinate ring of the upper-triangular subgroup of $GL_4$, thereby verifying that every cluster variable resides within the Mirkovic-Vilonen basis.

This paper introduces a novel deep learning framework designed to separate face identity features from expressive 3D facial data. For any given 3D face, the method extracts a disentangled identity representation and simultaneously generates a realistic 3D face with a neutral expression while identifying the subject. The architecture comprises three main modules: (1) a Graph Convolutional Autoencoder (GCA) that encodes 3D faces into latent vectors, (2) a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) which transforms latent representations of expressive faces into those of neutral faces, and (3) an identity recognition sub-network that leverages the neutralized latent space for 3D face recognition. The entire system is trained end-to-end, and experiments on three public datasets demonstrate the approach's efficacy.

An object detection system consists of a camera capturing the scene and a detector processing the resulting images, where image quality significantly influences detection performance. Current research often addresses either image enhancement or detector improvement in isolation, overlooking the benefits of jointly optimizing both subsystems. This paper aims to enhance the accuracy and throughput of existing object detectors in remote sensing by tailoring input images specifically for the detector. To achieve this, we empirically evaluate the impact of two camera calibration settings (distortion correction and gamma correction) and five image parameters (quantization, compression, resolution, color model, and additional channels). Our extensive assessment utilizes three UAV datasets from diverse domains alongside a mix of large and small state-of-the-art detector models. Furthermore, we developed an embedded prototype of the detection pipeline for UAVs and provide practical recommendations based on our results. We demonstrate that parameters do not affect accuracy or throughput equally; by finding an optimal balance, we can improve detection accuracy for lightweight models without compromising data throughput.

Contemporary research increasingly explores non-traditional data sources to develop innovative methodologies for addressing open questions within the human mobility framework regarding migration trends. In this context, we introduce the Multi-aspect Integrated Migration Indicators (MIMI) dataset, a new collection of migration drivers derived from acquiring, transforming, and merging official data on international flows and stocks with unconventional indicators, such as online social networks. This study outlines the process of collecting, embedding, and integrating both traditional and novel features to create this multidisciplinary dataset, which we believe will significantly enhance the ability to nowcast and forecast current and future bilateral migration trends.

This paper introduces a broad framework for establishing Lipschitz regularity in solutions to a wide spectrum of nonautonomous, vector-valued variational problems characterized by nonuniform ellipticity. The scope of the analyzed functionals spans from those with unbalanced polynomial growth to those exhibiting rapid, exponential growth. Our findings are sharp across all considered data points and establish novel, optimal regularity criteria, even within the traditional uniformly elliptic setting. Furthermore, we classify various forms of nonuniform ellipticity, pinpointing the appropriate conditions required to derive corresponding regularity theorems.

Across all local low-dimensional models, critical scaling typically diverges from mean-field predictions, with one notable exception. This unique model, which exhibits "ordinary" behavior, was investigated previously by H.-M. Broker and the author. Early simulations of its two-dimensional variant indicated that two critical exponents adhered to mean-field theory, while a third displayed only minimal deviations; furthermore, numerical results aligned almost exactly with an explicit mean-field model. In this study, we report simulations with significantly enhanced statistics for both 2D and 3D versions. In each dimension, we observe that deviations of all critical exponents from their mean-field values represent non-leading corrections, confirming that the scaling is precisely of the mean-field type. Consistent with the original work, we attribute this phenomenon to "confusion," defined as a strong randomization of feedback phases inherent to non-equilibrium systems.

Visualizing results is crucial for interpreting biomedical analyses, with interactive networks being a common tool. However, the data's high dimensionality and dense connectivity often cause information overload, hindering interpretation. Current approaches to mitigate this issue rely on data reduction, limited interactivity, or costly hardware. We propose utilizing the affordable Oculus Quest Virtual Reality (VR) headset for visualizing large-scale biological networks interactively. We introduce GeneNet VR, detailing its design and implementation, and assess its scalability and usability with extensive gene-to-gene interaction networks. Our system meets the Oculus performance requirement of 72 FPS for the largest network tested (2,693 genes) using both a GPU and the standalone Oculus Quest. Interviews with biomedical researchers indicate that GeneNet VR is perceived as innovative, engaging, and user-friendly for those new to VR. We believe affordable VR hardware holds significant potential for biological data analysis, though further research is needed to quantify its benefits for real-world knowledge discovery. GeneNet VR is open-sourced at https://github.com/kolibrid/GeneNet-VR, and a demonstration video is available at https://youtu.be/N4QDZiZqVNY.

Drawing inspiration from computability logic\cite{Jap03}, we refine the definitions of recursive functions into two distinct categories: blindly-quantified (BQ) and parallel universally quantified (PUQ). BQ definitions align with traditional approaches where recursive structures remain static, whereas PUQ definitions are dynamic and evolve during computation, thereby enabling automatic memoization. Furthermore, building upon this concept, we introduce a novel high-level object-oriented language.

For the first time, the 12C(20Ne,16O)16O alpha-transfer reaction at Elab=150 MeV has been employed to determine the ANC for the 6.92 MeV and 7.12 MeV states of 16O. Additionally, potential parameters for the 20Ne+12C system were derived from elastic scattering data. Using the direct reaction code FRESCO, the alpha-spectroscopy factor (Sα) was calculated for three 16O states (6.92 MeV, 7.12 MeV, and 11.52 MeV), while the ANC was determined for the two lower-energy states (6.92 MeV and 7.12 MeV). The extracted ANC and Sα values show good agreement with prior measurements.

This paper details the design, fabrication, and simulation of a compact, low-cost external cavity diode laser operating at 852 nm, which exhibits a measured free-running frequency drift of 1.4(1) MHz/h. This performance is realized through a nearly monolithic aluminum assembly engineered to suppress temperature variations within the cavity. Thermal finite element simulations quantify these gradient effects and indicate that the observed drift is likely constrained by the aging of the laser diode.

Kuleshov and Orlov established structure theorems regarding exceptional objects and collections within the bounded derived category of coherent sheaves on del Pezzo surfaces. This paper extends these findings to weak del Pezzo surfaces through a set of conjectures. Unlike their del Pezzo counterparts, exceptional objects on weak del Pezzo surfaces are not necessarily shifts of sheaves and cannot be uniquely identified by their classes in the Grothendieck group. Our conjectures address these complexities by utilizing spherical twists, which represent the categorification of $(-2)$-reflections acting on the derived category.

The primary focus of this work is resolving these conjectures for the prototypical weak del Pezzo surface $\Sigma_{2}$, the Hirzebruch surface of degree 2. We demonstrate that any exceptional object can be mapped to the unique exceptional vector bundle (up to shift) via a product of spherical twists that acts trivially on the derived category's Grothendieck group. Furthermore, we show that every exceptional collection on $\Sigma_{2}$ is contained within a full exceptional collection. Additionally, we prove that the braid group on four strands acts transitively on the set of exceptional collections of length four, modulo shifts.
By employing sieves and basic techniques, we demonstrate that the signs of partial sums of M\"obius-type quantities across divisors exhibit a strong form of equidistribution.

The High Altitude Water Cherenkov (HAWC) observatory is an air-shower detector engineered to investigate TeV gamma rays and cosmic rays. It consists of an array covering $22,000 \, m^2$, comprising $300$ water Cherenkov tanks ($4.5 \, m$ deep and $7.3 \, m$ in diameter), each equipped with four photomultipliers (PMTs). During events, the system records the count of triggered PMTs, timing data, and the total charge accumulated. These measurements allow for the estimation of key shower parameters, including arrival direction, ground core position, lateral age, and primary energy. This study examines the relationship between shower age and primary energy using data collected by HAWC from June 2015 to June 2019. By applying a shower-age cut derived from QGSJET-II-04 predictions, the researchers isolated a subsample of events dominated by hydrogen and helium nuclei. Through a specialized analysis of this data, the cosmic ray spectrum for H+He was reconstructed between $6$ and $158$ TeV, revealing a softening feature near $24$ TeV with a statistical significance of $4.1\sigma$.

A primary hurdle in cell-free (CF) massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) networks is establishing backhaul connections for numerous distributed access points (APs). Typically, deploying fiber-optic backhaul for these APs proves cost-prohibitive and hinders network scalability. Wireless backhauling offers a viable alternative, capable of being merged with wireless access links to enhance spectrum efficiency. This paper examines the implementation of integrated access and backhaul (IAB) within millimeter-wave (mmWave) CF massive MIMO environments. In this setup, access and backhaul links operate on shared mmWave spectrum, utilizing hybrid beamforming for signal transmission in both directions. The study optimizes bandwidth allocation between the two link types and the corresponding beamforming matrices to maximize end-to-end data rates. This optimization results in a non-convex problem, for which an efficient solution method is introduced. Simulation outcomes demonstrate the efficacy of the IAB technique and the proposed scheme in CF massive MIMO systems. Furthermore, these simulations compare the proposed hybrid beamforming approach against a fully digital solution regarding the count of radio frequency (RF) chains and backhaul traffic volume. Finally, the analysis explores how increasing the number of APs impacts user data rates under constraints of both wireless access and backhaul links.

This work investigates a potential calibration method for the nEXO experiment, which utilizes a $^{127}$Xe electron capture source. nEXO represents a next-generation effort to detect neutrinoless double beta decay ($0\nu\beta\beta$) employing a 5-tonne, monolithic liquid xenon time projection chamber (TPC). The xenon serves dual roles as both the source and detection medium and is enriched to 90% in $^{136}$Xe. To enhance event reconstruction and energy resolution, calibrations are required to account for the detector's position- and time-dependent response. Given the 36.3-day half-life of $^{127}$Xe and its significantly lower $Q$-value relative to the $^{136}$Xe $0\nu\beta\beta$ transition, a low-level activity can be sustained continuously within the detector during standard operations without adding background noise. This capability facilitates in-situ calibration and monitoring of the detector's response. The paper outlines the procedures for fabricating this source and presents preliminary experimental results. Furthermore, simulations are employed to estimate the precision with which such a source can calibrate spatial corrections for the light and charge signals in the nEXO TPC.

Adaptive remote instruction has yielded critical lessons for the future, such as reinterpreting established pedagogical principles within novel contexts and generating fresh insights for supporting distance learning. Focusing on a single computer science department serving both residential and remote undergraduate and graduate populations, we gathered data through interviews with 26 departmental stakeholders and a survey of 102 students across four academic quarters, from spring 2020 to spring 2021. This case study details instructor actions, synthesizes feedback from both faculty and students regarding courses during this timeframe, and offers guidance for similar CS departments moving forward. Key findings address: (1) optimal structuring of instructional components for students; (2) methods for assessing student learning; and (3) strategies for supporting student-initiated learning activities. The study institution is a major U.S. research university with an established history of online initiatives, including remote enrollment for on-campus classes and large-scale open-access courses. Consequently, our recommendations for instructors within this department may also prove valuable for other institutions offering technology-enhanced in-person instruction, remote enrollment options, and hybrid course models.

Typeface styles frequently evoke specific impressions, such as heaviness, modernity, or elegance, suggesting a correlation between font morphology and perceived attributes. To elucidate this relationship, the paper constructs a shared latent space where both fonts and their associated impressions are embedded in proximity. A primary challenge lies in the inherent noise of impression words, which stem from their subjective and varied nature; furthermore, irrelevant descriptors can disrupt the formation of this shared space. Consequently, the study employs DeepSets to automatically reinforce shape-relevant terms and filter out irrelevant ones during the training of the latent space. Experimental results on a large-scale dataset, both quantitative and qualitative, confirm that the proposed method effectively captures these correlations, particularly for impression words directly tied to font shapes.

We present an experimentally demonstrated, resource-efficient realization of the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) leveraging four-dimensional photonic states derived from single photons. This four-dimensional encoding is achieved by exploiting both the polarization and path degrees of freedom of individual photons. Our photonic VQE incorporates a quantum error mitigation (QEM) protocol designed to effectively suppress Pauli noise within the quantum processing unit. We utilized this approach to calculate the ground state energy of the He--H$^{+}$ cation. Both simulation and experimental data confirm that our resource-efficient photonic VQE can precisely determine the bond dissociation curve, maintaining accuracy despite significant noise in the quantum processing unit.

We demonstrate the existence of a suitable $C_2$-fixed points functor mapping calculus with Reality to Weiss's orthogonal calculus, thereby recovering the latter "up to a shift." This process mirrors the recovery of real topological $K$-theory from Atiyah's $K$-theory with Reality through the use of appropriate $C_2$-fixed points.

The human capacity for continual learning (CL) is intrinsically linked to the Stability-Plasticity Dilemma, which explains the balance between retaining acquired knowledge and acquiring new skills. Since the inception of artificial intelligence (AI), the concept of CL has remained central. This paper offers a comprehensive review of CL, distinguishing itself from prior surveys that primarily addressed catastrophic forgetting by adopting a broader, macroscopic perspective grounded in the Stability-Plasticity mechanism. Drawing parallels to biological systems, advanced AI agents must i) recall past knowledge (information retrospection), ii) continuously adapt to new data (information prospection), and iii) leverage useful insights (information transfer) to realize high-level CL. The study subsequently outlines a taxonomy, evaluation metrics, algorithms, applications, and outstanding challenges. Key contributions include re-examining CL through the lens of artificial general intelligence, delivering an exhaustive overview of CL domains, and proposing innovative directions for future development.

Deriving semantic representations directly from raw speech signals is a difficult yet valuable endeavor for speech mining and spoken language understanding. This research addresses the challenge of unsupervised learning for spoken utterances by introducing WavEmbed, a multimodal sequential autoencoder that predicts hidden units derived from acoustic discovery within a dense speech representation. Additionally, we propose S-HuBERT, which induces meaning via knowledge distillation: a sentence embedding model is first trained on these hidden units and then transfers its knowledge to a speech encoder through contrastive learning. The top-performing model achieves a moderate correlation (0.5–0.6) with human evaluations without requiring any labels or transcriptions. Moreover, these models can be readily extended to utilize textual transcriptions for learning superior speech embeddings that align closely with human annotations. The proposed methods are suitable for creating purely data-driven systems for speech mining, indexing, and search.

We have created and offer AnalyticLC, a new analytical framework and software tool designed for modeling planetary system dynamics. This method incorporates non-coplanar interactions using a disturbing function expanded to the fourth order in eccentricity and inclination. AnalyticLC simulates three-dimensional system dynamics to generate light curves, radial velocity curves, and astrometric signatures, facilitating the simultaneous fitting of these datasets. Our research demonstrates that in a near-resonant three-planet chain with closely spaced super-periods, the transit timing variations (TTVs) from pairwise interactions cannot be simply summed to represent the total system TTVs due to resonance between the super-periods themselves. Consequently, we derived a correction for simultaneous three-planet interactions and integrated it into AnalyticLC. By comparing our model against synthetic data from an N-body integrator, we validated its accuracy. Depending on the highest order of expansion terms retained, AnalyticLC can be up to ten times faster than the state-of-the-art TTVFast N-body integrator, though this speedup diminishes slightly at higher orders. The computational advantage becomes more pronounced over long observation periods since our method's runtime is independent of the data time-span. Photometric accuracy typically reaches a few parts per million (ppm), which is significantly lower than the uncertainties inherent in Kepler and other observatory data. This highly efficient and precise implementation enables the full inversion of numerous observed systems to determine planetary physical and orbital parameters, as detailed in a companion paper.

Amid the rising prevalence of interconnected devices, there is a critical demand for enhanced computing resources tailored to delay-sensitive applications. This paper introduces a Fog computing architecture grounded in priority queues, integrated with dynamic scalability of Fog devices. This approach not only minimizes latency for time-critical tasks by distinguishing between delay-sensitive and delay-insensitive workloads but also adaptively distributes Fog devices based on network computation loads to optimize power efficiency. The findings demonstrate that the proposed algorithm achieves substantially reduced delays for both task categories compared to existing schemes, while lowering power consumption by 14.5%.

When consecutive blocks of $N$ letters from a semi-infinite individual sequence $X$ over a finite alphabet are compressed into binary strings via a one-to-one mapping, the encoder lacks prior knowledge of $X$ and must employ a universal data-compression method. It is established that successively applying the universal LZ77 algorithm to these $N$-blocks yields the optimal error-free compression for the specific sequence $X$ as $N$ approaches infinity.
