Our analytical findings and numerical illustrations demonstrate that this framework is orthogonal to traditional transition matrix methods, yielding more granular and refined estimates. Furthermore, to support empirical implementation, we present a publicly accessible statistical methodology and demonstrate its utility using data on income dynamics in the USA. These findings enhance our comprehension of income temporal properties in real-world economies and offer instrumental tools for crafting policy interventions.

The unprecedented population of GRBs observed by Fermi-LAT reveals novel high-energy gamma-ray characteristics, offering intriguing and unforeseen insights into the mechanisms driving both prompt and afterglow emissions. Over the past six years, Swift has established a robust dataset of UV/optical and X-ray afterglow data, illuminating various components of GRB emission structures. The connection between LAT-detected GRBs and the well-studied, fainter, less energetic bursts identified by Swift-BAT is only starting to be investigated through multi-wavelength analyses. This study examines large samples of GRBs detected exclusively by BAT, by both BAT and Fermi-GBM, or by GBM and LAT, analyzing these groups separately to identify statistically significant population differences. By restricting the analysis to GRBs with measured redshifts, we aim to physically characterize these objects. Furthermore, we distinguish between instrumental selection biases and intrinsic properties to better comprehend the unique nature of LAT bursts.

Effective models describing strongly interacting matter must align with astrophysical constraints on compact stars. By employing the (axial-)vector meson extended linear sigma model as the equation of state, we calculate the mass-radius relationship and evaluate its consistency with observational limits, assuming quark matter dominates the stellar interior. Furthermore, we examine how variations in the model's parameters influence this mass-radius relation.

Recent proposals indicate that specific perturbations to integrable spin chains result in a weak integrability breaking, where integrability remains intact to first order in the coupling constant. This assertion is investigated here through the analysis of level spacing distributions. Our findings reveal a distinct volume-dependent crossover between integrable and chaotic level spacing statistics, which signals the emergence of quantum chaos, depending on whether the integrability breaking is weak or strong. Specifically, in the gapless regime, the crossover coupling as a function of system size $L$ follows a $1/L^2$ scaling law for weak breaking, contrasting with the $1/L^3$ scaling previously observed for strong breaking.

This study investigates a solution resembling the Bardeen metric, augmented by a cosmological constant and enveloped by quintessence, demonstrating that it arises from Einstein's equations coupled with nonlinear electrodynamics. We identify the specific conditions required for the solution to remain regular, noting that regularity is not guaranteed in all cases. Furthermore, we examine the associated thermodynamics by deriving the Smarr formula and the first law of thermodynamics. Key thermodynamic properties—including pressure, temperature, heat capacity, and isothermal compressibility—are calculated to determine the existence and nature of phase transitions. Our analysis reveals that for certain parameter values, the solution undergoes a first-order phase transition, behaving similarly to a van der Waals fluid.

This study presents a search for the Higgs boson decaying into two oppositely charged muons using data from the CMS experiment at CERN's LHC, collected in 2016 at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV with an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$. The observed data aligns with the predicted background. For a Higgs boson mass of 125.09 GeV, the 95% confidence level observed (and background-only expected) upper limit on the production cross section times branching fraction to muon pairs is 3.0 (2.5) times the Standard Model prediction. When combined with data from center-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV, the background-only expected upper limit tightens to 2.2 times the Standard Model value, yielding an expected significance of 1.0 standard deviation. The corresponding observed upper limit is 2.9 with an observed significance of 0.9 standard deviations. These results translate to an observed upper limit on the Standard Model Higgs boson branching fraction to muons of $6.4 \times 10^{-4}$ and an observed signal strength of $1.0 \pm 1.0$ (stat) $\pm 0.1$ (syst).

This study explores magnetic monopoles capable of generating multimagnetic structures, achieved by extending the $\rm{SU(2)}$ gauge group. The analysis relies on a modified relativistic framework incorporating multiple gauge and matter fields, which establishes a Bogomol'nyi bound and enables a first-order formalism for constructing stable multimagnetic solutions. We demonstrate these results through various examples of stable magnetic monopoles exhibiting multimagnetic characteristics.

We address the random energy model under the condition that configuration energies are restricted to integer values. In the thermodynamic limit, average overlaps exhibit size dependence and oscillate as the system grows. Although the extensive component of the free energy can still be derived using a standard replica calculation with one step replica symmetry breaking, this method fails to recover the overlaps. A viable adaptation of the replica approach involves permitting fluctuations in the sizes of the blocks within the Parisi matrix and allowing these blocks to assume complex values.

The electronic structure of twisted bilayer GeSe, characterized by a rectangular moiré pattern, is investigated using a $\bm{k}\cdot\bm{p}$ effective continuum model. This model is built upon a local approximation approach, wherein the twisted bilayer's local lattice is modeled as an untwisted bilayer with parallel displacement, and the necessary parameters are determined via first-principles calculations. By examining how physical properties vary with the twist angle, we establish a connection between the effective potential within the moiré pattern and the alignment of Ge atoms, as well as the emergence of a resultant one-dimensional flat band that exhibits stronger flattening in a specific direction compared to the perpendicular one. Given the relatively large effective mass of the constituent monolayers, this narrow flat band, with a width of only a few meV, appears at relatively large twist angles, thereby offering a unique opportunity to study dimensional crossover within twisted bilayer systems.

To explore how end-users conceptualize the consequences of cybersecurity attacks, we conducted a card sorting study, a recognized method in Cognitive Science. In this open-ended task, participants freely grouped the consequences of selected cyber attacks into as many categories as they deemed appropriate based on their own rationales. The results revealed significant variation among participants, prompting the research team to investigate how these individuals comprehended security attack outcomes. Seeking to determine if Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques could elucidate user mental models and behaviors, the team compared the card sorting data against outputs from various Natural Language Processing (NLP) methods. The objective was to understand how participants perceived and interpreted natural language descriptions of cyber attack consequences. The NLP-based analysis yielded an intriguing finding: participants primarily grouped consequences by checking individual keywords within sentences rather than considering the underlying semantics of the descriptions. The findings presented in this paper are deemed valuable for understanding cyber attacks from a user perspective. To our knowledge, this study is the first to introduce AI techniques for explaining and modeling user behavior and perceptions regarding a specific context. The novel contribution of this work lies in utilizing AI to explain user cognition.

Estimating subsurface velocity fields is a critical component of seismic processing, reservoir characterization, and hydrocarbon volume estimation within the Oil and Gas sector. While Full-Waveform Inversion (FWI) offers an advanced, iterative method for generating highly accurate and detailed velocity models, it incurs substantial computational expenses due to the physics-based numerical simulations required at every iteration. This study introduces a method to produce velocity field models with a level of detail comparable to FWI results by employing a conditional generative adversarial network (cGAN) utilizing multiple inputs. The primary objective of this approach is to eliminate the prohibitive costs associated with traditional FWI velocity modeling. The proposed network architecture was trained and validated using real-world data, with quality assessed through three metrics: percent error, structural similarity index measure (SSIM), and visual analysis. Evaluation against a test set demonstrates that the GAN successfully replicates real FWI outputs, effectively capturing key geological structures and lateral velocity variations from input data. Experimental findings suggest that deploying this method could significantly accelerate geophysical reservoir characterization, thereby reducing both time and computational resource requirements.

According to WHO data, as of August 12, 2021, there were over 204,617,027 confirmed global COVID-19 cases and 4,323,247 fatalities, leading to widespread mask usage during the pandemic. Traditional face recognition methods typically rely on unobstructed facial features like the eyes, nose, and mouth. Requiring individuals to remove masks for verification in secure settings like airports or labs significantly raises infection risks, presenting a major hurdle for existing recognition systems. In response to this gap and the lack of real-world masked face recognition (MFR) benchmarks, we established the Face Bio-metrics under COVID Workshop and the Masked Face Recognition Challenge at ICCV 2021. Leveraging the massive WebFace260M dataset and the Face Recognition Under Inference Time conStraint (FRUITS) protocol, this challenge aims to advance practical MFR capabilities. To address the limitations of existing noisy or saturated public datasets, we curated a new test set featuring 2,478 celebrities and 60,926 faces, alongside the largest real-world collection of masked test images. In the first phase, 69 teams submitted 833 solutions, with 49 surpassing our baseline performance. The challenge continues through October 1, 2021, with an active leaderboard and plans for future report updates.

Wavefront errors, specifically non-common path aberrations (NCPAs), constrain the performance of high-contrast imaging instruments. Focal-plane wavefront sensing (FPWFS) is well-suited for addressing NCPAs because it measures aberrations at the critical science focal plane. However, phase retrieval from focal-plane images suffers from a sign ambiguity regarding even modes of the pupil-plane phase. Current phase diversity methods used to resolve this ambiguity often reduce the science duty cycle, thereby limiting the fraction of observing time available for science. This study investigates combining vortex coronagraph phase diversity with modern deep learning to achieve efficient FPWFS without sacrificing observing time. We employed the state-of-the-art convolutional neural network EfficientNet-B4 to infer phase aberrations from simulated focal-plane images, evaluating both scalar (SVC) and vector (VVC) vortex coronagraphs using either a single post-coronagraphic point spread function (PSF) or two PSFs derived from splitting circular polarization states. The sign ambiguity was successfully resolved in both configurations, even at low signal-to-noise ratios. Performance with either the SVC or VVC matched that of phase diversity with a defocused PSF across most scenarios, though the SVC slightly underperformed at very high aberration levels. The models demonstrated robustness when trained on data spanning a wide range of wavefront errors and noise levels. Ultimately, the proposed FPWFS technique offers a 100% science duty cycle for vortex coronagraph instruments and requires no additional hardware when using an SVC.

The rapid evolution of drug repositioning for COVID-19 treatment has inspired this study, which develops computational models to support this process. The primary objective is to provide clinicians with a resource for identifying promising antiviral therapies, particularly given the virus's high mutation rate, ensuring the right antivirals are selected for specific viral isolates.

The central contribution is a publicly accessible, manually curated database containing known associations between viruses and antivirals. This database leverages both drug chemical structures and viral genomic sequences to gather similarity data. Accompanying the database are state-of-the-art computational drug repositioning tools based on matrix completion techniques. These tools were initially validated using standard experimental protocols for drug-target interactions, with the top performers subsequently applied to reposition antivirals for COVID-19.

The analysis identified six candidate drugs: four are currently in various trial stages—Remdesivir (for cure), Ribavirin (in combination for cure), Umifenovir (for prophylaxis and cure), and Sofosbuvir (for cure). Additionally, Tenofovir alafenamide, a novel prodrug designed to enhance renal safety compared to tenofovir disoproxil, was unanimously predicted; both are under trial, the former as a cure and the latter as prophylaxis. These findings confirm that the computational methods align with current practices. Furthermore, the study illustrates how selected drugs shift as SARS-CoV-2 mutates, highlighting the critical value of such predictive tools.

The dataset and software are available at https://github.com/aanchalMongia/DVA, while the user-friendly prediction tool can be accessed at http://dva.salsa.iiitd.edu.in.

This study quantifies the field-aligned anisotropy of solar wind turbulence, defined by the ratio of parallel to perpendicular correlation and Taylor length scales, using simultaneous two-point correlation measurements spanning 2001 to 2017. The findings indicate that at both solar maximum and minimum, the correlation scale is greatest along the magnetic field and smallest in the field-perpendicular directions. Conversely, the Taylor scale exhibits inconsistent behavior across different solar cycle phases: from 2001 to 2004, it was slightly larger in the parallel direction, whereas from 2004 to 2017, it was larger in the perpendicular direction. To assess the impact of solar activity on turbulence anisotropy, the correlation coefficient between sunspot numbers and the anisotropy ratio was analyzed. Results reveal a higher correlation coefficient for Taylor scale anisotropy (0.65) compared to correlation scale anisotropy (0.43), suggesting that Taylor scale anisotropy is more responsive to solar activity. Additionally, the effective magnetic Reynolds number, derived from both scales, is consistently larger in the field-parallel direction than in the field-perpendicular direction, with a correlation coefficient of -0.75 between sunspot numbers and the magnetic Reynolds number anisotropy ratio. These results offer valuable insights into solar wind turbulence anisotropy and its long-term variability within the context of solar activity.

Monocular 3D object detection (Mono3D) has seen significant advancements driven by large-scale autonomous driving datasets and the rapid evolution of deep learning. Nevertheless, severe domain gaps—such as differences in field of view, pixel size, and object dimensions across datasets—hinder the generalization of Mono3D detectors, causing substantial performance drops on unseen domains. To address these challenges, we integrate position-invariant transforms, multi-scale training, and a pixel-size depth strategy to establish an effective unified camera-generalized paradigm (CGP) that fully accounts for variations in image FOV and pixel size. Furthermore, through an exhaustive systematic study, we identified a critical obstacle in quantitative metrics during cross-dataset inference: a size bias in predictions leads to significant failure. Consequently, we propose the 2D-3D geometry-consistent object scaling strategy (GCOS), which bridges this gap through instance-level augmentation. Our proposed method, DGMono3D, achieves outstanding performance across all evaluated datasets, outperforming state-of-the-art unsupervised domain adaptation schemes even without access to target domain data.

We present a new module designed to simulate physical systems where particle motion is influenced by stochastic forces, phenomena anticipated in turbulent circumstellar or remnant planetesimal disks. This implementation provides a straightforward method for generating correlated noise with user-defined amplitude and auto-correlation times for individual particles. The module operates with minimal memory demands and is freely accessible through the REBOUNDx additional effects library.

We demonstrate that the lower-semicontinuous envelope of a non-convex double integral might fail to possess a representation as a double integral. By constructing an integrand that equals $+\infty$ everywhere except at three specific points (e.g., $-1$, $0$, and $1$), we provide a straightforward proof and an explicit formula for the relaxation, which may offer new insights into such problems. This work presents a simplified adaptation of examples by Mora-Corral and Tellini, as well as Kreisbeck and Zappale, who characterized the lower-semicontinuous envelope using Young measures.

This study examines the integer quantum Hall effect in Cd3As2 thin films subjected to strong and moderate quantum confinement, utilizing sample thicknesses of 10, 12, and 15 nm. Across all films, we detect the integer quantum Hall effect within the spin-polarized lowest Landau level at a filling factor of $
u = 1$, as well as at spin-degenerate higher-index Landau levels characterized by even filling factors ($
u = 2, 4, 6$). As quantum confinement increases, we observe the removal of spin degeneracy at $
u = 3$, evidenced by anomalies in both longitudinal and Hall resistivity. Tight-binding simulations indicate that the resulting enhancement of the g-factor stems from a synergy between quantum confinement and corrections from adjacent subbands. Additionally, we discuss the magnetic field-driven transition from an insulating state to a quantum Hall liquid occurring when the chemical potential is positioned near the charge neutrality point.

We directly derive multidimensional bosonization from the electron gas within a low-energy, low-momentum regime where $\omega\gg \frac{k^2}{k_F}$, allowing for the linearization of the dispersion relation. To achieve this limit, we simultaneously scale the Fermi momentum and the number of patches while maintaining a finite width for each patch. Applying this approach yields an exact low-energy solution for a Fermi surface coupled to a gapless boson, free from disorder and electron-electron scattering. Contrary to existing literature, we demonstrate that the bosonized theory precisely reproduces the $\omega^{2/3}$ scaling of electrons previously found in large-$N$ theories. Furthermore, we argue that corrections to the self-energy arising from tangential dispersion are subdominant at sufficiently low energies, specifically when $v_F k\gg \left(\frac{g^4 v_F}{k_F}\right)^{1/3} \omega^{2/3}$, with $g$ representing the coupling constant.

Driven by the hypothesis that new physics could appear as extremely massive particles, the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) primarily operates with proton-proton ($pp$) collisions at peak energies and luminosities. However, the resulting high collision rates necessitate stringent trigger conditions, such as high transverse momentum ($p_T$) thresholds for final-state particles, and introduce significant background noise from pileup events occurring within the same bunch crossing. This approach may be suboptimal for certain well-motivated new physics scenarios where particles are relatively light and weakly coupled, causing them to evade the online selection criteria of the LHC's multi-purpose detectors. A viable alternative involves utilizing complementary datasets routinely gathered by the experiments, including heavy ion collisions, low-pileup runs optimized for precision measurements, and specialized "parking" and "scouting" datasets. Although these datasets serve various physics objectives, they share the common advantage of employing lower $p_T$ thresholds at the trigger level. This study evaluates the effectiveness of these datasets for a representative model characterized by clean signatures of long-lived resonances that produce displaced dimuon vertices. Using the Delphes simulation to model Run 2 and Run 3 LHC data, we compare the discovery reach across these datasets with a straightforward analysis. Our results indicate that scouting and parking datasets, which achieve low $p_T$ triggers by utilizing partial detector information and delaying event reconstruction respectively, offer sensitivity comparable to the standard $pp$ dataset with conventional thresholds. Conversely, we find that heavy ion and low-pileup datasets are significantly less competitive for this specific signature.

The Leding-Logarithmic (LL) gluon Sudakov formfactor emerges from rapidity-ordered BFKL evolution that incorporates longitudinal-momentum conservation. This approach not only elucidates the connection between High-Energy and TMD factorizations but also allows for extensions beyond the LL-approximation.

This paper aims to establish a specific result regarding the moduli of curve families within the Heisenberg group. Let $\Omega$ denote a domain in the Heisenberg group that is foliated by a family $\Gamma$ of Legendrian curves. Suppose there exists a quadratic differential $q$ defined on $\Omega$ that lies in the kernel of the operator described in \cite{Tim2}, such that every curve in $\Gamma$ follows a horizontal trajectory of $q$. Define $l_\Gamma : \Omega \rightarrow ]0,+\infty[$ as the function assigning to each point $p\in \Omega$ the $q$-length of the leaf passing through $p$. Consequently, the modulus of $\Gamma$ is given by the formula:
\[ M_4 (\Gamma) = \int_\Omega \frac{|q|^2}{(l_\Gamma) ^4} \mathrm{d} L^3. \]

We investigate neutrinoless double beta ($0\nu \beta\beta$) decay triggered by an ultralight dark matter field interacting with neutrinos. If this interaction violates lepton number, the $\Delta L=2$ transition is directly mediated by the dark matter field, bypassing the suppression typically caused by small neutrino masses, thereby producing a significant effect on decay rates. Because ultralight dark matter behaves as a classical field, the resulting decay events exhibit a periodic modulation. However, we observe that in the early Universe, such a coupling would likely disrupt standard cosmological models. Specifically, the necessity for neutrinos to free-stream prior to matter-radiation equality imposes strict constraints on the parameter space, rendering the detection of any signal in future $0\nu \beta\beta$ experiments extremely unlikely, even with meV-level sensitivity to the effective neutrino mass.

**Aims.** This study seeks to determine the contribution of various Type Ia supernova (SN Ia) sub-classes to the Galaxy's chemical enrichment by analyzing iron and manganese abundances in Galactic stars. We examine four distinct SN Ia categories: the classical single-degenerate near-Chandrasekhar mass ($M_{\text{ch}}$) events, the fainter SN Iax systems linked to helium accretion from companions, and two sub-Chandrasekhar mass (sub-$M_{\text{ch}}$) models. The latter comprise double-detonation scenarios involving helium-rich accretion and violent white dwarf mergers.

**Methods.** Chemical abundances in Galactic stars are derived using Gaia eDR3 astrometry and photometry alongside publicly available spectra from the Gaia-ESO large spectroscopic survey. Spectroscopic analysis employs non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE) models. Galactic chemical evolution (GCE) models have been revised to incorporate detailed delay time distributions from binary population synthesis simulations, accounting for diverse SN Ia channels, as well as updated yields for core-collapse supernovae and AGB stars. A Markov chain Monte Carlo framework is utilized for data-model comparison, enabling an exploration of the full parameter space defined by varying explosion mechanisms and Galactic SN Ia rates, while integrating observational uncertainties.

**Results.** Comparing new data with GCE models indicates that observations can only be reconciled if the fraction of sub-$M_{\text{ch}}$ SNe in the models ranges from 50% to 73%. While standard $M_{\text{ch}}$ SNe are not the dominant channel, they remain necessary to explain the elevated [Mn/Fe] ratio in the thin disc. Our findings exhibit only weak dependence on assumptions regarding AGB and core-collapse SN yields, providing robust evidence that sub-$M_{\text{ch}}$ SNe play a pivotal role in the chemical evolution of the Galaxy.

Although deeper and wider Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) typically enhance performance in deep learning, they often yield diminishing returns per added parameter. This paper explores whether the benefits of increased depth stem solely from the expansion of optimization parameters or if the network's physical dimensions also contribute. We introduce a novel rescaling strategy for CNNs utilizing learnable parameter repetition. By applying this approach, we can scale CNNs without altering their parameter count, demonstrating that learnable weight sharing alone can significantly boost model performance. Our findings indicate that small base networks, when rescaled, can achieve performance comparable to much deeper models using as few as 6% of the optimization parameters. Furthermore, we examine group-equivariant CNNs to highlight the importance of weight sharing, revealing that improvements over standard CNNs on classification tasks are only partially attributable to equivariance; the remainder arises from learnable weight repetition. Specifically, on the rot-MNIST dataset, we find that up to 40% of the relative gains reported by state-of-the-art rotation-equivariant methods may actually result from this learned weight repetition rather than equivariance alone.

This study analyzes the proper motion of the Andromeda galaxy (M31) using the Early Third Data Release from the Gaia mission. By selecting young blue main sequence stars via Gaia photometry and applying rigorous quality filters, we generated clean tracer samples. After adjusting for the internal rotation of M31's disk, we calculated an apparent motion of 52.5 +/- 5.8 muas/yr relative to the Gaia reference frame. Following zero-point corrections derived from nearby quasars and adjustments for systemic biases, this value shifts to 61.9 +/- 9.7 muas/yr. When accounting for Solar reflex motion, the relative velocity between Andromeda and the Milky Way (in a non-rotating frame at the Sun's current position) is determined to be 42.2 +/- 39.3 km/s along right ascension (40.0 +/- 39.3 km/s along galactic longitude) and -59.4 +/- 30.3 km/s along declination (-60.9 +/- 30.3 km/s along galactic latitude), yielding a total transverse velocity of V_trans = 82.4 +/- 31.2 km/s. These results align with, yet improve upon, earlier Hubble Space Telescope measurements that anticipate a future galactic merger. Additionally, we observed a significant discrepancy in proper motion between blue stars in M31 and samples of red stars within the same galaxy. While we proposed several hypotheses to address this inconsistency, current data do not support any single explanation over the others.

PDDLStream solvers have recently become a viable option for Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) by extending PDDL to handle continuous action spaces. Previous research demonstrated that PDDLStream problems can be decomposed into a sequence of standard PDDL planning tasks solvable by existing planners, though this method often results in lengthy runtimes. This paper introduces LAZY, a PDDLStream solver that performs a single, integrated search over action skeletons, becoming increasingly geometrically informed as possible motions are lazily sampled during the planning process. We investigate how to incorporate learned goal-directed policies and current motion sampling data into LAZY to adaptively guide the task planner. Our results show that this approach significantly accelerates the search for feasible solutions across unseen test environments with varying object counts, goals, and initial states. Furthermore, we evaluate our TAMP methodology by comparing it against existing PDDLStream solvers on a diverse set of simulated 7DoF rearrangement and manipulation tasks.

This paper extends Theorem 5.1.1 from \cite{Helein} by H\'elein to a rescaled sequence of branched conformal immersions, as presented in Theorem 1.5. Leveraging this local convergence result, we investigate the blowup behavior of sequences of branched conformal immersions of closed Riemannian surfaces in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$, where both the areas and Willmore energies remain uniformly bounded. Additionally, we establish the validity of the integral identity for Gauss curvature.

A fundamental aspect of making sequential decisions under uncertainty involves balancing exploitation—selecting the optimal action based on current knowledge—with exploration—gathering information regarding the values of alternative actions. The multi-armed bandit problem, a classic task that embodies this trade-off, has historically driven the development of bandit algorithms in machine learning, which have proven highly valuable across various industrial applications. In contrast, the active inference framework, a recently developed approach in neuroscience aimed at understanding human and animal behavior, is characterized by a sophisticated strategy for resolving the exploration-exploitation dilemma. This distinction positions active inference as a promising alternative to established bandit methods. In this work, we present an efficient and scalable approximate active inference algorithm and evaluate it against two state-of-the-art bandit approaches: Bayesian upper confidence bound and optimistic Thompson sampling. The comparison spans two bandit environments: stationary and dynamic switching scenarios. Our empirical findings indicate that while the active inference algorithm fails to achieve efficient long-term behavior in stationary bandits, it significantly outperforms the two competing bandit algorithms in the more complex switching bandit problem. These results highlight new avenues for research in both theoretical and applied machine learning and further bolster the credibility of active inference as a comprehensive framework for studying human and animal behavior.

Gun violence remains a critical global issue, especially within the United States. Researchers have explored deep learning techniques to identify firearms in surveillance and smart IP camera feeds, enabling real-time notifications for security personnel. A primary obstacle in advancing gun detection algorithms is the scarcity of extensive public datasets. This study introduces a new resource comprising 51,000 annotated images for gun detection and an additional 51,000 cropped gun chip images for classification, aggregated from various sources. To our knowledge, this constitutes the largest dataset available for gun detection research, accessible at www.linksprite.com/gun-detection-datasets. We also present a detection system utilizing a smart IP camera as an embedded edge device, paired with a cloud server to manage devices, data, and alerts, thereby minimizing false positives. Our research addresses solutions for gun detection on embedded hardware and classification across both edge and cloud environments. This edge-cloud architecture facilitates the practical deployment of gun detection systems in real-world scenarios.

Recent benchmark studies indicate that despite reported advancements, certain machine learning sub-fields have stagnated. This lack of progress stems partly from the irreproducibility of numerous model comparison studies, which often fail to account for known sources of irreproducibility. Consequently, these results cannot be independently verified by others. Our goal is to survey the literature to present an overview and taxonomy of reported irreproducibility sources, discuss these issues, and propose three avenues for future research.

We demonstrate that the M\"obius function is linearly disjoint from a specific family of distal skew products defined on the product space $\mathbb{T}\times\Gamma\setminus G$, where $\mathbb{T}$ denotes the unit circle and $\Gamma\setminus G$ represents the 3-dimensional Heisenberg nilmanifold. This finding extends upon recent research conducted by Huang, Liu, and Wang.

Define $\Delta_d^{(a,-)}(n) = q_d^{(a)}(n) - Q_d^{(a,-)}(n)$, where $q_d^{(a)}(n)$ represents the count of partitions of $n$ into parts with a minimum difference of $d$ and a minimum size of $a$, while $Q_d^{(a,-)}(n)$ counts partitions into parts congruent to $\pm a \pmod{d+3}$, excluding the part $d+3-a$. Inspired by an effort to extend a conjecture by Kang and Park, Duncan, Khunger, Swisher, and the second author proposed that $\Delta_d^{(3,-)}(n) \geq 0$ for all $d \geq 1$ and $n \geq 1$, a result they verified when $d \geq 31$ is a multiple of 3. They also conjectured a similar inequality for larger $a$ values, defining the modified difference function $\Delta_{d}^{(a,-,-)}(n) = q_{d}^{(a)}(n) - Q_{d}^{(a,-,-)}(n) \geq 0$, where $Q_{d}^{(a,-,-)}(n)$ counts partitions into parts $\equiv \pm a \pmod{d + 3}$ excluding both $a$ and $d+3-a$. This inequality was proven for infinitely many classes of $n$ and $d$. In this work, we demonstrate that $\Delta_{d}^{(3,-)}(n) \geq 0$ holds for all but a finite number of $d$. Furthermore, we prove the generalized conjecture for all but finitely many $d$ when $a$ is fixed, thereby strengthening previous results by Duncan, Khunger, Swisher, and the second author. We also offer a conditional proof of a linear lower bound on $d$ for the generalized conjecture, refining our unconditional finding which relied on a conjectural adjustment to a recently established theorem by Alder. Leveraging this modification, we derive an enhanced version of the generalization of Kang and Park's conjecture that notably permits $a$ as a valid part. Finally, we present asymptotic evidence supporting the validity of this strengthened conjecture.

This work introduces direct inversion techniques to deduce fluid rheology from observations of shallow flows. Initially, we derive the evolution equation for inertia-less currents with general constitutive laws governing free-surface flow. A single function, $F(\tau_b)$, which relies solely on the constitutive law, links basal stress ($\tau_b$) to volume flux. The inversion process involves three steps: (i) deriving flux and basal stress from free-surface evolution, (ii) comparing these to constrain $F$, and (iii) determining the constitutive law from $F$. Examples of both steady and transient flows illustrate that various constitutive laws can be directly inferred. Additionally, for cases where free-surface velocity is known, we present an alternative approach that eliminates the requirement to calculate flux.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) are highly vulnerable to minute adversarial perturbations, often leading to incorrect predictions. Although various strategies, such as adversarial defenses and uncertainty inference (UI), have emerged to mitigate these threats, this paper introduces a novel Multi-Head Uncertainty Inference (MH-UI) framework specifically designed to identify adversarial examples. The proposed approach utilizes a multi-head architecture featuring multiple classifiers to generate predictions from various depths within the DNN, thereby incorporating shallow information into the UI process. By employing independent heads at different layers, the normalized outputs are modeled as following a shared Dirichlet distribution, with its parameters estimated through moment matching. This method allows cognitive uncertainty induced by adversarial attacks to be captured and amplified within the distribution. Experimental findings demonstrate that the MH-UI framework surpasses all compared UI methods across diverse settings in the task of detecting adversarial attacks.

This study examines a cohort of 600 engineering students enrolled in three sequential physics courses of varying difficulty levels within the curriculum. The research concentrates on identifying the most prevalent misconceptions regarding Newtonian mechanics among these students. The Force Concept Inventory (FCI) was administered at the start of each academic term. Utilizing the FCI's taxonomy of misconceptions, the authors investigated correlations between the number of course attempts to determine if specific misconceptions persist across multiple attempts. Data analysis employed the method of dominant incorrect answers. The findings indicate no significant difference in the frequency of common misconceptions between students on their first attempt and those on their third or subsequent attempt within each course.

This paper details the design, implementation, and assessment of FLSys, a mobile-cloud federated learning (FL) framework tailored for deep learning applications on mobile devices. FLSys serves as a foundational element for establishing an open ecosystem of FL models and applications. The system is engineered to process mobile sensing data from smartphones, optimize the trade-off between model performance and device resource usage, handle communication failures, and ensure cloud scalability. Within FLSys, multiple deep learning models utilizing various FL aggregation techniques can be trained and accessed simultaneously by different applications, alongside a unified API that enables third-party developers to train their own FL models. Implemented on Android and AWS, the system was co-designed with a Human Activity Recognition (HAR) model trained in the wild. Data collection involved over 100 college students across two locations over five months. The resulting HAR-Wild model, a CNN optimized for mobile hardware, incorporates data augmentation to address non-Independent and Identically Distributed (non-IID) data challenges common in real-world FL scenarios. Additionally, a Sentiment Analysis (SA) model trained on a dataset of over 46,000 tweets from 436 users demonstrates FLSys's capacity to support concurrent model operations. Extensive experiments conducted on Android phones and emulators confirm that FLSys delivers both high model utility and practical system performance.

The most prevalent metrics for assessing trajectory prediction models are the Best-of-N (BoN) Average Displacement Error (ADE) and Final Displacement Error (FDE). However, BoN fails to account for all generated samples, offering an incomplete assessment of model performance. To address this, we introduce the Average Mahalanobis Distance (AMD), which measures the proximity of the entire set of generated samples to the ground truth. Additionally, we propose the Average Maximum Eigenvalue (AMV) metric to evaluate the overall spread of predictions. Empirical validation demonstrates that while ADE/FDE remain insensitive to distribution shifts—leading to a biased accuracy perception—our AMD and AMV metrics provide a more robust evaluation. We further present Implicit Maximum Likelihood Estimation (IMLE) as an alternative to traditional generative models for training our architecture, Social-Implicit. The IMLE training framework aligns with the AMD/AMV objectives by ensuring predicted trajectories remain close to the ground truth with a compact distribution. Social-Implicit is a memory-efficient deep model featuring only 5.8K parameters, capable of real-time inference at approximately 580Hz with competitive results. An interactive demonstration is available at https://www.abduallahmohamed.com/social-implicit-amdamv-adefde-demo, and the source code can be found at https://github.com/abduallahmohamed/Social-Implicit.

Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) offer a practical solution for deploying mobile base stations to quickly establish communication services for ground users. However, unlike terrestrial networks, UAVs typically lack fiber optic back-haul connections unless tethered to the ground, which limits their mobility. In scenarios without back-haul infrastructure—such as in remote regions, during emergencies, or on battlefields—it is essential to maintain connectivity among UAVs while ensuring ground user coverage to form local area networks. This paper presents a distributed and dynamic control strategy based on UAV formations to achieve both user coverage and network connectivity. By employing flocking dynamics, the method constructs tailored UAV formations dynamically. Simulation results indicate that with an adequate number of aerial base stations, the proposed approach creates a strongly connected UAV network capable of supporting both backhaul and fronthaul communications. Furthermore, this approach can be expanded to develop multi-tier extra-terrestrial networks suitable for large-scale applications.

As the global COVID-19 crisis unfolds, successful outcomes rely heavily on constructive relationships between the public and policymakers. In the UK, this dynamic was tested early on with uncivil tweets directed at MPs regarding delays in implementing lockdown measures. While the pandemic has heightened scrutiny of ministers involved in the crisis, the majority of public engagement has remained civil. An exception occurred when Prime Minister Boris Johnson fell severely ill, triggering an atypical surge of supportive messages on Twitter. Statistical analysis revealed a significant negative correlation: MPs receiving more mentions regarding COVID-19 in replies tended to face less abuse. However, following Johnson's recovery, abuse levels climbed in May, driven by economic anxieties and public anger over lockdown violations by prominent individuals. The study identified 1,902 replies containing conspiracy hashtags or terms denying the virus's existence (such as #coronahoax or #coronabollocks); these comprised 0.04% of the 4.7 million total replies but accounted for 9% of mentions related to "stay home save lives." Notably, these conspiracy-laden replies were more frequently abusive. Additionally, evidence surfaced of conspiracy theories among the public, with higher abuse rates linked to hashtags that blamed China for the pandemic.

The standard Dobrushin approach fails to derive the mean-field limit for systems of self-propelled agents interacting via topological rules. Instead, we achieve a result in this area by extending Trocheris's 1986 techniques for the one-dimensional Vlasov-Poisson equation to the multidimensional setting.
We establish tight and efficient bounds for the distance separating tori of a constant injectivity radius within a Margulis tube in a hyperbolic 3-manifold.

This paper emphasizes the influence of human social and mobility behaviors on the ongoing development of sustainable socio-technical systems. Our methodology connects human traits and intentions with system objectives to model these interactions. By doing so, we align architectural design and quality of service (QoS) with human quality of experience (QoE). We have created a simulation environment that integrates agent-based social simulation (ABSS) with architectural models produced via a model-driven engineering process. This modeling framework enables the selection of the most suitable architectural model and system configuration to improve sustainability for both people and the system. We applied this approach to the Uffizi Galleries crowd management system, utilizing real-world data to simulate various scenarios affecting QoE. Subsequently, we evaluated different architectural models across diverse software/hardware configurations to recommend the optimal model based on specific QoS-QoE requirements under varying scenarios.

This study introduces a stochastic representation grounded in physical transport principles to model how mesoscale eddies influence large-scale ocean circulation. The proposed framework decomposes Lagrangian velocity into a smooth temporal component and a highly oscillatory noise term. A key feature of this random model is its ability to conserve the total energy of the resolved flow across all realizations. This energy-preserving approach has been effectively integrated into a well-established multi-layered quasi-geostrophic dynamical core. The spatial correlation of the unresolved noise is empirically calibrated using eddy-resolving simulation data. Notably, a stationary correction drift can be incorporated into the noise via a Girsanov transformation; this seemingly counterintuitive term proves essential for accurately reproducing the eastward jet of the wind-driven double-gyre circulation on a coarse grid. Furthermore, a projection method has been developed to restrict the noise to the iso-surfaces of vertical stratification. Consequently, the resulting noise enhances the intrinsic low-frequency variability of the large-scale currents.

Recent years have seen word and sentence embeddings become standard preprocessing for diverse NLP tasks, significantly boosting performance. However, these embeddings inadvertently inherit biases from their training data, propagating societal prejudices into NLP systems. Numerous studies have attempted to measure this bias to evaluate debiasing techniques or compare models, frequently relying on cosine-based metrics. Yet, some research has questioned the reliability of these scores, demonstrating that even when they indicate low bias, underlying prejudices often persist and become evident through alternative tests. Consequently, the literature offers a wide array of bias metrics without reaching a consensus on the optimal approach. There remains a gap in research regarding the behavior of these scores, specifically their pros and cons. This work investigates various cosine-based bias scores by establishing a bias definition grounded in existing literature and deriving new requirements for such metrics. We conduct a thorough analysis of current cosine-based scores to explain why they fail to detect biases in certain scenarios. Finally, we introduce a novel score, SAME, designed to overcome the limitations of existing methods, with empirical evidence showing that SAME is more effective at quantifying bias in word embeddings.

This study investigates the finite-dimensional distributions of the second-order scattering transform applied to a specific class of non-Gaussian processes as all scaling parameters approach infinity simultaneously. For commonly utilized wavelets, we identify a coupling rule linking the scale parameters between the first and second layers of the wavelet transform to ensure the existence of the limit. This rule is explicitly defined using the Hurst index of the long-range dependent inputs. Significantly, the spectral density function of the resulting limiting process can also be expressed explicitly in terms of the Hurst index and the Fourier transform of the mother wavelet. To derive these findings, we first demonstrate that for sufficiently large scale parameters, the scattering transform of non-Gaussian processes can be approximated by the second-order scattering transform of Gaussian processes. Subsequently, employing the moment method, we establish the existence of the doubling scaling limit for each resulting non-Gaussian approximation. The long-range dependent non-Gaussian model examined here is grounded in real data, with all assumptions validated by numerical results.

This note examines a topological implementation of a quantum teleportation protocol, where (non-)locality is defined as a discrete, isotopy-invariant property. This framework offers enhanced control over the transfer of quantum states between causally disconnected regions. An entropy linked to these disconnected regions characterizes the various stages of the protocol, allowing for the introduction of a Page curve analog for Hawking radiation entropy. Furthermore, the paper describes a generalized topological protocol as a toy model of black hole evaporation, demonstrating unitary behavior in the Page curve.

Biased bilayer graphene, characterized by its readily adjustable band gap, serves as an optimal platform for investigating excitonic effects in graphene-based materials. This study examines the excitonic optical response of such a system by integrating a tight-binding model with a semi-analytical solution to the Bethe-Salpeter equation, which relies on a single numerical quadrature to ensure transparent calculations. Our methodology first derives the optical selection rules analytically and then computes the absorption spectrum for a hexagonal boron nitride-encapsulated biased bilayer graphene, a configuration recently explored experimentally. The resulting theoretical predictions demonstrate excellent agreement with existing experimental data.

The stability of graph filters has emerged as a pivotal theoretical attribute underpinning the success of graph convolutional neural networks (GCNs). This stability quantifies how topology perturbations influence a graph filter's output, which serves as a core component of GCNs. While prior research largely addressed scenarios involving minor perturbations with few edge rewires, many practical applications involve a significantly larger number of rewires. To address this, the present study introduces a novel stability bound for graph filters based on their frequency response. Specifically, for low-pass filters, we demonstrate that stability is contingent upon perturbations to the community structure. As an application, we establish that for graphs generated by the stochastic block model, the distance between graph filters converges to zero as the node count approaches infinity. Numerical simulations confirm these theoretical results.

We construct a minimalist compartmental model to evaluate the effects of mobility restrictions imposed in Italy during the COVID-19 outbreak. Our findings indicate that an early lockdown merely delays the epidemic, whereas exceeding a critical threshold of restriction intensity causes the outbreak to resurge once measures are lifted, necessitating tailored mitigation strategies. To assess the relative efficacy of various broad approaches, we account for two primary sources of heterogeneity: geography and demography. First, by treating Italian regions as distinct administrative units with internal age-class interactions, we observe that due to sparse inter-regional mobility, the epidemic tends to evolve independently across areas, supporting the implementation of region-specific or clustered solutions. Second, we demonstrate that inter-age-class social contacts are crucial, and incorporating population age structures into measures significantly helps prevent rebound effects. While our general model does not detail specific strategies, it underscores the importance of key parameters in non-pharmaceutical interventions for epidemic control.

We present 21 cm absorption and emission observations from Arecibo aimed at characterizing the physical properties of neutral hydrogen (HI) near five giant molecular clouds (GMCs): Taurus, California, Rosette, Mon OB1, and NGC 2264. Significant HI absorption was identified toward all 79 background continuum sources within the approximately 60x20 square degree area. Gaussian decomposition techniques were applied to determine temperatures, optical depths, and column densities for both the cold and warm neutral media (CNM, WNM). The characteristics of individual CNM components resemble those found along random Galactic sightlines and near GMCs, implying a universality in cold HI properties. The CNM spin temperature ($T_s$) histogram peaks at approximately 50 K. CNM turbulent Mach numbers show wide variation, with a typical value of ~4, indicating supersonic motions. Roughly 60% of the total HI gas consists of WNM, with nearly 40% of this WNM located in the thermally unstable regime of 500–5000 K. The observed CNM fraction is higher around GMCs than in diffuse regions and rises with increasing column density ($N_{HI}$), reaching a maximum of ~75%. On average, the optically thin approximation ($N^*(HI)$) underestimates the total $N(HI)$ by ~21%, although we observe substantial regional variations in the relationship between $N(HI)$ and the correction factor $f = N(HI)/N^*(HI)$. We evaluated two correction methods for opacity effects using emission data from the GALFA-HI survey: a linear fit of $f$ versus $\log_{10}(N^*(HI))$ and a uniform $T_s$ approach. We favor the uniform $T_s$ method because the linear fit fails to produce convincing results for all subregions.

The USPTO maintains one of the world's most extensive publicly available databases of scientific, technical, and commercial information. Historically, USPTO data has been widely utilized in patent analytics, economics, and litigation and prosecution tools. This article focuses on a new category of applications centered on the research, development, and deployment of artificial intelligence. These applications encompass both providing AI capabilities for practical intellectual property uses and facilitating cutting-edge AI research through USPTO data products. The text includes case studies drawn from examples both inside and outside the USPTO.

The sigma model defined on an $AdS_3\times S^3$ background, sustained by both NS-NS and R-R fluxes, stands out as a highly significant integrable system. In this study, we investigate a specific set of classical string solutions corresponding to $N$-spike strings propagating in $AdS_3 \times S^1$, carrying angular momentum $J$ within the $S^1 \subset S^5$ subspace, under conditions of mixed flux. Our analysis reveals that introducing either angular momentum $J$ or a winding number $m$ causes the spikes to become rounded rather than terminating in a cusp. Furthermore, the inclusion of flux does not modify this rounding behavior. Additionally, we examine the large $N$ limit of these $N$-spike strings in a fluxed $AdS_3 \times S^1$ setting and demonstrate that the resulting Energy-Spin dispersion relation mirrors that obtained for periodic spikes in a fluxed $AdS_3$-pp-wave $\times S^1$ background.

Text-to-Graph extraction focuses on automatically deriving information graphs comprising mentions and types from natural language inputs. While current methods, including table filling and pairwise scoring, have demonstrated strong results in various extraction tasks, they struggle to scale to longer texts due to their second-order space and time complexities relative to input length. To address this, we introduce Hybrid Span Generator (HySPA), which invertibly converts information graphs into alternating sequences of nodes and edge types. This approach utilizes a hybrid span decoder capable of recurrently generating both spans and types in linear time and space. Extensive evaluations on the ACE05 dataset reveal that our method significantly surpasses state-of-the-art performance on joint entity and relation extraction.

Advanced cell culture methods, including 3D bio-printing and hydrogel-based cell embedding, offer promising avenues for investigating cells in environments that closely mimic in-vivo conditions. While researchers frequently employ fluorescence microscopy to visualize protein localization within these 3D structures, accurately quantifying concentration gradients in the microenvironment has proven challenging. This study introduces a technique for continuously monitoring time-dependent concentration gradients of diverse biomarkers in 3D cell culture assays. By utilizing bead-based immunoassays to capture and amplify the fluorescence signal of tagged proteins, this method facilitates near real-time, in situ biomarker detection and enables spatiotemporal quantification. Researchers can capture static snapshots of concentration profiles or conduct time-series analysis to estimate time-varying biomarker production. The approach is demonstrated through an osteosarcoma tumoroid case study, featuring both a quantitative single-plexed gel-encapsulated assay and a qualitative multi-plexed 3D bioprinted assay; both successfully measured a time-varying cytokine gradient. By fitting an analytical function describing continuous point source diffusion to the observed concentration gradients, the study estimated that each osteosarcoma cell produces approximately two IL-8 cytokines per second. Furthermore, the assay's proper calibration and application are thoroughly examined in the context of diffusion-limited Langmuir kinetics involving a spherical adsorber.

We develop a novel seven-dimensional gravity theory by incorporating two topological terms into the Einstein-Hilbert action. For specific values of the coupling constants, these terms correspond to the R^4 correction in the 3-form field equation of eleven-dimensional supergravity. We derive the complete set of equations of motion and discover that static, spherically symmetric black holes remain unaffected by these topological additions. Furthermore, we identify solutions in Euclidean signature, including squashed AdS_7, squashed seven-spheres, and Q^{111} spaces.

Recent research [Bret, EPL **135** (2021) 35001] assessed quantum electrodynamic (QED) impacts on the two-stream instability, specifically addressing perturbations with wave vectors aligned with the flow in a collisionless counter-streaming setup. This study broadens the analysis to encompass all possible wave vector orientations. It confirms the prior findings for the two-stream instability and demonstrates that, even within a 3D framework incorporating QED effects, the instability remains fundamentally one-dimensional. Conversely, the filamentation instability, occurring for wave vectors perpendicular to the flow, experiences only minor QED modifications. Similar to the classical scenario, its growth rate saturates at high $k_\perp$, with both the saturation level and the minimum unstable $k_\perp$ remaining unaffected by QED corrections. Unexpectedly, unstable modes associated with oblique wave vectors deviate from this trend; while QED corrections lower the growth rate for some modes, they enhance it for others. Finally, the potential role of QED effects in unmagnetized systems is examined, though pair production driven by gamma emission from particles oscillating in exponentially growing fields is excluded from consideration.

Hawking radiation represents a quantum phenomenon of black holes, conceptualized as quantum tunneling across the event horizon, yet it remains extremely challenging to observe directly from astrophysical black holes. Although remarkable experiments utilizing analogue black holes across different platforms have been conducted, verifying Hawking radiation and its quantum aspects, such as entanglement, has proven difficult due to the experimental hurdles of accurately simulating curved spacetime and precisely measuring thermal spectra. Leveraging recent breakthroughs in tunable couplers for superconducting processors, we have experimentally realized an analogue black hole using a custom chip featuring a chain of 10 superconducting transmon qubits interacting via 9 tunable couplers. By employing efficient techniques to engineer qubit couplings, we successfully simulate both flat and curved spacetime backgrounds. The quantum walks of quasi-particles within these curved spacetimes mimic gravitational effects around a black hole, producing Hawking radiation behavior. Through state tomography measurements of all 7 qubits located outside the analogue event horizon, we confirm the presence of Hawking radiation. Furthermore, we prepared an entangled pair within the horizon and directly measured the evolution of entanglement in curved spacetime. These findings are expected to spur greater interest in investigating the information paradox, entropy, and other related black hole properties using programmable superconducting processors equipped with tunable couplers.

This study introduces innovative approaches for estimating Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) in nonlinear systems characterized by high-dimensional, dependent random inputs. Central to our methodology is the DD-GPCE-Kriging surrogate, which combines dimensionally decomposed generalized polynomial chaos expansion with Kriging to precisely model nonlinear and nonsmooth random outputs. We integrate this surrogate into two distinct frameworks: (1) Monte Carlo simulation (MCS) and (2) multifidelity importance sampling (MFIS). The MCS approach samples directly from the DD-GPCE-Kriging surrogate, offering an efficient and accurate solution for high-dimensional dependent inputs. To mitigate the bias inherent in surrogate models, we developed an MFIS-based method where DD-GPCE-Kriging efficiently generates the biasing density, allowing the high-fidelity model to estimate CVaR from these biased samples. Furthermore, we accelerate the construction of the biasing density by computing the DD-GPCE-Kriging surrogate using a computationally inexpensive low-fidelity model. Numerical experiments on mathematical functions demonstrate that the MFIS-based approach yields superior accuracy compared to the MCS-based method when dealing with nonsmooth outputs. The scalability and practical applicability of these methods are validated on complex engineering cases, specifically a two-dimensional composite laminate with 28 partly dependent random inputs and a three-dimensional composite T-joint with 20 partly dependent random inputs. In the laminate case, the proposed MFIS-based method achieves a 104-fold speedup over standard MCS using the high-fidelity model while maintaining a CVaR estimation error of only 1.15%.

Recently, integrating sparse and dense image matching into a single functional correspondence framework has gained significant attention. However, current research primarily targets matching accuracy, often overlooking efficiency, which is vital for real-world deployment. To address this, we introduce the Efficient Correspondence Transformer (ECO-TR), an optimized structure that enhances the efficiency of functional correspondence models by adopting a coarse-to-fine correspondence search strategy. This approach connects multiple transformer blocks in stages to progressively refine predicted coordinates using a shared multi-scale feature extraction network. For any given pair of images and arbitrary query points, the model predicts all correspondences in a single feed-forward pass. Additionally, we develop an adaptive query-clustering mechanism and an uncertainty-driven outlier detection module to further accelerate and improve prediction quality. Experimental results across various sparse and dense matching benchmarks demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in both efficiency and effectiveness.

The problem of inserting a row or column into a totally positive matrix between two existing lines while preserving total positivity was initially addressed and resolved by Johnson and Smith, who developed an algorithm to generate a single valid insertion. This study revisits the issue by demonstrating that any totally positive matrix corresponds to a specific vertex-weighted graph, where matrix entries represent sums over particular paths; we term this graph the matrix's scaffolding. Leveraging this framework, we provide a complete characterization of all feasible line insertions, defining them as the strongly positive solutions to a specific homogeneous system of linear equations.

Recent research highlights hybrid quantum systems utilizing magnonics as a promising avenue for creating macroscopic quantum states comprising numerous spins. This study demonstrates the entanglement of two magnon modes within large yttrium-iron-garnet (YIG) spheres via cavity optomagnonics, where magnons interact with high-quality optical whispering gallery modes inherent to the spheres. These spheres can reach diameters of up to 1 mm, each housing over $10^{18}$ spins. The proposal leverages the asymmetry between Stokes and anti-Stokes sidebands produced by magnon-induced Brillouin light scattering within the cavity optomagnonics framework. This asymmetry enables the distinct use of Stokes and anti-Stokes scattering processes for both generating and verifying entanglement. Consequently, our findings suggest that cavity optomagnonics represents a viable platform for preparing macroscopic quantum states.

Face parsing involves predicting pixel-level labels for specific facial components within an image. Current methods typically crop the target face using a pre-computed bounding box, limiting analysis to internal Regions of Interest (RoIs) while ignoring peripheral elements like hair and potentially causing interference from nearby faces. Furthermore, these approaches are trained and assessed primarily on near-frontal portraits, leaving their efficacy in real-world ("in-the-wild") scenarios largely unexamined. To overcome these limitations, this paper offers three key contributions. First, we present the iBugMask dataset, designed for in-the-wild face parsing, comprising 21,866 training images and 1,000 test images. The training set is generated by augmenting an existing dataset with diverse face poses, while the test set features manual annotations of 11 facial regions, exhibiting significant variations in size, pose, expression, and background. Second, we introduce the RoI Tanh-polar transform, which warps the entire image into a Tanh-polar format with a fixed ratio between the face area and its context, guided by the target bounding box. This representation preserves all original image information and enables rotation equivariance in Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). Third, we propose the HybridBlock, a hybrid residual representation learning module that incorporates convolutional layers in both Tanh-polar and Tanh-Cartesian spaces, facilitating CNNs with receptive fields of varying shapes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method advances the state-of-the-art for in-the-wild face parsing without requiring facial landmarks for alignment.

The absence of observed ultra-high energy (UHE) photons and the constraints of current identification methods necessitate investigations into alternative simulation techniques and observational strategies. This report proposes one such novel approach, focusing on new observables that enable the indirect detection of UHE photons via cosmic ray phenomena characterized by numerous spatially correlated extensive air showers or primary cosmic rays detected simultaneously. The research relies on simulations of UHE photon interactions with the Sun's magnetic field using the PRESHOWER program with key modifications. A primary outcome of these interactions is the creation of cosmic ray ensembles (CRE) manifesting as extremely thin and elongated cascades of secondary photons across the entire cosmic ray energy spectrum. Upon reaching Earth's atmosphere, these cascades—or their segments—can produce distinctive walls of spatially correlated extensive air showers, an effect anticipated even when primary UHE photons are not aimed directly at Earth. The particle distributions within these multi-primary UHE photon footprints are predicted to have meter-scale thicknesses and elongations extending up to hundreds of millions of kilometers, rendering them potentially detectable through a global, multi-experiment framework that includes re-analyzing historical data. This approach is expected to yield an event rate surpassing the capacity of even the largest cosmic ray observatories. The methodologies outlined in this report facilitate the simulation of potentially observable quantities associated with UHE photon-induced CREs, including particle densities, energy spectra, and geographical orientations at the top of Earth's atmosphere.

The widespread adoption of FIDO2 standards, browser compatibility, and the proliferation of biometric verification on smartphones has galvanized major technology firms regarding the prospect of a passwordless future. While this vision seems ideal, this position paper argues that despite the advantages of passwordless authentication in specific contexts, completely eliminating passwords from the web remains unfeasible in the foreseeable future. We substantiate this stance with five key arguments, drawing upon recent academic literature as well as our own technical and business insights. Furthermore, we propose that this discussion can serve as a research agenda, highlighting promising directions for future work in user authentication.

Multifactor HCI experiment data frequently deviate from the normality required by parametric tests. While the Aligned Rank Transform (ART) is a widely used nonparametric method capable of detecting main and interaction effects in such nonconforming data, it yields inaccurate results when applied to contrast tests. To address this, we developed ART-C, a novel algorithm designed for conducting contrasts within the ART framework, which was validated across 72,000 datasets. Our findings demonstrate that ART-C avoids inflating Type I error rates—a flaw present in ART-based contrasts—and exhibits superior statistical power compared to t-tests, Mann-Whitney U tests, Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, and standard ART. We also integrated ART-C into the ARTool utility, making it available for both Windows and R environments. However, our validation study had specific constraints, including testing only six distribution types, excluding mixed factorial designs and random slopes, and noting that ART-C should not be used for data derived from Cauchy distributions.

Using the ab initio no-core shell model with importance truncation, we investigate the ground-state and excitation energies of singly-strange hypernuclei across the helium and lithium isotopic chains, ranging from $^5_\Lambda$He to $^{11}_\Lambda$He and from $^7_\Lambda$Li to $^{12}_\Lambda$Li. Our calculations utilize two- and three-baryon interactions derived from chiral effective field theory, applying a similarity renormalization group transformation consistently up to the three-baryon level to enhance model-space convergence. Although the absolute energies of hypernuclear states exhibit systematic dependence on the regulator cutoff of the hyperon-nucleon interaction, the calculated neutron separation energies remain highly stable and align well with existing data for both nucleonic parents and their daughter hypernuclei. We present predictions for the spectra and neutron separation energies of neutron-rich hypernuclei that have not yet been observed experimentally. Additionally, our results indicate that adding a hyperon does not alter the neutron drip lines within the helium and lithium isotopic chains.

Petrov-Galerkin methods utilizing optimal test functions provide stabilization for finite element simulations. Specifically, for a given discrete trial space, the optimal test space generates a numerical scheme that achieves the best possible approximation within a problem-specific energy norm. However, this ideal strategy faces two main challenges: the explicit knowledge of optimal test functions is required, and these functions often possess large supports, leading to costly dense linear systems. Despite these issues, parametric families of PDEs justify the offline computational investment needed to generate stabilized linear systems that can be solved efficiently during the online phase for specific parameters. To address the first challenge, we explicitly compute an offline function that maps any PDE parameter to the coefficient matrix of the optimal test functions expressed in a basis expansion. To mitigate the second challenge, we apply low-rank approximation to hierarchically compress the non-square coefficient matrix of these optimal test functions. To further accelerate this compression, we train a neural network to learn a critical bottleneck within the algorithm for the given set of PDE parameters. When solving the resulting compressed Petrov-Galerkin formulation online, we utilize a GMRES iterative solver, benefiting from inexpensive matrix-vector multiplications due to the low-rank structure of the compressed matrix. Experimental results demonstrate that the complete online procedure is as fast as the original, unstable Galerkin approach. Essentially, we achieve stabilization using hierarchical matrices and neural networks at negligible practical cost. Our findings are illustrated through 2D Eriksson-Johnson and Helmholtz model problems.

This work offers a theoretical examination of the Feedback Alignment (FA) algorithm, a computationally efficient alternative to backpropagation for training neural networks. We establish convergence guarantees with specific rates for deep linear networks under both continuous and discrete dynamics. Furthermore, we investigate incremental learning behaviors in shallow linear networks. Notably, we identify that certain initializations cause negligible components to be learned prior to principal ones, which may undermine the algorithm's efficacy; we term this phenomenon "implicit anti-regularization." Conversely, we propose initialization schemes where problem components are learned in decreasing order of importance, thereby inducing a form of implicit regularization.

We investigate the dynamics of two topological defects trapped within a sharp activity gradient, which divides an active circular domain from a surrounding passive nematic fluid. Using continuum simulations, we elucidate how the balance between energy injection, hydrodynamic interactions, and frictional forces dictates the motion of the self-propelling $+1/2$ defects required by topology. Our results are organized into a phase diagram mapping defect dynamics against activity levels and frictional damping, revealing six distinct dynamical regimes: immobile defects (ID), steady rotation (SR), bouncing (TB), bouncing-cruising (BC), dancing (DA), and multiple defects with irregular behavior (MD). These varied dynamic states suggest potential for creating synchronized defect arrays in microfluidic contexts.

Nonlocal gravity (NLG) represents a classical, nonlocal extension of Einstein's gravitational theory, modeled after the analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics in media. Within this framework, historical dependence is introduced through a constitutive relation that utilizes a causal kernel, which must ultimately be derived from observational data. This paper aims to reformulate nonlocal gravity so that the nonlocal components of the constitutive relation directly link measurable quantities, mirroring the approach found in nonlocal electrodynamics. The derived constitutive relation aligns with a recent proposal by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl [25]. Utilizing this updated constitutive relation for NLG, it is demonstrated that de Sitter spacetime does not constitute a valid solution.

Generating natural language descriptions that are syntactically and semantically accurate, while maintaining contextual relevance to the image, constitutes a challenging task known as Image Captioning. Current significant research in Bengali Image Captioning (BIC) relies on encoder-decoder frameworks. This study introduces an end-to-end image captioning system employing a multimodal architecture that integrates a one-dimensional Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for encoding sequential data with a pre-trained ResNet-50 model to extract region-specific visual features. We evaluated the system's performance on the BanglaLekhaImageCaptions dataset using standard metrics and conducted a human evaluation for qualitative assessment. Results indicate that our language encoder effectively captures fine-grained caption details, which, when combined with image features, produces accurate and diverse descriptions. Our approach surpasses all existing BIC methods, establishing a new state-of-the-art (SOTA) with scores of 0.651 on BLUE-1, 0.572 on CIDEr, 0.297 on METEOR, 0.434 on ROUGE, and 0.357 on SPICE.

The initial few hundred million years following the Big Bang, occurring at redshifts $z>10$, represent the final major unexplored era in cosmic history, currently known only through a single spectroscopically confirmed galaxy, GNz11 ($z\approx11$). This study utilizes $JWST$/NIRCam photometry covering $\approx1-5\mu$m across a $49$ arcmin$^{2}$ area from the public Early Release Science programs (CEERS and GLASS) to search for luminous galaxies at $z>10$. We identify two high-confidence candidates, GLASS-z12 and GLASS-z10, both with absolute UV magnitudes near $M_{\rm{UV}}\approx-21$. Their spectral energy distributions exhibit sharp breaks of $\gtrsim1.8$ magnitudes, indicative of full absorption of light blueward of the Lyman-$\alpha$ line, which corresponds to redshifts of $z=12.4^{+0.1}_{-0.3}$ and $z=10.4^{+0.4}_{-0.5}$, respectively. The absence of flux in multiple bands rules out lower-redshift interlopers, such as quiescent galaxies with strong Balmer breaks, which would be detected at $>5\sigma$. SED modeling indicates these systems have assembled approximately $10^9$ solar masses in stars within the first $\lesssim300-400$ Myr of the Universe. The high brightness of these sources allows for morphological analysis; notably, GLASS-z10 displays a clearly extended exponential profile, suggesting it may be a disk galaxy with a half-light radius of $r_{\rm{50}}\approx0.7$ kpc. If confirmed, these findings challenge number density predictions based on Schechter UV luminosity functions, which would require a survey area ten times larger to detect such luminous objects at these redshifts. Furthermore, these results extend evidence of minimal evolution in the bright end of the UV luminosity function from lower redshifts into the cosmic dawn, implying that galaxy formation began earlier than previously thought and suggesting that future deep $JWST$ observations could reveal bright galaxies from even earlier epochs.

We construct a family of GSp(2g)-parameterized ring isomorphisms between the cohomology of moduli spaces of stable Higgs bundles for any two degrees coprime to the rank; these isomorphisms preserve the perverse filtrations. Consequently, we establish two structural results regarding Higgs moduli cohomology that align with the P=W conjecture within non-abelian Hodge theory: (1) Galois conjugation on character varieties maintains the perverse filtrations for their corresponding Higgs moduli spaces, and (2) restricting the Hodge-Tate decomposition of a character variety to each segment of the perverse filtration of the associated Higgs moduli space yields a valid decomposition.
