While aggregating these local views is standard for conducting graph learning tasks, doing so often raises privacy issues due to the sensitive information contained within them. This paper aims to achieve private graph learning within a decentralized network. To this end, we introduce {\em Solitude}, a novel privacy-preserving framework built on graph neural networks (GNNs) that offers formal guarantees through edge local differential privacy. The core of {\em Solitude} lies in a series of refined mechanisms designed to calibrate the noise added to decentralized graphs collected from users, leveraging intrinsic properties common in real-world graphs, such as sparsity. Unlike prior work on locally private GNNs, our framework simultaneously safeguards both node feature and edge privacy and integrates seamlessly with any GNN that supports privacy-utility trade-offs. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that {\em Solitude} maintains the generalization capabilities of learned GNNs while effectively preserving user data privacy within specified privacy budgets.

We examined HST images of 31 nearby (z <~ 0.1) 3CR radio galaxies, comparing their UV and optical data to identify signs of recent star formation. Six targets were removed due to strong nuclear activity or insufficient UV counts. Following the subtraction of nuclear and jet emission, 12 of the remaining 25 objects displayed NUV - r colors brighter than 5.4, marking them as potential star-forming candidates. After accounting for contamination from AGN processes—such as UV emission lines, nebular continuum, and scattered nuclear light—only six "blue" galaxies remain as confirmed star-forming systems.

We subsequently classified the radio galaxies into Low Excitation Galaxies (LEG) and High Excitation Galaxies (HEG) based on radio morphology, power, and optical diagnostic line ratios. While FR type and radio power showed no correlation with color, FR type clearly linked to spectroscopic type. Notably, all HEG (with one possible exception) exhibited morphological evidence of recent star formation in UV compact knots spanning 5–20 kpc. In contrast, only one LEG out of 19, which included FR I galaxies, was "blue."

Synthesizing data on color, UV/optical properties, and dust morphology reveals that recent star formation is linked exclusively to these relatively powerful AGN in HEG, likely triggered by recent major wet mergers. Conversely, the fraction of actively star-forming objects in LEG galaxies does not exceed that of quiescent galaxies; their AGN activity is likely self-sustained by a hot interstellar medium.

Electromagnetic Vlasov simulations investigate the kinetic damping of low-frequency transverse perturbations traveling parallel to the magnetic field within a magnetized warm electron plasma. These simulations deterministically recover the short-timescale damping of electron magnetohydrodynamic whistler modes and analyze the influence of finite electron temperature on the wave's real frequency. The damping mechanism emerges from an interaction between global, phase-space-wide effects and the more conventional resonant-electron-specific kinetic processes; both conserve entropy but leave distinct signatures on the initially coherent, finite-amplitude modification of the warm electron equilibrium distribution. Ultimately, the net damping is driven by a deterministic thermalization or phase-mixing process that significantly complements the resonant acceleration of electrons occurring over shorter timescales, which is pertinent to transient turbulent electromagnetic fluctuations. Additionally, a kinetic model for the evolving initial transverse electromagnetic perturbation is introduced and utilized to identify signatures of the whistler wave phase-mixing process in the simulation results.

Over-parameterized deep neural networks can attain high training accuracy with minimal generalization error, a capability that allows them to fit arbitrary labels, a behavior known as memorization. This study investigates memorization using turn-over dropout, an efficient technique for assessing influence and memorization, applied to both real data with true labels and random data with arbitrary labels. The primary findings are: (i) Networks optimize both easy examples (such as real data) and difficult examples (such as random data) simultaneously, prioritizing the easier ones with greater speed; (ii) In the context of real data, a difficult example that is correctly labeled provides more information than an easy one. By demonstrating that memorization occurs in both real and random datasets, we underscore the consistency between them regarding optimization processes and highlight the significance of memorization during training.

With restricted quantum computers gradually becoming feasible, the quest for significant initial applications is accelerating. In this field, a prominent strategy involves utilizing a specialized quantum circuit known as a quantum neural network (QNN) as the foundation for machine learning models. While QNNs function analogously to classical neural networks, there remains a scarcity of knowledge regarding optimal circuit architectures and hyperparameters necessary for effective learning performance within machine learning contexts. This study employs the functional ANOVA framework to evaluate QNNs, specifically identifying which hyperparameters most significantly impact predictive performance. We focus on one of the most common QNN architectures and apply it to seven open-source datasets from the OpenML-CC18 classification benchmark, selected for having a feature count low enough to be processed by quantum hardware with fewer than 20 qubits. The functional ANOVA analysis of hyperparameter rankings revealed three primary tiers of importance. Our experiments validated anticipated patterns while uncovering novel insights; notably, the learning rate was identified as the most critical hyperparameter regarding marginal contribution across all datasets, whereas the specific selection of entangling gates proved the least significant, with the exception of a single dataset. This research introduces novel methodologies for investigating quantum machine learning models and offers fresh perspectives on quantum model selection.

This paper introduces a kinetic adaptation of the Watanabe-Strogatz (WS) transform applicable to vector models. Leveraging this generalized transform, we derive cross-ratio type constant of motion functionals for kinetic vector models under appropriate conditions and establish the sufficient and necessary criteria for their existence. Furthermore, we utilize these functionals to demonstrate the instability of bipolar states within the kinetic swarm sphere model. Additionally, we extend the WS-transform and the corresponding constant of motion functional to cases involving non-identical kinetic vector models.

Reproducing the statistical properties of realistic turbulence in initial or inflow synthetic turbulent velocity or scalar fields remains a significant challenge. The synthetic eddy method, originally developed for large eddy simulations under inflow conditions, operates on the premise that turbulence can be modeled as a superposition of coherent structures. This paper introduces a novel synthetic eddy method where the fundamental eddy is formed by superimposing three Hill's vortices with mutually orthogonal axes. By distributing these Hill's vortices, an anisotropic turbulent velocity field is synthesized that satisfies the incompressibility condition and aligns with a specified Reynolds stress tensor. The amplitudes of the constituent vortices within the fundamental eddy are determined by transforming known Reynolds stress profiles from the physical reference frame to the principal-axis reference frame. Consequently, this approach yields divergence-free anisotropic turbulent velocity fields capable of reproducing a given Reynolds stress tensor. The model was evaluated using both isotropic and anisotropic turbulent velocity fields within the contexts of grid turbulence decay and turbulent channel flow, respectively. In all tested scenarios, the transition from artificial to realistic turbulence near the inflow boundary was found to be minimal.

Few-shot learning, which involves learning and generalizing from scarce examples, is fundamental to numerous real-world vision tasks. A primary approach to achieving this is constructing an embedding space where samples from different classes are clearly distinct. Recent research indicates that hyperbolic geometry is particularly well-suited for few-shot learning due to its ability to represent hierarchical and structured data with minimal distortion. In this paper, we introduce a context-aware hyperbolic metric designed to measure the distance between a point and a set, utilizing a learned set-to-set distance. We formulate this metric as a weighted sum on the tangent bundle of hyperbolic space and develop a mechanism to adaptively determine these weights based on the spatial arrangement of the points. This approach renders the metric both local and task-dependent, allowing it to adapt dynamically to the specific samples being compared. Empirical results demonstrate that this metric offers robustness against outliers and delivers significant performance gains over baseline models, achieving state-of-the-art results across five prominent few-shot classification benchmarks: mini-ImageNet, tiered-ImageNet, Caltech-UCSD Birds-200-2011 (CUB), CIFAR-FS, and FC100.

This study systematically examines the interaction-induced electric dipole properties of all molecular dimers within the S66 benchmark set, utilizing CCSD(T)-F12b/aug-cc-pVDZ-F12 as the reference theoretical framework. For electric field strengths up to approximately 5 GV m$^{-1}$, response effects beyond the second order are negligible. Significant interaction dipole moments, defined as dipole changes resulting from van der Waals binding, occur specifically in hydrogen-bonded dimers aligned along the intermolecular axis, whereas dimers held together by $\pi$-stacking or London dispersion forces exhibit predominantly small interaction dipoles. Interaction polarizabilities—the changes in polarizability due to van der Waals binding—are generally small; however, they consistently feature one positive principal component aligned with the intermolecular axis and two negative components. Energy decompositions via symmetry-adapted perturbation theory (SAPT0/jun-cc-pVDZ) indicate that electrostatics is the primary driver of the interaction dipole moment. Furthermore, first-order SAPT0 decompositions into monomer-resolved contributions provide a quantitative connection between the electric properties of individual monomers and their dimer complexes. Additionally, using the aug-cc-pVQZ basis set and non-empirical PBE exchange-correlation kernels, we evaluated the impact of nonlocal exchange and correlation on predictive accuracy. While dRPA@PBE0 predictions align excellently with coupled cluster results, the computationally efficient LC-$\omega$PBE0-D3 method also delivers reliable outcomes with relative errors under 5%. In contrast, PBE alone, even with dispersion corrections, yields larger errors in both interaction dipole moments and polarizabilities.

We present ROS-X-Habitat, a software interface that connects the AI Habitat platform for embodied learning agents with other robotics resources through ROS. Beyond providing standardized communication protocols between agents and simulators, this interface facilitates physically and photorealistic simulations that enhance the training and testing of vision-based embodied agents. This tool allows roboticists to evaluate their Habitat reinforcement learning agents within alternative ROS-based simulators or to utilize Habitat Sim v2 as a testbed for their robotic algorithms. Our in silico experiments demonstrate that ROS-X-Habitat has negligible effects on the navigation performance and simulation speed of a Habitat RGBD agent, confirms that a standard suite of ROS mapping, planning, and navigation tools can operate within Habitat Sim v2, and verifies that a Habitat agent can function inside the standard ROS simulator, Gazebo.

The ramification of a polyhedral space is defined as the metric completion of the universal cover of its regular locus. This work primarily examines two types of polyhedral spaces: quotients of Euclidean space by a discrete group of isometries and polyhedral metrics on the complex projective plane featuring singularities along a set of complex lines. Regarding the former, we conjecture that such quotient spaces invariably possess a CAT[0] ramification, a claim proven in multiple instances. For the latter, we demonstrate that the ramification is CAT[0] provided the metric exhibits non-negative curvature. Consequently, we conclude that the complements of complex line arrangements in the complex projective plane, as analyzed by Hirzebruch, are aspherical.

To address challenges posed by increasing variable smart loads and distributed generation, distribution system operators (DSOs) have mandated that prosumers utilizing inverters adhere to predefined operational rules. Specifically, the maximum active and reactive power set points are determined by local voltage measurements to prevent voltage violations caused by inverter output. However, this study observes that such constraints limit local energy management flexibility, resulting in greater losses of arbitrage profits for prosumers situated further from the substation. The paper aims to: (a) create an optimal local energy optimization algorithm for activating load flexibility, inverter-interfaced solar PV, and energy storage under time-varying electricity prices; (b) quantify the impact of location on prosumer arbitrage gains due to existing inverter injection rules across various energy markets; and (c) propose a computationally efficient hybrid inverter control policy that ensures voltage regulation while significantly reducing locational disparities. Numerical simulations on three identical prosumers located at different points along a radial feeder demonstrate that the proposed control policy reduces locational disparity in arbitrage gains between customers at the feeder's start and end to 1.4%, while decreasing PV curtailment by 91.7% compared to the base case utilizing restrictive volt-Var and volt-watt policies.

Neutrinos interact within the atmosphere (downward-going) or the Earth's crust (Earth-skimming), generating air showers detectable by ground-based detector arrays. The Pierre Auger Observatory's surface detector is capable of identifying these cascades, distinguished by their very inclined trajectories close to the ground, indicating they have traversed a significant thickness of atmosphere. To date, no neutrino candidates have been identified by the Observatory. Detecting such rare events poses a significant challenge, necessitating sophisticated algorithms and high-resolution hardware. This work presents a trigger system utilizing a pipeline artificial neural network (ANN) deployed on a large FPGA to recognize specific event traces after a learning phase. The ANN algorithm, originally developed in MATLAB, has been integrated into the fast logic of a large Cyclone V E FPGA within the prototype Front-End Board for the Auger-Beyond-2015 initiative. Various algorithms were evaluated, with the Levenberg-Marquardt method proving most efficient. The network was trained in two stages: first, to identify "old" showers using real very inclined Auger showers as positive markers and real standard showers (Time over Threshold) as negative markers; second, to recognize "young" showers using simulated "young" events as positives and standard Auger events as negatives. A three-layer network trained on real very inclined showers demonstrated high efficiency in pattern recognition, successfully identifying 16-point traces with profiles characteristic of "old" showers.

The response of Michelson interferometers to weak plane gravitational waves is calculated to one order higher than the eikonal equation. This analysis incorporates the modulation of electromagnetic field amplitude and polarization by solving geometrical optics transport equations with boundary conditions tailored for laser interferometry. For both DC and balanced homodyne readout methods, explicit expressions for the interferometer output signals are derived. These signals include perturbations in optical path length, frequency, and amplitude, and are demonstrated to be unaffected by polarization perturbations.

This paper extends the interpretation of time based on conditional probability, where time evolution arises from the entanglement between a clock and a system of interest. The approach conditions a solution to the Wheeler-DeWitt equation on a specific subsystem acting as a clock, defined by a state corresponding to time $t$, thereby assigning a conditional state $|\psi_S(t)\rangle$ to the remainder of the Universe. We show that when the total Hamiltonian in the Wheeler-DeWitt equation includes an interaction term coupling the clock and the system, the resulting conditional state obeys a time-nonlocal Schrödinger equation. In this equation, the system's Hamiltonian is substituted by a self-adjoint integral operator. We solve this equation using perturbation theory and analyze three distinct clock-system interaction scenarios. One such case involves Newtonian gravitational interaction, which induces corrections to the system's Hamiltonian on the order of $G/c^4$, inversely proportional to the separation distance between the clock and the system.

Vehicular Edge Computing (VEC) offers a promising approach for caching vast amounts of data and multimedia near vehicles. However, designing optimal caching policies is difficult due to vehicle high mobility and fluctuating wireless channel conditions. Additionally, vehicles may be reluctant to store content with sensitive personal information on untrusted providers. Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) provides an emerging solution for handling high-dimensional and time-varying features, while permissioned blockchain creates a secure, decentralized peer-to-peer environment. This paper integrates DRL and permissioned blockchain into vehicular networks for intelligent and secure content caching. We introduce a blockchain-enabled distributed caching framework where vehicles handle caching tasks and base stations manage the permissioned blockchain. Next, we utilize advanced DRL to design an optimal caching scheme that accounts for mobility. Finally, we propose a novel Proof-of-Utility (PoU) method for block verifier selection to speed up verification. Security analysis confirms that our blockchain-empowered caching ensures privacy and security. Numerical results using a real Uber dataset demonstrate that the DRL-based caching scheme significantly outperforms two benchmark policies.

Given the lingering misconceptions in existing literature regarding powder diffraction phenomena in small nanocrystals ($D<10$ nm), we present a systematic and concise review of these issues through the lens of atomistic simulations. Contemporary phenomenological tools in powder diffraction can now be validated by constructing realistic atomistic models that track their thermodynamics and influence on diffraction patterns. These models range from small segments of perfect lattices to relaxed nanocrystals featuring typical strains and defects, which experimental evidence suggests approximate real nanocrystals. The discussion focuses specifically on metal nanocrystals. We elucidate the origins of peak shifts, noting that for perfect lattice cuts, these are primarily caused by multiplying broad profiles with steep slope factors related to atomic scattering and the Lorentz effect, with a detailed examination of the Lorentz factor within the Debye summation. For models relaxed using realistic force fields and actual nanocrystals, peak shifts also incorporate contributions from surface relaxation, facilitating the development of an experimental *in situ* method sensitive to surface states, with brief reviews of such results provided. Regarding small fcc nanocrystals, we examine the significance and impact of multiple (111) cross twinning on peak shifts and intensity. Furthermore, we explain and visualize strain and size effects in perfect multitwinned clusters, specifically decahedra and icosahedra. Finally, the manuscript proposes new methodologies for interpreting powder diffraction patterns of real, defective (twinned) fcc nanoparticles and highlights the inadequacy of the Rietveld method for this purpose.

Recently, a novel protocol known as mirror benchmarking was introduced to assess the system-level performance of quantum computers. These protocols utilize circuits composed of random gate sequences followed by a mirroring step, where each gate in the sequence is inverted. We provide a straightforward proof demonstrating that, under the assumption of uniform noise and provided the twirling group constitutes a 2-design, mirror benchmarking results in an exponential decrease of survival probability as the sequence length increases. The rate of this decay is governed by a quantity that is a quadratic function of the error channel and corresponds to unitarity for specific error types, offering a new approach to estimating noise coherence. Furthermore, we present experimental data from mirror benchmarking runs on the Honeywell System Model H1, which includes performance curves showing the success probability of random circuits relative to qubit count and circuit depth.

An increasingly popular strategy for tackling time-dependent scientific and engineering challenges is the space-time finite-element method, which employs finite elements across both spatial and temporal dimensions. Typically, the domain is discretized into temporal slices known as space-time slabs, which are weakly coupled in time via a Discontinuous Galerkin formulation. The associated jump term, essential for enforcing weak continuity between these slabs, poses significant computational difficulties, especially when dealing with deforming geometries. Enforcing conforming discretizations at the temporal boundaries of these slabs greatly simplifies the calculation of this term; otherwise, one must resort to costly and error-prone projections of the solution between time levels. However, achieving conforming meshes in simulations involving deformable domains, such as free-surface flows, is notoriously difficult. One existing remedy involves extruding the spatial mesh through time at every step to create the time-discontinuous prismatic space-time (D-PST) method, though this is limited to first-order temporal elements. This work introduces a new algorithmic framework for meshes of arbitrary discretization by inverting the mesh in the time direction at each step. This approach ensures a straightforward evaluation of the jump term because the mesh remains conforming throughout. The computational expense of flipping the mesh around its temporal symmetry plane scales linearly with the number of nodes, making it more efficient than either updating the mesh to enforce conformity or performing solution projections. The method's validity is demonstrated across various physical scenarios, including those with and without deforming boundaries.

Combinatorial optimization stands as a primary target for near-term and fault-tolerant quantum computing. This study examines the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), a well-known method for solving combinatorial problems, specifically applied to the MaxCut problem on 3-regular graphs. We investigate enhancing the outcomes of the most basic QAOA variant (depth-1) through a specific postselection technique that allows for efficient simulation via state preparation. Our theoretical analysis establishes upper and lower bounds, confirming that a modest but constant improvement in the fraction of satisfied edges is feasible. Numerical experiments on large-scale instances, which exceed classical simulation capabilities, corroborate these theoretical findings. Additionally, we explore local updates, a versatile strategy applicable to various optimization algorithms. For QAOA without postselection, the theoretical gains from local updates can be precisely quantified for large problems. While combining postselection with local updates renders the theoretical analysis intractable, numerical evidence indicates that the benefits of both approaches can be synergistically combined.

This brief note examines the null-dimensional reduction of the M5-brane covariant action. We analyze how longitudinal reduction yields a non-relativistic D4-brane, while transverse reduction results in an NS5-brane within the framework of non-relativistic string theory.

Most proposals for scaling quantum technology utilize modular or distributed architectures, connecting individual quantum processors, known as nodes, to create a large multinode quantum computer (MNQC). A primary method for building such systems involves superconducting quantum devices linked by optical interconnects. However, a significant bottleneck is the internode gate, which can be two to three orders of magnitude noisier and slower than local operations. Overcoming these limitations requires diverse strategies, such as enhancing entanglement generation, implementing entanglement distillation, and optimizing software and compilers. Yet, it is currently uncertain how improvements in these components interact to influence overall system performance, what specific performance levels are needed from each, or how to quantify them individually. This paper adopts a "co-design" approach to evaluate MNQC performance by modeling internode links, entanglement distillation, and local hardware architectures. Specifically, for superconducting MNQCs using microwave-to-optical links, we identify a tradeoff between entanglement generation and distillation that risks degrading system performance. We demonstrate how to navigate this tradeoff, outline compiler strategies for balancing local and internode gates, and analyze scenarios where noisy quantum links outperform purely classical ones. Based on these findings, we present a roadmap for realizing early MNQCs, highlighting potential hardware and software advancements and establishing criteria for evaluation, ranging from progress in entanglement generation and quantum memory to specialized algorithms like distributed quantum phase estimation. Although our focus is on superconducting devices with optical interconnects, our methodology is broadly applicable to various MNQC implementations.

As digital currency systems increasingly utilize blockchain for ledger security, the capacity for cross-chain transactions has become an essential interoperability feature. These transactions facilitate not only the transfer of funds between blockchains, similar to atomic swaps, but also enable one blockchain to confirm the inclusion of events on another. Cross-chain bridges are protocols designed to handle on-chain cryptocurrency exchanges, move assets to sidechains, and verify events across sharded blockchains, often relying on Byzantine fault tolerance (BFT) to ensure scalability. However, current bridge protocols that transfer funds from BFT blockchains impose substantial computational burdens on the destination blockchain, leading to elevated gas costs for smart contract event verification. This paper introduces Horizon, a gas-efficient cross-chain bridge protocol capable of transferring assets from a BFT blockchain to another blockchain, such as Ethereum, that supports fundamental smart contract execution.

Despite significant advancements in all-in-one multilingual neural machine translation (multilingual NMT), the inconsistency in joint training convergence remains overlooked, where different language pairs reach stability at varying epochs. This disparity causes the trained model to overfit low-resource language translations while underfitting high-resource ones. To address this, we introduce LSSD (Language-Specific Self-Distillation), a new training strategy designed to mitigate convergence inconsistencies and enable MNMT models to optimize performance across all language pairs simultaneously. Specifically, LSSD dynamically selects language-specific best checkpoints to guide the current model during training. Additionally, we systematically investigate three sample-level techniques for knowledge transfer. Experiments on three datasets demonstrate that LSSD yields consistent improvements across all language pairs, achieving state-of-the-art results.

This paper introduces a novel method for addressing job shop scheduling problems via deep reinforcement learning. To manage the intricacies of production environments, graph neural networks are utilized to model the diverse relationships within these systems. Additionally, the Job Shop Scheduling Problem (JSSP) is formulated as a distributed optimization task, where individual learning agents are assigned to specific resources, thereby enhancing flexibility in response to dynamic production conditions. The proposed distributed reinforcement learning agents, tasked with optimizing schedules for single resources, operate alongside a production environment co-simulation framework to generate the necessary data. This approach is tested on both a multi-robot setup and a complex production scheduling benchmark, with initial results demonstrating the method's applicability and performance.

Active faults alleviate tectonic stress generated by plate movement through various slip mechanisms, ranging from slow, non-seismic sliding to rapid, seismic ruptures. Slow earthquakes frequently manifest as tectonic tremor, characterized by non-impulsive signals that are often obscured by seismic noise and remain undetected. This study introduces a novel method to enhance the detection and localization of tremors concealed within such noise. The process begins with identifying tremors using a standard convolutional neural network, followed by employing neural network attribution to isolate core tremor features and denoise the input waveforms. These refined waveforms are then utilized with conventional array-based techniques to pinpoint tremor locations. Applied to the Cascadia subduction zone, this approach identifies tremor patches that align with current catalogs. Notably, the cleaned signals derived from the neural network attribution analysis reveal waveforms propagating through the Earth's crust and mantle at velocities consistent with local estimates. By successfully extracting these minute signals from the noise, this methodology enables the localization of more tremors than previously recorded in existing catalogs.

Training graph neural networks (GNNs) for large-scale node classification presents significant challenges, primarily due to the difficulty of deriving accurate hidden node representations while circumventing the neighborhood explosion issue. To address this, we introduce a novel method called feature momentum (FM), which utilizes a momentum mechanism to integrate historical embeddings during the update of feature representations. We have formulated two specific algorithms, GraphFM-IB and GraphFM-OB, designed to handle in-batch and out-of-batch data, respectively. GraphFM-IB applies the FM technique to in-batch sampled data, whereas GraphFM-OB applies it to out-of-batch data comprising the 1-hop neighbors of the in-batch set. We offer a convergence analysis for GraphFM-IB and provide theoretical insights for GraphFM-OB. Empirical results indicate that GraphFM-IB effectively mitigates the neighborhood explosion problem found in existing approaches, while GraphFM-OB demonstrates promising performance across multiple large-scale graph datasets.

The prospect of designing a novel fusion device arises from the theoretical potential of resonant ion confinement. Specifically, a Deuteron cloud within a Penning-Malmberg trap equipped with a uniquely configured rotating wall could enable nuclear fusion reactions in certain trap configurations, thereby satisfying Lawson's criterion for reactor efficiency. Additionally, this reactor design could be compact, eliminating the need for large-scale facilities and allowing it to operate as a fusion cell containing a pure ion thermal gas.

Quantum Machine Learning (QML) has not yet clearly or extensively proven its superiority over classical machine learning. Currently, only specific instances of quantum-inspired methods have yielded minor incremental gains, and a limited number of hybrid quantum computing experiments show promise for the near future, excluding pure optimization achievements via quantum-classical algorithms. Existing quantum hardware is characterized by noise and a scarcity of qubits, which hinders the demonstration of both current and potential quantum advantages in QML. This study demonstrates that applying Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) during data preprocessing can enhance classical encoding and the performance of quantum classifiers. Consequently, Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQA) utilizing LDA achieve improved balanced accuracy and surpass baseline classical classifiers.

Identifying personal statements regarding employment status on social media holds significant value for connecting job seekers with appropriate roles, enhancing social safety nets, and analyzing labor market dynamics. Nevertheless, detecting these disclosures remains difficult due to their scarcity amidst vast amounts of content and the diverse linguistic expressions used. This study evaluates three Active Learning (AL) approaches within real-world scenarios characterized by extreme class imbalance, identifying five specific categories of employment status disclosures (such as job loss) across three languages using BERT-based classifiers. Results indicate that even under such extreme imbalance, a limited number of AL iterations can yield substantial and statistically significant improvements in precision, recall, and result diversity compared to supervised baselines with equivalent labeling counts. Furthermore, the study finds that no single AL strategy consistently surpasses the others. Qualitative analysis reveals that AL aids the BERT attention mechanism in concentrating on key terms and refining semantic boundaries, underscoring the necessity of interpretable models to maintain greater oversight and control over this dynamic learning process.

This paper introduces the concept of unit reducibility for number fields, defined as fields where every positive unary form achieves its nonzero minimum at a unit. Additionally, we explore the relationship between unit reducibility and the count of homothety classes of perfect unary forms within a specific number field, and we provide a proof for an open conjecture by D. Yasaki regarding the number of such classes in real quadratic fields.
This paper introduces novel symmetry identities for q-Bernoulli polynomials, which are derived from p-adic q-integrals on Zp within the symmetric group of degree n.

An observer traveling relative to the cosmic rest frame would expect to see galaxies cluster and brighten in the direction of motion while spreading and fading in the opposite direction. The velocity derived from this dipole should align with the cosmic microwave background (CMB) temperature dipole, assuming galaxies are, on average, stationary relative to the CMB rest frame. However, recent investigations have reported a significant amplification of galaxy counts and flux toward the solar motion direction compared to CMB predictions, which challenges standard cosmological models. This study demonstrates that the distribution and luminosity of extragalactic radio sources are consistent with both the direction and velocity of the CMB dipole. By analyzing the first epoch of the Very Large Array Sky Survey alongside the Rapid Australian Square Kilometer Array Pathfinder Continuum Survey, we estimated the dipole using multiple methods, all yielding comparable outcomes. Typical fits indicate a velocity dipole of $331^{+161}_{-107}$ km s$^{-1}$ with an apex at $(\ell,b) = (271^{+55}_{-58}, 56^{+13}_{-35})$ in Galactic coordinates based on source counts, and $399^{+264}_{-199}$ km s$^{-1}$ toward $(\ell,b) = (301^{+30}_{-30}, 43^{+19}_{-17})$ based on radio fluxes. These results align with the CMB-solar velocity of 370 km s$^{-1}$ directed toward $(\ell,b) = (264, 48)$, confirming that galaxies are, on average, at rest relative to the early universe's rest frame as predicted by canonical cosmology.

This paper reviews numerical approximation techniques for solving elastic wave scattering in semi-infinite domains. The approach represents the half-space using boundary conditions derived from two-dimensional boundary element discretizations. Initially, classical BEM matrices are reformulated as dense dynamic stiffness matrices and subsequently approximated into banded matrices. This resulting banded matrix functions similarly to a standard finite element, enabling the solution of wave scattering problems with reduced memory demands. The accuracy of these methods is validated against benchmark cases of semi-circular and rectangular canyons, with results presented across time and frequency domains along with relative error analyses. The primary objective is to provide analysts with a practical method for obtaining approximate solutions sufficient to support engineering decisions.

We employed molecular simulations utilizing the SPC/E potential to evaluate how electric fields influence water's properties across diverse states and conditions. Fields exceeding approximately $0.1\,\text{V/\AA}$ significantly alter the grand-canonical partition function, causing chemical potential shifts at vapor-liquid equilibrium of up to $20\%$. Consequently, a field of $0.2\,\text{V/\AA}$ raises critical temperatures by nearly $7\%$, reduces vapor pressure, and substantially increases the entropy of vaporization (by as much as $35\%$). These findings are attributed to enhanced structural order and greater density fluctuations at the transition induced by the field. Furthermore, we examined the thermodynamics of compressed liquids and supercritical water across a broad pressure range, identifying the Zeno line and the ideal enthalpy curve within the supercritical region. By rescaling phase diagrams for various field strengths according to their critical properties, we established a correspondence among systems subjected to fields up to $0.2\,\text{V/\AA}$.

This study introduces attention as a cutting-edge mechanism for classifying radio galaxies using convolutional neural networks. We present an attention-based model that matches the performance of previous classifiers while utilizing more than 50% fewer parameters than the smallest classic CNN approach in this domain. We quantitatively demonstrate how choices in normalization and aggregation methods within attention-gating influence individual model outputs and show that the resulting attention maps enable interpretation of the model's classification decisions. Our observations reveal that the salient regions identified by our model closely align with those an expert human classifier would focus on to reach equivalent conclusions. We further show that while normalization and aggregation selection may have minimal impact on individual model performance, it significantly affects the interpretability of the corresponding attention maps; therefore, selecting a model that aligns well with how astronomers visually classify radio sources allows users to employ the model more effectively.

Interwell correlation is a primary step in investigating geological formations, serving as the foundation for building geological models and evaluating hydrocarbon reserves by revealing structural details. Currently, detailed interwell correlation depends on manually analyzing well-logging data, a process that is both time-intensive and subjective. Fundamentally, this task involves assessing the similarities between geological profiles. Although numerous past attempts have sought to automate interwell correlation using rule-based methods, classic machine learning, and deep learning, most solutions remain limited and often retain inherent expert subjectivity. We introduce a novel framework for estimating geological profile similarity using a deep learning model. This model accepts well-logging data as input and outputs the similarity between wells. The proposed framework facilitates (1) the extraction of key patterns and characteristics from geological profiles within wells and (2) unsupervised model training, eliminating the need for manual data interpretation. For validation, we utilized two open datasets from New Zealand and Norway. Our data-driven similarity models demonstrate superior performance, achieving an accuracy of 0.926 compared to 0.787 for baselines based on the popular gradient boosting method. Consequently, oil and gas professionals can enhance the quality of interwell correlation while reducing operational time.

The detection of certain variable X-ray sources in the Galactic Centre that have not exhibited outbursts over a ten-year monitoring period has led to the hypothesis of a substantial population of stellar-mass black holes in this area. A fundamental premise of this argument is the assertion that neutron stars in low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) do not experience long intervals between transients. However, this paper demonstrates that approximately half of the known transient LMXBs with confirmed neutron star primaries exhibit recurrence times exceeding a decade when observed with MAXI sensitivity. Furthermore, we show that to align the expected total number of neutron star LMXBs with both current observations and the galaxy's millisecond radio pulsar population, the dominant class of these systems must have recurrence times far surpassing a century for MAXI-detectable outbursts, implying that few such systems have been identified to date.

This paper constructs a min-max framework for minimal surfaces utilizing sweepouts of surfaces with genus $g\geq 1$ and at least $m\geq 1$ ideal boundary components. We demonstrate that the width associated with the area functional is realized by a bubble tree limit, which comprises branched genus $g$ free boundary minimal surfaces with nodes, alongside potentially a finite number of branched minimal spheres and free boundary minimal disks.

To resolve issues arising from incomplete information regarding the game environment in simulating non-complete information dynamic countermeasure modeling for intelligent games, a hierarchical analysis confrontation strategy based on OODA (Observation, Orientation, Decision, Action) theory is introduced. Aligning with the future trends of unmanned warfare, NetLogo software is employed to simulate dynamic tank-on-tank confrontations. During validation, OODA theory characterizes the operational dynamics between opposing forces (Red and Blue), executing a four-stage cycle of observation, judgment, decision, and action contingent on the armor counts of both sides. Following the initial cycle, the OODA system refines judgment and decision time coefficients for subsequent engagements based on the outcomes obtained. Unlike traditional simulation approaches that focus on objective metrics like loss and support rates, this OODA-driven hierarchical game analysis offers a more comprehensive assessment of confrontation scenarios.

Extensive research has investigated the conditions required for $k$ graphs, $G_1, \dots, G_k$, sharing a vertex set of size $n$, to contain a "colorful" copy of a graph $H$ (a copy where each edge originates from a distinct $G_i$). Keevash, Saks, Sudakov, and Verstra\"{e} established a lower bound on the sum of the edges of these graphs that guarantees such a copy and defined $\operatorname{ex}_k(n,H)$ as the maximum total edge count for a configuration avoiding a colorful $H$. They fully characterized $\operatorname{ex}_k(n,K_r)$ for large $n$, demonstrating that one of two natural constructions is always extremal depending on $k$. Furthermore, they conjectured this dichotomy holds for all color-critical graphs, proving it for the 3-color-critical case. This work confirms the conjecture for 4-color-critical graphs and for almost all $r$-color-critical graphs when $r > 4$. Additionally, it is shown that for non-color-critical, non-bipartite graphs, neither natural construction is extremal for specific values of $k$, thereby resolving a question posed by Keevash, Saks, Sudakov, and Verstra\"{e}te.

This paper derives several sufficient conditions ensuring the normality of a family of holomorphic mappings from a domain $D\subseteq\mathbb{C}$ into $\mathbb{P}^n$. These findings represent refinements to the Montel-Carathéodory Theorem concerning families of $\mathbb{P}^n$-valued holomorphic curves.

Metal photocathodes serve as a critical source of high-brightness electron beams, essential for both large-scale accelerators and compact microscopes. By nano-engineering metal surfaces with features comparable to the optical wavelength, one can excite and confine surface plasmon polariton waves. This study demonstrates that applying plasmonic nanogrooves to gold photocathodes yields a tenfold increase in fourth-order photoemission efficiency relative to linear processes. These cathodes achieved sustained average currents exceeding 100 nA and withstood optical intensities above 2 GW/cm² without performance degradation. A high-precision fabrication method is detailed to ensure reproducible results. Various nano-structured surfaces were evaluated optically and via electron yield, exhibiting excellent alignment with their theoretical designs. Furthermore, electron beam brightness was assessed through measurements of mean transverse energy; the observed asymmetry was attributed to surface roughness and validated against numerical simulations. These findings confirm that nano-engineered surfaces function as enhanced photocathodes, offering a robust, air-stable source of high-average-current electron beams with significant potential for both scientific and industrial applications.

Transformer architectures serve as the fundamental building blocks for large-scale autoregressive language models, yet identifying designs that optimally balance task performance (measured by perplexity) against hardware constraints such as peak memory usage and latency remains a significant challenge, particularly given the rapid proliferation of diverse hardware. We capitalize on the counterintuitive empirical finding that, regardless of architectural topology, the number of decoder parameters in autoregressive Transformers exhibits a strong rank correlation with task performance. This insight naturally gives rise to a straightforward, training-free Neural Architecture Search (NAS) algorithm that utilizes decoder parameters as a proxy for perplexity. Named Lightweight Transformer Search (LTS), this algorithm's search phase can execute directly on target devices without requiring GPUs. By leveraging on-device measurements, LTS identifies the Pareto frontier between perplexity and various hardware costs. Evaluated across a range of devices from ARM CPUs to NVIDIA GPUs using GPT-2 and Transformer-XL backbones, LTS demonstrates that 16-layer models can match the perplexity of larger counterparts while achieving up to 2.5x faster runtime and 1.2x to 2.0x reduced peak memory usage. In zero-shot and one-shot evaluations, LTS-generated Pareto-frontier models outperform the 350M parameter OPT model in average accuracy across 14 tasks, with latency reductions of up to 1.6x. Furthermore, LTS generates these frontiers in under three hours on a standard laptop, effectively eliminating the hundreds of GPU hours typically required for search and establishing a robust, efficient baseline for future NAS approaches in autoregressive language modeling.

A \emph{primitive hole} refers to a cycle of length 3 within a graph $G$. The count of such holes in a specific graph $G$ defines its primitive hole number. Additionally, the primitive degree of a vertex $v$ in $G$ represents the quantity of primitive holes connected to that vertex. This paper introduces the concept of Pythagorean holes in graphs and begins exploring significant findings regarding them, including those applicable to general graphs as well as set-graphs and Jaco graphs.

Source-Free Domain Adaptation (SFDA) focuses on transferring a pre-trained source model to an unlabeled target domain without requiring access to the labeled source data, a setup that is highly practical given concerns regarding data privacy, security, and transmission. To compensate for the lack of source data, most current approaches utilize feature prototype-based pseudo-labeling for self-training adaptation. However, since these prototypes are derived from instance-level clustering, they often exhibit category bias and generate noisy labels, particularly when visual domain gaps vary across categories. Furthermore, relying on a single central prototype per category can be ineffective, potentially causing negative transfer, especially for difficult transfer cases. To overcome these limitations, we propose a general Class-Balanced Multicentric Dynamic prototype (BMD) strategy for SFDA. Specifically, for each target category, we first employ a global inter-class balanced sampling method to gather representative target samples, followed by an intra-class multicentric clustering approach to generate more robust prototypes. Unlike existing methods that update pseudo-labels at fixed intervals, we introduce a dynamic pseudo-labeling mechanism that integrates network update information throughout the adaptation process. Extensive experiments demonstrate that this model-agnostic BMD strategy significantly enhances state-of-the-art SFDA methods. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ispc-lab/BMD.

Recent decades of humanoid research indicate that achieving high dynamic performance necessitates a stiff structure alongside an optimal mass-inertial distribution. Humanoid robots utilizing a purely tree-type architecture often become bulky and are typically limited in terms of velocity and force/torque capabilities. This paper introduces RH5, a novel series-parallel hybrid humanoid standing 2 meters tall and weighing 62.5 kg, designed to execute heavy-duty dynamic tasks while carrying 5 kg payloads in each hand. The robot's analysis and control rely on a whole-body trajectory optimization method based on differential dynamic programming (DDP). Furthermore, we propose an enhanced soft-constrained DDP algorithm for contact stability, which generates physically consistent walking trajectories that can be tracked using simple PD position control within a physics simulator. Finally, preliminary experimental results on the RH5 humanoid are presented.

Recent advancements in machine learning have facilitated data-driven autonomous navigation for mobile robots. However, because most learning-based systems rely on data from artificially constructed environments, robots often face unseen scenarios during large-scale real-world deployment that fall outside the training distribution, resulting in suboptimal performance. Conversely, direct real-world training is typically unsafe and inefficient. To mitigate this, we propose Self-supervised Environment Synthesis (SES), a framework where autonomous robots, after initial safe and efficient real-world operation, leverage their deployment experiences to reconstruct and synthesize representative training scenarios in simulation. Utilizing these synthesized environments for further training enhances future real-world navigation capabilities. The efficacy of SES in generating representative simulation environments and improving real-world performance is validated through a large-scale evaluation in a high-fidelity, realistic simulator and a small-scale test on a physical robot.

Cell-free networks are viewed as a promising solution for enhancing network capacity due to their robust interference management capabilities. Nevertheless, achieving further capacity gains typically necessitates deploying additional base stations (BSs), which incurs high costs and energy consumption. To mitigate this, we introduce the concept of RIS-aided cell-free networks, leveraging the recently developed reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) technology to boost capacity with reduced cost and power usage. The core strategy involves substituting certain required BSs with cost-effective and energy-efficient RISs. In a wideband context, we formulate a joint precoding optimization problem at both the BSs and RISs aimed at maximizing network capacity. Given the non-convex nature and computational complexity of this problem, we propose an alternating optimization framework. Specifically, we decouple the problem using fractional programming and solve the resulting subproblems iteratively. Notably, while many existing studies address specific scenarios that are subsets of the general case presented here, our proposed joint precoding framework offers a versatile solution for maximizing capacity across most current RIS-aided configurations. Finally, simulation results indicate that the proposed scheme significantly outperforms conventional cell-free networks in terms of network capacity.

This study examines the structural characteristics and morphology of galaxies brighter than $19.5^m$ in the $F814W$ band within the Coma Cluster's core, utilizing data from the HST/ACS Coma Cluster Treasury Survey. By relying primarily on spectroscopic redshifts, we identified 132 cluster members from an initial sample of 219 galaxies. Among these 132 members, there are 51 non-dwarfs and 81 dwarfs, whereas the 32 non-members consist of 4 dwarfs and 28 non-dwarfs; redshift data remains unavailable for the remaining 55 galaxies. We performed bulge-disc decomposition on the sample using GALFIT to derive key parameters and conducted a morphological classification through visual inspection of residuals. Our analysis investigates the relationships between morphological types and the Bulge-to-Total light ratio ($B/T$), Color-Magnitude Relation (CMR), S\'ersic index ($n$), the Kormendy relation, and cross-correlations among these parameters for both bulges and galaxies. Specifically, six members were classified as E/SO based on residuals and contour maps revealing central boxy/peanut bulges, leading us to categorize them as E/SO to minimize ambiguity between elliptical and S0 types. This research elucidates critical connections between parameters such as $B/T$, color, and $n$, offering insights into the merger histories of these galaxies as reflected in their positions on the Kormendy Diagram and their S\'ersic indices. Statistical methods reveal a significantly higher prevalence of E/SO and S0 galaxies among members compared to non-members.

The time delay experienced by light signals within the quadrupole field of a stationary body has been calculated to the second post-Newtonian (2PN) order using harmonic coordinates. For light rays grazing the Sun, Jupiter, and Saturn, the 2PN quadrupole contribution to this delay reaches approximately 0.004, 0.14, and 0.04 picoseconds, respectively. When compared against results from the first post-Newtonian (1PN and 1.5PN) approximations, it is determined that achieving a measurement accuracy of 0.001 picoseconds in the solar system necessitates the inclusion of the first eight mass multipoles and the spin-dipole for these massive bodies. Furthermore, to maintain this level of precision, the spin-hexapole of Jupiter must also be accounted for.

The Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer (AMS-02) is currently measuring electron and positron fluxes in cosmic rays with unparalleled accuracy up to the TeV range, offering a distinctive means to investigate local Galactic characteristics. While the interpretation of these spectra remains a subject of debate, particularly regarding the positron surplus above 10 GeV, the pulsar hypothesis has gained strong support following the detection of TeV gamma-ray halos around the Geminga and Monogem pulsars. Nevertheless, key aspects regarding the spatial and energetic distribution of pulsars, as well as the specific mechanisms of positron production, acceleration, and release, remain incompletely understood. This presentation outlines how high-precision AMS-02 positron data can be leveraged to constrain the primary attributes of the Galactic pulsar population and the requisite positron acceleration models to account for observed fluxes. By simulating extensive populations of Galactic pulsars based on the latest self-consistent models of spin-down and evolution—calibrated against catalog data—we fit the AMS-02 positron spectrum alongside a secondary component arising from primary cosmic ray interactions with the interstellar medium. This approach allows us to identify the pulsar physical parameters that dominate the positron flux and evaluate how varying assumptions concerning radial distributions, spin-down characteristics, Galactic propagation models, and positron emission timing influence the results.

This study examines a system of two convection-diffusion boundary value problems featuring small positive parameters multiplying the highest derivatives and discontinuous source terms. The solutions to these problems display both boundary and weak interior layers. We introduce a numerical approach utilizing the finite element method, specifically employing Shishkin and Bakhvalov-Shishkin meshes. Theoretical analysis yields an energy norm error estimate of order $O(N^{-1}\ln^{3/2}{N})$ relative to the perturbation parameter. Additionally, numerical experiments are provided to validate these theoretical findings.

This article offers a global and generalized outlook on electrodynamic metamaterials created through space and time engineered modulations, termed Generalized Space-Time Engineered Modulation (GSTEM) Metamaterials or GSTEMs. Adopting a unified spacetime framework, the work introduces accelerated metamaterials as a novel category of dynamic metamaterials. Initially, it situates GSTEMs within the wider context of electrodynamic systems involving non-modulated moving sources in a vacuum and moving bodies, distinguishing the moving-matter characteristics of the latter from the moving-perturbation nature of GSTEMs. The text categorizes various GSTEM types, including Space EMs (SEMs), Time EMs (TEMs), Uniform Space-Time EMs (USTEMs), and Accelerated Space-Time EMs (ASTEMs). Subsequently, it defines the physics governing related interfaces, covering direct-spacetime scattering and inverse-spacetime transition transformations. Furthermore, it elucidates the physics of GSTEM metamaterials formed by stacking these interfaces and homogenizing the resulting crystals; this section features a novel explanation of light deflection by USTEMs as a spacetime weighted averaging phenomenon and demonstrates ASTEM capabilities for light curving and black-hole light attraction. The article concludes by outlining future prospects, with supplementary material providing useful complementary information and animations.

We introduce the AID-purifier, an auxiliary network designed to enhance the robustness of adversarially-trained models by cleansing their inputs. Functioning as a lightweight add-on to an existing classifier, it is trained as a discriminator using binary cross-entropy loss to maintain computational efficiency. Leveraging information maximization principles, the architecture feeds two layers of the main classification network into the auxiliary system to extract valuable insights from adversarial samples. To facilitate iterative purification optimization, the auxiliary network employs AVmixup during training. The AID-purifier can be combined with other purification methods, such as PixelDefend, for further improvement. Experimental results demonstrate that the most robust adversarially-trained networks are significantly enhanced by top-tier purification techniques, positioning the lightweight and robust AID-purifier as a highly competitive solution.

The S{\o}rensen--Dice Coefficient, often referred to as Dice loss, has gained significant traction as a loss function because of its resilience in scenarios where negative samples vastly outnumber positive ones, including semantic segmentation, natural language processing, and sound event detection. Traditional polyphonic sound event detection models trained with binary cross-entropy often suffer from suboptimal performance due to being dominated by updates from negative samples. This study examines how Dice loss, along with intra- and inter-modal transfer learning, data augmentation, and recording formats, influences the performance of multichannel input polyphonic sound event detection systems. Our findings indicate that systems trained with Dice loss consistently surpass those using cross-entropy loss in terms of F1 score and error rate across various training configurations and recording types. Additionally, we secured further improvements by employing transfer learning and strategically combining different data augmentation methods.

It is a well-established fact that uniform resolvent estimates lead to spectral cluster estimates; however, we demonstrate that this implication holds in reverse under certain conditions. Specifically, the universal spectral cluster estimates provided by Sogge \cite{MR930395} for the Laplace--Beltrami operator on compact Riemannian manifolds without boundary directly entail the uniform Sobolev inequality of Dos Santos Ferreira, Kenig, and Salo \cite{MR3200351}, bypassing the need for parametrices. This insight further generates novel resolvent estimates for manifolds featuring boundaries or nonsmooth metrics, leveraging spectral cluster bounds from Smith--Sogge \cite{MR2316270} and Smith, Koch, and Tataru \cite{MR2443996}, respectively. Additionally, we transform the recent spectral cluster results of Canzani and Galkowski \cite{Canzani--Galkowski} into enhanced resolvent bounds. Finally, we prove that these resolvent estimates remain stable under perturbations, utilizing this property to derive uniform Sobolev and spectral cluster inequalities for Schr\"odinger operators with singular potentials.

Some cosmic inflation models generate significant perturbations at small scales that can eventually form primordial black holes. Determining the statistical properties of these perturbations and the resulting black holes requires moving beyond linear perturbation theory. Stochastic inflation offers a method to incorporate the most prominent non-linear effects. This paper reviews recent advancements in numerically simulating stochastic inflation. Unlike analytical methods, numerical approaches can account for a broader range of non-linearities and are applicable to single-field inflationary models regardless of their specific potential.

Asteroid families typically originate from the catastrophic disruption of a larger parent body, meaning their members are expected to reflect the parent's composition and mineralogical history. Recent releases of extensive datasets have enabled detailed investigations into the physical characteristics of numerous asteroids, including many within identified families. This review examines these new datasets and the aggregated properties of asteroid families derived from them, while also addressing current data limitations and outstanding questions in the field.

We investigate the theoretical formation of quantum droplets within a two-component Bose-Hubbard system subject to an external trapping potential. In this setup, a central superfluid region, encircled by a double-filled Mott insulator, constitutes a self-bound droplet stabilized by the discontinuous nature of the phase transition between these two states. Utilizing time-dependent Gutzwiller simulations in two dimensions, we demonstrate how manipulating the trap potential can elicit the droplet's characteristic dynamics. Both the static and dynamical attributes of this droplet are qualitatively captured by an effective Ginzburg-Landau field theory featuring cubic-quintic nonlinearities; notably, this framework yields an attractive cubic nonlinearity despite all underlying bare interparticle interactions being repulsive.

This paper introduces a precise two-phase millimeter-Wave (mmWave) beamspace channel tracking framework. In the initial phase, we train an extreme reservoir machine (ERM) to capture and forecast historical mmWave beamspace channel features for future time steps. To enhance prediction accuracy, we refine the ERM using the Xavier initialization method, which sets input weights based on a zero-mean, finite-variance Gaussian distribution. This approach reduces the prediction variance of a standard ERM by 49%. Numerical results demonstrate that this method improves the achievable spectral efficiency (SE) of current alternatives by 13% at a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 15dB. In the second phase, we employ ensemble learning by sequentially integrating multiple ERMs to create an adaptive boosting (AdaBoost) model. This strategy further cuts the prediction variance of conventional ERMs by 56% and boosts the achievable SE by 21% compared to existing schemes at an SNR of 15dB.

This study examines the performance of a microscopic quantum heat engine composed of V- or Lambda-type emitters, which interact either collectively or independently while coupled to thermal reservoirs. Although Carnot's cycle maintains a higher efficiency than these specific configurations, our findings indicate that under comparable conditions, a cooperative Lambda-type engine can outperform a V-type engine. In the Lambda setup, emitter cooperativity is crucial, substantially enhancing performance, whereas it has a negligible impact on V-type engines. This distinction arises because the population inversion on the working atomic transition and its off-diagonal elements exhibit different behaviors in these two atomic ensembles.

We examine statistical models derived from the shared solutions of sparse polynomial systems with general coefficients. The maximum likelihood degree represents the count of critical points for the likelihood function when restricted to these models. We demonstrate that this degree for a sparse polynomial system is dictated by its Newton polytopes and is equivalent to the mixed volume of an associated Lagrange system of equations.

This review examines theoretical models featuring extended Higgs sectors that permit tree-level flavor-changing neutral currents (FCNCs) mediated by scalar particles. Following a concise overview of models lacking such tree-level FCNCs, the discussion focuses on those that exhibit them. A widely used mass-matrix ansatz, which posits that flavor-changing couplings equal the geometric mean of individual flavor couplings, is detailed. Although this framework served as a benchmark for experimentalists for thirty years, it is now facing significant experimental challenges; couplings previously expected to be of order one must be much smaller, rendering the ansatz disfavored. The hypothesis of minimal flavor violation is subsequently introduced, followed by an analysis of specific models, including the Branco-Grimus-Lavoura models. While these models have not yet been ruled out by experiments, they are highly predictive and await testing upon the discovery of heavy Higgs bosons. The review then addresses flavorful models and the flavor-changing decays of heavy Higgs bosons, demonstrating that in many such scenarios, heavy Higgs bosons may predominantly decay via flavor-changing channels (e.g., $ct$ or $\mu\tau$), urging experimentalists to incorporate these possibilities into their search strategies.

This report details the measurement of prompt D$^0$, D$^+$, D$^{*+}$, and D$^+_s$ meson production in proton-lead (p-Pb) collisions occurring at a nucleon pair center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$ = 5.02 TeV, utilizing an integrated luminosity of $292\pm 11$ $\mu$b$^{-1}$. Differential production cross sections were determined at mid-rapidity ($-0.96<y_{\rm cms}<0.04$) as a function of transverse momentum ($p_{\rm T}$) across specific ranges: $0< p_{\rm T} < 36$ GeV/$c$ for D$^0$, $1< p_{\rm T} <36$ GeV/$c$ for D$^+$ and D$^{*+}$, and $2< p_{\rm T} <24$ GeV/$c$ for D$^+_s$. The nuclear modification factor $R_{\rm pPb}$ was derived for each meson type as a function of $p_{\rm T}$, referencing proton-proton (pp) data taken at the same energy. These results align with unity across the entire $p_{\rm T}$ spectrum. The average $R_{\rm pPb}$ for non-strange D mesons was evaluated against theoretical models incorporating initial-state effects and parton transport predictions. Additionally, the $p_{\rm T}$ dependence of $R_{\rm pPb}$ for D$^0$, D$^+$, and D$^{*+}$ was analyzed within the $1< p_{\rm T} < 36$ GeV/$c$ interval as a function of collision centrality, with central-to-peripheral ratios calculated from D-meson yields in various centrality classes. These findings show a trend consistent with charged-particle measurements across all centrality bins. Ratios of the $p_{\rm T}$-differential cross sections for the four meson species are also presented. Finally, D$^+_s$ and D$^+$ yields were compared relative to charged-particle multiplicity across several $p_{\rm T}$ intervals, revealing no modification in the relative abundances of the four species compared to pp collisions within statistical and systematic uncertainties.

Our previous research demonstrated that multiple Local Group (LG) galaxies exhibit radial velocities (RVs) significantly exceeding predictions from standard cosmological dynamical models. In this study, we reveal that six of these seven galaxies form a remarkably thin plane with a root mean square thickness of just 101 kpc, despite spanning nearly 3 Mpc—a scale far exceeding the conventional virial radii of the Milky Way (MW) or M31. This structure passes approximately 70 kpc from the MW-M31 barycenter and is inclined at 16° relative to the MW-M31 line. We propose a toy model suggesting that a past MW-M31 flyby within Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND) could have generated tidal dwarf galaxies that settled into the recently identified satellite planes around both galaxies. This scenario remains viable only for a specific MW-M31 orbital plane, which aligns closely with the plane containing LG dwarfs showing anomalously high RVs. Furthermore, restricted $N$-body simulations of the LG under MOND illustrate how a rapid past encounter between the MW and M31 could gravitationally eject test particles at high speeds. The most distant particles tend to cluster within the MW-M31 orbital plane, likely because those achieving the highest RVs were ejected nearly parallel to the perturber's motion. This offers a dynamical explanation for the observed trend in the real LG, a pattern unlikely to result from a random alignment of galaxies within an isotropic or mildly flattened distribution (probability = 0.0015).

During the NISQ era, the limited number of controllable hardware qubits prevents the implementation of quantum error correction (QEC). Consequently, quantum error mitigation (QEM) offers an alternative approach by suppressing measurement errors through repeated experiments and data postprocessing. However, standard QEM techniques, such as quasi-probability decomposition, often overlook correlated errors across different gates. In this work, we present a QEM strategy utilizing the matrix product operator (MPO) representation of quantum circuits, which characterizes noise channels with polynomial complexity. We validate this technique on a fully parallel circuit with a depth of 20 and up to 20 qubits subjected to both local and global noise. Results show that circuit errors are reduced by several magnitudes using a minimal bond dimension ($D^{\prime} = 1$) for the noise channel. By enhancing noise modeling accuracy without demanding additional experimental resources, our method improves QEM performance and expands its applicability. Furthermore, this approach holds promise for addressing higher-dimensional circuits involving more qubits and greater depth.

This study introduces Con$^{2}$DA, a straightforward framework that adapts recent semi-supervised learning advancements to address the semi-supervised domain adaptation (SSDA) challenge. By applying stochastic data transformations to inputs, the framework creates pairs of associated samples, which are then projected into a feature representation space via a feature extractor. We employ various loss functions to ensure consistency between the feature representations of these paired samples. Our results demonstrate that these learned representations effectively handle data distribution discrepancies inherent in domain adaptation. Experimental analysis of the model's core components reveals that (i) learning consistent and contrastive feature representations is vital for extracting robust discriminative features across domains, and (ii) the model gains significant advantages from strong augmentation strategies. Consequently, our approach achieves state-of-the-art results on three benchmark datasets for SSDA.

Vision Transformers (ViTs) have achieved state-of-the-art results across numerous visual tasks, prompting adversaries to target them with backdoor attacks. While the susceptibility of traditional Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to such attacks is well-documented, research into ViT-specific backdoors remains limited. Unlike CNNs, which rely on convolutions to capture local pixel features, ViTs utilize patches and attention mechanisms to extract global context. Consequently, directly adapting CNN-based backdoor strategies to ViTs results in poor performance, characterized by low clean data accuracy and a low attack success rate. To address this, we introduce $TrojViT$, a stealthy and practical attack tailored specifically for ViTs. Instead of employing area-based triggers common in CNN attacks, $TrojViT$ creates patch-level triggers that identify vulnerable bits within the ViT's DRAM-stored parameters. This process leverages patch salience ranking and attention-target loss to construct a Trojan, which is then minimized through parameter updates to reduce the number of altered bits. Once these vulnerable bits are flipped to embed the Trojan, the model maintains normal inference accuracy on benign inputs but is compelled to classify triggered inputs into a specific target class. We demonstrate that $TrojViT$ can effectively backdoor a ViT by flipping only a few bits identified through the RowHammer technique. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets and ViT architectures confirm the method's efficacy; for instance, on ImageNet, flipping just 345 bits allowed $TrojViT$ to direct 99.64% of test images to the target class.

This course was held at Peking University during the Fall 2019 semester. The curriculum covers the following topics:

(1) An overview of general topology, hyperspaces, metric and pseudometric spaces, and graph theory.
(2) Graphs within metric spaces, including minimum spanning trees, Steiner minimal trees, and Gromov minimal fillings.
(3) The Hausdorff distance, Vietoris topology, limit theory, and the inheritance of completeness, total boundedness, and compactness through hyperspaces.
(4) The Gromov-Hausdorff distance, the triangle inequality, positive definiteness regarding isometry classes of compact spaces, and counterexamples concerning boundedly compact spaces.
(5) The Gromov-Hausdorff distance for separable spaces defined via their isometric images in $\ell_\infty$, correspondences, and the formulation of this distance using correspondences.
(6) Epsilon-isometries and their relationship to the Gromov-Hausdorff distance.
(7) Irreducible correspondences and their connection to the Gromov-Hausdorff distance.
(8) Gromov-Hausdorff convergence and the preservation of metric and topological properties under such convergence.
(9) The Gromov-Hausdorff space (GH-space), optimal correspondences, the existence of closed optimal correspondences for compact metric spaces, and the fact that the GH-space is geodesic.
(10) The cover number, packing number, total boundedness, completeness, and separability within the context of the GH-space.
(11) The mst-spectrum expressed through GH-distances to simplexes and the Steiner problem formulated in the GH-space.
(12) GH-distances to simplexes containing more points versus those containing at most the same number of points.
(13) The Generalized Borsuk problem, its resolution using GH-distances, the clique covering number and chromatic number of simple graphs, their dualities, and methods to calculate these numbers via GH-distances.

Event extraction has traditionally been approached as a sentence-level task within the Information Extraction community. However, we contend that this perspective misaligns with human information-seeking patterns, resulting in extraction outputs that are both incomplete and uninformative. To address this, we introduce a document-level neural model for event argument extraction, framing the problem as conditional generation based on event templates. Additionally, we present WikiEvents, a newly compiled benchmark dataset for document-level extraction that features comprehensive event and coreference annotations. Our model achieves an absolute F1 score improvement of 7.6% and 5.7% over the next-best methods on the RAMS and WikiEvents datasets, respectively. Furthermore, on the more demanding task of informative argument extraction, which necessitates implicit coreference reasoning, we secure a 9.3% F1 gain compared to the strongest baseline. Finally, to showcase the model's adaptability, we developed the first end-to-end zero-shot event extraction framework; utilizing only 10 of 33 event types from the ACE dataset, it attains 97% of the fully supervised trigger extraction performance and 82% of the argument extraction performance.

Graph-based semi-supervised learning integrates graph topology with labeled examples to categorize unlabeled ones. This study investigates how a noisy oracle impacts classification, specifically by deriving the Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimator for clustering within a Degree Corrected Stochastic Block Model (DC-SBM) when a noisy oracle discloses a subset of labels. We subsequently introduce an algorithm based on the continuous relaxation of this MAP estimator and demonstrate its consistency. Empirical results on both synthetic and real-world datasets indicate that our method delivers strong performance, even under conditions of highly noisy labeling.

Surges represent cool, dense ejections commonly detected in chromospheric lines and are closely linked to other solar events such as UV bursts and coronal jets. This study aims to fill the gap in inverted models and diagnostics for surges while characterizing their plasma properties. We analyzed surges associated with UV bursts observed by the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph (IRIS) on April 2016. Using the k-means algorithm, we identified representative Mg II h&k line profiles to examine the mid- and low-chromosphere and performed inversions with the STiC code.
