Additionally, we investigated far-UV spectra, specifically the O IV 1399.8 and 1401.2 \r{A} lines, to conduct density diagnostics and determine transition region properties, comparing our findings with Bifrost code simulations. Thanks to the k-means clustering, we reduced the number of Mg II h&k profiles requiring inversion by a factor of 43.2. The inversions of these representative profiles indicate that the mid- and low-chromosphere of surges exhibit temperatures primarily around T = 6 kK within the optical depth range of $-6.0 \le \log_{10}(\tau) \le -3.2$. For electronic number density ($n_e$) and line-of-sight velocity ($V_{\mathrm{LOS}}$), the most reliable inversion results fall within $-6.0 \le \log_{10}(\tau) \le -4.8$, where $n_e$ varies from $\sim1.6 \times 10^{11}$ to $10^{12}$ cm$^{-3}$ and $V_{\mathrm{LOS}}$ is a few km s$^{-1}$. For the first time, we provide observational evidence of enhanced O IV emission within surges, suggesting these phenomena significantly impact the transition region even in the weakest far-UV lines. The layers emitting O IV show electron number densities ranging from $2.5\times 10^{10}$ to $10^{12}$ cm$^{-3}$, a finding supported theoretically by simulations regarding the topology and location of this emission.

Offensive material is widespread across social media platforms, raising significant concerns for both corporate and governmental entities. Numerous recent studies have explored techniques for identifying various types of such content, including hate speech, cyberbullying, and cyberaggression. However, the majority of this research focuses on English, largely due to the availability of annotated English datasets. This paper leverages existing English data by utilizing cross-lingual contextual word embeddings and transfer learning to generate predictions for languages with limited resources. Specifically, we project our findings onto Bengali, Hindi, and Spanish datasets, achieving macro F1 scores of 0.8415, 0.8568, and 0.7513, respectively. Furthermore, our approach demonstrates competitive performance compared to top systems in recent shared tasks for these languages, validating the robustness of cross-lingual contextual embeddings and transfer learning for offensive content detection.

Extracting cause-and-effect entities from medical literature is a critical component of medical information retrieval. Solutions to this task facilitate the compilation of diverse causal relationships, including those between diseases and symptoms, medications and side effects, and genes and diseases. Current extraction methods perform adequately when causes and effects are represented as named entities, single nouns, or short noun phrases (two to three words). However, medical texts often feature complex, multi-word phrases for these entities, causing existing methods to fail. Partial extraction yields low-quality, uninformative, or contradictory facts compared to the intended meaning. To address this, we introduce PatternCausality, an unsupervised method tailored for medical literature. Our approach first employs a set of cause-effect dependency patterns as templates to identify head words, followed by a novel phrase extraction technique to derive complete and meaningful cause-and-effect phrases. Experimental results on a dataset derived from PubMed articles demonstrate that PatternCausality significantly outperforms existing methods, achieving an order-of-magnitude improvement in F-score.

Visual recognition systems constantly process vast amounts of images and videos. Similar to the human visual system (HVS), machine vision systems (MVS) are highly sensitive to image quality, as degradation causes information loss and recognition failures. Recently, image and video processing techniques specifically tailored for MVS have gained prominence. However, current approaches focus on individual machines rather than the broader machine community, failing to meet the needs of all device types. Additionally, MVS characteristics are underutilized, restricting compression efficiency. This paper introduces a novel concept, the Satisfied Machine Ratio (SMR), to resolve these challenges. SMR statistically evaluates image quality from a machine's perspective by aggregating satisfaction scores from a diverse array of machines, accounting for MVS characteristics. We have established the first large-scale SMR dataset, comprising over 22 million annotated images for SMR research. Moreover, we propose a deep learning model capable of predicting SMR for any compressed image or video frame. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the SMR model significantly enhances the performance of image and video compression designed for machine recognition. Furthermore, the model exhibits strong generalization across unseen machines, compression frameworks, and datasets.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have proven highly effective for medical image segmentation. However, this study tackles several persistent challenges associated with these models. Training CNNs on limited medical datasets remains difficult, often necessitating transfer learning. Additionally, these models are notorious for generating over-confident predictions and failing silently when encountering out-of-distribution (OOD) data during testing. This paper advocates for multi-task learning, which involves training a single model across multiple datasets covering various organs and imaging modalities. We demonstrate that this approach enables a single CNN to automatically recognize context and accurately segment target organs, while also yielding more accurate and better-calibrated predictions than dedicated models trained on individual datasets. Our experiments indicate that multi-task learning can surpass transfer learning in medical image segmentation tasks. For OOD detection, we propose a method utilizing spectral analysis of CNN feature maps. We show that datasets representing different organs or modalities possess distinct spectral signatures, allowing the identification of whether a test image aligns with the training data. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this spectral approach is significantly more accurate than OOD detection based on prediction uncertainty. The methods introduced in this paper substantially enhance the accuracy and reliability of CNN-based medical image segmentation.

Contemporary e-commerce is deeply embedded in daily routines, causing the shopping process to evolve from a single transaction into a sequence of multiple actions, including browsing, adding to a cart, and purchasing. Consequently, leveraging interaction data alongside auxiliary behavioral data has garnered significant attention in e-commerce recommender systems. However, current models overlook two critical types of intrinsic heterogeneity essential for capturing variations in user preferences and item attributes. First, intra-heterogeneity arises because users possess multiple social identities with distinct characteristics, leading to diverse interaction preferences. Second, inter-heterogeneity involves each item converting a specific proportion of score from lower-level to higher-level behaviors, reflecting the gradual progression among actions. Neglecting these heterogeneities degrades recommendation ranking performance. To address this, we introduce a novel approach called the intra- and inter-heterogeneity recommendation model (ARGO). This method embeds each user into multiple vectors representing their various identities, using the maximum identity score to determine interaction preferences. Additionally, we treat the item-specific transition percentage as a trainable probability governing the shift between different behaviors. Extensive experiments on two real-world datasets demonstrate that ARGO significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in multi-behavior scenarios.

In \cite{km2}, Kudla and Millson utilized Howe's differential operators to construct a $q$-form $\varphi_{KM}$ on an orthogonal symmetric space, which serves as a fundamental component of their theta lifting theory. This form can be interpreted as the Thom form of a real oriented vector bundle. While Mathai and Quillen \cite{mq} developed a {\em canonical} Thom form, we demonstrate how the Kudla-Millson form can be recovered through their framework. Building on a similar result by \cite{garcia} for signature $(2,q)$ in the hermitian symmetric space case, we extend this finding to arbitrary signatures.

Although deep reinforcement learning has secured significant achievements across diverse fields, the majority of current research prioritizes maximizing the expected total return, often overlooking its intrinsic stochasticity. This randomness, termed aleatoric uncertainty, is intrinsically linked to risk assessment. This study pioneers the investigation of risk-sensitive deep reinforcement learning within an average reward framework, specifically employing variance as the risk metric. We concentrate on a variance-constrained policy optimization challenge aimed at identifying a policy that maximizes the long-run average expected reward while ensuring the long-run variance of this average remains below a specified threshold. By leveraging Lagrangian and Fenchel dualities, we convert the original constrained problem into an unconstrained saddle-point policy optimization task and introduce an actor-critic algorithm capable of iteratively and efficiently refining the policy, the Lagrange multiplier, and the Fenchel dual variable. Furthermore, when both value and policy functions are modeled using multi-layer overparameterized neural networks, we demonstrate that our proposed actor-critic algorithm produces a sequence of policies that converges to a globally optimal policy at a sublinear rate.

The study demonstrates a high prevalence of twisted (vortex) particle production in noncentral heavy-ion collisions. In these events, photons generated by the rotation of charges exhibit significant twist. Furthermore, charged particles emerge in nonspreading multiwave states with substantial orbital angular momentum. It is anticipated that the emission of any twisted particles, characterized by specific effects, is a widespread phenomenon.

Okuyama and Sakai recently introduced a new holomorphic anomaly equation for the partition function of 2d Yang-Mills theory on a torus, grounded in an anholomorphic modification of the propagator within the bosonic framework. Leveraging the boson-fermion correspondence, we establish the corresponding formula for the deformed partition function in the fermionic representation and provide a proof for the holomorphic anomaly equation.

We introduce a new class of Yang-Mills solutions defined on Minkowski space with an SO(1,3) gauge group, categorized geometrically into interior and exterior regions relative to the lightcone. This distinction is achieved by foliating the interior with SO(1,3)/SO(3) cosets and the exterior with SO(1,3)/SO(1,2) cosets, followed by an analytical solution to the Yang-Mills equations for an SO(1,3)-invariant gauge field. Although the resulting fields and their stress-energy tensor exhibit divergence at the lightcone within Minkowski space, we demonstrate that this divergence can be regularized owing to the tensor's unique algebraic properties.

We present EventNarrative, a dataset converting open-world knowledge graphs into text. While recent event-driven Information Extraction (IE) advances have highlighted a gap in prior graph-to-text research, which focused solely on entity-driven graphs, this work prioritizes event-centric data. Although our generation framework is adaptable to other KG types, it specifically addresses this underrepresented area. Unlike existing large-scale graph-to-text datasets that lack parallel KG-text pairs, or small-scale paired datasets that are manually created, lack rich ontologies, and suffer from sparse graphs and unlinked entities, EventNarrative offers a significant improvement. It comprises approximately 230,000 graph-text pairs—six times the size of the current largest parallel dataset—utilizing a rich ontology where every KG entity is linked to the text. Manual annotations further validate its high quality. Our objectives are twofold: to advance event-centric research by addressing data scarcity and to provide a robust, large-scale benchmark for evaluating current and future knowledge graph-to-text models. Additionally, we assess two baseline approaches on EventNarrative: a specialized graph-to-text model and two state-of-the-art language models previously shown to be adaptable to this domain.

This study investigates electronic correlation within confined H$^{-}$, He, and Li$^+$ atoms in their ground states through the lens of informational entropies. Various variational wavefunctions are utilized to more accurately capture Coulomb correlation effects. The resulting $S_r$, $S_p$, and $S_t$ entropy values demonstrate significant sensitivity to these Coulomb correlation effects. However, in the strong confinement regime, Coulomb correlation becomes negligible, rendering models based on independent particles and two non-interacting electrons confined by an impenetrable spherical cage particularly relevant. Finally, the calculated energy values align well with existing literature.

MTProto 2.0 serves as the cryptographic foundation for instant messaging within the widely used Telegram application. This study evaluates MTProto 2.0 using the symbolic verification tool ProVerif. We present fully automated proofs demonstrating the soundness of its authentication, standard chat, end-to-end encrypted chat, and rekeying mechanisms against various security attributes, such as authentication, integrity, secrecy, and perfect forward secrecy. However, our analysis also reveals that the rekeying protocol is susceptible to an unknown key-share (UKS) attack. The investigation follows an incremental approach, where each protocol is assessed independently, depending solely on the assurances offered by preceding protocols and the strength of fundamental cryptographic primitives. Ultimately, our research confirms the formal correctness of MTProto 2.0 regarding most critical security properties and can act as a benchmark for the implementation and analysis of both client and server components.

The Fourth Industrial Revolution has significantly boosted industrial productivity and efficiency by integrating data aggregation and cyber-physical systems for optimized planning and scheduling. However, current decision-making processes often fail to accurately account for environmental uncertainties and the imprecise nature of human operators. This oversight results in shipment delays and inaccurate budget forecasts, indicating a flaw in prevailing industrial models that necessitates correction. While previous studies have attempted to address these issues using stochastic or fuzzy set models, this paper introduces a comprehensive approach to logically and realistically quantify non-deterministic uncertainty via probabilistic modeling. This method is highly versatile, applicable to virtually all industrial datasets because it is self-adjusting and employs epsilon-contamination to handle limited or incomplete data. Numerical validation using an industrial dataset from Flanders, Belgium, confirms the efficacy of this robust scheduling method, demonstrating tangible performance improvements.

To enhance the widespread adoption of machine learning, automation is essential. This approach is cost-effective because it reduces the time experts spend on tuning, thereby accelerating development. However, while automated methods generate highly accurate architectures, they often function as "black boxes" that, despite yielding low conventional errors, fail to capture the underlying input-output relationships or ground truth. This paper investigates the application of the Fit to Median Error metric within automated machine learning regression, leveraging evolutionary computation to better approximate the ground truth. When combined with standard error measures, this technique enhances interpretability by regularizing learned relationships toward the conditional median. Compared against traditional regularizers, the Fit to Median Error method produces regression neural networks that model more consistent input-output dynamics. The study focuses on predicting ship power for a stochastic fuel-saving air lubrication system. Results demonstrate that networks optimized for Fit to Median Error approximate the ground truth more consistently while maintaining conventional Minkowski-r error performance.

Diode laser self-injection locking (SIL) into a high-quality factor resonator's whispering gallery mode is a prevalent technique for narrowing laser linewidths and suppressing high-frequency noise. This method has previously enabled ultra-low-noise photonic microwave oscillators and soliton microcomb generation, indicating broad applicability. To date, however, SIL demonstrations have been limited to single lasers, whereas modern telecommunication, quantum, and microwave photonics systems urgently require multi-frequency sources with narrow linewidths. In this work, we experimentally achieve dual-laser SIL by locking two multifrequency laser diodes to distinct modes of an integrated Si$_3$N$_4$ microresonator. Our results reveal simultaneous spectrum collapse, enhanced linewidth narrowing, and high-frequency noise reduction for both lasers, alongside strong nonlinear interactions between the two fields. Furthermore, locking both lasers to a shared mode yields simultaneous frequency and phase stabilization, enabling the coherent addition of their outputs. We also present a comprehensive theory of dual-SIL and analyze the mutual influence of the lasers mediated by nonlinear effects within the microresonator.

The "Rendezvous" game involves two players, Facilitator and Divider, operating on a graph. The Facilitator controls two agents with fixed starting positions, while the Divider commands a team of $k \ge 1$ agents and chooses their initial locations. Players alternate turns moving their agents to adjacent vertices or remaining stationary; the Facilitator aims to coordinate both her agents on the same vertex, whereas the Divider strives to prevent this. The central computational challenge is determining whether the Facilitator possesses a winning strategy against a Divider with $k$ agents. Fomin, Golovach, and Thilikos [WG, 2021] introduced this game, establishing its PSPACE-hardness and co-W[2]-hardness when parameterized by the number of agents. This difficulty suggests exploring structural parameterizations. The original authors demonstrated an FPT algorithm based on modular width and the number of allowed rounds but left open the complexity regarding other structural parameters, specifically asking about the treewidth. We resolve this by proving the problem is co-NP-hard even for graphs with constant treewidth. Additionally, we establish co-W[1]-hardness when parameterized by the feedback vertex set size and the number of agents, and indicate that a polynomial kernel is unlikely when parameterized by the vertex cover number and the number of agents. Conversely, we prove that the problem is FPT when parameterized by both the vertex cover number and the solution size. Finally, for graphs with treewidth at most two and grids, we demonstrate that the problem can be solved in polynomial time.

Contract-based design offers a promising approach to managing the complexity of building sophisticated systems. In this framework, a formal contract separates assumptions—constraints imposed by the component designer on its safe operating environment—from guarantees—promises made by the implementing team. This theory of formal contracts can be structured as an interface theory, facilitating the composition and refinement of both assumptions and guarantees. While existing contract-based methods address various functional and non-functional properties, we introduce the first interface theory specifically designed to ensure system-wide security properties, thereby advancing the science of co-engineering safety and security. Our framework includes a refinement relation and a composition operation that enable incremental design and independent implementation. We develop this theory for both stateless and stateful interfaces and demonstrate its utility through an example drawn from the automotive sector. Furthermore, we define three plausible trace semantics for stateful information-flow interfaces; we show that only two align with temporal logics for specifying hyperproperties, while the third introduces a novel class of hyperproperties situated between the other two.

The quantum speed limit defines the minimum duration required for a quantum system to transition from an initial to a final state under a specific dynamical process, offering crucial insights into the maximum rate of state transformations essential for designing and controlling quantum technologies. This paper establishes speed limits for various correlations, including entanglement, Bell-CHSH correlations, and quantum mutual information, within systems evolving under dynamical processes. Our primary contribution is a derived speed limit for negativity, an entanglement monotone applicable to arbitrary-dimensional bipartite quantum systems and processes. Additionally, we obtain speed limits for other correlation measures such as concurrence, quantum mutual information, and Bell-CHSH correlations. To demonstrate the effectiveness of these bounds, we analytically and numerically calculate the speed limits for negativity, concurrence, and Bell-CHSH correlations across several practically relevant quantum processes. We further show that for the cases examined, certain derived speed limits are attainable, indicating that these bounds are tight.

This study presents XMM-Newton and TESS data on V496 UMa, an AM Herculis-type cataclysmic variable. XMM-Newton observations indicate that while the white dwarf's two poles sometimes accrete simultaneously, accretion at the secondary magnetic pole is irregular and can almost stop within a single binary orbit (1.5 hours). Spectral modeling of the primary maximum shows that accretion structures on the primary pole remain unchanged even when secondary accretion is disrupted, implying that the disruption likely stems from mass-transfer fluctuations originating from the donor star. Additionally, an eight-week TESS observation with a two-minute sampling rate reveals a stable, double-peaked orbital modulation caused by cyclotron emission from the post-shock region; however, the times of maximum light exhibit a slow, systematic drift uncorrelated with the system's total brightness.

This paper introduces the concept of circular $r$-flows within mono-directed signed graphs $(G, \sigma)$. A circular $r$-flow is defined as a pair $(D, f)$, where $D$ represents an orientation of $G$, and the function $f: E(G)\to (-r,r)$ assigns values such that for positive edges $e$, $|f(e)|$ lies in $[1, r-1]$, while for negative edges $e$, $|f(e)|$ falls within $[0, \frac{r}{2}-1]\cup [\frac{r}{2}+1, r)$. Additionally, the sum of in-flows must equal the sum of out-flows at every vertex. The circular flow index, denoted $\Phi_c(G,\sigma)$, refers to the smallest $r$ for which a signed graph $(G, \sigma)$ lacking a positive bridge admits such a flow. This notion serves as the dual to the recently introduced circular colorings and chromatic numbers for signed graphs [Naserasr, Wang, and Zhu, 2021] and differs from circular flows in bi-directed graphs previously studied. The study provides multiple equivalent definitions, examines fundamental properties of these flows, investigates their relationship with standard graph flows, and establishes upper bounds for $\Phi_c(G,\sigma)$ based on the edge-connectivity of $G$. Furthermore, the authors observe that for specific values $r_{_k}=\frac{2k}{k-1}$, restricted to two natural subclasses of signed graphs, the existence of a circular $r_{_k}$-flow is tightly linked to the existence of a modulo $k$-orientation; notably, in planar graphs, this connection, via duality, relates to homomorphisms to $C_{-k}$.

The Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) features a large plate scale of 21"/px, which frequently results in light curves capturing blended light from multiple stars. This blending poses a significant risk of incorrectly attributing observed variability to the wrong source, thereby compromising any subsequent analysis. To address this, we have developed a technique capable of pinpointing the sky location of variability to an accuracy better than one-fifth of a pixel. By analyzing the measured frequencies of variability (such as those derived from periodogram analysis), we demonstrate that the amplitudes of best-fit sinusoids applied to raw light curves extracted from individual pixels match the light distribution of the variable source. The method's primary assumption is that neighboring stars do not exhibit variability at the same frequencies. Essentially, we leverage TESS's high frequency resolution to mitigate its low spatial resolution constraints. We have implemented this approach in an open-source Python package, TESS Localize (github.com/Higgins00/TESS-Localize), which identifies the position of a variable source on the sky using TESS pixel data and observed variability frequencies. Our method incorporates TESS Pixel Response Function models and evaluates systematics within the residuals of these model fits. Given how common source blending is in TESS light curves, verifying the origin of observed variability should become a standard procedure in TESS analyses.

We introduce an algorithm for parsing regular expressions and extracting submatches utilizing tagged deterministic finite automata, compatible with various disambiguation strategies. Detailed pseudocode is provided, incorporating key practical optimizations, alongside a step-by-step example illustrating the transformation from regular expressions to optimized automata. The approach covers both ahead-of-time and just-in-time determinization, with specific algorithmic variants tailored to each context. Benchmarks demonstrate the algorithm's high practical speed, supported by two independent implementations: the open-source lexer generator RE2C and an experimental Java library.

The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider conducted a search for heavy, long-lived charged particles using a dataset of 36.1 fb$^{-1}$ from proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. This analysis relies on ionization energy loss and time-of-flight measurements to detect heavy charged particles moving significantly slower than light speed. To ensure model independence, multiple search strategies covering various lifetimes and path lengths of several meters were established, referencing representative scenarios from supersymmetric models, including gluinos/squarks ($R$-hadrons), charginos, and staus. No significant excesses over the predicted Standard Model background were found. Consequently, 95% confidence level upper limits were set on the production cross sections for long-lived $R$-hadrons, as well as for directly pair-produced staus and charginos. These findings establish lower mass limits of 2000 GeV for long-lived gluino, sbottom, and stop $R$-hadrons, and 1250 GeV, 1340 GeV, 430 GeV, and 1090 GeV for staus and charginos, respectively.

Global linear analysis and nonlinear numerical simulations were employed to investigate Rossiter modes within an open cavity featuring a length-to-depth ratio of two and Reynolds numbers near 1000 based on cavity depth, with a specific focus on the influence of Mach number. Global analysis indicated that for thick boundary layers, only R1 and R2 modes become unstable within the Mach range of 0.1 to 0.9, whereas thin boundary layers allow instability up to the R4 mode. Compressibility proved highly destabilizing at low Mach numbers; at moderate Mach numbers, instability either saturated or exhibited irregular dependence. Eigenfunction analysis revealed that acoustic feedback scales with Ma^3, accounting for the strong destabilizing impact of compressibility. The irregular dependence was linked to resonances between Rossiter modes and acoustic cavity modes, explaining why such irregularities occur only in higher-order modes. In this parameter region, three-dimensional modes remain stable or marginally unstable. Two-dimensional simulations assessed the extent to which the nonlinear regime could be predicted by linear stability results. As instability increased, the final flow state became progressively more complex, yet the spectra retained distinct tones closely matching linear predictions. However, a detailed examination showed that while linear theory predicts R2 as the most unstable mode, the dominant frequency in the saturated state corresponds to R1. This discrepancy is attributed to nonlinear thickening of the mixing layer. Furthermore, the observed frequencies align much more closely with empirical Rossiter predictions than with linear instability forecasts. Even under these critical conditions, the spectra are well characterized by the R1 mode and a cascade of nonlinearly generated harmonics, showing no trace of the linear instability.

We examine the classical, randomized Ranking algorithm, which is established as $(1 - \frac{1}{e})$-competitive in expectation for the Online Bipartite Matching Problem. We derive a tail inequality demonstrating that Ranking achieves $(1 - \frac{1}{e} - \alpha)$-competitiveness with a probability of at least $1 - e^{-2\alpha^2 n}$, where $n$ represents the size of the maximum matching in the instance. Furthermore, we extend these findings to establish analogous concentration results for both the Fully Online Matching Problem and the Online Vertex-Weighted Bipartite Matching Problem.

The general expression for the surface stress tensor of an infinitesimally thin shell situated on a rotating null horizon is derived, where distinct interior and exterior geometries are joined. While the induced metric must remain continuous across the surface, its first derivatives may differ, creating discontinuities that result in a Dirac $\delta$-distribution within the Einstein tensor, localized at the horizon. For any general stationary axisymmetric configuration, the surface stress tensor is defined by two geometric invariants representing the surface: the jumps $[\kappa]$ in surface gravity and $[\cal J]$ in angular momentum density. Using coordinates aligned with the Killing symmetries, the Komar energy and angular momentum are calculated, with their surface contributions expressed via $[\kappa]$ and $[\cal J]$. Based on these findings, a simplified modification of the standard Israel junction conditions is confirmed directly through the Einstein tensor density, yielding the correct finite surface stress even as the normal vector $\boldsymbol n$ approaches a null vector continuously. The connection to Israel's original conditions—which are invalid for null surfaces—is clarified. These modified conditions are applicable for matching a rotating "black hole" exterior to any interior geometry at the Kerr null horizon, regardless of whether the surface normal is discontinuous or the Barrab\`es-Israel formalism is inapplicable. This junction on a rotating null horizon represents a matter shell configuration exclusively and involves no propagating gravitational shock waves.

We examine the feasibility of negative mass particles, determining whether current physical laws permit or forbid them and outlining their potential properties under such constraints. Our findings indicate that nothing precludes their existence; indeed, a more symmetric universe would necessitate them. Furthermore, within relativistic quantum mechanics, the negative mass bispinor in the rest frame exhibits a distinct structure compared to its positive mass counterpart.

Automatically generating medical reports for retinal images offers a promising approach to assist ophthalmologists in reducing their workload and enhancing efficiency. This study introduces a novel context-driven encoding network designed for this purpose. The proposed model consists primarily of a multi-modal input encoder and a fused-feature decoder. Experimental results demonstrate that the method effectively utilizes the interactive information between the input image and context, specifically keywords. Compared to baseline models, the proposed approach produces more accurate and meaningful reports for retinal images, achieving state-of-the-art performance. This superiority is evidenced across several standard metrics for medical report generation: BLEU-avg increased by 16%, CIDEr by 10.2%, and ROUGE by 8.6%.

Cloud architectures require the isolation of application components alongside efficient data sharing among those components running on the same physical hardware. Conventional approaches rely on the Memory Management Unit (MMU) to enforce isolation and enable sharing at the page level. However, MMU-based solutions often result in large Trusted Computing Bases (TCBs) within the kernel and necessitate inefficient operating system interfaces for data exchange. Emerging CPUs equipped with hardware support for memory capabilities present a new avenue for implementing isolation and sharing at a finer granularity.

This paper introduces cVMs, a novel VM-like abstraction that leverages memory capabilities to isolate application components and facilitate efficient data sharing, all without requiring application code to be explicitly capability-aware. Each cVM operates within a shared virtual address space safely, possessing capabilities solely to access its own memory. A cVM can incorporate a library operating system, thereby reducing its reliance on the broader cloud environment. Data exchange between cVMs occurs efficiently through two capability-based primitives, supported by a compact trusted monitor: (i) an asynchronous read-write interface for shared buffers, and (ii) a call interface for transferring control. These primitives enable the construction of more expressive mechanisms for efficient inter-cVM communication. A prototype implementation utilizing CHERI RISC-V capabilities demonstrates that cVMs can isolate services such as Redis and Python with minimal overhead while significantly enhancing data sharing capabilities.

As the economy and society expand, enterprises, particularly those in the FinTech sector, face surging demands for outbound calls related to debt collection, marketing, anti-fraud efforts, and more. However, human agents are often consumed by repetitive, mechanical tasks, leading to a corresponding rise in operational costs regarding labor and equipment. Concurrently, advancements in artificial intelligence over the last few decades have made it increasingly common for companies to leverage technologies like Big Data and AI to enhance outbound call operations. The intelligent outbound robot stands as a prime application of AI in this domain, designed to communicate with customers to achieve specific objectives. Characterized by low costs, high reusability, and ease of compliance, this technology has garnered significant industry attention.

Currently, two types of intelligent outbound robots exist, yet both possess substantial room for improvement. The first type relies on a finite state machine, utilizing manually configured jump conditions and nodes based on human experience; this is often referred to as a flow-based robot. For instance, Figure \ref{fig:label} illustrates the working model of a flow-based robot used in debt collection. In each interaction cycle, the robot responds to the user with predefined text corresponding to each node in the workflow.

Sampling binding processes in molecular dynamics (MD) simulations is challenging, often resulting in incomplete exploration of the state space. While evaluating interaction energies on a grid bypasses this issue, it is typically constrained by high dimensionality. This work introduces initial steps toward a low-dimensional grid-based model for molecular binding by discretizing the relative positions and orientations of two molecules under the rigid body assumption. The accompanying software, released as the Python package `molgri`, evaluates various algorithms for the rotational grid component—using Euler angles, polyhedra, and quaternions—and identifies polyhedra-based methods as the most uniform. The program generates sequences of molecular structures compatible with standard MD software for energy calculations. The approach is validated on a water dimer and a coiled-coil protein interacting with a chloride anion; for the latter, the rigid-body constraint is relaxed, and grid point energy accuracy is enhanced via energy minimization. In both scenarios, the resulting oriented bonding patterns and energies align with chemical intuition and MD findings. Additionally, the study illustrates how grid-based energy contribution analysis can be conducted, demonstrating that point-energy calculations effectively resolve electrostatically driven associations. Ultimately, grid-based models represent a promising complement to traditional sampling methods, with potential for extension into quantum chemistry and flexible docking applications.

Current advanced methods for mitigating scaling-induced main memory errors rely on the memory controller to detect and fix vulnerable bits. However, the internal use of on-die error-correcting codes (ECC) in modern memory chips obscures the controller's visibility into these errors, thereby hindering effective error profiling. To analyze this issue, we examine how on-die ECC alters the manifestation of memory errors to the controller, revealing that it creates statistical dependencies between errors in different bit positions. This introduces three significant obstacles for practical error profiling. To overcome these hurdles, we propose Hybrid Active-Reactive Profiling (HARP), a novel algorithm designed to rapidly achieve comprehensive coverage of at-risk bits in chips utilizing on-die ECC. HARP operates in two stages: first, it employs modified existing profiling techniques that interact with the on-die ECC to quickly locate a subset of vulnerable bits; second, it utilizes a secondary ECC within the controller to safely identify any remaining at-risk bits upon failure. Evaluation results demonstrate that HARP attains full coverage of all at-risk bits significantly faster than two leading baseline algorithms, which occasionally fail to reach complete coverage. Furthermore, a case study comparing the impact of each profiler on the system's overall bit error rate (BER) when employing a repair mechanism for DRAM data-retention errors shows that HARP outperforms the best baseline by a factor of 3.7x at a raw per-bit error probability of 0.75.

Multiple empirical studies have compared the in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (ODD) performance of various models, frequently reporting positive correlations in computer vision and NLP benchmarks. Surprisingly, these studies have never observed inverse correlations that would indicate necessary trade-offs, a finding that is crucial for determining if ID performance can serve as a proxy for OOD generalization. This paper demonstrates that inverse correlations between ID and OOD performance do indeed occur in real-world benchmarks, potentially having been overlooked in previous research due to biased model selection. We illustrate this using the WILDS-Camelyon17 dataset, analyzing models across various training epochs and random seeds. Our findings are especially pronounced when models are trained with a regularizer designed to diversify solutions to the ERM objective. Consequently, we refine previous recommendations and conclusions: (1) High OOD performance may occasionally necessitate sacrificing ID performance; (2) Focusing exclusively on ID performance may not optimize OOD results, potentially yielding diminishing and eventually negative returns; (3) Our example underscores that empirical studies only map achievable regimes given current methods, warranting caution when deriving prescriptive recommendations.

Designing adaptive structures offers a strategy to enhance building sustainability by enabling them to adjust to varying loads, environmental conditions, or evolving needs through shape modifications of any scale. In instances involving significant deformation, the mechanics and properties governing the deformation process are critical for the structure's energy efficiency. The authors' group previously developed the method of variational motion design, which identifies optimal deformation paths between two specific geometrical states based on a defined quality function. In this initial academic context, the method assumes that every degree of freedom can be controlled by arbitrary external actuation forces to achieve the optimized motion; these nodal forces are subsequently determined. The current study extends this motion design method by imposing the constraint that motion must be executed using a predefined set of actuation forces, which may include external forces or prescribed length changes of discrete internal actuators. Furthermore, static stability at each intermediate configuration during the motion is enforced by ensuring the stiffness matrix has a positive determinant.

This paper establishes a convergence rate for the periodic homogenization of Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equations featuring nonlocal diffusion. This outcome relies on the regularity of the corresponding effective problem, with convexity being essential. These regularity estimates, drawn from existing literature, become feasible after deriving a representation formula for the effective Hamiltonian, a finding that holds independent significance.

The distribution of relative velocities in wide binary (WB) stars offers a sensitive probe of gravitational laws under the low accelerations found in galactic outskirts. I assess the viability of the wide binary test using the "line velocity" approach, which isolates velocity components along the sky plane direction orthogonal to each WB's systemic proper motion. Applying this method to the Hernandez et al. (2019) sample while rigorously accounting for large-angle effects at the next order beyond the leading term, I find via Monte Carlo simulations that the uncertainty in one-dimensional velocity dispersion is roughly 100 m/s when using sky-projected relative velocities. However, utilizing line velocities lowers this uncertainty to approximately 30 m/s, as these measurements are far less susceptible to distance errors. My findings do not substantiate the Hernandez et al. (2019) assertion of a distinct deviation from Newtonian dynamics beyond a radius of about 10 kAU, largely due to my application of $2\sigma$ outlier rejection to purify their dataset beforehand. Nevertheless, the derived uncertainties are sufficiently small that current WB data are nearly adequate to differentiate between Newtonian and Modified Newtonian Dynamics; I estimate that approximately 1,000 WB systems would be needed if relying solely on line velocities. Beyond expanding the sample size, it is crucial to manage systematics such as undetected companions and moving groups, which could be addressed statistically. Contamination can be minimized by restricting analysis to a narrow, theoretically justified parameter range and examining how various theories predict differing proportions of WBs within that specific region.

We present the identification of three previously unidentified cataclysmic variables (CVs) within the first year of data from the SRG orbital observatory's all-sky X-ray survey. These sources were chosen based on their high brightness in the 4--12 keV range observed by the ART-XC telescope and were also detected by eROSITA, which supplied precise localization and spectral information for broad-band analysis. Although all three had been cataloged as X-ray sources in previous ROSAT and XMM-Newton surveys, their physical nature was previously unclear. Spectral data from eROSITA and ART-XC indicate optically thin thermal emission, with temperatures exceeding approximately 15 keV for SRGAJ194638.9+704552 and SRGAJ225412.8+690658, and above 5 keV for SRGAJ204547.8+672642. Combined with high inferred X-ray luminosities ($2\times 10^{32}$-$3\times 10^{33}$ erg s$^{-1}$), these findings strongly imply that all three objects are CVs. Optical photometry and spectroscopy obtained with the 1.6-m AZT-33IK telescope at Sayan Observatory further confirmed their CV classification. Specifically, SRGAJ194638.9+704552 is identified as an intermediate polar, SRGAJ204547.8+672642 is likely a polar or intermediate polar, and SRGAJ225412.8+690658 appears to be either a magnetic or non-magnetic CV. Additionally, an orbital period of 2.98 hours was measured for SRGAJ204547.8+672642 using TESS data. With three of the planned eight SRG all-sky surveys now complete, we anticipate discovering numerous new CVs and will continue our optical follow-up efforts.

Previous research utilizing asteroseismic ages and spot-based rotation rates suggests that standard age-rotation relationships may fail approximately midway through a star's main sequence life, a phenomenon known as weakened magnetic braking. Although determining rotation from spots is challenging for older, less active stars, asteroseismic rotational splitting offers a method to measure rotation for both active and quiescent stars, thereby validating whether this effect genuinely occurs on the main sequence. We measured asteroseismic rotation rates for 91 main sequence stars exhibiting high signal-to-noise oscillation modes. By combining these new rates with effective temperatures, metallicities, seismic masses, and ages, we constructed a hierarchical Bayesian mixture model to test if the data better supports a standard rotational evolution model or one involving weakened magnetic braking. The analysis revealed that the weakened magnetic braking scenario is 98.4% more probable for our stellar sample, contributing further evidence for this phase of stellar evolution. This study presents the most extensive catalogue of seismic rotation on the main sequence to date, enabling more detailed ensemble analyses of rotational evolution using Kepler data.

Let $k$ be an uncountable algebraically closed field, and let $Y$ be a smooth projective $k$-variety that lacks a decomposition of the diagonal. We demonstrate that $Y$ is not stably birational to a very general hypersurface of any specified degree and dimension. This result allows us to investigate how the stable birational types of Fano hypersurfaces vary across fields of any characteristic, building upon work initiated by Shinder, whose approach is restricted to characteristic zero.

Chandra's sub-arcsecond imaging of X-ray emission in the type 2 AGN Mrk 78 reveals complex structures exhibiting spectral variations across scales ranging from approximately 200 pc to 2 kpc. The X-ray emission is generally aligned east-west with the 3.6 cm radio source and the [OIII]-mapped narrow-line region, displaying significant east-west asymmetry. The eastern X-ray emission is predominantly found in a compact knot at the location where the radio source is deflected, whereas the western emission forms a loop or shell situated roughly 2 kpc from the nucleus with a radius of about 0.7 kpc. Suggestive evidence of shocks exists in both the eastern knot and the western arc, corresponding to substantial changes in the velocities of the [OIII] outflow at these locations. We explore potential reasons for the western X-ray shocks occurring approximately 1 kpc farther from the nucleus than their eastern counterparts. Furthermore, we estimate that the thermal energy injected by these shocks into the interstellar medium amounts to 0.05–0.6% of the AGN's bolometric luminosity.

To determine the magnetic field distribution within the KATRIN main-spectrometer using sensors positioned outside the vessel, one can exploit the absence of magnetic rotation inside the spectrometer volume. This condition allows for the definition of a scalar magnetic potential, $V(\vec{x})$, which satisfies the Laplace equation. By moving and fixed sensors, numerous magnetic field values can be sampled on the outer surface of the main-spectrometer; these samples serve as boundary conditions to relax the Laplace equation for the potential and the internal magnetic field components. Simulations of the KATRIN reference solenoid chain, incorporating both a global magnetic field and an external perturbing solenoid, demonstrate that this method can reconstruct the original field with an accuracy of within 2%.

Resiliency is defined as the capacity to rapidly recover from a violation and prevent future occurrences for an extended period. This attribute is critical for Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS), yet no universally accepted formal framework for CPS resiliency currently exists. We introduce an STL-based framework for reasoning about CPS resiliency, where resiliency is syntactically characterized by an STL-based Resiliency Specification (SRS). For any STL formula $\varphi$, along with time bounds $\alpha$ and $\beta$, the SRS $R_{\alpha,\beta}(\varphi)$ is formulated as $\neg\varphi\mathbf{U}_{[0,\alpha]}\mathbf{G}_{[0,\beta)}\varphi$. This specification ensures that recovery from a violation of $\varphi$ occurs within time $\alpha$ (recoverability), followed by the maintenance of $\varphi$ for a duration of $\beta$ (durability). These $R$-expressions, serving as atomic elements in our SRS logic, can be combined using STL operators to define composite resiliency requirements, such as the simultaneous satisfaction of multiple SRSs or the eventual resilience of a system. We establish a quantitative semantics for SRSs through a Resilience Satisfaction Value (ReSV) function $r$, proving its soundness and completeness relative to STL's Boolean semantics. The $r$-value for $R_{\alpha,\beta}(\varphi)$ atoms consists of a singleton set containing a pair that quantifies both recoverability and durability. For composite SRS formulas, the $r$-value yields a set of non-dominated recoverability-durability pairs, accounting for scenarios where subformula ReSVs are incomparable (e.g., one subformula offers better durability but poorer recoverability than another). To our knowledge, this represents the first multi-dimensional quantitative semantics for an STL-based logic. Two case studies illustrate the practical applicability of this approach.

Stylistic analysis plays a crucial role in research domains spanning from authorship attribution to forensic investigations and personality profiling. However, current methods suffer from significant drawbacks, including topic bias, poor discriminability when dealing with many authors, and a heavy reliance on large, diverse datasets. This paper identifies the origins of these limitations and argues for a cognitive approach to understanding authorial style as a solution. To this end, we introduce a new feature representation named Trajectory-based Style Estimation (TraSE). Experimental results from an authorship attribution task involving over 27,000 authors and 1.4 million samples in a cross-domain setting achieved 90% accuracy, demonstrating that TraSE is resistant to these negative factors and is highly effective for stylistic analysis. Furthermore, a qualitative evaluation of TraSE using physical human attributes, such as age, supports its ability to capture underlying cognitive traits.

Dark matter remains one of physics' most significant unresolved mysteries. Since it is established that dark matter interacts gravitationally with visible matter, searches utilizing accelerometers are particularly promising. This article outlines recent and prospective investigations into dark matter candidates—including feebly interacting particles trapped within the Earth, scalar-matter domain walls, and axion quark nuggets—by employing accelerometer networks. Furthermore, it provides an outlook on how emerging atomic-interferometry-based accelerometer networks can further advance these dark matter detection efforts.

This paper investigates the tomographic reconstruction of quantum states within Schwinger's picture of Quantum Mechanics, where each system is associated with a groupoid. The study specifically addresses spin tomography, utilizing a groupoid of pairs over a finite set. Fundamentally, this groupoid comprises transitions between all possible outcome pairs of that finite set, equipped with a partial composition rule that extends the concept of groups. The primary objective is to derive a reconstruction formula for states on the groupoid-algebra linked to the system's observables. By employing a frame defined through the group of bisections of this groupoid—special subsets corresponding one-to-one with outcomes—the validity of the tomographic reconstruction is demonstrated. The analysis details the specific case where outcomes form the set of integers modulo $n$, with $n$ being an odd prime. In this scenario, a subgroup of discrete affine linear transformations, whose graphs constitute linear subspaces of the groupoid, serves as a *quorum*, drawing a close analogy to the continuous case.

Consider a complete, non-compact Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$ whose $m$-dimensional Bakry-\'{E}mery Ricci curvature is bounded below by a non-positive constant. This paper establishes a localized Hamilton-type gradient estimate for positive, smooth, and bounded solutions to the nonlinear diffusion equation $u_t=\Delta u-\nabla\phi\cdot\nabla u-au\log u-bu$, where $\phi$ is a $C^2$ function and $a$ (non-zero) and $b$ are real constants. The findings extend the work of Souplet and Zhang (Bull. London Math. Soc., 38 (2006), pp. 1045-1053) and Wu (Preprint, 2008).

This study investigates a generalized length-preserving flow applied to convex curves in the plane. It demonstrates that the flow persists globally and transforms convex curves into circles as time approaches infinity.

This paper introduces a Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework for autonomous driving that utilizes a path velocity decomposition approach. The MPC optimization employs a two-layer structure: first determining a suitable trajectory for the vehicle, and subsequently calculating the optimal forward velocity along that path. The inherent design of this decomposition ensures seamless integration between the two optimization layers. A significant advantage of this method is that it delegates the majority of collision avoidance tasks to the velocity optimization layer, enabling the derivation of computationally efficient formulations. Specifically, we build upon our previously established time scaled collision cone (TSCC) constraints to formulate the forward velocity optimization as a convex quadratic programming problem. Validation is conducted on various autonomous driving scenarios, where the proposed MPC repeatedly solves both optimization layers in a receding horizon fashion to execute lane changes, overtaking, and merging maneuvers amidst multiple dynamic obstacles.

Quantum emitters interacting with structured photonic reservoirs exhibit unique individual and collective behaviors driven by the interplay of dimensionality and complex photon energy dispersions. This study systematically investigates various representative three-dimensional structured environments that differ qualitatively in their bath spectral densities. We identify non-Markovian individual and collective phenomena missing from simplified models, including ideal subradiant states and long-range anisotropic interactions. Additionally, we demonstrate how to realize these models using cold atoms in state-dependent optical lattices and outline methods to observe these unconventional dynamics within such systems.

Pre-trained language models have demonstrated remarkable efficacy in few-shot learning via in-context learning. However, their substantial size often hinders deployment on edge devices like smartphones and sensors. Smaller models typically require task-specific fine-tuning through data annotation, which imposes significant time and financial costs, particularly for startups, small research teams, and companies. This paper investigates various prompt-based fine-tuning techniques to enhance performance on both causal language and multimodal transformer models. We evaluate these methods using a dataset centered on temporal visual commonsense reasoning. Our findings indicate that simple, model-agnostic prompt-based fine-tuning can achieve comparable results using only 35%-40% of the training data. These approaches offer substantial reductions in both time and expense. Furthermore, since the proposed methods rely on minimal architectural assumptions, they are easily adaptable for other transformer models. Finally, we intend to release the source code openly to facilitate community adoption and contribution.

Accurate diagnosis and severity assessment of COVID-19 rely heavily on the automated segmentation of lung lesions within chest CT scans. However, conventional U-shaped encoder-decoder models and their derivatives often struggle with significant issues: pooling and upsampling operations degrade contextual information, widening semantic gaps between encoded and decoded feature maps, and triggering vanishing gradient problems due to sequential propagation, all of which lead to sub-optimal results. Furthermore, processing 3D CT volumes exacerbates these challenges by exponentially increasing computational complexity, thereby hindering optimization. To address these constraints, this paper introduces CovSegNet, an efficient neural network architecture for automated COVID-19 lesion segmentation. The proposed method employs a two-phase training strategy: a deeper 2D network first generates an ROI-enhanced CT volume, which is then refined by a shallower 3D network to incorporate additional contextual details without escalating computational costs. Beyond the standard vertical expansion of the U-Net, we implement horizontal expansion using multi-stage encoder-decoder modules to maximize performance. Additionally, multi-scale feature maps are incorporated into the scale transition process to mitigate information loss, while a novel multi-scale fusion module utilizes a pyramid fusion scheme to minimize semantic gaps between encoder/decoder stages and enable efficient parallel gradient optimization. Extensive testing on three public datasets demonstrates that the proposed scheme significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, this framework is readily adaptable for achieving optimal segmentation results across a broad range of applications.

We present TOI-1268b, a transiting Saturn-mass planet identified by the TESS mission. At an age under one billion years, determined through multiple indicators, TOI-1268b represents the youngest known Saturn-mass planet and adds to the limited group of well-characterized young planetary systems. The planet orbits an early K-dwarf star with a period of $P\,=\,8.1577080\pm0.0000044$ days. The host star has a mass of $0.96 \pm 0.04$ $M_{\odot}$, a radius of $0.92 \pm 0.06$ $R_{\odot}$, an effective temperature of $5300\pm100$ K, and a metallicity of $0.36\pm0.06$ dex. By integrating TESS photometry with high-resolution spectra obtained from the Tull spectrograph at McDonald Observatory, as well as instruments at Tautenburg and Ondrejov observatories, we determined the planet's mass to be $96.4 \pm 8.3\,M_{\oplus}$ and its radius to be $9.1 \pm 0.6\,R_{\oplus}$. TOI-1268 serves as an optimal system for investigating star-planet tidal interactions in non-inflated Saturn-mass planets. Utilizing the system parameters established in this study, we constrained the planet's tidal quality factor to a range of $10^{4.5-5.3}$. Compared with other non-inflated Saturn-mass planets, TOI-1268b emerges as a leading candidate for transmission spectroscopy investigations.

The lack of a dedicated library for evaluating non-linear functions means that current general-purpose secure multi-party computation (MPC) systems do not live up to the "general" expectations of programmers. Existing approaches either inefficiently reuse plaintext methods—leading to poor performance and potential errors—or rely on custom, ad-hoc approximations tailored to specific functions or platforms. We introduce NFGen, a universal technique that leverages pre-computed discrete piecewise polynomials to accurately approximate arbitrary functions using fixed-point arithmetic. Implemented via a performance-prediction-driven code generator, our solution supports diverse platforms. Extensive evaluations across 23 non-linear functions, six MPC protocols, and two platforms demonstrate that NFGen significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of performance, accuracy, and versatility.

We derive the relativistic classical radial action from scattering amplitudes within the probe limit, valid to all orders in perturbation theory. Our analysis covers point charges and monopoles, alongside Schwarzschild and pure-NUT gravitational backgrounds. By utilizing all-order amplitudes, we recover a distinct relativistic phenomenon: the ability of scattering trajectories to wind around these sources any number of times. Specifically, we demonstrate that the scattering amplitude for a probe interacting with a pure NUT is determined by the solution to a transcendental equation featuring continued fractions, and we detail the method for solving this equation to any specified loop order.

The massive datasets generated by sequencing complex environments present significant hurdles for current analysis methods. While *de novo* metagenomic assembly helps reduce the data volume, it demands substantial computational power. To address this, we implemented two pre-assembly filtering techniques—digital normalization and partitioning—to improve the computational feasibility of assembling large metagenomes. Validation using a human gut mock community revealed that these approaches yield assemblies nearly identical to those derived from unprocessed data. Subsequently, we assembled two extensive soil metagenomes from matched Iowa corn and native prairie soils. Analysis of the resulting contigs' predicted functional content and phylogenetic origins highlighted notable taxonomic differences despite functional similarities. These assembly strategies are broadly applicable to any metagenome, with full source code available under a BSD license.

Hierarchical domain-specific classification schemas, also known as subject heading vocabularies, are frequently employed to identify, categorize, and disambiguate concepts found in scholarly articles. In this study, we designed, implemented, and assessed a human-in-the-loop workflow that initially generates a category tree from crowd-sourced Wikipedia data, followed by the application of community detection, machine learning, and custom heuristics or rules to refine the tree. This process yielded WikiCSSH, a large-scale, hierarchically structured vocabulary specifically for the computer science (CS) domain. Our evaluation indicates that WikiCSSH surpasses other CS vocabularies in both vocabulary size and the effectiveness of lexicon-based key-phrase extraction from academic data. Furthermore, WikiCSSH is capable of distinguishing between coarse-grained and fine-grained CS concepts. The workflow described here can serve as a model for constructing hierarchically organized subject heading vocabularies for other domains represented in Wikipedia.

In the dense metal-organic framework Na[Mn(HCOO)$_3$], Mn$^{2+}$ ions with a spin of $S=\frac{5}{2}$ are situated at the nodes of a `trillium' hyperkagome network. We demonstrate that this material displays diverse behaviors typical of geometric frustration: the N\'eel transition is strongly suppressed relative to the characteristic magnetic interaction energy, short-range magnetic order remains stable well above the N\'eel temperature, and the magnetic susceptibility shows a pseudo-plateau at $\frac{1}{3}$-saturation magnetisation. We establish that a simple nearest-neighbour Heisenberg antiferromagnet model quantitatively explains each of these observations, marking Na[Mn(HCOO)$_3$] as the first experimental realization of this model on a trillium net. Furthermore, we construct a mapping between the trillium model and the two-dimensional Shastry-Sutherland lattice, illustrating how both systems connect geometric frustration within the classical spin liquid regime to a pronounced magnetocaloric response at low magnetic fields.

This work aims to advance both the theory and application of robot locomotion by tackling key hurdles in biomimicking bat aerial flight. Bat wings are notable for their rapid articulation, capable of mobilizing up to 40 joints per wingbeat. Replicating this flight has proven difficult; existing design approaches have fallen short because they rely solely on sensors and conventional actuators for closed-loop feedback, neglecting the computational functions inherent in morphology. To address this, we introduce a framework named Morphing via Integrated Mechanical Intelligence and Control (MIMIC), which utilizes small, low-energy actuators to steer the robot by altering its morphology. By applying the dynamic model of Northeastern University's Aerobat—a platform built to validate the MIMIC framework—we demonstrate that computational structures combined with closed-loop feedback can effectively emulate the stable flight mechanisms of bats.

We present a full algebraic classification of all complex nilpotent algebras in four dimensions. The resulting list contains 234 isomorphism classes (including parametric families), with 66 of these being novel to the existing literature.

Question Generation (QG) seeks to automate the creation of questions based on a passage and its corresponding answers. Although recent neural generation models have significantly enhanced question quality compared to traditional heuristic-based methods, existing evaluation metrics are often criticized for failing to align well with human judgment. To address this, we introduce QAScore, a novel reference-free metric designed to offer a more effective evaluation mechanism. Unlike approaches that fine-tune language models to match human preferences, QAScore assesses a question by calculating the cross-entropy of the probability that a language model can reconstruct the masked words within the answer. Additionally, we conducted a new crowd-sourced human evaluation study to examine the correlation between QAScore, other metrics, and human judgments. Our experiments demonstrate that QAScore achieves a stronger alignment with our human evaluation results than traditional word-overlap metrics like BLEU and ROUGE, as well as the pretrained-model-based BERTScore.

Estimating networks from multi-variate point processes or time series data is of fundamental importance. Previous research has largely relied on parametric methods that necessitate a known parametric model, rendering estimation procedures less robust to model mis-specification, non-linearities, and heterogeneities. This paper introduces a semi-parametric approach grounded in the monotone single-index multi-variate autoregressive model (SIMAM) to address these issues. We offer theoretical guarantees for dependent data and propose an alternating projected gradient descent algorithm. Notably, we do not explicitly assume mixing conditions on the process (though we require conditions analogous to restricted strong convexity) and achieve convergence rates of $O(T^{-\frac{1}{3}} \sqrt{s\log(TM)})$—which are optimal for independent design cases—where $s$ denotes the threshold for the maximum in-degree reflecting sparsity, $M$ represents the number of actors, and $T$ is the number of time points. Furthermore, we demonstrate superior performance on both simulated data and two real-world examples, showing that our SIMAM approach outperforms state-of-the-art parametric methods in terms of both prediction accuracy and network estimation.

Circular (or cyclic) proofs have garnered significant attention recently and have been suggested as a novel framework for investigating (co)inductive reasoning. Specifically, multiple type systems leveraging circular reasoning have been introduced. Nevertheless, the complexity-theoretic dimensions of circular proofs remain largely unexplored, particularly given their intricate loop structures that differ from standard 'recursion schemes'. This study aims to connect circular proofs with implicit computational complexity by developing a circular proof system grounded in Bellantoni and Cook's safe-normal function algebra. Furthermore, we establish appropriate proof-theoretic constraints to define the classes of polynomial-time and elementary computable functions.

Supplier selection represents a classic multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) challenge often characterized by inherent uncertainty. To tackle this, a novel approach grounded in interval data fusion is introduced. While adhering to the conventional method for generating classical basic probability assignments (BPA) based on the distance between evidences, this study retains criterion weights as interval numbers to produce and fuse interval BPAs. Subsequently, the alternatives are ranked, and a decision is formulated based on these interval BPAs. A numerical case study on supplier selection demonstrates the feasibility and validity of the proposed technique. This method is specifically designed to address multi-criteria decision-making scenarios where criterion weights or expert inputs are expressed through fuzzy data, such as linguistic terms or interval values.

We introduce a comprehensive investigation of ${\cal N}=(2,2)$ supersymmetric non-linear sigma models defined on $S^2$ with a K\"ahler manifold as the target space. We explore their reformulation within the framework of cohomological field theory, employing a new variant of 2D self-duality that incorporates a $U(1)$ action on $S^2$. Beyond the general case, we examine the theory featuring target space equivariance, which corresponds to a supersymmetric sigma model interacting with a non-dynamical supersymmetric background gauge multiplet. We analyze the localization locus and execute a one-loop computation centered on constant maps. Finally, we propose that the theory can be reduced to an exotic model defined over the moduli space of holomorphic disks.

The afterglow radiation of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), spanning from radio frequencies to GeV energies, arises from the interaction between a relativistic jet and the surrounding medium. While synchrotron radiation from shock-accelerated electrons is generally accepted as the primary emission mechanism, several critical factors remain uncertain, including the contribution of inverse Compton scattering, particle acceleration dynamics, and the specific properties of both the environment and the jet itself. Although the potential for afterglow emission to extend into the TeV range has long been theorized, it remained unobserved until recently. Cherenkov telescopes MAGIC and H.E.S.S. have now definitively demonstrated that this radiation persists above 100 GeV, reaching at least a few TeV. The future Cherenkov Telescope Array (CTA) is poised to significantly enhance access to this high-energy spectral window. This review first revises the current afterglow models, highlighting their limitations and unresolved questions. It then details recent detections of very high-energy emission and explores its origins. Furthermore, the article investigates the implications of these findings for understanding afterglow physics and constraining the underlying processes, emphasizing how upcoming observations by the CTA Observatory will be pivotal in elucidating these elusive sources.

Given curiosity's pivotal role in human life, theoretical frameworks like information gap theory and compression progress theory have attempted to elucidate its mechanisms. Information gap theory posits that curiosity drives the acquisition of missing information, whereas compression progress theory views it as the urge to develop a more concise mental model of reality. To address the limitations of these approaches, we introduce conformational change theory, which suggests that curiosity fosters mental models characterized by high conceptual flexibility. We formalize curiosity as the construction of an expanding knowledge network to quantitatively analyze all three theories. Within this network framework, information gaps correspond to topological cavities, compression progress is measured by network compressibility, and flexibility is quantified by the count of conformational degrees of freedom. Utilizing data from the Wikipedia online encyclopedia, we assessed the extent to which each theory accounts for the growth of knowledge networks formed by both individuals and collectives. Our results support a pluralistic understanding of curiosity, indicating that intrinsically motivated information gathering simultaneously fills knowledge gaps and enhances the compressibility and flexibility of knowledge networks. By identifying the specific contexts where each theoretical model applies across individuals and groups, we clarify their distinct yet complementary explanations. Ultimately, our findings provide a novel network-theoretic perspective on intrinsically motivated information acquisition that may refine or expand the traditional taxonomy of curiosity.

For the last ten years, rest-frame color-color diagrams have served as effective instruments for identifying quiescent galaxies at high redshifts by resolving the color degeneracy between dusty star-forming and quiescent populations. This study examines the rest-frame $U-V$ versus $V-J$ diagram using mock observations derived from cosmological galaxy formation simulations. Specifically, we perform numerical experiments to evaluate trends in UVJ space and the color evolution of massive galaxies as they transition to quiescence between redshifts $z\sim 1$ and $2$. Our models successfully replicate the observed UVJ diagram at these redshifts, notably reproducing the population of highly dust-reddened galaxies in the upper-right corner for the first time in a cosmological simulation. However, our simulations predominantly populate this region with low-mass galaxies and fail to generate the distinct bimodality between star-forming and quiescent galaxies seen in real data. These discrepancies arise because low-mass galaxies exhibit excess dust and high-mass galaxies show relatively gray attenuation curves, while the green valley is overpopulated in the SIMBA simulation. Regarding temporal evolution, we find that the quenching trajectory on the UVJ diagram depends primarily on the average specific star formation rate during the 1 Gyr preceding quenching, rather than the quenching timescale itself. These findings support the view that different quenching pathways reflect the divergent evolution of post-starburst and green valley galaxies.

We suggest identifying phonon and roton excitations in a two-dimensional Bose-Einstein condensate featuring Raman-induced spin-orbit coupling by introducing a weak barrier to perturb the atomic cloud. By translating this barrier along various directions within suitable parameter ranges, both excitation modes become observable. Phonon excitations manifest as solitary waves, whereas roton excitations produce characteristic spatial density variations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this approach enables the measurement of the anisotropic critical velocities of superfluidity.

The paper establishes sharp affine fractional Sobolev inequalities for functions defined on $\mathbb{R}^n$. For every $s$ in the interval $(0,1)$, these newly derived inequalities are substantially stronger than, and directly entail, the sharp fractional Sobolev inequalities previously formulated by Almgren and Lieb. Furthermore, as $s$ approaches 1 from below, these results imply the sharp affine Sobolev inequality established by Gaoyong Zhang. Consequently, this work yields fractional Petty projection inequalities that surpass the fractional Euclidean isoperimetric inequalities and provides a proof for a natural conjecture regarding radial mean bodies.

This study re-examines the construction of one-dimensional acoustic black holes by adopting Timoshenko's beam theory rather than the Euler-Bernoulli model, the latter of which is less accurate at higher frequencies. The objective is to minimize the reflection coefficient subject to constraints on the normalized wave number variation. By applying the calculus of variations, we analytically derive the corresponding Euler-Lagrange equation and subsequently employ numerical techniques to determine the optimal height profiles across various frequencies. When comparing these results with profiles previously obtained using Euler-Bernoulli theory, we observe that in the lower dimensionless frequency range ($\Omega$, defined by the plate's maximum height), the optimal profiles are nearly identical, as anticipated. However, at higher frequencies—even those where Euler-Bernoulli theory might still be considered marginally applicable—the profiles predicted by the two theories diverge significantly, with the Timoshenko results being the more accurate representation. A likely explanation for this discrepancy is that, unlike in cases of constant height, the wave numbers in our configuration also depend on the ratio of the smallest to the largest plate heights.

The advancement of Open-Domain Dialogue Systems (ODS) has become a prominent research area driven by significant societal and business implications, numerous technical challenges, and recent technological breakthroughs. However, building effective ODS necessitates two critical components: first, automated evaluation frameworks that strongly correlate with human assessments across various dialogue dimensions, offering explainable metrics to provide constructive feedback for rapid model iteration; and second, control mechanisms capable of mitigating toxicity, intelligently managing harmful user inputs, and maintaining conversational flow and engagement. This track at the 10th Dialogue System Technology Challenge (DSTC10) contributes to the broader initiative of fostering scalable and safe dialogue systems. The paper details the datasets and baseline models provided to participants, along with the evaluation results for both proposed subtasks.

We associate with each proof structure in multiplicative linear logic an ideal that encodes the proof's logical content as polynomial equations. We demonstrate that cut-elimination within multiplicative proof nets corresponds to specific instances of the Buchberger algorithm used to compute Gröbner bases in elimination theory.

We extend the principles of effective field theory to nonrelativistic quantum mechanics. By employing an artificial boundary of ignorance as a computational device, we construct the effective theory, using boundary conditions to represent short-ranged effects that are intentionally omitted; consequently, these boundary conditions function analogously to the effective action in field theory. Although this method temporarily violates unitarity, unitarity is maintained on average.
