As a proof of concept, we examine the Coulomb interaction and demonstrate that this effective quantum mechanics can predict bound state energies with exceptional precision using only a few fitting parameters. Furthermore, we show its equivalence to the theory of quantum defects, though derived within an effective framework. The approach adheres to electromagnetic gauge invariance and can also model decays arising from short-ranged interactions, such as those occurring in positronium. Effective quantum mechanics proves applicable to systems that possess analytically describable long-range behaviors but lack reliable or efficient models for their short-range effects. Potential applications span atomic and condensed matter systems, and the method may also offer valuable insights into the study of black holes.

The study of polarization in radio sources driven by Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) has garnered significant interest due to the critical role of magnetic fields in their physics, their utility as tracers of intergalactic plasma, and their potential impact on cosmic microwave background polarization measurements. Understanding the statistical relationship between polarization and source characteristics is essential for all these applications. In this work, we calculate the median fractional polarization ($\Pi_{0, \rm med}$) for extensive samples of radio sources with 1.4 GHz flux densities between 6.6 and 70 mJy. This is achieved by stacking polarized intensity data from the NVSS survey at 1.4 GHz, correlated with angular sizes derived from the FIRST survey. We analyze five groups of sources with mean deconvolved angular sizes ranging from 1.8" to 8.2", along with two groups of symmetric double sources, which collectively represent the majority of mJy radio sources smaller than or near the median angular size. Our findings indicate that $\Pi_{0,\rm med}$ at 1.4 GHz varies strongly with angular size for sources smaller than approximately 5", but shows only a weak dependence for larger sources up to ~8". We attribute these results to depolarization occurring within the AGN host galaxy and its circumgalactic medium. Furthermore, we observe an anti-correlation between the curvature of the low-frequency radio spectrum and $\Pi_{0,\rm med}$, providing additional evidence that depolarization is intrinsically linked to the source.

MultiWOZ 2.0 (Budzianowski et al., 2018) is a recently released multi-domain dialogue dataset spanning 7 distinct domains and containing over 10,000 dialogues. Despite being immensely useful and one of the largest resources of its kind to-date, MultiWOZ 2.0 has a few shortcomings. Firstly, there is substantial noise in the dialogue state annotations and dialogue utterances which negatively impact the performance of state-tracking models. Secondly, follow-up work (Lee et al., 2019) has augmented the original dataset with user dialogue acts. This leads to multiple co-existent versions of the same dataset with minor modifications. In this work we tackle the aforementioned issues by introducing MultiWOZ 2.1. To fix the noisy state annotations, we use crowdsourced workers to re-annotate state and utterances based on the original utterances in the dataset. This correction process results in changes to over 32% of state annotations across 40% of the dialogue turns. In addition, we fix 146 dialogue utterances by canonicalizing slot values in the utterances to the values in the dataset ontology. To address the second problem, we combined the contributions of the follow-up works into MultiWOZ 2.1. Hence, our dataset also includes user dialogue acts as well as multiple slot descriptions per dialogue state slot. We then benchmark a number of state-of-the-art dialogue state tracking models on the MultiWOZ 2.1 dataset and show the joint state tracking performance on the corrected state annotations. We are publicly releasing MultiWOZ 2.1 to the community, hoping that this dataset resource will allow for more effective models across various dialogue subproblems to be built in the future.

This paper leverages the fact that for any real numbers $a_{j}, b_{j}\in \mathbb{R}$ where $j=1,2,\ldots,n$, there exist $\lambda_{j}\in [0,1]$ summing to 1 such that \[ \min_{1\leq j\leq n}\{a_{j}\}-\min_{1\leq j\leq n}\{b_{j}\}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\lambda_{j}(a_{j}-b_{j}). \] Using this property, new error bounds for the extended vertical LCP under the row $\mathcal{W}$-property are derived; these bounds encompass those presented in [Math. Program., 106 (2006) 513-525] and [Comput. Optim. Appl., 42 (2009) 335-352]. Furthermore, unlike the row rearrangement technique used in the latter reference to reduce computational effort, these new bounds effectively circumvent the associated inconveniences. Additionally, two novel sufficient and necessary conditions regarding the row $\mathcal{W}$-property are established.

Addressing range anxiety for private electric vehicle (EV) drivers through charging recommendations that balance user preferences with dynamic external conditions offers a cost-effective solution. While prior research emphasizes centralized strategies suitable for privacy-insensitive taxi fleets and fixed-route public transit, private EV drivers require personalized, resource-conscious guidance tailored to their specific timing and location needs while adapting to spatiotemporal supply-demand mismatches. This study introduces a novel Regularized Actor-Critic (RAC) approach enabling individual drivers to optimally reconcile their historical charging habits with external rewards, such as driving distance and waiting time. Empirical evaluations on two real-world datasets confirm the distinct advantages and superior performance of this method compared to existing alternatives.

We examine the Modular Subset Sum problem: determining whether a multiset $X$ of integers from $\mathbb{Z}_m$ contains a subset summing to $t \pmod{m}$. Recent independent studies by Cardinal and Iacono (SOSA'21) and Axiotis et al. (SOSA'21) introduced near-linear algorithms for this task. Cardinal and Iacono presented a randomized approach with $O(m \log m)$ complexity, whereas Axiotis et al. offered a deterministic solution running in $O(m \text{ polylog } m)$ time. Both approaches rely on reducing the problem to a text problem solved via dynamic string data structures. In this paper, we introduce a specialized data structure called the "shift-tree," a simple modification of a segment tree tailored to the specific text problem in Modular Subset Sum algorithms. We offer both hashing-based and deterministic versions of this structure. Applying the shift-tree to the problem yields two new algorithms: a Monte-Carlo randomized algorithm matching the $O(m \log m)$ runtime of the Las-Vegas method by Cardinal and Iacono, and a fully deterministic algorithm executing in $O(m \log m \cdot \alpha(m))$ time, where $\alpha$ denotes the inverse Ackermann function.

When dark matter possesses a mass below approximately 1 GeV, it typically fails to generate sufficient energy for detectable nuclear recoils in standard direct-detection setups. Nevertheless, if cosmic ray collisions accelerate this dark matter to high energies, it could become observable in both direct-detection and neutrino experiments. This study presents findings from a specialized search for such boosted dark matter within the PROSPECT reactor antineutrino experiment. We demonstrate that an upscattered dark matter flux would exhibit a distinctive diurnal sidereal modulation, utilizing this feature to establish novel experimental limits on sub-GeV dark matter with significant interaction cross-sections.

Deep metric learning has achieved remarkable success in clustering and image retrieval by utilizing neural networks to generate highly discriminative feature embeddings for grouping samples. Significant research efforts have focused on designing intelligent loss functions or data mining strategies to train these networks. However, most existing approaches rely on pairs or triplets within a mini-batch to compute distance-based losses. We introduce Group Loss, a differentiable label-propagation-based loss function that ensures embedding similarity across all samples in a group while simultaneously encouraging low-density regions between different groups. Guided by the smoothness principle that similar objects should share the same group label, this loss trains the network for classification by enforcing consistent labeling within classes. Furthermore, we develop specialized inference strategies called Group Loss++ to enhance our model's performance. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art results in clustering and image retrieval across four datasets and delivers competitive outcomes on two person re-identification datasets, offering a unified framework for both retrieval and re-identification tasks.

The accelerating dissemination of COVID-19 information online necessitates automated quality assurance mechanisms. Consequently, this work assesses news credibility through specific linguistic markers and evaluates the practicality of graphical interfaces designed for such assessments via two empirical studies. A moderated qualitative interview with six participants identified rating scales, sub-criteria, and algorithm authorship as key predictors of usability. Furthermore, a subsequent quantitative online survey involving 50 participants highlighted a tension between transparency and conciseness in interface design, alongside a perceived hierarchy in metadata where the authorship of the news text is deemed more significant than the authorship of the algorithm evaluating its credibility. Finally, the study proposes future research directions, including the proactive documentation of credibility-related metadata for Natural Language Processing and language technology services, as well as the development of an explicit hierarchical taxonomy of usability predictors for automatic credibility assessment.

To measure the entanglement of a tripartite GHZ state within noninertial frames subjected to phase damping, phase flip, and bit flip noise, the one-tangle and {\pi}-tangle are employed. Results indicate that the two-tangles function as if the system were isolated. However, the one-tangle and {\pi}-tangle exhibit distinct dynamics across the three noise channels. Under phase damping, the occurrence of sudden death for both measures depends on the specific coupling type, whereas sudden death in the phase flip channel is inevitable. Additionally, decoherence effects become negligible when the system interacts with a bit flip channel at infinite acceleration. Finally, in the presence of a phase flip channel, both one-tangle and {\pi}-tangle experience a sudden rebirth, an event that can be postponed by activating collective coupling.

Multi-view data involves partitioning features into distinct sets, often representing different data sources. Stacked penalized logistic regression (StaPLR) is a recently developed approach for classification that automatically identifies the most predictive views. This work extends StaPLR to handle hierarchical multi-view structures and introduces a novel view importance metric, enabling comparisons of view significance across any hierarchical level. The extended algorithm is applied to Alzheimer's disease classification using MRI measures derived from three scan types: structural MRI, diffusion-weighted MRI, and resting-state fMRI. The method successfully determines which scan types and specific derived measures are most critical for classification, achieving superior performance compared to elastic net regression.

Privacy has become a global priority concerning activities involving sensitive data, prompting numerous countries and territories to enact regulations that limit how organizations can utilize personal information. While fields like machine learning and natural language processing have effectively implemented privacy-preserving techniques to protect data in many applications, information retrieval (IR) remains vulnerable to privacy risks, including attacks and accidental exposure of documents and search histories. These threats can compromise user security and lead to legal penalties under data protection laws. This study aims to examine open challenges in IR privacy found in recent literature, specifically focusing on tasks involving user-generated text. Our contribution consists of three parts: first, an overview of privacy threats facing IR tasks; second, a discussion of applicable privacy-preserving mechanisms to mitigate these risks; and third, an analysis of the trade-offs between maintaining privacy and preserving utility performance in IR tasks.

For positive integers $u$ and $v$, define $L_u=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ u & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ and $R_v=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & v \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, and let $G_{u,v}$ denote the group generated by these matrices. In prior work, the authors characterized matrices $M=\begin{bmatrix}a & b \\c & d\end{bmatrix}$ within $G_{u,v}$ for $u,v\geq 3$ using the short continued fraction expansion of $b/d$. This study extends that characterization to the case where $u,v\geq 2$, excluding the specific instance where $uv=4$.

This study presents the initial findings of a time-resolved CCD photometric and time-series investigation into NSV 13601, a variable star located in the Pegasus constellation. Observations were conducted using the 14-inch Schmidt telescope at Maharaja Krishnakumarsinhji Bhavnagar University (MKBU). Data analysis was carried out using both Vstar and Period04 software, with a comparison of their respective outcomes. Key results include the following periods: approximately 77.784 days (MKBU Data V via VStar), 77.632 days (MKBU Data Ic via VStar), 77.058 days (MKBU Data V via Period04), and 49.560 days (MKBU Data Ic via Period04). The mean V and I magnitudes for the MKBU data are 12.203 and 11.292, respectively. These findings confirm NSV 13601 as a variable star.

Keywords: Stars: individual: NSV 13601; stars: oscillations; techniques: photometric.

An incoherent Thomson scattering system featuring multiple lines of sight has been installed at the Gas Dynamic Trap (GDT) to measure radial profiles of plasma electron temperature and density. Utilizing an Nd:YAG laser operating at $1064 nm$, the diagnostic employs a $90^\circ$ scattering geometry with a total of eleven viewing angles. Currently, six of these lines of sight are fitted with interference filter spectrometers. Initial results from a one-month experimental run at the GDT indicate that radial profiles can be determined with an accuracy of a few percent for electron temperatures $T_e \geqslant 20 eV$ and densities $n_e \geqslant 10^{19} m^{-3}}. Future plans involve upgrading the system with a pulse burst laser to investigate the rapid dynamics of plasma parameters during each GDT shot.

Most uncertainty quantification techniques for deep object detectors, including variational inference, rely on network outputs. In this study, we investigate gradient-based epistemic uncertainty metrics to generate dependable confidence scores for these detectors. We demonstrate that these metrics provide predictive insights and capture information orthogonal to that obtained by standard output-based approaches like Monte-Carlo dropout and deep ensembles. To evaluate this, we apply meta-classification and meta-regression to produce confidence estimates using gradient metrics alongside other baselines applicable to any object detection architecture. Specifically, we analyze false positive detection rates and localization quality predictions to assess the uncertainty content of our metrics, while also calculating calibration errors for the meta-classifiers. Furthermore, we integrate these metrics as a post-processing filter within the object detection pipeline and compare detection performance. Our findings indicate that gradient-based uncertainty performs comparably to output-based methods across various detectors and datasets. More importantly, meta-classifiers that combine both gradient and output-based metrics outperform standalone models. These results confirm that gradient uncertainty contributes orthogonal information to output-based methods, suggesting that variational inference can be enhanced by incorporating gradient-based uncertainty. This combination yields improved confidence measures, thereby boosting the probabilistic reliability of deep object detectors and benefiting downstream applications.

This work presents a stochastic adaptation of the cutting-plane method tailored for a broad range of data-driven Mixed-Integer Nonlinear Optimization (MINLO) problems. Under minimal assumptions, we demonstrate that this stochastic approach converges to an $\epsilon$-optimal solution with high probability. Numerical experiments on various problems indicate that stochastic cutting planes achieve a speedup of multiple orders of magnitude compared to the conventional method. Additionally, we investigate the minimum sampling requirements and find that a sample size of $O(\sqrt[3]{n})$ often suffices to obtain high-quality solutions for many instances.

Presently, the sole methods for jointly governing deep learning models are homomorphic encryption and secure multiparty computation. However, both approaches are impractical for training large-scale neural networks due to excessive computational and communication costs. To address this, we propose a scalable solution: partitioning a deep learning model across multiple parties. This paper empirically evaluates the security implications of this approach, framed as the "model completion" problem. This problem asks how much training is needed to restore a model's original performance given either the full training dataset or an environment simulator, along with a subset of the model's parameters. We introduce a metric to assess the difficulty of model completion and analyze it empirically across supervised learning on ImageNet and reinforcement learning on Atari and DeepMind Lab. Our findings indicate that (1) model completion is more challenging in reinforcement learning than in supervised learning, primarily because the trained agent's trajectories are unavailable; and (2) the difficulty of the problem relies less on the quantity of missing parameters and more on their specific type and location. Consequently, our results suggest that splitting models could be a viable strategy for shared governance in scenarios where training is prohibitively expensive.

This study presents a notation for $\varepsilon$-weakened robustness to evaluate the reliability and stability of deep neural networks (DNNs). In contrast to traditional robustness, which prioritizes a "perfect" safe zone devoid of adversarial examples, $\varepsilon$-weakened robustness targets the region where the fraction of adversarial instances remains within a user-defined limit of $\varepsilon$, with lower $\varepsilon$ values indicating reduced failure probabilities. Based on this definition, we provide definitive findings for areas previously overlooked by conventional robustness analyses. We demonstrate that the decision problem for $\varepsilon$-weakened robustness is PP-complete and propose a statistical decision algorithm featuring a user-adjustable error margin. Additionally, we develop a method to compute the maximum $\varepsilon$-weakened robustness radius. Our algorithms exhibit polynomial time complexity regarding the network's dimension and size, ensuring scalability to large-scale real-world models. Furthermore, we highlight the potential of this approach in addressing quality-related issues.

Floquet engineering, which involves driving systems with periodic Hamiltonians, offers significant versatility for analog quantum simulation and enables a rich variety of phase structures. It has been suggested that Floquet systems can exhibit a phase breaking discrete time-translation symmetry (TTS), known as the discrete time crystal (DTC). This concept and its associated exotic phase have garnered substantial interest within the quantum simulation community. In this work, we report the observation of a DTC in a one-dimensional chain of superconducting qubits. We successfully demonstrated long-time stroboscopic quantum dynamics in a periodically driven spin system comprising eight transmon qubits, achieving a DTC order lifetime constrained only by the coherence time of the physical platform. Furthermore, we investigated the transition between discrete TTS-broken and unbroken phases through multiple physical indicators. Our findings expand the application of superconducting circuits in simulating many-body physics and offer an experimental framework for studying non-equilibrium dynamics and phase structures.

Drawing inspiration from the stochastic block model, we examine a specific class of Wigner-type matrices characterized by distinct block structures. By leveraging large-deviation bounds derived from the local law alongside the cumulant expansion formula, we prove a Central Limit Theorem for their corresponding linear spectral statistics. We then apply these findings to the stochastic block model, demonstrating that a particular class of renormalized adjacency matrices falls within the category of block-Wigner-type matrices. Furthermore, we establish that certain estimators for these renormalized matrices, although they no longer conform to the Wigner-type classification, exhibit long-range non-decaying weak correlations among their entries. Despite these differences, the linear spectral statistics of such estimators maintain the same limiting behavior as those of the block-Wigner-type matrices, thereby facilitating hypothesis testing for the stochastic block model.

Complex Word Identification (CWI) focuses on locating words within a text that readers might struggle to comprehend. Research indicates that CWI systems enhance text simplification, readability forecasting, and vocabulary acquisition modeling. However, word difficulty is a highly individual concept, varying based on a reader's native language, proficiency level, and reading background. This paper demonstrates that personalized models are superior for predicting word complexity for specific readers. We employ a novel active learning framework to customize models for individuals and provide a dataset of complexity annotations alongside trained models as a benchmark for future studies.

Numerous scientific challenges involve pinpointing a limited subset of covariates linked to a target response and quantifying their impacts. Frequently, these impacts are nonlinear and involve interactions, causing linear and additive approaches to yield suboptimal variable selection and estimation. Regrettably, techniques capable of jointly handling sparsity, nonlinearity, and interactions face computational hurdles, with runtimes scaling at least quadratically relative to the number of covariates, and often exceeding this. This study addresses that computational barrier by demonstrating that appropriate interaction models admit a kernel representation, enabling a "kernel trick" that facilitates variable selection and estimation in linear time relative to the number of covariates. The resulting model aligns with a sparse orthogonal decomposition of the regression function within a Hilbert space—specifically, a functional ANOVA decomposition—in which interaction effects capture all variation unaccounted for by lower-order terms. Across various synthetic and real-world datasets, this method surpasses current techniques for large, high-dimensional data while maintaining runtime efficiency that is either competitive or significantly superior (by orders of magnitude).

While formal specifications offer numerous advantages for software development, instructing students in this area can be challenging, as formal methods courses are often perceived as dull. To address this, we introduce FormalZ, a game designed to inject variety into classroom instruction. By allowing students to enjoy the gameplay while learning the fundamentals of writing formal specifications—specifically pre- and post-conditions—FormalZ aims to enhance engagement. Unlike other software engineering educational games such as Pex and Code Defenders, FormalZ adopts a deep gamification strategy where gameplay is central. This paper outlines our work in progress, presenting the first functional and tested implementation of FormalZ alongside preliminary user evaluation results; however, further refinement of the user interface remains future work.

We investigate the potential for detecting a light, invisible axion-like particle (ALP) $a$ through leptonic $Z$ boson decays at the proposed high-energy $e^+e^-$ colliders, CEPC and FCC-ee. Both facilities intend to operate at the $Z$ pole, gathering $10^{12}$ to $10^{13}$ observable $Z$ decays. Our analysis demonstrates that by searching for invisible ALP emission from leptons within these leptonic $Z$ decays, this vast dataset could constrain ALP-lepton couplings to a level previously unattainable in laboratory settings. Specifically, using a Monte Carlo simulation framework, we project that CEPC/FCC-ee could detect couplings of an invisible ALP to muons up to $f_a/C^A_{\mu\mu} \approx 1$ TeV (where $f_a$ represents the ALP decay constant), corresponding to a branching ratio of ${\rm BR}(Z \to \mu^+\mu^-\,a) \approx 2\times 10^{-11}$.

While observations of luminous quasars and their supermassive black holes at redshift z~6 imply formation within dense matter peaks of the early universe, definitive observational evidence for this has been scarce, contrasting with theoretical predictions. This study presents new data suggesting that the radio-loud quasar SDSS J0836+0054 at z=5.8 resides within an unexpectedly rich galactic structure. By synthesizing existing literature—specifically redshift measurements of three companion galaxies by Bosman et al. (2020) that validate an overdensity of i-dropouts previously identified by Zheng et al. (2006)—we demonstrate that the environment surrounding SDSS J0836+0054 represents one of the densest structures known at z~6-7. Notably, one spectroscopic companion is a highly massive, star-forming galaxy (log M_*/M_sun ~ 10.3), confirmed by its clear detection in Spitzer 3.6 μm imaging. This indicates that the quasar's field contains at least two rare, massive dark matter halos (log M_halo/M_sun > 12), implying a galaxy overdensity of no less than 20. After examining the characteristics of the young radio source, we conclude that the conditions in the SDSS J0836+0054 environment qualitatively align with the theoretical requirements for the direct collapse of a massive black hole seed.

Quantum walks play a vital role in advancing quantum algorithms and simulations. This work presents a novel one-dimensional quantum walk within a $d$-dimensional quantum domain ($d>2$), demonstrating its equivalence to circuit implementations in arbitrary finite-dimensional quantum logic. By leveraging a larger state space, this approach reduces the runtime of quantum walks compared to traditional binary systems. We detail efficient quantum circuits for realizing discrete-time quantum walks (DTQW) in one-dimensional position spaces across any finite-dimensional system, achieved through a logical mapping of position states onto multi-qudit states. Using example circuits for diverse qudit state spaces, we investigate scalability within $n$-qudit $d$-ary systems. Additionally, we examine the extension of one-dimensional DTQW to $d$-dimensional DTQW utilizing a $2d$-dimensional coin space on a $d$-dimensional lattice (where $d \ge 2$), followed by the presentation of circuit designs for scalable $d$-dimensional DTQW in $d$-ary systems. Finally, we illustrate circuit architectures for implementing DTQW with various coins across different search spaces.

Effective search-and-rescue (SaR) operations in unknown settings demand rapid, accurate, and optimal decision-making. Robots are emerging as ideal candidates for autonomously executing these tasks. While humans rely on heuristics to navigate uncertainty, optimizing multiple objectives under physical and control constraints poses a mathematical challenge best addressed by machine computation; consequently, SaR robots benefit from integrating both human-inspired and mathematical control mechanisms. Additionally, achieving low-computation-cost coordination among robots in large-scale missions remains an unresolved issue, and real-world sensor data often introduces further uncertainties. This paper introduces a hierarchical multi-agent control architecture that leverages the non-homogeneous and imperfect perception of SaR robots, combining the computational efficiency and fault tolerance of decentralized methods with the global performance gains of centralized approaches. The proposed framework integrates human-inspired and mathematical decision-making strategies in a coordinated, computationally efficient manner. Simulation results indicate that while the proposed method achieves area coverage comparable to existing coverage-focused heuristic techniques, it significantly outperforms them in locating trapped victims. Moreover, with similar computation times, the approach effectively prevents conflicts common in non-cooperative methods. These findings validate that the proposed multi-agent system successfully balances and coordinates both coverage-oriented and target-oriented SaR objectives.

We introduce a method to infer arm and hand dynamics from monocular video by leveraging the strong relationship between these body parts. Despite recent advancements in monocular full-body motion capture, accurately recovering realistic arm twists and hand gestures from uncontrolled, in-the-wild videos remains difficult. Our approach addresses this by capitalizing on the high correlation between arm poses and hand gestures observed in most real-world scenarios. To fully utilize both arm-hand correlations and inter-frame temporal information, we developed a Spatial-Temporal Parallel Arm-Hand Motion Transformer (PAHMT) that simultaneously predicts arm and hand movements. Additionally, we implemented novel loss functions to ensure the generated estimations are both smooth and precise. Furthermore, we curated a motion capture dataset containing 200,000 frames of hand gestures to train our model. By combining a 2D hand pose estimator with a 3D human pose estimator, our method effectively generates plausible arm and hand dynamics from single-view video. Comprehensive evaluations indicate that our approach outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods and demonstrates robustness across various challenging conditions.

Marginalized importance sampling (MIS) is a promising method for off-policy evaluation that estimates the density ratio between the state-action occupancy of a target policy and a sampling distribution. However, existing state-of-the-art MIS techniques depend on intricate optimization strategies and generally succeed only on simple toy problems. We bridge the gap between MIS and deep reinforcement learning by noting that the density ratio can be derived from the target policy's successor representation. This representation can be learned using deep reinforcement learning approaches, effectively separating reward optimization from environmental dynamics, which renders the resulting algorithm stable and suitable for high-dimensional domains. We empirically assess our method's performance across various challenging Atari and MuJoCo environments.

Framing exerts significant yet nuanced influences on public sentiment and policy. We introduce an NLP framework designed to quantify entity-centric frames, applying it to analyze media reporting on police violence in the U.S. through a novel Police Violence Frames Corpus comprising 82,000 news articles covering 7,000 police killings. Our analysis identifies over a dozen distinct framing devices and highlights substantial divergences between liberal and conservative outlets in how they frame both the issue of police violence and the specific entities involved. Conservative media tend to emphasize instances where victims were armed or attacking officers and frequently reference criminal records, whereas liberal sources prioritize systemic injustice, underscoring the victims' race and lack of weapons. We observe temporary surges in injustice-related frames following high-profile shootings and demonstrate that protest volume both correlates with and anticipates shifts in media framing strategies.

Big Data processing frameworks manage vast volumes of both structured and unstructured data by utilizing cluster analysis to store, process, and analyze information, thereby revealing hidden patterns and relationships. Within big data technologies, clustering applied across shared machines facilitates decision-making by deriving contextual relations from the data. These systems are capable of handling all data formats, including raw, tabular, structured, semi-structured, and unstructured inputs, without requiring linearity. Instead, they capture associative and correlative groupings. The primary objective and findings of this paper involve collecting and summarizing contemporary big data clustering techniques, along with evaluating their respective strengths and weaknesses within distributed environments.

This paper addresses a recent problem posed by Wang and Chu regarding series that contain the squares of finite sums defined as $1 + \frac{1}{3} + \cdots + \frac{1}{2n-1}$. We also present numerous closely related and equally complex evaluations of series and integrals. The primary proof relies on an identity originating from Wilf--Zeilberger theory, alongside methods drawn from the theory of colored multiple zeta values.

We examine the behavior of D and D_s mesons across increasing temperatures through lattice QCD simulations featuring N_f=2+1 dynamical flavors on anisotropic lattices. Accessing five temperatures within the hadronic phase, we analyze the impact of rising heat by studying ratios of mesonic correlators relative to the groundstate mass determined at the lowest temperature, eliminating the necessity for additional fitting or spectral reconstruction. Our results show that in the pseudoscalar and vector channels, temperature-induced changes are minimal, occurring at the percent level and well-described by a slight decrease in groundstate mass as the thermal crossover nears. Conversely, in the axial-vector and scalar channels, significant temperature effects are observed throughout the entire hadronic phase.

Although recent progress has been made in out-of-distribution detection, anomaly detection, and uncertainty estimation, a task-agnostic, post-hoc solution remains absent. To overcome this gap, we introduce Task Agnostic and Post-hoc Unseen Distribution Detection (TAPUDD), a novel clustering-based ensembling technique that leverages features from models trained on specific tasks. Specifically, TAPUDD incorporates TAP-Mahalanobis, which clusters training data features and calculates the minimum Mahalanobis distance between test samples and these clusters. Additionally, we propose an Ensembling module that aggregates iterative TAP-Mahalanobis computations across varying cluster counts to ensure reliable and efficient processing. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our method effectively identifies unseen samples across diverse tasks, achieving performance equal to or superior to existing baselines. Consequently, our approach removes the need to manually determine the optimal number of clusters, proving more suitable for large-scale classification applications.

The blending of vocabulary and syntax from multiple languages within a single utterance is known as Code-Mixing, a phenomenon particularly prominent in multilingual communities. This paper presents a system developed for SemEval 2020: Task 9, focusing on sentiment analysis for code-mixed social media content. The approach begins by generating two distinct types of embeddings: character-level embeddings to capture granular details and manage out-of-vocabulary items, and FastText word embeddings to represent morphology and semantics. These embeddings are fed into an LSTM network, resulting in a system that surpasses the baseline model's performance.

Grassmann Phase Space Theory (GSPT) is utilized to investigate the BEC/BCS crossover in cold fermionic atomic gases, specifically to track the evolution of Quantum Correlation Functions (QCF) over time or temperature. These QCFs define two key configurations: (a) the spatial arrangement of spin-up and spin-down atoms within a single Cooper pair, and (b) the spatial arrangement of two spin-up and two spin-down atoms across two Cooper pairs. The first QCF characterizes how the size of a Cooper pair shifts as the fermion-fermion coupling constant varies from the BEC side (small pairs) to the BCS side (large pairs). The second QCF addresses inter-pair correlations, which are negligible at the BEC or BCS limits but become significant in the strong interaction unitary regime, where pair size rivals the separation distance between pairs. In GSPT, QCFs are derived as stochastic averages of products of Grassmann stochastic momentum fields. The theory demonstrates a linear relationship between these stochastic averages at later times (or lower temperatures) and those at earlier times (or higher temperatures), with linear matrix elements consisting entirely of c-numbers. Analytical expressions for these matrix elements over small time or temperature increments have been derived, supplying the necessary formulas for future numerical studies of this evolution. Various initial conditions are examined, such as a non-interacting fermionic gas at zero temperature and a high-temperature gas where interactions are negligible initially. These scenarios are pertinent to analyzing the temporal evolution of Cooper pair formation upon switching on interactions via Feshbach resonance, or the evolution as temperature decreases for specific coupling constants, particularly in the large-coupling unitary regime. Complete derivations of these expressions are provided in the Appendices.

Executing analytics on extensive video datasets is becoming ubiquitous across numerous applications. These operations typically rely on costly machine learning models for object detection and tracking, prompting the recent development of systems designed to optimize video query execution and lower associated costs. Nevertheless, previous approaches often focus on a single dimension of execution speed by prioritizing one optimization technique while neglecting other acceleration opportunities, resulting in a suboptimal balance between speed and accuracy. We introduce MultiScope, a versatile video pre-processor for object detection and tracking that investigates multiple optimization pathways to extract video tracks, achieving a superior speed-accuracy tradeoff compared to existing solutions. Evaluated against three recent systems across seven diverse datasets, MultiScope demonstrates a 2.9x average speedup over the best-performing baseline while maintaining equivalent accuracy.

This paper investigates the design of optimal resource allocation algorithms for large intelligent reflecting surface (IRS)-assisted simultaneous wireless information and power transfer (SWIPT) systems. To enable efficient system design for large IRSs, we avoid jointly optimizing all IRS elements; instead, we divide the IRS into multiple tiles and utilize a scalable optimization framework consisting of offline and online stages. During the offline stage, elements within each tile are jointly configured to support various phase shift settings, termed transmission modes, while the online stage selects the optimal transmission mode for each tile from this set. With a given set of transmission modes, our objective is to minimize total base station (BS) transmit power by jointly optimizing beamforming and the transmission mode selection policy, subject to quality-of-service constraints for information decoding and non-linear energy harvesting. Although the resulting resource allocation problem is a non-convex combinatorial optimization task, we solve it optimally using the branch-and-bound (BnB) method, which incurs high computational complexity. To balance optimality with computational efficiency, we also propose an efficient suboptimal algorithm leveraging the penalty method and successive convex approximation. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed designs achieve significant power savings compared to several baseline schemes. Furthermore, our findings indicate that appropriately tuning the number of tiles and transmission modes allows the scalable optimization framework to effectively facilitate online design for large IRSs.

This work examines the weak-field approximation of General Relativity incorporating matter, along with potential quantization approaches. The goal is to develop a predictive quantum framework that offers a first-principles explanation of gravitational interactions within macroscopic quantum systems. This scope covers recent experimental proposals involving Newtonian gravitational forces generated by quantum matter distributions, as well as phenomena such as gravity-induced entanglement, gravitational cat states, Rabi oscillations driven by gravity, and the quantum causal ordering of events. Our primary findings are as follows: (i) We demonstrate that these effects do not rely on genuine gravitational degrees of freedom. (ii) We establish that, in contrast to full General Relativity, weak gravity coupled with matter functions as a parameterized field theory, achieved by treating spacetime coordinates as dynamical variables. (iii) Quantization through gauge-fixing yields an effective field theory that explains certain phenomena but introduces gauge dependence, particularly affecting spacetime observables; this ambiguity reflects the problem of time, which remains relevant even in weak gravity. (iv) We argue that a consistent quantization of parameterized field theories is crucial for constructing a predictive, spacetime-covariant theory of weak gravity capable of describing gravitational effects in macroscopic quantum systems. Additionally, we explore the implications of these results for gravitational decoherence theories, the concept of locality in gravity relative to quantum information theory, and the intriguing prospect that solutions to the problem of time could be empirically tested using weak-gravity quantum experiments.

Cross-correlation analysis serves as a potent instrument for deciphering the mutual dynamics within time series. This research presents an innovative approach to forecasting the future synchronization states of two financial time series. Specifically, we employ cross-recurrence plot analysis as a nonlinear technique to quantify multidimensional coupling in the time domain and assess synchronization levels. By utilizing a deep learning framework, we predict synchronization states based on features derived from dynamically sub-sampled cross-recurrence plots. We validate our methodology through extensive experiments involving multiple stocks, including key components of the S&P100 index. Our findings indicate that while predicting synchronization between two time series is generally challenging, it can be achieved with highly satisfactory results for specific stock pairs.

Let $K$ be a number field and $f \in K[X]$ an irreducible monic polynomial with coefficients in $O_K$, the ring of integers of $K$. We seek to establish an effective criterion, based on the Galois group of $f$ over $K$ and a linear recurrence sequence linked to $f$, that can sometimes characterize the prime ideals of $O_K$ modulo which $f$ splits completely. Consequently, if $\alpha$ is a root of $f$, this criterion identifies the prime ideals of $O_K$ that split completely in the extension $K(\alpha)$. This approach is applicable when the degree of $f$ is at least $4$ and its Galois group over $K$ is either the symmetric group or the alternating group.

This research focuses on gradient Gibbs measures (GGMs) for a SOS model defined on Cayley trees, featuring a countable spin set $\mathbb Z$ and alternating magnetism, governed by a nearest-neighbor gradient interaction potential. Leveraging the K\"ulske-Schriever argument derived from boundary law equations, we establish multiple $q$-height-periodic, translation-invariant GGMs for the cases where $q=2, 3, 4$.

Graph coloring is a core concept in graph theory involving the assignment of labels or colors to vertices or edges under specific constraints. This paper specifically examines harmonious coloring, a type of proper vertex coloring where, for any two distinct colors $i$ and $j$, at most one pair of adjacent vertices receives these colors. Because this method distinguishes edges, it holds promise for applications in transportation, computer, and airway network systems.

The study is divided into two main areas. The first section addresses the computational complexity of finding a minimum harmonious coloring, demonstrating that the problem is APX-hard for general graphs, that a standard greedy algorithm yields an $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$-approximation, and that a connection exists between vertex cover and the harmonious chromatic number. The second section establishes the exact harmonious chromatic number for specific graph classes, including all 3-regular planar graphs with a diameter of 3, certain non-planar regular graphs, and graphs related to cycles.

This study examines the Stueckelberg-modified two-dimensional (2D) Proca theory interacting with Dirac fields, focusing on its continuous and discrete symmetries. We demonstrate that this specific interacting field-theoretic model serves as a tractable example of Hodge theory, where its symmetries and associated conserved charges realize the de Rham cohomological operators of differential geometry at an algebraic level. The physical state within the quantum Hilbert space is defined as the harmonic state from the Hodge decomposition, which is annihilated by both the conserved, nilpotent (anti-)BRST and (anti-)co-BRST charges. A key finding is that the 2D anomaly at the quantum level does not compromise the theory's consistency or unitarity. Consequently, despite the presence of local chiral symmetry (linked to nilpotent (anti-)co-BRST transformations) alongside local gauge symmetry (linked to nilpotent (anti-)BRST transformations), the model remains compatible with a particle interpretation. The physicality condition imposed by the (anti-)co-BRST charges renders the 2D anomaly term trivial, ensuring the theory is consistent, unitary, and suitable for particle description.

Image animation involves creating a video sequence where an object from a source image moves in sync with the motion of a driving video. Our approach solves this challenge without requiring any annotations or prior knowledge about the specific object being animated. After training on a collection of videos featuring objects from the same category (such as faces or human bodies), the method can be applied to any instance of that class. To accomplish this, we separate appearance and motion data using a self-supervised framework. To handle complex movements, we employ a representation based on learned keypoints and their corresponding local affine transformations. A generator network simulates occlusions that occur during target motions, merging the appearance extracted from the source image with the motion derived from the driving video. Our framework achieves top performance across various benchmarks and object categories, and the source code is open to the public.

Leveraging their extensive tunability and control, quantum emulators enable the study of intricate details within closed quantum many-body systems, specifically examining regimes of thermalization and those arrested by disorder. The latter, known as many-body localization (MBL), is characterized by non-ergodic dynamics marked by the retention of local information and sluggish entanglement expansion. In this work, we precisely observe this same phenomenon under conditions where the on-site energy landscape is linearly graded rather than disordered, effectively simulating Stark MBL. We achieved this using a quantum processor comprising thirty-two superconducting qubits, which accurately replicates the relaxation dynamics of a non-integrable spin model. Our findings detail real-time evolution at system scales exceeding the capabilities of classical exact simulations, indicating the emergence of quantum advantage and paving the path for utilizing quantum computing to address out-of-equilibrium many-body challenges.

Hydrogen deuteride (HD) is abundant across diverse astrophysical settings, and quantifying its large-scale distribution across different cosmic epochs could reveal key properties of these environments. This study examines the feasibility of mapping this distribution via line intensity mapping of HD's lowest rotational transition, with a specific focus on the epoch of reionization ($z\sim6-10$) and earlier times. Our findings indicate that the reionization era offers the most promising signal, potentially accessible through cross-correlations with existing [CII] intensity mapping surveys. Although our predicted signal exceeds the capabilities of current-generation instruments, planned future upgrades should enable the detection of reionization-era HD without requiring new observational campaigns, thereby constraining the properties of star-forming galaxies central to the reionization process. We also explore various methods for detecting HD during "cosmic dawn" ($z\sim10-30$), a period where HD might serve as a crucial complementary observable to 21$\,$cm intensity maps. Ultimately, we conclude that both current and planned facilities are ill-suited for the specifications required for a significant detection, though such a measurement may become feasible with sustained future development. Finally, we argue that mapping HD in the intergalactic medium during the cosmic dark ages ($z\gtrsim 30$) remains beyond the reach of any conceivable experiment.

We present a straightforward and intuitive two-stage active learning framework designed for training $k$-nearest neighbors classifiers. We establish consistency guarantees for a modified $k$-nearest neighbors classifier when samples are acquired using our proposed method. Furthermore, we demonstrate that under conditions where the conditional probability function $\mathbb{P}(Y=y|X=x)$ is sufficiently smooth and the Tsybakov noise condition is satisfied, our actively trained classifiers converge to the Bayes optimal classifier at an asymptotic rate that surpasses that of passively trained $k$-nearest neighbor classifiers.

Decompilation, the process of reversing software compilation, serves as a vital tool in reverse engineering. While recent research has leveraged neural machine translation techniques to automate decompilation—offering potential for broader language support—current efforts have largely focused on C code. This paper argues that existing neural decompilers sacrifice retargetability for accuracy by relying on language-specific components like tokenizers and parsers to construct abstract syntax trees (ASTs), thereby increasing overhead for new languages. Instead, we propose a tradeoff that treats assembly and source code primarily as plain text, enabling the creation of a decompiler that is easily adaptable to new languages. We evaluated our prototype, Beyond The C (BTC), across Go, Fortran, OCaml, and C, analyzing how parameters such as tokenization and training data affect output quality. Our results demonstrate that BTC achieves decompilation performance comparable to prior neural methods while requiring significantly less domain knowledge. To foster further research in language-agnostic decompilation, we will release our training data, trained models, and source code.

As experimentally detectable signatures of Majorana bound states (MBSs) grow, the challenge of utilizing them to manipulate qubits becomes increasingly vital. This study proposes integrating a quantum dot (QD) with Majorana Josephson junctions (MJJs), demonstrating that the parity properties of Majorana qubits can be controlled by tuning the QD energy levels. By examining voltage generation through both fast and adiabatic evolution methods, we identify a distinctive $4\pi$-periodic hopping behavior of electrons in the QD, occurring within a robust $4\pi$-period voltage regime, which holds promise for constructing hybrid quantum circuits. Additionally, we analyze Landau-Zener-Stückelberg interference across various driving frequencies, revealing a cosinoidal QD occupation probability that remains unchanged during parity flips, alongside a controllable voltage state that induces parity flipping. Finally, we observe that Rabi oscillations in this system are damped. These findings offer pathways for detecting MBSs and advancing quantum computation.

Calculating response functions in correlated electronic systems represents a central challenge in condensed matter physics. Securing a physically accurate response function requires simultaneously maintaining the Ward-Takahashi identity and the fluctuation-dissipation theorem. In this work, we introduce a self-consistent many-body approach within the GW framework to compute response functions based on the fluctuation-dissipation theorem, ensuring compliance with the Ward-Takahashi identity as well. The efficacy of this method is validated using the two-dimensional one-band Hubbard model, where numerical results confirm adherence to both the Ward-Takahashi identity and the fluctuation-dissipation theorem. Furthermore, when compared to the precise spin susceptibility derived from the determinantal Monte Carlo method, our approach yields highly satisfactory results while significantly lowering computational costs.

Extending the interrogation time of optical clocks to several seconds to minimize statistical uncertainties requires phase-stable laser light. We present a laser system capable of delivering over 50 µW of phase-stabilized ultraviolet light at 267.4 nm for an aluminium ion optical clock. This light is produced by frequency-quadrupling a 1069.6 nm fibre laser through two cascaded non-linear crystals in a single-pass arrangement. First, a 10 mm PPLN waveguide crystal converts 1 W of fundamental light into more than 0.2 W at 534.8 nm. Subsequently, a 50 mm DKDP crystal generates more than 50 µW at 267.4 nm. The passive short-term phase stability upper limit was determined via beat-note measurements against an existing phase-stabilized quadrupling system using the same source laser. This yielded a fractional frequency instability of less than 5 × 10⁻¹⁷ after 1 second, supporting lifetime-limited probing of the ²⁷Al⁺ clock transition with a sufficiently stable laser. Future improvements in the fourth harmonic's stability are anticipated through interferometric path length stabilization of the pump light by back-reflecting it through the setup to correct frequency deviations. The in-loop error signal suggests an electronically limited instability of 1 × 10⁻¹⁸ at 1 second.

This study examines the generalized emergent dark energy (GEDE) model, a phenomenological framework proposed by Li and Shafieloo [Astrophys. J. {\bf 902}, 58 (2020)], analyzing its evolution through linear perturbations and various cosmological probes. The model features a free parameter, $\Delta$, which distinguishes between the $\Lambda$CDM scenario ($\Delta=0$) and the phenomenologically emergent dark energy (PEDE) scenario ($\Delta=1$), thereby enabling the identification of the model best supported by observational data. Our results indicate support for GEDE when using Planck data alone or in conjunction with R19; however, Bayesian model comparison yields inconclusive outcomes when Type Ia Supernovae or BAO data are incorporated. Specifically, the $\Lambda$CDM model is disfavored at greater than $2\sigma$ confidence levels for most datasets examined, whereas the PEDE model remains consistent with the Planck 2018+BAO+R19 combination within $1\sigma$ confidence levels.

Computing plays an increasingly significant role in data science and statistics curricula. Courses, particularly those led by faculty with statistical training, often utilize R as the primary programming language. Many educators have chosen to center their instruction on the tidyverse, a collection of R packages defined by its developers as sharing a unified high-level design philosophy and consistent low-level grammar and data structures. This coherence ensures that proficiency with one package facilitates learning others, driving the widespread adoption of the tidyverse ecosystem. A key driver of this popularity is the intentional design of these tools to simplify the learning curve, allowing users to master new functions as they explore the broader system. Furthermore, tidyverse packages cover the entire data science lifecycle, encompassing data import, visualization, wrangling, modeling, and communication. Consequently, we argue that the tidyverse offers a highly effective and efficient route for undergraduate students across all disciplines to acquire the computational skills and mindset essential for data science. This paper presents the tidyverse from an educational standpoint, offering a concise overview, demonstrating how fundamental statistics and data science tasks are performed using the tidyverse, and highlighting its strengths specifically within teaching and learning contexts.

Natural policy gradient methods have gained popularity in reinforcement learning for enhancing the stability of policy gradients through second-order approximations that precondition the gradient using the inverse Fisher-information matrix. Despite this, no prior study has systematically examined the impact of various second-order approximations. To fill this gap, we evaluated and compared five distinct approximations across critical metrics such as performance, stability, sample efficiency, and computational time. Additionally, we investigated often-overlooked hyperparameters, including batch size variations and the optimization of critic networks via natural gradients. Our findings indicate that, on average, improved second-order approximations yield superior performance, and carefully tuned hyperparameters can significantly boost performance and sample efficiency by up to 181%. The code for this research is publicly available at https://github.com/gebob19/natural-policy-gradient-reinforcement-learning.

When phenotypic diversity arises without underlying genetic differences, it typically indicates complex energy landscapes governed by gene regulatory networks (GRNs). In this framework, distinct phenotypes correspond to alternative states within complex nonlinear systems, representing either stable attractors in deterministic frameworks or modes of stationary distributions in stochastic contexts. This study offers both theoretical and practical analyses of these landscapes, with a specific emphasis on stochastic slow promoter kinetics—a timescale pertinent when transcription factor binding and unbinding are modulated by epigenetic mechanisms such as DNA methylation and chromatin remodeling. Unlike previously explored only through numerical simulations, adiabatic approximations of promoter kinetics are deemed unsuitable here. Contrary to current literature, we present rigorous analytic descriptions of multiple modes. A comprehensive formal approach elucidates how system parameters influence outcomes and predicts how alterations in GRN architecture, whether via mutations or artificial intervention, affect the quantity, position, and probability of alternative states. By adapting singular perturbation theory from mathematics, we model the stationary distributions of Chemical Master Equations for GRNs as mixtures of Poisson distributions, yielding explicit formulas for the locations and probabilities of metastable states based on system parameters. To demonstrate the theory, we examine the role of cooperative binding in stochastic versus deterministic models and apply the framework to various systems, including isolated and communicating toggle switches, a synthetic oscillator, and a trans-differentiation network.

Let $G$ be a simple graph with maximum degree $\Delta(G)$. A subgraph $H$ of $G$ is termed overfull if $|E(H)|>\Delta(G)\lfloor \frac{1}{2}|V(H)| \rfloor$. In 1986, Chetwynd and Hilton conjectured that for any graph $G$ satisfying $\Delta(G)>\frac{1}{3}|V(G)|$, the chromatic index equals $\Delta(G)$ precisely when $G$ lacks an overfull subgraph. Given $0<\varepsilon <1$ and a large graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with minimum degree at least $\frac{1}{2}(1+\varepsilon)n$, previous work established the conjecture for even $n$. This paper extends that finding to cases where $n$ is odd. To our knowledge, this represents the initial result addressing the conjecture for graphs of odd order under a minimum degree constraint.

This study details the contribution of Araguaia Medical Vision Lab to the 2017 International Skin Imaging Collaboration Skin Lesion Challenge. We employed deep convolutional neural networks to classify images of Melanoma and Seborrheic Keratosis lesions. By utilizing finetuned GoogleNet and AlexNet architectures, we achieved AUC scores of 0.950 and 0.846 for Seborrheic Keratosis and Melanoma, respectively.

E. Ghys established that the linking numbers of modular knots and the absent trefoil $K_{2,3}$ within $S^3$ correspond to values of the widely recognized Rademacher symbol for ${\rm SL}_2\mathbb{Z}$. In this work, we substitute ${\rm SL}_2\mathbb{Z}=\Gamma_{2,3}$ with the triangle group $\Gamma_{p,q}$ for any coprime integers $p, q$ satisfying $2\leq p<q$. By applying the theory of harmonic Maass forms defined on $\Gamma_{p,q}$, we define the Rademacher symbol $\psi_{p,q}$ and offer multiple characterizations. Furthermore, we extend Ghys's result concerning modular knots to any missing torus knot $K_{p,q}$ in $S^3$ and in lens spaces.

Argument mining necessitates a broad spectrum of linguistic phenomena ranging from simple to complex, alongside commonsense knowledge. Prior research indicates that pre-trained language models excel at capturing syntactic and semantic features when utilized with transfer learning and diverse pre-training strategies. However, a critical question remains regarding the extent to which these models cover the multifaceted demands of argument mining. Through experimentation, we investigate how language models derived from various lexical semantic families influence performance in identifying argumentative discourse units. The findings demonstrate that transfer learning enhances task performance, yet current approaches appear inadequate for fully exploiting commonsense knowledge across different lexical semantic families.

This study employs commercially available text analysis tools to process interview transcripts from a computational social science project. We demonstrate that topical clustering and terminological enrichment facilitate the efficient exploration and quantification of responses, enabling hypothesis generation and testing, the comparison of textual and non-textual variables, and a reduction in analyst workload. We advocate for the adoption of text analysis in social science research, particularly for exploratory open-ended inquiries. We also address how these technologies satisfy replicability standards. However, we caution that recent learning models often lack transparency, necessitating that models remain editable and their decisions explainable. Furthermore, we observe that current tools, including the one utilized here, are not specifically optimized for interview text processing. While many variables can be quantified through lexical statistics, we found that certain intriguing and potentially valuable features remain difficult or impossible to automate reliably at this time. We also highlight the potential of traditional natural language processing mechanisms, such as named entity recognition and anaphora resolution, within this domain. Finally, we recommend that language technologists investigate the comprehensive processing of interview data, specifically the dynamic interplay between questions and responses, and we urge social science researchers to confidently utilize text analysis tools, especially during the exploratory stages of interview data processing.

The reaction between carbon atoms and vinyl cyanide (CH₂CHCN) serves as a pathway to form the interstellar 3-cyano propargyl radical (CH₂C₃N), which has recently been identified in space. Although the 1-cyano propargyl radical (HC₃HCN), an isomer of CH₂C₃N, is theoretically predicted to be generated at least twice as efficiently in this reaction, it has not yet been observed. Consequently, HC₃HCN remains a viable candidate for future detection. Our objective is to produce the HC₃HCN radical in the gas phase to analyze its rotational spectrum. The resulting spectroscopic parameters will facilitate accurate frequency predictions to aid in its astronomical identification. We synthesized the HC₃HCN radical via electric discharge and characterized its rotational spectrum using a Balle-Flygare narrowband Fourier-transform microwave spectrometer within the 4–40 GHz range. Supported by high-level *ab initio* calculations, we measured a total of 193 hyperfine components arising from 12 *a*- and *b*-type rotational transitions. This analysis enabled the precise determination of 22 molecular constants, encompassing rotational, centrifugal distortion, fine, and hyperfine parameters. Using these transition frequency predictions, we searched the TMC-1 region with the QUIJOTE survey (30.1–50.4 GHz) but failed to detect HC₃HCN, establishing a 3σ upper limit on its column density of 6.0 × 10¹¹ cm⁻².

A key challenge in advancing Airborne Wind Energy (AWE) toward commercial viability is ensuring that system safety requirements are satisfied. However, the high-dimensional complexity of AWE systems makes calculating formal mathematical robustness guarantees difficult. We leverage research on Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability analysis to determine an optimal control policy for flight path tracking while enforcing safety constraints. Additionally, the zero-sublevel set of the resulting value function identifies the backward reachable set, representing all states from which the system can be safely driven to a target set within a specific timeframe without entering unsafe states. Moreover, we develop a switching law that allows the safety controller to operate alongside arbitrary, least-restrictive controllers, creating a safe hybrid control strategy. In this configuration, the safety controller engages only when the system nears the limits of its maneuverability envelope. This hybrid approach represents a significant advancement over existing robust control methods that degrade performance by assuming worst-case environmental and system conditions continuously. We validate our findings through extensive simulation studies.

We establish a unified operator framework for quantum holonomies arising in bosonic systems. For Hamiltonians that are bilinear in creation and annihilation operators, we identify a holonomy group governed by a specific set of orthonormal modes satisfying an enhanced adiabatic theorem. This photon-number independent approach yields both deeper conceptual understanding and computational benefits relative to conventional geometric phase formalisms. Notably, it reveals a strong parallel between quantum holonomies and linear optical networks. This correspondence offers a concrete method to render any linear optical quantum computation robust against errors by leveraging either adiabatic or nonadiabatic geometric phases.

Beyond merely occupying the extreme, diffuse tail of the dwarf galaxy population, Ultra-Diffuse Galaxies (UDGs) serve as a critical laboratory for investigating star formation within extremely low-density environments. In this second paper, we compare the spatially resolved star formation activity of 22 HI-selected UDGs against 21 "normal" dwarf galaxies within 120 Mpc, testing these observations against predictions from the pressure-regulated, feedback-modulated (PRFM) theory of star formation. Utilizing a joint SED fitting method applied to UV-optical imaging, we derive estimates for star formation rates and stellar mass surface densities. Our findings indicate that the PRFM framework successfully extends to the UDG regime; although the UDGs in our sample exhibit unusually low star formation rate surface densities relative to their HI content, this reduced efficiency is naturally accounted for by their diffuse structure. Indeed, when analyzed through the PRFM lens, the correlation between midplane pressure and star formation in the UDG sample aligns well not only with the "normal" dwarf reference but also with data from more massive galaxies. Consequently, our results suggest that despite their low efficiencies, HI-rich UDGs do not necessarily form stars via exotic mechanisms. Furthermore, we find that UDGs are likely deficient in molecular hydrogen (H$_2$) compared to the broader dwarf galaxy population.

This study introduces a framework utilizing $A_4$ discrete flavor symmetry, which employs both inverse and type-II seesaw mechanisms. These mechanisms are designed to yield TeV-scale right-handed neutrino masses accessible at the LHC and to generate a one-zero texture in the Majorana neutrino mass matrix. The model's implications for both neutrino physics and dark matter are explored. The spontaneous breaking of the non-Abelian $A_4$ symmetry into a $Z_2$ subgroup offers a stable dark matter candidate. To restrict the Yukawa Lagrangian, cyclic symmetries $Z'_2$, $Z_3$, and $Z_4$ are imposed alongside the $A_4$ flavor symmetry, with cosmological parameter updates from PLANCK 2018 incorporated into the analysis. For a dark matter mass between 45 GeV and 55 GeV, the corresponding mediator particle mass (right-handed neutrinos) is calculated to lie between 138 GeV and 155 GeV, while Yukawa couplings range from 0.995 to 1 to match the observed dark matter relic abundance. Furthermore, contributions from both inverse ($X\equiv\frac{F^2n}{z^2}$) and type-II ($X^{'}\equiv f_1 v_{\Delta_{1}}$) seesaws to the $0\nu\beta\beta$ decay amplitude $|M_{ee}|$ are derived, remaining consistent with low-energy experimental limits. Notably, for normally ordered neutrino masses, the type-II seesaw contribution to $|M_{ee}|$ is significantly larger than that of the inverse seesaw.

We establish the scaling limit for non-cascading 2-GREM Hierarchical Random Hopping dynamics under low-temperature conditions and time scales near equilibrium. The phenomenon of fine-tuning influences the system (depending on specific parameter choices), resulting in three distinct dynamical regimes. Unlike the cascading scenario, fluctuations in the energy pairs of the first and second levels scale with volume, creating a spectrum of time scales during which the dynamics explores only a segment of the complete low-temperature energy landscape.

We introduce a generalized architecture for reactive mobile manipulation, allowing a robot to execute tasks while its base moves toward the next high-level goal. By performing operations on-the-move, this approach significantly reduces overall cycle times compared to methods that require the base to pause during manipulation. The reactive control of the manipulator facilitates grasping objects with unpredictable motion and enhances robustness against perception errors, environmental disturbances, and inaccuracies in robot control, outperforming open-loop, trajectory-based planning methods. We provide an example implementation of this architecture and evaluate its performance on pick-and-place tasks involving both static and dynamic objects, benchmarking it against baseline methods. In real-world tests with a physical robot system, our method achieved a success rate exceeding 99%, with only one failure out of 120 attempts. The architecture is also demonstrated on other mobile manipulator platforms in simulation. Our approach cuts task time by up to 48% while improving reliability, gracefulness, and predictability compared to existing mobile manipulation architectures. Supplementary materials are available at https://benburgesslimerick.github.io/ManipulationOnTheMove.

This work introduces a non-local hidden variables theory for non-relativistic quantum mechanics that offers a realist interpretation, providing a complete description of individual events. The proposed fundamental framework extends an energetic causal set theory, positing that time, events, causal structure, momentum, and energy are foundational, whereas space and the wave function emerge from them. In this model, the "beables" are the perspectives of events, defined as subsets of their causal pasts; consequently, the universe is conceptualized as a causal network where each event contains a partial view of the cosmos derived by looking backward from that point. The fundamental dynamics rely on an action where potential energy scales with variety—a metric for the diversity of event views—and kinetic energy scales with the rate of change of this variety. The Schrödinger equation emerges as the leading-order term in an expansion based on the density of events within fundamental histories. At higher orders, the theory yields computable, non-linear corrections to the wave function, which could predict novel physical phenomena.

Linear Transformers, which utilize linearized attention, have successfully validated the practical scalability and efficacy of outer product-based Fast Weight Programmers (FWPs) introduced in the 1990s. Nevertheless, the original FWP framework is more versatile than current linear Transformers, as it allows a slow neural network to dynamically reprogram the weights of a fast neural network with any architecture, whereas existing linear Transformers restrict both networks to single-layer feedforward structures. This work investigates novel variations by incorporating recurrence into both the slow and fast networks. We assess these new recurrent Fast Weight Programmers (RFWPs) across synthetic algorithmic challenges (code execution and sequential ListOps), the Wikitext-103 language modeling task, and the Atari 2600 2D game environment. The resulting models combine characteristics of both Transformers and RNNs. In reinforcement learning scenarios, our approach achieves significant performance gains over LSTM across multiple Atari games, and our implementation is publicly available.

This paper introduces our approach for the two subtasks of the shared Arabic propaganda detection challenge at WANLP'2022. Subtask 1 involves a multi-label classification task to identify the propaganda techniques present in a tweet; our system leverages XLM-R to estimate the probability of each technique occurring in the target tweet. Subtask 2 extends this by requiring the localization of the specific text spans for each identified technique, which is modeled as a sequence tagging problem. For this second task, we employ a multi-granularity network built upon an mBERT encoder. In total, our system achieved second place in both subtasks, competing against 14 and 3 participants, respectively. Furthermore, our empirical analysis indicates that utilizing a larger English corpus annotated with propaganda techniques does not yield improvements, whether the data is used in its original English form or translated into Arabic.

The quantum-mechanical process of light-by-light scattering ($\gamma\gamma\rightarrow\gamma\gamma$), which is prohibited by classical electrodynamics, becomes observable at the Large Hadron Collider due to the intense electromagnetic fields produced by ultra-relativistic lead (Pb) ion collisions. The ATLAS Collaboration has presented evidence for this reaction using 480 $\mu$b$^{-1}$ of Pb+Pb collision data collected at a nucleon pair center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV. The analysis identified 13 candidate events against an expected background of 2.6$\pm$0.7 events. Following background subtraction and applying analysis corrections, the fiducial cross section for the process $\textrm{Pb+Pb}\,(\gamma\gamma)\rightarrow \textrm{Pb}^{(\ast)}\textrm{+}\textrm{Pb}^{(\ast)}\,\gamma\gamma$ was measured at 70 $\pm$ 24 (stat.) $\pm$ 17 (syst.) nb. This measurement applies to photons with transverse energy $E_{\mathrm{T}}>$3 GeV, absolute pseudorapidity $|\eta|<$2.4, and diphoton invariant masses exceeding 6 GeV, with diphoton transverse momentum below 2 GeV and acoplanarity under 0.01. The result aligns with Standard Model predictions.

Cloud-Radio Access Networks (Cloud-RANs) partition base station functionalities into three distinct units, with the interconnecting link designated as the fronthaul. This study illustrates the transmission of user data transport blocks between the distributed Medium Access Control (MAC) layer and the local Physical (PHY) layer within the radio unit via a Passive Optical Network (PON). While PON offers economic and flexible advantages for Cloud-RAN fronthaul transport, its upstream scheduling mechanisms can generate latency that may violate Cloud-RAN functional split requirements. To address this, we demonstrate how a virtual Dynamic Bandwidth Allocation (DBA) concept, utilizing the established cooperative DBA mechanism to interact with the mobile Long Term Evolution (LTE) scheduler, can reduce PON latency to acceptable levels. Consequently, our findings confirm the viability of employing PON as a fronthaul transport medium for the MAC/PHY functional split within a fully virtualized setting. By incorporating additional background traffic to simulate a more realistic environment, round-trip time measurements indicate that PON usage in a synchronized scenario is limited to approximately 11 km, whereas a non-synchronized scenario fails to meet compliance standards.

This article outlines the rationale and design of a 10-week graduate course focused on developing research software. Although situated within an engineering program, its curriculum is applicable to any scientific discipline involving software creation. Key topics cover local and remote version control, licensing and copyright, Python module structuring, testing and coverage, continuous integration, packaging and distribution, open science, software citation, and reproducibility fundamentals. The instruction combines lectures with in-class activities and discussions, with all materials freely available on GitHub. Assessment centers on a semester-long project where students individually build a software package for their specific research area, requiring all contributions to be submitted as pull requests for peer review and merging. The course launched in Spring 2018 with 17 participants and is scheduled to repeat in Spring 2019.

The Nash social welfare (NSW) is a recognized metric for social welfare that harmonizes individual utilities with overall efficiency. In the realm of fair allocation for indivisible goods, Caragiannis et al. (EC 2016 and TEAC 2019) demonstrated that an allocation maximizing the NSW satisfies the envy-free up to one good (EF1) property.
