This paper investigates the fairness of the NSW within a budget-feasible allocation setting, where items carry costs borne by the receiving agents, and each agent faces a budget constraint limiting the total cost of their assigned items. We establish that a budget-feasible allocation maximizing the NSW achieves a 1/4-approximation of EF1, and this bound is tight. Furthermore, the approximation ratio improves smoothly as item costs become small relative to agent budgets, converging to 1/2 when the budget-to-cost ratio approaches infinity.

We propose Reduced Density Matrix Functional Theory (RDMFT), centered on the first-order reduced density matrix (1-RDM), as a novel method for efficiently capturing correlation effects within relativistic quantum systems. This study first establishes the theoretical groundwork necessary to extend RDMFT into the relativistic regime. Subsequently, employing the no-pair (np) approximation, we develop an approximate framework for relativistic effects that relies on electronic wavefunctions while disregarding explicit positron contributions. Under the np approximation, the theory mirrors the nonrelativistic case, differing only in the unknown functional governing electron-electron interactions via the 1-RDM. Consequently, we construct functional approximations and introduce relativistic counterparts to several standard nonrelativistic RDMFT approximations, analyzing their specific properties.

The relaxed dynamics of stars and gas within galactic discs are effectively modeled by a rotational velocity dependent solely on radial distance, indicating that individual elements have erased memories of their initial conditions. Thermodynamically, this equilibrium corresponds to a microcanonical ensemble at maximum entropy, defined by a lognormal probability distribution. Applying this assumption to the surface density produces rotation curves that align closely with observational data across diverse galaxy types and masses, serving as a robust framework for modeling theoretical disc densities. The model yields a universal disc spin parameter, offering a precise virial mass estimator with a strong correlation between angular momentum and disc mass; this suggests a formation mechanism where the proto-disc shed excess mass to the core or transferred excess angular momentum to satellite galaxies. For high-mass galaxies, the baryonic-to-dynamic mass ratio approaches unity, whereas it remains generally below 1 for low-mass discs, a trend mirroring recent findings on the radial acceleration relation (RAR). While this supports Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND) over dark matter (DM) halos, it does not rule out the presence of undetected baryonic matter or a gravitational DM component within the disc.

This paper introduces a method for generating binary hash codes tailored for image retrieval. We employ Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) to construct two distinct loss functions that train a neural network to maximize correlation between two views. The initial loss function optimizes the correlation between hash centers and the learned hash codes, while the second enhances the correlation between class labels and classification scores. Additionally, we present a novel hash center update mechanism based on weighted means and thresholding, which adapts centers within each epoch. Our results indicate that the training loss converges to the theoretical lower bound of the proposed losses, demonstrating that correlation coefficients are maximized and confirming the creation of an efficient feature space for retrieval. Furthermore, mean average precision evaluations reveal that our approach surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods on both single-labeled and multi-labeled image datasets.

This work demonstrates that subpresentations of aspherical prounipotent presentations over fields of characteristic zero, as well as subpresentations of aspherical pro-$p$-presentations, are themselves aspherical, with an additional application extended to subpresentations of aspherical discrete presentations. In line with the approaches of Bousfield-Kan, Quillen, and Sullivan, these findings are interpreted as affirmative resolutions to the rational and $p$-adic counterparts of J.H.C. Whitehead's conjecture.

The Semantic Publishing Challenge series seeks to explore innovative methods for enhancing scholarly publishing through Linked Data technology. Initiated in 2014, the first effort concentrated on extracting data from non-semantic computer science workshop proceedings to evaluate their quality. This second edition aims to refine information extraction capabilities and connect the 2014 dataset with other related collections within the LOD Cloud, thereby enabling advanced services for end users.

We demonstrate that infinite families of non-relativistic spin-3 symmetries in 2+1 dimensions—including higher-spin versions of the Bargmann, Newton-Hooke, non-relativistic Maxwell, and non-relativistic AdS-Lorentz algebras—can be derived through Lie algebra expansions of two distinct spin-3 extensions of the Nappi-Witten symmetry. These higher-spin Nappi-Witten algebras themselves arise via İnönü-Wigner contractions of appropriate direct product extensions of $\mathfrak{sl}(3,\mathbb{R})$. Conversely, we establish that identical results are achievable by contracting expanded $\mathfrak{sl}(3,\mathbb{R})$ algebras. This approach provides a systematic framework for defining non-relativistic higher-spin Chern-Simons gravity theories in 2+1 dimensions.

This paper details the computation of difference Galois groups for order three equations across a broad spectrum of difference operators, specifically covering the shift operator (Case S), q-difference operator (Case Q), Mahler operator (Case M), and the elliptic case (Case E). We establish criteria to identify whether these Galois groups are irreducible or imprimitive. Furthermore, we provide a sufficient condition ensuring the differential transcendence of solutions to order three difference equations. Additionally, we calculate the difference Galois group for an equation proposed by Wadim Zudilin.

Power system transmission line failures often propagate and cascade across non-local areas, a well-known but counter-intuitive characteristic that significantly complicates the optimal and reliable operation of these intricate networks. This study introduces a comprehensive framework grounded in spectral graph theory that rigorously models the propagation of multiple simultaneous line failures, specifically distinguishing between non-cut and cut set outages. By utilizing this spectral representation, we pinpoint the critical graph sub-structure responsible for localizing line failures, known as the network bridge-block decomposition. Building on this theoretical foundation, we propose an adaptive network topology reconfiguration strategy employing a two-stage algorithm: the first stage identifies optimal clusters based on network modularity, while the second stage refines these clusters through optimal line switching actions. The efficacy of our proposed methodology is demonstrated through extensive numerical simulations on standard IEEE networks, alongside discussions on various extensions and algorithmic variants.

The RICOCHET reactor neutrino observatory is scheduled for installation at the Laue Langevin Institute (ILL) by mid-2022. Its primary scientific objective is to conduct high-precision, low-energy measurements of the coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering (CE$\nu$NS) spectrum to investigate exotic physics possibilities. The facility will feature two cryogenic detector arrays operating at 10 mK: CryoCube, which utilizes a 1 kg Germanium (Ge) target, and Q-ARRAY, which uses a Zinc (Zn) target. The CryoCube comprises 27 Ge crystals equipped with NTD-Ge thermal sensors and charge collection electrodes, enabling simultaneous readout of heat and ionization to effectively reject electromagnetic backgrounds such as gammas, betas, and x-rays. This report details the current status of the front-end electronics. The initial amplification stage employs High Electron Mobility Transistor (HEMT) devices developed by the CNRS/C2N laboratory, which are optimized for ultra-low noise performance at 1K with a power dissipation as low as 15 $\mu$W per channel. Our noise model indicates that 10 eV heat and 20 eVee RMS baseline resolutions are achievable, supported by a high dynamic range for energy deposition up to 10 MeV via loop amplification schemes. These resolutions are essential for achieving high discrimination power between nuclear and electron recoils at the lowest energy levels.

We examine a degenerate version of Einstein's Brownian motion model where the time interval $\tau$ between particle jumps prior to collision is inversely proportional to the particle density $u(x,t) > 0$ at position $x$ and time $t$. The parameter $0 < \tau \leq C < \infty$ characterizes a fluid property that approaches zero as $u \rightarrow \infty$. This degeneration results in the localization of particle propagation within the medium. In this report, we establish a structural relationship between the free-jump interval $\tau$ and the frequency of these jumps $\phi$ as functions of $u$, ensuring the finite speed of propagation for $u$.

This paper presents a hybrid chaos map designed for an image encryption method characterized by high sensitivity. The proposed map exhibits sensitivity to minor variations in both initial conditions and control parameters, thereby increasing computational complexity. Furthermore, its uniform distribution enhances the system's resistance to attacks in security contexts. Various tests and plots are provided to illustrate the enhanced chaotic behavior of the proposed system. Finally, we present additional results demonstrating the effectiveness of this chaotic map within existing image cryptography frameworks.

In high-energy physics, the standard convention for expressing physical quantities involves natural units. This paradigm establishes $c = \hbar = \epsilon_0 = 1$, thereby implicitly rescaling all physical quantities that depend on unit derivatives of these constants. We present $\texttt{NatPy}$, a straightforward Python module that defines user-friendly unit objects capable of usage and conversion within any predefined system of natural units. In this note, we will first introduce and then overview the algebraic methods employed by the $\texttt{NatPy}$ module.

Under-approximations of reachable sets and tubes have gained significant research interest because of their critical functions in verification and control synthesis. Existing methods for continuous-time linear systems often rely on the exact computation of transition matrices and their integrals, a requirement that is generally unfeasible, or they incur prohibitive computational costs. This note addresses these limitations for a specific class of linear time-invariant (LTI) systems by introducing a novel approach to under-approximate finite-time forward reachable sets and tubes using approximations of the matrix exponential and its integral. Specifically, we focus on continuous-time LTI systems featuring an identity input matrix, with uncertain initial states and inputs defined within full-dimensional sets that are affine transformations of closed unit balls. When implemented via zonotopes, the proposed method delivers computationally efficient under-approximations of reachable sets and tubes, ensuring first-order convergence with respect to the Hausdorff distance. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through three numerical examples involving linear systems of dimensions spanning from 2 to 200.

Multi-view detection leverages multiple camera perspectives to mitigate occlusion in dense environments; however, current state-of-the-art methods rely on homography transformations to map multi-view features onto the ground plane. We observe that these 2D transformations fail to account for object height, causing features from the same object along the vertical axis to project to different ground plane locations and resulting in impure feature representations. To address this, we introduce VFA (Voxelized 3D Feature Aggregation), a method for transforming and aggregating features in multi-view detection. Our approach involves voxelizing the 3D space, projecting these voxels onto individual camera views, and linking 2D features to the corresponding projected voxels. This enables the identification and aggregation of 2D features along identical vertical lines, significantly reducing projection distortions. Furthermore, to accommodate varying ground-plane shapes across different object types (e.g., humans versus cattle), we employ oriented Gaussian encoding, which enhances both accuracy and efficiency. Experiments on both multiview 2D and 3D detection tasks across four datasets—including a newly created MultiviewC dataset—demonstrate that our system performs competitively against existing state-of-the-art approaches. Our code and data, including the MultiviewC dataset, are available at https://github.com/Robert-Mar/VFA.

Generative adversarial learning (GAN) has become a leading area in artificial intelligence, renowned for its superior performance in demanding tasks like creating photorealistic images and videos. Although a quantum variant of GAN has appeared with the promise of exponential superiority over classical methods, its practical implementation using accessible quantum hardware and its potential applications remain largely unexplored. This study presents an experimental realization of quantum GAN enhanced by adaptive feedback driven by a stochastic gradient descent algorithm. We evaluated its efficacy by applying it to the adaptive characterization of quantum dynamics and the concurrent estimation of multiple phases. These findings highlight the promising benefits of quantum GAN even under adverse noise conditions, establishing a foundation for future quantum-enhanced information processing applications.

This research examines finite-time optimal consumption-investment scenarios involving power, logarithmic, and exponential utilities within a regime-switching market featuring random coefficients, under coupled constraints on both consumption and investment strategies. We derive explicit optimal strategies and values expressed through solutions to specific diagonally quadratic backward stochastic differential equation (BSDE) systems and linear BSDE systems with unbounded coefficients. Several of these BSDEs represent novel contributions to the literature; a primary theoretical achievement of this work is resolving them. This is achieved by employing a truncation and approximation technique to establish a priori uniformly bounded lower and upper limits for their solutions.

This study focuses on predicting a set of salient questions from a paragraph without prior knowledge of their specific answers. We present two primary contributions. First, we introduce a novel evaluation method that employs the Hungarian algorithm to match predicted questions against reference questions before scoring the pairs. We demonstrate that this approach offers superior theoretical and practical advantages over existing methods by effectively addressing reference coverage. Second, we analyze various strategies for leveraging a pre-trained seq2seq model to generate and select questions related to a given paragraph. The source code is publicly available.

We present DarkNews, a lightweight Python tool designed as a Monte-Carlo generator for neutrino-nucleus scattering beyond the Standard Model. This generator simulates the production and decay of heavy neutral leptons facilitated by extra vector or scalar mediators, as well as transition magnetic moments. By utilizing pre-calculated cross sections for neutrino-nucleus upscattering and heavy neutrino decay rates, DarkNews generates dilepton and single-photon events relevant to accelerator neutrino experiments. We provide two case studies featuring differential distributions for models capable of accounting for the MiniBooNE anomaly. Ultimately, this code aims to support both theoretical and experimental neutrino communities in conducting searches and sensitivity analyses for new particles arising from neutrino upscattering.

The Python Sky Model (PySM) is a Python library designed for Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) experiments to generate HEALPix pixelized maps of diffuse Galactic emission components—specifically dust, synchrotron, free-free, and Anomalous Microwave Emission—as well as the CMB itself. These maps can be convolved with specific instrument beams and integrated across defined bandpasses. Released in 2016, PySM 2 has established itself as the industry standard for simulating Galactic emission, evidenced by its adoption by major projects such as CMB-S4, Simons Observatory, LiteBird, PICO, CLASS, and POLARBEAR, and supported by over 80 citations. However, as upcoming experiments demand higher resolutions, PySM 2 has encountered performance bottlenecks. To address these challenges, PySM 3 was developed from the ground up with a focus on efficiency and scalability. Key enhancements include utilizing the Numba Just-In-Time compiler to optimize Python code and reduce memory usage, integrating MPI via mpi4py for multi-node execution coordination, leveraging libsharp for distributed spherical harmonic transforms, and employing Astropy's data utilities to manage and cache input templates. PySM 3 maintains full backward compatibility with PySM 2 by implementing identical astrophysical emission models and naming conventions. Furthermore, an extensive test suite validates this compatibility by directly comparing the output of each PySM 3 model against the corresponding results from PySM 2.

We investigate the von Neumann algebra formulation of inflationary quasi-de Sitter (dS) space. Distinct from ideal dS space, quasi-dS space permits a non-zero energy flux across the horizon, corresponding to the expectation value of the static time translation generator. Since the dS isometry linked to static time translation is spontaneously broken, temporal fluctuations accumulate, thereby generating fluctuations in the energy flux. Given that the inflationary duration is $(\epsilon_H H)^{-1}$, with $\epsilon_H$ representing the slow-roll parameter that quantifies the expansion rate of the Hubble radius, both the energy flux and its associated fluctuations diverge as $G \to 0$. By incorporating both the fluctuations in energy flux and the observer's energy, we propose that inflationary quasi-dS space is characterized by a Type II$_\infty$ algebra. Unlike the Type II$_1$ description of perfect dS space, where entropy is capped at a maximum due to maximal entanglement, our framework yields unbounded entropy. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these findings align with the interpretation of von Neumann entropy for the relevant density matrix as the generalized entropy, accounting for the aforementioned fluctuations.

This study introduces Attentive PixelHop (A-PixelHop), a new approach for identifying images generated by Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). The method offers three key benefits: minimal computational cost and compact model size, superior detection accuracy across various generative models, and mathematical transparency. A-PixelHop operates on the premise that synthesizing high-quality, high-frequency details in local areas is challenging. Its architecture comprises four modules: 1) isolating edge and texture blocks with prominent high-frequency content, 2) utilizing multiple filter banks to generate rich spatial-spectral features, 3) inputting these features into several binary classifiers to produce soft predictions, and 4) implementing an ensemble strategy to combine these predictions into a final decision. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that A-PixelHop surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques in detecting CycleGAN-generated images and exhibits strong generalization to unseen generative models and datasets.

Differential privacy has emerged as the practical standard for releasing data while maintaining privacy. Developing a differentially private algorithm typically begins with a noise-free base algorithm, requiring the designer to determine where to inject noise and the appropriate magnitude. This task is complex; improper implementation can lead to violations of differential privacy or result in poor utility.

This paper introduces DPGen, a program synthesizer that accepts non-private code and automatically generates its differentially private counterpart with precisely calibrated noise. Internally, DPGen employs novel algorithms to create a sketch program containing candidate noise locations, then simultaneously optimizes the privacy proof and noise scales. Additionally, DPGen can synthesize sophisticated adaptive mechanisms that process queries until a defined privacy budget is depleted. When tested against standard benchmarks, DPGen successfully generates differentially private mechanisms optimized for simple utility functions within 120 seconds, demonstrating sufficient power to also synthesize adaptive privacy mechanisms.

Training 3D convolutional neural networks presents challenges due to their high parameter count and extensive data requirements. To address these issues, we introduce a straightforward approach for efficiently learning 3D convolutional kernels that necessitates less training data. This is accomplished by factorizing the 3D kernel along the temporal axis, which reduces the total number of parameters and enhances training efficiency. Furthermore, we present a new dataset, Video-MNIST, to evaluate our method's performance. Our approach significantly surpasses traditional 3D convolution when data is scarce (1 to 5 videos per class). Moreover, in scenarios with abundant data (>10 videos per class), our model delivers competitive results while utilizing up to 45% fewer parameters.

This theoretical study investigates Weiss oscillations within the magnetoconductivity of bilayer graphene. We examine a bilayer graphene system subjected to a perpendicular magnetic field and a weak, unidirectional electric modulation, specifically calculating the $\sigma_{yy}$ component of the magnetoconductivity tensor, which displays these oscillations. Our findings indicate that Weiss oscillations in bilayer graphene are more robust against temperature variations than those in conventional two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) systems, yet less robust than those in monolayer graphene. Furthermore, we observe phase differences of $\pi$ and $2\pi$ in the oscillations relative to both monolayer graphene and standard 2DEG systems, a phenomenon attributed to the chiral nature of graphene's quasiparticles.

We introduce an optimal low-resolution precoding strategy designed to minimize symbol error probability. In contrast to existing methods that depend on QPSK modulation, our approach derives the minimum symbol error probability objective function to accommodate any PSK modulation order. Furthermore, we resolve the associated discrete optimization problem optimally using an advanced branch-and-bound algorithm, while also presenting greedy search-based methods for practical implementation. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the proposed minimum symbol error probability criterion outperforms established MMDDT and MMSE approaches regarding symbol error rate.

This paper introduces an algorithm designed to correct optical light curves generated by the Zwicky Transient Facility Forced Photometry Service. We apply this method to study the optical variability of 136 active galactic nuclei (AGN) powered by "light-weight" supermassive black holes ($M_{BH}$ < 2×10^6 $\odot$), a sample that includes 24 intermediate-mass black holes (IMBH; $M_{BH}$ < 2×10^5 $\odot$). Variability was detected in almost all sources, and for 101 objects, we examined its relationship with X-ray luminosity. Additionally, we identified a previously unknown candidate tidal disruption event (TDE) in SDSS~J112637.74+513423.0.

We evaluate the typical behavior of diverse arithmetic functions at the values of degree d polynomials f, ordered by height, with probability 1. This approach enables us to derive averaged formulations of the Bateman-Horn conjecture and the polynomial Chowla conjecture, while also tackling a fundamental question regarding the integral Hasse principle for norm form equations. Furthermore, we can determine the error term in the asymptotic behavior and the magnitude of the exceptional set for f, both achieving arbitrary logarithmic power savings.

The paper demonstrates that the mechanism for reducing top squark contributions to the Higgs mass, previously detailed in "Supersoft Top Squarks" (Phys. Rev. Lett. 125, no.15, 151801 (2020)), closely mirrors the approach outlined by the author in "Loop Suppressed Electroweak Symmetry Breaking" (Phys. Rev. D 95, no.1, 015002 (2017)), yielding identical results at leading order. Additionally, the study explores more general configurations of Yukawa and soft mass squared matrices that achieve the same outcome.

Segmenting pulmonary airways, arteries, and veins using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) presents significant challenges due to sparse supervision arising from the severe imbalance between tubular structures and the background. We introduce a CNN-based approach designed for precise segmentation of airways and arteries/veins in non-contrast computed tomography scans. This method demonstrates superior sensitivity to delicate peripheral structures, including bronchioles, arterioles, and venules. First, a feature recalibration module optimizes the utilization of features learned by the network by integrating spatial information to maintain the relative priority of activated regions, thereby enhancing subsequent channel-wise recalibration. Next, an attention distillation module strengthens the representation of tubular objects by recursively propagating fine-grained details from high-resolution attention maps in one layer to the previous one, enriching the context. Additionally, we incorporate a lung context map and a distance transform map as anatomical priors to improve the model's ability to differentiate between arteries and veins. Extensive experiments show that these components yield substantial performance improvements. Compared to state-of-the-art methods, our approach extracts significantly more vascular branches while maintaining competitive overall segmentation accuracy. The code and models are accessible at http://www.pami.sjtu.edu.cn/News/56.

This study applies a nonconforming rotated bilinear tetrahedral element to the Stokes problem in $\mathbb{R}^3$. We demonstrate that this element remains stable when paired with a piecewise linear, continuous pressure approximation. The resulting approximation resembles the well-known continuous $P^2-P^1$ Taylor-Hood element but requires fewer degrees of freedom. As a stable non-conforming low-order element that satisfies Korn's inequality, it ensures stability even when the Stokes equations are expressed in stress form, which is particularly useful for free surface flow applications.

This paper introduces a robust secrecy transmission scheme for communication systems aided by intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRS). Unlike prior studies that assume a fixed IRS location, we treat the IRS position as a variable to maximize the secrecy rate (SR) while satisfying an outage probability constraint. This is achieved by jointly optimizing the IRS location, transmit beamformer, and IRS phase shifts, even under imperfect channel state information (CSI) regarding the eavesdropper (Eve). We analyze two scenarios: a) where Eve's location is known, and b) where only a suspicious area for Eve is available. We identify a key insight that CSI models differ before and after IRS deployment, allowing the optimization problem to be decomposed and solved using a two-stage framework. In scenario a), the first stage derives universal upper bounds on outage probabilities dependent solely on the IRS location, which are optimized via successive convex approximation (SCA). The second stage employs an alternating optimization (AO) algorithm to iteratively refine the beamformer and phase shifts. For scenario b), we propose a Max-Min SR scheme within the same two-stage framework, optimizing the IRS location based on Eve's worst-case position. Simulation results demonstrate the critical importance of optimizing the IRS location.

Dynamical systems, defined as devices that accept time-varying inputs, evolve their internal state, and generate outputs, can be interconnected to create more intricate architectures. Earlier research demonstrated that collections of such machines could dynamically reconfigure their wiring based on their collective state, a concept termed "mode dependence." Although this framework was compositional—organizing re-wiring diagrams into an operad and mode-dependent systems into an associated algebra—its formulation felt more artificial than natural. In this paper, we demonstrate that the theory of mode-dependent dynamical systems can be more naturally reformulated within the category Poly of polynomial functors. This category possesses an exceptionally rich structure, featuring four interacting monoidal structures $(+,\times,\otimes,\circ)$, two of which ($\times,\otimes$) are monoidal closed, and whose comonoids for $\circ$ correspond exactly to standard categories. We examine how these diverse structures manifest within dynamical systems theory. Furthermore, we establish that the conventional coalgebraic formalism for dynamical systems operates within Poly, revealing that coalgebras represent a specific subclass of dynamical systems—those that do not retain historical records—which are formally analogous to how contractible groupoids relate to categories.

Let $p$ and $q$ be distinct prime numbers, and let $\ell$ be an odd prime. Consider a quadratic number field $F$. Let $K$ be an extension of $F$ where either $K$ forms a dihedral extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ with degree $\ell$ over $F$, or $K$ is an abelian $\ell$-extension unramified over $F$, provided that $\ell$ divides the class number of $F$. This paper provides a complete characterization of the division quaternion algebras $H_{K}(p, q)$ defined over $K$.

We investigate online inductive transfer learning, moving feature representations from a radial basis function network utilizing Gaussian mixture model hidden units to a direct, recurrent reinforcement learning agent. This agent was deployed in a trading experiment involving major spot currency pairs, with transaction and funding costs accurately factored in. Through a quadratic utility function, the agent learns to directly target positions while accounting for profit and loss sources, including currency market price trends. We advance previous research by addressing risk position targeting within an online transfer learning framework. Despite being forced to execute trades at 5 pm EST—the time when trading costs are statistically highest—our agent achieved a compound return of 9.3% and an annualized portfolio information ratio of 0.52 over a seven-year test period, all net of execution and funding costs.

Although recent investigations into spin-orbit torque-induced magnetization dynamics suggest a weak correlation between the critical switching current and the damping constant of a ferromagnetic free layer, this study demonstrates that the damping constant is nonetheless pivotal for such switching. Specifically, an undesirable phenomenon known as back switching—where the magnetization reverts to its initial state in a ferromagnet with an easy axis aligned with the current direction—is significantly mitigated by a large damping constant, as confirmed by both numerical and theoretical analyses.

In this brief note, we establish the cyclotomic expansion formula for the colored HOMFLY-PT invariant of double twist knots, thereby verifying the $SU(N)$-invariant cyclotomic expansion conjecture introduced in \cite{CLZ}.

In recent years, the integration of Deep Learning and Computer Vision has gained significant traction within the Cultural Heritage sector, driving applications such as interactive museums, augmented reality experiences, and smart audio guides. These technologies depend heavily on extensive datasets to function effectively and provide value to users. However, in the realm of art, gathering this data—specifically collecting artwork images and expert-annotated description sheets for tasks like Visual Question Answering—is a costly and time-intensive endeavor. This paper introduces a novel approach to Visual Question Answering that dynamically generates description sheets at runtime, capable of addressing both visual and contextual inquiries about artworks without requiring image collection or manual annotation. To achieve this, we explore the application of GPT-3 for creating artwork descriptions, assessing their quality using captioning metrics. Finally, we evaluate the system's performance on both captioning and Visual Question Answering tasks.

Black-box models typically rely on large multivariate functions, often constructed using generic basis expansions like polynomials, with parameters tuned to fit the data. This pragmatic approach is frequently necessary given the opaque nature of black-box problems. Once a suitable function is identified, however, there is no requirement to remain bound to the initial basis. Decoupling techniques address this by transforming multivariate functions into an alternative basis, which simultaneously reduces parameter count and uncovers underlying structures. This work introduces a filtered canonical polyadic decomposition (CPD), a non-parametric method capable of recovering decoupled functions even in scenarios involving non-unique decompositions. Overcoming this challenge enables a wide range of modeling applications.

Unbiased Learning to Rank (ULTR), which aims to rank documents using biased user feedback, remains a significant challenge in information retrieval. Current ULTR approaches predominantly depend on click modeling or Inverse Propensity Weighting (IPW). However, search engines often encounter severe long-tail query distributions, where both click modeling and IPW struggle to perform effectively. Click modeling is hindered by data sparsity, as query-document pairs in tail queries appear infrequently, while IPW suffers from high variance due to its sensitivity to low propensity scores. Consequently, there is an urgent need for a general debiasing framework capable of handling tail queries. To address this, we introduce a model-based unbiased learning-to-rank framework. Specifically, we design a general context-aware user simulator to generate pseudo clicks for unobserved ranked lists, thereby mitigating data sparsity. Furthermore, to account for the discrepancy between pseudo and actual clicks, we treat the observation of a ranked list as a treatment variable and integrate IPW with pseudo labels in a doubly robust manner. Theoretical analysis of the resulting bias and variance demonstrates that our proposed model-based approach is more robust than existing methods. Finally, extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, comprising both simulated data and real click logs, show that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art techniques across various scenarios.

This work introduces a Chandra investigation into surface brightness fluctuations within the diffuse intracluster medium of the Perseus Cluster. Leveraging deep archival imaging of the cluster core alongside a novel mosaic composed of 29 short (5 ks) exposures extending in eight directions out to approximately $2.2r_{2500}$, we analyze the data. Assuming log-normal density distributions at specific radii, the width of these distributions allows us to derive two key parameters: the density bias (defined as the square root of the clumping factor, $C$) and the one-dimensional turbulent velocity ($v_{k, 1D}$). Our analysis forward-models all surface brightness contributions, accounting for both astrophysical and particle backgrounds, while addressing the Poisson statistics of the signal. By measuring fluctuations across $1 \text{ arcmin}^2$ regions from $0.3$ to $2.2 r_{2500}$ ($7.8$–$57.3$ arcmin), we identify a small to moderate average density bias of roughly 3% at radii smaller than $1.6r_{2500}$. Furthermore, we infer an average one-dimensional turbulent velocity of $v_{1D} < 400 \text{ km s}^{-1}$ in this region. Future confirmation of these velocity inferences using X-ray calorimeter spectrometers on the XRISM and Athena observatories is expected to be feasible.

This paper introduces a computational algorithm to determine a global solution for the maximum rank correlation estimator via a mixed integer programming (MIP) framework. By converting all indicator functions into binary parameters to be estimated, we formulate a new constrained optimization problem and demonstrate its equivalence to the original formulation. Furthermore, we apply this method to best subset rank prediction, reformulating the initial optimization task as an MIP. We also establish a non-asymptotic bound for the tail probability of the predictive performance metric. Finally, the efficacy of the proposed MIP algorithm is evaluated through an empirical case study and Monte Carlo simulations.

Controlling the behavior of artificial neural networks, particularly generative language models, is widely recognized as a significant challenge. We reframe the task of steering natural language generation as learning to interface with a pretrained model, drawing a parallel to how Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) manage program behavior by adjusting hyperparameters. Within this new framework, a dedicated neural network—termed a Neural Programming Interface (NPI)—learns to manipulate the hidden activations of a pretrained model to generate specific outputs. Crucially, this approach requires no permanent modifications to the original model's weights, enabling the repurposing of pretrained models for new tasks without altering their core characteristics. Furthermore, we introduce a novel data construction algorithm and a GAN-inspired loss function designed to train NPI models to regulate outputs in autoregressive transformers. Experimental results comparing our methods against other state-of-the-art techniques, utilizing OpenAI's GPT-2, demonstrate their effectiveness. These experiments show successful control over elements such as noun selection, topic avoidance, and offensive speech filtering, all while largely preserving the model's fluency under deterministic conditions.

For the past thirty years, the cosmological constant, $\Lambda$, has served as a fundamental component of the standard $\Lambda$CDM concordance model. Despite inherent theoretical issues, this framework effectively describes general cosmological observations. However, a significant theoretical advancement and refinement in phenomenological modeling emerge when recognizing that vacuum energy density, $\rho_{\textrm{vac}}$, behaves as a "running quantity" within quantum field theory in curved spacetime. Research indicates that this approach can rival the $\Lambda$CDM model with a fixed $\Lambda$ term. Known as "running vacuum models" (RVM), these theories define $\rho_{\textrm{vac}}$ as an evolving function composed of even powers of the Hubble parameter and its derivatives, a structure previously motivated by renormalization group arguments. This review examines a recent detailed calculation by the authors regarding the renormalized energy-momentum tensor of a non-minimally coupled scalar field, utilizing adiabatic regularization. The outcome is significant: $\rho_{\textrm{vac}}(H)$ adopts the exact RVM structure, consisting of a constant term and a dynamical component proportional to $H^2$ (potentially observable today), alongside higher-order terms of order $\mathcal{O}(H^4)$ relevant to the early universe. Notably, this renormalized form of $\rho_{\textrm{vac}}$ avoids the problematic terms proportional to $m^4$—the quartic mass powers of fields that typically generate excessively large vacuum energy contributions and necessitate fine-tuning to address the cosmological constant problem.

Multiple manufacturers have begun commercializing near-bank Processing-In-Memory (PIM) architectures. By positioning simple cores adjacent to DRAM banks, these architectures significantly enhance performance and energy efficiency in parallel workloads by mitigating data access overhead. Real-world PIM systems offer substantial parallelism, high aggregate memory bandwidth, and reduced memory access latency, making them ideal for accelerating memory-bound Sparse Matrix Vector Multiplication (SpMV), a widely used kernel. This paper delivers the first comprehensive analysis of SpMV execution on a real PIM architecture and introduces SparseP, the inaugural SpMV library designed for such systems. Our contributions are threefold: first, we implement diverse software strategies for SpMV on multithreaded PIM cores to characterize their computational boundaries; second, we develop load balancing schemes across multiple PIM cores and two data partitioning approaches for execution on thousands of cores: (1) 1D-partitioned kernels that rely exclusively on PIM cores for the full SpMV computation, and (2) 2D-partitioned kernels that optimize the trade-off between computation and data transfer to PIM-enabled memory; third, we benchmark SpMV execution on a real PIM system featuring 2,528 cores against leading CPU and GPU systems to evaluate performance and energy efficiency. The SparseP package includes 25 SpMV kernels tailored for real PIM systems, supporting four dominant compressed matrix formats and various data types. Our extensive evaluation offers new insights and recommendations for both software designers and hardware architects to effectively accelerate SpMV on real PIM architectures.

Version space algebras offer a method for representing program spaces that can be manipulated via union, intersection, and cross-product (or "join") operations. When reified as Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs) containing explicit union and join nodes, these algebras can compactly encode exponentially large sets of programs, making them the dominant technique in enumerative program synthesis since FlashFill's introduction in 2010. We introduce a constructive, linear-time, semantics-preserving embedding of version space algebras into nondeterministic finite tree automata, demonstrating that the former are merely a subset of the latter. Coupled with recent findings establishing a correspondence between e-graphs and minimal deterministic tree automata, this indicates that tree automata strictly generalize all current major approaches to efficiently represent extensive program spaces through sharing.

A digital holographic microscopy system utilizing a lateral shear interferometer has been developed to quantitatively analyze the morphological dynamics of human red blood cells. This setup integrates a conventional microscope with a lateral shear interferometer and a CMOS sensor, creating a lateral-shearing digital holographic microscope capable of recording image-plane holograms. These holograms can be numerically reconstructed to estimate the sample's 3D profile, providing depth information alongside bright-field imaging. To resolve the issue of duplicate images, object information is filtered from one beam without compromising fringe contrast; this is achieved by increasing the reflectivity of the shear plate's back surface, which ultimately enhances the system's resolution.

Transfer learning seeks to boost performance in data-limited target domains by utilizing models pretrained on data-abundant source domains. A budget-friendly approach known as linear probing freezes the pretrained source model and trains a new classification head for the target task; however, this method is surpassed by the more expensive yet state-of-the-art technique of fine-tuning all parameters. Fine-tuning likely excels because it allows the model to utilize informative signals from intermediate layers that linear probing discards. We hypothesize that these intermediate layers can be directly leveraged and introduce Head-to-Toe probing (Head2Toe), a method that selects features from every layer of the source model to train a target-domain classifier. Evaluations on VTAB-1k show that Head2Toe matches fine-tuning's average performance while cutting training and storage costs by over a hundred times. Crucially, for out-of-distribution transfer scenarios, Head2Toe actually outperforms fine-tuning.

Self-testing certifies devices based on Bell test outcomes. While noise-tolerant self-testing examples exist, efficiently certifying a device's average quality with finite experimental data remains unclear without assuming identical behavior across runs. Consequently, prior results with finite statistics only guarantee correct operation for a single trial, restricting their practical use. We present a method that certifies a device produces states averaging close to a Bell state, independent of the specific state at each run, thereby removing the need for the independent and identically distributed (I.I.D.) assumption. Applying this analysis to data from a recent loophole-free Bell experiment, we demonstrate the successful distribution of Bell states over 398 meters, achieving an average fidelity of at least 55.50% with 99% confidence. Since this certification relies on a Bell test free from detection and locality loopholes, it is inherently device-independent, requiring no trust in or knowledge of the devices. This ensures the link can be integrated into a quantum network for long-distance quantum communications with security guarantees independent of specific implementation details.

This paper investigates linear codes $C_D$ over the non-chain ring $\mathcal{R} = \mathbb{Z}_2[u]/\langle u^3 - u\rangle$, where $m$ is a natural number and $L, M, N$ are subsets of $[m] = \{1, 2, \dots, m\}$. For any $X \subseteq [m]$, the set $\Delta_X$ is defined as $\{v \in \mathbb{Z}_2^m : \text{Supp}(v)\subseteq X\}$. The defining set $D$ is constructed as $(1+u^2)D_1 + u^2\big(D_2 + (u+u^2)D_3\big)$, a subset of $\mathcal{R}^m$, with $D_1, D_2, D_3$ chosen from the pairs $\{\Delta_L, \Delta_L^c\}$, $\{\Delta_M, \Delta_M^c\}$, and $\{\Delta_N, \Delta_N^c\}$ respectively. The study analyzes the Lee weight distribution of $C_D = \{\big(v\cdot d\big)_{d\in D} : v \in \mathcal{R}^m\}$. Furthermore, utilizing the Gray map $\Phi: \mathcal{R} \longrightarrow \mathbb{Z}_2^3$ defined by $\Phi(a+ub+u^2d) = (a+b, b+d, d)$, we derive the corresponding binary linear code $\Phi(C_D)$. We establish sufficient conditions for the minimality of these binary codes; notably, these conditions are quite mild, such as requiring $|L|, |M|, |N| < m-2$. Additionally, if $L$, $M$, and $N$ are all nonempty, the resulting binary codes are self-orthogonal.

Despite extensive research on backdoor attacks and their detection, critical questions remain unanswered regarding the boundaries of adversarial attack capabilities and defender detection capabilities. We posit that addressing these issues requires a deep comprehension of the relationship between the primary task intended for a benign model and the backdoor task executed by a compromised model. To achieve this, we utilize similarity metrics from multi-task learning to formally define "backdoor distance"—a measure of similarity between these two tasks. Our analysis of current stealthy backdoor attacks reveals that most fail to effectively minimize this distance, and even those that succeed leave significant room for enhancing stealthiness. Consequently, we introduce TSA, a novel method designed to automatically generate backdoor models within a specified distance constraint. We demonstrate that TSA outperforms existing attacks, advancing our understanding of attacker limitations. Most significantly, we provide both theoretical insights and experimental evidence across various datasets confirming a positive correlation between backdoor distance and detectability. This validates our task similarity analysis as a crucial tool for understanding backdoor risks and identifying more effective mitigation strategies.

Community detection within social media has garnered significant attention over the years. However, current approaches fail to identify the relationships between these communities, which can form alliances or exhibit antagonism due to shared or conflicting goals and values. Revealing such inter-community dynamics offers deeper insights into community structures and the broader social media landscape. Drawing from social science research, which suggests that attitudes between members of different groups are heavily influenced by their community affiliations, we hypothesize that user-expressed inter-community attitudes on social media can serve as indicators of these underlying relations. We first validate this hypothesis within the social media context. Subsequently, inspired by this finding, we propose a framework that simultaneously models user attitudes and social interactions to detect both communities and their relational ties. Experimental results across three real-world social media datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach.

Let $L_{q,\mu}$, where $1\le q<\infty$ and $\mu\ge0$, represent the weighted $L_q$ space defined by the classical Jacobi weight $w_\mu$ on the unit ball $\Bbb B^d$. This study examines the weighted least $\ell_q$ approximation problem relative to a given $L_{q,\mu}$-Marcinkiewicz-Zygmund family on $\Bbb B^d$. We derive weighted least $\ell_q$ approximation errors for the weighted Sobolev space $W_{q,\mu}^r$ with $r>(d+2\mu)/q$, demonstrating that these errors are order optimal. Additionally, we analyze the least squares quadrature generated by an $L_{2,\mu}$-Marcinkiewicz-Zygmund family and establish quadrature errors for $W_{2,\mu}^r$ where $r>(d+2\mu)/2$, which are likewise order optimal. Finally, we present the corresponding weighted least $\ell_q$ approximation theorem and least squares quadrature errors for the sphere.

Non-radiative losses significantly constrain the open-circuit voltage and, consequently, the power conversion efficiency of organic photovoltaic devices. The primary non-radiative loss originates within the active layer and is derived from the quasi-Fermi level splitting (QFLS) relative to the radiative thermodynamic limit of photovoltage. However, measuring QFLS in thin-film devices with low mobility is difficult because of the excitonic nature of photoexcitation and extra non-radiative losses tied to device architecture. This study presents an experimental technique utilizing electro-modulated photoluminescence to directly quantify intrinsic non-radiative voltage losses and determine the QFLS. Drift-diffusion simulations confirm that this approach accurately predicts bulk QFLS irrespective of device-specific non-radiative losses. Using state-of-the-art PM6:Y6-based organic solar cells as a test case, the method quantifies QFLS and demonstrates its independence from device architecture. Ultimately, this work offers a protocol for quantifying QFLS under operational conditions, fully dissecting the various non-radiative loss contributions. Beyond characterizing organic solar cells, this method is applicable to other platforms, including light-emitting diodes and photodetectors.

Blockchain and Internet of Things (IoT) technologies are driving the agricultural sector into its fourth revolution by significantly enhancing food safety, efficiency, and traceability throughout the supply chain. Despite these benefits, widespread adoption faces hurdles, primarily a workforce lacking the skills to utilize these tools effectively and an insufficient infrastructure for their training. This paper examines these adoption barriers within the agricultural supply chain and analyzes the transformative impact of Blockchain and IoT, offering strategies for greater adaptability by governments and corporations. By reducing imports and bolstering demand for local produce, developing nations can foster sustainable, localized agricultural ecosystems. Additionally, collaborative public and private research and development efforts are vital for expanding global technological knowledge and refining food supply chain operations. Ultimately, both governmental and corporate entities play a pivotal role in accelerating the integration of advanced technologies and improving the overall food supply chain.

The Sun could generate abundant hypothetical light particles, including axions and dark photons, a possibility that helioscopes are designed to detect. This study examines how the angular and spectral distribution of solar dark photons influences the sensitivity of these instruments. For the first time, we assess the spectral and angular dependence of the dark photon flux across the entire mass range and apply these findings to existing data from the Hinode Solar X-Ray Telescope. Specifically, we utilize calibration images for standard helioscope analysis and data from a solar eclipse, which offers sensitivity to very large oscillation lengths. We demonstrate that leveraging specific signal features can enhance constraints on the mixing parameter by more than an order of magnitude compared to a simple counting experiment.

This study investigates acoustic pulse and wave train shocks within general one-dimensional flows, focusing on their application to super-Eddington outbursts in massive stars. By employing approximate adiabatic invariants, we extend the classical equal-area method into both integral and differential formats. We forecast shock evolution for initially sinusoidal yet finite wave trains, deriving distinct solutions for internal shocks and head or tail shocks, which align closely with numerical simulations. Our internal shock findings suggest refined expressions for shock heating rates, while our analysis of head and tail shocks reveals that they conserve significantly more wave energy at large radii, enhancing their capacity for direct matter ejection; this contrast underscores the critical role of waveform in shock dynamics. Furthermore, our weak-shock analysis determines the conditions under which shocks intensify, providing a framework to study this transition. We apply these insights to estimate mass ejection resulting from sudden sound pulses and weak central explosions.

This study presents the development of the inaugural low-threshold cryogenic detector utilizing diamond as an absorber for astroparticle physics. We evaluated two 0.175$\,$g CVD diamond samples, each equipped with a W-TES, which exhibited transitions at approximately 25 mK. We detail the performance of these diamond-based detectors, focusing on the superior sensor that achieved an energy threshold of just 16.8 eV. This encouraging outcome establishes a foundation for employing diamond in various applications demanding low thresholds and high energy resolution, such as light dark matter searches and BSM physics involving coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering.

Cooperative effects characterize atomic ensembles that exchange photonic excitations, such as through dipole-dipole interactions. A specific instance of this phenomenon is superradiance, which occurs when this exchange causes constructive interference during spontaneous emission. In this work, we present an integrated approach for investigating cooperative radiation within many-body systems. This technique, capable of analyzing extended systems with an arbitrary number of particles, is defined by an effective, nonlinear two-atom master equation. This equation utilizes a closed-form expression that treats single-body and many-body dynamics equally. We apply this framework to a homogeneous gas of initially inverted two-level atoms, demonstrating the emergence of both superradiance and subradiance and identifying a many-body coherence term as the origin of these cooperative behaviors. Furthermore, we characterize many-body induced broadening—analytically determined to scale with the system's optical depth—and light shifts, distinguishing between spontaneous and induced effects. Additionally, we provide theoretical predictions regarding the time evolution of subradiance and the phase shift of the radiated field during cooperative decay.

Although manipulating the spin polarization of electron beams with light is highly desirable, it remains extremely difficult because prior methods relying on free-space light typically demand prohibitively high laser intensities. This study proposes utilizing an electric-field-polarized optical near field extended over nanostructures to efficiently trigger spin flips in a neighboring electron beam, leveraging strong inelastic electron scattering within phase-matched optical near fields. Our calculations demonstrate that a significantly lower laser intensity ($\sim 10^{12}\,$W/cm$^2$) combined with a short interaction length ($16\,\mu$m) yields an electron spin-flip probability of roughly $12\%$. Notably, the parallel and antiparallel spin components of an unpolarized incident electron beam are spin-flipped and inelastically scattered into distinct energy states, effectively creating an analog of the Stern–Gerlach experiment within the energy domain. These results hold significant importance for the optical manipulation of free-electron spins, the generation of spin-polarized electron beams, and applications ranging from material science to high-energy physics.

This brief paper extends a finding by Diamond and Sasaki regarding the equivalence between the geometric modularity of algebraic and non-algebraic weights. Specifically, we demonstrate that if non-algebraic weights are geometrically modular, then multiple algebraic weights are as well, a result that is straightforward. More notably, we establish that under certain conditions, the geometric modularity of several algebraic weights entails the geometric modularity of a non-algebraic weight. This finding bridges the work of Diamond and Sasaki with previous research on generalizing the weight component of Serre's conjecture.

This paper investigates the temporal robustness of temporal logic specifications and demonstrates methods for designing temporally robust control laws for time-critical control systems. This area is especially relevant for connected and interleaved processes, such as multi-robot and human-robot systems, where uncertainties in individual agent or human behavior can lead to timing variations. Although time-critical systems are significant, the temporal robustness of their logical specifications has remained underexplored, particularly regarding control design. We introduce concepts of synchronous and asynchronous temporal robustness, defining them as measures of robustness against synchronous and asynchronous time shifts within the predicates of temporal logic specifications. Furthermore, we establish that synchronous temporal robustness serves as an upper bound for asynchronous temporal robustness. The study then addresses the control design problem aimed at maximizing the temporal robustness of a dynamical system through a control law. Our proposed solution utilizes a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) formulation to generate sequences of optimal control inputs. Although asynchronous temporal robustness offers greater nuance, we demonstrate that designing control based on synchronous temporal robustness provides superior computational efficiency. This trade-off allows designers to select the appropriate approach depending on the specific application. Finally, the paper concludes with multiple case studies.

The engineering and manufacturing sectors are currently transitioning into a new era of digitized production. Various regions refer to these initiatives by different names, including "Industrie du futur" in France, "Industrial Internet" in the US, and "Industry 4.0" in Germany. Although the vision of digitizing production has gained significant momentum, the practical implementation using specific standards and technologies remains somewhat ambiguous. To address this within the German Industry 4.0 framework, the concept of an Administrative Shell was introduced. This concept aims to create a digital representation of all information associated with an object, whether it is a hardware system or a software platform. This paper outlines an approach to developing such a digital representation using semantic knowledge representation formalisms like RDF, RDF Schema, and OWL. We introduce the concept of a Semantic I4.0 Component, which leverages semantic technologies to tackle communication and comprehension challenges in Industry 4.0 scenarios. Finally, our approach is demonstrated through a concrete example that highlights its advantages in a real-world use case.

This research addresses the challenge of deploying multilingual automated reply suggestion (RS) models across numerous languages concurrently. Such models frequently struggle with limited capacity and significant data distribution imbalances among languages. Although previous studies have primarily concentrated on monolingual approaches, we introduce Conditional Generative Matching (CGM) models, which are optimized using a Variational Autoencoder framework to overcome these specific multilingual RS hurdles. CGM achieves this through expressive message-conditioned priors, mixture densities to improve multi-lingual data representation, latent alignment for language discrimination, and efficient variational optimization strategies for training. These advancements yield performance that surpasses competitive baselines by an average of over 10% in relevance (measured by ROUGE scores), with a 16% improvement specifically for low-resource languages. Furthermore, CGM demonstrates notable gains in diversity (80%), highlighting its strong capability to represent multi-lingual data.

The integration of machine learning into constraint optimization and combinatorial problem-solving has emerged as a vibrant field of inquiry within both computer science and operations research. This study focuses on leveraging advanced machine learning techniques to forecast high-quality solutions for constraint optimization tasks. Building upon \cite{abbasi2020predicting}, the paper extends previous efforts to predict solutions for large-scale stochastic optimization models by evaluating sophisticated algorithms and diverse costs linked to the predicted decision variables. Furthermore, it analyzes the critical role of loss functions and error criteria when applying machine learning models to optimization solution prediction. The blood transshipment problem serves as the empirical case study. Results indicate that LightGBM yields promising outcomes, surpassing other models employed by \cite{abbasi2020predicting}, particularly when the mean absolute deviation criterion is applied.

We build holographic superconductors at zero density, utilizing a model with the distinct advantage that the geometry dual to its ground state is known analytically. This geometry features an asymptotically AdS structure in the UV and a hyperscaling-violating form in the IR, offering fresh perspectives on supergravity solutions when classified by their IR behavior. We numerically generate finite-temperature hairy black hole solutions and confirm the phase transition by adjusting a double-trace deformation parameter. Furthermore, for an M-theory-based holographic superconductor, we derive an analytic expression for the AC conductivity, which clearly exhibits a superconducting delta function alongside a hard gap.

This paper investigates the correspondence theory of intuitionistic modal logic within the framework of modal Fairtlough-Mendler semantics (modal FM semantics), which serves as the intuitionistic analogue to possibility semantics \cite{Ho16}. We isolate the fragment of inductive formulas \cite{GorankoV06} within this language and adapt the $\mathsf{ALBA}$ algorithm \cite{CoPa12} to this specific semantic context. The study highlights two key contributions: first, in the expanded modal language, nominal variables—previously understood as atoms in perfect Boolean algebras, complete join-prime elements in perfect distributive lattices, and complete join-irreducible elements in perfect lattices—are reinterpreted here as the refined regular open closures of singletons, aligning with the approach in classical normal modal logic's possibility semantics \cite{Zh21d}. Second, by omitting conominals and diamond operators, we significantly constrain the scope of inductive formulas. We establish the soundness of $\mathsf{ALBA}$ regarding modal FM frames and demonstrate that the algorithm successfully processes inductive formulas, consistent with prior work in settings such as \cite{CoPa12,Zh21d,Zh22a}.

We examined the light curves of 1,376 nearby M dwarfs spanning early to late spectral types to detect white-light flares using All-Sky Automated Survey for Supernovae (ASAS-SN) photometry. A simple statistical method identifying sudden $V$-band flux increases revealed 480 candidate M dwarfs with potential flares. Following rigorous verification, we confirmed 62 individual flares occurring on 62 distinct stars, with amplitudes ranging from $0.12 <\Delta V < 2.04$ mag. Applying classical flare models, we established lower energy limits, finding $V$-band energies between $2.0\times10^{30}$ and $6.9\times10^{35}$ erg. The incidence of flaring stars rises with later spectral types, and the majority exhibit moderate to strong H$\alpha$ emission. Furthermore, 14 of these flaring stars are rotational variables; compared to non-flaring rotational variable M dwarfs, they display shorter rotation periods and more intense H$\alpha$ emission.

We investigate the mass spectra and wave functions for heavy pseudoscalar ($P$) and vector ($V$) mesons in both $1S$ and $2S$ states using the light-front quark model. Our analysis relies on two key empirical constraints: the experimental mass-gap relation $\Delta M_P > \Delta M_V$ (where $\Delta M_{P(V)}=M^{2S}_{P(V)}-M^{1S}_{P(V)}$) and the decay constant hierarchy $f_{1S}>f_{2S}$ for $1S$ versus $2S$ states. In our variational calculation of the Hamiltonian, which includes Coulomb and confining potentials, we enforce orthogonality between the trial wave functions of the $1S$ and $2S$ states. Furthermore, the hyperfine interaction is treated perturbatively for both heavy-heavy and heavy-light $P$ and $V$ mesons, consistent with heavy quark symmetry. Since satisfying the empirical constraints requires mixing between $1S$ and $2S$ states, we determine a lower bound for the mixing angle $\theta$ as $\theta_c = {\rm cot}^{-1}(2\sqrt{6})/2\simeq 6^{\circ}$ and identify an optimal mixing angle of approximately $12^\circ$ applicable to both charm and bottom flavors. The study reveals that mixing effects impact $2S$ state mesons more significantly than $1S$ state mesons. We compute various properties, including mass spectra, decay constants, twist-2 distribution amplitudes, and electromagnetic form factors, finding our results align well with existing data and lattice simulations. Notably, we predict a mass of $2600$ MeV for the $2S$ pseudoscalar $D_s$ meson, closely matching the recently discovered $D_{s0}(2590)^+$ meson by the LHCb Collaboration, thereby supporting the interpretation of this observed state as a radial excitation of the $D^+_s$ meson.

The attention mechanism has become highly popular because of its ability to deliver high accuracy across various domains. However, attention operates opportunistically and lacks justification based on content relevance or usability; consequently, Transformer-like structures generate all possible attention patterns. To address this, we introduce segregating strategies designed to prioritize content for specific applications, thereby enhancing performance. We propose two such strategies: the Self-Segregating Transformer (SST) and the Coordinated-Segregating Transformer (CST), applied to solve Visual Question Answering (VQA) tasks. The self-segregation strategy improves the understanding and filtering of information most relevant to answering questions, fostering greater diversity in visual reasoning. These approaches are easily adaptable to other applications involving repetitive tasks or multiple feature frames, significantly reducing attention redundancy. Since VQA demands the coordination of both visual and textual interpretations, our experiments show that applying segregation strategies to cascaded multi-head transformer attention outperforms many prior methods, achieving substantial improvements on the VQA-v2 benchmark.

This paper investigates leveraging Internet-scale image data and models to enable robot vision adaptation without additional labels. We introduce Self-supervised Embodied Active Learning (SEAL), a framework that employs perception models trained on web images to derive an active exploration policy. Observations collected by this policy are annotated via 3D consistency to refine the perception model. Furthermore, we construct and leverage 3D semantic maps to facilitate completely self-supervised learning of both action and perception. These maps generate an intrinsic motivation reward for the exploration policy and label agent observations through spatio-temporal 3D consistency and label propagation. We demonstrate that SEAL successfully closes the action-perception loop: it enhances object detection and instance segmentation performance of a pretrained model merely by navigating training environments, and this improved perception subsequently boosts Object Goal Navigation capabilities.

We establish the validity of Bogoliubov's approximation for translation-invariant Bose gases within the mean-field regime. Specifically, we demonstrate that the ground state energy $E_N$ satisfies $E_N=Ne_\mathrm{H}+\inf \sigma\left(\mathbb{H}\right)+o_{N\rightarrow \infty}(1)$, where $N$ denotes the particle count, $e_\mathrm{H}$ represents the lowest Hartree energy, and $\mathbb{H}$ refers to the Bogoliubov Hamiltonian. As a preliminary finding, we prove the existence of approximate ground states $\Psi_N$ such that $\langle H_N\rangle_{\Psi_N}=E_N+o_{N\rightarrow \infty}(1)$, which display full Bose--Einstein condensation relative to one of the Hartree minimizers.

Terahertz radiation enables the controlled excitation of vibrational modes within molecules and crystals. We demonstrate that the circular motion of ions generates inertial influences on electrons. Mirroring classical Coriolis and centrifugal forces, these phenomena include spin-rotation coupling, centrifugal field coupling, centrifugal spin-orbit coupling, and centrifugal redshift. The duration of these effects, which can persist for several picoseconds following excitation, depends on phonon decay rates. Enhancing these effects could establish a promising platform for manipulating localized quantum states or chemical reaction barriers through vibrational control.

This paper examines two distinct methods for defining the entropy of a quantum channel. The first approach utilizes the von Neumann entropy of the associated Choi-Jamio{\l}kowski state, whereas the second relies on the relative entropy between the output of the extended channel and that of the extended completely depolarizing channel, optimized across all possible input states. Our findings demonstrate that the former entropy serves as an upper bound for the latter. Furthermore, we establish that this bound is achieved for unital qubit channels. Finally, we propose a conjecture supported by numerical evidence suggesting that the bound may also be saturated for random channels as their dimension approaches infinity.

Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) are mathematical representations of Markov processes where the underlying state remains concealed yet allows for information leakage, typically modeled as 3-way joint-probability distributions. We employ HMMs to denote probabilistic sequential programs with hidden states by reformulating them as "abstract" HMMs within the Giry monad $\mathbb{D}$ and equipping them with a partial order reflecting increasing security. To encode the monadic type involving hidden state $\mathcal{X}$, we utilize $\mathbb{D}\mathcal{X}\to \mathbb{D}^2\mathcal{X}$ instead of the standard $\mathcal{X}{\to}\mathbb{D}\mathcal{X}$ used for non-hidden Markov models, a construction we demonstrate via a small Haskell prototype. Subsequently, we introduce uncertainty measures as a generalization of existing probabilistic entropy variants, highlighting their specific analytic properties and their interaction with the security order. Additionally, we provide a "backwards" uncertainty-transformer semantics for HMMs that is dual to the "forwards" abstract HMMs, mirroring the duality between relational and predicate-transformer semantics for imperative programs with demonic choice. Finally, we contend that this new denotational-semantic perspective reveals the Dalenius desideratum for statistical databases as a compositional issue, proposing a method to address it.

Cyber-physical systems (CPS) are widely utilized in safety-critical sectors, including automotive, avionics, and medical fields. Recently, Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become increasingly common for controlling these systems. However, public benchmarks for AI-enabled CPS remain scarce, and there is limited understanding of their performance and reliability across various industrial applications. To address this gap, we have initiated the creation of a public benchmark covering seven industry domains and developed AI controllers for them using state-of-the-art deep reinforcement learning (DRL) techniques. We then conducted a systematic evaluation of these AI-driven systems against traditional counterparts to identify current challenges and future opportunities. Our key findings reveal that (1) AI controllers do not consistently outperform traditional ones, (2) existing CPS testing methods, particularly falsification, are insufficient for analyzing AI-enabled CPS, and (3) hybrid systems that strategically combine and switch between AI and traditional controllers can achieve superior performance across domains. These results underscore the urgent need for new testing methodologies for AI-enabled CPS and further research into hybrid systems to optimize performance and reliability.

Deep Unfolding Networks (DUNs) have shown remarkable success in compressive sensing (CS) by mapping optimization algorithms into neural network architectures. While DUNs benefit from the well-defined, interpretable structure of iterative optimization steps, most current designs rely on traditional image-domain unfolding. This approach processes single-channel images between stages, leading to limited information transmission and unavoidable loss of image details. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a generalized dual-domain optimization framework applicable to inverse imaging problems. This framework combines the advantages of both image-domain and convolutional-coding-domain priors to restrict the feasible solution space. By unfolding this framework into deep neural networks, we developed a novel Dual-Domain Deep Convolutional Coding Network (D3C2-Net) for CS imaging. Unlike previous methods, D3C2-Net enables high-throughput feature-level image representation across all unfolded stages. Experimental results on natural and MRI images confirm that D3C2-Net outperforms state-of-the-art methods, delivering superior accuracy and a more favorable trade-off between performance and complexity.

A primary challenge for quantum-enabled technologies is environmental noise, which induces decoherence, erodes quantum properties, and generates errors during system operations. Although various mitigation strategies exist, many are tailored to specific environments and tasks, restricting their general utility. We introduce a protocol that renders arbitrary environments effectively noise-free by leveraging non-local superposition during evolution as a quantum resource. This approach ensures complete safeguarding of quantum information and entanglement against decoherence, facilitating flawless quantum communication over any noisy channel for finite-dimensional systems. Furthermore, we outline experimental methodologies to realize this protocol within linear optical and atomic platforms.

Dirac semimetals exhibit unique physical characteristics and can support exotic quantum phases, such as Weyl semimetals and topological insulators, under specific external conditions. In this study, we integrate angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) with first-principles calculations to demonstrate that the Zintl-phase compound SmMg$_2$Bi$_2$ resides in close proximity to a topological Dirac semimetallic state. ARPES data reveal a Dirac-like band crossing at the zone center near the Fermi level ($E_\mathrm{F}$), a finding corroborated by theoretical computations. Furthermore, these studies classify SmMg$_2$Bi$_2$ as a $Z_2$ topological material hosting spin-polarized states around $E_\mathrm{F}$. Although Zintl theory anticipates a Sm$^{2+}$ valence state, our detection of multiple Sm-4$f$ multiplet states (flat-bands) indicates the coexistence of both Sm$^{2+}$ and Sm$^{3+}$ ions based on their energy positions. Additionally, these flat-bands and other dispersive states exhibit strong hybridization upon crossing. The presence of Sm$^{3+}$ ions results in a Curie-Weiss-like contribution to the low-temperature magnetic susceptibility $\chi(T)$, complementing the Van Vleck-like behavior expected for Sm$^{2+}$ ions. This research contributes to a deeper understanding of the electronic structure, magnetism, and transport properties of related materials.

Current pretraining approaches are usually assessed by measuring linear classifier accuracy, transfer learning capabilities, or by visually examining lower-dimensional projections of the representation manifold (RM). In contrast, this study demonstrates that a deeper analysis of the RM itself offers a clearer understanding of methodological differences and enables a more granular comparison. To achieve this, we introduce a novel framework and metric designed to evaluate and compare various RMs. Furthermore, we analyze and report on the specific characteristics of RMs across different pretraining techniques. These characteristics are quantified by applying progressively larger local perturbations to input data—specifically through white noise injections and Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) adversarial attacks—while tracking the trajectory of each data point. We compute the total displacement for every point and the relative change in distance between consecutive perturbations. Our findings indicate that self-supervised methods produce RMs where perturbations result in large yet consistent displacement magnitudes, suggesting a smoother manifold compared to fully supervised methods. Finally, we integrate these observations into the Representation Manifold Quality Metric (RMQM), where higher scores reflect larger and more stable step sizes, demonstrating a positive correlation with downstream task performance.

This study investigates the conditions under which convex sets maintain disjointness following random projection.
