Utilizing concepts from high-dimensional convex geometry, we derive an analysis specifically for ellipsoids, offering a bound based on the separation distance between them and straightforward functions of their polynomial coefficients. Applying this theorem to compressive classification, we establish bounds for convex sets without requiring the data to be sparse; instead, our findings indicate that linear separability can be preserved even when acquired through a minimal number of measurements. We validate the practical viability of this methodology within hyperspectral imaging applications.

Large language models have excelled across numerous tasks, including code generation and question answering. Fundamentally, these models complete input sequences in statistically probable ways, allowing users to achieve various downstream goals through language instructions or few-shot examples. Advanced prompting techniques can even facilitate interactions between the model, the user, and external tools like calculators. However, achieving state-of-the-art results or adapting models for specific applications often necessitates complex, task-specific programming that may still involve ad-hoc interactions.

To address this, we introduce Language Model Programming (LMP), a novel approach that extends traditional text-based prompting by combining it with intuitive scripting. LMP further enables the specification of constraints on model outputs, offering high-level semantics while abstracting internal complexities for easy task adaptation. To operationalize LMP, we developed LMQL (Language Model Query Language), which utilizes control flow and constraints from prompts to generate efficient inference procedures that minimize costly calls to the underlying model. We demonstrate that LMQL can intuitively capture a broad spectrum of state-of-the-art prompting strategies, particularly excelling at implementing interactive flows that are difficult to manage with current high-level APIs. Our evaluation confirms that LMP maintains or improves accuracy on various downstream tasks while significantly reducing computational costs and API expenses, achieving savings of 13% to 85%.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) are a prominent approach in machine learning, yet their status as black-box models limits their ability to explain predictions. To address this, neural additive models (NAMs) have been introduced to combine interpretability with high predictive accuracy. This paper presents a new NAM framework designed for multivariate nowcasting (NC), a key area within machine learning. In NC tasks involving multivariate time-series data, it is crucial to provide explanations for each input value across distinct time steps. By utilizing generalized additive models, our proposed NAM-NC method effectively quantifies the importance of every input value for multiple variables and time points. Experiments on a toy dataset and two real-world datasets demonstrate that NAM-NC matches the prediction accuracy of state-of-the-art neural networks while offering interpretability for each input. Additionally, we investigated parameter-sharing networks using NAM-NC to reduce complexity and evaluated the hard-tied feature net of NAM-MC, which also yielded robust performance with clear explanations.

Current Click-Through Rate (CTR) prediction models primarily rely on behavior ID features derived from historical user-ad interactions. However, these features fail to effectively represent new ads that lack prior interaction history. To address this limitation, we leverage ad visual content to enhance CTR prediction performance. Our approach maps each ad into a set of visual IDs based on its imagery, which are then used to generate visual embeddings that augment the prediction model. We frame the learning of these visual IDs as a supervised quantization task. Given the absence of class labels for commercial images, we utilize image textual descriptions as supervision to optimize the image extractor for producing effective visual IDs. Furthermore, to enable end-to-end training, we replace non-differentiable hard quantization with a soft quantization operation. Once images are mapped to visual IDs, we learn embeddings for each ID using accumulated historical user-ad interactions. Because visual ID embeddings depend solely on visual content, they generalize well to new ads and complement existing behavior ID embeddings. Consequently, this integration significantly boosts CTR prediction performance for both new and well-known ads. When applied to Baidu's online advertising system, incorporating visual ID embeddings increased the average ad CTR by 1.46% and total charge by 1.10%.

Training novice excavator operators to master various skills typically demands the presence of expert instructors. However, due to the task's complexity, sourcing such skilled professionals is costly, time-intensive, and requires intense concentration. Additionally, human evaluators are prone to bias, resulting in noisy assessments and high variance in scores for operators with comparable abilities. This study tackles these challenges by introducing a novel method for the automated evaluation of excavator operators. Our approach incorporates the machine's internal dynamics and safety criteria at every time step to assess performance. To further validate this method, we employ the resulting score prediction model as a reward signal for a reinforcement learning agent tasked with maneuvering an excavator in a simulation that closely mirrors real-world physics. Our results indicate that policies trained using these external reward prediction models yield safer solutions that adhere strictly to dynamic constraints, outperforming those trained solely on task-based rewards and bringing practical application closer to reality. For future research, we have made our codebase available at https://github.com/pranavAL/InvRL_Auto-Evaluate and video demonstrations at https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jR1otOAu8zrY8mkhUOUZW9jkBOAKK71Z/view?usp=share_link.

Social concepts describing non-physical entities—such as revolution, violence, or friendship—serve as potent instruments for describing, indexing, and querying visual data, particularly within the expanding archives of art in the Cultural Heritage (CH) sector. Although computer vision has advanced significantly toward comprehensive image comprehension, automatically identifying the social concepts evoked by images remains a formidable challenge. This difficulty stems partly from the well-documented semantic gap, which is exacerbated for social concepts due to their absence of distinct physical attributes and their dependence on less specific features compared to concrete ones. This paper proposes translating recent cognitive theories regarding social concept representation into a software framework that models them as multimodal frames by incorporating multisensory data. Our approach centers on extracting, analyzing, and integrating multimodal features from visual art materials tagged with target concepts. We introduce a conceptual model and a novel ontology for formally representing social concepts as multimodal frames. Using the Tate Gallery's collection as an empirical foundation, we tested our method on a corpus of art images to demonstrate its potential as a proof of concept. Finally, we outline future research directions and make all software, data sources, and results publicly available.

We present a category of stochastic advection problems suitable for analyzing turbulent transport. The flow field's statistics are modeled as a continuous-time Markov process, reflecting the conceptual view of turbulence as transitions between distinct coherent structures. We derive closed-form expressions for the turbulent transport operator without relying on approximations. In the limit where the operator becomes local in both space and time, we recover the classical diffusivity tensor estimate, whose components correspond to the integrated auto-correlation of the velocity field.

This study examines the 3D spin orientations of galaxies relative to large-scale filaments using data from the MaNGA survey. The cosmic web structure is mapped using the Sloan Digital Sky Survey via the Disperse algorithm, while the 3D spins of MaNGA galaxies are derived from integral field spectroscopy kinematics under the thin disk approximation. Results indicate that late-type spiral galaxies exhibit spin axes parallel to the nearest filament. This alignment effect is primarily driven by low-mass spirals. In contrast, S0-type galaxies tend to align perpendicularly to the filament axes. This orthogonal preference is largely attributed to S0s with significant misalignment between stellar and ionized gas kinematic components, as well as low-mass S0s possessing lower rotational support than their high-mass equivalents. Similar trends emerge when categorizing galaxies by the degree of ordered stellar rotation: those with high spin magnitudes align with filaments, whereas those with low spin magnitudes orient perpendicularly. These findings, interpreted through conditional tidal torque theory, imply that galaxy spins retain a memory of their large-scale environment. Consistent with hydrodynamical cosmological simulations, the signal at low redshift is weak but statistically significant. Ultimately, the dependence of spin-filament orientation on stellar mass, morphology, and kinematics underscores the critical role of sample selection in detecting this alignment signal.

We introduce an integrated stellar mass-metallicity relation (MZR) derived from over 1,700 galaxies within the SDSS-IV MaNGA integral field survey. Utilizing spatially resolved data, we calculated metallicity at a consistent physical scale (the effective radius, $\mathrm{R_{eff}}$) employing a diverse collection of ten abundance calibrators. Beyond scale factors, the MZR shape remains consistent across all calibrators, aligning with prior findings from both single-fiber and integral field spectroscopy. We examined the residuals of this relation against star formation rate (SFR) and specific SFR (sSFR). Unlike earlier single-fiber studies, we detected no strong secondary dependence of the MZR on either SFR or sSFR for any calibrator. These findings support a model where metal enrichment occurs at local scales, with global outflows playing a minor role in galactic chemical evolution, while cold-gas inflows govern star formation.

Predicting outcomes at unobserved locations is a core challenge in spatial statistics. Due to the complexities of modeling spatial dependence, particularly in non-stationary scenarios, traditional model-based prediction intervals often suffer from misspecification bias, compromising their reliability. This paper introduces a novel, model-free nonparametric approach for spatial prediction utilizing conformal prediction methods. The central insight is that spatial data can often be considered exactly or approximately exchangeable across diverse settings. Specifically, under an infill asymptotic framework, we demonstrate that response values exhibit local approximate exchangeability for a wide variety of spatial processes. Based on this, we developed a local spatial conformal prediction algorithm that generates valid prediction intervals without relying on stringent model assumptions such as stationarity. Empirical results using both simulated and real datasets validate the proposed intervals and demonstrate their superior efficiency compared to existing model-based techniques, especially for large datasets involving non-Gaussian and non-stationary conditions.

Max-point-tolerance graphs (MPTG), introduced by Catanzaro et al. in 2017 as an extension of interval graphs, find significant utility in human genome analysis and network signal processing. This class was previously examined under the designation p-BOX(1) graphs by Soto and Caro in 2015. Our work focuses on a natural subclass known as proper max-point-tolerance graphs (proper MPTG), wherein vertex-associated intervals do not properly contain one another. We establish the first characterization theorem for this class by introducing a specific linear ordering of the vertex set. Furthermore, we demonstrate that proper MPTGs are asteroidal triple-free and perfect, and we show their equivalence to unit max-point-tolerance graphs. Additionally, we observe that both MPTG (and proper MPTG) and max-tolerance graphs (and their proper variants) are incomparable. Finally, we elucidate the relationships between proper MPTGs and other variations of MPTG and max-tolerance graphs.

We report the inaugural search for branon dark matter (DM) in the very high-energy gamma-ray regime, utilizing data from the dwarf spheroidal galaxy Segue~1 collected by the Major Atmospheric Gamma Imaging Cherenkov (MAGIC) telescope. Branons represent new degrees of freedom arising from brane fluctuations in flexible brane-world models and function as weakly interacting massive particles, making them viable DM candidates. Given the lack of a detected gamma-ray signal in the Segue~1 observations, we established constraints on the branon DM parameter space through a binned likelihood analysis. Our most stringent limit on the thermally-averaged annihilation cross-section, set at the $95\%$ confidence level, yields $\langle \sigma v \rangle \simeq 1.4 \times 10^{-23}~\text{cm}^{3}\text{s}^{-1}$ for a branon DM mass of approximately $0.7~\text{TeV}$.

Recent research highlights the critical impact of task distribution on meta-learner performance. While it is commonly believed that increasing task diversity enhances meta-learning outcomes, our study presents contrary evidence. First, our experiments challenge the effectiveness of learned models by demonstrating that similar manifolds can be acquired using subsets of data with lower task diversity, thereby questioning the benefit of supplying more data. Second, we show that increasing task diversity can sometimes impede model performance rather than yield the expected significant improvements. To substantiate these conclusions, we offer both empirical and theoretical support.

Determining the properties of a curve defined by $C_{f,g} = \{(x,y) \mid f(x) - g(y) = 0\}$ necessitates analyzing the genus 0 and 1 components of its projective normalization, $\tilde C_{f,g}$. In the case where $f$ and $g$ are polynomials and $f$ is indecomposable, [Fr73a] distinguished between components of $\tilde C_{f,g}$ where $u=1$ and those where $u>1$, addressing Schinzel's problem. While [Prop. 1, Fr73b] provided a direct genus formula for the $u=1$ case, determining the genus for $u>1$ previously required an ad hoc approach.

[Pak22] relaxed the indecomposable and polynomial constraints but assumed $\tilde C_{f,g}$ is irreducible ($u=1$). He demonstrated that for a fixed $f$, unless the Galois closure of the cover for $f$ has genus 0 or 1, the genus increases linearly with $\deg(g)$. Methods I and II extend [Prop. 1, Fr73b] by utilizing Nielsen classes to generalize Pakovich's formulation for the $u>1$ scenario. Method I operates on the covers of $f$ and $g$ mapping to the $z$-line ($P^1_z$) to compute the fiber product, whereas Method II relies on projecting to the $y$-line ($P^1_y$) through the explicit calculation of branch cycles for this cover.

Hurwitz families elucidate the importance of these components, expanding on [Prop. 2, Fr73a] to address Pakovich's problem. Without loss of generality, one begins with pairs $(f^*, g^*)$ sharing the same Galois closures but possessing entangled canonical representations, which generate multiple components on the fiber product. These component types, denoted as $W$, are then classified on $\tilde C_{f^*,g^*}$ using branch cycles derived via Method II. This yields a Nielsen class formulation that explicitly identifies which $g_1$ values must be avoided to ensure the component genuses of $\tilde C_{f^*,g^*og_1}$ grow as $\deg(g_1)$ increases. Notably, this approach leverages and extends Nielsen classes alongside the resolution of the genus 0 problem, which involves classifying the monodromy groups of indecomposable rational functions.

The rapid evolution of content generation technologies, commonly referred to as DeepFakes, combined with the widespread online spread of altered media, has made detecting these manipulations increasingly critical. Although numerous DeepFake detection methods exist, few address the influence of dataset preprocessing and the aggregation of frame-level predictions into video-level outputs on model efficacy. This paper introduces a preprocessing technique to enhance training data quality and investigates its impact on detection performance. Additionally, we propose and assess various video-level prediction aggregation strategies. Experimental findings demonstrate that the suggested preprocessing method significantly improves detection model performance, while the proposed aggregation scheme further enhances detection efficiency, particularly in videos containing multiple faces.

A novel, gauge-independent electromagnetic gyrokinetic framework has been established, where the equations governing gyrocenter motion and the associated phase-space transformation are formulated using perturbed electromagnetic fields rather than the conventional perturbed potentials. Gyrocenter polarization and magnetization are explicitly derived from the gyrocenter Hamiltonian up to the first order of the perturbation expansion. Additionally, expressions for the sources within Maxwell's equations have been developed in a format optimized for simulation studies and kinetic-gyrokinetic hybrid modeling.

In recent years, the prevalence and intricacy of political Twitter bots have grown, complicating the distinction between them and genuine human users. This study addresses the question of whether temporal activity patterns differ qualitatively between fake and human accounts. We gathered a substantial dataset of tweets from the post-2020 US election conflict and applied both supervised and unsupervised statistical learning methods to measure the predictive value of time-series features for human-bot classification. Our findings indicate no significant differences, implying that contemporary political bots are highly adept at emulating human behavior. Consequently, this underscores the necessity for developing new, more advanced bot-detection methodologies.
An invited research highlight article exploring searches for charged lepton flavor violation within the charmonium system.

This study presents a closed-form solution to the Schrödinger equation for the Bohr Hamiltonian under the minimal length framework. Drawing inspiration from Heisenberg algebra and the generalized uncertainty principle (GUP), this formalism is implemented within the geometric collective Bohr-Mottelson model (BMM) of nuclei using deformed canonical commutation relations and the Pauli-Podolsky prescription. The problem is addressed simultaneously through the asymptotic iteration method (AIM) and a quantum perturbation method (QPM), focusing on transitional nuclei near the critical point symmetry Z(4), which represents the phase transition between prolate and $\gamma$-rigid triaxial shapes. A scaled Davidson potential serves as the restoring potential to ensure a physical minimum. The theoretical outcomes show excellent agreement with experimental data.

Top quarks offer a unique high-energy environment for investigating fundamental quantum mechanics, as their measurable spin correlations allow the use of qubits at particle colliders. This work outlines the general framework for the quantum state of a top-antitop ($t\bar{t}$) pair generated via quantum chromodynamics (QCD) in high-energy collisions. We posit that the total probed quantum state in a collider is defined by the production spin density matrix, which inherently results in a mixed state. By calculating the quantum state of $t\bar{t}$ pairs arising from elementary QCD processes, we identify regions of phase space where entanglement and CHSH inequality violations occur. Furthermore, we demonstrate that realistic hadronic production of $t\bar{t}$ pairs constitutes a statistical mixture of these elementary processes. Focusing on proton-proton and proton-antiproton collisions at the LHC and Tevatron, respectively, we analyze how the quantum state varies with collision energy and provide experimental observables for detecting entanglement and CHSH violations. Specifically, at the LHC, entanglement is indicated by the violation of a Cauchy-Schwarz inequality through a single observable. We also extend the quantum tomography protocol for $t\bar{t}$ pairs to broader quantum states and production mechanisms found in the literature. Finally, we argue that observing CHSH violation in a collider represents only a weak form of Bell's theorem violation, as it inevitably involves several loopholes.

Measuring epicyclic frequencies is a prevalent astrophysical method for deducing properties of self-gravitating systems and their associated gravitational backgrounds. In this work, we derive the explicit formulas for these frequencies within static, spherically symmetric wormhole spacetimes. We examine the application of these theoretical findings to: (1) identify wormholes and differentiate them from black holes; (2) reconstruct wormhole solutions by fitting observational data. Finally, we explore the physical consequences of the proposed epicyclic approach.

We provide a cosmological examination of the Gauss-Bonnet quasi-dilaton massive gravity framework, which constitutes a gravitational theory featuring a non-vanishing graviton mass. We derive the full set of background equations of motion and identify self-accelerating background solutions, alongside constraints on parameters to ensure their correct signs. Furthermore, we analyze tensor perturbations, compute the graviton mass, and determine the dispersion relation for gravitational waves across two distinct scenarios. Ultimately, we explore the propagation of gravitational perturbations within FLRW cosmology under this specific Gauss-Bonnet quasi-dilaton massive gravity model.

Temporal hyperproperties define relationships among multiple execution traces. While model checking algorithms support these properties in finite-state hardware, and tools for general temporal logics such as HyperLTL are available, their analysis in infinite-state software has historically been restricted to $k$-safety properties, which ensure no bad interactions occur among any $k$ traces. This paper introduces an automated verification method for $\forall^k\exists^l$-safety properties within infinite-state systems. A $\forall^k\exists^l$-safety property requires that for every set of $k$ traces, there exist $l$ additional traces such that the combined $k+l$ traces avoid undesirable interactions. By combining universal and existential quantification, this approach captures properties beyond standard $k$-safety, such as generalized non-interference and program refinement. The proposed method utilizes a strategy-based instantiation of existential trace quantification alongside program reduction, both operating under a fixed predicate abstraction. Distinctively, the framework supports mutual dependence between the strategy and reduction components.

This paper examines two-species Lotka-Volterra prey-predator systems defined on finite connected graphs under Neumann boundary conditions and scenarios without boundary constraints. We demonstrate the global stability of the unique constant equilibrium solution for each corresponding parabolic system.

The theory of $\tau$-tilting was introduced by Adachi, Iyama, and Reiten at the start of the last decade and has rapidly emerged as a central and vibrant field within the representation theory of finite dimensional algebras. These notes serve a dual purpose: first, to provide an accessible introduction to $\tau$-tilting theory for those with a modest background in representation theory, and second, to address the lack of a comprehensive survey by consolidating many of the field's most significant results into a single resource.

Utilizing functionals based on Skyrme interactions, the time-dependent formulation of nuclear density functional theory offers an approximate description of nuclear dynamics. This work presents time-dependent calculations of dipole resonances, focusing on valence neutron excitations relative to a proton-plus-neutron core within the neutron-rich, doubly-magic $^{132}$Sn nucleus, alongside findings on collision dynamics. These dynamics highlight possible pathways to ternary fusion, illustrated by a $^{48}$Ca+$^{48}$Ca+$^{208}$Pb collision that yields a compound nucleus of element 120 capable of resisting immediate fission.

The Mars 2020 mission will deploy a helicopter alongside traditional ground rovers. This aerial vehicle's high-resolution imagery assists the rover in detecting small obstacles like steps and sharp rocks, while also supplying detailed data to forecast perception capabilities. This paper examines a three-agent configuration involving a Mars rover, a helicopter, and an orbiter. The primary objective is to enhance rover localization by determining an optimal trajectory that reduces the accumulation of localization uncertainty throughout the rover's journey. To accomplish this, we define localizability as a quality metric tied to the map and perform a joint-space search across the rover's path and the helicopter's sensing actions, utilizing prior data from the orbiter. We simultaneously determine where the helicopter should map and where the rover should drive using an iterative copter-rover path planning algorithm. Finally, numerical simulations based on the Mars 2020 landing site map were executed to validate the effectiveness of this proposed planner.

This work details an ab initio investigation into the rovibronic spectra of sulfur monoxide ($^{32}$S$^{16}$O), employing the internally contracted multireference configuration interaction (ic-MRCI) method alongside aug-cc-pV5Z basis sets. The study encompasses 13 electronic states—specifically $X^{3}\Sigma^{-}$, $a^{1}\Delta$, $b^{1}\Sigma^{+}$, $c^{1}\Sigma^{-}$, $A^{\prime\prime 3}\Sigma^{+}$, $A^{\prime 3}\Delta$, $A^{3}\Pi$, $B^{3}\Sigma^{-}$, $C^{3}\Pi$, $d^{1}\Pi$, $e^{1}\Pi$, $C^{\prime 3}\Pi$, and $(3)^{1}\Pi$—extending up to 66,800 cm$^{-1}$. The resulting ab initio spectroscopic model comprises 13 potential energy curves, 23 dipole and transition dipole moment curves, 23 spin-orbit curves, and 14 electronic angular momentum curves. To address avoided crossings between the spatially degenerate pairs $C^{3}\Pi - C^{\prime 3}\Pi$ and $e^{1}\Pi - (3)^{1}\Pi$, a diabatic representation was constructed using a property-based diabatisation approach. Additionally, both non-adiabatic and diabatic couplings for these interacting systems are provided. With all coupling curve phases defined consistently, this work establishes the first fully reproducible spectroscopic model for SO valid for wavelengths longer than 147 nm. Ultimately, an ab initio rovibronic spectrum of SO is calculated.

High-speed downflows have been detected in the solar transition region (TR) and lower corona for decades, yet identifying their signatures in the solar chromosphere has proven challenging. This study focuses on an enhanced network region exhibiting frequent rapid spicular downflows in the H$\alpha$ spectral line, which may correspond to high-speed downflows in the TR. We utilized the $k$-means algorithm to classify spectral profiles of on-disk spicules in H$\alpha$ and Ca II K data from the Swedish 1-m Solar Telescope (SST) and applied an automated detection method based on advanced morphological image processing to identify these features alongside rapid blue-shifted and red-shifted excursions (RBEs and RREs). For the first time, we report a new category of RREs, termed "downflowing RREs," which, contrary to previous interpretations, are linked to chromospheric field-aligned downflows moving toward strong magnetic field regions. Statistical analysis of nearly 20,000 RBEs and 15,000 RREs (including the downflowing variants) from a 97-minute dataset reveals that downflowing RREs are highly similar to standard RBEs and RREs, differing only in their oppositely directed plane-of-sky motion. Additionally, we find that RBEs, RREs, and downflowing RREs exhibit a wide variety of spectral profiles with varying Doppler offsets and H$\alpha$ line core widths along and perpendicular to the spicule axis, suggesting they represent multiple co-evolving substructures. We hypothesize that these rapid plasma downflows may indeed be the chromospheric counterparts of the commonly observed TR downflows.

The prevalent issue of Emergency Department (ED) overcrowding is typically addressed in existing research by modeling patient flow within individual EDs, often neglecting the potential benefits of inter-ED cooperation. Conversely, this paper argues that overcrowding must be analyzed through the lens of an ED network rather than in isolation. Utilizing a Simulation-Based Optimization approach via Discrete Event Simulation models, the study examines an ED network under various conditions, specifically focusing on the Ambulance Diversion problem and evaluating different diversion policies. These models are built upon real data gathered from six major EDs in the Lazio region of Italy. The primary objective is to optimize overall network performance to deliver superior patient care without incurring excessive costs. Experimental results identify the most effective diversion policies regarding both patient waiting times and service provider expenses.

Utilizing VVV near-infrared extinction maps, we have identified new transparent regions within the Galactic plane, facilitating an investigation into the Milky Way's disk structure. The primary objective is to chart spiral arms in the distant, less-explored regions of our Galaxy by employing red clump (RC) giants as distance markers. Specifically, we searched for near-IR clear windows at low Galactic latitudes ($|b|< 1$ deg) and discovered two new areas, VVV WIN 1607-5258 and VVV WIN 1475-5877, which supplement the existing VVV WIN 1713-3939 window. By analyzing the spatial distribution and line-of-sight number density of RC stars across these three windows, we detected overdensities and determined their distances. Subsequently, we utilized VVV proper motions to assess the kinematics of RC stars at varying distances. Our analysis reveals enhancements in the RC giant distance distributions across all studied windows, which we interpret as evidence of spiral arms in the Milky Way disk; notably, these structures are missing from current synthetic population models for these specific lines of sight. Through this work, we successfully traced the termination of the Galactic bar, as well as the Norma and Scutum-Centaurus arms in the far disk. Furthermore, measurements of proper motions confirm that these Galactic features participate in the bulk rotation of the disk.

This research investigates quantum chromodynamics featuring two-index symmetric or anti-symmetric quarks (QCD(Sym/ASym)) on a small $\mathbb{R}^2\times T^2$ manifold equipped with an appropriate magnetic flux. We initially examine the 't Hooft anomaly of these models, asserting that the discrete chiral symmetry must be spontaneously broken entirely to fulfill the anomaly matching requirement. The compactification of $T^2$ with magnetic flux conserves the 't Hooft anomaly, thereby constraining the resulting $2$d effective theory to share the same anomaly as $4$d QCD(Sym/ASym). We provide evidence for the spontaneous chiral symmetry breaking via a dilute gas of center vortices, which validates the 't Hooft anomaly prediction. Furthermore, we observe that every vacuum preserves charge conjugation symmetry, offering strong support for the nonperturbative large-$N$ orientifold equivalence between QCD(Sym/ASym) and $\mathcal{N}=1$ supersymmetric $SU(N)$ Yang-Mills theory.

A deterministic framework incorporating infected individual testing has been developed to examine the effects of various testing strategies. The model's global dynamics reveal that, when infected recruitment is zero, the system possesses a disease-free equilibrium and a unique endemic equilibrium determined by the basic reproduction number; however, if recruitment is non-zero, the disease-free equilibrium disappears, and the disease persists indefinitely. Model parameters were estimated via maximum likelihood analysis using early COVID-19 data from India, with practical identifiability analysis confirming unique parameter estimation. Sensitivity results indicate that increasing the testing rate by 20% and 30% above baseline reduces peak weekly cases by 37.63% and 52.90%, respectively, while delaying the peak by four and fourteen weeks. Similarly, a 12.67% increase in testing efficacy lowers peak cases by 59.05% and postpones the peak by fifteen weeks. These findings demonstrate that enhanced testing rates and efficacy mitigate disease burden by curbing new infections and align with real-world scenarios. Furthermore, both factors alleviate epidemic severity by expanding the final susceptible population size. Notably, the testing rate proves more impactful when testing efficacy is high. Finally, a global sensitivity analysis employing partial rank correlation coefficients (PRCCs) and Latin hypercube sampling (LHS) identified the critical parameters necessary to either exacerbate or contain the epidemic.

Efficient frequency-domain Full Waveform Inversion (FWI) for long-offset or wide-azimuth node data can be achieved using a limited set of discrete frequencies. Nevertheless, 3D frequency-domain seismic modeling remains difficult because it necessitates solving a large, sparse, linear indefinite system for every frequency. When addressing these systems with direct methods or hybrid direct/iterative solvers equipped with domain decomposition preconditioners, finite-difference stencils on regular Cartesian grids must balance compactness and accuracy. Compactness is essential to reduce the fill-in caused by Lower-Upper (LU) factorization, while accuracy is achieved by optimizing weights for stiffness and consistent mass matrices to minimize numerical dispersion across various grid points per wavelength ($G$). Traditionally, this is done by combining multiple second-order stencils around a collocation point to create a 27-point stencil; however, using uniform weights at every point results in suboptimal accuracy within heterogeneous media. This study introduces a simple method to enhance the accuracy of the 27-point stencil. The process involves first creating a detailed table of $G$ values that covers the wavelength range of the subsurface model and frequency. Next, a standard dispersion analysis in homogeneous media is used to determine optimal weights that minimize dispersion for each specific $G$, with Tikhonov regularization applied to ensure these weights vary smoothly. Finally, the impedance matrix is constructed by assigning optimal weights based on the local wavelength at each collocation point, resulting in a wavelength-adaptive stencil.

A limitation of the standard chain rule is its inability to iterate; it provides the derivative for $f(g(x))$ but does not directly yield second or higher-order derivatives. In this work, we introduce iterated differentials and a multivariable chain rule variant capable of iterating to any required derivative level. We initially present these concepts informally before addressing the necessary rigor, which involves touching upon the formal foundations of calculus. Furthermore, we propose a chain rule for finite calculus, challenging Graham, Knuth, and Patashnik's assertion that no such rule exists within that framework.

Let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a finite-dimensional simple Lie algebra over $\mathbb{C}$, where a $\operatorname{Y}(\mathfrak{g})$-module is defined as weight if it is also a weight $\mathfrak{g}$-module. This work presents a comprehensive classification of simple weight modules for $\operatorname{Y}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ that possess a one-dimensional weight space, identifying four distinct categories: finite, highest weight, lowest weight, and dense modules. Diverging from classical $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ representation theory, we demonstrate the existence of a specific class of $\operatorname{Y}(\mathfrak{sl}_{2})$ irreducible modules characterized by uniformly 2-dimensional weight spaces.

The fashion sector stands as one of the world's most dynamic and competitive industries, producing millions of goods annually to reach vast audiences. While numerous business processes drive this large-scale operation, effective supply chain management and retail strategies are vital due to the short life cycles of clothing. Accurately gauging consumer demands, resolving logistical challenges, and promoting the right products represent complex, high-level problems characterized by significant uncertainty stemming from multiple influencing factors and the inherent unpredictability of the future. Consequently, forecasting methods that predict future trends are essential for optimizing various business processes, all aimed at fashion's core mission: ensuring widespread adoption of specific products or styles to make items, people, and brands fashionable. This paper offers an overview of three specific forecasting tasks applicable to fashion companies to enhance their industrial and market influence. We examine the advancements and challenges inherent in these tasks, arguing for their significance and potential industrial impact. Finally, we discuss current issues and future research directions, considering how learning-based forecasting approaches can further support the fashion industry.

Let $G$ be a finite group, where $\pi(G)$ represents the set of prime factors of $|G|$ and $\pi_e(G)$ denotes the spectrum, defined as the set of element orders in $G$. We define $w_o(G) = |\pi(G)|$ as the width of the order of $G$ and $w_s(G) = \max\{|{\pi}(k)| \mid k \in \pi_e(G)\}$ as the width of the spectrum of $G$. This paper examines scenarios where $w_o(G)$ and $w_s(G)$ are small, establishes several new theorems, and provides a survey on these two group widths.

We have determined the characteristics of compact objects, such as neutron stars, utilizing an equation of state (EOS) derived from a core-envelope model of superdense stars. These superdense stars were investigated by solving Einstein's equations under pseudo-spheroidal and spherically symmetric space-time geometries. The resulting stellar properties were compared against those derived from nuclear matter equations of state. Based on the obtained mass-radius ($M-R$) relationship, compact stars are categorized into three groups: (i) highly compact self-bound stars indicative of exotic matter with radii under 9 km; (ii) normal neutron stars with radii ranging from 9 to 12 km; and (iii) soft matter neutron stars with radii between 12 and 20 km. Additionally, Keplerian frequency, surface gravity, and surface gravitational redshift were calculated for all three classifications. This research offers valuable insights for studying highly compact, neutron-like stars composed of exotic matter.

This study examines symmetry-protected toroidal dipole resonances and their excitation requirements within a novel class of electromagnetic metamaterials. These materials consist of all-dielectric planar periodic arrays featuring dielectric disks arranged on a dielectric substrate. The fundamental components of the array are trimers organized within hexagonal unit supercells, which possess the highest geometrical symmetry of C6v. We employ group representation theory, specifically applying magnetic group theory—a new method for addressing such challenges—to conduct our analysis. Our findings indicate that accessing the array's toroidal supermodes requires breaking the unit supercell symmetry twice: first by reducing the trimer's C3v symmetry, and second by lowering the unit supercell's C6v symmetry. We establish selection rules for both symmetric and antisymmetric orders of toroidal dipole moments in these arrays. Specifically, we demonstrate that reducing the unit supercell symmetry to the C2v group results in toroidal dipole resonance with an antitoroidal order, while arrays with lower Cs symmetry support resonances exhibiting both toroidal and antitoroidal orders. Furthermore, we show that these arrays are inherently polarization sensitive. Both full-wave simulations and experimental results validate our theoretical predictions. These proposed metamaterials can enhance light-matter interaction by confining light spatially and temporally within resonant systems characterized by very high quality factors.

Floquet engineering enables the generation of novel topological states that have no equivalents in static systems. This work details the experimental creation and analysis of new anomalous topological states using high-precision Floquet techniques on ultracold atoms within a shaken optical Raman lattice. By adjusting driving-induced band crossings, known as band inversion surfaces (BISs), we manipulate the topology of the Floquet bands; the arrangement of these BISs completely defines the topology of the resulting states. Through measurements of BIS configurations that reflect the bulk Floquet topology, we reveal various exotic anomalous topological states. Notably, we discover an unprecedented anomalous Floquet valley-Hall state featuring valley-protected, anomalous helical edge modes, alongside a chiral state exhibiting a high Chern number.

Non-intrusive load monitoring (NILM) serves as a vital, cost-effective technology for tracking power usage and addressing key challenges in establishing an efficient, sustainable, and competitive energy environment. This study introduces a smart NILM framework utilizing a novel local power histogramming (LPH) descriptor, which converts appliance power signals into a 2D space to extract short histograms representing each device. Specifically, these local histograms capture individual appliance consumption signatures, enabling the robust extraction of device-level data from aggregated power signals. Additionally, an enhanced k-nearest neighbors (IKNN) algorithm is developed to minimize computational learning time and boost classification accuracy, significantly improving the system's ability to distinguish between appliances in different categories. A comprehensive evaluation of the proposed LPH-IKNN solution across various datasets demonstrates promising performance, achieving accuracies of up to 99.65% and 98.51% on the GREEND and UK-DALE datasets, respectively, and exceeding 96% on both WHITED and PLAID datasets. These results validate the efficacy of 2D descriptors for precise appliance identification and offer new avenues for advancing NILM research.

We utilize the measured spatiotemporal responses of diverse physical phenomena to deduce the governing partial differential equations (PDEs). We introduce SimultaNeous Basis Function Approximation and Parameter Estimation (SNAPE), a parameter estimation technique for PDEs that achieves nearly 100% robustness against high noise levels by simultaneously fitting basis functions to observed data and estimating parameters for both ordinary and partial differential equations. General multidimensional domain knowledge serves as a constraint within the optimization framework. SNAPE demonstrates applicability across various complex dynamic systems spanning wide scientific fields, including the Schrödinger equation, chaotic Duffing oscillator, and Navier-Stokes equation, while also deriving an analytical approximation of the process response. This method systematically integrates established scientific theories with data science concepts to infer process properties from observed data.

This paper aims to establish novel conditions for the smooth linearization of nonautonomous systems, covering both discrete and continuous time frameworks. The proposed results rely on the assumption that the linear component possesses a nonuniform polynomial dichotomy, characterized by specific spectral gap and spectral band constraints within the associated polynomial dichotomy spectrum. This approach stands in stark contrast to the majority of prior literature, which typically required the linear part to exhibit an exponential dichotomy. Our methodology leverages the connection between polynomial and exponential dichotomies by employing a specific time reparametrization technique.

We present BenchCLAMP, a benchmark designed to assess Constrained Language Model Parsing. This process generates semantic outputs by analyzing input text through the constrained decoding of either prompted or fine-tuned language models. Although current evaluations for pretrained language models focus on classification, span extraction, and free-text generation, semantic parsing has been overlooked due to the complexities of managing task-specific architectures and representations. However, recent studies indicate that generation from prompted or fine-tuned models can excel at semantic parsing if the output is restricted to valid semantic representations. BenchCLAMP features context-free grammars for six datasets with diverse meaning representations and offers a constrained decoding interface to produce outputs adhering to these grammars. To facilitate accurate comparisons across different data regimes, we provide low, medium, and high resource splits for each dataset. Furthermore, the benchmark supports both prompt-based learning and fine-tuning, offering developers an accessible toolkit for evaluating their models on semantic parsing tasks.

This paper details findings from a pilot study investigating Morse code as a viable text entry method for mobile devices. Participants with no prior Morse code experience achieved an average speed of 6.7 wpm using a Morse code keyboard across three brief sessions. Improvements in both entry speed and accuracy were observed, indicating that keyboard performance is expected to enhance with continued practice.

The symmetries of certain materials can enforce a nodal-line semimetal phase, a state that holds significant interest for both fundamental physics and practical applications. We show that such a phase can be engineered through a straightforward approach: creating vacancies in specific arrangements within common symmorphic materials transforms them into nonsymmorphic polymorphs. These new structures possess symmetry-enforced nodal lines that remain stable against symmetry-preserving perturbations, including spin-orbit coupling. Additionally, the resulting spectrum features accidental nodal lines with even greater robustness to external disturbances. We explain these phenomena using a symmetry analysis of a minimal two-dimensional effective model that captures the essential symmetries of the proposed structures. This theoretical framework is validated by first-principles calculations on vacancy-engineered borophene polymorphs, covering cases with both negligible and strong Rashba spin-orbit coupling. Our results provide an alternative route to designing robust nodal-line semimetals; instead of relying on complex nonsymmorphic compounds, one can simply remove atoms from a simple symmorphic monoatomic material.

The study examines the classification of linear ordinary differential equations of the $n$-th order (where $n \geq 2$). Following a point transformation that reduces the equation to the \textit{Laguerre-Forsyth} form, subsequent computations are performed on this transformed version. This approach was developed by \textit{V.A. Yumaguzhin}.

Adversarial training (AT) has proven highly effective in safeguarding models against adversarial examples. Recent research indicates that not all examples contribute equally to a model's robustness during AT; specifically, "hard" examples, which are vulnerable to attacks, exert a greater influence on final robustness than robust ones. Consequently, ensuring the robustness of these hard examples is essential for enhancing overall model performance. However, developing effective heuristics to identify such examples remains a challenge. Drawing inspiration from the information bottleneck (IB) principle, we discover that examples exhibiting high mutual information between their input and associated latent representation are more susceptible to attacks. Leveraging this insight, we introduce InfoAT, a novel and efficient adversarial training method that prioritizes identifying and utilizing high mutual information examples to boost model robustness. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that InfoAT outperforms several state-of-the-art methods, achieving superior robustness across various datasets and models.

Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) have seen rapid adoption in recent years due to their versatility and affordability, with applications spanning from military missions and land mapping to search-and-rescue operations and disaster relief. Properly designing and operating these vehicles requires a thorough understanding of flight mechanics across various flight phases. Although the physics governing aircraft flight are well-established within Classical Mechanics, the extensive data required for analysis makes computational tools essential. This work introduces APT (Aircraft Performance Toolbox), a solution designed to facilitate preliminary flight mechanics and performance calculations. To accomplish this, a series of Matlab scripts were developed to execute the computations, accompanied by a graphical interface that consolidates these tools into a clear and intuitive platform for end-users. The potential of the toolbox is demonstrated through its application in analyzing a UAV developed for the 2014 SAE Brasil AeroDesign competition.

The classic problem of gradient percolation has been re-examined to analyze the probability distribution of island sizes. It was observed that, similar to ordinary percolation, this distribution follows a power-law decay function, yet the associated critical exponents differ. Due to the gradient in occupation probability, the mean island size also exhibits a gradient. This variation of the average island size with respect to the occupation probability along the gradient, along with its scaling analysis, has been investigated. Additionally, gradient bond percolation was introduced and studied; analysis of the island size distribution statistics yielded very similar results. The characteristics of the diffusion profile for a particle system on a lattice, initially half-filled and half-empty, were also examined, revealing the same value for the island size probability distribution exponent. Finally, this study was repeated for nonlinear gradient percolation, where the island size distribution exponent was found to depend on the strength of the nonlinear parameter.

The improper design and deployment of machine learning (ML) systems generate adverse social and ethical consequences, termed "social and ethical risks," affecting users, society, and the environment. Although there is an increasing demand for ML regulation, existing methods for evaluating and addressing these risks remain fragmented and inconsistent. Through interviews with 30 industry professionals regarding their current risk management strategies and initial responses to adapting safety engineering frameworks—specifically System Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA) and Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA)—our findings indicate that STPA and FMEA offer a suitable structure for assessing and mitigating social and ethical risks. Nevertheless, significant challenges arise when integrating these frameworks into the rapid-paced culture of the ML sector. We urge the ML research community to enhance existing frameworks and evaluate their effectiveness to ensure greater safety for all people.

Vyb\'{\i}ral's [\textit{Adv. Math.} 2020] striking finding establishes that the Schur product of positive matrices is bounded below by the matrix dimensions and the row sums of the resulting Schur product, a result Vyb\'{\i}ral leveraged to prove Novak's conjecture. This paper introduces the concept of the Schur product for matrices within arbitrary C*-algebras, deriving the corresponding theorems attributed to Schur and Vyb\'{\i}ral. As an application, we present a C*-algebraic formulation of Novak's conjecture and resolve it for the case of commutative unital C*-algebras. Furthermore, we articulate the P\'{o}lya-Szeg\H{o}-Rudin question regarding the C*-algebraic Schur product of positive matrices.

Wireless sensor networks employ randomly deployed nodes to monitor specific areas or targets, yet sustaining continuous surveillance remains difficult due to the restricted battery life of individual sensors. Wireless power transfer offers a dependable remedy by utilizing a mobile charger (MC) to replenish sensor energy. However, determining an optimal charging trajectory for the MC is complex, primarily because of network uncertainties. Sensor energy consumption rates can vary drastically due to unforeseen topology changes, such as node failures, which also alter the relative importance of each sensor—a factor often treated as uniform in current literature. This paper tackles these issues by introducing a new adaptive charging strategy based on deep reinforcement learning (DRL). Specifically, we equip the MC with a charging policy that selects the next target based on the network's current state, utilizing a deep neural network to parameterize and train this policy via reinforcement learning. This model enables adaptation to sudden shifts in network topology, and empirical results demonstrate that our algorithm significantly surpasses existing on-demand approaches.

Individual nuclear spin states, characterized by their potential for long lifetimes, offer promising applications as qubits. Significant strides in this field were made on the MgO/Ag(001) surface by detecting the hyperfine interaction (HFI) of Fe, Ti, and Cu adatoms through scanning tunneling microscopy (STM). Earlier work systematically quantified, from first principles, the HFI across the entire series of 3d transition metal adatoms (Sc–Cu) on various ultra-thin insulators, revealing trends linked to the filling of magnetic s- and d-orbitals and the nature of substrate bonding. This study extends the investigation to dimers by analyzing the relationship between HFI and the magnetic states of free-standing Fe dimers, isolated Fe adatoms, and Fe dimers placed on a bilayer of MgO(001). We demonstrate that the HFI magnitude can be regulated by toggling the dimer's magnetic state. Specifically, at short Fe–Fe separations, the antiferromagnetic state yields a larger HFI compared to the ferromagnetic state, whereas increasing the interatomic distance reverses this trend. Additionally, we show that atomic-level positioning of adatoms on the substrate allows for substantial modulation of the HFI. These findings define the boundaries of the conventional hyperfine Hamiltonian and suggest an extension incorporating multiple scattering processes.

ALICE primarily processes large datasets via the distributed Grid infrastructure. During LHC Runs 1 and 2, the experiment established "LEGO trains"—analysis systems allowing users to configure tasks, or "wagons," to run on identical data. This architecture leverages existing ALICE tools, including the analysis framework and Grid submission/monitoring systems. The centralized LEGO approach enhanced resource efficiency and introduced a graphical user interface (GUI) alongside bookkeeping capabilities, now utilized by approximately 90% of ALICE analyses. To address the projected two-order-of-magnitude increase in Pb-Pb collision data for LHC Run 3, the experiment has adopted the Online-Offline Computing System (O$^2$). Analysis trains remain central to Run 3 operations, supported by a new infrastructure called Hyperloop, which refines the LEGO concept. The Hyperloop system features a modern, responsive web-based GUI, advanced bookkeeping, instant automated testing, and the generation of skimmed derived data. To date, roughly 800 Hyperloop trains have been successfully submitted to Grid and ALICE facilities using converted Run 2 data. This overview examines the ALICE train system concept, emphasizing the enhancements introduced by the Hyperloop framework for Run 3.

This study addresses supervised learning using linear methods in scenarios where both features and labels may be corrupted, such as through heavy-tailed distributions or row-level corruptions. We propose a learning algorithm that combines coordinate gradient descent with robust estimators for partial derivatives. This approach yields robust statistical learning methods that maintain a numerical complexity nearly equivalent to non-robust empirical risk minimization techniques. The core concept is straightforward: whereas robust gradient descent typically demands the computational expense of estimating the full gradient for parameter updates, coordinate gradient descent allows for immediate updates using a robust estimator for just a single partial derivative. We establish upper bounds on the generalization error for these algorithms, which account for both optimization and statistical errors under both strong and non-strong convexity assumptions. Furthermore, we present an efficient implementation of this methodology within a new Python library named linlearn. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate that our approach offers a novel balance between robustness, statistical performance, and computational efficiency for this specific problem.

This study examines how external noise and detection thresholds influence simulation data for systems evolving through metastable states. Using the nonequilibrium athermal random field Ising model as a representative example, we introduced two noise types—uniform white noise and Gaussian white noise with varying standard deviations—to the response signals generated by model simulations. By analyzing these signals across a broad spectrum of detection thresholds, we demonstrate how these factors alter the scaling exponent $\gamma_{S/T}$ (which characterizes the relationship between average avalanche size and duration), the shift in waiting times between avalanches, and the collapse of waiting time distributions. These findings were derived from extensive numerical simulations conducted on equilateral three-dimensional cubic lattices of diverse sizes and disorder levels.

This study outlines an end-to-end Quality of Service (QoS) methodology designed to ensure performance guarantees within the SELENE platform, a high-performance heterogeneous System on Chip (SoC) based on RISC-V architecture for safety-critical real-time applications. The proposed QoS framework integrates intelligent interconnect solutions for both buses and Network-on-Chip (NoC) structures, alongside multicore interference-aware statistics units, working collaboratively to realize end-to-end QoS.

This technical report catalogs two enhanced applications designed to advance vehicular networking research. The first application was previously detailed in our work [21], whereas the second is a desktop application originally built as a publicly hosted web service, enabling any internet-connected device to remotely monitor roadway intersections via HTTP. This collaborative effort was conducted for and by ETSU's Vehicular Networking Lab, offering a foundation for future advancements in connected and autonomous vehicles.

Addressing the non-ideal behaviors in electrolyte-gated transistors (EGTs) that cannot be captured by a single theoretical framework, we developed a charge carrier transport model capable of describing both standard and anomalous operation modes in electrolyte-gated field-effect transistors (EGOFETs) and organic electrochemical transistors (OECTs). This analysis incorporates 2D and 3D percolation transport mechanisms as well as the impact of shallow exponential trap distributions, which can result in a non-uniform accumulation layer thickness along the channel. We integrated this variability by making the effective mobility parameter dependent on the accumulation thickness, which may exhibit 2D, 3D, or transitional percolation characteristics. Such transitions can generate non-ideal output profiles, specifically a lump or protuberance between the linear and saturation regions. Additionally, the model explains the non-linear behavior observed at low drain voltages, even with ohmic contacts, attributing it to the trap distribution profile and the minimal accumulation layer thickness near the injection contact. The model further allows for the determination of conditions where linear-field-effect mobility exceeds or falls below saturation mobility. Ultimately, successful fitting of experimental data from both EGOFETs and OECTs demonstrates the model's versatility.

This work analyzes the Kantorovich exponential sampling series specifically at jump discontinuities within bounded measurable signals, denoted as f. A representation lemma for the series is developed, which is then utilized to prove specific approximation theorems for discontinuous signals. The study examines the degree of approximation using the logarithmic modulus of smoothness. Additionally, a method for linearly predicting signals based on historical sample values is derived. Finally, numerical simulations are conducted to verify the accuracy of the sampling series in approximating discontinuous signals f.

We determine the parallel upper critical magnetic field $H_{\parallel}(0)$ for an in-plane isotropic quasi-two-dimensional (Q2D) chiral triplet superconductor at absolute zero ($T=0$). Specifically, we define the ratio $H_{\parallel}(0)/(|dH^{GL}_{\parallel}/dT|_{T=T_c}T_c) = 0.815$, where $|dH^{GL}_{\parallel}/dT|_{T=T_c}$ represents the Ginzburg-Landau slope of the upper critical field and $T_c$ denotes the superconducting transition temperature at zero field. We demonstrate that this theoretically derived value significantly conflicts with experimental measurements obtained from Sr$_2$RuO$_4$, a candidate material for chiral triplet superconductivity, thereby offering additional evidence against the chiral triplet scenario in this compound. Furthermore, our findings could assist in confirming chiral triplet superconductivity in other Q2D candidates exhibiting this phenomenon.

This study presents data on elastic $pp$ scattering at both ISR and LHC energies, employing an analytical model where the amplitude is represented as the sum of three exponentials with complex phases. The model incorporates Coulomb and Coulomb-nuclear interactions across the full momentum transfer range, alongside strong perturbative contributions for large transfers. We have derived updated values for key scattering parameters, including the total and elastic cross sections, the $\rho_0$-parameter, and the diffraction cone slope, while also examining the $t$-dependence of the total complex amplitude phase. Notable shifts in amplitude behavior are observed when transitioning from ISR to LHC energies. Finally, these findings are used to discuss the internal structure of colliding protons.

This study offers a comprehensive comparison of the rheological properties of sheared sediment beds within a pressure-driven, straight channel. The analysis utilizes fully coupled, grain-resolved direct numerical simulations alongside previously published experimental data by Aussillous et al. (J. Fluid Mech., vol. 736, 2013, pp. 594-615). Unlike experiments, the high-resolution simulation data enables the calculation of the suspension's stress balance in streamwise and vertical directions, as well as the stress exchange between fluid and particle phases—details previously inaccessible experimentally and essential for determining rheology. By applying these insights to both datasets, we derive statistically stationary, depth-resolved profiles of key rheological parameters. We examine the scaling behavior of shear and normal viscosities and the effective friction coefficient, comparing them against rheometry data and established rheological correlations. Our findings indicate that rheological properties previously attributed to annular Couette flows with neutrally buoyant particles also apply to our Poiseuille flow sediment transport setup; specifically, in the dense regime, the results align well with empirical relationships derived from those flows. Furthermore, decomposing total stress into contributions from particle contacts and hydrodynamics identifies a critical particle volume fraction of 0.3 as the threshold separating dense and dilute regimes. In the dilute regime, corresponding to the sediment transport layer, long-range hydrodynamic interactions are screened by the porous medium, causing the effective viscosity to follow the Einstein relation.

Refinement bridges the gap between abstract system models and concrete, executable programs, ensuring that properties proven for the abstract version hold true for the implementation. Although this approach has enabled the successful development of significant verified systems, current techniques face limitations that hinder their practical application. Some methods automatically generate code, often resulting in sub-optimal performance, while others rely on bottom-up verification of efficient implementations but demand rigid constraints on code structure, proof architecture, and the specific verification logic or tools used. This paper introduces a new refinement technique designed to overcome these barriers. By leveraging separation logic to analyze efficient concurrent systems, our method enforces only a loose coupling between the abstract model and the concrete code. This flexibility accommodates diverse program structures, data representations, and proof styles. Furthermore, we impose minimal assumptions on the underlying program logic, enabling compatibility with various logics and automation via standard separation logic verifiers. We provide a formalization of the technique, prove the core trace inclusion property, and validate its effectiveness through multiple case studies.

EdgeML accelerators, such as the Intel Neural Compute Stick 2 (NCS), facilitate efficient edge-based inference by running complex pre-trained models that are loaded on a host device like a Raspberry Pi before being transferred to the NCS. This paper presents practical, low-cost cold boot attacks against NCS to recover both the model architecture and weights loaded from the host. Our approach achieves 100% success in recovering the architecture and recovers weights with a mere 0.04% error rate. Consequently, the recovered model exhibits a maximum accuracy loss of only 0.5% compared to the original and can successfully transfer adversarial examples with high fidelity. We also evaluated other cold boot attack configurations from existing literature, which demonstrated higher error rates and accuracy losses up to 70%. To address these errors, we propose a knowledge distillation-based methodology capable of correcting erroneous weights in the recovered model without requiring access to the original training data. Furthermore, our attack remains effective despite the model encryption features present in the OpenVINO and NCS frameworks.

We introduce AdaFamily, a new approach for training deep neural networks that constitutes a family of adaptive gradient techniques. Conceptually, it can be viewed as a hybrid of the optimization algorithms Adam, AdaBelief, and AdaMomentum. Experiments conducted on standard image classification datasets demonstrate that our proposed method surpasses the performance of these existing algorithms.

Although the concept of a Dyson Sphere was first introduced in Olaf Stapledon's 1937 novel *Star Maker* and later popularized by Freeman Dyson in the 1960s, it describes an engineering marvel designed to encircle a star and capture its total radiated energy. This analysis examines the feasibility, scale, and probable design of such a structure, investigating each phase of its construction and operation. The study concludes that a Dyson Swarm—a vast collection of individual satellites orbiting a planet—is a superior design compared to the traditional solid shell surrounding the sun.

In our solar system, a Dyson Swarm constructed around Mars could meet Earth's 2019 global power consumption of 18.35 TW within fifty years, with construction potentially beginning as early as 2040. This system would consist of over 5.5 billion satellites built on the Martian surface and launched into orbit via electromagnetic accelerators. The swarm would capture between 0.74% and 2.77% of the Sun's $3.85\times10^{26}$ W output, with significant room for efficiency improvements as current technologies advance and new concepts are realized during and after construction. Beyond providing an almost limitless, renewable energy source for Earth, a Dyson Swarm would facilitate major expansions in human space exploration and the growth of our civilization.

This study examines the analysis, control, recovery, and operation of mobile robot networks maintaining time-varying formations under deception attacks targeting global positioning. To enhance resilience and maintain network redundancy and functionality, the paper introduces local and global tracking control algorithms. Lyapunov stability analysis is employed to demonstrate the boundedness of tracking errors and network stability across different attack scenarios. Furthermore, a performance metric is developed to evaluate the efficiency of the proposed algorithms in both attacked and unattacked environments. The research then presents a communication-free decentralized cooperative localization strategy based on extended information filters for recovering positioning estimates, utilizing Kullback-Leibler divergence to identify attacks. Finally, a gain-tuning resilient operation method is proposed to strategically integrate formation control with cooperative localization, ensuring accurate and swift recovery from positioning attacks. These methods are validated through numerical simulations and experimental tests using a quadrotor team.

Clustering is a fundamental technique in unsupervised learning. Most current self-supervised representation learning approaches cluster samples primarily based on visually dominant features. While effective for image-based tasks, this method often falls short for videos, which require analyzing motion rather than static backgrounds. Incorporating optical flow alongside RGB data can mitigate this issue; however, a simple fusion of these two views yields negligible improvements. This paper introduces a principled approach to integrating multiple views. Specifically, we propose a new clustering strategy that utilizes the initial cluster assignments from each view as priors to guide the final assignments of the other view. This mechanism enforces consistent cluster structures across views, resulting in semantically abstract clusters that are robust to noise inherent in individual views. Furthermore, we introduce a novel regularization strategy to tackle feature collapse, a common challenge in cluster-based self-supervised learning. Extensive evaluations demonstrate the efficacy of our learned representations on downstream tasks such as video retrieval and action recognition. Notably, we achieve state-of-the-art performance, surpassing existing methods by 7% on UCF and 4% on HMDB for video retrieval, and by 5% on UCF and 6% on HMDB for video classification.

Let $\M$ be a type ${\rm II}_1$ factor equipped with a faithful normal tracial state $\tau$, and denote its ultrapower algebra by $\M^\omega$. This paper establishes that for any operator $T \in \M^\omega$, there exists a family of projections $\{P_t\}_{0\leq t\leq 1}$ in $\M^\omega$ satisfying $TP_t = P_t T P_t$, the monotonicity condition $P_s \leq P_t$ for $s \leq t$, and the trace normalization $\tau_\omega(P_t) = t$. We define the set $\mathfrak{M} = \{Z \in \M \mid \exists \text{ a family of projections } \{P_t\}_{0\leq t\leq 1} \text{ in } \M \text{ such that } ZP_t = P_t Z P_t, P_s \leq P_t \text{ for } s \leq t, \text{ and } \tau(P_t) = t\}$. As an application, we demonstrate that for every $T \in \M$ and any $\epsilon > 0$, there exists an operator $S \in \mathfrak{M}$ with $\|S\| \leq \|T\|$ and $\|S - T\|_2 < \epsilon$. Furthermore, we prove that the ultrapower $\prod_n^\omega M_n(\mathbb{C})$ is not $\ast$-isomorphic to the ultrapower algebra of the hyperfinite type ${\rm II}_1$ factor.

There has been growing recent interest in developing verification methods for learning-enabled controllers (LECs) that operate within safety-critical systems. Due to the opacity and poor interpretability of the neural policies driving these controllers, many current solutions enforce safety via a "shield"—a dynamic monitoring and repair mechanism that prevents the LEC from generating actions violating safety constraints. However, these approaches face substantial scalability challenges, as verification expenses escalate with increased problem dimensionality and objective complexity. This paper introduces a novel automated verification pipeline capable of synthesizing high-quality safe controllers even in domains involving hundreds of dimensions or complex non-functional requirements such as stochastic perturbations and liveness considerations. Our central insight involves decoupling safety verification from neural controller training by utilizing pre-computed verified safety shields to constrain the training process. Experimental results across various high-dimensional benchmarks demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in both stochastic linear time-invariant and time-variant systems.

*Drosophila melanogaster* hemocytes are highly motile cells essential for successful embryogenesis and the organism's immune response. Researchers measured hemocyte movement using selective plane illumination microscopy, tracking every cell in one half of an embryo throughout development with a deep learning neural network. The cells' anomalous transport was accurately modeled by heterogeneous fractional Brownian motion, varying across both time and space, with persistence decreasing over time. Mutations in *LanB1* and *SCAR* disrupted collective motion and reduced persistence by altering viscoelasticity and actin-based motility, respectively. Hemocyte motility exhibited temporal oscillations, featuring alternating periods of varying persistence. Furthermore, touching hemocytes displayed synchronized contact inhibition of locomotion, described as an "anomalous tango." The study presents a quantitative statistical framework for hemocyte motility that yields new biological insights.

Although outdoor spaces are increasingly becoming the new frontier for indoor workplaces, a vast amount of real-world tasks, such as road construction, still require human labor in open environments. Given the potential of smart workplace technologies to enhance productivity and safety, we sought to apply these tools to a collaborative outdoor project aimed at boosting efficiency and minimizing worker injuries. However, our initial trials revealed several challenges, ranging from conceptual confusion among stakeholders to technical hurdles in extending the lifespan of underground devices. These issues prompted a reevaluation and deeper discussion of the concept of the "smart workplace." Consequently, recognizing the distinct nature of outdoor work—including more complex workflows and heightened safety requirements compared to office settings—we contend that a "safety-centric and smart outdoor workplace" warrants dedicated research efforts within the broader field of smart environments. Furthermore, the technical challenges identified can serve as catalysts for advancing various research dimensions in this unique area.

This paper examines the Logjam attack targeting TLS. Under specific circumstances, Logjam undermines the security guarantees of TLS by coercing servers and clients into employing obsolete export-grade cryptography, thereby compromising the Diffie-Hellman key exchange. We analyze the conceptual mechanics of the attack and the specific vulnerabilities within TLS that enable it. Additionally, we outline the prerequisites for executing this attack and provide an assessment of its potential impact. Finally, we propose several effective mitigation strategies.

This paper introduces "Look and Diagnose" (LAD), a hybrid deep learning system designed to assist medical professionals in effectively diagnosing Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV). By capturing visual data from both eyes during the Dix-Hallpike and lateral head turn tests, LAD analyzes the input to classify patients into one of six potential disorders. The system operates through two parallel streams: the first utilizes an RNN-based approach to process raw RGB images of both eyes, extracting visual features and optical flow to perform a ternary classification distinguishing between left/right posterior canal (PC) involvement and other conditions. The second stream employs a pupil detector that activates when a Non-PC classification is made, subsequently identifying the direction and intensity of nystagmus to categorize the four remaining Non-PC types: Geotropic BPPV (left and right) and Apogeotropic BPPV (left and right). Experimental validation demonstrates that, considering patient postures, the system achieves a 91% accuracy rate in classifying BPPV disorders across all six categories. Furthermore, the method attains specific accuracy rates of 93% for Posterior Canal disorders and 95% for both Geotropic and Apogeotropic disorders, offering a promising avenue for future research utilizing medical data.

Traditional business process management has primarily addressed structured, imperative workflows, but the growing significance of knowledge work has brought semi-structured processes to the forefront. Current methods for modeling knowledge-intensive business processes incorporate data objects yet inadequately address their cardinalities; consequently, these methods cannot ensure adherence to cardinality constraints or leverage them to manage concurrency and multiple activity instances during execution. This paper enhances an existing case management framework by integrating data object associations and cardinality constraints. The resulting capabilities enable refined data access semantics, defined lower and upper bounds for process activities, and synchronized handling of multiple data objects. Execution semantics are formally defined using colored Petri nets, and the approach's efficacy is demonstrated through a compiler that translates case models into colored Petri nets, alongside a specialized process execution engine.

We contend that in numerous cases, elastic scattering data fits, which have historically and often still been deemed acceptable, are actually inadequate. When the phenomenology of elastic scattering lacks sufficient ambition, crucial information regarding the dynamics of nucleon-nucleus and nucleus-nucleus interactions is lost. Consequently, we argue that an alternative phenomenological approach is warranted for the study of nuclear elastic scattering involving nucleons and other light nuclei.
