While Fréchet regression offers a method for estimating the conditional mean of such objects given Euclidean vectors, it lacks traditional regression parameters like slopes or intercepts because metric space-valued responses cannot undergo linear operations. We demonstrate that for multivariate Euclidean predictors, the parameters defining a single index and its associated projection vector can effectively compensate for the absence of standard parameters in Fréchet regression. Specifically, we establish the asymptotic consistency of appropriate parameter estimates under an identifiability constraint. Furthermore, we achieve consistent estimation of the link function in the proposed single index Fréchet regression model via local Fréchet regression. Simulation studies, covering special cases like probability distributions and graph adjacency matrices, illustrate the model's finite sample performance. Additionally, we apply the method to resting-state functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) data from the ADNI study.

We examine two-dimensional, periodic ornaments from the Late Hellenistic (several centuries BCE) and Early Roman (CE) classical eras discovered across various sites in Asia Minor, Turkey, and categorize them into mathematical wallpaper groups according to their symmetry. The artifacts originate from the Terrace Houses in Ephesus, Izmir; the Zeugma Museum in Gaziantep; and a newly uncovered bathing pool at Antiochia ad Cragum near Gazipa\c{s}a, Antalya. Based on these items, we first identify the frequency of each symmetry group. Subsequently, we compare this distribution with patterns from medieval Middle Eastern cultures—specifically Armenian, Byzantine, Arab, and Seljuk Turk—by computing pairwise Euclidean distances between their wallpaper group distributions. Multi-dimensional scaling and hierarchical cluster analysis of these findings confirm that Armenian and Byzantine art are heavily influenced by classical precedents, as well as Seljuk creations attributed to Arab artists.

We investigate the $C^{0}$-formulation of the strong cosmic censorship conjecture (SCC) through a quantum complexity-theoretic lens. We contend that for generic black hole parameters serving as initial conditions for the Einstein equations—representing the anticipated geometry of a hyperbolic black hole—the metric admits a $C^{0}$ extension to a broader Lorentzian manifold across the Cauchy horizon. To illustrate the inconsistencies arising from a hypothetical $C^{0}$ SCC validity, we demonstrate that it contradicts the "complexity=volume" conjecture for a low-temperature hyperbolic AdS$_{d+1}$ black hole, which is dual to a CFT residing on a ($d-1$)-dimensional hyperboloid $H_{d-1}$. In doing so, we enforce a lower bound on the interior metric's extendability, commensurate with the classical recurrence time, to maintain gauge/gravity duality.

We expand the traditional word analogy task into a one-to-X framework that accommodates one-to-none scenarios where no valid answer exists. Formulated as a relation discovery problem, this approach analyzes historical armed conflict datasets to predict novel `location:armed-group` relationships based on past events. Utilizing diachronic word embedding models trained on English news articles as the semantic foundation, we demonstrate a straightforward method to enhance performance over time: applying a cosine distance-based threshold to reduce false positives. This strategy proves advantageous across two distinct corpora. Additionally, we release a ready-to-use test set designed for evaluating one-to-X analogies within the context of historical armed conflicts.

In their 2022 *Nature Physics* paper titled "Time-reversal-based quantum metrology with many-body entangled states," Colombo et al. assert that they have measured an unknown phase and a 290 Hz oscillating magnetic field with precision exceeding the standard quantum limit—the threshold achievable by independent particles. By utilizing an ensemble of approximately 300 entangled atoms to determine the rotation angle from a known initial state and detect the magnetic field oscillations, the authors claim to have reached a precision roughly four times better than that possible with the same number of independent atoms, reporting gains of 12.8 dB and 11.8 dB respectively. However, these claims are false. Colombo et al. did not surpass the precision bound for 300 independent particles, nor did they exceed the bound for a single particle. Although the authors reference multiple experiments that purportedly beat the standard quantum limit using entanglement, every cited study employs the same type of incorrect, incomplete, or misleading comparisons identified here. Consequently, the single-particle precision bound has never been experimentally surpassed using entanglement.

Traditional adversarial attacks on deep neural networks typically depend on a constrained optimization paradigm to derive a single perturbation for a specific input. In contrast, this study reframes the challenge as learning a distribution of adversarial perturbations, allowing for the generation of varied attack distributions from an unperturbed input. We demonstrate that this approach is domain-agnostic, capable of targeting diverse input types with minimal adjustments. Across three distinct domains—images, text, and graphs—our method produces whitebox attacks with success rates that match or exceed current state-of-the-art techniques, notably achieving a new record in the graph domain. Furthermore, we show that the framework can efficiently produce a diverse array of attacks for a single input and possesses the ability to generalize to unseen test instances in a zero-shot manner.

Cascading failures (CFs) in electrical power grids exhibit nonlocal propagation, meaning subsequent failures can occur far from the initial disturbance. Investigating the avalanche dynamics and mitigation strategies for these nonlocal CFs requires numerical simulation, yet such simulations often involve high computational complexity. To address this, we first introduce avalanche centrality (AC), a metric derived from the Motter and Lai model that correlates with avalanche size. Subsequently, we train a graph neural network (GNN) using AC data from small-scale networks. This trained GNN is then applied to predict AC rankings in significantly larger networks and real-world electrical grids, providing an effective tool for avalanche mitigation. Furthermore, the proposed framework is adaptable to other complex processes where large-scale simulations are computationally prohibitive.

This study extends the EUCLID framework, a computational approach for automated material model discovery, to the domain of linear viscoelasticity. We implement a priori model selection using a generalized Maxwell model represented by a Prony series and apply EUCLID for parameter identification. The methodology integrates four core components: i) full-field displacement and net force data; ii) an extensive library of material models, specifically a large number of Prony series terms; iii) the linear momentum balance constraint; and iv) a sparsity constraint. The proposed strategy operates in two stages. Stage 1 utilizes sparse regression to enforce momentum balance on the data and employs sparsity-promoting regularization to significantly reduce the number of Prony series terms while identifying material parameters. Stage 2 employs k-means clustering; using the reduced term set from Stage 1, it further minimizes the terms by grouping Maxwell elements with similar relaxation times and summing their moduli. Automated procedures are established for selecting the regularization parameter in Stage 1 and the number of clusters in Stage 2. The overall strategy is validated using artificial numerical data, both with and without added noise, demonstrating its ability to efficiently and accurately identify a linear viscoelastic model with five relaxation times spanning four orders of magnitude, selected from a library of hundreds of terms covering seven orders of magnitude.

Music possesses hierarchical structures that extend beyond simple beats and measures. Although annotating these hierarchies aids music information retrieval and computer musicology, such data remains scarce in existing digital databases. This paper investigates a data-driven method for automatically deriving hierarchical metrical structures from musical scores. We introduce a novel model utilizing a Temporal Convolutional Network-Conditional Random Field (TCN-CRF) architecture. Given a symbolic score in beat-quantized form containing any number of voices, the model predicts a four-tiered metrical hierarchy ranging from downbeat to section levels. To support training and evaluation, we annotated a dataset using RWC-POP MIDI files. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed approach outperforms rule-based methods across various orchestration configurations. Additionally, we conducted preliminary musicological analyses on the model's outputs. All demos, datasets, and pre-trained models are accessible via our public Github repository.

This study introduces an adaptive digital autopilot for quadcopters, supported by experimental validation. The system is built by integrating retrospective cost adaptive control (RCAC) laws into the PX4 autopilot framework. To evaluate its effectiveness, the experiment deliberately scales down the fixed-gain autopilot's default parameters, significantly impairing its performance; this setup allows for assessing the adaptive autopilot's capacity to correct such detuned conditions. Both simulation and real-world flight tests were conducted to analyze the resulting performance enhancements.

Future and current surveys like Gaia, ZTF, and LSST will generate light curves for billions of astronomical objects, creating new challenges in detecting significant variability patterns. Gathering enough labeled data for training is particularly difficult, especially at the beginning of a survey. To overcome this data scarcity, we developed a single-band light-curve classifier using deep neural networks and applied transfer learning to share knowledge across datasets. Initially, we trained a network on 16 variability features derived from OGLE and EROS-2 light curves. We then fine-tuned this model using a small subset (approximately 5%) of periodic variable light curves from the ASAS dataset, effectively transferring insights from OGLE/EROS-2 to the ASAS domain. This approach yielded strong classification results for ASAS, demonstrating successful knowledge transfer between datasets. We also validated similar transfer learning capabilities using Hipparcos and ASAS-SN data. Consequently, we conclude that it is not necessary to train neural networks from scratch for every new survey; instead, transfer learning remains effective even when only limited labeled data is available in the new dataset.

This study introduces a Segregated Temporal Assembly Recurrent (STAR) network designed for weakly-supervised multiple action detection. Trained on untrimmed videos using only video-level labels, the model predicts the timing intervals of various actions. First, an attention mechanism with class-variable weights assembles video clips based on their labels, effectively filtering out background noise and irrelevant actions. Second, temporal relationships between these actions are established by processing the assembled features through an enhanced recurrent neural network (RNN). Third, the RNN's output is converted into an action distribution. To refine temporal proposals, we introduce a score term known as Segregated Temporal Gradient-Weighted Class Activation Mapping (ST-GradCAM), which integrates attention weights. Experiments conducted on the THUMOS'14 and ActivityNet1.3 datasets demonstrate that our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art weakly-supervised techniques and achieves performance comparable to fully-supervised approaches.

Given an Abelian surface $A$ admitting a finite group $G$ with a symplectic action, we define the partition function for $G$-invariant Hilbert schemes as $Z_{A, G}(q) = \sum_{d=0}^{\infty} e(\text{Hilb}^{d}(A)^{G})q^{d}$. We demonstrate that the reciprocal $Z_{A,G}^{-1}$ constitutes a modular form of weight $\frac{1}{2}e(A/G)$ for the congruence subgroup $\Gamma_{0}(|G|)$, providing explicit representations via eta products. Additionally, we derive refined formulas for the $\chi_{y}$-genera of $\text{Hilb}(A)^{G}$. Specifically, for the group generated by the standard involution $\tau : A \to A$, our results stem from the enumerative geometry of the orbifold Kummer surface $[A/\tau]$. We establish that a virtual count of curves within the stack is dictated by $\chi_{y}(\text{Hilb}(A)^{\tau})$. Furthermore, the coefficients of $Z_{A, \tau}$ represent actual (weighted) counts of rational curves, aligning with hyperelliptic counts established by Bryan, Oberdieck, Pandharipande, and Yin.

The question of whether a separating operator between semiprime f-algebras constitutes a weighted composition operator remains an open problem ( <cite>AAB</cite>). We demonstrate that this holds true if and only if the separating operator is almost contractive. Consequently, we generalize and reinforce several established results concerning separating operators.

This study examines a state estimation scenario involving multiple sensors whose data travels through a lossy wireless network to a central base station, where a Kalman filter generates estimates. The objective is to identify the optimal placement of this base station within a specific framework of packet loss probability models. Analysis of a two-sensor configuration demonstrates that the base station achieves optimality when situated at one of the sensor locations, with empirical data indicating that this principle likely extends to more general cases.

Drawing inspiration from recent experiments detecting strongly coupled polaritons in Moiré heterobilayers, we investigate a model featuring dipole-interacting excitons confined to lattice sites and coupled to planar cavity photons. By analyzing fluctuations around the mean field and assessing the stability of the excitation spectrum, we map out the system's phase diagram. Our results reveal that the transition from a normal state to a polariton condensate is mediated by multiple ordered states occurring at partial exciton lattice fillings, which are stabilized by exciton interactions. Notably, we predict the emergence of a supersolid phase characterized by the coexistence of a polariton condensate and spatial order.

In this study, we examine the $2$-nilpotent multiplier $\mathcal{M}^{(2)}(L)$ of finite-dimensional nilpotent Lie algebras to derive additional results. Specifically, we determine the structure of $\mathcal{M}^{(2)}(H)$ for a Heisenberg Lie algebra $H$. Furthermore, we establish certain inequalities regarding $\mathrm{dim}~ \mathcal{M}^{(2)}(L)$ to minimize the established upper bound for the $2$-nilpotent multiplier. Finally, we demonstrate that $H(m)$ is $2$-capable if and only if $m=1$.

Model predictive control (MPC) is an optimal control strategy that forecasts a system's future states and calculates the ideal control inputs necessary to guide those states toward a target reference. MPC computations occur at fixed intervals over a defined finite time horizon, where the horizon length and sampling frequency dictate both performance and computational load. While a longer horizon with more samples improves input estimation for rapidly changing states—yielding superior performance at the cost of higher computation—it is often unnecessary for slowly varying systems. In such cases, a shorter horizon with fewer samples can achieve comparable performance with significantly reduced computational effort. This paper introduces an adaptive, regression-based MPC that determines the optimal minimum horizon length and sample count by analyzing features derived from time-varying state changes. The method generates a synthetic dataset using the system model to train a support vector regressor for prediction purposes. Experimental comparisons against state-of-the-art methods on both linear and non-linear models demonstrate that the proposed technique achieves a superior reduction in computational time, decreasing processing duration by approximately 35-65% without compromising performance.

The compositional and morphological changes of minor Solar System bodies are largely governed by their heliocentric distance evolution, as solar radiation levels dictate cometary activity. This study examines the dynamical migration of Centaurs into the inner Solar System, a process driven by mean motion resonances with Jupiter and Saturn. Specifically, we focus on the recently discovered object P/2019 LD2, which is projected to move from the Centaur region into the inner Solar System in 2063. To provide context for LD2, we conducted N-body simulations of a Centaur and Jupiter-family comet (JFC) population. Our results indicate that objects located between Jupiter and Saturn with a Tisserand parameter relative to Jupiter ($T_J$) of approximately 3 can be efficiently transferred to orbits with perihelia ($q$) less than 4 AU within the next millennium. Simulations suggest that additional objects similar to LD2 will likely transition into the inner Solar System soon, all possessing low $\Delta$V relative to Jupiter. We analyzed the orbital element distributions resulting from a single encounter with Jupiter, demonstrating that objects starting with perihelia near Jupiter are effectively scattered to $q<4$ AU. Furthermore, about 55% of the transitioning objects in our simulated group undergo at least one Jovian encounter before reaching $q<4$ AU. We conclude that a spacecraft positioned near Jupiter would be ideally situated to rendezvous, match orbits with, and accompany LD2 into the inner Solar System, offering a unique chance to observe the initiation of vigorous activity in a pristine comet *in situ*. Finally, we explore the potential for identifying further targets for similar studies using upcoming observational capabilities.

This paper presents algorithms to determine whether two finite-dimensional Lie algebras are isomorphic and, if so, to compute the corresponding isomorphism. It also introduces methods for identifying algebraic parameter relations to assess the isomorphism of parameterized Lie algebras. All Lie algebras discussed are defined over a field $\F$, where $\F$ is either the complex numbers ($\C$) or the real numbers ($\R$). The paper includes several illustrative examples demonstrating the practicality and efficacy of these proposed algorithms.

Recent progress in Virtual Reality (VR) technology, coupled with the growing availability of VR hardware, has facilitated numerous consumer-focused applications. However, novice developers often find creating interactive VR scenes a difficult and labor-intensive process due to the high technical expertise required, which they frequently lack. This barrier prevents novices from effectively creating, modifying, and running their own interactive VR environments. While existing authoring tools for interactive VR are promising, they predominantly target expert professionals, overlooking novices with limited programming skills. To reduce this entry barrier, we introduce VREUD, an open-source, web-based End-User Development (EUD) tool designed for the rapid construction and execution of interactive VR scenes. Regarding scene creation, VREUD allows users to define VR environments, including interactions and tasks. Additionally, it supports the execution and immersive experience of these scenes on VR head-mounted displays. Through a user study, we evaluated VREUD's effectiveness, efficiency, and user satisfaction, finding promising results that demonstrate its potential to empower novices in building their own interactive VR experiences.

Let G and K be groupoids. We introduce the concept of a (G_{\alpha},K_{\beta})-set and establish a corresponding duality theorem, thereby generalizing the duality theorem for graded algebras over groups. Specifically, for a unital G-graded algebra A and a finite split G-set X, we demonstrate an isomorphism between the category of left A-modules graded by X and the category of left A \#_{\alpha}^{G}X-modules. Leveraging this isomorphism, we construct a Morita context.

Word embeddings offer a static, distributional representation of word contexts within a corpus, derived from word co-occurrence patterns. Although these models have demonstrated significant utility in machine learning, they can produce uneven semantic and syntactic representations and inadvertently encode biases inherent in their training data. Research indicates that post-processing embeddings using information from lexical dictionaries can enhance semantic associations and overall quality. Building on this concept, we introduce a system called "interactive refitting," which adapts post-processing techniques to tackle some of the most significant qualitative flaws in word embeddings. Our method enables humans to interactively identify and resolve potential quality issues. This approach bypasses the debate over who defines bias or other quality concerns affecting downstream tasks, allowing organizations to address specific issues at a granular level through an iterative process. Furthermore, it provides deeper insights into the impact of both original word embeddings and their refinements on machine learning pipelines.

This paper presents a 2021 update to a phenomenological framework for inelastic scattering of neutrinos and electrons off nucleons. The model employs effective leading-order parton distribution functions alongside a novel scaling variable, $\xi_w$, which effectively captures non-perturbative effects when combined with multiplicative $K$ factors at low $Q^2$. It successfully describes all available inelastic charged-lepton-nucleon scattering data from HERA, NMC, BCDMS, SLAC, and JLab, spanning from extremely high $Q^2$ down to the $Q^2=0$ photo-production limit. Designed for analyzing neutrino oscillation experiments in the few GeV range, the 2021 revision specifically addresses the distinction between axial and vector structure functions, significantly improving agreement with total neutrino-nucleon cross-section measurements. While primarily intended for hadronic final state masses $W$ exceeding 1.8 GeV, the inclusion of additional parameters allows the model to also describe average neutrino cross sections within the resonance region down to $W$=1.4 GeV.

The classification of equilibria for the spatially homogeneous Boltzmann equation involving Fermi-Dirac particles is established for any $n$-dimensional velocity space where $n\ge 2$. While this classification was previously proven for $n=3$ in \cite{Lu2001}, the current proof for $n\ge 2$ relies on a recent finding regarding the characterization of Euclidean balls across all dimensions $\ge 2$.

Continual or lifelong learning has long posed a significant challenge in machine learning, particularly within natural language processing (NLP). While state-of-the-art models like BERT have revolutionized the field with exceptional performance in multitask settings, they struggle with catastrophic forgetting when encountering continuous data streams characterized by shifting distributions. This paper presents DRILL, a new continual learning architecture designed for open-domain text classification. DRILL employs a biologically inspired, self-organizing neural structure to selectively gate latent representations from BERT in a task-incremental fashion. Experimental results show that DRILL surpasses existing methods in realistic scenarios involving imbalanced, non-stationary data without requiring prior knowledge of task boundaries. To our knowledge, DRILL represents the first application of a self-organizing neural architecture for open-domain lifelong learning in NLP.

The architecture of dwarf galaxies serves as a critical tool for investigating stellar feedback and environmental impacts. Leveraging a unique dataset of 223 low-mass satellites from the Exploration of Local VolumE Satellites (ELVES) Survey, we analyzed the structures of dwarfs within the stellar mass range $10^{5.5}<M_\star<10^{8.5}$M$_\odot$. Our survey covers approximately 80% of massive Local Volume hosts ($M_K<-22.4$ mag), with a sample of dwarf satellites that is complete down to luminosities of $M_V<-9$ mag and surface brightnesses of $\mu_{0,V}<26.5$ mag arcsec$^{-2}$ within roughly 200 projected kpc. By categorizing satellites into early- and late-type populations, we discovered that their mass-size relations are nearly identical, differing by only $\sim5\%$. This consistency suggests that the transition and quenching of a late-type dwarf into an early-type involves minimal size evolution. Based on apparent ellipticity distributions, we deduced the intrinsic shapes of both samples. When combined with existing literature data, our findings indicate that both dwarf types become thicker at lower luminosities, though early-types remain rounder at a fixed luminosity. Furthermore, comparing Local Volume satellites with those from the cores of the Virgo and Fornax clusters reveals that cluster dwarfs share similar scaling relations with Local Volume early-types but are approximately 10% larger at fixed mass, a discrepancy attributed to tidal heating in cluster environments. These structural insights provide a valuable benchmark for simulations concerning dwarf galaxy formation and the evolution of irregulars into spheroidals.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become the primary solution for graph machine learning tasks due to their capacity to generate high-quality representations from graph-structured data. However, aggregating vast amounts of real-world graph data for GNN training is often impractical because of privacy issues, regulatory constraints, and commercial competition. Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as the standard approach for collaboratively training models across distributed edge devices without centralization. Despite this, applying GNNs within a federated context remains poorly defined and presents significant statistical and system-level challenges. This paper introduces SpreadGNN, an innovative multi-task federated training framework that uniquely operates without a central server and handles partial labels. SpreadGNN adapts federated multi-task learning to realistic serverless environments for GNNs and employs a new optimization algorithm, Decentralized Periodic Averaging SGD (DPA-SGD), which offers convergence guarantees for decentralized multi-task learning. Empirical evaluations on various non-I.I.D. distributed datasets for graph-level molecular property prediction with partial labels demonstrate the framework's effectiveness. Results indicate that SpreadGNN surpasses GNN models trained via traditional central server-dependent federated learning, even under constrained topologies. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/FedML-AI/SpreadGNN.

This presentation offers a broad, non-technical overview of supersymmetry and its contemporary applications within strong-coupling quantum field theories and phenomenology. It was delivered as an invited talk at the conference {\sl Frontiers of Fundamental Physics, FFP16, May 23-26, 2022, Istanbul, T\"urkiye}.

Conventional MXenes have garnered significant attention due to their fascinating electronic and mechanical characteristics, as well as the versatility of their elemental makeup and chemical functionalization. Nevertheless, semiconducting MXenes featuring direct band gaps remain exceptionally scarce in the existing literature. Consequently, expanding the MXene family beyond carbides and nitrides to include materials with distinctive properties continues to be an extraordinary and captivating area of research.

Colloidal gels represent a significant class of materials with broad applications across various contexts. However, existing as matter far from equilibrium, they display a diverse array of perplexing time-dependent behaviors, such as strengthening just before catastrophic failure. Notably, an exceptionally simple model known as "sticky spheres" accurately captures these intricate phenomena. This review examines recent advances in understanding colloidal gels through real-space analysis and particle-resolved studies. We address the difficulties in establishing appropriate experimental systems where colloidal particles match the solvent's refractive index and density. Furthermore, we explore efforts to elucidate the particle-level mechanisms behind gel rigidity and trace the evolution of our understanding of time-dependent dynamics, ranging from initial aggregation to ageing. The discussion then shifts to how colloidal gels respond to deformation, followed by an examination of more complex systems involving anisotropic particles and mixtures. Finally, we highlight certain exotic materials that exhibit similar properties.

This study investigates the potential of a mismatched transmission line segment for bandpass filtering applications and provides a corresponding analytical model. The results indicate that the transfer characteristics of this mismatched section closely mimic those of a narrow bandpass filter, featuring a steeper roll-off. It was demonstrated that the response's center frequency is determined by both the length of the mismatched section and the dielectric material of the line. Furthermore, the center frequency can be tuned to a specific target value by modifying the dielectric profile along the line's length. These findings were validated using parallel wire transmission lines of varying lengths filled with liquid dielectrics. The research also revealed that mismatched transmission lines can be utilized to create a highly sensitive sensing mechanism capable of detecting minute variations in small volumes of liquid dielectrics.

Advanced driver assistance and automated driving systems depend on risk estimation modules to anticipate and prevent hazardous scenarios. Existing approaches often rely on costly sensor configurations and intricate processing workflows, which restricts their accessibility and reliability. To overcome these limitations, we propose a new deep learning framework for action recognition that classifies risky lane-change maneuvers within brief video segments captured by a single camera. Our designed deep spatiotemporal classification network leverages the pre-trained, state-of-the-art instance segmentation model, Mask R-CNN, to extract spatial features. The Long-Short Term Memory (LSTM) components and subsequent classification layers were trained using a semi-synthetic lane-change dataset featuring annotated risk labels. We conducted an extensive evaluation of various state-of-the-art feature extractors to identify the optimal network architecture and training methodology. The proposed network achieved the highest performance with an Area Under the Curve (AUC) score of 0.937. Our source code and trained models are freely available as open-source resources.

Determining the greatest common divisor (GCD) for polynomials with real or complex coefficients, represented in any specific basis, is an ill-posed problem. Despite this, solutions remain necessary for numerous applications, driving significant interest in the hybrid symbolic-numeric domain toward computing the GCD of approximate polynomials—where the term explicitly signifies minor coefficient uncertainties. This paper presents an algorithm, derived from work by Victor Ya. Pan, to compute an approximate GCD for a pair of such polynomials defined in a Lagrange basis. Specifically, the polynomials are provided via their approximate values at distinct, known points. The method proceeds by determining the roots of each polynomial using a Lagrange basis companion matrix, clustering these roots to detect multiplicity, and subsequently combining the polynomials to identify their GCD. Crucially, the algorithm never converts to the monomial basis, thereby maintaining the favorable conditioning inherent to the original Lagrange representation. We examine both the benefits and limitations of this approach. The computational expense is primarily dictated by the root-finding phase; absent specialized eigenvalue algorithms, the cost scales cubically with the polynomial degrees. While this complexity could theoretically be lowered, the current implementation does not pursue such optimizations.

This paper determines the attainable set for a control system defined on a free Carnot group of rank 3 and step 2, utilizing positive controls. Such systems are relevant to free Lie semigroup theory, probability estimates involving inequalities for independent random variables, nilpotent approximations of robotic controls, and cusp-free contour recovery in image processing. By applying the Pontryagin maximum principle to the time-optimal control problem, we analyze the boundary of this set. Our study covers extremal trajectories associated with bang-bang, singular, and mixed controls, and we derive upper bounds on the number of switchings for optimal controls. These findings enable a parametrization of the faces comprising the attainable set's boundary.

Quantum metrology seeks to enhance measurement precision by leveraging quantum resources, with quantum criticality emerging as a particularly efficient tool. While criticality-based protocols typically function effectively in decoherence-free environments, this study investigates whether the divergence of inverted variance remains achievable under noisy conditions near a quantum phase transition (QPT). Using the quantum Rabi model (QRM) as a case study, we derive an analytical expression for the inverted variance and demonstrate that noise can cause this variance to converge over time. As the system approaches the critical point, the maximum inverted variance increases according to a power law with an exponent of -1.2; notably, the absolute value of this exponent is smaller than the noise-free value of 2. Furthermore, we observe that the maximum inverted variance exhibits power-law dependencies on both the relaxation rate and temperature. Given the high sensitivity of metrological precision to noise, we propose applying squeezing operations to the initial state as a strategy to mitigate decoherence. Additionally, we examine criticality-based metrology under two-photon relaxation. Unlike single-photon relaxation, the quantum dynamics of the inverted variance display distinct behavior, failing to oscillate at a consistent frequency relative to rescaled time across different dimensionless coupling strengths. Remarkably, while the maximum inverted variance still follows a power-law relationship with the energy gap, the exponent becomes positive and varies with the coupling strength. These findings suggest that, in the presence of two-photon relaxation, criticality may degrade rather than enhance precision, a phenomenon attributable to the non-linearity introduced by this type of relaxation.

Music Emotion Recognition (MER) stands as a pivotal challenge within Music Information Retrieval (MIR) research. Due to inherent subjectivity and genre-specific variations in emotional cues, creating robust and generalizable models remains difficult. A crucial advancement involves elucidating what models learn from data and how specific predictions are generated. Our prior research demonstrated how to explain model outputs by mapping spectrogram segments to high-level emotion predictions through interpretable perceptual features; however, this approach lacked intuitive musical clarity at the spectrogram level. This study addresses that limitation by integrating audioLIME, a source-separation-based explainer, with mid-level perceptual features to establish a clear, intuitive pathway from raw audio to emotion predictions. We validate the efficacy of this methodology by utilizing it to identify and correct biases in an emotion prediction model.

Accurately identifying phenotypes is crucial for advancing disease biology, with significant practical implications for healthcare and the life sciences. The inherent complexities and noise found in electronic health records (EHRs) have driven the integration of machine learning into phenotypic discovery. While recent studies have prioritized developing predictive subtypes for clinical decision support, this work shifts focus to the noise causing phenotypic misclassification, a factor that can diminish a phenotype's capacity to reveal associations in genome-wide association studies (GWAS). By integrating anchor learning with transformer architectures in our proposed model, AnchorBERT, we successfully detect genomic associations that were previously identifiable only in large consortium studies involving five times more cases. Furthermore, even when the number of available controls is reduced by 50%, our model retains 40% more significant genomic associations from the GWAS catalog compared to standard phenotype definitions.

\keywords{Phenotyping \and Machine Learning \and Semi-Supervised \and Genetic Association Studies \and Biological Discovery}

When titanium nitride (TiN) Microwave Kinetic Inductance Detectors (MKIDs), cooled to temperatures $T \le T_c / 20$ (where $T_c \simeq 4.6~\text{K}$), are irradiated with optical pulses ($\lambda=405~\text{nm}$), we detect a significant phase response revealing two distinct yet interconnected modes. The initial mode represents the standard transition from Cooper-pair breaking to quasi-particles, generating an expected phase shift. This is succeeded by a substantial inverse response persisting from hundreds of microseconds to several milliseconds, varying with temperature. We suggest modeling this inverse pulse as a thermal perturbation of the superconductor coupled with two-level systems (TLS), which lowers the dielectric constant, alters the capacitance, and consequently shifts the resonance frequency. The proportion of TLS activated by illumination is comparable to the ratio of the inductor's area to the total resonator area.

We present a novel method for object characterization, designed to precisely describe small, isolated inclusions within potential field inverse problems, including those in electrostatics, magnetostatics, and related low-frequency Maxwell scenarios. Key applications encompass detecting ferrous unexploded ordnance (UXO) via magnetostatic measurements, modeling small conducting inclusions for electrical impedance tomography (EIT) in medical imaging, conducting geological surveys using electrical resistivity imaging (ERT), enabling electrosensing fish to identify food and navigate, and determining the effective properties of dilute composites. Building upon the concept of the generalised polarizability tensor (GPT), this approach offers an alternative to the compacted GPT (CGPT). We term these new characterisations harmonic GPTs (HGPTs), as their coefficients represent products of harmonic polynomials. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the number of independent HGPT coefficients required for object characterization can be substantially reduced by leveraging the object's symmetry group. We propose a systematic method to identify the subspace of symmetric harmonic polynomials invariant under the group and calculate its dimension, thereby allowing for the determination of independent HGPT coefficients across various symmetry groups.

We present polynomial couplings, an extension of probabilistic couplings, to create an algorithm for computing equivalence relations that elevates probabilistic bisimulation to polynomial differential equations, a common framework for dynamical systems in science and engineering. This algorithm operates in polynomial time and complements traditional partition-refinement methods by: (a) performing local system exploration, potentially deriving equivalences without examining the entire set of differential equations; (b) supporting enhancement via up-to techniques; and (c) enabling the specification of pairs to exclude from the output. A prototype demonstrates these benefits through case studies in systems biology for model reduction and comparison. Significantly, we report runtimes four orders of magnitude faster than partition-refinement approaches when disproving equivalences between Markov chains.

Although supersymmetry is powerful, deriving exact closed-form expressions for the protected operator spectra of interacting superconformal field theories (SCFTs) remains challenging. This paper advances a solution for the "simplest" interacting 4D $\mathcal{N}=2$ SCFT, the minimal Argyres-Douglas (MAD) theory, by presenting two findings that extend beyond the well-known Coulomb and Schur sectors. First, we determine the exact closed-form spectrum of multiplets containing operators chiral under any $\mathcal{N}=1\subset\mathcal{N}=2$ superconformal subalgebra. We contend that this "full" chiral sector (FCS) represents the simplest configuration permitted by unitarity for a theory possessing a Coulomb branch. Up to a rescaling of $U(1)_r$ quantum numbers and the absence of a finite number of states, the MAD FCS is isospectral to the FCS of a free $\mathcal{N}=2$ Abelian gauge theory; in terms of superconformal representation theory, this reduces the unknowns to the spectrum of the poorly understood $\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{R,r(j,\bar j)}$ multiplets. Our second result provides an exact closed-form count for the number of $\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{0,r(j,0)}$ multiplets for any $r$ and $j$ within the MAD theory. We argue that this sub-sector is likewise as simple as unitarity allows for a theory with a Coulomb branch and admits a natural mapping to the corresponding sector of the free $\mathcal{N}=2$ Abelian gauge theory. These findings support a conjecture regarding the complete local operator algebra of the MAD theory.

This study examines the interaction between collective optical responses and both static and dynamic molecular disorder using simplified effective Hamiltonians for ensembles of two-level emitters situated within and outside a single-mode cavity. Environmental disorder is simulated by randomly varying molecular transition frequencies and the coupling between emitters and the electromagnetic field, while also accounting for intermolecular interactions and orientational disorder. The research explores how these factors influence new features in steady-state absorption (outside the cavity), transmission spectra (inside the cavity), and the yield of local molecular processes, such as unimolecular reactions. Outside the cavity, collective behavior is evident in the linewidths of absorption and emission spectra, as well as local chemical yields. In contrast, inside the cavity, collective behavior mainly dictates Rabi splitting. The effects of intermolecular interactions under orientational disorder are also analyzed. Generally, increasing disorder reduces the collective nature of the molecular response (decreasing the effective N), leading to a contraction of the Rabi splitting, particularly with orientational disorder. Furthermore, static disorder is found to be more detrimental to collective behavior than dynamic disorder.

This paper investigates the electrostatic and structural characteristics of pH-responsive polyelectrolyte brushes using a strong stretching theory that incorporates excluded volume interactions, the density of chargeable sites, and the Born energy difference across the brush layer. Within a free energy framework, we derive self-consistent field equations to analyze the electrostatic properties between two such brushes. Our findings reveal that in the space separating two pH-responsive polyelectrolyte brushes, both the central electrostatic potential and the osmotic pressure rise with increasing excluded volume interactions and the density of chargeable sites on the polymer molecules. Crucially, we demonstrate that as two pH-responsive polyelectrolyte brushes approach one another, the brush thickness decreases; furthermore, larger excluded volume interactions and higher densities of chargeable sites lead to more significant brush contraction. Additionally, we examine how factors such as pH, the number of Kuhn monomers, charge site density, lateral separation between brushes, and Kuhn length influence the electrostatic and structural properties, specifically in relation to the exclusion volume interaction. Finally, we explore the impact of the Born energy difference on both the brush thickness and the osmotic pressure between two pH-responsive polyelectrolyte brushes.

Decanol droplets within a thin sodium decanoate layer containing sodium chloride display bifurcation branching growth driven by the interplay of osmotic pressure, diffusion, and surface tension. This study investigates whether applying an electrical potential difference alters the morphology of these branching droplets. By analyzing the graph-theoretic structure and applying various complexity metrics, we determined that the applied current generally increases droplet complexity, as evidenced by a rise in the number of connected components and nodes in their graph representations, alongside enhanced morphological complexity and reduced compressibility.

The dynamics of a propagating quantum radiation pulse interacting with a localized quantum system can be modeled using a cascaded master equation featuring distinct initially and finally populated input and output field modes [Phys. Rev. Lett. 123, 123604 (2019), arXiv:1902.09833v3]. By shifting to a suitable interaction picture, we reveal the standard Jaynes-Cummings Hamiltonian acting between the scatterer and a superposition of the initial and final modes, with coupling strength determined by the amplitude of the traveling pulse. This transformation also uncovers a coupling between the scatterer and an orthogonal combination of these two modes. The resulting transformed master equation provides valuable insights into the system's dynamics and enables numerically efficient computations.

Reinforcement learning with neural networks (RLNN) has shown significant potential across various domains, including quantum information theory. This study applies RLNN to quantum hypothesis testing to identify optimal measurement strategies for distinguishing among multiple quantum states $\{ \rho_{j} \}$ while minimizing error rates. However, when candidate states involve systems with numerous qubit subsystems, performing the optimal measurement on the entire system is practically unfeasible. Instead, we utilize RLNN to derive locally-adaptive strategies that are experimentally viable, measuring only one subsystem per round. Numerical results confirm that RLNN effectively identifies the optimal local approach even for systems comprising up to 20 subsystems, and its performance matches or surpasses a modified locally greedy method in random trials. Although RLNN excels at designing adaptive local strategies, a substantial performance gap often exists between locally-adaptive and optimal collective measurements. Building on prior research, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions under which collective protocols strictly outperform local ones. Furthermore, we present a new example that represents the simplest known state set displaying a significant disparity between local and collective protocols. This finding highlights intriguing new questions regarding the divide between theoretically optimal and practically implementable measurement strategies.

Optimizing ranking-based metrics like Average Precision (AP) is notoriously difficult because their non-differentiable nature prevents direct optimization via gradient descent. To address this, we propose Smooth-AP, a plug-and-play objective function that optimizes a smoothed approximation of AP, enabling straightforward end-to-end training of deep networks. We also provide an analysis demonstrating why directly optimizing AP yields advantages over other deep metric learning losses. Our experiments apply Smooth-AP to standard retrieval benchmarks (Stanford Online Products and VehicleID) as well as larger-scale datasets (INaturalist for fine-grained retrieval, and VGGFace2 and IJB-C for face retrieval). In every scenario, Smooth-AP outperforms the state-of-the-art, particularly on large-scale datasets, thereby validating its effectiveness and scalability in real-world applications.

This work presents MaRF, a new framework designed to synthesize the Martian environment using multiple sets of images from rover cameras. The goal is to create a 3D representation of Mars' surface to tackle critical challenges in planetary exploration, including geology, simulated navigation, and shape analysis. While various methods exist for reconstructing the Martian surface, they typically depend on traditional computer graphics techniques that demand substantial computational resources and struggle to generalize to unseen scenes or adapt to new rover imagery. MaRF overcomes these drawbacks by leveraging Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs), a technique that renders complex scenes by optimizing a continuous volumetric function based on a sparse collection of images. To accelerate the learning phase, we substituted the sparse set of rover images with Neural Graphics Primitives (NGPs)—fixed-length vectors trained to retain original image information in a much more compact format. The experimental section validates this approach by generating environments from real Mars datasets collected by the Curiosity rover, Perseverance rover, and Ingenuity helicopter, all accessible via the Planetary Data System (PDS).

Let $ES_{d}(n)$ denote the minimum integer such that every set of $ES_{d}(n)$ points in general position within $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ includes $n$ points forming a convex position. In 1960, Erd\H{o}s and Szekeres demonstrated that $ES_{2}(n) \geq 2^{n-2} + 1$ and famously conjectured that their construction is optimal. This conjecture was nearly resolved by Suk in 2017, who proved that $ES_{2}(n) \leq 2^{n+o(n)}$. In this work, we establish that $ES_{d}(n) = 2^{o(n)}$ for all dimensions $d \geq 3$. Specifically, this result confirms that in higher dimensions, a significantly smaller number of points is required to guarantee a convex polytope with $n$ vertices compared to the planar case.

We utilized Keck NIR spectroscopy on a sample of nine dwarf galaxies with stellar masses below 10$^{10}$ M$_\odot$ to verify AGN activity and identify galaxy-wide, AGN-driven outflows via coronal line (CL) emission. Strong CL detections were confirmed in five of these galaxies (55%), exhibiting line ratios inconsistent with shocks, thereby validating the presence of AGNs. This detection rate aligns with findings from larger samples of more massive galaxies hosting type 1 and 2 AGNs. To explore the link between CLs and global outflows, we analyzed the kinematics of the CL regions and examined how gas velocity scales with the ionization potential of various CLs. Furthermore, complementary Keck KCWI observations revealed that outflow velocities measured in [Si VI] are typically higher than those in [O III]. Notably, galaxies exhibiting the fastest [O III] outflows also display the highest [Si VI] luminosities. Additionally, the absence of $J$-band CN absorption features—commonly linked to younger stellar populations—offers further support for the conclusion that AGNs drive these outflows in low-mass galaxies.

Self-similar approximation theory enables the construction of effective sums for asymptotic series. By utilizing the method of self-similar factor approximants, researchers calculate critical temperatures and exponents for the three-dimensional $O(N)$-symmetric $\varphi^4$ field theory through the summation of asymptotic $\varepsilon$ expansions. This approach proves to be significantly simpler than alternative summation methods that rely on complex numerical computations, yet it maintains comparable levels of accuracy.

Nitrogen stands as one of the most plentiful elements within the interstellar medium (ISM), making it an ideal probe for investigating diverse astrophysical settings, from novae to active galactic nuclei. This study offers a comprehensive examination of the gaseous N K-edge by utilizing high-resolution {\it XMM-Newton} spectra from 12 Galactic and 40 extragalactic sources. For each object, we determined column densities for the ionic species {\rm N}~{\sc i} through {\rm N}~{\sc vii}, which correspond to the cold, warm, and hot phases of the local Galactic ISM. Our results indicate that the column densities of the cold-warm component diminish as Galactic latitude increases, whereas the hot component remains constant. Additionally, the distribution of cold column densities aligns well with UV observations. This work represents the inaugural detailed analysis of nitrogen K-edge absorption in the ISM conducted using high-resolution X-ray spectra.

Magnetic skyrmions represent promising topological spin textures for the development of future high-density, nonvolatile memory devices. Gaining a clear understanding of how skyrmions move under current drive when subjected to deformation is essential, yet an analytical framework for this phenomenon has been elusive. In this work, we expand upon Thiele's model by incorporating both radial and tangential forces. We attribute skyrmion deformation to current-induced breaking of rotational symmetry, encompassing effects such as magnetization canting and changes in domain wall width. Our model's predictions regarding skyrmion radius and nonlinear behavior align well with micromagnetic simulation data. Furthermore, we demonstrate that applying an in-plane magnetic field can suppress skyrmion deformation and even induce compression. Ultimately, our model offers a general approach for analyzing skyrmion deformation and may stimulate new applications rooted in nonlinear skyrmion dynamics.

We derive precise analytical formulas for the spatial Fourier spectrum of the fundamental bright soliton solution to the $(1+1)$-dimensional nonlinear Schrödinger equation. Like the Gaussian profile, the hyperbolic secant shape exhibits shape preservation under Fourier transformation. We additionally verify that the fundamental soliton adheres to key properties, including Parseval's relation and the stretch-bandwidth reciprocity principle. These fundamental bright solitons have extensive applications in nonlinear fiber optics and optical telecommunications.

We present a vast collection of strongly regular graphs (SRGs) defined by parameters $(n, k, \lambda, \mu)$ where $n < 100$. This collection is generated using Godsil-McKay (GM) switching with a $4,n-4$ partition and Wang-Qiu-Hu (WQH) switching with partitions of type $3,3,n-6$ or $4,4,n-8$. Typically, the process begins with highly symmetric graphs derived from finite geometries. A significant number of these graphs are novel; for example, we identified 16,565,438 SRGs with parameters $(81, 30, 9, 12)$, whereas only 15 appear to have been previously documented in existing literature. Additionally, we offer statistical data regarding the sizes of the associated automorphism groups and successfully identify the recently discovered Kr\v{c}adinac partial geometry, thereby establishing a third construction method for it.

Envy-freeness up to any good (EFX) offers a robust and intuitive fairness guarantee for allocating indivisible items, yet the questions of their universal existence and efficient computation remain unresolved. This paper investigates EFX alongside other economic properties under lexicographic preferences—a prominent model in AI and economics. Contrasting with findings for additive valuations, we demonstrate not only that EFX and Pareto optimal allocations exist in this setting but also provide an algorithmic characterization for both. Furthermore, we identify mechanisms that are additionally strategyproof, non-bossy, and neutral. However, when efficiency is elevated to rank-maximality, we establish non-existence and computational hardness; conversely, we show that tractability is regained by relaxing EFX to the maximin share guarantee (MMS).

To date, topological band theory has primarily focused on systems defined by standard eigenvalue problems. In this work, we extend this framework to encompass generalized eigenvalue problems (GEVPs). Our investigation reveals that non-Hermitian topological band structures can arise even when the underlying matrices in a GEVP are Hermitian. This finding is substantiated through the analysis of a two-dimensional toy model, which exhibits symmetry-protected exceptional rings (SPERs) despite involving only Hermitian matrices. Notably, these SPERs are safeguarded by an emergent symmetry specific to GEVP-based systems. Additionally, these structures provide insight into the characteristic dispersion observed in hyperbolic metamaterials during experiments.

The ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider analyzed 36.1 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data from 2015 and 2016, acquired at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV, to search for a heavy neutral Higgs boson, $A$, decaying into a $Z$ boson and a heavier Higgs boson, $H$. The analysis targeted the decay chain where the $Z$ boson produces electrons or muons and the $H$ boson decays into a $b$-quark pair. No significant evidence for $A$ boson production was observed. At the 95% confidence level, the upper limits on the product of the production cross-section and the branching ratio for $H\rightarrow bb$ were determined to be between 14 and 830 fb for gluon-gluon fusion and between 26 and 570 fb for $b$-associated production, covering $H$ boson masses from 130 to 700 GeV and $A$ boson masses from 230 to 800 GeV. These findings are discussed within the framework of the two-Higgs-doublet model.

Although recent neural vocoders typically employ WaveNet-like architectures to model long-term waveform dependencies, they demand substantial parameters to achieve adequate performance. This paper introduces an efficient network called location-variable convolution to address this issue. Unlike WaveNet's reliance on unified convolution kernels for arbitrary waveform dependencies, location-variable convolutions utilize a kernel predictor to generate multiple kernel sets derived from the mel-spectrum; each set is then applied to specific waveform intervals. By integrating this approach with WaveGlow, we developed an efficient vocoder named MelGlow. Experimental results on the LJSpeech dataset demonstrate that MelGlow outperforms WaveGlow at smaller model sizes, confirming both the effectiveness and the optimization potential of location-variable convolutions.

We introduce a selection of radio-loud (RL) quasi-stellar object (QSO) candidates at high redshifts ($z\gtrsim5.7$) by combining data from the radio Rapid ASKAP Continuum Survey (RACS) at 888 MHz and the optical/near-infrared Dark Energy Survey (DES). Specifically, we identified six candidates with flux densities exceeding $S_{\rm 888MHz}>1$ mJy beam$^{-1}$ and DES magnitudes brighter than 21.3 in the $i$-band, utilizing the dropout technique. From this group, we confirmed the high-redshift nature ($z\sim6.1$) of two sources, placing them among the highest-redshift RL QSOs identified to date. Our observations with Gemini-South/GMOS revealed that neither object displays a prominent Ly$\alpha$ emission line, suggesting they are likely weak emission-line QSOs with radio jets. This finding supports the emerging trend of an increasing fraction of weak emission-line QSOs in recent literature. However, additional multiwavelength observations are required to better constrain the properties of these QSOs and their relativistic jets. Based on these discoveries, we estimated the space density of RL QSOs between redshifts 5.9 and 6.4 to be $0.13^{+0.18}_{-0.09}$, a value consistent with expectations derived from our current understanding of the blazar population up to $z\sim5$.

We present a generalized theory of optical beam shifts, covering both the Goos-Hanchen and Imbert-Fedorov effects, specifically for near-normal incidence where the incident angle approaches the beam's angular divergence. This regime naturally accounts for the strong enhancement of these shifts previously reported in literature [ACS Photonics 6, 2530 (2019)], with our experimental findings offering a rigorous validation of the theory. Furthermore, the developed framework reveals that the anomalous enhancement of beam shifts originates from a unified Berry phase singularity. We also introduce a straightforward experimental setup utilizing a quarter-wave plate to simultaneously detect giant transverse and longitudinal spatial and angular beam shifts. These findings hold significant potential for applications in spin-orbit photonics, polarization optics, sensing technologies, and quantum weak measurements.

We introduce a novel empirical template for iron emission in active galactic nuclei (AGN) spanning the $4000-5600$ Å range. This template is derived from the spectrum of the narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxy Mrk 493, observed using the Hubble Space Telescope. Unlike the canonical iron template object I Zw 1, Mrk 493 exhibits narrower broad-line widths, reduced reddening, and a less extreme Eddington ratio, rendering it an optimal candidate for template creation. Through multicomponent spectral decomposition, we constructed a template that includes all permitted and forbidden Fe II lines identified in the Mrk 493 spectrum within this wavelength range, alongside lines from Ti II, Ni II, and Cr II. We validated the template by fitting it to AGN spectra with diverse iron emission characteristics and provided a comprehensive comparison against other commonly used monolithic and multi-component iron emission templates. Our analysis indicates that the new template generally achieves the best fit (lowest $\chi^2$) relative to other widely used monolithic empirical templates. Furthermore, it delivers more precise spectral measurements, notably offering a significantly improved match for derived Balmer line profiles (H$\beta$, H$\gamma$, H$\delta$) compared to alternative templates. Our comparative tests reveal that the selection of an iron template can induce systematic biases in H$\beta$ line width measurements, which in turn affects single-epoch black hole mass estimates by approximately $0.1$ dex on average, with individual cases potentially varying by $0.3-0.5$ dex.

Modeling noise from turbulent jets is challenging due to their low acoustic efficiency, as only a minuscule portion of near-field turbulent kinetic energy converts to far-field sound waves. Consequently, jet-noise models must precisely isolate this small, acoustically efficient component amidst largely inefficient fluctuations. This study identifies that efficient near-field source using large-eddy-simulation data to inform a predictive model. The methodology employs the resolvent framework, where the source manifests as nonlinear fluctuation terms acting as forcing functions on linearized Navier-Stokes equations. First, the forcing required to generate the dominant spectral proper orthogonal decomposition modes in the acoustic field for a Mach 0.4 jet is determined. Second, radiating components are isolated by retaining only those with supersonic phase speeds. Although this specific component accounts for less than 0.05% of the total forcing energy, it drives the majority of the acoustic response, particularly at peak downstream radiation angles. Finally, an empirical model is proposed for these identified acoustically efficient forcing components. Validated across various Mach numbers and flight-stream conditions, the model predicts noise with within 2 dB accuracy over a broad range of frequencies, downstream angles, and flight scenarios.

The TRAPUM collaboration utilized the MeerKAT telescope to investigate the young Small Magellanic Cloud pulsar J0058-7218, located within the supernova remnant IKT 16 and previously identified in X-rays by XMM-Newton, for pulsed radio emissions. After conducting three 2-hour L-band observations using MeerKAT's core dishes, we found no significant dispersed, pulsed radio signal, establishing an upper flux density limit of 7.0 μJy at 1284 MHz. This sensitivity surpasses prior Parkes L-band searches by nearly a factor of seven. These results imply that PSR J0058-7218's radio beam may not be directed toward Earth, or that it resembles a rare class of Pulsar Wind Nebulae systems with extremely low radio efficiency, similar to PSR B0540-6919 or the Large Magellanic Cloud Crab pulsar analogue. Additionally, we searched for bright, dispersed single radio pulses but detected no candidates exceeding a fluence of 93 mJy ms at 1284 MHz.

Accurately predicting vehicle paths is a critical yet difficult task for ensuring the safety of autonomous driving systems. Although numerous research efforts have addressed path prediction, most approaches fail to incorporate lane information and do not leverage the Transformer architecture. To address these gaps, we introduce Multi-modal Transformer Path Prediction (MTPP), a system designed to forecast the long-term trajectories of target agents by integrating diverse sensor data from self-driving vehicles. Our model employs the Transformer architecture to enhance prediction accuracy. Furthermore, we optimize lane usage by filtering out lanes traveling in the opposite direction of the target agent, as these are unlikely to be chosen, and by concatenating consecutive lane segments to ensure sufficient input length for effective prediction. Comprehensive evaluations on the nuScene, a real-world trajectory forecasting dataset, demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed system.

Identifying and analyzing calcifications in mammograms is vital for effective breast cancer diagnosis, as timely management of suspicious cases to determine their benign or malignant nature can lead to improved patient outcomes. Recent research indicates that deep learning algorithms are capable of learning robust features to detect these anomalies. This study demonstrates that applying random histogram equalization to calcification patches as a data augmentation strategy significantly enhances classification performance. Validated using the CBIS-DDSM dataset across two classification tasks, the proposed method achieved over a 1% increase in both mean accuracy and F1-score when data was equalized with a probability of 0.4, compared to baseline models without this technique. Furthermore, t-tests yielded a p-value of less than 0.0001, confirming the statistical significance of these findings.

Reasoning with equivalences is intuitive for mathematicians, yet in type-theoretic proof assistants, equality remains overly syntactic, making the use of equivalences difficult. While parametricity and univalence offer mechanisms to move programs and proofs across equivalent types, neither achieves seamless automation on its own. This research identifies the individual limitations of these concepts and combines them into "univalent parametricity," a heterogeneous extension that fully enables programming and proving modulo equivalences. We also introduce a lightweight Coq framework that allows users to transparently transfer definitions and theorems between equivalent types as if they were identical. This capability facilitates easy switching between representations that are either easier to reason about or more computationally efficient, provided an equivalence is established. Furthermore, the integration of parametricity and univalence supports a modular approach to transport: basic transport derived from type equivalences can be augmented with additional proofs about function equivalences to lift more programs and proofs while generating more efficient terms. We demonstrate this approach through various examples, including the recent integration of native integers in Coq.

Let $\Omega$ be an open, bounded, and Lipschitz domain within $\mathbb{R}^2$. We examine the torsion problem for the Laplace operator on $\Omega$ subject to Robin boundary conditions. Specifically, we analyze the equality condition in a Talenti-type comparison result, originally established in arXiv:1909.11950. Our findings demonstrate that equality holds if and only if $\Omega$ is a disk and the corresponding torsion function $u$ is radially symmetric.

We present Submillimeter Array (SMA) observations of CO transitions (J=2--1, 3--2, and 6--5) and their isotopologues ($^{13}$CO, $^{18}$CO, and $^{17}$CO) within the disk surrounding the Herbig Ae star HD 163296, achieving a resolution of approximately 2" (250 AU). These data are interpreted using a model that determines the radial and vertical locations of line emission. Initially, we construct a physically consistent accretion disk model featuring an exponentially tapered edge that aligns with the spectral energy distribution and spatially resolved millimeter dust continuum. Subsequently, we refine the disk's vertical structure by utilizing a broad range of excitation conditions probed by the CO lines, especially the seldom-observed J=6--5 transition. By fitting $^{13}$CO data within this framework, we constrain the vertical distribution of CO to exist between a lower limit where CO freezes onto dust grains at T ~ 19 K and an upper limit where CO undergoes photodissociation (corresponding to a hydrogen column density from the disk surface of ~10$^{21}$ cm$^{-2}$). This freeze-out at 19 K causes a marked decrease in gas-phase CO column density beyond a radius of roughly 155 AU, marking a "CO snow line" that we resolve directly. Through fitting the abundances of all CO isotopologues, we derive isotopic ratios for $^{12}$C/$^{13}$C, $^{16}$O/$^{18}$O, and $^{18}$O/$^{17}$O that align with quiescent interstellar gas-phase values. This comprehensive model of the HD 163296 disk illustrates the efficacy of a staged, parametric approach for building unified gas and dust structure models and constraining molecular abundance distributions using resolved, multi-transition, multi-isotope observations.

Modern deep neural networks are notoriously fragile when encountering unseen data, making the recognition of such instances a persistent challenge. Although continual-learning systems inevitably face these unknown concepts, existing research predominantly focuses on mitigating catastrophic interference within learned representations rather than addressing this detection issue. This paper introduces a probabilistic framework that unifies these perspectives through variational inference within a single deep autoencoder. Specifically, we propose constraining the approximate posterior by identifying high-density regions derived from correctly classified data. These constraints serve a dual function: they enable the distinction between unseen out-of-distribution data and known tasks to ensure robustness, while simultaneously allowing a generative replay process to be restricted strictly to in-distribution samples. This approach significantly reduces catastrophic interference while preserving previously acquired knowledge.

We investigate electronic transport in Weyl semimetals featuring spatially varying nodal tilt configurations. Our findings indicate that electron flow can be accurately steered by selecting appropriate tilt profiles. Across a broad parameter range, we demonstrate that electron dynamics are effectively modeled by semiclassical equations of motion analogous to those describing gravitational attraction. This gravitational analogy offers a physically intuitive framework for designing tilt-tronic components, such as electronic lenses. While this approach simplifies the complex description of inhomogeneous solids, comparisons with microscopic lattice simulations reveal that it remains valid only for trajectories sufficiently distant from analogue black holes. Finally, we discuss Berry curvature-induced transverse motion and connect it to the physics of spin precession.

Transforming sequencing reads into a lossless, compact structure that retains all essential biological data remains a significant challenge. While classical methods rely on either string graphs or de Bruijn graphs, each offers specific advantages depending on the use case, the optimal solution would be an index that is both efficient to construct and adaptable to various biological analyses. This paper introduces rBOSS, a novel data structure that approximates this ideal. Although functionally similar to a de Bruijn graph, rBOSS simulates any node label overlap of at least size *m* and supports *k*-length contexts, where *k* and *m* are tunable parameters. Setting *k* to match read length allows rBOSS to emulate a complete string graph. Like most Burrows-Wheeler Transform (BWT) based structures, rBOSS is unidirectional; however, it leverages DNA reverse complement properties to simulate bidirectionality, albeit with specific time and space trade-offs. We developed a genome assembler built upon rBOSS to validate its utility. Experimental findings indicate that with *k* = 100, rBOSS can assemble 185 MB of reads in under 15 minutes while consuming only 110 MB of memory. Furthermore, it generates contigs with an average size exceeding 10,000 bases, doubling the length achieved by a standard de Bruijn graph with a fixed *k*.

This work introduces magic state factory designs for generating $|CCZ\rangle$ and $|T\rangle$ states. The $|CCZ\rangle$ factory adapts Fowler et al.'s surface code lattice surgery methods for fault-tolerant Toffoli gates, achieving a $12d \times 6d$ footprint and yielding one $|CCZ\rangle$ state every $5.5d$ surface code cycles. The $|T\rangle$ factory leverages the output of the $|CCZ\rangle$ unit along with a catalyst $|T\rangle$ state to convert a single $|CCZ\rangle$ into two $|T\rangle$ states. Compared to Fowler et al.'s design, our $|T\rangle$ factory reduces its footprint by 25% while doubling the production speed. We demonstrate that this catalyzed approach generalizes to arbitrary phase angles, with $\theta=22.5^\circ$ offering an especially efficient method for creating $|\sqrt{T}\rangle$ states. Relative to Fowler et al.'s $12d \times 8d \times 6.5d$ $|T\rangle$ factory, our $|CCZ\rangle$ factory can accelerate Toffoli-dominated algorithms—such as Shor's algorithm and Babbush et al.'s chemistry algorithm—by a factor of five. At a physical gate error rate of $10^{-3}$, the CCZ factory generates approximately $10^{10}$ states before an error, which suffices for classically intractable chemistry simulations. For more rigorous applications like Shor's algorithm, expanding the factory footprint by roughly 20% can raise the mean number of states before failure to $\sim 10^{12}$.

Natural, social, and artificial multi-agent systems typically function within dynamic environments, making the capacity to adapt to shifting conditions essential. Achieving an effective collective response hinges on appropriate information exchange between agents, which relies fundamentally on their interaction network. To explore how network topology influences collective responses, we examine the leader-follower linear consensus, a standard model for distributed decision-making, focusing on the system's ability to track a dynamic driving signal across various topologies and scales. The analysis uncovers a complex relationship between the optimal network structure and the frequency of the driving signal. Notably, peak performance occurs when each agent interacts with a specific number of neighbors that decreases monotonically as signal frequency increases and, in sufficiently large systems, becomes independent of system size. This phenomenon was validated through experiments involving collective motion in swarms of land robots, where the emergent responses to both slow and rapid changes in the leader were measured and analyzed across different interaction topologies. These findings offer significant practical insights for designing and understanding distributed systems, emphasizing that dynamically rewiring the interaction network is critical for effective multi-agent operations across diverse time scales.

This work examines the online bin packing problem within two stochastic frameworks. In bin packing, the objective is to minimize the number of unit-sized bins required to store $n$ items with sizes between 0 and 1. First, we analyze the independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) model, where item sizes are drawn independently from an unknown distribution on (0,1]. Items arrive sequentially with revealed sizes, necessitating immediate and irreversible placement into bins. We introduce a straightforward meta-algorithm that converts any offline $\alpha$-asymptotic approximation algorithm into a polynomial-time $(\alpha + \varepsilon)$-competitive online algorithm for the i.i.d. setting. By leveraging the asymptotic Fully Polynomial-Time Approximation Scheme (AFPTAS) for offline bin packing, we achieve a linear-time $(1+\varepsilon)$-competitive algorithm for online bin packing under the i.i.d. model, thereby resolving this problem.

Next, we investigate the random-order model, where an adversary determines the item set, but their arrival order is a uniform random permutation. Kenyon's foundational work [SODA'96] established that the Best-Fit algorithm achieves a competitive ratio of at most 3/2 in this model, while conjecturing a ratio near 1.15; however, breaking the 3/2 barrier remained an open challenge even for restricted cases. Recently, Albers et al. [Algorithmica'21] improved this bound to 5/4 for items larger than 1/3. For this specific case, we refine the analysis to prove that Best-Fit attains a competitive ratio of 1. Furthermore, we advance the field by surpassing the 3/2 threshold for the 3-Partition problem, a difficult special case where all item sizes fall within the interval (1/4, 1/2].

QuaPy is an open-source Python framework dedicated to quantification, also known as supervised prevalence estimation. This process involves training quantifiers—predictors that estimate the relative frequencies of specific classes within unlabelled data—using supervised learning. Although quantification can be simply achieved by applying a standard classifier to unlabelled items and tallying the class assignments, specialized methods designed specifically for this task have demonstrated superior performance. QuaPy offers implementations of various baseline and advanced quantification techniques, tools for model selection tailored to quantification, widely accepted evaluation metrics, and robust evaluation protocols standard in the field. Additionally, the software provides access to commonly used test datasets and visualization utilities to aid in analyzing and interpreting results. QuaPy is open-source, distributed under a BSD-3 license, and can be found at https://github.com/HLT-ISTI/QuaPy or installed via pip at https://pypi.org/project/QuaPy/.

By determining closed-form expressions for geometric elements like covariant derivatives and parallel transport within exponential coordinates, we establish an explicit formulation of the Cucker-Smale (CS) model on the special orthogonal group $\mathrm{SO}(3)$. Utilizing a Lyapunov functional approach combined with La Salle's invariance principle, we investigate the resulting emergent dynamics.
