Parametric analysis of realistic scenarios indicates that in certain nearshore environments, CBIID's contribution to net Lagrangian drift can rival that of Stokes drift, suggesting significant implications for cross-shelf tracer transport.

The Kepler-Heisenberg problem involves analyzing planetary motion around a sun within the Heisenberg group, modeled as a three-dimensional sub-Riemannian manifold. In this framework, the sub-Riemannian Hamiltonian represents kinetic energy, while the gravitational potential corresponds to the fundamental solution of the sub-Laplacian. The system exhibits partial integrability, featuring two first integrals and a dilational momentum conserved by zero-energy orbits. It is established that closed orbits exist for any rational rotation number, all residing within the fundamental zero-energy integrable subsystem. This work demonstrates that, under mild conditions, zero-energy orbits display self-similarity. As a result, these orbits are categorized into three distinct families: future collision, past collision, and quasi-periodicity without collision. Notably, any collision that occurs happens within finite time.

Scalar fields, such as the dilaton, emerge in Quantum Field Theory (QFT) as a consequence of scale symmetry breaking and are also significant in modified gravity frameworks like $F(R)$ gravity and Hořava-Lifshitz gravity. In unified theories, they arise via the compactification of extra dimensions. Beyond addressing compactification scale and size issues, the particles associated with these fields serve as promising candidates for explaining dark energy (DE) and dark matter (DM). This study investigates the mixing dynamics between dilatonic scalar fields ($\phi$) and photons within a magnetized medium, specifically incorporating the parity-violating component of the photon polarization tensor evaluated at finite density. Although this parity-violating term is generally odd with respect to the external magnetic field strength ($eB$), we retain terms up to order $O(eB)$. We demonstrate that in a magnetized environment, a dilatonic scalar field can excite both transverse degrees of freedom (DOF) of photons: one through direct coupling and the other indirectly via the parity-violating term induced by the magnetized medium. Consequently, the mixing dynamics are described by $3 \times 3$ mixing matrices, rendering the medium optically active. This work focuses on the spectro-polarimetric signatures of these particles on the electromagnetic spectra of Gamma-Ray Bursters (GRBs). By analyzing a range of parameters—including magnetic field strength, plasma frequency ($\omega_p$), magnetized volume size, photon coupling strength, and particle mass—we aim to guide the design of space-borne detectors to maximize detection prospects.

This presentation examines the scientific drivers, inherent challenges, and recent breakthroughs in cosmology driven by X-ray cluster number counts. Our forward modelling demonstrates that numerous practical and conceptual limitations can now be resolved. We showcase recent findings from the XMM-XXL survey. The subsequent phase involves applying artificial intelligence to simulations, which circumvents the need for overly complex scaling relation formalisms. This approach yields a substantial reduction in free parameters and grants direct access to cosmological parameters alongside physical mechanisms like AGN feedback, ultimately enabling cluster cosmology without the explicit calculation of cluster masses.

Recent pre-trained language models have achieved state-of-the-art performance in relation extraction (RE) within the biomedical field. This paper investigates the integration of domain-specific knowledge, specifically drug molecular structures, to enhance Drug-Drug Interaction (DDI) prediction from textual data. We introduce BERTChem-DDI, a method that efficiently merges drug embeddings derived from chemical structures with a standard BioBERT-based RE framework. Results from experiments on the DDIExtraction 2013 corpus demonstrate that this approach outperforms strong baseline architectures by 3.4% in macro F1-score.

We present Bayesian Optimization with Fictitious Play (BOFiP), an algorithm designed for optimizing high-dimensional black-box functions. BOFiP partitions the original high-dimensional space into multiple non-overlapping sub-spaces defined by randomly generated sets of dimensions that collectively cover the entire dimensionality. The algorithm navigates the original space by alternating between performing Bayesian Optimization within these sub-spaces and exchanging information between them to refine sub-space evaluations. The core concept involves distributing high-dimensional optimization tasks across low-dimensional sub-spaces, treating each sub-space as a player in a game of equal interest. During each iteration, Bayesian Optimization generates approximate best responses to update the players' belief distributions, a process that alternates with belief updates until a stopping criterion is reached.

High-dimensional problems frequently arise in practical applications, and existing research in Bayesian Optimization has underscored the challenges of scaling to such dimensions due to the computational complexity of estimating model hyperparameters. This complexity grows exponentially with problem dimensionality, leading to significant performance degradation in most techniques as input dimensionality increases.

We evaluate BOFiP against several state-of-the-art methods in high-dimensional black-box optimization. Numerical experiments demonstrate its performance on three benchmark objective functions ranging from 20 to 1,000 dimensions. Additionally, a neural network architecture design problem was tested with configurations ranging from 42 to 911 nodes across 6 to 92 layers, yielding networks with between 500 and 10,000 weights. These empirical results indicate that BOFiP surpasses its competitors, maintaining consistent performance across various problems and demonstrating robustness as problem dimensionality increases.

Federated learning (FL) represents a burgeoning machine learning approach suitable for mobile edge environments, where a central server and numerous clients jointly train a statistical model by leveraging client data and computational power while safeguarding privacy-sensitive information. This study demonstrates that executing stochastic gradient descent (SGD) within this framework effectively introduces a momentum-like component to the global aggregation mechanism. Building on this insight, we evaluate the convergence rate of federated learning systems by considering the impacts of parameter staleness and communication constraints. These findings deepen the comprehension of the Federated SGD algorithm and establish a connection between staleness analysis and federated computing architectures, offering valuable guidance for system designers.

Moral foundations theory offers insights into how moral perspectives vary across different cultures. This study introduces a model designed to forecast moral foundations based on trending social media topics and examines whether variations in these foundations impact emotional traits. Our findings are encouraging and suggest several promising directions for future investigation.

In the West Atlantic Ocean, the distribution of dissolved aluminium displays a pattern that is the inverse of dissolved silicic acid, suggesting complex interactions between the oceanic cycles of Al and Si. The biogeochemistry of aluminium in marine environments is significant due to its potential influence on the remineralisation of diatom opal and, consequently, silicon availability. Additionally, surface dissolved aluminium concentrations serve as a tracer for dust input, which is the primary source of the bio-essential trace element iron. Previous simulations of dissolved aluminium concentrations achieved reasonable accuracy by considering only dust as a source and adsorption onto settling biogenic debris as the sole removal mechanism. This study investigates the effects of (i) a sediment source of aluminium in the Northern Hemisphere (particularly north of ~40°N), (ii) the imposed velocity field, and (iii) biological uptake of aluminium on modelled aluminium distributions. The inclusion of a sediment source notably enhances model performance, while varying the velocity field highlights the critical role of advection in shaping simulated aluminium patterns. Although biological incorporation emerges as a potentially significant removal pathway, a lack of independent data to constrain the Al:Si incorporation ratio in growing diatoms prevents a definitive conclusion. Consequently, this study cannot determine whether aluminium removal via incorporation is more or less important than removal through adsorptive scavenging.

This paper computes two components of the representation theory of Brauer configuration algebras: the Cartan matrix and the lengths of their associated indecomposable projective modules. We then define the subgroup-occurrence of an element within a group and leverage these calculated aspects to establish combinatorial identities valid for all finite groups.

In 2017, the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) captured the first image of the M87 galaxy's center, revealing a ring structure and dimensions that align with theoretical predictions for the light pattern surrounding a weakly accreting supermassive black hole of approximately 6.5 billion solar masses. Concurrently, a comprehensive multi-wavelength (MWL) campaign utilizing both ground-based and space-based observatories was conducted, spanning from radio frequencies to the TeV energy range. This note provides an overview of the findings from that campaign, which identified M87 in a historically low state where X-ray emission from the core exceeds that of HST-1. Additionally, we present the most complete simultaneous MWL spectrum of the active nucleus recorded to date.

We introduce a new method for detecting the elusive gravitational-wave memory predicted by general relativity, which manifests as a permanent offset in space-time strain during black hole mergers. Unlike prior techniques that require modeling and separating both the "chirp" and memory components, this approach offers several benefits: it focuses on the signal feature containing nearly all its Shannon information, maintains high simplicity, avoids the necessity for precise modeling of the full time evolution of gravitational wave components, and relies primarily on data largely devoid of the complex chirp signal. Although the frequency spectrum of the predicted memory signal resembles that of the chirp signal, its presence in lower frequencies—where noise and calibration issues are significant—makes detection challenging yet feasible. We applied this novel analysis, executed via a template-like algorithm, to 67 observations of 41 black hole mergers from the LIGO/Virgo Gravitational Wave Transient Catalog. Statistical significance was evaluated by examining numerous time-shifted intervals. The findings indicate a few potential detections (at $2\sigma-4\sigma$ levels) alongside many upper limits. The probability that a random ensemble of 67 strain time series, possessing identical noise characteristics but lacking memory signals, would produce a specific figure-of-merit matching the actual data is approximately 0.1. Various validation checks proved ineffective, largely due to substantial measurement and theoretical uncertainties, suggesting these results should be interpreted cautiously. The appendices provide MatLab code for various operations, including an algorithm for performing complex Fourier transforms on data with arbitrary spacing.

Experience and reasoning span various temporal scales, ranging from milliseconds to days, yet most computer vision research currently concentrates on individual images or brief clips lasting only a few seconds. This limitation exists because processing longer videos demands more scalable methods. In this study, we introduce a framework that allows researchers to analyze hour-long videos using the same hardware capable of handling second-long clips. By substituting traditional compression standards like JPEG with neural compression, we enable direct input of compressed videos into standard video networks. This approach enhances efficiency across the entire pipeline—including data transfer, speed, and memory usage—facilitating faster training on significantly longer video datasets. However, processing compressed signals can inadvertently prevent the use of standard augmentation techniques if handled improperly. We resolve this issue by proposing a lightweight network capable of applying transformations to latent codes, effectively replicating common augmentations used in the original video space. Our results demonstrate that this compressed vision pipeline allows for more efficient training of video models on benchmarks such as Kinetics-600 and COIN. Furthermore, we present proof-of-concept experiments involving novel tasks defined over hour-long videos at standard frame rates, proving that processing such extensive video durations is unfeasible without leveraging compressed representations.

The Pacific Ocean Neutrino Experiment (P-ONE) is a proposed cubic-kilometer neutrino telescope intended for deployment in the deep sea of the north-east Pacific. Working in tandem with Ocean Networks Canada's optical deep-sea data and communications infrastructure, an international research team plans to install kilometer-long mooring lines at approximately 2,660 meters depth within the Cascadia Basin—a relatively flat area located about 300 miles west of Vancouver Island. As the design and development phases continue, the P-ONE collaboration invites scientists from the oceanographic and marine communities to join, offering their expertise to implement additional or inclusive instrumentation and measurement strategies for oceanographic studies. Beyond monitoring optical bioluminescence and deep-ocean dynamics and thermodynamics, the array can accommodate active and passive acoustic sensors. This letter outlines the P-ONE detector and provides a non-exhaustive list of potential research topics of interest for the oceanographic and marine sciences.

We introduce a versatile deep architecture designed to learn functions across multiple permutation-invariant sets. Furthermore, we extend this framework to accommodate elements of arbitrary dimensions through dimension-wise equivariance. Our model is proven to be a universal approximator for these functions and outperforms existing methods on diverse tasks, such as counting, alignment, distinguishability, and statistical distance estimation. The latter task holds significant importance in Machine Learning. Despite its broad applicability, our approach also excels at generating more accurate approximations of KL divergence and mutual information compared to prior techniques specifically engineered for these statistical metrics.

This study offers a mathematical analysis of a reaction-diffusion model used to simulate acid-mediated tumor invasion. The framework tracks the spatial distribution and temporal dynamics of tumor cells, normal cells, and elevated lactic acid levels, operating under the assumption that tumor-induced shifts in microenvironmental pH serve as a straightforward yet comprehensive driver of cancer spread. Furthermore, we establish the existence and uniqueness of solutions for both Neumann and Dirichlet boundary conditions, accompanied by numerical simulations illustrating the results under each scenario.

This study examines a Finsler manifold $(M, F)$ and its associated curvature tensor, interpreted as 2-forms on the bundle of non-zero tangent vectors. Subspaces within the tangent spaces of $M$, defined by the curvature, are termed $k$-nullity foliations of the curvature operator. It is demonstrated that when the dimension of these foliations remains constant, the resulting distribution is involutive, and every maximal integral manifold is totally geodesic. The text provides a characterization of the $k$-nullity foliation along with findings regarding the constancy of flag curvature and the completeness of their integral manifolds, which implies the completeness of $(M, F)$. Furthermore, the introduced $k$-nullity space represents a natural generalization of the nullity space in Riemannian geometry—originally defined by S. S. Chern and N. H. Kuiper and expanded to the Finsler context by H. Akbar-Zadeh—serving as a special case of this broader framework.

Counting galaxy or star pairs based on distance forms the foundation of real-space correlation analysis in astrophysics and cosmology. Future surveys like LSST and Euclid will characterize billions of galaxies, pushing the limits of current counting methods within the minute-scale timeframe required for simulation workflows. Since the primary constraint is efficient data access, this challenge falls squarely within the realm of big data. We employ the Apache Spark framework to tackle this issue, creating a high-throughput algorithm capable of processing hundreds of millions to billions of data points. To enhance performance, we re-examined non-hierarchical sphere pixelization using cube symmetries, resulting in a novel approach called "Similar Radius Sphere Pixelization" (SARSPix), which features nearly square pixels and offers optimal indexing for distance-based calculations. Utilizing LSST-like fast simulations, we computed autocorrelation functions on tomographic bins ranging from 100 million to 1 billion data points. In every scenario, we generated a standard pair-distance histogram in approximately two minutes using a scalable, straightforward algorithm distributed across a moderate cluster of 16 to 64 nodes. This demonstrates the promise of these new techniques in astronomy, where data accessibility is increasingly the limiting factor. Furthermore, the method is easily adaptable to other applications such as nearest-neighbor searches, catalog cross-matching, and cluster identification. The software is publicly accessible at https://github.com/astrolabsoftware/SparkCorr.

The expected value and variance of the occurrences of a specific subgraph $H$ within an Erd\H{o}s--R\'enyi random graph of $n$ nodes are rational polynomials in $n$. We introduce software called Polcovar (derived from "polynomial" and "covariance"), which calculates the precise rational coefficients of these polynomials based on the structure of $H$.

This study examines a system comprising a polarizable atom situated near a nanosphere within an external electrostatic field, demonstrating that the attractive dispersive force can be counteracted by electrostatic interactions. Consequently, beyond the ability to actively tune the resultant force using an external agent without physical contact, the force can also be rendered repulsive. We explore this phenomenon across various distance regimes and analyze interactions between different atoms and both metallic and dielectric spheres to identify scenarios that are more amenable to control. Additionally, our findings indicate that these repulsive forces are attainable with field intensities feasible for laboratory settings.

This work introduces the inaugural Recurrent Neural Network architecture designed to learn Signal Temporal Logic formulas and offers the first comprehensive comparison of formula inference techniques. While legacy systems incorporate significant expert knowledge that remains unformalized, there is substantial interest in automatically deriving formal specifications—temporal logic formulas satisfied by system outputs—that describe ideal behavior. These specifications aid in understanding system dynamics and refining future designs. Unlike prior methods that relied on predefined formula templates or heuristic enumeration of possibilities, this approach employs a neural network to infer formula structure through gradient descent, thereby removing the constraint of specific templates. By unifying the learning of both formula structure and parameters within a single optimization process, the proposed method achieves mis-classification rates comparable to or superior to those of enumerative and lattice-based approaches. Furthermore, the observation that distinct formulas can yield similar mis-classification rates empirically highlights the under-determinism inherent in temporal logic inference.

The momentum of the $B^-$ meson in partially reconstructed decays can be determined without assumptions regarding its decay products by analyzing the decay of the narrow resonance $\overline{B}{}_{s2}^{*0}\!\rightarrow B^- K^+$. For the first time, this method is applied to separate contributions from $D^0$, $D^{*0}$, and higher-mass charmed states ($D^{**0}$) in semileptonic $B^-$ decays via the missing-mass distribution. The analysis utilizes a data set with an integrated luminosity of 3.0 fb${}^{-1}$ recorded by the LHCb detector in $pp$ collisions at center-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV. The measured branching fractions relative to the inclusive $B^- \!\rightarrow D^0 X \mu^- \overline{\nu}_\mu$ mode are $f_{D^0} = 0.25 \pm 0.06$ and $f_{D^{**0}} = 0.21 \pm 0.07$, where the remaining fraction is attributed to $D^{*0}$ states ($f_{D^{*0}} = 1 - f_{D^0} - f_{D^{**0}}$).

To address midhaul capacity constraints in Cloud Radio Access Networks (C-RAN), a Hybrid Cloud RAN (H-CRAN) architecture has been introduced. This framework employs functional splitting to distribute processing tasks between central and edge clouds. By allowing flexible selection of split points, H-CRAN designers can optimize for reduced midhaul bandwidth, lower latency, energy efficiency, or computational distribution based on available resources. Additionally, caching techniques are implemented to decrease content delivery latency and bandwidth requirements; however, these techniques introduce new constraints on functional splitting. This study formulates a constraint programming problem within the H-CRAN context to minimize total power consumption by determining the optimal functional split and content placement, subject to content access delay limits. Furthermore, the trade-off between overall power usage and occupied midhaul bandwidth is analyzed. The findings indicate that combining functional splitting with edge cloud caching effectively reduces both content access delays and fronthaul bandwidth usage, albeit at the cost of increased power consumption.

We examine the potential for insider arbitrage within a framework prohibiting short sales, utilizing a stock price process. This analysis introduces the concept of a minimal supermartingale measure and investigates its relationship with the minimal martingale measure. Specifically, we derive conditions under which neither measure exists, a scenario occurring when an insider's information set contains non-null events that uninformed investors perceive as having zero probability. These findings have various applications, particularly in local risk-minimization problems for insiders executing strategies without the ability to short sell.

Several years ago, Baker \cite{baker} introduced a metric that transitions smoothly from the Schwarzschild solution at small scales to the Friedmann-Robertson-Walker (FRW) solution at large scales; however, this proposal was discarded due to its inconsistency with Newtonian predictions for the solar system. We have identified a solution within similar variants of this framework that circumvents this issue. This resulting metric generates a MOND-like non-Newtonian acceleration, wherein the standard MOND acceleration $a_0$ is substituted by a cosmological acceleration determined by the background matter density.

Consider a random sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ drawn from a Gamma distribution with density $f(x)=\lambda^{\alpha}x^{\alpha-1}e^{-\lambda x}/\Gamma(\alpha)$ for $x>0$, where both the shape parameter $\alpha>0$ and the reciprocal scale parameter $\lambda>0$ are unknown. The primary finding establishes that the uniformly minimum variance unbiased estimator (UMVUE) for the shape parameter $\alpha$ exists if and only if $n\geq 4$; additionally, this estimator possesses finite variance if and only if $n\geq 6$. Specifically, the explicit form of the UMVUE is provided for various parametric functions, including $\alpha$, $\lambda$, $1/\alpha$, and $1/\lambda$. Moreover, a highly efficient estimation procedure for the two-parameter Beta distribution is presented. This approach relies on a Stein-type covariance identity specific to the Beta distribution, complemented by the application of $U$-statistics theory and the delta-method.

MSC: Primary 62F10; 62F12; Secondary 62E15.
Key words and phrases: unbiased estimation; Gamma distribution; Beta distribution; Ye-Chen-type closed-form estimators; asymptotic efficiency; $U$-statistics; Stein-type covariance identity; delta-method.

A charge density wave (CDW) with a nonzero ordering vector $\mathbf{q}$ statically couples electronic states at $\mathbf{k}$ and $\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q}$, inducing band folding that creates a reduced Brillouin zone (RBZ). Defined by an irreducible representation of the little group of $\mathbf{q}$, the CDW's structure alters the system's symmetry and electronic configuration, potentially driving a topological phase transition via band inversion. This study investigates monolayer 1\textit{T}-TiSe$_2$, which exhibits an unconventional CDW phase characterized by a triple-$q$ $M_1^-$ structure. Furthermore, the interaction among the triple-$q$ components of the $M_1^-$ CDW inevitably generates a minor $M_1^+$ CDW. While the CDW induces band inversion in 1\textit{T}-TiSe$_2$, distinct CDW types influence the electronic structure and system topology differently. To analyze these effects, a symmetrization-antisymmetrization technique was employed to isolate the $M_1^-$ and $M_1^+$ contributions within a DFT-based tight-binding model. The resulting findings align with parity considerations, thereby enhancing the understanding of topological properties in CDW systems both with and without parity symmetry.

We introduce explicit expressions for Macdonald polynomials of types $C_n$ and $D_n$ within the one-row context, designating them as "tableau formulas" due to their underlying combinatorial nature. These formulas are derived by utilizing transformation identities for basic hypergeometric series, specifically those involving very well-poised balanced ${}_{12}W_{11}$ series. Furthermore, we observe that the correlation functions of the deformed $\mathcal{W}$ algebra generators naturally yield these tableau formulas upon the principal specialization of the coordinate variables.

A benchmark brown dwarf (BD) is defined as one with precisely and independently determined properties, such as mass and chemical composition. These objects are essential for validating theoretical evolutionary models, spectral synthesis techniques, and atmospheric retrieval methods for sub-stellar bodies. In this study, we present atmospheric retrieval results for both a synthetic spectrum and the benchmark BD HR 7672~B using the \petit framework. Initially, we evaluated the retrieval framework against a synthetic PHOENIX BT-Settl spectrum with solar composition. While the retrieved carbon (C) and oxygen (O) abundances aligned with solar values, the C/O ratio was overestimated by 0.13–0.18, a discrepancy approximately four times larger than the formal uncertainty. Subsequently, we conducted retrievals on HR 7672~B utilizing high-resolution spectroscopic data (R=35,000) from the Keck Planet Imager and Characterizer (KPIC) alongside near-infrared photometry. The resulting values for [C/H], [O/H], and C/O were determined to be $-0.24\pm0.05$, $-0.19\pm0.04$, and $0.52\pm0.02$, respectively. These figures agree with those of HR 7672~A within 1.5$\sigma$. Consequently, HR 7672~B joins a select group of benchmark BDs—including Gl 570~D and HD 3651~B—that exhibit elemental abundances consistent with their primary stars. This work establishes a practical methodology for testing and executing atmospheric retrievals and highlights potential systematic errors in future analyses involving both high- and low-resolution data.

In \cite{Gazaki2015}, the author introduced a Bloch-Beilinson type filtration $\{F^r(A)\}_{r\geq 0}$ on the Chow group of zero-cycles, $\text{CH}_0(A)$, for an abelian variety $A$ over a perfect field $k$, where the successive quotients are associated with a Somekawa $K$-group. This paper examines the specific scenario where $A$ is isogenous to a product $X=E_1\times\cdots\times E_d$ of elliptic curves and investigates the relationship between this filtration and one defined by Raskind and Spiess (\cite{Raskind/Spiess2000}) for $\text{CH}_0(X)$. When $k$ is a finite extension of $\mathbb{Q}_p$, and provided certain conditions regarding the reduction type of the $E_i$, we demonstrate that the Albanese kernel of $A$ decomposes into the direct sum of its maximal divisible subgroup and a torsion group of finite exponent; notably, this torsion group is finite if $A$ is an abelian surface. An analogous result is established for products $C_1\times \cdots\times C_d$ of smooth projective curves whose Jacobians are isogenous to products of elliptic curves. These findings provide fresh support for a conjecture proposed by Raskind and Spiess and Colliot-Th\'{e}l\`{e}ne. Furthermore, by utilizing Jacobians of genus $2$ hyperelliptic curves, we construct infinitely many new instances that satisfy this conjecture.

Due to the small magnitude of the ratio A_2/A_0 in I=2 to I=0 K -> pipi decay amplitudes (a consequence of the Delta I=1/2 rule), electromagnetic effects on A_2 could be approximately 20 times larger than those predicted by a naive O(alpha) estimation. Consequently, to reach 10% accuracy in future computations of A_2 and epsilon'/epsilon, these electromagnetic contributions must be accounted for. This work outlines the initial steps toward incorporating electromagnetism into lattice QCD calculations of standard model K -> pipi decay amplitudes.

Amplitude analysis serves as a potent method for investigating hadron decays, yet it faces substantial challenges in addressing instrumental factors—such as background noise and fluctuations in selection efficiency—across multidimensional kinematic phase spaces. This paper surveys traditional approaches for estimating efficiency and background distributions while introducing density estimation techniques based on Gaussian processes and artificial neural networks. Although these methods are widely employed in other fields, they remain underutilized in amplitude analyses. The study concludes by proposing innovative applications of these models, specifically for estimating background density within the signal region using sidebands across multiple dimensions, as well as a broader framework for model-assisted density estimation via artificial neural networks.

Numerous practical applications, including learning to rank and recommender systems, entail addressing multiple related tasks. A representative case involves developing recommendation policies for users with analogous movie tastes, despite minor variations in their individual rankings. These tasks can be structured hierarchically, linking similar problems via a common framework. This study frames the issue as contextual off-policy optimization within a hierarchical graphical model derived from logged bandit data. To address this, we introduce HierOPO, a hierarchical off-policy optimization algorithm that estimates model parameters and subsequently acts conservatively based on them. We apply HierOPO to linear Gaussian models, providing both an efficient implementation and theoretical analysis. We establish per-task suboptimality bounds demonstrating significant gains from utilizing the hierarchical structure compared to independent task solving. Empirical evaluations further support these findings. Both theoretical and experimental results confirm the distinct advantages of employing a hierarchy over addressing tasks in isolation.

Hastings and Haah recently proposed a quantum memory based on the honeycomb lattice, characterized by weight-six parity checks implemented through two-local measurements. This architecture offers sparse connectivity and local measurement capabilities, which are advantageous for specific hardware platforms, while the weight-six checks ensure robustness within the circuit model. This study quantifies the resilience of logical qubits in the honeycomb code using a correlated minimum-weight perfect-matching decoder. By employing Monte Carlo sampling across various error models, we evaluate the code's threshold and assess its potential to achieve the "teraquop regime," where trillions of reliable quantum logical operations are feasible. We compare these findings with the rotated surface code, identifying a honeycomb code threshold of $0.2\%-0.3\%$ versus $0.5\%-0.7\%$ for the surface code under a controlled-not circuit model. In a circuit model featuring native two-body measurements, the honeycomb code reaches a threshold of $1.5\% < p <2.0\%$, where $p$ represents the collective error rate of the measurement gate, encompassing both measurement errors and correlated data depolarization. Assuming a physical error rate of $10^{-3}$ for these gates, we project that the honeycomb code can attain the teraquop regime utilizing merely 600 physical qubits.

In the framework of the HL-LHC upgrade, the CMS Collaboration is designing a High Granularity Calorimeter (CE) to substitute the current endcap calorimeters. This sampling calorimeter features exceptional transverse and longitudinal readout capabilities for both its electromagnetic (CE-E) and hadronic (CE-H) sections. The detector will consist of approximately 30,000 hexagonal silicon modules. Prototype units were fabricated using 6-inch hexagonal silicon sensors with 1.1~$cm^2$ cell areas and the SKIROC2-CMS readout ASIC. In 2017 and 2018, beam tests utilizing various sampling configurations were performed on these prototypes at DESY and CERN. This article details the construction and commissioning of the CE prototype, outlines the silicon modules employed, presents their fundamental performance metrics, and explains the calibration techniques applied.
A concise overview of the hadronic calorimeter calibration systems and their performance outcomes is provided for the ATLAS detector at the LHC.

The nonlinear fractional Boussinesq equations hold a significant position within the class of fractional differential equations in mathematical physics. This study employs the (G'G^2)-extension method, a highly effective analytical technique for deriving exact solutions, to investigate nonlinear Boussinesq equations featuring conformable time-fractional derivatives. Compared to other analytical approaches, this method proves exceptionally useful. By utilizing this proposed technique, three distinct solution types are obtained: hyperbolic, trigonometric, and rational. Furthermore, this approach demonstrates potential applicability to other nonlinear fractional models.

This work launches a systematic investigation into Dynamic Influence Maximization (DIM). The objective is to manage a seed set $S$ of no more than $k$ nodes within a social network that evolves over time, aiming to maximize expected influence spread while minimizing the amortized cost of updates. We examine two evolution scenarios. Under the incremental model, where the network expands by adding new users and links, we present an algorithm that delivers a $(1-1/e-\epsilon)$-approximation of the optimal solution with an amortized running time of $k \cdot \mathsf{poly}(\log n, \epsilon^{-1})$, thereby matching the performance of state-of-the-art offline algorithms with only poly-logarithmic overhead. In the fully dynamic model, where users join or depart and influence propagation strengths fluctuate in real time, we demonstrate that, assuming the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH), achieving a $2^{-(\log n)^{1-o(1)}}$-approximation is impossible unless the amortized running time reaches $n^{1-o(1)}$. Technically, our approach utilizes innovative adaptive sampling techniques to transform DIM into the dynamic MAX-k coverage problem, for which we devise an efficient $(1-1/e-\epsilon)$-approximation algorithm. Furthermore, our lower bound proof relies on the recently developed distributed PCP framework.

Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) connectivity research is increasingly aggregating data from multiple locations. Although this approach facilitates faster recruitment and larger sample sizes, it can also introduce systematic biases in connectivity metrics across different sites. This study quantifies the inter-site effect on connectivity and assesses its influence on detecting both individual and group-level differences. Using real multisite fMRI data from the 1000 Functional Connectome Project involving 345 healthy young adults scanned across eight sites with 3T scanners and varying protocols, we first demonstrated that typical functional networks were reliably identified at the group level at all sites. The inter-site effects were found to be small to moderate, with an average Cohen's effect size below 0.5 across brain connections. Subsequently, we conducted Monte-Carlo simulations based on these real datasets to evaluate how multisite effects impact statistical power in group comparisons using a general linear model (GLM) and the accuracy of group label prediction using a support-vector machine (SVM). As a baseline, identical simulations were run using single-site data with the same sample size. Results indicated that while heterogeneous multisite data slightly reduced the ability to detect changes compared to a single-site study using GLM, it had a more pronounced effect on prediction accuracy. Collectively, these findings suggest that multisite rs-fMRI studies are feasible, provided the sample size is sufficiently large.

Experimentally verifying the topological protection of Andreev states in Josephson junctions presents significant difficulties, particularly because the characteristic $4\pi$ periodicity in the current-phase relation of topological junctions has remained elusive due to rapid parity-breaking processes. Previous predictions suggested that low-temperature ac susceptibility measurements linked to current thermal noise could detect the topological protection of quantum Spin Hall edge states \cite{Fu2009} by investigating their low-energy Andreev spectrum. We conducted microwave probing of the Andreev spectrum in a phase-biased Josephson junction constructed around a bismuth nanowire, which was previously established to support one-dimensional ballistic edge states. Our results reveal absorption peaks corresponding to Andreev level crossings, with temperature and frequency dependencies indicating protected topological crossings, limited in accuracy only by the electronic temperature of our experimental setup.

Building upon a previous study, this work applies realistic probability distributions to reconstruct particle tracks within a constant magnetic field. Both the complete mathematical forms and their schematic approximations yield superior momentum estimates compared to standard fitting methods. A simplified derivation of one of these distributions is presented. The performance of these reconstructions is evaluated against standard least-squares fits using two distinct positioning algorithms: the eta-algorithm and the two-strip center of gravity. The superiority of our results is quantified by the necessary increases in magnetic field strength and signal-to-noise ratio required to match the quality of our best distributions. The data and simulations were calibrated using the tracker from an active experiment featuring double-sided microstrip detectors, where each side simulates magnetic bending measurements. To achieve parity with our optimal distributions, the magnetic field must be increased by a factor of 1.5 for the eta-algorithm based on least squares, and by 1.8 and 2.0 for the two-strip center of gravity method on the low and high noise sides, respectively. Similarly, the signal-to-noise ratio must be boosted by 1.6 for the low noise side and 2.2 for the high noise side when using the eta-algorithm. Notably, fits derived from the center of gravity positioning method remain unaffected by reductions in the signal-to-noise ratio.

We provide a constructive proof, valid to all orders, demonstrating that every element of the non-commutative potential Korteweg-de Vries (ncpKdV) hierarchy constitutes a Fredholm Grassmannian flow, thereby ensuring linearisability. This result holds for any linear combination of fields within the hierarchy. Consequently, the integrability of these members implies that time-evolving solutions can be derived by combining the solution to the corresponding linear dispersion equation with the solution to an associated linear Fredholm equation, specifically the Marchenko equation. Furthermore, we establish that within the class of polynomial partial differential fields, each member of the ncpKdV hierarchy is unique at every order; indeed, we prove to all orders that each such member aligns with the non-commutative Lax hierarchy field, which is itself a polynomial partial differential field. We achieve this by constructing the underlying abstract combinatorial algebra of the ncpKdV hierarchy. This algebra is defined as the non-commutative polynomial algebra over the real line generated by the set of all compositions, equipped with the Poppe product. This product serves as the abstract representation of the product rule for Hankel operators, a concept pioneered by Ch. Poppe for integrable equations such as the Sine-Gordon and Korteweg-de Vries equations. The integrability of the hierarchy's members translates, within this combinatorial algebra, into proving the existence of a "Poppe polynomial" expansion for basic compositions in terms of "linear signature expansions." Proving the existence of these Poppe polynomial expansions reduces to solving a linear algebraic problem for the expansion coefficients, which we resolve constructively to all orders.

We present examples of smooth, proper rigid-analytic varieties that possess a formal model with a projective special fiber and exhibit a violation of Hodge symmetry in cohomology for degrees three and higher. This finding provides a negative answer to a question posed by Hansen and Li.

We introduce and examine branched analogs of SL(r,C)-opers and their characteristics. While the underlying holomorphic vector bundle for standard SL(r,C)-opers remains invariant across different oper structures, the corresponding bundle for branched SL(r,C)-opers varies with each oper. For any given branched SL(r,C)-oper, we construct an associated holomorphic vector bundle equipped with a logarithmic connection that is independent of the specific oper. Furthermore, we characterize these branched SL(r,C)-opers by analyzing the logarithmic connections defined on this fixed holomorphic vector bundle.

Regularization plays a crucial role in preventing overfitting during network optimization, thereby enhancing the generalization capabilities of trained models. Introducing label noise serves as a potent form of implicit regularization by substituting ground truth labels with uniform random values. However, this approach can generate misleading gradients due to the substantial losses incurred from incorrect labels. To address this, we introduce Label-Noised Trim-SGD, a first-order optimization technique that combines label noise with example trimming to eliminate outliers based on loss values. This straightforward algorithm allows for the application of significant label noise, yielding a superior regularization effect compared to existing methods. We conduct a quantitative analysis by evaluating the individual behaviors of label noise, example trimming, and our proposed algorithm. Furthermore, empirical results across major benchmarks and foundational networks demonstrate the method's efficacy, showing that it outperforms current state-of-the-art optimization techniques.

Speech synthesis could be pivotal in advancing low-resource speech recognition. Although data augmentation has become a cornerstone of modern training pipelines, current methods are often simplistic and fail to mimic real-world scenarios. Conversely, speech synthesis is rapidly approaching the ability to generate human-like audio. This study explores whether synthesized speech can serve as an effective augmentation strategy to reduce the resources required for building speech recognizers. We evaluated three distinct synthesizer types: statistical parametric, neural, and adversarial. The results are promising and suggest new avenues for future research.

Hierarchical galaxy formation models predict that stellar tidal streams should be ubiquitous around most galaxies. While these structures offer valuable diagnostics for the $\Lambda$CDM framework, their observational characteristics remain largely unconstrained due to detection difficulties, interpretive challenges, and limited study coverage across the galaxy population. There is a clear need for more rigorous, systematic methodologies. This paper advocates for a statistical examination of the abundance and properties of these features within archival wide-field imaging surveys to enable direct comparison with numerical simulations. Specifically, we aim to systematically investigate the occurrence frequency and other observational traits of tidal features surrounding nearby galaxies. The resulting dataset will serve as a fundamental resource for statistical comparisons with cosmological galaxy formation models. Our methodology employs visual classification of diffuse features around a volume-limited sample of nearby galaxies, utilizing post-processed Sloan Digital Sky Survey imaging optimized for detecting low-surface-brightness stellar structures. At a limiting surface brightness of $28\ \mathrm{mag~arcsec^{-2}}$, we find that 14% of galaxies in our sample show evidence of diffuse features likely caused by minor mergers. This technique successfully recovers all known streams within our sample and identifies numerous new candidates. Consistent with prior research, coherent arc-like features and shells are the most prevalent tidal structures identified. We conclude that while some detections remain ambiguous and require confirmation from deeper imaging, our approach establishes a robust foundation for the statistical analysis of diffuse circumgalactic features in wide-area surveys and for selecting targets for follow-up observations.

This study employs a non-linear conjugate gradient optimization method to determine excitation energies under the Random Phase Approximation (RPA). By utilizing a modified Thouless functional grounded in an asymmetric Rayleigh quotient within an orthogonalized atomic orbital framework, the approach locates solutions to the RPA eigenvalue equation. This strategy circumvents the computational bottleneck associated with calculating molecular orbitals. Projections are applied to restrict the variational space to physically significant transitions. The investigation examines the feasibility of an RPA implementation that scales linearly with system size (N) by analyzing convergence relative to initial guess quality and sensitivity to noise under thresholding across both well- and ill-conditioned scenarios. Results indicate that this molecular-orbital-free algorithm is both robust and computationally efficient, marking a significant step toward large-scale, low-complexity calculations of time-dependent optical properties and linear response. Furthermore, the method is adaptable to other time-dependent perturbation theories, such as time-dependent Density Functional Theory.

Cytometry generates high-dimensional point cloud data that resists manual interpretation. Currently, analysis relies on Boolean gating and comparing the relative abundances of cellular subsets. However, this standard method fails to detect subtle topological features, particularly when they are obscured by data transformations, batch effects, or donor-to-donor variability in clinical samples. An examination of public cytometry data regarding non-naïve CD8+ T cells in COVID-19 patients versus healthy controls reveals systematic structural differences in single-cell protein expression. We identified key proteins using a decision-tree classifier, randomly sampled data points, and calculated persistence diagrams from these samples. These diagrams highlighted regions of varying density and protruding structures, such as "elbows." By computing Wasserstein distances between the diagrams of random pairs from both groups, we confirmed structural differences in the expression of T-bet, Eomes, and Ki-67 between patients and controls. Further analysis indicated that T-bet and Eomes expression was significantly downregulated in the non-naïve CD8+ T cells of COVID-19 patients compared to healthy controls. This counter-intuitive result suggests that canonical effector CD8+ T cells may be less prevalent in patients with COVID-19. This topological data analysis approach is applicable to any cytometry dataset to uncover novel insights that standard gating strategies or existing bioinformatic tools might miss.

We present an experimental study characterizing a spatially extended Josephson junction formed within a coherently coupled two-spin-component Bose-Einstein condensate. By confining the cloud in an elongated potential, transverse spin excitations are suppressed. Using three distinct manipulation protocols, we determine the non-linear parameter; the results from all methods align with a simple local density approximation of spin hydrodynamics, specifically the Bose-Josephson junction equations. Furthermore, we demonstrate a technique for generating states characterized by a well-defined uniform magnetization.

This study explores the theoretical framework of direct A(d,p)B reactions and examines the relationship between practical three-body models and optical model potentials that describe the interaction between the deuteron's constituents and target nucleus A. A novel definition of the nucleon optical potential is proposed, which requires a rigorous analysis of the boundary conditions inherent to the associated coupled channels problem. This new definition proves advantageous for linking theory with (d,p) reaction dynamics. Conducted within an antisymmetrised, translationally invariant formalism, the analysis establishes a robust many-body foundation for the three-body force effects previously calculated by Dinmore, Timofeyk, Al-Khalili, and Johnson.

Age-of-Information (AoI), a metric for data freshness, is critical for real-time Internet-of-Things (IoT) applications, which also urgently demand energy conservation for power-limited devices. This paper investigates the tradeoff between energy consumption and AoI for status updates transmitted from a sensor to a monitor over a noisy channel. The sensor operates by choosing to sleep, sense, transmit a fresh update, or retransmit, accounting for both sensing and transmission energy costs. The problem is modeled as an infinite-horizon average cost Markov decision process (MDP) aimed at minimizing the weighted sum of average AoI and average energy usage. By solving the corresponding discounted cost problem and analyzing the Markov chain under the optimal policy, we demonstrate that a threshold optimal stationary policy exists, defined by two specific thresholds: one for the AoI at the transmitter (AoIT) and another for the AoI at the receiver (AoIR). These thresholds can be efficiently determined using line search. Numerical simulations illustrate the performance of the optimal policies and the resulting tradeoff curves across various parameters. Comparisons with conventional approaches reveal that incorporating sensing energy significantly impacts policy design, while the introduction of a sleep mode substantially widens the achievable tradeoff range.

Precise estimation of thermosphere mass density is essential for understanding satellite orbital evolution and effectively managing space missions. While empirical models are frequently used for this task, they often carry significant uncertainties. This study outlines a Kalman filter approach designed to calibrate such models along a specific satellite's path. The method was utilized to adjust the NRLMSISE-00, JB2008, and DTM-2020 models based on density measurements from the Swarm-C satellite. Results showed significant reductions in root mean squared density residuals compared to both uncalibrated outputs and linear regression-based calibration on prior data. Additionally, further enhancements were achieved by integrating estimates from multiple models via a best linear unbiased estimator.

Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) has demonstrated significant potential for enhancing model generalization by guiding optimizers toward flat minima. However, its practical application is hindered by the computational burden of performing two forward-backward propagations for every parameter update. To address this, we introduce Stochastic Scheduled SAM (SS-SAM), a novel and efficient training framework. In SS-SAM, a predefined scheduling function governs the optimizer to conduct random trials at each step, dynamically choosing between standard SGD and SAM optimization. This stochastic approach substantially reduces the total number of propagation pairs required. We empirically evaluate four distinct scheduling functions, analyzing both their computational efficiency and their influence on model performance. Our results indicate that with appropriate scheduling, models can achieve performance comparable to, or even surpassing, pure SAM training while incurring significantly lower computational costs.

In observational astronomy, noise interferes with the detection of significant signals. As large-scale astronomical surveys expand in size and complexity, they generate vast amounts of data, thereby increasing data processing demands. Consequently, developing automated denoising tools, such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs), has emerged as a promising research direction. This study examines the viability of CNN-based self-supervised learning algorithms, specifically Noise2Noise, for cleaning astronomical images. Experiments were conducted using simulated noisy astronomical data, with performance evaluated based on the accuracy of flux and morphology recovery. The results indicate that this algorithm effectively recovers flux for Poisson noise (98.13${\raisebox{0.5ex}{\tiny$^{+0.77}_{-0.90} $}$\large\%$}) and for Gaussian noise in images featuring smooth signal profiles (96.45${\raisebox{0.5ex}{\tiny$^{+0.80}_{-0.96} $}$\large\%$}).

According to the third law of thermodynamics, entropy should vanish as temperature ($T$) approaches absolute zero. However, materials like glass display nonzero entropy at $T=0$, appearing to violate this principle. For over a century, this discrepancy has been circumvented by classifying glass as a nonequilibrium state, a workaround that introduces significant inconsistencies into thermodynamic theory. This paper offers resolutions to these contradictions and formulates a rigorous, exception-free statement of the third law. To identify the source of entropy, the subjective or anthropomorphic nature of entropy must be addressed; since entropy is uniquely defined only when thermodynamic coordinates (TCs) are specified, identifying the correct TCs is essential. This necessitates an unambiguous, structure-independent redefinition of equilibrium for solids. Based on this, it is deduced that the TCs of solids correspond to the equilibrium positions of their atoms. These coordinates define a thermodynamic space where entropy takes a unique value. In solids, equilibrium states are represented by discrete points in this space, each defining a specific atomic configuration. At sufficiently low temperatures, only one configuration is thermally active, while others remain frozen and do not influence entropy's temperature dependence in that regime. The rigorous third law is thus established by stating that the entropy of the active configuration approaches zero at $T=0$. Residual entropy occurs when entropy is calculated over an extended space that includes previously active configurations now frozen at low temperatures. This reconciliation of conflicting perspectives is clarified through an examination of various debates surrounding the glass transition.

Performance isolation serves as a fundamental pillar for ensuring Service Level Objectives (SLOs) in cloud and datacenter settings that utilize shared resources. Current best practices depend on hardware Quality of Service (QoS) mechanisms, such as Intel RDT, to distribute shared assets like last-level caches and memory bandwidth among co-located latency-sensitive applications. Consequently, the volume of such applications deployable on a single physical machine is constrained by the hardware's allocation capacity, which is inherently limited. For instance, Intel Xeon E5 v3 processors allow a maximum of four partitions for last-level caches, permitting only four applications to receive dedicated resource allocation. This paper investigates the viability and potential hurdles of extending SLO guarantees beyond these hardware-imposed limits. We introduce CoCo, a transparent software layer that schedules applications to time-share interference-free partitions, demonstrating both feasibility and significant advantages. Our evaluation reveals that CoCo surpasses both non-partitioned and round-robin strategies by up to 9x and 1.2x, respectively.

Driven by fairness needs in communication networks, we present a natural extension of the online paging problem known as \textit{min-max} paging, which aims to minimize the highest fault count among any single page. Although the standard paging problem, focused on minimizing total faults, allows for $k$-competitive deterministic and $O(\log k)$-competitive randomized solutions, we demonstrate that min-max paging lacks a $c(k)$-competitive algorithm for any function $c$. Specifically, we establish that the randomized competitive ratio is $\Omega(\log(n))$ and the deterministic ratio is $\Omega(k\log(n)/\log(k))$, with $n$ representing the total number of distinct pages requested. Furthermore, we develop a fractional algorithm that minimizes an $n$-variate differentiable convex function of the fault vector. This yields an $O(\log(n)\log(k))$-competitive fractional algorithm for min-max paging. By rounding this fractional solution with at most a $k$-fold loss in competitiveness, we achieve a deterministic $O(k\log(n)\log(k))$-competitive algorithm, which aligns with our lower bound up to a $\mathrm{poly}(\log(k))$ factor. Additionally, we provide a randomized rounding technique that produces an $O(\log^2 n \log k)$-competitive algorithm.

Over the past few years, artificial neural networks (ANNs) have proven effective in nuclear physics and related fields. This research calculates {\alpha}-decay half-lives for certain neutron-deficient nuclei using the Coulomb and proximity potential model (CPPM), the temperature-dependent variant (CPPMT), the Royer empirical formula, the new Ren B (NRB) formula, and a trained ANN model (TANN). When compared to experimental data, the ANN model provides an excellent description of these half-lives. Additionally, CPPMT outperforms CPPM, highlighting the significance of incorporating temperature-dependent nuclear potentials. To predict half-lives for unmeasured neutron-deficient nuclei, a separate ANN algorithm was trained to estimate Q {\alpha} values, with its results benchmarked against the Weizs\"acker-Skyrme-4+RBF (WS4+RBF) formula. Subsequently, half-lives for these unmeasured nuclei were predicted using CPPM, CPPMT, Royer, NRB, and TANN, utilizing the ANN-predicted Q {\alpha} values as inputs. The study concludes that ANNs can successfully forecast {\alpha}-decay half-lives for neutron-deficient nuclei, aiding in the identification of nuclei near the driplines.

Carrillo and Pares introduced Compact Approximate Taylor (CAT) methods for systems of conservation laws in 2019. These techniques, which extend high-order Lax-Wendroff approaches to nonlinear systems without relying on the Cauchy-Kovalevskaya procedure, achieve arbitrary even-order accuracy ($2p$) using $(2p + 1)$-point stencils, where $p$ is any positive integer. In 2021, Carrillo, Macca, Pares, Russo, and Zorio developed a strategy to eliminate the spurious oscillations near discontinuities inherent in CAT methods, resulting in Adaptive CAT (ACAT) methods. ACAT methods adapt both the order of accuracy and stencil width according to the local smoothness of the solution. This paper aims to generalize CAT and ACAT methods to systems of balance laws by expressing the source term as the derivative of its indefinite integral, which is formally treated as a flux function. The study discusses the well-balanced nature of these methods and presents a variant capable of preserving any stationary solution. Numerical tests on various systems, ranging from linear scalar conservation laws to the 2D Euler equations with gravity (including Burgers equations with sources and 1D shallow water equations), demonstrate and verify the order and well-balanced properties of the proposed methods.

Turán's Theorem states that an extremal graph free of $K_{r+1}$ is $r$-partite. The Stability Theorem by Erdős and Simonovits demonstrates that if a $K_{r+1}$-free graph with $n$ vertices possesses a number of edges nearly equal to the maximum possible, $t_r(n)$, it is structurally close to being $r$-partite. This paper precisely identifies the $K_{r+1}$-free graphs with at least $m$ edges that are most distant from being $r$-partite, for any $m \ge t_r(n) - \delta_r n^2$. The findings extend previous research by Erdős, Győri, and Simonovits and confirm a conjecture proposed by Balogh, Clemens, Lavrov, Lidický, and Pfender.

We perform 2D and 3D PIC simulations to model the expansion of a magnetized plasma that initially occupies a half-space, featuring a semi-cylindrical zone of heated electrons aligned along the boundary. This setup mirrors scenarios such as the ablation of a planar target by a femtosecond laser under quasi-cylindrical focusing. Our results indicate that the dissipation of the inhomogeneous plasma-vacuum interface is significantly influenced by an external magnetic field oriented parallel to the boundary. We identify several transient effects, notably the anisotropic scattering of electrons and the associated Weibel instability, alongside diverse spatial configurations of the resulting magnetic fields and currents. These include multiple separating filaments of the z-pinch variety and gradually evolving current sheets with varying orientations. The strength of the self-generated magnetic field can match or substantially surpass that of the external field. These dynamics are anticipated in both laser-driven and cosmic plasmas, ranging from explosive events in planetary magnetospheres to processes within stellar coronal arches.

The mechanism behind the FLASH effect—where ultra-high dose rate (UHDR) radiation spares normal tissue while maintaining tumor control comparable to conventional dose rate (CDR) radiation—remains unidentified. This study examines how interspur interactions, defined as collisions between radiolytic species within individual particle tracks, contribute to overall radiochemistry across various irradiation parameters, proposing that enhanced interspur interactions may explain tissue sparing in FLASH therapy. We developed an analytical model that maps the spatiotemporal distribution of spurs in a target volume based on factors such as dose, dose rate, and linear energy transfer (LET), quantifying their impact on radiochemical processes. Using a simplified reaction-diffusion equation calibrated with Monte Carlo simulations, the model calculates expected interspur overlap. Results indicate that a minimum critical dose and dose rate are required to trigger significant interspur interactions, which correlate negatively with beam LET at a constant dose. Furthermore, the model identifies optimal beam parameters to maximize these interactions. Given that radical scavenging rates limit interspur overlap, the findings suggest that the specific irradiation conditions needed to produce the FLASH effect coincide with the onset of substantial interspur interactions, supporting the hypothesis that interspur interactions underlie the FLASH phenomenon.

The Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) and the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) have driven a more in-depth investigation into quark-gluon plasma (QGP), specifically focusing on its perturbations. Our research centers on the temporal evolution of fluctuations in baryon and energy densities. If a localized baryon density pulse can travel significant distances through the QGP while maintaining its shape and localization, this phenomenon would have profound implications for both relativistic heavy ion physics and astrophysics. Mathematically, demonstrating this possibility involves deriving a Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) equation from the QGP's hydrodynamical equations under specific conditions; the solution to this equation represents a KdV soliton. This derivation relies heavily on the equation of state (EOS) of the QGP. While the standard MIT bag model EOS fails to produce KdV solitons, we recently formulated a new EOS that incorporates both perturbative and non-perturbative corrections to the MIT model while remaining simple enough for analytical manipulation. Using this refined EOS, we successfully derived a KdV equation applicable to cold QGP.

An investigation using the Ultra-relativistic Quantum Molecular Dynamics (UrQMD) model examines how the in-medium correction factor ($F$) influences nucleon-nucleon elastic cross sections. The study analyzes the impact of $F$'s beam energy dependence on directed and elliptic flow, as well as nuclear stopping, in $^{197}$Au+$^{197}$Au collisions across a range of $0.09$ to $0.8A$ GeV. Results indicate that at lower energies, these observables are highly sensitive to variations in $F$, with this sensitivity diminishing as beam energy increases. Furthermore, the beam energy-dependent in-medium correction factor $F$ is determined by comparing calculated excitation functions for flow and stopping against FOPI experimental data.

Building on the success of neural networks in designing auctions—where they learn optimal allocations and payment rules to satisfy desirable properties—we turn our attention to learning fair resource division without monetary transactions. Our objective is to distribute items, goods, and/or chores efficiently among fair allocations, defined here as those that are Envy-free (EF). However, EF allocations do not always exist for indivisible resources, so we adopt the relaxed concept of Envy-freeness up to one item (EF1), which is guaranteed to exist. Merely ensuring EF1 is insufficient because allocations with empty bundles also satisfy this condition; thus, we impose an additional efficiency constraint by maximizing utilitarian social welfare (USW). Generally, finding USW allocations within the EF1 framework is NP-Hard, even with additive valuations. To address this, we introduce EEF1-NN, a neural network designed for this task. We propose a UNet-inspired architecture, a Lagrangian loss function, and a specific training procedure to achieve our goals. Our results demonstrate that EEF1-NN identifies allocations near-optimal in USW while ensuring EF1 with high probability across various input valuation distributions. Compared to existing methods, EEF1-NN empirically achieves higher USW, and it is both scalable and significantly faster than solving the problem via constrained optimization.

We establish a foundational theory of cocartesian fibrations within the context of Segal spaces, following the approach outlined in arxiv:2102.05190, and leverage this framework to prove Barwick's theorem (the primary result of arxiv:1404.0108). Please note that this research was originally the author's master's thesis, submitted on 21.09.2020.

This paper introduces a closed-form method to restrict flow within a specified volume and around objects, ensuring the flow converges to a single fixed point. We demonstrate that the obstacle avoidance problem can be inverted to maintain flow confinement within a volume bounded by a polygonal surface. It is formally guaranteed that this flow will never touch the boundaries of the enclosing volume or obstacles and will asymptotically approach an attractor. Additionally, we generate smooth motion fields around obstacles with edges, such as tables. Both obstacles and enclosures can be time-varying, including moving, expanding, or shrinking. This technique allows a robot to navigate an enclosed corridor while avoiding both static and moving obstacles. It was tested on an autonomous robot (QOLO) in a complex static indoor setting and in simulations involving dense crowds. The final proof of concept occurred in an outdoor environment in Lausanne, where the QOLO robot successfully traversed a central marketplace amidst a diverse crowd exhibiting non-uniform motion patterns.

The quadratic Wasserstein metric effectively quantifies differences between probability densities, offering optimization objectives with enhanced convexity and robustness against data noise. However, adapting seismic signals for comparison using this metric remains a critical challenge. Squaring scaling is a promising approach as it ensures convexity in the presence of data shifts. Nevertheless, as noted in [Commun. Inf. Syst., 2019, 19:95-145], this technique can compromise uniqueness and introduce additional local minima into the misfit function. While our prior research [J. Comput. Phys., 2018, 373:188-209] demonstrated the successful application of the quadratic Wasserstein metric with squaring scaling to earthquake location, it was limited to inverse problems with few degrees of freedom. This study provides a more comprehensive investigation into combining squaring scaling with the quadratic Wasserstein metric. By filtering inapplicable data, selecting seismic phases, and establishing a novel normalization method, we have successfully inverted the seismic velocity structure using this framework. Numerical experiments indicate that this proposed method yields a highly efficient and accurate approach for inversion.

Fluctuations influence nanoporous transport through intricate mechanisms, complicating the optimization of signal-to-noise ratios in engineered designs. This study examines the most fundamental nanopore configuration, involving non-interacting particles diffusing through a channel connecting two reservoirs. We demonstrate that the concentration gradient across the pore—comparable to an osmotic pressure drop—displays fractional temporal noise, with a mean square average increasing as $t^{1/2}$. This phenomenon stems from the diffusive exchange of particles between the two regions. Using both particle simulations and analytical solutions, we fully explain this effect and identify the controlling parameters, such as pore radius and thickness. Consequently, we show that the particle count within the pore also exhibits fractional noise. This type of noise leads to a noise spectral density scaling of $1/f^{3/2}$ with respect to frequency $f$, and we calculate its amplitude. Our theoretical framework extends to more complex nanoporous systems (e.g., those involving adsorption) and significantly streamlines both particle simulations and analytical calculations.

Techniques, concepts, and insights drawn from linear algebra, abstract algebra, and functional analysis prove highly valuable across engineering, science, and social sciences, particularly in fields like signal processing and system theory. These disciplines find extensive application in areas such as approximation, optimization, parameter identification, and big data analysis. Indeed, numerous significant concepts emerge from the fundamental operator equation $A x = b$ when examined through diverse perspectives. When $x$ and $b$ represent vectors within the same or distinct vector spaces, and $A$ acts as an operator, three compelling inquiries arise that establish a framework for a comprehensive study.

We derive the sampling probability density function (pdf) for an ideal, localized random electromagnetic field, covering scenarios where the field is either statistically homogeneous in a quasi-statically time-varying environment or statistically inhomogeneous and static. These findings facilitate the estimation of field statistics and confidence intervals when randomization stems from a single spatial or temporal stochastic process. We present results for both coherent and incoherent detection methods, applicable to Cartesian, planar, and full-vectorial fields. We demonstrate that the functional form of the sampling pdf varies depending on whether the random variable is dimensioned (such as the sampled electric field itself) or expressed as a dimensionless, standardized, or normalized quantity (such as the sampled field divided by its standard deviation). For dimensioned quantities, the electric field, its amplitude, and intensity follow distinct types of Bessel $K$ sampling pdfs; these differ significantly from asymptotic Gauss normal and $\chi^{(2)}_{2p}$ ensemble pdfs when $\nu$ is relatively small. In contrast, the corresponding standardized quantities yield Student $t$, Fisher-Snedecor $F$, and root-$F$ sampling pdfs, which display heavier tails than comparable Bessel $K$ pdfs. We further show that statistical uncertainties derived from classical small-sample theory for dimensionless quantities are overestimated relative to those for dimensioned quantities. Additionally, we identify differences in sampling pdfs resulting from de-normalization versus de-standardization.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have garnered significant attention from the machine learning community for tackling relational reasoning problems, broadly categorized into spatial and spectral methodologies. Spatial methods rely on learned message-passing mechanisms that compute local vertex interactions, allowing information to propagate across longer distances through multiple steps. In contrast, spectral approaches utilize eigendecompositions of the graph Laplacian to generalize spatial convolutions to graph-structured data, accessing both short and long temporal scales simultaneously. This work introduces the Spectral Graph Network, which integrates message passing across both spatial and spectral domains. The model projects spatial graph vertices onto Laplacian eigenvectors, treating each as a node in a fully connected "spectral graph," before applying learned message passing to these representations. Evaluated on various benchmarks—including graph-based MNIST classification, molecular property prediction on MoleculeNet and QM9, and shortest path problems on random graphs—the Spectral Graph Network demonstrates efficient training, achieving high performance with fewer iterations despite a higher parameter count. Additionally, the model exhibits robustness against edge dropout and surpasses baseline methods in classification tasks. Finally, we investigate how these performance advantages correlate with specific dataset properties.

Electroweak Symmetry Breaking (EWSB) is established as the mechanism responsible for generating the massive universe we inhabit, yet it also potentially delineates critical boundaries for the freeze-in or freeze-out dynamics of dark matter (DM) interacting with the Standard Model through a Higgs portal. This distinction arises because DM relic abundance processes evolve differently across this boundary. Our investigation focuses on a two-component DM scenario wherein a massive $U(1)_X$ gauge boson undergoes freeze-in, while a scalar singlet DM experiences freeze-out, with both components inheriting EWSB effects in a correlated manner. We examine two specific scenarios: one where both components transition from the thermal bath prior to EWSB, and another where these transitions occur subsequent to EWSB. After satisfying relic density requirements and accounting for the latest direct detection limits from XENON1T, we identify notable distinctive features within the model's parameter space for these two cases, several of which offer model-independent insights.

Normalized distance and similarity measures, functioning as dual concepts, are essential tools for decision-making and pattern recognition within the intuitionistic fuzzy sets (IFS) framework. To enhance effectiveness in these applications, a robust normalized distance measure must ensure that its corresponding dual similarity measure adheres to the required axiomatic definition. This paper first presents examples demonstrating that the dual similarity measures associated with two nonlinear distance measures introduced in previous works ([IEEE Trans. Syst., Man, Cybern., Syst., vol.~51, no.~6, pp. 3980--3992, 2021] and [Int. J. Intell. Syst., vol.~24, no.~4, pp. 399--420, 2009]) fail to satisfy this axiomatic definition. Specifically, we show that (1) these measures cannot effectively distinguish intuitionistic fuzzy values (IFVs) that possess an obvious size relationship, and (2) aside from endpoints, there exist infinitely many pairs of IFVs where these distances achieve the maximum value of 1, resulting in counter-intuitive outcomes. To address these limitations, we introduce the concepts of strict intuitionistic fuzzy distance measure (SIFDisM) and strict intuitionistic fuzzy similarity measure (SIFSimM), and propose an improved intuitionistic fuzzy distance measure based on Jensen-Shannon divergence. We prove that (1) the proposed measure qualifies as a SIFDisM; (2) its dual similarity measure is a SIFSimM; and (3) its induced entropy constitutes a valid intuitionistic fuzzy entropy. Comparative analysis and numerical examples confirm that the proposed distance measure is entirely superior to existing methods.

Semiconductor quantum dots are regarded as promising non-classical light sources for future quantum applications, distinguished by several emission characteristics. The ability to align with the telecom C-band is particularly vital for long-distance transmission and silicon-based on-chip processing, whereas source brightness and high single-photon purity remain essential for nearly all quantum implementations. This study introduces an InAs/InGaAs/GaAs quantum dot that emits within the telecom C-band and is integrated with a circular Bragg grating. The resulting Purcell enhancement facilitates high brightness, achieving a fiber-coupled single-photon count rate of 13.9 MHz under an excitation repetition rate of 228 MHz (with a first-lens collection efficiency of approximately 17% for NA = 0.6), all while sustaining a minimal multi-photon contribution of g(2)(0) = 0.0052. Furthermore, the system's compatibility with temperatures up to 40 K, achievable via compact cryogenic coolers, reinforces its potential for practical, out-of-laboratory deployment.
