Urban planners are increasingly leveraging deep learning-based computer vision models to inform decisions regarding the design of urban environments. These models forecast public perceptions of urban quality, such as safety and aesthetics. However, the opaque nature of deep learning hinders planners from identifying which specific landscape elements drive high or low quality perceptions. This study explores how computer vision can be utilized to derive policy-relevant insights into public urban space perception. Specifically, we trained two prominent architectures—a Convolutional Neural Network and a transformer—and applied GradCAM, a standard post-hoc explainable AI method, to identify image regions critical to the model's predictions. By manually annotating objects based on these GradCAM visualizations, we uncovered novel objects that existing object detection models used in prior research have failed to capture. Furthermore, our methodological findings indicate that transformer architectures are better paired with GradCAM techniques. The project code is accessible via Github.

A novel model is introduced that employs a general radiation energy expression to elucidate afterglow dynamics. The study demonstrates that this framework effectively applies to both ultra-relativistic and non-relativistic phases, as well as to the investigation of radiative and adiabatic fireballs.

A geometric wedge model representing the near-Earth nightside plasma sheet is employed to derive a wave equation for low-frequency shear flow-interchange waves. These waves facilitate the transmission of $\vec{E} \times \vec{B}$ sheared zonal flows along magnetic flux tubes toward the ionosphere. The study examines inconsistencies between this derived equation and the one utilized by Kalmoni et al. (2015) regarding shear flow-ballooning instability. The shear flow-interchange instability is identified as the likely driver of substorm onset. By applying the wedge wave equation, rough estimates for dispersion relations and local growth rates are calculated for the midnight region of the nightside magnetotail, where this instability triggers the formation of auroral beads characteristic of geomagnetic substorms. Furthermore, stability analysis of these modes indicates that nonlinear analysis is essential for achieving quantitative accuracy and reveals the spatial scale over which the instability evolves.

In prior research, the authors proposed a Lin-Lu-Yau style Ricci curvature for directed graphs based on the Chung Laplacian formulation. This note aims to establish a von Renesse-Sturm type characterization of the lower Ricci curvature bound through a gradient estimate for the heat semigroup and a transportation inequality along the heat flow. As an application, we derive a concentration of measure inequality for directed graphs exhibiting positive Ricci curvature.

A persistent obstacle in scaling crowdsourced NLP datasets is that human annotators frequently rely on repetitive patterns, resulting in insufficient linguistic variety. We propose a new dataset creation framework that synergizes the generative capabilities of AI with the evaluative expertise of humans. Building upon the MultiNLI dataset for natural language inference (NLI), our method employs dataset cartography to automatically pinpoint examples exhibiting complex reasoning patterns and directs GPT-3 to generate new instances mirroring these patterns. These machine-generated samples undergo automatic filtering before being refined and labeled by human crowdworkers. The final output, WANLI, comprises 107,885 NLI examples and exhibits distinct empirical advantages over current NLI benchmarks. Notably, models trained on WANLI outperform those trained on the four times larger MultiNLI across eight out-of-domain test sets, achieving an 11% improvement on HANS and a 9% gain on Adversarial NLI; furthermore, WANLI remains superior even when MultiNLI is augmented with other NLI datasets. These findings highlight the potential of integrating natural language generation techniques and redefining human involvement in the dataset creation lifecycle.

We examine classical spin systems undergoing continuous-time evolution on locally tree-like interaction graphs. While various approximate analysis techniques based on the Belief Propagation or cavity method have previously been proposed, we present a novel approach derived more systematically that demonstrates superior performance across several key problem classes.

Ullman et al.\cite{ullman2018does} recently proposed a modern, multidimensional framework for trust in human-robot interaction (HRI). This model posits that trust comprises two distinct dimensions: performance aspects, analogous to trust in human-automation systems, and moral aspects, comparable to trust in human-human relationships. However, the specific impacts of violating each dimension remain unclear. Specifically, it is unknown how trust shifts when a robot breaches moral versus performance trust, or whether physiological signals can effectively measure gains or losses in these separate trust categories. Consequently, this study aims to design an experiment within a search and rescue scenario to investigate the distinct effects of performance-trust and moral-trust violations. The research seeks to determine if two robot failures of equal magnitude elicit different responses in human trust, depending on whether the failure stems from a performance or a moral breach.

Irregular applications have become a critical workload area across diverse domains such as bioinformatics, chemistry, physics, social sciences, and machine learning. Consequently, optimizing both performance and energy efficiency for these emerging applications is essential. This dissertation investigates the fundamental sources of inefficiency in irregular applications within modern computing systems and addresses them by introducing low-overhead synchronization methods for parallel threads, paired with optimized data access strategies.

The research delivers four key contributions aimed at accelerating irregular applications across various contexts, including CPU and Near-Data-Processing (NDP) or Processing-In-Memory (PIM) architectures. First, we present Color$^{\text{TM}}$, a new parallel graph coloring algorithm for CPU systems that prioritizes reduced data access costs over synchronization overhead. Second, we develop SmartPQ, an adaptive priority queue capable of delivering high performance under diverse contention scenarios in Non-Uniform Memory Access (NUMA) CPU environments. Third, we introduce SynCron, the first practical hardware synchronization mechanism specifically designed for NDP systems. Fourth, we create SparseP, the inaugural library for high-performance Sparse Matrix Vector Multiplication on actual PIM systems.

Our findings demonstrate that co-designing lightweight synchronization mechanisms with tailored data access policies can substantially speed up irregular application execution on both CPU and NDP/PIM architectures. This work bridges the divide between processor-centric CPU systems and memory-centric PIM systems within the vital domain of irregular applications. We hope this dissertation motivates future research into co-designing software algorithms with advanced computing platforms to significantly enhance the performance of emerging irregular applications.

We theoretically demonstrate that a bilayer consisting of a three-dimensional (3D) topological insulator (TI) and a thin-film ferromagnetic metal (FMM) can function as a quantum anomalous Hall (QAH) insulator possessing a broad global band gap. Through an analysis of band structures and eigenstate weight distributions, we show that attaching a metallic thin film to a 3D TI shifts the topologically non-trivial state into the metallic layer via band hybridization near the original Dirac point. By incorporating magnetic exchange interactions within the thin-film layers, we calculated the anomalous Hall conductivity and magnetic anisotropy, suggesting that this bilayer configuration yields a wider gap for the QAH effect compared to conventional materials like magnetically doped 3D TI thin films or 3D TI/ferromagnetic insulator heterostructures. Our findings imply that the 3D TI/thin-film FMM bilayer could realize the QAH effect at room temperature, thereby facilitating the experimental observation of other exotic topological quantum phenomena.

In Release 14, the 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) introduced Vehicle-to-Vehicle (V2V) mode-3, a technology where the eNodeB facilitates resource allocation by assigning sidelink subchannels to vehicles. Consequently, vehicles broadcast their signals independently without prior coordination. The eNodeB plays a pivotal role in subchannel assignment, effectively managing V2V traffic and avoiding allocation conflicts, which is essential for reliable signal reception by other vehicles. To address this, we propose two suboptimal resource allocation schemes with reduced complexity compared to exhaustive search: Bipartite Graph Matching-based Successive Allocation (BGM-SA) and Bipartite Graph Matching-based Parallel Allocation (BGM-PA). Both methods include constraints to prevent conflicts. This study focuses on overlapping clusters, such as those occurring at intersections or highway merges. Simulation results indicate that BGM-SA achieves near-optimal performance, whereas BGM-PA offers lower complexity but inferior performance. Furthermore, since BGM-PA relies on inter-cluster vehicle pre-grouping, we investigate various metrics to effectively represent the channel conditions of these groups. While this approach sacrifices optimal system capacity due to the use of simplified surrogate information, it significantly lowers computational complexity.

This study examines quantum phase transitions, criticality, and Berry phases within the ground state of a system comprising non-interacting two-level atoms in a non-linear optical medium, coupled to a single-mode quantized electromagnetic field. External pumping via a classical electric field induces degenerate parametric amplification, significantly altering field dynamics while leaving the atomic sector unaffected. Using a semiclassical approach, the various phases of this extended Dicke model are characterized. Quantum phase transitions are identified by analyzing expectation values of specific system observables, as well as the Berry phase and its first derivative, which function as order parameters. Notably, the model demonstrates that quantum criticality can be controlled by appropriately selecting parameters of the non-linear optical medium, potentially enabling experimental access to the superradiant region using low-intensity lasers.

Let $H$ be a graph with $h$ vertices. The vertex arboricity $ar(H)$ denotes the smallest integer $r$ such that the vertex set $V(H)$ can be divided into $r$ subsets, each inducing a forest. We demonstrate that for sufficiently large $n \in h\mathbb{N}$, every $n$-vertex graph $G$ satisfying $\delta(G) \geq \max\left\{\left(1-\frac{2}{f(H)}+o(1)\right)n, \left(\frac{1}{2}+o(1)\right)n\right\}$ and $\alpha(G)=o(n)$ contains an $H$-factor, where $f(H)$ equals either $2ar(H)$ or $2ar(H)-1$. This finding serves as an analogue to the Alon--Yuster theorem \cite{MR1376050} within Ramsey--Tur\'{a}n theory, extending the work of Balogh--Molla--Sharifzadeh~\cite{MR3570984} and Knierm--Su~\cite{MR4193066} regarding clique factors. Specifically, the derived degree conditions are asymptotically optimal for infinitely many graphs $H$ that are not cliques.

A theoretical framework involving a maverick top partner that decays into a dark photon has been proposed. When the dark photon mass is approximately 100 GeV, it decays into two overlapping electrons, creating a signature known as a lepton-jet. This process also yields a top quark, resulting in events characterized by two boosted objects: one heavy and one light. We introduce a search strategy that leverages this distinctive signal topology. Our analysis demonstrates that, with specific kinematic cuts applied to both the hadronic and leptonic decay channels of the Standard Model top quark, nearly all background can be suppressed. This leaves a sufficient number of signal events to make the search viable at the LHC for top partner masses reaching approximately 3 TeV.

Selective classification, also known as classification with a reject option, couples a classifier with a selection mechanism to decide if a prediction should be accepted. This framework balances coverage—the likelihood of accepting a prediction—against predictive performance, which is often evaluated using distributive loss functions. However, in various practical contexts like credit scoring, performance is assessed via ranking metrics, such as the Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC). We introduce a model-agnostic method designed to pair a selection function with a probabilistic binary classifier, specifically to optimize AUC. Our work includes theoretical support and presents a new algorithm named $AUCross$ to achieve this. Experimental results demonstrate that $AUCross$ effectively manages the trade-off between coverage and AUC, outperforming existing selective classification techniques that focus on accuracy.

The orientable genus of a graph $G$ represents the minimum count of handles needed to embed the graph onto a surface. Although determining this genus is a foundational problem, it is frequently challenging. We demonstrate that for any integer $d \geq 2$, the genus of a random $d$-regular graph with $n$ vertices equals $\frac{(d - 2)}{4}n(1 - \varepsilon)$ with high probability, for any $\varepsilon > 0$.

Medical image segmentation plays a critical role in diagnostics, necessitating automatic, robust, and valid outcomes for physicians. Hidden Markov Random Fields (HMRF) offer a powerful modeling approach by framing segmentation as the minimization of an energy function. The Cuckoo Search (CS) algorithm is a recent nature-inspired meta-heuristic that has demonstrated significant efficiency across various engineering optimization tasks. This study employs three variants of the Cuckoo Search algorithm to perform medical image segmentation.

Advanced LIGO interferometers exhibit time-varying responses [arXiv:1608.05134], necessitating that accurate calibration procedures track and adjust for fluctuations in model parameters. During the first three observing runs, these variations were monitored, and compensation for several was integrated into the calibration workflow. Specifically, during the second run, multiplicative corrections were applied to the interferometer response for both real-time and high-latency calibrated strain data. Following the second run and throughout the third, high-latency calibration incorporated filter updates to address the time dependence of the coupled cavity pole frequency $f_{\rm cc}$. New methods have since been established to handle time-dependent variations in the response, including dynamic adjustments to filters, gains, poles, zeros, and time delays. This compensation for well-modeled temporal variations has reduced systematic calibration errors to less than 2% in magnitude and less than 2° in phase within LIGO's most sensitive band (20–2000 Hz) [arXiv:2005.02531, arXiv:2107.00129]. Furthermore, this approach has been demonstrated to decrease uncertainty and bias in sky localization for simulated binary neutron star mergers.

The semiconducting behavior of regioregular poly(3-hexylthiophene) is evaluated through impedance measurements spanning 40 Hz to 100 MHz. X-ray diffraction reveals the material contains both ordered and disordered domains. Nyquist plot analysis of the impedance data displays two semi-circular arcs, the dimensions of which decrease under d.c. bias. Furthermore, changes in carrier concentration induced by light or chemical doping modify both the shape and size of these arcs. Fitting the data to equivalent circuits indicates significant variations in resistive, capacitive, and constant-phase element parameters as carrier density rises. Specifically, increasing carrier density shortens the relaxation time in ordered regions, while having a minimal effect on disordered regions.

The impact of qubit channels on projective measurements applied to qubit states is employed to demonstrate an equivalence between these channels and the characteristics of generalized measurements, specifically those defined by bias and sharpness parameters. This relationship can be viewed as a transition from the Schrödinger to the Heisenberg picture in describing measurement dynamics. Notably, unital quantum channels are demonstrated to generate unbiased measurements, whereas Markovian channels correspond to scenarios where measurement sharpness decreases monotonically over time. These findings are exemplified through an analysis of various noise channels. Additionally, the influence of bias and sharpness parameters on the energetic cost of measurements, along with their interaction with the non-Markovian nature of the dynamics, is examined.

Integrating external language models (LMs) into end-to-end (E2E) speech recognition systems for domain adaptation remains a difficult challenge. Recently, Internal Language Model Estimation (ILME)-based fusion has demonstrated substantial reductions in Word Error Rate (WER) compared to Shallow Fusion by subtracting a weighted internal LM score from the interpolation of E2E and external LM scores during beam search. However, optimal LM interpolation weights fluctuate significantly across different test sets, necessitating extensive tuning on well-matched validation data. This work proposes performing LM fusion directly within the Minimum WER (MWER) training of an E2E model to eliminate the need for weight tuning during inference. In addition to MWER training with Shallow Fusion (MWER-SF), we introduce a novel MWER training approach using ILME (MWER-ILME), where ILME-based fusion generates N-best hypotheses and their posteriors, inducing additional gradients when the internal LM is utilized in the MWER-ILME loss calculation. During inference, the LM weights determined during MWER training ensure robust integration across diverse test domains. Experiments conducted on 30K-hour trained transformer transducers show that MWER-ILME achieves average relative WER reductions of 8.8% and 5.8% compared to MWER and MWER-SF training, respectively, across six different test sets.

The magnetorotational instability (MRI) serves as a cornerstone mechanism governing the large-scale behavior of astrophysical accretion disks. In collisionless flows surrounding supermassive black holes, MRI-induced plasma turbulence that cascades down to microscopic kinetic scales can drive enhanced angular-momentum transport and redistribution, facilitate nonthermal particle acceleration, and create a two-temperature regime where electrons and ions heat unevenly. Nevertheless, standard magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) methods, commonly used to investigate the MRI, fail to capture this underlying microscopic physics. This study investigates the nonlinear evolution of MRI turbulence within a pair plasma using fully kinetic Particle-in-Cell (PIC) simulations in both two and three dimensions. Initially, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of axisymmetric MRI using 2D simulations to elucidate how and why this geometry yields outcomes significantly divergent from MHD predictions. Subsequently, we execute the largest 3D simulations to date, utilizing a new shearing-box technique, which demonstrates that sufficiently large 3D PIC models can replicate mesoscale (MHD-level) MRI dynamics. Leveraging these fully kinetic simulations, we characterize the nonthermal particle acceleration and angular-momentum transport generated by collisionless MRI. Given that these microscopic mechanisms ultimately produce potentially observable radiation in accreting plasmas, our work is crucial for interpreting current and future observations from first principles, transcending the constraints of fluid models. Although this initial study focuses on pair plasmas for simplicity, our findings constitute a vital step toward developing more realistic electron-ion simulations, which will be the subject of future research.

The identification of the Higgs boson has established a fresh pathway for investigating physics that extends beyond the Standard Model. This review examines the cosmological implications of the most straightforward Higgs interactions with a hidden sector, referred to as the Higgs portal. We specifically analyze the consequences of these couplings for inflation, vacuum stability, and dark matter, covering both conventional weakly interacting massive particles and feebly interacting scalars. Notably, the cosmological effects arising from the Higgs portal can remain significant even when the coupling values are extremely small.

We introduce a metallic-silicon architecture featuring a complex optical potential modulated along the waveguide to achieve robust higher harmonic generation. Specifically, for right-propagating fields where the non-Hermiticity strength matches the real component of the optical potential, the dynamical equations governing modal field amplitudes adopt a Jordan form Hamiltonian. This configuration enables unidirectional generation of higher frequencies that reach a peak value at a particular waveguide length, remaining unaffected by geometric imperfections. Additionally, the phase of the generated higher harmonic becomes decoupled from the interaction between the fundamental and higher frequency modes. Distinct from other spatiotemporal modulated systems with Jordan form Hamiltonians, this setup maintains reciprocity in the fundamental mode while ensuring non-reciprocity in harmonic generation. As a result, although the device is unsuitable for optical isolation, it is well-suited for applications such as laser cavities, interferometry, and holography.

Building upon our companion study [Phys. Rev. D 103 (2021) 10, [2101.02951]], where we established short-ranged potentials for massless spins $(0,1/2,1,2)$ within the Teukolsky equations under general spherically-symmetric, static metrics, this work applies those findings to numerically calculate Hawking radiation spectra for particles emitted by black holes (BHs) across three distinct scenarios: charged BHs, higher-dimensional BHs, and polymerized BHs emerging from quantum gravity models. To validate the robustness of our numerical approach, we demonstrate its consistency with recently derived analytic formulas for cross-sections in both low and high energy regimes. Furthermore, we illustrate how integrating these short-ranged potentials and precise radiation rates into the $\texttt{BlackHawk}$ code enables predictions of future primordial BH evaporation signals for a broad spectrum of BH solutions, including regular BH solutions from loop quantum gravity. Notably, we establish the first Hawking radiation constraints on polymerized BHs using AMEGO data. Additionally, we demonstrate that the mass window of $10^{16}-10^{18}\,$g, previously closed for all dark matter candidates as primordial BHs, can be reopened when the polymerization parameter—representing the scale and strength of quantum gravity corrections—is sufficiently large.

Software fault localization is a costly, labor-intensive, and time-consuming aspect of debugging that becomes particularly difficult in Software Product Line (SPL) systems due to the variability of failures. These unexpected behaviors stem from variability faults, which manifest only under specific combinations of system features, as interactions among these features trigger system failures. While bug localization in single-system engineering has been extensively studied, variability fault localization in SPL contexts remains largely unexplored. This article introduces VarCop, a novel and effective approach for localizing variability faults. When an SPL system fails due to variability bugs, VarCop isolates suspicious code statements by analyzing test results from sampled products alongside their source code. These isolated statements are those involved in feature interactions necessary for bug visibility. The suspiciousness of each statement is evaluated based on both the aggregate test results of products containing it and the detailed outcomes of test cases executed by that statement. Empirical evaluation on a large dataset of buggy SPL systems demonstrates that VarCop significantly outperforms two state-of-the-art fault localization techniques, improving the ranking of incorrect statements by 33% and 50% in single-bug scenarios. In approximately two-thirds of cases, VarCop places buggy statements within the top three positions. For multiple-bug scenarios, VarCop exceeds state-of-the-art methods by factors of two and ten regarding the proportion of bugs localized at the top position. Furthermore, VarCop correctly ranks at least one bug in the top-1 and top-5 positions in 22% and 65% of buggy versions, respectively.

The symbol serves to describe the Springer correspondence for classical groups. We introduce uniform, equivalent definitions of symbols for rigid partitions within the $B_n$, $C_n$, and $D_n$ theories. By analyzing this new definition in detail, we establish construction rules for partition symbols that are both intuitive and easy to apply. We also introduce formal partition operations that simplify the proof of these construction rules. Leveraging these rules, we derive a unified closed formula for symbols across all theories. As applications, the construction rules provide a clearer illustration of previous results.

To compare the photometric characteristics of galaxies across various redshifts, fluxes must be adjusted for shifts in effective rest-frame filter wavelengths, known as $k$-corrections. When $z>0.3$, this wavelength shift is substantial enough that typical broadband bands move into adjacent rest-frame regions; at $z=0.6-0.8$, the shift spans two or even three bands. Consequently, $k$-corrections must be applied between different observed bandpasses. This study expands upon the methodology introduced by Chilingarian et al. (2010) by fitting cross-band $k$-corrections using smooth, low-order polynomial functions of one observed color and redshift. While a version without cross-band capabilities is already available as standard functions in {\sc topcat} for galaxies with $z<0.5$, we also derived analytic approximations for WISE bands, which were previously unavailable. We now possess a comprehensive set of $k$-correction coefficients enabling the processing of photometric data for galaxies out to $z=1$. These standard and cross-band corrections were calculated for approximately 4 million galaxies in the second Reference Catalog of Spectral Energy Distributions (RCSEDv2). Our analysis demonstrates that, for commonly used UV, optical, and near-infrared filters, our analytic approximations are highly accurate and suitable for extragalactic data from future wide-field surveys.

This study reports a measurement of the polarisation of $W$ bosons originating from top-quark decays, utilizing proton-proton collision data recorded at a centre-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV. The dataset, gathered by the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider, comprises an integrated luminosity of 139 fb$^{-1}$. The analysis focuses on $t\bar{t}$ events characterized by final states containing two charged leptons (electrons or muons) and a minimum of two jets identified as originating from $b$-quarks. The polarisation fractions are derived from the differential cross-section distribution of the $\cos{\theta^{*}}$ variable, defined as the angle between the $W$ boson decay lepton's momentum and the opposite direction of the $b$-quark momentum, both evaluated within the $W$ boson rest frame. Corrected parton-level results for the $\cos{\theta^{*}}$ angle are provided. The observed fractions for longitudinal, left-handed, and right-handed polarisation states are determined to be $f_{0} = 0.684 \pm 0.005\,\mathrm{(stat.)} \pm 0.014\,\mathrm{(syst.)}$, $f_{\mathrm{L}} = 0.318 \pm 0.003\,\mathrm{(stat.)} \pm 0.008\,\mathrm{(syst.)}$, and $f_{\mathrm{R}} = -0.002 \pm 0.002\,\mathrm{(stat.)} \pm 0.014\,\mathrm{(syst.)}$, respectively, consistent with Standard Model expectations.

A single-hop beeping network is a distributed communication framework where all nodes interact by transmitting single-bit messages, known as beeps. This paper addresses two core challenges in distributed computing: naming and counting. Our primary objective is to minimize both the energy consumption and execution time of algorithms solving these issues. We present randomized algorithms that achieve optimal performance for both naming and counting on networks of $n$ stations, with a running time of $O(n \log n)$ and an energy complexity of $O(\log n)$.

Dark radiation (DR) emerges as a potential new physics candidate across various scenarios extending the Standard Model. Although perturbations in DR are frequently assumed to be adiabatic, the presence of multiple fields during inflation—whose decay products fail to fully thermalize—can readily introduce isocurvature components. By applying specific isocurvature initial conditions, we establish constraints on both uncorrelated and correlated DR density isocurvature perturbations using solely the full Planck 2018 dataset, as well as in conjunction with other cosmological observations. Our investigation into free-streaming DR (FDR) revises and expands existing limits on neutrino density isocurvature perturbations by accounting for a variable number of relativistic degrees of freedom, while we present the first-ever bounds for coupled DR (CDR) isocurvature. Furthermore, we demonstrate that CDR introduces qualitatively distinct physical effects compared to FDR; notably, under isocurvature initial conditions, FDR produces larger CMB anisotropies than CDR, which contrasts with the adiabatic scenario. Overall, our findings indicate a preference for a blue-tilted DR isocurvature spectrum, which yields a higher Hubble constant ($H_0$) relative to the standard $\Lambda$CDM+$\Delta N_{\rm eff}$ model with adiabatic spectra, thereby alleviating the $H_0$ tension.

This paper establishes the non-uniqueness of the three-dimensional magneto-hydrodynamic (MHD) system within the space $C([0,T];L^2(\mathbb{T}^3))$ for any initial data belonging to $H^{\bar{\beta}}(\mathbb{T}^3)$ where $\bar{\beta}>0$. We achieve this by demonstrating that both total energy and cross helicity remain controllable over a specified positive time interval. These findings broaden the scope of non-uniqueness results from the ideal MHD system to include viscous and resistive variants. Unlike the ideal case, the dissipation inherent in viscous and resistive MHD prevents the nonlinear term from offsetting the stress error $(\RR_q,\MM_q)$ as previously shown in \cite{2Beekie}. To address this, we employ box-type flows and construct a perturbation composed of six distinct flow types within a convex integral framework, ensuring the iteration process functions correctly and ultimately proving non-uniqueness.

Retinopathy of Prematurity (ROP) is a fibrovascular proliferative condition impacting the developing peripheral retinal vasculature in premature infants. Early identification is feasible in stages 1 and 2, which are defined by a demarcation line or ridge of specific width that distinguishes vascularized retina from the peripheral retina. Identifying this ridge within neonatal retinal images is challenging due to low contrast. This paper focuses on detecting this critical landmark for ROP diagnosis using a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). Our contribution involves employing a Mask R-CNN model to detect the demarcation line/ridge, thereby aiding clinicians in more accurately identifying stage 2 ROP. To address poor image quality, the proposed system incorporates an image enhancement pre-processing step. We utilized labeled neonatal images to explore CNN-based ridge localization, drawing from the KIDROP project dataset containing 220 images from 45 infants. The system was trained on 175 retinal images with ground truth ridge segmentation and tested on the remaining 45 images, achieving a detection accuracy of 0.88. These results demonstrate that deep learning combined with pre-processing via image normalization enables robust detection of ROP in its early stages.

A vast array of challenging combinatorial problems can be represented through systems of polynomial equations. N. Alon introduced the concept of the polynomial method to denote the application of nonlinear polynomials in addressing these issues. This work extends the investigation into the polynomial method by demonstrating how the algorithmic theory of polynomial ideals facilitates the detection of k-colorability, unique Hamiltonicity, and automorphism rigidity within graphs. Our approach employs a variety of techniques, including Nullstellensatz certificates, linear algebra over finite fields, Groebner bases, toric algebra, convex programming, and real algebraic geometry.

Kernel herding and herding are deterministic techniques for selecting samples that summarize a probability distribution, a task closely related to choosing samples for integral estimation via Bayesian quadrature. We demonstrate that the criterion minimized during sample selection in kernel herding is mathematically equivalent to the posterior variance in Bayesian quadrature. Furthermore, we establish that sequential Bayesian quadrature can be interpreted as a weighted variant of kernel herding that outperforms any other weighted herding approach. Empirical results confirm a convergence rate exceeding O(1/N), and our findings also provide an upper bound on the empirical error of the Bayesian quadrature estimate.

This paper demonstrates that the Vietoris-Rips complex $\mathcal R(n,r)$, constructed from $n$ points randomly sampled from a uniformly positive probability measure on a convex body $K\subseteq \mathbb R^d$, is almost surely contractible when $r \geq c\left(\frac{\ln n}{n}\right)^{1/d}$, where $c$ is a constant determined by $K$ and the specific probability measure. This result resolves a query posed by Kahle in 2011. Furthermore, we generalize the proof to show that if $K$ is a compact, smooth $d$-manifold with boundary (which need not be convex), then $\mathcal R(n,r)$ is almost surely homotopy equivalent to $K$ provided $c_1\left(\frac{\ln n}{n}\right)^{1/d} \leq r \leq c_2$, with $c_1$ and $c_2$ depending on $K$. Our methodologies reveal a link to the game of cops and robbers.

Formal methods offer systematic and rigorous approaches to software development, and we firmly advocate for their inclusion in computer science curricula. This paper outlines the pedagogical justification and the practical execution of two courses focused on formal methods, including shared instructional materials. These courses emphasize formal verification to guarantee software safety and security, with a specific focus on the Internet of Things domain.

Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) poses a significant threat of vision loss or blindness, especially among the elderly. In exudative AMD, abnormal blood vessels grow from the choroid beneath the macula, penetrating the blood-retina barrier (composed of Bruch's membrane and the retinal pigment epithelium), and leaking fluid and blood that displace photoreceptors. This study presents a computational model of angiogenesis using a cellular Potts approach to simulate interactions between choroidal vessels, Bruch's membrane, retinal pigment epithelium cells, drusen, and photoreceptors. The findings suggest that mitigating AMD involves restoring impaired lateral adhesion between retinal pigment epithelium cells and Bruch's membrane, alongside reducing levels of Vessel Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF) and Jagged proteins involved in the Notch signaling pathway. Numerical simulations indicate that while anti-VEGF and anti-Jagged therapies may provide temporary relief, correcting defective cellular adhesion could offer more sustained long-term efficacy.

Plant water stress arises from either insufficient water availability in the soil or heightened transpiration rates. These conditions negatively impact plant physiology and photosynthesis, ultimately inhibiting growth and yield [18]. Detecting water stress early allows for timely corrective actions to secure anticipated crop yields. Furthermore, enhancing crop productivity through precision agriculture aligns with climate policies and the UN Sustainable Development Goals [1]. Leaf Water Content (LWC) serves as a metric to estimate water levels and detect stressed plants; during early growth stages, LWC is a critical indicator of potential productivity and yield. Water stress effects can be immediate, disrupting gaseous exchange [15], or long-term, causing significant reductions in performance [9, 18, 22]. Consequently, identifying stress during the initial growth phase is essential for implementing corrective irrigation and mitigating damage [15]. Additionally, LWC helps identify genotypes tolerant to water stress and salinity by assessing LWC stability under artificially induced stress conditions [18, 25]. However, traditional LWC measurement often requires destructive sampling, which is labor-intensive and time-consuming. To address this, the current research proposes a non-destructive approach to estimate LWC using UAV-based hyperspectral data.

We establish a uniform variant of Varadhan's decomposition for shift-invariant closed uniform forms linked to large-scale interacting systems across general crystal lattices. This finding specifically encompasses translation-invariant processes on Euclidean lattices $\mathbf{Z}^d$ with finite range. Our work extends the results from arXiv:2009.04699, which were limited to systems on transitive graphs. Future research will leverage this article's findings to demonstrate Varadhan's decomposition of closed $L^2$-forms for large-scale interacting systems on general crystal lattices.

When a quantum emitter operates within a dynamic environment, its energy levels can drift uncontrollably due to fluctuations in the surrounding bath. This phenomenon broadens the emission and absorption spectrum across a wide frequency range, posing significant challenges for practical applications. In this study, we examine a quantum emitter whose environment induces energy shifts, causing the emission frequency to follow a Gaussian random distribution characterized by a specific mean, standard deviation, and correlation time. We investigate how the system's emission spectrum behaves when subjected to a periodic sequence of finite-width $\pi$ pulses. Our findings demonstrate that this external control protocol can effectively mitigate spectral diffusion by refocusing the majority of the emission spectrum onto the pulse carrier frequency. Furthermore, we analyze two emitters situated in distinct noisy environments and show that applying the same pulse sequence to both enables efficient two-photon interference. Finally, we illustrate that an ensemble of nominally identical emitters, each experiencing a unique environment and thus a randomly shifted frequency, can have its collectively inhomogeneously broadened spectrum refocused into a lineshape featuring a well-defined central peak. This peak's linewidth matches that of a single isolated emitter free from noise. Collectively, these results confirm that for this specific model of noisy environments, an external control protocol—represented here by a periodic sequence of finite-width pulses—can successfully protect spectral properties.

The objective of stable sparse recovery involves reconstructing a $k$-sparse approximation $x*$ of a vector $x$ based on linear measurements. Specifically, we aim to find $x*$ such that $||x-x*||_p \leq C \min_{k\text{-sparse } x'} ||x-x'||_q$ for a constant $C$ and specific norm parameters $p$ and $q$. It is established that when $p=q=1$ or $p=q=2$, this can be achieved with $m=O(k \log (n/k))$ non-adaptive measurements [CRT06], a bound proven to be tight [DIPW10,FPRU10,PW11]. In this work, we demonstrate that allowing adaptive measurements significantly reduces the required number of measurements. Specifically, for $C=1+\epsilon$ and $p=q=2$, we present: (1) a scheme requiring $m=O((1/\epsilon)k \log \log (n \epsilon/k))$ measurements across $O(\log^* k \log \log (n \epsilon/k))$ rounds, and (2) a two-round scheme using $m=O((1/\epsilon) k \log (k/\epsilon) + k \log (n/k))$ measurements. Both approaches offer substantial improvements over non-adaptive limits and represent the first results of their kind. Additionally, as a separate application, we address finding a duplicate in a data stream of $n$ items from $\{1, \dots, n-1\}$ using $O(\log n)$ space and $O(\log \log n)$ passes, thereby improving upon the space complexity achievable with a single pass.

We establish a functional transcendence theorem regarding the integrals of algebraic forms within families of algebraic varieties. This result enables us to demonstrate a geometric formulation of Andr\'e's extension of the Grothendieck period conjecture, expressed through the framework of Nori motives. Specifically, we prove an Ax--Schanuel conjecture concerning the relationship between flat and algebraic coordinates for any admissible graded polarizable variation of integral mixed Hodge structures. This finding can be viewed as a broadening of recent Ax--Schanuel theorems by \cite{chiu,GaoKlingler} that address mixed period maps.

Recent years have seen a surge in Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications designed for code-mixed (CM) or multilingual text, driven largely by the widespread use of language mixing in social media within diverse, multilingual regions such as India, Mexico, parts of Europe, and the USA. Although word embeddings are fundamental components of modern NLP systems, creating them for CM languages remains an uncharted area. The primary challenge lies in "switching points"—locations where one language transitions to another—which suffer from a lack of contextual information and statistical reliability due to high variance in observed data. This paper outlines initial findings on applying switching-point-based positional encoding techniques to CM languages, specifically focusing on Hinglish (Hindi-English). While the results offer only marginal improvements over the state-of-the-art, they suggest that positional encoding is a promising approach for training position-sensitive language models on CM text.

Achieving significant advancements in perovskite solar cells requires divalent cation-incorporated lead halide perovskites that exhibit improved performance, greater stability, and lower toxicity. Although mixing strategies exist, they have not been widely explored to reduce lead content. This study investigates the structural, electronic, and optical characteristics of RbPb{1-x}MxI3 (where M represents Sn or Ge, and x equals 0.25, 0.50, or 0.75) via B-site alloying using density functional theory. Calculated formation enthalpies for all compositions confirm the stability of these structures. A detailed analysis of energy bandgaps and density of states (DOS) reveals that the bandgap narrows as Sn/Ge content increases, reaching a minimum of 1.850 eV at x = 0.50 for the RbPb{1-x}GexI3 system. Additionally, effective masses, exciton binding energies, and spectroscopic limited maximum efficiency (SLME) were determined for all mixed systems. Notably, the exciton character transitions from Mott-Wannier to Frenkel type as Sn and Ge concentrations rise. An efficiency of 23% is attained with an active layer composed of an equal mixture of Sn, Ge, and Pb. These findings align with existing literature on similar systems.

We employed density functional calculations alongside linearized Migdal-Eliashberg equations and the functional derivative method, which incorporates the energy-dependent variation of the density of states at the Fermi level ($N(\varepsilon)$) across phonon energy scales. This methodology was used to trace the pressure-dependent evolution of the critical temperature ($T_{c}$) and isotope effect coefficient ($\alpha$) for H$_{3}$S within its $lm\bar{3}m$ crystal structure, spanning pressures from 162 to 250 GPa. Compared to the constant $N(\varepsilon)$ approximation, this approach yields significantly better agreement with experimental $T_{c}$ values across the entire pressure range. For $\alpha$, we accounted for two primary components: a positive electron-phonon (el-ph) contribution and a negative electron-electron (el-el) term. Our results show a monotonic decrease in $\alpha$ with increasing pressure, regardless of whether the $N(\varepsilon)$ or constant $N(0)$ scheme is used. However, including the energy dependence of $N(\varepsilon)$ induces significant renormalization in both el-ph and el-el contributions, thereby enhancing consistency with experimental data, particularly at high pressures. Consequently, the observed pressure-driven changes in $T_{c}$ and $\alpha$ underscore the pivotal role of energy-dependent $N(\varepsilon)$ in accurately modeling the superconducting state of high-$T_{c}$ metal hydrides like H$_{3}$S, especially regarding their van Hove singularities.

This letter extends Spekkens' concept of measurement non-contextuality (NC). We demonstrate that any ontological model adhering to this non-contextual definition cannot account for the statistical outcomes of a single, specifically designed POVM performed sequentially on a quantum system. This POVM functions as a unified measurement apparatus, where the measurement context is defined by the various configurations in which the device is utilized. We derive an inequality based on non-contextual ontic models and identify corresponding quantum scenarios where the device's measurement results violate this NC inequality. Our findings highlight previously unexamined consequences of contextuality regarding a single measurement device and establish a foundation for further investigating the implications of contextuality in sequential measurements.

We introduce a framework designed to analyze layered quantum algorithms, including quantum alternating operator ansätze. This framework connects quantum cost gradient operators—derived from mixing and cost Hamiltonians—to classical cost difference functions that capture the neighborhood structure of cost functions. By examining QAOA circuits through the Heisenberg picture, we obtain exact general expressions for expectation values as series expansions involving algorithm parameters, cost gradient operators, and cost difference functions. These derivations provide new interpretability and insights into QAOA behavior across various parameter regimes. For single-level QAOA1, we explicitly demonstrate leading-order changes in output probabilities and cost expectations in terms of classical cost differences for arbitrary cost functions. This shows that with sufficiently small positive parameters, probability flows on average from lower to higher cost states, and that parameter signs can control this flow direction. Using these findings, we derive a classical random algorithm that emulates QAOA1 in the small-parameter regime, producing bitstring samples with identical probabilities up to negligible error. For deeper QAOA$p$ circuits, we apply the framework to derive similar and supplementary results, proving that QAOA consistently outperforms random guessing. We also explain how the framework integrates cost Hamiltonian locality for specific problem classes, such as causal cone approaches, and applies to performance analysis with arbitrary parameters. Finally, we illustrate these results with examples covering QUBO problems, MaxCut, and MaxSat variants, as well as applications to constrained optimization problems like Max Independent Set and Graph Coloring using mixing unitaries beyond the standard transverse-field mixer.

For affine-type quantum groups, Lusztig established an explicit construction of the affine canonical basis through simple perverse sheaves. In this study, we derive a bar-invariant basis utilizing a PBW basis generated by representations of the associated tame quiver. We demonstrate that this bar-invariant basis aligns with Lusztig's canonical basis and establish a specific bijection between their respective elements. The indexing sets for these bases are systematically organized by modules within preprojective, regular non-homogeneous, and preinjective components, alongside irreducible characters of symmetric groups. Our findings build upon the work of Lin, Xiao, and Zhang and are closely connected to the research of Beck and Nakajima. A pivotal technique employed in our construction involves a generalization of the method proposed by Deng, Du, and Xiao.

Streamline tracing within conical hypersonic flows is critical for the design of high-performance waveriders and intakes. Traditionally, streamline equations are resolved following the calculation of the velocity field from an axisymmetric conical flow solution. Waverider geometries are typically constructed by repeatedly applying streamline tracing across multiple planes based on the base conical flow. However, this approach becomes computationally costly when exploring design spaces for optimization. This study introduces a novel strategy: first, the Taylor-Maccoll equations for inviscid axisymmetric conical flow and the streamlines originating from the shock are solved across a broad spectrum of cone angles and Mach numbers to create a comprehensive database. These streamlines are then fitted with third-order polynomials, and an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) is trained to predict the polynomial coefficients for any given combination of Mach number, cone angle, and shock-origin streamline location. This method was applied to design a cone-derived waverider, with results compared against both standard conical and simplified waverider design methods. The ANN technique demonstrated high accuracy, yielding coordinate differences of only 0.68% relative to the standard method. Furthermore, RANS simulations revealed that the ANN-derived waverider avoids the severe leading-edge flow spillage seen in designs generated by the simplified method. Ultimately, this new ANN-based approach is 20 times faster than conventional techniques.

We demonstrate that the $k$-th positive integer moment of partial sums of Steinhaus random multiplicative functions on the interval $(x, x+H]$ coincides with the corresponding Gaussian moment, provided that $H\ll x/(\log x)^{2k^2+2+o(1)}$ and $H$ increases as $x$ grows. Furthermore, we establish that appropriately normalized partial sums of typical multiplicative functions derived from random multiplicative function realizations exhibit a Gaussian limiting distribution within short moving intervals $(x, x+H]$ where $H\ll X/(\log X)^{W(X)}$ and $H$ tends to infinity with $X$. In this context, $x$ is selected uniformly from $\{1,2,\dots, X\}$, and $W(X)$ increases with $X$ at an arbitrarily slow rate. These findings represent initial progress toward answering a recent question posed by Harper.

This study investigates a linear quadratic (LQ) leader-follower stochastic differential game involving regime-switching diffusions with mean-field interactions. A key contribution is the inclusion of conditional mean-field terms within both the state dynamics and the cost functionals. Utilizing stochastic maximum principles (SMPs), the followers' and leaders' optimization problems are addressed sequentially to derive an open-loop Stackelberg equilibrium. Furthermore, by applying a four-step scheme, the associated Hamiltonian systems for both players are decoupled; consequently, the open-loop Stackelberg equilibrium can be expressed in state feedback form, provided that specific new-type Riccati equations are solvable.

Conventional clustering analyses of galaxy redshift surveys transform clustering data into a collection of late-time physical parameters in a manner independent of any specific model. This methodology has recently been enhanced by incorporating an extra shape variable that captures information regarding early-time physics. By applying this novel technique, ShapeFit, to SDSS-III BOSS data, we demonstrate that it achieves constraining power comparable to alternative, model-dependent methods that directly limit model parameters based on a cosmological framework from the start. ShapeFit offers several advantages: it is approximately 30 times faster, remains model-independent, inherently separates early- and late-time variables, and provides superior control over observational systematics.

This study employs first-principles calculations to examine how chemical disorder influences magnetic exchange interactions and the Curie temperature ($T_{\text{c}}$) within L1$_0$-ordered FeNi. By utilizing supercells, we capture the specific symmetry-broken local environments surrounding individual atoms. Our results reveal significant fluctuations in the dominant first-nearest neighbor Fe-Fe interaction across different inequivalent pairs, varying from approximately 5 meV to 37 meV, which contrasts with the 27 meV coupling strength observed in the ordered state. To assess the impact of these substantial variations in magnetic coupling constants on the $T_{\text{c}}$ of disordered or partially ordered systems, we analyzed a simple Heisenberg model featuring random Gaussian-distributed nearest neighbor couplings on an fcc lattice. Monte Carlo simulations of this model suggest that highly variable exchange couplings, similar to those found in FeNi, can reduce the Curie temperature by roughly 10% compared to calculations based solely on the average coupling.

We introduce a framework for modeling conversational negation by integrating worldly context (prior knowledge) into logical negation within compositional distributional semantics. This approach generates word negations that align with human perception, adjusting logical negation to prioritize meanings that are closer in the entailment hierarchy over those further apart. The framework is adaptable, supporting various choices for logical negation, composition, and worldly context generation; notably, we propose and justify a new logical negation based on matrix inversion. To validate the framework's effectiveness, we conducted experiments using density matrices to represent graded entailment information. Our results indicate that combining subtraction negation with a phaser in the basis of the negated word achieves the highest Pearson correlation of 0.635 with human ratings.

To establish the Fundamental Theorem of Natural Selection, Fisher introduced the concepts of average excess and average effect of a gene substitution. Because these ideas were often viewed as obscure, some scholars suggested recasting Fisher's framework using the classical statistical tools of covariance and regression. We contend, however, that Fisher originally designed these two averages to highlight the difference between correlation and causation. Specifically, the average effect represents a specific weighted average of actual phenotypic shifts resulting from the physical alteration of allelic states in homologous genes. We demonstrate that the statistical and causal interpretations of the average effect—seen by Falconer as contradictory—can be harmonized provided that specific relationships between genotype frequencies and non-additive residuals remain constant. Furthermore, internal theoretical considerations support Fisher's causal formulation; for instance, the frequency-weighted mean of average effects summing to zero at each locus emerges as a derivable outcome rather than an arbitrary restriction. More generally, Fisher's separation of correlation and causation holds critical significance for gene-trait mapping research and the foundational principles of evolutionary biology.

Research into Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) using third-person video inputs has demonstrated promising potential for eliminating the necessity of manually designing rewards for robotic tasks. Nevertheless, existing studies remain constrained by their reliance on limited video domains. This paper posits that the genuine promise of third-person IRL is realized through enhancing video diversity to facilitate better scaling. To derive reward functions from such varied data, we introduce a method that applies graph abstraction to videos and subsequently performs temporal matching within the graph domain to assess task progression. Our core insight is that tasks can be characterized by entity interactions structured as graphs; this abstraction filters out non-essential details like textures, thereby yielding more robust reward functions. We evaluate our proposed framework, GraphIRL, on cross-embodiment learning within X-MAGICAL and on learning from human demonstrations for real-robot manipulation. Our results indicate substantial improvements in robustness regarding diverse video inputs compared to prior methods, and we even surpass manual reward design on a real-robot pushing task. The video dataset is accessible at https://sateeshkumar21.github.io/GraphIRL.

This work addresses many-electron polar and $s-d(f)$ exchange models within the framework of developing magnetism theories for transition and rare-earth metals and their compounds. Significant focus is given to deriving the many-electron Heisenberg, Hubbard, Anderson, and $t-J$ models, along with elucidating their interconnections. Key subjects include many-electron methodologies for $d$- and $f$-electron systems, atomic representations of Hubbard's $X$-operators, slave-particle formulations, issues regarding strong itinerant magnetism and local moment formation, and the significance of non-quasiparticle (incoherent) states. The text further explores the application of these concepts to strongly correlated systems, specifically half-metallic ferromagnets and Kondo lattices, and offers a comparison with contemporary field-theoretical and topological approaches.

This study introduces a new method for localizing neuronal current sources, leveraging a Deep Prior that utilizes convolutional networks to model a more intricate prior distribution of current sources. As an unsupervised learning technique, the Deep Prior relies on randomly initialized neural networks to refine source locations based on single observations, without the need for training data. While our prior research proposed a Deep-Prior-based localization technique for brain activity, its performance lagged behind conventional methods like sLORETA. To address this limitation, the current paper incorporates a depth weight into the Deep Prior framework, which applies greater penalties to superficial currents. The efficacy of this enhanced approach is validated through experiments estimating current sources using simulated MEG data.

Crop residue burning represents a significant contributor to air pollution globally, particularly in South Asia. Although policymakers, practitioners, and researchers have dedicated resources to quantifying its impacts and implementing reduction strategies, assessing these efforts depends heavily on precise location data, which is difficult and costly to gather in the field. This study leverages ground-based monitoring records from Punjab, India, to investigate the potential of accessible satellite imagery for detecting such fires. We evaluated both high-frequency PlanetScope data (3m resolution, up to daily) and spectrally rich Sentinel-2 data (weekly resolution) to determine the most effective spectral bands and burn indices for distinguishing between burned and unburned plots. Using these optimized features, we developed a Random Forest model validated against ground-truthed data, achieving an overall accuracy of 82%, a favorable result given the inherent measurement difficulties. Drawing on these findings, we examine the technical hurdles associated with identifying crop residue burning via satellite and the broader challenges involved in measuring the impacts of both the burning itself and policy interventions.

Fifth Generation (5G) New Radio (NR) and subsequent technologies are designed to support enhanced mobile broadband, ultra-low latency, and connectivity for vast numbers of devices. Consequently, maintaining seamless mobility during cell transitions is critical for high-speed users. Given the density of mobile devices, managing high mobility within such networks is essential. Furthermore, dynamically adjusting the Time-to-Trigger (TTT) and hysteresis margins is necessary, as these parameters significantly influence handover latency and overall throughput. To address these challenges, this paper introduces Learning-based Intelligent Mobility Management (LIM2), an online learning mechanism for 5G and beyond that intelligently adapts TTT and hysteresis values. LIM2 employs a Kalman filter to forecast future signal quality for serving and neighboring cells, selects the target cell via SARSA-based reinforcement learning, and adjusts TTT and hysteresis using an epsilon-greedy policy. A prototype of LIM2 was implemented in NS-3 and evaluated extensively, demonstrating that the algorithm substantially improves handover performance in scenarios involving very high-speed mobility.

Salient Object Detection (SOD) identifies significant elements within an input image. However, RGB-only approaches struggle due to a lack of complementary depth information, leading to suboptimal performance in complex situations. While RGB-D models utilize both color and depth data, their reliance on depth inputs often limits practical application when such data is unavailable during testing. This study addresses these limitations by utilizing solely RGB images, estimating depth from them, and incorporating intermediate depth features. We introduce a pyramidal attention architecture that extracts multi-level convolutional-transformer features to refine initial representations and enhance subsequent stages. At each level, the backbone transformer generates global receptive fields through parallel computation to achieve fine-grained global predictions, which are further optimized by a residual convolutional attention decoder for precise saliency mapping. Experimental results demonstrate significant performance gains over 21 and 40 state-of-the-art SOD methods across eight RGB and RGB-D datasets, respectively. This work establishes a novel SOD paradigm that simulates RGB-D capabilities without requiring depth data during training or inference, thereby augmenting RGB methods with depth cues for superior results. The code and trained models are accessible at https://github.com/tanveer-hussain/EfficientSOD2.

We introduce a novel method for identifying human-like social biases within word embeddings by employing representational similarity analysis. This approach investigates both contextualized and non-contextualized embeddings to uncover intersectional biases targeting Black women. Our results indicate that these embeddings depict Black women as being less feminine compared to White women and less Black compared to Black men. This outcome supports intersectionality theory, which posits that overlapping identity categories (such as race and gender) combine to produce distinct forms of discrimination that do not exist within any single category alone.

Video object detection represents a core challenge in computer vision with diverse applications. Driven by deep learning, research in this field aims to maximize both detection speed and precision. To mitigate computational expenses, we propose sampling only key frames from a video sequence, classifying the remaining frames as non-key frames. This approach employs a large, deep network for key frame feature extraction while utilizing a lightweight network for non-key frames. To enrich the features of non-key frames, we introduce a novel short-term feature aggregation technique that rapidly transfers rich information from key frames. This fast aggregation leverages readily available motion cues in compressed video data, complemented by optical flow-based aggregation for key frames. The resulting propagated deep features are fused with directly extracted features to facilitate object detection. Both feature extraction and integration parameters are optimized through an end-to-end process. Evaluated on the ImageNet VID benchmark, the proposed network achieves 77.2% mAP, matching state-of-the-art accuracy while reaching 30 FPS on a Titan X GPU. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/hustvl/LSFA.

This article generalizes the compactness theorems established by Sprouse and Hwang-Lee to weighted manifolds, assuming the weighted Ricci curvature is bounded below by its weight function. Utilizing the $\varepsilon$-range, we address scenarios where the effective dimension is no greater than 1, as well as cases where it is at least the manifold's dimension. To prove these results, we extend the Cheeger-Colding segment inequality to the setting of weighted manifolds.

Recently, the block-term decomposition (BTD) tensor model, particularly its rank-$(L_r,L_r,1)$ variant, has garnered significant interest for its superior capability in representing systems and signals comprising multi-rank block components, a scenario prevalent across diverse applications. While the uniqueness and approximation properties of this model have been extensively investigated, the critical challenge of estimating its structure—specifically determining the number of block terms and their individual ranks—has only recently become a focal point. In data-streaming and big data contexts, where tensor dimensions expand over time or require incremental processing, it is vital to perform model selection and computation recursively. Although existing literature offers one incremental method for the general rank-$(L,M,N)$ BTD model, it relies on a-priori knowledge of the BTD and block ranks that remain time-invariant. This preprint introduces a novel approach for selecting and tracking rank-$(L_r,L_r,1)$ BTD models by enforcing joint column sparsity on the factors and estimating ranks as the count of non-negligible factor columns. An online alternating iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS) algorithm is developed, demonstrating high computational efficiency and rapid convergence, while accommodating time-varying model ranks. Evaluations of time and memory efficiency favorably contrast this method against batch approaches. Simulation results confirm the scheme's effectiveness in both accurately selecting and tracking the BTD model.

The initial stage of table recognition involves identifying the tabular region within a document, followed by a second phase where the structure is analyzed to extract data from individual cells. Both table detection and structural recognition are critical challenges in the field of table understanding. However, analyzing tables remains a complex endeavor due to their vast diversity and asymmetrical nature, making it an active area of research in document image analysis. Recent improvements in graphical processing unit capabilities have allowed deep neural networks to surpass traditional machine learning methods, significantly advancing the field of table understanding. Despite these breakthroughs, there is currently no consolidated overview of deep learning techniques specifically for table detection and structural recognition. This review paper offers a comprehensive examination of modern deep neural network methodologies, providing a clear understanding of the current state-of-the-art and associated challenges. Additionally, it details leading datasets, their complexities, and quantitative results, while also outlining promising future directions to guide further enhancements in table analysis for document images.

We demonstrate that the dynamics driving the variation of Standard Model fermion Yukawa couplings generically induces a robust first-order electroweak phase transition, provided these couplings are initially large (order 1) prior to the transition and evolve to their current values afterward. While there are compelling reasons to suggest that flavor structure emerges during electroweak symmetry breaking—such as if Froggatt-Nielsen field dynamics are coupled to the Higgs field—this study requires no specific flavor theory. Instead, we present a model-independent argument showing that the nature of the electroweak phase transition fundamentally shifts when Standard Model Yukawas vary concurrently with the Higgs acquiring its vacuum expectation value. Specifically, the thermal contributions from fermions generate a barrier between the symmetric and broken phase minima of the effective potential, thereby triggering a first-order phase transition. This mechanism opens new avenues for generating baryon asymmetry at the electroweak scale, with significant implications for flavor models.

This work outlines advancements in applying physics-informed deep learning to reservoir simulation. The proposed approach utilizes a neural network jointly trained to adhere to governing physical laws and satisfy boundary conditions. This methodology is demonstrated through the simulation of a 2-phase immiscible transport problem, specifically the Buckley-Leverett scenario. The resulting model generates accurate physical solutions, correctly capturing both shock and rarefaction phenomena while strictly honoring the underlying partial differential equations, initial states, and boundary constraints. By testing various hypotheses, including uniform and non-uniform initial conditions, we demonstrate that properly implemented physical constraints enable the training of robust solutions within a reasonable timeframe and number of iterations. We address limitations identified in prior work \cite{Fuks2020} and extend the method's applicability to forward, purely hyperbolic setups. Additionally, we provide practical insights into using Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), reviewing existing network architectures and offering recommendations to enhance convergence and accuracy. The proposed framework offers a straightforward and elegant means of embedding physical knowledge into machine-learning algorithms, thereby mitigating two major drawbacks of standard ML: the need for extensive datasets and the unreliability of extrapolation. These principles are highly generalizable and pave the way for a new class of algorithms capable of solving both forward and inverse physical problems.

Transformation optics has proven to be a potent instrument for manipulating physical fields, provided that the governing equations remain formally invariant under coordinate transformations. Nevertheless, controlling hydrodynamics remains unsatisfactory because there is a scarcity of rigorous validation regarding the application of transformation theory across different fluid categories. This study systematically examines the viability of applying transformation optics to fluid mechanics. Our findings indicate that the Stokes and Navier-Stokes equations, which govern Stokes flow and general flow respectively, change their mathematical forms when subjected to curvilinear transformations. In contrast, Hele-Shaw flow, defined by shallow geometries, strictly preserves the form of its governing equations under arbitrary transformations. Utilizing the derived transformation rules, we propose designing multilayered structures with spatially varying cell depths rather than manipulating the rank-2 shear viscosity tensor to achieve the necessary anisotropy in transformation Hele-Shaw hydrodynamic metamaterials. The theoretical validation and fabrication techniques presented in this work may open new pathways for precisely regulating flow distribution through artificial structural design.

This study reports the initial observation of the decay processes $\Lambda_b^0 \to \chi_{c1} p K^-$ and $\Lambda_b^0 \to \chi_{c2} p K^-$, utilizing a dataset with an integrated luminosity of $3.0$ fb$^{-1}$ gathered by the LHCb experiment from $pp$ collisions at center-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV. The measured ratios of branching fractions are as follows:
\begin{eqnarray*}
  \frac{{\cal B}(\Lambda_b^0 \to \chi_{c1} p K^-)}{{\cal B}(\Lambda_b^0 \to J/\psi p K^-)} = 0.242 \pm 0.014 \pm 0.013 \pm 0.009,
  \frac{{\cal B}(\Lambda_b^0 \to \chi_{c2} p K^-)}{{\cal B}(\Lambda_b^0 \to J/\psi p K^-)} = 0.248 \pm 0.020 \pm 0.014 \pm 0.009,
  \frac{{\cal B}(\Lambda_b^0 \to \chi_{c2} p K^-)}{{\cal B}(\Lambda_b^0 \to \chi_{c1} p K^-)} = 1.02 \pm 0.10 \pm 0.02 \pm 0.05,
  \end{eqnarray*}
where the first uncertainty represents statistical error, the second denotes systematic error, and the third arises from uncertainties in the branching fractions of the $\chi_{c1}\to J/\psi\gamma$ and $\chi_{c2} \to J/\psi\gamma$ decays. Furthermore, by combining both decay channels, the mass of the $\Lambda_b^0$ baryon is determined to be $m_{\Lambda_b^0} = 5619.44 \pm 0.28 \pm 0.26$ MeV/$c^2$, with the first and second uncertainties corresponding to statistical and systematic contributions, respectively.

The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) is poised to deliver the first high-resolution images of the Galactic Centre's supermassive black hole (SMBH) candidate, Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*), allowing researchers to explore gravity within the strong-field regime. Beyond analyzing accretion processes in extreme conditions, the resulting data and images will help investigate the fundamental structure of spacetime. Currently, the EHT can differentiate between a rotating Kerr black hole and a horizon-less alternative like a boson star, but future upgrades will enhance this ability to distinguish various spacetimes. This study examines an advanced EHT concept featuring an orbiting space antenna to image and discriminate among different spacetimes surrounding Sgr A*. Utilizing GRMHD simulations of accreting compact objects—including Kerr and dilaton black holes, as well as boson stars—we calculated their radiative signatures using general relativistic radiative transfer methods. To ensure comparability with future observations, we generated realistic synthetic data that accounts for source variability, diffractive and refractive scattering, and the full observing array configuration, including the space-based component. Using regularised Maximum Entropy methods, we dynamically reconstructed black hole shadow images from these synthetic observations. Additionally, we employed a genetic algorithm to optimize the space antenna's orbit for enhanced imaging capabilities and u-v-plane coverage, and developed a novel technique to analyze source variability in Fourier space. Our findings indicate that incorporating an orbiting space antenna significantly improves the EHT's capacity to distinguish the spins of Kerr and dilaton black holes based on reconstructed radio images and complex visibilities.

This survey examines recent rigorous findings regarding large $N$ problems in quantum field theory, stochastic quantization, and singular stochastic PDEs, with a specific focus on their mean field limits. We concentrate on the $O(N)$ linear sigma model defined on two- and three-dimensional tori. The stochastic quantization approach generates a coupled system of $N$ interacting $\Phi^4$ equations. In dimension $d=2$, we establish $N$-uniform bounds for the dynamics and demonstrate convergence to a mean-field singular SPDE. Under conditions of sufficiently large mass or small coupling, the invariant measures of the $O(N)$ linear sigma model converge to the massive Gaussian free field—the unique invariant measure of the mean-field dynamics—in terms of Wasserstein distance. Furthermore, we prove tightness for specific $O(N)$-invariant observables as random fields within appropriate Besov spaces as $N \to \infty$, providing exact characterizations of the limiting correlations. In $d=3$, the analysis is more complex due to the heightened singularity of the equation; we outline the methodology for proving convergence to the massive Gaussian free field in this context. These proofs leverage advancements in singular SPDE theory and integrate novel techniques, including uniform $N$ estimates and dynamical mean field theory, drawing upon joint research with Scott Smith, Rongchan Zhu, and Xiangchan Zhu.

Cyber-physical systems introduce significant security challenges due to the integration of heterogeneous devices with constrained processing, communication, and power resources. Furthermore, the convergence of physical and cyber domains complicates the creation of a unified security strategy. Security researchers frequently face an overwhelming volume of daily cyber-alerts, many of which are false positives. This paper proposes the use of machine learning and natural language processing to forecast the outcomes of cyberattacks, thereby equipping researchers with tools to effectively convey these risks to stakeholders lacking cybersecurity expertise. Additionally, the proposed approach aims to alleviate researcher cognitive load by automatically predicting consequences for newly discovered attacks. We evaluated various machine learning models utilizing word vectors derived from both tf-idf and Doc2Vec methods. Experimental results indicate an accuracy of 60% with tf-idf features and 57% with the Doc2Vec method when employing LinearSVC-based models.

By leveraging the modified Bonora-Tonin superfield approach (MBTSA) alongside the (anti-)chiral superfield approach (ACSA) within the Becchi-Rouet-Stora-Tyutin (BRST) framework, we establish the full set of off-shell nilpotent (anti-)BRST symmetry transformations associated with the classical two $(1 + 1)$-dimensional (2D) diffeomorphism symmetries on the world-sheet of a bosonic string model. While previous literature has exclusively addressed the BRST transformations for this system, our work derives the (anti-)BRST invariant Curci-Ferrari (CF) type constraints via MBTSA, identifying them as the fundamental source of the absolute anticommutativity of these transformations. Furthermore, we encapsulate the invariance of the (anti-)BRST symmetric Lagrangian densities under the ACSA. The novel contributions of this study include the derivation of the proper anti-BRST transformations—complementary to the known BRST transformations—and the establishment of the (anti-)BRST invariant CF-type restrictions.

Hashed Timelock Contracts (HTLCs) within the Lightning Network are vulnerable to griefing attacks, where adversaries can obstruct multiple channels and delay transactions. While the Hashed Timelock Contract with Griefing-Penalty (HTLC-GP) offers a robust defense under the classical assumption of purely honest or malicious actors, it proves ineffective against rational participants. To bridge this gap, we develop a game-theoretic framework to analyze griefing strategies in HTLCs and HTLC-GP. Our analysis leads to the conjecture that, given Bitcoin's current scripting capabilities, no efficient protocol can adequately penalize malicious actors. We further examine how penalties influence attack costs, noting that HTLC-GP only weakly deters attackers under specific conditions. To amplify the economic cost of such attacks, we propose "guaranteed minimum compensation," denoted as $\zeta$, and integrate it into HTLC-GP to create $\textrm{HTLC-GP}^{\zeta}$.
