Additionally, we utilized a technique less reliant on theoretical hfs accuracy to transform HD 4306's lines into what would be observed if its atmospheric parameters (Teff, log g, turbulence, Vsin i, and Ba abundance) matched those of HD 6268. **Results.** Both methods indicate that the hfs-affected barium lines in HD 4306 align with an s-process composition, whereas HD 6268 displays a distinct profile suggestive of an r-process isotopic pattern. **Conclusions.** The barium lines in HD 6268 and HD 4306 support theoretical predictions that the ancient Galactic halo has been enriched by both r-process events and s-process contributions from rotating massive stars.

This research explores self-supervised representation learning for speaker verification (SV). Initially, we analyze a straightforward contrastive learning method (SimCLR) integrated with a momentum contrastive (MoCo) framework, which employs a queue to store a vast collection of negative samples; our findings indicate that MoCo yields superior speaker embeddings. Subsequently, we investigate alternative augmentation techniques designed to normalize extrinsic speaker variations across two random segments of the same utterance, revealing that waveform-level augmentation significantly enhances speaker representations for SV. Furthermore, introducing a prototypical memory bank to the proposed MoCo system further refines performance by utilizing an intermediate clustering step to align embeddings closer to their designated prototypes. Additionally, we extend this self-supervised framework to a semi-supervised setting where only a limited portion of the data is labeled. Extensive experiments on the VoxCeleb dataset confirm that our approach achieves competitive results against existing methods and can attain performance levels comparable to fully supervised models using partially labeled data.

Predicting the behavior of large, complex networks based on historical time-series data is crucial across many fields. This work introduces a machine learning framework utilizing a parallel architecture that replicates the topology of the target network. We validate the method's effectiveness and scalability by applying reservoir computing to a chaotic oscillator network. The study evaluates two scenarios regarding prior knowledge: (i) where network connections are known, and (ii) where connections are unknown and estimated through a data-driven approach to enhance prediction accuracy.

The absence of a detailed, high-resolution cerebellar atlas has impeded research into the cerebellum's role in both normal brain function and pathology. Accurately representing the cerebellar cortex's tightly foliated structure is challenging due to its highly convoluted surface and the excessive time required for manual delineation. Furthermore, manual segmentation quality depends on human expertise, while current automatic labeling methods are limited by the robustness of existing algorithms. The 20μm isotropic BigBrain dataset offers a resolution far superior to the 1000μm (1mm) capability of standard magnetic resonance imaging, providing an ideal framework for semantic segmentation. To eliminate the need for manual annotation, we propose training a model to adaptively transfer annotations from the cerebellum in the Allen Brain Human Brain Atlas to the BigBrain in an unsupervised manner, accounting for differences in staining and section spacing. Existing methods fail to generate meaningful segmentation masks due to visual discrepancies between the Allen Brain and BigBrain datasets, while artifacts from sectioning and histological preparation in the BigBrain data add further complexity. To overcome these issues, we introduce a two-stage framework: first, we transfer the Allen Brain cerebellum into a space that shares visual similarity with the BigBrain; second, we employ a self-training strategy using a confidence map to iteratively guide the model's learning from noisy pseudo-labels. Qualitative results confirm the approach's effectiveness, and quantitative experiments demonstrate that our method achieves over 2.6% loss reduction compared to other techniques.

This research examines high-precision three-dimensional surface detection within smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) simulations of free-surface flows. Initially, a novel geometric approach is introduced to improve the accuracy of identifying free-surface particles in intricate flow scenarios. This technique locates surface particles by conducting a continuous global scan within a sphere centered on each particle, utilizing a cone-shaped region with its vertex at the particle's position; a particle is classified as free-surface if an empty cone region exists. Subsequently, an efficient semi-geometric method is developed to lower computational expenses by first identifying particles near the surface through position divergence and then applying the geometric method to confirm their status. The accuracy and robustness of these proposed techniques are validated through various model problem tests.

This note addresses the design of distributed reference trajectories for a group of nonholonomic vehicles, transforming their cooperative behavior into single-vehicle tracking problems. Since nonholonomic vehicles cannot asymptotically stabilize infeasible reference signals, modifications to the virtual trajectory design are required. By employing reduced-order design, time-varying techniques, and straightforward geometric methods, the authors derive dynamic reference trajectories.

This study investigates four-top-quark ($t\bar{t}t\bar{t}$) production using proton-proton collision data recorded by the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. The dataset comprises 36.1 fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity collected at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV during 2015 and 2016. The analysis covers the single-lepton and opposite-sign dilepton channels, which feature one or two isolated high-transverse-momentum electrons or muons alongside multiple jets. A data-driven approach estimates the primary background arising from top-quark pair production with jets. No significant deviation from Standard Model predictions is found. Combining these findings with prior ATLAS searches in same-sign dilepton and multilepton channels yields an observed (expected) 95% confidence level upper limit of 5.3 (2.1) times the Standard Model cross section. Furthermore, constraints on anomalous four-top-quark production are established within an effective field theory framework.

Text recognition for irregular content remains a difficult challenge. To stimulate research in this area, we introduce COO, a new dataset featuring Japanese comic onomatopoeia. This dataset includes highly distorted text, such as severely curved, partially shrunk, or arbitrarily positioned characters. Additionally, some text is fragmented into multiple truncated segments that lack individual meaning and must be connected to convey the intended message. Consequently, we propose a novel task focused on predicting links between these fragmented texts. We evaluate three specific tasks—text detection, text recognition, and link prediction—to identify onomatopoeia regions and recover their full meaning. Extensive experiments were conducted to analyze the unique characteristics of the COO dataset. Our data and source code are accessible at \url{https://github.com/ku21fan/COO-Comic-Onomatopoeia}.

Photoacoustic tomography (PAT), leveraging the photoacoustic effect, has rapidly evolved into a vital imaging modality for both clinical and preclinical applications. By employing a sufficient array of ultrasound transducers surrounding biological tissue, PAT achieves high image contrast and deep penetration through the combined utilization of light and sound. However, spatial and environmental constraints often necessitate a limited-angle transducer arrangement, resulting in significant information loss on the uncovered side. Traditional reconstruction algorithms struggle with this limited-view scenario, leading to artifacts and data gaps that can contribute to diagnostic errors such as misdiagnosis or missed diagnoses. To address limited-view PA image reconstruction, we propose integrating both time-domain and frequency-domain algorithms to generate delay-and-sum (DAS) and k-space images, respectively. Although these dual-domain images share similar textural features, they exhibit distinct artifact patterns, enabling the network to differentiate between valid information and artifacts at the input stage. This paper introduces the Dual Domain Unet (DuDoUnet), equipped with a specially designed Information Sharing Block (ISB) to further integrate and distinguish information across domains. Additionally, we employ an auxiliary network utilizing mutual information (MI) with ground-truth inputs and outputs to incorporate prior knowledge regarding limited-view PA data. Validated on a public clinical database, the proposed method demonstrates superior performance, achieving an SSIM of 93.5622% and a PSNR of 20.8859.

Following the AGILE and Fermi-LAT teams' announcement of gamma-ray flares from the Crab Nebula in late 2010, an international collaboration began regularly monitoring the source's X-ray emission using the Chandra X-Ray Observatory, observing approximately once a month when feasible. The program's objectives are to deeply analyze X-ray variations within the Nebula and, if possible, pinpoint the gamma-ray flares' origins more precisely. In April 2011, coinciding with the most intense gamma-ray flare observed to date, we initiated a series of Chandra Target-of-Opportunity observations. This text provides a brief summary of the April X-ray data and the insights gathered so far.

In this study, $\eta(G)$ is defined as the count of conjugacy classes of maximal cyclic subgroups within $G$. We establish that for any $p$-group $G$ of order $p^n$ and nilpotence class $l$, the value of $\eta(G)$ is bounded from below by a linear function of $n/l$.

Atmospheric flow patterns that persist over time, including weather fronts, mid-latitude blockings, and tropical cyclones, frequently generate extreme weather events. Consequently, describing, detecting, and tracking these phenomena has garnered significant attention in recent years. Comparable goals exist across various disciplines such as turbulence and combustion studies, image analysis, and medical diagnostics, where tasks like "feature tracking," "coherent structure detection," and "image registration" are common. Numerous methods have been created and effectively deployed to address these often similar underlying challenges. This work summarizes, extends, and applies several representative approaches to meteorological datasets. Furthermore, it establishes a unified framework for defining "persistent structures" based on shared abstract operational steps, which encompass specifying the system's physical state, identifying the features of interest, and determining metrics for measuring their persistence.

This brief note aims to clarify a frequent misunderstanding regarding convolutional neural networks (CNNs). While CNNs consist of convolutional layers that exhibit shift equivariance through weight sharing, these layers do not possess translation equivariance, even if boundary effects are disregarded and pooling or subsampling are excluded. This distinction arises because shift equivariance pertains to discrete symmetries, whereas translation equivariance involves continuous symmetries. Although this concept is well-established among researchers in equivariant machine learning, it is often ignored by non-experts. To reduce confusion, we recommend distinguishing between `shift equivariance' for discrete pixel shifts and `translation equivariance' for continuous translations.

This work introduces a first-order aggregation model defined on a group ring and investigates its long-term dynamical behavior. Under conditions of positive coupling strength, we demonstrate that the system's trajectory approaches an equilibrium manifold asymptotically. To establish this, we construct a Lyapunov functional that does not increase along the flow; by leveraging the temporal decay of this nonlinear functional alongside LaSalle's invariance principle, we prove the asymptotic convergence to the equilibrium manifold. Furthermore, we show that the architecture of this equilibrium manifold is intrinsically linked to the structure of the underlying group.

GRBAlpha is a 1U CubeSat mission scheduled for launch in the first half of 2021. Its payload includes a 75 x 75 x 5 mm CsI(Tl) scintillator coupled with a dual-channel multi-pixel photon counter (MPPC) to detect gamma-ray bursts. This detector serves as an in-orbit demonstration for the Cubesats Applied for MEasuring and LOcalising Transients (CAMELOT) mission. Although GRBAlpha offers only one-eighth of the effective area anticipated for CAMELOT, comparing its observed light curves with data from other GRB monitoring satellites will validate CAMELOT's primary concept: the feasibility of timing-based localization.

DUNE operates as a dual-site experiment designed for long-baseline neutrino oscillation research, neutrino astrophysics, and the search for nucleon decay. The ProtoDUNE Dual Phase (DP) serves as a 6x6x6m³ liquid argon time-projection chamber (LArTPC) prototype for the DUNE Far Detector, having collected cosmic-muon data at the CERN Neutrino Platform between 2019 and 2020. Within this LArTPC, propagating charged particles generate both ionization and scintillation light; the latter can act as a trigger for non-beam events while also enhancing timing precision and calorimetric accuracy. In ProtoDUNE-DP, photomultiplier tubes positioned up to 7 meters from the ionization tracks collected scintillation and electroluminescence light produced by cosmic muons. This paper evaluates the performance of the ProtoDUNE-DP photon detection system, specifically examining the impact of various wavelength shifters like PEN and TPB, as well as Xe-doped liquid argon, in preparation for future giant LArTPCs. Furthermore, the study analyzes scintillation light production and propagation, comparing simulation results with data to deepen the understanding of liquid argon properties.

$\Z_p\Z_{p^2}$-additive codes function as subgroups within $\Z_p^{\alpha_1} \times \Z_{p^2}^{\alpha_2}$ and correspond to linear codes over $\Z_p$ when $\alpha_2=0$, $\Z_{p^2}$-additive codes when $\alpha_1=0$, or $\Z_2\Z_4$-additive codes specifically when $p=2$. A $\Z_p\Z_{p^2}$-linear generalized Hadamard (GH) code is defined as a GH code over $\Z_p$ obtained via the Gray map from a $\Z_p\Z_{p^2}$-additive code. This study extends established results for $\Z_p\Z_{p^2}$-linear GH codes where $p=2$ to any prime $p\geq 3$ under the condition that $\alpha_1 \neq 0$. Initially, we present a recursive method for constructing $\Z_p\Z_{p^2}$-additive GH codes of type $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2;t_1,t_2)$ with $t_1,t_2\geq 1$. Subsequently, we identify the specific code types for which the resulting $\Z_p\Z_{p^2}$-linear GH codes exhibit non-linearity over $\Z_p$. Finally, based on computational findings, we observe that, in contrast to $\Z_4$-linear GH codes, when $p\geq 3$ is prime, the family of $\Z_{p^2}$-linear GH codes is not contained within the set of $\Z_p\Z_{p^2}$-linear GH codes where $\alpha_1 \neq 0$.

This work examines the current state of collinear and Transverse Momentum Dependent (TMD) densities utilizing the Parton Branching method. Furthermore, we assess the efficacy of PB-TMD evolution and PB-TMD parton showers across various hard process configurations within both four- and five-flavour schemes.

Social science and psychological research indicates that an argument's persuasiveness is determined not merely by its language, but also by the communicator's attributes, the audience, and the strength and appropriateness of the claims within their specific pragmatic and discourse contexts. However, existing NLP literature has not explicitly examined how these contextual factors influence argument quality. To address this gap, this paper introduces a new dataset designed to study this dimension of argumentation, featuring over 47,000 claims across 741 controversial topics. Additionally, we develop predictive models that integrate pragmatic and discourse context, demonstrating that they surpass models relying solely on linguistic features of individual claims when predicting the perceived impact of arguments.

Radio Access Network (RAN) virtualization is increasingly becoming central to the re-architecture of next-generation cellular networks. Current studies and solutions primarily focus on sharing communication capacity, often mandating uniform Physical (PHY) and Medium Access Control (MAC) layers across all network slices. This method fails to address scenarios where distinct slices require diverse PHY and MAC layers, such as for radically different services or within wireless living labs that conduct whole-stack research by deploying novel layers alongside existing ones on shared physical infrastructure. To facilitate whole-stack slicing with heterogeneous PHY and MAC layers, we introduce PV-RAN, the first open-source virtual RAN platform that allows multiple slices to share the same Software Defined Radio (SDR) physical resources. Utilizing API Remoting, PV-RAN enables the execution of paravirtualized OpenAirInterface (OAI) instances across different slices without necessitating modifications to the OAI source code. By leveraging Xen's inter-domain communication mechanisms to transport time-sensitive I/Q samples through shared memory, PV-RAN ensures that virtualization overhead in communication is nearly negligible. We performed comprehensive performance benchmarking of PV-RAN, demonstrating its low overhead and high efficiency. Additionally, we integrated PV-RAN with the CyNet wireless living lab to support applications in smart agriculture and transportation.

FPGA accelerators tailored for graph processing are becoming increasingly prevalent. While Domain Specific Language (DSL) frameworks can lower the complexity and cost of designing graph algorithms, developing for specific accelerators still demands specialized technical skills and substantial effort to create, implement, and verify the system. Consequently, the high cost of acquiring hardware programming expertise often renders FPGA accelerators inaccessible or economically unviable for most algorithm designers. Although general-purpose High-Level Synthesis (HLS) tools facilitate mapping high-level languages to Hardware Description Languages (HDLs), the resulting code is frequently inefficient and verbose compared to highly optimized graph accelerators, preventing the full utilization of FPGA capacity at a low development cost. To address this, we introduce JGraph, a graph programming system designed to enable easy algorithm programming while maintaining acceptable performance. JGraph comprises two primary components: 1) a DSL for graph atomic operations paired with a library offering high-level abstractions, such as parameterized user-defined functions, and 2) a lightweight HLS translator that generates high-performance HDL code in collaboration with a communication manager and runtime scheduler. To our knowledge, JGraph represents the first graph programming system combining a DSL and translator on the FPGA platform. Our system achieves BFS traversal rates of up to 300 MTEPS within tens of seconds.

This study employs statistical and differential geometric frameworks to derive prior knowledge regarding an artificial neural network's learning capacity on specific datasets. It examines a wide range of neural architectures capable of generalized regression via stochastic gradient descent (SGD), focusing on system dynamics at two pivotal stages of the learning trajectory. The analysis reveals that during certain training epochs, the system achieves equilibrium corresponding to peak generalization performance, whereas it may also enter coherent, localized non-equilibrium states marked by Hessian matrix stabilization. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates that networks with superior generalization capabilities exhibit slower convergence rates and explores the link between generalization ability and network stability. By bridging high-energy physics principles with neural learning theory, the work formulates a Complexity-Action conjecture from the perspective of artificial neural networks.

This paper details our winning entry for SemEval 2018 Task 4, Character Identification on Multiparty Dialogues. It employs a straightforward, standard model featuring a single key advancement: an entity library. Our findings demonstrate that this innovation significantly improves the identification of infrequent characters. Given the model's generic nature, this insight may be applicable to any task requiring effective learning from sparse or unbalanced data.

A dynamic iteration approach for linear differential-algebraic port-Hamiltonian systems is introduced, utilizing Lions-Mercier-type operator splitting techniques. This iteration scheme is monotone, characterized by a decreasing error rate without the need for stability conditions. Notably, this specific iteration method is novel even for linear port-Hamiltonian systems. The resulting algorithm is applied to analyze multibody systems and electrical networks.

The OGS for non-abelian groups extends the foundational concept of bases used in finite abelian groups. According to the OGS definition, each group element possesses a unique representation as an ordered product of powers of specific generators. Regarding symmetric groups $S_n$, R. Shwartz established a significant link between the OGS and the standard Coxeter presentation, designating the latter as the standard OGS for $S_n$. This paper extends that standard OGS to the finite classical Coxeter group $D_n$. We detail the exchange laws governing this generalized standard OGS for $D_n$ and relate it to the Coxeter lengths of the group's elements.

Realistic lightcone mocks play a crucial role in the clustering analyses of extensive galaxy surveys. In simulations where only discrete snapshots are accessible, approximate lightcones are typically generated by stitching these snapshots together into spherical shells. We evaluated the two-point clustering statistics of central galaxies in approximate lightcones derived from the Millennium-XXL simulation, varying the number of snapshots used in their construction. Our results show that the monopole and quadrupole of the real-space correlation function are significantly enhanced on small scales (below 1 Mpc/h) because certain galaxies are duplicated at the boundaries between snapshots. Although increasing the number of snapshots keeps the total count of duplicated galaxies roughly constant, it shifts them to smaller separations. However, this effect remains negligible in redshift space provided the snapshots are sliced into shells in real space. Randomly removing these duplicated galaxies effectively mitigates the excess clustering signal. Furthermore, incorporating satellite galaxies lessens the impact of duplicates, as many small-scale pairs originate from satellites within the same halo. To address galaxies missing at the shell boundaries, a small overlap can be introduced between adjacent shells. This correction is particularly vital for analyses relying on very small-scale clustering measurements or for mocks designed to test the effects of fibre collisions.

Identifying global patterns and monitoring changes frequently relies on semantic segmentation of satellite imagery. While most cutting-edge models utilize Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) trained via full supervision, these networks often struggle to generalize across diverse satellite data characterized by varying landscapes, resolutions, and limited labeled samples across different geographies and seasons. Consequently, CNN performance fails to transfer effectively to unseen regions or temporal periods. Drawing inspiration from Conditional Generative Adversarial Networks (CGANs) used for high-resolution image-to-image translation, we introduce a CGAN framework designed for land cover classification using medium-resolution Sentinel-2 data. Our results demonstrate that this CGAN model significantly outperforms a similarly complex CNN on an imbalanced test set comprising unseen data.

We introduce a novel ES-BGK model for diatomic gases that incorporates translational-rotational and translational-vibrational energy exchanges, modeled through the Landau-Teller and Jeans relaxation equations. This approach aligns with the standard definitions of vibrational and rotational collision numbers frequently employed in DSMC simulations. Furthermore, the model is demonstrated to satisfy the H-theorem and yield accurate transport coefficients, including volume viscosity.

We present a low-power amplification mechanism within cavity optomechanics (COM) that relies on nonlinear position-modulated self-Kerr interactions. This nonlinear term causes the effective coupling to scale significantly with photon number, thereby producing a substantial increase in cooperativity. Consequently, even with minimal nonlinearity, the system achieves the amplification threshold under weak driving conditions, enabling low-power phonon lasing. This phase-preserving amplifier offers practical benefits by addressing power consumption challenges. These findings pave the way for developing efficient, low-power amplifiers in optomechanics and associated domains.

The ambiguities inherent in Thiemann regularization within Loop Quantum Cosmology allow for multiple choices in formulating a quantization scheme; three distinct proposals have been identified in the literature. While two of these have already been analyzed in detail, this thesis applies the existing methodology to examine the third proposal, designated as mLQC-II, with particular focus on the mathematical characteristics of the quantum operator for the full Hamiltonian constraint. These properties suggest that the system's evolution is uniquely defined. Additionally, the dynamics are explored by calculating the expectation value of volume as a function of the scalar field and constants of motion, which is then compared to trajectories derived from effective dynamics. Finally, the key features of this prescription are contrasted with those of the previously investigated alternatives.

Plasma jets are a pervasive feature within the Earth's magnetotail, where their fronts (JFs) serve as the primary sites for particle acceleration and energy conversion. These fronts are typically linked to dipolarization fronts (DFs), which manifest as solitary, sharp spikes in the northward magnetic field component. Nevertheless, MHD and kinetic instabilities can arise at JFs, disrupting the front's structure and challenging the assumption that DFs always occur there. Utilizing five years (2017–2021) of Magnetospheric Multiscale Mission data from the central plasma sheet, we analyzed the structure of JFs across a compiled database of 2,394 jets. Our findings indicate that approximately 42% of JFs exhibit large-amplitude variations in $B_z$. Among these significant events, only 25% correspond to classical DFs, whereas the remainder display more complex magnetic field configurations. Consequently, the traditional view of DFs appearing at JFs does not represent the most frequent scenario.

We propose a Tamm states variant within metal-insulator-metal (MIM) waveguides, analyzing and optimizing it using an impedance-based transfer matrix method. The involvement of plasmonic Tamm states enables a dual enhancement of fields: the first arises from coupling between a conventional waveguide and a nanoscale plasmonic waveguide, while the second results from the strong localization and field enhancement inherent to Tamm states. In our demonstrated 2D coupling setup, |E|^2 reaches an enhancement factor of up to 1050 when 1550 nm light is coupled from a 300 nm Si slab waveguide into a 40 nm MIM waveguide.

We present a comprehensive metric characterizing the gravitational field of a static, axisymmetric thin disk surrounding a Schwarzschild black hole, where the disk lacks radial pressure. The disk's density profiles are astrophysically plausible, extending from the event horizon to radial infinity while decaying rapidly at both extremes. These metric functions are formulated as finite series of Legendre polynomials. Key benefits of this solution include: (i) the absence of disk edges, ensuring the fields remain regular everywhere outside the horizon, and (ii) the provision of all non-trivial metric functions in closed, analytical forms. Furthermore, we analyze and demonstrate the fundamental properties of these black hole-disk space-times.

Over the last few decades, light field (LF) acquisition and processing have become essential to media production. The extensive data contained within LFs has facilitated innovative applications such as post-capture depth-of-field manipulation, 3D reconstruction, segmentation, matting, saliency and object detection, and mixed reality experiences. However, the success of these applications relies on specific underlying conditions that are frequently overlooked. For instance, tasks like noise reduction or hyperfan filtering are feasible only if a scene point behaves as a Lambertian radiator, whereas removing obstacles or viewing behind objects requires at least one ray to capture the specific scene point. Therefore, the ray distribution associated with a given scene point is a critical factor for assessing processing potential. The core objective of this paper is to define a relationship between the capture configuration and the rays of the LF. To achieve this, we discretize the view frustum. While traditional methods employ uniform discretization, creating voxels that represent single samples on a regularly spaced 3D grid, we propose using frustum-shaped voxels (froxels) through a discretization method dependent on depth and the capture setup. Using this approach, we count the number of rays mapping to the same pixel on the capture device(s). Based on these counts, we introduce histograms of ray counts over froxels, termed "fristograms." These Fristograms serve as analytical tools to uncover key characteristics of the LF, such as the quantity of rays originating from a scene point and their color distribution. As a demonstration, we illustrate their utility by significantly reducing the ray count for noise reduction while preserving realistic rendering of non-Lambertian or partially occluded areas.

Active learning minimizes the need for labeled data by efficiently gathering informative unlabeled instances for annotation. In this study, we introduce an acquisition function that incorporates local sensitivity and hardness awareness to retrieve unlabeled samples. Our approach creates data replicas via local perturbations and identifies points with the greatest divergence in predictive likelihood compared to these copies. Additionally, we enhance the acquisition function by integrating a select-worst case perturbation. Experiments across various classification tasks show consistent improvements over standard active learning methods. Moreover, our method yields steady gains over baselines in prompt selection for prompt-based few-shot learning. These results confirm that an acquisition strategy guided by local sensitivity and hardness is both effective and advantageous for numerous NLP applications.

In a recent mathematical study, Netzel (2018) introduces a technique for calculating the statistical error of spectral line equivalent widths. By employing various approximations, he formulates a determination equation that diverges substantially from previous methods developed by Vollmann & Eversberg (2006) and Chalabaev & Mailard (1983), subsequently evaluating those earlier works through his new framework. Several critical factors emerge that significantly impact the assessment of this approach.

Building on a recent study by Liu, Zhu, and Wu (2015) regarding force theory in two-dimensional, viscous, compressible, and steady flows, this companion work extends the analysis to three-dimensional flow. By utilizing the fundamental solution of the linearized Navier-Stokes equations, we refine Goldstein's (1931) and Milne-Thomson's (1968) incomplete incompressible force formulas into their complete final form, which is proven to hold universally across subsonic and supersonic regimes. We designate this outcome as the \textit{unified force theorem}, asserting that forces are invariably dictated by the vector circulation $\pGamma_\phi$ of longitudinal velocity and the scalar inflow $Q_\psi$ of transverse velocity. Since this theorem is not directly observable in experiments or computations, we also derive a testable variant applicable to the linear far field, termed the \textit{testable unified force formula}. Finally, we propose a general principle for enhancing the lift-drag ratio.

We investigate the stability of black holes within Einstein-Aether theory against odd-parity perturbations on a static, spherically symmetric background. For these odd-parity modes, two dynamical degrees of freedom emerge from the tensor gravitational sector and the Aether vector field. We establish general criteria ensuring the absence of ghosts and Laplacian instabilities in these fields. Applying these findings to specific black hole solutions documented in existing literature, we demonstrate that certain solutions are ruled out due to stability condition violations. Specifically, the exact Schwarzschild solution valid when $c_{13} = c_{14} = 0$—where $c_i$ denotes the four coupling constants of the theory and $c_{ij} = c_i + c_j$—exhibits Laplacian instabilities along the angular direction outside the horizon. Conversely, we identify that odd-parity instabilities associated with high radial and angular momentum modes do not occur in black hole solutions satisfying $c_{13} = c_4 = 0$ and $c_1 \geq 0$.

We utilize the Relativistic Mean Field (RMF) model, specifically the NL3 parametrization, to examine the ground state characteristics of the superheavy nucleus with Z = 124. Among the complete isotopic series, the selected nuclei for detailed analysis exhibit very low central nucleon density, classifying them as semi-bubble nuclei. Significant shell gaps observed at neutron numbers N = 172, 184, and 198 indicate the magicity associated with these values. Where feasible, these findings are contrasted with results from the macro-microscopic Finite Range Droplet Model (FRDM).

Driven by growing concerns regarding data privacy and ownership, the field of machine learning (ML) has undergone a significant paradigm shift in recent years. Federated learning (FL), an emerging approach, has attracted considerable attention as an innovative framework for ML deployment. FL facilitates model training within data silos under the guidance of a central server, thereby avoiding the transmission of raw data and reducing communication costs. This paper reviews the FL paradigm, specifically comparing its types, network architectures, and global model aggregation techniques. Furthermore, we present a comprehensive survey of FL applications within the energy sector, with a focus on smart grids. We offer a thematic classification of FL to tackle diverse energy challenges, such as demand response, identification, prediction, and federated optimization. The taxonomy is detailed, and the paper concludes with a discussion on various aspects, including challenges, opportunities, and limitations in energy informatics applications like system modeling, design, privacy, and evolution.

We investigate the modular Hamiltonian for a Gaussian state defined on the Weyl algebra. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the local equivalence of Gaussian states, achieving this independently of earlier classical findings by Araki and Yamagami, Van Daele, and Holevo. Furthermore, we provide a criterion determining when a Bogoliubov automorphism is weakly inner within the GNS representation. The primary application of our analysis is characterizing the vacuum modular Hamiltonian for a time-zero interval in a two-dimensional spacetime scalar, massive, free quantum field theory, thereby extending recent results from higher dimensions. Specifically, we derive formulas for the local entropy of a one-dimensional Klein-Gordon wave packet and Araki's vacuum relative entropy concerning a coherent state on a double cone von Neumann algebra. Additionally, we demonstrate the type III_1 factor property. Incidentally, our work identifies certain positive selfadjoint extensions of the Laplacian with outer boundary conditions that appear to be previously unexamined.

Aspect-based Sentiment Analysis (ABSA) focuses on identifying sentiment polarity regarding specific aspects. Due to the scarcity and high cost of labeled data, pretraining has become the standard approach for ABSA. However, significant domain discrepancies often exist between pretraining corpora and downstream ABSA datasets, which impedes effective knowledge transfer during direct fine-tuning and results in sub-optimal performance. To address this domain shift, we propose a unified alignment pretraining framework integrated into the standard pretrain-finetune pipeline, featuring both instance-level and knowledge-level alignment. First, we develop a novel coarse-to-fine retrieval sampling method to select target domain-relevant instances from large-scale pretraining data, thereby aligning instances across domains (Stage 1). Second, we employ a knowledge guidance strategy to bridge the domain gap at the knowledge level. Practically, the model pretrained on sampled instances serves as both a knowledge guidance model and a learner model. On the target dataset, we implement an on-the-fly teacher-student joint fine-tuning approach to progressively transfer knowledge from the guidance model to the learner model (Stage 2), enabling the learner to retain more domain-invariant knowledge while acquiring new information. Finally, in Stage 3, the learner model is fine-tuned to better adapt its acquired knowledge to the target dataset. Extensive experiments on multiple ABSA benchmarks validate the effectiveness and universality of our framework, with our method pushing several strong baselines to new state-of-the-art results. We have made our code and models publicly available.

This study employs first-principles calculations to investigate the electronic characteristics of polycrystalline lead oxide, which comprises a network of single-crystalline $\alpha$-PbO platelets, and examines the formation of native point defects within the $\alpha$-PbO crystal lattice. The $\alpha$-PbO lattice is composed of coupled layers with insufficient interaction to facilitate efficient interlayer charge transfer. Consequently, the polycrystalline structure of $\alpha$-PbO leads to a high concentration of lattice defects, making defect-mediated conductivity the primary mechanism for interlayer charge transitions. Our findings indicate that oxygen vacancies have low formation energies; in their neutral state, these vacancies are occupied by two electrons and tend to donate them to lead vacancies, resulting in the ionization of both defects. These vacancies introduce localized states within the band gap that influence charge transport. Specifically, oxygen vacancies create a defect state at 1.03 eV above the valence band, acting as deep electron traps, whereas lead vacancies form shallow hole traps situated just 0.1 eV above the valence band. Furthermore, the release of trapped charge from oxygen vacancies provides an explanation for the experimentally observed dark current decay in ITO/PbO/Au devices.

Traditionally, mass flow modeling relies on hydrostatic balance equations. However, when momentum transfers scale comparably along the slope and flow depth, gravity and acceleration exert effects of similar magnitude, necessitating a non-hydrostatic formulation. This study extends single-phase Boussinesq-type models by introducing a novel non-hydrostatic model for multi-phase mass flows comprising solids, fine particles, and viscous fluids (Pudasaini & Mergili, 2019). The proposed model incorporates enhanced gravity and dispersion mechanisms that account for diverse interfacial momentum exchanges. We detail new contributions regarding non-hydrostatic Boussinesq-type multi-phase gravity waves arising from phase interactions and present a robust, structured framework for simulating these flows with improved gravity and dispersion capabilities. We examine scenarios where non-hydrostatic and dispersive effects are particularly significant, demonstrating through reduced models the critical role of non-hydrostatic terms. Simplified analytical solutions illustrate how the new dispersive model can be simplified to non-dispersive forms while generalizing existing approaches. We introduce a novel, spatially varying dissipative force termed the "prime-force," which precisely governs mass flow dynamics and run-out, offering practical utility for engineers and practitioners and highlighting the necessity of incorporating this force into momentum equations. A derived dispersion equation underscores the fundamental impact of dispersion on mass flow dynamics; specifically, dispersion generates a wavy velocity field around a non-dispersive reference state, marking the first such phenomenon for avalanching debris. Furthermore, dispersion intensity increases energetically as solid volume fraction or friction decreases.

Currently, deep neural networks exceed human capabilities in numerous tasks, yet their effectiveness plummets when input data diverges from training distributions. Recent studies indicate that adjusting model parameters during inference can alleviate this performance decline. Consequently, this paper introduces a new variant of the SwAV self-supervised training framework capable of adapting to individual test instances. By leveraging SwAV's existing prototypes alongside a derived test-time loss function, we align the representations of novel test samples with learned prototypes. Our approach demonstrates significant success on the CIFAR10-C benchmark dataset.

Microtubule networks (MTs) serve as cellular indicators of various chemical compounds and can reveal properties like treatment resistance, making their image classification vital for cell diagnostics. However, human experts struggle to accurately assess the extent of chemical exposure in cells. Enhancing accuracy through automated methods could significantly advance cell therapy. This paper introduces a Deep Learning approach for classifying MT images, evaluated on a large dataset of animal cells featuring three distinct levels of chemical exposure. The findings show that the trained deep network matches or surpasses human expert performance in cell classification. Specifically, the neural network demonstrates a substantial advantage over human experts in identifying varying degrees of chemical agent exposure.

Achieving superconductivity that induces a substantial energy gap in semiconductors even under strong magnetic fields is a critical objective for advancing semiconductor-superconductor hybrid materials in future quantum information technologies. This study examines devices comprising InAs nanowires connected to molybdenum-rhenium (MoRe) superconducting alloys, which feature thin films with transition temperatures near 10 K and critical fields surpassing 6 T. Through normal/superconductor tunnel spectroscopy, we confirmed that the induced superconductivity persists up to approximately 10 K. Additionally, MoRe-based Josephson junctions demonstrated supercurrents and multiple Andreev reflections. Our analysis reveals an induced superconducting gap smaller than anticipated based on the transition temperature, alongside observed gap softening at finite magnetic fields; these characteristics may be typical for hybrids utilizing large-gap, type-II superconductors. These findings support the continued development of MoRe-based hybrid systems.

This paper introduces a dynamical simulation framework designed to model the highly correlated excited state behavior of linear polyenes, specifically applied to internal conversion processes in carotenoids following photoexcitation. The approach utilizes the extended Hubbard-Peierls model ($\hat{H}_{\textrm{UVP}}$) to represent the $\pi$-electronic system interacting with nuclear degrees of freedom, augmented by a Hamiltonian ($\hat{H}_{\epsilon}$) that explicitly breaks both particle-hole and two-fold rotation symmetries inherent to idealized carotenoids. Electronic dynamics are handled quantum mechanically through the adaptive time-dependent density matrix renormalization group (tDMRG) method applied to the time-dependent Schr\"odinger equation, whereas nuclear motion is governed by Ehrenfest equations of motion. By defining adiabatic excited states as eigenstates of the total Hamiltonian ($\hat{H}=\hat{H}_{\textrm{UVP}}+\hat{H}_{\epsilon}$) and diabatic states as eigenstates of $\hat{H}_{\textrm{UVP}}$, we establish a computational protocol to track internal conversion from the initial photoexcited state to singlet triplet-pair states. Additionally, Lanczos-DMRG is integrated into the tDMRG-Ehrenfest scheme to compute transient absorption spectra from the evolving photoexcited state. We outline the accuracy and convergence criteria for DMRG, demonstrating that this methodology accurately captures carotenoid excited state dynamics. The study further examines the impact of $\hat{H}_{\epsilon}$ on internal conversion, showing that its influence on conversion extent follows a Landau-Zener-type transition. This methodological work complements our more detailed discussion on carotenoid excited state dynamics in *Photoexcited state dynamics and singlet fission in carotenoids*, D. Manawadu, T. N. Georges and W. Barford, *J. Phys. Chem. A* (2023).

Topological insulators featuring intrinsic magnetic order, which may host rare quantum phenomena, have recently garnered significant interest, with MnBi$_2$Te$_4$ being the first confirmed instance. The Sb-doped variant, Mn(Bi$_{1-x}$Sb$_x$)$_2$Te$_4$, exhibits a wide range of electronic behaviors dependent on the Sb concentration $x$, including Fermi level shifts, variations in the Neel temperature $T_{\mathrm N}$, and a transition from $n$- to $p$-type conductivity at high substitution levels. In this study, we examine the impact of magnetic ordering on the bulk electronic structure of Mn(Bi$_{1-x}$Sb$_x$)$_2$Te$_4$ with high Sb content ($x=0.93$) using temperature-dependent reflectivity measurements across a broad frequency spectrum. Our results reveal anomalies in the optical response occurring at $T_{\mathrm N}$ upon the establishment of antiferromagnetic order, indicating a coupling between magnetic ordering and the material's electronic structure.

Hot accretion flows are thought to host collisionless plasmas capable of accelerating particles to extreme energies via turbulence driven by the magnetorotational instability (MRI). To investigate particle diffusion and stochastic acceleration, we performed unstratified shearing-box simulations of ideal magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) MRI turbulence, injecting relativistic test particles into simulation snapshots. These simulations utilized varying levels of net vertical magnetic flux to explore different saturated disk magnetization states, with resolution sufficient to resolve the gyro-radii ($R_g$) of most particles. Our results indicate that particles with large $R_g$ ($\gtrsim0.03H$, where $H$ is the disk scale height) exhibit spatial diffusion coefficients approximately 30 and 5 times the Bohm limits in the azimuthal and poloidal directions, respectively. By applying the Fokker-Planck equation to momentum evolution, we measured the momentum diffusion coefficient $D(p)$; for these larger particles, turbulent fluctuations drive a $D(p) \propto p$ scaling, whereas shear acceleration dominates for $R_g \gtrsim 0.1H$, yielding a $D(p) \propto p^3$ relationship. Conversely, particles with smaller $R_g$ ($\lesssim 0.03H$) display spatial diffusion coefficients scaling roughly as $\sim p^{-1}$ and show tentative evidence of $D(p) \propto p^2$ momentum diffusion, though with significant uncertainties. We conclude that stochastic acceleration and deceleration result from multiple interacting effects and are likely influenced by intermittency within the MRI turbulence, further discussing the potential for generating PeV cosmic rays in the hot accretion flows surrounding supermassive black holes.

This study examines the Euler equations for gas dynamics, incorporating an incomplete equation of state that links internal energy to mass density and pressure. We demonstrate that any sufficiently smooth solution can be obtained as the vanishing viscosity and heat conductivity limit of the Navier--Stokes--Fourier system, provided the temperature is appropriately defined. This finding holds unconditionally for Navier-type (slip) boundary conditions and extends to no-slip velocity conditions under additional hypotheses of Kato's type regarding fluid behavior within the boundary layer.

Accurately estimating scene geometry using affordable sensors is essential for robotics and autonomous driving. This paper investigates predicting dense depth from a single RGB image (monodepth), optionally incorporating sparse data from low-cost active depth sensors. We present Sparse Auxiliary Networks (SANs), a novel module that allows monodepth models to handle both depth prediction and completion, adapting dynamically based on whether only RGB images or combined RGB and sparse point cloud data are available during inference. Our approach first separates image and depth encoding stages, employing sparse convolutions to process only valid depth pixels. Subsequently, we integrate this information into the skip connections of the prediction network when available, thereby enriching its feature representation. Extensive experiments on one indoor (NYUv2) and two outdoor (KITTI and DDAD) benchmarks demonstrate that the SAN architecture successfully learns both tasks simultaneously, establishing a new state-of-the-art in depth prediction with a significant performance margin.

Semidefinite programming serves as a versatile optimization framework with extensive applications, including the approximation of challenging combinatorial problems. We present a variational quantum algorithm for these programs that requires only $n$ qubits, a constant number of circuit setups, and $O(n^2)$ expectation value measurements to handle instances with up to $N=2^n$ variables and $M=2^n$ constraints. Optimization efficiency is realized by encoding the objective matrix into a parameterized unitary conditioned on an auxiliary qubit via the Hadamard Test; this approach allows the objective function to be optimized by estimating just one ancilla expectation value, avoiding the need to separately calculate exponentially many values. Furthermore, we show that constraints can be effectively enforced through a second Hadamard Test combined with approximately $n^2/2$ Pauli string amplitude constraints. The protocol's efficacy is demonstrated by implementing an efficient quantum version of the Goemans-Williamson algorithm, a key approximation tool for NP-hard problems like MaxCut. Our method outperforms comparable classical approaches on a varied subset of well-known MaxCut instances from the GSet library.

In this paper, we construct an initial datum $u_{0}\in B^{\sigma}_{p,\infty}$ satisfying $\sigma-2>\max\{1+\frac 1 p, \frac 3 2\}$ and demonstrate that the corresponding solution to the higher dimensional Camassa-Holm equations becomes discontinuous at $t=0$ within the $B^{\sigma}_{p,\infty}$ norm, thereby establishing the ill-posedness of these equations in that space.

Let $q$ denote a prime power and let $V$ represent a $2$-dimensional column vector space defined over the finite field $\mathbb{F}_{q}$. Given a group $G$ such that $SL_2(V) \leq G \leq GL_2(V)$, this paper establishes an Erdős-Ko-Rado theorem for intersecting subsets of $G$. We demonstrate that any maximum intersecting set within $G$ is either a coset of a point stabilizer or a coset of $\mathcal{G}_{\langle w\rangle}$, where $\mathcal{G}_{\langle w\rangle}=\{M\in G:\forall v\in V, Mv-v\in \langle w\rangle\}$ for some non-zero $w \in V$. Furthermore, we prove that every intersecting set of $G$ is a subset of a maximum intersecting set.

Although recent gamma-ray and radio investigations have established tight constraints on annihilating dark matter, X-ray analyses have been limited. This study utilizes X-ray data from the Omega Centauri cluster to analyze annihilating dark matter. If dark matter accounts for the non-luminous mass in Omega Centauri, conservative lower limits on the mass of thermal dark matter annihilating through $\tau^+\tau^-$, $b\bar{b}$, and $W^+W^-$ channels can be substantially refined to 104(43) GeV, 650(167) GeV, and 480(137) GeV, respectively, under the assumption that the diffusion coefficient $D_0 \le 10^{26}(10^{27})$ cm$^2$/s. These findings robustly exclude recent assertions regarding dark matter explanations for the gamma-ray and anti-proton excesses observed in the Galaxy. Overall, the conservative lower limits derived for non-leptophilic annihilation channels are significantly stricter than those achieved via gamma-ray studies of nearby dwarf galaxies, suggesting the potential to open a novel avenue for constraining annihilating dark matter.

Detecting anomalies is a crucial research area because they often reveal vital insights into unusual data behaviors. One specific approach, dependency-based anomaly detection, identifies irregularities by detecting violations of normal variable dependencies. These methods excel at uncovering subtle, interpretable anomalies. While existing dependency-based techniques vary in implementation and exhibit distinct strengths and weaknesses, their underlying theoretical foundations and general workflows remain insufficiently explored. This paper introduces DepAD, a unified framework that streamlines the dependency-based anomaly detection process. DepAD breaks down unsupervised tasks into feature selection and prediction components, leveraging standard tools to create adaptable instantiations for diverse domains. To assess performance, the authors evaluated 128 variations of DepAD across 32 real-world datasets. Comparative experiments pitting two DepAD methods against nine state-of-the-art anomaly detection approaches demonstrate that DepAD outperforms competitors in the majority of cases. Ultimately, this framework offers valuable guidance for future research in dependency-based detection and establishes a benchmark for evaluation.

This study examines how the COVID-19 pandemic, specifically the lockdown of an economic sector, may have shifted consumer habits and consequently altered demand for certain goods even after markets reopened. Within a two-sector infinite horizon economic model, we demonstrate that demand for goods from the locked-down sector could either contract or expand relative to pre-pandemic levels, contingent upon the lockdown's duration and the balance between satiation and substitutability effects. Furthermore, we outline the conditions under which this sector might remain dormant post-lockdown and offer policy insights to prevent such an outcome.

Exciton-polaritons represent hybrid light-matter quasiparticles formed by the strong coupling of exciton resonances with photonic cavity modes. Acting as bosons, they can undergo a phase transition into a condensed state that emits coherent light without requiring population inversion, making them promising candidates for thresholdless lasers. However, their short lifetimes have historically hindered condensation at low power densities. Consequently, long-lived symmetry-protected states offer a solution to the limitations imposed by the finite reflectivity of monolithic microcavities. This study demonstrates state-of-the-art polariton condensation thresholds in GaAs/AlGaAs waveguides by utilizing a photonic symmetry-protected bound state in the continuum coupled to an excitonic resonance. Crucially, we investigate the impact of fabrication precision and show that surface passivation through atomic layer deposition effectively mitigates exciton quenching at grating sidewalls.

Obtaining downlink channel state information at the base station (BS) in time-varying massive MIMO systems presents a significant challenge, primarily due to the excessive overheads of downlink training and uplink feedback. This paper investigates a hybrid precoding architecture at the BS and explores channel extrapolation within the antenna-time domain. We propose a latent ordinary differential equation (ODE) network integrated into a variational auto-encoder (VAE) framework to learn the mapping from partial uplink channels to complete downlink channels at the BS. Specifically, the encoder utilizes a gated recurrent unit, while the decoder employs a fully-connected neural network. Network parameters are optimized through end-to-end learning. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed network can effectively infer full downlink channels from partial uplink data, thereby substantially reducing channel training overhead.

One-dimensional interacting particle systems, 1+1 random growth models, and two-dimensional directed polymers all generate two-dimensional height fields. The KPZ universality conjecture suggests that, after appropriate scaling, the height function of a broad class of these models converges to a universal random field that is independent of the specific model details. This survey examines limit theorems for several models and highlights variations across different domains, with a specific focus on recent findings regarding periodic domains. Additionally, the discussion touches upon integrable probability models, integrable differential equations, and the concept of universality.

We employed a semianalytic galaxy formation model to evaluate two quenching mechanisms: halo quenching versus black-hole (BH) quenching. Following calibration to match the galaxy mass function, the BH quenching scenario aligns more closely with observations regarding the passive galaxy fraction across stellar mass ($M_*$) and the morphological distribution on a star-formation-rate versus $M_*$ plot. Beyond this primary conclusion, the study yields two additional insights. First, a viable BH-quenching model necessitates that minor mergers drive the growth of supermassive black holes; otherwise, simulations would produce an excessive number of high-mass blue galaxies if such mergers did not trigger quenching. Second, to accurately reproduce the $M_{\rm BH}$–$M_*$ correlation and the passive fraction as a function of $M_*$, BH growth during mergers must be less efficient at lower masses, consistent with the hypothesis that supernovae inhibit BH growth in systems with low escape velocities. These results support a quasar-feedback framework where black holes grow until their mass is sufficient to expel cold gas from host galaxies and heat the circumgalactic medium to high entropy, extending its cooling time. Furthermore, the findings suggest that quenching and maintenance operate under distinct feedback regimes.

Spatially distributed systems, such as the Internet of Things, complex sensor networks, and multi-agent cyber-physical systems, continuously evolve over time and produce vast quantities of spatio-temporal data. While system designers frequently aim to analyze and uncover structural patterns within this data, significant research has focused on learning causal and logical properties of temporal data using frameworks like Signal Temporal Logic (STL). In contrast, work on discovering such relations specifically for spatio-temporal data remains limited. We introduce the first suite of algorithms designed for unsupervised learning of spatio-temporal data. Our approach automatically extracts features by projecting the data onto the parameter space of a parametric spatio-temporal reach and escape logic (PSTREL). Furthermore, we propose an agglomerative hierarchical clustering method that ensures each resulting cluster adheres to a unique STREL formula. We demonstrate that our technique generates STREL formulas with bounded description complexity through a novel decision-tree approach that extends prior unsupervised learning methods for Signal Temporal Logic. Finally, we validate the efficacy of our approach through case studies spanning diverse fields, including urban transportation, epidemiology, green infrastructure, and air quality monitoring.
This paper briefly examines the ethical concerns surrounding target advertising and underscores the significance of designing algorithms with ethical considerations.

Many mesoscopic and macroscopic flocking theories are derived by coarse-graining microscopic models where binary interactions serve as the primary alignment mechanism. Although these theories appear to predict polar order solely through binary interactions, actomyosin motility assays demonstrate that such interactions are inadequate for generating polar order, particularly at high densities. To resolve this contradiction, we present a solvable one-dimensional flocking model and develop its stochastic hydrodynamics. Our analysis reveals that two-body interactions cannot produce polar order unless the noise is non-Gaussian. Furthermore, we demonstrate that incorporating noisy three-body interactions into the microscopic framework captures all essential dynamical characteristics of the flocking transition, enabling orientational order to emerge above a critical density.

This study examines the space-time derived from quotients of $AdS_4$, specifically analyzing quotients under certain $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetries. By considering first-order metric perturbations, we estimated how matter fields backreact on the geometry. The expected value of the stress-energy tensor was computed by mapping it back to the covering space. Under appropriate boundary conditions, the average null energy turns negative, thereby enabling the formation of a traversable wormhole.

This work extends a classical second Ray-Knight theorem to spectrally positive stable processes. We demonstrate that local time processes satisfy specific stochastic Volterra equations driven by Poisson random measures and fall within a newly defined class of non-Markov branching processes termed \textit{rough continuous-state branching processes}. Furthermore, we establish the weak uniqueness of solutions to these stochastic Volterra equations by deriving explicit exponential representations of their characteristic functionals based on the unique solutions to related nonlinear Volterra equations.

This paper introduces a novel approach for generating spatial constraints to facilitate motion planning within dynamic environments. Standard motion planning techniques for autonomous vehicles and mobile robots typically depend on map-based global planners to produce collision-free trajectories. However, these approaches often fail in the absence of offline maps or when maps become invalid due to environmental dynamics like road blockages, construction, or traffic jams. While triangulation-based methods can provide spatial constraints, they struggle in dynamic settings and may cause motion planners to reach unrecoverable states. To overcome this, we propose a new technique that generates a sequence of channels across varying triangulation mesh topologies to serve as spatial constraints, applicable to motion planning for autonomous vehicles and robots in cluttered, unstructured settings. The method is evaluated against other triangulation-based approaches using synthetic data and complex scenarios sourced from a real-world autonomous driving dataset. Results demonstrate that our proposed method yields more stable, long-term plans with higher task completion rates, faster arrival times, a greater frequency of successful plans, and fewer collisions compared to existing solutions.

To combat pandemics like COVID-19, essential resources such as personal protection equipment (PPE) are critical for lowering infection rates and safeguarding those near patients (Heymann and Shindo, 2020; Klompas et al., 2021). As the number of infected individuals rises, the demand for these products grows exponentially, surpassing the capacity of local manufacturing to keep up (Ranney et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2020). Furthermore, global supply chain disruptions caused by factory closures or reduced transportation can exacerbate shortages (McMahon et al., 2020). While the initial phase of the pandemic triggered a "our people first" reflex across many regions (Baldwin and Evenett, 2020), this paper demonstrates that a cooperative sharing mechanism can significantly enhance epidemic response capabilities. We introduce a stylized model where communities share resources, ensuring access during local outbreaks, which may prevent local depletion and lower the total number of infections. However, we find that successful resource sharing relies heavily on a sufficiently long time lag between epidemic onsets in different communities, implying that global sharing must be paired with measures to slow cross-community transmission. This study represents a foundational step toward designing a resilient global supply chain that proactively addresses future pandemics, moving away from the current coincidental and unequal distribution of opportunities.

The excitation of a microwave cavity by an axion field has been rigorously analyzed using the Boundary Integral - Resonant Mode Expansion (BI-RME) 3D technique. In this framework, the electromagnetic field arising from axion-photon coupling is modeled as being driven by equivalent electrical charge and current densities. These densities are incorporated into the general BI-RME 3D equations, which define the cavity's RF electromagnetic field as an integral of the cavity's Dyadic Green functions (under the Coulomb gauge) and the aforementioned densities. This approach accommodates arbitrary spatial and temporal variations in both the magnitude and phase of the axion field. Consequently, a simplified network driven by the axion current source was derived to represent the coupling between the axion field and the cavity's resonant modes. Using this method, the extracted and dissipated RF power can be calculated across a broad frequency range without relying on Cauchy-Lorentz approximations, even for modes near the axion resonance. Furthermore, this technique provides complete knowledge of the extracted signal, including both its magnitude and phase, which is particularly valuable for future analyses where the axion phase is a critical parameter.

The pressure-dependent magnetization of the three-dimensional antiferromagnetic coordination polymer Mn(N(CN)$_{2}$)$_{2}$ was investigated using dc and ac magnetometry from 8 K up to 12 kbar. The magnetic transition temperature ($T_c$) rises significantly under pressure, shifting from 16.0 K at ambient conditions to 23.5 K at 12.1 kbar. Furthermore, a distinct change in magnetic behavior occurs at 7.1 kbar. Below this threshold ($P < 7.1$ kbar), the pressure increase leads to a reduction in the differences between field-cooled and zero-field-cooled magnetizations, as well as decreases in the coercive field and remanent magnetization. Conversely, for pressures exceeding 7.1 kbar, this trend reverses. Additionally, minor hysteresis loops appear when the pressure surpasses 8.6 kbar. These observations collectively indicate that applied pressure enhances the superexchange interaction and introduces increased exchange anisotropy.

We present an L-series connected to harmonic Maass forms and demonstrate their functional equations. Furthermore, we derive converse theorems for these series and apply them to formulate and prove a summation formula for the holomorphic component of a harmonic lift of a specified cusp form.

This paper tackles the design of receding horizon control algorithms for linear discrete-time systems subject to parametric uncertainty, excluding stochastic forcing or process noise. The parametric uncertainty is treated as probabilistic with known probability density functions, and generalized polynomial chaos theory is employed to develop these stochastic receding horizon control strategies. Within this framework, the stochastic problem is transformed into a deterministic one within a higher-dimensional space. The effectiveness of the proposed algorithms is evaluated using a linear two-state model.

We present the Synchronized Planarity problem, which takes as input a loop-free multi-graph along with synchronization constraints. These constraints, for instance, define a bijection between the edges of vertex pairs sharing the same degree. The core question is whether such a graph can be embedded in the plane without crossings while maintaining consistent edge ordering around synchronized vertices. On one hand, we demonstrate that Synchronized Planarity is solvable in quadratic time. On the other, it functions as a versatile modeling framework, enabling the straightforward formulation of various constrained planarity problems as instances of Synchronized Planarity. Specifically, this approach allows us to solve Clustered Planarity in quadratic time, significantly improving upon the best previously known algorithm, which had an upper bound of $O(n^{8})$.

This study examines phase transition patterns within a coupled two-scalar field model, accounting for the combined influences of finite size and temperature. The scalar fields propagate in a $D=4$ Euclidean space, featuring standard periodic compactification along the Euclidean time direction (where the dimension corresponds to the inverse temperature) and an additional compact spatial dimension of size $L$. In this spatial case, Dirichlet boundary conditions are applied. The research investigates the occurrence of reentrant phase transitions and the persistence of symmetry breaking as functions of temperature and finite size effects, with potential applications to relevant physical systems also explored.

Recently \cite{Horowitz:2022rpp,Horowitz:2022uak}, a denominator regularisation (Den. Reg.) scheme was introduced to address divergences in quantum field theory. Demonstrated through multiple field theory examples, it produces results as straightforward as those from dimensional regularisation and proves compatible with the minimal subtraction scheme. In this article, we highlight distinctive features of this regularisation method that arise from the necessity of gauge invariance, specifically by re-examining QED vacuum polarisation and $H\to\gamma\gamma$ decay within this framework.

This paper presents our work on designing closed-loop feedback for thruster-assisted bipedal robot walking. Assuming well-tuned supervisory controllers, we concentrate on refining desired joint trajectories to meet specific performance goals. To ensure these constraints are met, we develop an intermediary filter grounded in reference governors. Since modifications and impact events cause deviations from desired periodic orbits, we robustly guarantee hybrid invariance by employing predictive schemes within a brief time window during the gait cycle. We achieve this hybrid invariance by utilizing the distinctive capabilities of our thruster-based model. The primary advantage of our approach is that, unlike existing optimization-based nonlinear control methods, it avoids expensive numerical computations when satisfying performance constraints during the single support phase. Furthermore, the proposed thruster-assisted gait control structure uniquely enables the exploitation of performance and robustness enhancements during specific segments of the gait cycle, a capability not previously reported.

The Advanced Wakefield (AWAKE) Experiment serves as a proof-of-concept for accelerating electron beams using proton-driven plasma wakefield acceleration. While Run 1 successfully accelerated electrons to 2 GeV, Run 2 aims to surpass this by reaching approximately 10 GeV with improved beam quality. To support this upgrade, the existing proton and electron beamlines will be modified, incorporating a second plasma cell and a novel 150 MeV electron beamline. This new line must deliver electron bunches with micron-scale stability and size into the second plasma cell, navigating the 1-meter gap separating the two cells. This paper outlines the methodologies—such as numerical optimizers and genetic algorithms—employed to design the 150 MeV electron line to satisfy these rigorous experimental requirements. Furthermore, it examines operational techniques for both electron transfer lines, including steering and alignment strategies that utilize numerical optimizers alongside beam measurement techniques based on neural networks.

Machine learning practitioners are increasingly required to build models that reflect the values and objectives of non-technical stakeholders, yet there remains a lack of guidance on how to effectively convert domain expertise into model updates. This paper proposes a systematic approach to capturing interactions between practitioners and experts by introducing a taxonomy that aligns specific types of expert feedback with corresponding practitioner updates. Feedback can occur at either the observation or domain level, leading practitioners to modify the dataset, loss function, or parameter space. We review relevant literature from machine learning and human-computer interaction to define this feedback-update framework and underscore the current neglect of non-technical expert input. Finally, we conclude with a series of open questions emerging from our proposed taxonomy and associated survey.

This study systematically explores short periodic orbits within the Lorenz system using the similarity signature curve, introducing a new approach to identify these orbits. Leveraging equivariant moving frame theory, we derive similarity invariants, which facilitate the emergence of the similarity signature curve. Compared to the original system, the Lorenz system's similarity signature curve exhibits more regular behavior. By integrating the sliding window method, we numerically detect quasi-periodic orbits, successfully identifying all periodic orbits with periods $p \leqslant 8$, and calculating their corresponding period lengths and symbol sequences.

This paper establishes two key findings related to the global and unramified geometric Langlands program. The first result serves as an analogue to the Ramanujan conjecture, asserting that every cuspidal D-module on Bun_G is tempered. We further demonstrate a broader claim: any D-module *-extended from a quasi-compact open substack of Bun_G possesses the tempered property. The specific case concerning cuspidal objects follows directly from a theorem by Drinfeld and Gaitsgory. Leveraging this foundation, we prove our second primary result: the automorphic gluing theorem for SL_2. This theorem posits that any D-module on Bun_{SL_2} is fully determined by its tempered component and its constant term. In broad terms, this acts as a geometric Langlands counterpart to Langlands' classification for SL_2(R), corresponding to the spectral gluing theorem developed by Arinkin, Gaitsgory, and the author.

Diffusion models represent a category of generative architectures that excel over other methods in producing lifelike images from natural datasets. We present DISPR, a diffusion-based framework designed to address the inverse challenge of inferring three-dimensional (3D) cell morphology from two-dimensional (2D) single-cell microscopy data. By conditioning the model on 2D images as priors, DISPR generates authentic 3D shape reconstructions. To validate its utility as a data augmentation technique for feature-based single-cell classification, we extracted morphological traits from cells categorized into six highly imbalanced classes. Incorporating DISPR-generated features for the three minority classes elevated the macro F1 score from $F1_\text{macro} = 55.2 \pm 4.6\%$ to $F1_\text{macro} = 72.2 \pm 4.9\%$. As the pioneering approach to utilize diffusion models for such 3D inverse problems, our work demonstrates their capability to learn and reconstruct 3D shapes with realistic morphological characteristics directly from 2D microscopy inputs.

Analyzing signals in cytometry is a difficult endeavor with substantial implications for uncertainty. Traditional cytometers typically rely on basic metrics like signal area, width, and height to characterize individual measurements. However, these methods struggle to differentiate between intrinsic biological variability and artifacts caused by instrument conditions or operational settings. Consequently, quantifying uncertainty for individual cell properties and executing tasks like doublet deconvolution remains problematic. To overcome these limitations, we employ signal analysis techniques utilizing scale transformations that: (I) isolate biomarker expression variations from influences of flow dynamics and particle size; (II) assess reproducibility within specific laser interrogation zones; (III) calculate per-event measurement uncertainty; and (IV) isolate singlets from multiplets. The core of this methodology involves modeling how fluctuating operating conditions distort signal shapes, then applying constrained optimization to reverse these deformations in measured signals, where the resulting residuals define reproducibility. Leveraging a newly developed microfluidic cytometer, we demonstrate that these techniques effectively mitigate variability from both instruments and measurands, achieving a residual uncertainty of under 2.5% in signal shape and below 1% in integrated area.

X-ray imaging is a standard method for securing devices within the quality inspection sector, and identifying signs printed on weld X-rays is critical for digital traceability in manufacturing. Nevertheless, significant variations in object scales within these images often impede satisfactory recognition performance. To address this, we introduce a convolutional neural network (CNN)-based framework for sign recognition in weld images. This framework begins with a shallow classification network designed to correct image pose. Furthermore, we propose a novel Spatial and Channel Enhancement (SCE) module to tackle the scale variation issue; this module integrates multi-scale features and adaptively weights each feature source. Building on the SCE module, a streamlined network is developed for the final recognition of weld information. To ensure practicality, the framework's architecture is optimized to minimize parameters and computational load. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that the framework achieves 99.7% accuracy with 1.1 GFLOPs during the classification phase, and 90.0 mean average precision (mAP) with 176.1 frames per second (FPS) during the recognition phase.

Face authentication systems necessitate a strong anti-spoofing component to prevent deception via fabricated images of authorized individuals.
