While contemporary anti-spoofing techniques primarily depend on optimized architectures and training goals to mitigate distribution shifts between training and testing users, historical data from users in real-world scenarios offers valuable insights to address this shift. Consequently, we present OAP (Online Adaptive Personalization), a lightweight approach that enables online model adaptation using unlabeled data. OAP can be integrated with most existing anti-spoofing methods without requiring the storage of original biometric images. Experimental results on the SiW dataset demonstrate that OAP enhances the recognition performance of current methods in both single-video and continual settings, the latter simulating spoofing attacks by interleaving spoof and live videos. Furthermore, ablation studies validate the design decisions underlying our solution.

This paper presents a visual relocalization approach leveraging geometric data from a 3D surfel map. Initially, a visual database is constructed using global indices derived from rendering the surfel map, establishing links between image points and 3D surfels. Surfel reprojection constraints are then applied to optimize keyframe poses and map points within this database. Subsequently, a hierarchical relocalization algorithm employs the visual database to estimate 6-DoF camera poses, with learned descriptors enhancing performance in difficult scenarios. Evaluations conducted in both real-world settings and simulations demonstrate the method's effectiveness and efficiency, ensuring that the final camera poses remain consistently well-aligned with the 3D environment.

Graphene-induced energy transfer (GIET) is an emerging fluorescence spectroscopy method capable of achieving sub-nanometer optical localization of fluorophores along the microscope's optical axis. This technique relies on near-field energy transfer from an optically excited fluorescent molecule to a single graphene sheet. GIET has proven effective for determining inter-leaflet distances in single lipid bilayers and analyzing the membrane organization of living mitochondria. In this research, we employed GIET to detect minute, cholesterol-driven alterations in membrane thickness at the nanoscale. We quantified these thickness variations in supported lipid bilayers (SLBs) by varying lipid composition and increasing cholesterol levels. Our results confirm that GIET serves as a highly sensitive instrument for probing nanometric structural changes within bio-membranes.

In our 2020 study (Huybrighs et al.), we examined energetic proton depletions during Galileo's Europa flyby E26. Through particle tracing, we hypothesized that these depletions result from a combination of perturbed electromagnetic fields, atmospheric charge exchange, and potential plumes. While Jia et al. (2021) later identified one specific depletion feature previously labeled as a plume signature as an artifact, this paper reaffirms that Huybrighs et al. (2020) successfully demonstrated that plumes can indeed cause proton depletions, which should continue to be investigated. The original conclusions regarding the critical roles of perturbed electromagnetic fields and atmospheric charge exchange remain valid. We propose that the artifact arose from the EPD instrument mistakenly classifying protons as heavier ions. Consequently, the artifact prevents us from definitively confirming or ruling out a depletion linked to a plume. Additionally, we address critiques of the MHD simulations, showing that energy losses between 540–1040 keV are not inherently inconsistent with those between 115–244 keV caused by plume-associated charge exchange.

Automated analysis of tissue sections enhances the comprehension of disease biology and can identify biomarkers to inform prognosis and treatment choices. In digital pathology, while rare cell types hold significant biological value, their scarcity often leads to biased and suboptimal detection models. To mitigate the impact of this class imbalance, we introduced a deep learning pipeline that integrates cell abundance during training. By generating cell weight images that assign higher weights to less frequent cells, we regularized the Dice overlap loss function. Trained and evaluated on myeloma bone marrow trephine samples, our model achieved a cell detection F1-score of 0.78, representing a 2% improvement over baseline models, and demonstrated superior performance in identifying rare cell types. These findings indicate that scaling the deep learning loss function according to cell abundance enhances detection accuracy, underscoring the necessity of embedding domain knowledge into deep learning approaches for pathological datasets characterized by class imbalance.

Although models of cardiac electrical excitation and recovery have grown increasingly sophisticated, they are not yet routinely employed in clinical practice to guide personalized interventions. A primary obstacle remains the calibration of these models using the limited patient data available during standard procedures. This study introduces a new framework for probabilistically calibrating electrophysiology parameters in the heart's left atrium based on local excitability measurements. We represent parameter fields as Gaussian processes defined on manifolds, linking them to observations through surrogate functions that translate local parameter values into measurements, thereby deriving the posterior distribution of the parameter fields. Our approach successfully recovers parameter fields used to generate synthetic localized measurements of the effective refractory period. Furthermore, this methodology is adaptable to various clinical measurement types and broader calibration scenarios where model parameters vary across a manifold.

In recent years, manifold techniques have gained prominence as tools for dimensionality reduction. These methods have yielded compelling results across various domains under the assumption that high-dimensional data resides on or near a low-dimensional nonlinear manifold; this assumption is also frequently valid for functional data, which represents continuously observed functions. Nevertheless, the efficacy of manifold methods recently developed for tabular or image data has not yet been systematically evaluated within the functional data context. Furthermore, assessing the quality of learned embeddings that do not produce invertible mappings remains problematic, as reconstruction error cannot serve as a performance metric for such representations. This paper addresses the specific challenges of nonlinear dimension reduction in functional data settings. The work offers three main contributions: first, it establishes a theoretical framework to systematically analyze unique challenges in functional data, adapts several nonlinear dimension reduction techniques from tabular and image domains to functional data, and demonstrates the successful application of manifold methods in this context. Second, it conducts a rigorous and systematic evaluation of performance assessment and tuning strategies across diverse functional data scenarios, highlighting previously unrecognized weaknesses and pitfalls that can compromise the reliable judgment of embedding quality. Finally, it proposes a refined approach to enable more objective and trustworthy decisions regarding competing nonconforming embeddings.

We introduce Apricot, an open-source Python library designed to select representative subsets from large datasets via submodular optimization. The library features an efficient greedy algorithm with robust theoretical guarantees regarding subset quality. It supports two submodular functions: facility location, which is widely applicable but demands quadratic memory relative to dataset size, and a feature-based function that, while less versatile, scales effectively to millions of examples. Apricot achieves high efficiency through algorithmic enhancements like lazy greedy methods and code optimization via Numba. We illustrate subset selection's utility by training machine learning models on representative subsets that match the accuracy of models trained on full datasets. This paper details submodular selection principles, outlines Apricot's capabilities, and applies the method to various datasets. Source code and tutorial Jupyter notebooks are accessible at https://github.com/jmschrei/apricot.

Methods like matching-adjusted indirect comparison (MAIC) are gaining traction for evaluating marginal treatment effects in scenarios characterized by cross-trial variations in effect modifiers and scarce patient-level data. However, MAIC relies on propensity score weighting, making it vulnerable to limited covariate overlap and restricting its ability to extrapolate outside the observed data range. Conversely, existing outcome regression-based alternatives allow for extrapolation but target conditional treatment effects that are not suitable for indirect comparisons. To derive a compatible marginal treatment effect when adjusting for covariates, one must integrate or average these conditional estimates across the target population. We introduce a marginalization technique grounded in parametric G-computation, which is straightforward to implement using generalized linear models or Cox models for outcome regression. This approach treats the covariate adjustment regression as a nuisance model, decoupling its estimation from the calculation of the marginal treatment effect. The method supports a Bayesian framework, seamlessly incorporating the analysis into a probabilistic setting. A simulation study validates the method's feasibility and compares its performance against MAIC and standard outcome regression. Results indicate that parametric G-computation delivers more precise and accurate estimates than MAIC, especially under poor covariate overlap, and produces unbiased marginal treatment effect estimates provided assumptions hold. Moreover, these marginalized regression-adjusted estimates surpass the precision and accuracy of conditional estimates from conventional outcome regression, which are inherently biased due to the non-collapsibility of the effect measure.

Achieving stable locomotion for legged robots on a dynamic rigid surface (DRS)—a rigid terrain moving within the inertial frame—presents a challenging planning and control task. This difficulty stems from the hybrid nonlinear dynamics of walking, which are further complicated by explicitly time-varying holonomic constraints induced by the surface's motion. This study introduces two primary contributions: first, it extends the concept of the capture point from static to dynamic surfaces and utilizes this metric for online motion planning; second, it develops a quadratic-programming (QP) based feedback controller that explicitly accounts for DRS movement. The stability and robustness of this control strategy are verified via simulations of a quadrupedal robot traversing a DRS with rocking motion. Furthermore, the simulation outcomes highlight superior walking performance compared to our prior approach, which relied on offline planning and input-output linearizing control without explicitly ensuring the feasibility of ground contact constraints.

This study details targeted searches within *RXTE* data from various accreting millisecond X-ray pulsars (AMXPs) for signatures of non-radial oscillation modes, specifically r- and g-modes. By eliminating phase delays caused by binary motion and calculating FFT power spectra of continuous light curves with up to $2^{30}$ time bins, we identified potential coherent signals in the neutron star's rest frame across the frequency range theoretically expected for these modes. Analysis of the discovery outburst data from the 435 Hz pulsar XTE J1751$-$305 yielded a single candidate: a coherent oscillation at $0.5727597 \times \nu_{spin}$ (249.332609 Hz) with a fractional Fourier amplitude of $7.46 \times 10^{-4}$. This feature exhibits a significance level of $1.6 \times 10^{-3}$, surpassing a $3\sigma$ detection threshold. Potential identifications include rotationally-modified g-modes linked to a helium-rich surface layer or a density discontinuity from electron captures on hydrogen in the accreted ocean. While the frequency could also correspond to an inertial mode or a crust-modified r-mode, the latter is unlikely because the required amplitude would produce a spin-down rate inconsistent with observed pulse timing. For AMXPs XTE J1814$-$338 and NGC 6440 X-2, no candidate oscillation signals were detected, leading to upper limits on fractional Fourier amplitudes of $7.8\times 10^{-4}$ and $5.6 \times 10^{-3}$, respectively, within the searched frequency range. Finally, we briefly outline the prospects and sensitivity for conducting similar searches using future X-ray missions with larger collecting areas.

This study explores the use of machine learning (ML) to help intelligent systems learn multi-party turn-taking patterns from dialogue logs. The core objective is to predict the next speaker based on the identity and content of previous utterances. To achieve this, the paper compares the performance of various ML methods, including Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE), Support Vector Machines (SVM), and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), utilizing both utterance content and speaker identity data. Three distinct datasets are introduced: one derived from an American sitcom featuring casual conversation, a second from a financial advice multi-bot system, and a third constructed from the Multi-Domain Wizard-of-Oz dataset, with the latter two being topic-oriented. The findings indicate that (i) corpus size significantly enhances the accuracy of content-based deep learning models, which excel on larger datasets, and (ii) for small, topic-oriented datasets with limited topic variety, agent-only MLE or SVM models are sufficient, though CNN models incorporating utterance content yield marginally higher accuracy.

The dark photon is a hypothetical massive particle that couples to the Standard Model through kinetic mixing with the visible photon. When the mixing parameter is small, dark photons can satisfy cosmological constraints and serve as a viable dark matter candidate. Because their electromagnetic signatures resemble those of axions, many existing limits on dark photons are effectively reinterpretations of historical axion haloscope results. However, dark photons possess an intrinsic polarization—a property absent in axions. Accurately modeling this polarization is complex, varying by experiment, and relies on assumptions regarding the production mechanism. This study demonstrates that incorporating both Earth's rotation and dark photon polarization into the analysis can boost an experiment's discovery potential by more than an order of magnitude. We outline optimization strategies, including the careful selection of experimental location and orientation, as well as the timing of repeated measurements. Specifically, experiments situated at latitudes of $\pm$35$^\circ$ or $\pm$55$^\circ$ that conduct three observations across different sidereal times can achieve fully optimized sensitivity that is independent of the dark photon's polarization state and production mechanism. Furthermore, we highlight that several established axion searches utilize signal testing methods that prevent them from establishing exclusion limits on dark photons, meaning these results should not be reinterpreted as such.

We critique the article "Quantifying sustainability: Resilience, efficiency and the return of information theory" (Ulanowicz et al., Ecological Complexity, 2009) regarding its exposition of information theory to ecologists. The authors argue that the presentation of fundamental IT concepts is needlessly obscure, deliberately misaligned with established terminology, and occasionally mathematically incorrect. This response aims to resolve the confusion by rectifying errors, clarifying ambiguities, and adopting standard terminology wherever feasible. We contend that clear and rigorous explanations are essential to facilitate a productive exchange between information theorists and ecologists.

Fomalhaut is known for hosting a narrow, eccentric debris disc and a highly eccentric companion, Fomalhaut b. A common argument suggests that Fomalhaut b cannot possess significant mass, as a massive body would rapidly disrupt the disc. However, we demonstrate that material trapped in internal mean-motion resonances with a massive, coplanar Fomalhaut b remains long-term stable and occupies orbits consistent with the observed debris. Additionally, dust generated by collisions among these resonant bodies can replicate the disc's observed width, shape, and orientation.

First, we re-evaluate the potential orbits of Fomalhaut b under gravitational influence alone. If the companion orbits near the disc midplane, its path intersects the disc with apsidal alignment, suggesting an active dynamical interaction. Using observationally permitted orbits, we modeled the interaction between a massive Fomalhaut b and the debris. While most debris in such an extreme setup is unstable, we identified specific resonant populations that remain stable throughout the star's lifetime, even while crossing Fomalhaut b's orbit. This debris resides on low-eccentricity orbits matching the observed ring. Although these resonant bodies are clumpy, dust released from their collisions would form a narrow, relatively smooth ring aligning with observations. We conclude that if Fomalhaut b has a mass between that of Earth and Jupiter, rather than destroying the debris, it could be sculpting it through resonant interactions.

In a p-wave topological superconductor, the coherence length between two Majorana zero energy modes scales inversely with the superconducting order parameter. However, our investigation into finite size effects on Majorana zero modes at vortices within a topological insulator/superconductor heterostructure revealed a distinct behavior: the coherence length of the two zero-energy modes at the vortex line's terminals remains independent of the superconducting order parameter, instead being governed by the intrinsic characteristics of the topological insulator. This anomalous finding indicates that the superconducting topological insulator is topologically trivial, distinguishing it from a p-wave topological superconductor.

This paper aims to derive novel inequalities for a broad class of generalizations of the Wiener Index and to identify the extremal graphs within this set. The primary findings establish upper and lower bounds for these topological indices specifically on unicyclic graphs.

Bayesian models incorporating Multi-Dirichlet (MD) priors, which blend several Dirichlet prior parameters, are increasingly popular. However, inferring the mixing weights and parameters of these distributions is challenging because summing over Dirichlet parameters complicates the joint distribution of model parameters. This paper introduces a novel auxiliary variable scheme that simplifies inference for models involving hierarchical MDs and MDPs. By employing this approach, researchers can easily derive fully collapsed inference schemes, enabling efficient inference.

In an N-party quantum network, non-classical correlations emerge when locally measuring k-party entangled states (where k < N) that are independently distributed; these correlations define quantum network nonlocality. This paper demonstrates that bipartite entanglement (k=2) is sufficient to generate all types of quantum network nonlocality when post-selection is permitted, a capability potentially absent in more general non-signaling devices. Furthermore, we show that quantum network nonlocality does not arise in networks restricted solely to pure stabilizer states and Clifford gates. These findings clarify the distinction between non-genuine and genuine network nonlocality by revealing that all known methods for producing the latter necessitate some form of non-Clifford operation.

Mapping Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) onto accelerators is a computationally intensive challenge that has spurred significant research into heuristic and learning-based solutions to improve tractability. Although numerous mappers exist, each claiming empirical superiority, the field currently lacks systematic understanding of how various search strategies traverse the solution space and how different mapping dimensions impact accelerator performance and efficiency. These insights are vital for designing mapping frameworks capable of handling the growing complexity of irregular and sparse DNNs resulting from neural architecture search. Instead of introducing another mapper, this study presents the first direct comparison of search techniques used by existing mappers. Based on these findings, we propose two novel augmentation techniques—warm-start and sparsity-aware—that enhance current mappers, demonstrating improvements in speed, scalability, and robustness across a diverse range of DNN models.

The rise of deep learning has popularized deep neural network architectures for monaural music source separation, with end-to-end waveform-based methods gaining significant research interest. Among these, transforming the input mixture into a learned latent space and applying a soft mask multiplicatively yields the best results but often introduces artifacts. To mitigate this issue, we propose HTMD-Net, a hybrid time-domain approach that integrates a lightweight masking component with a denoising module utilizing skip connections to refine the masked source estimates. Evaluations on the musdb18 dataset for monaural singing voice separation demonstrate that our method achieves competitive performance compared to pure masking approaches under identical training conditions, particularly improving behavior during silent segments while maintaining higher computational efficiency.

At finite temperatures, the stable equilibrium configurations of a coupled two-component superfluid with equal masses—examined through holographic real-time dynamics in both non-rotating and rotating scenarios—are defined as the final, time-invariant states reached during evolution. In the absence of rotation, when the Josephson coupling $\epsilon$ is disabled, spatially phase-separated states become more stable than miscible condensates once the direct repulsive inter-component coupling constant exceeds a critical threshold of $\eta_c = 0.05$ ($\eta > \eta_c$). Conversely, a finite $\epsilon$ invariably prevents spatial separation of the two species. Under rotational conditions with vanishing $\epsilon$, varying $\eta$ from negative to positive causes the quantum fluid to exhibit diverse vortex equilibrium structures; specifically, interlaced vortex lattices undergo a phase transition into vortex sheets, where each component consists of chains of single quantized vortices.

The Migdal effect, which involves the excitation and ionization of a recoiling atom during dark matter elastic scattering, allows ionization electrons to contribute additional energy deposition alongside the nuclear recoil. This mechanism enables the detection of dark matter particles with masses below 1 GeV/c². Utilizing the dual-phase liquid argon time projection chamber of the DarkSide-50 experiment, we establish new constraints for such sub-GeV dark matter based on an exposure of (12306 ± 184) kg d. By relying solely on the ionization signal, our analysis significantly boosts the experiment's sensitivity, extending the reach to dark matter masses as low as 40 MeV/c². Moreover, these results set the current most stringent upper limits on the spin-independent dark matter-nucleon cross section for masses under 3.6 GeV/c².

This study tackles the persistent challenge of determining the observability of mass and inertia parameters within adaptive identification (AID) for second-order nonlinear models of 6-degree-of-freedom rigid-body systems under external forces and moments. While previous research has established stable methods for AID and direct adaptive trajectory tracking for these systems, none have analytically proven that parameter estimates converge to their true values. This paper establishes the necessary and sufficient conditions for uniform complete observability (UCO) of 6-DOF inertial parameters, ensuring that the adaptive estimates converge to the true values when these conditions are met. To the authors' knowledge, this constitutes the first proof of UCO and parameter convergence for this specific class of systems. Furthermore, a numerical simulation demonstrates that the UCO condition can be satisfied for both fully-actuated and underactuated plants through appropriate control inputs, confirming the convergence of estimates. Finally, the authors conjecture that this methodology can be generalized to other rigid body model parameters, such as drag, buoyancy, added mass, bias, and actuator characteristics.

We define the primary object of the Partite Lemma as the colimit of a specific diagram. This approach offers a purely categorical perspective on the lemma, ensuring the object's canonicity. Furthermore, this categorical framework enables the unification of the direct Partite Lemma found in the Ne\v{s}et\v{r}il--R\"odl Theorem with Solecki's dual Paritite Lemma.

Assume a hypersurface exists with a Newton polytope $\Delta$ that contains a specified set of subvarieties. By employing tropical geometry, we map each subvariety to a corresponding subset of $\Delta$. We demonstrate that a weighted sum of the volumes of these subsets provides a lower bound for the volume of $\Delta$.

As a specific application, we examine a planar algebraic curve $C$ passing through generic points $p_1, \dots, p_n$ with assigned multiplicities $m_1, \dots, m_n$. Given that the minimal lattice width $\omega(\Delta)$ of the curve's Newton polygon satisfies $\omega(\Delta) \geq \max(m_i)$, we utilize tropical floor diagrams—a degeneration of the points onto a horizontal line—to establish the inequality:
$$\mathrm{area}(\Delta)\geq \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^n m_i^2-S,\ \ \text{where } S=\frac{1}{2}\max \left(\sum_{i=1}^n s_i^2 \Big| s_i\leq m_i, \sum_{i=1}^n s_i\leq \omega(\Delta)\right).$$
When the multiplicities are uniform, i.e., $m_1 = \dots = m \leq \omega(\Delta)$, this estimate simplifies to $\mathrm{area}(\Delta)\geq \frac{1}{2}(n-\frac{\omega(\Delta)}{m})m^2$, which translates to the degree bound $d\geq (\sqrt{n}-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2\sqrt n})m$ for curves of degree $d$.

Our framework applies to any toric surface (arbitrary $\Delta$), with the base field being an infinite field of any characteristic or a sufficiently large finite field. The requirement for a large finite field stems from the lack of a clear definition for "generic points" in small finite fields. We explicitly construct such point collections for sufficiently large fields, a development that may also hold significance for coding theory.

Spin glasses are characterized by magnetic moments that freeze into random orientations at low temperatures, lacking long-range order. Since frustration and disorder are typically considered essential for such systems, it was unexpected that the stoichiometric compound PrAu2Si2, which possesses a well-ordered crystal structure, was found to display spin glass freezing. This article presents inelastic neutron scattering data on crystal field excitations, revealing that PrAu2Si2 features a singlet ground state and an exchange coupling nearly at the critical threshold for magnetic ordering. We suggest that the observed spin glass freezing arises from dynamic fluctuations in crystal field levels, which destabilize induced moments and hinder the formation of long-range magnetic correlations. This proposed mechanism for generating a frustrated ground state may offer a means to test the concept of "avoided criticality" within glassy systems.

Accelerator mass spectrometry (AMS) is a prevalent technique utilized across geology, molecular biology, and archaeology; however, its reliance on tandem accelerators and large magnets restricts it to major laboratories despite its high precision. We introduce interferometric mass spectrometry (IMS), a new mass separation approach based on quantum interference. By exploiting the wave-like nature of samples, IMS complements AMS, which operates on particle-like samples. This duality yields two key advantages: (i) IMS separates based on absolute mass ($m$) rather than the mass-to-charge ratio ($m/q$) as AMS does; and (ii) IMS operates in the low-velocity regime, unlike the high-velocity regime of AMS. Consequently, IMS is well-suited for compact mobile devices, for fragile molecules that decompose during acceleration, and for neutral samples that are challenging to ionize.

In wireless multi-hop environments, including wireless sensor networks, link quality (LQ) stands as a critical metric extensively utilized by upper-layer protocols like routing algorithms. Accurate prediction of link quality can significantly enhance the overall performance of these networks. Although numerous prediction models have been developed recently, the dynamic and stochastic characteristics of wireless transmission continue to make link quality prediction a formidable challenge. This article primarily investigates how the stochastic nature of wireless transmission impacts link quality prediction models and examines the advantages of applying performance-constrained prediction models within wireless multi-hop network applications.

Untreated retinopathy, a cluster of retinal disorders, can lead to significant vision loss or total blindness. While numerous researchers have created autonomous systems to detect this condition using fundus and optical coherence tomography (OCT) images, most rely on traditional transfer learning and fine-tuning methods that demand substantial amounts of well-annotated data for accurate diagnostics. This paper introduces a novel incremental cross-domain adaptation framework that enables any deep classification model to progressively identify abnormal retinal pathologies in OCT and fundus imagery through few-shot learning. Distinct from existing approaches, the proposed system utilizes a Bayesian multi-objective function; this mechanism ensures the candidate network retains its previously acquired knowledge during incremental training while also grasping the structural and semantic connections between old and new disease categories to facilitate effective recognition during inference. When evaluated across six public datasets sourced from three different scanners to screen thirteen retinal pathologies, the framework surpassed state-of-the-art methods, achieving an overall accuracy of 0.9826 and an F1 score of 0.9846.

Common envelope evolution (CEE) physics is fundamental to the formation of binary systems, including merging stellar gravitational wave sources, pulsar binaries, and Type Ia supernovae. With the advent of large-scale surveys and gravitational wave detectors, precise constraints on CEE have become increasingly vital. This study employs an adiabatic mass loss model to investigate how a donor's total energy varies with remnant mass, offering a more self-consistent method for calculating binding energy. For comparison, we also derive binding energy by integrating total energy from the core to the surface. The outcome of CEE is determined by total energy conservation at the moment when both components' radii contract within their Roche lobes. We apply these findings to a sample of 142 hot subdwarf binaries. For sdBs with shorter orbital periods, the binding energy shows high consistency; however, for those with longer periods, the binding energy can differ by up to a factor of two. The CE efficiency parameter $\beta_\mathrm{CE}$ falls below $\alpha_\mathrm{CE}$ when the final orbital period satisfies $\log_{10} P_{\mathrm{orb}}/\mathrm{d} > -0.5$. Additionally, we observe a linear correlation between mass ratios $\log_{10} q$ and CE efficiency parameters $\log_{10} \alpha_{\mathrm{CE}}$ and $\log_{10} \beta_\mathrm{CE}$ in sdBs, a trend consistent with findings by De Marco et al. (2010) for post-AGB binaries.

Building on Becker-Denef-Lipschitz's (1979) observation that, for a finite field $k$, the total residue map $\text{res}:k(\!(t)\!)\to k$ (which extracts the constant term of a Laurent series) is definable in the language of rings with a parameter for $t$, we investigate the theory $\text{VF}_{\text{res},\iota}$ of valued fields augmented with a linear form $\text{res}:K\to k$ that agrees with the residue map on the valuation ring. We demonstrate that $\text{VF}_{\text{res},\iota}$ lacks a model companion. Furthermore, we establish that the power series field $(k(\!(t)\!),\text{res})$, endowed with such a total residue map, is undecidable for any infinite field $k$. Consequently, it follows that $(\mathbb{C}(\!(t)\!), \text{Res}_0)$ is undecidable, where $\text{Res}_0:\mathbb{C}(\!(t)\!)\to \mathbb{C}$ assigns to each function $f$ its complex residue at $0$.

We present a self-contained proof of a formula for the Fredholm index of asymptotically non-degenerate Cauchy-Riemann operators on punctured surfaces with boundaries, utilizing the technique of large antilinear deformations. Originally introduced by Taubes for closed surfaces and later extended by Gerig to include interior punctures, this method yields a novel feature in our proof: the Euler characteristic term in the index formula incorporates a non-standard weighted count of boundary zeros. We anticipate that this specific formulation of the index formula will prove beneficial for other researchers.

Identifying page components like tables, figures, and equations is the fundamental initial step in extracting data from document images. We introduce CDeC-Net, a novel end-to-end trainable deep network designed for table detection. This architecture features a multi-stage extension of Mask R-CNN equipped with a dual backbone and deformable convolutions, enabling the detection of tables across varying scales with high accuracy even at stringent Intersection over Union (IoU) thresholds. We empirically validated CDeC-Net across all publicly available benchmark datasets—including ICDAR-2013, ICDAR-2017, ICDAR-2019, UNLV, Marmot, PubLayNet, and TableBank—through extensive experimentation. Our approach offers three key advantages: (i) the single trained model, CDeC-Net, delivers strong performance across all major benchmarks; (ii) we achieve excellent results across multiple IoU thresholds, including higher ones; and (iii) adhering to the protocols of recent studies, we consistently demonstrate superior quantitative performance. To ensure reproducibility, our code and models will be made publicly available.

We utilize an empirical, data-driven methodology to model crop yield as a function of monthly temperature and precipitation, employing generative probabilistic models with parameters estimated via Bayesian inference. While our approach is demonstrated using state-level maize yield and meteorological data from the US Corn Belt between 1981 and 2014, it is easily adaptable to other crops, regions, and spatial resolutions. Testing various models reveals that maize growth rates can be effectively represented by a two-dimensional Gaussian function of temperature and precipitation, with monthly contributions accumulating throughout the growing season. This method captures non-linear responses to individual meteorological variables and accounts for interactions between them. Our models confirm that temperature and precipitation exert the greatest influence on yield during the six months preceding harvest, aligning with the typical US maize growing season (April to September). Optimal growth rates occur at a monthly mean temperature of 18–19°C (corresponding to a daily maximum of 24–25°C) and a monthly total precipitation of 115 mm, figures that broadly match prior research. Furthermore, this framework offers a self-consistent means to assess the impacts of climate change on current US maize varieties without assuming adaptation measures. With precipitation and growing area held constant, a 2°C temperature increase relative to the 1981–2014 baseline leads to an 8% reduction in mean yield and a threefold increase in yield variance. Consequently, we present a flexible, data-driven framework for examining the effects of natural climate variability and climate change on globally significant crops based on observed behaviors. When combined with other methods, this work can help guide the development of adaptation strategies to ensure food security in a changing climate.

Anatomical entities like the liver, hippocampus, and bones can be modeled as orientable, closed surfaces, enabling the calculation of volume, surface area, mean and Gaussian curvatures, and the Euler-Poincaré characteristic, even across structures with varying topologies. Typically, these structures are represented implicitly in curve evolution as zero level sets of an embedding, often achieved by embedding binary images via a signed distance transform. However, the quantization inherent in this approach hampers accurate curvature computation, resulting in significant morphometric errors. This study introduces a rapid and straightforward embedding technique that achieves precise local morphometry by identifying the zero crossing of a Gaussian-blurred binary image. Validation was conducted using femoral and fourth lumbar vertebrae from 50 clinical CT datasets. Findings indicate that the signed distance transform introduces substantial quantization errors in local curvature calculations. Global validation through regression and Bland-Altman analysis demonstrated that the coefficient of determination for average mean curvature rose from 93.8% with the signed distance transform to 100% with the proposed method. Regarding surface area, proportional bias shifted from -5.0% to +0.6%, and the accuracy of the Euler-Poincaré characteristic improved from being unusable to 98%. Consequently, this method facilitates enhanced local and global curvature evaluation for morphometry on closed, implicit surfaces.

This study addresses strongly convex-strongly concave (SCSC) saddle-point problems formulated as $\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d_x}}\max_{y\in\mathbb{R}^{d_y}}f(x,y)$, where the objective function $f$ is $L$-smooth, $\mu$-strongly convex in $x$ for any fixed $y$, and $\mu$-strongly concave in $y$ for any fixed $x$. These problems are prevalent in machine learning, particularly within robust empirical risk minimization (ERM) such as distributionally robust ERM, where gradients are approximated via mini-batches. Utilizing an unbiased stochastic first-order oracle, we examine the stochastic accelerated primal-dual (SAPD) algorithm introduced by Zhang et al. [2021] as a robust solution to gradient noise. SAPD generalizes stochastic gradient descent ascent (SGDA); when the momentum parameter is zero, it reduces to SGDA, but with an optimally tuned momentum, it achieves an accelerated convergence rate, reducing the dependency on the condition number $\kappa \triangleq L/\mu$ from $\kappa^2$ to $\kappa$. Furthermore, we introduce efficient variance-reduction techniques for SAPD leveraging Richardson-Romberg extrapolation, demonstrating that our approach outperforms the original SAPD method both theoretically and empirically.

We investigate the fractional quantum Hall effect in bilayer systems featuring a charge-imbalance distribution, potentially caused by a bias gate voltage. These bilayers may be intrinsic or arise spontaneously within wide quantum wells as a result of electron Coulomb repulsion. Specifically, we examine the fractional quantum Hall effect in asymmetric bilayer configurations at a filling factor of ν=4/11, demonstrating that an asymmetric Halperin-like trial wavefunction accurately describes the system's ground state.

Despite the proven success of various Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architectures in quantifying cardiac index, they remain susceptible to minor input disturbances, such as spatial shifts, image distortions, and adversarial attacks. This fragility undermines confidence in automated CNN-based diagnoses for cardiovascular conditions. This study introduces a straightforward yet effective technique for training robust CNNs to quantify the left ventricle (LV), covering cavity and myocardium areas, directional dimensions, and regional wall thicknesses. The core of our method relies on the biologically-inspired steerable pyramid transform (SPT) as a fixed preprocessing step, offering three distinct computational benefits for LV quantification. First, SPT basis functions align with the LV's anatomical structure and the geometric traits of the target indices. Second, SPT facilitates parameter regularization by allowing a single CNN to handle multiple orientations while naturally capturing scale variations. Third, the residual highpass subband can be easily discarded to promote more robust feature learning. We also propose a concise metric called the Robustness Ratio to assess performance under diverse perturbations. Extensive testing on 145 cardiac sequences demonstrates that our SPT-enhanced approach not only matches or exceeds state-of-the-art algorithms in prediction accuracy but also exhibits significantly greater robustness against input perturbations.

Intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRSs) represent a transformative technology in wireless communications, enabling the creation of a controllable propagation environment. This study introduces the deployment of an IRS at the boundary between multiple cells to support downlink transmissions for cell-edge users while simultaneously reducing inter-cell interference, a critical challenge in multicell networks. The objective is to maximize the weighted sum rate (WSR) of all users by jointly optimizing active precoding matrices at the base stations (BSs) and the phase shifts at the IRS, adhering to power constraints for each BS and unit modulus constraints for the IRS. Since both BSs and users utilize multiple antennas to leverage spatial multiplexing gains and improve spectral efficiency, the resulting optimization problem is non-convex. To address this, we first reformulate the problem and solve it using a block coordinate descent (BCD) algorithm, which alternately optimizes precoding matrices and phase shifts. Closed-form solutions for the optimal precoding matrices are derived when phase shifts are fixed. Furthermore, two efficient algorithms—the Majorization-Minimization (MM) Algorithm and the Complex Circle Manifold (CCM) Method—are proposed to solve the phase shift optimization problem, with both guaranteed to converge to at least locally optimal solutions. The proposed methods are also extended to cover more complex scenarios involving multiple IRSs and network MIMO. Finally, simulation results validate the benefits of integrating IRSs for improving the performance of cell-edge users.

While prior AI achievements in complex games typically addressed scenarios with no more than hundreds of actions per decision point, Diplomacy presents a significantly larger challenge, featuring over 10^20 possible actions per turn. Previous efforts to tackle games with such massive branching factors, including Diplomacy, StarCraft, and Dota, relied on human data to initialize policies or employed manually crafted reward shaping. This paper introduces an algorithm designed for action exploration and equilibrium approximation within games characterized by combinatorial action spaces. The method concurrently executes value iteration and learns a policy proposal network, utilizing a double oracle step to identify additional actions for inclusion in the proposals. For each state, the target state value and policy required for model training are derived through an equilibrium search procedure. Leveraging this algorithm, we trained an agent named DORA entirely from scratch on a popular two-player Diplomacy variant, demonstrating superhuman performance. Furthermore, we extended these methods to full-scale no-press Diplomacy, marking the first instance of training an agent from scratch without any human data. We provide evidence that this agent employs strategies incompatible with those bootstrapped from human data, offering the first strong indication of multiple equilibria in Diplomacy and suggesting that self-play alone may not be sufficient to achieve superhuman results in the game.

Performance degradation techniques serve as a crucial complement to side-channel attacks. This study introduces HyperDegrade, a novel method that integrates prior strategies with simultaneous multithreading (SMT) architectures. Beyond this new technique, we identify a previously unrecognized source of slowdown by analyzing cache eviction as a root cause. The resulting performance degradation is substantially greater than previous methods, thereby enhancing the time granularity available for Flush+Reload attacks. We evaluated HyperDegrade across various Intel microarchitectures, achieving significant slowdowns that, in specific microbenchmark scenarios, represent a three-order-of-magnitude improvement over state-of-the-art solutions. To assess the effectiveness of performance degradation in amplifying side channels, we introduced and validated specific leakage metrics. Our findings indicate that HyperDegrade improves time granularity without compromising trace quality. Furthermore, we conducted a fair comparison of three performance degradation strategies when paired with Flush+Reload from an attacker's viewpoint. We also devised an attack targeting an underutilized vulnerability in OpenSSL, where HyperDegrade demonstrated superior performance by reducing the number of required Flush+Reload traces needed for success by a factor of three. In terms of cryptographic contributions, we revisited the recently proposed Raccoon attack on TLS-DH key exchanges, extending its application to other protocols. Leveraging HyperDegrade, we constructed an end-to-end attack proving that Raccoon-like exploits can succeed with real data, addressing a gap left by earlier research.

We conduct a non-perturbative lattice study of decay rates for inclusive semi-leptonic transitions in charmed mesons. Given the persistent discrepancy between exclusive and inclusive methods in extracting CKM matrix elements $|V_{ub}|$ and $|V_{cb}|$, lattice QCD has recently been applied to describe inclusive decays. Because determining hadronic parameters via QCD requires independent validation, we concentrate on the charm sector, which benefits from both available experimental data and precisely known CKM values. We present a pilot lattice simulation for $D_s \rightarrow X_s \ell\nu$, investigating enhancements to current methodologies. Our approach utilizes Möbius domain-wall formulations for charm and strange quarks, with masses tuned to approximate physical values across the entire kinematical range. Additionally, we detail our progress in evaluating systematic uncertainties, including the extrapolation of the kernel function for Chebyshev approximation and the impact of results near the kinematic limit.

Given any two non-negative integers $h$ and $k$ where $h > k$, an $L(h, k)$-colouring of a graph $G$ assigns colours to vertices such that adjacent vertices have colours differing by at least $h$, and vertices at distance two have colours differing by at least $k$. The smallest positive integer $\lambda$ for which an $L(h, k)$-colouring exists with a maximum colour value of $\lambda$ is defined as the $L(h, k)$-chromatic number, or $L(h, k)$-colouring number, denoted by $\lambda_{h,k}(G)$. This paper explores several invariants in hypergraphs, specifically examining the relationship between the spectral gap and the $L(2, 1)$-chromatic number. We establish inequalities connecting the $L(2, 1)$-chromatic number of a $k$-regular simple graph to its spectral gap and expansion constant. Furthermore, we derive an upper bound for the $L(h, k)$-chromatic number using various hypergraph invariants, including the strong chromatic number, strong independent number, and maximum degree. We also determine a sharp upper bound for the $L(2, 1)$-chromatic number of hypertrees based on their maximum degree. The paper concludes with a discussion on $L(2, 1)$-colouring within the Cartesian products of specific hypergraph classes.

We demonstrate that the units identified by Gardam in torsion-free group rings are twisted unitary elements. This insight validates certain seemingly arbitrary decisions in Gardam's construction and generates additional examples of units. Furthermore, we observe that every unit discovered to date possesses non-trivial symmetry.

We introduce "opportunistic evaluation," a framework designed to speed up dataframe interactions, a critical factor for human-in-the-loop, iterative data analysis workloads. This approach drastically cuts interactive latency by: 1) prioritizing computations essential to immediate user actions, and 2) utilizing periods of user inactivity to perform asynchronous background processing for non-critical operators that may become relevant later. Empirical analysis demonstrates that existing user behavior offers significant optimization potential, which our proposed solutions effectively exploit.

The accretion of rocky planetary material onto a star can be inferred from the subsequent enrichment of refractory elements in the star's photosphere. However, these chemical signatures are subject to dilution through stellar interior mixing, specifically thermohaline mixing driven by an inverse mean-molecular-weight gradient between the radiative core and convective envelope. Utilizing MESA stellar models, we determined the intensity and lifespan of these engulfment signatures. Our findings indicate that thermohaline mixing is the dominant process for approximately 5 to 45 million years after engulfment, reducing the signal strength by a factor of roughly two before gravitational settling causes depletion over longer periods. For solar-metallicity stars between 0.5 and 1.2 solar masses, observable signatures persist for timescales ranging from 1 million to 8 billion years, contingent upon the star's mass and the quantity of material accreted. Early-type stars display more pronounced initial refractory enhancements but experience faster depletion. Solar-like stars (0.9–1.1 $M_{\odot}$) retain detectable signatures (greater than 0.05 dex) for approximately 20 million to 1.7 billion years following the engulfment of a 10 Earth-mass object; however, these signatures last longer in low-metallicity or hotter stars (e.g., ~2–3 Gyr for a 1 $M_{\odot}$ star). Furthermore, engulfment events occurring significantly after the zero-age main sequence generate stronger signals because gravitational settling of helium suppresses thermohaline mixing (e.g., ~1.5 Gyr for a 1 $M_{\odot}$ star). Consequently, detecting engulfment signatures in solar-like stars that are several billion years old may be challenging.

**Purpose:** Inter-scan motion significantly degrades $R_1$ estimation accuracy, a problem likely to worsen at 7T due to greater $B_1$ inhomogeneity. Existing correction techniques fail at 7T because they rely on body coil references. We present two superior alternatives that bypass this requirement by calculating relative sensitivities without needing body coil images.

**Theory:** The new approaches derive relative coil sensitivities from coil-combined magnitude images. The first method employs a straightforward ratio for efficient computation, while the second utilizes a more complex generative model fitting process.

**Methods:** $R_1$ maps were generated using the variable flip angle (VFA) technique. Datasets were collected at both 3T and 7T, both with and without motion occurring between VFA volume acquisitions. Map reconstruction was performed without correction, using the proposed methods, and (at 3T) with the standard correction scheme.

**Results:** At 3T, the proposed methods surpassed the baseline. At 7T, inter-scan motion artifacts were similarly reduced. However, reproducibility matched the no-motion baseline only when position-specific transmit field effects were included.

**Conclusion:** These methods streamline inter-scan motion correction for $R_1$ maps, offering applicability at both 3T and 7T where body coils are often unavailable. Open-source code for all techniques is now publicly accessible.

A key implication of the cosmic censorship conjecture is that any topological feature eventually collapses within the horizons of black holes, rendering it inaccessible to external classical observers. Nevertheless, a single two-level quantum system (a UDW detector) positioned outside the horizon can differentiate between a black hole and its associated geon counterpart by observing distinct response rates. This study expands upon that inquiry by examining the entanglement structure of the vacuum state for a quantum scalar field in the spacetime of an $\mathbb{RP}_2$ geon, contrasting it with the BTZ black hole. Using an entanglement harvesting protocol that transfers field entanglement to a pair of UDW detectors, we discover that the classically concealed topology of the geon leads to significant differences in harvested entanglement compared to the BTZ spacetime, particularly for small masses. Specifically, detectors with small energy gaps harvest more entanglement in the BTZ spacetime, whereas those with larger energy gaps harvest more in the geon spacetime. The crossover energy gap varies with black hole mass, appearing at lower values for smaller masses. These findings also influence the "entanglement shadow"—the region near the horizon where harvesting fails. In geon spacetimes, small-gap detectors experience a larger shadow, while large-gap detectors encounter a larger shadow in BTZ spacetimes.

Extensions of the Standard Model (SM) frequently incorporate large fermionic multiplets to explain small neutrino masses, the dark matter relic density, and the muon $(g-2)$ anomaly. Among these, models featuring fermion quintuplets ($\Sigma$) alongside other scalar multiplets can resolve recent flavor sector anomalies while adhering to electroweak constraints. Typically, exotic fermions in such frameworks couple directly to SM particles, resulting in stringent mass limits from collider searches like the LHC. However, this study examines a specific scenario where quintuplet fermions are heavier than the scalars—a hierarchy naturally suggested by the muon $(g-2)$ data. A distinctive feature of these models is the prediction of non-standard collider signatures, as the quintuplet fermions decay through scalars after production. We analyze these non-standard interactions and propose alternative search strategies for the LHC and future linear colliders (e.g., $e^+e^-$ machines), discussing both exclusion and discovery prospects. Specifically, the doubly charged quintuplet fermion ($\Sigma^{\pm\pm}$) could be discovered at the 14 TeV LHC with $5\sigma$ significance using 3000 fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity if $M_\Sigma \leq 980$ GeV. Conversely, discovering the singly charged quintuplet fermion ($\Sigma^\pm$) at the LHC remains difficult, though a $5\sigma$ discovery might be achievable at an $e^+e^-$ collider with 1000 fb$^{-1}$ luminosity for $M_\Sigma \leq 700$ GeV.

This study introduces two novel constraint-handling strategies for the DMulti-MADS algorithm, a blackbox extension of the Mesh Adaptive Direct Search (MADS) method tailored for multiobjective optimization. These strategies aggregate constraints into a single violation function applied in two distinct modes: a two-phase approach that prioritizes finding feasible points before refining the solution set, and a progressive barrier approach that discards trial points exceeding a threshold, which is gradually lowered over iterations. Similar to single-objective optimization, it is demonstrated that both variants produce sequences of feasible or infeasible points that converge to a set of local Pareto optima in feasible scenarios or to Clarke stationary points based on the violation function in infeasible scenarios. Computational results indicate that these methods perform competitively against other leading algorithms.

Restoring realistic images in high-texture regions, such as removing face masks, remains a significant challenge. Current state-of-the-art deep learning approaches struggle to ensure high fidelity, often suffer from training instability caused by vanishing gradients (resulting in minimal weight updates in early layers), and lose spatial information. Furthermore, these methods rely on intermediate stages like segmentation, necessitating external masks. This paper introduces a blind mask face inpainting technique utilizing a Residual Attention UNet to eliminate face masks and restore facial features with fine details, closely aligning with the ground truth structure. By feeding information from a residual block to subsequent layers and those two hops away, the model addresses vanishing gradients. Additionally, the attention mechanism enables the model to concentrate on relevant masked areas, conserving computational resources and enhancing speed. Extensive experiments on the public CelebA dataset demonstrate the feasibility and robustness of the proposed model. The code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/mdhosen/Mask-Face-Inpainting-Using-Residual-Attention-Unet}.

This study employs an Effective Field Theory (EFT) framework to assess whether the Higgs boson can resolve the $g-2$ anomaly. Despite the Standard Model (SM) contribution of the Higgs to the muon's magnetic dipole moment being negligible, our \textit{bottom-up} EFT analysis demonstrates that the Higgs remains a viable candidate if its couplings to other SM particles are permitted to deviate from SM expectations, provided current experimental constraints on the Higgs sector are satisfied. By applying unitarity arguments, we determine that such a scenario implies a New Physics (NP) scale of approximately 10–18 TeV, which could drop to around 5 TeV if the Higgs couplings to $W$ and $Z$ bosons adhere to SM predictions. Furthermore, we show that this framework could significantly enhance di-Higgs production at muon colliders, offering additional motivation for exploring this possibility. A primary conclusion of this work is the critical need to measure the $\bar{\mu} \mu hh$ coupling in upcoming experiments.

**Context.** Uranus's extreme 98-degree axial tilt is traditionally explained by giant impacts during the planet's formation, yet this model has notable limitations.

**Aims.** Research indicates that over a billion-year span, tidal evolution of Jupiter's and Saturn's moons significantly influences their spin dynamics. This study re-evaluates the tilting of Uranus by applying this mechanism.

**Methods.** We examined Uranus's precession spectrum to pinpoint potential secular spin-orbit resonances capable of causing the tilt. Additionally, we characterized the hypothetical ancient satellite necessary for capture and simulated its dynamics numerically.

**Results.** A single satellite with a minimum mass of 4e-4 times Uranus's mass, migrating across more than 10 Uranian radii, can tilt the planet from a low obliquity toward 90 degrees. To achieve this tilt within the Solar System's age, the satellite's orbital drift rate must match the Moon's current expansion rate; under these conditions, simulations show Uranus can easily tilt beyond 80 degrees. Beyond this threshold, the satellite becomes highly unstable, inducing chaotic motion in the planet's spin axis. This chaos concludes when the satellite collides with Uranus, locking the planet's obliquity into either a prograde or retrograde state similar to today's Uranus. Such Uranus-like spin states can occur with up to an 80% probability, though a larger satellite (mass $\ge$ 1.7e-3 Uranus masses) is preferred. Nevertheless, smaller ancient satellites are not definitively excluded, and future research may refine this scenario, particularly by considering interactions among multiple pre-existing satellites.

This study investigates the magnetoanisotropic properties and magnetocaloric effect in layered ferromagnetic Cr$_4$Te$_5$ single crystals through a critical behavior analysis of magnetization isotherms. Utilizing modified Arrott plots, we determined critical exponents of $\beta$=0.485(3), $\gamma$=1.202(5), and $\delta$=3.52(3), alongside a Curie temperature of $T_C \approx 340.73(4)$ K. A significant magnetocrystalline anisotropy of $K_u$=330 kJ/$m^3$ was observed at 3 K, exhibiting a gradual decline as temperature rises. Near $T_C$, with the magnetic field applied parallel to the $\it{ab}$-plane, the maximum entropy change (-$\Delta S_{M}^{max}$) and relative cooling power (RCP) reached 2.77 $J/kg-K$ and 88.29 $J/kg$, respectively. The rescaling of -$\Delta S_M (T, H)$ data across various temperatures and fields into a single universal curve validates the second-order magnetic transition. Furthermore, renormalization group theory analysis indicates that the spin coupling follows a 3D Heisenberg-type model, $\{d:n\}=\{3:3\}$, characterized by long-range exchange interactions that decay according to $J (r) = r^{-(d+\sigma)}= r^{-4.71}$.

This presentation details the LHCb method for accurately determining the CKM angle $\gamma$ through tree-level decays. The LHCb experiment currently offers up to 16 independent measurements derived from various decay channels of beauty and charm mesons, though their sensitivity to $\gamma$ varies. Optimal precision is achieved by combining all available results. These proceedings examine several of the individual determinations included in this combination and report the most recent combined value as of Summer 2018.
This passage provides a concise overview of direct tests for T, CP, and CPT symmetries in transitions involving entangled neutral kaons generated at a $\phi$-factory.

This study introduces a method based on the quantum multistream model to investigate the electronic band structure of plasmonic excitations within a streaming electron gas, accommodating any level of degeneracy. By employing the multifluid quantum hydrodynamic model, we derive a system of $N$-coupled pseudoforce differential equations to compute the energy band structure. Our findings indicate that the unavoidable emergence of energy bands separated by gaps arises from discrete velocity filaments and their electrostatic mode coupling within the electron gas. Additionally, the current framework offers an alternative perspective on collisionless damping and phase mixing, describing them as collective scattering phenomena occurring within band gaps due to the coupling between wave-like and particle-like oscillations. We further extend the quantum multistream model to incorporate virtual streams, enabling the calculation of electronic band structures for one-dimensional plasmonic crystals. Notably, unlike the empty lattice approximation in the free electron model, energy band gaps in plasmon excitations result from collective electrostatic interactions among electrons. We also demonstrate that the plasmonic band gap size at the first Brillouin zone boundary reaches its maximum near the reciprocal lattice vector $G$ corresponding to metallic densities. Finally, we discuss the impacts of electron-lattice binding and electron-phonon coupling strengths on the electronic band structure, concluding that the inevitable formation of such band structures is a general characteristic of various quantum multistream systems coupled electromagnetically or gravitationally.

To enhance the awareness and impact of soft robotics, the field must move beyond laboratory settings and become accessible to individuals lacking robotic expertise. Currently, however, standard manufacturing methods rely on professional equipment or specialized materials that are unavailable to the general public, limiting widespread adoption. This paper introduces the BPActuator, a lightweight and affordable soft bending actuator that can be easily constructed using common plastics and balloons. We fabricated various actuator morphologies to characterize their deformation and load-bearing capabilities, demonstrating that they can achieve up to 35 degrees of bending while exerting a tip force of approximately 0.070 ± 0.015 N—more than five times their average weight. Additionally, we developed a three-fingered gripper using these actuators, which successfully performs human-like grasps on a variety of everyday objects and can lift loads at least eight times its own weight. With each unit costing only about 0.22 USD, the BPActuator offers significant cost efficiency. These advantages suggest that BPActuators will substantially improve the accessibility of soft robotics for a broader audience without requiring specialized knowledge.

We employ repeat measurements to calculate the mean values and uncertainties of parameters derived from light curve solutions of contact binaries. This approach utilizes the Monte Carlo algorithm within the Wilson-Devinney code to simultaneously determine both random and systematic errors. Analysis of 48 models indicates that systematic errors are typically smaller than random errors. Numerical results show that relative errors in photometric mass ratios remain below 1% for totally eclipsing contact binaries, whereas they generally range from 10% to 20% for partly eclipsing systems. The influence of third light on photometric solution errors was also examined; its presence can elevate errors in totally eclipsing binaries to approximately 10%. Specifically, if the third light is very faint (contributing less than 1% to the luminosity), it is preferable to set it to zero in the flux, as including such a faint component can significantly increase errors in the light curve solutions.

To date, LHC data collected at 7, 8, and 13 TeV have provided no evidence for new particles beyond the 125 GeV Higgs boson, specifically showing no signs of Supersymmetry (SUSY). Nevertheless, the complementary role of $e^+e^-$ collisions continues to offer promising avenues for discovering SUSY at the International Linear Collider (ILC). These prospects rely on the unique ability of $e^+e^-$ machines to detect events with missing four-momentum—a signature inaccessible at hadron colliders, which can only measure transverse momentum imbalance. Furthermore, the low background levels and trigger-less operation of $e^+e^-$ detectors allow for the observation of events with significantly lower visible energy compared to hadron colliders. This contribution details simulation studies conducted using the ILC detector concept. The simulations encompass the complete Standard Model background and realistic accelerator conditions. We present findings regarding the expected discovery and exclusion sensitivities for the most difficult SUSY channels, such as low-mass higgsinos or winos. Additionally, we evaluate the precision achievable in measuring model parameters upon discovery and demonstrate how these measurements can constrain sparticle spectra beyond direct detection limits and distinguish between various high-scale SUSY-breaking models.

We examine the challenge of forecasting chaotic dynamical systems using data, specifically when input consists of noisy partial observations of the system's past and current states. Recent machine learning methods have shown great promise in this domain, with hybrid approaches proving particularly effective by integrating machine learning with knowledge-based models. In these hybrids, machine learning corrects deficiencies within the knowledge-based model, which often arise from incomplete understanding or limited resolution of physical processes like those in the atmosphere or ocean. Unlike previous data-driven methods that typically require full measurements of all variables for training, we propose a method that relaxes this constraint by merging data assimilation with machine learning. We illustrate this approach using the Ensemble Transform Kalman Filter (ETKF) to assimilate synthetic data for both the 3-variable Lorenz system and the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky system, simulating model errors through misspecified parameters. Our results demonstrate that even with partial state measurements, a machine learning model can be trained to enhance the predictive accuracy of an imperfect knowledge-based model.

This work investigates the geometric evolution of entire graphs driven by fractional mean curvature. Specifically, we analyze the nonlocal quasilinear evolution equation governing the family of graph functions. Employing an analytic semigroup framework, we prove the short-time existence, uniqueness, and optimal Hölder regularity (in both time and space) for classical solutions, with results contingent upon the regularity of the initial graph. Furthermore, this methodology provides $C^\infty$-smoothness estimates for the evolving graphs at any positive time.

The VST Photometric Halpha Survey of the Southern Galactic Plane and Bulge (VPHAS+) is currently mapping the southern Milky Way using u, g, r, i, and Halpha filters with an angular resolution of 1 arcsec. Its primary coverage extends across Galactic longitudes south of the celestial equator between latitudes -5 and +5, with extensions reaching +/-10 degrees around the Galactic Centre to encompass much of the Bulge. Initiated on December 28, 2011, as a public ESO survey, VPHAS+ achieves a depth of 20th magnitude (10-sigma) and aims to deliver single-epoch digital optical photometry for approximately 300 million stars. The publication details the observing strategy and data processing pipeline, alongside an evaluation of the segmented narrowband Halpha filter employed. Utilizing model atmospheres and spectral libraries, the authors calculate main-sequence stellar colours—(u - g), (g - r), (r - i), and (r - Halpha)—within the Vega system. Preliminary validation of the photometry is reported using test data from two overlapping pointings with the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, accompanied by sample (u - g, g - r) and (r - Halpha, r - i) colour-magnitude diagrams for a complete survey field. The high image quality enables significant research opportunities regarding compact nebulae and their morphologies. Furthermore, the utility of the u band in identifying planetary nebula central stars is highlighted by the detection of the central star of NGC 2899 within the survey data. Thanks to the superior imaging capabilities of the VST/OmegaCam combination, this survey is ideally suited for automated searches for reddened early-type stars and will facilitate the discovery and analysis of compact binaries, white dwarfs, and transient sources.

We examine how high-energy quantum fluctuations influence the ultimate geometry of compact extra dimensions. During the inflationary epoch, these fluctuations generate a diverse array of initial extra-dimensional metrics within causally disconnected regions, known as pocket universes, across the Multiverse. This collection of initial configurations evolves into a set of inhomogeneous metrics observable at the present time, resulting in distinct low-energy physical conditions in different pocket universes. Furthermore, the probability of identifying a specific metric is numerically estimated using a model based on a compact two-dimensional extra space.

The $^{22}$Ne($\alpha$, n)$^{25}$Mg reaction is crucial for the neutron flux in the weak s-process nucleosynthesis path within AGB stars with masses $M \geq 8M_\odot$. A recent evaluation by Philip $\it{et al.}$, utilizing updated $^{26}$Mg nuclear data from various sources, revealed significant uncertainties and notable discrepancies with existing literature at low temperatures. Furthermore, Philip $\it{et al.}$ proposed that $R$-matrix modeling is necessary to determine $^{26}$Mg resonance state parameters and investigate interference patterns between distant levels. In this study, an $R$-matrix analysis was conducted to examine interference effects and constrain resonance spin and parity by fitting direct measurement data. The resonance parameters proposed by Philip $\it{et al.}$ fail to adequately explain the data due to strong interference among states of identical spin and parity. However, by adjusting the spin-parity assignments of certain states, the current $R$-matrix calculations successfully reproduce the experimental data within the 0.8 to 1.45 MeV energy range.

Self-supervised learning (SSL) has become essential for progress in natural language processing (NLP) and computer vision (CV), enabling state-of-the-art performance on diverse tasks through pretraining on vast amounts of unlabeled data with minimal fine-tuning. In contrast, the speech processing field has lacked a comparable framework to systematically investigate this approach. To address this, we introduce SUPERB (Speech processing Universal PERformance Benchmark), a leaderboard designed to evaluate shared models across numerous speech tasks with minimal architectural modifications and labeled data. While the shared model serves multiple purposes, our primary focus is on leveraging the reusable representations learned via SSL. We propose a straightforward framework that tackles SUPERB tasks by attaching lightweight, task-specific prediction heads to a frozen shared model. Our findings indicate that this approach is highly promising, demonstrating that SSL representations offer both competitive generalizability and accessibility across various speech tasks. We have released SUPERB as a challenge, complete with a leaderboard and benchmark toolkit, to advance research in representation learning and general speech processing.

Addressing challenges in neuroimaging where traditional "mass univariate" methods ignore spatial structure but full joint modeling is computationally prohibitive, this work introduces a new technique for handling spatial dependence within a broad family of model-selection tasks. Spatial relationships are represented using a Markov random field model, enhanced by a modified pseudo-marginal Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm that expands the underlying state space. This strategy enables the use of existing unbiased marginal likelihood estimators designed for spatially independent settings, allowing spatial dependence to be integrated with minimal additional effort. The proposed algorithm is practical for analyzing subsets of large-scale image data, such as 2D slices from 3D dynamic PET brain scans or other regions of interest. Various principled approximations and simple extensions based on the augmented spaces are explored, demonstrating performance comparable to the full pseudo-marginal method. These variations achieve the benefits of incorporating spatial dependence at negligible extra cost. An application to actual PET image data confirms that this approach significantly improves the detection of underlying spatial structures compared to current methods that assume spatial independence.

Just as general relativity necessitated the departure from Euclidean geometry, quantum theory demands the relinquishment of classical logic. We demonstrate that the Hilbert space framework of quantum mechanics is a logical necessity and that no fundamental principles underpin the theory itself. Instead, we identify an unavoidable extension of classical logic in which conjunctions can assume negative values, reverting to classical behavior only for order-invariant measurements. This generalized joint probability, derived from the expectation of conjunctions, similarly permits negative values. A commutative conjunction specifically yields the standard Hilbert space formalism. While quantum theory governs both microscopic and macroscopic systems, classicality is characterized by the non-negativity of this generalized joint probability. We further illustrate this logic by applying it to elucidate counterintuitive findings within quantum cognition.

Networked-Control Systems (NCSs), a subset of cyber-physical systems, integrate computing, communication, and control technologies closely. Although these environments offer significant flexibility, they remain susceptible to computing and network-based attacks, a vulnerability highlighted by recent hacking incidents that have prompted a need for enhanced cyber-physical security research. Concerns regarding quantum computing's potential to dismantle current cryptographic systems have exacerbated these risks. While the quantum threat has spurred new fields like post-quantum cryptography, other domains, specifically cyber-physical defense research, have often neglected the possibility of quantum-enabled adversaries. Cyber-physical defense is a distinct yet complementary discipline to protection, focusing on the ability to detect and respond to cyber-physical attacks. This involves integrating mechanisms to identify adverse events and formulate response plans both during and after incidents. This paper assumes that future quantum computers will grant adversaries an advantage unless defenders also adopt the technology. We propose a paradigm shift where the increase in adversarial resources due to quantum supremacy does not necessarily lead to a higher probability of disruptions. Aligning with current system design practices in other sectors, such as using artificial intelligence to bolster attack detection, we outline a vision for next-generation cyber-physical defense layers that leverage quantum computing and machine learning concepts. Through an illustrative example, we demonstrate how NCS defenders can learn and refine their strategies to anticipate and recover from attacks.

Utilizing the color glass condensate effective theory, we investigate azimuthal asymmetries in the diffractive production of $J/\psi$ mesons during ultraperipheral heavy-ion collisions at RHIC and LHC energies. Our theoretical framework accurately reproduces the azimuthally averaged $J/\psi$ production cross sections observed by STAR and ALICE. Additionally, we forecast substantial $\cos 2\phi$ and $\cos 4\phi$ azimuthal asymmetries for diffractive $J/\psi$ production across UPCs at RHIC and LHC energies, as well as in eA collisions at EIC energies. These newly identified polarization-sensitive observables could offer complementary data to better constrain the transverse spatial distribution of gluons within large nuclei. Distinct from all prior analyses of diffractive $J/\psi$ production, our calculations incorporate three essential new components: the double-slit interference effect, the linear polarization of coherent photons, and the impact of final-state soft photon radiation.

**Aims.** This study seeks to acquire near-ultraviolet to visible (NUV-VIS, 0.35–0.95 μm) reflectance spectra of primitive asteroids, specifically targeting members of the Themis and Polana-Eulalia complex families. This characterization aims to investigate the origins of two recent sample return mission targets: (162173) Ryugu and (101955) Bennu.

**Methods.** We acquired low-resolution visible spectra extending down to 0.35 μm using telescopes at the Roque de los Muchachos Observatory and reanalyzed previously published spectroscopic data. Our analysis focuses on the NUV-VIS reflectance properties of primitive asteroids within the Themis and Polana-Eulalia family complexes. Furthermore, we compared the NUV characteristics of these families with those of Ryugu and Bennu.
