The package includes data from hundreds of simulations covering core-collapse, thermonuclear, and pair-instability supernovae. This output can be utilized by event generators like sntools or event rate calculators such as SNOwGLoBES. Furthermore, SNEWPY contains additional routines that automate the processing of generated data through SNOwGLoBES and compile the results into the observable channels for each detector. This paper outlines the package's contents, the underlying physics of SNEWPY, its code organization, and provides examples of its capabilities.

We present Permutation and Structured Perturbation Inference (PSPI), a novel problem formulation designed to generalize various graph matching tasks prevalent in systems biology. PSPI serves as a robust extension of standard permutation inference or graph matching, aiming to identify a permutation between two graphs while accounting for potential edge perturbations caused by underlying factors. For instance, when comparing gene regulatory networks X and Y from diseased versus normal tissues, PSPI can detect structural alterations between them, offering a potential signature of the disease. In addition to this formulation, we introduce an ADMM-based algorithm named STEPD to solve a relaxed version of the PSPI problem. An extensive case study on comparative gene regulatory networks (GRNs) demonstrates that STEPD accurately infers structured perturbations, providing computational biologists with a tool to identify new prognostic markers. Furthermore, spectral analysis confirms that STEPD can recover small clique-like perturbations, establishing it as a valuable method for detecting permutation-invariant changes within graphs.

VPNs create secure tunnels that enable service providers to transmit data across unsecured networks. A wide range of VPN solutions exists, each with varying impacts on target architecture, as well as distinct performance limitations or advantages. This technical report evaluates Wireguard and OpenVPN across different SATCOM deployment scenarios and topologies.

Automatic fault detection remains a significant challenge across various sports. In race walking, officials currently rely on visual inspection to identify rule violations, making objectivity and fairness critical. While previous research has explored using sensors and machine learning for automation, these methods face issues such as intrusive equipment attachments and high-speed cameras that interfere with human judgment, alongside concerns regarding model interpretability. This study introduces a non-contact fault detection system leveraging pose estimation and machine learning models trained on the consensus of multiple qualified referees to ensure equitable rulings. The system was validated using smartphone footage of both compliant and intentionally faulty race walking by various athletes, including a Tokyo Olympic medalist. Results indicate that the proposed system achieves an average fault detection accuracy exceeding 90% and adheres strictly to race walking regulations. Furthermore, the study revealed distinct differences in the intentional faulty movements of the medalist compared to university-level walkers, insights that support the development of more generalized detection models. The associated code and dataset are accessible at https://github.com/SZucchini/racewalk-aijudge.

In numerical simulations of laser welding and additive manufacturing, material absorptivity represents a significant source of uncertainty, often requiring time-consuming trial-and-error calibration. This uncertainty compromises the predictive capability of simulations for process behavior and impedes the realization of fully digitized manufacturing processes, a key objective of "Industry 4.0." This study introduces an improved absorption model that accounts for laser properties, incident angles, surface temperature, and material composition to predict internal heat and fluid dynamics during the laser melting of stainless steel 316L. Utilizing this physically realistic variable model is superior to assuming a constant absorptivity and reduces calibration costs. High-fidelity three-dimensional simulations were conducted using both variable and constant absorptivity approaches, with results validated against experimental data. The findings reveal the critical influence of absorptivity on internal flow physics in laser material processing, explain the differences in melt-pool morphology between fiber and CO$_2$ laser sources, and discuss the factors governing local energy absorption.

Music Structure Analysis (MSA) involves segmenting songs into distinct parts like verses, choruses, and solos, effectively mapping the song's simplified organization. This paper introduces the Convolutive Block-Matching (CBM) algorithm, a novel approach designed for MSA. Specifically, CBM is a dynamic programming method that operates on autosimilarity matrices, a standard instrument in MSA. In this study, these matrices are derived from the feature representation of audio signals, with time sampling occurring at the bar level. We evaluate three different similarity functions for calculating these matrices. Our findings indicate that the proposed algorithm achieves performance levels comparable to supervised state-of-the-art methods across three out of four metrics, all while remaining fully unsupervised.

This research investigates the continuous-time Kyle-Back model featuring a risk-averse informed trader, demonstrating that an equilibrium exists in a multi-asset market characterized by non-Gaussian price distributions. This equilibrium is derived by solving a Fokker-Planck equation alongside a system of coupled partial differential equations, which are linked by an optimal transport constraint at the terminal time.

This study introduces a new method for determining melodic originality, building upon Simonton's (1994) research. This formula is subsequently utilized on a dataset comprising 428 Romantic-era classical compositions to examine the connection between melodic originality and thematic fame.

The field of vision science, especially machine vision, has undergone a transformation driven by the adoption of massive image datasets and statistical learning methods. However, human neuroimaging research on visual perception continues to depend on limited image sets (approximately 100) because of time restrictions in experimental protocols. To effectively merge neuroscience with statistical learning, the volume of images in neuroimaging studies must expand substantially. We introduce BOLD5000, a functional MRI (fMRI) experiment featuring nearly 5,000 unique real-world scene images. Beyond drastically outpacing previous fMRI studies in dataset size, BOLD5000 ensures high image diversity by integrating images from established computer vision repositories such as Scene UNderstanding (SUN), Common Objects in Context (COCO), and ImageNet. The combination of this large-scale, diverse imagery with a slow event-related fMRI design facilitates a detailed investigation of neural representations across various visual features, categories, and semantic meanings. Simultaneously, BOLD5000 advances the realization of Marr's vision for a unified discipline—the integrated study of biological and computational vision.

Driven by the growing demand for interpretable machine learning, there is an increasing need for human involvement in providing diverse explanations for model decisions. To enhance the trust and transparency of AI systems, the field of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has emerged, divided primarily into feature attribution and counterfactual explanation methods. While feature attribution explains the rationale behind a model's decision, counterfactual explanations identify the minimal input changes required to alter that decision. This paper aims to foster trust and transparency in time series models by utilizing motifs to generate counterfactual explanations. We introduce Motif-Guided Counterfactual Explanation (MG-CF), a novel approach that produces intuitive post-hoc counterfactuals by fully leveraging significant motifs to offer interpretive insights into decision-making. To our knowledge, this is the first study to employ motifs to guide the generation of counterfactual explanations. We evaluated MG-CF using five real-world time-series datasets from the UCR repository. Our experimental results demonstrate that MG-CF outperforms other state-of-the-art baselines in balancing the desirable properties of counterfactual explanations.

Previous self-supervised learning studies have primarily relied on image-level instance discrimination as a pretext task, achieving classification accuracy comparable to supervised methods. However, these approaches suffer from reduced performance when transferred to downstream tasks like object detection. To address this gap, we introduce a new object-level self-supervised method named Contrastive learning with Downstream background invariance (CoDo). This method shifts the focus of the pretext task to modeling instance locations across diverse backgrounds, a capability essential for effective object detection. Our approach involves three key components: first, a data augmentation strategy that pastes instances onto background images and jitters their bounding boxes to incorporate contextual information; second, architectural alignment between the pretraining network and standard detection pipelines; and third, a hierarchical, multi-view contrastive learning framework to enhance visual representation. Experiments on the MSCOCO dataset demonstrate that CoDo, when paired with common backbones such as ResNet50-FPN, delivers robust transfer learning results for object detection.

This work examines two classes of second-order-in-time partial differential equations: semilinear wave equations and semilinear beam equations. To address these using exponential integrators, we introduce a method for efficiently calculating the action of the matrix exponential and associated matrix functions. Several numerical simulations are provided to demonstrate the efficacy of this approach.

High-throughput density functional theory (DFT) enables a systematic search for conventional superconductors. Motivated by the growing interest in two-dimensional (2D) superconductivity, we employed a high-throughput workflow to screen more than 1,000 2D materials within the JARVIS-DFT database, calculating electron-phonon coupling and the superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$) via the McMillan-Allen-Dynes formula for 170 candidates. Among these, we identified 34 dynamically stable structures exhibiting $T_c$ values exceeding 5 K, such as W$_2$N$_3$, NbO$_2$, ZrBrO, TiClO, NaSn$_2$S$_4$, Mg$_2$B$_4$C$_2$, and the newly reported Mg$_2$B$_4$N$_2$ ($T_c$ = 21.8 K). Furthermore, we conducted experiments to measure the $T_c$ of selected layered superconductors (2H-NbSe$_2$, 2H-NbS$_2$, ZrSiS, FeSe) and analyzed the findings in relation to our DFT predictions. We anticipate that this workflow's results will serve as a roadmap to guide future computational and experimental investigations into new and emerging 2D superconductors by leveraging high-throughput DFT data.

Differentially private federated learning (DP-FL) has gained significant traction as a method to address privacy concerns in federated learning environments. Despite various proposed schemes, a utility gap persists. Central Differential Privacy in FL (CDP-FL) offers a strong privacy-utility balance but relies on a trusted server, whereas Local Differential Privacy for FL (LDP-FL) operates without one but suffers from poor privacy-utility trade-offs. While recently introduced shuffle DP-based FL aims to bridge the divide between CDP-FL and LDP-FL without requiring a trusted server, it still exhibits a utility gap when handling models with numerous parameters. This paper introduces OLIVE, a system that merges the advantages of CDP-FL and LDP-FL through the use of a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE). Our primary technical contributions involve analyzing and developing countermeasures against TEE vulnerabilities within OLIVE. First, we theoretically examine memory access pattern leakage in OLIVE, identifying risks associated with sparsified gradients common in federated learning. Second, we design an inference attack to demonstrate how memory access patterns can be correlated with training data. Third, we develop oblivious yet efficient algorithms to mitigate memory access pattern leakage in OLIVE. Experiments on real-world datasets confirm that OLIVE remains efficient even when training models with hundreds of thousands of parameters and is effective against side-channel attacks targeting TEE.

We introduce previously unseen high-fidelity radio images of the M87 jet, derived from broadband, full-polarization data collected by the Jansky Very Large Array (VLA) across 4 to 18 GHz. Utilizing the most extended A-configuration, these observations enable the study of jet emission up to kiloparsec scales with a linear resolution of approximately 10 pc, sufficient to resolve the jet's width. We confirm a double-helix morphology in the jet material spanning roughly 300 pc to 1 kpc. Our analysis reveals a polarization degree gradient, with minima along the projected axis and maxima at the jet edges, alongside a Faraday depth gradient exhibiting opposite signs at the edges. Furthermore, the frequency-dependent behavior of these polarization properties aligns with internal Faraday depolarization. Collectively, these features strongly indicate the presence of a helical magnetic field in the M87 jet extending up to 1 kpc from the central black hole, despite the jet likely being particle-dominated at these large scales. Consequently, we propose a scenario where Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities are responsible for maintaining this helical magnetic field configuration over such extensive distances.

Machine Learning relies heavily on extensive labeled datasets to train models. Although numerous public datasets exist, this availability often restricts machine learning applications to specific domains, creating a data scarcity challenge as these algorithms expand into new fields. To address this, this thesis explores active learning as a strategy to minimize manual data processing by selecting only the most informative data points for training robust models. A novel framework, which formulates active learning as a reinforcement learning problem, is adapted for image classification and tested through three sequential experiments. Each experiment is analyzed to identify potential issues, with subsequent iterations proposing and evaluating improvements to the framework. Ultimately, the study concludes that the hypothesis is invalid; the current reinforcement learning-based framework fails to enhance active learning for image classification.

We demonstrate enhanced fine-grained hardness for two fundamental lattice problems under the $\ell_p$ norm: Bounded Distance Decoding to within an $\alpha$ factor of the minimum distance ($\mathrm{BDD}_{p, \alpha}$) and the (decisional) $\gamma$-approximate Shortest Vector Problem ($\mathrm{SVP}_{p,\gamma}$), contingent upon variants of the Gap (Strong) Exponential Time Hypothesis (Gap-(S)ETH). Specifically, our findings are:
1. For every $p \in [1, \infty)$, solving $\mathrm{BDD}_{p, \alpha}$ for any constant $\alpha > \alpha_\mathsf{kn}$ requires more than $2^{o(n)}$ time, where $\alpha_\mathsf{kn} = 2^{-c_\mathsf{kn}} < 0.98491$ and $c_\mathsf{kn}$ denotes the $\ell_2$ kissing-number constant, unless non-uniform Gap-ETH fails.
2. For every $p \in [1, \infty)$, any constant $\alpha > \alpha^\ddagger_p$ precludes a $2^{o(n)}$-time solution for $\mathrm{BDD}_{p, \alpha}$. Here, $\alpha^\ddagger_p$ is an explicit value such that $\alpha^\ddagger_p = 1$ when $1 \leq p \leq 2$, $\alpha^\ddagger_p < 1$ for $p > 2$, and $\alpha^\ddagger_p$ approaches $1/2$ as $p \to \infty$, assuming randomized Gap-ETH holds.
3. For all non-even integers $p \in [1, \infty)$ and any $C > 1$, $\mathrm{BDD}_{p, \alpha}$ cannot be solved in $2^{n/C}$ time for any constant $\alpha > \alpha^\dagger_{p, C}$. The explicit constant $\alpha^\dagger_{p, C}$ converges to 1 as $C \to \infty$ for any fixed $p$, provided non-uniform Gap-SETH is true.
4. For all $p > p_0 \approx 2.1397$ where $p$ is not an even integer, and for any $C > C_p$, there exists a constant $\gamma > 1$ such that $\mathrm{SVP}_{p, \gamma}$ lacks a $2^{n/C}$-time algorithm. The explicit constant $C_p > 1$ satisfies $C_p \to 1$ as $p \to \infty$, unless randomized Gap-SETH is false.

This paper establishes key properties and formulates criteria for the existence of subquasigroups within finite quasigroups. Leveraging these findings, we introduce an efficient algorithm that either proves the nonexistence of a subquasigroup in a finite quasigroup or identifies all its proper subquasigroups, a capability crucial for evaluating cryptographic fitness. Additionally, we present a binary operation grounded in finite field arithmetic to generate quasigroups of order $p^r$. We derive conditions ensuring these structures possess favorable cryptographic traits, specifically polynomial completeness and the absence of proper subquasigroups, followed by a practical construction method. The proposed approaches are demonstrated through academic examples, and all algorithms have been implemented using the computer algebra system {\sc{Singular}}.

The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN operates as a 7 TeV proton synchrotron with a design stored energy of 362 MJ per beam, a figure projected to rise to 675 MJ per beam following the high-luminosity (HL-LHC) upgrade. To safeguard superconducting magnets and other delicate components from damage caused by quenches and beam losses, a multi-level collimation system is essential. Detailed simulations are necessary to determine where particles scattered by collimators are lost throughout the ring across various machine configurations. Merlin++ is an extended simulation framework incorporating detailed scattering physics to forecast local particle loss rates around the LHC. This study compares Merlin++ simulations of losses occurring during the squeeze—the dynamic reduction of the $\beta$-function at interaction points prior to collision—with loss maps recorded from Run 1 and 2 beam squeezes. The squeeze phase is critical due to simultaneous adjustments in collimator positions and quadrupole magnet currents. By utilizing Merlin++, we can predict expected losses for the HL-LHC to guarantee sufficient machine protection.

This paper addresses safe longitudinal control for a connected automated truck following another connected vehicle. A controller is developed using control barrier function theory and predictor feedback to ensure provably safe, collision-free operation, specifically accounting for the truck's significant response time as input delay and its dynamical model uncertainties as input disturbances. Numerical simulations demonstrate the advantages of this proposed controller over existing designs that either ignore the delay or treat it merely as a disturbance.

This study presents a speech recognition system utilizing electroencephalography (EEG) signals captured via dry electrodes, trained on a restricted English vocabulary of three vowels and one word using a deep learning approach. The model achieved a test accuracy of 79.07% on a subset containing two English vowels. These findings confirm the viability of employing dry electrode-recorded EEG signals for speech recognition tasks.

The one-inclusion graph algorithm developed by Haussler, Littlestone, and Warmuth achieves an optimal in-expectation risk bound within the standard PAC classification framework. In an early open problem at COLT, Warmuth conjectured that this prediction strategy invariably guarantees an optimal high-probability risk bound, thereby qualifying as an optimal PAC algorithm. We refute this conjecture in its strongest form: for any practically significant Vapnik-Chervonenkis class, we demonstrate an in-expectation optimal one-inclusion graph algorithm whose high-probability risk bound is limited to what Markov's inequality permits. Our construction of these suboptimal one-inclusion graph algorithms relies on Varshamov-Tenengolts error-correcting codes. This negative result carries several implications. First, it reveals that the same deficient high-probability performance is inherited by several recent prediction strategies that generalize the one-inclusion graph algorithm. Second, our analysis highlights another statistical problem where an estimator is provably optimal in expectation through a leave-one-out argument but fails in the high-probability regime. This discrepancy persists despite the boundedness of the binary loss, a condition under which concentration inequalities typically yield sharp high-probability risk bounds.

This study examines a specific class of non-doubling manifolds $\mathcal{M}$, defined as the connected sum of finitely many $N$-dimensional manifolds of the type $\mathbb{R}^{n_{i}} \times \mathcal{M}_{i}$. Building upon the work of Hassell and the second author \cite{hs2019}, we employ a particular decomposition of the resolvent operators $(\Delta + k^{2})^{-M}$ (where $M \in \mathbb{N}^{*}$) to establish that the vertical square function operator
$$ Sf(x) := \left( \int^{\infty}_{0} \left|t \nabla (I + t^{2} \Delta)^{-M}f(x)\right|{2} \frac{dt}{t}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}} $$
is bounded on $L^{p}(\mathcal{M})$ for $1 < p < n_{min} = \min_{i} n_{i}$ and of weak-type $(1,1)$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the reverse inequality $\left\Vert f \right\Vert_{p} \lesssim \left\Vert S f\right\Vert_{p}$ is valid for $p \in (n_{min}',n_{min})$, and that $S$ becomes unbounded for $p \geq n_{min}$ under the condition $2 M < n_{min}$. Similarly, for $M > 1$, this proof technique confirms that the horizontal square function operator
$$ sf(x) := \left(\int^{\infty}_{0} \left|t^{2}\Delta (I + t^{2} \Delta)^{-M}f(x)\right|^{2} \, \frac{dt}{t}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}} $$
is bounded on $L^{p}(\mathcal{M})$ for all $1 < p < \infty$ and of weak-type $(1,1)$. Consequently, for $p \geq n_{min}$, the vertical and horizontal square function operators are not equivalent, and their associated Hardy spaces $H^p$ do not coincide.

Deformable medical image registration is crucial for clinical diagnosis and treatment. While recent deep learning (DL) approaches have been extensively studied and demonstrate superior computational speed, they often lack sufficient registration accuracy due to an inability to effectively capture both global and local features in the moving and fixed images. To overcome this limitation, this paper introduces a transformer-based image registration framework. Leveraging the unique capabilities of the transformer architecture, this method extracts both global and local features to generate deformation fields, subsequently producing the registered image in an unsupervised manner. By employing a self-attention mechanism and bi-level information flow, our approach significantly enhances registration accuracy. Experiments conducted on brain MR datasets, specifically LPBA40 and OASIS-1, show that compared to various traditional and DL-based methods, our technique achieves superior performance in terms of Dice values.

Recent angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy experiments indicate that incorporating a significant strong nearest-neighbor attraction into the Hubbard model improves the accuracy of describing doped cuprates. A defining characteristic of these materials is the stripe-ordered pattern, which arises from the inhomogeneous distribution of spin, charge, and pairing correlations within the CuO$_{2}$ planes. This study investigates the combined effects of nearest-neighbor attraction and stripe phases using the constrained path quantum Monte Carlo method applied to a repulsive Hubbard model on a two-dimensional square lattice. Calculations were performed to determine ground-state spin correlations along and across stripe regions, as well as $d$-wave pairing correlations. The results show that spin-spin correlation peaks when the interstripe region is near half-filling, and that the presence of stripe patterns alongside strong nearest-neighbor attraction enhances $d$-wave superconducting correlations on neighboring sites, underscoring their critical importance for superconductivity in doped cuprates.

This study performs the inaugural analysis of adversarial robustness in self-supervised Vision Transformers trained with DINO. Initially, we assess whether features derived from self-supervision offer greater resilience to adversarial attacks compared to those from supervised learning. Next, we examine the characteristics of attacks occurring within the latent space. Finally, we investigate whether three established defense mechanisms—Adversarial Training, Ensemble Adversarial Training, and Ensemble of Specialized Networks—can enhance robustness in downstream tasks through fine-tuning only the classification head, thereby achieving protection even under constrained computational resources.

This work primarily examines superquadratic minimization issues concerning splitting-type variational integrals defined on a bounded Lipschitz domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$. We establish higher integrability of the gradient near the boundary by utilizing a suitable weight function that accounts for the solution's distance from the boundary data. Consequently, we quantify the local Hölder coefficient relative to an enhanced Hölder continuity using the function ${\rm dist}(\cdot,\partial \Omega)$. Furthermore, these findings are generalized to anisotropic problems lacking a splitting structure, provided natural growth and ellipticity conditions are met. In both scenarios, our arguments rely on variations of Caccioppoli's inequality that incorporate small weights.

The past ten years have witnessed significant advancements in stellar physics and asteroseismology, driven by new space missions. Thanks to the high precision and richness of modern oscillation spectra, advanced seismic methods now enable us to identify the boundaries of current stellar structure and evolution models. Nevertheless, the reliability of these seismic diagnostics is contingent upon the accuracy of pulsation models. In solar-like oscillations, the primary source of error stems from the near-surface layers, where oscillations are non-adiabatic and heavily influenced by turbulent convection. Additionally, rapid rotation in some pulsating stars must be accurately incorporated into their modeling, while magnetic fields or dynamic tides may also play a role in others. This overview highlights both the remarkable achievements and existing limitations of asteroseismology.

This study establishes a hypercontractive inequality for matrix-valued functions on large alphabets, extending a finding by Ben-Aroya, Regev, and de Wolf (FOCS'08) originally limited to the Boolean alphabet. Our approach builds upon the generalized $2$-uniform convexity inequality for trace norms introduced by Ball, Carlen, and Lieb (Inventiones Mathematicae'94). We demonstrate two primary applications of this inequality.

First, regarding Locally Decodable Codes (LDCs), we derive a lower bound for LDCs over large alphabets. An LDC $C:\mathbb{Z}_r^n\to \mathbb{Z}_r^N$ encodes an input $x\in\mathbb{Z}_r^n$ into a codeword $C(x)$, allowing the recovery of any coordinate $x_i$ with probability at least $1/r+\varepsilon$ through a small number of queries to a corrupted codeword. The central issue involves the trade-off between the block length $N$ and the message length $n$. Leveraging hypercontractivity, we show that for $2$-query (potentially non-linear) LDCs over $\mathbb{Z}_r$, the block length satisfies $N=2^{\Omega(\varepsilon^4 n/r^4)}$. Prior to this, exponential lower bounds existed only for the case $r=2$ (Kerenidis and de Wolf, JCSS'04) and for linear codes (Dvir and Shpilka, SICOMP'07).

Second, in the domain of streaming algorithms, we provide both upper and lower bounds for the communication complexity of the Hidden Hypermatching problem on large alphabets, which extends the well-known Boolean Hidden Matching problem. Furthermore, we examine streaming algorithms for approximating the value of Unique Games on a $t$-hyperedge hypergraph. A straightforward edge-counting method yields an $r$-approximation using $O(\log{n})$ space. Conversely, utilizing our communication lower bound, we prove that any streaming algorithm in the adversarial model achieving a $(r-\varepsilon)$-approximation necessitates $\Omega(n^{1-1/t})$ classical space or $\Omega(n^{1-2/t})$ quantum space. These findings simplify and generalize the landmark contributions of Kapralov, Khanna, and Sudan (SODA'15) and Kapravol and Krachun (STOC'19) specifically when $r=2$.

We investigate bond and site percolation models across various three-dimensional lattices, specifically the diamond, body-centered cubic, and face-centered cubic structures. Consistent with findings on the simple-cubic lattice [Phys. Rev. E, \textbf{87} 052107 (2013)], we find that specific wrapping probabilities demonstrate less sensitivity to finite-size effects compared to dimensionless ratios derived from cluster-size distributions. Furthermore, these wrapping probabilities show greater responsiveness to deviations from the percolation threshold $p_c$, making them highly effective tools for its determination. By analyzing the numerical data for these wrapping probabilities concurrently and assuming shared universal parameters across the studied models, we achieve significantly refined estimates for $p_c$.

We demonstrate through both analytical and numerical methods that circularly polarized helical (Laguerre-Gaussian) laser pulses, utilizing plasma mirror injection, can accelerate highly collimated, dense electron bunches to energies exceeding several hundred MeV with existing laser technology. These beams possess a distinctive field configuration where transverse components form helical wavefronts that vanish on-axis, resulting in significant longitudinal electric and magnetic fields at the focus. Analysis indicates that the radial mode number critically influences electron acceleration near the axis. Three-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations reveal that a 0.6 PW circularly polarized helical beam generates multiple dense attosecond bunches. Specifically, the bunch located near the laser envelope's peak achieves an energy of 0.47 GeV, a charge of 26 pC, a duration of approximately 400 as, and an exceptionally low divergence of 20 mrad, with an energy spread as narrow as 10%. The confinement provided by longitudinal magnetic fields in the near-axis region enables electrons to be accelerated by longitudinal electric fields over an extended duration following initial reflection. Both the longitudinal electric and magnetic fields are proven to be indispensable for this acceleration mechanism. These findings suggest new pathways for generating attosecond electron beams or radiation at numerous global laser facilities.

There exists an absolute constant $C$ such that for any subset $A$ of the finite field $\mathbb{F}_p$ (where $p$ is prime), if the size of $A$ satisfies $|A| > C p^{5/8}$, then the product set $(A \pm A)(A \pm A)$ contains at least $p/2$ distinct elements.

The primary objective of this note is to measure the rate at which a conditioned process approaches its Q-process, contingent upon specific assumptions regarding the process's quasi-stationary distribution. In contrast, we demonstrate that if a conditioned process converges uniformly to an ergodic, conservative Markov process, it possesses a unique quasi-stationary distribution and exhibits uniform exponential convergence toward it, regardless of the initial distribution. As a practical application, we establish a conditional ergodic theorem.

Currently, the growing interaction between humans and robots necessitates real-time human motion recognition systems. However, most existing temporal action detection and recognition methods operate offline by classifying segmented videos as complete units. This paper investigates the effective use of temporal context and human movement dynamics for online action detection, leveraging the recently proposed Temporal Recurrent Networks framework. Our method integrates various state-of-the-art architectures and strategically combines extracted features to enhance detection performance. We assess our approach on the widely used THUMOS'14 dataset for temporal action localization. Experimental results demonstrate significant improvements over baseline methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance on THUMOS'14.

This dissertation investigates the interaction of high-intensity lasers with plasmas to generate radiation and accelerate electrons through both computational simulations and experimental work. The study utilizes ultrashort laser pulses (lasting less than 100 fs) spanning near-infrared to mid-infrared wavelengths (0.8 $\mu$m, 2 $\mu$m, or 3.9 $\mu$m), with energies in the millijoule range and high repetition rates of either 480 Hz or 20 Hz. Experiments employ solid-density (overdense) and gaseous (underdense) plasma sources. Leveraging the system's high-repetition-rate capability, statistical methods are applied to refine specific experimental parameters and elucidate underlying physical phenomena.

Managing broadband electromagnetic energy at the nanoscale remains a pivotal hurdle in optoelectronics. While surface plasmon polaritons (plasmons) enable subwavelength light confinement, they suffer from substantial losses. Conversely, dielectric materials fail to provide a robust response in the visible spectrum required to trap photons like metallic counterparts. Overcoming these constraints appears difficult, seemingly requiring a way to bypass causality within quantum-mechanical matter. However, we show that this challenge can be met using a novel strategy involving suitably deformed reflective metaphotonic structures. The engineered complex geometries of these reflectors mimic nondispersive index responses, allowing for inverse design according to arbitrary form factors. We present the fabrication of key components, including resonators featuring an ultra-high refractive index of $n=100$ across various profiles. These structures facilitate light localization via bound states in the continuum (BIC), which are fully confined in air within a platform where all refractive index regions are physically accessible. We explore sensing applications by designing sensors where the analyte directly interfaces with ultra-high index areas. Exploiting this capability, we achieve differential sensitivities reaching $350$~nm/RIU in structures with footprints of about one micron, outperforming the nearest competitor with a similar form factor by a factor of two. Inversely designed reflective metaphotonics thus presents a flexible technology for broadband light control, enabling optoelectronic integration with large bandwidths in miniaturized circuitry.

The highly contagious COVID-19 pandemic poses a severe risk to human health and survival. To automate the tracking of individuals in close proximity to infected persons and to analyze associated data, researchers have developed various ad-hoc programs designed to run on users' smartphones. However, current solutions suffer from two main drawbacks: (1) a lack of generality, where specific data types must be transmitted to an analyst for each distinct analytical task; and (2) a lack of transparency, meaning that data providers are not necessarily infected individuals, allowing infected users' information to be shared with analysts without their fine-grained, direct consent. This paper introduces Glass-Vault, a protocol that resolves both issues at once. It enables analysts to execute authorized programs on data collected from infected users without accessing the underlying input data. Glass-Vault is built upon a novel variant of generic Functional Encryption, termed DD-Steel, which introduces two key properties: dynamic and decentralized capabilities. We demonstrate the security of both Glass-Vault and DD-Steel within the Universal Composability framework. Glass-Vault represents the first UC-secure protocol facilitating the privacy-preserving analysis of Exposure Notification user data. As a practical demonstration, we show how it can be applied to generate "infection heatmaps."

We construct non-flat cosmological models for dust and radiation scenarios within Møller's tetradic theory (MTT) of gravitation by employing a tetrad that yields the non-flat Friedmann-Robertson-Walker (FRW) metric. These models depend on the free dimensional parameter $\lambda$ inherent to MTT, which vanishes in the limit of flat spacetime. By applying standard thermodynamic definitions, we determine the horizon radius, Hawking temperature, and entropy for these non-flat systems, illustrating the impact of $\lambda$ on both open and closed universes. Subsequently, we utilize the first law of thermodynamics to build non-flat cosmological models through a non-extensive thermodynamic framework. These resulting models are influenced by $\lambda$ and the extensive parameter $\delta$, which measures non-extensive effects. Setting $\lambda=0$ and $\delta=1$ recovers the models of Einstein's general relativity. We analyze the evolution of these models under collisionless non-relativistic matter, deriving specific forms for dark energy density and the equation-of-state parameter that constrain the non-extensive parameter. Our findings demonstrate that incorporating the non-extensive parameter alters the dynamics of the non-flat FRW universe significantly compared to standard thermodynamics. Furthermore, we show that in the future epoch, as redshift approaches $z \approx -1$, the deceleration of an open universe mimics the behavior of dark energy.

Null hypothesis statistical significance testing (NHST) remains the primary method for analyzing randomized controlled trials. Although NHST offers guarantees regarding long-run error rates, its central tool—the $p$-value—serves only as an indirect indicator of evidence against the null hypothesis. This limitation exists because the $p$-value is calculated under the assumption that the null hypothesis is true, while disregarding the likelihood of the data under any alternative hypothesis. Consequently, to quantify the strength of evidence for or against the null, specifying an alternative hypothesis is necessary (Goodman & Royall, 1988). Paradoxes emerge when researchers misinterpret $p$-values as direct evidence; for example, data that seem surprising under the null may be equally surprising under a plausible alternative, meaning a result of $p=.045$ (leading to rejection of the null) does not necessarily reduce the null's plausibility. Thus, $p$-values are often criticized for overstating evidence against the null. Conversely, statistically non-significant results ($p>.05$) can still offer support for the alternative hypothesis. Therefore, it is essential for researchers to understand when statistical significance and evidentiary strength diverge, which necessitates computing and reporting a direct measure of evidence alongside the traditional $p$-value.

Although deepfake and spoofing detection research for automatic speaker verification has advanced over recent years, the specific artifacts classifiers rely on to differentiate genuine from spoofed speech remain largely unknown, yet understanding them is vital for creating trustworthy and explainable systems. This paper extends our prior research by employing SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to analyze classifier behavior. Our objective is to pinpoint the artifacts that define utterances produced by various attack algorithms. By utilizing two classifiers—one processing raw waveforms and the other magnitude spectrograms—we demonstrate that SHAP visualizations effectively reveal attack-specific artifacts, as well as the distinctions and consistencies between synthetic speech and voice conversion spoofing attacks.

We recently identified a novel supergravity D-term, independent of gauged R-symmetry, and leveraged it to build fresh supergravity models. This paper extends that concept, applied in earlier studies, to develop a slow-roll inflation supergravity model incorporating the observable sector of the minimal supersymmetric standard model. In this framework, supersymmetry breaks at a high energy scale within the hidden sector and transfers to the observable sector via gravity mediation. The newly introduced D-term includes adjustable parameters capable of generating substantial masses for scalar superpartners of quarks and leptons and for higgsinos, while keeping the masses of observed particles unchanged. Meanwhile, gauginos acquire mass through a non-canonical kinetic term for the vector supermultiplets. Furthermore, we provide a straightforward, fully general argument demonstrating that the cutoff $\Lambda$ of effective theories featuring new D-terms can never surpass the supersymmetry breaking scale. Specifically, within our theory, the connection between the D-term and the Hubble constant during inflation necessitates the universal constraint $\Lambda \lesssim \sqrt{H M_{Pl}}$.

The third iteration of the International Celestial Reference Frame (ICRF3) comprises 4536 quasars observed via Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) at S/X bands. These high-redshift quasars, typically with $1<z<2$, are thought to harbor active galactic nuclei (AGN) at their cores, with compact radio sources allowing for more precise positional determination than those with significant extended structure. This study presents data from a series of 20 observations conducted between January and December 2017, aimed at achieving high-precision astrometry and monitoring the structural characteristics of ICRF3 sources. During this one-year campaign, 3627 sources were targeted; among the 2697 detected at S-band, the median flux density was 0.13 Jy, while 3209 detections at X-band yielded a median flux density of 0.09 Jy. Results indicate that 70% of the detected sources are compact at X-band, making them ideal for ICRF applications, and 89% of the 2615 sources detected at both frequencies exhibit a flat spectral index ($\alpha>0.5$).

This research investigates the optical binding of a dimer consisting of dielectric particles situated near a graphene sheet. Employing a rigorous electromagnetic approach, we computed the optical force exerted on each nanoparticle. Furthermore, we derived analytical formulas to assess the impact of graphene surface plasmons (GSPs) on optical binding. Our findings indicate that graphene plasmon excitations create multiple equilibrium positions where inter-particle distances are tens of times smaller than the photon wavelength. Additionally, these positions can be dynamically tuned by modifying the graphene's chemical potential, with analyses covering both normal and oblique incidence scenarios.

This study details the development and evaluation of a fabric-constructed soft pneumatic actuator designed for low-pressure operation, specifically targeting infant upper limb assistive applications. The primary objective is to facilitate shoulder abduction and adduction while maintaining freedom of movement in other directions and avoiding interference with elbow articulation. Initially, simulations were conducted to assess a range of actuator configurations featuring internal air cells, with variations defined by cell count and width. Following simulation, physically feasible designs underwent hardware validation. Two specific prototypes were evaluated on a custom-built model calibrated to infant anthropometric data. The selection of the optimal design for pediatric wearable assistive devices was determined by analyzing metrics such as lifting force, motion smoothness, trajectory length, and maximum shoulder flexion, alongside additional insights for future research.

We present a nearly-linear time algorithm for solving the linear system $L_1x = b$, parameterized by the first Betti number, where $L_1$ represents the 1-Laplacian of a simplicial complex $K$ that is a subcomplex of a collapsible complex $X$ linearly embedded in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$. This approach extends the work of Black et al. [SODA2022], which addressed the same problem but was restricted to complexes with trivial first homology. Our method accommodates complexes $K$ with arbitrary first homology, achieving nearly-linear runtime relative to the complex size and polynomial runtime with respect to the first Betti number. The core of our solver relies on a novel algorithm for computing the Hodge decomposition of 1-chains in nearly-linear time. Furthermore, our technique yields nearly quadratic solvers and Hodge decompositions for the 1-Laplacian of any simplicial complex $K$ embedded in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$, since any such $K$ can be expanded into a collapsible embedded complex with quadratic complexity.

This paper investigates the abstraction of finite-state transition systems within the context of control synthesis. We re-examine alternating simulation equivalence (ASE), a relaxation of alternating bisimulations, to establish relationships between systems and their abstractions. Similar to alternating bisimulations, ASE ensures that a controller exists for the original system if and only if one exists for the abstraction. Furthermore, as a less restrictive condition, ASE enables more aggressive system reduction, yielding smaller abstractions. We present an algorithm capable of generating minimal abstractions that are ASE-equivalent. These theoretical findings are subsequently applied to derive (un)schedulability certificates for periodic event-triggered control systems utilizing a shared communication channel, with a numerical example demonstrating the proposed approach.

The kinetics of dilute heterogeneous traffic on a two-lane road are modeled using the Ben-Naim Krapivsky framework, with stationary state properties derived analytically in the asymptotic limit. Heterogeneity is modeled as quenched disorder in vehicles' desired speeds. The model posits that each vehicle or platoon moves ballistically until encountering a slower entity, at which point it merges; conversely, vehicles leave their platoons at a constant rate by changing lanes, with each lane having a distinct escape rate. As the system reaches a stationary state, platoon densities equalize across both lanes, while vehicle densities and fluxes are higher in the lane with the lower escape rate. Most vehicles experience free-flow when the harmonic mean of the lane escape rates matches the road's average initial flux, and the average platoon size remains near unity in this regime. If the harmonic mean falls below the average initial flux, a threshold speed $v^*$ emerges: vehicles with desired speeds below $v^*$ maintain free-flow, whereas those exceeding it encounter congestion and form platoons behind slower vehicles. This characteristic speed relates to the mean escape time $R = (R_1 + R_{-1})/2$ (for lanes labeled 1 and -1) via $v^* \sim R^{-\frac{1}{\mu+2}}$, where $\mu$ is the exponent of the quenched disorder distribution for low desired speeds. When $v^* \ll 1$, the average platoon size in a lane scales proportionally to $R^{\frac{\mu+1}{\mu+2}}$ with an additional lane-specific correction. Furthermore, the kinetics of the platoon size distribution for two-lane traffic are analyzed, revealing that a stationary state featuring platoons as long as the road itself can only exist if the mean escape rate remains independent of platoon size.

An analytic framework for the electron-phonon spectral function is developed within the adiabatic limit. When the chemical potential is large and negative ($\mu \to -\infty$), the ground state lacks adiabatic deformation, and the spectral function follows standard perturbation theory; in this regime, we provide a fourth-order calculation in the electron-phonon coupling constant that satisfies sum rules up to the fifth moment. Conversely, when the chemical potential is fixed at the polaron binding energy, the ground state exhibits nonzero adiabatic deformation. We compute the spectral function for finite polaron density under these adiabatic conditions and illustrate the evaluation of higher-moment sum rules in this limit. Unlike the zero-density case, the spectral function with finite polaron concentration includes contributions distinct to polarons.

This paper investigates the Assouad and quasi-Assouad dimensions of dominated rectangular self-affine sets in two dimensions. Unlike prior research on the dimension theory of such sets, we impose specific separation conditions only on projections to the principal axis, while allowing for arbitrary overlaps within the plane. We define and analyze the regularity of a particular symbolic non-autonomous iterated function system that corresponds to "symbolic slices" of the self-affine set. Subsequently, we derive dimensional formulas for these sets by combining the dimension of the projection with the maximal dimension of slices orthogonal to it. Our findings are novel even under the strong separation condition; notably, as an application, we demonstrate that self-affine sets satisfying this condition can possess distinct Assouad and quasi-Assouad dimensions, thereby resolving a question posed by the first author.

Scanned Receipt OCR and Key Information Extraction (SROIE) involve recognizing text from scanned receipts, extracting essential details, and storing them in structured formats. While SROIE is vital for numerous document analysis applications and offers significant commercial potential, the field has seen limited research and advancement. Acknowledging these technical challenges, importance, and market opportunities, we organized the ICDAR 2019 competition on SROIE. This competition featured three specific tasks: Scanned Receipt Text Localisation (Task 1), Scanned Receipt OCR (Task 2), and Key Information Extraction from Scanned Receipts (Task 3). To support these tasks, a new dataset comprising 1,000 annotated whole scanned receipt images was created. This report details the competition's motivation, dataset, task definitions, evaluation protocol, submission statistics, method performance, and result analysis.

The Earth Mover's Distance quantifies the cost of converting one distribution, $P$, into another, $S$, both sharing equal total mass, where the expense is defined by the distance traveled per unit of mass. This work presents approximation algorithms for calculating this distance between various collections of geometric shapes. Specifically, we achieve a $(1 + \varepsilon)$-approximation when $P$ consists of weighted points and $S$ comprises line segments, triangles, or $d$-dimensional simplices. In cases where both $P$ and $S$ are composed of the same types of objects—such as line segments, triangles, or simplices—we provide a $(1 + \varepsilon)$-approximation augmented by a small additive term. All proposed algorithms operate in polynomial time relative to the sizes of $P$ and $S$ and explicitly compute the transport plan, detailing exactly how mass is moved, rather than merely estimating the cost. To the best of our knowledge, these represent the inaugural combinatorial algorithms offering provable approximation ratios for Earth Mover's Distance involving continuous objects instead of discrete points.

Understanding the behavior of nuclear symmetry energy near saturation density is crucial for comprehending dense nuclear matter. This density dependence is typically characterized by the symmetry energy and its derivatives at nuclear saturation density. This study demonstrates that the core-crust interface mode of a neutron star is sensitive to these parameters, mediated by the (density-weighted) shear speed within the crust, which relies on the symmetry energy profile of dense matter. We compute the frequency required for the neutron star's quadrupole ($\ell = 2$) crust-core interface mode to be excited by the tidal field of a binary companion in order to induce a Resonant Shattering Flare (RSF). Furthermore, we show that coincident multimessenger observations of an RSF and the gravitational wave chirp from a neutron star merger would allow for constraints on symmetry energy parameters that rival those obtained from existing nuclear experiments.

In the modern era, innovation stands as a primary driver of economic growth, with patents serving as a critical metric for gauging the inventive output of nations, firms, and technologies. This study examines the causal consequences of European Union (EU) enlargement by analyzing patent performance in the 13 new member states (EU-13). Utilizing data from the OECD database spanning 1985 to 2017 and employing a Bayesian structural time-series model developed by Google, the findings indicate that EU accession significantly influenced patent performance in Romania, Estonia, Poland, the Czech Republic, Croatia, and Lithuania; however, this impact was negative in Croatia and Lithuania. Conversely, no statistically significant effect was observed for the remaining EU-13 nations. Regardless of these specific accession effects, the EU-13 group lags substantially behind the EU-15 (countries that joined prior to 2004) regarding patent performance. Specifically, 98.66% of patents were assigned to the EU-15, while the EU-13 accounted for only 1.34% of assignees.

This study examines the physics capabilities of long-baseline experiments T2HK, T2HKK, and ESS$
u$SB within the framework of invisible neutrino decay. Assuming normal mass ordering and that the $
u_{3}$ state is unstable, decaying into sterile states during propagation, we derive constraints on the neutrino decay lifetime ($	au_3$). Our results indicate that T2HK, T2HKK, and ESS$
u$SB can probe the decay rate of $
u_{3}$ for $	au_{3}/m_{3} \leq 2.72	imes10^{-11}$s/eV, $	au_{3}/m_{3} \leq 4.36	imes10^{-11}$s/eV, and $	au_{3}/m_{3} \leq 2.43	imes10^{-11}$s/eV, respectively, at a 3$\sigma$ confidence level. We analyze and compare the sensitivities of these three experiments, with a specific focus on the influence of the mixing angle $	heta_{23}$. We observe that experiments peaking near the second oscillation maximum exhibit weaker constraints on the decay lifetime due to reduced sensitivity to $	heta_{23}$. However, T2HKK achieves superior decay sensitivity despite one detector being near the second maximum, because its second detector is positioned at the first oscillation maximum. Furthermore, we identify a synergy between T2HKK's two baselines that enhances sensitivity to $	heta_{23}$ in the higher octant. Investigating octant sensitivity in the presence of decay, we note an improvement driven by the survival probability $P_{\mu\mu}$, which is particularly significant for experiments operating at the second oscillation maximum. Finally, we present the combined sensitivity for T2HK+ESS$
u$SB and T2HKK+ESS$
u$SB as $	au_{3}/m_{3} \leq 4.36	imes10^{-11}$s/eV and $	au_{3}/m_{3} \leq 5.53	imes10^{-11}$s/eV, respectively, at 3$\sigma$ C.L.

The ALICE experiment at the LHC has determined a refined lifetime for the (anti-)hypertriton by analyzing a dataset of Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}} = 5.02$ TeV. By reconstructing the (anti-)hypertriton through its charged two-body mesonic decay, researchers derived the lifetime from an exponential fit applied to the d$N$/d($ct$) distribution. The resulting measurement, $\tau$ = 242$^{+34}_{-38}$ (stat.) $\pm$ 17 (syst.) ps, aligns with existing theoretical predictions, thereby helping to resolve the long-standing puzzle regarding hypertriton lifetime.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) are currently central to artificial intelligence research, yet designing their architecture remains a significant challenge. Traditionally, architectures are manually constructed by exploring hyperparameters and remain static during training, a process that is both time-consuming and inefficient. Furthermore, modern networks often require millions of parameters, making them unsuitable for applications or devices that need compact inference models; migrating DNNs to such constrained environments usually results in a substantial drop in accuracy. To overcome these hurdles, we introduce DR+SCANN, a two-step neural network synthesis methodology that integrates two complementary strategies to create DNNs that are both compact and accurate. The core of this framework is the SCANN methodology, which employs three fundamental architecture-modifying operations—connection growth, neuron growth, and connection pruning—to generate feed-forward networks with arbitrary structures. SCANN applies a repeated grow-and-prune paradigm across three distinct architectural starting points. DR+SCANN further enhances this by combining SCANN with dataset dimensionality reduction to mitigate the curse of dimensionality. We validate the effectiveness of both SCANN and DR+SCANN across various image and non-image datasets, specifically evaluating SCANN on the MNIST and ImageNet benchmarks, as well as DR+SCANN on nine small to medium-sized datasets. Our results demonstrate that this synthesis approach produces neural networks that navigate the trade-off between accuracy and energy efficiency far more effectively, thereby enabling neural network-based inference on Internet-of-Things sensors.

The interaction between two counter-rotating beams can generate coherent dipole modes. When impedance is present, these beam-beam modes may couple with higher-order head-tail modes, resulting in significant instabilities. To investigate this novel coupled mode instability and explore potential solutions like transverse dampers and high chromaticity, a fully self-consistent methodology incorporating both beam-beam effects and impedance was employed.

X-ray spectra from certain active galactic nuclei (AGN) exhibit a soft X-ray excess, defined as emission surpassing the extrapolated primary continuum below 2 keV. Recent research indicates this feature may arise from relativistic ionized reflection—where reprocessed light from the accretion disk's innermost region is severely blurred—or from Comptonization within an optically thick, warm "warm corona," where electron scattering dominates opacity. To determine the source of this soft excess in the Seyfert 1 galaxy Mrk 926, we conducted a multi-epoch spectral analysis using data from Suzaku (2009), XMM-Newton, and NuSTAR (2016), as well as NuSTAR and Swift-XRT (2021). The broadband X-ray spectra of Mrk 926 reveal a thermally Comptonized primary continuum, a variable soft excess, and distant reflection. Similar to many other sources, the data in Mrk 926 do not allow for a definitive conclusion regarding the cause of the soft excess; while a warm coronal-like component is slightly favored, a reflection origin remains a viable possibility. Furthermore, archival radio data identified an optically-thin radio component in our broadband study of Mrk 926. Although this component aligns with an optically-thin radio jet, future multi-wavelength observations, particularly high spatial resolution radio imaging at multiple frequencies, are necessary to further investigate the origin of this radio emission.

As the demand for computational tools among scientists increases, software created in isolation can no longer meet these requirements. Often, this gap is filled by communities of practice, where domain experts develop software to achieve practical objectives and address specific, identifiable scientific needs. This discussion highlights methods that have effectively fostered and sustained such communities, with particular focus on the yt and Enzo projects.

Gradual argumentation frameworks model arguments and their interconnections within a weighted graph. Their intuitive semantics and graphical structure make them a promising tool for interpretable machine learning. Recent observations highlight a strong mechanical resemblance to neural networks, enabling the learning of framework weights from data using standard deep learning techniques. As an initial proof of concept, we introduce a genetic algorithm designed to concurrently learn the structure of argumentative classification models. To ensure high interpretability, the fitness function optimizes a balance between classifier accuracy and sparsity. We detail the proposed algorithm and report preliminary experimental results on standard benchmarks from the UCI machine learning repository. Our prototype successfully generates argumentative classification models that match decision trees in both learning performance and interpretability.

A study based on the tight-binding model examines persistent currents in one-dimensional non-superconducting mesoscopic rings subjected to a slowly varying magnetic flux $\phi$. The analysis explores the behavior of these currents across three specific scenarios: (a) the presence of a single hopping impurity, (b) an in-plane electric field, and (c) the inclusion of foreign atoms.

Branching processes are frequently employed to model population and evolutionary dynamics, as well as the transmission of infectious diseases. A key metric for characterizing these dynamics is the basic reproduction number, $R_0$. In the context of epidemics, $R_0$ is typically defined as the average number of secondary infections generated by a single infectious individual within a fully susceptible population. Generally, an $R_0$ greater than 1 suggests an outbreak will persist and grow exponentially, whereas an $R_0$ less than 1 implies the outbreak will eventually die out.

This study demonstrates that temporal fluctuations in dynamics can sustain outbreaks even when the expected number of secondary cases per individual falls below 1. Such variability is often overlooked in disease modeling approaches that rely on ordinary differential equations, such as the standard SIR model. We present three specific examples: 1) extinction governed by an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, 2) extinction rates that randomly switch between two distinct values, and 3) the interaction of two populations with differing $R_0$ values. Our analytical results are supported by computer simulations.

This paper demonstrates that integrating a 1-cocycle $I(X)$, defined on the space of long knots in $\mathbb{R}^3$, over Fox-Hatcher 1-cycles yields a Vassiliev invariant of precisely order three. This finding extends the earlier work of the second author, which established that integrating $I(X)$ over Gramain 1-cycles produces the Casson invariant—the sole nontrivial Vassiliev invariant of order two, modulo scalar factors. The current result parallels aspects of Mortier's findings; however, it diverges from and is inspired by Mortier's approach because our 1-cocycle $I(X)$ is constructed via configuration space integrals linked to graphs, whereas Mortier's cocycle was derived combinatorially.

This work addresses the Dirichlet Problem for the Monge-Ampère equation in the vicinity of an isolated Klt singularity, extending the findings of Eyssidieux, Guedj, and Zeriahi \cite{EGZ}, who solved the equation on singular varieties lacking boundaries. As a consequence, we establish the existence of solutions to the Monge-Ampère equation featuring isolated singularities within a strongly pseudoconvex domain $\Omega$ in $\mathbb{C}^n$.

Space-based gamma-ray telescopes face intense bombardment from charged particles, photons, and secondary neutrons, which jeopardize satellite functionality and restrict the sensitivity of detection instruments. The background noise produced by these impinging particles consistently overwhelms the astrophysical signals of interest. This chapter outlines various orbital configurations suitable for gamma-ray missions, evaluating their pros and cons, while also assessing the utility of stratospheric balloon experiments. Furthermore, it examines the physical characteristics of all background components across different orbits and within the stratosphere.

This study focuses on estimating user locations within a spatially distributed antenna system (DAS) using uplink channel state information (CSI). However, as the number of remote radio heads (RRHs) grows, aggregating CSI at a central unit (CU) drastically raises fronthaul overhead and computational demands. To address this, we propose a deep learning framework that selects a subset of RRHs for wireless localization. Our approach utilizes an RRH selection layer co-trained with the rest of the network to simultaneously optimize model parameters and identify the optimal RRH subset. We demonstrate that this selection strategy incurs only a minor localization performance penalty. Furthermore, compared to a basic method relying on channel gain maximization, our proposed technique achieves substantial performance improvements in non-line-of-sight dominated propagation environments.

In 2013, Nebe and Villar constructed a family of ternary self-dual codes with length $2(p+1)$, where $p$ is a prime satisfying $p \equiv 5 \pmod{8}$. This construction led to the discovery of the third ternary extremal self-dual code of length $60$. We establish that for primes $p \equiv 5 \pmod{24}$, the codewords of these ternary self-dual codes form a Hadamard matrix of order $2(p+1)$, and furthermore, the codes are generated by the rows of these matrices. Additionally, we prove that the third ternary extremal self-dual code of length $60$ encompasses at least two inequivalent Hadamard matrices.

We outline universal design principles for engineering and identifying periodic systems characterized by flat bands. Our approach leverages spin-orbit assisted orbital frustration within a lattice to generate band structures featuring multiplets of narrowly dispersing bands, where the bandwidth is smaller than all other relevant energy scales, including the gap surrounding the flat bands. We introduce a series of 1D and 2D models across various lattices, incorporating distinct intracellular spin-orbit-like potentials that hybridize unit cell degrees of freedom. Serving as an alternative to machine learning-driven exhaustive searches, these principles and models enable the discovery of flat band systems in diverse physical contexts and facilitate the investigation of weakly dispersing, highly orbitally frustrated degrees of freedom in regimes where interactions dominate kinetic energy.

We establish the divisibility conjecture regarding sums of even powers of $q$-binomial coefficients, a problem recently formulated by Guo, Schlosser, and Zudilin. Our demonstration is grounded in two congruences for $q$-harmonic series derived by Shi and Pan.

The LHCb detector has observed $J/\psi$ mesons produced alongside open charm, as well as pairs of open charm hadrons, in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV, utilizing an integrated luminosity of $355\text{ pb}^{-1}$. The study presents model-independent measurements of absolute cross-sections, along with their ratios relative to the measured $J/\psi$ and open charm cross-sections. Additionally, the characteristics of these events are analyzed and compared against theoretical predictions.

This paper examines numerical approaches for strictly convex unconstrained optimization using linesearch Newton-CG methods. The study concentrates on techniques that utilize inexact objective function evaluations, along with inexact and potentially stochastic gradient and Hessian approximations. These derivative estimates do not need to meet strict accuracy thresholds at every iteration; instead, they must satisfy them with high probability. Regarding objective function evaluation, we initially consider scenarios where noise is bounded in absolute terms, followed by an analysis of cases where errors adhere to specific dynamic accuracy constraints. For both scenarios, we present a complexity analysis and establish expected iteration complexity bounds. Finally, we address the specific context of finite-sum minimization, a common requirement in machine learning applications.

This study examines a class of parabolic economic optimal control problems featuring pointwise state constraints regularized by a parameter, effectively converting pure state constraints into mixed control-state ones. While classical (semismooth) Newton methods suffer from deteriorating convergence as the regularization parameter decreases, this issue is addressed through the introduction of a nonlinear preconditioner. This preconditioner relies on an overlapping optimized waveform-relaxation approach defined by Robin transmission conditions. Numerical results demonstrate that selecting suitable values for the overlap and Robin parameter enables a preconditioned Newton method to achieve robust convergence independent of the state constraints' regularization parameter.

Elegant Objects (EO) is a programming language grounded in the concepts of pure objects and the Decorator pattern, which Bugayenko proposed as an intermediate representation for object-oriented code. This paper describes a dynamic dispatch model within EO and identifies a problem regarding unjustified assumptions in decorator objects, mirroring similar issues found in subclasses. Subsequently, we propose a method to detect these problems in EO programs through technique of method inlining and constrained property inference. Finally, the paper discusses a prototype implementation of this approach using the Scala programming language.

Retrieval-based conversational systems rank response candidates for a specific dialogue context by calculating the similarity of their vector representations. However, relying on a single textual form of the multi-turn context restricts a model's capacity to learn representations that generalize to natural variations encountered during inference. This paper introduces a framework that integrates augmented versions of the dialogue context into the learning objective. We employ contrastive learning as an auxiliary task to derive robust dialogue context representations that remain invariant to perturbations introduced via our augmentation strategy. Experiments across four benchmark dialogue datasets reveal that our framework effectively complements existing augmentation techniques and significantly outperforms baseline BERT-based ranking architectures. Additionally, we propose a novel data augmentation method called ConMix, which introduces token-level perturbations through the stochastic mixing of tokens from other contexts within the batch. Our results demonstrate that this proposed augmentation method surpasses prior approaches and yields dialogue representations that are more resilient to common perturbations observed during inference.

This study investigates push recovery for bipedal robot locomotion, introducing a robust planning and reactive decision-making framework designed to withstand external disturbances. While rejecting perturbations is a well-researched and critical capability for bipedal robots, adversarial forces and aggressive turns can induce negative lateral step widths—resulting in crossed-leg scenarios that pose stability risks and potential self-collisions. These computationally challenging motion planning issues have not previously been addressed using a hierarchically integrated task and motion planning approach. We propose a framework that tightly couples linear temporal logic-based reactive synthesis with trajectory optimization, fully accounting for the robot's dynamics, kinematics, and leg collision avoidance constraints. Behavior trees function as a reactive interface between high-level discrete symbolic decisions and low-level continuous motion planning, managing perturbations at any stage of locomotion. Experimental results demonstrate the method's effectiveness in producing resilient recovery behaviors against diverse perturbations from various directions with bounded magnitudes.

Fixed-event forecasting is a standard approach in economic policy, characterized by a series of predictions for the same target variable, which inherently reduces the forecasting difficulty over time. Typically, these fixed-event point forecasts are released without accompanying quantitative uncertainty metrics. To address this gap, we examine postprocessing techniques specifically designed for fixed-event scenarios. We introduce heteroscedastic and quantile regression methods that incorporate parametric constraints derived from the specific nature of the problem, applying them to generate prediction intervals for GDP growth in both the US and Germany.

A novel noise model, grounded in vortex structures within both 2D (point vortices) and 3D (vortex filaments) contexts, is presented. Defined as the scaling limit of a jump process that navigates these vortex configurations, this noise can be established across any domain, including those with boundaries. The text examines its relationship with classical Kraichnan noise and a solenoidal variant of the Gaussian Free Field. Ultimately, the vortex noise is demonstrated to be effective for analyzing eddy dissipation resulting from small-scale turbulence.

Recently, link prediction within large-scale knowledge graphs has attracted significant interest. The OGB-LSC initiative established the OGB Large-Scale Challenge (OGB-LSC), providing three real-world datasets to push the boundaries of large-scale graph machine learning. This paper details our team's GraphMIRAcles submission for the WikiKG90M-LSC track of the OGB-LSC @ KDD Cup 2021. In this track, the objective is to automatically infer missing links within WikiKG90M, a massive knowledge graph derived from Wikidata. To tackle this problem, we developed a framework combining three elements: a base model (ComplEx-CMRC), a rule miner (AMIE 3), and an inference model for predicting links. Experimental results show our approach attained an MRR of 0.9707 on the test set. However, since the inference model's knowledge distillation relied on test tail candidates that are inaccessible in real-world scenarios, we performed ablation studies. These studies revealed that our model excluding knowledge distillation achieved an MRR of 0.9533 on the complete validation dataset.

A sequence $u_0u_1 \ldots u_{k-1}u_k$ is defined as a \textit{weakly toll walk} if the presence of edges $u_0u_i$ requires $u_i = u_1$, and edges $u_ju_k$ require $u_j = u_{k-1}$. A vertex set $S$ in a graph $G$ is termed \textit{weakly toll convex} if every vertex lying on any weakly toll walk between two non-adjacent vertices $x$ and $y$ within $S$ is also contained in $S$. The concept of \emph{weakly toll convexity} refers to the graph convexity space formed by these sets. Significant research focuses on identifying whether a graph endowed with a specific convexity space constitutes a {\em convex geometry}. An \emph{extreme vertex} is an element $x$ of a convex set $S$ such that removing $x$ leaves the remaining set $S\backslash\{x\}$ convex. A graph convexity space qualifies as a convex geometry if it adheres to the Minkowski-Krein-Milman property, meaning every convex set equals the convex hull of its extreme vertices. It is established that chordal, Ptolemaic, weakly polarizable, and interval graphs can be characterized as convex geometries relative to monophonic, geodesic, $m^3$, and toll convexities, respectively, with other notable graph classes also fitting this framework. This paper demonstrates that a graph is a convex geometry under weakly toll convexity if and only if it is a proper interval graph. Additionally, the study investigates various well-known graph invariants in the context of weakly toll convexity.

This paper reviews recent developments in defining access control mechanisms for collaborative settings, specifically within WebdamLog, an extension of datalog designed for distributed environments. We examine two approaches: a fine-grained access control system for intentional data that relies on provenance, and a mechanism for handling delegation, which involves deploying rules at remote peers.

We introduce a change-point detection method designed for large-scale multiple testing scenarios involving data with clustered signals. In contrast to traditional change-point models, our approach accommodates varying signal magnitudes within clusters. This clustering structure facilitates the precise identification of boundaries between signal and non-signal segments. We propose novel test statistics for observations derived from single or multiple realizations and derive their asymptotic distributions. Additionally, we address the challenge of variance estimation, allowing for heteroscedasticity in the multiple realization context, which significantly broadens the method's applicability. Simulation results indicate that the proposed approach exhibits favorable performance, and the procedure is demonstrated on an array-based Comparative Genomic Hybridization (aCGH) dataset.

Third-generation nanopore sequencers include a "Read Until" feature, also known as selective sequencing, which enables real-time analysis and immediate discarding of genomic reads that do not match regions of interest. This capability facilitates crucial applications like rapid, low-cost genetic testing. For selective sequencing to be effective, analysis latency must be minimized to reject irrelevant reads as early as possible. However, current approaches using the subsequence Dynamic Time Warping (sDTW) algorithm are computationally demanding; even powerful workstations with multiple CPU cores struggle to match the data throughput of a MinION sequencer. This paper introduces Hardware Accelerated Read Until (HARU), a resource-efficient method based on hardware-software co-design that utilizes a portable, low-cost heterogeneous MPSoC platform with an on-chip FPGA to accelerate sDTW-based Read Until. Experimental results indicate that HARU running on a Xilinx FPGA with an embedded 4-core ARM processor is approximately 2.5 times faster than a highly optimized multi-threaded software version (and roughly 85 times faster than an unoptimized multi-threaded version) executed on a high-end 36-core Intel Xeon server using a SARS-CoV-2 dataset. Furthermore, HARU consumes two orders of magnitude less energy than the same application on the 36-core server. The open-source source code for the HARU sDTW module is available at https://github.com/beebdev/HARU, along with an example application at https://github.com/beebdev/sigfish-haru.

Cognitive neuroscience frequently employs extensive feature sets—ranging from human annotations to deep neural network representations—to predict and decode brain activity. Central to this process is the mapping model, which establishes the potential relationships between these features and neural data. While encoding and decoding studies historically relied on linear models, the recent surge in data availability and computational power has enabled the use of more flexible nonlinear alternatives; yet, the scientific utility of these nonlinear models remains a subject of debate. This discussion evaluates the selection of a mapping model based on three core criteria: predictive accuracy, interpretability, and biological plausibility. Contrary to common assumptions, these criteria do not strictly align with a linear versus nonlinear dichotomy; rather, each criterion encompasses multiple research goals that impose distinct constraints on the model.
