Furthermore, we contend that models should not be rigidly categorized as linear or nonlinear, but instead evaluated by estimating their complexity. We demonstrate that complexity often better reflects the specific limitations dictated by various research objectives. Finally, we present several metrics for assessing model complexity to facilitate effective evaluation.

We introduce a property equivalent to that of being semi-Kelley. Leveraging this equivalence, we demonstrate that the semi-Kelley property is hereditary within atriodic continua. Furthermore, we establish that semi-Kelley remainders are atriodic; we also show that semi-Kelley continua function as semi-Kelley remainders for chainable, circularly chainable, and arc continua. Additionally, we provide an example of an atriodic Kelley continuum that is a semi-Kelley remainder but not a Kelley remainder. Finally, we prove that hereditarily semi-Kelley dendroids are smooth.

The function of cities varies based on their placement within the transport network; for instance, two urban centers of comparable size may exhibit different traits if one sits on a corridor linking two capitals while the other lies adjacent to a barrier like a mountain range. This positional attribute is termed "intermediacy," which we quantify for African cities by utilizing a road infrastructure network derived from OpenStreetMap. This network facilitates the calculation of urban metrics such as degree and centrality. To estimate the volume of traffic flowing through each network edge, we employ a mathematical model grounded in the gravitational attraction between city pairs. Crucially, our model incorporates the additional time required to cross international borders as a parameter, thereby accounting for the economic costs of fragmented regions and political barriers. Our findings reveal that small cities display a broad spectrum of intermediacy. We identify a phase transition where cities with populations under one million exhibit centrality determined by both their size and degree. Conversely, for cities exceeding one million inhabitants, centrality is predominantly driven by population size rather than network degree.

This study employs density functional theory to fully relax the bulk ferrite structure containing monoatomic interstitial chromium at a 12.5% concentration, periodically situated at the boundaries of the bcc Fe$_\alpha$ unit cell. We demonstrate that structural relaxation in these artificially engineered alloys induces substantial atomic displacements, yielding new, highly stable configurations characterized by parallel chains of octahedrally arranged iron atoms. The enhanced magnetic polarization observed in the low-symmetry metallic state of these alloys can be externally modulated by incorporating nonmagnetic impurities such as nitrogen. Furthermore, we explore potential applications of these interstitial alloys in spintronic devices and suggest evaluating them as a foundation for developing novel, durable stainless steel variants.

Entanglement represents a distinctive feature of quantum systems and serves as a vital resource for numerous quantum technologies. The capacity to transfer or exchange entanglement between systems constitutes a crucial protocol within quantum information science. Since photon entanglement underpins distributed quantum networks, demonstrating photonic entanglement swapping is fundamental to their implementation. This work presents an experiment that achieves entanglement swapping from two independent multimode time-frequency entangled sources, yielding multiple heralded temporal-mode Bell states. The entanglement present in these heralded states is confirmed through measurements of conditional anti-correlated joint spectra and quantum beating in two-photon interference. This proof-of-concept setup successfully distinguishes up to five orthogonal Bell pairs, with its ultimate capability theoretically limited only by the entanglement quality of the source.

Building a meaning bank—a semantically annotated corpus designed for semantic parsing or generation—presents a significant challenge. While constructing a complex meaning representation is straightforward, crafting a simple one that effectively captures numerous nuances proves difficult. This paper outlines key insights gained from nearly a decade of meaning annotation efforts, specifically within the development of the Groningen Meaning Bank (Bos et al., 2017) and the Parallel Meaning Bank (Abzianidze et al., 2017). The paper adopts an unconventional structure, omitting standard sections such as related work, methodology, results, and discussion; instead, it serves as an introductory preface and draws structural inspiration from Traum (2000) and Bender (2013). The content begins with a brief overview of existing meaning banks (Section 1), followed by items organized into three main categories: corpus collection (Sections 2–3), annotation methods (Sections 4–11), and the design of meaning representations (Sections 12–30). We hope this overview provides inspiration and guidance for developing enhanced meaning banks in the future.

Medical records hold a vast amount of valuable data for researchers, yet protecting patient privacy requires the removal of Protected Health Information (PHI) before release, a process called de-identification. The primary goal of such systems is to maximize recall. Although recent neural-network-based approaches have achieved state-of-the-art performance by avoiding reliance on human-engineered features—which facilitates rapid deployment—they also fail to utilize expert knowledge or data from Electronic Health Records (EHRs). This study investigates integrating both human-engineered and EHR-derived features into a neural-network framework. Our findings demonstrate that adding these features, particularly those sourced from EHRs, enhances current de-identification standards, including the handling of highly sensitive PHI like patient names. Given that patient notes often accompany EHRs in real-world scenarios, we advise developers to exploit the additional information available within EHRs to improve their systems.

Surface plasmons enable extreme light confinement but are hindered by significant intrinsic electronic losses. While stimulated electron emission has been demonstrated to supply energy to plasmons and offset these losses, existing implementations depend on coupling external gain media to the plasmons. We propose an alternative approach wherein plasmons in two-dimensional materials, characterized by closely spaced electron and hole Fermi pockets, can achieve gain through an applied electrical current bias aligned with the displaced pockets, eliminating the requirement for external gain media. Using WTe$_2$ from the 1T$'$-MX$_2$ family as a prototype—whose electronic structure is modeled by a type-II tilted massive Dirac framework—we observe that the nonlocal plasmonic response exhibits substantial gain at experimentally feasible currents around mA$\mu$m$^{-1}$. Additionally, analysis of the isofrequency curves reveals that the plasmon group velocity indicates highly collimated amplification along a direction perpendicular to the Dirac node tilt when the current is oriented along that tilt.

We establish a specific isomorphism linking the permutohedral variety to the regular semisimple Hessenberg variety corresponding to the Hessenberg function $h_+(i)=i+1$ for $1\le i\le n-1$. During the definition of this isomorphism, we define a sequence of intermediate structures termed prepermutohedral varieties. Initially, we analyze the toric properties of these varieties and calculate their Euler characteristics and Betti numbers via toric variety theory. Subsequently, we characterize their cohomology, utilizing Stembridge's codes to naturally represent the one-dimensional cohomology components. By applying our constructed isomorphisms, we further elucidate the geometric structure of regular semisimple Hessenberg varieties associated with the function $h_k= (2,3, \cdots, k+1, n,\cdots,n)$ where $1\le k\le n-3$, including the explicit formulation of their cohomology rings. Finally, we identify the dot representation of the symmetric group ${\frak S}_n$ acting on these Hessenberg varieties.

The study focuses on non-degenerate real hypersurfaces within almost Hermite-like manifolds, introducing the concept of tangential real hypersurfaces and deriving their primary identities. Leveraging these identities, the paper analyzes specific contact metric structures, namely K-contact and cosymplectic cases.

Rooted trees serve as a representation for routing tables in ad hoc and wireless protocols. Given the persistent requirements for storing and transmitting these trees, there is a critical need for efficient coding algorithms. This efficiency is quantified by average code length, with optimality assessed by comparing this length against the source entropy. This paper introduces TreeExplorer, a straightforward-to-implement and nearly optimal algorithm for encoding rooted tree structures. The method leverages the tree's leaf count to select the most appropriate coding strategy. We demonstrate how TreeExplorer can enhance current routing protocols for wireless and ad hoc systems, thereby substantially reducing communication overhead.

Identifying distinct threads within conversations, known as conversation disentanglement, serves as a crucial preprocessing stage for multi-party conversational NLP tasks like question answering and summarization. By treating this as a classification problem where the goal is to link a specific utterance of interest (UOI) to its preceding reply, we evaluated several transformer-based architectures and determined that BERT augmented with handcrafted features remains a robust baseline. We subsequently developed a multi-task learning framework that simultaneously optimizes for utterance-to-utterance and utterance-to-thread classification. Noticing that incorrect predictions often include the correct ground truth label among the top candidates, we introduced bipartite graphs as a post-processing mechanism to optimally match sets of UOIs to historical utterances. Experiments on the Ubuntu IRC dataset demonstrate that this method can surpass the standard greedy strategy of independently selecting the highest-probability candidate for each UOI, suggesting a fruitful avenue for future research.

The observation of gravitational waves from compact binary coalescence by Advanced LIGO and Advanced Virgo offers a unique opportunity to investigate the strong-field, highly relativistic domain of gravity. Standard gravitational-wave tests of general relativity (GR) typically rely on the assumptions of Gaussian and stationary detector noise, thereby neglecting non-Gaussian, transient noise features known as glitches. This study presents results from parametrized GR tests applied to simulated binary-black-hole coalescence signals overlaid with three common classes of instrumental glitches that exhibit distinct morphologies. We subsequently review and implement three glitch mitigation strategies to assess their impact on minimizing false deviations from GR. By analyzing nine scenarios involving glitches overlapping with simulated signals, we demonstrate that the short-duration, broadband blip and tomte glitches considered here can induce spurious violations of GR. However, we find that employing an inpainting filter and glitch model subtraction consistently removes these false violations without generating additional artifacts.

Selecting effective positive examples is a critical component in training convolutional neural network-based object detectors. However, in the context of anchor-based detectors trained on images with sparse annotations, the process of identifying these examples can inadvertently degrade performance. Standard anchor-based methods, which select positive examples based on Intersection over Union (IoU) thresholds relative to ground truth boxes, often introduce false positives from other classes or fail to sample relevant objects as positives. To address these challenges, we employed two strategies: utilizing an anchorless object detector and implementing a semi-supervised learning framework that leverages a single object tracker. Our proposed technique performs single object tracking by treating sparsely annotated bounding boxes as temporal anchors across successive frames. Based on these tracking results, we automatically generated dense annotations for training images, which were then used to train the detector. We applied this single object tracking-based semi-supervised approach to the Epic-Kitchens dataset, achieving first place in the "Seen" section and runner-up status in the "Unseen" section of the Epic-Kitchens 2020 object detection challenge, evaluated under an IoU > 0.5 criterion.

New experimental data have prompted a re-examination of the magnetic, thermal, and transport characteristics of the non-centrosymmetric material Eu$_2$Pd$_2$Sn. Within its paramagnetic state, the defining characteristic of this compound is the creation of Eu$^{2+}$ dimers, which clarify why the magnetic susceptibility $\chi(T)$ departs from the Curie-Weiss law below roughly 70 K, why the field-dependent magnetization $M(B)$ shifts below approximately 80 K, and why the entropy at the ordering temperature is reduced to $S(T_N)= 0.64R\ln(8)$. Notably, the exchange interactions undergo a marked transformation between $T\approx 70$ K (where $\theta_P = 18$ K) and the Néel temperature $T_N = 13.3$ K (where $\theta_P = -4.5$ K). The strong electronic overlap, resulting from a shorter Eu-Eu distance than in pure Eu$^{2+}$, is anticipated to drive the formation of these quasiparticles and necessitate a substantial revision of the magnetic structure. By analyzing the derivatives of magnetic parameters—$\partial \chi/\partial T$ and $\partial M/\partial B$—along with the specific heat's field dependence, a complex magnetic phase diagram emerges. This analysis identifies two critical points and offers a preliminary model for the magnetic structures. Furthermore, theoretical investigations into hexagonal structures with analogous interaction patterns suggest the potential emergence of a skyrmion lattice, likely stemming from magnetically frustrated regions within the phase diagram.

Every singular level within a completely integrable system (c.i.s.) that possesses non-degenerate singularities features a singular affine structure. We demonstrate how to build a straightforward c.i.s. around such a level, preserving this affine structure. This construction utilizes the cotangent bundle of the desingularized level, resulting in a c.i.s. that resembles the most fundamental system associated with the given affine structure. We apply this construction method to generate multiple examples of c.i.s. characterized by various types of non-degenerate singularities.

This note serves as a crucial extension to the author's arXiv paper arXiv:2001.01070, which addresses general multiplicative systems of random variables. By applying specific lemmas and the approach outlined in \cite{Kar4}, we derive a broad extreme inequality, alongside corollaries that cover Rademacher chaos sums and their equivalents for multiplicative systems. Notably, we demonstrate that a system of functions formed by bounded products of a multiplicative system constitutes a convergence system.

The spin Hall effect (SHE), traditionally understood as converting charge current into a transverse spin current via spin-orbit coupling, is proposed here to arise instead from a chiral magnetic structure that breaks spin rotation symmetry. Unlike the topological Hall effect, this mechanism does not require spin-orbit coupling, even when scalar spin chirality is zero. For instance, in established chiral antiferromagnetic compounds like Mn$_3$X (where X = Ga, Ge, and Sn), our *ab initio* calculations demonstrate substantial spin Hall conductivities. Beyond enhancing the theoretical framework of the SHE, this research offers a novel approach to designing spin Hall materials that avoid heavy elements, potentially benefiting technological applications.

Blockchain technology is increasingly applied across diverse sectors, such as supply chain finance and digital governance, making smart contract confidentiality a critical requirement for practical use. Despite the emergence of new privacy techniques, securely integrating Multi-party Computation (MPC) into confidential smart contracts remains an understudied challenge. Current state-of-the-art solutions are hindered by high on-chain costs, limited flexibility, and security vulnerabilities, making them inaccessible to general users. This paper introduces TENET, a pluggable and configurable framework for confidential smart contracts. TENET addresses the challenges of supporting off-chain MPC-enabled contracts via a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) network by proposing specific solutions, including anonymous negotiation among unknown participants, fair and atomic distribution of MPC outputs, and secure evaluation of MPC programs with constant on-chain transactions. TENET secures MPC operations using only three transactions. Evaluation across both illustrative examples and real-world applications involving 2 to 11 parties demonstrates that TENET requires 0.55–0.98X gas (0.91X on average) compared to existing solutions.

Federated Learning facilitates model training on distributed devices without centralizing data, thus preserving privacy. Effectively managing data heterogeneity (non-IID distributions) is crucial for expanding Federated Learning adoption. This paper introduces a novel Divide-and-Conquer training approach that allows the widely used FedAvg algorithm to function effectively in non-IID settings by addressing its known limitations. We propose utilizing a Cosine-distance based Weight Divergence metric to precisely identify where to split a Deep Learning network into class-agnostic initial layers and class-specific deep layers for this Divide-and-Conquer strategy. Our results demonstrate that this method achieves accuracy comparable to, and in some instances superior to, state-of-the-art aggregation techniques such as FedProx and FedMA. Furthermore, we show that under specific conditions, this approach optimizes both computational resources and bandwidth usage.

This work addresses the solution of linear systems derived from three distinct fields: kernel methods in machine learning, the discretization of boundary integral equations in mathematical physics, and Schur complements resulting from the factorization of large sparse matrices. The coefficient matrices in these applications are frequently data-sparse, characterized by off-diagonal blocks with low numerical ranks; specifically, our focus lies on "hierarchically off-diagonal low-rank (HODLR)" matrices. We present algorithms designed to factorize HODLR matrices and apply these factorizations on a GPU. By utilizing the efficiency of batched dense linear algebra, these methods achieve nearly linear scaling with matrix size when numerical ranks remain constant. Since the accuracy of the HODLR approximation is adjustable, the approach supports both high-accuracy fast direct solvers and low-accuracy robust preconditioners. Numerical experiments demonstrate the capability to resolve problems involving millions of unknowns within seconds using a single GPU.

This paper introduces a novel surface trap design that couples ion motion within ten selected wells by adjusting DC-voltages across a set of electrodes. We demonstrate and characterize various phonon mode spectra for two ion types, Calcium (Ca) and Beryllium (Be), across different voltage configurations within a 10-ion architecture. Our findings indicate that ions can be grouped into segments with distinct phonon mode frequencies to enable parallel MS-gate operations. Furthermore, we model the fidelity of MS-gate operations for two-ion segments, accounting for two primary sources of infidelity: the limited frequency difference between segment phonon modes and the finite drift of these frequencies expected in experimental settings. Finally, we examine how the number of ions per individual trap and anharmonic potential terms influence the coupling between the two wells.

During the second extended LHC shutdown in 2019–2020, the Inner Tracking System (ITS) of the ALICE experiment is set for an upgrade. The primary objective of this upgrade is to facilitate high-precision measurements of low-momentum particles (below 1 GeV/c) by capturing large event samples, taking advantage of the anticipated rise in instantaneous luminosity for Pb-Pb collisions to $\mathcal{L} = 6 \cdot 10^{27} cm^{-2} s^{-1}$ in Run 3. To achieve this, the project aims to enhance the readout rate, refine the impact parameter resolution, and improve both tracking efficiency and position resolution. The core modification involves replacing the existing ITS with seven layers of silicon pixel detectors. For this purpose, the ALPIDE chip—a CMOS Monolithic Active Pixel Sensor (MAPS)—was developed, providing a spatial resolution of 5 $\mu$m. Combining MAPS technology with a rigorous mechanical design reduces the material budget to 0.35% $X_0$ in the innermost layers and 1% $X_0$ in the outer layers. The detector design was validated during the research and development phase through various tests confirming reliable operation throughout the full mission lifetime. With the production phase nearing completion, all newly assembled components are undergoing tests to characterize modules and staves and establish their qualification levels. This paper details the detector design, results from the research and development measurements, and the current production status.

Lately, particle-based variational inference (ParVI) techniques have attracted significant attention due to their ability to bypass the restrictive parametric assumptions typical of standard variational inference. Nevertheless, most existing ParVI methods restrict arbitrary posterior sampling, and those rare methods that permit it often yield suboptimal results. This study introduces a novel approach for learning to approximate samples from the posterior distribution. We develop a neural sampler trained on the functional gradient of the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the empirical sampling distribution and the target distribution, under the assumption that this gradient exists within a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. Our proposed Generative ParVI (GPVI) framework retains the asymptotic performance benefits of ParVI while providing the adaptability of a generative sampler. Through rigorous experiments, we demonstrate that GPVI surpasses prior generative ParVI techniques, such as amortized SVGD, and performs competitively against both standard ParVI methods and gold-standard algorithms like Hamiltonian Monte Carlo when fitting both tractable and intractable target distributions.

Just as six-membered rings are prevalent, five-membered rings are fundamental building blocks in organic chemistry, particularly in biochemistry. By combining laboratory rotational spectroscopy with a sensitive radio spectral survey of the starless cloud core TMC-1, we report the astronomical detection of 1-cyano-1,3-cyclopentadiene ($c$-C$_5$H$_5$CN), a highly polar cyano derivative of cyclopentadiene ($c$-C$_5$H$_6$). The derived abundance of this molecule significantly exceeds predictions from existing astrochemical models, which successfully account for the abundances of many carbon chains. This discrepancy suggests that either a previously unaccounted production mechanism or a substantial reservoir of aromatic material must be considered. The non-detection of its closely related isomer, 2-cyano-1,3-cyclopentadiene, may result from lower stability or indicate a selective formation pathway for the 1-cyano isomer, potentially originating from acyclic precursors. Furthermore, the lack of N-heterocycles like pyrrole and pyridine is examined in the context of these astronomical findings.

Addressing the algebraic dichotomy conjecture for constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) over structures first-order definable in countably infinite, finitely bounded homogeneous structures hinges on the efficacy of local-consistency techniques within this framework. This study investigates the requisite degree of consistency, quantified by relational width, necessary to resolve CSPs for first-order expansions $S$ of countably infinite homogeneous graphs possessing bounded strict width. Specifically, for these structures, local consistency not only determines the existence of a solution but also guarantees that any solution can be derived from a locally consistent instance through greedy variable assignment without backtracking.

The primary finding establishes that the relational width of the considered structures $S$ is exactly $(2, L)$, where $L$ represents the maximum size of a forbidden subgraph in a homogeneous graph under study, provided $L \geq 3$. This result surpasses the existing upper bound of $(2m, 3m)$, where $m = \max(\text{arity}(S)+1, L, 3)$ and $\text{arity}(S)$ denotes the maximum arity of relations in $S$, a bound derived from a known sufficient condition for bounded relational width. Furthermore, because $L$ can be arbitrarily large, this finding highlights a distinction from the relational bounded width hierarchy for finite structures, where a finite relational width is strictly limited to at most $(2,3)$.

This theoretical study examines the low-energy continuous states of electrons within a heterostructure featuring periodically arranged quantum-dot sheets. The electron Green's function is described by the Dyson equation, utilizing a self-energy function derived from boundary conditions at the quantum-dot sheets, assuming weak damping in the low-energy regime. The superlattice parameters, composed of these quantum-dot sheets, are established using a short-range model for the quantum dots. Both the density of states and the spectral dependencies of the anisotropic absorption coefficient during mid-IR transitions from doped quantum dots to superlattice miniband states exhibit strong reliance on dot concentration and sheet periodicity. These relationships facilitate the characterization of multi-layer structures and define the parameters for various optoelectronic devices that rely on vertical carrier transport through the quantum-dot sheets.

This work offers a structured summary of adaptation techniques for neural network-driven speech recognition, addressing both hybrid HMM/NN architectures and end-to-end models, with specific attention to speaker, domain, and accent adaptation. The analysis categorizes these methods into three primary approaches: embeddings, model parameter adaptation, and data augmentation. Furthermore, we provide a meta-analysis evaluating the efficacy of these adaptation strategies by examining relative error rate reductions documented in existing literature.

Client-Side Scanning (CSS), particularly within the context of Child Sexual Abuse Material Detection (CSAMD), constitutes ubiquitous mass surveillance. Although Apple initially proposed scanning for such imagery, the CSAMD initiative was delayed; however, the European Union subsequently advocated for mandatory CSS to combat child abuse, albeit at the expense of encryption. This approach represents the mass inspection of personal data, images, and text, disregarding privacy, cybersecurity, and legal standards. The paper first argues against the necessity and efficacy of CSS, examining cryptographic handling of images and how CSAMD purportedly preserves privacy. Subsequently, it analyzes potential human rights violations under the European Convention on Human Rights, focusing on individual harm and commenting on the proposed Child Abuse Regulation. The authors conclude that CSS is problematic because it rarely achieves its intended goals, similar to the limitations observed in antivirus software. The costs of attempting to address CSAM outweigh the benefits, a situation unlikely to improve. The proposed CSAMD fails to maintain privacy or security as described in source materials. Furthermore, CSS generally risks violating the Right to a Fair Trial, Right to Privacy, and Freedom of Expression. Images may be obtained in ways that render trials against legitimate perpetrators inadmissible or violate fair trial rights; the absence of national legal safeguards compromises the Right to Privacy; and it remains unclear if such scanning can satisfy legal requirements for Freedom of Expression. Finally, the proposed Regulation presents significant issues due to its reliance on techno-solutionist arguments while ignoring established cybersecurity knowledge.

Dwarf galaxies serve as promising environments for testing models regarding the seeding and evolution of supermassive and intermediate-mass black holes (MBHs) through their black hole occupation fraction (BHOF). However, separating seeding mechanisms from the complexities of mass assembly remains difficult. This study employs semi-analytical models (SAMs) to evaluate how diverse surveys can differentiate between various seed and growth scenarios. By examining BHOF variations across different black hole mass and AGN luminosity thresholds, we establish a framework to rigorously compare SAMs—including their inherent uncertainties—with X-ray data. We demonstrate that distinguishing between seeding models requires detecting or modeling all AGNs brighter than $10^{37}\ \rm{erg \ s^{-1}}$ in galaxies with stellar masses $M_* \sim 10^{8-10} \ \rm{M_{\odot}}$. Shallower missions, such as eRASS, fail to differentiate seed models even when accounting for a significantly larger survey volume. Our analysis indicates that the AMUSE survey strongly supports heavy seed models, evolving under empirically driven growth scenarios such as a power-law Eddington Ratio Distribution Function (ERDF) or accretion linked to star-formation rates (AGN-MS). These two growth pathways can be distinguished via the AGN luminosity function below $10^{44}\ \rm{erg \ s^{-1}}$. Furthermore, these models predict distinct radio scaling relations, which we quantify using the fundamental plane of black hole activity. The paper concludes with recommendations for designing future multi-wavelength campaigns to optimally detect MBHs in dwarf galaxies.

This study investigates how phonemes are represented and encoded within a recurrent neural network designed for grounded speech. The model processes both images and their spoken descriptions, projecting visual and auditory inputs into a shared semantic space. We analyze how information regarding individual phonemes is encoded in the MFCC features derived from the speech signal as well as in the model's layer activations. Experiments involving phoneme decoding and discrimination reveal that phoneme representations are most prominent in the lower layers, where fine-grained low-level signals are processed, despite significant phonological information persisting in the top recurrent layer. Additionally, we observe that the attention mechanism situated after the top recurrent layer substantially reduces phonological encoding, resulting in utterance embeddings that are highly invariant to synonymy. Finally, hierarchical clustering of the phoneme representations learned by the network demonstrates an organizational structure of phonemes that aligns with those proposed in linguistics.

Research interest in tensegrity robotics is currently experiencing significant growth. Robots designed within this framework offer distinct benefits, including enhanced structural compliance, dexterity, safety, and weight efficiency. This study introduces a novel robotic mechanism that combines tensegrity principles with reconfigurable modular robotics. The paper details specific actuation strategies for this multi-degree-of-freedom tensegrity system. It presents an easy-to-assemble 350 mm prototype constructed by stacking rigid struts connected via tensegrity joints, which maintain separation without direct rigid contact. The functionality of this device is confirmed through experiments, utilizing a polyhedral parallel structure as its skeleton alongside a series of tensegrity joints. The resulting manipulator achieves bending angles of up to 76 degrees. Furthermore, an adaptive, cable-driven underactuated gripper has been designed and integrated with the tensegrity manipulator to enable the grasping of objects varying in shape, weight, and size.

**Aims.** Interacting galaxies often exhibit unique irregularities within their kinematic structures. By analyzing the spatially resolved kinematics and stellar population characteristics of galaxies displaying such irregularities, we can construct a comprehensive understanding of the formation and evolutionary mechanisms that have shaped them over time. **Methods.** This study focuses specifically on galaxies characterized by a kinematically distinct stellar core (KDC), particularly those with counter-rotation where the core and the main body rotate in opposing directions. We visually identified eleven MaNGA galaxies possessing a KDC based on their stellar kinematics and investigated their spatially resolved stellar and gaseous kinematic properties, including two-dimensional velocity and velocity dispersion ({\sigma}) maps for both components. Furthermore, we examined stellar population attributes and recent star formation histories by analyzing spatially resolved gradients in Dn4000 and H{\delta}. **Results.** The galaxies exhibit multiple off-centered, symmetrical peaks in their stellar {\sigma} maps, whereas their gaseous velocity and {\sigma} maps display regular characteristics. Stellar population properties and their gradients vary according to the outcomes of spatially resolved emission line diagnostics, with some galaxies exhibiting inside-out quenching while others do not. Star formation histories also differ significantly based on these diagnostics, though most galaxies indicate recent star formation either in their cores or outskirts. **Conclusions.** Our findings reveal distinct differences in kinematic and stellar population properties among galaxies with counter-rotating stellar cores, contingent upon their classification via spatially resolved emission line diagnostics.

This paper presents K-FACE, a newly established large-scale face database from KIST, alongside a specialized capturing apparatus developed to acquire the data. Comprising over one million high-quality images of 1,000 subjects, the dataset ensures a balanced representation of gender and age groups. It features diverse attributes, including 27 poses, 35 lighting conditions, three facial expressions, and occlusions created by five different types of accessories. Built through a hemispherical capturing system with sophisticated lighting control and multi-camera setups, K-FACE enables precise analysis of factors that degrade performance, such as variations in pose, lighting, and accessories. The database maintains equilibrium in external environmental conditions and personal characteristics, with an equal gender split and subjects uniformly distributed across age groups from their 20s to 50s for both genders. We anticipate that the systematic diversity and uniformity of K-FACE will significantly advance various vision tasks, including face recognition, frontalization, illumination normalization, age estimation, and 3D face model generation, thereby fostering progress in these research areas.

This work examines the large-scale dynamics of non-equilibrium dense soliton gases within the Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) framework, specifically under the "condensate" limit. We demonstrate that in this regime, the integro-differential kinetic equation governing spectral density simplifies to the $N$-phase KdV-Whitham modulation equations previously established by Flaschka, Forest, and McLaughlin (1980) and Lax and Levermore (1983). Furthermore, we analyze Riemann problems involving soliton condensates to derive explicit solutions for the kinetic equation, which describe generalized rarefaction and dispersive shock waves. Finally, we provide numerical data for "diluted" soliton condensates that reveal complex incoherent behaviors linked to integrable turbulence.

Theoretical physics has firmly established that shadows are not exclusive to black holes; other compact objects, including naked singularities, gravastars, and boson stars, can also produce them. A key insight is that neither an event horizon nor a photon sphere is strictly required for a shadow to appear. Consequently, if two compact objects of equal mass generate shadows of identical size, they become challenging to distinguish visually. However, because their underlying spacetime geometries differ, the behavior of null and timelike geodesics around each object will vary, leading to distinct intensity distributions in the light emitted by surrounding accreting matter. This paper investigates this phenomenon, demonstrating that a naked singularity spacetime—specifically the first type of Joshi-Malafarina-Narayan (JMN1) geometry—can be differentiated from a Schwarzschild black hole based on light intensity patterns, despite sharing the same mass and shadow dimensions. By applying image processing techniques to theoretical intensity data, we illustrate these differences. The resulting patterns serve as theoretical templates for intensity variations, which can aid in analyzing observational data of compact objects.

This study investigates how the isovector-scalar $\delta$-meson field influences finite nuclei, infinite nuclear matter, and neutron stars using the Relativistic Mean Field (RMF) model with non-linear couplings. To evaluate the $\delta$-meson's impact on neutron star characteristics, several parameter sets (SRV's) were developed. These sets feature varying $\delta$-meson nucleon coupling constants, while other parameters are tuned to match experimental data for finite nuclei and nuclear matter. Results indicate that fitting nuclear and matter properties in the presence of the $\delta$ field necessitates a stronger coupling between isovector-vector $\rho$ mesons and nucleons. Additionally, the $\delta$-meson significantly alters the radius of canonical neutron stars. The resulting dimensionless tidal deformability (${\Lambda}$) for these stars aligns with constraints derived from the GW170817 binary neutron star merger waveform analysis. Finally, a covariance analysis was conducted to determine statistical uncertainties for the model parameters and to assess correlations among parameters and key observables.

Transformer-based models have achieved significant success in image captioning by encoding object regions and attending them into vector representations to guide decoding. However, these vector representations capture only region-level details, neglecting global information that reflects the entire image, thereby limiting the model's ability to perform complex multi-modal reasoning. To address this, we propose the Global Enhanced Transformer (GET), which extracts a more comprehensive global representation to adaptively guide the decoder in generating high-quality captions. GET consists of a Global Enhanced Encoder and a Global Adaptive Decoder. The encoder embeds global features by leveraging a proposed Global Enhanced Attention mechanism and a layer-wise fusion module to model both intra- and inter-layer global representations. The decoder incorporates a Global Adaptive Controller that dynamically fuses global information to direct caption generation. Extensive experiments on the MS COCO dataset demonstrate that our GET outperforms many state-of-the-art methods.

This study examines the valuation of variable annuities (VAs) featuring diverse fee structures within widely used stochastic volatility frameworks, including Heston, Hull-White, Scott, $\alpha$-Hypergeometric, $3/2$, and $4/2$ models. Specifically, we investigate how various VIX-linked fee mechanisms influence the optimal surrender strategy for a VA contract that includes a guaranteed minimum maturity benefit (GMMB). Assuming early surrender is permitted, pricing the VA contract translates into an optimal stopping problem characterized by an unbounded, time-dependent, and discontinuous payoff function. To address this, we devise efficient pricing algorithms utilizing a two-layer continuous-time Markov chain approximation for the fund value process. Furthermore, when the contract is held to maturity under a general fee structure, we demonstrate that the contract's value can be approximated by a closed-form matrix expression. Additionally, we present a straightforward recursive algorithm to quickly calculate early surrender values and an accessible method to approximate the optimal surrender surface. Numerical results indicate that the optimal surrender strategy exhibits greater robustness to fluctuations in account value volatility when fees are tied to the VIX index.

This paper introduces a generalized Dirichlet fundamental domain, denoted as $\mathcal{F}^{*}$, for Fuchsian groups $G$ that include parabolic generators. Using this concept, we demonstrate that a quasisymmetric homeomorphism $h$ compatible with a first-kind convergence Fuchsian group $G$ is strongly quasisymmetric if and only if it admits a quasiconformal extension $f$ to the upper half-plane $\mathbb{H}$ such that the measure $\lambda_{\mu}=|\mu|^{2}/Im(z)dxdy$, derived from the Beltrami coefficient $\mu$ of $f$, constitutes a Carleson measure on $\mathcal{F}^{*}$. Furthermore, we establish that this property remains valid for Carleson-Denjoy domains.

In 2D multi-slice magnetic resonance (MR) acquisitions, through-plane signals generally exhibit lower resolution compared to in-plane signals. Although current super-resolution (SR) techniques strive to reconstruct high-resolution volumes, they rely on end-to-end data-driven training to implicitly infer high-frequency details rather than explicitly targeting them. To overcome this limitation, we reformulate the SR problem using perfect reconstruction filter banks, allowing for the direct identification and estimation of missing information. We introduce a two-stage method to approximate the completion of a perfect reconstruction filter bank tailored to the anisotropic nature of specific scans. The first stage estimates missing filters via gradient descent, while the second stage employs deep networks to map coarse coefficients to detail coefficients. Furthermore, our formulation operates without external training data, thereby eliminating the need for domain shift correction. Consequently, SR performance is notably enhanced, especially in "slice gap" scenarios, attributed to the constrained solution space defined by our framework.

Cold atom fountain clocks offer superior long-term stability by extending interrogation time, albeit with increased physical dimensions. We introduce a compact cold atom fountain that employs a grating magneto-optical trap (GMOT) for laser cooling and atom launching within a streamlined optical configuration. Evaluated through coherent population trapping, the system exhibits enhanced single-shot stability immediately following launch. Ramsey interrogation times reaching 100 ms were achieved, corresponding to a fringe linewidth of 5 Hz. This approach holds the potential to enhance both short- and long-term stability in cold atom clocks while maintaining a compact form factor suitable for portable applications.

The temporal evolution of nonlinear equations governing coupled modes is utilized to investigate the mean-field optical phase transition in multimode photonic networks with uniform coupling. Drawing analogies to statistical mechanics models of interacting classical spins—based on the mapping between complex-valued modes and two-component spins—this study defines both single- and two-component order parameters. A thorough finite-size scaling analysis estimates the critical points and exponents associated with a second-order phase transition driven by optical energy per mode, with equilibrium properties validated against exact results where feasible. Across various parameter configurations, the findings confirm the transition's mean-field character and delineate the critical line within the nonlinearity versus energy-density phase diagram. Furthermore, critical scaling indicates an upper critical dimension of $d_c=4$. By introducing a kinetic temperature with a suitable zero-temperature limit, the system's connection to thermodynamic quantities is clarified. Specifically, in the low-temperature regime (low energy per mode), spins exhibit alignment, whereas in the high-temperature regime (high energy per mode), spins rotate independently.

RR Tel is a symbiotic nova consisting of an interacting binary where a hot white dwarf accretes material from a Mira-type variable star through the gravitational capture of its stellar wind. This system exhibits strong Raman-scattered O VI lines at 1032 Å and 1038 Å, appearing at 6825 Å and 7082 Å, respectively. We utilized the Magellan Inamori Kyocera Echelle (MIKE) spectrograph on the Magellan-Clay telescope in Chile to obtain high-resolution optical spectra of RR Tel during 2016 and 2017. Our objective was to analyze stellar wind accretion by examining the profiles of these O VI Raman features. By fitting an asymmetric O VI disk model, we determined a representative Keplerian velocity exceeding 35 km s⁻¹ and a corresponding scale smaller than 0.8 au. The optimal fit for the Raman profiles yielded a Mira mass loss rate of approximately $2 \times 10^{-6} \, M_{\odot} \, \text{yr}^{-1}$ and a wind terminal velocity near 20 km s⁻¹. We further compared the MIKE observations with an archival spectrum from 2003 obtained using the FEROS spectrograph at the MPG/ESO 2.2m telescope, revealing variations in the O VI feature profiles that suggest changes in the O VI disk's density distribution over the past two decades. Additionally, we detected O VI recombination lines at 3811 Å and 3834 Å, which are blended with other emissions. Profile decomposition indicates that O VII recombination occurs closer to the white dwarf than the region producing the O VI 1032 Å and 1038 Å emission.

u_	au$ and $\Lambda^*_c(2625)	au ar
u_	au$ to investigate their potential significance in probing lepton flavor universality violation. Employing an effective field theory framework, we examine various observables accessible via the visible kinematics of charged particles from tau decays, specifically analyzing the $\pi^-
u_	au,ho^-
u_	au$, and $\mu^- ar
u_\mu
u_	au$ modes. Our comparison between Standard Model predictions and scenarios involving new physics (NP) with either left-handed or right-handed neutrino operators reveals a discriminating capability similar to that of the $\Lambda_b	o \Lambda_c$ transition, though somewhat limited by the larger uncertainties in the $\Lambda_b	o\Lambda^*_c$ lattice form factors. Despite these challenges, the current analysis can already distinguish between certain NP models, with its efficacy expected to increase significantly as more precise form factors become available.

An intriguing monogamy relation resembling the Pythagorean theorem has been identified for pure states in $2\otimes 2\otimes n$ dimensions, elucidating the interplay between bipartite concurrence, concurrence of assistance, and genuine tripartite entanglement. Concurrently, a genuine tripartite entanglement monotone, extending the concept of the 3-tangle, is derived for these same $(2\otimes 2\otimes n)$-dimensional pure states using a novel approach. For mixed states, the monogamy equation transforms into a monogamy inequality. Furthermore, these findings regarding tripartite quantum states can be extended to multipartite systems.

This paper details the adaptation of the Monte Carlo event generator ReneSANCe, originally designed for $e^+e^-$ collisions, to handle hadron-hadron ($pp$ and $p\bar{p}$) collision modes. The extended version of ReneSANCe currently implements neutral and charged current Drell-Yan processes, specifically $pp[p\bar{p}] \to ZX \to \ell^+\ell^- X$, $pp[p\bar{p}] \to W^+X \to \ell^+\nu_\ell X$, and $pp[p\bar{p}] \to W^-X \to \ell^-\bar{\nu}_\ell X$. These calculations incorporate full one-loop electroweak and QCD corrections. Built upon the SANC (Support for Analytic and Numeric Calculations for experiments at colliders) framework, the generator is architected to facilitate the easy addition of new processes. The study provides a theoretical overview of the SANC methodology, includes numerical validation results, and offers a user manual.

Achieving synchronization in few-level quantum systems is crucial for comprehending the deep quantum regime, where the feasibility of synchronizing the smallest unit, a two-level system, has long been debated. In this study, we present the first experimental demonstration that a qubit can be synchronized to an external drive using a trapped-ion setup. Through the engineering of fully controllable gain and damping mechanisms, we successfully locked an ion qubit's oscillation frequency and phase to a driving signal. We systematically mapped the parameter space for synchronization, observing the characteristic Arnold tongue features, and found that our experimental results align remarkably well with numerical simulations grounded in recent theoretical models. By synchronizing this fundamental unit of quantum information, our work paves the way for extending quantum synchronization to large-scale quantum networks.

Inverse methods are employed to derive atmospheric properties of exoplanets, yet these approaches can yield biased outcomes if the underlying forward model is inadequate. A common simplification in forward modeling assumes a planet's radius remains constant across wavelengths, whereas a more physically accurate approach recognizes that the photospheric radius changes with wavelength. This study investigates the bias introduced when retrieving molecular abundances from emission spectra generated under a variable-radius assumption. Our findings indicate that for low-gravity planets, retrieval models relying on a constant radius fail to fit the data. Additionally, we observe biased results when analyzing typical hot Jupiters within the MIRI LRS wavelength range. Conversely, high-gravity planets are not subject to this bias. We recommend that future spectral retrieval efforts interpreting exoplanet emission spectra incorporate a variable radius to ensure accuracy.

Over the past decade, quantitative analytics has revolutionized sports. Currently, these statistical methods primarily describe historical and current states to inform future decisions. However, because team sports like baseball, hockey, and soccer are often perceived as binary win-or-lose scenarios, modeling them as zero-sum games appears intuitive. This paper proposes such a framework for a specific category of matchups: the baseball at-bat, a contest between a pitcher and a batter. We introduce a novel zero-sum stochastic game model where the batter aims to reach base while the pitcher strives to stop them, with the game's value defined as the on-base percentage. Although classical methods could theoretically solve this stochastic game, significant technical hurdles remain, including predicting pitch locations based on pitcher intent, estimating outcome distributions when a batter swings, and quantifying a batter's patience. To overcome these issues, we develop new representations for both batters and pitchers alongside a specialized deep neural network architecture for outcome prediction. Experiments utilizing Kaggle data from the 2015–2018 MLB seasons confirm the effectiveness of this approach.

Autonomous vehicles operate within high-risk, dynamic, and uncertain environments that necessitate the constant updating of sensory data and knowledge bases. The high frequency of encountering unknown objects renders classical Artificial Intelligence (AI) classification models, which typically depend on the closed-world assumption, ineffective. Consequently, an open-world AI approach is better suited to address the challenge of object classification in this domain. We propose an algorithm capable of identifying all known entities that may appear before the vehicle, while also detecting and learning the classes of rare, unknown objects (such as a crate dropped from a truck on a highway). Our methodology builds upon the DOC algorithm by Lei Shu et al., as well as the Query-by-Committee algorithm.

Monitoring of energetic particles near Earth has been ongoing since the 1970s. As quantifying radiation risks becomes increasingly critical for human missions to the Moon and Mars, it is vital to sustain and enhance these observations. Since 1995, the Electron Proton Helium INstrument (EPHIN) aboard SOHO has continuously supplied these datasets to the solar science and space weather communities. This paper introduces the various data products generated over the years and highlights their applications in space weather. Additionally, key design features contributing to EPHIN's success, along with lessons learned and potential improvements for future particle detectors, are discussed.

Investigating magnetic phenomena on stars beyond our Sun is crucial for accurately analyzing exoplanet atmospheres and characterizing stellar activity across diverse stellar populations. Modeling surface features across various spectral types and rotation rates is essential for comprehending this magnetic activity. Leveraging Kepler data, we employed the STarSPot (STSP) modeling program to determine the location and dimensions of starspots on KOI-340, an eclipsing binary system comprising a subgiant primary ($\rm T_{\rm eff} = 5593 \pm 27 \, K; R_{*} = 1.98 \pm 0.05 \, R_{\odot}$) and an M-dwarf companion ($M_{*} = 0.214 \pm 0.006 \, M_{\odot}$). STSP utilizes a unique methodology that leverages the transiting secondary to model individual active regions via high-precision photometry. Our findings indicate that the average spot size on KOI-340's primary is approximately 10% of the stellar radius, which is double the mean size of sunspots during solar maximum. These spots are distributed across all longitudes and exhibit potential signs of differential rotation. The minimum fractional spotted area of KOI-340's primary is estimated at $2^{+12}_{-2}\%$, compared to a maximum of 0.2% for the Sun. Additionally, one transit event revealed a signal consistent with a plage immediately preceding a dark spot, suggesting that these features may be co-located on the star's surface.

Determining the sound speed $c_s$ within compact stars remains a significant open problem with far-reaching implications for high-density matter behavior and gravitational-wave emission from neutron stars. In this study, we generate over $10^7$ equations of state (EOSs) featuring continuous sound speeds and construct more than $10^8$ nonrotating stellar models that align with nuclear theory, perturbative QCD, and astronomical observations. Our analysis reveals that while EOSs with sub-conformal sound speeds ($c^2_s < 1/3$) are theoretically permissible, they are practically improbable, constituting merely $0.03\%$ of our dataset. Consequently, it is reasonable to anticipate that $c^2_s > 1/3$ occurs somewhere within the stellar interior. Leveraging our extensive sample, we derive $95\%$ credibility estimates for the radii of representative $1.4$ and $2.0$ solar mass neutron stars ($R_{1.4}=12.42^{+0.52}_{-0.99}\,{\rm km}$, $R_{2.0}=12.12^{+1.11}_{-1.23}\,{\rm km}$) and the binary tidal deformability for the GW170817 event ($\tilde\Lambda_{1.186}=485^{+225}_{-211}$). Notably, our lower-bound radius estimates closely match predictions derived from independent arguments, specifically the threshold mass. Additionally, we present simple analytic formulas to calculate the minimum and maximum values of $\tilde\Lambda$ as a function of chirp mass.

Numerous natural phenomena display stochastic characteristics, which are typically modeled using various types of stochastic processes. A central goal in this context is often to analyze the memory properties of the phenomenon, usually achieved by calculating the autocorrelation function of the numerical series representing the data. When dealing with real-world data, this computation is frequently performed using a single time series via a time-averaging approach. This paper introduces a novel method for evaluating the time-average autocorrelation function, which relies on first estimating the quantity $N(\tau, g\mu, g\nu)$. Apart from normalization factors, this quantity serves as a numerical estimate of the two-point joint probability density function $P(x_2, \tau; x_1, 0)$ derived from a single realization of the process. The primary benefit of this approach is its ability to quantify the error introduced by the finite length of simulated time series when numerically assessing the autocorrelation function. Specifically, we demonstrate that for a broad class of stochastic processes governed by nonlinear Langevin equations with white noise and describable via Fokker-Planck equations, the convergence of the numerical autocorrelation estimate to its theoretical counterpart is influenced by the tails of the probability density function. Furthermore, knowledge of $N(\tau, g\mu, g\nu)$ facilitates the easy computation of process histograms and the characterization of systems with multiple timescales. Finally, we illustrate the efficacy of this new methodology by examining three stochastic processes where both the autocorrelation function and the two-point probability density function are known analytically or numerically, enabling direct comparisons.

This work investigates the rates of noise-driven transitions between stable states and extinction in dissipative dynamical systems with delay, which serve as models for population dynamics. We focus on a specific class of systems where evolution relies on variables from a fixed prior time, termed "hard delay." In the regime of weak noise, both switching and extinction rates are exponentially small. Determining these rates to logarithmic precision is equivalent to solving variational problems, whose solutions identify the most probable trajectories for switching or extinction. We demonstrate that the equations governing these most probable paths are acausal and establish the necessary boundary conditions. For delays that are small relative to the relaxation rate, we derive explicit general results. Furthermore, we introduce a direct variational approach to calculate these rates, showing that our analytical findings align closely with numerical simulations for both switching and extinction.

This study introduces the lowest-order nonconforming virtual element method, which generalizes the Morley triangular element to polygonal domains for approximating the weak solution $u\in V:=H^2_0(\Omega)$ of the biharmonic equation. The proposed abstract framework accommodates two local discrete space examples, $V_h(P)$, including a mixture of smoother and rougher spaces, thereby permitting rough source terms $F\in V^*=H^{-2}(\Omega)$. The paper's a priori and a posteriori error analysis avoids second derivatives by employing a computable conforming companion operator $J:V_h\to V$ that maps the nonconforming virtual element space $V_h$. Since $J$ acts as a right-inverse to the interpolation operator, it yields optimal error estimates in piecewise Sobolev norms without requiring additional regularity assumptions on $u\in V$. Furthermore, utilizing the companion operator as a smoother to adjust the discrete right-hand side enables quasi-best approximation. The explicit, residual-based a posteriori error estimator is demonstrated to be both reliable and efficient, accounting for data oscillations. Finally, numerical experiments confirm the predicted empirical convergence rates for both uniform and adaptive mesh-refinement strategies.

This study introduces the concept of slant helices within three-dimensional Lie Groups equipped with a bi-invariant metric and establishes their defining characteristics. Furthermore, we explore the connections between slant helices and their corresponding involutes and spherical images.

This study assesses the Large Hadron Collider's (LHC) sensitivity to light lepton portal dark matter with masses under 10 GeV. The framework incorporates an additional scalar doublet and singlet Dirac dark matter interacting via Yukawa couplings to left-handed leptons. Achieving the correct thermal freeze-out abundance necessitates a significant mass splitting among the extra scalars, resulting in a light neutral scalar below ${\cal O}(10)$ GeV alongside heavy neutral and charged scalars at the electroweak scale. We concentrate on the electroweak pair-production of these extra scalars and their subsequent model-specific decays, analyzing current constraints from LHC Run 2 data and the discovery potential at the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC). Our findings indicate that a substantial portion of the theoretically viable parameter space can be probed at the HL-LHC by leveraging the complementarity between slepton searches and mono-$Z$ plus missing transverse energy analyses. Furthermore, we examine same-sign charged scalar production as a distinctive prediction of this model and explore the implications of collider searches within the thermal dark matter context.

Utilizing matrices to model problems is fundamental to Computer Science. Disciplines such as computer graphics, graph theory, and machine learning rely heavily on matrix operations to address their specific challenges. Among these, matrix multiplication is the most frequently performed operation; however, it can become computationally expensive when dealing with large datasets. Consequently, parallel computing has emerged as a necessary solution to mitigate this performance bottleneck. This report presents a comparative analysis of sequential and parallel approaches to matrix multiplication, implemented using CUDA and OpenMP. The findings demonstrate that parallelization is particularly critical for achieving optimal performance with large-scale matrices.

Young stars (t $\lesssim$ 10 Myrs) exhibit powerful magnetic fields that direct ionized gas from their circumstellar discs onto the stellar surface. When this gas strikes the star, it shocks, recombines, and produces hydrogen spectral lines. To determine the density and temperature of this accreting material, we analyzed the equivalent widths of Brackett (Br) 11–20 emission lines found in 1101 APOGEE spectra of 326 probable pre-main sequence accretors. For targets with repeated observations, we observed median variations in line strength of 10% for Br11 and 20% for Br20 between epochs. We compared our measured line ratios against radiative transfer model predictions by Kwan & Fischer. Our best-fit results yield characteristic electron densities of $n_e$ = 10$^{11} - 10^{12}$ cm$^{-3}$ and excitation temperatures that decrease as electron density increases, ranging from approximately 12,500 K at $n_e \sim 10^{11}$ cm$^{-3}$ down to 5,000 K at $n_e \sim 10^{12}$ cm$^{-3}$. These findings align well with hydrodynamic and radiative transfer models of accretion streams. Additionally, we provide a supplementary catalog containing line measurements from 9,733 spectra of 4,255 Brackett emission line sources within the APOGEE DR17 dataset.

Plasma injection mechanisms are essential for generating high-quality electron beams within laser-plasma accelerators. This paper outlines the fundamental principles of plasma injection. It begins by presenting a Hamiltonian model that describes particle trapping and acceleration in plasma waves, using this framework to detail ionization injection and colliding-pulse injection. The discussion then advances to examine injection processes occurring within plasma density gradients.

We introduce the Optimization Method for the Acquisition System of the SPARC4 Electron Multiplying Charge-Coupled Devices (OMASS4). This system evaluates the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and acquisition rate (AR) based on the CCD's operational mode. OMASS4 incorporates three distinct optimization strategies: (1) maximizing SNR alone, (2) maximizing AR alone, and (3) simultaneously optimizing both SNR and AR. The first two approaches utilize analytical maximization of the cost function, while the third employs Bayesian optimization to identify the optimal operating mode. We applied OMASS4 to observations from the Pico dos Dias Observatory in Brazil, comparing the recommended operational modes and their performance against those chosen by human observers. Had OMASS4 been utilized to optimize the CCDs for all observation nights, efficiency could have been enhanced by 97.17%, 65.08%, and 77.66% for optimization modes 1, 2, and 3, respectively.

This study examines the evolution of the complex order parameter's modulus and phase during a field-induced phase transition (FIPT) of the vacuum interacting with a time-dependent Sauter pulse, analyzing stages such as the quasi electron-positron plasma (QEPP), transient, and residual electron-positron plasma (REPP). By revisiting FIPT under single-sheeted and multi-sheeted pulse conditions, we identify the transient stage as a result of nonlinear coupling within the differential equations governing the order parameter's dynamics. The rapid oscillations observed in the modulus are linked to an abrupt phase shift during this transient phase. Additionally, FIPT is investigated using multi-sheeted Sauter pulses with linear and quadratic frequency chirps. The QEPP stage exhibits complex dynamics characterized by fast, irregular oscillations caused by frequency chirping. Specifically, quadratic chirping induces a pre-transient region in the accelerating phase of the QEPP stage, prior to the electric field reaching its peak. As the quadratic chirp intensity increases, the pre-transient and transient stages converge closer to the electric field maximum, reducing the temporal separation between them. This earlier onset of the transient stage, and consequently the REPP stage, leads to an enhanced pair production rate.

We introduce GarNet, a Garment Similarity Network designed to learn geometric and physical similarities among garments by continuously monitoring a robot as it lifts a garment from a table. The objective is to encode these characteristics into a manifold capable of supporting decisions, such as classifying the garment's shape or estimating its perceived weight. Our method employs an early stopping strategy, allowing GarNet to generate predictions without requiring the garment to transition from a crumpled to a hanging state. Experimental results demonstrate that GarNet achieves 92% accuracy in shape classification and 95.5% in weight prediction, improving upon state-of-the-art approaches by 21% for shape classification.

Spiky coatings, alternatively termed nanoforests or Fakir-like surfaces, have been widely utilized in biotechnology, material sciences, and chemical physics for applications including filtration, sensing, selective protein separation, and superhydrophobic materials. This paper presents a systematic investigation of steady-state diffusion toward a periodic arrangement of absorbing cylindrical pillars extending from a flat surface. By approximating a periodic unit cell as a circular tube with a single pillar, we derive an exact solution to the governing Laplace equation and obtain a simple, precise formula for the total particle flux onto the pillar. The study thoroughly examines how this flux varies with the model's geometric parameters, specifically analyzing several asymptotic limits: thin pillars, disk-shaped pillars, and infinitely long pillars. Ultimately, this research illuminates the trapping efficiency of spiky coatings and clarifies the impacts of pillar anisotropy and diffusional screening.

By measuring the specific heat of herbertsmithite single crystals under high magnetic fields (up to $34$ T), we can separate the low-temperature kagome contribution from extrinsic Schottky-like effects. The kagome component adheres to a unique power law, $C_{p}(T\rightarrow0)\propto T^{\alpha}$ where $\alpha\sim1.5$, and remains constant between $28$ and $34$ T for temperatures ranging from $1$ to $4$ K. These findings impose strict constraints on attempts to replicate the data using low-temperature extrapolations of high-temperature series expansions. We successfully reproduce the experimental results only when approximately $10$ % of the kagome sites are assumed non-contributing. From $0$ to $34$ T, the calculated specific heat exhibits negligible field dependence, supporting an algebraic temperature dependence in zero field characteristic of a critical spin liquid ground state. We discuss the necessity of effective dilution within the kagome planes, which likely arises from copper ions occupying interplane zinc sites. Additionally, at very low temperatures and moderate fields, we observe minor field-induced anomalies in the total specific heat and begin to construct a phase diagram.

We examine the latest intersections between the mathematical framework of two-dimensional topological order and operator algebras, with a specific focus on the Jones theory of subfactors. Our discussion highlights the significance of representation theory within tensor categories and explores links to two-dimensional conformal field theory. Furthermore, we analyze anyon condensation, gapped domain walls, and matrix product operators through the lens of operator algebras.

Cache side-channel attacks reveal secrets by analyzing how victim software interacts with the cache. While practical attacks on cryptographic systems and media libraries have been demonstrated in various scenarios—inferring secret keys and reconstructing private data like images—this work introduces a new approach. First, we define eight criteria for designing a comprehensive detector for cache side-channel vulnerabilities. Subsequently, we propose CacheQL, a novel detector that satisfies all these criteria. CacheQL precisely measures information leakage in binary code by characterizing the distinguishability of logged side-channel traces. Furthermore, it models leakage as a cooperative game, enabling the precise distribution of information leakage to specific program points susceptible to cache side channels. CacheQL is highly optimized to analyze entire side-channel traces from production software, which can contain millions of records, and it mitigates randomness caused by cryptographic blinding, ORAM, or real-world noise.

Our evaluation quantifies side-channel leaks in production cryptographic and media software. We not only localize vulnerabilities previously reported by other detectors but also identify hundreds of new leakage sites in recent versions of OpenSSL (3.0.0), MbedTLS (3.0.0), and Libgcrypt (1.9.4). Many of these newly identified program points reside within cryptosystem pre-processing modules, which existing works have overlooked due to scalability constraints. Additionally, we localize vulnerabilities in Libjpeg (2.1.2) that result in the leakage of input image privacy.

This study examines the global H\"older regularity of weak solutions for a specific class of problems featuring the fractional $(p,q)$-Laplacian, expressed as $(-\Delta)^{s_1}_{p}+(-\Delta)^{s_2}_{q}$, where $1<p,q<\infty$ and $s_1,s_2\in (0,1)$. By utilizing an appropriate Caccioppoli inequality alongside a local boundedness result, we demonstrate a weak Harnack type inequality. Subsequently, through a tailored iteration process, we derive interior H\"older regularity for local weak solutions without assuming they are bounded. The established global H\"older regularity result extends and refines the findings of Giacomoni, Kumar, and Sreenadh (arXiv: 2102.06080) by addressing the subquadratic case ($q<2$) and more general right-hand sides, necessitating a novel methodological approach. Additionally, we prove a nonlocal Harnack type inequality for weak solutions, a contribution of independent significance.

Common deep learning models exhibit significant vulnerability to robustness failures, where minimal noise can deceive state-of-the-art systems into erroneous predictions. Although numerous high-performance attack generation techniques exist, most simply superimpose perturbations onto raw data measured via $L_p$ norms, often disrupting the underlying data structure and resulting in ineffective attacks. This paper introduces a black-box attack strategy that bypasses direct data modification by altering latent features extracted through an autoencoder, thereby measuring noise within the semantic space to preserve data integrity. Autoencoders were trained on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, with optimal adversarial perturbations identified using a genetic algorithm. The proposed method achieved a 100% success rate on the initial 100 samples of both datasets while introducing less perturbation than FGSM.

Given a cover $\mathbb{U}$ of smooth complex algebraic varieties, we define a class $\mathcal{U}$, which includes $\mathbb{U}$, consisting of structures locally definable within an o-minimal expansion of the real numbers. We demonstrate that this class is stable and $\aleph_0$-homogeneous over submodels, leading to the conclusion that $\mathcal{U}$ is categorical in cardinality $\aleph_1$. Furthermore, in the one-dimensional setting, we establish that a minor adjustment to $\mathcal{U}$ forms an abstract elementary class that is categorical across all uncountable cardinals.

We present findings from Canberra-ATCA Doppler-only continuous wave (CW) radar observations of the near-Earth asteroid (163899) 2003 SD220, conducted at a receiving frequency of 7159 MHz (4.19 cm) on December 20, 21, and 22, 2018, during its close approach to within 0.019 au (7.4 lunar distances). Analysis of the echo power spectra suggests the asteroid possesses a significantly elongated, asymmetric shape featuring at least one prominent concavity. The average radar cross section (OC) for opposite sense of circular polarization across the three observation tracks was measured at 0.39, 0.27, and 0.25 km$^{2}$, respectively, with an uncertainty of 35%. A variation in limb-to-limb bandwidth by approximately a factor of two over the three-day period indicates the rotation of an elongated body. Furthermore, we determined a circular polarization ratio of 0.21 $\pm$ 0.07, which aligns with, though is slightly below, the mean values observed for other S-class near-Earth asteroids via radar.

This note introduces a straightforward technique for incorporating count (or quantile) constraints into regression neural networks. Given a training set of $n$ samples, this approach ensures that the predictions for $m$ samples ($m<n$) exceed their corresponding actual values. Distinct from standard quantile regression networks, which rely on minimizing mean absolute differences via specific loss functions, this method is compatible with any loss function. Because the count constraint yields zero gradients almost everywhere, it resists optimization through standard gradient descent. To address this, we propose an alternation scheme grounded in conventional neural network optimization techniques, accompanied by theoretical analysis.

While numerous general-purpose benchmarks exist for Semantic Textual Similarity, none specifically target technical concepts found in patents and scientific literature. This study addresses that gap by introducing a new dataset of human-rated contextual phrase-to-phrase pairs. Comprising nearly 50,000 rated pairs, each annotated with a Cooperative Patent Classification (CPC) code as context, the paper details this dataset alongside several baseline models.

The primary theoretical foundation for the concepts presented in this paper is the theory of cellular automata. This framework consists of a uniform grid where each cell occupies a finite, predefined state, with the initial configuration established at time zero. Subsequent cell states are governed by a set of straightforward rules. This study aims to construct a cellular automaton dedicated to prime numbers and to derive associated axioms, theorems, and conjectures.

We examine a charged Brownian particle situated within an asymmetric bistable electrostatic potential, subject to either an externally applied or magnetically induced time-periodic electric field. A key distinction lies in the field amplitudes: while the applied field's amplitude remains constant regardless of frequency, the amplitude of the magnetically induced field varies with frequency. Adopting terminology from protein channel research, we define the open probability as the fraction of time the particle resides on a specific side of the potential barrier. Our findings reveal that varying the frequency of the applied field and the potential's bias (depolarization) does not produce a peak in open probability. In contrast, when using the induced field, a sharp peak in open probability emerges within a specific, narrow range of low frequencies and low bias values. This observation of stochastic resonance aligns with experimental data regarding voltage-gated Iks and KCNQ1 potassium channels in biological membranes, as well as findings in cardiac myocytes.

This study examines the conformal mapping of a rectangular dam section containing porous material onto the upper half-plane, a scenario relevant to fluid flow calculations in hydraulic structures. The solution employs a representation of the Christoffel-Schwarz elliptic integral using Weierstrass functions. The computation relies on the Taylor series expansion of the sigma function, with its coefficients determined through a recursive process. A straightforward conformal mapping formula is derived, dependent on four parameters and incorporating the sigma function. A numerical experiment was conducted for a specific domain, and the limiting case where the dam width approaches zero was analyzed, demonstrating that the formula converges to the solution of the limiting problem. Additionally, a refined proof of the Weierstrass recursive formula for the Taylor series coefficients of the sigma function is provided.

Recent deep learning advancements have notably improved named entity recognition (NER), yet most current approaches rely on clean data, overlooking the substantial noise present in real-world scenarios from sources like pseudo, weak, or distant annotations. This research addresses NER within a noisy labeling framework by incorporating calibrated confidence estimation. Drawing on empirical insights regarding the distinct training dynamics of noisy versus clean labels, we introduce strategies to derive confidence scores using both local and global independence assumptions. Additionally, we employ a Conditional Random Field (CRF) model to partially marginalize low-confidence labels and propose a calibration technique tailored to the structural properties of entity labels. Finally, we embed this approach into a self-training pipeline to enhance performance. Experiments across four languages in general noisy and distantly labeled contexts validate the method's efficacy; the source code is available at https://github.com/liukun95/Noisy-NER-Confidence-Estimation.
