Drawing upon Frolicher structures, we introduce a definition of a diffiety. This approach yields a natural Vinogradov sequence, and provided a suitable derivation exists, we can construct a well-posed Kadomtsev-Petviashvili hierarchy on this sequence.

Recently, the Computer Vision field has predominantly favored achieving marginal performance gains at the cost of significant complexity increases. To counter this trend, we introduce a novel method designed to enhance image classification accuracy without escalating complexity. By revisiting ensembling—a powerful yet underutilized technique hindered by its inherent computational and training overhead—we made it viable through specific architectural choices. First, we employed bagging by training two end-to-end EfficientNet-b0 models (recognized for their superior accuracy-to-complexity ratio) on disjoint data subsets. Subsequently, we constructed an efficient adaptive ensemble by fine-tuning a trainable combination layer. This approach enabled us to surpass state-of-the-art results by an average of 0.5% in accuracy while maintaining restrained complexity. Specifically, we achieved a reduction in parameter count by 5 to 60 times and in Floating Point Operations Per Second (FLOPs) by 10 to 100 times across several major benchmark datasets, thereby fully aligning with the principles of green AI.

This paper introduces Shallow Aggressive Decoding (SAD), a method designed to enhance the online inference efficiency of Transformers for instantaneous Grammatical Error Correction (GEC). SAD achieves this through two key innovations: first, it enables aggressive parallel decoding of multiple tokens rather than processing them sequentially to maximize computational parallelism; second, it employs a shallow decoder architecture instead of the standard balanced encoder-decoder Transformer structure to lower inference computational costs. Experiments conducted on English and Chinese GEC benchmarks demonstrate that aggressive decoding matches greedy decoding in prediction accuracy while significantly accelerating online inference. When combined with the shallow decoder, this approach delivers even greater speedups over powerful Transformer baselines without compromising quality. Our method not only enables a single model to achieve state-of-the-art performance on English GEC benchmarks—scoring 66.4 F0.5 on the CoNLL-14 test set and 72.9 F0.5 on the BEA-19 test set with nearly a 10x speedup over the Transformer-big model—but is also easily adaptable to other languages. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/AutoTemp/Shallow-Aggressive-Decoding.

This study investigates the cosmic model incorporating GGPDE and matter within a Locally Rotationally Symmetric (LRS) Bianchi type-I spacetime, utilizing a novel holographic dark energy framework under Saez-Ballester theory. We analyze three distinct scenarios: Type Ia supernovae union data; Type Ia supernovae combined with Baryon Acoustic Oscillations (BAO) and Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) observations; and a combination of Hubble Parameter data (H(z)) and Joint Light-curve Analysis (JLA) observations. These analyses reveal a universe model transitioning from a deceleration to an acceleration phase. Our results indicate that cosmological parameters—including energy density ($\rho$), equation of state (EoS), squared speed of sound ($v_s^2$), the term $(\omega_D-\omega_D^{'})$, and the $(r-s)$ plane—are consistent with recent observational findings. Furthermore, we examine the trajectories of $(\omega_D-\omega_D^{'})$ in both thawing and freezing regions, alongside the correspondence between the quintessence field and GGPD dark energy, while highlighting key physical aspects of the GGPDE models.

Although dietary supplements (DS) are extensively consumed, fragmented and incomplete data regarding their efficacy and safety hinder consumers from accessing effective information. While conversational agent (CA) systems are already utilized in healthcare, no such system currently exists to address consumer inquiries about DS usage despite their popularity. This study introduces the development of the first CA system dedicated to DS use.

The Ultraviolet Transient Astronomical Satellite (ULTRASAT) is a scientific space mission equipped with an astronomical telescope. Led by the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel and the Israel Space Agency, the project involves the German Deutsches Elektronen Synchrotron, which designed and constructed the focal plane camera. The mission's primary objectives are to identify counterparts to gravitational wave sources and supernovae, with a planned 2024 launch to geostationary orbit. The telescope offers a field-of-view of approximately 200 square degrees and is optimized for the near-ultraviolet spectrum ranging from 220 to 280 nm. Its focal plane array consists of four backside-illuminated CMOS sensors, each with 22.4 megapixels, totaling an active area of 90x90 mm². Before the final flight sensors were manufactured, smaller test sensors were evaluated to inform critical design choices; these prototypes share the same epitaxial layer and anti-reflective coating (ARC) architecture as the flight units. This paper details the characterization of these test sensors, including the analysis of dark current and read noise across varying device temperatures. A temperature-independent noise component is identified as stemming from on-die infrared emission and self-heating within the read-out electronics. Using a high-precision photometric calibration system referenced against PTB/NIST standards (220–1100 nm), the study determined the quantum efficiency (QE), quantum yield for wavelengths below 300 nm, system non-linearity, and conversion gain, alongside a discussion of uncertainties regarding the setup's performance parameters. Among three ARC options (Tstd, T1, and T2), option T2 was selected for the final ULTRASAT UV sensor as it maximizes out-of-band rejection and achieves peak efficiency within the operational waveband, reaching a maximum QE of approximately 80% at 245 nm.

We introduce a Poisson-Bikerman (PBik) framework to determine the differential capacitance (DC) of electrical double layers (EDLs) within aqueous electrolytes and ionic liquids. This theory extends the classical Poisson-Boltzmann model by incorporating distinct steric energies for ions and water molecules of varying sizes, analogous to how it handles electrical energies for ions with different charges. In this molecular mean field approach, the physical volumes of water and ions, including interstitial voids, align with those observed in molecular dynamics simulations. Derived from Fermi distributions applicable to ions and water of arbitrary shapes and volumes, the PBik formula simplifies to the Bikerman-Freise equation when assuming a lattice model of uniformly sized ions. While the Gouy-Chapman formula predicts U-shaped DC curves for point-like ions in dilute solutions, the PBik model shows these curves evolving into a camel (Bactrian) shape and finally a bell shape as the volume fraction of ions and water increases from zero to large values. This transition is defined by critical and inflection voltages related to particle volume fraction, which govern the steric and electrical energies describing the competition between space and charge, as well as saturation properties, within the condensed EDL layer under high fields. Under these conditions, steric energy is as significant as electrical energy. The PBik model generates symmetric DC curves reflecting the delicate balance of steric interactions between asymmetric-sized ions and water, matching experimental results for KPF6 in aqueous solutions. Furthermore, it calculates asymmetric curves that capture the nuanced balance of steric or electrical interactions among ions with differing volumes or charges in ionic liquids.

The bipartite entanglement of the antiferromagnetic mixed spin-(1/2, $S$) Heisenberg dimer (MSHD) is investigated via exact analytical diagonalization using the negativity metric. Assuming uniaxial single-ion anisotropy influences only the higher spin-$S$ components ($S > 1/2$), the initial $2S$-fold ground-state degeneracy is partially lifted, resulting in a two-fold degenerate ground state characterized by total magnetization per dimer of $\pm(S - 1/2)$. Findings indicate that maximum quantum entanglement occurs in the antiferromagnetic ground state of MSHD for any arbitrary half-odd-integer spin $S$, independent of exchange and single-ion anisotropy parameters. In contrast, for integer spin $S$ under easy-plane single-ion anisotropy, the degree of quantum entanglement displays an increasing trend with a distinct spin-$S$ driven crossing point. The increase in spin magnitude is identified as a critical factor enhancing the threshold temperature above which thermal entanglement disappears. Furthermore, the combination of easy-plane single-ion anisotropy and increased spin-$S$ magnitude serves as another significant mechanism for boosting thermal entanglement in the MSHD.

We re-examine the magnetic behavior of the antiferromagnetic Kondo lattice CeNiAsO using $^{75}$As nuclear magnetic resonance. Our findings validate two sequential antiferromagnetic phase transitions of the Ce moments occurring at $T_{N1}=9.0(3)$ K and $T_{N2}=7.0(3)$ K. Below $T^*\sim15$ K, we detect a Knight shift anomaly marked by the breakdown of $K(T)-\chi(T)$ scaling, indicating the emergence of coherent $c-f$ correlations; this energy scale is corroborated by the spin-lattice relaxation rate ($1/T_1$). Furthermore, an analysis of spin dynamics demonstrates that spin fluctuations in CeNiAsO exhibit a quasi-two-dimensional nature. This study establishes a foundation for future pressure-dependent $^{75}$As NMR investigations.

The characteristics of newly predicted thermally fissile thorium and uranium isotopes are investigated using the relativistic mean field (RMF) model with an axially deformed basis. Ground states, first intrinsic excited states, and matter densities were computed for highly neutron-rich isotopes of both elements. Decay pathways, including $\alpha$- and $\beta$-decay, were examined; results indicate that while these neutron-rich isotopes are stable against $\alpha$-decay, they are highly unstable toward $\beta$-decay, with predicted lifetimes on the order of tens of seconds. If utilized prior to decay, these nuclei could generate substantial energy via multi-fragmentation fission, holding significant implications for astrophysics. Nucleonic density distributions were analyzed to identify internal clusters. Additionally, isomeric states ranging from 2 to 3 MeV were discovered in certain cases, and three minima were identified in the potential energy surfaces of $^{228-230}$Th and $^{228-234}$U isotopes.

Given a string $T$ of length $n$ drawn from an alphabet $\Sigma$ of size $\sigma$, where $\Sigma \subset \{1,2,\ldots,n^{O(1)}\}$, we aim to preprocess $T$ such that for any specified range $[i,j]$, we can efficiently return a representation of the shortest string over $\Sigma$ missing from the substring $T[i]\cdots T[j]$. We introduce an $O(n)$-space data structure that constructs in $O(n\log_\sigma n)$ time and responds to these queries in constant time.

This paper employs canonical bundle formulas to extend an established theorem by Kawamata regarding the semiampleness of nef and abundant log canonical divisors. Specifically, we demonstrate that for klt pairs $(X,B)$ where $K_X+B$ is effective, if $L \in Pic(X)$ is nef, then the nefness and abundance of $K_X+B+L$ guarantee its semiampleness. This result effectively broadens Kawamata's theorem to the context of generalized abundance.

Real-world audio environments comprise time-varying collections of sound sources, each producing distinct events that blend together in recordings. These constituent events are semantically linked within the scene: while the scene represents a union of source classes, not every class naturally co-occurs. Motivated by this, the paper investigates using unsupervised automatic sound separation to break down unlabeled audio scenes into multiple semantically connected views, facilitating self-supervised contrastive learning. We observe that training models to associate input mixtures with their automatically separated outputs generates more robust representations than previous methods relying solely on mixtures. Furthermore, we find that perfect source separation is unnecessary for effective contrastive learning, as various convergence states of separation systems produce useful and often complementary data transformations. Our top-performing system integrates these unsupervised separation models into a unified augmentation front-end, jointly optimizing objectives for similarity maximization and coincidence prediction across different views. Consequently, this approach yields an unsupervised audio representation that matches the performance of state-of-the-art alternatives on the standard shallow AudioSet classification benchmark.

The distinctive characteristics of topological semimetals stem from their nontrivial band structure, yet the influence of strong electron correlations on these states in actual materials has been largely uninvestigated. In this study, we examine the magnetotransport properties of YbCdSn single crystals. We identify two primary experimental signatures of electron correlations via magnetic susceptibility and specific heat measurements. These correlations result in an intermediate valence state and an increase in the effective mass of charge carriers. Consequently, this correlated state displays large nonsaturating magnetoresistance, low carrier density, a magnetic field-induced crossover from semiconductor-like to metallic behavior, and a resistivity plateau at low temperatures. Additionally, a cusp-like magnetoconductivity observed at low magnetic fields suggests the presence of weak antilocalization. Finally, band structure calculations for the Yb$^{2+}$ state predict that YbCdSn is a topological nodal-line semimetal.

This work addresses the class of bounded-degree graphs within any minor-closed family, including planar graphs. For a graph with $n$ vertices and degree bound $d$, these classes admit hyperfinite decompositions: by removing $\epsilon dn$ edges for a sufficiently small $\epsilon$, the remaining connected components have sizes independent of $n$. A key instrument for sublinear algorithms and property testing in these settings is the partition oracle, first introduced by Hassidim, Kelner, Nguyen, and Onak (FOCS 2009). This oracle is a local mechanism that provides consistent access to a hyperfinite decomposition without preprocessing; given a vertex $v$, it returns the component containing $v$ in time independent of $n$, ensuring all responses align with a single decomposition. The original oracle by Hassidim et al. operates in $d^{\text{poly}(d/\epsilon)}$ time per query and posed the open question of whether poly$(d/\epsilon)$-time oracles exist. While Levi-Ron (ICALP 2013) improved this to $d^{\log(d/\epsilon) \cdot \text{poly}(1)}$ time, this paper resolves the open problem by presenting poly$(d/\epsilon)$-time partition oracles for bounded-degree graphs in any minor-closed family. Departing from prior combinatorial approaches, we utilize spectral graph theory, building on a recent toolkit developed by the authors for efficient property testing. Our findings enable poly$(d/\epsilon)$-query testers for any monotone and additive property in these families, such as bipartiteness in planar graphs. Furthermore, our results yield poly$(d/\epsilon)$-query algorithms for additive $\epsilon n$-approximations of problems including maximum matching, minimum vertex cover, maximum independent set, and minimum dominating set.

Machine learning classifiers that achieve high test accuracy often struggle against adversarial attacks, a problem typically thought to be solved by adversarial training. However, this paper reveals that the opposite can occur: while adversarial training improves performance with ample data, it can actually impair robust generalization when sample sizes are small. We first establish this phenomenon in a high-dimensional linear classification setting with noiseless data, offering insights that likely extend to feature learning models. Additionally, experiments on standard image datasets show that this behavior also manifests in perceptible attacks—such as mask attacks and object corruptions—that significantly degrade class information.

A quantum channel is classified as a mixed-unitary channel if it can be represented as a convex sum of unitary channels. We demonstrate that, given the Choi representation of a quantum channel, determining whether it qualifies as a mixed-unitary channel is NP-hard under polynomial-time Turing reductions. This computational hardness remains true even if the channel is not situated within an inverse-polynomial distance (relative to the space dimension) from the boundary of the set of mixed-unitary channels.

Based on data from SOHO, STEREO, and Hinode, this study examines magnetic field evolution within an equatorial coronal hole. Two dipoles emerge sequentially; the negative polarity of the first dipole vanishes following an interaction with the second dipole's positive polarity, a process accompanied by a jet and plasma eruption. The second dipole's opposite polarities initially separate before canceling each other out, marking the first such observation in a coronal hole. Over two days, as the second dipole's unsigned magnetic flux decreased from 9.8 × 10^20 Mx to 3.0 × 10^20 Mx, 171 Å brightness dropped by 75% and coronal loops contracted significantly. At the cancellation sites, strong transverse fields directed from positive to negative elements were detected alongside Doppler red-shifts averaging 0.9 km s⁻¹, a value comparable to the 1.0 km s⁻¹ horizontal velocity of the cancelling island. Several days later, the northeastern sector of the coronal hole, hosting the dipoles, appeared as a quiet region. These findings support the hypothesis that the dipole interaction results from flux reconnection, whereas the cancellation of the second dipole's opposite polarities is driven by the submergence of original loops, thereby enhancing our understanding of coronal hole evolution.

The interplay among unconventional superconductivity, antiferromagnetism, and nematic order in iron-based superconductors (FeSCs) remains a subject of intense debate. While many FeSCs exhibit superconductivity near states characterized by nematic and magnetic ordering, LiFeAs stands out as an exceptional stoichiometric compound that becomes superconducting below 18 K without undergoing any structural or magnetic transitions. Despite this, recent experiments have hinted at the presence of finite nematic fluctuations and potentially a nematic superconducting phase. This study utilizes elastoresistance to quantify nematic fluctuations in pristine LiFeAs, comparing these results with data from LiFeAs doped with low concentrations of Co and V, as well as with NaFeAs, which displays both magnetic and nematic ordering. Our findings indicate that both pristine LiFeAs and Co-doped LiFeAs are situated far from a nematic instability.

This note offers an overview of geometric symmetries governing spin-0 perturbations in four-dimensional black hole and de Sitter spacetimes. For black holes, we examine static perturbations, which possess exact geometric symmetries forming an SO(1,3) group. This group comprises three spatial rotations and three conformal Killing vectors satisfying a specific melodic condition. The resulting static perturbation solutions constitute a unitary principal series representation of this group. Recent ladder symmetries, derived from this representation, account for the established vanishing of black hole Love numbers. In contrast, dynamical perturbations around de Sitter space exhibit symmetries consistent with the SO(1,4) isometry group. As previously noted, quasinormal solutions in this context form a non-unitary representation of the isometry group, for which we derive explicit ladder operator expressions. In both scenarios, these ladder structures bridge the boundary conditions at the horizon versus infinity (for black holes) or the origin (for de Sitter space), appearing explicitly as contiguous relations within the hypergeometric solutions.

We demonstrate the optimal protection of quantum states and entanglement at non-zero temperatures through measurement reversal following weak measurement, providing explicit formulas for this protection.

It is widely accepted in linguistics and discourse studies that discourse relations are understood through explicit content and the shared or implicit knowledge of the speaker and listener. Yet, the specific role of the lexical semantics of arguments remains ambiguous. We introduce a computational method for analyzing contrast and concession relations within the PDTB corpus. Our research illuminates how much lexical semantics aids in signaling both explicit and implicit discourse relations and clarifies the distinct contributions of various parts of speech in doing so. Furthermore, this study helps bridge the divide between corpus and computational linguistics by developing transparent and explainable models of discourse relations grounded in the synonymy and antonymy of their arguments.

This work presents a numerical investigation into amorphous counterparts of a two-dimensional photonic Chern insulator. These disordered lattices are composed of gyromagnetic rods that violate time-reversal symmetry, with positions determined by a close-packing algorithm that ensures short-range order is tunable while eliminating long-range order. Results indicate that the topologically nontrivial gaps characteristic of the photonic Chern insulator remain stable within the amorphous phase, provided adequate short-range order exists. Consequently, strongly nonreciprocal and robust transmission arises through edge states that propagate ballistically without long-range order and remain exponentially localized at the lattice boundaries. Notably, nonreciprocal transmission is enhanced even at minimal levels of short-range order, a condition where distinct spectral gaps are no longer observable.

Symbolic music generation heavily depends on a generative model's ability to represent context, with Transformer-based architectures currently dominating this field. However, existing research often neglects the structural components of music, such as intros, verses, and choruses, which are essential for learning musical context. This paper introduces a hierarchical Transformer model designed to capture multi-scale contexts. During the encoding phase, we implement a Fragment Scope Localization layer to segment music into chords and sections, followed by a multi-scale attention mechanism to learn contexts at the note, chord, and section levels. For decoding, we propose a hierarchical Transformer utilizing fine-decoders to generate sections in parallel and a coarse-decoder to synthesize the complete piece. Additionally, a Music Style Normalization layer ensures stylistic consistency across generated sections. Evaluated on two open MIDI datasets, our model surpasses current state-of-the-art music generators. Notably, visual assessments reveal our approach excels in melody reuse, producing more realistic music.

The nonscattering optical anapole state corresponds to radiationless field distributions within open resonators, providing novel degrees of freedom for customizing light-matter interactions. Traditional approaches to achieving this state depend on complex manipulation of electromagnetic multipolar moments of all orders to ensure superpositions of vanishing moment strengths at a specific wavelength. In contrast, this study demonstrates the excitation of an optical radiationless anapole hidden within a resonant state of a silicon nanoparticle using a tightly focused radially polarized (RP) beam. The simultaneous existence of a magnetic resonant state and anapole condition at the same wavelength allows for triggering the resonant state with a tightly focused azimuthally polarized (AP) beam, even when the corresponding electric multipole coefficient is zero. Consequently, high-contrast transitions between the radiationless anapole condition and ideal magnetic resonant scattering can be experimentally realized in the visible spectrum. This proposed mechanism is versatile and applicable to various nanostructure types. Our findings illustrate that the unique synergy between structured light and structured Mie resonances offers new avenues for tailoring light-matter interactions, potentially advancing functional meta-optics.

While a sequence of segments where each subsequent segment is $n$ times larger than the preceding one offers a straightforward geometric representation of the natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$, this paper explores the inverse scenario. We endow the set of similar triangles with parallel sides with an algebraic structure, introduce a geometric method for triangle addition, and apply this approach to dissect a triangle into fifteen triangles with distinct side lengths.

Under the assumption that both the target variable $Y$ and the model $F$ are subgaussian, we derive sharp oracle inequalities for empirical risk minimization (ERM) in regression. When $F$ is convex, our bound achieves sharpness in the minimax sense. Furthermore, under mild conditions on $F$, the ERM error rate remains optimal even if the procedure succeeds with only constant probability. Our analysis also includes a novel proof of minimax results for the Gaussian regression model.

This paper introduces multiple quantum models utilizing algebraic geometry. It depicts the Universe as a presheaf defined on the "space of ultimation" (representing the branching future) and taking values in a category that extends the one opposite to C*-algebras. The presented models demonstrate how ordinary space-times from both Special and General Relativity can be derived from ultrametric spaces.

Although Wikipedia is available in 287 languages, its content is not evenly distributed across them. This study explores the creation of open-domain Wikipedia summaries for underrepresented languages by leveraging structured data from Wikidata. We introduce a neural network architecture featuring copy mechanisms that generates concise, understandable single-sentence summaries derived from Wikidata triples. The efficacy of our method is validated by comparing it against baseline models on two distinct languages: Arabic, which is morphologically complex with a vast vocabulary compared to English, and Esperanto, a constructed language noted for its ease of learning.

Historically, calculating the thermal conductivity of glasses from first principles has been considered prohibitively difficult. Previous studies have demonstrated significant hurdles in achieving convergence regarding time and length scales when utilizing either the Allen-Feldman or Green-Kubo approaches, suggesting that atomistic models with thousands of atoms—sizes unattainable by standard first-principles methods—are required. Furthermore, these traditional methods either ignore anharmonicity (Allen-Feldman) or fail to incorporate Bose-Einstein statistics for atomic vibrations (Green-Kubo), leaving the significance of these factors unresolved. In this work, we introduce a first-principles framework capable of computing thermal conductivity in glasses above the plateau, fully accounting for structural disorder, anharmonicity, and quantum Bose-Einstein statistics. Our approach integrates the Wigner formulation of thermal transport with convergence-acceleration techniques and is validated on vitreous silica using both first-principles calculations and a quantum-accurate machine-learned potential. We demonstrate that models of vitreous silica with fewer than 200 atoms can accurately predict macroscopic thermal conductivity and that anharmonicity has a negligible impact on heat transport in this material. Finally, we examine the microscopic factors driving conductivity trends at high temperatures, confirming that our calculations align with experimental data in the range above the plateau (50 < T < 450 K), where radiative effects are insignificant.

Eukaryotic cells utilize flagella for locomotion and fluid transport. We introduce the inaugural three-dimensional, time-resolved visualization of the *Chlamydomonas reinhardtii* flagellar waveform, featuring a freshwater model alga. Our findings indicate that during the power stroke, the flagella exhibit rotational symmetry around the cell's central axis, whereas the recovery stroke demonstrates mirror symmetry along the same axis. Leveraging our 3D imaging data, we evaluated the validity of resistive force theory by approximating a force-free state with a cell attached to a micropipette. The derived swimming velocities and rotation rates align well with experimental observations of freely swimming cells.

Beam-beam interactions in the proposed BNL ERL-based Electron-Ion Collider (eRHIC) exhibit unique characteristics that distinguish them from those found in both lepton and hadron colliders. By utilizing the electron beam for a single pass, we anticipate achieving a luminosity approximately ten times higher than that of a comparable ring-ring collision scheme. Nevertheless, without appropriate mitigation strategies, beam-beam interactions can degrade or even cause the loss of both electron and hadron beams. This discussion will cover detrimental effects such as electron beam disruption and mismatch, ion beam kink instability and noise heating, along with potential countermeasures.

This paper investigates the stability of an Einstein static universe within the DGP braneworld framework, examining two distinct branches characterized by $\epsilon=\pm1$. Under the assumption of a perfect fluid with a constant equation of state, $w$, the analysis reveals that no stable Einstein static solution exists for the $\epsilon=1$ branch. Conversely, for the $\epsilon=-1$ branch, the Einstein static universe is stable provided that $-1<w<-1/3$. In this stable regime, the universe can persist eternally into the past and may experience an infinite series of non-singular oscillations, thereby resolving the big bang singularity issue inherent in standard cosmological models.

Introducing adsorbed atoms (adatoms) as impurities into solid-state host matrices can profoundly alter their characteristics, particularly within low-dimensional structures like one-dimensional organic polymer chains or quasi-one-dimensional graphene nanoribbons, where the optical properties, including absorption cross-sections, can be uniquely manipulated. While the Purcell effect remains the predominant method for linking quantum emitters to optical antennas, it exclusively addresses spontaneous emission into a modified photonic environment and neglects charge transfer between the emitter and the antenna. To address this limitation, we introduce a tight-binding framework that couples an adatom, modeled as a two-level system, to a finite Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain acting as the optical antenna. Our systematic analysis investigates how coupling strength and adatom location affect the optical behavior of these molecular chains. The model incorporates inter-system hopping to account for charge transfer in both directions, alongside Coulomb interactions occurring within the antenna and between the adatom and antenna. Our results demonstrate that attaching an adatom to a bulk site within the linear chain induces significant optical changes even at relatively weak coupling strengths. Furthermore, we find that the adatom's position is a critical factor determining whether and to what extent the chain's optical properties are modified. Consequently, we propose this adatom-chain hybrid system as a versatile, tunable platform for nanoscale light-matter interactions.

This study estimates average response curves regarding treatment duration in the Emergency Department (ED), proposing that extending this time could improve admission decisions. However, empirically validating this approach is challenging because treatment duration is a continuous time-to-event variable, heavily influenced by unobserved patient health needs, jointly determined with the admission decision, and only potentially modifiable via a shift in realized time. By formalizing the admission process as a directed acyclic graph, we demonstrate that nonparametric identification of these response curves is impossible due to unmeasured confounding from patient health needs. Consequently, we employ a parametric model featuring a latent variable for health needs and a threshold regression model for the admission process. Applied to observational data from 28,862 abdominal pain patients at a large tertiary teaching hospital, our results indicate that standardizing ED treatment time to two hours instead of one would lower admission rates from 41.6% (95% CI: [40.6, 42.7]) to 32.7% (95% CI: [32.2, 33.2]). Furthermore, increasing realized treatment time by 30 minutes could reduce admission rates by 1.1% (95% CI: [-1.1, 3.2]), with minimal impact on 30-day revisit or readmission rates.

This project is dedicated to researching and prototyping an extension to Distributed MARF that enables its services to be managed via SNMP, the widely recognized management protocol. The decision to adopt SNMP over MARF's proprietary protocols is driven by the need for seamless integration with standard network service and device management practices. By utilizing SNMP, administrators can oversee MARF nodes using familiar tools and methods, allowing them to monitor performance, collect statistics, and configure settings just as they would with other network devices and application servers.

The study investigates the production of (anti)hypertriton nuclei, $\rm ^3_{\Lambda}H$ and $\rm ^3_{\overline \Lambda}\overline H$, in Cu+Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm{NN}}}=200$ GeV across three centrality intervals (0-10%, 10-30%, and 30-60%) using a dynamically constrained phase-space coalescence model combined with [PACIAE] simulations. The results compare the yields of $\rm ^3H(^3\overline H)$ and $\rm ^3He(^3\overline {He})$, revealing that light nuclei and hypernuclei production rises sharply from peripheral to central collisions, whereas the ratios of anti-particles to particles remain constant across different centrality bins. The calculated strangeness population factor, $S_3=\rm{{^3_{\Lambda}H}/({^3{He}}\times \Lambda/p)}$, is found to be approximately unity, aligning with both STAR experimental data and theoretical predictions. This agreement indicates that the phase-space occupancy of strange quarks is comparable to that of light quarks and supports the formation of deconfined, high-temperature quark matter in these Cu+Cu interactions.

Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) is an NLP task focused on identifying the appropriate meaning of a word within a sentence from a set of predefined options. While existing systems have achieved remarkable performance, they often struggle with rare word senses due to the uneven distribution of senses in training data. To address this, we employ data augmentation to boost the frequency of least frequent senses (LFS), thereby mitigating distributional bias. We introduce Sense-Maintained Sentence Mixup (SMSMix), a novel word-level mixup technique that preserves the sense of a target word. SMSMix utilizes mask prediction to smoothly blend two sentences while retaining the specific span identified by saliency scores to ensure the target word's meaning remains intact. To our knowledge, this marks the first application of mixup in NLP designed to maintain the semantic integrity of a specific word. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our augmentation approach effectively provides richer information regarding rare senses during training while keeping the target sense label consistent.

**Background:** Following the early 2020 coronavirus outbreak, global policymakers and local governments were forced to design Non-Pharmaceutical Interventions (NPIs) under conditions of significant uncertainty. In the absence of vaccines or treatments during the initial epidemic phase, algorithmic prediction emerged as a vital tool for guiding local policy. However, replicating a leading epidemiological model used by a southern Brazilian region revealed that it depended excessively on manually set covariates and reacted too slowly to shifting data trends.

**Methods:** We developed four variations of the original approach to incorporate daily reported infection data and more explicitly address case under-reporting. Two of these versions also accounted for delays in test reporting. We simulated weekly death forecasts spanning from May 31, 2020, to January 31, 2021. This workflow enabled the use of a streamlined model version after the initial calibration week, utilizing weekly updated Google Mobility data as covariates for each simulation run.

**Findings:** The modifications resulted in a model that was significantly less reactive and faster at adapting to scenarios following a death peak. Accounting for substantial under-reporting greatly enhanced model stability, while modeling retroactively added data (due to the "hot" nature of the dataset) had a negligible effect on performance.

**Interpretation:** Although death statistics remain more reliable than case counts, modeling cases alongside an "overestimate" parameter offers a robust alternative for enhancing forecasting accuracy. This approach is particularly effective for long-range predictions and in the aftermath of an infection wave's peak.

We derive a family of coercive Korn-type inequalities tailored to generalised incompatible fields within the superlinear growth regime, adhering to precise criteria. This work optimally extends and unifies various established inequalities that are fundamental to the existence theory across numerous continuum mechanics models. Distinct from our prior research (ArXiv 2206.10373), which addressed the $p=1$ case with incompatibilities defined by the matrix curl, the current study focuses on $p>1$. This shift leverages substantially stronger results from harmonic analysis while accommodating more general incompatibilities. Specifically, we achieve sharp generalisations of recently established inequalities by the last two authors and M\"{u}ller (Calc. Var. PDE 60 (2021), 150) regarding incompatible Korn-type inequalities with conformally invariant dislocation energy. Furthermore, our methodology, which applies to higher-order scenarios, yields the first and sharp inequalities involving Kr\"{o}ner's incompatibility tensor $\mathrm{inc}$.

A direct numerical simulation examines an oblique shock wave impacting a turbulent boundary layer at Mach 2.28 and moderate Reynolds numbers, replicating the flow conditions of the experiment by Dupont et al. (2006). The study investigates low-frequency shock unsteadiness—a subject of significant prior research—using the Morlet wavelet transform. Due to the transform's compact support in both physical and Fourier domains, it enables the tracking of the time evolution across various scales of wall-pressure fluctuations. This capability also allows for the definition of a local intermittency measure, expressed as a frequency-dependent flatness factor, to identify energy bursts that define the shock's intermittent behavior at different scales. A key finding is that wavelet decomposition reveals broadband shock movement as a series of sparse temporal events, each with a distinct time scale, a detail obscured by classical Fourier analysis which only captures time-averaged behavior. Furthermore, a proposed procedure processes relevant time series, such as wall-pressure history or separation bubble extent, using a local intermittency-based condition to filter turbulent content near the shock foot and isolate the intermittent signal component. Additionally, wavelet analysis uncovers intermittent behavior in the breathing motion of the recirculation bubble behind the reflected shock and identifies a direct, partial correspondence between the most significant intermittent events in the separation region and those at the shock foot wall-pressure.

The extensive availability of large-scale datasets on scholarly work has allowed science to be examined quantitatively. In this study, we utilize established cognitive models from anthropology to characterize the personal collaboration networks of scientists—specifically their ego networks—from the perspective of individual researchers, quantifying the cognitive effort invested in each collaboration. Building on these models, we explore the relationship between the structure of academic collaborations, academic performance, and mobility across various career stages, considering both purely academic mobility (changes in affiliation) and geographical mobility (physical relocation). Our analysis relies on a geo-referenced dataset of publications from 81,500 authors sourced from Scopus. Our primary finding reveals a strong correlation between co-authorship ego network structure and academic performance: higher publication counts and impact factors correspond to larger collaboration networks. However, we identify a capacity bound effect, where beyond a certain threshold, increased performance shows diminishing correlation with network size. Additionally, while international migrants are more effective at expanding their networks than those moving only within a country, domestic migrants are better at leveraging collaborations to achieve higher impact. Furthermore, high levels of academic mobility do not necessarily lead to improved performance or larger networks.

Anomaly detection within attributed networks has garnered significant attention across various domains, including cybersecurity and financial fraud prevention. Although deep learning has been widely adopted for graph representation, current methods often rely on Euclidean graph encoders as their primary architecture, potentially discarding crucial hierarchical details, particularly in intricate network structures. To address this limitation, we introduce a streamlined anomaly detection framework grounded in hyperbolic self-supervised contrastive learning. Our method begins with data augmentation via subgraph sampling, followed by the exploitation of hierarchical information within hyperbolic space through exponential and logarithmic mappings. An anomaly score is subsequently derived by contrasting negative and positive pair scores through a discriminative mechanism. Comprehensive experiments across four real-world datasets confirm that our approach outperforms existing representative baselines.

We model the phase space of a system comprising $n$ identical qudits (each of prime dimension $d$) as a grid containing $d^{n} \times d^{n}$ points, labeling the axes using the finite field $GF(d^{n})$. Within this framework, displacement operators enable the definition of $s$-parametrized quasidistribution functions that mirror the properties of their continuous analogs. These same displacements facilitate the construction of finite coherent states, provided a fiducial state is selected; we choose this reference as an eigenstate of the discrete Fourier transform to analyze the factorization characteristics of the resulting states. Furthermore, we generalize these concepts to discrete squeezed states, revealing their fascinating connection to entanglement across different qudits.

We have derived the commutation relation for a cavity mode that is driven by coherent light and coupled to a two-level atom. Our findings indicate that the commutation relation for a free cavity mode, whether containing photons or not, remains the standard one. In contrast, the commutation relation for a cavity mode interacting with a two-level atom deviates from the usual form.

This chapter explores avalanches within glasses and disordered systems, examining the macroscopic dynamics they drive. We provide a concise overview of three distinct systems where avalanches occur: the depinning of disordered interfaces, the yielding of amorphous materials, and the jamming transition. Avoiding heavy formalism, we present findings from theoretical frameworks such as mean-field theory, scaling laws, exponent relations, the renormalization group, and selected results from replica theory. Our discussion highlights both the intricate physics underlying avalanches and emerging perspectives on the macroscopic flow behavior observed beyond the depinning or yielding thresholds.

Humans can quickly grasp structural word properties and apply their syntactic knowledge consistently across various grammatical situations. This study evaluates whether modern neural language models can replicate this human-like behavior in English, specifically examining the impact of structural supervision on learning. First, we investigate few-shot learning by designing controlled experiments that test models' generalization of syntactic nominal number and verbal argument structures using tokens encountered as few as twice during training. Second, we examine the invariance of learned representations: the capacity to transfer syntactic generalizations from a base context, such as a simple declarative active-voice sentence, to a transformed context, like an interrogative sentence. The evaluation involves four models trained on identical data: an n-gram baseline, an LSTM, and two LSTM variants enhanced with explicit structural supervision (Dyer et al., 2016; Charniak et al., 2016). Results indicate that in most scenarios, neural models successfully derive appropriate syntactic generalizations after minimal exposure, often requiring only two training examples. Furthermore, the two structurally supervised models demonstrate superior generalization accuracy compared to the standard LSTM. Finally, all neural models prove capable of using information from base contexts to inform expectations in transformed contexts, suggesting they have acquired certain invariance properties of syntax.

Word embeddings serve as robust feature representations that enable high-quality outcomes across numerous NLP tasks. Uncontextualized embeddings remain prevalent in many applications, particularly in resource-constrained environments lacking the memory capacity and GPUs necessary for more advanced methods. Building on the historical efficacy of these techniques, this paper offers a retrospective analysis of prominent word embedding algorithms. We deconstruct methods such as Word2vec and GloVe into a unified framework, revealing shared prerequisites for achieving high performance. We posit that the theoretical insights derived from this study will lay the groundwork for the more informed design of future models.

Models utilizing dust reference fields within relational formalism have proven valuable for constructing gauge-invariant perturbation theory to arbitrary orders in the canonical framework. While these reference fields alter the dynamical equations governing perturbations, significant questions persist regarding their connection to conventional perturbation theories for inflatons coupled to gravity and multi-fluid systems, as well as the interpretation of these modifications in terms of physical degrees of freedom. This manuscript addresses those gaps for Brown-Kucha\v{r} and Gaussian dust models, each characterized by three scalar physical degrees of freedom. By introducing a specific set of gauge-invariant variables on the reduced phase space of these dust reference models, we establish their relationship with standard inflationary and multi-fluid systems involving ordinary dust. We derive the modifications to the Bardeen equation in the longitudinal gauge and the Mukhanov-Sasaki equation in the spatially-flat gauge caused by dust clocks, expressed explicitly in terms of physical degrees of freedom. Consequently, we obtain a closed system of equations encompassing all necessary degrees of freedom to investigate the evolution of scalar perturbations. Our analysis demonstrates, for the first time, that even in two-fluid systems, there exists a natural selection of gauge-invariant variables for any given gauge; this choice provides a direct physical interpretation and simplifies the dynamical equations.

This study examines Markovian queues monitored by a controller at random intervals governed by a Poisson process. Upon each observation, the controller adjusts the service rate to the lesser of the current queue length or a predefined maximum, a setting that remains in effect until the subsequent inspection. We analyze the resulting two-dimensional Markov process tracking both queue size and server speed, focusing on two distinct time-scale separation regimes: those with infinitely frequent and those with infinitely long examination periods. While the intermediate regime presents significant analytical challenges, we further explore the system's dynamics by investigating two model variants where the controller acts solely as an observer without modifying the server's speed.

We provide an in-depth numerical study of the head-on collision between a two-kink and two-antikink system. Our findings reveal that the escape of oscillon-like structures corresponds to a pair of standard $\phi^4$ kinks moving apart. New evidence suggests that lump-like defects can arise from two-kink interactions to create metastable states. Furthermore, these configurations indicate escape windows possessing a fractal structure akin to the $n$-bounce sequence observed in $\phi^4$ kink interactions. Finally, our numerical experiment demonstrates that by appropriately perturbing a lump-like defect, one can recover another metastable lump-like configuration.

Recent efforts to implement full-duplex (FD) communication in millimeter-wave (mmWave) systems have attracted considerable attention due to their promising potential. This paper introduces a cost-effective design for mmWave FD systems that dynamically minimizes the RF beam codebook in a computationally efficient way, ensuring the codebook consists only of RF beams that avoid saturating the receiver (Rx) chain from self-interference (SI). The analog beamformer suppresses SI to a level where the remaining interference can be entirely eliminated through digital SI cancellation, enabling the digital beamformer to focus on the target channel without SI contamination. To minimize the computational burden of this approach, we propose two practically tight sufficient conditions that prevent Rx saturation. Performance evaluations in realistically modeled mmWave FD scenarios demonstrate that the proposed design achieves performance comparable to ideal FD systems and other benchmarks while incurring significantly lower costs.

Multi-access edge computing (MEC) and network virtualization serve as critical enablers for fifth-generation (5G) networks to support a wide array of applications and services. These services are typically delivered as fully connected virtual network functions (VNFs) via service function chaining (SFC). However, allocating SFC resources at the network edge remains challenging due to complexities in VNF placement, chaining, and scheduling. To address these issues, this paper introduces a game-theoretic approach aimed at minimizing service latency within the edge SFC context. The resource allocation challenge is decomposed into two subproblems: VNF placement and routing, and VNF scheduling. For the placement and routing subproblem, we model it as a mean field game (MFG), treating VNFs as entities competing for edge resources to lower MEC node consumption and user latency. We implement this using a reinforcement learning technique based on the Ishikawa-Mann learning algorithm (IMLA). For the scheduling subproblem, we formulate it as a matching game between VNFs and edge resources to determine the optimal execution order while reducing latency. To solve this efficiently, we propose an enhanced multi-step deferred acceptance algorithm (eMSDA), a modified version of the many-to-one deferred acceptance algorithm (DAA). Extensive simulations demonstrate that the proposed approaches outperform existing benchmarks and other state-of-the-art methods.

This research investigates the relationship between magnetization profiles in scalar field models with marginal interactions within bounded domains and the solutions to the Yamabe problem—specifically, finding metrics with constant curvature—within those same domains. Using the slab as a reference domain, we first analyze magnetization profiles at the upper critical dimensions ($d=3$, $4$, and $6$) under various scale-invariant boundary conditions. By examining the saddle-point equations for magnetization, we derive general formulas expressed via Weierstrass elliptic functions, which extend existing exact results and yield new findings for percolation cases. The zeros and poles of these elliptic solutions correspond directly to the imposed boundary conditions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for any dimension $d$, the magnetization profiles satisfy the corresponding integer Yamabe equation at that dimension with identical boundary conditions. In the specific case of the four-dimensional Ising model with fixed boundaries, our profiles show strong agreement with Monte Carlo simulations. These findings explicitly validate recent results at the upper critical dimension presented in reference [1].

Combining multiple decision-makers creates sophisticated systems, though it necessitates addressing specialization and division of labor. This study examines whether information constraints within hierarchies of experts can serve not only as a principled regularization method but also to enforce specialization. Specifically, we introduce an information-theoretically inspired online learning rule that partitions the problem space into sub-problems solvable by individual experts. We demonstrate two application strategies: (i) partitioning based on individual data samples, which enables the system to solve complex problems by optimally combining local experts, and (ii) partitioning based on data sets representing tasks, which creates experts specialized in task families to address meta-learning challenges. We validate the broad applicability of this approach across classification, regression, density estimation, and reinforcement learning, covering both standard and meta-learning configurations.

Recent research has leveraged natural-language prompts to guide pretrained language models in executing various AI tasks, utilizing either a fill-in-the-blank framework (Petroni et al., 2019) or a few-shot extrapolation approach (Brown et al., 2020). For instance, these models possess factual knowledge within their training data that can be retrieved by requesting a "fill in the blank" response to a sentence. Yet, the origin of these prompts remains an open question. This work investigates learning prompts through gradient descent, either by fine-tuning existing prompts or initiating them from random weights. Unlike traditional word embeddings, our prompts consist of "soft words," which are continuous vectors. Additionally, for every task, we optimize a combination of prompts to determine the most effective ones and how to ensemble them. Our method significantly surpasses prior techniques across diverse English language models and tasks, demonstrating that the implicit factual knowledge within these models was previously undervalued. Furthermore, extracting this knowledge is cost-effective, as random initialization yields results nearly as strong as those from informed initialization.

Recently, hyperbolic neural networks have attracted considerable interest for their strong performance on various graph tasks, such as node classification and link prediction, largely because hyperbolic space effectively captures the hierarchical nature of graph data. However, these networks face limitations regarding generalization, scalability, and performance on non-hierarchical datasets. This paper introduces a distinct perspective on modeling hyperbolic networks by utilizing the Poincaré disk not only to represent hyperbolic geometry but also as a tangent space at the origin. This approach allows us to substitute non-scalable Möbius gyrovector operations with a Euclidean approximation, thereby simplifying the hyperbolic model into a Euclidean model followed by a hyperbolic normalization function. Although our method does not rely on Möbius mathematics, it operates within a Riemannian manifold, leading us to term it the "Pseudo-Poincaré framework." We applied our non-linear hyperbolic normalization to leading homogeneous and multi-relational graph networks, demonstrating performance gains over both Euclidean and traditional hyperbolic models. The core contribution of this work is its capacity to capture hierarchical features within Euclidean space, enabling the replacement of hyperbolic networks without sacrificing performance metrics while simultaneously benefiting from Euclidean advantages like interpretability and efficient component execution.

Mixture Density Networks (MDNs) are an established method for modeling conditional probability distributions, making them an ideal baseline for new approaches. While the standard MDN formulation outputs parameters for a Gaussian mixture model with restricted covariance components, covariance remains a critical factor in the conditional modeling challenges we address. Consequently, I developed and implemented an MDN variant that allows for unrestricted covariances. Although this may have been done previously, no online resources were found. Therefore, this technical report documents my approach, hoping it will assist others encountering similar issues.

Recent decades have seen a significant surge in interest regarding the brain-body connection. Specifically, within psychoneuroimmunology, numerous studies link stress—stemming from various sources—to alterations in the immune system, examined through medical, immunological, and biochemical lenses. This paper identifies key behaviors of the stress-immune system interplay documented in medical literature and aims to represent them qualitatively using a simple, paradigmatic mathematical model. To achieve this, we construct a two-equation differential equation system tracking infection levels and immune response, incorporating stress as an additional parameter. Our model successfully replicates a stable healthy state under low stress, an oscillating dynamic between health and infection under high stress, and a stable "burn-out" or sick state under extreme stress. These distinct dynamical regimes are governed by two saddle-node in cycle (SNIC) bifurcations. Additionally, the model captures induced infections occurring when stress drops from moderate to low levels and predicts that infection periods lengthen as stress increases before culminating in a burn-out state.

Numerous machine and deep learning approaches have been developed to address various tasks in predictive process monitoring, such as forecasting the next event, suffix, remaining duration, or outcome-related variables for ongoing cases. Among these, Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), particularly Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, are the most widely adopted. This study examines an LSTM's ability to learn the underlying structural model of an event log. We propose an evaluation framework that integrates variant-based resampling with custom metrics for fitness, precision, and generalization. Four hypotheses were tested regarding LSTM learning capabilities, the impact of overfitting mitigation strategies, the degree of training set incompleteness, and the level of parallelism in the process model. Our findings confirm that LSTMs often struggle to grasp process model structures, even with simple data and permissive configurations. While appropriate anti-overfitting measures can help, they do not necessarily yield optimal results when hyperparameters are selected solely based on prediction accuracy. Furthermore, reducing the information available to the LSTM during training leads to a significant decline in generalization and precision. Finally, while our experiments did not reveal a direct link between model parallelism and generalization performance, they suggest that process complexity may still play a role.

Stance detection involves determining whether an author supports, opposes, or remains neutral toward a specific target. This task faces two primary challenges: the scarcity of data for diverse targets due to few-shot learning constraints and the insufficient contextual information available about those targets. While previous research has largely addressed the lack of context through attention mechanisms or noisy external knowledge, the few-shot learning aspect remains largely unexplored. Drawing on the ability of pre-trained language models (PLMs) to act as both knowledge repositories and few-shot learners, this paper introduces prompt-based fine-tuning for stance detection. By utilizing prompts, PLMs can supply necessary target context and facilitate learning from limited examples. Given the target's pivotal role, we develop target-aware prompts and a new verbalizer strategy. Unlike traditional methods that map labels to specific words, our verbalizer maps each label to a vector, selecting the one that best reflects the relationship between the stance and the target. Furthermore, to mitigate the limitations of relying on a single hand-crafted prompt for varying targets, we propose distilling knowledge from multiple prompts. Experimental results demonstrate that our model outperforms existing approaches in both full-data and few-shot settings.

The rationality of the ratios of critical values for Rankin-Selberg L-functions associated with GL(n) x GL(n') over a totally imaginary field F is established by analyzing rank-one Eisenstein cohomology within the group GL(N)/F, where N = n + n'. This approach extends methods and findings from earlier work conducted with Guenter Harder, which was limited to totally real base fields. Unlike the totally real scenario, the specific internal architecture of the totally imaginary base field exerts a subtle influence on the resulting rationality properties.

Despite experimental verification and application in quantum computing, sensing, and networks, current entanglement measures often fail to characterize it accurately. This study leverages the Schmidt decomposition of a bipartite state $|\psi\rangle_{AB}$ to establish a one-to-one relationship between the characteristic polynomial of the reduced state $\rho_A$ and its trace polynomials. We propose a new family of entanglement measures based on the complete eigenvalues of the system's reduced density matrices, exemplified by Informationally Complete Entanglement Measures (ICEMs). These ICEMs demonstrate superior ability to distinguish and characterize entanglement compared to established metrics, providing criteria for state transformations under local operations and classical communication. Furthermore, ICEMs can be efficiently estimated on quantum computers, enabling the faithful detection of fully separable states, entanglement, and genuine multipartite entanglement.

This study investigates the degree and manner in which high-$p_\perp$ data and theoretical predictions mirror the geometry and anisotropy of the QCD medium created during ultrarelativistic heavy-ion collisions. Utilizing our newly introduced DREENA-A framework, which supports arbitrary temperature profiles within the dynamical energy loss formalism, we demonstrate that the ratio of high-$p_\perp$ $v_2$ to $(1-R_{AA})$ predictions converges to a specific saturation limit. This limit is directly proportional to the time-averaged anisotropy of the evolving QGP as perceived by the jets.

By integrating the Lee and $E(-1)$ differentials into a version of Khovanov homology, we define a $1$-parameter family of concordance homomorphisms analogous to the Upsilon invariant derived from knot Floer homology. This invariant provides lower bounds for the slice genus and enables the demonstration that specific infinite families of pretzel knots are linearly independent within the smooth concordance group.

While every Lagrangian torus in a K3 surface with a Maslov index of zero possesses a non-trivial homology class, this note generalizes that finding to tori with even Maslov indices. Conversely, it is demonstrated that any homologically non-trivial Lagrangian torus must have a Maslov index of zero.

Recently, particle-based optimization algorithms have emerged as iterative sampling techniques that refine a collection of particles to approximate target distributions. Among these, Stein variational gradient descent has garnered significant interest within the approximate inference community due to its flexibility and precision. This work empirically investigates the method's capacity to sample from multi-modal distributions, highlighting two critical challenges: (i) particles becoming trapped in local modes and (ii) the method's struggle to accurately reproduce density across different regions. To address these limitations, we introduce an annealing schedule. Through extensive experimentation, we demonstrate that this straightforward approach substantially enhances mode coverage while maintaining all theoretical guarantees of the original algorithm.

We describe an asymmetric, high-energy dual optical parametric amplifier (OPA) capable of maintaining relative phase locking among idlers, signals, and depleted pumps at both commensurate and incommensurate wavelengths. Idler and signal locking achieves an rms stability of approximately 200 mrad or better, equivalent to 212 as jitter at $\lambda$=2$\mu$m. The high-energy arm delivers a combined 3.5 mJ of signal and idler energy, while the low-energy arm provides 1.5 mJ, all pumped by a 1 kHz, 18 mJ Ti:Sapphire laser. Both arms offer independent tunability ranging from 1080 nm to 2600 nm. This system's unique combination of relative phase locking, high output power and peak intensity, and extensive tunability makes it an ideal platform for difference frequency generation (DFG) under strong pump conditions and for high peak field waveform synthesis in the near-infrared. Demonstrating this capability, we generated terahertz radiation via two-color waveform synthesis in air plasma, illustrating how relative phase affects the resulting terahertz intensity. The capacity to phase-lock multiple incommensurate wavelengths at high energies unlocks numerous possibilities for strong pump DFG and waveform synthesis.

We introduce and validate a laser frequency stabilization technique that produces a tunable Doppler-free dichroic lock (TDFDL) signal with dispersion-like characteristics. This signal provides a broad range for adjusting the lock point (specifically the zero-crossing) without sacrificing the locking signal's slope. The approach relies on detecting magnetically induced dichroism in an atomic vapor using a weak probe laser beam in conjunction with a counter-propagating strong pump laser beam. A straightforward model is provided to elucidate the fundamental principles behind generating the TDFDL signal. By tuning the pump beam's frequency, the spectral shift in the locking signal is realized. Furthermore, the TDFDL signal demonstrates utility for stabilizing the frequency of a cooling laser employed in a magneto-optical trap (MOT) for $^{87}Rb$ atoms.

This study examines the sample complexity of bounded two-layer neural networks across various activation functions. Specifically, we analyze the hypothesis class:
\[
\mathcal{H} = \left\{\textbf{x}\mapsto \langle \textbf{v}, \sigma \circ
W\textbf{x} + \textbf{b} \rangle :
  \textbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^d, W \in \mathbb{R}^{T\times d}, \textbf{v} \in
\mathbb{R}^{T}\right\}
\]
where the spectral norms of $W$ and $\textbf{v}$ are bounded by $O(1)$, the Frobenius norm of $W$ remains bounded by its initialization $R > 0$, and $\sigma$ represents a Lipschitz activation function. We demonstrate that when $\sigma$ operates element-wise, the sample complexity of $\mathcal{H}$ is independent of the network width, and we establish that this bound is tight. Furthermore, we prove that the element-wise nature of $\sigma$ is critical for achieving width-independent bounds; specifically, we identify non-element-wise activation functions for which the sample complexity is demonstrably dependent on the width. To derive the upper bound, we employ the recent Approximate Description Length (ADL) method for norm-based bounds (arXiv:1910.05697). Additionally, we introduce novel techniques and tools for this approach, aiming to inspire future research.

Coordination serves as a vital capability in multi-agent systems, enabling the completion of objectives that single agents cannot achieve alone. This study examines how a team of strategic agents selects among multiple tasks within a stochastic framework, specifically focusing on two tasks with randomly distributed and partially observable difficulties. We demonstrate that when prior distributions regarding task difficulty are diffuse, a Nash equilibrium with a straightforward, intuitive linear structure emerges. Conversely, we find that if the prior distribution is not diffuse, an agent's best response to an affine strategy profile may become nonlinear. Furthermore, we present an algorithm capable of efficiently calculating a data-driven Nash equilibrium restricted to the class of affine policies.

We investigate the relativistic liquid hydrodynamic theory developed by \"{O}ttinger and colleagues within the GENERIC framework. By applying the maximum entropy principle, we establish the criteria for linear stability across any reference frame and ensure relativistic causality. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the field equations, when linearized, can be transformed into a symmetric-hyperbolic structure. This reformulation reveals that the resulting equations constitute a specific instance of the Israel-Stewart theory, with certain Israel-Stewart parameters subject to constraints. Consequently, this approach enables a reinterpretation of the GENERIC framework through the lens of Extended Irreversible Thermodynamics (EIT).

This paper presents a comprehensive global analysis of Type-II two-Higgs-doublet models (2HDM), examining how anticipated precision measurements of SM-like Higgs bosons and Z-pole observables will influence the viable parameter space. Utilizing the GAMBIT framework, our study incorporates current constraints from theoretical requirements (unitarity, perturbativity, and vacuum stability), collider Higgs searches, electroweak physics, and flavour physics. Furthermore, we assess the potential of upcoming facilities—including the HL-LHC, CEPC, ILC, and FCC-ee—to probe the 2HDM parameter space more deeply.

To facilitate the application of the Generator Coordinate Method to extensive configuration spaces, we introduce a straightforward approximate formula for calculating diabatic many-body matrix elements, thereby eliminating the need to evaluate two-body interaction matrix elements. This approach is demonstrated using two analytically solvable Hamiltonians derived from the harmonic oscillator.

Using the Green's function technique within a tight-binding framework, we investigate the electron transport characteristics of specific molecular wires and an atypical disordered thin film. Our findings demonstrate that electron transport is heavily influenced by quantum interference among electronic wave functions, the coupling strengths between molecules and electrodes, the length of the molecular wire, and the degree of disorder. These model calculations offer physical insights into the conduction behavior across bridge systems.

Software effort is quantified using story points [35]. Existing automated methods for estimating these points typically rely on deep learning and pre-trained embedding models for text regression, often incurring high computational costs. We introduce HeteroSP, a tool designed to estimate story points from textual Agile project issues. Our baseline for comparison includes GPT2SP [12] and Deep-SE [8]. Analysis of the story point dataset [8] reveals that software issues consist of natural language mixed with quoted code snippets and suffer from large vocabulary sizes. To address this, we developed a text normalization module that processes both words and code tokens. Subsequently, we designed an algorithm to transform software issues into graphs featuring diverse node and edge types. We then constructed a heterogeneous graph neural network model, leveraging fastText [6] for initial node embeddings, to learn and predict story points for new issues. We evaluated our approach across three estimation scenarios: within a project, cross-project within the same repository, and cross-project across different repositories. The results yielded average Mean Absolute Errors (MAE) of 2.38, 2.61, and 2.63, respectively. HeteroSP outperformed GPT2SP in two of the three scenarios and surpassed Deep-SE in the most challenging scenario while requiring significantly less execution time. Furthermore, comparisons with homogeneous graph neural network models demonstrated that our heterogeneous approach yields superior estimation accuracy. In terms of efficiency, the total time required for node embedding initialization, model construction, and story point estimation across all three processes is approximately 570 seconds.

Recovering global rankings from pairwise comparisons has broad applications ranging from time synchronization to sports team evaluation. These comparisons, akin to matches in a competition, can be modeled as edges in a directed graph where nodes represent competitors with unknown ranks. This paper introduces GNNRank, a trainable graph neural network framework utilizing digraph embeddings to address ranking recovery. We propose new objectives designed to encode ranking upsets or violations. The framework employs a ranking score estimation method and incorporates an inductive bias by unfolding the computation of the Fiedler vector from a graph built on a learnable similarity matrix. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves competitive and often superior performance compared to baselines, exhibiting strong transferability. The code and preprocessed data are available at: \url{https://github.com/SherylHYX/GNNRank}.

The dual holographic framework has proven highly effective in elucidating fundamental characteristics of the initial phases of relativistic heavy ion collisions, extending through the creation of a minimal-viscosity quark-gluon plasma. Nevertheless, efforts to apply this approach beyond this specific epoch remain scarce. This work investigates the potential for extending such applications past the hadronization phase. Our analysis leverages recent advances regarding the duality between entanglement properties of field theory states at the boundary of Anti-de Sitter space and the non-trivial horizon topologies in the bulk, commonly known as the ER = EPR correspondence. We examine these issues through the lens of heavy-ion phenomenology, review pertinent concepts, and chart a course toward integrating them into a comprehensive, at least semiquantitative, description of relativistic heavy ion collisions. Finally, we delineate potential future directions for this research.

The field of machine learning has seen a surge in interest regarding algorithmic fairness. Although numerous definitions exist in the literature, the relationships and distinctions between them remain ambiguous. This paper reviews existing fairness concepts and explores their links to moral and political philosophy, particularly theories of justice. We also examine fairness through a dynamic lens, assessing the long-term consequences of current predictions and decisions. To address variations in how fairness is characterized, we introduce a flowchart that maps the implicit assumptions and anticipated outcomes of different fairness inquiries across three dimensions: the data generation process, the predicted results, and the resulting impacts. Ultimately, this work highlights the necessity of aligning the specific fairness goal with the appropriate analytical framework to achieve the desired objective.

Optical pumping enables the control of chemical reactions across a broad spectrum of rotational energies. This study investigates the hydrogen abstraction reaction SiO$^+$ + H$_2$ $\rightarrow$ SiOH$^+$ + H within an ion trap environment. Using a broad-band optical pumping technique, the SiO$^+$ cation was prepared with a narrow distribution of rotational states, reaching super-rotor levels with quantum numbers ($j$) up to 170. Experimental results demonstrate that these super-rotor states significantly boost the reaction rate, a finding corroborated by parallel theoretical modeling. The underlying mechanism for this rotational enhancement is identified as a strong coupling between the SiO$^+$ rotational mode and the reaction coordinate at the transition state along the primary dynamical pathway. This research presents the first kinetic characterization of a chemical reaction driven by such extreme rotational excitation of a reactant.

The increasing demand for dependable communication across untrusted networks has revitalized research into adversarial channel models, which frequently exhibit behaviors distinct from traditional stochastic models. A particularly relevant practical scenario involves a \textit{causal} or \textit{online} adversary, restricted to knowing the transmitted codeword only up to the current time. This study examines stochastic-adversarial mixed noise scenarios where a transmitter (Alice) seeks to convey information to a receiver (Bob) over either a binary erasure channel (BEC) or a binary symmetric channel (BSC). This communication is hindered by an online adversary (Calvin) capable of flipping or erasing a limited number of bits at the channel input. Calvin is aware of the encoding scheme and possesses causal access to Bob's received data via \textit{feedback snooping}. Regarding erasures, we establish a full capacity characterization both with and without transmitter feedback. For bit-flips, we derive significant achievability bounds and converse limits.

Since the 19th century, logical methods have been used to develop and assess computational models for quantifier words, yet current Natural Language Understanding (NLU) systems continue to struggle with capturing their semantics. We utilize Generalized Quantifier Theory to create language-independent semantic representations, allowing us to measure how quantifiers contribute to NLU model errors. Our findings indicate that quantifiers are widespread in NLU benchmarks and their presence during testing correlates with performance declines. While multilingual models also demonstrate poor quantifier reasoning capabilities, this deficit does not necessarily affect non-English languages more severely than English. To enable direct probing, we introduce an adversarial Generalized Quantifier Natural Language Inference (GQNLI) task, demonstrating that pre-trained language models lack robustness in generalized quantifier reasoning.
