Consequently, every beam step requires scanning the entire corpus, rendering $k$NN-MT approximately two orders of magnitude slower than vanilla MT models and hindering its deployment in real-world, particularly online, scenarios. To overcome this limitation, we introduce Fast $k$NN-MT, which builds a much smaller datastore. For each source word, Fast $k$NN-MT first identifies token-level neighbors restricted to matching query tokens. During decoding, instead of searching the whole corpus, the method limits the search space to target tokens associated with the previously selected source tokens. This approach eliminates the need to traverse the entire datastore, drastically boosting decoding efficiency. Fast $k$NN-MT achieves this two-orders-of-magnitude speedup without sacrificing performance, resulting in a system only twice as slow as standard NMT models. This advancement enables the practical application of $k$NN-MT in real-world settings. The code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/ShannonAI/fast-knn-nmt}.

Although real music signals exhibit high variability, they possess robust statistical structures. Bayesian modelling techniques can effectively unify prior knowledge regarding the physical mechanisms of sound generation and the rules governing complex musical organization, such as notes, chords, and full scores. While existing Automatic Music Transcription algorithms typically handle distinct tasks like multiple-F0 detection and beat tracking separately, the significant challenge lies in achieving joint estimation of all these parameters. This paper introduces a Bayesian framework for music audio modelling and content analysis. Utilizing Gaussian processes, our methodology aims to jointly estimate various musical concepts by integrating prior information about non-stationary behavior, dynamics, and rich spectral content directly into the kernel. We demonstrate the advantages of this approach through two specific applications: pitch estimation and the inference of missing segments within polyphonic audio recordings.

Online handwriting recognition has been researched extensively yet yielded limited practical outcomes when applied to standard paper. Earlier sensor-based methods faced constraints that hindered their deployment in real-world scenarios. This study introduces a writer-independent system capable of recognizing characters written on plain paper using a sensor-integrated pen. Designed for practical application, the system requires no user-specific training. The pen captures linear acceleration, angular velocity, magnetic field data, and applied force, functioning as a digitizer that converts these analog signals into time-series data during writing on regular paper. Our collected dataset includes Latin uppercase and lowercase alphabets. We demonstrate the efficacy of a convolutional neural network for letter classification, showing that this approach yields promising results for writer-independent recognition. Ultimately, this work aims to deliver a real-time handwriting recognition solution suitable for use on normal paper.

Software vulnerabilities often stem from flaws, bugs, or errors within the architecture, design, or implementation of computer systems, which attackers can exploit to compromise security. To address this, the Common Weakness Enumerations (CWE) serve as a hierarchical dictionary defining software weaknesses, detailing their potential impact and mitigation strategies. Conversely, Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) offer concise, unique identifiers for specific vulnerabilities found in particular products or protocols. Mapping CVEs to CWEs allows for a deeper understanding of impact and facilitates mitigation; however, since manual mapping is impractical, automated solutions are necessary yet difficult to achieve. This paper introduces V2W-BERT, a novel Transformer-based framework leveraging natural language processing, link prediction, and transfer learning. Our method surpasses prior approaches in accuracy, excelling even with rare CWE classes that have limited training data. Furthermore, our approach effectively utilizes historical data to predict links for future CVE instances, offering a practical solution for real-world applications. Utilizing datasets from MITRE and the National Vulnerability Database, we achieved up to 97% accuracy on randomly partitioned data and 94% accuracy on temporally partitioned data. We anticipate that this work will inspire improved method designs and training models, ultimately aiding in solving increasingly complex cybersecurity challenges.

Data has been the primary driver of machine learning (ML) advancements over the last ten years, yet acquiring high-quality, labeled data remains difficult and costly. To utilize vast amounts of unlabeled data, self-supervised learning—specifically contrastive learning—has emerged. This approach aims to bring representations of different views from the same training sample (generated via augmentation) closer together in representation space, while pushing representations of different samples further apart. Consequently, contrastive models learn informative data representations that facilitate downstream ML tasks. Although recent studies indicate that ML models are susceptible to various privacy attacks, most existing research focuses on supervised learning models. However, the expressive representations learned by contrastive models also pose significant privacy risks. This paper presents the first privacy analysis of contrastive learning using membership and attribute inference attacks. Our experiments reveal that, compared to supervised models, contrastive models trained on image datasets are more resistant to membership inference attacks but more vulnerable to attribute inference attacks. This resistance stems from reduced overfitting in contrastive models, whereas the vulnerability arises from their ability to create expressive data representations. To address this, we introduce Talos, the first privacy-preserving contrastive learning mechanism based on adversarial training. Empirical results demonstrate that Talos effectively mitigates attribute inference risks while preserving membership privacy and model utility.

Logic programming's semantic foundations are typically divided into two distinct approaches: operational semantics, which employs SLD-resolution to compute answers, and declarative semantics, which interprets logic programs as formulas with models. In this work, we introduce a novel operational framework known as TSLD-resolution (Typed SLD-resolution). This method incorporates a specific "wrong" value to signal type errors detected during runtime, facilitated by a newly defined typed unification algorithm. Furthermore, we establish the correctness of TSLD-resolution by relating it to a typed declarative semantics.

We examined the thermodynamics and phase transitions of a renormalized group-improved, asymptotically safe Schwarzschild black hole. This geometry incorporates quantum gravitational effects through a running gravitational constant, defined as $G(r) \equiv G(k=k(r))$. Our analysis of various thermodynamic quantities—including entropy, specific heat, and Hawking temperature—was conducted for the general parameter $\gamma$ within the quantum-corrected Schwarzschild metric. We observed that the leading logarithmic quantum correction coefficient is influenced by $\gamma$. Furthermore, we investigated thermal stability, local temperature, and free energy within a cavity surrounding the black hole. Based on the local specific heat, three black hole states were identified, with the large and tiny states being thermally stable. Analysis of the on-shell free energy revealed no Hawking-Page phase transition, contrasting with ordinary Schwarzschild black holes; instead, the black hole state persists across all temperatures. Additionally, two critical points, $T_{c1}$ and $T_{c2}$, were identified, marking phase transitions between different black hole states.

Uncertainty estimation in object detection is crucial for ensuring safety in autonomous driving. While deep learning has become the standard for object detection and numerous probabilistic detectors have emerged, there remains a lack of comprehensive summaries regarding uncertainty estimation. Current methods vary significantly in network architectures and uncertainty approaches, and are tested on diverse datasets using a broad spectrum of metrics. Consequently, comparing these methods and selecting the most suitable model for specific applications is difficult. This paper addresses this issue by offering a review and comparative analysis of probabilistic object detection methods tailored for autonomous driving. We begin by outlining general uncertainty estimation in deep learning, followed by a systematic survey of existing probabilistic detection methods and their evaluation metrics. Subsequently, we conduct a rigorous comparative study using an image detector across three public autonomous driving datasets. Finally, we discuss outstanding challenges and future research directions. The code is accessible at https://github.com/asharakeh/pod_compare.git.

The entanglement of spin pairs in top quarks generated at a collider offers a means to test a (generalized) Bell inequality at energy levels previously unexamined. We demonstrate that measuring just one observable can confirm the violation of this inequality with 98% confidence using existing data from the Large Hadron Collider, and with 99.99% confidence utilizing the increased luminosity anticipated in the next run.

Let $(M,g)$ be a smooth, compact, orientable two-dimensional Riemannian manifold (a surface) equipped with a smooth metric tensor $g$ and a smooth, connected boundary $\Gamma$. The associated Dirichlet-to-Neumann (DN) map, denoted as $\Lambda_g: {C^\infty}(\Gamma)\to{C^\infty}(\Gamma)$, corresponds to the forward elliptic problem $\Delta_gu=0$ in $M\setminus\Gamma$ with boundary condition $u=f$ on $\Gamma$. This operator is defined by $\Lambda_g f:=\partial_\nu u^f$ on $\Gamma$, where $\Delta_g$ represents the Beltrami-Laplace operator, $u^f(x)$ is the solution, and $\nu$ denotes the outward normal to $\Gamma$. The corresponding inverse problem seeks to reconstruct the surface $(M,g)$ from its DN-map $\Lambda_g$. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for an operator acting on ${C^\infty}(\Gamma)$ to qualify as such a DN-map. Unlike the existing conditions formulated by G. Henkin and V. Michel using multidimensional complex analysis, our approach relies on the connections between this inverse problem and commutative Banach algebras.

Traditional queuing network control methods generally depend on precise information regarding model parameters, specifically arrival and service rates. Nevertheless, this data is often unavailable or subject to temporal variations. To overcome this limitation, we examine a category of model-data-independent (MDI) control policies that function based solely on traffic state observations and network topology. Our focus is on MDI policies capable of stabilizing multi-class Markovian queuing networks under both centralized and decentralized frameworks, with control actions encompassing routing, sequencing, and holding. By extending routes and developing piecewise-linear test functions, we establish a practical criterion for verifying the stability of a multi-class network under a specific MDI policy. We demonstrate that for stabilizable multi-class networks, a centralized stabilizing MDI policy is guaranteed to exist. Furthermore, for stabilizable single-class networks, we prove the existence of a decentralized stabilizing MDI policy. Additionally, for both scenarios, we formulate explicit policies that achieve maximum throughput and provide numerical examples to validate our findings.

Document image classification continues to be a prominent research field due to its extensive commercial potential across various enterprise sectors. While recent breakthroughs in large pre-trained vision and language models, as well as graph neural networks, have provided powerful tools for this task, the heavy computational demands of these large models often undermine the cost-efficiency benefits of automation. To address this, we introduce an efficient document image classification framework that leverages graph convolutional neural networks while integrating textual, visual, and layout data. Our approach has been rigorously evaluated against several state-of-the-art vision and language models using both public datasets and a real-world insurance document classification set. Empirical results demonstrate that our method achieves performance nearly on par with state-of-the-art solutions while significantly reducing the computing resources and time required for training and inference. Consequently, our approach offers superior cost advantages, particularly for scalable enterprise deployments. Furthermore, we provide detailed comparisons of computing resources, model sizes, and training/inference times between our method and baseline models, along with a breakdown of the cost per image for both our approach and existing alternatives.

If dark energy arises from the dynamics of a scalar field, that field is generally expected to couple to matter. While couplings to standard model particles are tightly restricted by local experiments, constraints on couplings to dark matter (DM) rely solely on cosmological data, making them significantly weaker. Recent insights suggest that such couplings may emerge only during the epoch of dark energy domination, driven by the dark energy's own evolution, which would induce a violation of the equivalence principle (EP) within the dark sector at late times. This paper examines a specific model and demonstrates that late-time EP violations in the DM sector are not severely limited by cosmological background evolution or linear regime observables, such as those from the cosmic microwave background. Consequently, a rigorous constraint on these late-time EP violations requires an investigation of perturbations in the non-linear regime.

Upon encountering such a query, mathematicians typically cite L.P. Eisenhart's 1926 result to assert that the answer is "one," referring to the sole constant defining constant Riemannian curvature. This paper, however, aims to demonstrate the opposite by examining two-dimensional Riemannian geometry through the lens of E. Vessiot's 1903 work, which remains entirely unrecognized today over a century later. Specifically, we will locally compute the Vessiot structure equations to establish that there are indeed "two" Vessiot structure constants subject to a single linear Jacobi condition; this necessitates that one constant vanishes while the other matches the established value. This finding relies on profound mathematical principles within the formal theory of Lie pseudogroups, encompassing both Spencer $\delta$-cohomology and diagram chasing in homological algebra. A further analogous example will support this assertion beyond the classical tensorial framework of the renowned "equivalence problem," with the case of contact transformations also being analyzed. Despite being surprising, our conclusion is that the mathematical foundations of both classical and conformal Riemannian geometry require reconsideration. The analysis of conformal geometry has been addressed in a recent arXiv preprint.

We derive recursive approximations for the action of the Morava stabilizer group at height $h \geq 2$ on the corresponding Lubin-Tate deformation ring. By specializing to $h=3$ and $p>2$, we determine this action explicitly. These findings are novel for heights $h>2$ and are consistent with Lader's computations at height $h=2$.

Domain adaptation addresses learning challenges in a target domain by utilizing knowledge from a related source domain. Despite significant progress, most current methods depend heavily on large volumes of unlabeled target data to learn domain-invariant representations, which is often unfeasible in real-world scenarios where such data is unavailable. This paper investigates the scenario where only well-labeled source domain data exists during training, a setting termed robust domain adaptation. To address this, we introduce a novel Causal AutoEncoder (CAE) based on the assumption that causal relationships between features and class labels remain consistent across domains. The CAE unifies deep autoencoding with causal structure learning to derive causal representations solely from a single source domain. Specifically, the deep autoencoder component extracts low-dimensional representations, while a dedicated causal structure learning module disentangles these into causal and task-irrelevant components. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed CAE outperforms eleven state-of-the-art methods.

Rising demands on next-generation wireless networks have driven recent investigations into multi-antenna transceiver hardware and smart communication protocols, with Full Duplex (FD) Multiple-Input Multiple-Output (MIMO) systems being a key focus. These architectures enable simultaneous uplink and downlink transmission across the full frequency spectrum. However, as antenna counts grow, self-interference leaking from the transmitter to the receiver in FD radios intensifies. This paper introduces a unified FD massive MIMO framework that integrates both analog and digital transmit and receive beamforming, alongside corresponding analog and digital self-interference (SI) cancellation techniques. These components are jointly optimized to meet diverse performance goals and complexity constraints. The study evaluates the proposed architecture in scenarios involving fully digital and hybrid analog-digital beamforming using advanced algorithms, as well as concurrent data and control signal transmission. Results demonstrate that the proposed design achieves enhanced spectral efficiency for FD communications across both small and large antenna arrays while requiring fewer analog cancellation elements than existing benchmark schemes. The article concludes by outlining open challenges and future research directions for FD massive MIMO systems and their potential applications.

Social technologies have enabled the spread of disinformation and mass manipulation on a scale never before seen. This poses a severe security risk, especially since humans often represent the weakest defense for critical infrastructure, with the power grid being particularly vulnerable. In this study, we examine an attack where an adversary manipulates energy consumer behavior by distributing fake discount alerts that encourage shifting usage to peak-demand times. We conducted surveys to evaluate individuals' likelihood of acting on these notifications and sharing them with friends, which allowed us to model the propagation of such disinformation through social networks. Using Greater London as a case study, we demonstrate that disinformation can successfully coordinate an attack where unsuspecting consumers synchronize their energy consumption, leading to city-wide blackouts. These results highlight that in an age where disinformation can be weaponized, vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure stem not only from hardware and software but also from consumer behavior.

This paper introduces two nonparametric approaches for forecasting functional time-dependent data: functional singular spectrum analysis (FSSA) recurrent forecasting and vector forecasting. Both methods leverage outcomes from FSSA alongside historical observations to generate future predictions; specifically, recurrent forecasting targets individual functions sequentially, whereas vector forecasting operates on functional vectors. Through evaluations using both simulated and real-world datasets, we benchmark these techniques against a gold-standard algorithm for functional time-dependent prediction, concluding that our methods outperform the standard when applied to periodic stochastic processes.

This study introduces a curated dataset derived from the NASA Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) mission, optimized for machine learning research. Starting with Level 1 scientific data, we applied various instrumental corrections, reduced spatial and temporal resolutions to manageable levels, and aligned observations both spatially and temporally. We demonstrate the dataset's utility through two applications: predicting future EVE irradiance based on current readings and converting HMI observations into AIA observations. For each use case, we provide performance metrics and baselines to enable future model comparisons. We expect this curated resource to advance machine learning research in heliophysics and broader physical sciences, thereby enhancing the scientific impact of the SDO mission. This project was directly supported by the 2018 NASA Frontier Development Laboratory Program. Access to the dataset is available in the appendix.

This study tackles optimal control issues by leveraging search trees. Initially, we examine multi-armed bandit problems featuring continuous action spaces and introduce LD-HOO, a limited-depth adaptation of the hierarchical optimistic optimization (HOO) algorithm. Our regret analysis demonstrates that LD-HOO asymptotically matches the cumulative regret of the original HOO algorithm but operates with greater speed and memory efficiency. Subsequently, we develop a Monte Carlo tree search method grounded in LD-HOO for optimal control tasks, showcasing its effectiveness across various control scenarios.

This review outlines general strategies for addressing complex problems that lack exact solutions and present two primary challenges. First, the absence of small parameters prevents the reliable application of perturbation theory; furthermore, even when such parameters exist, the resulting perturbative series often diverge strongly. Second, these series are typically too short for standard resummation techniques to produce viable approximations or remain applicable at all. The review focuses on methods pioneered and refined by the author, including {\it Optimized Perturbation Theory}, now widely utilized across physics, chemistry, and applied mathematics, as well as {\it Self-Similar Approximation Theory}, which enables the simple yet accurate summation of divergent series. Both approaches share significant conceptual similarities with the renormalization group method, which is briefly discussed to highlight these connections and their interrelations.

Optical metasurfaces consist of flat substrates featuring custom nanoscale structures designed to selectively manipulate incoming light based on its direction, wavelength, and polarization. When integrated with photodetectors and subsequent computational processing, these surfaces enable the creation of highly compact imagers and sensors with unique functionalities. We present D-Flat, a fully differentiable TensorFlow framework that generates physically accurate simulations of images formed by metasurface systems. This tool allows for simultaneous optimization of both the metasurface geometry and post-capture processing parameters against nearly any sensor performance metric. Capable of simulating metasurfaces ranging from millimeters to centimeters in diameter on standard computers, D-Flat is modular, supporting diverse wave optics models for both scattering at the surface and propagation to sensors. We validate the framework through comparison with symbolic calculations and prior experimental data, and demonstrate its utility by simulating novel computational sensor designs for single-shot depth sensing and single-shot spatial frequency filtering.

The increasing abundance of counterfeit narratives online has sparked considerable interest within the machine learning community regarding the rapid and scalable identification of fake news. Although various machine learning methods have been developed for this task, it is evident that assessing the effect of noise—defined as news articles incorrectly classified as either fake or real—on their performance remains necessary. This study advances that goal by investigating how noise influences a state-of-the-art structural model utilizing BiLSTM (Bidirectional Long-Short Term Model) for fake news detection, specifically the Hierarchical Discourse-level Structure for Fake News Detection proposed by Karimi and Tang (Reference no. 9).

Satellite remote sensing of trace gases, including carbon dioxide (CO$_2$), has significantly enhanced our capacity to monitor and comprehend Earth's climate. Nevertheless, remote sensing datasets, particularly Level 2 retrievals, often exhibit irregularity in space and time, necessitating spatio-temporal prediction to estimate values for any given location and moment. These inferences are crucial not only for addressing key climate questions but also for validating satellite instruments, as Level 2 retrievals are typically not co-located with ground-based sensors. This discussion outlines statistical methods for generating Level 3 products from Level 2 retrievals, highlighting both the advantages and potential pitfalls of statistical prediction in this domain. Subsequently, we apply a spatio-temporal modeling framework called fixed rank kriging (FRK) to derive global predictions and associated standard errors for column-averaged CO$_2$ using Version 7r and Version 8r retrievals from the Orbiting Carbon Observatory-2 (OCO-2). These FRK predictions enable the statistical validation of Level 2 retrievals globally, despite discrepancies between satellite and ground-based observation locations and times. Critically, this validation incorporates prediction uncertainty, which depends on the time-varying density of observations near ground sites and the unmodeled spatio-temporal high-frequency variations in the trace gas field. For validating remotely sensed CO$_2$ data, we utilize measurements from the Total Carbon Column Observing Network (TCCON). We demonstrate that the FRK product derived from Version 8r exhibits superior agreement with TCCON data compared to the product based on Version 7r.

Multivalent associative proteins featuring robust complementary interactions are essential for the phase separation of intracellular liquid condensates. Our research investigates the internal dynamics of these "bond-network" condensates, formed by two complementary proteins, using both scaling analysis and molecular dynamics. We observe that at balanced stoichiometry, relaxation decelerates significantly because bond breaks leave a shortage of alternative binding partners. This microscopic retardation profoundly impacts bulk properties such as diffusivity, viscosity, and mixing, thereby offering a pathway to experimentally validate our findings.

Inspired by kidney exchange programs, we investigate a mechanism-design challenge on a directed graph representing transplant compatibilities. The goal is to identify a simple path originating from a designated altruistic donor that maximizes the total length, thereby benefiting the highest number of patients. However, the mechanism lacks direct access to the full graph; instead, vertices are distributed among multiple players (hospitals), each of whom reports only a subset of their vertices. A player might strategically withhold vertices to manipulate the mechanism into selecting a path that includes more of their own nodes.

Our aim is to design mechanisms that discourage such manipulation while still achieving long paths. Unfortunately, in worst-case scenarios, it is impossible to approximate the longest possible path while simultaneously ensuring approximate truthfulness—specifically, preventing a player's utility from increasing by more than a factor of $1 + o(1)$ by hiding nodes. Consequently, we adopt a semi-random model where a small ($o(n)$) number of random edges are introduced to these worst-case instances. Although truthful mechanisms still cannot match the overall longest path in this setting, we present a truthful mechanism that performs against a weaker yet significant benchmark: the length of any path where the subpaths within each player maintain a minimum average length. Furthermore, our mechanism adheres to a stronger truthfulness concept termed "matching-time incentive compatibility," which mandates that players not only report their nodes honestly but also refrain from terminating the returned path at their own nodes to redirect it into their subgraph.

This paper outlines our system designed for the SemEval2022 challenge focused on aligning dictionary glosses with word embeddings. We concentrate on the Reverse Dictionary Track, which involves mapping multilingual glosses back to reconstructed vector representations. Specifically, our models transform input sentences into three distinct embedding types: SGNS, Character, and Electra. We conducted various experiments incorporating neural network cells, general multilingual and multitask architectures, and language-agnostic techniques. Additionally, we offer comparisons across different embedding types and ablation studies to identify effective strategies. While our initial transformer-based model yielded relatively modest performance, exploring different retokenization methods led to improvements. Ultimately, our proposed Elmo-based monolingual model achieved the best results, with its multitask and multilingual variants also demonstrating competitive performance.

We demonstrate that bandlimited signals can be uniquely reconstructed, aside from a constant global phase factor, from the magnitudes of their Gabor transforms when sampled at twice the Nyquist rate across two frequency bins.

This work introduces diffeomorphisms of wild blender-horseshoes that reside within the $C^r$ closures ($1\leq r<\infty$) of two distinct diffeomorphism types: one featuring a historic contracting wandering domain, and the other possessing a non-trivial Dirac physical measure supported by a saddle periodic orbit. These results extend Colli-Vargas' model [CV01] to higher-dimensional dynamics by employing wild blender-horseshoes.

Recent years have seen the acquisition of numerous impressive polarimetric images using adaptive optics (AO) systems on large telescopes, leveraging their superior spatial resolution. This paper outlines the fundamental principles of AO polarimetry, examines the associated challenges and constraints, and presents findings that demonstrate the effectiveness of AO polarimeters in studying circumstellar disks, dusty winds from evolved stars, and in the search for reflecting exoplanets.

This demo paper introduces RhythmEdge, an affordable, deep-learning-driven system designed for contactless heart rate (HR) monitoring. RhythmEdge surpasses current methods by leveraging contactless capabilities, real-time or offline functionality, and the use of low-cost, accessible sensors and computing hardware. The system is portable and readily deployable for dependable HR estimation in moderately controlled indoor or outdoor settings. By utilizing Remote Photoplethysmography (rPPG), RhythmEdge extracts HR data from facial videos to deliver immediate assessments via standard, commercially available, resource-constrained edge devices and cameras. We validate the system's scalability, flexibility, and compatibility by implementing it across three distinct architectures (NVIDIA Jetson Nano, Google Coral Development Board, and Raspberry Pi) and three varied cameras (web, action, and DSLR) with different sensitivities and resolutions. Additionally, RhythmEdge archives longitudinal cardiovascular data and offers instant user notifications. Finally, we comprehensively evaluate the prototype's stability, latency, and feasibility on three edge platforms by analyzing their runtime, memory consumption, and power usage.

We present the spherical wedge billiard, a dynamical system where a particle travels along geodesics on a closed, non-Euclidean surface shaped like a spherical wedge. We derive the analytic expression for the associated Poincaré map and observe highly complex dynamics that span from fully chaotic to extremely regular, displaying fractal characteristics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that altering the billiard parameter causes the fixed points of the Poincaré map to merge in intricate patterns, a phenomenon rooted in the spherical aberration of the mapping. Additionally, we provide a detailed analysis of the regular regime, noting that the phase space diagram bears a close resemblance to Talbot carpets.

This paper examines the iterative resolution of regularized saddle-point systems. When the dominant block is symmetric and positive semi-definite within a suitable subspace, Dollar, Gould, Schilders, and Wathen (2006) demonstrated the efficacy of combining the conjugate gradient (CG) method with a constraint preconditioner for optimization tasks. We explore the creation of constraint-preconditioned alternatives to other Krylov methods for these systems by analyzing the basis-generation mechanism. Drawing on the framework established by Gould, Orban, and Rees (2014), we offer general guidelines to adapt any Krylov method for regularized saddle-point problems. Specifically, we derive constraint-preconditioned versions of Lanczos and Arnoldi-based algorithms, such as the Lanczos adaptation of CG, MINRES, SYMMLQ, GMRES(m), and DQGMRES. Additionally, we present MATLAB implementations intended to serve as a foundation for more advanced software development. Lastly, we demonstrate the numerical performance of these constraint-preconditioned Krylov solvers on both symmetric and nonsymmetric systems derived from constrained optimization.

This paper introduces MIXANDMIX, a tool based on Anderson mixing designed to compute the empirical spectral distribution of random matrices arising from population mixtures. Under the population mixture model, the relationship between population distributions and the limiting spectral distribution is established by solving a system of non-linear equations, for which an efficient implementation is presented. Key contributions include an accelerated fixed-point convergence method, a homotopy continuation strategy to avoid non-admissible solutions, a blind non-uniform grid construction for detecting and approximating distribution support, and a parallel computing architecture. Performance is evaluated against existing packages for single-population cases and against simulation results for the more general model, demonstrating competitive performance and enhanced flexibility.

Machine translation (MT) stands as a primary task within natural language processing, aiming to automatically convert text from one natural language into another. Currently, deep neural networks have garnered significant interest for MT applications. These networks demand substantial data to learn abstract input representations and encode them as continuous vectors. This study introduces the first relatively large-scale Amharic-English parallel sentence dataset. Leveraging this compiled data, we developed bi-directional Amharic-English translation models by fine-tuning the pre-existing Facebook M2M100 model, achieving a BLEU score of 37.79 for Amharic-to-English translation and 32.74 for English-to-Amharic. Furthermore, we investigated the impact of Amharic homophone normalization on machine translation performance. The findings indicate that normalizing Amharic homophone characters enhances translation performance in both directions.

This paper details the design and implementation of an embedded optimal control strategy tailored for autonomous driving on a Ford Focus. We developed and deployed a non-linear model predictive control (NMPC) system capable of meeting hard real-time constraints, demonstrating the suitability of sequential quadratic programming (SQP) solvers for driving tasks. The proposed algorithms were validated through a standard automotive XiL development cycle, encompassing model-in-the-loop (MiL) simulations with high-fidelity dynamics, hardware-in-the-loop (HiL) testing with vehicle actuation and embedded hardware, and full vehicle-hardware-in-the-loop (VeHiL) trials. The testing environment combined virtual simulations with physical proving grounds. Furthermore, the NMPC algorithms and optimal control formulations were optimized using deployable C code generated via toolchains compatible with the target embedded systems. Ultimately, the developed system was successfully applied to high-speed autonomous collision avoidance, trajectory tracking, and lane changes on city and highway roads, as well as low-speed maneuvering in parking environments.

This study details the integration of conflict graph-based algorithms and data structures into the COIN-OR Branch-and-Cut (CBC) solver. Key contributions include: $(i)$ a robust framework for efficiently constructing and managing conflict graphs; $(ii)$ a preprocessing routine utilizing a clique strengthening scheme that reduces constraint counts and yields stronger formulations; $(iii)$ a clique cut separator that achieves dual bounds at the root node LP relaxation $19.65\%$ superior to those of a leading commercial solver's equivalent generator, $3.62$ times better than GLPK's clique cut separator, and $4.22$ times stronger than the COIN-OR Cut Generation Library's routine; and $(iv)$ an odd-cycle cut separator featuring a novel lifting module to generate valid odd-wheel inequalities. Performance evaluations indicate that this updated CBC version closed the average optimality gap up to four times more effectively than its predecessor, while increasing the number of mixed-integer programs solved within a three-hour time limit by $23.53\%$.

Interactions between planetary nebulae (PNe) and the interstellar medium (ISM) represent a critical topic in astrophysics. This study aims to validate the interaction mechanisms for planetary nebulae previously identified in literature as interacting PNe (IPNe). Utilizing recent parallax and proper motion data from the Gaia space mission's early third data release, we analyzed the motion of the central stars (CS) of these nebulae relative to the interaction regions. Our analysis confirmed the interaction process for 68 PNe while disproving it for 33 others. Although all 101 objects were previously classified as genuine interacting systems, the 33 rejected cases are now identified as false positives that merely mimic the structural appearance of IPNe. For the verified group of 68 PNe, we computed physical and kinematic properties and classified their galactic populations using high-precision proper motion and parallax measurements. Results indicate that 41% of the verified group belong to the galactic thin disk and 41% to the thick disk, with an additional 18% classified as members of either disk type. Furthermore, kinematic analysis reveals that thin-disk members exhibit smaller vertical heights, space velocities, and peculiar velocities compared to their thick-disk counterparts.

The chemical variety observed in low-mass protostellar sources is widely attributed to environmental influences, making the study of isolated sources, free from nearby object interference, particularly significant. This paper presents the chemical and physical characteristics of the low-mass Class 0 protostar IRAS 16544$-$1604 within the Bok globule CB68, utilizing 1.3 mm ALMA observations with a spatial resolution of approximately 70 au from the FAUST large program. We detected three interstellar saturated complex organic molecules (iCOMs)—CH$_3$OH, HCOOCH$_3$, and CH$_3$OCH$_3$—toward the protostar. For CH$_3$OH, the derived rotation temperature and emitting region size are $131\pm11$~K and $\sim$10~au, respectively. The presence of these iCOMs near the protostar suggests that CB68 contains a hot corino. Kinematic analysis of C$^{18}$O, CH$_3$OH, and OCS lines supports an infalling-rotating envelope model, yielding estimated protostellar masses of $0.08-0.30$~$M_\odot$ and a centrifugal barrier radius of less than 30 au. The small size of this centrifugal barrier appears correlated with the compact emitting regions of the iCOMs. Furthermore, emission lines from c-C$_3$H$_2$ and CCH associated with the protostar indicate warm carbon chain chemistry (WCCC) extending over a 1000~au scale. Consequently, the chemical structure of CB68 is characterized as a hybrid chemistry. Finally, molecular abundances are discussed in relation to other hot corino sources and existing chemical models.

Although general relativity restricts gravitational wave polarization to two tensor modes, broader metric theories of gravity permit up to four additional modes: two vector and two scalar modes. Detecting these polarization states offers a direct means to test modified gravity theories. The stochastic gravitational wave background (SGWB), potentially observable by space-based laser interferometers at their design sensitivity, presents a unique opportunity to directly measure these alternative polarizations. This paper examines the detection performance of the LISA-TianQin network regarding alternative polarizations in stochastic backgrounds. First, we extend the small antenna approximation to calculate overlap reduction functions for SGWB with arbitrary polarization, a method applicable to any time-delay interferometry combination. Subsequently, we evaluate the network's detection capabilities for SGWB across various polarization types. Leveraging the specific orbital characteristics of LISA and TianQin, we propose a technique to disentangle distinct polarization modes from mixed observational data. Compared to ground-based instruments, space-based detectors demonstrate superior capability in resolving SGWB polarizations; notably, they possess the potential to isolate two scalar modes that remain inaccessible to ground-based facilities.

This paper introduces a scalable and efficient neural waveform coding system designed for speech compression. The speech coding challenge is framed as an autoencoding task, utilizing a convolutional neural network (CNN) to handle both encoding and decoding as a neural waveform codec (NWC) within its feedforward pass. The proposed NWC incorporates quantization and entropy coding as trainable components, ensuring that coding artifacts and bitrate management are optimized simultaneously. Efficiency is achieved through compact model architectures, including gated residual networks and depthwise separable convolutions. Additionally, the system features a scalable architecture known as cross-module residual learning (CMRL), enabling operation across a broad spectrum of bitrates. This approach leverages residual coding by chaining multiple NWC autoencoding modules, where each module compensates for reconstruction errors introduced by its predecessors. To support lower bitrates, CMRL integrates a linear predictive coding (LPC) module as the initial autoencoder. This hybrid design redefines LPC quantization as a differentiable process, facilitating end-to-end training. The decoder configuration varies by bitrate: it uses a single NWC (0.12 million parameters) for low to medium rates (12–20 kbps) and two NWCs for high rates (32 kbps). While decoding complexity remains higher than traditional codecs, it is substantially lower than that of other neural coders like WaveNet-based vocoders. In terms of wide-band speech quality, the system matches or exceeds the performance of AMR-WB and Opus on TIMIT test data at low and medium bitrates, with the capability to scale to higher bitrates for near-transparent audio quality.

This paper advances the resolution of an open question posed by Tsurumi (Arch. Ration. Mech. Anal. 234:2, 2019) regarding the well-posedness of the stationary Navier-Stokes equations in $\R^d$ from $\dot{B}_{p, q}^{-2}$ to $\mathbb{P} \dot{B}_{p, q}^{0}$ where $p=d$ and $1 \leq q \leq 2$. We demonstrate that for $1 \leq q < \frac d2$ with $d\geq4$, the system is ill-posed from $\dot{B}_{d, q}^{-2}(\R^d)$ to $\mathbb{P} \dot{B}_{d, q}^{0}(\R^d)$. This ill-posedness is established by constructing a sequence of external forces that reveals a discontinuity in the solution map at zero; specifically, there exists a sequence of forces converging to zero in $\dot{B}_{d, q}^{-2}$ that generates solutions failing to converge to zero in $\dot{B}_{d, q}^{0}$. Furthermore, we prove that the equations are well-posed from $\dot{B}_{d, 2}^{-2}(\R^d)$ to $\mathbb{P} \dot{B}_{d, 2}^{0}(\R^d)$ when $d=3$ or $d=4$. Combining these findings, we conclude that the open question concerning dimensions $d\geq4$ is now fully resolved.

The relic abundance of thermal dark matter in the MeV mass range is established during the complex phases of neutrino decoupling and electron annihilation. Previous attempts to fully address this problem were hindered by the computational challenges of solving Boltzmann equations for multiple sectors that are simultaneously relativistic and non-relativistic. In this work, we present the first calculation of light dark matter freeze-out that comprehensively accounts for energy exchange between the dark sector, neutrinos, and the electromagnetically interacting plasma through both annihilation and elastic scattering. We introduce a numerically efficient framework capable of tracking photon and neutrino temperatures throughout freeze-out, yielding precise predictions for $N_{\rm eff}$ across arbitrary dark matter annihilation branching ratios. Furthermore, our approach uniquely resolves the temperature evolution of dark matter across freeze-out within a three-sector system. We find that velocity-dependent annihilation efficiencies impact these dynamics, and specifically for a flavor-blind $p$-wave annihilation into electron- and neutrino-pairs of all generations, current Planck data rules out a complex scalar dark matter particle with a mass $m_\phi \leq 7$ MeV.

This study presents quantum transport calculations detailing how electrons scatter from an extended line defect in graphene, incorporating potentials from local magnetic moments recently predicted to exist on sites neighboring the defect. The derived transmission probability is formulated as a function of the incident electron's valley, spin, and angle of incidence at the Fermi level. The results indicate that the previously anticipated valley polarization in transmitted electron beams remains largely unaffected by these magnetic moments. However, the moments do introduce additional spin polarization alongside the valley polarization, contributing no more than approximately 20%.

Although deep neural networks demonstrate impressive performance, their integration into clinical settings remains limited, largely due to their lack of explainability. This study applies attribution techniques to a pre-trained deep neural network designed for 12-lead electrocardiogram classification, aiming to illuminate the "black box" by elucidating the connection between model predictions and learned features. By processing data from a public dataset, the attribution methods assign a "relevance score" to each signal sample, enabling an analysis of the network's training outcomes through quantitative metrics: average relevance scores calculated across a) classes, b) leads, and c) average beats. Evaluations of relevance scores for atrial fibrillation (AF) and left bundle branch block (LBBB) against healthy controls reveal that mean values a) rise with increased classification confidence and approach zero during false classifications, while b) align with clinical guidelines on which leads to prioritize. Additionally, c) the presence of visible P-waves and concordant T-waves generates distinctly negative relevance scores in AF and LBBB classification, respectively. In conclusion, our findings indicate that the DNN has acquired features consistent with standard cardiology textbook knowledge.

Superhydrophobic surfaces are crucial for advancing new product coatings, including automotive applications, as well as mechanical engineering fields like the design of turbines and compressors. Consequently, a key aspect of developing these surfaces involves computationally simulating them, with a specific focus on how variations in the shape and size of microscopic pits and grooves on flat surfaces affect performance. In this study, the relationship between contact angle and fluid-wall dispersive energy is established through molecular simulation, while the static and dynamic properties of nonpolar fluids interacting with highly rough surfaces are also characterized.

Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) has previously localized repeating fast radio bursts (FRBs) across diverse environments, ranging from nearby star-forming regions to globular clusters. This study reports the VLBI localization of FRB 20201124A using a temporary array of dishes linked to the European VLBI Network (EVN). Our observing campaign identified 18 bursts from FRB 20201124A across two distinct epochs. By merging visibility data from both epochs, we localized the source with a 1-$\sigma$ uncertainty of 4.5 milliarcseconds (mas). Leveraging the substantial burst sample, we assessed astrometric accuracy and determined that using $\gtrsim20$ baselines ($\gtrsim7$ dishes) enables robust milliarcsecond precision even with single-burst datasets. Furthermore, sub-arcsecond precision remains achievable for individual bursts with as few as $\sim$ six baselines (four dishes). We compared two techniques for determining individual burst positions: identifying peaks in dirty maps versus applying a Gaussian fit to the cross-fringe pattern on those maps. The Gaussian fit proved more reliable, yielding lower mean and standard deviations in positional offsets. Our VLBI results place FRB 20201124A at $705 \pm 26$ mas (1-$\sigma$) from the optical center of its host galaxy, consistent with its origin within a recently identified extended radio structure linked to star formation. Future high-resolution optical observations, such as those from the Hubble Space Telescope, will clarify the proximity of our VLBI position to nearby star-forming knots.

This paper investigates bearing-based tracking for leader-follower formations that vary over time. The required constraints among agents are defined by bearing vectors, with multiple leaders following bounded reference velocities. Each follower measures the relative positions of its neighbors and its own velocity while receiving data from them. Assuming the target formation is infinitesimally bearing rigid and that the local reference frames of followers are aligned, this work proposes two control laws utilizing a sliding mode control approach. The stability of these laws is analyzed using Lyapunov stability theory and validated through numerical simulations.

While Machine Learning (ML) has proven effective for detecting network attacks within single organizations, developing an ML-based detection system using heterogeneous data from multiple sources remains a significant challenge. This difficulty stems primarily from privacy concerns and the absence of a universal data format. To address these hurdles, this paper introduces a collaborative federated learning scheme. The proposed framework enables multiple organizations to jointly design, train, and evaluate a robust ML-driven network intrusion detection system. This approach relies on two key elements: the availability of network traffic in a common format to facilitate pattern extraction across diverse sources, and the use of a federated learning mechanism to eliminate the need for sharing sensitive user data. Consequently, organizations gain access to each other's cyber threat intelligence while preserving internal data privacy. The model is trained locally, with only updated weights shared among participants via a federated averaging process. The framework was evaluated using two NetFlow datasets, NF-UNSW-NB15-v2 and NF-BoT-IoT-v2, under two scenarios: centralized training involving local data sharing and localized training with no intelligence exchange. The results confirm the efficiency and effectiveness of the proposed framework in creating a universal ML model that accurately classifies benign and malicious traffic from multiple organizations without requiring the exchange of local data.

This paper introduces and examines a streamlined model for the vertical movement of individuals within a high-rise structure via elevators, specifically targeting start-of-day scenarios where occupants arrive at the ground level at a constant rate. Upon an elevator's arrival, passengers board until capacity is full before being dispatched to their respective floors. The study calculates the distribution of individual wait times, the queue size of people awaiting transport, and the conditions under which multiple elevators achieve synchronization at high arrival rates. Furthermore, numerous theoretical predictions are confirmed through event-driven simulations.

We demonstrate the significance of continuous in-situ star formation within the Brightest Cluster Galaxy (BCG) of the massive cool-core CLASH cluster MACS 1931.8-2635 at z=0.35. By employing a multi-wavelength strategy, we evaluate the stellar and warm ionized medium components using spatially resolved VLT-MUSE spectroscopy and correlate them with molecular gas data from sub-mm ALMA observations. Analysis of strong emission line fluxes allows us to derive the physical conditions of the warm ionized gas. The peak brightness of the ionized gas aligns with the supermassive black hole, while a diffuse tail of warm ionized gas extends 30 kpc toward the north-east. The ionized and molecular gases are co-spatial and co-moving; the gas in the tail is falling inward, supplying fuel for both star formation and accretion-driven nuclear activity. Ionization arises from a combination of star formation and other energetic processes producing LINER-like emission, though active galactic nucleus emission dominates only in the BCG core. We calculate a star formation rate of 97 Msun/yr, peaking at the BCG core, yet star formation contributes only 50-60% of the energy required to ionize the warm gas. In-situ star formation, driven by thermally unstable intracluster medium cooling and/or dry mergers, dominates stellar mass growth at z<0.5 and accounts for 20% of the system's total mass buildup. Our findings indicate that the BCG's most central regions have the lowest gas-phase oxygen abundance, while the tail shows slightly higher values. The galaxy is dispersion-dominated, characteristic of massive ellipticals, with gas and stellar kinematics decoupled; the gas velocity fields align more closely with the bulk motions of the intracluster medium.

The classical bond-fluctuation model (BFM) serves as an efficient lattice Monte Carlo method for coarse-grained polymer chains, wherein each monomer is restricted to occupying a specific number of lattice sites exclusively. This paper introduces a generalized BFM that relaxes this restriction, permitting monomer overlap subject to a finite energy penalty $\overlap$. This modification allows for the systematic variation of the dimensionless compressibility $g$ of the solution, facilitating an investigation into how density fluctuations within dense polymer melts affect various static properties at a constant overall monomer density. The compressibility is derived directly from the low-wavevector limit of the static structure factor. For instance, we examine the intrachain bond-bond correlation function, $P(s)$, for two bonds separated by $s$ monomers along the chain. Our findings indicate that excluded volume interactions are never completely screened for very long chains. When distances smaller than the thermal blob size are considered ($s \ll g$), the chains exhibit swelling consistent with the classical Fixman expansion, such as $P(s) \sim g^{-1}s^{-1/2}$. More significantly, at larger distances ($s \gg g$), the polymers behave akin to swollen chains composed of incompressible blobs, following $P(s) \sim g^0s^{-3/2}$.

Extending the methodology used for grid homology of links in $S^3$, we establish combinatorially that the grid homology of links in lens spaces, as defined by Baker, Grigsby, and Hedden, constitutes a link invariant. Additionally, by applying the sign assignment proposed by Celoria, we demonstrate that the extension of grid homology to integral coefficients also yields a link invariant.

Photon emission from quark-gluon plasma (QGP) serves as a probe for medium interactions, exhibiting distinct qualitative differences between weakly and strongly coupled plasmas in the soft-photon limit. This emissivity arises from the product of kinematic factors and a spectral function linked to the two-point correlation of the electromagnetic current under lightlike conditions. In lattice QCD, a specific Euclidean correlator evaluated at imaginary spatial momentum can be computed; this quantity corresponds to an integral over the aforementioned spectral function at lightlike kinematics. This work presents the first exploratory lattice calculation of such a correlator. Furthermore, it demonstrates that Euclidean correlators at imaginary spatial momenta can also investigate the deep inelastic scattering regime of QGP, thereby revealing its parton distribution function.

We investigate a mesoscopic model of a liquid crystalline brush designed to act as a photoswitchable aligning surface for inducing preorientation in bulk low molecular weight liquid crystals. This brush consists of grafted polymer chains featuring a side-chain architecture, where side chains are capped with chromophores mimicking azobenzene units attached to a substrate. Upon exposure to ultraviolet light, these chromophores photoisomerize into a non-mesogenic cis state, transforming the system into a standard polymer brush lacking orientational order; it exists in either a collapsed or straightened state based on grafting density. Conversely, visible light irradiation triggers photoisomerization into a mesogenic trans state, creating a transient network between chains due to strong chromophore attraction. Under these conditions, spontaneous self-assembly yields an orientationally isotropic polydomain structure. However, uniaxial planar ordering of chromophores within the brush can be achieved at specific temperature and grafting density ranges through a two-stage preparation protocol. In the first stage, an external stimulus induces uniaxial alignment of the chromophores. During the second stage, the system is equilibrated at a set temperature with the external stimulus removed. Whether the preoriented chromophores retain or lose their alignment depends on the strength of the memory effect inherent to the transient network formed in the first stage, analogous to the covalent crosslink-induced effects observed in liquid crystalline elastomers.

We investigate the stability of perturbations within a homogeneous non-Abelian electric field configuration that is immune to Schwinger pair production. Our analysis pinpoints unstable modes and determines a specific parameter range where instabilities are absent. Finally, we explore the potential implications of these findings for confining strings in non-Abelian gauge theories.

Protecting the privacy of medical imaging data presents significant challenges. Even after stripping metadata, brain scans remain susceptible to attacks that match facial renderings against image databases. Existing de-identification methods, which attempt to obscure or excise facial regions from diagnostic scans, often either fail to reliably conceal patient identity or are so aggressive that they degrade subsequent medical analyses. We introduce a novel category of de-identification techniques that remodels facial features rather than removing them. Our approach utilizes a conditional multi-scale Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) architecture. Taking a patient's MRI as input, the system generates a 3D volume conditioned on the patient's brain; this output preserves the brain structure exactly while de-identifying the face through remodeling. We demonstrate that our method offers superior privacy protection compared to current techniques without compromising downstream medical analyses, validated through evaluations on the OASIS-3 and ADNI datasets.

Optical coherence tomography (OCT) serves as a widely adopted non-invasive 3D imaging technique in ophthalmology for visualizing the retina. Automating the segmentation of retinal layers in a way that maintains anatomical coherence is crucial for diagnosing and tracking conditions such as Age-related Macular Disease (AMD) and Diabetic Retinopathy. Nevertheless, most current state-of-the-art segmentation approaches rely entirely on supervised deep learning, which necessitates extensive pixel-level annotated data that is both costly and difficult to acquire. To address this, we propose a semi-supervised framework for retinal layer segmentation that leverages information from large-scale unlabeled datasets alongside anatomical priors. Specifically, we employ a novel fully differentiable method to transform surface position regression into pixel-wise structured segmentation, enabling the coupled training of the model using both 1D surface and 2D layer representations. These 2D segmentations function as anatomical factors that, combined with learned style factors, create disentangled representations for input image reconstruction. Concurrently, we introduce a set of anatomical priors to enhance network performance when labeled data is scarce. Our evaluations on real-world scans of intermediate and wet-AMD demonstrate that our method surpasses state-of-the-art techniques using our complete training set; more significantly, it substantially outperforms existing methods when trained on only a fraction of the labeled data.

This study presents estimates of the effective reproduction number ($R_e$) for Athens, Greece, during the initial pandemic wave (February 26–May 15, 2020). Utilizing a comparative framework, we applied the two most prevalent $R_e$ estimation techniques: those developed by Wallinga and Teunis, and by Cori et al. Data were sourced from Greece's national SARS-CoV-2 infection database. Our findings indicate that the expected $R_e$ value fell below 1 around March 15, shortly following the nationwide suspension of educational institutions on March 10 and the closure of retail venues, including cafes, bars, museums, shopping centers, sports facilities, and restaurants, on March 13. By May 4, when the strict lockdown began to ease, the expected $R_e$ remained slightly below 1, though with considerable uncertainty attributable to the low number of reported cases during that interval. Lastly, we address the limitations and potential pitfalls of the employed methods, emphasizing that policymakers should interpret these results merely as indicative.

Since voltage phase angle data are frequently missing from sensors at transmission boundaries and within distribution networks, this study investigates how to estimate the sensitivities of voltage magnitudes to complex power injections (both active and reactive) using available measurements. These sensitivities correspond to specific submatrices of the inverse power flow Jacobian. Building on prior work, we demonstrate that the sensitivity of a bus voltage magnitude to active power injections is distinct from its sensitivity to reactive power injections. Utilizing the classical Newton-Raphson power flow model, we derive a new formulation expressing bus voltage magnitudes as an underdetermined linear operator of power injections, parameterized by bus power factors. We establish two criteria that guarantee the existence of unique complex power injections for a given set of voltage magnitudes, effectively narrowing the solution space: a sufficient condition relying on bus power factors and a necessary and sufficient condition based on system eigenvalues. Furthermore, by applying matrix completion theory, we develop methods to estimate sensitivity matrices despite varying degrees of sensor availability. Simulations confirm the validity of these findings and illustrate their practical engineering applications.

Recently, anisotropic bulk Dirac (or Weyl) cones in three-dimensional systems have attracted significant research attention due to their status as materials exhibiting tilted Dirac (or Weyl) cones, which signal a violation of Lorentz invariance. Conversely, investigations into anisotropic surface Dirac cones in topological materials, which influence anisotropic carrier mobility, remain scarce. Utilizing angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy combined with first-principles calculations, we uncover anisotropic surface Dirac dispersion in the tetradymite material Ti2Te2P within the (001) plane of the Brillouin zone. We identify quasi-elliptical Fermi pockets at the M-point of the Brillouin zone that constitute these anisotropic surface Dirac cones. Furthermore, our calculations of the Z2 indices demonstrate that the system is topologically non-trivial, hosting multiple topological phases within the same material. Additionally, the presence of a nodal-line-like feature formed by bulk bands renders this system topologically rich.

The maritime sector is undergoing a technological transformation that impacts ship construction, the operation of both inland and ocean-going vessels, cargo handling, and harbor workflows. This shift is motivated by the goal of creating a more sustainable and cost-effective ecosystem. Digitalization and automation facilitate these objectives by making shipping and cruising significantly more energy- and cost-efficient while reducing carbon footprints. Central to this process are always-on connectivity and content delivery services, which not only enhance operational efficiency and lower emissions for shipping companies but also improve crew well-being and passenger satisfaction. Thanks to recent breakthroughs in high-capacity, ultra-reliable terrestrial and non-terrestrial networking, ubiquitous maritime connectivity is now achievable. To manage the growing complexity of these integrated systems, this article recommends employing artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques to satisfy service demands and energy efficiency goals across various maritime communication scenarios.

We present the identification of a long-timescale negative time lag in the nearby Seyfert 1 galaxy Fairall 9, where blue light trails red light. Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) exhibit variability across diverse timescales, and measuring lags between wavelengths allows researchers to probe the otherwise hidden kinematics and structure of the accretion disk. While reverberation mapping is a standard technique used to quantify lags that increase outward at the speed of light—thereby revealing the disk's size and temperature profile—we are inspired by numerical simulations to look for longer lags that travel inward over extended periods, tracing the accretion process itself. By analyzing Fairall 9's light curves in both temporal and frequency domains, we detect these inward-propagating long-timescale lags ($\sim -70$ days), which move opposite to typical reverberation lags. We also confirm a short continuum lag ($<10$ days) that aligns with previously reported literature values. When fitting the longer lag against frequency using a model based on the thin disk theory, we conclude that the disk scale height likely increases toward the outer regions. This discovery offers a promising avenue for mapping accretion disk structures across a broad spectrum of AGN parameters.

Universal Style Transfer (UST) integrates styles from arbitrary reference images into content images. Although existing methods have achieved significant practical success, they fail to explain experimental findings, such as the varying ability of UST algorithms to maintain the spatial structure of content. Furthermore, current approaches rely on cumbersome global controls, necessitating extra spatial masks to achieve desired stylization. This study offers a systematic Fourier analysis of a general UST framework, presenting an equivalent frequency-domain formulation. This formulation reveals that existing algorithms treat all frequency components and feature map pixels uniformly, with the sole exception of the zero-frequency component. We establish a connection where Fourier amplitude corresponds to Gram matrices and Fourier phase relates to content reconstruction loss in style transfer. Leveraging these equivalences and connections, we interpret the differing structure preservation behaviors among algorithms based on Fourier phase. Building on these insights, we propose two practical manipulations to enhance structure preservation and achieve desired stylization. Both qualitative and quantitative experiments demonstrate that our method competes favorably against state-of-the-art approaches. Additionally, we conduct experiments to validate the proposed equivalence, the interpretability derived from Fourier amplitude and phase, and the controllability linked to specific frequency components.

This work introduces a slave rotor-Hartree Fock framework to investigate the p-d model characterizing perovskite transition metal oxides, alongside a flexible and efficient numerical approach for solving it. The methodology successfully reproduces key features of the rare earth nickelate phase diagram within a unified formulation, capturing both the paramagnetic metallic state of LaNiO3 and the correct magnetic ground state of insulating compounds. Furthermore, the method elucidates ground-state transitions as morphology shifts from bulk to strained and unstrained thin films. In ultrathin films, the study demonstrates that epitaxial strain and charge transfer to apical out-of-plane oxygen sites exert a substantial influence on the phase diagram.

In robust geometric computation, exact decisions frequently rely on inexact floating-point arithmetic. A prevalent strategy involves recording the computation history within an arithmetic expression DAG and re-evaluating it at higher precisions until an exact result is achieved. This study demonstrates that exact-decision number types utilizing expression DAGs can be processed more efficiently in practice by leveraging parallelization across multiple cores. Furthermore, we analyze how various DAG restructuring techniques influence execution time within a parallel computing environment.

This study investigates the null controllability of the heat equation featuring an inverse square potential and a memory component. We begin by proving null controllability for a nonhomogeneous singular heat equation using a novel Carleman inequality with weights that remain bounded at t=0. Subsequently, under a specific condition regarding the kernel, we demonstrate the null controllability of the singular heat equation with memory via Kakutani's fixed-point Theorem.

Accurate determination of material positions within the LHCb vertex locator (VELO) is crucial for suppressing background noise in searches for long-lived exotic particles and for distinguishing jets from beauty and charm quarks. By analyzing secondary hadronic interactions resulting from beam-gas collisions, researchers construct a map of this material distribution. Combining this map with the characteristics of a reconstructed secondary vertex and its associated tracks allows for the calculation of a $p$-value testing the hypothesis that the vertex stems from a material interaction. The validity of this method is demonstrated through its application to photon conversions into dimuons.

4H-silicon-carbide (4H-SiC) presents a promising material for high-rate particle detectors due to its distinctive electrical and material characteristics. Unlike the commonly utilized silicon (Si), 4H-SiC provides a superior carrier saturation velocity and higher breakdown voltage, which facilitate excellent intrinsic time resolution and reduce pile-up effects. Furthermore, as radiation hardness standards become stricter, wide-bandgap materials like 4H-SiC are expected to deliver enhanced performance. This study evaluated the performance of 50-micron-thick 4H-SiC p-in-n planar pad sensors at room temperature using a 241Am alpha source under reverse biases reaching 1100 V. The investigation also incorporated samples exposed to neutron irradiation with fluences up to 1e16/cm^2 to assess radiation hardness, comparing the findings against prior UV-TCT studies. Results indicate that charge collection efficiency (CCE) declines as irradiation fluence increases, though this drop is partially offset at high reverse bias voltages exceeding the full depletion threshold. While an unirradiated reference detector shows a charge plateau corresponding to the depletion volume traversed by alpha particles, this plateau in irradiated samples emerges only at higher reverse biases. At the maximum fluence tested, CCE increases nearly linearly with reverse bias. Compared to UV-TCT data, the reverse bias needed to deplete the sensitive volume for full alpha energy deposition is lower, attributed to the shallow penetration depth of alpha particles. However, at the highest reverse bias, the measured CCE values align closely with previous UV-TCT results, with discrepancies ranging between 1% and 5%.

This study addresses the estimation of the epidemic reproduction number $R_t$ for populations where case detection probability is influenced by a known covariate. We demonstrate that standard empirical estimators may fail when case prevalence varies across groups over time. To address this, we introduce a Bayesian approach, alongside a simplified solution for scenarios with a high volume of cases. We validate these methods using a realistic simulation study and examine the broader implications for the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic.

A new Monte Carlo approach has been created to measure the lifetimes of excited states within the tens-to-hundreds femtosecond range. This technique was applied to low-energy heavy-ion binary reactions that populate nuclei exhibiting complex velocity distributions. Its utility is illustrated through the $^{18}$O(7.0 MeV/u) + $^{181}$Ta experiment conducted at GANIL using the AGATA+VAMOS+PARIS apparatus to investigate neutron-rich oxygen, carbon, nitrogen, and other nuclei. Known lifetimes of excited states in $^{17}$O and $^{19}$O served to validate the method across a sensitivity window of approximately 20–400 fs. Particular emphasis is placed on the exceptional position resolution offered by $\gamma$-tracking arrays, a critical factor for achieving the necessary accuracy in Doppler-shift corrections, which underpins the detailed analysis of $\gamma$-ray lineshapes and subsequent lifetime determinations. This technique is expected to become a vital instrument for studying lifetimes in exotic neutron-rich nuclei generated via intense ISOL-type beams.

This paper introduces a novel method for Boolean matrix factorization (BMF) that avoids solving the BMF problem directly. Instead, it addresses a nonnegative optimization problem constrained by an auxiliary matrix sharing the same Boolean structure as the original data; the resulting solution is then thresholded to yield the BMF solution. The authors provide proofs demonstrating the equivalence of the two solution spaces when an exact solution exists, as well as evidence of the algorithm's nonincreasing property. Furthermore, experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets illustrate the method's effectiveness and computational complexity relative to existing approaches.

This study introduces approximate analytic formulas for muon survival probability within a $3+1$ mixing framework that incorporates matter effects via the S-matrix formalism. We demonstrate that the various terms constituting the muon survival probability can be substantially condensed into just three components. The dominant term originates from the standard three-flavor muon survival probability, succeeded by two sub-leading terms derived from active-sterile mixing. To further streamline the findings, we utilize established series expansions regarding the mass-hierarchy parameter $\alpha = \Delta m^2_{21} / \Delta m^2_{31}$ and the mixing angle $\sin \theta_{13}$ under the assumption that $\alpha^2$ approaches zero. We examine the significance of muon survival probability for investigating CP and T-violation signals potentially arising from new physics. Additionally, we contrast the analytic relationship between vacuum and matter contributions to the muon survival probability at the leading order. Finally, we address the probability's behavior across various long baselines, which is essential for analyzing the atmospheric-neutrino sector and addressing the current mass-hierarchy issue.

This paper introduces a framework for integrating optical-orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (O-OFDM) and index-modulated O-OFDM (O-OFDM-IM) within optical wireless systems. While both methods have distinct drawbacks—specifically, O-OFDM lacks flexibility in balancing spectral efficiency (SE) and energy efficiency (EE), whereas O-OFDM-IM suffers reduced EE with higher-order modulation alphabets—combining them overcomes these limitations. To validate the proposed approach, we apply it to asymmetrically clipped O-OFDM and ACO-OFDM-IM. The findings demonstrate that unifying these schemes not only enables a configurable SE/EE trade-off but also achieves higher SE and superior EE compared to O-OFDM-IM in high-SE scenarios.

Frauchiger and Renner demonstrated that quantum theory creates a contradiction when simple reasoning principles are applied to observers modeled as physical systems, utilizing a thought experiment that generates a multi-agent paradox. This work extends those conditions to any physical theory, specifically focusing on generalized probabilistic theories (GPTs). When applied to the GPT known as box world, we identify a deterministic contradiction arising if agents can share a PR box; this result surpasses the quantum paradox because it does not depend on post-selection. Establishing such an inconsistency within the GPT framework expands the range of theories where classical reasoning rules fail when applied to physical agents. Furthermore, we illustrate how observer memories can evolve in box world in accordance with Barrett's criteria for valid operations.

In recent years, the field of natural language processing has experienced remarkable growth and sophistication, driven by the emergence of highly scalable artificial neural networks for text representation. Leveraging the distributional hypothesis, these methods enable the conversion of complex linguistic data into multidimensional dense numeric vectors. Consequently, the rapid evolution of text representation techniques has left the research community struggling to keep track of these methods and their interconnections. To address this gap in compilation, organization, and systematization, we present a three-part contribution: a survey of current approaches, a genealogical arrangement of these methods, and a conceptual taxonomy designed to analyze and explain state-of-the-art techniques. This work serves as an essential guide and reference for AI researchers and practitioners working on NLP applications, including sentiment analysis, chatbots, and recommender systems.
