Following a 49-year quiescent period, the source 4U~1730--22 reactivated with two outbursts in 2021 and 2022, during which ten thermonuclear X-ray bursts were identified by Insight-HXMT. One of the faintest bursts exhibited a double-peaked profile, designating this object as the fifth accreting neutron star (NS) to display double or triple-peaked type-I X-ray bursts, while the remaining bursts demonstrated photospheric radius expansion (PRE). The characteristics of the double-peaked non-PRE burst suggest a connection to a stalled burning front. Regarding the five bright PRE bursts, residuals were detected in both the soft ($<$3 keV) and hard ($>$10 keV) X-ray bands beyond the emission from the NS surface. Time-resolved spectroscopy attributes this excess to either enhanced pre-burst or persistent emission, or to the Comptonization of burst emission by the corona or boundary layer. Observations indicate that burst emission rises as the photosphere recedes to the NS surface, deviating from the theoretical prediction of constant Eddington luminosity. The deficit of burst emission during the early rising phase exceeds what can be explained by disk occlusion. We hypothesize that this discrepancy arises because the obscured portion of the NS surface (including areas other than the lower section) becomes visible due to the evaporation of obscuring material caused by the burst emission, or because the burst emission is anisotropic ($\xi>1$) in the early phase. Furthermore, utilizing the average flux of PRE bursts at the moment of touch-down, we estimate the source's distance to be 10.4 kpc.

Recent findings indicate that bacteria like *E. coli* and *P. putida* exhibit distinct motility patterns within porous media compared to dilute or free-space environments. This observation supports a proposed strategy for active particles in disordered settings: suppressing reorientations in locally sparse areas while enhancing them in densely packed ones. Consequently, local geometry dictates the optimal trajectory for these agents, significantly accelerating their dynamics by up to two orders of magnitude. Furthermore, we detect a non-monotonic relationship between the diffusion coefficient and the tumbling rate, alongside a localization transition triggered by either increasing obstacle density or reducing the reorientation rate.

Consider the group $G$, which represents either the piecewise-affine circle homeomorphisms ${\rm PAff}_+({\bf S}^1)$ or the smooth circle diffeomorphisms ${\Diff}^{\infty}(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)$. A constructive demonstration is provided showing that every irrational rotation is distorted within $G$.

Identifying partial differential equations (PDEs) from scarce, noisy spatio-temporal data is crucial across various scientific domains, yet it remains unclear when sparse regression-based algorithms can successfully uncover the true physical mechanisms. This study demonstrates that design matrices generated for sparse regression can breach the Lasso's irrepresentability condition (IRC), even when constructed from exact analytical PDE solutions devoid of extra noise. Consequently, there is a need for sparse regression methods capable of handling violated IRC conditions, prompting the development of the randomised adaptive Lasso. When this method is incorporated into the DeepMod deep learning framework for model discovery, it successfully recovers a broad range of nonlinear and chaotic canonical PDEs. Specifically, it achieves performance up to $\mathcal{O}(2)$ times better in noise-to-sample ratios compared to current state-of-the-art algorithms and operates with a single set of hyperparameters, advancing the goal of fully automated model discovery.

Our earlier work examined the optical characteristics of multi-layered nanocomposites fabricated via Sputtering Atomic Layer Augmented Deposition (SALAD), comprising 300 alternating pairs of AlOx and Cu layers. These samples exhibited anomalous spectral reflectance that defied conventional descriptions and could not be attributed to a simple interpolation of their constituent materials, necessitating computational modeling to both interpret the results and forecast other properties. We employed the transfer-matrix method to model spectral reflectance based on the individual materials and utilized the dispersion method to determine the composite refractive index. While the models accurately represented pure Cu, they faced minor challenges with AlOx; consequently, further research is required to either adapt the current algorithm for non-holomorphic materials like AlOx or develop a superior model capable of adequately describing both components. The implemented dispersion model suggests that these numerous thin-film metal-dielectric structures exhibit semiconductor-like behavior, indicating that SALAD's integration of sputtering and ALD enables the creation of novel metal-dielectric semiconductors.

Current nuclear fuel cycle simulations are typically highly customized, necessitating a modular design to accommodate diverse user needs. Cyclus was created specifically to overcome the rigidity of earlier simulators by employing an agent-based infrastructure and discrete time steps. Its kernel supports "archetypes"—models with varying fidelity and functionality tailored to specific user requirements. Consequently, users must create their own archetypes if none exist within the Cyclus ecosystem, thereby becoming archetype developers. Developing these archetypes manually is challenging for newcomers without automation. This paper introduces the Cyclus preprocessor (cycpp), a framework designed to simplify archetype creation. By handling algorithmic software development and computer science tasks, cycpp enables developers to concentrate on modeling physics, social policies, and economics. The tool processes code in three stages: C preprocessor normalization, notation accumulation, and code generation. This approach reduces the required code volume by roughly an order of magnitude and ensures automatic validation of the resulting archetypes.

We investigate the parameter space of effective two-scalar inflationary models within modified $(R+R^2)$ supergravity, focusing on double inflation scenarios. In these models, the initial inflationary phase is driven by Starobinsky's scalaron arising from $R^2$ gravity, followed by a second stage propelled by another scalar from the supergravity multiplet. An ultra-slow-roll phase separating these two stages generates a significant peak in the scalar power spectrum, facilitating efficient primordial black hole (PBH) formation. Both inflation and PBH production are generic features of our framework, with the resulting PBHs potentially constituting a substantial portion or entirety of dark matter. While earlier models in this category exhibited tensions ($>3\sigma$) with the observed scalar spectral index $n_s$, we examine more general, multi-parameter models to analyze how cosmological tilts $(n_s, r)$ and power spectrum enhancements depend on these parameters. We also compute PBH masses and their density fraction relative to dark matter. Achieving consistency with the observed $n_s$ (within $2\sigma$ to $3\sigma$) necessitates fine-tuning and is specifically realized in $\delta$-models. Our framework unifies the gravitational origins of inflation, PBHs, and dark matter, offering testable predictions through future precision observations of the cosmic microwave background and gravitational waves induced by PBHs.

Graph connectivity serves as a crucial metric for assessing reliability. Concepts such as structure and substructure connectivity, component connectivity, and $k$-restricted connectivity represent well-established generalizations of standard connectivity that have been widely examined through a combinatorial lens. However, aside from recent findings regarding the computational complexity of $k$-restricted edge-connectivity, very few results exist concerning their complexity. This paper focuses on determining the complexity of structure and substructure connectivity, component connectivity, and $k$-restricted connectivity, demonstrating that each is NP-complete.

This paper examines the decoding of Gabidulin codes and demonstrates how to adapt standard decoders for any supercode of a Gabidulin code, albeit with a substantial reduction in the decoding radius. Leveraging this modified decoder, the authors present polynomial-time attacks against the rank-metric encryption schemes RAMESSES and LIGA.

We introduce a technique for tracing implicit real algebraic curves defined by polynomials possessing rank-deficient Jacobians. For a specified curve $f^{-1}(0)$, the method initially employs regularization to identify at least one witness point within each connected component; we enhance this process by deriving a sufficient condition to verify the emptiness of $f^{-1}(0)$. Furthermore, we examine the convergence speed and perform an error analysis regarding the refinement of these witness points. These points are generated by calculating the minimum distance from a random point to a smooth manifold that embeds the curve, simultaneously penalizing the residual of $f$ at local minima. To trace the curve from these starting points, we demonstrate that dragging a random point along a trajectory within a tubular neighborhood of the embedded manifold yields a unique projection onto the manifold, which can be determined via numerical continuation. We subsequently illustrate how to select such a trajectory to approximate the curve by computing eigenvectors of specific matrices. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through various examples.

The connection between an arbitrary frequency distribution and the expected values derived from its samples is examined. A broad range of measurable quantities, termed "invariant moments," are developed; these possess expectation values that generally remain independent of sample size. These results are demonstrated by applying them to the Ewens sampling formula. Invariant moments prove particularly valuable when sampling systems lacking an intrinsic scale. The text explores distribution functions capable of parametrizing samples from such scale-free distributions and calculates their invariant expectation values, while also outlining the conditions required for the existence of a scaling limit for these distributions.

The direct measurement method is employed to determine the nuclear reactor antineutrino spectrum. We propose isolating the partial spectra of fissile isotopes by applying the technique of extracting antineutrino spectra from the inverse beta decay positron spectrum, as demonstrated in the Rovno experiment. This approach enhances the precision of the partial antineutrino spectra that constitute the total reactor spectrum. Such accuracy is crucial for analyzing the reactor core's fuel composition and holds potential applications in non-proliferation efforts.

Increasing the size of convolutional neural networks (CNNs), such as their width and depth, is a proven method for enhancing model accuracy. However, the resulting large model sizes hinder training on resource-limited edge devices. For example, federated learning (FL) can impose excessive computational demands on these edge nodes, despite its critical importance for privacy and confidentiality. To overcome the limitations of edge devices, we reframe FL as a group knowledge transfer training algorithm named FedGKT. FedGKT employs a modified alternating minimization strategy to train compact CNNs on edge nodes, periodically transferring their learned knowledge via knowledge distillation to a larger server-side CNN. This framework integrates multiple benefits: it minimizes edge computation requirements, reduces communication bandwidth for large models, and supports asynchronous training, all while achieving accuracy levels comparable to FedAvg. We evaluated CNNs based on ResNet-56 and ResNet-110 across three datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and CINIC-10), including their non-I.I.D. variants. Our findings indicate that FedGKT achieves accuracy comparable to or slightly exceeding that of FedAvg. Crucially, FedGKT makes edge training feasible; compared to FedAvg, it reduces edge computational power (FLOPs) by 9 to 17 times and decreases the number of parameters in edge CNNs by 54 to 105 times. Our source code is available at FedML (https://fedml.ai).

By addressing the second boundary value problem for the Lagrangian mean curvature equation, we establish the existence and uniqueness of a smooth, uniformly convex solution, thereby extending Brendle-Warren's theorem on minimal Lagrangian diffeomorphisms within Euclidean metric space.

The "paradox of progress" refers to the observed trend where increased education correlates with heightened income inequality. This phenomenon stems from two competing drivers: the convex nature of the Mincer equation, which connects wages to education, and the variation in returns across different income levels, as identified through quantile regressions. To assess the relative impact of each factor, we introduce a statistical framework combining least-squares and quantile regressions, utilizing a "functional derivative" approach for estimation. This decomposition method is applied to analyze data from Argentina between 1992 and 2015.

Artificial superlattice (SL) potentials have been widely utilized to engineer the band structure of the two-dimensional (2D) Dirac electron gas in graphene. Although these engineered electronic structures can alter graphene's optical or plasmonic characteristics, no emergent polaritonic behavior beyond weak perturbative effects—such as anisotropic Drude weights—has previously been observed. In this study, we demonstrate that extreme modulation of one-dimensional (1D) SL potentials in monolayer graphene distorts the fundamental Dirac band dispersion and creates ladder-like energy levels near the Fermi surface. These features give rise to emergent intersubband polaritonic responses in optical conductivity. The proposed system consists of hBN-encapsulated graphene positioned atop a 1D periodic metagate, with a second backgate located beneath the metagate to further modulate carrier density in regions of graphene not directly screened by the metagate. Under strong carrier density modulation, graphene electrons encounter an array of deep potential wells; at sufficiently large momenta perpendicular to the modulation direction, Dirac electrons are waveguided through total internal reflection. These waveguided modes manifest as flat subbands with nearly equidistant energy levels, leading to the formation of hybrid intersubband-polaritons exhibiting ultra-strong coupling within plasmonic dispersions. Consequently, this research paves the way for investigating emergent polaritons in two-dimensional materials featuring gate-tunable electronic band structures.

We aim to semantically characterize a collection of images, encompassing both individual image attributes and the variations present within the group. Our approach mirrors Principal Component Analysis (PCA), substituting projection vectors with generated phrases. Initially, we generate a centroid phrase that maximizes average semantic similarity to the image set, utilizing pretrained vision-language models for both similarity calculation and phrase generation. Subsequently, we generate a phrase that yields the highest variation in similarity scores, again using these models. Following this, each subsequent phrase maximizes variance while maintaining orthogonality in the latent space relative to the previously generated high-variance phrase, continuing this iterative process. Experimental results demonstrate that our method effectively captures the core essence of image sets and provides semantically meaningful descriptions of individual elements within the broader context of the collection. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/OdedH/textual-pca.

This study investigates a general framework comprising multiple ordinary differential equations coupled with a reaction-diffusion equation within a bounded domain subject to zero-flux boundary conditions, specifically focusing on pattern formation. The associated initial-boundary value problems may admit regular (sufficiently smooth) stationary solutions. This category of "close-to-equilibrium" patterns encompasses stationary states generated by the Turing instability of a spatially uniform stationary solution. The primary finding of this work establishes that all such regular patterns are unstable. This result implies that stable stationary solutions in models containing non-diffusive components must be "far-from-equilibrium" and exhibit singularities. These discontinuous stationary solutions have been examined in our concurrent work [\textit{Stable discontinuous stationary solutions to reaction-diffusion-ODE systems}, preprint (2021)].

We examine the singular Yamabe obstruction $\mathcal{B}_3$ for a hypersurface situated within a four-dimensional general background. Starting from its fundamental definition, we derive several explicit expressions for $\mathcal{B}_3$ and compare them with analogous formulas found in existing literature. The accompanying proofs are straightforward.

We introduce SpectroMap, an open-source Python repository dedicated to audio fingerprinting. This tool utilizes a peak search algorithm to identify topological prominences within spectrograms by analyzing time-frequency bands. The paper details the algorithm's operation through two experimental applications, demonstrating its efficacy using high-quality urban sound datasets and environmental audio recordings.

This work consists of two main components. The initial section examines the long-term asymptotic behavior of solutions to the heat equation on Riemannian symmetric spaces $G/K$ of noncompact type and arbitrary rank. We demonstrate that solutions with bi-$K$-invariant $L^{1}$ initial data asymptotically resemble the mass multiplied by the fundamental solution, while also presenting a counterexample for the non bi-$K$-invariant scenario, thereby addressing questions recently posed by J.L. V\'azquez. The second section explores the long-time asymptotic properties of solutions to the heat equation linked to the distinguished Laplacian on $G/K$. Notably, this part reveals phenomena akin to those in Euclidean space, characterized by $L^1$ asymptotic convergence without requiring bi-$K$-invariance and strong $L^{\infty}$ convergence.

When long, flexible polymer solutions are exposed to strong velocity gradients, they display chaotic motion and flow instabilities known as elastic turbulence. Unlike the well-understood inertia-driven turbulence in Newtonian fluids, the mechanism behind elastic turbulence remains unclear. In this study, we show that the dynamics of purely elastic pressure-driven channel flows in dilute polymer solutions are governed by exact coherent structures manifesting as two-dimensional travelling waves. Our findings indicate that these travelling wave solutions do not require linear instability to persist and originate solely from elastic effects. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the associated stress profiles feature thin, filament-like polymer stretches maintained by a solitary pair of vortices. Finally, we explore the implications of these travelling wave solutions for the onset of elastic turbulence in straight channels and suggest methods for their experimental detection.

Faces are fundamental to both the combinatorial and computational study of polyhedra. This paper introduces the first formalization of polyhedral faces within the Coq proof assistant, extending an existing library that covers basic polyhedral constructions such as projections, convex hulls, and images under linear maps. We also develop a specialized mechanism that automatically selects the most suitable representation for a polyhedron or face based on the proof context. The utility of this method is demonstrated by verifying key combinatorial properties of faces, specifically that they form graded atomistic and coatomistic lattices closed under interval sublattices. Additionally, we provide a proof of Balinski's theorem regarding the $d$-connectedness of the adjacency graph for polytopes of dimension $d$.

This study introduces a quantum framework for field propagation in three-dimensional dielectrics, incorporating third-order dispersion and attenuation coefficients. A specific Lagrangian is formulated to derive the corresponding equations of motion and classical Hamiltonian, under the assumption that the dielectric exhibits combined inhomogeneity, dispersion, and nonlinearity. Utilizing a constraint quantization method, the resulting Hamiltonian is expanded using appropriately defined annihilation and creation operators. These operators are then employed to determine the quantum fields (photon-polaritons) propagating through the medium with the specified dispersion and attenuation effects. The number operator within the final Hamiltonian represents the count of photon-polaritons in the medium, while the nonlinear component of the Hamiltonian is derived by expressing the displacement field operator in terms of these same annihilation and creation operators. As a demonstration, this quantum theory is applied to analyze field propagation through a one-dimensional slab.

This study presents thermodynamic data, $^{31}$P NMR results, and density-functional band-structure calculations for the quantum magnet $\varepsilon$-LiVOPO$_4$. Characterized by a singlet ground state, this material consists of two alternating types of spin-$\frac12$ chains, evidenced by double peaks in magnetic susceptibility and specific heat, as well as a two-step magnetization curve featuring an intermediate $\frac12$-plateau. Analysis of thermodynamic properties and band-structure computations yields estimates for the primary exchange couplings $J_1\simeq 20$ K and $J_2\simeq 60$ K, alongside alternation ratios of $\alpha_1=J_1'/J_1\simeq 0.6$ and $\alpha_2=J_2'/J_2\simeq 0.3$ for the respective chains. A zero-field spin gap of $\Delta_0/k_{\rm B}\simeq 7.3$ K, identified through thermodynamic and NMR measurements, originates from the $J_1$-$J_1'$ spin chains and is closed by an applied field of $\mu_{0}H_{\rm c1}\simeq 5.6$ T, triggering field-induced long-range order. Low-temperature NMR data indicate dominant three-dimensional spin-spin correlations. The magnetic ordering transition observed above $H_{c1}$ is ascribed to the Bose-Einstein condensation of triplons within the sublattice composed of the $J_1$-$J_1'$ chains, which possess weaker exchange interactions.

Although coupled dynamical systems are common in nature, their causal structures often remain unclear without specific domain knowledge. This challenge is particularly acute when analyzing observational time series data, such as climate variables, where controlled experiments are impossible. While various methods exist to infer causal relationships from data—including Granger causality, convergent cross mapping, and causal graph learning techniques like PCMCI—path signatures and their associated signed areas offer a novel perspective. These tools enable a model-free, data-driven approach to algorithmic causal discovery. This paper investigates the application of path signatures in causal discovery and introduces confidence sequences to evaluate the statistical significance of the signed area magnitudes between variable pairs. As sampling length increases, these confidence sequence regions converge; combined with an analysis of pairwise signed areas across time-shifted series, they facilitate the identification of lag and lead causal relationships. Consequently, this methodology offers a new means to quantify the confidence of causal links between time series and may establish a framework for hypothesis testing to determine whether one series causes another.

Cosmic-ray particles striking the atmosphere generate high-energy cascades known as Extensive Air Showers (EAS), which produce coherent radio signals. These signals are influenced by strong electric fields present during thunderstorms. To retrieve the atmospheric electric field from the observed radio footprint of an EAS, this study employs the analytic MGMR3D model. We conduct a comprehensive comparison between MGMR3D and the microscopic CoREAS model to derive an enhanced parametrization for MGMR3D under thunderstorm conditions, including confidence intervals. The method for extracting electric field structures was successfully applied to a complex radio footprint recorded by LOFAR during a thunderstorm. This demonstrates that the improved MGMR3D parametrization enables the effective extraction of atmospheric electric field structures.

Achieving high performance for both Integrated Sensing and Communications (ISAC) and efficiently utilizing resources is a compelling goal, yet a major hurdle remains in using channel-coded communication signals (c.c.s) for sensing. This paper examines the sensing capabilities of c.c.s within multi-user, interference-limited environments, revealing that performance is constrained by sidelobes in the range-Doppler map, which vary depending on whether single-carrier or OFDM waveforms are employed. While uncoded signals composed of independent symbols yield asymptotically zero sidelobes due to the law of large numbers, it was unclear if this applied to c.c.s, given that structured channel coding introduces symbol dependence. We demonstrate that c.c.s also produce asymptotically zero sidelobes for both waveform types by deriving upper bounds on sidelobe tail probabilities that decay exponentially with the product of the code rate and block length. Consequently, c.c.s prove to be robust sensing signals effective against multi-user interference at sufficiently large block lengths, with negligible performance differences between single-carrier and OFDM modulations. Simulations confirm this, showing that a QPSK-modulated c.c.s (code rate 120/1024, block length 1024) achieves detection and false-alarm probabilities comparable to an interference-free FMCW waveform even at high interference levels (SIR of -11dB) for both waveform structures.

This paper advances the understanding of Principal Component Analysis (PCA) in unsupervised clustering by examining its role beyond mere dimensionality reduction. We investigate a specific property termed "compressibility," demonstrating that PCA substantially decreases distances between points within the same cluster while only mildly affecting inter-cluster distances. This disparity accounts for numerous empirical findings, such as the observed enhancement in K-means accuracy following PCA application in single-cell RNA-sequencing, a key vector clustering task in biology. Our research addresses this compression gap through both theoretical analysis and practical verification. Theoretically, we evaluate PCA within a broad probabilistic framework known as the random vector model. Practically, we confirm PCA's compressibility across various single-cell RNA-seq datasets.

Understanding how young star clusters and OB associations form and evolve is crucial for grasping star formation, the environments of young binaries and planetary systems, and the origins of long-lived open and globular clusters. However, our knowledge of the physical mechanisms driving this evolution was previously constrained by the static nature of most observational data. This limitation is being overcome by a surge in kinematic data quality resulting from large-scale radial velocity surveys and modern astrometric instruments like Gaia. In this summary, I review recent investigations into multiple OB associations using data from both Gaia and ground-based astrometric surveys. These findings reveal significant kinematic substructure within OB associations and provide no support for the radial expansion predicted by theories such as residual gas expulsion. Consequently, contrary to the conventional view of OB associations as expanded star clusters, these systems likely never existed as dense clusters; instead, they were probably born as extended, highly substructured groups. This insight imposes strict constraints on the initial clustering of young stars and the conditions surrounding young planetary systems.

Quantum repeaters are essential for enabling long-distance quantum communications and the quantum Internet, relying on entanglement swapping that typically demands controlled quantum gates. While frequent measurements of a quantum system can inhibit its evolution through the quantum Zeno effect (QZE), this phenomenon can also be harnessed to steer system dynamics by inserting specific operations between measurements. This study introduces an entanglement swapping protocol grounded in the QZE that attains near-unit fidelity. Our approach necessitates only straightforward frequent threshold measurements and single-particle rotations, eliminating the need for controlled gates and thereby reducing the circuit complexity of quantum repeaters. Furthermore, we generalize this protocol to a chain of repeater stations, creating quantum Zeno repeaters that maintain almost unit fidelity irrespective of the network size. This work holds promise for advancing long-distance quantum communications and quantum computing by leveraging the quantum Zeno effect.

This paper details our efforts to develop a generic framework for multi-modal embedding and multi-label binary classification in the context of SemEval 2022 Task 5 (Multimedia Automatic Misogyny Identification). Because training deep models from scratch is resource-intensive and data-hungry, our methodology relies on three primary strategies. First, we integrate various state-of-the-art architectures to capture a broad range of semantic signals from multi-modal inputs. Second, we utilize a multi-task learning scheme to leverage multiple datasets within the same knowledge domain, thereby enhancing model performance. Third, we employ multiple objectives to regularize and fine-tune different components of the system.

Although anyons serve as fundamental units for topological quantum computation, individually creating and controlling them remains a significant hurdle. This study demonstrates that dissipative dynamics within cavities can deterministically generate droplets of light in targeted fractional quantum Hall states. Within these droplets, the count and positions of anyons are precisely adjustable without the need for additional potentials to imprint or localize these quasiparticles. Furthermore, anyonic statistics become easily accessible through the light's density profile. Additionally, coupling a quantum spin valve to these droplets enables direct measurement of braiding statistics. Our findings outline a promising pathway for quantum optics to address difficult challenges in quantum Hall physics.

Automating nuclei segmentation is a cornerstone of digital pathology, typically achieved through deep learning; however, these approaches demand extensive datasets with precise annotations, which are difficult to acquire. To alleviate annotation burdens, training on weakly labeled data has emerged as a popular strategy. This paper introduces a novel meta-learning framework for nuclei segmentation that adheres to a label correction paradigm, effectively utilizing data containing noisy masks. Specifically, we develop a fully conventional meta-model capable of refining noisy masks using a minimal set of clean meta-data, thereby generating corrected masks to supervise the segmentation model's training. Furthermore, we employ a bi-level optimization technique to alternately update the parameters of both the primary segmentation model and the meta-model in an end-to-end manner. Extensive experiments on two nuclear segmentation datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance, even matching the results of models trained on fully supervised data under certain noisy conditions.

This study investigates the eruption of a coronal mass ejection (CME) magnetic flux rope (MFR) originating from active region (AR) NOAA 11719 on April 11, 2013, using data from SDO, STEREO, SOHO, and WIND spacecraft. The source AR features a pre-existing sigmoidal structure superimposed on a filament channel, interpreted as an MFR system. Low-corona EUV observations indicate the MFR system evolved through the addition of axial flux via tether-cutting reconnection at the sigmoid's center, driven by continuous slow flux motions over the preceding two days. Our findings suggest the MFR system began moving upward due to kink instability and was subsequently propelled by torus instability. Analysis of the CME morphology from simultaneous three-point coronagraph data, fitted with the Graduated Cylindrical Shell (GCS) model, reveals an MFR topology oriented along the source AR's magnetic neutral line. The MFR expanded self-similarly, displaying source AR twist signatures within the associated near-Earth magnetic cloud (MC). We derived the CME propagation kinematics using various stereoscopic and single-spacecraft reconstruction techniques. Although stereoscopic methods yielded less accurate results than other approaches, fitting methods proved superior for estimating the CME's arrival time compared to in-situ measurements. By combining constrained solar wind velocity, drag parameters, and 3D kinematics from the GCS fit, we constructed a drag-based CME kinematic model that aligns with the in-situ MC arrival.

The Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory (LHAASO) has identified numerous photon events in the multi-TeV range, including several PeV-scale gamma rays reaching up to 1.4 PeV, with extragalactic origins remaining a viable possibility. This paper proposes an axion-photon conversion mechanism to explain how very-high-energy (VHE) and ultra-high-energy (UHE) photons could travel and reach Earth-based detectors. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this conversion process offers an alternative explanation, alongside Lorez invariance violation threshold anomalies, for the distinct VHE characteristics observed in the recent gamma-ray burst GRB 221009A.

To examine the stability of Itô stochastic differential equations featuring multiplicative noise, we propose the stochastic logarithmic norm. Originally formulated by G. Dahlquist in 1958 as a mechanism for analyzing solution growth in ordinary differential equations and assessing error accumulation in discretization schemes, this concept is now extended to address stability in Itô SDEs with multiplicative noise. We derive stability estimates for linear Itô SDEs utilizing one, two, and $\infty$-norms within the $l$-th mean (for $1 \leq l < \infty$), and we demonstrate the utility of the stochastic logarithmic norm through illustrative examples.

The BLMSSM extends the minimal supersymmetric standard model (MSSM) by introducing an additional local gauge group, $SU(3)_C \times SU(2)_L \times U(1)_Y \times U(1)_B \times U(1)_L$. Assuming the lightest scalar neutrino serves as the dark matter candidate, this study investigates the relic density and the spin-independent cross-section of sneutrino-nucleon scattering. Through detailed numerical calculations, we identify viable regions within the parameter space. These findings help constrain the model's parameters and offer valuable guidance for future dark matter research.

Consider a connected graph $G$ with $n$ vertices. A cyclic base ordering of $G$ is defined as a cyclic arrangement of all its edges where every set of $n-1$ consecutive edges in this cycle forms a spanning tree of $G$. This project investigates cyclic base orderings within triangular grid graphs, series compositions of graphs, generalized theta graphs, and circulant graphs.

This paper examines the transverse momentum spectra and their evolution relative to the azimuthal angle of particles linked to the leading particle, alongside an analysis of spherocity distribution within identical azimuthal bins. The investigation utilized proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}$ = 13 TeV, employing the PYTHIA8 Monte Carlo event generator. Furthermore, the multiplicity and midrapidity transverse momentum spectra of charged hadrons were evaluated using the non-extensive statistical framework, with findings regarding the Underlying Event also presented.

This study examines noise-resilient Boolean networks characterized by majority functions and varied topologies. These diverse configurations are modeled using a stochastic blockmodel. Within this framework, the system's dynamics consistently exhibit a phase transition: shifting from a non-ergodic regime, which retains a memory of previous states, to an ergodic regime, where memory is lost and all microstates become equally probable. The analysis provides analytical derivations for both the average network error and the critical noise threshold triggering this transition, with findings validated against numerical simulations. Furthermore, results concerning "partially dense" networks—composed of a small number of highly influential nodes with significantly higher input counts than the network average—establish broad upper limits on the maximum noise resilience achievable in globally sparse systems.

Precise computational modeling of the antigen processing pathway is essential for advancing personalized epitope vaccine design in cancer. A critical component of this pathway involves the proteasome degrading the vaccine into peptides, some of which are subsequently presented to T cells via the MHC complex. Although predicting MHC-peptide binding has garnered significant recent interest, forecasting proteasomal cleavage remains largely underexplored, particularly amidst recent breakthroughs in high-throughput mass spectrometry-based MHC ligandomics. Furthermore, since current experimental methods cannot definitively identify non-cleavable regions, recent predictors often generate artificial decoy negative samples to train on, mistakenly classifying some potential positives as negatives. To address this, we introduce a novel predictor built upon an expanded dataset and the robust theoretical framework of positive-unlabeled learning, achieving a new state-of-the-art in proteasomal cleavage prediction. These enhanced capabilities will facilitate more accurate vaccine development, thereby boosting the efficacy of epitope-based therapies. Pretrained models are accessible via GitHub.

The established concept of graph domination models the protection of specific locations using guards. This paper proposes a novel graph invariant, the autonomous domination number, which represents the defense of a set of locations by autonomous agents. These agents adhere to a straightforward protocol that enables them to coordinate their defensive efforts based solely on local information.

Stencil computation serves as a critical kernel across numerous scientific and engineering domains. Prior research has primarily targeted vectorization and tiling methods to leverage in-core data parallelism and locality, respectively. This paper examines the limitations of current vectorization approaches, noting that they either cause data alignment conflicts or degrade locality when combined with tiling. Consequently, we introduce a novel transpose layout that maintains data locality for tiling while minimizing data reorganization overhead for vectorization. Additionally, to enhance register-level data reuse, we develop a time loop unroll-and-jam strategy to execute multi-step stencil operations along the time dimension. Experiments conducted on AVX-2 and AVX-512 processors demonstrate that our method achieves competitive performance.

This study examines how the frequency, intensity, and geographic reach of extreme temperatures in Ireland evolved between 1960 and 2019. We constructed an extreme value model designed to account for both spatial and temporal non-stationarity in daily maximum temperature records. Specifically, we modeled the tails of marginal distributions using the generalised Pareto distribution and represented spatial dependence via a semi-parametric Brown-Resnick r-generalised Pareto process, allowing all parameters to vary over time. We relied on weather station data for modeling extreme events because climate models can oversmooth such phenomena due to abstraction; however, climate models offer essential insights into Ireland's detailed physiography. To address the limitations of sparse and biased observational sampling, we introduced novel methods that leverage climate model data. Our findings reveal significant temporal shifts in the marginal behavior of extreme temperatures, though the dependence structure remained stable. These characteristics explain the observed expansion in the spatial coverage of events surpassing critical temperature thresholds.

In Part I, I begin by deriving the coordinate transformation for a uniformly accelerating observer within a flat background, which facilitates the construction of Rindler space-time and the analysis of its extended geometry. Subsequently, I examine the relationship between Fourier modes of free scalar fields in Minkowski and Rindler spacetimes using Bogoliubov transformations. In Part II, I investigate the physical viewpoint of an accelerated observer relative to the Minkowski vacuum, deriving a Bose-Einstein distribution with a temperature proportional to the acceleration of the non-inertial frame. Finally, in Part III, I employ Euclidean techniques to develop the necessary tools for constructing, in detail, the Thermofield-double state.

This study theoretically investigates the electro-optical response of graphene arising from carrier heating and drift. The real and imaginary components of the dynamic conductivity tensor are computed under conditions of effective momentum relaxation, where anisotropic effects are negligible. The analysis employs a quasiequilibrium distribution for electrons and holes, defined by an effective carrier temperature and concentrations regulated by gate voltage and in-plane electric fields. Focusing on the normal propagation of probe radiation, the work examines the spectral and field dependencies of the reflection coefficient and relative absorption. Additionally, the degree of ellipticity in both reflected and transmitted radiation is calculated, accounting for the small birefringence induced by current in the graphene sheet.

The notion of Artificial Intelligence for Social Good (AI4SG) is rapidly gaining traction within both the AI community and information societies. While AI-driven advancements offer effective solutions to societal challenges, there remains only a basic understanding of the fundamental principles of socially beneficial AI, its practical reality, and the necessary policies to govern it. This paper addresses that gap by exploring the ethical dimensions critical for future AI4SG initiatives. Some of these ethical characteristics are novel to the field of AI, while others assume greater significance due to AI's specific applications.

A fundamental challenge in multi-label classification involves capturing the structural relationships among classes. Utilizing probabilistic and interpretable methods to model this structure facilitates applications across diverse domains, including zero-shot learning and scenarios with incomplete data. This paper introduces the probabilistic rule stacking learner (pRSL), which integrates predictions from multiple base classifiers using probabilistic propositional logic rules and belief propagation. We develop algorithms for both exact and approximate inference and learning, demonstrating that pRSL achieves state-of-the-art results on various benchmark datasets. Furthermore, we propose a novel multicategorical extension of the noisy-or gate and present simulation findings regarding the efficacy of loopy belief propagation algorithms for approximate inference within bipartite noisy-or networks.

This work presents a robust model order reduction framework tailored for parametric analysis in electromagnetics, with a primary focus on certifying the accuracy of the resulting reduced-order models. To achieve this, a new sharp state error estimator is introduced. Conventional a posteriori error estimation for model reduction depends on the inf-sup constant; however, in parametric systems, this constant varies with parameters. When the inf-sup constant is extremely small or vanishes, standard estimation becomes problematic because the error bound is inversely proportional to this constant, yielding excessively pessimistic and practically useless results. This scenario is common in electromagnetics, where inf-sup values approach zero near resonant frequencies. The proposed method offers a novel a posteriori state error estimator that circumvents the need to calculate the inf-sup constant. Comparative analysis against both standard and recently published estimators demonstrates that the proposed approach significantly outperforms existing methods. Numerical experiments conducted on real-world microwave components—including narrowband and wideband antennas and a dual-mode waveguide filter—validate the efficiency and effectiveness of this methodology.

Human life holds immense value, making robotic platforms ideal substitutes for humans when undertaking hazardous or life-endangering duties. This study specifically addresses Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD), where robot telepresence offers significant safety advantages, supported by the proven robustness of mobile robots across various environments. While full autonomy remains risky and complex at this stage compared to direct human control, teleoperation serves as a viable middle ground between complete robot independence and human presence. We introduce a cost-effective solution for EOD telepresence and teleoperation utilizing a legged manipulator—specifically a quadruped robot equipped with a manipulator and RGB-D sensors. To address the complex challenge of whole-body control for quadruped manipulators, we propose a novel system integration. Our approach combines a wearable IMU-based motion capture system for teleoperation with a VR headset for visual immersion. We experimentally validate this method in real-world scenarios involving loco-manipulation tasks that demand comprehensive whole-body control and visual telepresence.

Spatial data are now prevalent across numerous scientific domains, including transportation and the social web. A current trend in spatial data analysis focuses on "exploratory analysis," where analysts are steered toward promising options through successive iterations. Typically, this guidance mechanism relies on explicit user feedback, such as selecting specific points or regions of interest. However, analysts often fail to explicitly express their preferences regarding what they find intriguing. To address this, our method captures implicit feedback by monitoring mouse movements and explicit interactions to identify spatial regions with high mouse density. In this paper, we define, formalize, and investigate Interesting Dense Regions (IDRs) that reflect analyst preferences to automatically detect significant spatial highlights. Our approach utilizes a polygon-based abstraction layer to model these preferences. Leveraging IDRs, we highlight key points to guide the analytical process. Finally, we evaluate the efficiency and effectiveness of our method through realistic examples and experiments using Airbnb and Yelp datasets.

We investigate the tidal dissipation-driven migration of hot Jupiters around solar-type pre-main sequence and main sequence stars, covering stellar masses between 0.6 and 1.3 $M_{\odot}$. Using newly developed prescriptions, we simulate orbital evolution across a broad parameter space, incorporating three tidal mechanisms: equilibrium tides, inertial waves, and gravity waves. By integrating our simulation results with observed distributions of stellar and planetary parameters, we calculate the infall rate of hot Jupiters in the Milky Way. Our findings indicate that 11–21% of the initial hot Jupiter population undergoes coalescence before the host star exhausts its main sequence fuel. If the planets are sufficiently massive, this event could generate powerful transients detectable by next-generation facilities. While orbital decay is theoretically observable via transit-timing variations, the predicted Galactic coalescence rate (340–650 events per million years) is too low to guarantee detection. Consequently, decaying systems formed by stars in specific mass ranges may be too rare for current space telescopes like TESS to identify within a decade, though upcoming missions such as PLATO offer more promising prospects.

This research focuses on exclusive charm and bottom hadrons that admit at least a partial non-relativistic description. Beginning with specific wave functions for quarkonia and tetra-quarks, we analyze their production cross sections, total decay widths, and other decay characteristics. Specifically, we calculate the production cross sections for ground-state scalar quarkonia, yielding results consistent with existing literature. We also determine the production cross sections for lower-energy charm and bottom tetra-quark states, alongside their decay widths and rates for decaying into two $\mu\bar\mu$ pairs and the $q\bar q\mu\bar\mu$ channel. Our findings on tetra-charm align with data from the LHCb Collaboration, while our tetra-bottom results show reasonable agreement with CMS Collaboration indications. These cross-section analyses rely on interpolations using gluon-gluon luminosity grids provided by the NNPDF and CTEQ Collaborations, with hard amplitude calculations performed within the tree-level approximation of QCD. We believe that refining our methodology and incorporating improved experimental data following the anticipated luminosity increase at the LHC will enable significant tests of QCD at intermediate energies.

Stochastic games serve as an effective formal framework for modeling systems where rational agents compete or cooperate within uncertain settings. Probabilistic model checking methods applicable to these models enable the formal definition of quantitative properties regarding individual or collective behavior, followed by the automatic synthesis of agent strategies that guarantee satisfaction of these specifications. Despite significant advancements in algorithms and tooling, efficiency and scalability continue to pose challenges. This paper explores a symbolic implementation utilizing multi-terminal binary decision diagrams. We detail the construction and verification of turn-based stochastic games against temporal logic specifications grounded in either zero-sum or Nash equilibrium principles. Furthermore, we present a benchmark suite for this category of games and assess our approach's performance, demonstrating superior results in several instances and highlighting that symbolically synthesized strategies can be significantly more compact.

This work introduces and examines the convergence of a new stochastic algorithm designed to solve monotone inclusions defined as the sum of a maximal monotone operator and a monotone, Lipschitzian operator. The proposed method relies solely on unbiased estimates of the Lipschitzian component. We establish an expected convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(\log(n)/n)$ for the strongly monotone scenario, alongside almost sure convergence for the general case. Additionally, within the framework of convex-concave saddle point problems, we analyze the convergence rate of the primal-dual gap, specifically achieving an $\mathcal{O}(1/n)$ rate in the deterministic setting.

We present a concise summary of current knowledge regarding Quadratic Gravity, a framework that incorporates curvature-squared terms within the fundamental action. This theory is suggested as a renormalizable ultraviolet completion for quantum gravity that retains the metric as the primary dynamical variable. Nevertheless, it presents atypical field-theoretic implications due to the quartic momentum dependence found in its propagators. Despite these complexities, Quadratic Gravity remains a promising candidate for a quantum gravity theory given our current level of understanding.

Utilizing 1.7 years of data from the COSINE-100 experiment, which employs a 106 kg target of tallium-doped sodium iodide (NaI(Tl)), we establish novel constraints on dark matter interactions. Designed to evaluate DAMA's dark matter claims using identical detector technology, this study benefits from an expanded dataset, refined event selection criteria, and a more accurate characterization of detector backgrounds, all of which significantly boost sensitivity. No evidence consistent with dark matter interactions was found; consequently, model-dependent interpretations of the DAMA signal are excluded within the framework of the standard halo model for the NaI(Tl) target across various interaction hypotheses.

Generative adversarial networks (GANs) currently achieve state-of-the-art performance in image generation; however, their training remains notoriously difficult due to a highly non-convex optimization landscape that fosters various instabilities. Mode collapse is among the most severe of these issues, occurring when a model captures only a subset of the data distribution's modes while neglecting the rest. This study addresses mode collapse by leveraging second-order gradient information. By analyzing the loss surface via its Hessian eigenvalues, we demonstrate that mode collapse stems from convergence to sharp minima, noting a direct correlation between the eigenvalues of the generator ($G$) and the phenomenon. Building on these insights, we propose a novel optimization algorithm, nudged-Adam (NuGAN), which incorporates spectral information to mitigate mode collapse and achieve empirically more stable convergence.

Using the Hurwitz Zeta Function, we derived a novel functional equation for the Riemann Zeta Function. By evaluating this equation at $s=1$ and $s=2$, we established a relationship among the values of the Riemann zeta function at positive integers. In this context, the matrix possesses two dimensions, with the second component being the vector $(1, -\zeta(2))$. Since the elements of this vector are linearly independent over the rationals, we conclude that $\zeta(j)$ is irrational for all integers $j \geq 3$.

We execute and analyze multiple supervised learning experiments focused on real quadratic fields possessing class numbers of 1, 2, and 3. From a data science standpoint, we measure the relative challenges in distinguishing between class numbers of matching and differing parity, employing feature analysis and principal component analysis. Furthermore, we utilize symbolic classification to construct machine-learned formulas for these specific class numbers that are applicable to our dataset.

This study presents a dynamic Gordon growth model enhanced by a Bayesian Markov-Switching Vector Autoregressive (MS-BVAR) framework. By applying risk-neutral valuation and a locally risk-minimizing strategy, we derive pricing and hedging formulas for dividend-paying European call and put options, Margrabe options, segregated funds, and unit-linked life insurance. The analysis assumes that the regime-switching mechanism operates as a homogeneous Markov process, while the residual process adheres to a heteroscedastic model.

Although nanotechnology theoretically allows for a direct translation from design to device, it has historically depended on human intuition and basic optimizations. A primary challenge in nanophotonics is creating devices where light-matter interaction is constrained solely by material properties and fabrication limits. This study addresses that by incorporating measured fabrication constraints into topology optimization to achieve maximal light-matter interaction within a compact silicon membrane. The result is an unprecedented photonic nanocavity supporting telecom photons at a $\lambda\sim 1550$ nm wavelength, characterized by a mode volume of $V\sim3\times10^{-4}\,\lambda^3$, a quality factor of $Q\sim1100$, and a footprint of $4\,\lambda^2$. We successfully fabricated this cavity, which traps photons within 8 nm silicon bridges, and utilized near-field optical measurements to provide the first experimental proof of confining photons to a single hotspot significantly smaller than the diffraction limit in dielectric materials.

I present two remarks regarding nuclear matter. First, I examine the interaction between the $O(4)$ chiral field, $\vec{\phi}$, and the $\omega_\mu$ meson, modeled as $\sim + \, \omega_\mu^2 \, \vec{\phi}^{\, 2}$. At any net baryon density, this coupling inevitably generates an $\omega_0$ condensate. I posit that rising density reduces both the chiral condensate and the effective $\omega_0$ mass, thereby stiffening the equation of state (EoS). To connect this to a softer EoS for quarkyonic matter, I employ an $O(N)$ field theory at large $N$, where quantum fluctuations at non-zero temperature disrupt any potential pion "condensate" into a quantum pion liquid (Q$\pi$L), as detailed in arXiv:2005.10259. This paper demonstrates that the Q$\pi$L phase persists even at zero temperature. If this framework holds qualitatively for $N=4$, the $\omega_0$ mass increases sharply, suppressing the $\omega_0$ condensate. This mechanism could produce a spike in the speed of sound at high densities, a feature relevant to neutron stars. Second, I propose a toy model involving a $Z(3)$ gauge theory with three fermion flavors, wherein $Z(3)$ vortices confine fermions into baryons. In $1+1$ dimensions, this model is amenable to numerical study using current techniques on both classical and quantum computers.

Neural architectures and hardware accelerators have served as the primary catalysts for deep learning advancements. Prior research generally focused on optimizing hardware for a static model architecture or vice versa, with Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) being the predominant hardware focus. In contrast, our study targets the optimization of both software and hardware configurations on a commercial-grade edge accelerator. We systematically investigate the significance and strategies of co-designing neural networks with hardware accelerators. Our findings highlight three key points: 1) the software search space must be tailored to maximize the potential of the specific hardware architecture, 2) jointly searching for both model and hardware architectures yields superior results compared to separate optimization, and 3) distinct use cases produce markedly different optimal solutions. Experimental results demonstrate that our joint search approach consistently surpasses prior platform-aware neural architecture search, manually designed models, and the state-of-the-art EfficientNet, improving ImageNet top-1 accuracy by approximately 1% across all latency targets. Furthermore, by co-adapting model architectures and hardware accelerator configurations, our method can reduce energy consumption on edge accelerators by up to 2x while maintaining the same accuracy levels.

We introduce a uniform block-diagonal preconditioner designed for condensed $H$(div)-conforming HDG schemes addressing parameter-dependent saddle point problems, such as the generalized Stokes and linear elasticity equations. Using the auxiliary space preconditioning (ASP) technique \cite{Xu96}, we achieve an optimal preconditioner for the stiffness matrix within the global velocity or displacement space. Furthermore, we construct a spectrally equivalent approximation for the Schur complement on the element-wise constant pressure space and derive an explicit, computable exact inverse using the Woodbury matrix identity. Numerical experiments confirm that the proposed preconditioner remains robust across variations in model parameters and mesh size.

Clustering with deep neural networks has been widely explored recently, with Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) being prominent frameworks. These models utilize encoder-decoder architectures to learn latent feature representations, which serve as an ideal foundation for clustering by simplifying data manifolds and reducing noise within the latent space. This article employs the VAE framework to examine how probability function gradient ascent can process data points to enhance clustering performance. While this approach yields classification improvements over unprocessed data, it does not match state-of-the-art results. Conversely, applying gradient descent leads to more distinct cluster separation, thereby simplifying the investigation of hyperparameters like the number of clusters. We propose a straightforward yet effective method for determining the appropriate number of clusters using the DBSCAN algorithm, demonstrating that gradient processing facilitates this determination. Additionally, our baseline comparison model—a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) applied to the t-SNE latent space of a VAE with a weight of one on reconstruction loss during training (acting as an autoencoder)—achieved state-of-the-art results on the MNIST dataset, to our knowledge, surpassing all other existing models.

Standard contrastive self-supervised methods typically rely on similarity metrics within latent space to guide learning by comparing positive and negative image pairs. Despite recent advancements in these algorithms, significant barriers like high computational costs remain. To address this, we introduce a supplementary objective within the contrastive learning framework designed to regress parameters for affine transformations or homographies alongside the standard contrastive goal. We demonstrate that this addition enhances both performance and training efficiency. Crucially, the module is designed to avoid enforcing invariance to affine components, as such invariance is not always desirable. We validate this approach on two prominent self-supervised algorithms and provide a comprehensive experimental analysis showing performance gains across all tested datasets. Furthermore, while both homography and affine regression yield improvements, affine transformations consistently outperform homographies in every scenario.

Emotion stimulus extraction is a specialized subtask within emotion analysis dedicated to pinpointing the textual cause of an expressed emotion (for instance, in "I am happy that I passed my exam," the stimulus is "passed my exam"). While prior research has primarily addressed Mandarin and English, there were no available resources or models for German. This study addresses that gap by creating a corpus of 2,006 German news headlines annotated with emotions and 811 instances specifically tagged with stimulus phrases. Acknowledging the high cost and time required for such annotation, we also propose a method to project the English GoodNewsEveryone (GNE) corpus into a machine-translated German version. We evaluate a Conditional Random Field (CRF) model—trained both monolingually on the new German data and cross-lingually via projection—against a multilingual XLM-RoBERTa (XLM-R) model. The results indicate that training the CRF model on the original German corpus yields higher F1 scores than using the projected data, while the XLM-R model consistently outperforms its respective CRF counterparts in all experiments.

Custom spatial accelerators for machine learning are gaining significant traction, utilizing arrays of processing elements (PEs) connected through bespoke buffer hierarchies and on-chip networks. Their efficiency stems from optimized dataflow strategies—specifically, the spatial and temporal partitioning of data across PEs alongside fine-grained scheduling—to maximize data reuse. This study evaluates such architectures using a tiled general matrix-matrix multiplication (GEMM) kernel. We introduce a framework that determines optimal dataflow and tile size mappings for tiled GEMM operations tailored to specific spatial accelerators and workloads, utilizing an analytical cost model to estimate runtime and energy consumption. Evaluations across five distinct spatial accelerators reveal that the tiled GEMM mappings systematically produced by our framework deliver high performance across diverse GEMM workloads and hardware configurations.

The well-documented inaccuracy of the classical magnetic field integral equation (MFIE) has prompted various investigations, including the use of higher-order discretization schemes. Although these schemes can enhance precision, our analysis shows that accuracy issues can persist. To address this, we introduce an advanced scheme utilizing a weak-form discretization of the identity operator, which significantly improves high-frequency MFIE accuracy without substantially increasing computational cost or complexity.

This study reports a search for eV-scale sterile neutrino oscillations using the MicroBooNE liquid argon detector, incorporating all potential appearance and disappearance effects within the $3+1$ active-to-sterile neutrino oscillation model. We examine neutrino candidate events from recent measurements of charged-current $
u_e$ and $
u_{\mu}$ interactions in MicroBooNE, utilizing data from an exposure of $6.37	imes10^{20}$ protons on target delivered by the Fermilab booster neutrino beam. No evidence for light sterile neutrino oscillations was found, leading to the derivation of $95\%$ confidence level exclusion contours in the $\Delta m^2_{41}$ versus $	heta_{\mu e}$ and $	heta_{ee}$ parameter plane, which rule out a portion of the parameter space previously suggested by experimental anomalies. The simultaneous consideration of $
u_e$ appearance and disappearance effects within the full $3+1$ framework results in a degeneracy for determining oscillation parameters, a phenomenon discussed here and slated for resolution in future analyses.

This paper investigates the optimal stopping problem within an exploratory framework, where actions are taken stochastically based on the current state and an entropy-regularization term is incorporated into the reward functional. This transformation converts the optimal stopping problem into a standard optimal control problem. We derive the associated Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation and establish its solvability. Additionally, we provide the convergence rate of policy iteration and compare this approach to classical optimal stopping problems. Guided by this theoretical analysis, we design a reinforcement learning algorithm and present numerical results for various models.

In high-dimensional omics studies, selecting variables is essential because it is biologically sound to assume that only a small subset of non-noisy features drives the underlying data structures. Nevertheless, this challenge is especially difficult in unsupervised contexts, leading to the continued reliance on ad hoc selection methods despite their known limitations and poor reproducibility. We introduce a Bayesian variable selection framework tailored for rank-based unsupervised transcriptomic analysis. By utilizing data rankings rather than raw continuous values, our approach enhances the robustness of conclusions compared to traditional statistical techniques, while integrating variable selection directly into inference ensures full reproducibility. Specifically, we present a new extension of the Bayesian Mallows model designed for variable selection, enabling comprehensive probabilistic analysis and consistent uncertainty quantification. Simulation results highlight the method's versatility and robustness across various scenarios, demonstrating its superiority over competing approaches when data dimensions or generating processes vary. We apply this novel technique to genome-wide RNA-seq data from ovarian cancer patients, successfully identifying genes influencing cancer development in a fully unsupervised manner. This underscores the method's utility for discovering gene signatures in cancer genomics, while the ability to quantify uncertainty proves vital for subsequent biological investigations.

This study investigates the varying asymmetries observed during the decay of sunspot groups. The research utilizes magnetic polarity data from the SoHO/MDI-Debrecen Database (SDD) sunspot catalog, covering the period between 1996 and 2010. A sample of 142 sunspot groups was analyzed to examine several asymmetry types. The leading-following asymmetry was found to increase across three distinct phases during decay and shows an anticorrelation with sunspot size. Additionally, it correlates with hemispheric asymmetry; during decay, the area asymmetry index yields higher values in the southern hemisphere, potentially attributed to the elevated activity levels in that hemisphere during solar cycle 23. The total umbral area demonstrates an inverse relationship with the umbra/penumbra ratio but a direct relationship with the umbral decay rate. Throughout the decay phase, the umbra/penumbra (U/P) ratio unambiguously decreases in trailing regions and decreases in most leading regions as well. These variations in the U/P ratio result from the differing depths of the umbral and penumbral magnetic fields.

We demonstrate that a quantum particle experiencing a positive force along one arm of a Mach-Zehnder interferometer and no force along the other can exhibit a negative average momentum transfer upon exiting via a specific port. In this setup, quantum interference enables an ensemble of particles to acquire an average momentum opposing the applied force, a phenomenon absent in classical physics. We outline experimental approaches capable of verifying this effect using current technology, involving electrons or neutrons in free-space Mach-Zehnder interferometers as well as atoms sourced from a Bose-Einstein condensate.

This study examines how magnon-magnon interactions influence magnon dispersion and polarization in collinear antiferromagnetic (AF) insulators at finite temperatures. Utilizing a self-consistent Hartree-Fock mean-field approach, we analyze nonlinear thermal interactions within two-sublattice AF systems exhibiting either uniaxial or biaxial magnetocrystalline anisotropies. These interactions decompose into intra- and interband scattering processes involving two magnons. Additionally, we calculate the temperature-dependent shifts in the magnon bandgap and AF resonance modes for square and hexagonal lattices, alongside the impact of these interactions on mode polarization. Our results reveal that while uniaxial noninteracting eigenmodes are circularly polarized, nonlinear thermal interactions break the Hamiltonian's local U(1) symmetry, causing low-energy modes to become elliptical due to attractive squeezing. Conversely, in biaxial systems, low-energy bare eigenmodes are already elliptically polarized, but thermal nonlinearities further compress them. The predicted temperature-dependent AF resonance modes and their polarization offer a measurable method to detect nonlinear interactions. Ultimately, these findings provide a framework for investigating thermal magnon effects in technologically relevant magnetic systems, including the stability of emerging two-dimensional magnetic materials, coherent magnon transport, magnon Bose-Einstein condensation, and magnonic topological insulators.

In millimeter-wave vehicular communications, acquiring the covariance matrices of spatially correlated channels enables the design of environment-aware beamforming codebooks. Due to their symmetric positive definite (SPD) nature, these matrices can be modeled on non-Euclidean Riemannian manifolds. Accordingly, this paper introduces a Riemannian-Geometric machine learning (G-ML) framework for estimating channel covariance matrices using an unsupervised K-Means approach. This proposed algorithm employs the Log-Euclidean metric (LEM) to measure distances between matrices on the Riemannian manifold. Results demonstrate that the K-Means G-ML model reduces error by up to 80% compared to traditional Euclidean-based K-Means, which clusters the channel vectors directly.

Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) has emerged as the preferred optimization technique for training large-scale deep neural networks, valued for its simplicity, low computational cost per update, and strong performance. Standard theoretical bounds suggest that SGD requires only a single pass over the training data, implying that additional passes offer no benefit. However, empirical observations indicate that multi-pass SGD significantly outperforms one-pass SGD regarding excess risk bounds, yet a theoretical explanation for this phenomenon remains elusive. This paper offers theoretical evidence to clarify why multiple passes can enhance performance under specific conditions. Specifically, we examine smooth risk minimization problems involving non-convex least squared loss. Under the Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) condition, we demonstrate that multi-pass SGD achieves a faster convergence rate for the excess risk bound compared to one-pass SGD.

Automatically detecting fake news on the internet presents a significant challenge within deception detection tasks. As online news spreads, it is frequently altered, with malicious actors distorting facts to fabricate misinformation. This continuous evolution creates unprecedented variations that can deceive models trained on original data. To address this, we introduce the Fake News Evolution (FNE) dataset, which tracks the progression of fake news. This dataset contains 950 paired entries, each featuring articles from three critical stages of the evolution: the original truth, the initial fake news, and the subsequently evolved fake news. Our analysis of features throughout this process includes disinformation tactics, text similarity, top 10 keywords, classification accuracy, parts of speech, and sentiment characteristics.

Autonomous and Robotics Systems (ARSs) are becoming increasingly prevalent, complex, and integrated into public spaces. Given that many of these systems are safety-critical, detecting software errors is essential to prevent harm. We introduce a new family of techniques designed to identify anomalous program executions and faulty behaviors. Our approach involves modeling execution patterns by gathering low-level runtime signals to train machine learning models, which can flag previously unseen executions likely to contain errors. We outline a practical method for collecting dynamic binary runtime signals on ARSs, minimizing overhead from dynamic instrumentation by leveraging the inherent architecture of these systems, which is well-suited to masking such costs. We validate the efficiency of these methods in simulations using ARDUPILOT, a widely used open-source autopilot, and HUSKY, an unmanned ground vehicle. By instrumenting these systems, we collect data to construct supervised machine learning models and assess their accuracy. Furthermore, we examine the quantity of training data required to achieve varying levels of accuracy, quantify the performance overhead introduced by the analysis tool, and determine which runtime signals are most effective at detecting unusual behavior. Finally, we investigate how timing delays impact the functional behavior of ARSs.

We introduce novel families of Tillich-Z\'emor hash functions by leveraging higher-dimensional special linear groups over finite fields as their underlying structure. The Cayley graphs associated with these groups exhibit rapid mixing and high girth, properties that collectively ensure robust preimage and collision resistance for the resulting hash functions. Furthermore, we substantiate the assertion that these constructed hash functions maintain security against quantum attacks.

Lightning and convection are typically modeled using proxies derived from expert knowledge, such as CAPE, wind shear, and charge separation mechanisms. However, recent advancements in machine learning, high-resolution reanalyses, and precise lightning detection now enable the creation of specialized proxies without relying on prior human expertise. To identify vertical profiles conducive to lightning, a deep neural network was developed to connect ERA5 vertical profiles of cloud physics, mass fields, and wind data with lightning strike records from the Austrian Lightning Detection & Information System (ALDIS). These records were converted into a binary classification system labeling ERA5 grid cells as either containing lightning or not. The model utilizes approximately 670 features derived from model levels above the tropopause as its input layer. Trained and validated on data from 2010 to 2018, the network demonstrated superior performance on independent 2019 test data compared to a reference model based on meteorological expertise. Shapley value analysis revealed that the network identified cloud ice and snow content in the upper and mid-troposphere as critical features. Since these patterns align with charge separation processes in thunderstorms, the deep learning model provides a physically interpretable description of lightning generation.

This study addresses the problem of determining, for a set of planar regions $\cal R$ and an integer $k$, whether a convex shape exists such that its boundary intersects at least $k$ regions from $\cal R$. We present a polynomial-time algorithm for the scenario where regions consist of disjoint line segments with a constant number of orientations. Conversely, we demonstrate that the problem is NP-hard when the regions are either intersecting axis-aligned rectangles or line segments with three orientations. The status of the problem remains open for several natural intermediate classes of shapes, including arbitrary disjoint segments and intersecting line segments with two orientations.

This paper investigates the interference cancellation performance of MIMO transmitters and receivers through both theoretical analysis and numerical simulations conducted in Quadriga. The study focuses on the Reduced Channel Zero-Forcing (RCZF) precoding scheme alongside Minimum MSE Interference Rejection Combiner (MMSE-IRC) and QR Maximum Likelihood Detection (QR-MLD) receivers. Using straightforward yet highly effective algebraic derivations, we analytically demonstrate and verify via simulations that these techniques are asymptotically equivalent. Our combined theoretical and experimental findings confirm that pairing MMSE-IRC and QR-MLD receivers with RCZF precoding achieves complete interference suppression in the asymptotic limit.

This paper explores the application of Stochastic Approximation for estimating high-dimensional sparse parameters. Our approach involves solving a penalized stochastic optimization problem at every step of a multistage algorithm, utilizing the non-Euclidean Composite Stochastic Mirror Descent (CSMD) method to achieve a specified accuracy for each sub-problem. Under assumptions of a smooth and quadratically minorated objective function and sub-Gaussian stochastic perturbations, we derive parameter settings that guarantee rapid convergence of the estimation error, defined as the radius of a confidence ball around the approximate solution. Convergence is linear in the initial "preliminary" phase and transitions to sublinear in the subsequent "asymptotic" phase.
