We apply this framework to sparse Generalized Linear Regression, demonstrating that the algorithm achieves optimal estimation error convergence even under weak assumptions regarding the regressor distribution. Finally, we include a numerical study that evaluates the algorithm's performance using high-dimensional simulated data.

The Human-Machine Interaction (HMI) domain has become a significant area of study within machine learning, driven by recent advances in computing capabilities. This progress has enabled the application of machine learning for image and video classification, surpassing the limitations of conventional computer vision techniques. This paper aims to create a synergistic integration of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) to identify Italian cultural and anthropological sign language gestures from video data. In this architecture, the CNN extracts critical features which are subsequently processed by the RNN. By leveraging RNNs, the model retains temporal information, utilizing context from preceding frames to improve prediction accuracy. Our innovative methodology employs various data augmentation strategies and regularization techniques applied exclusively to RGB frames to mitigate overfitting and minimize generalization errors.

Quantum key distribution (QKD) is now a mature technique for generating secure, long-distance keys with information-theoretic security, as its protection stems from the laws of quantum physics rather than computational complexity. To advance QKD into industrial applications, there is a pressing need for cost-effective, mass-producible, and practical systems, making the integration of photonic and electronic components for both transmitters and receivers a focal point. This study introduces a high-speed (2.5 GHz) integrated QKD system comprising a silicon photonics transmitter chip capable of precise state preparation and high-speed modulation, alongside a polarization-independent, low-loss receiver chip in aluminum borosilicate glass created via femtosecond laser micromachining. Our system demonstrates raw bit error rates, quantum bit error rates, and secret key rates that match the performance of significantly more complex state-of-the-art setups utilizing discrete components.

This study details findings from a survey of one of the deepest X-ray fields ever observed by the XMM-Newton satellite. The 1.75 Ms Ultra Narrow Deep Field (XMM175UNDF) project comprises 13 observations spanning two years, achieving a total exposure of 1.75 Ms (1.372 Ms after filtering out flares) centered on the blazar 1ES 1553+113 within a $30' \times 30' $ area. By stacking these 13 observations, we reached flux sensitivity limits of $4.03 \times 10^{-16}$, $1.3 \times 10^{-15}$, and $9.8 \times 10^{-16}\, erg\, s^{-1}\, cm^{-2}$ in the soft $(0.2 - 2\, \mathrm{keV})$, hard $(2 - 12\, \mathrm{keV})$, and full $(0.2 - 12\, \mathrm{keV})$ energy bands, respectively. Applying a conservative detection threshold of Maximum Likelihood significance $ML \geq 6$ (equivalent to $3\sigma$), we identified 301 point sources and calculated their positions, multi-band fluxes, and hardness ratios. Through optical follow-up using the 10.4m Gran Telescopio Canarias (GTC) in the $u'g'r'i'z'$ bands, combined with WISE/2MASS infrared data, we matched 244 optical/IR candidates to our X-ray sources. This allowed us to estimate their X-ray luminosities, redshift distribution, flux ratios (X-ray/optical and X-ray/IR), and absolute magnitudes. Ultimately, this subsample was categorized into 40 non-active sources and 204 AGNs, further divided into 139 Seyfert galaxies and 41 Quasars.

Multi-source domain adaptation seeks to utilize knowledge from various tasks to predict outcomes in a related target domain, making the proper integration of diverse sources based on their relationships a critical component. This paper investigates the challenge of aggregating source domains with varying label distributions, an area where most recent source selection methods struggle. Our proposed algorithm distinguishes itself from prior approaches in two primary aspects: first, it aggregates multiple sources primarily by measuring the similarity of their semantic conditional distributions rather than marginal ones; second, it introduces a \emph{unified} framework capable of selecting relevant sources across three common scenarios, namely domain adaptation with limited target labels, unsupervised domain adaptation, and partially unsupervised label adaptation. Through extensive experimentation, we demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms baseline approaches.

Accurate wound segmentation is essential for clinical diagnosis and timely treatment, with deep learning currently serving as the primary methodology. However, performance is often enhanced by pre-processing steps like illumination correction, traditionally applied before training. Because this correction and the model training operate independently, a fixed correction strategy may fail to suit all images, resulting in sub-optimal outcomes. To overcome this, we propose an end-to-end dual-view segmentation framework that integrates a learnable illumination correction module directly into the deep segmentation model. This allows the module's parameters to be automatically optimized during training, while dual-view fusion effectively leverages features from both original and enhanced images. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate the framework's effectiveness and robustness, yielding results that significantly outperform state-of-the-art methods.

When dielectric particles come into close contact, induced surface charges seem to diverge. Numerically resolving this singularity is computationally prohibitive due to the requirement for high spatial resolution. This study demonstrates that the singularity's strength varies logarithmically with both the inter-particle separation and the dielectric permittivity. We introduce a regularization method to isolate this singularity, enabling the precise calculation of cohesive energy for clusters of contacting dielectric particles. Our findings reveal that at high permittivity levels, polarization energy stabilizes open cluster configurations, mirroring the behavior of conducting particles; conversely, at low permittivity levels, it favors compact configurations.

This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the spectrum for a constant coefficient differential operator acting on a scale of localized Sobolev spaces, $H^{s}_{loc}(I)$, which are Fréchet spaces. This approach contrasts with existing literature, where spectral results are primarily restricted to Banach spaces. Our objective is to examine the behavior of all three spectral types—point, residual, and continuous—and their relationships with the dual operator. The principal finding reveals that the resolvent set of such operators contains no complex numbers, suggesting a novel method for defining the spectrum to align with classical Spectral Theory theorems within Fréchet spaces.

Effective data characterization is crucial for selecting learning algorithms and estimating model performance. Meta-learning has generated extensive research on characterizing data through various meta-feature families, including statistical, model-based, information-theoretic, and topological approaches. This paper builds upon the wealth of existing meta-features to introduce a method that derives new abstract meta-features as latent variables within a deep neural network. We highlight the limitations of applying traditional meta-features directly and emphasize the necessity of learning high-level task properties. Our approach utilizes a deep neural network as a feature extractor, demonstrating that 1) meta-models mapping these abstract features to generalization performance achieve an average improvement of approximately 18% over other methods, and 2) these abstract meta-features exhibit high relevance scores.

Consider a two-dimensional canonical system defined by $y'(t)=zJH(t)y(t)$ on the half-line $(0,\infty)$, where the Hamiltonian $H$ is almost everywhere positive semidefinite. Let $q_H$ represent its Weyl coefficient. According to De Branges' inverse spectral theorem, the mapping $H\mapsto q_H$ establishes a bijection between trace-normalized Hamiltonians and Nevanlinna functions. We demonstrate that $q_H$ exhibits asymptotic behavior toward $i\infty$ with a leading term proportional to a regularly varying function if and only if the primitive $M$ of $H$ is regularly or rapidly varying at the origin and its off-diagonal elements exhibit limited oscillation. Explicit formulas link the leading coefficient of this asymptotic expansion to the behavior of $M$ near zero. Specifically, the magnitude of the growth rate is determined solely by the diagonal entries of $M$, whereas the argument of the leading coefficient reflects the relative proportions of the off-diagonal entries.

This paper introduces an Adaptive Realized Hyperbolic GARCH (A-Realized HYGARCH) process designed to capture long memory in high-frequency time series data, accounting for potential structural breaks. Structural changes are incorporated by allowing the intercept to adhere to the smooth and flexible functional form proposed by Gallant (1984). Furthermore, the study examines the stability conditions of the process and conducts a Monte Carlo simulation to evaluate the performance of the A-Realized HYGARCH model against standard Realized HYGARCH models with and without structural changes.

This paper presents twisted Rota-Baxter operators on Lie algebras, establishing them as an operator counterpart to twisted r-matrices. We construct an appropriate $L_\infty$-algebra where the Maurer-Cartan elements correspond to these twisted Rota-Baxter operators, thereby enabling the definition of their cohomology. This cohomology is interpreted as the Chevalley-Eilenberg cohomology of a specific Lie algebra with coefficients in a suitable representation. From a cohomological perspective, we investigate the deformations of twisted Rota-Baxter operators and provide applications involving Reynolds operators and twisted r-matrices. Furthermore, we introduce a novel algebraic structure known as NS-Lie algebras, which relate to twisted Rota-Baxter operators analogously to how pre-Lie algebras relate to Rota-Baxter operators. The paper concludes by examining twisted generalized complex structures on modules over Lie algebras.

Federated learning (FL) represents a promising machine learning framework for distributed data that preserves privacy by keeping information local to each user. While this safeguards user privacy, it complicates server-side verification of data quality, particularly regarding label correctness. Since training with corrupted labels severely hinders FL tasks, yet label noise remains largely overlooked, this paper addresses this gap by proposing a learning-based reweighting strategy to mitigate noisy label effects. Specifically, we adjust weights for individual training samples to maximize the model's generalization performance on a validation set, formally framing this as a Federated Bilevel Optimization problem. Bilevel optimization involves two entangled levels of decision-making; while non-distributed variants have recently seen significant algorithmic advancements, their application in FL settings remains under-explored. We identify that the high communication overhead associated with hypergradient calculation is the primary bottleneck. To address this, we introduce \textit{Comm-FedBiO}, a solution for general Federated Bilevel Optimization that employs two communication-efficient subroutines for estimating the hypergradient. We provide convergence analysis for these algorithms and apply them to the noisy label problem, demonstrating superior performance across various real-world datasets compared to existing baselines.

More than 300 million individuals globally suffer from retinal diseases, which can be detected through noninvasive Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) scans by identifying structural abnormalities such as retinal lesions. Automated localization of these lesions is crucial for early disease detection. To address the scarcity of manual annotations required for deep supervised learning, this paper introduces the first study applying semi-supervised object detection (SSOD) for lesion localization in OCT images. We established a taxonomy to unify and structure existing SSOD methods, thereby identifying their core components. To assess the impact of these modules, we created the OCT-SS dataset, comprising over 1,000 expert-labeled OCT B-scans and more than 13,000 unlabeled scans. Extensive experiments on this dataset determined that the Unbiased Teacher (UnT) method is the most effective current SSOD approach for this task. Furthermore, we enhanced this strong baseline, raising the mean Average Precision (mAP) from 49.34 to 50.86.

This research examines the connection between specific non-degenerate lower Hessenberg infinite matrices $\mathcal{G}$ and the existence of orthogonal polynomial sequences defined under Sobolev inner products, thereby generalizing the classic Favard theorem for Sobolev orthogonality. Furthermore, we describe the structural properties of both the matrix $\mathcal{G}$ and its corresponding formal moment matrix $\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{G}}$ using particular matrix operators.

Na$_{4-\delta}$NiTeO$_{6}$ stands as a rare instance within the transition-metal tellurate family where an $S$ = 1 spin-chain architecture is achieved. Through neutron powder diffraction, researchers have identified its ground-state magnetic configuration. The data indicate that below a Néel temperature of approximately 6.8(2) K, Ni$^{2+}$ moments organize into a screwed ferromagnetic (FM) spin chain along the crystallographic $a$ axis; however, these FM chains interact antiferromagnetically along the $b$ and $c$ directions, resulting in a magnetic propagation vector of $k$ = (0, 1/2, 1/2). This zigzag magnetic ordering is corroborated by first-principles calculations. At 3 K, the Ni$^{2+}$ spin moment is measured at 2.1(1) $\mu$$\rm_{B}$, implying substantial quenching of the orbital moment caused by the crystalline electric field (CEF). The previously observed metamagnetic transition near a critical field of roughly 0.1 T is interpreted as a field-induced spin-flip event. Due to the relatively facile tuning of its magnetic dimensionality via external parameters, Na$_{4-\delta}$NiTeO$_{6}$ emerges as a promising material for investigating diverse novel spin-chain phenomena.

At the Laboratori Nazionale del Gran Sasso, researchers utilized a modified ultra-low-background high-purity detector with optimized geometry to measure a hafnium foil. The study meticulously examined the radiopurity of the stock Hf foil and analyzed 310 days of data to investigate rare processes within natural hafnium isotopes. First, limits on alpha decays of all natural Hf isotopes to the first excited states of their daughter nuclides were established, ranging from $10^{16}$ to $10^{18}$ years at 90% C.L. Second, a search for double electron capture and electron capture with positron emission in $^{174}$Hf was conducted, resulting in half-life limits of $10^{16}$-$10^{18}$ years (90% C.L.). Finally, the investigation explored novel dark matter-induced nuclear excitations in hafnium isotopes; for dark matter with a mass of 1 TeV/$c^2$, leading constraints were set on the inelastic dark matter--nucleon cross section for mass splittings between 428 keV and 473 keV.

In biomedical optics, researchers often statistically model speckle amplitude using distributions whose parameters serve as biomarkers. This paper proposes a paradigm shift toward a distributional model-free approach. Specifically, it evaluates various distances across different domains between an empirical nonparametric distribution of normalized speckle amplitude samples and the standard Rayleigh distribution. Based on OCT images from phantoms, two ex-vivo porcine cornea experiments, and one in-vivo human cornea experiment, evidence is presented showing that this model-free method, despite its simplicity, can outperform the best-fitted distributional model among a range of options. In conclusion, for practical applications, the distributional model-free approach should be prioritized as the primary method for speckle modeling before resorting to distribution-based techniques.

This work introduces a method for initializing the internal state values of LSTM recurrent neural networks by learning an intrinsic data manifold, thereby ensuring alignment with observed input data. Leveraging the concept of generalized synchronization, we posit that converged, mature internal states function as mappings on this learned manifold, where the manifold's dimensionality determines the necessary length of observed time series for consistent initialization. We demonstrate this approach using a partially observed chemical model, showing that such initialization significantly enhances performance. Furthermore, we illustrate that learning this manifold allows for the conversion of partially observed dynamics into fully observed ones, opening new identification pathways for nonlinear dynamical systems.

The normal ordering of integral powers of the number operator using boson operators is formulated via Stirling numbers of the second kind. Treating this as a degenerate case, we examine the normal ordering of degenerate integral powers of the number operator in terms of boson operators, which is expressed through degenerate Stirling numbers of the second kind. As an application, we derive two defining equations for these degenerate Stirling numbers and a Dobinski-like formula for degenerate Bell polynomials.

This study addresses the optimal utilization of $N$ resources, each existing in an unknown binary state that can be estimated through noisy, state-dependent observations. Depending on the resource's state, usage yields either a reward or a penalty per unit time. The goal is to define a sequential strategy for sensing and exploitation at each time step to maximize expected utility—defined as total rewards minus penalties and sensing costs—over a finite horizon $L$. We model this scenario as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP), demonstrating that the optimal approach relies on two time-varying thresholds per resource and an optimal rule for selecting which resource to sense. Since fully characterizing the optimal strategy is typically intractable, we propose a low-complexity policy that simulations show delivers near-optimal performance. This framework is applicable to opportunistic spectrum access, marketing strategies, and other sequential resource allocation challenges.

Amidst the rapid pace of modern life, stress has emerged as a significant health issue. Although wearable and mobile devices now offer increasingly automated stress monitoring, there remains a gap in understanding how these tools function in daily routines. This paper reports an empirical investigation into the usage of automatic stress-tracking technologies in China, utilizing semi-structured interviews with 17 participants. The research identifies three barriers to effectively engaging with stress-tracking data: insufficient immediate awareness, a deficit in necessary background knowledge, and a lack of communal support. By examining the stress-tracking behaviors revealed in the study, we challenge prevailing assumptions in self-tracking literature regarding data engagement. Finally, we advocate for re-evaluating data engagement as an integral component of self-tracking practices, moving beyond a sole focus on the user interface.

Time series models frequently encounter extreme events and anomalies, which are common in real-world data. These models often require precise probabilistic forecasting, a critical capability for managing risks associated with phenomena like pandemics and hurricanes. However, automatically detecting and utilizing such anomalies in large-scale datasets is difficult and typically demands manual intervention. To address this, we introduce an anomaly-aware forecasting framework that utilizes historical anomaly impacts to enhance prediction accuracy during and following extreme events. Specifically, the system automatically identifies anomalies and integrates them via an attention mechanism to boost performance for future extremes. Additionally, it employs a dynamic uncertainty optimization algorithm that minimizes forecast uncertainty in an online fashion. Experimental results across three diverse datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves consistently superior accuracy with reduced uncertainty compared to existing prediction models.

Wavelet frames have emerged as a valuable instrument for time-frequency analysis and image processing. Numerous researchers have contributed to this domain, establishing various necessary and sufficient conditions. Ron and Shen [17] provided a characterization of wavelet frames, while Benedetto and Treiber [3], along with Ron and Shen [17], offered distinct presentations of the subject. It is well-known that any function $f \in L^2(R)$ can be expressed as an orthonormal wavelet series, and the pointwise and uniform convergence of such series have been extensively examined by various authors [9, 17]. In this study, we examine the pointwise convergence of orthogonal wavelet series in Pringsheim's sense. Additionally, we explore the Cesaro $|C,1,1|$ summability and the strong Cesaro $|C,1,1|$ summability of wavelet series.

This study introduces a modified Morris-Lecar model that integrates the sodium inward current and analyzes its dynamical behavior across key parameters. By varying these values, the model demonstrates diverse excitability properties. We specifically assessed how alterations in maximum ion conductances and external current influence membrane potential dynamics through a comprehensive numerical bifurcation analysis. The bifurcation structures identified in this work differ from those found in previous studies of the original Morris-Lecar model. These findings offer insights into the electrical activity of excitable cells and serve as a foundation for future research.
Our goal is to establish the integration formula on the noncommutative (Moyal) plane using singular traces in the style of Connes.

While face recognition has reached levels of accuracy that exceed human performance in specific contexts, these automated systems are not yet viable for production due to their vulnerability to simple identity spoofing attacks. Although significant research has focused on developing face anti-spoofing models, these solutions often struggle with generalization in real-world environments. This paper presents a novel method that redefines the Generalized Presentation Attack Detection (GPAD) task through the lens of anomaly detection. Technically, we propose a deep metric learning framework that employs triplet focal loss as a regularization mechanism for a new loss function termed "metric-softmax," which directs the learning process to generate highly discriminative feature representations within an embedding space. Furthermore, we validate the efficacy of this deep anomaly detection architecture by implementing a few-shot a posteriori probability estimation method that requires no additional classifier training on the learned features. Extensive experiments conducted using the GRAD-GPAD framework—the largest aggregated dataset available for face GPAD—demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms all current state-of-the-art methods.

We obtain the chiral effective Lagrangian for excited heavy-light mesons by applying appropriate approximations to QCD. Our analysis concentrates on chiral partners with $j_l^P=\frac{3}{2}^+$ and $j_l^P=\frac{3}{2}^-$, corresponding to ($1^+,2^+$) and ($1^-,2^-$) states, respectively. We calculate the low-energy constants, including the masses of these partners, and find that the resulting spectrum aligns reasonably well with experimental observations. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the quantum numbers of $B_J(5970)$ can be assigned as either $1^-$ or $2^-$.

Most research on Twitter influence campaigns has depended on detecting malicious activity within public tweets retrieved via official APIs, which only include posts that remain undeleted. However, adversaries can strategically remove content to manipulate the platform, and estimates derived from public data often significantly underestimate the actual volume of deleted tweets. This study presents the first comprehensive, large-scale investigation into anomalous deletion patterns, analyzing over a billion deletions across more than 11 million accounts. We discovered that a tiny fraction of accounts are responsible for deleting a massive number of tweets each day. Furthermore, we identified two abusive tactics that leverage these deletions: first, bypassing tweet volume limits to flood the network with more than 26,000 daily posts; and second, coordinated networks performing repetitive likes and unlikes on content slated for deletion to manipulate ranking algorithms. These methods enable abusers to amplify content and inflate popularity while evading detection, offering platforms and researchers novel approaches to identify social media abuse.

We extend Ogg's theorem regarding supersingular $j$-invariants to supersingular elliptic curves possessing level structure. While Ogg noted that the level one case characterizes the primes dividing the monster group's order, we demonstrate that analogous analyses for higher levels yield similar characterizations of primes dividing the orders of other sporadic simple groups, such as the baby monster and Fischer's largest group, thereby broadening the scope of Ogg's result. More broadly, we characterize, via supersingular elliptic curves with level, the primes that appear as orders of Fricke elements within centralizer subgroups of the monster. Additionally, we explore the link between supersingular elliptic curves and umbral moonshine and provide a method for explicitly computing the invariants of supersingular elliptic curves with level structure.

For decades, traditional deep inelastic scattering (DIS) experiments have investigated dimuon events arising from charm-quark production in neutrino interactions. Recent advancements in neutrino telescopes now enable the search for such events at energies significantly exceeding laboratory scales. This paper presents a simulation framework designed to compute the yields and distributions of dimuon signals within an IceCube-like kilocubic-meter neutrino telescope. Due to limitations in resolving the lateral separation of double tracks, the analysis considers only dimuons produced outside the detector volume. Detailed simulation results covering a ten-year exposure period are provided. Comparing our findings with a previous study [1] on a similar scenario, we use that work as a baseline. We further evaluate the effects of varying muon energy loss calculation methods, discovering that the average energy loss formula employed in the prior study yields a higher event count compared to Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we assess the experimental potential for dimuon searches assuming a background consisting solely of single-muon events. Our results, based on a simplified double-track reconstruction, suggest moderate sensitivity, particularly with the ORCA configuration. Consequently, further research into both reconstruction algorithms and potential detector designs is necessary and currently underway.

We introduce a cutting-edge neural framework for the unsupervised reconstruction of archaic word forms. While prior research in this area relied on expectation-maximization to forecast basic phonological shifts between ancient terms and their modern cognates, our approach leverages neural models capable of capturing more intricate phonological and morphological transformations. Concurrently, we retain the inductive biases inherent in classical techniques by integrating monotonic alignment constraints into the model and intentionally underfitting during the maximization phase. Our method is evaluated on reconstructing Latin using a corpus of cognates spanning five Romance languages, yielding a significant decrease in edit distance relative to earlier methods.

This study examines quickest change detection within a sequence of independent observations, assuming a known pre-change distribution but an entirely unknown post-change distribution. A novel window-limited leave-one-out (LOO) CuSum test is proposed; this method requires no knowledge of the post-change distribution and eliminates the need for post-change training data. Under specific convergence conditions regarding the density estimator, it is demonstrated that the LOO-CuSum test achieves first-order asymptotic optimality as the false alarm rate approaches zero. Numerical experiments validate this analysis by comparing the LOO-CuSum test against baseline methods that rely on known distributional information.

Ionospheric path delays affect single-band Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) group delays, thereby restricting their utility for absolute astrometry. This study examines two specific scenarios: observations conducted simultaneously at two frequencies where delays are available for only one band in a subset of data, and observations designed exclusively for a single band. Optimal data analysis procedures were developed for both situations by integrating Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) ionosphere maps, incorporating a stochastic model for ionospheric errors, and assessing their influence on source position estimates. The results indicate that the stochastic model is accurate to approximately 15%. It was determined that using GNSS ionospheric maps without modification introduces significant biases in declination estimates; however, a new procedure was created that nearly eliminates these biases. Additionally, an unexpected finding revealed that GNSS ionospheric maps contain multiplicative errors and must be scaled by a factor of 0.85 to mitigate declination bias—a similar scaling factor was observed when comparing vertical total electron content from satellite altimetry with GNSS maps. This scaling is interpreted as evidence of the limitations inherent in the thin shell model. The study demonstrates that ionospheric path delays can be modeled sufficiently to prevent systematic errors and to accurately evaluate the impact of ionosphere-induced random errors on source positions, rendering single-band absolute astrometry a viable method for determining source coordinates.

The nonlinear scattering of linear optical waves by conservative solitons has long been investigated in optical fibers as a method for nonlinear frequency conversion. In this work, we expand this analysis to examine the scattering of an externally injected probe wave from a dissipative Kerr cavity soliton circulating within a Kerr microresonator. Through both theoretical modeling and experimental verification, we show that this nonlinear interaction can be utilized to effectively broaden the soliton frequency comb by generating a secondary idler comb. We investigate the underlying physics, demonstrating that the phase detuning of the injected probe relative to a cavity resonance is critical in determining the central frequency of the idler comb, thereby offering a convenient parameter for controlling the comb's spectral envelope. Our findings clarify the dynamics governing the interplay between dissipative Kerr cavity solitons and external probe waves, and they may prove valuable for designing future Kerr frequency comb systems by enabling the generation of high-power comb lines in specific spectral regions simply through the injection of an appropriately selected probe.

Messages often convey opinions regarding events, products, services, political stances, or the author's emotional state. Sentiment analysis has been applied in various contexts, such as assessing the social network impact of events, evaluating consumer opinions, and understanding communication dynamics within Online Social Networks (OSNs). While numerous methods exist for measuring sentiment—ranging from lexical-based techniques to supervised machine learning—there is currently no consensus on which approach best identifies message polarity (positive or negative), as existing literature lacks comparative studies. Conducting such comparisons is vital for understanding the strengths and weaknesses of popular methods in analyzing OSN content. This study addresses that gap by comparing eight widely used sentiment analysis methods based on coverage (the proportion of messages with identified sentiment) and agreement (the alignment of identified sentiments with ground truth). Furthermore, we introduce a novel method that integrates existing approaches, achieving superior coverage and competitive agreement. Additionally, we offer a free Web service named iFeel, which provides an open API to access and compare results from various sentiment methods for any given text.

This paper explores finite-time distributive synchronization of complex networks using a single nonlinear pinning controller, with applicability extending to heterogeneous dynamic networks. Unlike many existing models that assume a symmetric coupling matrix or an undirected graph, this study considers asymmetric coupling matrices corresponding to directed graphs.

Recent years have seen significant interest in graph representation learning, yet most existing research concentrates on embedding single-layer graphs. Only a limited number of studies address multilayer structures, and these typically depend on the assumption that inter-layer connections are known, thereby restricting their practical utility. We introduce MultiSAGE, an extension of the GraphSAGE algorithm designed to embed multiplex networks. Our findings demonstrate that MultiSAGE effectively reconstructs both intra-layer and inter-layer connectivity, surpassing the performance of GraphSAGE, which is tailored for simple graphs. Furthermore, extensive experimental analysis reveals how embedding quality varies in both simple and multiplex networks, highlighting that graph density and link randomness are critical factors influencing performance.

We investigate the detailed derivation of the multiple D2-brane effective action arising from multiple M2-branes within the Bagger-Lambert-Gustavsson (BLG) and Aharony-Bergman-Jafferis-Maldacena (ABJM) frameworks by utilizing a new Higgs mechanism. Our analysis explicitly demonstrates that high-order $F^3$ and $F^4$ terms take the form of commutators, leading us to conjecture that all such high-order terms are commutator-based. Since these commutator terms can be interpreted as covariant derivative terms, they do not contribute to the multiple D2-brane effective action. Drawing inspiration from the derivation of a single D2-brane from an M2-brane, we extend our approach to curved M2-branes by introducing an auxiliary field. Upon integrating out this auxiliary field, we successfully recover the correct high-order $F^4$ terms in the D2-brane effective action derived from BLG theory and ABJM theory with $SU(2) \times SU(2)$ gauge symmetry. However, we fail to obtain the correct high-order $F^4$ terms from ABJM theory when considering $U(N) \times U(N)$ and $SU(N) \times SU(N)$ gauge symmetries for $N > 2$. We also provide a brief discussion on (gauged) BF membrane theory.
We enhance the conventional error term within the truncated Perron formula used for the logarithm of an $L$-function, ensuring that all constants remain explicit.

For Run 3, scheduled between 2022 and 2024, the LHC will raise its center-of-mass energy from 13 TeV to 14 TeV. Following this run, the High-Luminosity-LHC (HL-LHC) upgrade program is set to begin operations in 2027, boosting instantaneous luminosity to 5.0 to 7.5 times the nominal level. To manage the resulting high event rates and maintain physics acceptance, the ATLAS trigger system will undergo continuous improvements, including the installation of new detectors during the pre-Run 3 long shutdown. Starting in Run 3, new trigger logic will integrate data from detectors both inside and outside the magnetic field to lower the trigger rate. A newly developed trigger processor board has been designed to process data from these diverse detectors. During the HL-LHC upgrade, the first-level hardware-based trigger and readout systems will be enhanced to transfer full-granularity information to the processor board, enabling more sophisticated, offline-like track reconstruction within the hardware. To handle this data volume and perform hardware-based track reconstruction, the board will feature an FPGA equipped with hundreds of transceiver pairs and extensive memory resources. The anticipated performance of the hardware-based endcap muon trigger for both Run 3 and the HL-LHC will also be discussed.

Upsilon Sagittarii is a hydrogen-poor binary system previously thought to be in a second phase of mass transfer, where the primary evolved into a helium supergiant after exhausting its core helium. A tentative ultraviolet detection of a faint companion suggested mass estimates that would make the helium star a prototypical immediate progenitor for a type Ib/c supernova. However, the lack of a consistent model for its complex spectrum cast doubt on this interpretation. This study presents the first composite spectral model fitting the ultraviolet data, identifying the companion as a rapidly rotating, slowly moving ~7 solar mass B-type star, contrary to earlier claims. The stripped helium supergiant is now found to be less luminous than previously estimated, and with a mass under 1 solar mass, it is ruled out as a core-collapse supernova progenitor. We offer a detailed binary evolution scenario explaining the temperature, luminosity, extremely low gravity (log g ~ 1.0 cm/s²), and severe hydrogen deficiency (atmospheric mass fraction XH ~ 0.001) of the primary. The best-fitting model involves a ~5 solar mass intermediate-mass primary with an initial orbital period of a few days and a secondary that has gained significant mass despite its high rotation. We conclude that Upsilon Sagittarii is a critical system for testing binary evolution mechanisms, particularly envelope stripping and mass accretion.

Optimizing a sequence of tasks for a robot, often referred to as multi-point manufacturing, is a well-researched challenge where many approaches rely on variants of the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) to minimize distance or time. However, methods seeking optimal solutions often fail to scale effectively or operate in real-time. In online planning scenarios involving rapid task execution, the time required to calculate the optimal ordering can become the dominant factor in total execution time. Consequently, the optimal outcome in this context is defined as the sum of planning computational time and actual execution time. To address this, the proposed algorithm balances solution quality against total execution time by identifying a locally optimal sequence through waypoint generation, spatial clustering, and waypoint optimization. Simulation studies and tests on a real UR5 robot demonstrated that this approach yields significant reductions in time compared to a baseline algorithm.

We establish novel sufficient conditions for the permutation and monomial equivalence of linear cyclic codes across diverse finite fields. Noting that monomial and isometric equivalence coincide for linear codes over finite fields, we also present a necessary and sufficient condition for the monomial equivalence of such codes via a shift map acting on their defining sets. Furthermore, we introduce fresh algebraic criteria for determining the monomial equivalence of constacyclic codes over $\mathbb{F}_4$. Additionally, we demonstrate that when $\gcd(3n,\phi(3n))=1$, every permutation equivalent constacyclic code of length $n$ over $\mathbb{F}_4$ arises from the action of multipliers. These findings enable the optimization of search algorithms for new linear codes and facilitate the discovery of record-breaking linear and quantum codes.

The study investigated $\gamma$-ray de-excitation from an isomeric state of $^{186}$Ta, which was generated via multinucleon transfer reactions using a $^{136}$Xe beam on a natural tungsten target and subsequently isolated by the KEK Isotope Separation System. For the first time, two $\gamma$ transitions with energies of 161.1(2) and 186.8(1) keV linked to the isomeric decay were detected, leading to a deduced half-life of 17(2) s for the neutral $^{186 \rm m}$Ta isomer. By comparing these findings with prior measurements from the ESR storage ring at GSI Darmstadt and considering the coupling of individual particle orbitals in odd-odd nuclei, a decay scheme for $^{186 \rm m}$Ta was proposed.

We introduce twisted fiber bundles defined over any compact topological space for the associative algebra $A(\mathfrak g)$ associated with an infinite-dimensional Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$. The fibers consist of elements from the algebraic completion of formal series in complex parameters, while the sections are represented by rational functions possessing specific analytic characteristics. We establish both homotopical invariance and covariance regarding trivial bundles of twisted $A(\mathfrak g)$-bundles. Additionally, we highlight further applications of these findings relevant to the cohomology of infinite-dimensional Lie algebras on smooth manifolds, $K$-theory, conformal field theory, deformation theory, and foliation theory.

The AI community has recently focused on numerical reasoning involving hybrid data, such as tables and lengthy text. Current state-of-the-art approaches employ a retriever-generator pipeline to produce executable programs combining mathematical and table operations to answer queries. However, these methods rely on static retrieval results, even though distinct generation steps often require different sentences. To address this, we introduce DyRRen, an extended retriever-reranker-generator framework that enhances each generation step through dynamic reranking of retrieved sentences tailored to their specific relevance. Our approach surpasses existing baselines when evaluated on the FinQA dataset.

Quantum measurements serve as our primary window into complex quantum systems characterized by numerous microscopic degrees of freedom. Yet, inherent measurement uncertainties and the exponentially vast Hilbert space create significant obstacles to straightforwardly interpreting experimental results. To address this, we introduce a nonlinear "measurement energy" derived from observed outcomes, combined with an iterative effective-Hamiltonian method. This approach efficiently and generally extracts the most probable states (maximum likelihood estimates), thereby reconciling non-commuting observables and maximizing the utility of quantum data. We demonstrate the robustness and precision of this framework on random long-range fermion models and Kitaev quantum spin liquid models, even in cases where definitive signatures were absent. Furthermore, our research establishes a foundation for advanced concepts like nonlinear-operator Hamiltonians and applications such as parent Hamiltonian reconstruction.

Time-frequency music source separation typically involves applying binary or soft masks to the magnitude of complex spectrograms, while the phase is merely copied from the mixture to the separated sources. Although this approach offers practical benefits, it limits system performance by introducing audible phase artifacts in the isolated sources. This paper tackles these limitations by directly estimating masks within the complex domain, adapting recent advancements from speech enhancement. This technique is especially effective for multi-instrument separation, as phase artifacts are more detrimental when spectrally overlapping instruments are present. We demonstrate that utilizing complex masks yields superior separation results compared to methods operating exclusively on magnitude.

For centuries, the high-energy physics community has struggled to confirm the existence of magnetic charges, though recent models suggest they could now be detected at current colliders. These entities manifest in field theories as either heavily suppressed, well-studied monopoles with soliton structures or the less-explored, point-like monopoles first proposed by Dirac to symmetrize Maxwell's equations via a singular magnetic field. Building on this, S. Baines et al. investigated these sources as matter fields with spins 0, 1/2, or 1 within a perturbative effective field theory applicable to threshold-produced monopoles where the coupling strength $g(\beta)$ is suppressed. The MoEDAL collaboration at CERN is currently exploring all three scenarios, using the kinematic distribution expressions derived in this work as guides. These cross-section distributions originate from a \emph{U}(1) invariant gauge theory. Unlike the electron, it is not assumed that the monopole's magnetic moment arises from minimal spin interactions, as its value could be substantial. Consequently, the analytical expressions for spin 1/2 and 1 cases remain fully general by incorporating a phenomenological parameter $\kappa$, linked to the gyromagnetic ratio $g_R=1+\kappa$. Furthermore, including this parameter ensures the effective theory's validity in the high-energy limit, provided the magnetic coupling scales with the particle's velocity $\beta=v/c$.

Optical navigation for a CubeSat depends on accurately extracting beacon directions from onboard imagery. This paper details an experiment on the European Space Agency's (ESA) OPS-SAT, a 3-unit CubeSat equipped with a proven Attitude Determination and Control System (ADCS) and imager, to characterize the onboard Angle-based Correlation (AbC) algorithm. The study utilizes selected star fields containing sufficient visible stars within a 10° field of view. During the experiment, OPS-SAT orients itself toward the most suitable star field available at the time. The imager captures the field, and sub-windows are extracted around the anticipated position of each star, determined by the attitude quaternion provided by the ADCS. The AbC algorithm reconstructs the absolute direction of the central body—effectively the known star used as a beacon in this test—by heavily employing quaternion algebra. The process first consolidates the beacon's location within the field of view using AbC, then finely positions the field of view against the sky using the same method, associating a covariance with the resulting beacon direction. The experiment manages the satellite's pointing and imager operations, processes the acquired images, and subsequently downloads the computed absolute directions and their covariances for comparison with actual directions. Following an intensive campaign, the algorithm's statistical performance will be evaluated against the onboard covariances. Additionally, this setup will provide an assessment of OPS-SAT's inertial pointing stability. Theoretically, AbC can eliminate both the platform's Attitude Control Error (ACE) and the Attitude Knowledge Error (AKE) estimated by the ADCS, potentially converging to...

We investigate the stresses generated during the drying of a colloidal drop containing silica nanoparticles. Specifically, we utilize the wrinkling instability of a thin floating sheet to quantify the net stress exerted by the deposit on the substrate, with a focus on the impact of particle polydispersity. For bidisperse suspensions, we demonstrate that even a small fraction of large particles significantly reduces the anticipated stress, an effect we attribute to the creation of pathways with lower hydrodynamic resistance within the porous material. Given that colloidal suspensions are typically polydisperse, we show that across various average particle sizes, the resulting stress is primarily governed by the largest particles in the distribution rather than the mean particle size.

The Solar Orbiter mission, which operates in an orbit inclined to the ecliptic and positioned outside the Sun-Earth line, enables the integrated analysis of data from solar imagers and spectrometers. For the first time, distinct space-based spectrometers will be situated at wide angular separations, making 3D spectroscopy of the solar atmosphere possible. This study aims to establish a methodology for reconstructing 3D vector velocities from two stereoscopic line-of-sight (LOS) Doppler measurements. This involves combining data from the Spectral Imaging of the Coronal Environment (SPICE) instrument on Solar Orbiter with near-Earth spectrometers located far apart in space. We adapt previously developed libraries from the STEREO mission, applying them to spectroscopic data from Hinode and the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO). The approach incorporates established techniques for static and dynamic solar rotation stereoscopy, as well as methods for EUV stereoscopic triangulation of optically thin coronal plasma. Additionally, we create new algorithms utilizing spatial analytical geometry to calculate 3D velocities within coronal loops. Our method is demonstrated by reconstructing 3D velocity vectors in plasma flows along both "open" and "closed" magnetic loops. This technique is designed for application during the nominal phase of the Solar Orbiter mission, involving two spacecraft with spectrometers (SPICE, the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph [IRIS], and the Hinode imaging spectrometer) at varying separations. Finally, we outline how these observations can be effectively coordinated.

Neural networks frequently demand extensive data to generalize effectively and are often inappropriate for modeling small, noisy experimental datasets. Consequently, standard architectures trained on such scarce and noisy data tend to produce predictions that contradict fundamental physical principles. This paper introduces techniques for incorporating even-odd symmetries and conservation laws directly into neural networks, alongside novel extensions and applications for physically constrained neural networks. We develop an even-odd decomposition architecture that separates a neural network's parameterized function into its even and odd parts, proving its ability to accurately infer symmetries without prior information. We emphasize the noise-resilient capabilities of these physically constrained networks, demonstrating their effectiveness as physics-informed noise regulators. Specifically, we applied a network embedding a conservation of energy constraint to serve as a physics-informed noise regulator for a symbolic regression task. Our results show that this approach yields a symbolic representation of the function that aligns closely with underlying physics and surpasses a baseline symbolic regression method.

We have compiled a sample of stars detected by both LAMOST and Gaia that exhibit colors indicative of temperatures exceeding 7000 K. By training a machine learning model on LAMOST spectroscopic data labeled with stellar classes and metallicities, we created a catalog of Blue Horizontal Branch (BHB) stars including metallicity details. A separate model, trained on Gaia parallaxes, was used to estimate the absolute magnitudes for these stars. The resulting catalog contains 13,693 BHBs, estimated to be approximately 86% pure, with uncertainties of $\sigma_{[Fe/H]}\sim$0.35 dex and $\sigma_{G}\sim$0.31 mag. These figures are validated against globular clusters, though a covariance error appears to influence our magnitude and abundance calculations. We further examined a subset of this catalog within the Galactic Halo. Our analysis reveals that BHB populations in the outer halo are redder, suggesting a younger population, and that the metallicity gradient remains relatively flat near [Fe/H] = -1.9 dex across our observed area. Additionally, we found that metal-rich BHB stars follow more radially anisotropic orbits ($\beta \sim 0.70$) at all radii compared to their metal-poor counterparts ($\beta \sim 0.62$).

The growing popularity of neural networks within reinforcement learning stems from their success in solving numerous complex benchmarks, with some AI algorithms even surpassing human experts. Typically, these networks feature multiple hidden layers, resulting in a substantial number of parameters that require optimization. While numeric methods like stochastic gradient descent are standard for this purpose, they often incur high computational costs, making them unsuitable for tasks where efficiency is paramount. Addressing this limitation, this paper proposes optimizing neural network parameters using estimation of distribution algorithms, specifically employing the univariate marginal distribution algorithm (UMDA) to evolve networks across various reinforcement learning scenarios. To validate this approach, the algorithm was tested on four OpenAI Gym benchmark problems and compared against a standard genetic algorithm. The results demonstrate that UMDA generally yields superior optimization outcomes compared to the genetic algorithm.

This study first proves that positive solutions to the fractional Kirchhoff equation $\Big(a+b{\int_{\mathbb{R}^{N}}}|(-\Delta)^{\frac{s}{2}}u|^2dx\Big)(-\Delta)^su+mu=|u|^{p-2}u$ in $\mathbb{R}^{N}$ are both unique and non-degenerate, given $a,b,m>0$, $0<\frac{N}{4}<s<1$, $2<p<2^*_s=\frac{2N}{N-2s}$, and where $(-\Delta )^s$ denotes the fractional Laplacian. Subsequently, by integrating this non-degeneracy finding with the Lyapunov-Schmidt reduction technique, we demonstrate the existence of semiclassical solutions for the singularly perturbed problem $\Big(\varepsilon^{2s}a+\varepsilon^{4s-N} b{\int_{\mathbb{R}^{N}}}|(-\Delta)^{\frac{s}{2}}u|^2dx\Big)(-\Delta)^su+V(x)u=|u|^{p-2}u$ in $\mathbb{R}^{N}$, provided $\varepsilon>0$ is sufficiently small and $V$ represents a potential function.

This study examines weakly confined particle systems in two dimensions, defined by a significant number of outliers situated far from the droplet where the majority of particles cluster in the many-particle limit. The asymptotic behavior of these outliers is analyzed for two families of point processes: Coulomb gases subject to regular background measures at determinantal inverse temperature, and a specific class of random polynomials. It is observed that the limiting outlier process relies solely on the geometry of the uncharged region housing them and the total net excess charge. Specifically, for a determinantal Coulomb gas confined by a sufficiently regular background measure, outliers within a simply connected uncharged region converge to the corresponding Bergman point process. In the case of a finitely connected uncharged region $\Omega$, a collection of limiting outlier processes emerges, indexed by the Pontryagin dual of the fundamental group of $\Omega$. Furthermore, outliers in distinct uncharged regions are asymptotically independent, even when the regions share boundary points; this finding illustrates the screening properties inherent to the particle system.

This article examines the relevance of the process matrix formalism and quantum causal modelling to current debates regarding causation's role in fundamental physics. We contend that the process matrix approach has accurately pinpointed a concept of "causal order" crucial to fundamental physics, yet this concept is less robust than the everyday understanding of causation because it lacks asymmetry. Furthermore, we argue that causal order serves as a foundation for more traditional causal phenomena. Applying these insights to quantum foundations, we assert that because no-signalling quantum correlations fail to display causal order, they should not be examined through classical causal models; this addresses an open issue concerning the interpretation of fine-tuning in such models. Finally, we note that a quantum extension of causal modelling can fulfill a function similar to standard causal reasoning, though we stress that this functional equivalence does not imply that quantum causal models provide new explanations for quantum processes.

We explicitly compute the quantum partition function for dissolving Abelian Higgs vortices by utilizing spectral information from the Beltrami Laplacian defined on the $N$-vortex moduli space $\mathbb{CP}^N$, equipped with a scaled Fubini--Study metric. This partition function allows for the derivation of the vortex gas pressure. The system exhibits three distinct asymptotic regimes: High, Intermediate, and Low Temperature. The transition from the Intermediate to the Low Temperature phase is described by a Bessel function, and within the Low Temperature regime, the free energy scales as $N^2$ rather than being extensive.

Neural networks and associated deep learning approaches currently lead the field in object classification; however, they typically require extensive training data and time, and their models often lack interpretability. This paper introduces FastMapSVM, an interpretable machine learning framework designed as a superior alternative to neural networks for general classification tasks. By integrating the complementary advantages of FastMap and Support-Vector Machines (SVMs), FastMapSVM extends SVM applicability to domains involving complex objects. FastMap is a linear-time, efficient algorithm that maps complex objects into Euclidean space while maintaining domain-specific pairwise distances. We demonstrate FastMapSVM's efficiency and effectiveness through seismogram classification, showing that its precision, recall, and accuracy match those of other state-of-the-art methods. In contrast, FastMapSVM requires significantly less time and data for training. Additionally, it offers clear visualizations of both the objects and the classification boundaries between them. We anticipate that FastMapSVM will be viable for classification tasks across numerous other real-world domains.

This work examines Lorentz-Karamata spaces, along with their small and grand variants, and the specific $\mathcal{L}$, $\mathcal{R}$, $\mathcal{LL}$, $\mathcal{RL}$, and $\mathcal{RR}$ spaces. The quasi-norms associated with a function $f$ in these spaces are defined using either the non-increasing rearrangement $f^*$ or the maximal function $f^{**}$. We analyze the conditions under which these quasi-norms are equivalent, with most proofs relying on Hardy-type inequalities. As an application, we show how these general findings enable the derivation of interpolation formulae for both grand and small Lorentz-Karamata spaces.

Trust serves as a cornerstone for large-scale distributed systems, including the Internet of Things (IoT), facilitating the transition from options to definitive decisions. However, calculating trust is inherently linked to the level of uncertainty within data sources; consequently, trust levels in an IoT network are inversely related to uncertainties arising from hardware failures, network instability, adversarial threats, and the characteristics of exchanged data. This relationship necessitates strategies that maximize trust while minimizing uncertainty. Regrettably, there remains no agreed-upon method for guaranteeing IoT network trustworthiness, especially regarding the fine-grained handling of uncertainty. This paper introduces a generalized framework for managing trust across IoT networks of diverse scales. Within this proposed framework, various uncertainty sources are quantified, trust ratings are assigned to individual entities, and a network model is developed to efficiently distribute workloads to reliable nodes. The study applies this approach to a practical scenario involving smart vehicular networks. Ultimately, this work aims to establish a standardized methodology for constructing trustworthy IoT networks, thereby providing a foundation for future research in trust management under conditions of uncertainty.

We investigate the issue of orbifold deconstruction, which involves determining, based solely on accessible data, if a specific conformal model corresponds to an orbifold, and subsequently identifying the associated twist group and the underlying conformal model.

We introduce an all-fiber emitter-cavity quantum electrodynamics (QED) setup comprising a nanofiber cavity and two two-level emitters. This configuration enables the observation of higher-order exceptional points through the interaction between the emitters and the cavity. The cavity's effective gain can be determined by weakly driving it with two identical laser fields, facilitating coherent perfect absorption (CPA) in experimental applications. Under feasible experimental conditions, the system's Hamiltonian exhibits pseudo-Hermiticity, allowing its eigenvalues to be either entirely real or consist of one real value and a complex conjugate pair. By adjusting the ratio of emitter-cavity coupling strengths and the decay rates of the emitters, we can identify both third-order (EP3) and second-order (EP2) exceptional points without requiring parity-time symmetry. These findings are corroborated by total output and transmission spectra. Furthermore, we observe that symmetric modes emerge when the coupling strength exceeds the critical threshold at EP3 points. This proposal offers a novel approach to achieving higher-order exceptional points.

This paper investigates the Mori fan and the corresponding secondary fan for the Dolgachev-Nikulin-Voisin family at degree $2$. The primary contribution is an enumeration of every maximal-dimensional cone within both fans.

This paper details the systems entered into the iSarcasm shared task, which aims to detect sarcasm in both Arabic and English text. Our team focused on the Arabic language component, submitting a multi-layer machine learning model designed for Arabic sarcasm detection. The system utilizes TF-IDF vectors for feature representation, remains simple in design, and requires no external resources. The experimental results demonstrate promising performance.

Federated learning (FL) is a privacy-preserving distributed machine learning approach that trains models without moving original data from local devices. Given that devices often face resource constraints, offloading computational tasks to edge servers can enhance FL performance. However, device mobility poses a challenge, as participants may leave the network and connect to different edge servers during training, necessitating the migration of offloaded computations. Addressing this gap, we introduce FedFly, the first known method to migrate deep neural networks (DNNs) when devices switch edge servers during FL training. Empirical evaluations on the CIFAR10 dataset, covering both balanced and imbalanced data distributions, demonstrate that FedFly reduces training time by up to 33% if a device moves after 50% completion, and by up to 45% if the move occurs after 90% completion, outperforming existing state-of-the-art offloading techniques. FedFly incurs negligible overhead of up to two seconds while maintaining accuracy. We also identify several open research directions for future study. The code for FedFly is available at https://github.com/qub-blesson/FedFly.

A recent study by the final three authors established that a game-theoretic $p$-harmonic function $v$ is uniquely determined by an asymptotic mean value property involving a variationally defined mean $\nu_p^r[v](x)$ over balls $B_r(x)$. Building on this, the present work examines the operator $\mu_p^\ve$ acting on continuous functions over $\ol{\Om}$ within a domain $\Om\subset\RR^N$ ($N\ge 2$), defined as $\mu_p^\ve[v](x)=\nu^{r_\ve(x)}_p[v](x)$, where $r_\ve(x)=\min[\ve,\dist(x,\Ga)]$ and $\Ga$ represents the boundary of $\Omega$. We first establish key properties of $\mu^\ve_p$, including continuity and monotonicity. Subsequently, we demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of a function $u^\ve\in C(\ol{\Om})$ that solves the Dirichlet-type problem:
$$
u(x)=\mu_p^\ve[u](x) \ \mbox{ for all } \ x\in\Om,\quad u=g \ \mbox{ on } \ \Ga,
$$
for any continuous boundary data $g\in C(\Ga)$. This result relies on the assumption of a suitable barrier function existing at every point in $\Ga$. We identify $u^\ve$ as the \textit{variational} $p$-harmonious function with Dirichlet data $g$, derived via a Perron-type method grounded in a comparison principle. Furthermore, we show that the family $\{ u^\ve\}_{\ve>0}$ serves as an approximation scheme for the viscosity solution $u\in C(\ol{\Om})$ of the equation
$$ \De_p^G u=0 \ \mbox{ in }\Om, \quad u=g \ \mbox{ on } \ \Ga, $$
where $\De_p^G$ denotes the game-theoretic (or homogeneous) $p$-Laplace operator. Specifically, we prove that $u^\ve$ converges uniformly to $u$ on $\ol{\Om}$ as $\ve\to 0$.

Combining the precise mass estimate of the supermassive black hole at the center of galaxy M87, obtained by the Event Horizon Telescope, with recent high-quality photometric and spectroscopic data, allows for a detailed decomposition of dark and luminous mass from the galactic core to its virial radius. This offers critical insights into major cosmological and astrophysical questions. For the first time, we can analyze the distributions of dark and standard matter within a galaxy region directly under the gravitational influence of a supermassive black hole. The established relationship between supermassive black hole mass and stellar dispersion velocity at the highest mass scales suggests an unusual growth mechanism for these black holes. This case may represent the first instance where supermassive black hole growth is attributed partly to the Dark Matter component. Furthermore, the presence of a massive dark matter halo core in a galaxy with inefficient baryonic feedback places constraints on the nature of dark halo particles. Finally, the previously observed complex interplay between dark and luminous structural properties in disk systems also manifests here.

We investigate an open molecular junction where electrons interact with multiple phonon modes. By employing a master equation approach for equilibrated phonons, we demonstrate that nearly-degenerate phonon modes can be effectively mapped onto a single mode, significantly lowering computational expenses. To illustrate this, we apply our theoretical framework to the OPV-5 molecule, achieving consistent conductance spectra while decreasing computational time by orders of magnitude.

This study examines a long-range random walk in a $1+1$ dimensional random environment, characterized by spatially independent but temporally correlated disorder. We demonstrate that the rescaled partition function converges weakly to the Stratonovich solution of a fractional stochastic heat equation driven by multiplicative Gaussian noise that is white in space and colored in time.
We present direct constructions for 226 group divisible designs featuring a block size of five, primarily of the type $g^u m^1$ where $m > 0$.

Around $x\approx0.25$, $\mathrm{Ba}_{1-x}\mathrm{K}_{x}\mathrm{Fe}_{2}\mathrm{As}_{2}$ exhibits a unique first-order transition from a four-fold symmetric double-Q magnetic state to a two-fold symmetric single-Q phase, an event previously proposed to coincide with the emergence of superconductivity (B\"ohmer et al., Nat. Comm. 6, 7911 (2015)). In this study, we utilize magnetic fields reaching 10T to examine the interaction between superconductivity and this magneto-structural transition through high-resolution thermal-expansion and heat-capacity measurements. Our findings indicate that magnetic fields suppress the reentrance of the single-Q orthorhombic phase more effectively than they suppress the superconducting transition, causing a splitting of the zero-field first-order transition. The suppression rate of the orthorhombic reentrance is more pronounced for out-of-plane fields compared to in-plane fields and correlates with the anisotropy of the superconducting state. A phenomenological Ginzburg-Landau model successfully describes these observations, strongly implying that the suppression of the reentrant orthorhombic single-Q phase is mainly driven by the field-induced weakening of the superconducting order. However, the model fails to account for the significant reduction in orthorhombic distortion observed under out-of-plane fields, an aspect requiring further theoretical investigation.

The primary objective of this study is to formulate a set-valued It\^{o}'s formula. By applying this result, we demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of solutions for general set-valued backward stochastic differential equations, thereby resolving an open problem raised by Ararat et al. (C. Ararat, J. Ma, and W.Q. Wu, *Set-valued backward stochastic differential equation*, arXiv:2007.15073).

This paper introduces the initial beam test outcomes for centimeter-scale AC-LGAD strip sensors, fabricated by Brookhaven National Laboratory and tested at the Fermilab Test Beam Facility. These sensors are designed to enable cost-effective, large-area 4D tracking, making them suitable for timing layers in the Electron Ion Collider (EIC) and space-based particle experiments. The study reviews various sensor designs to optimize electrode geometry for enhanced spatial resolution and timing performance, addressing key considerations for preserving signal quality as electrode sizes increase. Performance data from multiple prototypes demonstrate simultaneous resolutions of 18 microns spatially and 32 ps temporally using 1 cm long strips with a 500 micron pitch. With minor adjustments, these sensors represent ideal candidates for implementing a 4D timing layer at the EIC.

This study investigates energy transport within a one-dimensional system consisting of two distinct Frenkel-Kontorova lattices linked by a time-modulated coupling and interfaced with heat reservoirs at varying temperatures via molecular dynamics simulations. We identify a specific driving frequency that maximizes heat flux, a phenomenon known as thermal resonance. Significant structural changes in the lattice substantially influence how external driving forces interact with phonon bands. Specifically, the overlap of these bands within the model's harmonic regime defines the frequency range where resonance occurs. Additionally, we analyze parameter dependencies that allow the incoming heat flux to be directed toward either reservoir. These findings could facilitate advancements in the design of thermal devices.

This work details the next-to-leading order (NLO) calculation of doubly-polarized $W^\pm Z$ pair production at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), incorporating both Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) and Electroweak (EW) corrections through a double-pole approximation method. Specific numerical results for the $W^- Z$ process in the $e^-\bar{\nu}_e \mu^+\mu^-$ channel are provided at 13 TeV, applying ATLAS fiducial cuts and defining polarized distributions within the $WZ$ center-of-mass frame. While NLO EW corrections relative to NLO QCD predictions remain below 5% for most kinematic variables, they can approach 10% in specific cases, such as lepton transverse momentum or the rapidity separation between the electron and the $Z$ boson. These corrections vary depending on the polarization state. Finally, the study compares the newly reported ATLAS measurement of polarization fractions against the corresponding theoretical predictions.

Integer lists are frequently utilized in database systems and inverted indexes, often requiring memory compression. Leveraging the SIMD instructions found in standard processors can accelerate these integer compression methods. Our proposed S4-BP128-D4 scheme achieves state-of-the-art compression rates while decoding integers in as few as 0.7 CPU cycles. However, optimizing decoding speed becomes inefficient if the subsequent processing of those integers is slow. To demonstrate that this trade-off is unnecessary, we (1) vectorized and optimized the intersection of posting lists and (2) developed the SIMD Galloping algorithm, which utilizes a single SIMD instruction to compare four integer pairs simultaneously. Experiments conducted on the GOV2 and ClueWeb09 (Category B) TREC text collections, utilizing logs from the TREC million-query track, reveal that our conjunctive query techniques can double the speed of current state-of-the-art approaches using only the SIMD instructions present in all modern CPUs.

While model-free reinforcement learning algorithms can calculate policy gradients from sampled environment transitions, they necessitate substantial data volumes. Conversely, model-based approaches leverage learned models to synthesize new data, yet they risk instability or suboptimality due to model errors and bias. This paper introduces a novel technique that merges real-world data with a learned model to capture the strengths of both paradigms. The central concept involves utilizing real-world data for on-policy predictions while employing the learned model solely for generalization across different actions. Specifically, we apply time-dependent on-policy correction terms derived from real data atop a learned model, ensuring data generation capabilities without the accumulation of errors over extended prediction horizons. We provide theoretical justification for this approach, demonstrating that it mitigates the error term associated with model-based policy improvement. Experimental results on MuJoCo and PyBullet benchmarks indicate that our method significantly enhances existing model-based strategies without requiring additional tuning parameters.

Under extreme pressure, the conventional periodic trends governing elements—such as oxidation states, compound stoichiometry, and reactivity—undergo profound changes. The application of pressure modifies the energetic arrangement of atomic orbitals, enabling core orbitals to participate in chemistry, generating unusual electron configurations, and even creating non-atom-centered orbitals within the voids of solid lattices. These conditions give rise to anomalous stoichiometries, structural arrangements, and bonding patterns. Crystal structure prediction methods, free from atmospheric-pressure biases, have been highly effective in mapping high-pressure phase diagrams and discovering new structures across various chemical systems. Many of these predicted phases have since been confirmed experimentally, thanks to advancements in diamond anvil cells and dynamic compression techniques that facilitate access to high-pressure environments. The synergy between theoretical modeling and experimental validation has yielded significant breakthroughs in high-temperature superconductivity, revealing numerous novel phases with superconducting transition temperatures nearing room temperature.

The connection between conservation laws and symmetries for solitons in a ferromagnet is intricate due to gyroscopic (precessional) forces, which are described within the Lagrangian framework using a background gauge field. This setup renders canonical momenta gauge-dependent and necessitates a meticulous application of Noether's theorem. We demonstrate that Cartan's theory of differential forms provides an ideal framework for this purpose. Employing this approach, we derive the conserved momenta for the Belavin--Polyakov skyrmion, accounting for its symmetries in translation, global spin rotation, and dilation.

As strategies for precision physics programs advance across the HL-LHC, FCC-ee, FCC-hh, ILC, CLIC, CEPC, and CPPC, it becomes increasingly evident that rigorous control of associated theoretical precision is essential. This discussion examines how amplitude-based resummation can address this need, illustrated through examples drawn from the LHC, upcoming collider proposals, and quantum gravity.

Every non-erasing monoid morphism $\sigma: {\cal A}^* \to {\cal B}^*$ generates a measure transfer map $\sigma_X^{\cal M}: {\cal M}(X) \to {\cal M}(\sigma(X))$ linking the measure cones ${\cal M}(X)$ and ${\cal M}(\sigma(X))$ for any subshift $X \subseteq {\cal A}^\mathbb Z$ and its corresponding image $\sigma(X) \subseteq {\cal B}^\mathbb Z$. This paper defines and analyzes this map, demonstrating that it possesses properties of continuity, linearity, and functoriality, and is also surjective. Additionally, an efficient method for calculating the value of the transferred measure $\sigma_X^{\cal M}(\mu)$ on any cylinder $[w]$ (where $w \in {\cal B}^\mathbb Z$) is provided.

**Theorem:** If a non-erasing morphism $\sigma: {\cal A}^* \to {\cal B}^*$ is recognizable within a subshift $X \subseteq {\cal A}^\mathbb Z$, then the map $\sigma^{\cal M}_X$ is bijective.

The concept of a "recognizable" subshift is fundamental in symbolic dynamics, having evolved through a rich history of refinement and playing a pivotal role in the field. To establish the aforementioned theorem, we prove the following proposition: A non-erasing morphism $\sigma: {\cal A}^* \to {\cal B}^*$ is recognizable in a subshift $X \subseteq {\cal A}^\mathbb Z$ if and only if:
(1) the mapping from the shift-orbits of $X$ to those of $\sigma(X)$ is injective, and
(2) $\sigma$ maintains the shift-period of every periodic word found in $X$.

This paper presents a comprehensive procedure for deriving a data-driven small-signal model designed for converter-based power system analysis. The study evaluates three modeling approaches—single Decision Tree (DT) regression, ensemble DT regression, and Spline regression—by comparing their accuracy, training duration, and computational efficiency. The proposed methodology outlines a detailed workflow encompassing data generation via conventional simulations and mathematical models, database organization, regression training and validation, and prediction for new scenarios. Initially developed using a basic network, the approach was subsequently validated on a more complex system to demonstrate its efficacy, with both test cases reflecting key features of converter-dominated grids, including high renewable penetration and HVDC connections. Furthermore, the article proposes a visual representation of small-signal stability results across diverse operating conditions by leveraging DT regressions. Finally, potential applications of this model are explored, emphasizing its utility for future research in power system small-signal dynamics.

Beginning in 2018, the LHCb detector underwent an upgrade to function at increased luminosity and broaden its discovery potential. As critical elements for particle identification within the LHCb, the Ring Imaging Cherenkov (RICH) detectors necessitated a redesign of their optoelectronic readout chain to meet these upgraded specifications. This work outlines the experimental configuration and presents the outcomes of beam tests conducted to evaluate and verify the performance of the new optoelectronic readout system.

The Bianchi IX cosmological model is examined within a generalized uncertainty principle framework. By applying the Arnowitt-Deser-Misner reduction to the dynamics, the volume of the Universe emerges as the natural time coordinate; this variable is handled conventionally, whereas anisotropies (the physical degrees of freedom) are modeled using a deformed Heisenberg algebra.
