In such tasks, modern machine learning approaches outperform traditional systems by offering superior adaptability to stochasticity and robustness against significant uncertainties. Specifically, supervised and imitation learning have delivered exceptional results, though they rely on supervision that is often unavailable in all scenarios. Conversely, while reinforcement learning (RL) demands only minimal supervision, it remains impractical due to inefficiency. To address this, we introduce and theoretically justify a new Unsupervised Reward Shaping algorithm derived from expert observations, which reduces the supervision burden on the agent and enhances RL performance for this specific task.
This paper demonstrates the embedding of regularly acting groups and diagonal groups into wreath products under their product action by utilizing Cartesian Decomposition.

The recent Gaia mission has identified an unexpected abundance of equal-mass "twin" wide binaries, characterized by mass ratios $q\gtrsim 0.95$ and separations reaching at least 1000 AU. The formation mechanism for this group remains puzzling: although twin binaries are believed to originate from correlated accretion within circumbinary disks, typical protostellar disks span only about 100 AU, which is significantly smaller than the distances separating the widest twins. In this study, we derive the eccentricity distribution of wide twins by analyzing the distribution of their $v$-$r$ angles—the angle formed between the separation vector and the relative velocity vector of the components. Our findings indicate that wide twins must reside on highly eccentric orbits. Specifically, for the excess twin population at separations of 400–1000 AU, we observe a sharp concentration of systems with extreme eccentricities, where $0.95 \lesssim e \leq 1$. Such high eccentricities imply pericenter distances of approximately 10 AU, suggesting that these systems were scattered through dynamical interactions during their formation. This supports a scenario where twins initially form in circumbinary disks and are subsequently widened. Furthermore, these results confirm that wide twin binaries constitute a distinct population and demonstrate their utility as tracers of the dynamical histories of stellar groups.

We present the first comprehensive spectral and temporal analysis of the newly identified Be/X-ray binary eRASSU J050810.4$-$660653 in the Large Magellanic Cloud, utilizing data from SRG/ART-XC, NuSTAR, and Swift/XRT collected between December 2021 and May 2022 across a broad energy band of 0.5–79 keV. The light curve reveals pulsations with a period of $40.5781 \pm 0.0004$ s, exhibiting a pulsed fraction that increases monotonically with energy. Long-term monitoring yielded an orbital period estimate of approximately 38 days. The source spectrum is well described by a power-law model featuring an exponential cutoff at high energies. Phase-resolved spectroscopy indicates significant variations in spectral parameters tied to the neutron star's rotation phase. No cyclotron absorption line features were detected in either the phase-averaged or phase-resolved spectra. Despite this, indirect methods suggest a neutron star magnetic field strength on the order of several $10^{13}$ G. Furthermore, we discuss the observed variations in the hardness ratio across the pulse phase in the context of the emitting region's physical and geometrical characteristics.

Our analysis reveals that dust clouds eclipsing young stars cover the stellar disk unevenly. Specifically regarding CQ Tau, we identify isolated optically thick structures with dimensions of less than approximately 0.6 stellar radii and calculate the typical vertical extinction gradient across the sky plane, which reaches several magnitudes per stellar radius. These significant extinction gradients and the intricate architecture of the obscuring material not only produce a distinct Rossiter-McLaughlin effect but also induce complex and variable distortions in the stellar absorption lines.

This study examines the one-dimensional isentropic compressible Euler equations featuring linear damping $\beta(t,x)\rho u$ within a bounded domain, a framework applicable to compressible flow through porous media. The model is subjected to a dissipative subsonic time-periodic boundary condition. Our primary findings demonstrate that such a boundary condition induces a unique, smooth subsonic time-periodic solution that remains stable against small perturbations in initial data. Furthermore, the regularity and stability of this time-periodic solution are enhanced when the boundary condition possesses higher regularity.

This chapter of the High Energy Physics Software Foundation Community Whitepaper examines the current status, best practices, and emerging trends regarding data and software preservation within high energy physics. It introduces a revised perspective on the motivation for preservation, emphasizing its role in facilitating reuse. Additionally, it outlines and discusses a set of research and development objectives aimed at enhancing software and cyberinfrastructure to support the reuse of particle physics analyses and production tools.

This study examines the nonequilibrium dynamics of entanglement entropy and out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs) for noninteracting fermions at half-filling, evolving from a product state to differentiate between delocalized, multifractal (specifically under nearest-neighbor hopping), localized, and mixed phases within the quasiperiodic Aubry-Andr\'e-Harper (AAH) model augmented by long-range hopping. In mixed phases with sufficiently strong long-range hopping, a secondary logarithmic behavior emerges in the entanglement entropy, contrasting with the primary power-law behavior, whose exponent varies across phases. The saturation value of entanglement entropy scales linearly with system size in delocalized, multifractal, and mixed phases, whereas in the localized phase (under short-range conditions), it remains independent of system size. OTOC dynamics reveal distinct power-law growth at early times when comparing nearest-neighbor versus long-range hopping, and late-time decay exhibits noticeably different power-law exponents across the various phases. Furthermore, the spatial profile of the OTOC and its dependence on system size offer unique characteristics for phase identification; notably, in mixed phases, the spatial profile displays two distinct spatial dependencies for short and long distances. Additionally, in the presence of multifractal states, the spatial profile exhibits significant fluctuations at specific locations tied to the quasiperiodicity parameter.

This study examines the $(n,k)$-Bernoulli--Laplace model involving two urns with an equal total count of red and white balls, where the selection size $k$ at each step scales asymptotically with the urn size $n$. The primary objective is to analyze the long-term dynamics of the associated Markov chain that monitors the red ball count in a specific urn. Assuming reasonable conditions on the limit of the $k/n$ ratio as $n$ approaches infinity, we demonstrate a cutoff phenomenon in total variation distance and derive the corresponding cutoff window. These findings partially address an open question previously raised by Eskenazis and Nestoridi.

Although near-wall blood flow and wall shear stress (WSS) are critical regulators of major cardiovascular diseases, obtaining high-fidelity measurements of them remains difficult. Existing patient-specific computational and experimental approaches to measuring WSS often struggle with noise, low resolution, and uncertainty. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) offer a flexible deep learning solution that integrates governing mathematical equations—specifically the Navier-Stokes equations for blood flow—with empirical data. By incorporating this physical knowledge, PINNs reduce the massive data requirements typical of standard deep learning. This study demonstrates the application of PINNs to enhance WSS quantification in diseased arterial flows, particularly in scenarios where inlet and outlet boundary conditions are unknown. Since uncertainty in boundary conditions is prevalent in patient-specific computational fluid dynamics, PINNs were shown to achieve very high accuracy in quantifying WSS using only sparse velocity measurements away from the wall, without needing complete boundary data. Examples using idealized stenosis and aneurysm models illustrate how combining partial knowledge of flow physics with limited measurements yields precise near-wall hemodynamic data. Ultimately, this hybrid framework, which merges data-driven methods with physics-based deep learning, holds significant promise for advancing high-fidelity modeling of near-wall hemodynamics in cardiovascular disease.

Recent research has proposed representing semantic relations through questions and answers, breaking down textual data into distinct interrogative natural language statements. This paper addresses three QA-based semantic tasks—QA-SRL, QANom, and QADiscourse, each focusing on a specific type of predication—and suggests they collectively offer a holistic representation of text. To achieve this, we explore the most effective ways to leverage sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) pre-trained language models within a semi-structured output framework comprising an unordered collection of question-answer pairs. We evaluate various input and output linearization methods, as well as the impacts of multitask learning and basic data augmentation techniques, particularly in scenarios with imbalanced training data. As a result, we introduce the first unified QASem parsing tool, designed to be practical for downstream applications that require an explicit, QA-based interpretation of textual information units.

This note establishes three distinct theorems. First, defining $\lfloor x \rfloor$ as the greatest integer not greater than $x$, it is shown that there exists an increasing sequence of positive integers $S=\{s_1,s_2,...\}$ satisfying $s_n<s_{n+1}\le 2s_n$ and a positive integer $m$ such that the set $\{2^i:0\le i\le m\}$ is never contained within $\{\lfloor\alpha s_n\rfloor: n=1,2,3,...\}$ for any $\alpha$ in the interval $0<\alpha<1$. Second, for any integers $r,\ell\ge 2$, there exists an integer $k\ge 1$ such that $\ell^m+k$ fails to be $r$--full for all positive integers $m$, where an integer $n$ is termed $r$--full if $p|n$ necessitates $p^r|n$ for every prime $p$. Third, it is proven that all but at most $O(n/\log n)$ of the $n$ numbers $2^n-i$ (where $1\le i\le n$) are composite, with the implied constant being absolute. The initial two findings resolve problems previously posed by Ma and Chen, as well as Chen and Ruzsa, respectively. The final result serves as a partial contribution toward a problem raised by Chen, who questioned whether infinitely many integers $n$ exist such that every number in the sequence $2^n-i$ ($1\le i\le n$) is composite; the author notes this specific question remains unsolved. A unifying feature of these three results is the availability of their elementary and straightforward proofs.

This paper classifies quadratically integrable systems of the cylindrical type within quantum mechanics under the influence of magnetic fields. Aligning with the direct method employed in classical mechanics by Fournier et al. (2020) to enable direct comparison, the analysis identifies two systems requiring no corrections and two that do. In every instance, the magnetic field $B$ remains identical to its classical counterpart, whereas the scalar potential $W$ may incorporate corrections dependent on $\hbar^2$. Among these, two systems possess both cylindrical integrals that are quadratic in momenta, rendering them non-separable. These findings establish a foundation for future investigations into superintegrability.

Phrase representation learning has been extensively investigated across numerous Natural Language Processing (NLP) domains, such as Sentiment Analysis and Machine Translation, yielding significant improvements. Existing approaches typically rely on either non-compositional representations derived from general word embedding techniques or compositional representations grounded in syntactic structures; however, the latter often demand extensive human annotation or struggle to generalize across all phrases. This study introduces a novel pairwise gated recurrent unit (pairwise-GRU) framework that leverages large-scale paraphrase databases to generate compositional phrase representations. This framework is designed to be reusable for representing any phrase. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple phrase similarity tasks.

Researchers frequently aim to understand not only how treatments influence outcomes but also the mechanisms driving these effects. A mediator is defined as a variable influenced by the treatment that subsequently impacts the outcome. Current penalized mediation approaches often fail to capture critical mediators, either by relying on finite-dimensional linear models to eliminate confounding bias or by neglecting confounding control entirely; however, these assumptions frequently do not reflect reality. To address this, we introduce a method that treats confounding functions as nuisance parameters estimated via data-adaptive techniques. We subsequently apply a new regularization strategy to the resulting objective function to pinpoint key mediators. We derive the asymptotic properties of our estimator and prove its oracle property under specific conditions. Furthermore, we present asymptotic results for a local setting, contrasting our approach with the standard adaptive lasso. Additionally, we propose a perturbation bootstrap technique to ensure asymptotically valid post-selection inference for the targeted mediated effects. Finally, we evaluate and demonstrate the performance of these methods through simulation studies.

We examine the parameter space of the recently proposed Littlest Higgs model with T-parity (NLHT), which was designed to resolve issues present in the original LHT framework. This model necessitates additional fermions and pseudo-Goldstone bosons. Although the heavy top quark sector remains similar, the NLHT introduces both T-odd and T-even heavy quarks and leptons whose masses depend on two sets of Yukawa matrices, compared to just one in the LHT. The new scalar sector consists of a T-odd real singlet and triplet, with masses determined by gauge and Yukawa couplings rather than the spontaneous symmetry breaking scale $f$, making them potentially light. By enforcing that no mass surpasses the cutoff scale, incorporating current lower limits on vector-like quarks, and adopting a simplified scenario with mass-degenerate heavy fermions suitable for heavy photon dark matter, we constrain $f$ to the range of 2–3 TeV. Furthermore, the common Yukawa coupling for heavy leptons is fixed, while the heavy quark Yukawa coupling becomes strongly correlated with the top quark's Yukawa coupling. Consequently, the particle spectrum is bounded: the lightest heavy photon sits near 0.5 TeV, close to heavy leptons; new scalars fall below 1 TeV; the complex scalar triplet aligns with heavy weak bosons at 1.5–2.5 TeV; and heavy quarks and top partners lie between 2 and 5 TeV. Finally, these new scalars primarily decay into a standard lepton and a T-odd lepton, exhibiting a decay width similar to that of the Higgs boson.

This paper introduces a new method to enhance distance-based formation controllers by adding a secondary constraint designed to eliminate 3D formation ambiguities. We define three controlled variables that span an orthogonal space, uniquely identifying a tetrahedron formation in three dimensions. This framework integrates constraints regarding inter-agent distances and the signed volumes of tetrahedral substructures. The system is modeled as a directed graph featuring a leader-follower architecture and single-integrator dynamics. We demonstrate that the proposed decentralized controller guarantees both global asymptotic stability and local exponential stability for the target formation in an n-agent system without any ambiguities. Distinct from prior research, this stability is achieved without imposing restrictions on the specific tetrahedrons constituting the desired formation or on the control gains.

This study examines the Hawking--Page phase transitions of Schwarzschild and charged black holes within an extended phase space, where the black holes are situated inside a spherical cavity of radius $r_B$ in asymptotically flat space. We introduce an effective thermodynamic volume, $V=4\pi r_B^3/3$, and define an effective pressure $p$ as its conjugate variable. Systematically analyzing the phase transition temperature $T_{\rm HP}$ and Gibbs free energy $G$ in a grand canonical ensemble with a fixed electric potential $\Phi$, we find that $T_{\rm HP}$ rises with increasing $p$ but falls as $\Phi$ increases. For a phase transition to occur, $\Phi$ must remain below a specific upper bound to ensure the cavity radius exceeds the black hole horizon radius. These findings are compared with phase transition behaviors in anti-de Sitter space, highlighting both significant similarities and distinct differences. Ultimately, this work elucidates the connection between black hole thermodynamic properties and their specific boundary conditions across various extended phase spaces.

Software has become central to academic inquiry. We contend that beyond its methodological significance, software should often be recognized as a research output equivalent to a traditional academic paper. This article explores the various functions software serves in research and emphasizes its connection to reproducibility and sustainability. It outlines the specific challenges involved in citing and reviewing software, noting that these processes differ from those applied to papers. We conclude that while software outputs do not currently fit seamlessly into existing publication models, substantial positive efforts are underway that are poised to address this issue effectively.

Reinforcement learning (RL) allows robots to acquire skills through real-world interactions. However, the unstructured, step-based exploration typical of Deep RL, which often succeeds in simulations, frequently results in jerky motion patterns when applied to physical robots. This shaky behavior leads to poor exploration or even hardware damage. To mitigate these problems, we adapt state-dependent exploration (SDE) for current Deep RL algorithms. By introducing two extensions—utilizing more general features and periodically re-sampling noise—we develop a new approach called generalized state-dependent exploration (gSDE). We evaluated gSDE in simulations using PyBullet continuous control tasks and on three distinct physical robots: a tendon-driven elastic robot, a quadruped, and an RC car. The noise sampling interval in gSDE offers a balance between performance and smoothness, enabling direct training on real robots without performance degradation. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/DLR-RM/stable-baselines3.

This work establishes a framework for analyzing how the expansion rate of the image of a bounded set evolves under a flow in Euclidean space, applying it to stochastic differential equations (SDEs) featuring singular coefficients. Specifically, if the SDE's singular drift can be decomposed into two parts—one singular and the other possessing a radial component with sufficient strength directed toward the origin—then the resulting random dynamical system is guaranteed to possess a pullback attractor.

Charge carriers in Dirac and Weyl semi-metals display behavior akin to that of relativistic particles. This study introduces a new form of intrinsic half-integer Quantum Hall effect in two-dimensional materials, which simultaneously provides a mechanism for topological current protection. This phenomenon arises from the two-dimensional parity anomaly and does not require an external perpendicular magnetic field. We hypothesize that it can emerge in perturbed honeycomb lattices where both time-reversal symmetry and spin degeneracy are broken. Such systems feature two separate gap-opening mechanisms; when they act concurrently, they generate slightly different energy gaps in each valley. This disparity results in a net anomalous conductivity when the chemical potential is adjusted to lie between these distinct gaps. Finally, we outline several promising material configurations that meet the necessary criteria, encouraging further numerical and experimental investigation into this effect.

This paper examines the Cauchy problem for the Riccati differential equation featuring constant coefficients and a modified Gerasimov-Caputo fractional differential operator of variable order. By employing Newton's numerical algorithm, solution curves are generated for various Cauchy problem parameters. These results are benchmarked against previously established findings, and the computational precision of the algorithm is analyzed. Furthermore, utilizing the Runge rule, it is demonstrated that the computational accuracy converges toward the accuracy of the numerical method as the number of grid nodes increases.

This study introduces the first numerically stable nonlinear evolution for the leading-order gravitational effective field theory, known as Quadratic Gravity, within the spherically-symmetric sector. The approach utilizes three key components: (i) harmonic gauge to transform the evolution system into a quasi-linear format, (ii) the Cartoon method to maintain spherical symmetry consistent with harmonic gauge, and (iii) reduction to first-order in time through the introduction of auxiliary variables. The well-posedness of the initial-value problem is validated numerically by evolving randomly perturbed initial data for flat space and black holes. This work serves as a proof-of-concept demonstrating that stable numerical evolution is feasible even in the presence of higher-order derivatives.

We introduce a novel compression framework for genomic data consisting of sequence fragments, or reads. This approach relies on a reference genome available solely at the decoder, thereby relieving the encoder from the need to store references or execute computationally expensive alignment tasks. Central to this scheme is a multi-layer coding structure that provides the decoder with the necessary data to align reads, correct deviations from the reference, verify reconstructions, and fix any errors. The method leverages the established principles of distributed source coding with decoder side information, enhanced by a generalized-concatenation code construction that efficiently embeds all required information for reliable reconstruction. We initially outline the scheme for handling only substitution errors between reads and the reference, subsequently extending it to accommodate reads containing a single deletion alongside multiple substitutions. A key component of this extension is a newly developed distance metric, which is demonstrated analytically to outperform existing metrics in alignment performance.

Human evaluation has become essential for assessing chatbot performance. However, existing off-the-shelf methods face significant reliability and replication challenges, largely due to the vast diversity of evaluation criteria. Consequently, there is an urgent need to establish standardized criteria and precise definitions. To address this, we conducted a comprehensive review of 105 papers on human evaluation for chatbots, resulting in the proposal of five standard criteria with exact definitions.

This Letter presents a complete orbital analysis of the two-planet system orbiting the nearby K0 dwarf star 14 Herculis (HD 145675, HIP 79248). Identified as a middle-aged ($4.6^{+3.8}_{-1.3}$ Gyr) star, 14 Her hosts two eccentric giant planets previously detected through radial velocity (RV) variations and long-term trends. By combining archival RV data from Keck/HIRES with *Gaia-Hipparcos* proper motion acceleration corrections, we have resolved the mass and inclination of planet b to ${9.1}_{-1.1}^{+1.0}$ $M_\mathrm{Jup}$ and ${32.7}_{-3.2}^{+5.3}$ degrees, respectively. Even with incomplete phase coverage for planet c, we successfully constrained its mass and orbital parameters to ${6.9}_{-1.0}^{+1.7}$ $M_\mathrm{Jup}$ and ${101}_{-33}^{+31}$ degrees. Our results indicate that the coplanarity of the b and c orbits is strongly disfavored. Given the system's age and the similar masses of its planets, these findings suggest that planet-planet scattering likely shaped the current system configuration.

Using the concept of quantization, we investigate the Helton-Howe trace and the Connes-Chern character associated with Toeplitz operators on weighted Bergman spaces. We establish a local formula for the large $t$-limit of the Connes-Chern character as the weight approaches infinity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Helton-Howe trace of Toeplitz operators remains invariant regardless of the weight $t$, and we derive a local formula for this trace across all weighted Bergman spaces by employing harmonic analysis and quantization techniques.

Estimating the value of a property within a large stochastic system proves challenging when sample sizes are too small to accurately determine the underlying probability distribution. The standard Bayesian estimator for such properties depends on knowing the prior distribution, yet selecting an appropriate prior is often ambiguous. Existing approaches have typically developed estimators with priors specifically tailored to individual properties, such as entropy, mutual information, or pairwise correlations. This paper introduces a universal framework for selecting priors applicable to any property. We first establish that only specific dimensions of the prior distribution influence the inference. Subsequently, we represent the desired prior as a linear combination of a one-dimensional family of indexed priors, where each member is derived via a maximum entropy approach constrained by the mean value of the target property. In many practical scenarios, only one or a few components of this expansion significantly impact the Bayesian estimator, allowing for the retention of a single component. The data itself determines the relevant component, eliminating the need for manually crafted priors. We validate this approximation using several paradigmatic examples, demonstrating performance comparable to, and in some cases superior to, previous ad-hoc methods. Furthermore, our approach illuminates the link between Bayesian inference and equilibrium statistical mechanics, as the most significant component of the expansion corresponds to the appropriate temperature.

This paper examines a buyer-seller scenario involving a new product where the seller initially lacks knowledge of production costs. Contracts can be finalized either before the cost is revealed (ex-ante) or after, provided both parties accept a costly delay, at which point the seller knows the cost. We demonstrate that for a profit-seeking seller, the ideal ex-ante agreement is a fixed-price contract with an "at-will" provision, permitting the seller to terminate the deal once the production cost is discovered. However, the seller may achieve higher profits by proposing a guaranteed-delivery price ex-ante, followed by a contingent second price if the buyer declines the initial offer. This "limited commitment" strategy increases profits by allowing partial dependence on cost without explicitly embedding it in the contract terms. Comparable findings apply to a model where the buyer is unaware of her valuation ex-ante and instead initiates a procurement contract with the seller.

We examine bulk-surface gapped Hamiltonians on lattices featuring corners and introduce a periodic table of topological invariants associated with corner states for investigating higher-order topological insulators. This framework relies on four key components: (1) defining topological invariants, (2) proving their connection to corner states, (3) calculating K-groups, and (4) creating explicit examples.

Integrating Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) into primary diagnosis workflows demands near-perfect accuracy alongside robust generalization across data variations and model transparency. Current CNNs often function as opaque "black boxes," failing to assure physicians that critical diagnostic markers are being utilized. Building upon established methods like multi-task learning, domain adversarial training, and concept-based interpretability, this study tackles the challenge of embedding specific diagnostic factors directly into training objectives. We demonstrate that our architecture, which learns an end-to-end uncertainty-weighted combination of multi-task and adversarial losses, prioritizes relevant pathology features—such as nuclear density and pleomorphism—while filtering out misleading indicators like staining inconsistencies. Experiments on breast lymph node tissue reveal significantly enhanced generalization in tumor detection, achieving a best average AUC of 0.89 (±0.01) compared to the baseline 0.86 (±0.005). Furthermore, by applying linear probing of intermediate representations, we confirm that the model successfully learns interpretable features like nuclei density, thereby increasing its transparency. This work establishes a foundation for developing robust, interpretable multi-task architectures capable of handling data heterogeneity. The source code is accessible at https://bit.ly/356yQ2u.
This paper introduces novel concepts of triangular Banach algebras and examines the derivations within these structures.

The rapid expansion of data has necessitated a corresponding focus on data quality, which is essential for ensuring information relevance and supporting organizational decision-making and planning. Since data quality is often assessed ad-hoc, existing concepts frequently lack practical application. This empirical study aims to develop a concrete automated platform designed to evaluate incoming datasets, generate quality labels and scores, and produce comprehensive reports. Using diverse datasets from healthdata.gov, opendata.nhs, and the Demographics and Health Surveys (DHS) Program, we analyzed variations in quality scores and formulated a labeling system based on Principal Component Analysis (PCA). The study identified a metric comprising nine key quality components: provenance, dataset characteristics, uniformity, metadata coupling, the percentage of missing cells and duplicate rows, data skewness, the ratio of inconsistencies in categorical columns, and correlations among these attributes. Additionally, the research includes an illustrative case study and validates the metric using Mutation Testing approaches. Ultimately, this work offers an automated solution that accepts incoming datasets and metadata to deliver a Data Quality (DQ) score, report, and label. These findings are particularly valuable for data scientists, as the confidence provided by the quality label can be crucial before deploying data in practical applications.

As the cornerstone of urban mobility, rail transit systems require a deep understanding of their vulnerability, specifically their capacity to sustain normal operations under operational disturbances of varying magnitudes. To address this, the paper introduces a network vulnerability assessment approach that integrates both static network topology and dynamic travel demand. This methodology employs an accessibility-based framework to identify critical stations based on time-varying passenger flows and introduces a novel dynamic vulnerability evaluation index. Using Beijing's rail transit system as a case study, empirical analysis reveals that the distribution of high-importance stations fluctuates throughout the day, driven by the interplay of static structure and hourly passenger volume. Furthermore, under operational delay scenarios, the influence of these key stations on network vulnerability escalates with increasing delayed travel demand. The study identifies that stations acting as essential bridges between origins and destinations, particularly those with high passenger throughput, exert the most significant impact on vulnerability. Additionally, network performance degradation during continuous interval failures exhibits distinct segmentation and stratification. The primary driver of system-wide performance decline is the disruption between different lines, where certain critical stations within a line function as catalysts that accelerate this degradation. Ultimately, this approach offers a reference for assessing dynamic, passenger-flow-related network vulnerability and provides the field with a new evaluation metric.

Viewing molecules as assemblies of smaller subunits or fragments is a fundamental principle in chemical and physical sciences, facilitating productive approaches in quantum chemistry. By employing fragmentation schemes, researchers can develop efficient algorithms to tackle challenges related to the formation and breaking of chemical bonds. We introduce a formally exact time-dependent density-functional theory designed for the electronic dynamics of molecular fragments with a variable electron count. This new framework extends our earlier research published in *Phys. Rev. Lett.* {\bf 111}, 023001 (2013). Furthermore, we propose a stable density-inversion method applicable to both time-dependent and ground-state density-functional theory, as well as their extensions, including the methodology presented here.

Reconstructing the visual structure of tomato plants via robotics presents significant difficulties in greenhouses due to substantial environmental variability and occlusion. Active vision offers a solution by leveraging prior data to systematically optimize camera viewpoints for acquiring new information. However, current active vision methods struggle with specific perception goals, such as 3D leaf node reconstruction, because they fail to differentiate between target plant components and the rest of the vegetation. This paper introduces an attention-driven active vision algorithm that focuses exclusively on relevant plant parts based on the specific task. Evaluated in a simulation for 3D reconstruction at varying attention levels (whole plant, main stem, and leaf nodes), the proposed method outperforms pre-defined and random strategies. Within the first three viewpoints, it improves 3D reconstruction accuracy by 9.7% and 5.3% for the whole plant, 14.2% and 7.9% for the main stem, and 25.9% and 17.3% for leaf nodes, respectively. Furthermore, it achieves 80% reconstruction of the whole plant and main stem in one fewer viewpoint, and 80% of leaf nodes in three fewer viewpoints compared to baseline approaches. The study also demonstrates the planner's robustness against variations in plant models, occlusion levels, candidate viewpoint counts, and reconstruction resolutions. By integrating an attention mechanism into active vision, efficient reconstruction of both entire plants and specific parts becomes feasible. Ultimately, incorporating attention into active vision is essential for significantly enhancing perception quality in complex agro-food settings.

We introduce Enhash, an efficient ensemble learning algorithm designed to identify \textit{concept drift} within data streams. This approach handles diverse drift scenarios, including abrupt, gradual, virtual, recurring, or mixed types. By utilizing projection hashing to integrate new samples, Enhash demonstrates empirically competitive performance compared to current ensemble methods, achieving these results with significantly reduced computation time and moderate resource consumption. Our evaluation involved performance comparisons across six artificial and four real-world datasets featuring various drift patterns.

Certain interactions involving classical or quantum fields and matter are recognized as irreversible processes. In this work, we define an entropy for the electromagnetic field using established concepts from statistical quantum mechanics, specifically diagonal entropy. Our approach centers on analyzing spontaneous emission and light diffusion. We derive a metric capable of quantifying irreversibility for both quantum and classical descriptions of the electromagnetic field, which we examine and interpret through a thermodynamic lens.

An interactive mechanism is an algorithm that retains a dataset and responds to adaptively selected queries. It is termed differentially private if no adversary can determine whether a specific individual belongs to the dataset by interacting with it. This paper investigates the composition properties of differential privacy within concurrent settings, where an adversary simultaneously engages with $k$ interactive mechanisms and can arbitrarily interleave its queries. While Vadhan and Wang [2021] established an optimal concurrent composition theorem for pure differential privacy, we significantly broaden and extend these findings. Specifically, we demonstrate optimal parallel composition properties for several prominent differential privacy frameworks, including approximate DP, Rényi DP, and zero-concentrated DP. Our findings indicate that adversaries derive no benefit from interleaving queries across independently operating mechanisms, suggesting that interactivity is a capability provided by differential privacy at no additional cost. Concurrently and independently, Vadhan and Zhang [2022] derived an optimal concurrent composition theorem for $f$-DP [Dong et al., 2022], which subsumes our results for the approximate DP scenario.

Line waves, recently identified as wave entities localized along two dimensions, serve as the one-dimensional analogs of surface waves. They can exist at discontinuities in the surface reactance or resistance of low-dimensional materials, including graphene and metasurfaces. This study examines a wider category of non-Hermitian surface-impedance junctions capable of supporting coupled line waves, offering a unified framework to explore various one-dimensional waveguiding mechanisms. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that under parity-time-symmetry conditions, exceptional points can arise in a flat-optics context, combining the unique properties of line waves with exceptional-point physics and illuminating phase transitions within these systems. Furthermore, the necessary surface-impedance parameters align with those achievable using standard models of photoexcited graphene metasurfaces in the terahertz range. Beyond advancing the nascent understanding of line wave physics, these findings open promising avenues in the largely uncharted domain of non-Hermitian flat optics, with potential applications spanning sensing, lasing, and on-chip optical signal processing.

Calculations regarding dark matter relic density from its freeze-out in the primordial plasma have become highly refined, supported by numerical tools that achieve observationally necessary precision. Conversely, dark matter produced via the freeze-in mechanism operates at significantly higher temperatures, presenting substantial technical and computational hurdles when striving for equivalent accuracy. We re-examine the formulation of freeze-in production to streamline the incorporation of in-medium effects such as plasma interactions and the spin statistics of relativistic quantum gases. Additionally, we address the temperature-dependent production rates driven by electroweak and strong phase transitions, and we thoroughly analyze the complexities introduced by $s$-channel resonances. Using Higgs portal models as a case study, we deliver the most precise calculation to date for the freeze-in abundance of Scalar Singlet dark matter. We specifically investigate scenarios with low reheating temperatures, where the couplings predicted by freeze-in could be probed at the LHC. Accompanying this paper, we release a major update (version 6.3) of DarkSUSY, which now includes the capability to perform comprehensive freeze-in calculations incorporating all the aforementioned complications.

Electromagnetic whistler-mode wave resonances are the main mechanism driving the creation and evolution of energetic electron populations across diverse space plasma environments, such as planetary radiation belts and shock waves. The standard theoretical model for describing the cumulative impact of multiple resonant interactions is quasi-linear theory, which relies on electron diffusion within velocity space. In this framework, the quasi-linear diffusion coefficient ($D_{QL}$) scales linearly with wave intensity ($B_w^2$) and must remain sufficiently low to maintain the theory's validity. However, spacecraft observations frequently reveal whistler-mode waves with intensities strong enough to drive nonlinear electron resonances. These nonlinear interactions introduce phenomena like phase trapping and bunching, which can alter electron fluxes rapidly through non-diffusive processes. While both diffusive and nonlinear regimes are well understood, no existing theory quantifies the transition between them. This paper characterizes the integral effect of nonlinear electron-wave interactions by analyzing the relaxation time-scale of the electron distribution, approximately $1/D_{NL}$. We derive how the nonlinear diffusion coefficient ($D_{NL}$) depends on wave intensity ($B_w^2$) and other key parameters, such as wave-packet dimensions. By comparing $D_{QL}$ and $D_{NL}$, we identify the specific ranges of wave intensity and packet size where diffusive and nonlinear regimes produce identical evolution rates for the electron distribution. Finally, these findings are discussed in relation to energetic electron dynamics within Earth's radiation belt.

Key characteristics of biological intelligence include energy efficiency, the ability to adapt continuously, and risk management achieved through uncertainty quantification. Consequently, neuromorphic engineering has primarily focused on creating energy-efficient machines inspired by the time-based computing mechanisms of biological brains. This paper advances the design of neuromorphic systems capable of adapting to evolving learning tasks while generating well-calibrated uncertainty estimates. To achieve this, we develop online learning rules for spiking neural networks (SNNs) grounded in a Bayesian continual learning framework. Within this framework, each synaptic weight is modeled using parameters that reflect current epistemic uncertainty derived from prior knowledge and observed data. The proposed online rules update these distribution parameters in a streaming manner as new data arrives. We implement this approach for both real-valued and binary synaptic weights. Experimental results on Intel's Lava platform demonstrate the advantages of Bayesian learning over frequentist learning regarding adaptation capacity and uncertainty quantification.

Learning from demonstration (LfD) offers a practical approach for endowing robots with dexterous abilities when demonstrations are available in the robot's intrinsic coordinates; however, the accumulation of errors in lengthy and intricate tasks hinders its broad adoption. Given that many complex skills consist of smaller movements combined together, modeling the target skill as a sequence of compact motor primitives appears logical. The core challenge addressed here is ensuring that each motor primitive concludes in a state conducive to the successful execution of the following primitive. This study tackles that issue by proposing the learning of an explicit correction policy to be activated when the anticipated transition state between primitives is not met. This correction policy is trained using behavior cloning, leveraging the state-of-the-art Conditional Neural Motor Primitives (CNMPs) architecture. The resulting policy can generate diverse movement trajectories in a context-dependent manner. The superiority of this proposed system over learning an entire task as a single action is demonstrated in a simulated table-top environment where an object must be pushed through a corridor in two stages. Furthermore, the method's applicability to real-world bi-manual knotting is illustrated by equipping an upper-body humanoid robot with the ability to tie knots over a bar in 3D space. Experimental results indicate that the robot can successfully perform knotting even when encountering correction scenarios that were not present in the original human demonstration dataset.

Text-guided image retrieval holds significant potential for various practical domains, including e-commerce. The objective involves taking a source image and textual instructions describing desired alterations, then identifying target images that match the source while incorporating those modifications through a multi-modal (image-text) query. To address this, we introduce Additive Attention Compositional Learning (AACL), a novel approach utilizing a multi-modal transformer architecture to effectively model image-text relationships. At its core is a new composition module based on additive attention, designed to integrate seamlessly into deep neural networks. Additionally, we present a new, challenging benchmark constructed from the Shopping100k dataset. Evaluated across three large-scale datasets—FashionIQ, Fashion200k, and Shopping100k—against robust baselines, AACL demonstrates new state-of-the-art performance on all three.

This study generalizes large sieve-type estimates to sums comprising pth powers of trigonometric polynomials. We present a methodology for deriving these estimates that avoids standard L^2 techniques, relying instead on comparing the norm and spectral radius of convolution operators defined on a normed space of trigonometric polynomials.

We demonstrate that spontaneous Raman scattering from incident radiation can be detected in cavity-QED systems without requiring external enhancement or interaction with vibrational degrees of freedom. These Raman processes manifest as resonances within the emission spectrum, becoming distinctly observable as the system enters the ultrastrong coupling regime. We offer a quantum mechanical framework for this phenomenon and establish that ultrastrong light-matter coupling is an essential prerequisite for observing Raman scattering. Furthermore, the sensitivity of this effect to system parameters creates new possibilities for characterizing cavity QED configurations and generating quantum states of light.

Accurate segmentation of small targets is vital for 3D medical image diagnosis, yet it remains a significant challenge. To address this, we introduce the Axis Projection Attention UNet (APAUNet), a specialized architecture for 3D medical image segmentation focused on small lesions. Given that 3D feature spaces are dominated by background data, we employ a projection strategy that maps 3D features onto three orthogonal 2D planes to capture contextual attention from multiple viewpoints. This approach effectively filters redundant information while mitigating the loss of critical details regarding small lesions. Subsequently, a dimension hybridization strategy fuses 3D features with multi-axis attention maps through weighted summation, enabling the adaptive learning of perspective importance. Furthermore, the APA Decoder concatenates high- and low-resolution features within the 2D projection workflow to generate precise multi-scale information, which is essential for segmenting small lesions. Experiments on two public datasets, BTCV and MSD, demonstrate that APAUNet outperforms existing methods. Specifically, it achieves an average Dice score of 87.84 on BTCV, 84.48 on MSD-Liver, and 69.13 on MSD-Pancreas, significantly surpassing state-of-the-art approaches for small target segmentation.

This research investigates the magnetic and quadrupole moments of $B_c$-like tetraquark states with quantum numbers $J^P = 1^+$ using QCD light-cone sum rules within both the molecular and diquark-antidiquark frameworks. The numerical analysis employs interpolating currents corresponding to these two configurations alongside photon distribution amplitudes to derive the moments. The calculated magnetic moments are $\mu_{Z_{{uc \bar u \bar b}}}^{Mol}=1.18^{+0.52}_{-0.40}~\mu_N$, $\mu_{Z_{{uc \bar u \bar b}}}^{Di}=3.05^{+1.19}_{-0.95}~\mu_N$, $\mu_{Z_{dc \bar d \bar b}}^{Mol}=0.32^{+0.18}_{-0.10}~\mu_N$, and $\mu_{Z_{dc \bar d \bar b}}^{Di}=2.38^{+0.95}_{-0.75}~\mu_N$. Alongside mass, magnetic and quadrupole moments serve as fundamental observables offering insights into the underlying quark structure and dynamics. Notably, the results derived from the two different pictures differ significantly. Experimental measurements of these magnetic moments could elucidate the internal composition of these states. Furthermore, the study yields small but non-zero quadrupole moments for $B_c$-like tetraquarks, indicating non-spherical charge distributions. We hope that the findings presented here will assist future experimental searches for these particles, representing a compelling area of research.

For the past twenty years, it has been proposed that the Lorentz transformation, which extends Newtonian classical mechanics into Einstein's special relativity, necessitates a corresponding deformation of standard statistical mechanics. Within this framework, the exponential function defining Boltzmann's factor undergoes a proper deformation, resulting in what is known as the $\kappa$-deformed exponential function. Building on this foundation, we define new categories of statistical distributions that represent $\kappa$-deformed versions of established distributions such as the Generalized Gamma, Weibull, and Logistic. These distributions are particularly suited for analyzing statistical data characterized by power-law tails.

This paper introduces PredNAS, a general and effective framework for Neural Architecture Search (NAS). The core motivation is that, given a differentiable performance estimator, architectures can be directly optimized for higher performance through simple gradient ascent. Specifically, the method employs a neural predictor to estimate performance. Surprisingly, PredNAS achieves state-of-the-art results on NAS benchmarks using fewer than 100 training samples. To demonstrate the method's universality, it is applied to large-scale tasks, comparing against RegNet on ImageNet and YOLOX on MSCOCO. These results show that PredNAS can discover novel architectures with competitive performance under specific computational constraints.

A $(k,g)$-cage is defined as a simple, $k$-regular graph with girth $g$ that possesses the minimum possible number of vertices. In this study, such cages that are also Moore graphs are termed minimal $(k,g)$-cages. A simple connected graph is classified as distance regular (DR) when every vertex shares an identical intersection array, whereas a bipartite graph is designated as distance biregular (DBR) if all vertices within the same partite set exhibit the same intersection array. It is established that minimal $(k,g)$-cages are DR graphs, and their subdivisions result in DBR graphs. This paper presents a formula for the distance spectral radius of minimal $(k,g)$-cages expressed through $k$ and $g$, and identifies polynomials of degree $[\frac{g}{2}]$—which corresponds to the graph's diameter. These polynomials yield all distance eigenvalues upon substituting adjacency eigenvalues for the variable. We demonstrate that a minimal $(k,g)$-cage with diameter $d$ possesses exactly $d+1$ distinct distance eigenvalues, thereby partially resolving a question raised in [5]. Furthermore, we prove that every DBR graph constitutes a 2-partitioned transmission regular graph and provide a corresponding formula for its distance spectral radius. Utilizing this formula, we derive the distance spectral radius for the subdivisions of minimal $(k,g)$-cages. Finally, we establish the complete distance spectrum for the subdivisions of specific minimal $(k,g)$-cages.

Neutron Resonance Transmission Analysis (NRTA) leverages resonant neutron absorption to determine the absolute isotopic makeup of a target, facilitating applications across archaeology, nuclear fuel analysis, and arms control verification. Historically, NRTA relied on large-scale facilities and intricate detector setups; however, recent improvements in the intensity of compact neutron sources have rendered compact neutron imaging designs increasingly viable. This study details a Monte Carlo (MC) driven design for a compact epithermal NRTA radiographic system utilizing a moderated, compact deuterium-tritium (DT) source and an epithermal detector. Such a device offers extensive application potential, particularly for nuclear inspections and arms control exercises where mobility and cost are critical. The MC simulations presented confirm accurate time-of-flight (TOF) reconstructions of transmitted neutron energies, enabling the high-precision differentiation of nuclear material isotopes. Future generations of miniaturized, high-intensity neutron sources will further enhance the technique's precision and speed, yielding significant benefits for diverse engineering and societal challenges.

We introduce a novel class of exact four-dimensional Taub-NUT spacetimes within Einstein-$\Lambda$ theory, featuring a conformally coupled scalar field with a power-counting super-renormalizable potential. The construction begins with a seed solution $(g_{\mu\nu},\phi)$ derived from a conformally coupled theory with a conformal potential. By applying a specific frame transformation alongside a simultaneous shift of the seed scalar, we generate a new configuration $(\bar{g}_{\mu\nu},\bar{\phi})$ that satisfies the field equations for a theory with the specified super-renormalizable potential; notably, the seed's solution spectrum is significantly enriched. We identify two distinct families of exact black bounces: de Sitter and anti-de Sitter geometries, each transitioning through three different phases. The de Sitter geometries evolve from a regular black hole possessing both event and cosmological horizons into a bouncing cosmology linking two de Sitter universes with varying asymptotic cosmological constants, passing through an intermediate phase of either a de Sitter wormhole or a bouncing cosmology connecting two de Sitter universes in the presence of a cosmological horizon. Conversely, anti-de Sitter geometries transition from a regular black hole with inner and event horizons to a wormhole connecting two asymptotic boundaries of differing constant curvatures, with an intermediate phase consisting of an anti-de Sitter regular black hole with a single event horizon appearing in two contexts: as a regular black hole embedded within an anti-de Sitter wormhole, or as a black hole exhibiting an internal cosmological bounce. These diverse geometries are smoothly connected solely by varying the mass parameter. Furthermore, additional solutions including black holes, bouncing cosmologies, and wormholes are also discovered.

Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) are extensively employed to accelerate applications in artificial intelligence, physics simulation, medical imaging, and information visualization. To enhance GPU performance, hardware designers must analyze vast quantities of simulator-generated traces to pinpoint performance bottlenecks. Visualizing these execution traces alleviates user cognitive load and aids in interpreting the behaviors of GPU components. This paper formalizes the GPU performance analysis process and defines the design requirements for visualizing execution traces through surveys and interviews with GPU hardware designers. We contribute a data and task abstraction framework for this analysis. Building on this task analysis, we introduce Daisen, a framework that collects data from GPU simulators and visualizes the resulting execution traces. Daisen features a specialized data abstraction and trace format capable of recording simulator outputs. It also provides a web-based visualization tool designed to help hardware designers examine traces, identify performance bottlenecks, and verify improvements. A qualitative evaluation with GPU hardware designers confirms that Daisen aligns with their typical workflows, enabling participants to effectively detect potential bottlenecks and opportunities for optimization. The open-source implementation of Daisen is available at gitlab.com/akita/vis. Additional resources, including a demo video, survey questions, evaluation guides, and post-study surveys, can be accessed at osf.io/j5ghq.

This study examines the potential of both the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) near detector and the proposed DUNE-PRISM movable near detector to detect sub-GeV dark matter, focusing on scalar dark matter that interacts with the Standard Model through a sub-GeV dark photon. The analysis considers dark matter generated within the DUNE target, which then travels to the detector to scatter off electrons. Utilizing DUNE-PRISM to conduct searches across multiple off-axis positions significantly enhances sensitivity to this scenario compared to relying on a single on-axis measurement.

Gender-neutral pronouns have been recently adopted across many languages to serve two purposes: a) representing non-binary individuals and b) functioning as a generic singular. New psycholinguistic findings indicate that humans do not experience processing difficulties with these pronouns in Swedish. However, we demonstrate that this ease of human processing stands in stark contrast to how automated systems handle them. Specifically, gender-neutral pronouns in Danish, English, and Swedish result in increased perplexity, more scattered attention distributions, and inferior downstream performance in language models. We contend that this conservative behavior in artificial intelligence could hinder the broad acceptance of gender-neutral pronouns, necessitating a resolution to this issue.

Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) is a pivotal technology for facilitating more natural human-machine interaction; however, it has historically been hindered by the scarcity of large-scale, publicly available labeled datasets. To address this limitation, we explore how unsupervised representation learning applied to unlabeled data can enhance SER. Our findings demonstrate that Contrastive Predictive Coding (CPC) can extract salient features from unlabeled corpora, thereby boosting emotion recognition accuracy. Experimental results indicate that this approach achieved state-of-the-art Concordance Correlation Coefficient (CCC) scores across all emotion primitives—activation, valence, and dominance—on the IEMOCAP dataset. Furthermore, on the MSP- Podcast dataset, our method yielded significant performance gains over existing baselines.

This paper details the evaluation of missing transverse momentum (${\vec p}_{\mathrm{T}}^\mathrm{miss}$) reconstruction algorithms within the CMS experiment, utilizing proton-proton collision data from the CERN LHC recorded in 2016 at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. The dataset comprises an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$. The study reports on the scale and resolution measurements of ${\vec p}_{\mathrm{T}}^\mathrm{miss}$, alongside an in-depth analysis of events exhibiting anomalous ${\vec p}_{\mathrm{T}}^\mathrm{miss}$. Furthermore, it assesses a reconstruction technique designed to reduce the impact of multiple proton-proton interactions by employing the "pileup per particle identification" approach. Finally, the performance of an algorithm used to determine the compatibility of the reconstructed ${\vec p}_{\mathrm{T}}^\mathrm{miss}$ with the hypothesis that it arises solely from resolution effects is presented.

This work examines a bi-objective optimization challenge defined by a positive real number $n$, seeking a non-negative vector $X = \{x_0,\cdots,x_{k-1}\} \in \mathbb{R}^{k}_{\ge 0}$ that satisfies $\sum_{i=0}^{k-1} x_i = n$. The goal is to simultaneously minimize the maximum of $k$ type-one functions, $\max_{i=0}^{k-1} f_i(x_i)$, and the sum of $k$ type-two functions, $\sum_{i=0}^{k-1} g_i(x_i)$. This problem is relevant for optimizing performance and energy efficiency on high-performance computing systems. Initially, we introduce an algorithm for the scenario where all type-one functions are continuous and strictly increasing, while all type-two functions are linearly increasing. Subsequently, we present an algorithm for a discrete variant where $n$ is a positive integer, all functions are discrete and defined by finite sets, with no specific constraints on their shapes. Both proposed algorithms operate with polynomial complexity.

Dirac Hamiltonians, characterized by linear energy dispersion crossings, have recently drawn significant attention. This linear behavior typically arises from approximations at band-touching points where higher-order terms are neglected. However, this paper demonstrates that regarding nonadiabatic transitions, specific quadratic terms cannot be disregarded even in the immediate vicinity of a touching point; these terms substantially influence transition probabilities, rendering the Hamiltonian irreducible to a purely linear form. Furthermore, we show that terms with exponents greater than two impact the transition probability only when moving away from the touching point. Finally, we examine the conditions under which oscillations may emerge in the transition probability profile.

Effective aero-optical beam control depends on rapid, low-latency forecasting methods to anticipate wavefront distortions caused by the Turbulent Boundary Layer (TBL) surrounding airborne optical systems, addressing diverse requirements from astronomy to microscopy for precise laser propagation. This study utilizes Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD), an equation-free, data-driven approach for detecting coherent flow structures and their spatiotemporal evolution, to project future wavefront phase aberrations for integration into adaptive optic (AO) control loops. Specifically, we apply the optimized DMD (opt-DMD) algorithm to a subset of the Airborne Aero-Optics Laboratory Transonic (AAOL-T) dataset, analyzing aberrated wavefront dynamics across 23 beam propagation directions through the method's inherent spatiotemporal decomposition. Crucially, we demonstrate that opt-DMD yields an optimally de-biased eigenvalue spectrum featuring imaginary eigenvalues, enabling robust long-term forecasting and accurate future-state predictions, whereas standard exact DMD fails to retain structural information due to modal decay rates.

This study examines an ideal Bose gas consisting of a finite number $N$ of particles. Exact formulas for the partition functions and occupation numbers are derived for the grand canonical, canonical, and microcanonical ensembles. Furthermore, asymptotic expressions for the partition functions and occupation numbers within the canonical and microcanonical ensembles are calculated for the limit $N\gg1$. The analysis demonstrates that the chemical potential $\mu$ of an ideal Bose gas can span the entire range $-\infty<\mu<\infty$, contradicting the commonly held belief that this potential must be negative.

A drop bouncing on a vertically oscillating surface can self-propel via Faraday waves while moving along a fluid interface. This phenomenon, known as a "walker," establishes a macroscopic wave-particle duality outside the quantum realm. Over the past decade, the dynamics of single walkers have sparked extensive research, yielding remarkable experimental findings. This study employs numerical simulations to examine the behavior of numerous walkers on an unbounded fluid interface under the influence of a confining potential. We demonstrate that despite erratic individual paths, the system exhibits a well-defined, ordered internal structure that remains stable across various parameter changes. By leveraging wave symmetry to explain this non-stationary self-organization, we reveal that oscillatory pair potentials generate a wavy collective state within this active matter system.

The paper examines the most straightforward method for bootstrapping within general relativity, which purports to reconstruct the infinite series of perturbative graviton interactions by recursively coupling metric perturbations to their energy-momentum tensor. We demonstrate that this method yields an erroneous expression for the three-graviton interaction term and further discuss additional challenges associated with the bootstrap approach.

The advent of polar codes represents a significant milestone in coding theory, primarily because of their capacity-achieving capabilities. This advantage relies on a quasilinear construction alongside encoding and successive cancellation list decoding methods derived from the Plotkin framework. These decoding procedures can be adapted with minor adjustments for Reed-Muller and eBCH codes, which also achieve capacity on erasure channels; however, the list size required for optimal performance increases too rapidly, rendering the decoding impractical even for moderate block lengths. The theoretical proof of capacity achievement for Reed-Muller and eBCH codes hinges on their symmetry groups, which can be integrated into Plotkin decomposition to create various permutation decoding algorithms. While these methods can surpass basic polar-like decoding, their computational complexity remains prohibitive. This paper demonstrates that while invariance under a large automorphism group is theoretically beneficial, it also necessitates an exponential growth in list size for good performance. Furthermore, we derive bounds associated with sacrificing certain symmetries. Although the theoretical analysis of list decoding algorithms remains unresolved, our findings offer valuable insights into the specific factors influencing decoding complexity.

Metric Temporal Logic (MTL) and Timed Propositional Temporal Logic (TPTL) serve as major real-time extensions of Linear Temporal Logic (LTL). Generally, determining satisfiability for these logics is undecidable when employing both future ($U$) and past ($S$) modalities. A classical finding establishes that satisfiability for MITL[U,S]—a non-punctual fragment of MTL[U,S]—is decidable, albeit with EXPSPACE-complete complexity. Since the concept of non-punctuality fails to restore decidability for TPTL[U,S], we introduce a broader notion termed \emph{non-adjacency} for TPTL[U,S], specifically analyzing its 1-variable fragment, 1-TPTL[U,S]. Although non-adjacent 1-TPTL[U,S] constitutes a seemingly minimal fragment, it exhibits strictly greater expressiveness than MITL. Our primary contribution demonstrates that the satisfiability problem for non-adjacent 1-TPTL[U,S] is decidable and possesses EXPSPACE-complete complexity.

Negative differential resistance (NDR) tunnel diodes represent a promising alternative for post-CMOS computing, particularly when integrated with transistors. We introduce a novel semiconductor-free NDR tunnel diode design featuring an exceptionally high peak-to-valley current ratio (PVCR). This device comprises two cold metal electrodes separated by a thin insulating barrier. The NDR phenomenon arises from the distinct electronic band structure of these cold metals, where the width of isolated metallic bands near the Fermi level and the energy gaps between higher and lower bands dictate the current-voltage ($I$-$V$) behavior and PVCR. By selecting specific cold metal materials, one can achieve either a conventional N-type or a ${\Lambda}$-type NDR effect. Two-dimensional (2D) materials provide an ideal platform for implementing this concept. Using the nonequilibrium Green function method alongside density functional theory, we calculated the $I$-$V$ characteristics of lateral (AlI$_2$/MgI$_2$/AlI$_2$) and vertical (NbS$_2$/h-BN/NbS$_2$) heterojunction tunnel diodes based on 2D cold metals. The lateral configuration demonstrated a ${\Lambda}$-type NDR effect with an ultra-high PVCR of $10^{16}$ at room temperature, whereas the vertical configuration showed a conventional N-type NDR effect with a lower PVCR of approximately $10^4$. This semiconductor-free approach offers a viable solution for creating NDR devices with tailored $I$-$V$ profiles and ultra-high PVCR values suitable for memory and logic applications.

Creating presentation slides that summarize scientific and technical papers is a highly efficient method for disseminating research, yet the manual process is labor-intensive. To address this, we introduce an automated approach for generating slides from scientific papers, trained on a dataset of 5,000 paper-slide pairs sourced from conference proceedings. Our methodology employs a sentence labeling module inspired by SummaRuNNer, a neural sequence model designed for extractive summarization. Unlike traditional methods that rank sentences based on global semantic similarity, our algorithm evaluates the importance and novelty of sentences by integrating semantic and lexical features within a local sentence window. Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms various baseline approaches, including SummaRuNNer, as measured by the ROUGE score.

We announce the identification of a probable outbursting Class I young stellar object located in the NGC 281-W star-forming region, approximately 2.8 kpc away. This source is detectable exclusively at infrared wavelengths, having been observed in both the Palomar Gattini InfraRed survey at 1.2 μm and the Near Earth Object Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer at 3.4 and 4.6 μm. Recent near-infrared imaging has uncovered a newly formed, extended nebula of scattered light. Furthermore, recent near-infrared spectroscopy aligns PGIR 20dci with FU Ori-type sources, evidenced by prominent molecular absorption features in CO, H$_2$O, and OH, diminished absorption in various atomic lines, and a warm wind or outflow suggested by a P Cygni profile in the HeI 10830 Å line. This object represents a rare instance of an FU Ori star exhibiting a well-documented, gradual long-term photometric increase preceding a sharper outburst, as well as the second known case of an FU Ori star displaying a two-step brightening pattern in the mid-infrared.

An expanding body of research focuses on determining optimal treatment rules, which assign interventions to individuals based on their characteristics to maximize desired outcomes. A related objective involves identifying those predicted to suffer from harmful indirect effects (the impact of treatment on an outcome via mediators), even when the overall treatment effect is beneficial. In certain scenarios, the probability of such adverse indirect effects may surpass the potential overall benefits, warranting caution against administering the treatment to specific individuals. Drawing upon existing mediation and optimal treatment rule literature, we propose a method to detect a subgroup experiencing harmful treatment effects through mediators. Our nonparametric approach accounts for post-treatment variables that could confound the mediator-outcome relationship and imposes no distributional restrictions on baseline covariates, mediating variables (jointly), or outcomes. We demonstrate this method by identifying a subgroup of boys in the Moving to Opportunity housing voucher experiment who are forecasted to face harmful indirect effects, despite the average total effect being favorable.

Research into astrophysical plasma lensing, particularly during extreme scattering events, has traditionally relied on the geometric optics limit, overlooking wave phenomena. Nevertheless, for coherent emitters like pulsars and fast radio bursts (FRBs), wave effects are significant. While asymptotic techniques, such as the Eikonal limit or stationary phase approximation, have been employed to capture first-order wave effects, they break down at Stokes lines. These lines are common across various lens models and represent parameter space regions where imaginary images start influencing the intensity modulation of lensed sources. By applying Picard-Lefschetz theory to calculate diffraction integrals, we contend that these imaginary images hold information equivalent to their geometric counterparts and could potentially be detected in observational data. Consequently, weak-lensing events exhibiting these imaginary images may prove just as valuable for determining lens parameters as strong-lensing events characterized by multiple geometric images.

Given that the Galactic globular clusters 47 Tuc and Omega Cen may be tidally stripped remnants of dwarf galaxies, they likely still harbor fractions of their original dark matter cores. This study utilized the ultra-wide band receiver on the Parkes telescope (Murriyang) to establish upper limits on the annihilation rate of exotic Light Dark Matter particles (X) through the XX/$e^+e^-$ channel, specifically by analyzing positronium (Ps) recombination rates. While this extends a method previously applied to the Galactic Centre, stacking spectral data across multiple line frequencies significantly enhanced our sensitivity. Consequently, we derived 3-sigma flux density upper limits for Ps recombination rates of 1.7 mJy (1.4x10$^{43}$ s$^{-1}$) and 0.8 mJy (1.1x10$^{43}$ s$^{-1}$) for 47 Tuc and Omega Cen, respectively. Considering the Parkes beam size at these cluster distances (ranging from 10 to 23 pc depending on frequency), we calculated upper limits for dark matter mass and root-mean-square density of <1.2-1.3x10$^5$ fn$^{-0.5}$ (mX/MeV c$^{-2}$) solar masses and <48-54 fn$^{-0.5}$ (mX/MeV c$^{-2}$) solar masses pc$^{-3}$, where fn=Rn/Rp represents the ratio of Ps recombination transitions to annihilations, estimated at 0.01. Radio limits for Omega Cen imply that, assuming a fiducial dark/luminous mass ratio of 0.05, any contribution from Light Dark Matter remains negligible unless the cross section exceeds 7.9x10$^{-28}$ (mX/MeV c$^{-2}$)$^2$ cm$^3$ s$^{-1}$. Furthermore, due to the clusters' compactness and proximity, archival 511-keV measurements yield tighter constraints than those allowed by CMB anisotropies, specifically <8.6x10$^{-31}$ (mX/MeV c$^{-2}$)$^2$ cm$^3$ s$^{-1}$. Ultimately, our recombination rate limits represent a substantial improvement over prior radio constraints for the Milky Way.

We present a proof of a soft variant of the $p$-converse to the Gross--Zagier and Kolyvagin theorem for non-CM elliptic curves exhibiting good ordinary reduction at primes $p > 3$, assuming the residual representation is irreducible. Notably, this approach imposes no constraints on the conductor. When integrated with existing results, it establishes that for every elliptic curve over the rationals, the Mordell-Weil rank equals one and the Tate-Shafarevich group is finite if and only if the analytic rank is one.

We present the DCH-2 dataset, comprising 4,390 Chinese customer-helpdesk dialogues alongside their English translations. This resource includes both dialogue-level and turn-level annotations derived independently from 19 or 20 annotators. Developed by our team as organizers of the NTCIR-14 Short Text Conversation and NTCIR-15 Dialogue Evaluation tasks, DCH-2 aims to assist researchers in defining effective helpdesk interactions, ultimately facilitating the creation of efficient, always-available customer support systems. Furthermore, DCH-2 serves multiple additional functions, such as acting as a corpus for retrieval-based dialogue systems or a parallel corpus for machine translation within the helpdesk domain.

This article introduces a class of special zonotopes generated by a matrix pair featuring finite-interval parameters. We examine the connection between the volume of these zonotopes and the controllability of specific aspects, particularly the volume of the controllable region, within dynamic systems. Additionally, we provide a corollary and establish an efficient recursive approach for calculating the volume of these special zonotopes. Furthermore, we devise two recursive and analytical methods for computing the volumes of finite- and infinite-time controllable regions when real eigenvalues are involved. Finally, we perform numerical experiments to validate the efficacy of these new volume-computation techniques for both zonotopes and regions.

Parametric amplifiers have been instrumental in advancing ultrafast, strong-field, and high-energy density laser science, serving as a critical component for expanding the frequency capabilities of emerging diode-pumped solid-state lasers. Nevertheless, their effectiveness has been constrained by intrinsically low quantum efficiency resulting from non-uniform light extraction. In this work, we introduce a novel parametric amplifier utilizing hybridized nonlinear optics. By combining parametric amplification with idler second harmonic generation, we achieve unique evolutionary dynamics characterized by saturating gain rather than the typical cyclic behavior, a phenomenon observed here for the first time. This innovation facilitates highly uniform light extraction, delivering unprecedented efficiency for a lossless amplifier that maintains Gaussian-like intensity profiles. Specifically, we achieved a 48-dB single-stage gain with 68% quantum efficiency and 44% pump-to-signal energy conversion, representing a several-fold improvement over conventional methods. By merging the laser-like high quantum efficiency of traditional amplifiers with the thermal-loading-free benefits of parametric systems, this straightforward approach offers broad implementation potential, significantly boosting the power available for scientific and industrial applications.

Publication rates are surging across numerous scientific disciplines, making it increasingly challenging to keep abreast of emerging research. Consequently, automatically summarizing recent findings and assisting scholars in synthesizing related work has become a compelling research goal. This paper examines citation text generation, a task where a model produces a citation based on a set of referenced papers and the surrounding citing context. Although previous studies have addressed citation text generation, the use of disparate datasets and varying task definitions has hindered systematic analysis. To overcome this, we introduce CiteBench, a unified benchmark that consolidates prior datasets to facilitate standardized evaluation of models across different domains and settings. Leveraging this benchmark, we evaluate several robust baselines, assess their transferability between datasets, and provide new insights into task definitions and evaluation metrics to steer future research. The CiteBench benchmark is now publicly accessible at https://github.com/UKPLab/citebench.

The LHCb experiment conducted a search for the $B^0_s \!\rightarrow D^{*\pm} D^\mp$ decay utilizing proton-proton collision data recorded at center-of-mass energies of $7$, $8$, and $13\,\text{TeV}$, amounting to an integrated luminosity of $9\,\text{fb}^{-1}$.
