Although theoretical optimality has been established for these agents, their behavioral characteristics have not yet been empirically studied. This work offers a concise, unified survey of these URL algorithms and presents experimental results that qualitatively demonstrate policy properties and comparative performance in partially observable gridworlds. Additionally, we provide an open-source reference implementation designed to encourage further exploration and experimentation with these concepts.

Extending Beurling's theorem regarding shift-invariant subspaces within the Hardy class $H^2$ of the unit disk to the realm of several complex variables remained an unresolved issue since at least 1964. This paper presents a generalization of Beurling's theorem to valuation Hilbert modules defined over valuation algebras. We utilize this abstract version to provide a comprehensive characterization of the closed invariant subspaces of $H^2$ on the polydisk. As demonstrated in a forthcoming publication, additional implications of our abstract theorem yield complete extensions of Beurling's result to a broader range of Hilbert spaces of analytic functions in several complex variables.

This study analyzes quiet-time oxygen measurements from the ACE spacecraft at 1 au, covering the energy range of 7.3 to 237.9 MeV nuc$^{-1}$, to compare anomalous cosmic rays (ACRs) and Galactic cosmic rays (GCRs) between 1997 and 2020. The results indicate that the shift from an ACR-dominated to a GCR-dominated spectrum occurs at energies between approximately 15 and 35 MeV nuc$^{-1}$. The transition energy ($E_t$) exhibits a strong anticorrelation with solar activity, marking the first investigation into how this transition depends on solar cycle variations. Below $E_t$, the power-law index of the ACR spectrum ($\gamma_1$) varies from -2.0 to -0.5, while the GCR spectrum's index ($\gamma_2$) shifts from 0.3 to 0.8 between $E_t$ and 237.9 MeV nuc$^{-1}$. Both indices show a positive correlation with solar activity. Furthermore, during the solar cycle 24/25 minimum, ACE recorded a peak GCR intensity roughly 8% higher than in 2009, establishing a new record since the beginning of the space age. In contrast, the peak ACR intensity remained comparable to those of the preceding two cycles, which shared the same solar magnetic polarity pattern, suggesting distinct modulation mechanisms for ACRs and GCRs.

Deploying wideband extremely large antenna arrays holds great promise for achieving terabits-per-second data rates in future communication networks. However, the combination of extremely wide bandwidth and large aperture causes a near-field beam-split effect that severely undermines transmission performance, a phenomenon that has not yet been explored in prior research. To tackle this challenge, we first uncover the nature of the near-field beam-split effect and evaluate the resulting array gain loss. Subsequently, we utilize a piecewise-far-field model featuring piecewise-linear phase characteristics to approximate the near-field channel. Leveraging this model, we propose a phase-delay focusing technique to mitigate the beam-split issue. Additionally, we introduce a novel metric called the "effective Rayleigh distance," which offers superior accuracy in distinguishing between near-field and far-field regions compared to the classical Rayleigh distance for practical applications. Finally, numerical simulations are presented to validate the efficacy of our proposed methods.

Scientific publications generally expand in proportion to funding levels and research interest within specific domains. Analyzing this body of work can uncover patterns that are not immediately obvious. The CORD-19 corpus constitutes an increasingly extensive collection of scientific documents related to COVID-19. We investigated the overlap between a set of potential therapeutics identified through a drug-repurposing study and the chronological data within the CORD-19 corpus to assess whether shifts associated with these candidates could be detected and quantified over time. We suggest that the methodologies employed here could serve as the foundation for a tool designed to pre-screen new therapeutic candidates at the early stages of research.

To facilitate a full simulation of the Thick GEM detector, this study provides a partial simulation of 6 keV X-ray interactions within a gas volume. The investigation utilized pure Argon, Xenon, and CO2, along with a 70%-30% mixture of each noble gas combined with CO2. At this energy level, the photoelectric effect is the dominant physical process; consequently, by accounting for atomic binding energies, the kinetic energy of the primary electrons was predicted. The resulting simulated spectrum of primary electron kinetic energy displays peaks associated with the ionization of inner atomic shells. Furthermore, the spectrum indicates a negligible Compton effect, which transfers only minimal energies (approximately eVs). It was concluded that the energy spectrum for the gas mixture represents a linear combination of the spectra of its individual components.

The `kedd` package extends the R statistical system with advanced smoothing methods. While numerous packages available on the Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN) offer tools beneficial for nonparametric statistics, `kedd` is designed to act as a centralized repository specifically for nonparametric functions and datasets. The package's capabilities are organized into four primary categories: calculating convolutions and derivatives of kernel functions, estimating kernel density functions and their derivatives, selecting bandwidths using various techniques, and visualizing both kernel estimators and bandwidth selection functions. Adhering to R's philosophy of working with model objects, the package returns structured objects containing relevant functions rather than simple values; these objects utilize S3 classes. This design allows users to freely manipulate results through dedicated extraction, summary, and plotting utilities. Furthermore, the developers strive to create a cohesive graphical user interface for the package's functions to enhance usability.

Advanced synthesis methods and experimental techniques now enable precise, reproducible measurements of nanoparticle magnetic properties, which can be accurately modeled theoretically. This study examines ferrite nanoparticles using Monte Carlo-based theoretical approaches. We present a macromagnetic model developed in three progressive stages of complexity. Initially, we analyze single nanoparticles using customized Hamiltonians. In the second stage, we account for internal structure by distinguishing between core and shell regions. Finally, we investigate assemblies of these core/shell nanoparticles. All relevant internal magnetic couplings, including inter- and intra-atomic exchange interactions and magnetocrystalline anisotropies, have been estimated. Hysteresis loops for all three scenarios were calculated and compared against recent experimental data. Specifically, for nanoparticle assemblies, the simulated hysteresis loops, zero-field cooling, and field cooling curves demonstrate excellent agreement with experimental results. This model serves as a vital tool for elucidating the internal structure and complex spin interactions within core-shell ferrite nanoparticles.

A classical method for addressing color reproduction challenges, including color adaptation and space transformation, relies on low-parameter spectral models. This approach's primary advantage lies in its flexibility to define specific model properties, such as extensive color triangle coverage or accurate representation of spectral addition and multiplication based solely on tristimulus values. However, a key drawback is that certain attributes of these models are currently supported only by empirical evidence. This study focuses on the theoretical validation of various spectral model properties. Specifically, we demonstrate that the banded model is the unique model capable of simultaneously satisfying closure under both addition and multiplication. Furthermore, we establish that the Gaussian model represents the limiting case of the von Mises model and prove that the von Mises protomer set unambiguously encompasses the color triangle for both convex and non-convex spectral loci.

This paper investigates an active target defense differential game involving an Attacker missile pursuing a Target aircraft. The aircraft is protected by a Defender missile, deployed by a wingman, which aims to intercept the Attacker before it reaches the Target. Consequently, the Target and Defender form a cooperative team striving to maximize the distance between the Target and the point of interception, while the Attacker seeks to minimize this distance. The study focuses on identifying the set of initial coordinates that guarantee the Target's survival, provided both the Target and Defender adhere to their optimal strategies. These optimal strategies are also detailed in this work.

This paper introduces a novel application of the minDSS tangential cover algorithm for the geometric reconstruction of noisy digital contours. Leveraging maximal primitives introduced in our prior research, we compute multi-scale, irregular isothetic representations of contours, converting them into one-dimensional intervals. These intervals are subsequently decomposed into maximal line segments or circular arcs. By adapting the minDSS algorithm to handle this sparse, irregular data supporting maximal primitives, we successfully reconstruct noisy inputs into cyclic contours composed of lines or arcs using the minimal number of primitives. We detail this complete pipeline and provide an experimental evaluation using both synthetic and real image data. Furthermore, we demonstrate the approach's robustness through comparisons with state-of-the-art references and a multi-scale noise evaluation process.

This study introduces a novel approach for locating critical points of differentiable functionals defined on Banach spaces that fall within a specific class, denoted as ($\mathcal{J}$). The core strategy involves constructing a real-valued function, $\zeta$, referred to as the {\it energy function}, which is intrinsically linked to a given functional $J$ in the class ($\mathcal{J}$). The method relies on the principle that if $\zeta$ possesses real critical points, then the original functional $J$ must also have critical points. Leveraging this technique, we resolve several variational elliptic problems where the corresponding energy functional belongs to ($\mathcal{J}$). Furthermore, we present a variant of the mountain pass theorem tailored for functionals in this class, enabling the derivation of mountain pass solutions without relying on the Ambrosetti-Rabinowitz condition.

The Resource Allocation (RA) approach enhances MOEA/D performance by sustaining a large population while updating only a few solutions per generation. However, existing RA research has predominantly focused on various allocation metrics, leaving the primary drivers of MOEA/D performance improvements under RA uncertain. This study examines the Partial Update Strategy within MOEA/D across an extensive range of multi-objective problems (MOPs) to clarify the relationships between this strategy and MOEA/D variants utilizing small versus large populations. We conduct a detailed analysis of population dynamics, evaluating final approximation Pareto sets, anytime hypervolume performance, attained regions, and the count of unique non-dominated solutions. Our findings demonstrate that MOEA/D with the Partial Update Strategy advances the search as rapidly as the small-population variant while exploring the search space as effectively as the big-population variant. Consequently, the Partial Update Strategy alleviates common issues associated with population size selection, offering superior convergence speed across most MOPs, as evidenced by hypervolume metrics, the number of unique non-dominated solutions, anytime performance, and the Empirical Attainment Function.

Accurate annotations for multimedia data are essential for advancing numerous Information Retrieval applications, particularly by facilitating the creation of automated systems capable of labeling vast and varied multimedia archives. In domains such as everyday sounds and online repositories, the material to be described is highly heterogeneous, encompassing a wide array of concepts typically arranged within extensive hierarchical taxonomies. Consequently, manually annotating such content proves to be a laborious undertaking. This paper details our user-centered approach to developing two tools designed for the manual annotation of diverse audio types. We performed an initial assessment of functional prototypes with actual users within a real-world setting, aiming to gather user insights and stimulate innovative concepts. This process involved a qualitative analysis comprising usability surveys and semi-structured interviews, which uncovered significant considerations for designing manual audio annotation tools that utilize labels from large hierarchical taxonomies.

In recent years, engineers and researchers have increasingly focused on the DUS transformation of lifetime distributions. This study presents a novel distribution class derived from exponentiating the DUS transformation, specifically utilizing the Exponential distribution as its baseline. The paper investigates the statistical properties of this new model and estimates its parameters via maximum likelihood. Furthermore, the model's suitability is validated through analysis of real-world data.

In 1948, Schwinger formulated a local, Lorentz-covariant version of relativistic quantum electrodynamics in space-time that inherently conflicts with delocalized interpretations of quantum mechanics. A compatible interpretation is proposed here, yielding identical empirical predictions to standard delocalized quantum theory in configuration space. This approach constitutes an explicit, unambiguous, and Lorentz-covariant "local hidden variable theory" within space-time, definitively demonstrating the viability of such frameworks. The apparent contradiction with Bell's theorem is resolved by identifying this as a local many-worlds theory. Every physical system is defined by a wave-field comprising a collection of indexed, piece-wise single-particle wavefunctions across space-time, each possessing its own coefficient, alongside a memory storing the distinct local Hilbert-space quantum state at every event. For fundamental systems, each single-particle wavefunction describes the motion of a segment of a conserved space-time fluid that decomposes into numerous classical point particles; each particle follows a world-line and maintains a local memory. Local interactions between two systems manifest as local boundary conditions between differently indexed segments of their respective wave-fields, with new indexes representing each orthogonal interaction outcome. The exposition introduces the general machinery, including local mechanisms for entanglement and interference, and addresses the phenomena of collapse, Born rule probability, and environmental decoherence, supplemented by various illustrative examples.

Local explanations for learning-to-rank (LTR) models aim to identify the key features driving a model's ranking prediction for individual data points. However, assessing the reliability of these explanations is difficult because ground truth feature importance scores are typically unavailable for most modern LTR architectures. This study introduces a systematic evaluation framework specifically for LTR explanations. Rather than relying on black-box models like neural networks, we focus on tree-based LTR models, allowing us to derive ground truth importance scores directly from decision paths. These scores are then compared against those produced by various explanation methods. We evaluate two recent explanation techniques applied to decision trees and gradient boosting models using the MQ2008 dataset. Our results demonstrate that explanation accuracy can vary significantly, depending on both the underlying model and the specific data point being analyzed.

The sizes of the proximity zones surrounding high-redshift quasars allow researchers to constrain the duration of quasar activity, a critical factor for comprehending the growth of the supermassive black holes (SMBHs) driving their emission. This study presents precise estimates for the ultraviolet (UV) luminous lifetimes of ten quasars located at $5.8< z< 6.5$. These targets were initially selected for their short lifetimes based on preliminary assessments of their proximity zone dimensions and subsequently observed with high-quality sub-mm, optical, and infrared data to refine these measurements and confirm their durations. By comparing the observed proximity zone sizes against mock quasar spectra derived from radiative transfer simulations across various lifetimes, we infer extremely brief lifetimes of $t_{\rm Q}<10^4$ years for four objects, while the others align with longer durations of $t_{\rm Q}\gtrsim 10^5$ years. These young quasars, characterized by small proximity zones, constitute less than 10% of the total quasar population. When compared with other research on quasar activity timescales, our findings support an average lifetime of $t_{\rm Q}\sim10^6$ years for the broader population, implying that newly activated quasars occur roughly 1–10% of the time. These recently ignited quasars offer a distinct chance to investigate SMBH triggering and feedback mechanisms, as their UV luminous phase began recently, leaving observable traces of these processes.

While semantic paradoxes typically arise from self-reference or referential circularity, certain infinitary variants, such as Yablo's paradox, exist without this circular feature. It is currently unresolved which specific reference relations among groups of sentences create the structural conditions required for paradox, often described as "dangerous" directed graphs. Drawing on the work of Rabern and colleagues (2013), we restate this issue using fixed points of particular functions, reducing the inquiry to a purely mathematical framework.

Neuromorphic sensors mimic the sparse, event-driven communication patterns found in biological sensory systems and brains. Current sensors are capable of generating millions of asynchronous events per second, a volume that strains conventional computing systems. To mitigate processing bottlenecks, it is essential to enhance concurrent and parallel event handling.

We introduce AEStream, a library designed to efficiently stream asynchronous events from inputs to outputs on standard computers. By utilizing cooperative multitasking primitives called coroutines, AEStream processes individual events concurrently, significantly streamlining integration with event-based peripherals like neuromorphic hardware and event-driven cameras. Benchmarking AEStream against traditional threading mechanisms reveals that coroutines offer at least double the throughput in concurrent environments. Furthermore, applying AEStream to a real-time edge detection task on a GPU demonstrates a 1.3-fold increase in processing speed while reducing memory operations by a factor of five.

We examine a simplified scenario involving a W' boson introduced into the Standard Model, featuring minimal interactions with quarks but broad couplings to leptons and electroweak bosons. We investigate the consequences of this framework for LHC investigations. As a result, we suggest an LHC search utilizing the vector boson fusion channel, capable of detecting such a new particle given the current proton-proton collision energies and accessible luminosity.

The Sun stands out as one of the most luminous and enigmatic gamma-ray sources in the sky, yet current models fail to fully account for its emission's luminosity, spectral characteristics, temporal variability, and spatial structure. This study presents the first comprehensive analysis of solar-disk gamma rays spanning an entire 11-year solar cycle, employing an advanced technique to isolate solar signals from astrophysical backgrounds. Our findings include: (i) a precisely measured spectrum between 100 MeV and 100 GeV, with accuracy reaching several percent in the 1–10 GeV band; (ii) evidence of an anti-correlation between solar activity levels and gamma-ray output; (iii) stringent limits on variability across timescales from hours to years; and (iv) new detections of equatorial and polar high-energy gamma-ray morphologies. Notably, we observe no significant energy dependence in the time variability of this emission, suggesting that magnetic fields near the solar surface, rather than heliospheric modulation, are the primary drivers of the flux and morphology of solar-disk gamma rays.

Adversarial training stands as a potent strategy for enhancing the robustness of pre-trained language models (PLMs), yet it often incurs higher costs than conventional fine-tuning due to the requirement of generating adversarial examples through gradient descent. By examining the optimization dynamics of adversarial training, we observed that robust connectivity patterns arise during the initial training phase (approximately $0.15\sim0.3$ epochs), well before parameters reach convergence. Leveraging this insight, we identified "robust early-bird tickets"—specific subnetworks—to create a more efficient adversarial training framework. This approach involves (1) identifying these robust tickets with structured sparsity at the outset and (2) fine-tuning them during the remaining training duration. To maximize the speed of ticket extraction, we introduced a ticket convergence metric that automatically halts the search process. Experimental results demonstrate that this efficient adversarial training method achieves training speedups of up to $7\times$ to $13\times$, while sustaining robustness levels that are comparable to or superior to the most advanced state-of-the-art adversarial training techniques.

We suggest that finite cutoff regions in holographic spacetimes correspond to quantum circuits connecting boundary states across varying times and Wilsonian cutoffs, where the circuit complexity is quantified by the gravitational action. The most efficient circuit minimizes this action, representing a broad extension of the "complexity equals volume" conjecture to unoptimized scenarios and an adaptation of path integral optimization to finite cutoffs. Leveraging tools from holographic $T\bar T$, we identify that surfaces of constant scalar curvature are pivotal in optimizing these quantum circuits. Furthermore, we uncover a significant link between our proposal and kinematic space, while exploring potential circuit representations and gate-counting interpretations of the gravitational action.

It is established that every nonzero Jordan ideal in a $2$-torsion free semiprime ring contains a nonzero ideal. This paper demonstrates that any square closed Lie ideal within a $2$-torsion free prime ring likewise contains a nonzero ideal. This result suggests that investigating identities over one-sided ideals represents the most effective approach for studying identities. Building on this insight, we extend certain findings by Dhara, Rehman, and Raza regarding Lie ideals and the action of generalized derivations in rings to the domain of nonzero left ideals.

Neural networks are increasingly central to healthcare, with some models achieving or exceeding expert-level accuracy. Nevertheless, these achievements are overshadowed by significant concerns regarding model opacity and bias toward specific patient groups or medical conditions. While explainable AI is viewed as the solution to these issues, this study reveals that generated explanations are highly unstable when models undergo training changes orthogonal to the classification task or structural modifications. This volatility casts doubt on the reliability of deep learning in medical settings, specifically questioning whether models learn genuine causal relationships or merely exploit spurious correlations that explanations happen to highlight. We demonstrate that explainability outputs from deep neural networks can fluctuate drastically with minor hyper-parameter adjustments, such as random seed variations or training set shuffling. To address this, we propose a metric for explanation consistency, applied to the MIMIC-CXR dataset, which shows that identical models trained differently yield explanations with only about 33% average consistency. In contrast, kernel methods prove robust against such orthogonal changes, maintaining a consistency rate of 94%. Consequently, we conclude that current approaches to model explanation are inadequate for mitigating the risks associated with deploying these systems in real-world healthcare applications.

A natural one-to-one correspondence exists between permutations achievable with a stack (those avoiding the pattern 312) and those achievable with a queue (those avoiding 321), a relationship equivalent to a bijection identified by Simion and Schmidt in 1985. We contend that this mapping could have been discovered as early as 1968 by readers of the first volume of Knuth's *The Art of Computer Programming*, had he not assigned difficulty ratings to his exercises.

As demonstrated by Sina Degenfeld-Schonburg in "On the Hausdorff-Young theorem for commutative hypergroups," the Fourier transform for a commutative hypergroup $K$ can be extended to $L^p(K)$ within the range $1\leq p \leq 2$, ensuring the validity of the Hausdorff-Young inequality. This article investigates the structural properties of non-zero functions in $L^p(K)$ that achieve equality in this inequality for $1<p<2$, and additionally offers a characterization of the fundamental uncertainty principle applicable to commutative hypergroups possessing a non-trivial centre.

Neural information retrieval (IR) has significantly enhanced search and various knowledge-intensive language tasks. Although numerous neural IR approaches encode queries and documents as single vectors, late interaction models generate multi-vector representations at the token level, breaking down relevance modeling into scalable computations. While this decomposition boosts effectiveness, it increases the model's memory usage by roughly tenfold. This work presents ColBERTv2, a retriever that combines a robust residual compression mechanism with a denoised supervision strategy to simultaneously enhance both the quality and efficiency of late interaction models. Extensive evaluations across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that ColBERTv2 achieves state-of-the-art performance both within and beyond its training domain, while reducing the memory footprint of late interaction models by 6 to 10 times.

Within the standard seesaw framework, flavor mixing and CP violation in the weak charged-current interactions of light and heavy Majorana neutrinos are linked and characterized by the $3	imes 3$ matrices $U$ and $R$, respectively. We demonstrate that the observed condition $ ig|U^{}_{\mu i} ig| =  ig|U^{}_{	au i} ig|$ (for $i = 1, 2, 3$), strongly supported by current neutrino oscillation data, inherently predicts the relation $ ig|R^{}_{\mu i} ig| =  ig|R^{}_{	au i} ig|$ (for $i = 1, 2, 3$). We establish that these equalities, alongside experimental evidence for leptonic CP violation, stem from a minimal flavor symmetry: the total neutrino mass term remains invariant when left-handed neutrino fields transform as $
u^{}_{e m L} 	o (
u^{}_{e m L})^c$, $
u^{}_{\mu m L} 	o (
u^{}_{	au m L})^c$, and $
u^{}_{	au m L} 	o (
u^{}_{\mu m L})^c$, while right-handed neutrino fields experience an arbitrary unitary CP transformation. This generalized $\mu$-$	au$ reflection symmetry offers a means to constrain the flavor structures of both active and sterile neutrinos within the seesaw mechanism.

Learning-based testing (LBT) represents a novel approach to automating iterative black-box requirements verification for software systems by integrating model inference with model checking. To ensure scalability when testing large-scale systems, various optimizations for model inference are required. This paper introduces the IKL algorithm, an active incremental learning method designed for deterministic Kripke structures, and provides a formal proof of its correctness. Furthermore, we examine the scalability-enhancing optimizations embedded within IKL and assess a black-box heuristic for test termination that relies on the convergence of the IKL learning process.

Determining the ideal timing for pulmonary valve replacement in Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) patients currently relies on ventricular volume and function as per established guidelines. These metrics are most accurately quantified through the segmentation of 3D cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) images. While U-Net architectures have demonstrated remarkable performance in recent grand challenges, clinical environments present greater variability due to diverse patient pathologies and scanner-specific image characteristics. Furthermore, training data for complex, rare conditions like TOF remains limited. This study addresses two objectives: 1) evaluating the performance gap when training on a public dataset (ACDC) and testing it on TOF data, and vice versa, and 2) determining if consistent results can be achieved on a more heterogeneous database. We trained multiple deep learning models using four-fold cross-validation and evaluated them on unseen CMR images from the alternative dataset. Our findings indicate that while current models yield excellent segmentation accuracy (left ventricle Dice of $0.951\pm{0.003}$/$0.941\pm{0.007}$ for train/validation within a single collection), they suffer from significant overfitting when applied to different pathologies, evidenced by a sharp decline in Dice scores to $0.072\pm{0.001}$ for the left and $0.165\pm{0.001}$ for the right ventricle.

The development of spectral theory on the $S$-spectrum was initially driven by the objective of establishing a rigorous mathematical framework for quaternionic quantum mechanics, as originally formulated by Birkhoff and von Neumann. Subsequently, the theory demonstrated significant utility in diverse areas, including fractional diffusion problems, and facilitated the definition of multiple functional calculi for $n$-tuples of noncommuting operators. This paper demonstrates that the spectral theory on the $S$-spectrum is notably more comprehensive, encompassing the complex, quaternionic, and Clifford settings as specific instances. Specifically, we establish that the $S$-spectrum is well-defined for elements within an algebra possessing a complex structure and for operators in general Banach modules. Furthermore, we illustrate that the abstract formulation of the $S$-functional calculus extends beyond the realms of quaternionic and Clifford analysis, exhibiting a particular {\em universality property}. This universality renders the spectral theory on the $S$-spectrum applicable to various domains of operator theory, enabling the definition of functions for noncommuting matrix and operator variables as special cases.

Self-testing serves as a method for characterizing quantum resources with the least amount of trust, previously functioning as a device-independent certification tool for specific quantum measurements, channels, and pure entangled states. This work extends the concept of self-testing to encompass more general entanglement structures. Specifically, we present the inaugural self-tests for entangled subspaces, namely the five-qubit code and the toric code. We demonstrate that any quantum state that maximally violates a specifically selected Bell inequality necessarily resides within the corresponding code subspace, a result that notably applies to mixed states as well.

We demonstrate that the ultradifferentiable-like function classes developed by S. Pilipović, N. Teofanov, and F. Tomić are particular instances within the broader framework of ultradifferentiable spaces characterized by weight matrices, as formulated by A. Rainer and the third author. Furthermore, we examine newly defined classes that extend beyond geometric growth factors, utilizing a combination of a weight sequence and an exponent sequence. We establish that these novel classes can be represented via weight matrices and successfully transfer established results from matrix-type theories to this non-standard ultradifferentiable context.

Achieving a band gap and static valley control in graphene-derived 2D materials has been a longstanding objective. Driven by recent advances in synthesizing Si-N passivated 2D materials, we introduce two novel graphene-based systems, C2SiN and CSiN, through first-principles calculations. The monolayer C2SiN exhibits metallic behavior and supports superconductivity at low temperatures, whereas the monolayer CSiN demonstrates superior stability and mechanical robustness as a semiconductor featuring a ternary valley structure for electron carriers. Unlike current valleytronic platforms, these valleys are manipulatable via applied uniaxial strain. This valley polarization results in significant variations in anisotropic conductivity, observable through straightforward electrical measurements. Furthermore, strong interaction effects generate substantial exciton binding energies and boost optical absorption in the ultraviolet spectrum. Our findings establish a novel pathway to simultaneously achieve superconductivity, a ternary valley structure, and enhanced optical absorption in 2D materials.

Emerging neutron scattering applications are intensity-constrained techniques that require minimizing neutron losses between the source and detectors. Concurrently, the nuclear sector seeks more precise data and methodologies for designing and optimizing advanced fission reactors, particularly regarding fuel and moderator materials. To address these needs, existing computational tools must be enhanced by developing superior models that accurately depict neutron interactions within target systems. The Neutron Physics Department at Centro Atomico Bariloche (CNEA, Argentina) has progressively created new models for slow neutron interactions with materials to generate scattering kernels and cross-section data in the thermal and cold neutron energy ranges. Beyond research on neutron moderators, the department has recently initiated investigations into materials capable of serving as efficient neutron reflectors within these energy bands. This study presents findings from simultaneous transmission and scattering experiments on diamond nanopowder and magnesium hydride conducted at the VESUVIO spectrometer (ISIS, UK), comparing the results against newly developed cross-section libraries.

This paper investigates the asymptotic behavior of phase-field functionals in the Am brosio and Tortorelli class, which permit small-scale oscillations within both the bulk and the diffuse surface components. These functionals represent a static gradient damage model applicable to heterogeneous materials. By utilizing Gamma-convergence, the effective behavior of the model is completely determined based on the relative rates at which the approximation and oscillation parameters vanish.

This note establishes a Trudinger-Moser inequality for conical metrics defined on the unit ball. Specifically, let $\mathbb{B}$ denote the unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^N$ where $N \geq 2$, and let $p > 1$. Consider the conical metric $g = |x|^{\frac{2p}{N}\beta}(dx_1^2 + \cdots + dx_N^2)$ on $\mathbb{B}$. We define $\lambda_p(\mathbb{B})$ as the infimum of $\int_\mathbb{B}|\nabla u|^Ndx$ over functions $u \in W_0^{1,N}(\mathbb{B})$ satisfying $\int_\mathbb{B}|u|^pdx = 1$. We demonstrate that for any $\beta \geq 0$ and $\alpha < (1+\frac{p}{N}\beta)^{N-1+\frac{N}{p}}\lambda_p(\mathbb{B})$, there exists a constant $C$ such that for all radially symmetric $u \in W_0^{1,N}(\mathbb{B})$ fulfilling the condition $\int_\mathbb{B}|\nabla u|^Ndx - \alpha(\int_\mathbb{B}|u|^p|x|^{p\beta}dx)^{N/p} \leq 1$, the following inequality holds:
$$ \int_\mathbb{B}e^{\alpha_N(1+\frac{p}{N}\beta)|u|^{\frac{N}{N-1}}}|x|^{p\beta}dx \leq C, $$
where $|x|^{p\beta}dx = dv_g$, $\alpha_N = N\omega_{N-1}^{1/(N-1)}$, and $\omega_{N-1}$ represents the surface area of the unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^N$. Furthermore, extremal functions for this inequality are shown to exist. Previous work by Adimurthi and Sandeep \cite{A-S} addressed the case where $p=N$, $-1<\beta<0$, and $\alpha=0$, while de Figueiredo, do \'O, and dos Santos \cite{F-do-dos} investigated the scenario with $p=N=2$, $\beta \geq 0$, and $\alpha=0$.

While the momentum distribution $n(k)$ in classical plasmas and ideal Fermi gases exhibits exponential decay at large $k$, the simultaneous influence of quantum and correlation effects predicts an algebraic decay of $n_\infty(k) \sim k^{-8}$. This behavior is significant for threshold processes and cross-sections in dense plasmas that rely on energetic particle counts. We provide extensive \textit{ab initio} findings regarding the momentum distribution of the nonideal uniform electron gas under warm dense matter conditions. Derived from first-principles fermionic path integral Monte Carlo (CPIMC) simulations, our data unequivocally validate the $k^{-8}$ asymptotic limit. This decay is intrinsically tied to short-range correlations, examined through the on-top pair distribution function (on-top PDF), which describes pairs of electrons with opposite spins. Furthermore, we detail the density and temperature dependencies of the on-top PDF and the momentum distribution across the full range of momenta.

This paper introduces a new model termed the Error Loss Network (ELN), designed to construct error loss functions for supervised learning tasks. Structurally resembling a radial basis function (RBF) neural network, the ELN takes error samples as input and generates corresponding loss values as output, thereby utilizing a nonlinear input-output mapper to define an error loss function. This proposed ELN serves as a unified framework for a broad category of error loss functions, encompassing various information theoretic learning (ITL) losses as specific instances. Key components of the ELN, including the activation function, weight parameters, and network architecture, can either be set in advance or learned directly from error samples. Building on this foundation, a novel machine learning paradigm is presented that splits the learning process into two phases: first, training an ELN to derive a loss function, and second, employing this learned loss function to drive the subsequent learning procedure. Experimental outcomes are provided to validate the superior performance of this approach.

Recommender systems have long served as the foundation for online retail. While they historically relied on rules, relevance metrics, ranking methods, and supervised learning, it is now possible to employ reinforcement learning to create significant recommendations. This study explores and establishes a reproducible testbed to assess various state-of-the-art algorithms within a realistic setting, encompassing a proposal, literature review, methodology, results, and commentary.

We compare exclusive $J/\psi$ photoproduction cross sections, computed at next-to-leading order (NLO) within the collinear factorization framework, against HERA and LHCb experimental data. By applying the optimum scale formalism and subtracting the low $k_t < Q_0$ contribution from the NLO coefficient function to prevent double counting, we demonstrate that current global parton distribution functions (PDFs) align with the data within their stated uncertainties. Nevertheless, uncertainties in these global PDFs remain substantial at low $x$. Conversely, the precision of the LHCb data is quite high, offering the opportunity to directly constrain the gluon PDF across the extensive $x$ range of $10^{-6} < x < 10^{-2}$ at a fixed low scale.

This research examines RNA folding and analyzes its topology by integrating knot theory with embedded rigid vertex graphs. While knot theory aids in modeling biomolecules, traditional knots focus primarily on entanglement, overlooking intrachain interactions. To address this limitation, we employ stuck knots and links, which allow for the simultaneous consideration of both entanglement and intrachain dynamics. We begin by establishing a generating set for oriented stuck Reidemeister moves applicable to oriented stuck links. Subsequently, we introduce an algebraic framework to axiomatize these moves. Leveraging this structure, we define a coloring counting invariant for stuck links and present explicit calculations. Finally, we compute this invariant for arc diagrams representing RNA foldings by utilizing stuck link diagrams.

In a two-stage research framework, the initial phase employs a statistical model to estimate unobserved exposures, which are subsequently used as covariates in epidemiological models during the second phase. Measurement errors from the imputation process in the first stage act as biases in the second, distorting exposure effect estimates. This study seeks to enhance the accuracy of these estimates by facilitating information exchange between the two stages. Central to our proposed estimator is the insight that certain second-stage observations are more critical for imputation than others. Drawing from optimal experimental design theory, we identify these high-priority individuals and refine their imputation using machine learning techniques based on domain adaptation. Simulation results demonstrate that our method yields more accurate exposure effect estimates than current best practices. An empirical application regarding the impact of particulate matter (PM) on hyperglycemia risk produced smaller effect estimates with narrower confidence intervals. Ultimately, this principled approach to information sharing between environmental scientists and epidemiologists improves health effect estimation and is applicable to any two-stage study.

We introduce a vision-grounded speech perception model that maps spoken language and images into a shared semantic space. By employing a multi-layer recurrent highway network to capture the temporal dynamics of speech, we demonstrate the model's ability to extract both form-based and meaning-based linguistic information from the input. Our comprehensive analysis of the trained model's internal representations reveals that semantic encoding becomes progressively richer across higher layers, whereas the encoding of form-related aspects initially rises before stabilizing or declining.

We outline a strategy for examining the relationship between potential future collider data and the detection of gravitational waves generated by a strong first-order electroweak phase transition within Beyond the Standard Model frameworks. This approach utilizes a dimensionally reduced three-dimensional effective field theory alongside findings from both perturbative calculations and non-perturbative lattice simulations. We apply these advanced techniques to the real scalar triplet extension of the Standard Model, which allows for a two-step thermal history of electroweak symmetry breaking. Our results indicate that (1) a first-order transition occurring during the second phase could produce a signal detectable by LISA-generation observatories, and (2) the resulting gravitational wave signal exhibits significant sensitivity to the portal coupling linking the new scalar to the Higgs boson. We demonstrate how combining direct and indirect measurements of the new scalar's properties with the presence or absence of a gravitational wave detection could validate the model and constrain its parameter values.

The atomic hydrogen spectrum has long served as a fundamental Rosetta stone for deciphering quantum mechanics across diverse physical, chemical, and biological domains. This work demonstrates that beyond its status as a basic quantum model, the hydrogen atom acts as a primary constituent of quantum information. By leveraging its electron and nuclear spin degrees of freedom, the hydrogen atom offers a physically grounded framework and an appropriate Hilbert space for bipartite entanglement. Notably, the two-qubit concurrence and quantum coherence within this system can be formulated using fundamental physical constants, including the Planck and Boltzmann constants, electron and proton masses, the fine-structure constant, the Bohr radius, and the Bohr magneton. We find that the intrinsic entanglement stored in the hyperfine-structure (HFS) states at low temperatures diminishes rapidly as temperature rises, disappearing entirely above a critical threshold of approximately 5.35 $\mu$eV. However, an external magnetic field can counteract this thermal degradation. A central result of this study is the demonstration that such a magnetic field can generate and maintain HFS entanglement despite thermal effects, even at temperatures exceeding the critical threshold. This capability paves the way for magnetic-field-assisted entanglement engineering in low-temperature gases and solids.

Recent progress in deep learning has shown promise for accurate chest X-ray analysis and expanding access to radiological expertise; however, poor generalization caused by data distribution shifts in clinical environments remains a major obstacle to deployment. This study evaluated the diagnostic performance of eight distinct chest X-ray models, developed by various groups and submitted to the CheXpert challenge, when applied without fine-tuning to (1) smartphone-captured X-ray images and (2) external datasets. Results indicated that while all eight models suffered a statistically significant performance drop on smartphone photos, only three performed significantly worse than radiologists on average. Conversely, on the external dataset, none of the models performed significantly worse than radiologists, and five outperformed them significantly. These findings suggest that under clinically relevant distribution shifts, some models achieve radiologist-level performance while others do not. Future research should focus on training procedures and dataset collection strategies to improve generalization amidst data distribution shifts.

Single particle imaging (SPI) at X-ray free electron lasers (XFELs) enables the determination of three-dimensional structures for nanoscale entities, such as biomolecules, by analyzing numerous diffraction patterns from identical objects oriented randomly. During an SPI experiment, millions of low signal-to-noise patterns with unknown orientations are acquired; these are subsequently processed and merged via reconstruction algorithms to yield the particle's complete 3D structure. The achievable resolution is constrained by background noise, the signal-to-noise ratio of the diffraction data, and the total dataset size. We previously proposed a reference-enhanced holographic SPI approach [Optica 7,593-601(2020)] capable of generating high signal-to-noise, background-tolerant patterns, alongside a reconstruction method that recovers missing parameters beyond orientation to directly obtain the sample's full Fourier model. In this work, we present MaxLP, a phase retrieval algorithm utilizing maximum likelihood estimation with pattern search. MaxLP offers superior scalability for fine sampling of latent parameters and delivers significantly improved performance in low-signal regimes. Additionally, we demonstrate that structural variations within the target particle are averaged in real space, markedly enhancing robustness against conformational heterogeneity compared to conventional SPI. Leveraging these computational advances, we posit that reference-enhanced SPI can achieve sub-nanometer resolution in biomolecule imaging.

It is established that any contact 3-manifold can be constructed via rationally contact Dehn surgery on a Legendrian link $L$ within the standard tight contact 3-sphere. This paper introduces and analyzes several variations of contact surgery numbers, defined as the minimum number of components required in a surgery link $L$ to represent a specific contact 3-manifold.

In the first section, we establish relationships between contact surgery numbers and other invariants through various inequalities. Specifically, we demonstrate that the contact surgery number of a contact manifold is bounded above by the topological surgery number of its underlying manifold plus three.

In the second section, we calculate the contact surgery numbers for all contact structures on the 3-sphere. Additionally, we provide a complete classification of contact structures with a contact surgery number of one on $S^1\times S^2$, the Poincaré homology sphere, and the Brieskorn sphere $\Sigma(2,3,7)$. Our findings reveal that there are infinitely many non-isotopic contact structures on each of these manifolds that cannot be achieved by a single rational contact surgery from the standard tight contact 3-sphere. We also derive results concerning the 3-torus and lens spaces.

As a component of the proofs for these results, we extend computations regarding the homotopical invariants of contact structures to include contact surgeries with more general surgery coefficients, a development that may hold independent interest.

Manipulating 3D objects within interactive settings remains a significant challenge in Reinforcement Learning (RL), particularly when developing policies that generalize across diverse semantic categories, varying geometric shapes, and multifaceted functionalities. Recently, visual affordance has emerged as a promising approach by supplying object-centric priors and actionable semantic information, enabling policies to learn complex actions, such as opening a door by applying force to a handle. However, traditional affordance learning often depends on manually defined action primitives, which restricts its applicability to a limited set of tasks. In this study, we leverage visual affordance by utilizing contact data generated during RL training to predict relevant contact maps. This approach facilitates an end-to-end affordance learning framework capable of generalizing across various manipulation tasks. Notably, the framework demonstrates robust performance in both multi-stage and multi-agent scenarios. We evaluated the method on eight distinct manipulation tasks, and results indicate that it significantly outperforms baseline algorithms—including both visual-based affordance techniques and standard RL methods—in terms of success rates. Further demonstrations are available at https://sites.google.com/view/rlafford/.

Metallic quantum criticality plays a pivotal role in numerous strongly correlated systems. Recent experimental findings have prompted a fundamental inquiry into how charge responses can exhibit singular behavior, even when the Landau framework restricts such singularities to the spin channel. Driven by this emerging challenge, we investigate the particle-hole-asymmetric regime of a Bose-Fermi Anderson model featuring power-law dependencies for both the bosonic bath spectrum and the fermionic band density of states. We identify a particle-hole-asymmetric quantum-critical state in which quasiparticles vanish due to the critical breakdown of Kondo screening, alongside the demonstration of dynamical Planckian scaling in the charge response. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for a novel regime of heavy-fermion quantum criticality and for Mott-Hubbard systems.

Human lives are increasingly shaped by algorithms, necessitating that these systems adhere to stricter standards regarding both accuracy and explainability, a requirement that is particularly critical in high-stakes domains like real estate valuation. Regrettably, existing methods in this field often face a trade-off between precision and interpretability. While case-based reasoning (CBR) offers an explainable framework by grounding decisions in specific historical cases, it frequently lacks accuracy. Conversely, unexplainable machine learning models typically deliver superior accuracy but remain opaque regarding their decision-making processes.

This paper proposes applying evolutionary algorithms (EAs) to enhance CBR predictors. Specifically, we utilize EAs to optimize similarity functions within CBR systems to better fit the available dataset. This approach yields higher accuracy than state-of-the-art deep neural networks (DNNs) while maintaining full interpretability and explainability. Our empirical evaluation on a substantial dataset of real estate offers compares standard similarity functions, their EA-optimized versions, and DNNs. Surprisingly, DNNs performed only on par with conventional CBR techniques; however, employing EA-learned similarity functions resulted in significantly improved performance.

We employ the Gauss decomposition of the generator matrix within the $R$-matrix formulation of the Yangian for the orthosymplectic Lie superalgebra ${\frak osp}_{N|2m}$ to derive its Drinfeld-type presentation. This work builds upon Gow's (2007) research on ${\frak gl}_{n|m}$ Yangians and our previous collaboration with Jing and Liu (2018) on orthogonal and symplectic Yangians, with the sole exception of the embedding theorem, which necessitated a distinct approach due to the super case.

**Context.** The Vista Variables in the Via Lactea (VVV) near-infrared variability survey investigates highly complex areas of the Milky Way's bulge and disk, characterized by significant extinction and crowding. **Aims.** Our objective is to augment the optical data from the American Association of Variable Star Observers International Variable Star Index (VSX-AAVSO) with a new wavelength dimension, thereby testing VVV near-infrared photometry to better characterize these objects. **Methods.** We performed a cross-match between the VVV and VSX-AAVSO catalogues, incorporating Gaia Data Release 2 photometry and parallax measurements. **Results.** We present a comprehensive catalogue featuring precise individual coordinates, near-infrared magnitudes (ZY JHKs), extinction values ($A_{Ks}$), and distances derived from Gaia parallaxes. Furthermore, we display near-infrared color-magnitude diagrams (CMDs) and spatial distributions for various VSX variable star types, including key distance indicators such as RR Lyrae stars, Cepheids, and Miras. Analysis of photometric flags revealed that approximately 20% of stars with verified variability are flagged as non-stellar sources, despite being outside saturation and noise regimes. Additionally, pairing our sample with the VIVA catalogue showed that over half of our sources are absent from the VVV variability list, primarily due to low signal-to-noise ratios or photometric issues, with only a small fraction attributed to selection failures. **Conclusions.** Our findings indicate that current understanding of Galactic variability is biased toward nearby stars with low extinction. This catalogue lays the foundation for characterizing results from future large-scale variability surveys, such as the Vera C. Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time, within the crowded and reddened regions of the Galactic plane, as well as supporting follow-up campaigns.

Coarse-to-fine Q-attention enhances sample efficiency in robot manipulation by discretizing translation space hierarchically, with resolution incrementally increasing at each layer. Despite its effectiveness, standard Q-attention is limited by "coarse ambiguity," making it difficult to differentiate visually similar objects when voxelization is too coarse without finer inspection. To address this, we conceptualize Q-attention as an expandable tree that accumulates value estimates across the top-k voxels at every Q-attention depth. By integrating our proposed Q-attention with Tree Expansion (QTE) into the Attention-driven Robot Manipulation (ARM) framework, we successfully execute a broader range of tasks, particularly those prone to coarse ambiguity. Beyond evaluating the method on 12 RLBench tasks, we demonstrate that the performance gains translate to real-world scenarios involving small objects.

Computational pathology poses significant hurdles for computer vision algorithms, primarily due to the massive scale of pathology images. To accommodate modern convolutional neural networks (CNNs), these large histopathology images must be segmented into smaller tiles or patches. This study introduces a novel approach to create an interpretable representation of computational pathology images using quadtrees, alongside a pipeline that leverages these representations for highly accurate downstream classification. To our knowledge, this represents the inaugural application of quadtrees for pathology image data. We demonstrate that this method achieves high accuracy, matching the performance of currently popular tissue mask patch extraction techniques while utilizing over 38% less data.

We introduce an extension of the Gravitational Decoupling algorithm tailored for Lovelock theory with Unique Vacuum (LUV), offering a straightforward method to solve the equations of motion. This approach decomposes the system's energy into the energy of the seed solution and the energy contributions from each quasi-LUV sector. Under specific assumptions, the total energy changes based on the input from these quasi-LUV sectors. Consequently, we present a novel solution whose energy deviates from the seed solution by an amount dependent on the number of additional sources. This new solution is characterized by the presence of two inner horizons. Moreover, its thermodynamic properties differ from those of the seed solution, as the derived solution remains stable and exhibits no phase transitions. Given that the presence of matter fields alters the first law of thermodynamics, we propose a revised version of this law for LUV, establishing a local definition for energy variation while ensuring that entropy and temperature remain consistent within the LUV framework.

J. Quintanilla has recently established a theorem that creates a one-to-one correspondence between zero-temperature static spin-spin correlators and coupling constants for a broad class of quantum spin Hamiltonians bilinear in spin operators, utilizing an argument analogous to the Hohenberg-Kohn theorem in density functional theory. This theorem provides a robust theoretical basis for learning quantum spin Hamiltonians using spin structure factors as input. In this work, we extend the theorem's applicability in two key ways. First, adopting Mermin's approach, we generalize the proof to finite-temperature spin structure factors, thereby validating the theorem's use with experimental data. Second, we demonstrate that the theorem applies to any Hamiltonian expressed as a sum of bilinear operators, enabling it to relate density-density correlators to Coulomb matrix elements for interacting electrons within the lowest Landau level.

We introduce a logical qubit constructed from the Blume-Capel model, which extends the Ising chain to higher spins and maintains rotational invariance around the Ising axis through on-site anisotropy. We demonstrate that a spin-3/2 variant of this model can host localized Majorana bound states at the chain's termini. Drawing inspiration from established braiding protocols for these states, we show that by appropriately tuning system parameters, one can implement a suite of universal gate operations acting on qubits encoded within the doubly degenerate ground states of the chain.

We examine the arrangements of lines and conics on a specific subset of Kummer octic surfaces. Specifically, we establish an upper limit of $176$ for the number of conics and demonstrate that a unique surface achieves this maximum, featuring $176$ irreducible conics that support a faithful action by a Mukai group. Consequently, our analysis extends to conics and lines on Mukai surfaces, where we identify a double plane—branched along a smooth sextic curve—that harbors $8910$ smooth conics.

The F-minor-free deletion problem seeks the smallest vertex set in a graph that intersects every minor model of graphs belonging to a family F. The Vertex planarization problem represents a specific instance of this where F consists of {K_5, K_{3,3}}. It is established that if F includes at least one planar graph, F-minor-free deletion admits both constant-factor approximation algorithms and polynomial kernelizations [Fomin, Lokshtanov, Misra, and Saurabh, FOCS'12]. Vertex planarization is considered the most basic scenario where F contains no planar graph, making the existence of such efficient algorithms a significant open challenge.

This study demonstrates that Vertex planarization allows for an algorithm that merges these two strategies. Specifically, we introduce a polynomial A-approximate kernelization (where A > 1 is a constant) utilizing the lossy kernelization framework [Lokshtanov, Panolan, Ramanujan, and Saurabh, STOC'17]. Essentially, given a graph G and an integer k, we construct a reduced graph G' with poly(k) vertices such that any B-approximate solution for G' can be transformed into an (A*B)-approximate solution for G, provided the condition A*B*OPT(G) <= k holds. To accomplish this, we devise a sparsification framework for planar graphs that roughly maintains all separators and near-separators among subsets of a designated terminal set.

Consequently, our findings enhance the state-of-the-art approximation methods for Vertex planarization. Previous approaches included a polynomial-time O(n^eps)-approximation algorithm (for any eps > 0) and a quasi-polynomial-time (log n)^O(1) approximation algorithm, both randomized [Kawarabayashi and Sidiropoulos, FOCS'17]. By integrating these algorithms with our approximate kernelization, we improve the approximation ratios to O(OPT^eps) and (log OPT)^O(1), respectively.

Information constitutes physical reality, implying that a universal physical theory must treat observers as physical systems possessing concrete memories to retain data gained from experimentation and reasoning. This paper examines these challenges within Spekkens' toy theory, a non-contextual, epistemically restricted framework that partially replicates quantum mechanical behavior. We introduce a method for modeling physical agents, memory storage, measurements, conditional operations, and information processing within this theory. Our findings reveal significant constraints on toy agents: despite the existence of non-orthogonal states, physical agents cannot consciously prepare them. Furthermore, memory limitations prevent agents from forgetting which of two arbitrary states a system occupies. We also formalize the inference process regarding other agents' experiments and model multi-agent scenarios such as Wigner's friend. Distinct from quantum theory or box world, the toy theory avoids inconsistencies when physical agents reason about one another's knowledge.

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) represent a potent method for image generation, yet they are plagued by training instability, particularly when applied to large and complex datasets. Although BigGAN has markedly enhanced image quality on ImageNet, its massive scale hinders deployment on resource-limited devices. To address this, we introduce a black-box knowledge distillation framework designed to compress GANs, ensuring a stable and efficient training workflow. Using BigGAN as the teacher, we successfully trained a significantly smaller student network to replicate its capabilities. This approach yields competitive Inception and FID scores while reducing the generator's parameter count by 16-fold.

Autoinducers act as small signaling molecules that facilitate intercellular communication within microbial communities, orchestrating synchronized gene expression through a process known as "quorum sensing." Gaining insight into the regulatory mechanisms governing autoinducer synthesis is therefore crucial for comprehending collective microbial behaviors, including virulence and bioluminescence. Recent experimental evidence reveals heterogeneous promoter activity in autoinducer synthase genes, implying that within an isogenic population, certain cells may produce autoinducers while others do not. Despite this observation, the specific mechanism driving this phenotypic diversity in quorum-sensing populations has remained unclear. Our theoretical framework proposes a model where cells synthesize and secrete autoinducers into their surroundings, enhance production based on these local environmental cues, and experience a fitness trade-off where non-producing cells replicate more rapidly than producers. We demonstrate that the interplay between ecological and population dynamics mediated by quorum sensing can generate phenotypic heterogeneity, offering an alternative explanation to stochastic gene expression within bistable regulatory circuits.

The Hofmann-Mislove theorem establishes a bijection between compact saturated sets in a sober topological space and the open filters of its lattice of open sets. This paper explores an analogous result within the context of approach spaces by introducing the concept of compact functions, which serve as the enriched equivalent of compact subsets. It demonstrates that for a sober approach space, there is a one-to-one correspondence between inhabited, saturated compact functions and the proper open $[0,\infty]$-filters of the metric space formed by its upper regular functions, thereby extending the Hofmann-Mislove theorem to approach spaces.

In transfer learning, the "head" (the network's final section) is typically the only component fine-tuned. Representation similarity analysis indicates that even when all weights are updated, the most substantial shifts still occur within the head. Conversely, recent findings in few-shot learning suggest that updating representations in early, predominantly convolutional layers offers significant benefits, particularly for cross-domain adaptation. This study investigates whether those benefits apply to transfer learning. Furthermore, we examine how representations evolve throughout both pre-training and fine-tuning phases, revealing that the pre-trained architecture is effectively discarded if its learned features are not utilized.

We investigated neighboring bin multiplicity correlations across varying pseudorapidities in Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 7.7-62.4$ GeV using the AMPT multi-phase transport model, which incorporates both initial partonic and hadronic interactions. Our results show that for $\sqrt{s_{NN}} < 19.6$ GeV, short-range correlations of final particles exhibit a trough at central pseudorapidity, whereas for $\sqrt{s_{NN}} > 19.6$ GeV, these correlations display a peak at the same region. These findings suggest that the pseudorapidity dependence of short-range correlations carries novel physical information and cannot be merely attributed to the pseudorapidity distribution of final particles. By comparing AMPT simulations with and without hadronic scattering, we determined that while hadronic scattering can enhance short-range correlations to a certain degree, it does not account for the distinct correlation shapes observed at different energies. Additional analysis indicates that the varying pseudorapidity dependence of short-range correlations is primarily driven by partonic evolution and the subsequent hadronization mechanism.

Direct decoding in task-oriented dialogue is recognized for suffering from the explaining-away effect, leading models to favor short and generic replies. We propose applying Bayes' theorem to decompose the dialogue task into two components: the likelihood of the context given a response and the prior distribution over responses. This method, which implements the noisy channel model, not only alleviates the explaining-away effect but also enables the principled integration of large pretrained models for the response prior. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the noisy channel model generates superior responses compared to direct decoding, and a two-stage pretraining strategy utilizing both open-domain and task-oriented data outperforms models with random initialization.

Cross-sections for the production of $^{68}$Ge, $^{69}$Ge, $^{65}$Zn, and $^{67}$Ga radioisotopes via alpha-induced reactions on $^{nat}$Zn were determined using the stacked foil activation method combined with off-line $\gamma$-ray spectroscopy, covering incident alpha energies from 14.47 to 37 MeV. This study reports data for the $^{nat}$Zn($\alpha$,x)$^{68}$Ge, $^{nat}$Zn($\alpha$,x)$^{69}$Ge, $^{nat}$Zn($\alpha$,x)$^{65}$Zn, and $^{nat}$Zn($\alpha$,x)$^{67}$Ga reactions. The measured cross-sections are evaluated against prior experimental data from the EXFOR library and theoretical predictions generated by the TALYS nuclear reaction code. Furthermore, a comprehensive uncertainty analysis was conducted, with the resulting covariance metrics provided. Given the significance of $\alpha$-induced reactions in astrophysics, nuclear medicine, and the refinement of nuclear reaction models, this study incorporates necessary corrections for coincidence summing and geometric factors during the data analysis.

This paper introduces an audio denoising technique that integrates processing within both the time and time-frequency domains. The approach employs a deep neural network to model a noisy audio segment. Although the network's approximation is partial, it more effectively captures the clean signal than the noise, enabling the separation of the clean audio from the remainder. This separation is achieved by calculating a fitting score for each time-frequency bin and subsequently applying time-frequency filtering based on these scores. The method operates entirely in an unsupervised manner, training exclusively on the specific audio clip requiring denoising. Experimental results indicate that our approach outperforms existing methods found in the literature. The associated code and samples can be accessed at github.com/mosheman5/DNP and are also provided as supplementary materials. Index Terms: Audio denoising; Unsupervised learning.

This study explores the steady-state movement of cylindrical droplets subjected to external body forces through both theoretical analysis and lattice Boltzmann simulations. Provided the droplet's shape remains invariant, the center-of-mass velocity increases linearly with both the force density and the square of the droplet's radius. Conversely, significant deformation leads to non-linear dynamics, specifically elongation driven by high external forces. Regardless of force density or droplet size, the center-of-mass velocity maintains a linear relationship with the inverse of dynamic viscosity. Furthermore, energy dissipation is predominantly localized near the substrate, especially around the three-phase contact line. The total viscous dissipation scales linearly with the inverse of dynamic viscosity and quadratically with the force density. Additionally, the influence of the equilibrium contact angle on the center-of-mass velocity is examined, supported by a simple analytic model that accurately reproduces the observed phenomena.

The swift rise in debilitating respiratory conditions, including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), necessitates a significant incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) into medical care. Although AI offers enhanced detection and monitoring capabilities for such disorders, these methods are typically "data-hungry," underscoring the critical need for generating physically accurate surrogate data. Domain-aware surrogates can facilitate a deeper understanding of how respiratory waveforms vary across different breathing disorders and improve machine learning training. To address this, we present a device constructed from PVC tubing and 3D-printed components, offering a straightforward yet efficient approach to simulating both obstructive and restrictive respiratory waveforms in healthy individuals. By independently adjusting inspiratory and expiratory resistances, the apparatus can replicate obstructive breathing disorders across the entire spectrum of FEV1/FVC spirometry ratios, spanning from normal levels to those indicative of severe COPD. Furthermore, the generated waveforms exhibit key characteristics of breathing disorders, such as altered inspiratory duty cycles and peak flow rates. In summary, this proposed apparatus delivers a simple, effective, and physically grounded method for producing faithful surrogate breathing disorder waveforms, which is essential for advancing AI applications in respiratory health.

For two unital C*-algebras with associated states and a positive operator within the enveloping von Neumann algebra of their minimal tensor product, we introduce three parameters quantifying the operator's capacity to align with a coupling of these states. We prove a duality formula demonstrating the equivalence of two of these parameters. When restricted to abelian C*-algebras, this framework recovers specific instances of Monge-Kantorovich duality and links to quantitative formulations of Arveson's Null Set Theorem. Conversely, in the context of matrix algebras, we recover and extend quantum analogues of Strassen's Theorem. Furthermore, we demonstrate that in this latter scenario, the defined parameters can identify both maximal entanglement and separability.

Planning for robots in partially observable environments presents significant challenges, as systems must simultaneously estimate their current state and formulate actions. This difficulty is amplified in domains containing numerous objects, where reasoning about the objects and their interrelationships becomes even more complex. This paper introduces an algorithm named Scene Analysis for Robot Planning (SARP), designed to leverage visual contextual information for achieving long-term goals despite uncertainty. SARP builds scene graphs—factored representations of objects and their relations—derived from images captured from various viewpoints, utilizing these structures to facilitate context-aware planning under partial observability. The method was evaluated through experiments in multiple simulated 3D environments and with a dataset gathered by a physical robot. Compared to standard planning and scene analysis approaches, SARP demonstrates superior efficiency and accuracy in task completion within target search domains. Additional materials are available at https://tinyurl.com/sarp22.

Pre-trained language models have become essential across various information retrieval (IR) paradigms, with late interaction—pioneered by ColBERT and enhanced in ColBERTv2—establishing state-of-the-art performance on numerous benchmarks. To significantly accelerate the search latency associated with late interaction, we present the Performance-optimized Late Interaction Driver (PLAID). PLAID maintains high retrieval quality while rapidly filtering out low-scoring documents through an innovative centroid interaction mechanism that conceptualizes each passage as a compact collection of centroids. By combining centroid interaction with centroid pruning to sparsify these collections, and deploying them within a highly optimized engine, PLAID reduces late interaction search latency by up to 7$\times$ on GPUs and 45$\times$ on CPUs compared to standard ColBERTv2. This efficiency enables the PLAID engine, paired with ColBERTv2, to achieve response times in the tens of milliseconds on GPUs and under a few hundred milliseconds on CPUs at scale, even when processing up to 140 million passages.

A central goal of NASA's Parker Solar Probe (PSP) mission is to comprehend the physical mechanisms driving heating, acceleration, and dissipation within the solar corona and wind. Evidence from coherent electromagnetic waves at ion scales indicates that both linear cyclotron resonance and non-linear dynamics play significant roles in the inner heliosphere. A wavelet-based statistical analysis of coherent waves during PSP's initial perihelion passage reveals transverse electromagnetic waves at ion-resonant scales occurring in 30–50% of radial field intervals. These events exhibit average amplitudes of roughly 4 nT and durations averaging around 20 seconds, although some events persist uninterrupted for hours. While ion-scale waves are more frequently detected during intervals with a radial mean magnetic field, constraints inherent to single-spacecraft sampling of quasi-parallel waves superimposed on anisotropic turbulence make the quasi-parallel ion-wave spectrum unobservable when the mean field is oblique to the solar wind flow. This suggests that coherent ion-scale waves are not restricted to radial field configurations. Furthermore, the absence of strong radial scaling in wave amplitude and duration implies an *in-situ* generation via plasma instabilities. Additionally, proton distribution function observations suggest that temperature anisotropy could be driving these ion-scale waves.

Fekete polynomials are associated with each prime number $p$, featuring coefficients of $-1$ or $1$ (except for the constant term, which is zero); these coefficients mirror the distribution of quadratic residues modulo $p$. Originally examined in the 19th century in the context of Dirichlet $L$-functions, our paper introduces two closely related polynomials. We derive expressions for their special values at various integers using specific class numbers and generalized Bernoulli numbers. Furthermore, we investigate the splitting fields and Galois groups of these polynomials, specifically proposing a conjecture regarding the structure of these Galois groups.

We introduce a method to substantially increase the strong coupling rate between photons within an optical cavity and a single quantum emitter, including atoms, quantum dots, or trapped ions. Our findings demonstrate that specifically engineered non-spherical mirrors can generate cavity eigenmodes featuring substantial field enhancement at the cavity's center. This configuration results in markedly reduced beam divergence, leading to lower round-trip losses and improved cooperativity compared to spherical-mirror cavities operating in the near-concentric regime. We validate these designs through mode matching theory and evaluate their resilience against various manufacturing imperfections.

Recently introduced "plug-and-play" (PnP) image recovery methods have demonstrated exceptional performance in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). While these algorithms resemble traditional iterative techniques such as FISTA, ADMM, or primal-dual splitting (PDS), they substitute the proximal update step with an invocation of a specialized image denoiser, like BM3D or DnCNN. However, the convergence of PnP algorithms relies on an algorithmic stepsize parameter that requires careful tuning for optimal results. This study introduces a rapid and resilient auto-tuning PnP-PDS method that leverages pre-scan measurement-noise variance data available in MRI. Experimental findings indicate that the proposed algorithm achieves performance nearly equivalent to genie-tuned benchmarks and does so considerably faster than current autotuning methods.
