We introduce MOLET, a self-consistent and flexible forward modelling package capable of generating pixel-level and time-series simulations for strongly lensed systems with time variability. Unlike existing methods, MOLET explicitly incorporates the time dimension, accounting for variability mechanisms like microlensing that are critical for time delay measurements, H0 determinations, and caustic crossing predictions. With the rise of time-domain surveys, such experiments are becoming more streamlined; therefore, a model-aware, physics-driven approach to understanding their systematic and statistical uncertainties is essential for enhancing accuracy and precision. We demonstrate the software's utility by investigating time delay measurements from lensed quasars and supernovae across multiple wavelengths, under various assumptions regarding microlensing and intrinsic variability. In this initial application, we determine that observation cadence and the integration of multi-wavelength data significantly influence the accurate recovery of time delays. The MOLET software package is available at: https://github.com/gvernard/molet

Polynomial multiplication represents a critical performance bottleneck in numerous public-key cryptography protocols, such as Elliptic-curve cryptography and various post-quantum algorithms currently under investigation. This paper introduces a library of diverse large integer polynomial multipliers tailored for hardware cryptocores. The collection offers both digitized and non-digitized multiplier options, enabling circuit designers to select the most suitable approach. Backed by a C++ generator, the library automatically synthesizes the multipliers' logic into Verilog HDL, facilitating integration into both FPGA and ASIC designs. Furthermore, it produces configurable and parameterizable synthesis scripts specifically for ASIC implementations. These generator capabilities streamline the simultaneous generation and evaluation of multiple architectures, allowing designers to efficiently navigate the complex optimization landscape of polynomial multiplication.

The magnetic dipole moment form factor, $G_M^{(2)}(Q^2)$, which characterizes electromagnetic transitions involving radial excitations from decuplet to octet baryons, along with the ratios $R_{SM} = -\frac{1}{4 m_2^2} \sqrt{4 m_2^2 Q^2 + (m_2^2 - Q^2 -m_1^2)^2} \frac{G_C^{(2)}(Q^2)}{G_M^{(2)}(Q^2)}$ and $R_{EM} = -\frac{G_E^{(2)}(Q^2)}{G_M^{(2)}(Q^2)}$, are computed using light-cone sum rules. Additionally, we assess the extent of U-spin symmetry violation. These calculated multipole form factors may prove valuable in investigating the characteristics of radially excited baryon states.

The widespread adoption of artificial neural networks (ANNs) across various scientific computing fields is causing a rapid surge in energy consumption within modern high-performance systems. A promising and potentially more sustainable solution lies in emerging neuromorphic paradigms, which execute ANNs directly in hardware. Nevertheless, the specific advantages of deploying ANNs on neuromorphic hardware for scientific applications remain largely unexplored. This study introduces a methodology for quantifying the energy expenditure and computation time required for ANN inference on traditional hardware. Furthermore, we developed a dedicated architecture and estimated corresponding metrics for a state-of-the-art analog in-memory computing (AIMC) platform, a cornerstone of neuromorphic technology. We compared these approaches using two distinct scientific use cases: quantum many-body physics in two-dimensional condensed matter systems and anomaly detection operating at 40 MHz at the Large Hadron Collider in particle physics. Our findings indicate that AIMC can reduce computation times by up to an order of magnitude while lowering energy costs by up to three orders of magnitude compared to conventional hardware. These results highlight the significant potential of neuromorphic hardware to enable faster and more sustainable scientific computing.

To monitor the real-time 3D positions and movement paths of surrounding traffic, contemporary autonomous vehicles utilize multiple cameras to capture their entire environment. However, existing camera-based 3D tracking approaches primarily optimize single-camera configurations and rely on post-hoc fusion when multiple cameras are employed. This paper introduces CC-3DT, a method for panoramic 3D object tracking that correlates and models trajectories across both time and different camera views, thereby enhancing tracking consistency. Specifically, our approach integrates 3D detections from multiple cameras prior to the association stage, which markedly reduces identity switches and refines motion modeling. Experiments conducted on extensive driving datasets demonstrate that fusing data before association yields substantial improvements over post-hoc fusion. On the competitive NuScenes 3D tracking benchmark, our method establishes a new state-of-the-art, achieving a 12.6% gain in average multi-object tracking accuracy (AMOTA) compared to other camera-based techniques. Furthermore, utilizing the same 3D detector as prior work, CC-3DT surpasses existing methods by 6.5% in AMOTA.

Let $M_R$ be a module and $\sigma$ an endomorphism of $R$. For any $m \in M$ and $a \in R$, we define $M_R$ as satisfying condition $\mathcal{C}_1$ (respectively, $\mathcal{C}_2$) if $ma=0$ implies $m\sigma(a)=0$ (respectively, $m\sigma(a)=0$ implies $ma=0$). We demonstrate that if $M_R$ is p.q.-Baer, then the skew polynomial module $M[x;\sigma]_{R[x;\sigma]}$ is also p.q.-Baer provided $M_R$ satisfies condition $\mathcal{C}_2$, with the reverse implication holding when $M_R$ satisfies condition $\mathcal{C}_1$. Furthermore, if $M_R$ satisfies both $\mathcal{C}_2$ and is $\sigma$-skew Armendariz, then $M_R$ is a p.p.-module if and only if $M[x;\sigma]_{R[x;\sigma]}$ is a p.p.-module, which in turn is equivalent to $M[x,x^{-1};\sigma]_{R[x,x^{-1};\sigma]}$ being a p.p.-module (assuming $\sigma \in Aut(R)$). The study yields numerous generalizations, with additional results established specifically when $M_R$ is a semicommutative module.

This study examines the maximum coding rate attainable by uniformly-random codes on the deletion channel. We establish an upper bound that lies within 0.1 of the best-known lower bounds across all deletion probabilities $d$, with the gap narrowing significantly for small and large $d$. Simulation results indicate that this upper bound is likely within 0.05 of the exact value for all $d$, and within 0.01 when $d > 0.75$. Although these bounds are derived from simulations, we conjecture that a positive rate remains achievable using uniformly-random codes for any deletion probability less than 1. Furthermore, our findings yield impossibility results for the equivalent problem of compressing i.i.d. sources correlated through the deletion channel, a model pertinent to DNA storage applications.

Let $X$ denote a compact, connected Riemann surface with genus $g \geq 2$, and let ${\mathcal M}_{\rm DH}$ represent the associated rank one Deligne-Hitchin moduli space. It is established that ${\mathcal M}_{\rm DH}$ serves as the twistor space for the hyper-K\"ahler structure defined on the moduli space of rank one holomorphic connections over $X$. This study examines the group $\operatorname{Aut}({\mathcal M}_{\rm DH})$, comprising all holomorphic automorphisms of ${\mathcal M}_{\rm DH}$. We determine the connected component of this group containing the identity. Additionally, we identify a natural element within $H^2({\mathcal M}_{\rm DH}, {\mathbb Z})$ and calculate the subgroup of $\operatorname{Aut}({\mathcal M}_{\rm DH})$ that preserves this second cohomology class. Given that ${\mathcal M}_{\rm DH}$ contains an ample rational curve, Verbitsky's theorem allows the extension of the algebraic dimension concept to this space. Finally, we demonstrate that ${\mathcal M}_{\rm DH}$ is Moishezon.

Recent proposals suggest that the theory space of effective field theories (EFTs) with consistent ultraviolet (UV) completions can be modeled as a positive geometry known as the EFThedron. This paper establishes that the fundamental structure of this geometry arises from the convex hull of the product of two moment curves. This finding connects to the extensively studied bi-variate moment problem, where known solutions allow for the generalization of Hankel coupling matrices into moment matrices. Consequently, we derive analytic expressions for bounds that align precisely with numerical outcomes from semi-definite programming. Additionally, we show that infrared crossing symmetry imposes significant constraints on the UV spectrum. Specifically, permutation invariance in identical scalar scattering necessitates that any UV completion extending beyond the scalar sector must include states of arbitrarily high spin, encompassing at least all even spins up to $\ell=28$. The ratios of spinning spectral functions are bounded from above, indicating strong spin suppression. Moreover, the spinning spectrum must contain at least one state satisfying the bound $m^2_{J}<M^2 \frac{( J^2-12) ( J^4 - 32 J^2 +204)}{8 (150 - 43 J^2 + 2 J^4)}$, where $J^2=\ell(\ell+1)$ and $M^2$ represents the mass of the heaviest spin-2 state.

When a $4D$ supersymmetric theory is defined on $S^3 \times \mathbb{R}$, its supersymmetric algebra is inevitably deformed to $su(2|1)$, resulting in a weak supersymmetric system. In such systems, the excited states of the Hamiltonian do not necessarily form complete pairs. Consequently, the Witten index, defined as Tr$\{(-1)^F e^{-\beta H}\}$, ceases to be an integer and instead becomes a function dependent on $\beta$. Nevertheless, this function remains invariant under any deformation of the theory that preserves the supersymmetry algebra. We provide a straightforward general proof of this invariance based on Hilbert space analysis and subsequently demonstrate its application to the two simplest weak supersymmetric quantum mechanical systems, each involving either a real or a complex bosonic degree of freedom.

Complex nonlinear dynamics are prevalent across numerous disciplines, yet we often lack access to all relevant state variables that govern these systems. While delay embedding theoretically addresses unobserved variables, we present an algebraic framework that enables explicit error approximation and defines the asymptotic relationship between first-order approximation errors and system size. Crucially, this formulation can be directly implemented via a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN), thereby enhancing the interpretability of both delay embedding and RNNs and allowing for the principled integration of structural constraints and other requirements.

This paper introduces finite element techniques to numerically solve the Risk-Adjusted Pricing Methodology (RAPM) Black-Scholes model for option pricing in the presence of transaction costs. The study formulates spatial finite element models utilizing P1 and/or P2 elements alongside group finite elements, employing numerical quadrature to address the nonlinear term, all paired with a Crank-Nicolson-type temporal scheme implemented via the Rannacher approach. The method's stability is managed by observing spatial-temporal mesh-size ratios. The findings demonstrate favorable comparisons against existing finite difference results in the literature for this model.

Microflares, representing small-scale solar phenomena, are thought to result from magnetic reconnection; however, their three-dimensional (3D) magnetic and thermodynamic architectures, as well as their physical connection to reconnection, have remained elusive. This Letter employs high-resolution 3D radiative magnetohydrodynamic simulations of the quiet Sun, covering the upper convection zone to the corona, to examine the 3D structures of three homologous microflares. Our findings indicate that these events arise from localized hot plasma within the chromosphere, situated 2–10 Mm above the photosphere, persisting for 3–10 minutes and releasing magnetic energies between $10^{27}$ and $10^{28}$ erg. The heated plasma aligns closely with regions of peak heating rates per particle. Analysis of the 3D velocity field uncovers converging flows reaching tens of km s$^{-1}$ directed toward the hot plasma, alongside outflows at approximately 100 km s$^{-1}$ moving away. These characteristics confirm that magnetic reconnection is essential for heating localized chromospheric plasma to coronal temperatures, thereby producing observed microflares. Furthermore, magnetic topology analysis reveals that the reconnection zone is situated near quasi-separators where both current density and squashing factors peak, although the specific topology can range from tether-cutting to fan-spine-like configurations.

In 2007, Primoz Moravec published a significant paper demonstrating that for any finite group $G$ with exponent $n$, the exponent of its Schur multiplier is bounded by a function $f(n)$ determined solely by $n$. Although Moravec did not specify a concrete value for $f(n)$, his proof establishes that $f(n) = ne$, where $e$ represents the order of the element $b^{-n}a^{-n}(ab)^{n}$ within the Schur multiplier of $R(2,n)$. In this context, $R(2,n)$ denotes the largest finite two-generator group of exponent $n$, with $a$ and $b$ serving as its generators. Manual calculations confirm that $e=n$ for $n=2,3$, and computations using the $p$-quotient algorithm verify this for $n=4,5,7$. However, $R(2,8)$ and $R(2,9)$ exceed the computational limits of the $p$-quotient algorithm, even on modern supercomputers; nonetheless, it has been shown that $e \geq n$ for these cases. Furthermore, Moravec's result extends to finite groups of exponent $n$ and nilpotency class $c$, indicating that the exponent of the Schur multiplier is bounded by $ne$, where $e$ is the order of $b^{-n}a^{-n}(ab)^{n}$ in the class $c$ quotient $R(2,n;c)$ of $R(2,n)$. Defining $e_{q,c}$ as the order of $b^{-q}a^{-q}(ab)^{q}$ in the Schur multiplier of $R(2,q;c)$ for a prime power $q$, we demonstrate that $e_{p^{k},p^{2}-p-1}$ divides $p$ for all prime powers $p^{k}$. Additionally, for $k>2$, $e_{2^{k},c}$ equals 2 when $c<4$, 4 when $4\leq c\leq11$, and 8 when $c=12$. For $k>1$, $e_{3^{k},c}$ equals 1 when $c<3$, 3 when $3\leq c<12$, and 9 when $c=12$. The study also examines the order of the commutator $[b,a]$ within a Schur cover for $R(2,q;c)$.

Evaluating the right ventricle (RV) structure and function is vital for diagnosing various cardiac conditions, yet RV segmentation remains more difficult than left ventricle (LV) segmentation. This study addresses the simultaneous segmentation of the RV in both short-axis (SA) and long-axis (LA) cardiac MRI scans. We introduce Tempera, a novel multi-input/output architecture described as a hybrid 2D/3D geometric spatial TransformEr Multi-Pass fEature pyRAmid. Our feature pyramid design advances existing methods by supporting multi-scale outputs as well as multi-scale SA and LA inputs. Tempera facilitates feature transfer between SA and LA images through shared layer weights and employs a geometric target transformer to map SA predictions into LA space. The model attained average Dice scores of 0.836 and 0.798 for SA and LA segments, respectively, with Hausdorff distances of 26.31 mm and 31.19 mm. These results suggest that RV segmentation models can be effectively integrated into clinical practice.

Optical flow is considered crucial for the agile flight of birds and insects. Despite its simplicity, it is seldom applied in computer vision for collision avoidance. This study implements a neural network-based collision avoidance system that was deployed and evaluated on a car refitted specifically for this purpose.

Recent years have witnessed substantial progress in autonomous driving. Nevertheless, developing a resilient control policy remains difficult, necessitating training data across diverse scenarios—including infrequent events like collisions—alongside a potent policy architecture and a streamlined learning approach. We introduce ADAPS, a framework designed to generate robust control policies for autonomous vehicles. ADAPS integrates two simulation environments dedicated to accident generation and analysis to automatically create labeled training data, coupled with a memory-equipped hierarchical control policy. Furthermore, ADAPS employs a more efficient online learning mechanism that minimizes the number of learning iterations compared to established methods like DAGGER. We provide both theoretical and experimental evidence; the latter, derived from simulated settings, offers qualitative and quantitative results that highlight the advantages of ADAPS.

This paper investigates Cohen-Macaulay local rings characterized by dimension $d$, multiplicity $e$, and a second Hilbert coefficient $e_2$ under the condition $e_2 = e_1 - e + 1$. Defining $h$ as $\mu(\mathfrak{m}) - d$, we establish that when $e_2 \neq 0$, the type $A$ satisfies $A \geq e - h - 1$. Furthermore, if the type equals $e - h - 1$, we demonstrate that the associated graded ring $G(A)$ is Cohen-Macaulay. In the subsequent scenario where type $A = e - h$, we identify all feasible Hilbert series for $A$ and prove that the Hilbert series of $A$ fully determines the depth of $G(A)$.

We present LIMES, a novel approach for learning from non-stationary streaming data, drawing inspiration from recent advances in meta-learning. Rather than attempting to train a single universal classifier or maintaining numerous separate models, LIMES employs a hybrid strategy: it learns a unified set of model parameters, from which a specific classifier for any given data distribution is derived through adaptation. In a multi-class classification scenario involving class-prior shifts, this adaptation can be executed analytically, affecting only the classifier's bias terms. Additionally, we introduce an extrapolation mechanism that forecasts appropriate adaptation parameters for future time steps based on historical data. Together, these components form a lightweight procedure for handling streaming data with shifting class distributions that requires no additional trainable parameters and incurs negligible memory or computational overhead compared to standard single-model training. Empirical evaluations on exemplary tasks utilizing Twitter data demonstrate that LIMES outperforms alternative methods, particularly regarding the critical real-world metric of lowest within-day accuracy.

This paper outlines the scientific motivations for developing Band 1 receivers within ALMA's current Development Program. We detail the newly defined frequency range of 35–52 GHz for Band 1, selected to optimize the scientific return of the receiver suite. Two primary drivers guide this effort: first, tracing the evolution of dust grains in protoplanetary and debris disks, and second, observing molecular gas in galaxies during the epoch of re-ionization. Utilizing Band 1 receivers will substantially advance ALMA's Level 1 Science Goals. Beyond these, numerous additional continuum and line science opportunities leverage ALMA's superior sensitivity and angular resolution. Specifically, Band 1 continuum observations will investigate the Sunyaev-Zel'dovich Effect in galaxy clusters, very small grains and spinning dust, ionized jets from young stars, spatial and flaring dynamics of Sgr A*, solar flare acceleration sites, pulsar wind nebulae, radio supernovae, and X-ray binaries. Furthermore, Band 1 line data will enable the study of chemical differentiation in cloud cores, complex carbon chain molecules, extragalactic radio recombination lines, masers, magnetic fields via Zeeman effect measurements, molecular outflows from young stars, the co-evolution of star formation and active galactic nuclei, and the molecular content of galaxies at redshifts around 3. While ALMA offers comparable or superior sensitivity to the JVLA across the 35–50 GHz range—with advantages growing at higher frequencies—its smaller antennas, shorter baselines, larger number of baselines, and single-dish capabilities provide a distinct advantage for observing extended emission, creating wide-field mosaics, and achieving the high image fidelity required by these scientific objectives.

This work introduces a novel resource allocation strategy for Simultaneous Wireless Information and Power Transfer (SWIPT), designed to enhance communication efficiency in next-generation mobile networks while reducing overall power consumption through green energy sourcing. First, a distinct architecture is proposed where receivers harvest energy from an Access Point (AP) without requiring a signal splitter; in this OFDMA model, specific spectrum portions are allocated for Information Decoding (ID) while others are dedicated to Energy Harvesting (EH). To evaluate performance gains, an optimization problem is formulated to maximize harvested energy in a multi-user single-cell OFDMA downlink while ensuring minimum data-rate requirements are met for all users, solved via optimization tools to find a locally optimal solution despite the problem's non-convex nature caused by integer variable coupling. Second, the system model is refined to address throughput maximization in an OFDMA multi-user multi-cell environment using a separated receiver architecture, resulting in a challenging Mixed-Integer Non-Linear Problem (MINLP) that jointly optimizes subcarrier assignment and power allocation. Finally, the study explores a state-of-the-art receiver technique based on antenna selection with a co-located architecture, termed the Generalized Antenna-Switching Technique, to optimize energy efficiency in SWIPT-enabled multi-cell multi-user OFDMA networks.

The cartoon domain has seen a surge in popularity, yet transforming portraits into cartoon styles remains challenging due to unaddressed constraints like the need for extensive training data or the inability to handle abstract facial features. While recent layer-swapping techniques reduce the training image requirement, their applicability remains limited as they fail to resolve these underlying issues. To address this, we introduce a novel approach termed Cross-domain Style mixing, which integrates latent codes from two distinct domains. This method enables the effective stylization of faces into diverse cartoon characters across various abstraction levels using a single generator, all without relying on a large dataset of training images.

Unitary synthesis serves as an optimization strategy capable of minimizing multi-qubit gate counts when mapping quantum circuits onto constrained qubit architectures. However, since synthesis algorithms face scalability hurdles due to exponentially increasing runtime and memory needs, circuits exceeding five qubits must be divided into smaller segments using a divide-and-conquer approach. This study investigates techniques to lower both circuit depth (execution time) and multi-qubit gate instructions for wide (16–100 qubit) circuits optimized via synthesis, thereby enhancing program performance and execution success rates on parallel quantum hardware.

We introduce TopAS, a topology-aware synthesis tool developed within the \emph{BQSKit} framework that preconditions quantum circuits prior to mapping. By optimizing and fitting partitioned subcircuits to sparse qubit subtopologies, TopAS balances the conflicting requirements of synthesis and mapping algorithms. This method effectively reduces depth and gate counts for wide quantum circuits mapped to the sparse topologies found in Google and IBM systems. Compared to large-scale synthesis algorithms that optimize circuits post-mapping, TopAS achieves an average depth reduction of 35.2% and a CNOT gate count reduction of 11.5% when targeting a 2D mesh topology. Furthermore, relative to traditional quantum compilers utilizing peephole optimization and mapping routines from Qiskit or $t|ket\rangle$ toolkits, our approach yields substantial performance gains, lowering CNOT counts by 30.3% and depth by 38.2% on average.

This study examines a parameterized eigenvalue problem within a two-dimensional stress wave scattering framework involving a phononic array, proposing a sensing application for source angle localization. The phononic domain comprises a periodic micro-structured medium where eigen-wavevector band structures and eigen-modes are utilized. These eigen-modes exhibit inherent angle dependence, driven by variations in phase and periodic mode shapes relative to the incident angle. Notably, the band displays angle-dependent transitions at exceptional points (EPs) and critical angles (CAs), where eigenvalues either coincide or vanish. Associated with these transitions, the eigen-modes undergo shifts in energy characteristics and symmetry patterns at these branch points, thereby amplifying angle sensitivity. Furthermore, since these eigen-modes form the basis functions for scattered waves, the medium's scattering response intrinsically holds angle-dependent properties, rendering the system ideal for sensing. An artificial neural network (ANN) is trained using randomly weighted eigen-modes to deeply learn these features and angular dependencies. The training dataset relies exclusively on the unit cell eigen-modes. Despite this, the trained ANN accurately determines the incident angle of unknown scattering signals, achieving minimal side lobe levels and a narrowed main lobe width. The ANN outperforms standard delay-and-sum techniques for angle-of-arrival estimation. This proposed integration of ANN and micro-structured media underscores the technological relevance of band structure topology and eigen-modes, strengthens current localization methodologies, and offers a robust foundation for future enhancements via rapidly advancing data-driven approaches.

Let $I\supsetneq J$ be squarefree monomial ideals in a polynomial algebra over a field where the generators have degrees at least $d$ and $d+1$, respectively. Assume $I$ is generated by three monomials of degree $d$. Then, if the Stanley depth of the quotient $I/J$ does not exceed $d+1$, the standard depth of $I/J$ is likewise bounded by $d+1$.

Accurate testing of superconducting circuits and characterization of material losses depend on robust techniques for extracting the internal and coupling quality factors of microwave resonators. While single-port reflection geometry is a widely used approach, often necessitated by constraints in device design or experimental setups, it requires careful calibration of the measurement chain at cryogenic temperatures to account for impedance mismatches. This paper presents a data-driven single-port calibration method utilizing commercial microwave standards and a vector network analyzer (VNA) with samples maintained at millikelvin temperatures within a dilution refrigerator, thereby enabling measurements of quantum phenomena. Furthermore, we validate this approach by cross-referencing our single-port calibration and reflection data with over-coupled two- and three-dimensional resonators against established two-port techniques.

Visual representations are characterized by the collective neuronal population responses to images, where an individual neuron's activation across the entire image domain is termed a "tuning landscape." This study investigates the structural properties of such landscapes within high-dimensional spaces by applying concepts from level sets and Morse theory. Building on recent in vivo measurements of two-dimensional tuning maps across various brain regions, we established a statistically robust signature based on topological transitions within these level sets. Our findings reveal that this topological signature evolves progressively through the cortical hierarchy, a pattern mirrored by units in convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Additionally, we examined the geometric characteristics of level sets on CNN tuning landscapes, proposing that while higher-order units can be approximated as isotropic radial basis functions locally, this does not hold globally. These results underscore the utility of level sets as a powerful conceptual framework for deciphering neuronal activation patterns across image space.

Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is primarily utilized to prevent or treat malaria transmitted by mosquito bites. Although the drug has recently been proposed as a treatment for COVID-19, this claim lacks scientific validation. However, misinformation regarding its efficacy has proliferated on social media, creating community risks by distorting public perceptions. This study examines social network users' responses to the recommendation of using HCQ for COVID-19 by analyzing tweet reaction patterns and sentiment. We gathered 164,016 tweets between February and December 2020, employing text mining to detect social reaction patterns and shifts in opinion over time. Descriptive analysis revealed irregularities in user reactions closely tied to social and news updates concerning HCQ and COVID-19 treatment. By correlating tweets with Google search trends, we identified varying community viewpoints on HCQ usage across different states. Furthermore, sentiment analysis demonstrated significant fluctuations in public opinion regarding HCQ for COVID-19 over the study period; while early support was high, it dropped significantly by October. Finally, benchmarking our sentiment analysis against a manual classification of 4,850 human-labeled tweets showed that the Google Cloud Natural Language algorithm surpassed the Valence Aware Dictionary and sEntiment Reasoner (VADER), particularly in categorizing sarcastic tweets.

Model predictive control (MPC) leveraging data offers two primary benefits compared to model-free approaches: enhanced sample efficiency via model learning and superior performance as the planning computational budget expands. Nevertheless, long-horizon planning remains computationally expensive, and acquiring an accurate environmental model poses significant challenges. This study integrates the advantages of both model-based and model-free techniques by employing a learned, task-oriented latent dynamics model for local trajectory optimization over short horizons and a learned terminal value function to approximate long-term returns; both components are trained jointly using temporal difference learning. The proposed TD-MPC method demonstrates improved sample efficiency and asymptotic performance over existing methods on both state and image-based continuous control benchmarks from DMControl and Meta-World. Source code and video demonstrations can be accessed at https://nicklashansen.github.io/td-mpc.

New applications operating over wireless networks require mathematical frameworks to systematically evaluate network reliability. We introduce two metrics for assessing the reliability of wireless mesh routing topologies: one tailored for flooding and another for unicast routing. The Flooding Path Probability (FPP) metric calculates the end-to-end packet delivery probability under a scheme where nodes broadcast a packet only after receiving it from all upstream neighbors. Conversely, the Unicast Retransmission Flow (URF) metric determines the end-to-end packet delivery probability when a relay node retransmits a unicast packet across its outgoing links until it secures an acknowledgement or exhausts all available links. Both metrics derive explicit expressions for end-to-end packet delivery probability from individual link probabilities and the underlying connectivity graph using specific packet forwarding models, avoiding heuristics. Furthermore, we propose a distributed, greedy algorithm that leverages the URF metric to build a reliable routing topology. This algorithm generates a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) from a weighted, undirected connectivity graph, assigning weights to links based on their success probabilities. It employs a vector of decreasing reliability thresholds to coordinate node entry into the routing topology. Simulation results indicate that, on average, this algorithm produces a more reliable topology than the standard minimum hop DAG.

The stellar surface density within the inner kiloparsec ($\Sigma_{1}$) has emerged as a key metric for investigating galaxy evolution and its link to the cessation of star formation. Current trends indicate that developing a dense central core is essential for quenching. Yet, it remains uncertain whether variations in $\Sigma_{1}$ correspond to shifts in stellar kinematics and the development of dispersion-dominated bulges. In this study, we integrate imaging data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey with kinematic information from the SAMI and MaNGA surveys to measure the relationship between $\Sigma_{1}$ and the stellar spin parameter proxy ($\lambda_{re}$) within one effective radius for 1599 nearby galaxies. Our findings reveal that, for galaxies on the star-forming main sequence at a fixed stellar mass, fluctuations in $\Sigma_{1}$ are reflected by changes in $\lambda_{re}$. While actively forming stars, main sequence galaxies maintain rotational dominance, exhibiting rising $\Sigma_{1}$ while their stellar spin remains stable or increases marginally. Below the main sequence, however, the correlation between $\Sigma_{1}$ and $\lambda_{re}$ breaks down. Passive systems display a restricted range of $\Sigma_{1}$ values but a broader distribution of $\lambda_{re}$ compared to star-forming counterparts. These results suggest that, structurally, passive galaxies constitute a more diverse population than star-forming ones, likely having undergone varied evolutionary histories. Furthermore, this implies that if dispersion-dominated bulges continue to grow significantly at $z\sim$0, such growth typically occurs during or following the quenching phase.

The fully heavy pentaquarks $cccc\bar{c}$ and $bbbb\bar{b}$ have been systematically analyzed using both the chiral quark model and the quark delocalization color screening model. The findings from these two frameworks align, highlighting that channel-coupling effects are essential for the formation of bound states within the fully heavy pentaquark system. Three specific candidates were identified: the $cccc\bar{c}$ state with $J^P = 1/2^-$ and a mass range of $7891.9 \sim 7892.7$ MeV; the $bbbb\bar{b}$ state with $J^P = 1/2^-$ and a mass range of $23810.1 \sim 23813.8$ MeV; and another $bbbb\bar{b}$ state with $J^P = 3/2^-$ and a mass range of $23748.2 \sim 23752.3$ MeV. These predicted fully heavy pentaquark states represent promising targets for future experimental searches.

Interpreting chest radiographs (CXR) in children is a complex task prone to errors, demanding extensive radiologic expertise. Although deep convolutional neural networks (D-CNNs) have demonstrated impressive results in adult CXR analysis, their ability to accurately identify multiple pediatric lung pathologies remains unproven. Developing diagnostic models for pediatric chest diseases is hindered by two primary obstacles: a scarcity of physician-annotated data and class imbalance issues. To address these challenges, this study retrospectively assembled a large cohort of 5,017 pediatric CXR scans, each manually labeled by an experienced radiologist for 10 common conditions. A D-CNN was trained on 3,550 of these annotated images to automatically classify multiple pediatric lung diseases. To mitigate class imbalance, we introduced and applied a "Distribution-Balanced loss" function, which adapts the standard Binary-Cross Entropy (BCE) loss to prioritize harder samples by reducing the weight assigned to majority classes. Evaluation on an independent test set of 777 studies yielded an area under the receiver operating characteristic (AUC) of 0.709 (95% CI, 0.690-0.729). At the optimal cutoff, the model achieved a sensitivity of 0.722 (0.694-0.750), specificity of 0.579 (0.563-0.595), and an F1-score of 0.389 (0.373-0.405). These metrics significantly surpassed previous state-of-the-art methods for most target diseases. Furthermore, ablation studies confirmed the superiority of our proposed loss function over standard alternatives like BCE and Focal Loss for this specific task. Collectively, these findings highlight the potential of D-CNNs in interpreting pediatric chest radiographs.

Processing historical documents using natural language techniques is challenging due to numerous spelling variations and a scarcity of labeled datasets. A prevalent solution involves converting archaic spellings into their contemporary equivalents. This study investigates the effectiveness of a deep neural network, specifically a character-level deep bi-LSTM, for this normalization task. When tested on a varied corpus of Early New High German texts, our model performs competitively against existing normalization algorithms. Furthermore, we demonstrate that incorporating additional normalization data through multi-task learning can enhance the model's performance even further.

This study examines a stochastic SIR (susceptible, infective, recovered) epidemic on a configuration model random graph, where infections spread only between connected neighbors during an infectious period governed by a specific, arbitrary distribution. Under the assumption that node degrees are bounded, we establish central limit theorems for the final epidemic size—the count of initially susceptible individuals who become infected—as the population size $n$ approaches infinity. These theorems provide explicit and computationally simple formulas for the asymptotic variance. The findings apply to both the Molloy-Reed random graph (with deterministic degrees) and the Newman-Strogatz-Watts random graph (with independent and identically distributed degrees). The analysis covers two scenarios regarding the initial number of infectives: (a) a quantity that grows to infinity, assuming the initial infection fraction converges to a limit (potentially zero), and (b) a fixed quantity, where the theorems are conditioned on the occurrence of a large outbreak (specifically, one reaching at least size $\log n$). Furthermore, our results immediately yield central limit theorems for the sizes of the largest cluster and the giant component in bond percolation on these graphs, as well as corresponding theorems for site percolation.

Robot manipulators frequently operate in semi-structured settings like logistics and manufacturing, often sharing space with humans or other robots. While these environments are mostly static, they may include movable obstacles that the robot must navigate around. Although tasks in these applications are typically repetitive, they demand rapid and dependable motion planning, frequently under tight time limits. Traditional preprocessing-based methods work well in highly structured scenarios but fail when movable obstacles are present, as these are not pre-modeled. We introduce a new preprocessing-based technique called the Alternative Paths Planner (APP), which offers provable fixed-time planning guarantees in semi-structured environments. APP pre-computes a set of alternative paths offline, ensuring that regardless of how movable obstacles are arranged, at least one path remains collision-free. During online execution, a valid collision-free path can be retrieved efficiently within microseconds. We evaluated APP on a 7-degree-of-freedom robotic arm across semi-structured domains of varying complexity, showing it is orders of magnitude faster than current state-of-the-art motion planners. Additionally, we confirmed the approach's effectiveness through real-time experiments on a physical robotic manipulator.

We demonstrate that large gauge transformations alter momentum conservation structures, resulting in non-zero three-point amplitudes within a simplified gravitational wave model. This mechanism reconciles an apparent conflict between perturbative scattering amplitude calculations and exact field theory methods. When large gauge effects are incorporated through a modified LSZ prescription, the tension vanishes to all orders in perturbation theory; conversely, omitting these effects causes perturbative approaches to recover only a fraction of the complete non-perturbative terms. While our findings stem from specific examples, various elements of this work have counterparts in dynamical gravitational scattering.

Although logarithmic conformation reformulations have mitigated the high Weissenberg number problem and enabled the study of highly elastic flows, their application within stabilized finite element frameworks remains underexplored. This study introduces stabilized formulations for the Saramito (2014) logarithmic reformulation of the Oldroyd-B model, utilizing both the Variational Multiscale framework and the Galerkin/Least-Squares method. The fully-implicit nature of this reformulation facilitates the direct solution of steady-state problems via Newton's method. The proposed stabilization techniques address convection and compatibility instabilities while maintaining a three-field structure. Accuracy assessments using the four-roll periodic box demonstrate comparable performance among the methods. Validation through benchmark flows involving a cylinder and a 4:1 contraction confirms excellent agreement with existing literature. Notably, the algebraic sub-grid scale method proves highly robust, as evidenced by its ability to handle high limiting Weissenberg numbers in these benchmark scenarios.

Identifying water vapor in the atmospheres of temperate rocky exoplanets represents a critical step toward assessing their habitability. While previous models indicate that cloud formation can obscure water vapor signals on Earth-like planets with surface oceans when observed by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), this study examines a distinct target class: arid planets. Through transit spectrum simulations, we demonstrate that detecting atmospheric H2O on arid worlds with cold-trapped surface ice deposits could be more feasible, as these planets lack the thick water cloud decks that typically diminish spectral feature depths in transit observations. Nevertheless, significant hurdles remain, including spectral line overlaps with CO2 and other gases, extinction caused by mineral dust, interference from stellar water lines, and the inherent noise limits of JWST. Consequently, a combined approach utilizing both space-based and ground-based spectroscopy will be crucial for reliably detecting water on rocky exoplanets in the future.

This paper investigates sufficient conditions for weight functions that enable norm approximations using analytic polynomials. The examined weights encompass radial, non-radial, and angular varieties.

We introduce a generalized formulation of the optical theorem based on Localized Waves, a representation frequently employed to produce Frozen waves, Xwaves, and other propagation-invariant beams. Through the examination of multiple scenarios involving various input beam sources measured on a circular detector, we determine the corresponding extinction cross-sections.

Mobile Edge Computing (MEC) utilizes geographically distributed edge servers located near base stations to deliver highly accessible and efficient computing resources to end-users. Within this framework, service providers can host their services on leased edge servers to minimize end-to-end latency for users assigned to those nodes. An ideal deployment strategy aims to maximize the number of served users while minimizing the count of hired servers, all while maintaining the necessary quality of service. This paper models the Edge User Allocation (EUA) problem as a bin packing challenge and proposes a novel, optimal solution using the Lexicographic Goal Programming technique. We evaluated the proposed method through three experimental series against two representative baseline approaches. The results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms both baselines.

Duplicate question detection (DQD) is crucial for enhancing the efficiency of community and automated question-answering platforms. However, collecting supervised data within a specific domain is often costly and time-intensive, and utilizing annotations from other domains remains limited. This study employs neural representations to investigate nearest neighbor approaches for cross-domain generalization in DQD. Specifically, we encode question pairs from both source and target domains into a rich representation space, then apply a k-nearest neighbor retrieval technique to aggregate neighbor labels and distances for ranking. Our results demonstrate robust performance across various cross-domain scenarios using StackExchange, Spring, and Quora datasets, surpassing cross-entropy classification in several instances.

Prompt Tuning, which relies on task-specific learned prompt vectors, has become a data- and parameter-efficient strategy for adapting large pretrained vision-language models to various downstream tasks. However, current methods typically learn these vectors independently for each task, neglecting the valuable shared knowledge available across different vision-language tasks. This paper introduces Multitask Vision-Language Prompt Tuning (MVLPT), a framework that integrates cross-task knowledge into the prompt tuning process. Specifically, we demonstrate that learning a single transferable prompt from multiple source tasks effectively initializes prompts for target tasks, and we show that many target tasks can mutually benefit from shared prompt vectors through joint multitask learning. We evaluate MVLPT against three representative prompt tuning approaches: text prompt tuning, visual prompt tuning, and unified vision-language prompt tuning. Experiments across 20 vision tasks reveal that our method surpasses all single-task baselines, establishing new state-of-the-art results on few-shot ELEVATER and cross-task generalization benchmarks. Furthermore, a large-scale study examining task transferability across 400 combinations for each method identifies that the most effective MVLPT configurations vary by prompt tuning type, with tasks benefiting from one another based on their visual and label similarities. The code is accessible at https://github.com/sIncerass/MVLPT.
We examine the maximum likelihood estimation of parameters for models controlled by a stochastic differential equation driven by a mixed fractional Brownian motion incorporating random effects.

This paper presents the first provably accurate algorithms for learning differentially private, top-down decision trees in a distributed environment, building on prior work by Balcan et al. (2012). We introduce DP-TopDown, a general framework for privacy-preserving decision tree learning, and offer two distinct distributed implementations. The first approach, NoisyCounts, adapts the single-machine algorithm by integrating the Laplace mechanism. The second method, LocalRNM, substantially lowers both communication overhead and added noise by executing local optimization at each data holder. We establish the first utility guarantees for differentially private top-down decision tree learning in both single-machine and distributed contexts, demonstrating that the error of the learned trees rapidly approaches zero as the dataset size increases. Furthermore, extensive experiments on real-world datasets highlight the trade-offs among privacy, accuracy, and generalization when constructing private decision trees in distributed settings.
This paper completes the stability analysis of the Schur decomposition based on the Jordan structure of the perturbation, an investigation originally initiated in \cite{MNO}.

Achieving precise motion control for multi-degree-of-freedom (DOF) robot manipulators remains a significant challenge owing to their nonlinear dynamics, disturbances, and uncertainties. Given that most manipulators operate using digital signals, this paper introduces a novel discrete-time higher-order sliding mode controller integrated with time delay estimation. The dynamic model employed in the design facilitates effective management of the system's nonlinearities, uncertainties, and disturbances. Specifically, time delay estimation addresses parametric uncertainties and external disturbances, while the controller's feedback structure manages the manipulator's inherent nonlinearity. By combining a terminal sliding mode surface with a higher-order control scheme, the proposed controller ensures a rapid response with minimal chattering. Furthermore, the implementation of a modified sliding mode surface and a variable-gain structure further enhances overall performance. The paper also derives the conditions required to ensure the stability of the closed-loop system. Ultimately, both simulation and experimental results demonstrate that the proposed control scheme achieves high precision in robot manipulator systems.

We have developed a basic prototype designed to detect short-duration optical transients using the innovative drift scan imaging method outlined by Tingay (2020). This setup employs two synchronized, aligned cameras with a shared field of view of roughly 3.7 square degrees, capturing more than 34,000 five-second exposures over a 24-hour period. With an effective pixel exposure time of 21 milliseconds, the system is sensitive to transients brighter than V magnitude 6.6. Across 89.7 square degree-hours of observation, no candidate astronomical transients were identified, establishing an upper rate limit of 0.8 per square degree per day, a figure that rivals other similar experiments. Although the system is triggered by satellite reflections and various instrumental artifacts, the dual-camera configuration allows these to be readily distinguished. Future advancements for this promising technique involve transitioning to systems featuring larger apertures and broader fields of view.

The Internet has evolved into a potent platform for the daily dissemination of varied medical information. Globally, there has been a significant surge in searches concerning symptoms, illnesses, medications, and other health-related topics. Typically, search engines generate results based solely on a single user query, often necessitating extensive manual filtering to arrive at the desired outcome. Existing search engines and recommendation systems currently lack real-time interaction capabilities that could facilitate more precise result generation. This paper introduces an intelligent and interactive system connected to extensive medical big data repositories on the web, demonstrating its potential for retrieving medical information.

We demonstrate that the Loop O(1) model, a recognized graphical representation of the Ising model, acts as a factor of i.i.d. on unimodular random rooted graphs under multiple conditions, even when a non-negative external field is present. As a practical application, we establish that the gradient of the free Ising model is a factor of i.i.d. on unimodular planar maps with a locally finite dual. Central to this work is the development of a theory regarding the local limits of uniform even subgraphs under various boundary conditions, proving these can be sampled as a factor of i.i.d. Additionally, we prove and utilize the fact that the wired uniform spanning tree on a unimodular transient graph constitutes a factor of i.i.d., thereby partially addressing questions raised by Hutchcroft.

Detecting novel objects for robotic manipulation in unstructured settings is a critical skill. While 2D grasp detection, which assumes grasps lie within a plane, often employs fully convolutional neural networks to predict grasps across an entire image in a single step, this approach fails for grasp pose detection where poses exist in SE(3). Consequently, the 3D problem is typically addressed in two stages: generating grasp candidates and classifying them. Since classification is computationally expensive, the focus shifts to efficiently identifying high-quality candidate grasps. This paper introduces a novel grasp candidate generation method that significantly surpasses leading 3D grasp detection baselines. Supplementary materials can be found at https://atenpas.github.io/psn/.

Since real-world graph data inherently contains noise, practical graph representations must be robust to such disturbances. While existing research typically addresses feature smoothing without modifying geometric structures, most approaches rely on the L2-norm to enforce global smoothness, thereby restricting the expressivity of graph neural networks. This paper introduces tailored regularizers designed to handle both feature and structural noise, utilizing the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) to efficiently solve the resulting objective function. The proposed framework supports multiple layers without risking over-smoothing and guarantees convergence to optimal solutions. Empirical results demonstrate that the model significantly outperforms standard graph convolutions, even when the graph data is heavily contaminated.

This research examines triangle decompositions of graphs. We investigate specific graph classes in which every edge belongs to a triangle, noting that adding the fewest possible multiple edges between existing adjacent vertices yields a graph that is both strongly triangle divisible and triangle decomposable. Our analysis covers various planar graph classes along with a category of toroidal graphs.

Although various allosteric regulation mechanisms are well understood, the specific nature of the "allosteric signal" and its propagation timescale remain unclear. The PDZ3 domain of the postsynaptic density-95 protein is a small domain featuring a terminal third alpha helix ($\alpha$3-helix), which exhibits allosteric activity. We engineered a photocontrollable PDZ3 variant by cross-linking this helix with an azobenzene group. This modification enables photoswitching to induce an allosteric transition, thereby altering the binding affinity of a peptide within a distant pocket. By employing time-resolved infrared and UV/Vis spectroscopy, we tracked the signal transduction process and reconstructed the 200 ns timeline for the propagation of the allosteric signal through the protein.
